It is on that basis that contemporary *batei din* are empowered to address the full range of *halachic* cases they handle.

---

## Kol & Rumors

### Mishna Kol

Following the discussion of *get me'useh*, the *gemara* turns to a new *mishna* dealing with a categorically different problem: the halakhic weight of rumors about a woman's marital status. The *mishna* states: *yatza shemah ba'ir mekudeshes harei zo mekudeshes* — if a rumor has spread in the town that a woman is married, she must be treated as married and cannot marry another man without receiving a *get*. *Megureshes harei zo megureshes* — if a rumor spread that she is divorced, she is treated as divorced; meaning, at minimum, if she is married to a *kohen*, the rumor that her husband divorced her would preclude her from remaining with him. The *mishna* adds the crucial qualification: *uvilvad shelo yehei sham amatla* — all of this applies only if there is no contextualizing explanation that neutralizes the rumor.

The *mishna* provides two examples of an *amatla*. If the rumor was that so-and-so divorced his wife, but it was said that he did so *al tenai*, on a condition, that does not constitute a rumor of divorce because one may simply assume the condition was not met. Alternatively, if the rumor was of a *kiddushin* in which it was unclear whether the object of value reached her — *safeik karov lo safeik karov lah* — the ambiguity built into the rumor itself constitutes an *amatla* that neutralizes it.

What immediately becomes apparent is that the *gemara* will work systematically and relentlessly to narrow the scope of this *mishna* until the cases to which it actually applies are extraordinarily limited. The stakes are high: how much disruption to a woman's life can be justified on the basis of rumors alone?

### Rav Assi Single

The *gemara* begins its narrowing. *V'amar Rav Assi kol kal dibatar nisuin lo chashinan lei* — any rumor about a woman that arises after she has already been married, we do not concern ourselves with it. The second case in the *mishna* — a woman married to a *kohen* and a rumor spreads that she was divorced — falls entirely under this principle. Rav Assi's position means we do not force a married woman to leave her husband on account of a rumor that she was divorced. The *mishna*, Rav Assi therefore clarifies, applies in full only to the first case: a single woman about whom a rumor spreads that she got married. In that case alone, we treat her as potentially married, and she may not marry another man without a *get*. The case of *mekudeshes u'megureshes* — a rumor that she both married and was divorced — cancels itself out as *kol v'shovro imo*, a rumor that carries its own refutation.

### Frivolous Gossip

The *gemara* continues further limiting the *mishna*. Rava rules: *yatza lah shem mezanah ba'ir ein chosheshin lah* — if a rumor circulates that a woman is promiscuous or sexually loose, we are not concerned with it. This would be relevant, for example, to a *kohen* who might otherwise have to avoid marrying her, as intercourse with a non-Jew would render her prohibited to *kehunah*. Rava's reason: *pritzuta b'alma hu d'chazu* — people have simply observed some minor behavioral impropriety and extrapolated wildly from it. *Rashi* illustrates the range: the "pritzuta" might have been something as minor as joking with men in the marketplace, or at the other end, some form of physical contact. The point is the same — once people observe behavior that slightly transgresses communal norms, they will embroider and amplify, and such rumors carry no halakhic weight.

### Tannaim Adultery

The *gemara* notes that the question of how much evidentiary weight to assign to behavior-based inferences was debated among the *Tannaim*. If a woman was observed eating in the marketplace, walking with an outstretched neck, or nursing her child in public, Rabbi Meir says *tetzei* — she must be divorced, as we infer adultery from such conduct. Rabbi Akiva is more lenient, requiring that the town gossips — those who knit in the moonlight, *mezasos balevana* — have already begun talking about her before we take any such action. Both, however, give significant halakhic weight to behavioral rumors.

### Ben Nuri Witnesses

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects sharply to both positions, and his is the voice of reason in this discussion. *Im kein lo hinachta bas l'Avinu sheyosheves tachas ba'alah* — with this approach, no woman will be allowed to remain married to her husband. The Torah explicitly requires *ki matza bah ervat davar*, a concrete matter of nakedness, and invokes the general evidentiary principle that *al pi shenayim eidim o pi shlosha eidim yakum davar* — it takes two or three witnesses to establish a fact. *Davar* appears in both: evidence must be clear and concrete, not inferential gossip.

Tosafot draws out the implication for our *mishna*: if we won't force a married woman to leave her husband based on behavioral rumors, then *a fortiori* we should not impose halakhic consequences on a single woman based on such rumors either — even though the threshold for consequences to a single woman (e.g., *kehunah* eligibility) might seem lower than forcing divorce. The *gemara*'s thrust is consistent: it is not the identity of the rumored act but the evidentiary quality of the rumor itself that determines whether it carries weight.

---

## Limiting Kol

### No Concern List

A *baraita* catalogs a sweeping series of cases in which we are categorically not concerned about a rumor: a rumor of sexual intercourse (*be'ula*), a rumor of marriage (*nesu'ah*), a rumor of *kiddushin* only (*arusa*), a rumor that identifies no specific person (*shelo l'ploni*), a rumor about an event in another city (*d'ir acheret*), a rumor that she is a *mamzeret*, and a rumor that she is a *shifcha*. The list extends to property-status rumors as well. In short, standing alone, none of these rumors are halakhically actionable. *Rashi* summarizes the operative principle: only a rumor that claims she married a specific, named person on this very day in this very city carries any weight at all. A rumor about the past, about an unidentified party, or about a distant location is simply discarded.

### Circumstantial Evidence

Ulla radically narrows the operative case of the *mishna* further still. The *mishna* is not concerned with a mere *kol havarah* — a disembodied echo, a rumor of uncertain origin that simply passed from mouth to mouth. Rather, the concern arises only when there is robust circumstantial evidence: candles are lit, couches are spread out, there is a catering van at the hall, and *uvnei adam nichnasim v'yotzim* — people are streaming in and out. It is in that context, where the entire town has witnessed what looks unmistakably like a wedding, that we take a rumor seriously. Levi's teaching parallels Ulla's, adding that women are knitting by candlelight and rejoicing.

### Nitkadshah Not Mitkad

Even with all of that circumstantial evidence, the *gemara* further demands precision in what is actually being said. If the townspeople say *plonit mitkadeshet hayom* — so-and-so is getting married today — *v'dilma lo ikadshah*: maybe it got called off at the last moment, and we have only evidence of a planned wedding, not an actual one. The concern arises only when people say *plonit nitkadshah hayom* — so-and-so *got* married today, an established fact and not merely an anticipated event. This distinction between *mitkadeshet* (getting married) and *nitkadshah* (got married) is determinative. Rav Papa and Bar Rav Papa citing Rabbi Yochanan both make this same point, with slight variations in the accompanying details.

The *gemara* then addresses a cryptic statement: if the people did say *nitkadshah*, that is a *kol*; if they did not say it, it is an *amatla* — an explanation that neutralizes the *kol*. This is puzzling: if they said nothing, there is no *kol* to neutralize in the first place. The *gemara* resolves that it means when an explanation emerges immediately alongside the rumor, it functions as though the rumor was never established. This stands in contrast to the position of Rav Abba bar Rav Huna, who holds that an *amatla* can neutralize an established *kol* even if it is offered as much as ten days later.

### Witness Tracing

Rav Papa and Rav Huna bar Minyomi citing Rav Abba citing Rav Huna citing Rav offer a second track for establishing a *kol*: even without the full battery of circumstantial evidence described by Ulla and Levi, if one can trace the rumor back through a chain of people — A heard it from B, B heard it from C — and at the end of the chain identify specific individuals who are claimed to have witnessed the event directly, that too constitutes a *kol* worthy of concern. The final version of this tradition adds the crucial detail: *v'halchu lahem l'medinat hayam* — those identified witnesses have gone overseas and cannot be questioned. If the tracing leads to a *davar barur*, a clearly established fact through identifiable witnesses who can actually testify, it is no longer a *kol* at all but direct testimony. It is specifically the case where the original witnesses have been identified but are unavailable that creates a *kol*. Tosafot observes that this and Ulla's approach represent two distinct tracks: circumstantial evidence from a community-wide wedding scene, or a traceable chain ending in named but absent witnesses.

---

## Bittul Kol

### Abaye Question

Having established the extremely narrow circumstances in which a *kol* is halakhically significant, the *gemara* turns to a related but distinct question: once a *kol* has been established, should the *beis din* proactively work to dispel it? Abaye poses this to Rav Yosef: *mevatlinan kola o lo mevatlinan?* One might assume that since *kol* is given relatively little weight, the *beis din* should have every interest in stamping out harmful rumors. On the other hand, one might argue that attempting to dispel a rumor could be counterproductive — if people believe the rumor, a *beis din* denying it will simply discredit itself.

### Witnesses Debate

The answer turns on a dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet regarding the standard for establishing a *kol* in the first place. Rav Chisda maintains that a *kol* is only significant if it is spread by *kesherim* — valid witnesses, or at least those who heard directly from valid witnesses. Since this is such a stringent standard, the *gemara* infers *shema mina mevatlinan kala*: because we are concerned about rumors only in very narrow circumstances, we would obviously not hesitate to proactively dispel them. Rav Sheshet disagrees and holds that *afilu mipi nashim havei kala* — even if the rumor is spread by women, who are not valid witnesses for such purposes, it constitutes a *kol* of concern, given that the other factual prerequisites are in place. From his broader standard, *shema mina lo mevatlinan kala*: since the circumstances creating concern are somewhat more expansive, we are more cautious about the underlying facts and do not rush to dispel rumors, lest there be some fire behind the smoke.

### Regional Practice

Rav Yosef resolves the tension practically: this is a matter of regional custom. *Be-Sura mevatli kala* — in Sura they proactively nullify rumors. *Be-Nahardea lo mevatli kala* — in Nehardea they do not. This reflects the respective positions of Rav (Sura) and Shmuel (Nehardea).

### Conditional Marriage

The *gemara* now presents a series of cases that test when nullification is effective. In the first case, a rumor spread that a woman had been betrothed to a *bar bei Rav*, a yeshiva student. Rav Chama brought the woman's father before him and asked what had happened. The father explained that the *kiddushin* had been performed *al tenai* — on the condition that the student would not travel to the region of *Bei Chuzai* — but the student subsequently went there, voiding the condition and thus the *kiddushin*. Rav Chama rejected this: *keivan de-be-idna de-havei kala lo havei amatla* — since this explanation was not offered at the time the rumor was established, *lav kol kaminach de-mechazket amatla* — the father cannot retroactively establish it as an *amatla* to neutralize the rumor. This directly applies the earlier dispute: can an explanation that comes after the *kol* was established neutralize it? Here the answer is no — once the *kol* is established, a later explanation does not suffice.

### Dates Case

The next case involves a woman about whom a rumor circulated that she had been betrothed at a specific wellspring, using what *Rashi* identifies as remnants of unripe dates — an object presumably worth less than a *shaveh perutah*, the minimum value required for valid *kiddushin*. The question was sent to Abaye: must we be concerned, or may we nullify this rumor? Abaye rules: *afilu le-man de-amar lo mevatlinan kola, be-ha mevatlinan kola* — even according to the position that in general we do not nullify rumors, here we would. Why? Because *meimar amri inhu be-derabbanan be-kidushin ve-lo havei bah shaveh perutah* — people will reason on their own that the object used was not worth a *shaveh perutah*, and so the *kiddushin* was never valid. The key principle is effectiveness: a *beis din* will only act to nullify a rumor when it can expect to be effective. If the *beis din*'s nullification directly contradicts public perception, it will discredit the *beis din* and accomplish nothing. But when the rumor itself contains internal elements — here, the specific detail of the unripe dates — that people will naturally use to explain away the *kiddushin*, then working with that internal logic can be effective, and the *beis din* will act.

### Unnamed Son

A parallel case: a rumor spread that a woman had become betrothed to one of the sons of a certain family, without specifying which son. Rava rules: *afilu le-man de-amar lo mevatlinan kola, be-ha mevatlinan kola* — even for those who hold we generally do not nullify, here we do. The reasoning: *meimar amri inhu be-rabbanan be-kiddushei u-vi-kiddushei katan havu* — people will reason that since the rumors don't specify which son, it was probably the minor son, and a minor cannot effect valid *kiddushin*. Again, the internal logic of the rumor provides the explanation that allows for effective dispelling.

### Mature Minor

A harder case: a rumor that a woman was betrothed to a minor who appeared physically mature — tall, husky, looking every bit like an adult. Here there is hesitation to work toward nullification. The difficulty is that public perception directly contradicts the halakhic reality. The *beis din* might say he was a minor, but people saw what appeared to be an adult. Rav Mordechai told Rav Ashi, however, that in a case like this, there was a precedent and people said *adayin lo higia le-phalgut Reuven* — he had not yet reached the stage of "the divisions of Reuven." This is a reference to the verse in *Shirat Devorah*, *li-flogos Reuven gedolim chikrei lev*, describing how mature adults engage in deep deliberation. The point is that even if someone looks physically adult, people can perceive from his behavior and intellectual immaturity that he is a minor. Therefore, if the *beis din* points out that the young man in question was clearly behaving in childish, immature ways — *gedolim chikrei lev* being the marker of adult capacity — people will understand and accept that he was a minor, making the nullification effective. The underlying principle throughout these cases is consistent: we will dispel a rumor when we think we can be effective in doing so; we will not if it will merely entrench it.

---

## Amatla Neutralizing

### Ten Days Later

Returning to the question of when an *amatla* can neutralize an established *kol*, the *gemara* cites Rabba bar Rav Huna who holds the lenient position: *amatla she-amru afilu mikan ve-ad asarah yamim* — an explanation, even if it comes as late as ten days afterward, is sufficient to neutralize the *kol*.

### Possible Amatla

Rav Zvid goes even further: *be-makom amatla chosheshin le-amatla* — in a place where an *amatla* is possible, meaning wherever an explanation is conceivable even hypothetically, that theoretical possibility alone is sufficient to neutralize the *kol*. One need not even produce an actual explanation; the mere availability of one neutralizes the rumor. The *gemara* at this stage does not present the more stringent view — that an *amatla* must come on the very day of the *kol* — but instead consistently cites the lenient positions, reflecting the overall *gemara*'s sustained effort to limit the halakhic consequences of rumors.

Rav Papa challenges Rav Zvid from the *mishna* itself, which says *uvilvad shelo tehe sham amatla* — the *kol* is only neutralized when there is an *amatla* present. This implies an actual *amatla* is needed, not merely a theoretical one. Rav Zvid responds: *bimkom amatla ka-amar* — the *mishna* means in a place where an *amatla* is conceivable. Rav Kahana then presses Rav Papa: surely you agree that a possible explanation suffices?

### Conditional Kiddushin

The question is adjudicated with a case from *Yevamos*. A woman remarried on the basis of a single witness's testimony that her first husband had died; her first husband then reappeared alive. If she had only received *kiddushin* from the second man and had not yet cohabited with him, *muteres lachzor* — she may return to her first husband. Why? The *gemara* suggests that people will naturally assume the *kiddushin* was done *al tenai*, on a condition, that proved not to be fulfilled. This reflects the rule that *kiddushin* without subsequent *nissu'in* is assumed to be conditional when circumstances call for it, while *kiddushin* that has led to *nissu'in* is not so easily unwound. No one explicitly stated the *tenai* — yet we read one into the situation because a plausible explanation exists. This appears to support Rav Zvid's position that the mere possibility of an *amatla* suffices.

### Husband Contest

The *gemara* deflects: *shani hasam de-asi ba'al ve-ka me'ar'er* — that case is different, because the first husband has appeared and is actively objecting, loudly contesting the claim that he ever died or that she was ever free to remarry. It is the husband's own presence and insistence that drives the *gemara* to accept that the *kiddushin* must have been conditional, not merely the theoretical availability of an explanation. The *gemara* then asks: if the husband's objection is the operative factor, why not allow her to return to him even if she had already cohabited with the second man? The answer leads to the final principle.

### Nisuin Issur

*Nisseis de-avdi issura knasu rabbanan, nitkadsha de-lo avdi issura lo knasu rabbanan* — once the woman has cohabited with the second man, she has unwittingly committed a violation, and the Rabbis imposed a consequence to give the initial *kiddushin* legal permanence and prevent a situation that would look like *machzir gerushaso*, a man taking back a woman he had divorced after she had been with another. Before cohabitation, there is no violation — she had only *kiddushin* — and therefore no rabbinic penalty applies, and she may return to her first husband. The husband's contestation provides the warrant for assuming the explanation, but that warrant operates differently depending on whether *nissu'in* has occurred.

The arc of this entire discussion is clear and consistent. The *mishna*'s seemingly expansive rule — that a *kol* creates halakhic consequences — has been narrowed at every stage. The circumstances that establish a valid *kol* are exceptional: all the hallmarks of a public wedding, or a traceable chain to named, absent witnesses. Even then, the *kol* may be dispelled when the *beis din* can do so effectively. And when the *kol* has been established, an *amatla* — actual or merely possible — can neutralize it. The *gemara*'s consistent movement is toward protecting women from the halakhic consequences of unverified communal rumor, a theme that will continue as the *masechet* concludes.

---

---

# Gittin 89

## Gett Me'useh

### Mishnah: Forced Get

The final *daf* of *Gittin* reserves its most consequential material for last. After three chapters devoted to the laws of *bifnei nichtav u'bifnei nechtam*, we arrive at a single *amud* addressing the compulsion of a husband to give a *get*. The *mishnah* opens with a foundational distinction: *get me'useh b'Yisrael kasher* — a *get* that is coerced by a Jewish *beit din* is valid. *B'ovdei kochavim pasul* — if non-Jews are the ones compelling it, the *get* is invalid.

The *mishnah* then adds that non-Jews may nonetheless beat the husband and say to him: "Do what the Jews tell you." The final word *v'kasher* appears in parentheses in many texts and is not universally accepted as part of the *mishnah*. *Tosafot* raises the possibility that even this arrangement — non-Jews doing the physical work while the Jewish *beit din* supervises — might be invalid, but ultimately rejects that reading. Since the *dayanim* themselves need not personally administer the coercion, what matters is under whose auspices the compulsion occurs. If the Jewish *beit din* is directing proceedings, the *get* is valid.

### Rav Nachman's Rule

The *gemara* refines the *mishnah*'s ruling through a statement of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel. *Haget me'useh b'Yisrael k'din kasher* — a *get* coerced by a Jewish *beit din* in a legally mandated case is valid. *Shelo k'din pasul u'posel* — if the court compelled the *get* without legal mandate, the *get* is invalid, but it generates the *re'ach haget* problem: should the husband subsequently die, the woman would be disqualified from marrying a *kohen*. Turning to the non-Jewish case: *b'ovdei kochavim k'din pasul u'posel* — even where the legal obligation to give a *get* exists, if the compulsion came from a non-Jewish court acting on its own authority, the *get* is invalid, yet still generates a *kehunah* disqualification. However, *shelo k'din* — where there is neither legal mandate nor Jewish auspices — *afilu re'ach haget ein bo*: there is not even a whiff of a *get*, and no *kehunah* problem arises at all.

A striking issue that the *gemara* does not directly analyze here is the threshold question of how a coerced *get* can be valid at all. Ordinarily, a coerced transaction is invalid. The *gemara* does address analogous cases elsewhere: *talu'ei v'zavin* — if someone was strung up until he agreed to sell property, the sale is valid (*zinei zinei*), because even under external compulsion, a person at some level is acting on his own volition; circumstances always compel us in various ways, and at the end of the day the act is performed. The *gemara* similarly validates a coerced *kiddushin*: *talu'ei v'kiddesh kiddushei kiddushin*. One could simply place the forced *get* in this same category. Yet the *Rambam* offers a further rationale specific to *gittin*.

### Rambam: Yetzer Hara

The *Rambam* explains that deep down, a person wants to do what *halachah* requires. It is only the *yetzer hara* standing in the way. When the *beit din* beats him, it is not overriding his genuine will; it is wearing down the *yetzer hara* and liberating his true desire to comply with the law. The compulsion thus frees, rather than supplants, authentic consent.

One might ask why the *Rambam* needed this additional rationale when the general principle of *talu'ei v'zavin* would seem sufficient. Some *acharonim* answer that there may be a heightened standard specific to *gittin*. The *Rambam* states at the outset of *Hilchos Gittin* that among the ten criteria for a valid *get* is the requirement that it be given *m'mirtsono* — of the husband's own genuine will — derived from the verse *ki matza bah ervat davar v'chasav lah sefer krisus*. Whereas ordinary transactions require only *da'as* — intent to perform the act — a *get* requires something more: the Torah's formulation implies the husband is *motivated* to give it, not merely that he consents. The *Rambam*'s explanation therefore does the necessary halachic work: by attributing the coercion to suppressing the *yetzer hara* rather than to overriding the husband's will, it establishes that deep down he genuinely wants to do the right thing, satisfying even this elevated standard.

This analysis also clarifies why a *get* that is not legally mandated is invalid: the entire justification for treating the coerced *get* as a genuine expression of will depends on the existence of a *halachic* mandate. Without that mandate, the theoretical underpinning collapses.

### Non-Jewish Court Get

The *gemara* now examines the intermediate cases — where compulsion comes from a non-Jewish court — through the lens of a *mah nafshach* argument. Either non-Jews have the capacity to meaningfully compel a *get*, in which case a *get* forced by them in a legally mandated case should be fully valid; or they do not, in which case there should be no *re'ach haget* whatsoever. What justifies the intermediate position?

Rav Marshisha proposes a bold answer: *dvar Torah*, as a matter of biblical law, a *get* coerced by a non-Jewish court in a legally mandated case is valid. The rabbinic invalidation was enacted as a protective measure — *shelo tehei kol achat v'achat holechet v'tola atzma b'ovdei kochavim u'mafka'as atzma miyad ba'alah* — lest every wife hire a non-Jewish court, which might be more susceptible to bribery, to pressure her husband into giving a *get* when no legal obligation exists. Since the invalidation is purely rabbinic, a legally mandated *get* compelled by non-Jews retains its biblical validity, which is why it generates a *re'ach haget* concern.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this position: if we accept that the non-Jewish court's compulsion is in principle valid, then a non-legally-mandated *get* forced by non-Jews should still carry a *re'ach haget* problem — analogous to a legally-mandated *get* forced by a Jewish court without authority. *Ela hadra Rav Marshisha bidusa hi* — the *gemara* dismisses Rav Marshisha's position as untenable. The compulsion of a non-Jewish court is intrinsically without force.

Why then does a legally mandated *get* forced by non-Jews still generate a *re'ach haget* problem? The *gemara* answers: *kidin k'chidin d'Yisrael michlaf* — where there is a legal obligation to give a *get*, a non-Jewish court's compulsion is similar enough to the case that actually works — a legally mandated *get* forced by a Jewish court — that it creates a *kehunah* concern. *Shelo kidin b'kidin d'Yisrael lo michlaf* — but if a non-Jewish court forces a *get* without legal mandate, it is two full degrees removed from the valid case, and not even *re'ach haget* applies.

### Four-Case Chart

The resulting framework can be mapped across two axes: whether the compulsion is legally mandated (*k'din*) or not (*shelo k'din*), and whether the compelling authority is a Jewish *beit din* (*Yisrael*) or a non-Jewish court (*goyim*). The only case that yields a fully valid *get* is the combination of legal mandate and Jewish court. Both the case of a Jewish court without legal mandate and the case of a non-Jewish court with legal mandate are one degree removed from the valid case and therefore each generates a *re'ach haget* problem. The case of a non-Jewish court without legal mandate is two degrees removed and generates no halachic concern whatsoever — *afilu re'ach haget ein bo*.

---

## Semicha & Authority

### Abaye's Challenge

The *gemara* records that Abaye found Rav Yosef sitting and compelling husbands who were legally obligated to give *gittin*, applying whatever pressure and leverage was available to compel compliance. Abaye challenged him: *ve'anan hedyotot anan* — are we not mere commoners? We lack the *semicha* that traces back to Moshe Rabbeinu. How can we presume to exercise this authority?

### Tanna: Semicha Needed

Abaye invokes a *tannaitic* source: wherever one finds non-Jewish courts (*aguriyot shel ovdei kochavim*), even if the substance of their law is identical to Jewish law, *af al pi shedineihem kedinei Yisrael, ee atah reshai lehizakek lahem* — one may not submit to their authority. The verse *ve'eleh hamishpatim asher tasim lifneihem* specifies *lifneihem* — before Jewish judges, and not before non-Jewish ones. This principle is not merely about the content of the law but about which institution is recognized as legitimately empowered. The text then adds: *davar acher lifneihem velo lifnei hedyotot* — "before them and not before commoners." To impose the law one must possess *semicha*; a *beit din* composed of those without ordained authority cannot exercise coercive legal power.

This raises obvious contemporary questions about the use of secular courts, which people do in practice even within observant communities — a subject with an extensive halachic literature of its own.

### Beit Din Agency

Rav Yosef responds: *anan shelichusaihu ka'avdinan* — we act as agents of the court that does possess *semicha*. We are not claiming independent authority; we are representing those who are properly empowered.

### Common vs. Rare Matters

The *gemara* draws an analogy: just as courts today handle cases involving loans and admissions (*hoda'os v'halva'os*) on this agency theory, so too can they handle the forcing of a *get*. The *gemara* immediately asks: if that is so, why not also handle cases of theft (*gezeilos*) and personal injury (*chavalos*)? The *gemara* answers: *ki avdinan shelichusaihu bemilsa d'shchichah* — we are considered agents of the ordained court only in common matters. *Bemilsa d'lo shchichah lo avdinan shelichusaihu* — in uncommon matters, we do not exercise that agency.

This generates substantial halachic literature about the precise scope of contemporary *beit din* authority. *Tosafot* notes that the *gemara* does treat courts as handling theft and injury in some passages, and works to reconcile this. There is also a distinction noted between matters of *knas* — punitive fines — where courts without *semicha* would not exercise *shelichut*, and matters of pure restitution (*mamon*), where they may. A further limiting principle is that *shelichut* may apply only where someone has actually suffered a monetary loss (*chisaron kis*).

What is particularly striking is that forcing a *get* — which involves physical compulsion and the halachic paradox of treating a coerced act as voluntary — should seemingly require the clearest possible credentialing. Yet the *gemara* not only affirms that contemporary courts were empowered to do this, but describes it as *milsa d'shchicha* — a common matter. That characterization is itself a sobering commentary: even in the time of the *gemara*, husbands who were legally obligated to give a *get* and refused were a sufficiently frequent occurrence to be classified as routine. This makes the contemporary failure of the Israeli rabbinical establishment — which possesses actual coercive power (including imprisonment) yet largely declines to use it — all the more difficult to understand.

### Tosafot: Gerim & Shtlich…

*Tosafot* raises two additional points of interest. The first concerns the acceptance of converts (*geirim*). The *gemara* in *Yevamos* establishes that conversion requires three expert judges with *semicha* (*mishpat kesiv bei*). *Tosafot* answers, in the name of the *Ri*, that we perform the conversion as agents of the ordained court (*d'avdinan shlichusaihu*), since the matter is considered sufficiently common (*d'chashiv k'shchiach*) — though the *Tosafot* acknowledges the irony, given that conversion to Judaism in medieval Christian or Muslim lands was punishable by death and was anything but common. Indeed, various *poskim* writing about the laws of *geirim* felt compelled to include disclaimers that the entire subject was theoretical, given the legal dangers of the time.

The second point concerns a deeper structural question: *shelichut* to an existing court with *semicha* makes sense, but how can anyone claim to represent a court that no longer exists? *Ve'im tomar heichi avdinan shlichusaihu? V'ha achshav ein mumchin b'Eretz Yisrael* — if there were a living court in Israel with *semicha*, we could be their deputies; but when no such court exists, who is authorizing us? *Tosafot* answers: *d'shlichus d'kama'ei avdinan* — we exercise the agency of the early, ancient *beit din* that once held *semicha*. We are the continuing authorized representatives of an authority that no longer exists as a living institution. It is a striking and far-reaching idea: contemporary halachic courts derive their legitimacy not from any presently constituted body but from their status as the ongoing expression of an ancient empowerment.

---

## Rumors About Status

### Mishnah: Rumor Status

The *gemara* now turns to an entirely different set of concerns, introduced by a second *mishnah*: *yatza shemah ba'ir mekudeshet harei zo mekudeshet* — if a rumor circulates in town that a woman is married, she must be treated as married. She cannot marry another man without receiving a *get* from her purported first husband. *Megureshes harei zo megureshes* — if there is a rumor that she is divorced, she is treated as divorced.

The second ruling is troubling in both directions. It does not mean we leniently assume she is free: primarily it means that if a married woman's husband is a *kohen* and a rumor circulates that he divorced her, we would not allow her to continue living with him. *Uvilvad shelo yehei sham amatla* — this applies only when there is no explanation that contextualizes or qualifies the rumor. *Eizo hi amatla?* What constitutes such an explanation? If the rumor was that he divorced her on a condition (*al tnai*), we assume the condition was not fulfilled, and the *get* therefore never took effect. Or if the rumor was that *kiddushin* occurred but there was uncertainty whether the object of value (*kesef kiddushin*) actually reached her — *safek karov la safek karov lo* — then the rumor is inherently uncertain and is neutralized.

### Rav Ashi: Post-Marriage

The *gemara* moves immediately to limit the *mishnah*'s scope. *Ve'asrinan la agavra?* — are we really going to forbid a woman to her husband on the basis of a rumor? Rav Ashi rules: *kol kala d'vatar nisuin lo hashishan leh* — any rumor that arises after a woman is already married carries no halachic weight. The *mishnah*'s ruling that *megureshes harei zo megureshes* therefore does not mean we force an already-married woman to separate from her husband. Rather, Rav Ashi reinterprets the *mishnah*: the case of a woman reported as married (*mekudeshet*) refers to an unmarried woman — a rumor that she became betrothed means she cannot now marry anyone else without a *get* from the first. The case of *mekudeshet u'megoreshet* — married and divorced — means the rumor contains both elements simultaneously, in which case *kol v'shovro imo*: the rumor carries its own cancellation within it. These two components obviously neutralize one another, and the result is no halachic concern.

### Pritzuta Rumors

Rava adds a further restriction: *yatza la shem mezana ba'ir ein chosheshin lah* — if a rumor circulates that a woman is sexually promiscuous, it carries no halachic weight. One might think that a rumor of promiscuity could, for example, disqualify an unmarried woman from marrying a *kohen* (if she were suspected of having relations with someone who would render her a *zona*). Rava dismisses this: *pritzuta b'alma hu d'hazu lah* — people simply observe behavior that strikes them as somewhat loose, and from that the rumor of serious sexual misconduct grows. *Rashi* illustrates the range of behaviors that might trigger such rumors: from *shichaka bashuk* — joking with men in the marketplace — to *michla bein dadei* — a sexual act of some kind. The spectrum is wide, and the connection between the observed behavior and the rumored conclusion is unreliable. Communal gossip, as always, has a tendency to amplify minor infractions into lurid accusations.

### Tannaim Debate

This reflects a dispute among *tanna'im*. If a woman was seen eating in the marketplace (*achla bashuk*), or walking with an outstretched neck in a manner designed to attract attention (*gargara bashuk*), or nursing her child in a public place (*henika bashuk*) — Rabbi Meir rules that she must be divorced from her husband, the assumption being that such behavior indicates adultery has occurred. Rabbi Akiva sets the threshold much higher: *mishe-yishiu ve-yitnu bah mezarot balevanah* — not until the women who spin wool by moonlight — the proverbial neighborhood gossips — have taken up the story. Even by Rabbi Akiva's account, however, communal yenta-talk carries some weight, which is itself a striking position.

### R. Yochanan: Two Witness…

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri finally provides the voice of genuine caution: *im ken lo hinachta bat le-Avraham Avinu she-yoshevet tachat ba'alah* — if we give this weight, no woman will remain with her husband. He then invokes a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *davar* appears both in the verse requiring a husband to find an *ervat davar* before writing a *get* and in the verse *al pi shenei edim o al pi sheloshah edim yakum davar* — establishing matters through two or three witnesses. *Mah le-halan davar barur af kan davar barur* — just as the latter verse requires clear, established evidence, so too does the former. Nothing short of clear evidence suffices.

This position also, *Tosafot* notes, implies that even rumors about a single woman prior to her marriage cannot simply be given halachic weight. If a *kohen* marries a woman unaware that rumors had circulated about her before the marriage, and those rumors then come to light, giving them weight now would retroactively harm him in his current marriage. Once we see that rumors are insufficient to compel a married woman to divorce, the same logic extends to their weight regarding a single woman's status. The *gemara* is thus progressively narrowing the *mishnah* from every direction.

---

## Narrowing Rumor Scope

### Baraita: No Concern

A *baraita* enumerates case after case in which rumors generate no halachic concern: *be'ulah ein chosheshin lah* — a rumor of sexual relations carries no weight. *Nesu'ah ein chosheshin lah* — a rumor that she got married carries no weight, directly contradicting the plain reading of the *mishnah*. *Arusah ein chosheshin lah* — even a rumor of *kiddushin*, which is a more private affair than a full wedding and might seem more believable, carries no weight. *Shelo l'Ploni ein chosheshin lah* — if the rumor does not name the specific person she allegedly married, it is disregarded. *V'ir acheret ein chosheshin lah* — if the rumored marriage took place in another city, it is disregarded.

*Rashi* draws the implication explicitly: the only rumor we are concerned about is one that says she got married *today*, *in this city*, *to this specific named person*. Anything that fails to specify all three elements — the immediacy, the location, and the identity of the husband — is insufficient to create a halachic concern.

### Baraita Extended

The *baraita* continues: *mamzeret ein chosheshin lah* — a rumor that she is a *mamzeret* carries no weight. *Shifcha ein chosheshin lah* — a rumor that she is a *shifcha* likewise. Similarly, a rumor that a certain person consecrated his property or renounced ownership of it does not affect the halachic status of that property. The general principle is stark: rumors, across a wide range of categories, carry essentially no halachic force.

### Ulla: Circumstantial

With the *baraita* having reduced the *mishnah*'s operative scope to almost nothing, the *gemara* through Ulla articulates precisely what would render a rumor halachically significant. *Lo sheshamu kol havarah* — the case of the *mishnah* is not where people merely heard an echo — that is, an unrooted report passed from person to person. Rather: *ela k'dei she'yoru nerot v'yatziu mitot u'vnei adam nichnasim v'yotzim* — only where the rumor is accompanied by substantial circumstantial evidence. Candles are being lit; bedding is being spread; people are going in and out of the hall. And amidst all of this: *v'omrim Plonit nitkadsha hayom* — people are saying that so-and-so got married today. Only under these conditions does the rumor rise to the level of halachic concern.

### Got Married Today

Even Ulla's formulation requires clarification. *Mitkadeshet hayom* — "she is getting married today" — leaves open the possibility that the marriage ultimately did not occur. *V'dilma lo ikadsha* — perhaps it was called off at the last moment. The *gemara* therefore insists: the statement must be *nitkadsha* — "she got married," in the past tense, completed, not merely anticipated. Levi's parallel teaching adds further texture: women knitting by candlelight (*nashim tavot l'or haner*), everyone rejoicing around the bride — and still the formulation must be *nitkadsha*, past tense. Rav Pappa confirms: the statement must be *Plonit nitkadsha hayom*. Anything less — a statement that she *will* be married, or a rumor that lacks any of the required specificity — does not rise to the level of a halachic *kol*.

### Named Witnesses

A statement of Rav in a chain transmitted through Rav Huna, Rav Abba, and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda identifies a second track by which a rumor may be established. It is not enough to have heard a disembodied report: one must be able to trace the rumor back — *Ploni me'heichan shama mi'Ploni u'Ploni mi'Ploni* — through an identified chain of sources. Taken to its logical conclusion, this chain would eventually reach the people who directly witnessed the event, in which case it would no longer be a rumor but actual testimony (*edut ma'alyata*).

The *gemara* therefore refines the ruling: *v'halchu lahem l'medinat hayam* — the chain leads back to specifically identified witnesses who are known but not currently available, having traveled overseas. In such a case, where we know who witnessed the event but cannot question them, there is enough substance to the rumor to create concern. *Tosafot* understands this as an alternative and independent track from Ulla's circumstantial-evidence approach. Either path suffices to establish a *kol*: either the extensive circumstantial evidence at the time of the event (even without knowing who the specific witnesses were), or the identification of specific witnesses who can be named but not presently questioned. One or the other is required; neither alone suffices without meeting its own threshold.

---

## Nullifying Rumors

### Abaye's Question

Abaye poses a question to Rav Yosef: *mevatlinan kala o lo mevatlinan* — when a rumor is circulating, should the *beit din* proactively work to stamp it out, or should it leave the rumor alone? The intuitive answer might be that since rumors can harm people's status, of course we should dispel them. But there is a practical counterargument: attempting to dispel a rumor may simply draw more attention to it, discredit those trying to dispel it, and ultimately make things worse. The question is therefore whether active nullification is wise policy.

### Chisda vs. Sheshes

Two *amora'im* offer divergent perspectives that bear on this question. Rav Chisda holds that a *kol* is only established when it is heard testified to by *kesherim* — people of unimpeachable credibility. Since *Rashi* understands this to mean credible people testifying to what they heard (not directly witnessed), it follows that the threshold for a halachically significant rumor is relatively high. From this, one might infer *shma mina mevatlinan kala*: since we generally do not credit rumors, it follows that we would actively work to dispel them.

Rav Sheshes disagrees: *afilu mipi nashim havei kala* — even a rumor spread by women (who are not qualified *edim*) can constitute a halachically significant *kol*, provided the other conditions of circumstantial evidence or identified witnesses are present. If we are willing to treat this as a meaningful *kol*, then *lo mevatlinan kala* — perhaps we do not proactively attempt to dispel it, since there may be some genuine substance behind it.

### Regional Practice

Rav Yosef resolves the exchange by noting that the question is itself regionally contested: *b'Sura mevatli kala* — in Sura, they proactively nullify rumors. *Benhardah lo mevatli kala* — in Nardah, they do not. This corresponds, broadly speaking, to the respective orientations of Rav (Sura) and Shmuel (Nardah).

### Unripe Dates Case

The *gemara* then presents a series of cases illustrating when active nullification is and is not appropriate. In the first, a rumor circulated that a certain woman had become betrothed to a *yeshiva* student using unripe dates (*atzifa d'tuchla*) at the wellspring of a place called Bei Shifei. Rav Idi bar Avin sent the case to Abaye: given these specific circumstances, should the rumor be nullified?

Abaye rules: *afilu man d'amar lo mevatlinan kala beha mevatlinan kala* — even according to those who ordinarily do not nullify rumors, here they would. Why? *Meimar amri* — people will naturally say that the Rabbis examined the dates at the time of the *kiddushin* and determined they were worth less than a *shavei pruta*, meaning the *kiddushin* was invalid. The key principle the *gemara* is articulating here is that active nullification is warranted not in every case, but specifically when the nullification will be *effective* — when it aligns with the existing rumor's own internal logic in a way that people will find credible. To directly contradict what people think they saw or heard would be counterproductive and self-defeating; but where the explanation flows naturally from within the rumor's own details, it can be deployed successfully.

### Unknown Son

A second case: a rumor circulated that a woman had become betrothed to one of the sons of a certain individual (*l'chad mibnei planya*), without specifying which son. Under normal circumstances, a rumor that does not name the husband is not a halachic concern. Here, however, the question is whether even this rumor warrants active nullification. Rava rules that even those who generally do not nullify rumors would do so here: *inhu barabbanan b'kiddushei v'kiddushei katan havi* — people will naturally say that when they heard she was betrothed to one of the sons, it was probably the minor among them, and *kiddushin* by a minor is invalid. Again, the nullification works because it can be advanced within the terms of what people already believe, without requiring anyone to abandon their perception.

### Minor Appears Grown

The third case draws the limit of this principle. A rumor circulated that a woman was betrothed to a minor who appeared physically like an adult (*katan hanireh k'gadol*). Here, explaining that the groom was a minor would directly contradict people's visual perception. Reality and perception diverge: the boy is truly a *katan*, but everyone sees a *gadol*. Would such an explanation be effective?

Rav Mordechai reports to Rav Ashi that a case of this kind was brought and people said the boy had not yet reached *palgus Reuven* — a reference to the verse in *Shiras Devorah* about the tribe of Reuven, *b'palgus Reuven gedolim chikrei lev*, which the *gemara* reads as referring to a distinct level of adult discernment. The point is that even if a young person is physically imposing, observers can nonetheless detect through his behavior and manner that he lacks adult judgment — *gedolim chikrei lev* describes the kind of mature understanding that makes adulthood recognizable. People would therefore accept an explanation that the groom was a minor, because his comportment would have revealed his age. The rumor can thus be nullified even in this case, because the explanation does not require people to disbelieve what they perceived, only to interpret it correctly.

---

## Amtalot (Explanations)

### Mishnah: Amtala

The *mishnah* had already established the principle that a rumor is halachically operative only *uvilvad shelo yehei sham amatla* — provided no explanation or qualification is present. The *gemara* now addresses the conditions under which an *amatla* successfully neutralizes an otherwise established rumor.

### Timing of Amtala

Rabba bar Rav Huna holds: *amatla she'amru afilu mikan v'ad asara yamim* — an explanation can neutralize a rumor even if it is offered as much as ten days later. The *amatla* need not be contemporaneous with the establishment of the *kol*.

### Possibility Suffices

Rav Zeira goes further still: *b'makom amatla chosheshin l'amatla* — in a context where an explanation is *possible*, even the mere possibility of an explanation is sufficient to neutralize the *kol*. One need not actually produce a named explanation or have anyone claim one; the fact that an explanation could theoretically exist is enough. This is a sweeping position: it means that wherever we can imagine a plausible benign interpretation of the events that gave rise to the rumor, the rumor carries no halachic weight.

The *gemara* at this point has effectively adopted the most permissive readings at each stage. Rather than requiring an explanation on the same day (the position that appeared earlier in the discussion), it now cites only Rabba bar Rav Huna's position that an explanation can come even ten days later. And beyond that, it entertains Rav Zeira's view that even a theoretical possibility of an explanation suffices. The consistent direction of the *gemara*'s movement throughout this entire discussion has been to limit, restrict, and ultimately minimize the halachic weight of rumors.

### Tenai Example

Rav Kahana challenges Rav Pappa to accept Rav Zeira's position, citing a proof from the *mishnah* in *Yevamos*. If a woman remarried on the basis of a single witness's testimony that her first husband died, and then the first husband reappeared alive, but she had only reached *kiddushin* with the second man — not yet *nisuin* — she is *muteres lachazor* to her first husband. The reason she cannot return to him after *nisuin* is that the situation resembles *machzir grushato* — a man remarrying his divorced wife after she has been with another — which is *asur*. But if she has only had *kiddushin* and not *nisuin* with the second man, she may return to the first.

Why is no objection raised about the appearance of *machzir grushato* even in the *kiddushin* case? It must be, argues Rav Kahana, because we assume the *kiddushin* with the second man was performed *al tnai* — conditionally — and since the first husband has returned alive, the condition retroactively failed. But this is merely a *possible* explanation, not one that was actually stated at the time of the *kiddushin*. This proves that the mere possibility of an explanation — *bemakom amatla* — is enough to neutralize a concern.

### Limits of Possibility

The *gemara* rejects this proof: *shani hasam de'asi ba'al veka m'arer* — that case is different because the first husband has actually arrived and is actively protesting, asserting that he was always alive and that she was always his wife. It is the husband's real-world protest and presence that creates the effective explanation, not simply the abstract theoretical possibility of a *tnai*. The proof therefore does not establish the general principle that a theoretical possibility of an explanation is sufficient.

### Consequence Doctrine

The *gemara* then asks: if the husband's protest is what matters, why not allow her to return to him even after *nisuin* with the second man? The answer establishes a doctrinal principle: *nises de'avdi issura kansu rabanan, niskadsha delo avdi issura lo kansu rabanan* — once she has lived with the second man, she has transgressed (albeit unwittingly), and the Rabbis imposed a consequence. Before *nisuin*, when no *issur* has actually occurred, there is no penalty and no reason to prevent her return to her first husband. This "consequence doctrine" — that rabbinic sanctions attach to situations where an *issur* has actually been committed, but not where the prohibition was avoided — represents the final limiting principle in this extended discussion.

The overall movement of the *gemara* across this entire topic is thus unmistakable. Beginning with a *mishnah* that seemed to give meaningful weight to rumors about a woman's status, the *gemara* has progressively narrowed the operative cases to an extraordinary degree: requiring specific circumstantial evidence or named witnesses, limiting concern to past-tense statements naming a specific person in a specific city on that very day, allowing proactive nullification wherever it can be effective, permitting explanations even after significant delay, and approaching the position that even the theoretical possibility of an explanation neutralizes a *kol*. Tomorrow's concluding *amud* will bring this discussion — and the tractate — to its close.

---

---

# Gittin 89b

## Kol & Substantiation

### Kol Requires Beit Din

We pick up on 89b in Gittin, approximately twenty lines down from where *Tosfos* cites the statement of *Amar Rav Huna*, and about five lines above that point, at the line beginning with the word *rabbanan*. At this stage in the sugya, the Gemara has already established several principles governing the *kol* — the rumor or public report that a woman has contracted a marriage. The *mishna* held that such a rumor requires us to be concerned, preventing the woman from marrying another man without receiving a *get* from the one she was rumored to have married. The Gemara's preceding discussion explored the degree of substantiating circumstances required for a *kol* to be treated as actionable, and whether *beit din* may proactively negate — *mevatlin* — a *kol* once it is determined to have been unfounded.

Into this discussion steps Rav Ashi with a foundational principle: *kol kola d'lo it'chazeik b'vei dina lav kola havei* — any *kol* that *beit din* has not examined and established as a matter warranting concern does not attain the status of a *kol*. This is consistent with the earlier requirement for substantiating evidentiary circumstances. As Rashi explains: we are not concerned about a rumor unless the local *beit din* has investigated — in accordance with the standards discussed earlier in the Gemara — and has formally declared this particular *kol* to be one we must heed.

### Kol After Marriage

Rav Ashi adds a second ruling: *kol kol d'basar nissuin lo chashinan lah* — any *kol* that arises after a woman is already married, we do not act upon. That is, a rumor emerging after *nissuin* — full cohabitation — that would impugn her status (for example, that she had previously been married to another man, or had committed an act rendering her forbidden to a *kohen*) is simply not heeded, since acting upon it would have a direct impact on the man to whom she is currently married. The Gemara then infers the converse: *ha d'basar eirusin chashinan lah* — a *kol* that arose after *eirusin* but before *nissuin* would still be heeded, since at that point only *kiddushin* has taken place and they are not yet living together as husband and wife.

### Rav Chaviva Ruling

Rav Chaviva disagrees even with that limited scope: *afilu d'basar eirusin nami lo chashinan lah*. Even a *kol* that arose after *eirusin* is not heeded, because here too there is already a relationship being directly impacted. The *halakha* follows Rav Chaviva: once a woman is in any stage of marriage — whether *eirusin* or *nissuin* — we disregard rumors about her prior status.

---

## Kol & Kiddushin

### Query Setup

The Gemara now records that a query was sent from the house of Rav to Shmuel: *yelamdenu rabbeinu* — let our master teach us. The case is as follows: a *kol* had gone forth that a woman was married to Reuven — a *kol* of the type and strength that would ordinarily require concern. Then Shimon came along and married her through explicit *kiddushei Torah*, in full public view. He did not merely create another *kol*; people actually witnessed him perform *kiddushin* with her. What is the ruling?

### Shmuel's Response

Shmuel's response is threefold: *taitzei* — she must leave Shimon; *v'amidu hadavar al buryo* — investigate and establish the facts; and *ve'odiuoni* — report the findings back to me.

The Gemara then unpacks what "clarifying the matter" means in practice, proceeding in two stages. The first possibility: the investigation reveals that the first marriage — the one underlying the *kol* — was in fact invalid. For instance, perhaps there were all the social trappings of a wedding (torches, candles, public celebration) sufficient to generate a strong *kol*, but no actual valid *kiddushin* — say, because the ring was not worth a *perutah*. In that case, *mevatlinan kala* — we would negate the *kol* and permit the woman to remain married to Shimon without requiring a *get*. The investigation has shown the *kol* to be baseless.

But this first resolution is immediately rejected: *ve'ha Nahardea atra d'Shmuel hu, v'lo mevatlinan kala* — Nahardea was Shmuel's own city, and Nahardea does not negate a *kol*. This is a striking point. Even if *beit din* determines through investigation that the *kol* was factually false, the *beit din* of Nahardea will not publicly annul it, because at a certain point, once a *kol* has achieved sufficient traction, it cannot simply be overridden by a contrary ruling without appearing to sanction what the public perceives as a real marriage. As one might put it: the only difference between reality and perception is that it is often easier to change reality than perception. And so even if the facts exonerate the first marriage, the second husband will still be required to give a *get* — because the community cannot be expected to simply disregard what it believes it knows.

The second possibility: the investigation reveals not that the first marriage was void, but that it was definitively valid. That is, we move from the realm of *kol* — substantiated rumor — to actual *edut*, direct testimony that she was truly married to Reuven. In that case, *lo tzricha get mishinei* — she does not need a *get* from Shimon at all. She is simply married to Reuven; Shimon's *kiddushin* was an act of no legal consequence, and she returns to Reuven directly.

To summarize: regardless of what the investigation yields, Shimon cannot remain married to her — *taitzei* applies in all scenarios. Whether she requires a *get* from Shimon depends on the outcome: if the investigation produces only a negated *kol* (Nahardea: she still needs a *get* from Shimon), or if the investigation yields actual *edut* establishing the first marriage as real (no *get* from Shimon needed).

### Rav Huna Dispute

The Gemara notes that this ruling stands in tension with the position of Rav Huna: *eishet ish she'pashat yadah ve'kiblah kiddushin mei'acher mekudeshet, mi'din d'Rav Hamnuna* — a married woman who extends her hand and accepts *kiddushin* from another man thereby becomes betrothed to him, based on the principle of Rav Hamnuna.

Rav Hamnuna had ruled: *ha'isha she'amra l'ba'alah geirashtani ne'emenet, chazakah ein isha me'izah paneha bifnei ba'alah* — a woman who says directly to her husband's face "you have divorced me" is believed, because we invoke the principle that a woman would not be so brazen as to make such a declaration in her husband's presence unless it were true. Rav Huna derives from this that a married woman who accepts *kiddushin* from another man is in effect making precisely such a declaration — she is treating herself as divorced — and therefore she is considered betrothed to the second man as well. Were we to rule in accordance with Rav Huna's principle, it would follow that even when we know with certainty that she was married to Reuven, her acceptance of *kiddushin* from Shimon carries evidentiary weight, and she would at minimum need a *get* from Shimon. But the Gemara above concluded that if we have actual *edut* of the first marriage, she needs no *get* from Shimon. This is therefore a dispute with Rav Huna.

### Rav Hamnuna Presence

The Gemara resolves the apparent tension by clarifying the precise scope of Rav Hamnuna's teaching: *ki m'deRav Hamnuna bifanav — shelo bifanav, mizeh umizeh* — Rav Hamnuna's principle applies only when the woman accepts *kiddushin* from the second man in the presence of her husband, or declares her divorce directly to him face to face. It is specifically in that context — in the first husband's presence — that we say a woman would not be so brazen unless it were true. But in our case, the woman accepted *kiddushin* from Shimon without Reuven being present. Therefore Rav Hamnuna's principle does not apply, and the acceptance of *kiddushin* from Shimon carries no evidentiary weight regarding her status vis-à-vis Reuven.

*Tosfos* notes that this point — that the evidentiary force of accepting *kiddushin* from another man applies only when done in the first husband's presence — was never actually in dispute. The Gemara's point here, then, is narrower: even granting that argument, one might still have thought that accepting *kiddushin* from Shimon outside Reuven's presence should at least require a *get* from Shimon as a matter of caution. The answer is no: if we know as a fact that she was married to Reuven, and Shimon's *kiddushin* was performed outside Reuven's presence, that act is entirely without legal significance, she needs no *get* from Shimon, and she simply returns to being married to Reuven.

---

## Rumor Unresolved

### Rav Huna Option

The Gemara now turns to the scenario where the investigation yields no clear resolution. There was a strong *kol* that she was married to Reuven. Shimon then performed *kiddushin* with her. The investigation is conducted, but the facts remain indeterminate — neither the truth nor the falsity of the first marriage can be established. We are left precisely where we began.

Rav Huna rules: *megaresh rishon venosay sheni — megaresh sheni venosay rishon lo*. Contrary to what the word *taitzei* might initially suggest — that she must leave the first arrangement — Rav Huna explains that *taitzei* means she must leave Reuven's sphere. Reuven is to be the one who divorces her, and she may then, if she chooses, marry Shimon. The reverse — Shimon divorcing her so she can return to Reuven — is not permitted. Why? *Asya l'maimar machzir grushaso min ha'erusin*: people will reconstruct the narrative as follows: the *kol* was true, she was married to Reuven, Reuven then divorced her, she married Shimon, Shimon divorced her, and now Reuven is remarrying his divorcée. This appearance of *machzir grushaso* is something Rav Huna wishes to avoid, even at the cost of foreclosing an otherwise valid legal option. This is an uncomfortable concession to perception over reality — we are closing off a permissible avenue simply to avoid what the community might think.

### Ameimar Resolution

Ameimar offers a different resolution: *aynei rabanan b'kidushei v'kidushei ta'ut havei* — the Rabbis examined the *kiddushin* and determined that it was a mistake from the outset. Rather than framing the situation as a chain of marriages and divorces — which would produce the appearance of *machzir grushaso* — the Rabbis retroactively characterize Shimon's *kiddushin* as an error, a marriage that was never valid. When the woman returns to Reuven, the community's understanding will simply be that she was always married to Reuven and that the marriage to Shimon never took legal effect.

According to *Tosfos*, this is the ruling we follow. It is, as noted, still somewhat unfortunate that we must accommodate the perception of reality at all — but Ameimar's approach at least avoids artificially restricting the available options by nullifying the second marriage conceptually rather than through a second *get*.

---

## Competing Rumors

### Rav Papa Initial

A new scenario: the case of two competing *kolot*. On one day, a strong *kol* emerged that the woman had married Reuven; on another day, an equally strong *kol* arose that she had married Shimon. These are pure rumors — there was no witnessed act of *kiddushin* as there was in the previous case — and we assume that the investigation has not resolved either rumor's truth or falsity.

Rav Papa's initial position, following Rav Huna's logic, is that even here the same restrictions apply: *af zu megaresh rishon venosay sheni* — even in this case, she is limited to the option of Reuven divorcing her and her then marrying Shimon. She may not have Shimon divorce her and return to Reuven, for the same concern about the appearance of *machzir grushaso*.

### Ameimar Two Rumors

Ameimar disagrees: *mutteres lishneihem* — she is permitted to either of them. With two competing rumors, the concern for *machzir grushaso* does not apply. Since both marriages rest entirely on the level of *kol*, the community will not construct a definitive narrative of married-divorced-married-divorced. One of the rumors must by necessity be false for any coherent story to emerge, and therefore no perception of *machzir grushaso* can credibly take hold.

### Two Rumors Ruling

The *halakha* follows Ameimar: *mutteres lishneihem* — when there are two competing rumors that remain unresolved, she is permitted to either man. We do not give both rumors such absolute weight that we impose the limitation of *machzir grushaso* on her options. She may receive a *get* from Shimon and remain with Reuven, or vice versa, as circumstances warrant. All of this, it bears noting, remains unfortunate to whatever degree — particularly according to the position that does not negate a *kol* even when the facts are established — that we must at all accommodate the perception of reality alongside the reality itself.

---

## Grounds for Divorce

### Beit Shammai

We now turn to the last *daf* of *Gittin*, 90a, and arrive at a *mishna* that forms a fitting capstone to the entire *maseches*: after an entire tractate devoted to the technicalities and legal mechanics of the *get* — its writing, delivery, agency, and conditions — we finally reach the question of which circumstances actually warrant a divorce in the first place.

The *mishna* records the famous three-way dispute. Beit Shammai states: *lo yegaresh adam et ishto ela im ken matza bah devar ervah* — a man should not divorce his wife unless he has found in her a matter of *ervah*, sexual sin. The scriptural basis is the verse in Deuteronomy that serves as the Torah's primary reference to divorce: *ki matza bah ervat davar*. The entire Torah's treatment of *get* is embedded within the laws of *machzir grushaso* — the prohibition on a man remarrying his divorced wife after she has wed another. In framing the initial divorce, the Torah describes two conditions: *ve-haya im lo timtza chen be-einav* — if she no longer finds favor in his eyes — and *ki matza bah ervat davar* — because he has found in her a matter of sexual impropriety. Beit Shammai focuses exclusively on the latter: actual adultery, or the equivalent thereof. Only when the woman has committed an act that renders it halachically forbidden for them to remain together — when there is real evidentiary basis for sexual transgression — is divorce truly warranted.

It is important to observe that Beit Shammai is not saying that a *get* given for lesser reasons is legally void. The entire framing of the *mishna* is one of guidelines — of what is appropriate — not of legal validity. A *get* does not require court approval; it is in essence an act between the two parties. It does not need to be judicially warranted for it to take effect. What Beit Shammai is articulating is a moral and normative standard: *lo yegaresh*, a man ought not divorce his wife except under these circumstances.

### Beit Hillel Leniency

Beit Hillel permits divorce for any matter that displeases the husband — *afilu hikdicha tavshilo* — even if she merely burned his soup or over-spiced his stew. Rashi notes that this can mean either that the food was actually scorched or simply that it was seasoned in a way he did not like. Either way, the most trivial domestic misstep suffices. The scriptural hook, as we will see in the Gemara's analysis, is the word *davar* in *ki matza bah ervat davar*: *matza bah davar* — he found something, anything, that he did not like.

One might note that the characterization of Beit Hillel as *le-kula* here requires some nuance. If the dynamic is one in which the wife wishes to remain married and the husband acts capriciously, Beit Hillel's ruling is hardly kind to the wife. At the same time, it is *le-kula* in the formal sense of operating with fewer restrictions — and of course the dynamic is not always as described, for it may be the wife who wishes the marriage to end.

### Rabbi Akiva Permissive

Rabbi Akiva extends the grounds for divorce even further: *afilu matza acheret na'ah heimena* — even if he has simply found another woman more beautiful, or more pleasing to him. His scriptural basis is the opening clause of the verse — *ve-haya im lo timtza chen be-einav*, if she no longer finds favor in his eyes — without requiring that she has done anything wrong at all. The wife may be entirely blameless and a model spouse; if her husband has become more attracted to another woman, that is sufficient grounds.

This is a genuinely difficult position to read with equanimity. Some have sought to connect Rabbi Akiva's view with what we know of his biographical relationship with his own wife, his famous deep and passionate love — reading him perhaps as a romantic who believes one must always follow one's heart and remain passionately devoted to one's spouse, so that a loss of that passion is itself grounds for dissolution. But that is a generous reading, and it is worth acknowledging the difficulty. Rabbi Akiva's position here also connects to his rulings in other areas — for instance, regarding a woman's appearance during periods when physical intimacy is restricted — which reflect an orientation that the wife bears a significant responsibility to ensure she remains attractive and pleasing to her husband. A position that allows a man to remarry anyone who pleases him more places a correspondingly heavy burden on the wife to remain perpetually desirable. These are matters that invite serious reflection in light of contemporary sensibilities.

---

## Textual Analysis

### Beit Hillel Exegesis

The Gemara now records a *baraita* that traces the hermeneutical exchange between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Hillel opens: *v'lo kvar neemar davar?* — does the verse not already say *davar*, which denotes any matter? Beit Shammai responds: *v'lo kvar neemar ervat?* — but does it not also say *ervat*, which denotes sexual sin?

Beit Hillel then offers the fuller argument. If the Torah had written only *ervat* and not *davar*, one might have thought: a man may divorce his wife on account of sexual sin, but not for any ordinary matter. And if the Torah had written only *davar* and not *ervat*, one might have thought: if he divorces her for some ordinary matter, she may go and remarry another man — but if he divorces her because she has committed adultery, perhaps she is not entitled to remarry at all. For the continuation of the verse reads *ve-halchah ve-haytah le-ish acher* — and she went and became the wife of another man. One might have supposed that this permission to remarry applies only to a woman divorced for trivial reasons, not for adultery. Therefore, says Beit Hillel, both terms are necessary: *ervat* teaches that even a woman divorced for adultery may remarry (any man other than the adulterer), and *davar* teaches that even the slightest matter suffices as a ground for divorce.

### Beit Shammai Witnesses

For Beit Shammai, the challenge is to account for the word *davar* without conceding Beit Hillel's reading. The Gemara asks: *Beit Shammai, hai davar mai avid lei?* — what do Beit Shammai do with the word *davar*? Their answer is a *gezerah shavah*: the word *davar* appears here, and the same word appears elsewhere — *al pi shnayim edim o al pi shlosha edim yakum davar* — a matter is established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. Just as in that context *davar* requires two witnesses, so too here: the *davar* of *ervat davar* teaches that adultery must be established through the testimony of two witnesses. The word *davar* is not a second independent ground for divorce; it is a procedural requirement attached to the sole ground, *ervah*.

### One vs. Two Grounds

The debate then sharpens into a linguistic question about the phrase *ervat davar* itself. Beit Hillel presses: *mi ktiv ervah b'davar?* — the text does not say *ervah* was found "through" *davar*, through testimony. It says *ervat davar* as a construct phrase. Therefore *davar* cannot be merely the mechanism for establishing *ervah*; it must be a separate item. Beit Shammai replies: *mi ktiv o ervah o davar?* — but the text does not say "either *ervah* or *davar*." The phrase is *ervat davar*, a single unified construct, not two alternatives.

Beit Hillel's final response: *hachi ktiv ervat davar, d'mashma hachi u'mashma hachi* — yes, it is written as a single phrase, but it is precisely this dual resonance that is the point. The phrase simultaneously conveys: *ervah* alone (adultery as grounds) and *davar* alone (any matter as grounds), with the construct form serving to indicate that even in the case of *ervah*, the subsequent permission to remarry applies. The phrase thus carries both meanings at once.

For Beit Shammai, this linguistic analysis reinforces that *davar* is not an independent ground at all: the requirement for *edut* — two witnesses — to establish adultery is the very content the word *davar* imports. Their reading is that *ervat davar* is a single concept: an actual, evidenced act of adultery. Only under those circumstances does the Torah envision divorce as truly warranted.

---

## Get Validity Issues

### Unjustified Divorce

Having established that the grounds for divorce are debated — *ervah* alone (Beit Shammai), any *davar* (Beit Hillel), or even mere loss of attraction (Rabbi Akiva) — the Gemara now addresses the threshold question underlying the entire *mishna*: what if a man divorces his wife with none of these justifications? There was no *ervah*, no *davar*, nothing at all by even Beit Hillel's standards. Does the *get* take effect, or is the man required to remarry her? Rav Papa poses this question to Rava.

### Get Effective

Rava responds by invoking the law of the rapist: the Torah states *lo yuchal leshalcha kol yamav* — the man who raped a woman and was compelled to marry her may never divorce her. If he does give a *get*, he is required to remarry her — *kol yamav b'omed ve-hachzir*. Rava's reasoning: the Torah had to state explicitly that the rapist cannot divorce his wife. This implies that in any other case, even if the divorce transgresses the guidelines articulated in the *mishna*, *mai de'avad avad* — what he has done is done. The *get* is valid. The *mishna* deals entirely with normative guidelines; it does not define the conditions under which a *get* legally functions.

### Secret Divorce Plan

Rav Mesharshiya then raises a related concern — not a legal one, but an ethical one. He poses the following to Rava: if a man has decided in his heart that he intends to divorce his wife, but conceals this from her — while she continues to live in his home, serve him, prepare his meals, share his bed — what is the moral status of that conduct?

Rava's response is a scriptural citation: *al tacharosh al re'acha ra ve-hu yoshev lavetach itach* — do not plot evil against your friend when he dwells with you in trust. The word *re'im* — friends — evokes *re'im ha-ahuvim*, the beloved companions of the marriage bond. The betrayal of plotting divorce while one's wife tends to the home in full trust constitutes a profound breach of the foundational human relationship. It is not a *halakhic* violation — the *get* will still work — but the moral condemnation is severe.

---

## Food & Wife Analogy

### Analogy Framework

A *baraita* is then cited: *haya Rabbi Meir omer, kashem she'hade'ot b'ma'achal kach de'ot banashim* — Rabbi Meir would say: just as people differ in their attitudes toward food, so too they differ in their attitudes toward wives. The comparison of food and marital intimacy as analogous areas of human desire is not uncommon in rabbinic literature, though here the analogy focuses less on desire per se and more on fastidiousness and standards of tolerance. Three types of men are described.

### Fastidious Type

The first is the extremely fastidious man. A fly falls into his cup and he throws out the entire cup — a minor contamination renders the whole thing unacceptable. The *baraita* identifies this with the behavior of Pappos ben Yehuda: when he left his house, he would lock the door and keep his wife confined inside. The analogy to extreme fastidiousness is clear — he could not bear the thought of his wife having any interaction with the outside world, anyone who might constitute, in his mind, any form of contamination. As Rashi notes at the end of his commentary on this passage: *umida she'eina hogenet hee zo shemitoch kach eiva nichneset beineihem umezana tachtav* — this is an unseemly trait, for from such conduct hatred and enmity enter between them, and it actually leads to the very outcome he feared most. By imprisoning his wife in jealousy and suspicion, he generates the conditions for what he dreads. And beyond that consequence, the controlling and abusive nature of such a relationship requires no commentary.

### Normal & Permissive

The second type is the ordinary person — *midat kol adam*. The fly falls into his cup; he removes the fly and drinks the cup. In the context of marriage: his wife speaks with acquaintances, neighbors, and relatives, and he is not troubled by it. He does not allow groundless jealousy to poison the relationship. This is presented as the normative standard.

The third type is the morally deficient man. The fly falls into the stew — the *tamchuy* — and he wrings the fly dry to extract all the juices absorbed from the stew, and then eats the stew. He is wholly indifferent to contamination, even when the contamination is substantial. In the marital context: his wife goes out with her head uncovered, spins in the marketplace in a way that draws attention and exposes her arms, wears clothing slit up the sides, and bathes in places shared with men — and he is unbothered. The Gemara clarifies: bathing literally together with men? Rather, she bathes in the same river or area where men bathe, overlapping in proximity in a way that is far too intimate. The *baraita* concludes: *zu mitzvah min hatorah le-garesha* — in such a case it is a *mitzvah* ordained by the Torah to divorce her.

---

## Immodest Conduct

### Improper Behaviors

The behaviors enumerated in the preceding *baraita* — going out with her head uncovered, spinning in the marketplace, wearing garments slit up the sides, bathing in shared spaces — constitute the category of *ervat davar* in a broad sense.
