This is the same rubric discussed in *Ketubot* under the categories of *dat Moshe* and *dat Yehudit*: behaviors that violate either Mosaic law or the standards of Jewish communal norms as they govern the conduct expected within marriage. It should be noted that while the *mishna* and this *baraita* address women's behavior exclusively, the same logic applies to conduct by husbands that draws inappropriate attention or constitutes disrespect toward the marital bond.

### Mitzva to Divorce

When a woman engages in the behaviors enumerated above, the *baraita* states that it is a *mitzvah min hatorah* to divorce her — *she-garsha, she-ne'emar ki matza bah ervat davar*. The verse *ki matza bah ervat davar* here is read not necessarily as evidence of actual adultery, but as encompassing the broader category of sexually immodest or inappropriate conduct that undermines the integrity of the marriage.

### Second Husband Fate

The *baraita* continues with a *midrashic* reading of the continuation of the verse: *ve-halchah ve-haytah le-ish acher* — she goes and becomes the wife of another man. *Hakatuv kera'o acher* — the Torah calls him *acher*, different or "other," to indicate that he is not of the same quality as the first husband. The first husband did the right thing — *hotzi rishah mibeito*, he removed this woman whose conduct was shameful from his house. The second man — the *acher* — *hichnis rishah le-toch beito*, brings her into his house. If the second man merits it, he will eventually also send her away — *she-ne'emar ve-saneiah ha-ish ha-acharon*. And if he does not merit it: *k'vartahu* — she will bury him, as the verse says *o ki yamut ha-ish ha-acharon*, or the last husband dies. *Kedai hu be-mitah*, he is deserving of death, for the first man expelled this wicked woman from his home, and this man brought her back in.

---

## Malachi Dispute

### Rabbi Yehuda

The Gemara now turns to a *pasuk* in *Malachi* — *ki sanei shalach* — which is read as bearing on the question of when divorce is appropriate. Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse permissively: *im saneisah shalach* — if you hate her, send her away. Rashi understands this as aligned with Rabbi Akiva — or perhaps Beit Hillel — that subjective aversion, even without any wrongdoing on the wife's part, suffices as grounds.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan reads the same verse in the opposite direction: *sanui ha-meshaleiach* — the one who sends her away is himself to be despised. On this reading, the act of divorce is condemned; a man who divorces his wife is hateful. This aligns with a Beit Shammai ethos: divorce without genuine justification is not merely inadvisable but morally contemptible.

### God's Hate Standard

An alternative textual reading (*girsa*) of the verse is: *snuah hi lifnei ha-makom shalach* — only if she is hated before God — i.e., if she has committed adultery, a sin that makes her hateful in God's eyes — should you send her away. This is the most restrictive reading, corresponding most closely to Beit Shammai's position.

### Marriage Distinction

The Gemara then offers a resolution: *v'lo pligi* — the *tannaim* do not ultimately disagree. Rather, their statements apply to different situations. *Ha b'zug rishon, ha b'zug sheini* — one refers to the first marriage, the other to the second. The permissive reading (Rabbi Yehuda) may be applied in the case of a second marriage; the restrictive reading (Rabbi Yochanan), which treats the one who divorces as despicable, is specifically addressed to the first marriage. This resolution flows naturally into the teaching of Rabbi Elazar that follows.

---

## First Marriage Sanctity

### Altar's Tears

Rabbi Elazar teaches: *kol ha-megaresh ishto rishonah afilu mizbe'ach morid alav d'maos* — whoever divorces his first wife, even the altar itself sheds tears over him. The image is striking: the physical altar, the site of sacrifice and divine service, mourns the dissolution of a first marriage.

### Malachi Midrash

The scriptural basis is the verse in *Malachi* (2): *ve-zos sheinis ta'asu, ksos d'mah et mizbe'ach Hashem b'chi va-anakah, mei-ein od penos el ha-minchah v'lakchas ratzon mi-yedchem* — this second thing you do, covering the altar of God with weeping and wailing, so that He no longer turns to the offering or accepts it with favor from your hands. And when the people ask *al mah*, on what account, the verse answers: *al ki Hashem he'id beinecha u-vein eishet neurecha asher atah bagadtah bah* — because God has testified between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have betrayed.

### Covenant Rupture

The theological weight of this verse is profound. The rupture of the marital bond — specifically the betrayal of the wife of one's youth — disrupts one's relationship with God. The altar weeps; God turns away from the offerings. The verse then identifies the wife with two terms: *v'hi chavertecha v'eishet britecha* — she is your friend, your companion, and the woman of your covenant. The marriage to the first wife is cast as a covenant — *brit* — a foundational relationship of partnership and commitment. Betraying that covenant sends ripples outward, all the way to the altar of God.

The resolution the Gemara offers — that Rabbi Yehuda speaks of a second marriage and Rabbi Yochanan of a first — is precisely calibrated to this teaching. When we speak of a second marriage, there is greater latitude; the standards of Beit Hillel or even Rabbi Akiva might apply. But when it is the first marriage — the *zug rishon*, the foundational relationship, the *eishet brit* — the bar is incomparably higher, and to dissolve it for trivial reasons is to be considered despicable, *sanui ha-meshaleiach*.

### Modern Balance

This is a beautiful and powerful teaching, and it is worth sitting with its imagery. At the same time, the principle must be handled with care in its practical application. The concern that divorce not be undertaken trivially must not become a cudgel used against people who have arrived at that painful decision through a long and responsible process. There is a real phenomenon — reflected in personal testimonies and public discourse, including in the Orthodox world — of people who have carefully deliberated and sought guidance over extended periods, who finally appear before a *beit din*, and are made to feel contemptible for being there at all. Sometimes divorce is the right and even necessary decision. The tradition's emphasis on the gravity of first-marriage dissolution must be balanced against sensitivity to the human beings who stand before the *dayan*, and against the reality that prolonging an irreparably broken marriage serves no one.

### Partnership Ideal

It is fitting to close on the phrase with which *Malachi* describes the wife: *chavertecha v'eishet britecha* — your friend and the wife of your covenant. Despite everything in this final chapter — the unilateral power of the husband to initiate divorce, the analogies to food and property, the male gaze that pervades so much of this discussion — this phrase articulates an ideal of marriage as equal partnership, as friendship, as covenant. Remarkably, *ketubot* discovered in the Cairo *Genizah* employ this very language to describe the marital bond: *ishti ve'eishet briti, chaverti ve'eishet briti* — my wife and the wife of my covenant, my companion and the wife of my covenant. Even in an era when many of the legal structures of marriage were heavily asymmetric, the covenantal ideal of *chevratcha v'eishet britecha* persisted as the animating vision of what marriage is meant to be. It is a fitting note on which to conclude *maseches Gittin*.

# Gittin 90

## Kol: Substantiation

### Kol Requires Beit Din

We pick up on 89b in Gittin, in the middle of a discussion about the *kol* — the rumor or report — that a woman has contracted a marriage. The *mishna* established that when such a *kol* circulates, we must be concerned about it and not permit the woman to marry someone else without a *get* from the man she was rumored to have married. The *gemara* has been probing exactly when that concern applies: how much substantiation a *kol* requires, whether we are *mevatlinan kala* — whether we proactively negate the *kol* once we discover it was unfounded — and what the practical consequences of a *kol* are once it has been established.

We now pick up with the ruling of Rav Ashi. The *gemara* states: *kol kol d'lo it-chazek b'vei dina lav kola hu* — any rumor that the *beis din* has not investigated and formally established as a matter of concern is not a *kol* to be reckoned with. This reinforces the earlier principle that substantiating circumstances alone are not sufficient; the *beis din* must actively examine the matter and declare it worthy of concern. Rashi explains: *lo chashinan lei ela im ken yadu beis din ha-ir she-kach yatza kol ploni me-hekhan shama ve-gazru she-yeichushu le-kol zeh* — we are not concerned about the *kol* unless the *beis din* of the city investigated the rumor, determined its source, and formally ruled that it must be attended to.

### Kol Achar Nisuin

Rav Ashi adds a second ruling: *kol kol d'vasar nisuin lo chashinan lei* — any *kol* that arises after the woman is already married is not a *kol* we attend to. Once she is already living with her husband, a rumor about her prior status — that she had been married to someone else, or had committed some act that would render her forbidden to a *kohen* — is disregarded, because acting on it would impact the man she is currently married to.

The *gemara* then qualifies: *d'vasar erusin chashinan lei* — but if the *kol* arose after *erusin* but before *nisuin*, when there is a formal bond but the couple has not yet begun living together, we would still be concerned. Rav Chaviva, however, goes further: *afilu d'vasar erusin nami lo chashinan lei* — even a *kol* arising after *erusin* is disregarded, since even at that stage there is already an existing relationship being impacted by the rumor. The *halacha* follows Rav Chaviva: once *erusin* has taken effect, a *kol* that emerges thereafter is not acted upon.

## Kol + Kiddushin

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a case sent from the academy of Rav to Shmuel: *yatza lah kol me-rishon u-va acher ve-kiddeshah kiddushei Torah mahu* — a *kol* went out that this woman had been married to Reuven, and then Shimon came and gave her *kiddushin* in a full and public manner — *kiddushei Torah*, witnessed *kiddushin* performed openly — in disregard of the existing *kol*. What should be done?

This is a case in which the *kol* was presumably of the serious, substantiated variety that would ordinarily require concern, and yet Shimon proceeded to marry her anyway. The question is how we now navigate the tangle of her status.

### Tetzei Response

Shmuel's reply is: *teitzei* — she must leave the second man. And then: *ve-ha-amidu ha-davar al buryo* — clarify the underlying facts. But what precisely does this instruction to "clarify" entail?

### Investigation: Eidus

A first reading: perhaps it means we investigate and discover that the first marriage was in fact not valid. There was, say, a strong *kol* supported by circumstantial evidence — everyone was carrying candles, everyone celebrated what looked like a wedding — but no formal *eidus*. Upon investigation we find, say, that the ring was not worth a *shaveh prutah* and the *kiddushin* was defective. In that case, *mevatlinan kala*, we would set aside the *kol* and allow the situation to resolve itself in Shimon's favor.

But this reading is rejected: *v'ha Neharde'a atreih de-Shmuel hu, v'lo mevatlinan kala* — Neharde'a was Shmuel's own city, and the practice of Neharde'a is that we are *not mevatlinan kala*. This is a striking ruling. Even when *beis din* determines that the *kol* was factually false, the practice in Neharde'a is still not to proactively negate it. The reason touches on a fundamental principle: the only difference between reality and perception is that it is far easier to change reality than perception. Even if *beis din* knows the truth, they cannot rule in a way that openly contradicts the public's settled understanding of the situation. Therefore, even in such a case, Shimon would still be required to give a *get*, since everyone believes the woman is married to someone else.

The correct reading of "clarify the matter" must therefore be the opposite: we investigate and find witnesses who can testify that the first marriage to Reuven was, in fact, genuine and valid. In that case, *lo tzricha get mi-sheni* — she does not need a *get* from Shimon at all. If the first marriage is proven by *eidus*, Shimon's *kiddushin* was simply void, and she returns to Reuven without any further action.

To summarize the ruling: the *teitzei* is absolute — she cannot remain with Shimon regardless. The only question is whether she needs a *get* from Shimon. If there is only a *kol* and no firm evidence of her marriage to Reuven, she needs a *get* from Shimon before returning. If the marriage to Reuven is established by testimony, she needs no *get* from Shimon whatsoever.

## Kol + Kiddushin (II)

### Perception Issue

This ruling is noted to be in conflict with the position of Rav Huna. Rav Huna holds, based on a principle of Rav Hamnuna, that if a married woman reaches out and accepts *kiddushin* from another man, she is considered at least *safek mekudeshes* to the second man — because a woman who does such a thing is, in effect, declaring to her husband that he has divorced her. Rav Hamnuna's principle is: *ha-ishah she-amrah le-ba'alah geirashtani ne'emenet, chazakah ein ishah me'izah paneha bifnei ba'alah* — a woman who tells her husband directly to his face "you have divorced me" is believed, since we presume no woman would be so brazen if it were untrue. Accepting *kiddushin* from Shimon is an act tantamount to making that declaration.

If we were to rule according to Rav Huna, then even in a case where we know for a fact that the woman is married to Reuven, the act of accepting *kiddushin* from Shimon would minimally require a *get* from Shimon. Yet Shmuel's ruling is that in such a case she does not need a *get* from Shimon at all.

The *gemara* resolves the tension: Rav Hamnuna's principle applies only when the act of accepting *kiddushin* — or making the declaration — occurs in her husband's presence, *be-fanav*. It is specifically because the husband is present and does not protest that we infer the divorce must be real. In our case, the woman accepted *kiddushin* from Shimon *she-lo be-fanav* — not in Reuven's presence — and therefore the act carries no such inferential weight. If we know as fact she is married to Reuven, Shimon's *kiddushin* is meaningless, no *get* is required from Shimon, and she simply returns to being married to Reuven. Tosafot notes that this point — that the principle of Rav Hamnuna requires the husband's presence — was never actually in dispute; the discussion here merely clarifies that even absent that concern, no *get* is needed from Shimon when the first marriage is established by evidence.

### Rav Huna View

Having addressed the confirmed-marriage scenario, the *gemara* turns to the unresolved case: *lo matza davar barur ve-ma hu* — investigation was conducted but no definitive conclusion was reached. The *kol* remains as it was, neither confirmed nor refuted, and Shimon has already given her *kiddushin*. What now?

Rav Huna rules: *megaresh rishon ve-nosei sheni* — the first man, Reuven, must divorce her, and then she may marry the second man, Shimon. This is how Rav Huna understands the instruction *teitzei*: she leaves Reuven (through a *get* from him), and that resolves the *kol*.

### Machzir Grushaso

But Rav Huna also rules: *u-megaresh sheni ve-nosei rishon lo* — we would not permit the reverse arrangement, whereby Shimon divorces her and she returns to marry Reuven. Why not? *Asi le-meimar machzir grushaso min ha-erusin* — people will say that Reuven had married her, then divorced her, then Shimon married her, then Shimon divorced her, and now Reuven is taking her back — which creates the appearance of *machzir grushaso*, a prohibited remarriage of a divorced wife. Even though there is no actual prohibition in this case, the appearance of impropriety forecloses this option according to Rav Huna. It is, to put it plainly, unfortunate that we must so constrain our practical options in order to manage public perception. Yet that is Rav Huna's position.

### Rav Idi Disagrees

The son of Rav Idi — identified in the discussion of competing rumors as Ashmeimar — disagrees: *af megaresh sheni ve-nosei rishon* — we are not concerned about the appearance of *machzir grushaso*. His reasoning: *meimar amri inei rabbanan be-kiddushei ve-kiddushei ta'us hava* — people will say the rabbis looked into the matter and determined that Shimon's *kiddushin* was an error, that it was never valid. Since there was already a *kol* that she was married to Reuven, and the investigation could not refute it, the public perception will naturally be that Shimon's marriage was mistaken from the outset — not that Reuven remarried a woman he had previously divorced. According to Tosafot, the *halacha* follows the son of Rav Idi on this point.

## Kol: Substantiation (II)

### Lo Mevatlinan Kala

This section of the discussion crystallizes the position of Neharde'a regarding *mevatlinan kala*. The Neharde'a position is that we do not negate a *kol* — *lo mevatlinan kala* — even after *beis din* has determined that the underlying facts do not support it. As noted above, this reflects the principle that perception, once formed, cannot simply be undone by legal decree. If the *kol* had the substantiating features that made it credible in the community's eyes, *beis din* cannot retroactively announce that nothing happened and expect that announcement to undo the public's settled understanding. The consequence is that even a woman who is in fact free of any prior marriage must still contend with the *kol* and all that it requires — including, in certain scenarios, a *get* from a man she was never truly married to.

## Competing Rumors

### Two Rumors Setup

The *gemara* now poses a further case: *yatza lah kol mi-zeh u-mi-zeh mahu* — suppose there were not a confirmed *kiddushin* by Shimon but rather two competing *kolot*. On Monday, a strong *kol* emerged that she had married Reuven; on Tuesday, a strong *kol* emerged that she had married Shimon. Both *kolot* are of the variety that would ordinarily demand concern. We were unable to clarify either one. What are her options?

### Rav Papa View

Rav Papa holds that even in this case of two competing rumors, she remains constrained in the same manner as the single-*kol* case under the approach of Rav Huna: *af zu megaresh rishon ve-nosei sheni* — even here, the *kol* tied to Reuven must be addressed by Reuven giving a *get*, and she may then remain with Shimon. The concern for *machzir grushaso* still limits the options to that one arrangement.

### Ashmeimar View

Ashmeimar disagrees: *muteres li-shneihem* — she is permitted in relation to both. When both marriages are based purely on rumors and neither is established by evidence, we cannot treat either *kol* as so definitive that we become worried about the appearance of *machzir grushaso*. Since it is enough for only one of the rumors to have been false in order for her to remain with Reuven without any taint of a prohibited remarriage, we do not impose that constraint here. Both competing *kolot* weaken each other, and the strict perception-management that drove Rav Huna's concern is simply inapplicable when everything is rumor.

### Halacha Ruling

*Ve-hilkheta muteres li-shneihem* — the *halacha* follows Ashmeimar: when there are competing *kolot* with no established facts, she retains full flexibility and is not restricted to any particular outcome. We must still attend to the *kolot* — they do not simply vanish — but we will not give both of them such absolute weight as to generate a concern of *machzir grushaso*. The understanding is that the public, seeing her return to Reuven, will naturally assume that the marriage to Shimon was never established. This remains, in any case, a less than ideal situation, particularly for those who rule *lo mevatlinan kala* — that even known falsehood must be accommodated as perception. That we are required to manage the appearance of reality even after knowing the truth is, one must acknowledge, genuinely unfortunate.

## Grounds for Divorce

### Beit Shammai View

Having concluded an entire tractate devoted to the technical legal act of divorce and the writing of the *get*, we arrive at the final *mishna* of Gittin, which addresses the circumstances that actually warrant a divorce. It is worth appreciating the framing: the *Torah* touches on divorce almost in passing, within the broader prohibition of *machzir grushaso*. The verse that frames the entire institution — *ve-hayah im lo timtza chen be-einav ki matza bah ervat davar*, "it shall be if she does not find favor in his eyes because he found in her *ervat davar*" — arises primarily to set the context for why the first husband divorced her, before the *Torah* goes on to forbid the first husband from remarrying her.

Beit Shammai reads: *lo yegaresh adam et ishto ella im ken matza bah devar ervah, shene'emar ki matza bah ervat davar* — a man should not divorce his wife unless he has found actual *ervat davar* in her, a matter of sexual sin, as it is written that "he found in her *ervat davar*." The language of *matza bah* — "he found in her" — suggests actual discovery, something known to have occurred. Beit Shammai therefore grounds the warrant for divorce in genuine adultery, or at the very least demonstrated sexual impropriety.

It is important to note what this discussion is and is not about. The question of whether a *get* is *valid* — whether it effects a divorce — is a separate matter entirely. The *get* is not like a court-issued civil divorce that requires fault; it is an act performed between husband and wife, and it does not require the approval or certification of *beis din*. The *mishna* is addressing what is *appropriate*, what is *warranted*, what the *Torah* is saying a man should do — not whether the *get* will take effect if he acts outside those parameters. The entire discussion is framed in terms of guidelines for proper conduct, not legal preconditions for validity.

### Beit Hillel View

Beit Hillel holds: *afilu hikdicha tavshilo* — even if she burned his soup, that is sufficient grounds for divorce. Rashi understands this broadly — too many spices, or simply something done to annoy him. The textual support: *shene'emar ki matza bah ervat davar* — the same verse, but Beit Hillel focuses not on *ervah* but on *davar*, "any matter," any small thing that offended him. One might note, and the *gemara* will address this, that Beit Hillel's position is lenient in the particular sense of expanding human freedom and reducing legal restrictions — though whether it is beneficial to the wife is another question entirely, depending on whose interests one has in view.

### Rabbi Akiva View

Rabbi Akiva goes furthest: *afilu matza acheret na'ah mimennah, shene'emar ve-hayah im lo timtza chen be-einav* — even if he simply found someone more beautiful or more pleasing than she is, that is grounds for divorce. The wife need not have done anything wrong whatsoever; she may be the perfect wife in every respect. Yet if the husband is attracted to another woman, the verse says "if she does not find favor in his eyes" — and that subjective failure of attraction is, according to Rabbi Akiva, sufficient.

This is a position that invites real reflection. Rabbi Akiva is, of course, the *tanna* whose love for his wife is among the most celebrated in all of rabbinic literature — the man whose wife Rachel sacrificed everything for him and whom he revered and adored in return. Some have tried to read his position here in that light: perhaps he is a romantic who believes one must always be passionately in love, and therefore if that feeling is gone, the marriage should end. But the position does create real difficulties in terms of protecting the interests of the wife, and it also connects to Rabbi Akiva's rulings elsewhere — regarding certain practices during *niddah* and on *Tisha B'Av* — where he emphasizes that a wife must take care not to become displeasing to her husband, *she-lo titganeh al ba'alah*. If a husband is understood to have the right to leave whenever he finds another woman more attractive, that places an enormous and asymmetric burden on the wife to always present herself favorably. This is something to genuinely reckon with in light of contemporary sensibilities.

## Gemara Analysis

### Davar vs. Ervah

The *gemara* now records a *baraita* in which Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai engage each other directly. Beit Hillel says to Beit Shammai: does it not say *davar* — "any matter" — which proves that even minor things suffice? Beit Shammai replies: does it not say *ervat* — sexual impropriety — which proves it must be something serious? Beit Hillel then explains why both words are necessary: had the verse said only *ervat* and not *davar*, I might have thought a woman can be divorced for *ervah* but not for some lesser *davar*. Had it said only *davar* and not *ervat*, I might have thought that if she remarries after being divorced for a *davar*, she is still permitted to marry anyone — but that if divorced for adultery, she is forbidden to marry anyone else. Since the verse goes on to say *ve-halkhah ve-haytah le-ish acher* — "she went and became the wife of another man" — we needed *ervat* precisely to teach that even in the case of adultery she may remarry. The double language thus serves two purposes: *davar* extends the grounds for divorce, and *ervat* teaches that even an adulteress may remarry (anyone other than the adulterer, as *halacha* specifies).

What then does Beit Shammai do with the word *davar*? They apply the *gezeirah shavah*: *ne'emar kan davar ve-ne'emar le-ilan davar al pi shnayim eidim o al pi shloshah eidim yakum davar* — the word *davar* appears here and also in the verse requiring two or three witnesses to establish "a matter." Just as there, a matter is established through testimony, so here, the *ervah* must be established through witnesses. Beit Shammai thus uses *davar* not to expand the grounds for divorce but to impose an evidentiary standard: adultery must be proven through formal testimony before it constitutes grounds for divorce.

### Interpretation of Pasuk

The *gemara* then asks: what is the underlying dispute? Reish Lakish had established that the word *ki* in the *Torah* carries four meanings: *im* (if), *dilma* (lest), *ela* (rather), and *de-ha* (because). Rashi illustrates these with several examples; notably, both *ela* and *de-ha* appear in proximity in the exchange between Sarah and Avraham — Sarah saying *ki yareti* (because she was afraid) and Avraham responding *lo ki tzachakt* (rather, you did laugh). The dispute between the positions turns on how one reads the word *ki* in this verse.

### Beit Shammai Reading

Beit Shammai reads the entire clause as a single, unified statement: *ve-hayah im lo timtza chen be-einav* describes the lack of favor, and *ki matza bah ervat davar* explains why she does not find favor — "because" (*de-ha*) he found *ervat davar* in her. On this reading, the *Torah* presents one scenario: she has committed adultery, and that is why he no longer finds favor with her. The lack of favor is not an independent ground; it is the consequence of the adultery. There is thus only one condition that justifies divorce.

### Rabbi Akiva Reading

Rabbi Akiva reads the verse as containing two entirely separate statements: *im lo timtza chen be-einav* — if she does not find favor — stands alone as an independent ground for divorce, and *ki matza bah ervat davar* — if he found *ervat davar* — is a second, separate ground. The *ki* here means *im*, "if." On this reading, the verse presents two distinct cases, either of which independently suffices. Beit Hillel's reading, it should be noted, is closer to Beit Shammai's in structure — they too do not read *lo timtza chen* as an independent clause — and it is only Rabbi Akiva who fully separates the two conditions into two freestanding grounds for divorce.

## Get Mechanics

### Get Validity

Rav Pappa asks Rava: if a man divorces his wife with no justification at all — no *ervah*, no *davar* even in Beit Hillel's broad sense — does the *get* take effect? The question itself confirms what was said earlier: the grounds for divorce discussed in the *mishna* are matters of propriety and guideline, not legal preconditions. Rava's answer, however, engages the question from a different angle.

### Rapist Cannot Divorce

Rava says: *degali Rachmana gabei ones* — the Torah made a specific disclosure regarding the rapist (*ones*), stating *lo yukhal leshalchah kol yamav* — "he may not send her away all his days." The *gemara* understands this as *bekum ve-hachzeir*: if a man who raped a woman and was compelled to marry her then divorces her, he must take her back. That is, the Torah explicitly imposes on the rapist not just the prohibition of divorcing but an obligation to re-marry if he does. The implication: *hatam hu de-gali Rachmana* — it was *there*, in the case of the rapist, that the Torah made explicit that the *get* does not stand; *aval hacha mai de-avad avad* — here, in the ordinary case of a divorce without grounds, whatever was done was done. The *get* takes effect, even if the motivation was improper.

### Hidden Intent

Rav Mesharshiya poses a different question to Rava: if a man has inwardly decided to divorce his wife but conceals this intention, allowing her to continue living in his home, serving him, and being intimate with him — what is the ruling on this? Rava does not answer in legal terms. Instead, he cites a verse: *al tacharosh al re'akha ra'ah ve-hu yoshev lavetach itakh* — "do not plot evil against your friend while he dwells securely beside you." The language *re'im ha-ahuvim* — beloved companions — captures the essence of the marriage bond, and to scheme a betrayal while one's spouse lives in trusting intimacy is precisely what this verse forbids. It is an act of profound treachery that the verse characterizes as plotting evil against one who reposes complete trust in you.

## Fastidious Man

### Rabbi Meir Parable

A *baraita* records: Rabbi Meir would say — *keshem she-ha-de'ot ba-ma'akhal kach de'ot ba-nashim* — just as people differ in their attitudes toward food, so they differ in their attitudes toward wives. The analogy, troubling as it may be in certain respects, is developed through three character types.

### Overly Fastidious

The first type: there is a person who, when a fly falls into his cup of wine, discards the entire cup — so fastidious that the slightest contamination renders the wine undrinkable. *Ve-zu hi middat Pappos ben Yehuda* — this is the character of Pappos ben Yehuda, who, when leaving his house, would lock his wife inside, keeping her completely secluded from the outside world. This is presented as extreme, and Rashi remarks directly on how counterproductive and harmful this is: *u-midah she-einah hogenet hi zo she-mi-tokh kakh eivah nikhneset beineihem u-mezanah tachtav* — it is an improper character trait, because it breeds terrible enmity between husband and wife and may lead, of all ironies, to the very infidelity he feared. The controlling dynamic of locking one's wife away does not produce fidelity; it produces hatred.

### Average Man

The second type: the ordinary person, when a fly falls into his cup, removes the fly and drinks the cup. *Ve-zo hi midat kol adam* — that is how most people behave. Correspondingly, most husbands allow their wives to speak with brothers and relatives and other familiar contacts, and do not become suspicious or jealous over normal social interaction.

### Least Fastidious

The third type: there is a person into whose stew a fly falls, who wrings out every drop of flavor from the fly and then eats the stew. *Zo hi midat adam ra* — this is the character of a bad person. Such a man sees his wife go out with her hair uncovered, spinning in the marketplace with her arms exposed, wearing clothing slit up the sides — and does not react. He tolerates everything.

## Women's Conduct

### Immodest Behavior

The *baraita* now enumerates the categories of women's public conduct that fall under the rubric of *ervat davar* in its broader sense — not necessarily adultery, but behavior that constitutes *dat Yehudit*, the norms of modest Jewish conduct within marriage. These include: going out with her hair uncovered, spinning in the marketplace in a manner that exposes her arms, and wearing clothing that is open at the sides.

### Public Bathing

The final and most striking example: *ve-rochetzet im bnei adam* — and bathes with men. The *gemara* objects immediately: literally with men? *Im bnei adam salka datcha* — can that really be meant? The clarification: *ela bemakom she-bnei adam rochtzin* — in a location where men bathe, with sufficient proximity to constitute impropriety even if not literal simultaneous bathing.

In such a case: *zo mitzva min ha-Torah le-garshah* — it is a *mitzvah* to divorce her. The *gemara* invokes *ki matza bah ervat davar* not in the narrow sense of proven adultery but in the broader sense of conduct that is sexually inappropriate and transgresses the norms of modest conduct in marriage. The discussion in *Ketubot* on *dat Moshe* and *dat Yehudit* addresses this at length. The *gemara* is careful to note that the verse then says *ve-halkhah ve-haytah le-ish acher* — she went and became the wife of another man — and the second man who takes such a woman, *hakatuv kera'o acher* — the verse calls him "different" — suggesting he is not of the same character as the first. The first man, *hotzi rasha mi-beito*, rid his house of a wicked woman. The second, *hichnis rasha le-tokh beito*, brought her into his. If the second man merits it, *shelakh* — he too will divorce her. If not, *kevertahu* — she will bury him. *Kedai hu ba-mitah* — death is fitting for him who should have known better.

## Ki Sane Shalakh

### Rabbi Yehuda

The *parasha* contains the phrase *ki sane shalakh* — which can be read as "if he hates, send away." Rabbi Yehuda understands this as a directive: *im sane'tah shalakh* — if you hate her, send her away. Rashi reads this as consonant with the position of Rabbi Akiva, though one might equally associate it with Beit Hillel's broader reading. The common thread is that subjective disaffection — the loss of positive feeling — constitutes grounds for ending the marriage.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan reads it entirely differently: *sanui ha-mishalei'ach* — the one who sends her away is the one who is to be despised. On this reading, the verse is not a permission but a condemnation: the man who divorces his wife is hateful. This aligns with a stricter, Beit Shammai–like sensibility that divorce without serious cause is an act of which one ought to be ashamed.

### Bezug Rishon/Sheni

The *gemara* says: *ve-lo peligi* — in fact they do not disagree. *Ha be-zug rishon ha be-zug sheni* — one statement applies to a first marriage, the other to a second. The context determines which is meant, as we will see in what follows.

## Altar Cries

### First Wife Tragedy

Rabbi Elazar states: *kol ha-megaresh ishto rishonah, afilu mizbe'ach morid alav dema'ot* — anyone who divorces his first wife — the *mizbe'ach*, the altar, sheds tears on his account. The verse is brought from the prophet: *ve-zot shenit ta'asu, kessut dim'ah et mizbe'ach Hashem be-bekhi ve-anakah* — "you cover the altar of God with tears and weeping and sighing." God no longer turns to the *minchah* and no longer wishes to receive the offering from your hands. And when you ask why — *al ki Hashem he'id beinekha u-vein eshet ne'urekha* — because God has testified between you and the wife of your youth, *asher atah bagadta vah* — that you have betrayed her.

### Chavratcha

The verse concludes with words of singular beauty: *ve-hi chavratekha ve-eshet beritecha* — she is your companion and the woman of your covenant. The word *chavratekha* — your friend, your partner — conjures an image of the marriage relationship that is strikingly egalitarian, especially in a context where so much of the tractate has dealt with the husband's unilateral power in matters of divorce. The word *berit* — covenant — suggests a sacred, binding relationship entered into by two parties with equal standing.

### Balance Issues

This brings us back to the tension between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan, resolved by the distinction between a first and second marriage. It is the divorce of the first wife — the wife of one's youth, the foundational relationship — that causes the altar to cry. Applying a Beit Shammai–like stringency to that relationship, insisting that divorce not be undertaken lightly and certainly not for trivial reasons, captures something profound and important. At the same time, it is worth acknowledging that this framework, applied rigidly and without sensitivity, can cause enormous harm. A woman who has carefully and thoughtfully determined that a marriage must end, after long deliberation and many steps in the process, should not be made to feel that she is doing something monstrous simply by appearing before a *beis din*. Sometimes divorce is the right decision. The challenge is to honor the genuine tragedy of the dissolution of a first marriage without weaponizing that recognition to obstruct, shame, or manipulate people who are trying to move forward with their lives.

### Closing: Partnership

It is perhaps fitting to close the tractate on the note of *chavratekha ve-eshet beritecha*. Amid all the discussion of the mechanics of *gittin*, the rules of agency, the conditions of the document, and the grounds for divorce, these words from the prophets remind us what marriage is at its deepest level: a partnership between two people bound by covenant. It is striking that in *ketubot* discovered in the Cairo *Geniza*, this very language is used to describe the marriage relationship — *chaverti ve-eshet briti*, my companion and the woman of my covenant. That the language of friendship and covenantal partnership found its way into those documents of daily life speaks to how central this vision of marriage was — and remains. On that note of *chavratekha ve-eshet beritecha*, we conclude *Masekhta Gittin*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 2

## Intro to Kiddushin

### Masechet Overview

We begin the final *masechet* of *Nashim*: *Masechet Kiddushin*. Like *Gittin*, this is a tractate studied intensively in *yeshivas*, with a rich tradition of *rishonim* and subsequent literature, owing in part to its practical *halachic* relevance to questions of marriage and *kiddushin*. Yet it is equally important to appreciate the remarkably diverse range of topics it encompasses — a diversity comparable to what we encountered in *Gittin*.

A few introductory observations are in order. *Gittin* contained eight or nine *perakim* and extended to ninety *dapim*. *Kiddushin*, by contrast, has only four *perakim* and runs to eighty *dapim* — nearly the same length with roughly half the *perakim*. Alongside the laws of *kiddushin* proper, one finds discussions of parental and filial obligations, *kibbud av va'em*, and other subjects a reader might not expect to encounter in *Masechet Kiddushin*.

### First Perek Structure

The first *perek* is, by any measure, the largest *perek* in *Shas* — forty *dapim*, half the entire *masechet* — and its scope extends well beyond *kiddushin*. The opening *mishna* reads *ha-isha nikneit b'shalosh drachim*, a woman is acquired in three ways, and by the end of that same *mishna* the topic shifts to *ha-yevamah nikneit*, how a *yevamah* is acquired. From there, the *mishnayot* of the first *perek* proceed systematically: how an *eved ivri* is acquired, how an *eved kena'ani* is acquired, how one purchases real estate, how one acquires chattel — all organized around the theme of *kinyanim*, of transactions and acquisitions. The operative word throughout is *nikneit* — acquired. So while the *masechet* is named *Kiddushin* and is named for the institution of betrothal, the first *perek* is devoted not solely, and perhaps not even primarily, to *kiddushin* itself, but to the broad question of how various things and persons are acquired.

The second *perek* returns to a direct focus on *kiddushin* with the formulation *ha-ish mekadesh*, the man betroths — and immediately after that, *bo u'vshlucho*, through himself or through his agent. Where *Gittin* took the institution of *shlichus* somewhat for granted (while raising particular questions about who qualifies as an agent), *Kiddushin* gives *shlichus* a sustained and direct treatment in the second *perek*. The third *perek* engages with questions of *tna'im*, conditions, which we also encountered extensively in *Gittin*. And the fourth *perek* — *asara yuchasin* — addresses lineage: questions of *mamzerut*, uncertain parentage, and related issues of status. A wide and diverse *masechet*, then, and hence even four *perakim* amounts to eighty *dapim*.

---

## Ha-Isha Nikneit Mishna

### Mishna Text

The first *mishna* reads: *ha-isha nikneit b'shalosh drachim*, a woman is acquired in three ways; *v'konah et atzmah b'shtei drachim*, and she acquires herself — her own freedom, if you will — in two ways. Then: *nikneit b'kesef b'shtar u'v'viah*, she is acquired through money, through a document, and through sexual relations.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi explains the phrase *v'konah et atzmah* — "acquires herself" — as meaning *lihyot birshutah*, to be under her own control, and specifically *lihinasay l'acher*, to be free to marry someone else. There are, of course, other dimensions to the change in her status — for instance, a husband may annul his wife's vows, and her earnings belong to him. But Rashi focuses on the most fundamental consequence of *kiddushin*: that she is now bound to her husband in the sense that she may not marry or have relations with another man. That is the core change effected by *kiddushin*, and accordingly that is what "she acquires herself" primarily refers to: the dissolution of that bond, restoring her freedom to remarry. The precision of Rashi's formulation will become clearer as we proceed.

### Three Methods

The three modes of *kiddushin* are *kesef*, *shtar*, and *biah* — money, document, and sexual relations.

### Kesef Method

*Kesef* involves giving an object of value accompanied by the declaration *harei at mekudeshet li* — behold, you are betrothed to me. Also essential, though not stated explicitly in the *mishna*, is the requirement of *eidim*, witnesses — not merely to prove that the act occurred, but to constitute it as a legally binding act, just as we saw by *gittin*.

### Ring Practice

The traditional practice of using a ring is not mentioned anywhere in the *Gemara*. Its first recorded appearance is in a work called *Sefer ha-Chilukim*, a Gaonic-era compilation that documents observed differences in practice between the Jews of *Mizrach* — Babylonia — and the Jews of *Eretz Yisrael*. There it states that the Jews of the East did not use a ring in *kiddushin*, whereas the Jews of *Eretz Yisrael* did. This appears to reflect a regional divergence. In any event, neither the Bavli nor the Yerushalmi mentions a ring; *kesef* simply means the giving of some object of value.

### Shtar Method

*Shtar* is a written document — at its simplest, a piece of paper on which is written *harei at mekudeshet li* — given to the woman in the presence of *eidim*. It is worth noting that while *shtar kiddushin* is fully treated as a valid *halachic* mechanism, there is virtually no evidence that it was ever actually practiced. The *Gemara* contains many accounts of *kesef kiddushin* — a man in a marketplace, for instance, handing a woman a basket of fruit and declaring *harei at mekudeshet li* — but no stories involving a *shtar kiddushin*. It appears never to have been used in practice.

One might be tempted to identify the *ketubah* as the *shtar* referred to here, or the *yichud* room as the *biah*. This is a common misunderstanding, but a complete *halachic* error: the *ketubah* and *yichud* pertain to *nisu'in*, not to *kiddushin*. That said, the ancient *ketubot* from the Cairo Genizah are instructive. Scholars such as Mordechai Friedman have noted that some of those documents include language in which the groom declares *harei at mekudeshet li*, and there is reason to think that at least some communities conceptualized the *ketubah* as bearing some relation to a *shtar kiddushin* — even though *halachically* it is not one, and even though the *ketubah* is fundamentally a document recording mutual obligations associated with *nisu'in*.

### Biah Method

*Biah* — sexual relations — constitutes the third mode of *kiddushin*. The witnesses presumably need not be in the room itself. Crucially, it must be an act of sexual relations performed specifically with the intention of creating *kiddushin*, of establishing the couple as betrothed. Not any act of intimacy — the intent must be directed toward this legal and personal transformation.

---

## Kiddushin vs. Nisu'in

### Kiddushin Defined

The mention of *biah* as a mode of *kiddushin* is an apt occasion to clarify — as it bears repeating — the fundamental distinction between *kiddushin* and *nisu'in*. *Kiddushin* is the act that renders a woman legally a married woman. This means that if she were to accept *kiddushin* from another man, it would have no effect; and if she were to be intimate with another man, it would constitute adultery. However, *kiddushin* does not yet mean that the husband and wife are living together, establishing a household, or having an ongoing sexual relationship. All of that belongs to *nisu'in*, to the moment of *chuppah*, when they actually begin life together.

### Nisu'in Defined

*Nisu'in* is treated in *Masechet Ketubot*, which addresses what constitutes *chuppah*, the obligations it creates — the husband's obligations of *shear, kesut, v'onah* (sustenance, clothing, and conjugal rights) as specified in the *Torah*, as well as the reciprocal obligations running in the other direction, including the wife's earnings going to the husband — and all the legal dimensions of actually establishing a shared household.

### Historical Context

The existence of *kiddushin* and *nisu'in* as two distinct stages reflects a social reality. In the *alte heim*, marriages were often arranged by parents when children were very young. What prevented one side from backing out? In later practice, *tna'im* — formal betrothal agreements with severe financial penalties for withdrawal — served that purpose. But originally, the binding mechanism was *kiddushin* itself. The groom, who had to be of age, would give an object of value, and the legal status of marriage was thereby created — even if the couple would not begin living together for years. The girl could have been betrothed by her father even as a minor. The actual commencement of married life, the *nisu'in*, might follow a decade later.

It is also worth noting that *Masechet Kiddushin* is ordered after *Ketubot* only because it is shorter — four *perakim* versus *Ketubot*'s many more — but conceptually *kiddushin* precedes *nisu'in*, and the ordering reflects size rather than logical sequence. *Sotah*, similarly, follows *Gittin* despite a different conceptual sequence.

### Rashi's Precision

This historical context illuminates the precision of Rashi's earlier comment. When Rashi says *v'konah et atzmah* refers specifically to the ability to marry another man, he is deliberately not mentioning vow annulment or the right to her earnings — because those consequences arise only from *nisu'in*, not from *kiddushin*. The only thing that *kiddushin*, in the absence of *nisu'in*, actually accomplishes is the prohibition on marrying or having relations with another man. All other ways in which a wife is legally under her husband's authority are products of *nisu'in*. Rashi is, as always, precise.

### Biah Distinction

The same precision applies to the *biah* of *kiddushin*. This is not the ongoing sexual relationship that characterizes *nisu'in* and married life. It is a single, discrete act performed with the specific intent of creating the status of *kiddushin* — after which the couple might not begin living together for years. The act of *biah* that constitutes *kiddushin* and the sexual relationship of *nisu'in* are entirely different in kind: the former is a one-time legal act, the latter is the ongoing reality of a shared life.

---

## Kesef Dispute

### Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

The *mishna* continues: *nikneit b'kesef* — acquired through *kesef*. What is meant by *kesef*? *Beit Shammai* say: a *dinar* or its equivalent. *Beit Hillel* say: a *perutah* or its equivalent. The *dinar* was the silver coin of the Roman Empire — and this usage of *kesef* was, literally, silver. The additional *chiddush* of the phrase "or its equivalent" is that the object need not actually be a coin or even metal; it need only be of equivalent value.

### Perutah Definition

*Beit Hillel*'s position — a *perutah* or its equivalent — involves a copper coin, or its equivalent. This of course already demonstrates that *kesef* need not mean silver at all. The *mishna* then provides a gloss on *Beit Hillel*'s view: *kamah hi perutah? Echad m'shmoneh b'isar ha-italki* — one-eighth of an Italian *isar*. The sources indicate that the Italian *isar* was itself a copper coin — *nechoshet* — a point worth noting. If *Beit Hillel* were trying to anchor the *perutah* in the language of silver (*kesef*), one would expect the reference coin to be silver. The fact that it is copper reinforces that according to *Beit Hillel*, *kesef* in this context simply means something of value, however minimal.

This also illuminates the structure of the *mishna* itself. The earlier, core formulation — *nikneit b'kesef, b'shtar, u'v'biah* — reads as a tight, apodictic statement. The discussion of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* is a gloss: a later layer of *tannaitic* commentary asking what that word *kesef* means. And the definition of the *perutah* as one-eighth of an Italian *isar* is, in turn, a gloss upon the gloss. Recognizing this layering is important not only for understanding the *mishna*'s structure but also for appreciating what *kesef* might have meant before *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* introduced their debate.

### Kesef Evolution

Without the *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* gloss, one reads simply: *ha-isha nikneit b'kesef* — a woman is acquired with money. How much money? One might naturally assume something like the *chamishim kesef* of the *Torah* — the standard *mohar ha-betulot*, the fifty silver pieces that constituted the standard bride-price paid, typically to the father, when a virgin was married. That would be a significant, meaningful sum — one that would make the transaction feel genuinely transactional, genuinely like a *kinyan*.

What happened to that fifty *kesef*, which became two hundred *zuz* in rabbinic reckoning? It migrated to the *ketubah*. It became not a sum paid upfront but a sum recorded as a debt, payable upon death or divorce — designed to protect the woman's financial interests and, according to *Chazal*, to slow a husband from divorcing precipitously by ensuring there would be real financial consequences. By moving this amount to the back end, the upfront act of *kiddushin* became symbolic rather than substantial. That is precisely what prompts *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*: if we are no longer giving the *mohar* upfront, what does *kesef* in *kiddushin* actually mean? A *dinar*? A *perutah*?

Once that shift occurs — once the act of *kiddushin* involves only something symbolic rather than a significant purchase price — the institution stops being referred to as *kinyan* and is called exclusively *kiddushin*. The linguistic change tracks an evolution in how the institution itself is conceptualized.

### Kesef in Context

The contrast with other applications of *kesef* as a mode of acquisition sharpens this point. When the *mishna* later teaches that *nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayut* — real estate — is acquired through *kesef, shtar, u'chazakah*, what does *kesef* mean there? Market value. Whatever is being asked for. Nobody imagines that a *perutah* suffices to purchase a house. The *kesef* of real estate acquisition is the actual going rate. So if the opening *mishna* had said simply *ha-isha nikneit b'kesef* without the *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* gloss, the natural reading would be: whatever the agreed-upon price is — presumably something like the *mohar* of the *Torah*. The introduction of a *dinar* or a *perutah* as the operative amount fundamentally transforms how we understand the nature of this transaction.

---

## Intro to Kiddushin (II)

### Kinyan vs. Kiddushin

This brings us to a foundational conceptual tension that will run throughout the entire first *perek*: the *kinyan* model versus the *kiddushin* model of understanding marriage.

*Masechet Kiddushin* is named *Kiddushin*. And in every *mishna* throughout the *masechet* — with a single exception — the institution of betrothal is referred to using the language of *kiddushin*: *mekadesh*, *mekudeshet*, *kiddushin*. The one exception is this very first *mishna*, which uses the language of *kinyan*: *nikneit*, acquired.

One model — the *kinyan* model — understands marriage as a form of acquisition. Not the acquisition of a slave in the full sense of an *eved kena'ani*, but an acquisition nonetheless: the man acquires the woman in certain defined ways. What would he be acquiring? Not her labor — that right is rabbinic, not biblical. But perhaps sexual rights: not only are other men prohibited from her, but he has a claim to her. The *Gemara* discusses the husband's *chiyuv* of *onah*, his obligation to have sex with his wife — but notably never derives from a verse that the wife is obligated to have sex with her husband. The obligation is simply assumed, perhaps because it is built into the very concept of what *kinyan* in marriage means. Similarly, children born of the marriage are considered his in a fundamental way — reflected in the *Torah*'s ruling that one who strikes a pregnant woman causing miscarriage pays the husband, not the mother.

The *kiddushin* model, by contrast, is not primarily about possession at all. It is about personal status — the transformation of a woman from single to married, the creation of an exclusive relationship that renders her *asurah* to other men. It is about a status that emerges through a relationship, not about ownership of a person.

The first *perek* of *Kiddushin* will be the arena in which this tension is worked through. The early, tight collections of *mishnayot* — *ha-isha nikneit*, *ha-yevamah nikneit*, *eved ivri*, *eved kena'ani*, *nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayut* — all structured around "here is the object, here are the modes of acquisition," reflect an early stratum in which the *kinyan* model predominated. The later development — moving the substantial monetary payment to the *ketubah*, reducing the upfront amount to something purely symbolic, and renaming the institution *kiddushin* — reflects a fundamental reconceptualization. A ring that is worth a *perutah* does not feel like a purchase price. It feels like a symbol. And once it becomes a symbol, the institution is no longer called *kinyan*. It is called *kiddushin*.

---

## Nikneit vs. Mekadesh

### Terminology Question

The *Gemara* opens with a direct question: *mai shna hacha detani ha-isha nikneit u'mai shna hatam detani ha-ish mekadesh?* What is the difference between here, where the *mishna* says *ha-isha nikneit* — the woman is acquired — and there, the second *perek*, where the language is *ha-ish mekadesh* — the man betroths? Why does the language of *kinyan* appear only here?

### Kinyan from Efron

The *Gemara* answers: *mishum dekaba'i lemisnei kesef* — because the *mishna* is about to discuss *kesef*, and the concept of *kesef* as a mode of acquisition is derived from the language of *kinyan* used in connection with Avraham's purchase of the field of Efron. That is why we open with the vocabulary of acquisition.

### Gezerah Shavah

The derivation is a *gezerah shavah* of *kicha kicha* — the word "taking" appearing in two contexts. *Ketiv hacha: ki yikach ish isha* — when a man takes a woman. *U'ketiv hatam: natatti kesef ha-sadeh kach mimeni* — I have given the money for the field, take it from me. The same root, *kicha*, appears in both the acquisition of a wife and the acquisition of Efron's field. This creates the hermeneutical link between *kiddushin* and the language of *kinyan*.

### Field Acquisition

To complete the *gezerah shavah*: not only is the same word *kicha* used in both contexts, but the field of Efron is explicitly referred to as a *kinyan* — *ha-sadeh asher kanah Avraham*, the field that Avraham purchased. And a further verse confirms that *kesef* is what effects the acquisition of fields: *sadot b'kesef yiknu* — fields are purchased with money. Tosafot raises the possibility that one might argue the money was merely the price, while the actual act of *kinyan* was accomplished through something else — *chazakah*, perhaps. The verse *sadot b'kesef yiknu* forecloses that: the giving of money is itself the act that acquires the field. So when we learn *kiddushin* from this parallel, we know both that *kesef* is a valid mode of acquisition for a wife and that the giving of *kesef* is itself the operative act.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

The *Gemara* then asks: why not be consistent and use *kinyan* language throughout the entire *masechet*? The answer: *me-ikara tani lishna d'Oraita* — at the outset, the *mishna* uses biblical language. *Kinyan*, as we have seen, is the biblical conceptualization, rooted in the *gezerah shavah* from Efron's field. *U'levasof tani lishna d'Rabbanan* — but subsequently, the *mishna* uses rabbinic language. The rabbinic vocabulary is no longer *kinyan* but *kiddushin*. Words are not arbitrary. The shift from *kinyan* to *kiddushin* across the *masechet* reflects a genuine conceptual evolution in how the institution was understood.

---

## Kiddushin Meaning

### Hekdesh Model

What does the rabbinic term *kiddushin* mean? The *Gemara* explains: *d'asar lah a'kuly alma k'hekdesh* — he renders her forbidden to all other men, as *hekdesh* renders an object forbidden. Just as sanctifying an animal or object to the Temple removes it from the domain of all ordinary use, so too a man who is *mekadesh* a woman renders her off-limits to all other men. This is the core of the *kiddushin* model: not ownership, not possession, but a status of exclusivity — she is removed from the general domain of eligibility.

### Tosafot Relationship

This formulation, while legally precise, is not entirely satisfying as a description of marriage. As one observes immediately: *hekdesh* is off-limits even to the person who sanctified it. If I sanctify an animal, it becomes *asur* to me as well. Furthermore, I can only sanctify something *to* the Temple if I already own it — the act of *hekdesh* flows from prior ownership. But a man does not own the woman before *kiddushin*. So what gives him the right to make her *hekdesh*? And she certainly does not become *asurah* to him.

Tosafot addresses this directly and adds the crucial missing piece. Tosafot asks: in the formula *harei at mekudeshet li*, what does the word *li* — to me — contribute? Tosafot answers: *li yehei li* — she becomes *mekudeshet* to the world *bishvili*, because of her connection to me. Just as one might say *harei hem mekudashim l'Shamayim* — these are sanctified to Heaven — meaning they belong to Heaven and therefore become forbidden to all else, so too *mekudeshet li* means: because you are mine, because you are in relationship with me, you are therefore forbidden to everyone else. Tosafot thus adds the relational dimension: the exclusivity that *kiddushin* creates is grounded not in a transfer of ownership but in a relationship that, once established, forecloses all other relationships.

### Kinyan to Status

What emerges is a fundamental transition: from a world of *kinyan* — possession, control, acquisition of objects — to a world of *kiddushin* — personal status arising through a relationship. The man is still the initiating party; *kiddushin* is still something the man does. But the framework shifts from "I am acquiring her" to "I am entering into an exclusive relationship with her, and the consequence is that she is removed from the domain of all other men." The *li* — the relational dimension — is what drives the prohibition, not an act of possession.

This is reinforced by the comparison to *hekdesh* itself. One might understand *hekdesh* as a transfer of ownership to God. But one can also sanctify an animal as a *korban* — a sacrifice — in a sense that is not simply about God owning the animal in the way a person owns property. The sanctification establishes a relationship of dedication. So too with *kiddushin*: the model of *kiddushin as hekdesh* can be read not as a transfer of ownership but as a dedication — an act of exclusive consecration that establishes a relationship and, as its consequence, shuts out all others.

### Woman's Agency

This leads directly to a further point the *Gemara* will make explicit. The *mishna* says *ha-isha nikneit* — the woman is acquired — using the passive voice and making the woman the grammatical subject. The *Gemara* observes that this is not accidental. While the entire structure of the first *perek*'s *mishnayot* focuses on the object being acquired (the woman, the *yevamah*, the *eved ivri*, the *eved kena'ani*, the real estate), the choice to say *ha-isha nikneit* rather than *ha-ish koneh* — the man acquires — has a deliberate legal implication: *kiddushin* requires the woman's *da'at*, her consent and desire. *Mida'atah in, she-lo mida'atah lo* — with her knowledge, yes; without it, no. The *mishna* makes her a subject, not merely an object.

This is a striking interpretive move. The same *mishna* that uses the language of *kinyan*, and whose derivation is from the purchase of a field, is read by the *Gemara* as emphasizing the woman's subjectivity and agency. The *Gemara* is aware, of course, that in the *Torah* the father could marry off his daughter entirely without her consent. *Chazal* interpreted that power as applying only to a *k'tanah*, a minor — once she reached maturity, she could not be married off without her own participation. And the *Gemara* reads the very language of *ha-isha nikneit* as encoding this requirement of consent, even within a *mishna* that speaks the language of acquisition.

---

## Tosafot Questions

### Tosafot Q1

Tosafot raises two pointed questions on the *gezerah shavah* of *kicha kicha* from Efron's field. The first: why is the elaborate invocation of the *Efron* account necessary? If we already know that *kesef* is the mechanism — as stated explicitly in *ki yikach ish isha* and in the verse *sadot b'kesef yiknu* — why do we need the entire parallel to the field of Efron to establish that *kiddushin* is a *kinyan*?

### Tosafot Answer

Tosafot's answer is subtle. *Kesef* by itself does not necessarily imply *kinyan*. Even if we know that a monetary payment is involved in *kiddushin*, we would not automatically conclude that this payment constitutes an act of *kinyan* in the full technical sense — the same kind of *kinyan* used to acquire a field. Perhaps *kesef* in *kiddushin* operates through some other model entirely, some mechanism that involves money but does not carry the full conceptual weight of *kinyan*. It is precisely the *gezerah shavah* from Efron's field that establishes the equation: the *kesef* of *kiddushin* is called *kinyan* in exactly the same sense that the purchase of a field is called *kinyan*. Without that parallel, the word *kesef* alone would not carry that implication. One could have *kesef* without *kinyan*; one needs the *gezerah shavah* to prove that here, *kesef* constitutes *kinyan*.

### Tosafot Q2

Tosafot's second question is a logical problem with the parallel itself. The *gezerah shavah* links *ki yikach ish isha* — the taking of a woman — with *kach mimenni* — take from me — from Efron's account. But in the *Efron* verse, what Avraham is taking is the *money* of the field — Efron is saying, take my money for the field. The *kicha* in Efron's account refers to the taking of the silver, not the taking of the field. Whereas in *ki yikach ish isha*, the *kicha* refers to taking the woman herself, not to any money. The parallel is therefore imperfect: in one case the *kicha* is of the price, in the other case the *kicha* is of the object acquired. This is simply a sharp observation on the limits of the *gezerah shavah* as deployed here, and Tosafot flags it as such.

---

## Kicha in Torah

### Biblical Kicha

A further and perhaps more fundamental difficulty with the *gezerah shavah* from *kicha* deserves attention. In the *Torah* itself, what does the word *kicha* actually mean when used in the context of a woman? The answer, on close reading, is that *kicha* in the *Torah* refers to *nisu'in* — to full marriage, cohabitation, and sexual relations — not to *kiddushin* or *erusin*. As Tosafot notes, *v'ish asher yikach et achoto* — a man who takes his sister — refers to sexual relations, not to betrothal. And *ki yikach ish isha u'va aleha* — when a man takes a woman and comes to her — the *kicha* and the *bi'ah* are not two sequential stages (first betrothal, then sex). Rather, *kicha* is the full taking into the household; *u'va aleha* is simply the natural consequence. The *kicha* of the *Torah* is the totality of *nisu'in*.

### Erusin

The word in the *Torah* that actually corresponds to what *Chazal* call *kiddushin* — *erusin*, betrothal — is not *kicha* at all. It is the root *eiras*: *asher eiras isha*, the man who has betrothed a woman. *Mi ha-ish asher eiras isha v'lo lekachah* — who is the man who has betrothed a woman but has not yet taken her — demonstrating clearly that in the *Torah*'s own usage, *eiras* comes first and *kicha* comes afterward. *Kicha* is *nisu'in*; *eiras* is *erusin*.

### Methodological Paradox

This creates a striking methodological paradox. *Chazal* derive the laws of *kiddushin* — betrothal — from the *pesukim* that use the language of *kicha*. But those very *pesukim* about *kicha*, in their plain biblical sense, refer to *nisu'in*, not to *kiddushin*. The *pesukim* that actually correspond to the institution *Chazal* are deriving — betrothal as distinct from full marriage — are the *pesukim* using the root *eiras*. Yet the *limudim* in this *masechet* will overwhelmingly draw on the *kicha* verses. This is not a flaw in the derivation but it is worth noting as a structural curiosity: the biblical language most naturally associated with *kiddushin* is *erusin/eiras*, while the language *Chazal* use as their primary hermeneutical tool — *kicha* — is, in the *Torah's* own usage, the language of *nisu'in*.

---

## Woman's Consent

### Voice Answer

The *Gemara* returns to the question of why the *mishna* says *ha-isha nikneit* — the woman is acquired, passive — rather than *ha-ish koneh* — the man acquires, active. The more substantive answer is structural: the entire sequence of *mishnayot* in the first *perek* is organized around the object being acquired. *Ha-isha nikneit, ha-yevamah nikneit, eved ivri, eved kena'ani, nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayut* — each *mishna* names the object and lists the modes of acquisition. Focusing on the object, not the acquirer, is the organizing principle of the entire *perek*. Moreover, the *mishna* must say *v'konah et atzmah* — she acquires herself — and so it is natural that it should also say *ha-isha nikneit*, making her the subject throughout.

### Voice Question

But the *Gemara* presses further: why not say *ha-ish koneh u'makneh* — the man acquires and then releases her — retaining the active, man-centered formulation throughout while still accommodating both halves of the *mishna*?

### Medatah Requirement

Because, the *Gemara* responds, when the husband dies, it is not he who releases her — *lav ihu ka-maknei lah, min shamayim hu d'ka-maknei lah* — it is Heaven that releases her. His death is not an act of *makneh* on his part. So the structure cannot be *ha-ish koneh u'makneh*.

But beyond this technical point, the *Gemara* adds a deeper reason: *iba'it eima* — if you prefer, the language *ha-isha nikneit* is used to make a substantive legal point. Had the *mishna* said *ha-ish koneh*, one might have thought that a man could perform *kiddushin* even without the woman's knowledge or against her will — *afilu be'al korchah*. The *mishna* says *ha-isha nikneit* precisely to emphasize that *kiddushin* is only valid *mida'atah* — with her desire and consent — and not *she-lo mida'atah*.

### Father's Rights

This is a striking move by the *stam*. In the *Torah*, *kiddushin* — or at least the *erusin* of the *Torah* — was not *mida'atah* in any general sense. The father married off his daughter; she was not asked. Only in the account of Rivkah's family (*nikra la-na'ara v'nish'ala et piha*) does the *Torah* depict the bride being consulted, and that itself is presented as exceptional. Ordinarily, in the *Torah*, the woman was entirely the object of a transaction between men — father and husband.

*Chazal* limited the father's authority to marry off his daughter to her minority alone. Once she became an adult, she could only be married with her own participation and consent. And what the *Gemara* does here is remarkable: it reads the language of *ha-isha nikneit* — a *mishna* that uses the most objectifying possible vocabulary, the *kinyan* of acquisition — as encoding the requirement of her consent. The same *mishna* that says "the woman is acquired" is read as insisting that she is a subject, not merely an object, that she must desire and agree to what is happening to her. The linguistic vehicle of *kinyan* is being turned, at the moment of its very first deployment, into an affirmation of her agency.

---

## Shalosh Grammar

### Grammar Question

The *Gemara* now turns to a grammatical question that will occupy the balance of the *daf*: why does the *mishna* say *bi-shalosh drachim* rather than *bi-shlosha drachim*? The number three takes different forms depending on the grammatical gender of the noun it modifies — *shalosh* for feminine nouns, *shlosha* for masculine. If the *mishna* says *shalosh*, it is treating *derech* as feminine. But is *derech* feminine?

### Derech Feminine

Yes: *derech* is a feminine noun. The proof: *v'hoda'ta lahem et ha-derech yelchu vah* — you shall make known to them the path that they shall walk *bah*, using the feminine pronoun *bah*. The feminine agreement of the pronoun confirms that *derech* is feminine, which is why *shalosh* is correct.

### Derech Contradiction

But then the *Gemara* notes an apparent contradiction. Another verse uses *derech* with masculine agreement: *be-derech echad yetz'u eilecha u've-shiva derachim yanusu lefanecha* — they shall come out against you by one way and flee before you by seven ways. Here *echad* (masculine) is used, not *achat* (feminine), suggesting *derech* is masculine. And there is a corresponding inconsistency in the *mishnayot*: our *mishna* says *shalosh drachim* (feminine), while another *mishna* — about checking a *zav* — says *shiva derachim* (masculine, using *shiva* rather than *sheva*).

So the *pesukim* seem to contradict one another, and the *mishnayot* seem to contradict one another.

### Context Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves: *kra'ei ahadadi lo kashya* — the verses do not actually contradict. The grammatical gender of *derech* is context-dependent. The verse *v'hoda'ta lahem et ha-derech yelchu vah* is speaking about the way of the *Torah*. And *Torah* itself is a feminine noun — *Torat Hashem temima meshivat nafesh*. A *derech* that represents *Torah* takes the feminine form; hence *bah*, and hence *shalosh*. The verse *be-derech echad yetz'u eilecha... be-shiva derachim yanusu* is about war — and war is the domain of men (*darko shel ish la'asot milchama, v'ein darchah shel isha la'asot milchama*). A *derech* that represents the masculine domain of warfare takes the masculine form, hence *echad* and *shiva*.

---

## Mishnah Application

### Ha-Isha Gender

The same principle resolves the inconsistency between the *mishnayot*. Our *mishna* — *ha-isha nikneit bi-shalosh drachim* — is about a woman. Since the subject is female, *derech* takes its feminine form, and the number three appears as *shalosh*.

### Zav Gender

The *mishna* about the *zav* — *bi-shiva derachim bodkim et ha-zav* — uses the masculine form *shiva* because the checking procedure applies exclusively to men.

### Zav Rationale

Why are only men subject to this examination? Because the investigation of whether a discharge constitutes *zivah* of the *Torah* — contingent on its not having been triggered by sleep, food, accident, or some other external cause — applies only to men. If a woman has a bleeding, she is automatically rendered *tamei*, whether it was caused by an outside force or not. The source of the bleeding does not determine her status. Therefore *d'darko shel ish le-hivadek, v'ein darchah shel isha le-hivadek* — the checking pertains to the male domain — and so *derech* takes masculine agreement: *shiva derachim*, not *sheva derachim*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 3

## Kinyan vs. Bi'ah Models

### Nikneit vs. Mekadesh

Today we take up *Kiddushin* daf 3, picking up towards the bottom of amud 2. The first *daf* of the *masechet* laid critical groundwork, and the *Gemara* continues here with what is, on its surface, a technical grammatical introduction — yet embedded within it are some of the most fundamental conceptual questions of the entire *masechet*.

The opening discussion centered on the verb *nikneit* — *ha'isha nikneit* — rather than what we find later in the *masechet*, where the language shifts to *mekadesh* or *mekudeshet*. This seemingly minor terminological difference opens onto a major conceptual fault line: is *kiddushin* to be understood as a type of *kinyan*, a property acquisition, in which the woman is essentially the object being purchased? The *Gemara* identified this as *lishna d'kra*, the Torah's own framing of the institution — rooted, as we saw, in the *gezeira shava* from the purchase of Ephron's field.

### Lishna D'Kra vs. Status

On the other side stands the rabbinic understanding encoded in the term *mekudeshet*. As *Tosafot* explains it, *mekudeshet* is not merely a passive status of being forbidden to others — it is *mekudeshet li*, forbidden to others specifically as a result of the relationship between this particular man and this particular woman. This is a status model rather than a property model, and the distinction could not be more consequential. These two frameworks — *kinyan* and *kiddushin* as status — will compete with one another throughout the first half of the first *perek*.

### Object vs. Subject

What makes the *Gemara*'s introduction even more striking is the way it reads the *Mishnah*'s language against itself. The *Mishnah* does indeed treat the woman as a kind of grammatical object — *ha'isha nikneit* sits alongside *yivama nikneit*, *eved ivri*, *eved kna'ani*, *nechasim she'yesh lahem achrayut*, the list moving between persons and things being acquired. And yet the *stama d'Gemara* insists that the choice of *nikneit* rather than *ha'ish koneh* is precisely to foreground her role as a subject — to emphasize that *kiddushin* cannot be done against her will, that she must be a consenting party. This is notably not the Torah model; in the Torah, the woman as an adult acting for herself is nowhere explicit. The *Gemara* here is registering a shift: from the Torah's model, in which the father gives her as a minor, to the world of *Chazal*, in which she is an adult participant.

---

## Drachim vs. Devarim

### Gender Agreement

Continuing along the bottom of the *daf*, the *Gemara* raises the question of gender agreement in the phrase *shlosha drachim*. Since *derech* can be either masculine or feminine in biblical Hebrew, and in fact appears both ways in different *mishnayot*, the *Gemara* asks *mai ta'ama tani shalosh* — why the feminine form *shalosh* rather than *shlosha*? The answer offered is that *derech* takes on a feminine character here because the woman, who is the subject of the *Mishnah*, inflects the gender of the word. This is, admittedly, a point that is difficult to get especially animated about. But behind it lies a more interesting question, to which the *Gemara* immediately pivots.

### Derech and Bi'ah

The deeper question is: why say *drachim* at all? Why not simply say *b'shlosha devarim* — in three things, or three matters? In English the difference between "a woman is acquired in three ways" and "a woman is acquired by three things" is not trivial, and the *Gemara* takes the distinction seriously. The answer: *mishum d'ka ba'ei l'mitni bi'ah* — because the *Mishnah* is going to list *bi'ah*, sexual union, as one of the three modes, and *bi'ah* is linguistically and conceptually associated with the word *derech*. As the *pasuk* says, *v'derech gever b'alma* — the way of a man with a young woman. And similarly, *ken derech isha menafet* — the way of an adulterous woman. The word *derech* is bound up with the concept of *bi'ah* in the biblical imagination.

### Derech Natural Way

But then the *Gemara* poses the obvious challenge: very well, *derech* may be the right word for *bi'ah*, but what about *kesef* and *shtar*? Why should those also be called *drachim*? The answer: *hanahu nami tzorech bi'ah ninhu* — those two also ultimately exist in service of *bi'ah*. All of *kiddushin*, on this reading, is oriented toward and framed by the eventual union of the couple. The word *derech*, applied to all three modes, reflects the fact that the entire institution is pointing toward *bi'ah* as its telos. This is a striking claim, and it parallels the earlier move with *nikneit*: just as the term *nikneit* frames the whole institution even though it is strictly appropriate only to *kesef*, so *derech* frames all three modes even though it is strictly appropriate only to *bi'ah*.

---

## Derech Framing

### Man Seeks Woman

This is where the *Gemara* turns from grammatical observation to something considerably more profound. The *stama d'Gemara* offers a second explanation for the word *drachim*, introduced with *ve'iba'it eima ha mani Rabbi Shimon hi* — an alternative reading attributed to Rabbi Shimon. The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *Rabbi Shimon omer, mipnei mah amrah Torah ki yikach ish isha v'lo k'tiv ki tilakach isha le'ish* — why does the Torah say "when a man takes a woman" and not "when a woman is taken by a man"? Why is the man framed as the active party in *kiddushin*?
