The answer: *mipnei shedarko shel ish lachazor achar haishah v'ein darkah shel ishah lachazor achar haish* — because it is the way of a man to seek out a woman, and it is not the way of a woman to seek out a man. Even in today's more egalitarian social landscape, this dynamic has not entirely disappeared — the expectation that the man is more often the initiator in courtship remains, however contested, a recognizable pattern. And this dynamic also has a direct *halachic* implication: the man is the active party in the act of *kiddushin* itself.

### Aveidah Metaphor

What follows is a beautiful and theologically rich *mashal*: *mashal l'adam she'avdah lo aveidah* — it is like a person who has lost an object. Why does he go looking for it? Because the object was lost from *him*. So too, *mi chozer al mi? Ba'al aveidah mechazer al aveidato* — the one who suffered the loss is the one who goes searching. The man seeks the woman because she is his lost half — the part of him taken away in *maaseh bereishit*, when woman was formed from man. The reference is to *al ken ya'azov ish et aviv ve'et imo v'davak b'ishto v'hayu l'vasar echad* — the two halves rejoining as one flesh.

This metaphor deserves careful attention, because it is doing something quite different from the *kinyan* model. Yes, the *aveidah* metaphor still contains a possessive element — it is something of his that he is reclaiming. But the emotional and conceptual valence is entirely different from the acquisition of an object. One's *aveidah* is not a commodity; it is something one is incomplete without. The resonance is with *bashert* — with the idea that the union is a restoration of something originally whole, not the purchase of something external.

### Beyond Kinyan

The *Gemara* is therefore introducing, right at the outset of the *masechet*, several competing models of what is actually happening in *kiddushin*. On one side sits the *kinyan* framework, with its emphasis on acquisition, property transfer, and the woman as object. On the other side sits the *bi'ah* framework, with its emphasis on natural union, biological and existential complementarity, and the man not as purchaser but as the one searching for his lost half. It is worth pausing to appreciate how powerful it is that both of these framings appear simultaneously in the *Gemara*'s introduction. Saying that all of *kiddushin* is ultimately about the *kinyan* model, or all about the *bi'ah* model, would be too simple. The *Gemara* is presenting both, letting them sit in tension.

There is a related and important observation about the man's role as active party. One might have said: of course the man is the active one, because she is merely the object being purchased. But Rabbi Shimon's answer reframes this entirely. The man is the active one not because she is a passive object, but because he is the one who has lost something and must go searching. This moves the dynamic from domination to longing.

### Natural Operation

The *Gemara* then broadens its inquiry into the word *drachim* by testing it against other *mishnayot* that use the same term. It asks: *vehasnan, be-zayin drachim bodkim et hazav* — we examine a *zav* in seven *drachim* to determine whether his flow results from natural causes. Why say *drachim* rather than *devarim*? The answer: *hasam kamashma lan de'orcha demichla yasira la'asuyei lidei ziva* — the word *derech* conveys that excessive eating naturally leads to a discharge; this is the way things work. Similarly with drink: *ve'orcha demishtaya yasira la'asuyei lidei ziva*. The word *derech* signals not merely a list of items but a natural causal relationship — these are the ways in which the body operates.

The *Gemara* then turns to the *mishnah*: *etrog shaveh le'ilan be-gimmel drachim* — the *etrog* resembles a tree in three *drachim*. Why not say *devarim*? The answer: *mishum de'ba'inan l'mitni seifa, v'leyarak be-derech echad* — because the *Mishnah* also needs to say that it resembles a vegetable in one *derech*. But this just shifts the question: why say *derech* there either? And the *Gemara*'s answer in both places is *de'orcha de'etrog keyarak* — the *way* of the *etrog* is like the *way* of a vegetable, in that it grows on all waters and goes by the time of its picking for *maaser* purposes.

Here it is worth stepping back to explain the underlying *halacha*. By trees, the year that determines which *maaser* applies is the year of blossoming. By vegetables, it is the year of picking. An *etrog* behaves like a tree for *shemita* purposes — we go by when it blossoms. But for *maaser* purposes, it behaves like a vegetable, because like a vegetable it grows continuously throughout the year and can be picked at any time; it is not fixed to one season. *Rashi* explains that the *etrog*'s similarity to a tree includes the *halachot* of *orlah* and *neta revai*, while its similarity to a vegetable includes that its *maaser* obligation follows the time of picking. The use of the word *derech* in both cases signals that these are not arbitrary classifications but reflect something about how each organism naturally operates — how it grows, how it fruits, what it requires.

This carries back to *kiddushin*. The insight that *drachim* is used when natural operation or natural causation is being invoked is significant. *Bi'ah* as a mode of *kiddushin* is not arbitrary — there is something deeply natural about physical union as the expression and actualization of marriage. There is a compelling argument, indeed, that among the three modes, *bi'ah* represents the most primordially natural one. The *Rambam* notes, based on the *Gemara*, that for *Bnei Noach* before the Torah was given, a man and woman who wished to marry would come together in sexual union and thereby be married. This is the *derech* in its most natural sense — not a societal formalism, not a written document, but the physical coming together that *Bereishit* itself describes in the words *v'davak b'ishto*.

This observation opens onto a further question raised in the course of the discussion: if *bi'ah* is the most natural and perhaps the most primordially valid mode of *kiddushin*, does that affect its *halachic* status relative to the others? *Rashi* already cites, in the name of his *rabotai*, a *shita* — associated also with the *Geonim* and reflected in a *sugya* at the beginning of *Ketubot* regarding *hafka'at kiddushin* — that *kiddushei kesef* is *d'rabbanan*. The *Rambam* himself says in several places that *kiddushei kesef* is *midivrei sofrim*. The most explicitly *d'oraissa* mode of *kiddushin* in the Torah may well be *bi'ah*, given the phrase *ki yikach ish isha u-ve'alah* — though we noted yesterday that *ki yikach ish isha* in the plain reading of the Torah refers to *nissuin* rather than *kiddushin*, and that *kiddushin* in the Torah is rooted in *asher eirastiv*. Still, the *Rambam*'s position invites the reading that *bi'ah* is the primary mode and *kesef* is in some sense derived or secondary. If so, then the *Gemara*'s framing — that *kesef* and *shtar* are themselves in service of *bi'ah*, that the whole institution is shadowed by *bi'ah* — is not merely a *drasha* about word choice but a substantive claim about the architecture of *kiddushin*.

One participant in the shiur raised a sharp point: the *Gemara*'s framing may not be merely that marriage is ultimately oriented toward *bi'ah* in the sense of physical intimacy within the marriage, but that *bi'ah* is the primary act of *kiddushin* itself — and the other two modes are in service of that primary act, not merely in service of the eventual marital union. This reading has real *halachic* weight given the positions of *Rashi*'s *rabotai* and the *Rambam*.

There is something else worth noting about how *derech* functions across these cases. As one sharp observation during the shiur put it: the *Gemara* opens by making strong claims about natural order — the natural way of a man is to seek a woman, the natural way of *bi'ah* is framed by the word *derech* — and then proceeds to bring cases of in-between things, like the *etrog* that is partly like a tree and partly like a vegetable. It is almost as if the *Gemara* is subverting its own invocations of natural order by immediately showing that nature is full of hybrids and edge cases. The *koi* — that creature the *Gemara* elsewhere identifies as a hybrid of uncertain classification — is *shaveh l'chaya* in some ways and *shaveh l'behema* in others, and in some ways like neither. *Derech* as natural order is the framework, and then immediately the *Gemara* illustrates how complex natural order really is.

---

## Drachim vs. Devarim (II)

### Drachim Alternatives

After surveying all these cases, the *Gemara* arrives at a clean resolution of the *drachim* versus *devarim* question. The rule is: *kol haycha d'ika plugta tani drachim* — wherever there are distinctions being drawn, wherever the point is that certain ways are specified as against alternatives, the *Mishnah* uses *drachim*. When one is listing matters without implying that alternative possibilities are being excluded, the word used is *devarim*. The proof: the *seifa* of the *mishnah* about *etrog* says *Rabbi Eliezer omer eser shaveh le'ilan l'chol davar* — similar to a tree in all matters — not *l'chol derech*. When the point is not contrast but comprehensive similarity, *devarim* is the right word. When the point is here are the paths as opposed to other possible paths, *drachim* is right.

This maps cleanly onto the usage in our *Mishnah*: a woman is acquired in three *drachim* — these three, and not others. The very phrasing signals that alternatives are being excluded. And this, of course, sets up the *Gemara*'s next move: what are those alternatives being excluded?

It is worth pausing on what these grammatical *sugyot* at the opening of a *masechet* actually accomplish. *Rav Sherira Gaon*, in his famous letter, notes that these opening passages are often characterized by an accumulation of Tannaitic material organized around seemingly trivial questions of grammar or terminology. The tendency in *yeshiva* study is to hyperfocus on every fine distinction; the opposite tendency, in survey learning, is to gloss over these passages as introductory filler. Neither extreme serves well. What the *Gemara* is doing, through these grammatical questions, is introducing the key conceptual vocabulary of the *masechet* — and, more than that, placing several competing models in tension with one another before the *halachic* analysis proper begins. The same move occurs at the opening of *Bava Kama*, where the question of whether *toladot* are equivalent to *avot* for purposes of liability serves as the frame for introducing every major category of damage in the first half of the tractate.

---

## Excluded Modes

### Minyana Resha

Having established that the counting in the *Mishnah* is designed to exclude alternatives, the *Gemara* now asks directly: *minyana derisha lema'utei mai* — what does the number three in the opening clause exclude? And correspondingly, what does the number two in the closing clause exclude?

### Chuppah Exclusion

The *Gemara* answers the first question: *minyana derisha lema'utei chuppah* — the three modes of acquisition exclude *chuppah* as a means of *kiddushin*. The case imagined is one where the father hands over his daughter, or perhaps where a man and woman proceed directly to *chuppah* without any prior *kiddushin*, and the question is whether standing under *chuppah* alone could effect *kiddushin*. *Rashi* here introduces the father specifically, perhaps because the act of *chuppah* alone — simply standing beneath it — is difficult to conceptualize as a significant legal act. What precisely is being done? *Rashi* may find it easier to frame the case if the father actively hands over his daughter, making the *chuppah* feel like something more concrete is occurring. Still, the question stands: might *chuppah* alone, as a symbol of marriage, suffice to create *kiddushin*?

The *Gemara* immediately notes: *u-lerav Huna de'amar chuppah konah* — Rav Huna in fact holds that *chuppah* does effect *kiddushin*, deriving it through a *kal vachomer*. We will encounter his position in the coming days. For Rav Huna, then, the question becomes: what does the number three exclude? To which the *Gemara* responds —

### Chalipin Excluded

— *lema'utei chalipin*. It would exclude *chalipin*, exchange or barter, as a mode of *kiddushin*. The *hava amina* is serious: *salka deitach amina, ho'il u'gamar kikha kikha misdei Ephron* — since we derive *kiddushin* through a *gezeira shava* of *kicha kicha* from the acquisition of Ephron's field, we might have thought that all modes of acquisition that work for a field should work for a woman. Since *chalipin* works for acquiring a field, perhaps it should work for *kiddushin* as well. *Kamashma lan* — the *Mishnah* tells us no.

### Chalipin Perutah

But the *Gemara* does not stop there. It asks *ve'eima hachi nami* — why not indeed? What is actually wrong with the *hava amina*? The *Gemara* answers: *chalipin itnehu b'fachot mishaveh perutah* — *chalipin* can be effected with an object worth less than a *perutah*. A *keli* of any value, even a toothpick, suffices. *Ve'ishah b'fachot mishaveh perutah lo mikanya nafshah* — a woman will not agree to give herself over for less than a *perutah*. *Rashi* adds: *degnai hu lah* — it is demeaning to her to be party to such a transaction.

Two distinct types of *chalipin* must be held in mind here. The first is classic barter — I give you my donkey, you give me your cow; objects are exchanged on the assumption of rough equivalence. This is in some ways more ancient and more *natural* than *kesef*, since commerce likely began as barter before abstract monetary value was established. The second type of *chalipin* — often called *kinyan* — is a formal legal act: one party takes an object (classically a handkerchief) as a symbolic gesture that expresses *gemar da'at*, the finalization of a commitment. This second type is more like a handshake than an exchange; in the context of a wedding, for example, the groom takes the rabbi's watch or handkerchief to obligate himself to the terms of the *ketubah*.

### Exchange Model Fails

For the exchange model, the inappropriateness for *kiddushin* is readily felt. To frame *kiddushin* as a swap — my pen for your daughter — thoroughly commodifies the woman. *Rashi*'s language of *degnai hu lah* maps cleanly onto this: it is demeaning because it turns *kiddushin* into barter. And this demeanor quality inheres in the transaction type itself, not merely in the value of the object. Consider: if a man were to say *harei at mekudeshet li* while handing a woman an iPhone worth several hundred dollars, that works perfectly well as *kiddushei kesef*. But if he were to say *be-chalifei iPhone zeh harei at mekudeshet li*, framing the same object as *chalipin*, it does not work. The object is identical; what changes is the framing. When the transaction is framed as *chalipin*, it is framed as exchange — we are swapping — and that framing is what makes it inappropriate. The *kesef* model, by contrast, allows the object to function symbolically: you give something of value, and that effectuates the institution, without the connotation of a commercial transaction.

The *gemar da'at* model of *chalipin* presents a harder case. Why should a formal act of commitment-expression be inappropriate for *kiddushin*? In some ways, *kiddushin* as *gemar da'at* seems conceptually apt — it expresses finality, mutual commitment, the completion of a decision. Yet even the *gemar da'at* form of *chalipin* ultimately hearkens back to the root concept of exchange and barter. Even if the handkerchief is purely symbolic, the institutional logic of *chalipin* remains that of swap. And it is that root logic — exchange, commodity, barter — that is incompatible with *kiddushin*.

### Tosafot Chalipin

*Tosafot* offers a narrower and more technically precise reading. According to *Tosafot*, the question was never whether all modes of field acquisition should work for a woman; it was specifically whether *chalipin* might be subsumed under *kesef* — that is, whether *chalipin* is simply a form of *kesef*. After all, in both cases you give something and the transaction is effected. Why not call *chalipin* a species of *kesef*?

The *Gemara*'s answer, on *Tosafot*'s reading, is that *chalipin* operates on fundamentally different parameters. *Kesef* works because of the *value* of what is given; it requires *shaveh perutah*, monetary worth. *Chalipin* works because of the *keli* — the object itself, regardless of value. Fruit, for example, would not work for *chalipin*. These are categorically distinct mechanisms. Once *chalipin* is shown to work *b'fachot mishaveh perutah* — with objects worth less than the minimum monetary unit — it is proven that *chalipin* is not a form of *kesef*. And since only *kesef*, *shtar*, and *bi'ah* effectuate *kiddushin*, *chalipin*, having been shown to be none of these, does not work.

This is a cleaner and more narrowly *halachic* argument than *Rashi*'s. For *Tosafot*, the issue is not primarily about dignity or demeanor but about categorical classification: *chalipin* and *kesef* are different legal instruments with different operative parameters, and *kiddushin* requires *kesef*, not merely any transaction that resembles it.

---

## Woman's Freedom

### Minyana Sifa

The *Gemara* turns from the first clause to the second: *minyana de-seifa lema'utei mai* — what does the number two exclude in the clause that says a woman acquires her freedom in two ways?

### Chalitza Exclusion

The answer: it excludes *chalitza*. The *hava amina* is constructed as a *kal vachomer*: *mah yevama she-eina yotza b'get yotza b'chalitza* — a *yevama*, a widow awaiting *yibum*, cannot be released from her obligation to the *yavam* by means of a *get* prior to *yibum*, and yet *chalitza* does release her. *Zu she-yotza b'get eino din she-yotza b'chalitza* — a regular married woman, whom a *get* does free, should *kal vachomer* be freeable by *chalitza* as well. The *Gemara* answers: *amar kra, sefer keritut* — the verse says a *sefer keritut*, a written bill of severance. Only a *get* dissolves a regular marriage.

This *kal vachomer*, it must be said, is one of a series of formally constructed but intuitively strained arguments that appear throughout the opening of *Kiddushin*. The whole force of *chalitza* in the context of *yibum* has everything to do with the specific bond created by the *yibbum* obligation — it is *kacha ye'aseh la'ish asher lo yivneh et beit achiv*, a specific ceremony for a specific relationship. To suggest via *kal vachomer* that *chalitza* might therefore dissolve a regular marriage is, as a practical matter, almost absurd. And yet the *Gemara* follows the formal logic of the argument to its conclusion, requiring a *pasuk* to rule it out. This is characteristic of how the *Gemara* operates in this section: it applies the structure of *kal vachomer* with full rigor even when the conclusion seems intuitively obvious. The need for *sefer keritut* — a verse that explicitly requires a written document — closes the argument definitively.

*Tosafot* continues the analysis by exploring further *kal vachomers* that might have been constructed and were not, asking why certain arguments were or were not raised. This mode of analysis reaches its apex in the *acharon* known as the *Atzmos Yosef*, who effectively performs *Tosafot* to the second power, raising hypotheticals upon hypotheticals. The point is not to mock the exercise but to recognize that the formal structure of *kal vachomer* as applied here is being pushed to its limits, and the limiting factor is always either a *pasuk* or an intrinsic incompatibility in the comparison.

---

## Kesef Source

### Menalan Kesef

Having established what *kiddushin* does not include, the *Gemara* now asks the foundational question: *menalan* — how do we know that *kesef* works for *kiddushin* at all? This might seem surprising given how much has already been built on this assumption, but the *Gemara* now turns to ground it properly.

### Father's Rights

The *Gemara* approaches this question through the lens of the father's rights, citing a *mishnah* in *Ketubot*: *zakai b'vito b'kiddusheha b'kesef b'shtar u-v'viah* — the father has rights over his daughter's *kiddushin* and can marry her off through *kesef*, *shtar*, or *bi'ah*. This is significant because you might have thought that only *kesef* would work when it is the father acting — since the transaction model, with money passing from the groom to the father, fits most naturally with *kesef*. The *mishnah* establishes that all three modes apply equally when the father acts on his daughter's behalf.

The emphasis on the father also carries a deeper conceptual weight. As noted above, the Torah's presentation of *kiddushin* is fundamentally the father's act — the woman in the Torah is a minor whose marriage is arranged by her father. The father model is where the *kinyan* framework is most at home: she is the object, he is the seller, the money comes to him. By beginning the derivation of *kesef* from the father's rights, the *Gemara* is in some sense returning to the foundational framework.

### Adon Zeh Adon

The actual derivation of *kesef* comes from a *pasuk* in the context of a Jewish slave-girl, the *amah haivrit*: *veyatza chinam ein kesef* — she goes free without money. The *Gemara* reads this as follows: *ein kesef le'adon zeh, aval yesh kesef le'adon acher* — there is no money going to *this* master when she leaves his control, but there is money going to *another* master. The verse cannot be referring merely to the explicit case of the slave-girl's sale — that is already stated explicitly. There must be another case in which a woman leaves the father's control and money is paid to him. That case must be *kiddushin*. Hence: when a man marries the daughter, money goes to the father.

### Father Active Agent

But how do we know the father is the one who receives the money, rather than the daughter herself? The *Gemara* cites: *et biti natati l'ish hazeh* — "I have given my daughter to this man." This verse, from the case of *motzi shem ra*, establishes that the father is the active agent who gives over his daughter in *kiddushin*. He performs the act; he hands her over. *Rashi* and *Tosafot* both note that the verse technically speaks of a *na'arah* rather than a *ketanah*, but the *Gemara* reads it as applying to a case where he married her off when she was a minor. In any event, if the father is the one performing the act of *kiddushin* — *et biti natati* — then obviously the money placed in his hand is his to keep.

### Ketanah Na'arah

The *Gemara* then introduces a complication. One might have argued: all of the above — that the father acts, that the money goes to him — applies clearly when she is a *ketanah*, a minor, because as a minor she has no legal personality of her own and no capacity to receive *kiddushin* herself. But what about when she is a *na'arah* — between twelve and twelve and a half, the stage at which she has attained some degree of her own personhood in *halacha*? At that stage she does have some capacity to accept *kiddushin* on her own. Perhaps, then, when she is a *na'arah*, she could accept the *kesef* herself and retain it: *tikadesh hi nafshah v'tishkol kasba* — she could betroth herself and pocket the money.

This question — how do we know the father retains his rights and his claim to the money when she is a *na'arah* — is where the *Gemara* leaves us. The status of the *na'arah* is the middle ground: not the *ketanah* over whom the father has total control, and not the *bogeret*, the adult woman twelve and a half and older who is entirely beyond the father's control. In the *na'arah* stage, *halacha* recognizes her as possessing *yad* — a hand, an agency — even while the father also retains certain rights. How those rights are defined, and how we know the father is entitled to the *kiddushin* money even when she has some independent standing, is the question that will open tomorrow's discussion.

---

---

# Kiddushin 4

## Father Sells Daughter

### Intro: Kesef & Father

The *daf* opens in the middle of an ongoing discussion about how we derive the rules of *kiddushei kesef* — betrothal effected through money. Although the *stam* of the *gemara* earlier introduced this topic through the famous *gezerah shavah* of *kicha kicha* from the field of Ephron, the *gemara* here focuses primarily on the *pasuk* dealing with a father selling his daughter into slavery. The thematic proximity of that sale to a father marrying off his daughter makes it a natural anchor for the derivation.

The *gemara* picks up approximately in the middle of 3b. The *gemara* establishes that from the *pasuk* in the context of *motzi shem ra* — *es biti natati la'ish hazeh*, "I gave my daughter to this man" — we see that the father has the authority to marry off his daughter. And from the *pasuk* of *ein kesef* in the context of the sale of a daughter as a slave, we learn that *kiddushin* is effected through money. These two sources together establish: *kiddushei kesef* exists, the father performs it, and the father keeps the proceeds.

### Ktana: Father Controls

But this raises an immediate question: from *es biti natati la'ish hazeh*, all we can demonstrate is the father's authority when she is a *ktana* — a minor. The *mishna* in *Ketubot* teaches that these rights apply even when she is a *na'arah*, a girl between twelve and twelve and a half years old, who already has some legal standing. How do we extend the father's rights to that later stage?

The *gemara* quotes the text: *v'eima hani mili ktana d'leit lah yad* — perhaps these rules apply only to a minor who has no independent legal hand. According to our *girsa*, the phrase *likabel kiddushin* is included: she has no hand to receive her own *kiddushin*. Rashi, however, appears not to have had that word, and understood the question more broadly — a *ktana* has no legal standing whatsoever.

### Na'arah Question

The *gemara* then presses the question: *aval na'arah d'it lah yad likabel kiddushin* — a *na'arah* who does have the capacity to receive her own *kiddushin*, perhaps *eima takdish ihi nafshah v'tishkol kaspah* — she should marry herself off and pocket the money herself? The scope of the question is somewhat ambiguous: is the *gemara* asking whether the father loses his right entirely when she is a *na'arah*, or merely whether she can act alongside him? In any case, the question is sharp: what is the source for the father's authority and his right to the money at this stage?

### Slave Sale Source

The *gemara* answers from the *pasuk*: *b'neureiha beit aviha* — "in her youth, in her father's house." This phrase appears in the context of the father's power to annul her vows. From it the *gemara* derives a broader principle.

### Neurim to Father

*Kol shevach neurim l'aviha* — all the benefit of her youth goes to her father. Therefore, any money she would receive through an act of *kiddushin* that she herself performs would flow to him. The *gemara* then cites a related teaching: Rav Huna said in the name of Rav — how do we know that a daughter's earnings go to her father? From the *pasuk* *v'chi yimkor ish et bito l'amah*: just as a female slave's labor belongs to her master, so a daughter's labor belongs to her father — *mah amah ma'aseh yadeiha l'rabbah af bat nami ma'aseh yadeiha l'aviha*.

As Rashi notes, when she is a *ktana*, one doesn't even need a *pasuk* for this — it follows by *kal va'chomer*: if he can sell her labor to someone else as a slave, obviously he himself is entitled to it. The novelty of the *pasuk* is that it extends this right even to the stage of *na'arah*, when he can no longer sell her as a slave.

## Three Categories

### Chart Three Rights

At this point it becomes useful to lay out the full picture. The father has three distinct categories of rights over his daughter. First, as a *ktana*, he can sell her as a slave — *v'chi yimkor ish et bito l'amah* — and this obviously entails his right to her *ma'aseh yadeiha*. Second, he can perform *kiddushin* on her behalf, derived from *es biti natati la'ish hazeh*. Third, he has the power of *hifrat nedarim*, annulment of her vows, from *b'neureiha beit aviha*.

Now the *gemara* asks: for the stage of *na'arah*, we know *hifrat nedarim* applies because the *pasuk* itself says *b'neureiha*. We know *ma'aseh yadeiha* applies from the *drasha* on *v'chi yimkor*. But we still need to establish that the father keeps the *kiddushei kesef* even when she marries herself as a *na'arah*. The *gemara* attempts several routes and rejects each.

### Why Not Nedarim?

Perhaps we could learn *kiddushei kesef* from the principle of *hifrat nedarim* — if he has all the rights of her youth generally, surely he gets her money. The *gemara* rejects this: *mamoni me'issuri lo yalfinan* — monetary law cannot be derived from laws of *issur v'heter*. The right to annul vows is a religious prerogative that tells us nothing about financial entitlements.

### Knas Distinction

What about the fact that in cases of *ones u'mifateh* — rape and seduction — and *motzi shem ra*, the Torah explicitly gives the *knas* to the father, *v'natnu l'avi ha-na'arah*? Surely that establishes that money flows to the father? The *gemara* again rejects this: *mamona miknasa lo yalfinan* — one cannot derive ordinary monetary law from a *knas*. A *knas* is a penal fine rooted in punishment, not compensation, and its rules carry no implications for a straightforward monetary transaction like *kiddushei kesef*.

### Boshet & Pegam

One might then suggest: what about *boshet* and *pegam* — the genuine compensation payments in a case of rape? These are not punitive fines but actual damages for the shame and physical injury suffered by the victim. If these real compensation payments go to the father, that should prove that *kiddushei kesef* goes to him as well.

## Three Categories (II)

### Father's Rights

The *gemara* responds: *d'avua shaich b'gufa* — the father has a stake in her body, meaning in his rights over her, that justifies his receiving *boshet* and *pegam*. But does this help us prove *kiddushei kesef*?

## Boshet/Pegam Logic

### Rashi: Lost Profit

Rashi explains the underlying logic in stark terms. The father has a direct financial interest in her body in the sense that he could have arranged her marriage and received money for doing so. By being raped or harmed, she is now worth less on the marriage market. The *boshet* and *pegam* compensate for that lost opportunity. This is a disturbing framing, but it is the *gemara*'s own logic as Rashi describes it. Notably, if the father's right to *boshet* and *pegam* is rooted in his ability to marry her off and profit from doing so, this very logic would seem to imply that *kiddushei kesef* should go to him as well.

### Why Not Boshet?

Yet the *gemara* struggles with this very point. If *boshet* and *pegam* go to the father because of his authority to marry her off, why can't we use that to prove he gets *kiddushei kesef*? The argument becomes murky here, and the *gemara* has difficulty cleanly distinguishing the cases.

### Tosafot Resolves

Tosafot resolves this by reframing the scenario. The argument is specifically about the case where she marries herself as a *na'arah*. Even in that case, the father retains the ability to marry her off himself — he has not lost that right. That is why he is entitled to *boshet* and *pegam*. But one might still argue: in the specific sub-case where she herself performs the act of *kiddushin*, perhaps in that moment she should get the money — not because he lacks rights generally, but because in this particular transaction she is the active party.

### Misavra: Ein Kesef

The *gemara* ultimately resolves the question not through a logical proof but through *misavra* — the weight of contextual reasoning. The *pasuk* of *ein kesef* establishes that when a slave goes free from her master, the master receives no money. The *gemara* notes that the implicit parallel is: when she leaves the domain of another authority figure, money does change hands. And when the *gemara* seeks who that authority figure is whose analogue receives the money, it is not her but the father. Whether he arranged the *kiddushin* or she did, the recipient on the father's side of the transaction is the father himself.

## Departure Parallel

### Still in Father House

The *gemara* immediately challenges this parallel. The model of *yetzi'ah* — departure from the master — does not translate cleanly to *kiddushin*, because after *kiddushin* a *na'arah* does not actually leave her father's house. *Hasha'm nafkah me'reshus adon legamrei* — in the case of the slave, she departs fully from her master's domain. *V'hacha achat michsra mesirah lechupah* — in the case of *kiddushin*, until she actually enters the husband's home at *nisuin*, she remains entirely under her father's control and within his household.

### Shared Vow Control

The *gemara* responds: *leafroshai nedarim mi'ha nafkah me'reshusei* — there is at least a partial departure in the domain of vow annulment. The *mishna* teaches that once a *na'arah* is betrothed, *aviha u'va'alah meferin nedareha* — both her father and her husband must jointly annul her vows. His authority in this area is no longer exclusive.

### Limited Status Change

This is, admittedly, a limited change of status. He still retains vow annulment power; he simply now shares it. It is therefore somewhat puzzling that the *gemara* treats this partial shift as sufficient to sustain the comparison to a slave's departure from her master. The point seems to be not a genuine parallel in terms of lived experience, but a formal change of status that the *halacha* recognizes. And once we see the *gemara* is working with a formal model rather than a realistic one, the question can be turned on its head: if she doesn't truly leave his domain, that is all the more reason why — once we accept *kiddushei kesef* in principle — the money should go to him rather than to her.

### Transactional Model

What emerges from this entire discussion is that the dominant model in the *gemara*'s analysis of *kiddushei kesef* is the sale of a daughter as a slave. The *gemara* repeatedly returns to that framework. The father has control over her, she is sold or transferred to another domain, and money changes hands. The model is transactional in a deep structural sense. One cannot read through this *sugya* — even if some of the arguments are difficult to follow — without absorbing the message that *kiddushei kesef* is being derived from and explained through the template of the father selling his daughter into slavery.

## Economics & Symbolism

### 50 Coins & Burden

It is worth pausing to acknowledge the economic reality underlying all of this. In the world of the Torah, the payment involved was fifty silver *shekalim* — equivalent to two hundred *zuz* — a substantial sum. In that context, one might understand the financial logic that daughters, who in the ancient world generally did not go out and earn wages for the household, were perceived as financial burdens, and the father's primary obligation was to marry them off to someone who would provide for them.

### Dowry Shift

The deep irony is that once *kiddushei kesef* became purely symbolic — reduced to a ring worth a *perutah* — the financial burden shifted entirely to the father. It is now the father who must provide a substantial dowry if he wishes to arrange a favorable match. The one who once received money now pays.

### Ketubah Balance

The *ketubah* reflects this more complex economic reality. On one side, the groom undertakes financial obligations payable in the event of divorce. On the other, the bride's family brings property into the marriage. The system is not a simple sale; it involves financial flows in both directions, and the *ketubah* functions as a kind of balance between these competing obligations.

## Ein Kesef Derasha

### Extra Yud Method

The *gemara* now turns to a textual puzzle. The *pasuk* regarding the release of a Hebrew slave-girl says both *yatz'ah chinam* — she goes free without payment — and *ein kesef* — there is no money. If *chinam* already tells me she goes free at no cost, what does *ein kesef* add? The *braita* teaches: *yatz'ah chinam elu yemei bagrut, ein kesef elu yemei na'arut* — the first phrase refers to her going free as a *bogeret*, the second to her going free already as a *na'arah*. But if that is what *ein kesef* teaches, how can the *gemara* also use *ein kesef* to derive *kiddushei kesef*?

### Rabina's Drasha

Ravina answers: had the Torah meant only to convey the law of *na'arut*, it could have written *an kesef* — without a *yud*. The fact that it writes *ein* with a *yud* allows us to derive two teachings simultaneously. The phrase itself — *ein kesef* — teaches that she goes free as a *na'arah*, and the extra *yud* teaches *ein kesef la'adon zeh v'yesh kesef la'adon acher u'manihu av* — there is no money to this master, but there is money to another master, namely the father. Thus from a single letter, two separate *halachot* are derived.

### Zera Ein Lah

The *gemara* validates this method of interpretation by analogy to the *pasuk* of *v'zera ein lah* — the *bat kohen* who married a *yisrael* and is now widowed without children returns to her father's house and may eat *terumah* again. The *braita* asks: I know only that her own children constitute *zera*; how do I know that grandchildren — *zera zarah* — would also bar her return? *Talmud lomar v'zera ein lah* — the *gemara* reads *ein* as *ayin lah*, "look into her" — investigate all connections. Furthermore, one might think only *zera kasher* — legitimate offspring — counts; how do I know that a *mamzer* would also constitute *zera*? Again from *zera ein lah*, *ayin lah*. The *gemara* then asks: how can you use *ein lah* for both grandchildren and *zera pasul*? For grandchildren you did not even need the *pasuk* — *benei vanim harei hem kevanim*, grandchildren are like children by a general principle. Therefore the *pasuk* is needed specifically for the case of *zera pasul*, and that is what the *ayin lah* comes to teach. The methodology of deriving multiple teachings from an extra *yud* is thus established.

### Both Verses Needed

The *gemara* confirms that both *pesukim* are in fact necessary — both the *ein kesef* teaching (that the father receives money) and the teaching that she goes free as a *na'arah*. Neither can be dispensed with.

## Why Both Verses

### If Only Kesef...

If the Torah had only written *kiddusheiha l'aviha* — that the *kiddushei kesef* goes to her father — one might have thought: this is because she didn't exert any effort to earn it, like *kesef metziah*, found money. Therefore it goes to him rather than to her. But from this I would not know that her ongoing earnings also go to him.

### If Only Yatzah...

Conversely, if the Torah had only taught *ma'aseh yadeiha l'aviha* — her earnings go to her father — the logic is clear: she lives in his house, he feeds her, and in exchange she works and he takes her earnings. This is an implicit reciprocal arrangement, the very model that *Chazal* later built into the marital relationship between husband and wife. But by that logic, *kiddushei kesef* would not obviously belong to him — it is not something she earns through ongoing labor. It falls, as the *gemara* puts it, *me'alma ka'ati*, out of the sky, unexpectedly.

### Reciprocity Model

The two *pesukim* together thus paint a complete picture: the father supports her, she provides her labor, and the reciprocal arrangement extends even to *kiddushei kesef*. Each *pasuk* provides what the other cannot.

### Unexpected Kesef

Precisely because *kiddushei kesef* is unexpected and not part of the regular rhythm of her labor and his support, it cannot be derived by inference alone — it requires explicit scriptural teaching. This is why both verses are indispensable.

## Na'arah Status

### Father Can Override

The *gemara* has been clear that the father can marry off his *na'arah* even against her will. His authority is not conditioned on her consent.

### Self-Marriage Debate

A closer question is whether a *na'arah* can marry herself off. The *gemara* appears to suggest that she can, given the entire discussion about what happens when she performs the act of *kiddushin* herself. But this requires examination in light of the *rishonim*.

### Rambam: Prior OK

The Rambam rules *lehalacha* that a *na'arah* cannot independently perform her own *kiddushin*. If she does, the validity is entirely contingent on her father. And crucially, the Rambam holds that even the father's subsequent approval — after the fact — does not validate the act. The only way her participation in *kiddushin* works is if the father gave his approval beforehand. In that framing, she is essentially acting as his *shaliach*; he grants her permission in advance, and she executes his decision.

### Retroactive Approval

Others disagree, holding that if she marries herself and the father subsequently ratifies the act, it may be valid. On this view, his approval after the fact is sufficient to confirm what she initiated.

## Double Language

### Redundancy Question

The *gemara* now addresses a related textual puzzle. The *pasuk* about the release of the Hebrew slave-girl mentions both *na'arut* and *bagrut* — the stages of *na'arah* and *bogeret*. Since a girl can only be sold as a slave when she is a *ktana*, she will necessarily go free either as a *na'arah* or as a *bogeret*, never later. So why does the verse need to mention *bagrut* at all? If we are told she goes free as a *na'arah*, she will obviously be free before reaching *bagrut*.

### Rabba: Both Stages

Rabba answers: *bazzeh u'limad al zeh* — one phrase teaches through the other. Without the double language, a reader would naturally apply the single phrase to the later, more extreme stage — *bagrut*. The presence of the second phrase is what allows us to extend the rule to the earlier stage of *na'arut* as well. Had there been only one phrase, we would not have derived *na'arut* independently.

### Bazzeh U'Limad

The *gemara* illustrates this principle through the case of *toshav v'sachir* in the laws of *terumah*. The Torah states that a *kohen*'s *toshav* and *sachir* may not eat his *terumah*. The *braita* establishes: *toshav* refers to an *eved ivri* acquired permanently — the one who had his ear pierced and serves until *yovel*; *sachir* refers to the *eved ivri* who serves for six years. One might ask: just say *toshav* — the more permanent one — and I would derive by *kal va'chomer* that the *sachir* certainly doesn't eat *terumah*. But had the Torah written only one term, one would have applied it to the more limited case — the *sachir* — and I would have concluded that the permanent *eved ivri*, the *toshav*, actually does eat *terumah*. The second term is necessary precisely to cover the case that would otherwise seem like the more extreme and more doubtful instance.

Abbaye, however, challenges this analogy. In the *toshav v'sachir* case, we are dealing with two different people — a *toshav* and a *sachir* are distinct individuals. Even if one were obvious, the Torah can reiterate it because the two statements are independent. But in the case of the slave-girl, it is one person. She cannot go free as both a *na'arah* and a *bogeret* — if she goes free at *na'arut*, she never reaches *bagrut* as a slave. So the two phrases cannot both refer to the same girl going free at two different stages. There must be a different explanation.

## Aylonit Case

### Aylonit Definition

Abbaye therefore proposes a new resolution: *ela amar Abbaye lo nitzrecha ela l'vagar de'aylonit* — the verse is needed for the case of the *aylonit*, a woman who never develops the normal signs of puberty and therefore never passes through the halachic stage of *na'arut*. The *aylonit* transitions from *ketana* directly to *bogeret* at age twenty, when she is legally recognized as an adult by default, having failed to develop the physical markers that would have defined her as a *na'arah*.

### Skips Freedom?

The concern is straightforward: since the *aylonit* skips *na'arut* entirely, one might have thought she also skips the liberation that occurs at *na'arut*. Perhaps she remains enslaved indefinitely, since the trigger for her freedom — reaching *na'arut* — never arrives.

### Aylonit Freed

The verse therefore teaches *ka mashma lan*: she does go free when she reaches *bagrut*, even though she never passed through *na'arut*. The stage of *bagrut* — whenever it arrives — is sufficient to effect her release.

### Kal Va'Chomer?

Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges this: *v'lav kal va'chomer hu*? Is this not simply a *kal va'chomer*? When a girl develops the signs of puberty — *simanim* — this does not free her from her father's domain; she remains a *na'arah* under his authority. Nevertheless, those same signs do free her from her master. Now, *bagrut* — which does free her from her father's domain entirely — surely frees her from her master as well. This seems so obvious that no *pasuk* should be needed to teach it.

### Chidush: Sell Her

Mar bar Rav Ashi himself resolves the difficulty: *lo nitzrecha ela l'ikar zevina de'aylonit* — the novel teaching of the *pasuk* is not about her liberation but about the permissibility of selling her in the first place. The *hava amina* would have been: only a girl who will become a *na'arah* can be sold; a girl who will never become a *na'arah* — like this *aylonit* — perhaps cannot be sold at all. *Ka mashma lan* that even an *aylonit* may be sold as a Hebrew slave. This is the genuine *chidush*, and since we have no need for the *pasuk* to tell us she goes free at *bagrut* — that follows from a *kal va'chomer* — we apply the *pasuk* to this more surprising teaching.

Tosafot raises the question of how we could know at the time of sale — before age twelve — that this girl is an *aylonit*. Tosafot notes that there is a discussion about whether *simanei aylonit* can be detected even at a young age. The *gemara* appears to assume that she would remain enslaved until age twenty. It is also worth noting the striking halachic point embedded here: this woman is nineteen years old, fully an adult by any intuitive measure, yet is legally classified as a *ketana* — because the *halacha* defines majority through specific physical markers rather than age alone. A twelve-year-old with minimal signs of puberty is a legal adult; a nineteen-year-old without them is not.

It is also worth stepping back to appreciate the broader significance of this discussion. The repeated emphasis on the father's sale of his daughter as a slave throughout this *sugya* is somewhat mitigated when one reflects on the actual purpose of that sale in the Torah's framework. The *gemara* itself implies that the *amah ivriyah* arrangement is ultimately oriented toward marriage — the master or his son is expected to marry her, and if neither does, she goes free. The labor of a young *ketana* is minimal; the real point of the transaction is the eventual marriage decision. Understood this way, the model is less about slavery and more about a structured arrangement for securing her marital future.

## Why Ein Kesef?

### Braita: Ki Yikach

The *gemara* now transitions to the *braita* that introduces the derivation of *kiddushei kesef* from the *pasuk* of *ki yikach ish isha u'va'alah* — "when a man takes a woman and has relations with her." The *braita* states: *ein kicha ela b'kesef* — the word *kicha* (taking) refers to acquisition through money, as evidenced by *natati kesef hasadeh kach mimeni* — Ephron's statement to Abraham that he should take the money for the field.

### Slave to Woman

But the *braita* immediately asks: why do I need a *pasuk* at all? Is this not derivable by *kal va'chomer*? *U'mah amah ivriyah she'eina niknes b'biah niknes b'kesef* — a Hebrew slave-girl, who is not acquired through an act of *biah*, is nevertheless acquired through money. *Zu she'niknes b'biah* — this woman, who is acquired through *biah* (as the continuation of the *pasuk* states, *u'va'alah*), *eino din she'tikne b'kesef*? Should it not follow all the more so that she can be acquired through money?

### Yevamah Contrast

The *gemara* immediately raises a counterexample: *yevamah tochiah* — the *yevamah* disproves this. A *yevamah* is acquired through *biah* — the act of *yibum* — yet she is not acquired through money. So the *kal va'chomer* breaks down: acquiring through *biah* does not guarantee acquiring through *kesef*.

### Yevamah Limited

The *braita* responds by distinguishing the *yevamah*: *mah l'yevamah she'ken eina niknes b'shtar* — the *yevamah* is a unique case in which only *biah* works, not even a *shtar*. The methods of *kiddushin* for a *yevamah* are radically limited. In contrast, marriage (*kiddushin*) works through both *biah* and *shtar* — as we are about to derive. If the methods of acquisition are broader for ordinary *kiddushin*, then money should certainly also be available as an avenue, and we can restore the *kal va'chomer* from *amah ivriyah*.

### Derive from Marriage

Since *shtar* works for *kiddushin* but not for *yibum*, the *yevamah* is not a valid parallel. And since the *kal va'chomer* from *amah ivriyah* can be restored, the *pasuk* of *ki yikach* — together with the *kicha-kesef* analogy from Ephron — serves to anchor *kiddushei kesef* and *kiddushei shtar* firmly in the realm of ordinary marriage, distinct from the narrow rules of *yibum*.

## Both Verses Needed

### Woman Keeps?

Having established that *ki yikach* is needed, the *gemara* asks why we need both *ki yikach* and *yatz'ah chinam ein kesef*. If the Torah had written only *ki yikach* — derived through the *kicha-kesef* analogy from Ephron — the *hava amina* would have been: *kiddushin d'yahiv ba'al dedidah havu* — the money of *kiddushin* belongs to her. This follows naturally from the *ki yikach* context, where there are only two parties and the woman herself appears to be the relevant figure in the transaction.

### Two-Party Model

The Ephron-Abraham model is significant here. In that narrative, there are only two parties: Abraham and Ephron. There is no third-party authority selling the woman as a father sells a daughter. The story therefore naturally suggests a model in which the woman herself is the central figure — a two-party transaction rather than a three-party arrangement with a father as intermediary. If *kiddushei kesef* were derived from this model alone, one might have assumed that the money goes to her.

### Ein Kesef Ambiguous

Had the Torah written only *ein kesef* — without *ki yikach* — the ambiguity would run in a different direction. *Ein kesef* tells us that money changes hands, but it does not specify who gives and who receives. The *pasuk* merely implies that in the analogous case of *kiddushin*, money is involved. But in which direction does it flow?

### Rashi: She Gives

Rashi identifies the *hava amina* explicitly: *heicha d'yahava ihi ledidei kesef v'kidashto d'amra lei hiskadesh li* — perhaps she gives the money to him and says "marry me." The *pasuk* of *ein kesef* alone would not rule this out; it simply asserts that money is part of the equation without specifying the direction.

### Ki Yikach: He Takes

*Ki yikach* resolves this: *ki yikach* — he takes, he is the active party. The grammatical and legal subject of the act is the man. *Ki tikach* — she takes — is not what the Torah wrote. The husband must be the one who effects the acquisition, not the woman. Thus the two *pesukim* are mutually necessary: *ein kesef* teaches that the father receives the money even when she is a *na'arah*, and *ki yikach* teaches that he — the man — is the active party who gives the money.

## Status Asymmetry

### She Becomes M'k

Tosafot raises a pointed observation about Rashi's *hava amina*. Rashi suggested that without *ki yikach*, one might have thought she gives the money and says *harei ata mekudash li* — "you are hereby betrothed to me." Tosafot challenges this: the language of *kiddushin* does not grammatically apply to the man, because *kiddushin* does not change his status. He is not rendered prohibited to other women by virtue of being married — polygamy was technically permitted. The status of *mekudeshet* — betrothed — is a status that applies to her, not to him. When he marries her, her relationship to all other men is transformed. His relationship to other women is not equivalently transformed. Therefore, saying *harei ata mekudash li* is not a coherent formulation.

### She Declares

Tosafot therefore reformulates: perhaps the *hava amina* was that she says *harei ani mekudeshet lach* — "I am hereby betrothed to you." She is still the speaker who articulates her own status change, even if the language is now correctly formulated.

### Tosafot Full

Tosafot takes this one step further. Tosafot argues that *d'yahava ihi ledidei* — "she gives the money to him" — was never meant literally. We have just established at length that the father receives the *kiddushei kesef*. How could the *hava amina* be that she gives money to the groom? Rather, Tosafot proposes, the *hava amina* was *natan hu v'amrah hi* — he gives the money and she speaks the declaration. The question was about who recites the formula of *kiddushin*, not about who physically transfers the money.

### Not Pshat

This is not, however, the plain reading of the *gemara*, as Tosafot acknowledges. Rashi's reading — that the *hava amina* was literally that she hands over the money — is the straightforward *pshat* of the text. Tosafot is reframing the entire discussion to make it consistent with the conclusion that the father receives the money. In doing so, Tosafot surfaces a deeper tension: the *gemara* has two very different models in play simultaneously — the father-centered model derived from *ein kesef* and the *amah ivriyah*, and the two-party transactional model derived from *ki yikach* and Abraham's purchase of the field. At the very last moment, the *gemara* suggests that even the *ki yikach* model, taken alone, could have generated an unexpected conclusion — not that she receives the money, but that she gives it. These two contrasting models, and the tension between them, run through the entire *sugya* and animate the *gemara*'s sustained need to derive *kiddushei kesef* from two independent *pesukim* rather than one.

---

---

# Kiddushin 5

## Three Methods Overview

### Opening

We begin toward the bottom of 4b, carrying into 5a. The daf finds us already in the midst of a larger discussion: what are the *limudim* — the derivations — for each of the three different ways of effecting *kiddushin*? Those three ways are *kesef*, *shtar*, and *biah*. The *gemara* has already worked through most of the proofs for *kiddushei kesef* and has begun its treatment of *kiddushei biah*.

### Mishnah vs. Gemara Order

One immediately notices a structural peculiarity: the order of derivations in the *gemara* differs from the order presented in the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* proceeds *kesef*, *shtar*, *biah*; the *gemara* treats *shtar* last. We will encounter this reordering directly as we work through the *sugyot* today.

---

## Kiddushei Biah

### Uv'alah Drasha

The *gemara* cites the *pasuk*: *ki yikach ish isha uv'alah* — "when a man takes a wife and *ba'alah*," where *uv'alah* functions as an active verb, meaning he becomes her *ba'al*, or in a more graphic sense, he consummates the relationship. From this word the *gemara* derives: *uv'alah melamed sheniknet b'biah* — the word *uv'alah* teaches that the *kinyan* of *kiddushin* can be effected through a sexual act.

### Kiddushin vs. Nissuin

It is worth noting at this juncture that several *dappim* later the *gemara* will raise a crucial question: *biah kiddushin oseh o biah nissuin oseh?* — does that initial act of *biah* effect both stages of marriage simultaneously, jumping across both *kiddushin* and *nissuin*, or does it effect only *kiddushin*, leaving *nissuin* to be completed through a separate step? We register this question here, as it bears on everything that follows.

### Kal Vachomer: Yevamah

But the *gemara* immediately asks: is the word *uv'alah* even necessary? Could we not derive *kiddushei biah* through *kal vachomer*? The *gemara* proposes: *v'halo din hu* — is this not a logical inference? A *yevamah* cannot be acquired through *kesef* and yet she is acquired through *biah* (the act of *yibbum* is effected exclusively through *biah*). Surely then, in a normal marriage, where we already know *kesef* works, *biah* should work *kal vachomer* — money being more broadly applicable demonstrates that the avenue is even wider, and *biah* should follow.

### Three Marriage Cases

The *gemara* throughout this *sugya* continually compares and contrasts three distinct cases: *yibbum*, *amah ivriyah*, and normal marriage. *Yibbum* is the situation where a man's brother has died childless; the surviving brother and the widow are already in a particular legal relationship — they must either consummate the *yibbum* or dissolve it through *chalitzah*. The *amah ivriyah* — a minor girl indentured by her father — occupies an intermediate position: it is primarily a labor arrangement, though as we shall see, the *gemara* insists it is not a marital relationship, while *tosafot* will complicate that picture considerably. These three cases interact with the three modes of *kiddushin* and with the comparison between *kiddushin* and *gerushin* — the *hekesh havayah l'yetziah* — and sorting out which comparisons are primary and which secondary goes to the core question of what the institution of *kiddushin* actually is and how it is effected.

### Amah Ivriyah Exception

The *kal vachomer* from *yevamah* is challenged: *amah ivriyah tochiach* — the case of the indentured servant refutes the inference. The *amah ivriyah* can be acquired through *kesef* and yet cannot be acquired through *biah*: the transfer of her labor rights cannot be effected through a sexual act. The *kal vachomer* thus collapses.

The *gemara* anticipates a reply: *mah l'amah ha'ivriyah she'ein kinyanah leshum ishut* — the *amah ivriyah* is not a marital relationship; perhaps we should limit her counter-example to non-marital contexts and allow the inference to proceed for relationships that are *leshum ishut*. The *gemara* responds that this is precisely why we need the *pasuk*: *talmud lomar uv'alah* — the word *uv'alah* is required to teach that a normal marriage can be effected through *biah*, because the *kal vachomer* cannot carry us there on its own.

### Rav Ashi Resolution

But why can the *kal vachomer* not carry us there? *Rav Ashi* explains: the difficulty lies not only with the *amah ivriyah* counterexample but with the *yevamah* premise itself. *Mah li'yevamah sheken zekukah ve'omedet* — what makes *yibbum* distinctive is the *zikah*, the pre-existing bond that forms between the *yavam* and the *yevamah* from the moment of the brother's death. The *yevamah* is already in a state of *zekukah ve'omedet* — she stands in a legal relationship with the *yavam* before any act of *biah* occurs. That antecedent *zikah* sets the stage and enables *biah* to consummate what is already, in some sense, a developing relationship. In normal marriage there is no such pre-existing *zikah*; the two parties are strangers in the legal sense. Therefore the *kal vachomer* fails from both ends: the *yevamah* premise is unique in its *zikah*, and the *amah ivriyah* counterexample undermines any broader application. All three cases — *yibbum*, *amah ivriyah*, and normal marriage — are legally distinct from one another. Hence: *talmud lomar uv'alah*.

It is worth noting the background *machloket tanna'im* of *yesh zikah o ein zikah*, and the question of how substantial that *zikah* really is — whether according to some *tanna'im*, including Rabbi Akiva, the *zikah* is comparable in force to *kiddushin* itself, such that *yibbum* brings the relationship from a quasi-*mekudeshet* state to completion of *nissuin*. That discussion lies in the background of *Rav Ashi*'s resolution.

### Tosafot Ye'ud

*Tosafot*, commenting toward the bottom of 4b, revisits the *amah ivriyah* and complicates the *gemara*'s categorical dismissal of her relationship as non-marital. One of the reserved rights of the master over an *amah ivriyah* is *ye'ud*: he may designate her to marry himself or to marry his son. In this arrangement, the *kesef kiddushin* is retroactively absorbed into the original purchase price — the money paid at the time of the sale serves double duty. This *ye'ud* is unmistakably a marital dimension of the *amah ivriyah*'s status. *Tosafot* therefore notes that while the *gemara* has categorically rejected the notion of *amah ivriyah she'einah leshum ishut*, the institution of *ye'ud* introduces genuine marital elements into the picture, and there are several additional points *tosafot* develops on this question.

---

## Kiddushei Shtar

### Shtar Derivation

Moving to 5a, the *gemara* turns to *kiddushei shtar*, introducing the question with the word *af* — "also": *u'minayin she'af b'shtar?* — from where do we know that *kiddushin* can be effected by giving a *shtar*, a document? The use of *af* signals that *shtar* is perhaps the least intuitive of the three methods, and we will see why throughout this *sugya*. The *gemara* follows the same structural template we have observed throughout: first propose a *kal vachomer*, then reject it, then introduce an independent *limud*. Only once all three independent *limudim* have been established will the *gemara* attempt to derive each method from the combination of the other two — the *tzad hashaveh* argument — and that discussion will unfold on *amud bet*. The underlying operating principle of the entire *sugya* is that it would be preferable to learn through *kal vachomer*, which requires no expenditure of *pesukim*, and resort to *drashot* only when necessary.

### Kal Vachomer: Kesef

The proposed *kal vachomer*: *mah kesef she'ein motzi machnis* — money, which cannot be used to effect divorce, can nonetheless be used to enter into marriage. A *get* can only be a document; one cannot give *kesef* for divorce. *Shtar*, by contrast, can end a marriage — it is the very instrument of divorce. If money, which lacks the power to dissolve, can create the marital bond, surely *shtar*, which has the power to dissolve, should *kal vachomer* be able to create it as well?

This is a striking argument, and worth pausing over. The *Rashba* frames it in terms of *koach deheteira adif*: the power required to create a *heter* where there was none is far greater than the power to create a prohibition. One can generate *issurim* relatively easily — through *nedarim*, through the principle of *shavei anafshei kachaticha de'issura*, and so forth. But to permit what is forbidden is impossible absent a genuine legal mechanism. The power of a *get* to accomplish exactly that — to permit a woman who would otherwise be a married woman to remarry — is extraordinary. *Shatarot* generally carry enormous legal weight in *halacha*: *Rabbi Yochanan* holds that witnesses who sign a *shtar* are treated as if their testimony had already been examined by a *beit din*, without requiring the usual *drisha ve'chakira*. So the suggestion that *shtar's* power to dissolve should yield *kal vachomer* a power to create is a serious argument, even if it will ultimately be rejected.

### Kesef Uniqueness

The *kal vachomer* fails because *kesef* has a unique quality that *shtar* lacks: *mah l'kesef sheken podim bo hekdesh u'ma'aser sheni* — money can be used for *pidyon*, to transfer the sanctified status of *ma'aser sheni* or *hekdesh* onto the coins themselves. *Ma'aser sheni*, which normally must be brought to Jerusalem and consumed there, can be redeemed onto a silver coin — *v'natan hakesef v'kam lo* — allowing the money to be brought instead and used to purchase food in Jerusalem. *Hekdesh* similarly can be redeemed. No *shtar* can accomplish this. *Rashi* raises the *hava amina*: what kind of *shtar* would one have imagined using for *ma'aser sheni*? Perhaps a *shtar chov* — a lien instrument, where one writes "I am obligated to bring five silver coins to Jerusalem for *ma'aser sheni*." The *Rashba*, however, objects strongly: a *shtar kiddushin* and a *get* are not *shtarot chov*. They are *shtarot kinyan* — documents that describe and effect the transaction directly, as when one writes *harei perot elu peduyim b'shtar zo*. The *Rashba*'s point is that the *hava amina* must be understood in terms of the correct category of *shtar*.

The *pidyon* comparison is also interesting in light of the earlier equation between *kiddushin* and *hekdesh* noted on 2b: *de'assar lah achulei alma kehekdesh* — the very word *kiddushin* draws on the parallel between marital sanctity and consecrated property, and the transfer of status that *kiddushin* effects is in some ways analogous to the transfer accomplished through *pidyon*. But the parallel remains imperfect, which is why the *kal vachomer* from *kesef* ultimately fails.

### Hekesh Havaya

Having rejected the *kal vachomer*, the *gemara* turns to an independent *limud*. The *pasuk* in the context of divorce reads: *v'yatza v'hayta l'ish acher* — she leaves and she can become the wife of another man. The *gemara* derives: *makish havayah l'yetziah* — comparing entry into marriage (*havayah*) to exit from marriage (*yetziah*). *Mah yetziah b'shtar af havayah nami b'shtar* — just as a woman is divorced through a *get*, so too she can be married through a *shtar kiddushin*. This is the *hekesh havayah l'yetziah*, and unlike the *kal vachomer*, it is a genuine *hekesh* drawn from the language of *mikra*.

### Sanigor Katigor

A natural question follows: could we not apply the *hekesh* in the reverse direction — *v'ikish nami yetziah l'havayah* — and derive from *kiddushei kesef* that divorce could also be accomplished through *kesef*? *Mah havayah b'kesef af yetziah b'kesef* — just as one enters marriage with money, perhaps one could also exit marriage with money?

*Abaye* rejects this: *yomru kesef machnis kesef motzi* — people would say the same mechanism that creates the marriage dissolves it. This is *sanigor ya'aseh katigor* — the defense attorney has become the prosecuting attorney. The instrument by which a woman is bound has become the instrument by which she is released. It is worth noting that *kiddushei kesef* is the only method of *kiddushin* actually practiced in the time of *Chazal*, which is precisely why this concern arises: people would readily associate the two acts if both involved giving money.

### Distinct Shtar Documents

The *gemara* then raises an analogous concern about *shtar*: does not the *hekesh* cut both ways? If we derive *kiddushei shtar* from the fact that *yetziah* is accomplished through *shtar*, have we not simultaneously derived that *yetziah* could also be accomplished through the *shtar* used in *kiddushin* — *katigor ya'aseh sanigor*? The *gemara* dismisses this concern: *milei d'hai shtar l'chud u'milei d'hai shtar l'chud* — these are two entirely different *shtarot*. The words written in a *get* are unmistakably those of a *get*; the words written in a *shtar kiddushin* are unmistakably those of *kiddushin*. No one could confuse them. Each document is a unique and explicitly identifiable object. The *hekesh* therefore derives *kiddushei shtar* without creating any confusion about the instruments of divorce and marriage.

### Fungibility Distinction

This resolution raises a further question: why can we not apply the same logic to *kesef* and say that *kiddushei kesef* coins are distinct from divorce coins, just as the two *shtarot* are distinct? The *gemara* answers: *tiba michad hu* — money has a single nature. Coins are fungible. A five-dollar bill is indistinguishable from any other five-dollar bill; if one is lost, any equivalent sum suffices as replacement. The very essence of *kesef* is its interchangeability. A *shtar*, by contrast, is a unique, specific object. One could never mistake a *get* for a *shtar kiddushin* because each is a particular document with particular language. But money given for *kiddushin* and money given for divorce would look and feel identical, and the principle of *ein kategor na'aseh sanegor* — which we apply, for instance, to prohibiting a cow's horn for a *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah*, and to prohibiting the *Kohen Gadol* from wearing gold into the *Kodesh Kodashim* on *Yom Kippur* — compels us not to use the same medium for such antithetical purposes.

### Rabbi Yose HaGalili

A loose end requires attention. *Rava* offers an alternative derivation that divorce cannot be accomplished through *kesef*: *amar kra v'chatav lah* — the *pasuk* explicitly says "and he shall write for her," meaning *b'chtivah mitgareshet ve'einah mitgareshet b'kesef* — she is divorced only through writing, not through money. We spent three months in Masechet Gittin on this principle.

But then: *ve'eima b'chtivah mitgareshet ve'einah mitkaddeshet b'chtivah?* — why don't we use the same *pasuk* to exclude *shtar* from *kiddushin* rather than from divorce? The *gemara* answers that the *pasuk* of *v'yatza v'hayta* — the *hekesh havayah l'yetziah* — connects *kiddushin* to *gerushin*, and the question of which direction the *mi'ut* runs, and from which domain to which, is precisely the substance of the back-and-forth we have traced.

This raises the question of *Rabbi Yose HaGalili*, whose *drasha* in Gittin 21a uses the verse *v'chatav lah* for an entirely different *derasha*, deriving that she cannot be divorced with money. Since he deploys that verse elsewhere, where does *Rabbi Yose HaGalili* learn the prohibition on *get b'kesef*? *Amar kra sefer keritut* — the *pasuk* says *sefer keritut*, a "bill of severance," implying *sefer kartah v'ein davar acher kartah* — only a document effects divorce, nothing else. *V'rabanan hai keritut mai avdi lei* — how do the Rabbis then use the word *keritut* rather than simply *karat*? *Mibaei lei l'davar hakoret beino l'beina* — they require the extra form to teach that the *get* must constitute a complete severance between the husband and wife at the time of divorce. This is the *baraita* we encountered recently: *harei zeh gitech al m'nat shelo tishti yayin al m'nat shelo telchi l'veit avich l'olam ein zeh keritut* — a divorce conditioned on permanent constraints is not a valid *keritut* because the husband retains residual power over her. *Kol shloshim yom harei zeh keritut* — if the condition is limited to thirty days, it is a valid severance. The *Rashba* in a *teshuvah* addresses the boundary cases — what about fifty years? What about conditions that end with the death of one of the parties? *Tosafot* here likewise engages with those questions. For *Rabbi Yose HaGalili*, by contrast, the doubled form *keritut* over *karat* yields both *drashot* simultaneously. *V'rabanan karat keritut lo mashma lehu* — the Rabbis do not read the derivation from singular to plural. *Chada mechada lo atya* — one cannot be derived from the other.

---

## Learned One from Two

### Deriving Shtar

Having established that each of the three methods cannot be derived from either of the other two individually — *chada mechada lo atya* — the *gemara* asks whether one might be derivable from the combination of the other two: *teiti chada mitarti*. Could *shtar* be derived from *biah* and *kesef* together?

### Hana'ah Distinction

No. *Biah* and *kesef* share a common feature that *shtar* lacks: *hana'atan merubah* — they both involve *hana'ah*, benefit or pleasure. Money has intrinsic value; there is tangible benefit in receiving it. *Biah* involves physical pleasure. A *shtar*, by contrast, is a purely legal object. It can be worth less than a *pruta*. It carries no intrinsic *hana'ah* whatsoever. Because *shtar* lacks this shared quality of *biah* and *kesef*, we cannot derive it from their combination.

This raises a subtle question addressed by the *Sha'ar HaMelech* in a different context: if *biah* works as a mode of *kiddushin* because it involves *hana'ah*, what would be the status of *kiddushin* effected through anal intercourse, which *Chazal* understand to involve diminished *hana'ah*? He suggests the resolution may be that *biah* does not actually work through a transfer of *hana'ah* at all — rather, it is the *ma'aseh kinyan* itself, the legal act, that matters. The *gemara*'s statement that *biah* is characterized by *hana'atan merubah* would then describe a general feature of the category, not a mechanism on which the *kinyan* depends. This is an important conceptual question about how much the *gemara*'s formulation reflects an intrinsic requirement versus a descriptive characterization.

### Deriving Kesef

Could *kesef* be derived from *biah* and *shtar* combined?

### Biah Not Normal Kinyan

No. *Biah* and *shtar* share a quality that *kesef* lacks: *kinyanan merubah* — *kesef* and *shtar* are general-purpose instruments of *kinyan*, applicable across many domains of acquisition including the purchase of land and the acquisition of slaves (topics the rest of the *perek* will address). *Biah*, by contrast, is not a normal mode of *kinyan*. One does not acquire a piece of land by *biah*. It is an act specific to particular marital and quasi-marital contexts. And since *biah* lacks the broader *kinyan* applicability shared by *kesef* and *shtar*, the combination cannot yield *kesef*.

### Biah Chazakah Analogy

*Tosafot* on 3a entertains — and rejects — the suggestion that *biah* might be compared to *chazakah* in the acquisition of land, whereby one demonstrates ownership by plowing, fencing, or traversing the property. Like *biah*, *chazakah* is a physical act that demonstrates the reality of a relationship between the acquirer and what is being acquired. The parallel is genuinely interesting, and it touches on sensitive questions about how the woman's role in *kiddushei biah* relates to the role of the field in *kinyan chazakah*. *Tosafot* rejects the analogy, noting that these are fundamentally different legal acts — though the comparison is serious enough to warrant extended treatment.

### Deriving Biah

Could *biah* be derived from *kesef* and *shtar* combined?

### Be'al Korchah

No. *Kesef* and *shtar* share a quality that *biah* lacks in the marital context: *yeshnan b'al korchah* — they can operate *b'al korchah*, without the woman's consent. A husband can give his wife a *get* against her will (prior to *Rabbeinu Gershom*'s *takkanah*). *Biah* as a mode of *kiddushin* in a normal marriage cannot occur *b'al korchah* — valid marital *biah* requires the woman's *da'at*.

The *gemara* notes that *yibbum* seems to complicate this: the *biah* of *yibbum* can be *b'al korchah* in some sense, because the *yevamah's* agreement to the legal entry into a marital relationship with this particular man is not required at the moment of *yibbum*, given that the *zikah* already creates a pre-existing bond. But that is specifically *yibbum*, not a normal marital *biah*, and the distinction holds.

Regarding *kesef b'al korchah*: *tosafot* raises the case of *amah ivriyah*, where a father sells his minor daughter into indenture — seemingly imposing the arrangement upon her. But *tosafot* resolves this by noting that the father in this case is the minor's legal agent; because she is not yet a *bar da'at*, there is no *ratzon* of her own that is being overridden. The father's *da'at* substitutes for hers, and it is therefore not classified as *b'al korchah* in the technical sense.

---

## Rav Huna Chuppah

### Chuppah Kal Vachomer

We have now concluded the discussion of the three established modes of *kiddushin*. Each requires its own independent *limud*; none can be derived from any other singly; and each possesses a unique quality — *shtar* has no *hana'ah*, *biah* is not a general-purpose *kinyan*, and *kesef* does not exist *b'al korchah* in a marital context — that defeats any attempt at *tzad hashaveh* derivation from the combination of the other two. It is striking to consider that three distinct processes all yield the same legal outcome and yet have such fundamentally different character.

*Rav Huna* now proposes something new: *chuppah koneh m'kal vachomer* — *chuppah* should be able to effect *kiddushin* through *kal vachomer*. *Chuppah* is the rabbinic term for *nissuin*, the second stage of marriage, and the *rishonim* have a wide-ranging *machloket* — something like seven positions — regarding what *chuppah* actually refers to: wrapping the couple in a shared garment (as in some *Sephardi* practice), spreading a canopy over them, veiling the bride, *yichud*, the act of *biah*, or entering the shared home. Each identification carries significant legal implications.

### Kesef Terumah

*Rav Huna*'s argument: *chuppah koneh m'kal vachomer umah kesef she'eino ma'achil b'terumah koneh, chuppah she'ma'achelet b'terumah eino din she'tikneh* — money, which does not grant the woman the right to eat *terumah*, nonetheless effects *kiddushin*. *Chuppah*, which does grant that right (when a woman enters *nissuin* with a *kohen*), should certainly effect *kiddushin kal vachomer*.

### Woman Eating Terumah

The *gemara* challenges the premise: does *kesef* truly not allow the woman to eat *terumah*? *V'ha amar Ulla devar Torah arusa bat Yisrael ochelet b'terumah* — *Ulla* holds that *mid'oraita*, a woman who is only *mekudeshet* — *arusah* — may eat *terumah*, because the *pasuk* states *v'kohen ki yikneh nefesh kinyan kaspo* — a *kohen's* wife is his *kinyan kaspo*, and since marriage is effected as *kinyan kaspo*, she is entitled to eat *terumah* from the point of *kiddushin*. She is *kinyan kaspo* already from that stage.

### Rabbinic Gezeirah

The reason *miderabbanan* an *arusah* cannot eat *terumah* is a *gezeirah*: *shema yimzegu lah kos b'veit aviha v'tashkeihu l'acheiha v'l'achayoteiha* — perhaps her family will pour her a cup of *terumah* wine in her father's house and she will share it with her siblings, who are not married to *kohanim* and may not eat *terumah*. The rabbinic prohibition on *terumah* for an *arusah* is thus a prophylactic measure, not a reflection of her actual status *mid'oraita*. So *kal vachomer*, the *kesef* also allows eating *terumah* — Rav Huna's premise is undermined.

### Biah Counter

The *gemara* then reformulates the *kal vachomer* correctly: *umah kesef she'eino gomer koneh, chuppah she'gomeret eino din she'tikneh* — money, which does not complete the marriage (it only effects *kiddushin*, not *nissuin*), nonetheless creates the *kinyan* of *kiddushin*. *Chuppah*, which completes the marriage by effecting *nissuin*, should *kal vachomer* be able to effect *kiddushin* as well. The counter from *biah* is raised: *biah tochiach* — *biah* shows that a mode of *kinyan* can work for *kiddushin*.
