And *mah l'biah sheken konah b'yevamah* — *biah* is distinctive in that it effects a *kinyan* in the context of *yibbum*, which has no parallel for *chuppah*. *Kesef yochiach* — and around the cycle we go, each counterexample being refuted by the other. *Lo rai zeh k'rai zeh v'lo rai zeh k'rai zeh* — each has its defects but they are not identical defects.

### Kesef Yochiach

The *gemara* works through the *tzad hashaveh*: *hatzad hashaveh shebahen shekonin b'alma v'koneh kan* — the common denominator of *kesef* and *biah* is that they are both instruments of *kinyan* in the general sense and they effect *kiddushin*. *Af ani avi chuppah shekonin b'alma v'koneh kan* — I will bring *chuppah* also as an instrument of *kinyan* in the general sense, and it too should effect *kiddushin*.

### Tzad HaShaveh

The *tzad hashaveh* argument is pressed further. *Mah l'tzad hashaveh shebahen sheken hana'ah merubah* — but the common denominator of *biah* and *kesef* is that they involve *hana'ah*, which *chuppah* does not. *Shtar yochiach* — let *shtar* serve as the refutation: *shtar* has no *hana'ah* and still effects *kiddushin*. *Mah l'shtar sheken motzi* — *shtar* is unique in that it can dissolve a marriage through *get*, which *chuppah* cannot do.

### Hana'ah Objection

*Kesef u'biah yochiach* — *kesef* and *biah* will show that the capacity to dissolve is not required. *V'hazar hadin* — the argument cycles again. *Lo rai zeh k'rai zeh v'lo rai zeh k'rai zeh* — each method, again, has a disqualifying factor the others lack.

### Unique Factors

*Mah l'tzad hashaveh shebahen sheken yeshnan b'al korchah* — the common denominator of *shtar* and *biah* is that both can exist in a context of *b'al korchah*, which *kesef* — and likewise *chuppah* — cannot. *V'Rav Huna kesef mi ha b'isha lo ashkechan b'al korchah* — and *Rav Huna* has no answer to the fact that *kesef* does not exist in a marital context that is *b'al korchah*. The *kal vachomer* cannot be completed.

### Rava Objection One

*Amar Rava shtei teshuvot b'davar* — *Rava* raises two independent objections to *Rav Huna*. First: *chada d'shalosh tnan v'lo arba* — the *mishnah* explicitly states *ha'isha niknet b'shalosh drachim*, a woman can be married in three ways, not four. *Chuppah* is not among the three.

### Rava Objection Two

Second, and more fundamentally: *v'od klum chuppah gomeret ela al yedei kiddushin* — *chuppah* only effects *nissuin* in the wake of prior *kiddushin*. It presupposes *kiddushin*; it does not operate independently. How then can *Rav Huna* propose a *kal vachomer* that *chuppah* — which can complete marriage — should be able to do what the other methods do? *Chuppah* completing marriage is a function that operates only once *kiddushin* has already occurred. It cannot be bootstrapped into being a method of *kiddushin* itself.

### Abaye Defense

*Abaye* defends *Rav Huna* against *Rava*'s first objection: *tana milta d'chtiva b'hedya katanei, milta delo chtiva b'hedya lo katanei* — the *mishnah* lists only what is explicitly derivable from *pesukim*. *Chuppah*, being derived through *kal vachomer* rather than from explicit scriptural language, was not listed — but this is *tana veshayer*, the *tanna* listed only a subset. The *mishnah*'s enumeration of three therefore does not refute the possibility of a fourth.

This is perhaps not the most compelling answer, and *Rava*'s second objection remains formidable.

### Rav Huna Response

*Abaye* then addresses the second objection on *Rav Huna*'s behalf: *Rav Huna* can actually incorporate *Rava*'s challenge into the *kal vachomer* and make it even stronger. *Mah kesef she'eino gomer achar kesef koneh* — money cannot effect *nissuin* even after *kiddushei kesef* has been performed; giving a second ring does not constitute *nissuin*. *Chuppah shegomeret achar kesef eino din shetikneh* — since *chuppah* does work after *kesef* (it effects *nissuin* following *kiddushei kesef*), should it not *kal vachomer* be able to effect *kiddushin* as well?

### Tosafot HaRosh

This leads into the *Tosafot HaRosh*'s question: when *Rav Huna* says *chuppah koneh m'kal vachomer*, does he mean *chuppah* effecting *kiddushin* and *nissuin* together in a single act, or does he mean *chuppah* effecting *kiddushin* alone — requiring some separate act for *nissuin* afterward? This is a fundamental question about the shape of *Rav Huna*'s position and it remains unresolved within the *sugya*.

We note that while *Rava*'s objections are serious and we generally rule like *Rava* over *Abaye*, the *Rif* may rule like *Rav Huna* — a notable exception. The practical *nafka minah* is rare, but one can imagine the question arising in a tragic case where, for example, a *kallah* collapsed and died immediately after *bede'ken* and before a conventional *kiddushin* — and the question becomes whether any form of *chuppah* was completed, and whether the *kohen* husband is permitted to be *mitamei* for her as a full wife. Such cases do not arise often, but the theoretical weight of *Rav Huna*'s position is not nothing.

---

## Kiddushei Kesef Mechanics

### Man's Action Required

The *gemara* now pivots to the practical mechanics of *kiddushei kesef*. A *baraita* is cited: *natan lah kesef o shaveh kesef v'amar lah harei at mekudeshet li, harei at me'ureset li, harei at li le'intu* — he gives her money or its equivalent and says one of several designated formulas: "You are *mekudeshet* to me," "You are betrothed to me," "You are my wife." *Harei zu mekudeshet* — she is thereby married. The *kiddushin* requires both the act of giving and an accompanying verbal declaration, an *amira*.

### Woman's Declaration Und…

The *baraita* continues: *aval hi she'natnah lo v'amrah hi* — but if she gives the ring to him and she is the one who speaks — *lo havei kiddushin* — they are not married. Two variables have changed: she gave rather than he, and she spoke rather than he. This reflects the *pasuk* of *ki yikach ish isha* — the man takes the wife, giving him the more active legal role in the process.

### Rav Pappa Question

*Rav Pappa* is troubled by the *baraita*: *ta'ama d'natan hu v'amar hu* — the reason the first case works is that he gave and he said. From the *reisha* one might infer: if he gave but she said — that would not work. From the *seifa* one might infer: the reason it fails is that she gave and she said — but if he gave and she said, it would work. The two halves of the *baraita* appear to contradict each other on this intermediate case, and *Rav Pappa* wants to know the answer.

### Reisha Davka

The *gemara* resolves: *reisha davka* — the first clause is precise. For valid *kiddushin*, the man must both give and declare. The *seifa* simply came along for parallel formulation and does not yield independent inferences.

### Woman's Amira Effect

But the *gemara* elaborates more carefully: if the man gives the money and the woman is the one who speaks, this is treated *ke'mi she'natnah hi v'amrah hi* — as if she had given it and said it. Her act of *amira* when he gives effectively makes the act hers, such that it is not *kiddushin*.

### Safek Kiddushin

An alternative reading: *natan hu v'amrah hi safeka hi v'chaishinan miderabbanan* — if he gives and she speaks, this may be *safek kiddushin*. That is, there is genuine doubt whether her declaration plays the role of the required *amira*. Under this view, were she to go and marry another man, she would require a *get* from both. The first view would say it is simply not *kiddushin* at all; the second view treats it as *safek*. This unresolved question about the *amira*'s role — and whether the woman's participation in the declaration can either substitute for or undermine the man's declaration — speaks to the broader question of what precisely the verbal component of *kiddushin* accomplishes.

---

## Shmuel Amira Rule

### Required Formulations

*Shmuel* addresses the *amira* requirements directly. If the man gives *kesef* or its equivalent and says *harei at mekudeshet* — "you are *mekudeshet*" — or *harei at me'ureset*, or *harei at le'intu* — "you are my wife" — she is married. These formulations share a common feature: they describe a change in the *woman's* status. She becomes *mekudeshet*, she becomes *me'ureset*, she becomes *le'intu*.

### Man Status Doesn't Change

But if the man says *hareini isheich* — "I am your husband" — or *hareini ba'aleich* — "I am your *ba'al*" — or *hareini aruseich* — "I am betrothed to you" — *ein kan beit michush* — there is not even cause for concern. This is simply not *kiddushin*. The man's status does not change through the act of *kiddushin*. He can go and marry another wife; nothing in his legal standing is transformed. It is the woman's status that changes: she becomes forbidden to all other men, she requires a *get* to remarry, and an entire structure of obligations and prohibitions attaches to her. When the man declares a change in his own status rather than hers, the declaration is legally inert.

### Status Change Principle

The same principle applies in *gerushin*: *v'chatav lah v'natan b'yadah* — the *pasuk* requires him to write *for her* and give it *into her hand*. If a man says *harei at meshulachat* — "you are sent away" — or *harei at megureshet* — "you are divorced" — or *harei at muteret l'chol adam* — "you are permitted to every man" — *harei zu megureshet*, she is divorced. These formulas change the woman's status. But if he says *eini ishech, eini ba'alech, eini aruseich* — "I am no longer your husband, I am no longer your *ba'al*, I am no longer betrothed to you" — this is again *ein kan beit michush*. He has described a change in his own status, not hers, and a divorce requires changing hers.

### Yadayim Question

*Rav Pappa* asks *Abaye*: does this ruling of *Shmuel* imply that *Shmuel* holds *yadayim she'einan mochiyot havyan yadayim* — that an indirect expression, even one that does not explicitly denote the intended legal act, constitutes a valid declaration? After all, *Shmuel* rules that saying *harei at mekudeshet* without specifying *li* — "to me" — is sufficient. Is this not accepting an incomplete expression?

### Nazir Yadayim Example

*Rav Pappa* raises the counterexample from *Nazir*: if a person sees a *nazir* passing by and says *aha* — pointing at him — is he himself a *nazir*? *Shmuel* rules: *ve'hu she'hayah nazir over lefanav* — only if the *nazir* was actually passing by at that moment. *Ta'ama d'nazir over lefanav hu, lav hachi lo* — the reason it works is that the *nazir* was physically present, making the reference unambiguous; without that context, the exclamation would not suffice. This suggests *Shmuel* holds *yadayim she'einan mochiyot einan yadayim* — imprecise expressions are not valid declarations.

### Status Change Resolution

The *gemara* resolves: *Shmuel*'s ruling about *kiddushin* teaches not that imprecise expressions are valid, but rather something about whose status must be described. The *chiddush* is that the man must declare a change in the *woman's* status — not his own. *Hacha k'siv ki yikach v'lo she'yikach et atzmo* — the *pasuk* says *ki yikach ish isha*, "a man shall take a wife" — the act of taking is directed toward her, not toward himself. He cannot "take himself" to her. And *v'hacha k'siv v'shilchah v'lo she'yishlach et atzmo* — the *pasuk* of divorce says *v'shilchah*, "and he shall send her away" — he cannot divorce himself from her. In both marriage and divorce, it is the woman's legal status that is the object of the act, and the verbal declaration must reflect that.

---

---

# Kiddushin 6

## Kiddushin Formulatio (II)

### Six Formulations

The *gemara* on Kiddushin 6a resumes mid-discussion with a *tanna rabbanan*, continuing the examination of which linguistic formulations (*lashonot*) constitute a valid *ma'amar* of *kiddushin*. The *beraita* presents six formulations, grouped in two sets of three. In the first set: *harei at ishti* ("you are my wife"), *harei at arusati* ("you are my *arusa*"), and *harei at knuya li* ("you are acquired to me") — in any of these cases, she is *mekudeshet*. In the second set: *harei at sheli* ("you are mine"), *harei at birshuti* ("you are in my domain"), and *harei at zekuka li* ("you are bound to me") — these, too, effectuate *kiddushin*. The term *zekuka* carries connotations similar to *zika* in the context of *yibbum*, conveying a sense of being halachically bound or attached.

The *gemara* asks why these six formulations are presented as two separate groupings rather than a single unified list. The answer is simply that this is how the tradition was received: *tana telat shmi'ineihu ve-garsineihu* — he heard them in sets of three and transmitted them that way. Grouping teachings in threes is a familiar mnemonic convention, even when the internal logic might not demand the division.

### Ambiguous Formulations

The *gemara* then turns to a series of more ambiguous formulations and poses the question *mahu* — is this effective or not? The list includes: *meiyuchedet li* ("singled out to me"), *meyu'edet li* ("designated to me," drawing on the language of *ya'adah* from the passage about the *bat la'amah*), *ezrati* ("my helpmate," from *ezer kinegdo* in *Bereishit*), *negdati* ("alongside me"), *atzurati* (from *atzeret*, suggesting being gathered together with him at home), *tzalati* (from *vayikach achat mitzal'otav*, God's taking of the *tzela* from *Adam*), *segurati* (from *vayisgor basar tachtena*, the enclosing of flesh), *tachtai* ("beneath me," from the same verse), and *tefusati* (from the language of *nitpasha* in the context of a *na'ara me'orasa* — carrying connotations of being seized, which, rightly or wrongly, implies the married relationship).

One of these ambiguous cases admits of a ready resolution. The formulation *lekuchati* — "my taken one" — is validated by a *beraita*: *omer lekuchati harei zu mekudeshet*, because the *Torah* itself uses the root *kicha* to describe betrothal: *ki yikach ish isha*. The term *likuchin* is the *Torah's* own word for this act, and so this formulation clearly works.

### Charufah Usage

The *gemara* then raises the case of *charufati* — a term derived from the passage *shifcha nechereset l'ish*, which describes a slave-woman who is *nechereset*, or designated, to a man. Does using this term constitute a valid *ma'amar* of *kiddushin*?

A *beraita* is cited: *omer charufati mekudeshet* — yes, it works. The *gemara* initially explains this on the basis that *bi-Yehudah korin l'arusa charufa* — in Judea, *arusa* is colloquially called *charufa*. The *gemara* challenges this: if we already have a *pasuk* supporting the term, why do we additionally need to appeal to regional Judean usage? And conversely, if the *pasuk* alone is sufficient, why does the regional usage matter?

After two rounds of revision, the *gemara* settles on the following reading: *omer charufa bi-Yehudah mekudeshet* — if one uses this formulation specifically *in Judea*, it is effective, because there the word is understood to mean *arusa*, likely by association with the *pasuk*. But if one uses this term outside of Judea, where the word does not carry that meaning, it would presumably not work.

### Context Requirement

This leads into a broader structural question: all these ambiguous formulations — *tzalati*, *segurati*, *atzurati*, and the rest — in what kind of case are we evaluating them? If the parties were not already engaged in conversation about *kiddushin* and related matters (*iskei gitta ve-kiddusheha*), how would she even know what he means? A bizarre formulation like *harei at segurati* or *harei at atzurati* would be unintelligible to her without context. And since, unlike a *get*, which can be given against the woman's will, *kiddushin* requires her knowing consent — if she has no idea what he is saying, she cannot meaningfully agree.

But if they *are* already talking about marriage-related matters, then — the *gemara* points out — even if he said nothing at all when giving her the money, it would be valid. This is the ruling of the Mishnah: if a man was speaking with a woman about the matters of her *get* and *kiddushin* and gave her the document or money without making any verbal declaration (*velo peireish*), Rabbi Yose says *dayo* — it is sufficient. Rabbi Yehudah disagrees and holds that one must explicitly state what the act is for.

The *gemara* cites Rav Huna in the name of Shmuel: *halachah ke-Rabbi Yose*. And since even silence is sufficient according to Rabbi Yose, the question about these ambiguous formulations becomes sharper — if you don't need to say anything, what does it add to say something ambiguous?

The *gemara* resolves this by identifying a middle case: the ambiguous formulation is actually more problematic than silence. When parties are engaged in conversation about marriage and one simply hands over the ring without speaking, an outside observer understands perfectly what is happening. But when one uses a strange, oblique phrase — *harei at segurati* or *harei at izmargadi* — one might wonder whether the speaker is trying to redirect the conversation. Perhaps he is now talking about hiring her for work. The ambiguous statement introduces doubt where silence would not.

## Silent Kiddushin

### Yossi vs. Yehudah

To review the Mishnah's dispute more carefully: *hayah medaber im ha'ishah al iskei gitta ve-kiddusheha ve-natan lah gitta ve-kiddusheha velo peireish* — he was speaking with the woman about matters of *get* and *kiddushin*, then gave her the document or the money, without specifying what it was for. Rabbi Yose says this is sufficient — *dayo*. Rabbi Yehudah says he must explicitly declare his intent — *tzarich le-fareish*.

### Halachah: Context Suffic…

Rav Huna reports in the name of Shmuel that *halachah ke-Rabbi Yose*. A further qualification is added by Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel: even Rabbi Yose concedes that this only applies *ve-hu she-asukin be-oto inyan* — provided they are still actively engaged in that same conversation when the act is performed. If they had moved on to other topics before he handed her the money, the contextual understanding that makes silent *kiddushin* effective is no longer present. Rav Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya concurs. A *beraita* also records Rabbi [Yehudah ha-Nasi] agreeing with this requirement.

Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon, however, holds that even if they are no longer discussing the same matter, the *kiddushin* can still be valid. The *gemara* asks: if they have already moved on to a different topic, how does she know what he means? Abaye explains: *mitoch inyan le-inyan* — not a completely unrelated topic, but a related one. So for example, if they had been discussing the *kiddushin* itself and then shifted to discussing the financial arrangements of the marriage — the dowry and assets — that peripheral conversation is close enough that the subsequent act of giving money is still understood in context, per Rashi.

The *halachah* follows Rabbi Yose: *amar Rav Huna amar Shmuel halachah ke-Rabbi Yose*. Rav Ami and Rav Assi then apply this in connection with another statement of Shmuel — that anyone who does not have thorough command of the laws of *gittin* and *kiddushin* should not involve himself in adjudicating such cases. They suggest that even ignorance of this specific *halachah* of Rabbi Yose would qualify one as insufficiently expert to sit on such a *beit din*.

## Kiddushin Formulatio (II)

### Witnesses & Intent

The *gemara's* analysis of ambiguous formulations prompts a deep examination in *Tosafot ha-Rosh ha-Zaken*. The issue is not merely what the two parties understood between themselves, but what an objective third party — specifically, the *edim*, the witnesses — would have understood at that moment.

*Tosafot ha-Rosh ha-Zaken* makes the following point: even if both parties afterward declare that they understood the exchange to constitute *kiddushin* — even if the man says he intended it for *kiddushin* and the woman says she understood it as such and consented — this is still insufficient. The reason is *harei edim lo nitbarer lahem amitat ha-lashon be-et she-shamu* — at the moment the witnesses heard the words, the true meaning of the formulation was not clear to them. The validity of *kiddushin* cannot rest purely on the subjective agreement of the two parties; it requires that the act be objectively comprehensible to outside observers at the time it occurs.

This is not because the witnesses' understanding supersedes that of the principals, but because *kiddushin* is a legally constituted act that requires objectively intelligible expression. If a stranger were dropped into the middle of the scene at that moment, would they understand what was taking place? That is the standard.

*Tosafot ha-Rosh ha-Zaken* then offers a path by which even an ambiguous formulation could work: *im techila amru la-edim* — if, before the act, he informed the witnesses in advance, explaining "I am going to give her *kiddushin* by means of this particular formulation," and she subsequently confirmed that she understood it as *kiddushin*, then *vadai havu kiddushin* — it is certainly valid *kiddushin*. Why? Because at the moment the witnesses heard the formulation, *nitbarer lahem she-hem kiddushin* — it had already been made clear to them that this is what they would be witnessing. The context was established in advance, and the act is therefore objectively understood.

The practical upshot is that there is an objective but flexible standard. It cannot be entirely subjective — the two parties' private mutual understanding is not enough on its own. But the objective understanding can be established through advance disclosure to the witnesses. What cannot work is an ambiguous phrase taken in isolation, with nothing establishing its meaning for outside observers at the time of the act.

This explains why the *gemara* found silence to be less problematic than an ambiguous statement. When the parties are *asukim be-oto inyan* and the man silently gives money or a ring, any witness present understands perfectly what is occurring — the entire conversation has provided the context. But an odd phrase inserted into the flow of that conversation could, paradoxically, disrupt the clarity of the situation: it might suggest a shift of subject, introducing ambiguity where the silent act would have left none.

## Get Formulations

### Divorce Language

Parallel to the *kiddushin* formulations, the *gemara* now surveys valid *lashonot* for a *get*. If a man gives his wife a *get* and says *harei at meshulachet* ("you are sent away"), *harei at megureshet* ("you are divorced"), or *harei at muteret le-chol adam* ("you are permitted to any man"), she is divorced. These are straightforward and clearly effective.

### Reversed Language

The *gemara* then considers switched formulations. If a man gives his wife a *get* and says *harei at bat chorin* ("you are free") — a phrase appropriate for freeing a slave — he has said nothing effective. Similarly, if he says to his *shifchah* *harei at muteret le-chol adam* — a phrase from the *get* context — that too is ineffective. Each formula was misapplied: you used the slave's formula for your wife, and the wife's formula for your slave. Neither effects the intended legal change.

### Le'Atzmaych Question

The *gemara* then raises an ambiguous case in the context of *gerushin*: if a husband says to his wife *harei at le-atzmekh* ("you are unto yourself"), what does this accomplish? Is he divorcing her — meaning "you are now your own person, detached from me" — or is he merely relinquishing his rights to *ma'aseh yadeha*, the fruits of her labor, while remaining married? The latter would be a permissible arrangement, under which he agrees not to support her in exchange for not claiming her earnings.

Ravina raises a proof from a *beraita* before Rav Ashi: *gufo shel get shichrur* — the body of a *get shichrur* for a slave includes the formulation *harei ata ben chorin harei ata le-atzmecha* — "you are free, you are unto yourself." From here, a *kal va-chomer* is constructed: with a *eved Kena'ani*, whom the master owns bodily (*kani lei le-gufeih*), when he says *harei ata le-atzmecha*, this clearly means complete freedom — not merely that the slave can keep his own earnings. How much more so when one says this to a wife, over whose body he has no ownership — it must certainly mean complete release. Therefore, *harei at le-atzmekh* said to a wife constitutes a valid *get*.

## Slave Manumission

### Ein Li Esek Bakh

The *gemara* continues with a question about freeing a slave: if a master says to his slave *ein li esek bakh* — "I have nothing more to do with you" — does this constitute manumission? The question is whether the phrase means he is entirely releasing the slave (full *shichrur*, which changes the slave's status entirely, making him, in effect, a Jew in the full sense) or whether it merely means he is relinquishing control over the slave's labor while the slave remains legally enslaved. For an *eved Kena'ani*, the distinction is not merely practical but one of fundamental personal status.

### Ono Document

Rav Nachman — and some report it as Rav Chanin from Chuza — raises this before Rav Ashi, citing a proof. The *mishnah* records that if a master sells his slave to a non-Jew, the slave goes free, but he still requires a *get shichrur* from his original master. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies: this applies only if the master did not write an *ono* at the time of sale. But if he wrote an *ono*, that document itself constitutes the *get shichrur*, and no separate document is needed.

Rav Sheshet explains: what is an *ono*? It is a document in which the master writes *kshe-tivrach mimeni, ein li esek bakh* — "when you flee from me, I have nothing to do with you." Since such a document is recognized as a *shtar shichrur* — proof that the slave goes free upon flight — it follows that the phrase *ein li esek bakh* does constitute full release. The question is thereby resolved.

## Kiddushin with Loan

### Loan Disqualified

Returning to *kiddushin*, Abaye presents a ruling that opens a substantial discussion: *ha-mekadesh be-malveh einah mekudeshet* — if a man attempts to be *mekadesh* a woman using a pre-existing loan (money he has already lent her), the *kiddushin* is not valid. The operative principle, derived from the model of *Sedei Ephron* — where Avraham gave Ephron money at the moment of the transaction — is that *kiddushin* must be effected by giving something at the time of the act. A loan is different: *hotza'ah nitnah, kevar hein shela* — once a loan is disbursed, the money is already hers. He no longer controls it; she merely owes him a debt. He cannot use money that is no longer his to effect *kiddushin*, for he is not giving her anything new. As Rashi explains the case: *de-amar hitkadshi li be-malveh she-yesh li be-yadeich* — he says "be betrothed to me through the loan I have in your hands." Since the money is already legally hers, he is not transferring anything, and the *kiddushin* fails.

### Extending Loan Term

However, Abaye continues: *be-hana'at malveh mekudeshet* — if he is *mekadesh* her with the *hana'ah* (benefit) derived from extending the loan term, the *kiddushin* is valid. The *gemara* clarifies what *hana'at malveh* means. It is not *arba be-chamesh* — loaning four to be repaid as five — because that would simply be the loan itself (and would constitute actual *ribit*). Rather, *lo tzricha de-arvach lah zimna* — it means he extended the repayment deadline. She was obligated to pay him back by a certain date; he grants her additional time. The *hana'ah* she derives from this extension — she would theoretically have been willing to pay someone a *perutah* to intercede and secure that extension — constitutes the monetary benefit with which he is *mekadesh* her. Rashi articulates this explicitly: *amar lah hitkadshi li be-hana'ah zu she-at hayit notenet perutah le-adam she-yefayeseni alayich* — the extension is worth a *perutah* to her, and with that value he betroths her.

### Ribit Problem

While this *kiddushin* is valid, Abaye cautions: *aval asur la'asot kein mipnei ha'aramat ribit* — one may not do this, because it has the appearance of *ribit*. The technical distinction is that it is not *ribit gamur* — he is not receiving money from her; he receives a wife. He takes nothing directly from the loan transaction. Nevertheless, he derives benefit from the loan — the *hana'ah* of the extension is transformed into *kiddushin* — and this creates the appearance of a lender profiting from a loan, which the Torah prohibits. The principle is that a Jewish loan must be neutral: you lend a hundred and receive a hundred back. Here, the lender is getting something more — a wife — out of the loan relationship, even if it is not cash payment.

The *Rosh* agrees that *hana'at malveh* in the sense of extending the time constitutes real monetary value that can serve as the basis for *kiddushin*. And as noted, the extension need not be the exclusive path — forgiving the loan entirely also qualifies as *hana'at malveh* according to this view. The *Rashba* adds a further nuance: the effectiveness of the extension may depend on its timing. When the loan is *kol ha-omed ligbot ke-gavuy dami* — effectively ready for collection — then the creditor truly has the power to extend or demand, and the extension is a tangible new benefit. But if the loan is far from due, the extension is still too abstract to function as real *hana'ah*, and may not support *kiddushin*.

### Loan Forgiveness

Abaye then adds: *ve-kol sheken im machala kol ha-malveh* — certainly if he forgives the entire loan, this too functions as *hana'at malveh* and would constitute valid *kiddushin* (though the same *ribit* concern would apply). The reason is that *mechilah* creates a genuinely new benefit: where before she owed him a hundred dollars, now she owes nothing. That release of obligation — *hana'at mechilah* — is a fresh and real economic benefit conferred upon her at the moment of *kiddushin*, unlike the original loan disbursement, which is already spent. As Rashi frames it: *hashta hu de-kaya ve-lav afshata de-at malveh* — it is something that exists now, not merely the residue of the original loan.

The *Ran*, however, disputes whether forgiving the loan truly works. His position is that *mechilah* of the loan is not a genuinely *new* benefit — it is simply the erasure of a prior debt. The woman's mind is on the hundred dollars that was given, not on some additional, abstract gain. To be valid, the *kiddushin* must be effected with something above and beyond the original loan, something new introduced at the moment of betrothal. On this view, only the *hana'ah* of the extended repayment term — something genuinely incremental and new — would work, while outright forgiveness of the principal would not. This represents a substantive disagreement between Rashi and the *Ran* about the nature of what constitutes a valid new benefit in this context.

## Conditional Gifts

### Conditional in Other Cas…

Rava raises the case of *matanah al menat lehachzir* — a conditional gift given on the understanding that it will be returned. The paradigmatic instance is the *arba minim* on *Sukkot*: if one person says to another *heilach etrog zeh al menat she-tachzirehu li* — here is my *etrog*, but give it back — and the recipient takes it and uses it and then returns it, he has fulfilled his obligation. Rava himself ruled this way: *netalo ve-hachziro yatza*; if he did not return it, he did not fulfill the obligation.

Rava then applies this principle across several domains. In a sale (*mecher*), if a buyer says "here is payment on condition you return it," no acquisition takes place. For *kiddushin*, if he gives her money on condition she returns it, she is not *mekudeshet*. For *pidyon haben*, if he gives the *kohen* the five *sela'im* on condition they be returned, the son is not redeemed. But for *terumah*, if he gives *terumah* to the *kohen* on condition it be returned — *yatza yedei netinah* — the obligation to give *terumah* is fulfilled, though the practice is forbidden because it creates the appearance that the *kohen* has made a deal or purchased the *terumah*, compromising the dignity of the gift and smacking of *armah* — evasion of the spirit of the law.

### Why It Fails for Kiddush…

The *gemara* finds this account internally inconsistent. Rava himself holds *matanah al menat lehachzir shemah matanah* — a conditional gift counts as a gift. If so, all these cases should work. And if it does not count as a gift, none of them should — including *terumah*, which the *beraita* says *does* work. The formulation in which some cases work and others do not seems untenable.

### Girsa Dispute

Rav Ashi resolves this by correcting the *girsa* of the *beraita*. The proper reading is not that *kiddushin*, *mecher*, and *pidyon haben* all fail while *terumah* alone works. Rather: *be-chulehu kani* — all of them work — *levar me-ishah* — except for the woman. *Mecher* works, *pidyon haben* works, *terumah* works (though one should not do it in practice for the reasons of *armah*), but *kiddushin* does not work. Why does *kiddushin* alone fail?

*She-ein ishah nikneit be-chalippin* — a woman cannot be betrothed through the mechanism of *chalippin*. The *kicha* of *kiddushin* was derived from the model of *Sedei Ephron*, in which Avraham gave Ephron a definitive, unconditional transfer of money. *Chalippin* — the mode of acquisition by exchange or barter, typified by the *sudar* (handkerchief) — operates on a different and incompatible logic. The *sudar* in a *kinyan chalippin* is taken and immediately returned; the exchange is instantaneous and the physical object passes back at once, much as the *etrog* in the *matanah al menat lehachzir* case is returned. Saying to a woman "here is money, give it back" is structurally identical to *chalippin*, and *ein ishah nikneit be-chalippin*. Avraham's gift to Ephron was a clean, permanent, one-directional transfer, and *kiddushin* must replicate that model.

Rav Huna bar Rav Nechemia of Rav Ashi confirms: this was indeed the tradition he had in the name of Rava — the corrected *girsa* is the right one. All the cases except *kiddushin* work; only *kiddushin* fails due to the inherent incompatibility with *chalippin*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 7

## Rava's Three Cases

### Problem Setup

The sugya opens at the very bottom of daf 6b, introducing three remarkable cases articulated by Rava involving unusual mechanisms for effecting *kiddushei kesef*. In a standard case of *kiddushin*, the man gives something of value to the woman — that object or sum of money constitutes the *kesef kiddushin* that effects the formal transactional change of status we call *kiddushin*. It is not a purchase in the simple sense, but there is nonetheless a formalized process that introduces both the prohibitive dimensions of marriage and its attendant obligations. The *sugya* here is concerned specifically with *kiddushei kesef* — and the cases Rava presents are, to put it plainly, strange.

To follow the cases clearly, three parties must be kept in mind: the *isha* (the woman), the *ba'al* (the prospective husband), and *Ploni* (a third party).

### Din Arev

The first case: *ten maneh l'Ploni ve-ekadesh lach, mekudeshet mi-din arev*. The man says to the woman — or, grammatically more precisely, she says to the man — "Give a *maneh* to Ploni, and I will be betrothed to you." The direction of the money is striking: it flows from the husband to a third party. The woman receives nothing; the husband does not give anything to his prospective wife. Yet Rava rules she is *mekudeshet*.

The Gemara explains via the analogy of an *arev* — a guarantor or co-signer on a loan. When a borrower seeks funds and the lender requires added security, the *arev* steps in to obligate himself to repay in the event of default, despite receiving no benefit whatsoever from the transaction. The Gemara applies this logic: *arev, af al gav d'lo mati hana'ah l'yadeih, kamshabd nafsheih* — the guarantor, even though no benefit reaches him, nonetheless obligates himself. So too the woman: even though no money reaches her, she obligates herself and effects the transfer of her person into the marital relationship.

### Arev Analysis

There is a major *machloket rishonim* about precisely how this case works, and indeed the underlying question touches on the most fundamental issues of what *kiddushei kesef* requires.

Rashi appears to take the position that each of these archetypical transaction-types — *arev*, *eved Kena'ani*, and the combined case — functions as a recognized transactional form, and because it works in those contexts, it can work for *kiddushin* as well. The later *rishonim* find this difficult.

The Rosh takes the view that what makes this good *kiddushei kesef* is simply the fact that money was transferred — regardless of direction or party. A formal act of monetary transfer occurred, and that transfer is what *kiddushin* attaches to. On this reading, *kiddushin* is not about the man purchasing the woman, but about a formal transactional event that gives legal content to the marital intention.

The Rambam's approach, which is perhaps the most conceptually coherent, is that the woman receives a psychological *hana'ah* — a benefit. Her agreement to do what the husband requests in a financial matter, or more precisely, the benefit she derives from the fact that he acted on her financial direction, constitutes *hana'ah* worth at least a *perutah*. This principle — that intangible psychological value can constitute *kesef kiddushin* — recurs later in the *masechta* in cases such as "do a dance for me and you will be *mekudeshet*." The difficulty with the Rambam's approach, as noted, is that none of this is articulated in the Gemara's formulation of the case itself.

Rashi and several other *rishonim* respond that for this mechanism to work, it must be articulated explicitly — otherwise, the woman handing money to a stranger is simply disconnected from *kiddushin* entirely. There is no inherent link unless something is stated to make the connection.

The Ritva stakes out a middle position: there is a monetary dimension in the sense that money was transferred, but some part of the mechanism is still anchored in the psychological value as well. The cases are genuinely difficult, and that difficulty is precisely the point — these are strange cases that push at the edges of what *kiddushei kesef* can mean.

One further clarification that emerges from discussion: in the first case, who actually gives the money? The text is ambiguous, and whether it is her money or his money being given to Ploni is itself part of the *machloket rishonim*. The textual formulation may be read either way. What is clear is that the woman is the one making the request — she says, in effect, give money to Ploni and I will be your wife — and the theoretical underpinning is the *arev* principle: a person can obligate themselves in a transaction from which they derive no direct benefit.

### Din Eved Kena'ani

The second case: *heilach maneh vehitkadshi l'Ploni, mekudeshet mi-din eved Kena'ani*. Here the directions are reversed. A third party gives the woman money, and the man — the *Ploni* here — marries her as a result, even though he has not spent a single coin. The Gemara grounds this in the law of the Canaanite slave.

When a slave seeks to purchase his own freedom, the *halacha* presents a structural problem: everything a slave owns belongs in principle to his master. Any money the slave accumulates is already the master's property. Therefore, the slave cannot technically purchase his own freedom using money in his possession. Instead, a third party must provide the purchase price, paying the master directly. Yet the transaction is the slave's — it is his freedom that is acquired, his status that changes, and the conceptual framework remains one of him acquiring himself.

*Eved Kena'ani yochiach*: the slave proves that a person can effect a change in his own status through a transaction in which he himself loses nothing — because someone else bears the financial cost. Applied to *kiddushin*: the husband does not lose money, someone else provides the funds to the woman, and yet the marriage is effected. It is a status change, not a purchase, and the status change attaches to the husband even without any financial outlay on his part.

### Din Shneihem

The third case combines both problems simultaneously: *ten maneh l'Ploni vehitkadshi ani lo, mekudeshet mi-din sheneihem*. The woman tells the husband, "Give money to Ploni, and I will be married to him." The husband gives money to a third party, and the woman becomes betrothed to that third party. Neither problem in isolation is sufficient to invalidate — the woman gets no money, and the prospective husband Ploni loses nothing — and Rava therefore invokes both principles together to validate the transaction.

The Gemara walks through the circular logic explicitly: *arev* addresses the woman's situation (she obligates herself despite receiving no *hana'ah*); *eved Kena'ani* addresses Ploni's situation (he acquires a wife without losing money). Each principle on its own would face the objection that the other half doesn't match — but together, the two principles cover all the anomalies of the transaction and the *kiddushin* is valid.

---

## Fourth Case & Agav

### Woman Gives to Husband

Rava then poses a question — *ba'ei Rava* — which is perhaps the most striking of all: *heilach maneh ve-ekadesh ani lach, mahu?* What is the rule when the woman gives money directly to the man and says, "I will be betrothed to you"? This is the case that Abaye had in mind when questioning the formulation of *hikadesh otach* — the language of marriage being initiated by the woman rather than the man. The Gemara takes it up as a genuine question rather than disposing of it categorically.

Mar Zutra, citing Rav Pappa, rules: *mekudeshet* — the marriage is valid.

### Agav Problem

Rav Ashi immediately objects. If the woman's giving of money to the man can effect *kiddushin*, that implies the woman is, conceptually, transferring herself to the man *agav* the money — as an incidental acquisition bundled with the primary transfer. But the *mishnah* teaches the rule of *kinyan agav* as follows: movable property (*nechasim she-ein lahem achrayut*) can be acquired along with real estate (*nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayut*), not the reverse. Land is the primary vehicle; chattels ride along for free. Here, money is movable property — and the woman would be the *karka*, real estate — so the transfer is going in the wrong direction. It would be as if one were purchasing a flock of sheep and claiming the field comes along with them, which is precisely the inverse of how *kinyan agav* works.

### Adam Chashuv

Mar Zutra deflects the objection entirely: *mi savart de-amari agav? hacha be-Adam Chashuv askinan* — who said I am invoking *kinyan agav* at all? We are speaking of a case involving an *adam chashuv*, a person of considerable social standing and reputation.

Rashi explains: an *adam chashuv* is someone who, on principle, does not accept gifts, based on the *pasuk* in Mishlei, *soneh matanot yichyeh* — the one who hates gifts will live. Refusing gifts is treated by *Chazal* as a mark of honor and is regularly invoked as a normative standard for distinguished individuals. If such a person accepts a gift, the psychological benefit to the giver is measurable and real: *de-be-hahi hana'ah de-ka mekaibel hana'ah minah, gamra u-maknya lei nafshah* — from the benefit she receives from the fact that this *adam chashuv*, who does not ordinarily accept gifts, has accepted hers, she resolves to betroth herself to him completely.

The analogy is apt: if one were to pay for dinner in the company of a distinguished personage who normally declines others' hospitality, the very fact of that acceptance confers a palpable benefit on the one who treated. That benefit is worth at least a *perutah*, and it is this psychological *hana'ah* — not any principle of *kinyan agav* — that provides the mechanism for the *kiddushin*.

This parallels the Rambam's reading of the first case, where the woman's benefit from being heeded in a financial matter constitutes the *hana'ah* that makes the *kiddushei kesef* functional. The difference is that in the *adam chashuv* case, the Gemara makes this explicit — unlike the first case, where the Rambam reads it in by inference.

In practice, the *adam chashuv* principle is extremely narrow. It applies only where the recipient is genuinely known to refuse gifts, and where the psychological benefit to the giver is therefore clear and recognized. The difficulty of assessing such benefit in any given case is considerable, which is part of why the reverse ring ceremony, while theoretically available in this framework, is not practically employed.

---

## Application to Mamona

### Kiddushin vs Mamona

After teaching the three cases of *arev*, *eved Kena'ani*, and *din sheneihem*, Rava adds: *ve-chen l'inyan mamona* — and the same principles apply in monetary transactions. That is, if one wishes to use any of these unusual mechanisms to effect a *kinyan kesef* in a standard financial transaction — purchasing a field, for example, which requires only a *perutah* of *kesef* — those mechanisms work there too.

One might wonder why this needs to be stated. The Gemara explains: *tzricha*.

### Mamona Same Rules

Had Rava taught only the *kiddushin* cases, one might have assumed the permissibility was limited to *kiddushin* because the threshold for *kesef kiddushin* is extremely low — a single *perutah* — and moreover because of the well-known presumption of Reish Lakish: *tav le-meitav tadu mi-le-meitav armelu* — it is better to dwell in partnership than to dwell alone, meaning women generally prefer a state of marriage. Given that preference, one might assume the *kiddushin* threshold is especially easy to meet on account of the woman's own inclination. Hence we might have thought these mechanisms work only for *kiddushin* and not for ordinary monetary transactions. Rava therefore teaches: no, they work for monetary transactions as well.

### No Mechila in Kiddushin

Conversely, had Rava taught only the monetary cases, one might have assumed the permissibility there flows from the fact that in monetary contexts, there is room for *mechila* — waiver. A creditor can simply forgive a debt: *arba me'ot shekel kesef beini u-veinecha mah hi* — four hundred shekels of silver between you and me, consider it a gift. In financial matters, if the parties are satisfied, the formal adequacy of the payment mechanism matters less.

But *kiddushin* has no room for *mechila*. The formal transactional event is constitutive of the *kiddushin* itself; without it, there is no marriage regardless of mutual consent. A man and a woman who simply agree to be married, without any *kinyan*, are not *mekudeshet*. Therefore, one might have thought these unusual mechanisms — good enough for *mamona* where *mechila* smooths over gaps — would not work for the more demanding formal requirements of *kiddushin*. Rava therefore teaches both: the mechanisms are valid for both *kiddushin* and *mamona*, and each teaching is necessary because neither can be derived from the other.

---

## Half-Marriage Cases

### Half Marriage

Rava then turns to a different class of problems: *hitkadshi li l'chetzi* — "be betrothed to half of me." Can a man offer to marry a woman only partially? Rava rules: *mekudeshet* — she is betrothed. The marriage is valid.

### Why Half Fails

Abaye challenges: if it is valid for a man to offer half of himself in marriage, why should the inverse case — *chetziyech mekudeshet li*, "half of you be betrothed to me" — be invalid? The verse says *ki yikach ish isha*, implying a whole woman must be taken. But it also says *ish* — implying, perhaps, a whole man must be the one taking. The same logic that invalidates half-*kiddushin* of the woman should apply to the man.

Rava responds: do not invoke *pesukim* at me; I am speaking of *svarot* — substantive logical reasoning. *Ititah le-vei terei lo chazya* — a woman cannot be married to two men simultaneously. Therefore, when a man says "half of you be betrothed to me," the implicit consequence is that the other half remains available for a second man to marry — which is forbidden. The statement is thus structurally self-defeating: it presupposes an arrangement that cannot legally exist.

But a man in a marriage? *Gavra mi lo chazi le-vei terei?* — can a man not be married to two women? In the period of the Gemara, polygamy, while not normative, was technically permitted. When a man says "half of me be betrothed to you," what he is expressing — using unconventional language — is that he reserves the right within this marriage to take a second wife. That is halachically permissible, and therefore the statement does not self-destruct in the same way. The *kiddushin* is valid.

It is worth pausing to note the interesting implication: the man here is entering marriage on the explicit understanding that he may take a second wife. One might consider the extent to which, in entering a polygamous arrangement, a man must stipulate this at the outset or whether it is a reserved right independent of the *kiddushin* formulation. The Gemara does not pursue that question, but the structure of the case raises it naturally.

### Hekdesh Analogy

Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari then poses a challenge to Ravina: even if we accept that *chetziyech mekudeshet li* fails, why should the *kiddushin* not spread through her entire person? This is an importation from the laws of *hekdesh*: if a person consecrates part of an animal for the altar, the sanctity can spread (*lifshot*) through the entire animal. Does the *kiddushin* not spread similarly?

The Gemara invokes a specific teaching on the matter: *ha-omer regla shel zo olah, tehei kulah olah* — if one says "the leg of this animal is an *olah*," the entire animal becomes an *olah*. Even according to the opinion in Masechet Temurah that such spreading does not always work, that restrictive view applies only where one consecrated a part from which the animal could survive — a leg, for instance. An animal can live without a leg. But if one consecrates something that the animal's life depends on — its heart, its brain — then the entire life of the animal is encompassed, and the *hekdesh* spreads throughout. By analogy, if one says "half of you" in a way that divides the woman down the middle — a division incompatible with survival — should not the *kiddushin* spread through all of her?

### Objects vs Persons

The Gemara's answer marks a fundamental distinction: *mi dami? hasam behemah, hacha da'at acheret* — can these cases be compared? There, it is an animal; here, there is *da'at acheret* — another consciousness, another will.

When an animal is consecrated for the altar, it is designated — it does not consent. An animal has no *da'at* to resist or limit the effect of *hekdesh*. The sanctity spreads because the animal is a passive object of the transaction.

Marriage is different in the most fundamental way: the woman's *da'at* is constitutive of the *kiddushin*. We have seen already in the *masechta* that at the moment of *kiddushin*, the husband articulates a verbal declaration of intent, and the woman's acceptance is her consent to that specific declaration. If the man says *chetziyech mekudeshet li* — "half of you be betrothed to me" — her acceptance is an acceptance of precisely that formulation. She may be agreeing only to what was said; her *da'at* does not expand beyond the terms she was offered. Unlike an animal, which has no consciousness to resist or delimit the spread of holiness, the woman's active *da'at* means the *kiddushin* takes effect only to the extent she has consented — and "half of you" is what she agreed to.

The emphasis here on the woman's *da'at* as a limiting and constitutive factor in *kiddushin* is striking. Even in a case where she seems broadly willing, her agreement is agreement to a particular articulation, and *kiddushin* cannot spread beyond what that articulation encompasses.

Before leaving this section, one important dispute between Rashi and Tosafot should be noted. The *hava amina* earlier — that the woman giving money to the man might operate via *kinyan agav* — raised the question of whether a human being can be analogized to land for transactional purposes. Rashi holds that human beings are in a certain general sense comparable to *karka* in transactional contexts. Tosafot strongly disagrees: the comparison to real estate applies to Canaanite slaves, who are explicitly equated to land by a *pasuk*, but does not extend to free persons. The *Shach* in Shulchan Aruch marshals extensive proofs against Tosafot's position — as is characteristic of his method when he is firmly convinced of one view. The underlying question — whether the *hekesh* between slaves and land extends conceptually to free persons — is a significant one and worth careful consideration.

The Gemara then draws additional lessons from a case involving an animal owned by two partners, one of whom consecrates his half, then purchases the other half and consecrates that as well. Such an animal is *kadosh* but cannot be brought as a sacrifice — *eina kreiva* — because it is, in conceptual terms, two half-animals joined together rather than one whole animal. Yet it has sufficient *kedushah* to effect *temurah*, the exchange of sanctity to another animal — which requires *kdushat haguf*. And the *temurah* itself is likewise *eina kreiva*.

From this case the Gemara derives three lessons — *shma mina tlat*, as is the Talmudic convention: that living animals can be subjected to *dichui* (disqualification that persists even after the disqualifying condition resolves); that *dichui me-ikara havei dichui* — even initial-state disqualification counts; and that *yesh dichui be-damim* — *dichui* applies even in cases of *kdushat damim*, value-based sanctification, not only *kdushat haguf*.

---

## Teiku Cases

### Half-Perutah

Rava then poses a series of progressively more strained cases, all left as *teiku* — unresolved. The general principle is that most *rishonim*, including the Rambam, rule *lechumra* in cases of *teiku* in *kiddushin*, though of course the precise application depends on how a given Gemara is read.

The first case: *chetzyeich be-chatzi perutah ve-chetzyeich be-chatzi perutah* — "half of you with half a *perutah* and half of you with another half a *perutah*." Can two statements of *chatzi pruta* combine to constitute the minimum value? *Keivan de-amar lah chatzi perutah, chatzi paska* — by saying "half a *perutah*," he has articulated an incomplete transaction, and the two halves may simply be two separate invalid acts. Or perhaps he is *moneh ve-holeich* — building up his count incrementally, in which case the transaction adds up. *Teiku*.

If one admits that *moneh ve-holeich* applies there, a more acute case follows: *chetzyeich be-pruta ve-chetzyeich be-pruta* — "half of you with one *perutah* and the other half with another *perutah*." Now each half is stated with a full *perutah* — a significant and discrete amount. Does stating a full *perutah* indicate a self-contained transaction, thus splitting the two statements into two independently invalid acts? Or does the same *moneh ve-holeich* principle apply — he is simply counting out the *kiddushin* in pieces? *Teiku*.

And if that case admits of combination: *chetzyeich be-pruta hayom ve-chetzyeich be-pruta le-machar* — "half of you today with a *perutah* and half tomorrow with a *perutah*." At this point the absurdity is evident; it seems nearly certain that this cannot work. *Keivan de-amar lah le-machar, paska* — the word "tomorrow" already severs the transaction entirely. Or perhaps, the Gemara entertains, what he is expressing is that the *kiddushin* begins now but is only completed tomorrow — conceptually drawing out what should be an instantaneous transactional moment across two days. It is worth noting that the time-scale here is days rather than minutes and hours, which themselves are known concepts — the coarse granularity is itself interesting to observe. *Teiku*.

Finally: *shenei chetzyeich be-pruta* — "your two halves be betrothed to me with this one *perutah*." This is a single statement, made at one moment, referring to the complete person by saying "both halves." Here the Gemara asks whether this single unified statement can save the transaction — *hacha vadai be-chad zimna ka'amar lah*, he said it at one time. Or perhaps there is a more fundamental principle: *ein ishah mitkadeshet le-chatzayin klal* — a woman simply cannot be married by halves in any form. Framing the *kiddushin* in terms of halves, even adding up to a whole in the same breath, reflects a flawed conception of what marriage is about, or signals to the woman an offer she is not able to meaningfully accept. *Teiku*.

### Two-to-Two Case

Rav Pappa then raises a separate case: *shenei benotayich li-shenei banai be-perutah* — a father, acting as agent for his two sons (having been properly appointed as *shaliach*, since a father cannot unilaterally marry off a son without the son's authorization), approaches another father and says: "Your two daughters be betrothed to my two sons with a single *perutah*." Does the single *perutah* suffice for both marriages?

The question is whether we follow the people actually conducting the transaction — the two fathers — making it in some sense a single unified exchange, with the money satisfying the minimum requirement. Or do we follow the men and women who are themselves being married, meaning each pair needs a separate *perutah*, and one *perutah* divided between two marriages is insufficient? *Teiku*.

### Daughter & Cow

Rav Ashi's case pushes further into the complexity of combining different categories of transaction: *bittacha u-faratcha be-perutah* — "your daughter and your cow with a single *perutah*." Are these being split into half a *perutah* each, making the *kiddushin* invalid for lack of minimum value? Or are they fundamentally different transactions — the *kiddushin* effected by a full *perutah* and the cow acquired by *meshicha* (the appropriate *kinyan* for movable property), the two simply uttered together but legally discrete? *Teiku*.

Rav Ashi then poses the closest variant: *bittacha be-karkacha be-perutah* — "your daughter and your field with a single *perutah*." Human beings and land are, in a certain conceptual sense, closer to each other in the transactional framework than a woman and a cow are. The *hava amina* that free persons might be analogized to real estate (whatever one concludes about the Rashi-Tosafot debate) gives this case a special texture. Is the *perutah* split half and half, or does the full *perutah* go to the *kiddushin* while the field is acquired by *chazakah*? *Teiku*.

---

## Silk & Valuation

### Silk Case

The final section of the *daf* is introduced by a real case: *hahu gavra de-akadish be-shirai* — a man who attempted to effect *kiddushin* using a piece of silk. Silk in this period was extraordinarily valuable — the product of silkworms from China, reaching the Near East only through long and costly trade routes. The historical note is apt: Rava and Rav Yosef are late-fourth-generation Amoraim, and silk was making its appearance in the markets of Babylonia precisely in this period, making it exactly the kind of novel, expensive, and imprecisely-valued commodity whose halachic implications needed to be worked out in real time.

### Raba vs Rav Yosef

Raba says: *lo tzricha shuma* — no assessment of value is required. We know silk is certainly worth more than a *perutah*; that is sufficient for *kiddushei kesef*, and the woman's consent stands on that basis.

Rav Yosef says: *tzricha shuma* — precise assessment is required. The woman is consenting to the marriage conditional on the object being worth what she believes it is worth. If she has no way of independently verifying the value, her *da'at* — her real consent — is not fully secured.

This dispute has direct practical ramifications and underlies the requirement, well-established in later *posekim*, to use plain metal rings of determinable value for *kiddushin* — avoiding gemstones or elaborately worked pieces whose market value fluctuates widely and which a non-expert cannot independently evaluate.

### Consensus

The Gemara clarifies that there are two cases in which everyone agrees. First: if the man explicitly says *be-kulo* — "be married to me for whatever minimal value exists in this silk," indicating that only a single *perutah*'s worth is being designated as the *kesef kiddushin*. Since it is beyond question that silk is worth at least a *perutah*, everyone agrees *lo tzricha shuma* — no assessment is needed. Second: if the man explicitly stated the silk was worth 50 and it was actually not worth 50 — *ha lo shavu* — everyone agrees that the *kiddushin* is invalid. She was misled about the value, her consent was based on a false representation, and the marriage does not stand.

### Core Dispute

The actual *machloket* between Raba and Rav Yosef concerns a case where the man said the silk was worth 50 and it actually was worth 50 — *d'amar chamishin ve-shavu chamishin* — but the woman did not know this independently and had no way to verify it.

Raba rules: *lo tzricha shuma* — no assessment is required. He said it was worth 50, it was worth 50; the statement was accurate, she agreed to it, the marriage is valid.

Rav Yosef rules: *tzricha shuma* — assessment is required. *Keivan de-ittata lo bekia'ah be-shuma, lo samcha da'atah* — since a woman would not normally know how to assess the value of silk, her mind is not settled. She did not really consent in the full sense because she had no way to evaluate the claim being made. Even if it turned out to be true, the *da'at* necessary for *kiddushin* was lacking at the moment of the transaction.

### Alternative View

An alternative reading of the *sugya* — introduced as *ika de-amrei* — extends the dispute further. On this view, Raba and Rav Yosef disagree even in the case of *be-kulo*, where the man designated only a minimal *perutah*'s worth. Rav Yosef holds: *shaveh perutah harei hu ke-kesef* — an object worth a *perutah* is treated as money for purposes of *kiddushei kesef*, and therefore it must conform to the qualities of money.

### Shaveh Kesef Rules

What is the essential quality of money? *Mah kesef de-kayatz* — money is precisely and fixedly valued. A coin has a determinate worth; there is no ambiguity about how much a *perutah* is worth. Rav Yosef therefore holds: *af shaveh kesef nami de-kayatz* — when *shaveh kesef* (property used in place of money) is employed for *kiddushin*, it too must be precisely measurable in value. Silk, whose price varies and which requires expert evaluation, does not meet that standard unless it is formally assessed.

The source for this principle is a *baraita*: *mi-kesef miknato* — in the context of the *eved Ivri*, the Hebrew bondsman who wishes to buy out the remaining years of his indentured servitude, the *pasuk* establishes that the redemption must be *be-kesef* — with money. The *baraita* derives that this excludes *tvu'ah* and *keilim* — produce and implements. Not because they cannot be used in transactions generally — the *pasuk* continues, *yashiv et geulato*, which the Gemara reads as extending *shaveh kesef ke-kesef*, equating property with money for transactional purposes — but because *tvu'ah* and *keilim*, even when they clearly exceed a *perutah* in value, lack the property of *kayitz*: their value is not fixed, not precisely defined, subject to fluctuation and market variation.

The analogy to *kiddushin* is thus direct: just as the redemption of the *eved Ivri* requires *kesef de-kayatz* or *shaveh kesef de-kayatz* — either actual money or property of precisely determinable value — so too *kiddushei kesef* requires that what is given, whether money or *shaveh kesef*, have a known and fixed value at the moment of the transaction. Where value is indeterminate, the woman's *da'at* is unsettled, and the *kiddushin* cannot stand.

A final note of historical interest connects the laws of *kiddushin* to the approaching holiday: the Rama in *siman* 695 rules, strangely, that a man should not send *mishloach manot* to a widow, owing to concern about *safek kiddushin*. The *acharonim* are puzzled — for *kiddushin* to result, both the man's intent and the woman's consent are obviously required. Yet the Rama states the concern. Looking closely at this ruling in light of today's *sugya* — which has established just how expansive the mechanisms of *kiddushei kesef* can be, including psychological *hana'ah* and gifts accepted by *adam chashuv* — provides the proper context for understanding what halachic concern the Rama may have in mind.

---

---

# Kiddushin 8

## Rabba vs. Rav Yosef

### Two Versions

The *gemara* on this daf centers on a dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef concerning a man who attempted *kiddushin* by giving a woman silk (*shiraim*), and whether the silk required a formal appraisal — *tzrichi shuma* — before the *kiddushin* could be valid. Rabba held that it did not; Rav Yosef held that it did. Crucially, the *gemara* presents two distinct versions of this debate, and they differ not only in outcome but in the underlying conceptual question each version raises.

In the first version, the man claimed a specific value for the silk — say, it was worth fifty — and it turned out to be exactly that amount, but no expert had verified this before the exchange. Rabba held that since the silk was in fact worth what he said, she is married. Rav Yosef countered that silk is not something a layperson can readily assess, and therefore even if it happened to be worth what he claimed, the woman could not have been genuinely confident (*samcha da'atah*) of its value at the time of acceptance. That absence of confident reliance is a deficiency in the *da'as* required for *kiddushin* to take effect.

The second version is conceptually richer. Here, the man makes no value claim at all — he simply says he is marrying her with whatever the silk is worth, which is certainly at least a *perutah*, but no specific amount is asserted. One can readily understand why Rabba would not require an assessment in this case, since no representation about value was made. Yet Rav Yosef holds that even here, an assessment is required. Understanding why brings us to the heart of the debate.

### Rav Yosef on Kayatz

Rav Yosef's position rests on a fundamental principle about how *shaveh kessef* — things of monetary value — function in halachic transactions. The principle that *shaveh kessef harei hu k'kessef*, that items of value may serve as money, is well established and applies across many contexts. We know a woman may be betrothed with *kessef* either from the verse concerning the sale of a daughter as an *amah ivriyah*, or from the purchase of Ephron's field by Avraham, where the text specifies payment that functioned as currency.

But Rav Yosef insists that the equation of *shaveh kessef* with *kessef* is not a blanket substitution — it means *shaveh kessef* must *function like* money. And the defining feature of money is that it has a fixed, determined value. The principle he articulates at the opening of daf 8a is: *ma kessef d'kaitz, af shaveh kessef nami d'kaitz* — just as money has a fixed value, so too *shaveh kessef* must have a fixed value. Silk whose value has not been established — which might be worth anywhere from ten to a hundred — cannot function as money, because money by definition is determinate. Therefore, without prior assessment that fixes the value, the silk cannot serve as *kessef kiddushin*.

### Eved Ivri Source

Rav Yosef then offers a *talmudic* source for this position from a *braita* dealing with the redemption of a *eved ivri*. The verse states *mikessef miknaso* — that a Hebrew slave is purchased and redeemed by means of money — and the *braita* derives from this that redemption works only with *kessef* and not with *tevuah* (grain) or *keilim* (vessels).

The *gemara* then interrogates this *braita*: in what circumstances does it exclude grain and vessels? If we say they simply cannot effect the transaction at all, that seems to contradict the well-established principle that *shaveh kessef* functions as *kessef*, learned from the word *geulato* — "his redemption" — which is general and inclusive. If on the other hand we say they are excluded only when they lack the value of a *perutah*, then the exclusion has nothing to do with being grain or vessels specifically — the same would apply to money itself. So why mention *tevuah* and *keilim* at all?

The *gemara* concludes: we must be dealing with grain and vessels that *do* have the value of a *perutah*, and yet they still fail — *kivan delo kaitz lehu* — because their values are indeterminate. This is Rav Yosef's proof: the *braita* is teaching that even objects of value fail when their value is not fixed. The principle of *kaitz* is therefore derived from the *eved ivri* context and applied to *kiddushin* as well.

### Rabba's Response

Rabba responds with a fundamentally different reading of the *braita*. In his view, the exclusion of *tevuah* and *keilim* has nothing to do with indeterminacy of value. Rather, the *braita* is teaching that the transaction must be structured *betorat kessef* — as an act of monetary payment — and not *betorat chaliphin*, not as an act of symbolic exchange. *Chaliphin*, in the relevant sense here, refers to the procedure of kinyan sudra, the handkerchief-type acquisition: one takes an object of significance — not for its monetary value but as a symbolic act of finalization — and that effects the transaction. The *braita*, says Rabba, is simply excluding framing the acquisition of an *eved ivri* as an act of *chaliphin* rather than as a monetary purchase.

The *gemara* pushes back: this reading works for *keilim*, which are paradigmatically used for *chaliphin*, but what about *tevuah* — grain? Rav Nachman rules that food items (*peirot*) cannot function as *chaliphin* at all. So the *braita's* exclusion of *tevuah* cannot be read as excluding *chaliphin* performed with grain, since that isn't a recognized form of *chaliphin* in the first place.

Cornered, Rabba retreats to the position that indeed the case is where *tevuah* and *keilim* lack the value of a *perutah*. But then, as the *gemara* objects, why specify those categories? Rabba answers with a *lo mibaya* construction: it goes without saying that actual *kessef* less than a *perutah* does not effect a transaction. The *chiddush* of the *braita* is that even *tevuah* and *keilim* — which one might think could function differently, since their value is direct and experiential (one eats the grain, one uses the vessel) — even those fail when they fall below a *perutah* in monetary value. *Kamashma lan* that in the end, value must be monetary value, not merely functional value.

This illuminates the deeper structure of the disagreement. For Rav Yosef, *shaveh kessef* functions as *kessef* precisely because it is quasi-money — it stands in for money, and therefore it must exhibit money's defining characteristic of determinacy. For Rabba, *shaveh kessef* functions not as a substitute for money but as an object of value in its own right. The underlying logic of the transaction is that something of value changes hands, not that something money-like changes hands. That is why the requirement of *kaitz* — a fixed, determined value — does not apply.

### Pidyon Ha-Ben

Rav Yosef then brings a second source from a *braita* concerning *pidyon ha-ben*. The *braita* states: if a man says to a *kohen*, "I am giving you this calf for my son's *pidyon*," or "this *tallis* for my son's *pidyon*" — without specifying a value — *lo amar klum*, it accomplishes nothing. But if he says, "I am giving you this calf valued at five *sela'im* for my son's *pidyon*," or "this *tallis* valued at five *sela'im*," then *bno paduy* — the son is redeemed.

The *gemara* asks: in what case are we dealing? If the object is actually not worth five *sela'im* in either scenario, then in the second case, merely saying the value does not make it so — *kol k'minei*, he has no power to magically assign worth beyond the item's true value. So it must be that in both cases the item actually is worth five *sela'im*. And yet when he fails to state a value, it does not work. *Ve-keivan de-lo kaitz* — since no fixed value was declared, the *pidyon* is invalid. This, says Rav Yosef, confirms the *kaitz* requirement.

Rabba responds with a different reading: the two cases differ not in what the item is actually worth, but in whether the *kohen* is willing to accept it at that valuation. *Lo le-olam de-lo shavi* — in fact, the item is not intrinsically worth five *sela'im*. *Ve-kheivan de-kibel lei kohen iluyei* — but the *kohen* was willing to evaluate it at five *sela'im* for himself. This is Rabba's *chiddush*: the question is not about standardized market value or official assessment. It is about whether this recipient — the *kohen* — subjectively values it at the required amount, and whether that subjective valuation is credible.

This is illustrated by the case of Rav Kahana, who — at the time of performing a *pidyon ha-ben* — took a *sudra* (handkerchief) and said that to him, personally, it was worth five *sela'im*. Tosafot notes, interestingly, that Rav Kahana may not himself have been a *kohen* but was perhaps married to the daughter of a *kohen*, implying that a *kohen's* daughter may also receive the *pidyon* payment.

Mar bar Rav Ashi adds a critical qualification: this principle — that a person may declare a subjective valuation — applies only to someone like Rav Kahana, who was a *gavra raba*, a man of stature, for whom it was genuinely undignified to go about without a head covering. One can understand how he would truly be willing to pay five *sela'im* for a *sudra* under those circumstances. But if a normal person, with no particular pressing need, simply asserts that a trivial object is worth five *sela'im*, the law applies the principle of *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* — his claimed valuation is simply discounted, because no reasonable person under those circumstances would pay that amount. A further illustration is the case of Mar bar Rav Ashi himself, who paid thirteen for a *sudra* worth ten, because it was of a quality appropriate to his standing and genuinely difficult to find.

The contrast between Rabba and Rav Yosef thus runs deeper than the question of formal assessment. Rav Yosef, who requires *shaveh kessef* to function as money, demands that the value be *kaitz* — fixed — in a way that reflects the objective determinacy of currency. Rabba, who holds that *shaveh kessef* functions as an object of value on its own terms, is comfortable with subjective valuation, provided it is a genuinely credible one. For Rabba, it need not fit the mold of money; it need only represent authentic value.

### Tosafot on Shiraim

The *gemara* concludes with the ruling: *vehilchesa shiraim lo tzrichi shuma* — silk does not require appraisal, and we rule like Rabba. Tosafot raises the well-known question: given that we generally rule like Rabba over Rav Yosef, why does the *gemara* need to state the ruling explicitly? This question also touches on which version of the debate the ruling addresses — the first version, concerning *smichat da'at* when a value is claimed, or the second version, concerning whether any *kaitz* is required at all.

Rabbeinu Tam offers a subtle and important distinction. The ruling that *shiraim* do not require *shuma* is specifically calibrated to the nature of silk: its value is roughly knowable — *shumasan yadu'a ketzat* — and the variance in how people assess it is not so wide as to undermine the woman's confidence. Silk is not the kind of item about which one can be dramatically mistaken.

But other items, such as precious stones and pearls, are a different matter entirely. With diamonds, the variance in valuation can be enormous — one must know not only whether the stone is genuine but also its cut, clarity, color, and carat weight, factors that can shift the price by orders of magnitude. In that case, *tzarich shuma mishum de-lo samcha da'atah* — an appraisal is required because the woman may be relying on a grossly inflated estimate of the stone's worth, and her *smichat da'at* is therefore compromised. Rabbeinu Tam's point thus operates on the terrain of the first version of the debate, focusing on the woman's subjective confidence rather than the abstract requirement of *kaitz*.

This distinction has direct practical implications. Tosafot states: *lefikach nahagu olam lekadesh betaba'at she-ein bah even* — and this is why the universal practice developed to perform *kiddushin* with a plain ring that contains no precious stone. A plain gold ring is valued by weight, and gold's weight-based valuation admits of no significant variance. The woman may not know the precise sum, but there is no concern about dramatic misjudgment, and therefore *smichat da'at* is not at issue and no assessment is required.

This also explains the practice at the *chuppah* whereby the rabbi confirms with the witnesses that the ring is worth at least a *perutah*, and asks the *chassan* accordingly. This is in part a way of framing the *kiddushin* so that the ring is not represented as worth any specific substantial amount — thereby removing the concern about *smichat da'at* entirely. As for common variations in ring shape or design — a square rather than a round band, an artistic cut — these do not generate meaningful indeterminacy in value, since anyone can verify the price through ordinary channels. A ring made by Picasso would present an entirely different problem.

---

## Maneh & Dinar

### Maneh Stam

Rabbi Elazar rules: if a man says to a woman, "Marry me with a *maneh*" — a hundred — and then hands her a single *dinar*, she is nonetheless betrothed, and he must eventually complete the payment. The reasoning, as the *gemara* explains, is that when he said *maneh* and immediately handed her a *dinar*, the context clarifies his intent: he was not proposing that a hundred coins constitute the *kessef kiddushin*. Rather, he was framing the full hundred as a *tenai* — a condition — while the *dinar* in her hand is the actual *kessef* of the *kiddushin*. The *gemara* invokes Rav Huna's ruling in the name of Rav: *kol ha-omer al menat, k'omer me-achshav dami* — one who says "on the condition" is regarded as having said "from now," meaning the *kiddushin* takes effect immediately with the *dinar*, subject to the condition of eventual full payment.

### Maneh Zu

The *gemara* then raises a challenge from a *braita*: if a man says "Marry me with a *maneh*" and begins counting out the coins one by one, and either party wishes to retract — even when only the last coin remains — the right to retract is in hand, and the *kiddushin* has not yet taken effect.
