Rav Pappa rules: *hilcheta malveh al peh goveh min ha'yorshim ve'eino goveh min ha'lokchot* — an oral loan can be collected from heirs but not from purchasers. The reasoning follows: *goveh min ha'yorshim* — *shibuda d'Oraisa* is in force, confirming that obligations create automatic Torah-level liens. *Ve'eino goveh min ha'lokchot* — but against purchasers it cannot be collected, *de'leis lei kala*, because since the loan was not recorded and publicly known, we protect the innocent purchasers who had no notice. The *yorshim*, by contrast, are not third-party purchasers who paid money in reliance on the debtor's unencumbered estate; they simply receive what their ancestor had, subject to his existing obligations.

---

## Woman's Release

### Get & Death Q

The Gemara now transitions to the next *mishnah*: *ve'konah et atzmah be'get u'be'misat ha'baal* — a woman acquires her own freedom through a *get* and through the death of her husband. The discussion of *kiddushin* naturally gives way to the question of how *kiddushin* is dissolved.

*Bishlama get* — that a *get* releases her is clear, as the Torah explicitly commands *ve'kasav lah sefer keritut*, a bill of severance. But the husband's death — *ela misat ha'baal, menalan* — where does the Torah ever explicitly state that she is released through his death?

### Arayot Problem

The Gemara first suggests a *sevara*, a logical inference: *hu asrah ve'hu sharya* — he made her forbidden (by marrying her), so when he dies he makes her permissible. The Gemara rejects this immediately: *de'arayot de'asru lehu ve'lo shari lehu* — the logic does not hold, because by many of the *arayot*, a woman becomes forbidden to a specific person through a relationship that no longer exists, yet the prohibition persists even after the death of the party who created the forbidden connection. The clearest example is a father's wife: she becomes forbidden to the son because of her marriage to the father. Yet even after the father dies, the prohibition does not lift. So death does not automatically dissolve forbidden relationships, and we cannot simply assume that a wife is released upon her husband's death.

### Yevamah Case

The Gemara attempts a derivation from the laws of *yibbum*: the Torah states that a *yevamah she'ein lah banim asurah* — a childless widow is forbidden to all other men because of her obligation to the *yavam*, the deceased husband's brother. This implies *ha yesh lah banim mutteret* — implicitly, if she has children and is exempt from *yibbum*, she is permissible. The Gemara pushes back: *vedilma* — perhaps even if she has children, she remains forbidden to the world at large; the only thing the childless case tells us is that she is also *forbidden* to non-*yavam* men, while the case with children merely removes the *yavam*'s claim, leaving the general question of her status unresolved. The inference therefore fails.

### Widow & Kohen

The Gemara tries yet another approach: the Torah forbids a *kohen gadol* from marrying a widow. The implication is *ha le'kohen hedyot sharya* — to an ordinary *kohen* and to the rest of the world she is permissible. Again the Gemara rejects the inference: *de'dilma l'kohen gadol be'lav* — perhaps the *kohen gadol* violates a specific negative commandment, *ve'le'chulei alma be'aseh* — while for everybody else there is merely an *issur aseh* prohibiting her from remarrying. The discussion of whether and how we can definitively derive the permissibility of a widow after her husband's death will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Kiddushin 14

## Opening & Context

### Opening Remarks

Dan Margulis is filling in for Rabbi Linzer. By way of introduction, he notes that it is *shoshon purim*, the fifteenth of Adar, which is, by the well-known principle, *shloshim yom kodem hachag* — thirty days before Pesach — the time when we begin *sho'alin vedorshin b'hilchot hapesach*. Though the tractate under study is *Kiddushin*, the spirit of Pesach is present: the essential act of Pesach is asking questions, and that spirit animates the entire enterprise of Talmud study. The sugya before us today is on 13b.

### Eternal Marriage Polemic

The sugya at hand addresses how we know that a husband's death permits his widow to remarry. This is not merely a technical halakhic question; it carries polemical weight against theological traditions — certain of them still present today — that maintain the concept of an eternal marriage bond persisting even after one spouse's death. The Gemara's sustained attention to deriving this permission from scriptural sources reflects a serious halakhic and philosophical commitment to establishing that death fully dissolves the marital bond.

---

## Widow Remarriage

### Kohen Gadol Source

The Gemara proposes that we may derive the widow's permission to remarry from the special prohibition applying to the *kohen gadol*: *ela mide'amar rachmana almanah le'kohen gadol asura ha le'kohen hedyot sharya* — the Torah specifically prohibits the *kohen gadol* from marrying an *almanah*, which implies that a regular *kohen* may do so, and therefore an *almanah* is in general permitted to remarry. The only one absolutely prohibited from marrying a widow would be the *kohen gadol*.

### Mitzvat Asei Proposal

The Gemara immediately challenges this derivation. Perhaps the prohibition for the *kohen gadol* is a *lav*, while for all others — *Yisraelim*, regular *kohanim*, and everyone else — there remains an *issur asei* derived from the verse *vedavak be'ishto*, the idea that one is bound by a positive commandment to be joined with one's wife. The *Ri* in *Tosafot* raises precisely this possibility: perhaps even after the husband's death, some residual *mitzvat asei* prohibits another man from marrying the widow. This is framed as the Gemara's *hava amina* — a position that will ultimately be rejected, but whose very consideration underscores how counterintuitive it would be to require explicit derivation for something as seemingly obvious as a widow's right to remarry. As the Gemara notes, the entire *shakla vetarya* here is designed to push against that intuition and demonstrate that the permission is in fact well-grounded in *psukim*.

### Lav vs Asei

The Gemara probes what this hypothetical *mitzvat asei* would actually accomplish. *Hai asei mai avid lei* — what does this *asei* do? Either *mitat habaal* completely releases her (*tishari legamri*), or it does not release her at all and she remains in her prior status (*tukma be'milta kamaisa*). The problem is that a *lav* and an *asei* operating together cannot produce a clean intermediate result. *Rashi* explains that if such an *issur asei* existed for everyone, there would be no reason for the *kohen gadol*'s prohibition to be expressed as the more severe *lav*.

The Gemara then entertains a further refinement: perhaps *mitat habaal* removes her from the category of capital crime (*chiyuv mitat beit din*) but leaves intact an *issur asei*. The analogy offered is *psulei hamukdashim* — animals consecrated for sacrifice that subsequently became disqualified by a permanent blemish. Before the blemish, there is a prohibition of *me'ilah* (using consecrated property) as well as prohibitions against shearing or using the animal for labor. Once an act of *me'ilah* occurs under certain circumstances, the *kedushah* is removed and *me'ilah* no longer applies — yet the prohibitions of shearing and labor (*giza va'avoda*) remain. Similarly, one might think that the husband's death removes the *issur* punishable by *chenek*, but an *issur asei* persists.

This analogy is ultimately rejected, and the Gemara arrives at a real *pasuk*: *pen yamut bamilchama ve'ish acher yikachena* — from the section of those exempt from military service, the Torah anticipates that a soldier recently betrothed might die in battle, and another man will marry her. The word *yikach* is recognized as language of marriage (*ki yikach ish isha*), proving incidentally that another man may marry her after the first husband's death. This *drasha*, however, applies only to *erusin*, not *nisuin*, which will require separate derivation.

### Rav Sheshet's Objection

*Matkif lah Rav Sheshet breih de'Rav Idi*: perhaps the verse does not prove that she may remarry any man she chooses; perhaps the only man permitted to marry her would be the *yavam* — her deceased husband's brother — to whom she has an existing obligation. This is a pointed challenge and one that proves highly relevant to deeper questions about the nature of *yibum*.

### Yavam Not Acher

*Amar Rav Ashi: shtei teshuvot badavar* — there are two answers. First, *yavam lo ikrei acher* — the *yavam* is not called "another" man. This is a significant statement about the nature of *yibum*: the *yavam* is, in some sense, a continuation of or stand-in for his deceased brother, not a new and unrelated third party. The *Rambam*, notably, highlights in the opening *halachot* of *Hilchot Yibum VeChalitzah* that the *ketubah* in *yibum* is paid *al nikhsei ba'ala harishon* — from the estate of the first husband — underscoring the continuity of the original relationship. Whether *yibum* constitutes a new relationship or the continuation of the prior one is a rich question in the *rishonim*.

### Death Like Divorce

The second answer: *ve'od kativ ve'sane'ah ha'ish ha'acharon* — the verse discussing *machzir grushato* (the prohibition against a man remarrying his divorced wife after she has been married to and divorced or widowed from another man) refers to the second husband as *ha'ish ha'acharon*. The verse contemplates that the second husband either divorces her or dies. If he dies, she is then permitted to remarry a third man — proof that death, like divorce, severs the marital bond entirely and permits remarriage. *Ve'hikish mita l'gerushin* — the Torah's juxtaposition of death and divorce in this verse establishes that just as *gerushin* completely severs the relationship and allows her to remarry (*ma gerushin sharya ve'gomar, af mita sharya ve'gomar*), so too death accomplishes the same full severance.

An aside of contemporary halakhic interest: the *rishonim* discuss the case of *Eliyahu HaNavi*, who ascended to heaven in a chariot and did not die in the ordinary sense. What is the status of *Eliyahu*'s wife? This serves as a theoretical construct for exploring the case of someone who has neither died nor is still present among the living. Related questions arise regarding persons who died and returned to life — whether through miraculous revival as recorded in *Tanakh*, or through modern resuscitation such as CPR. The *Pitchei Teshuva* addresses this, and the *Ben Ish Chai* has a *teshuva* distinguishing between *techiyat hameitim al yedei nes* — miraculous revival that might characterize modern medicine — and *techiyat hameitim* in the messianic era, which is categorically different. Whether cardiac death followed by resuscitation would in principle dissolve a marriage is thus at least a *hava amina* in the *poskim*, even if practical ruling consistently forecloses that conclusion.

---

## Yibbum Mechanism

### Yibbum Not Kesef

The *mishnah* taught: *hayevamah nikneit be'viah* — a *yevamah* is acquired through *biah* alone, and she acquires her freedom through *chalitzah* or the *yavam*'s death. The Gemara now asks: *be'viah minalan?* The question, as the *rishonim* clarify, is not merely how we know *biah* works, but specifically how we know that *kesef* and *shtar* do not work. The only effective mechanism for *yibum* is *biah*, and this requires derivation.

### Yavo Aleha Source

*Amar kra: yevamah yavo aleha ulekachah lo le'ishah* — the verse in *Ki Tetze* states that her brother-in-law will come upon her and take her as his wife. The expression *yavo aleha* is the Torah's euphemism for a sexual encounter. One might have thought that since the verse concludes *ulekachah lo le'ishah*, comparing her to any other wife, all the mechanisms of standard *kiddushin* — *kesef*, *shtar*, and *biah* — would apply. *Rashi* makes this explicit: *dilma ke'ishah, mah ishah kesef ushtar ke'viah, af yevamah kesef ushtar ke'viah* — just as a wife can be acquired through *kesef* and *shtar* in addition to *biah*, perhaps the same is true of the *yevamah* precisely because the verse says *le'ishah*. This is why an explicit exclusionary *drasha* is necessary.

### Veyibmah Redundancy

A *braita* is cited: one might have thought that *kesef* and *shtar* complete the acquisition of the *yevamah* just as *biah* does. *Talmud lomar: veyibmah* — the verse contains an apparently redundant word: after stating *yavo aleha ulekachah lo le'ishah*, it adds *veyibmah*, "and perform *yibum* with her." This redundancy teaches: *biah gomeret bah ve'ein kesef ushtar gomerin bah* — only *biah* completes the acquisition; *kesef* and *shtar* do not.

This reflects a fundamental difference between *yibum* and ordinary *kiddushin*. The mechanisms differ, and more profoundly, the *chalos* — the legal status created — differs. *Yibum* is predicated on a pre-existing relationship; it is a very different kind of bond from *kiddushin*, which brings together two people with no prior legal connection.

### Implicit Consent

The Gemara then asks: perhaps the word *veyibmah* is needed to teach not the exclusion of *kesef* and *shtar*, but rather that *yibum* may be performed *baal karkhah* — without the explicit present consent of the woman? The Gemara resolves this by noting that the verse could have said *veyabem* (masculine verb); the fact that it says *veyibmah* (with the feminine suffix, creating an additional textual redundancy) allows us to derive both principles simultaneously: *shema mina tartei* — we learn two things from the single word. *Biah* is the exclusive mechanism, and *yibum* may proceed *baal karkhah*.

The halakhic understanding of *baal karkhah* here is nuanced. The woman's *da'at* — her consent — at the time of her initial marriage is understood to carry with it an implicit legal acceptance of *yibum* should her husband predecease her without children. She entered marriage knowing the *halacha*; her consent to the marriage therefore encompasses implicit consent to the potential *yibum* obligation. This raises profound questions, discussed at length in the *rishonim* and *acharonim*, about how much voice the woman genuinely has in choosing between *yibum* and *chalitzah*, particularly given the question — debated in the first *perek* of *Yevamot* and in *Bechorot* — of whether we practice *yibum* today at all.

---

## Chalitzah Release

### Chalitzah Permits Remarr…

The *mishnah* also taught that the *yevamah* acquires her freedom through *chalitzah*. The Gemara asks: *minalan d'chalutzah muteret lehinnase?* — how do we know that a woman who has undergone *chalitzah* is permitted to remarry? One might think that after *chalitzah* she remains unable to remarry anyone: she has been rejected by the *yavam* (or has rejected him), but that alone does not necessarily permit her to marry a stranger. The death of her first husband left strings attached; her only options were *yibum* or *chalitzah*, and it is not self-evident that performing *chalitzah* entirely dissolves the bond and opens the door to any other marriage.

### Shoe Removal Source

The Gemara derives the permission from the verse: *ve'nikra shemo be'Yisrael beit chalutz hana'al* — the *yavam* who submitted to *chalitzah* will be known in Israel as "the house of him whose shoe was removed." From the phrase *shemo be'Yisrael*, the Gemara infers: *keivan shechalaẓ bah na'al, hutrah le'chol Yisrael* — once she removes his shoe, she is permitted to marry any member of *Klal Yisrael*. This does not, of course, include a *kohen*, since a *chalutzah* is prohibited to a *kohen* — though the *rishonim* largely hold that the prohibition of *chalutzah le'kohen* is only *d'rabbanan*, since *chalitzah* resembles but is not identical to *gerushin*.

### Beth Din Jurisdiction

The Gemara immediately challenges this derivation: is the word *Yisrael* in this verse really needed to teach her permission to remarry, or does *Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah* need it to teach something else? *Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah* holds that the word *Yisrael* teaches that *chalitzah* must be performed before a *beit din shel Yisrael* — a Jewish court — and not before a non-Jewish court.

The alternative text discussed, following the *Hagahot HaBach*, reads *beit din shel geirim* rather than *beit din shel ovdei kochavim*. The question of whether converts may serve as *dayanim* for *chalitzah* is significant: it touches on the nature of *chalitzah* as a proceeding — is it a formal legal act requiring a fully qualified *beit din*, or is the *beit din* present primarily as witnesses to a ceremony? The *hava amina* that *chalitzah* might be valid before a non-Jewish court is striking and points to a genuine ambiguity about what kind of authority the *dayanim* present at *chalitzah* are exercising.

This line of reasoning connects to broader questions about civil law in *agunah* cases. Rav Kook, in a *teshuva* dealing with an *agunah* case, made the radical suggestion that at the *d'Oraisa* level, a civil divorce might qualify as a *get pasul*, employing this as one *snif le'hakeil* in a broader *diyun*. Similarly, questions arise about how much weight to give civil marriage or common-law marriage in Jewish legal contexts.

### Multiple Yisrael Uses

The resolution: *trei be'Yisrael kesivi* — the word *Yisrael* appears twice in the *parsha* of *chalitzah*, and therefore we may derive multiple *halachot* from the multiple occurrences.

### Rabbi Tarfon Procedure

A *braita* quoted by *Rabbi Yehuda* teaches that he and others once sat before *Rabbi Tarfon* when a *yevamah* came to perform *chalitzah*. *Rabbi Tarfon* instructed all those present to call out *chalutz hana'al, chalutz hana'al* — "the one whose shoe was removed" — immediately upon the completion of the ceremony. This raises the question of how literally to understand the verse *ve'nikra shemo be'Yisrael beit chalutz hana'al*: is the formal public calling of this name a required act, to be performed right then by those present, or is it merely a figurative description of how he will be known going forward?

### Calling Him by Name

The Gemara resolves this: *hahu mi've'nikra shemo nafka* — that particular *halacha* (the public calling of his name) is derived from the phrase *ve'nikra shemo*, not from the word *Yisrael*. Therefore, all three *halachot* can be derived independently: (1) the *beit din* must be a Jewish court; (2) the *chalutzah* is permitted to remarry any *Yisrael*; and (3) upon completion of the ceremony, those present must call out *chalutz hana'al*.

---

## Yavam's Death

### Kal Vachomer Logic

The *mishnah* further states that the *yevamah* acquires her freedom through the death of the *yavam*. The Gemara asks: *minalan?* And proposes a *kal vachomer* from *eishet ish*: if an *eishet ish* — a fully married woman whose violation carries the penalty of *chenek* — is released by the death of her husband, then a *yevamah* whose prohibition carries only the lesser penalty of a *lav* (punishable by lashes) should certainly be released by the death of her *yavam*.

### Get vs Chalitzah

The *kal vachomer* is challenged: *mah le'eishet ish she'ken yotzah be'get* — the *eishet ish* is different in that she can be released through a *get*, which is not available to the *yevamah*, who can only be released through *chalitzah*. This asymmetry may undermine the comparison. The response is: *ha nami yotza be'chalitzah* — the *yevamah* too has a release mechanism, namely *chalitzah*, and perhaps *chalitzah* and *get* are sufficiently analogous to preserve the *kal vachomer*.

### Yavam's Dual Role

A deeper challenge: *mah le'eishet ish she'ken oserah matirah* — in the case of *eishet ish*, the one who created the prohibition (the husband) is the same one who releases her (through death or *get*). Can this be compared to the *yevamah*, where at first glance it seems the deceased husband created the prohibition while the *yavam* releases her through *chalitzah*?

*Amar Rav Ashi: ha nami osrah u'matirah* — Rav Ashi resolves this by pointing out that in the case of *yibum* as well, the same party both creates and dissolves the prohibition. The *yavam* himself is the one who creates the *issur*: if the *yavam* did not exist — if there were no brothers — the woman would be permitted to remarry immediately upon her husband's death. It is the very existence of the *yavam* that creates the prohibition of *yevamah lashuk*. Therefore, it is the *yavam* who both creates the *issur* and, through *chalitzah* or *yibum*, dissolves it.

### Reverse Kal Vachomer

The Gemara now explores the mirror image: can we run the *kal vachomer* in reverse? *Vetehei eishet ish yotza be'chalitzah mikal vachomer* — perhaps an *eishet ish* could also be released through *chalitzah*? The reasoning would be: if a *yevamah*, who cannot be released by a *get*, can be released by *chalitzah*, then surely an *eishet ish*, who can be released by a *get*, should also be releasable by *chalitzah*. *Amar kra: sefer kortah ve'ein davar acher kortah* — the Torah specified that only a written document severs the marriage of an *eishet ish*; nothing else can serve that function.

Similarly, one might argue in the other direction: *vetehei yevamah yotza be'get mikal vachomer* — if an *eishet ish*, who cannot be released by *chalitzah*, can be released by a *get*, surely a *yevamah* who can be released by *chalitzah* should also be releasable by a *get*?

### Kacha & La

The Gemara invokes two separate scriptural limitations. By the laws of *chalitzah*, the Torah used the word *kacha* — *kacha ye'aseh la'ish asher lo yivneh et beit achiv* — and *kacha ikuva*: the word *kacha* creates a restriction, limiting the procedure to precisely this form and no other. This would seem to preclude learning from a *kal vachomer* that a *get* could work for a *yevamah*. But can *kacha* truly block a *kal vachomer*?

### Yom Kippur Example

The Gemara addresses whether a term of restriction (*chukkah* or *kacha*) can entirely block a *kal vachomer* inference, and brings the example of *Yom Kippur* and the two goats. The Torah states that only the *goral* — the lottery — designates which goat becomes the *korban chatat* and which is sent to *Azazel*; *kriyat shem* (verbal declaration) does not work for this designation. Yet a *kal vachomer* argument is conceivable: in other cases where a *goral* does not work, *kriyat shem* does work; so where *goral* does work (on *Yom Kippur*), surely *kriyat shem* should work as well. The Torah needed a specific verse — *ve'asahu chatat, hagoral oseh chatat ve'ein hashem oseh chatat* — to exclude this. This proves that even when the Torah employs a limiting term like *chukkah*, the *hava amina* of a *kal vachomer* still arises and must be defeated by an explicit verse. Therefore, *kacha* alone is not sufficient to block the *kal vachomer* that a *get* might work for a *yevamah*; an explicit verse is needed.

That verse is *la* — *ve'chatav lah*, "and he shall write it for her." *La v'lo le'yevamah*: the Torah's use of *lah* specifies that the *get* is written for his wife, not for a *yevamah*. This is the explicit scriptural exclusion that prevents a *get* from working for a *yevamah*.

A student raises the question: is not the word *lah* needed for the *drasha* that a *get* must be written *lishmah* — for the specific woman for whom it is intended? *Trei lah ketivi* — the word appears twice, and therefore both *drashot* can be sustained. A further question: does the second *lah* teach *la v'lo le'yevamah* or *la v'lo lah ve'lachavertah* — that a husband cannot divorce two wives with a single *get*? The Gemara resolves this by turning to the *parsha* of *chalitzah*: *naal, naal — naal ein midi achrina lo* — just as there is a *drasha* that only a written document severs an ordinary marriage (*sefer kortah ve'ein davar acher kortah*), so too in *chalitzah* the Torah specifies the shoe, teaching that only the shoe effects *chalitzah* and nothing else can substitute for it.

The underlying theme of this entire *sugya*, as the discussion makes clear, is the *chachamim*'s insistence on the primacy of *psukim* over *kal vachomer*. *Kal vachomer* is a powerful tool for deriving *halacha*, yet the Gemara works strenuously to ground each rule in explicit scriptural derivation rather than purely logical inference. The reason is that *yibum*, *gerushin*, *eishet ish*, and *amah ivriyah* are not simply variations on a single theme; each is a unique and distinct legal institution, and the Torah's precise language in each context reflects those distinctions. Logical analogy alone cannot safely be used to import rules from one domain into another, because the apparently similar categories are in fact genuinely different.

---

## Chalitzah Shoe

### Whose Shoe Works

The word *naal* in the *chalitzah* verse implies the *yavam*'s own shoe — *na'alo*. But the *drasha* of *naal* (unmodified) teaches expansively: *naal shel kol adam* — any person's shoe may be used. The *yavam* need not own the shoe; it may be borrowed or provided by the *beit din*.

### Shoe Exclusions

The *braita* provides three exclusions. *Prat le'gadol she'ein yachol lehalech bo* — a shoe so large that the *yavam* cannot walk in it (the image of clown shoes makes the point) is invalid. *Prat le'katan she'eino chofeh rov raglo* — a shoe so small that it does not cover the majority of his foot is likewise invalid. The legal principle of *rubo ke'kulo* (the majority counts as the whole) is operative, though practically speaking a shoe that covers only the majority of the foot would still be uncomfortable; the criterion is a legal one. *Prat le'mesulyah she'ein lo akeiv* — certain sandal types lacking a proper heel cup (effectively, flip-flops) are also excluded.

### Proper Fit

The general principle is *na'alo hara'uy lo* — the shoe must be appropriately fit for him. A flip-flop, lacking the structural cup to hold the heel, is not considered a proper shoe in the relevant halakhic sense.

### Veyibmah Teaches All

*Im kein nechtov kra naal — mai hanaal? Shema mina tartei*: had the Torah written only *naal*, the word *hanaal* (with the definite article, creating apparent redundancy) would be unnecessary. From this redundancy we derive two things: first, that *chalitzah* can only be effected through the shoe and no other mechanism; and second, all the specifications regarding the shoe's fitness and physical requirements are also derived. The detailed laws governing the *chalitzah* shoe are treated at length in *Masechet Yevamot*.

---

## Eved Ivri Intro

### Three Sources

The *mishnah* now shifts to a new subject: *eved ivri*, the Jewish indentured servant. The laws of *eved ivri* appear three times in the Torah: in *Parshat Mishpatim*, in *Parshat Behar*, and in *Parshat Re'eh* in *Sefer Devarim*. Each passage has a different emphasis and focus. Biblical critics have argued that these three sections reflect different literary sources. Professor Aaron Koller of Yeshiva University has argued persuasively, drawing on both traditional sources and Ancient Near Eastern parallels, that the three sections are entirely compatible, mutually complementary parts of a unified legal system. A recurring failure of modern biblical scholarship, on this view, is to identify apparent tensions and attribute them to source pluralism without adequately examining analogous legal structures in the ancient world, which demonstrate that such complexity is entirely expected within a coherent legal code.

### Two Paths

There are two paths by which a Jew could become an *eved ivri*. The first is *mocher atzmo* — a man in financial distress voluntarily sells himself into indentured servitude. The second is *mecharu beit din* — a *beit din* sells a person as a servant when he has stolen and is too poor to repay the principal (*keren*) of what he stole. The thief can be sold to cover the *keren* but not the *keifel* (the double payment), since the *keifel* is a punitive fine rather than a restitutionary obligation, and one cannot be sold into servitude to pay a penal surcharge.

### Mishnah Overview

The *mishnah* states: *eved ivri nikne be'chesef uve'shtar* — an *eved ivri* is acquired through money or a document — *ve'koneh atzmo be'shanim* — and acquires his freedom through the passage of years (specifically six years, as the verse states *ve'avadcha sheish shanim*), *uve'yovel* — or through the arrival of the Jubilee year, which releases him even mid-term — *uve'giraon kesef* — or through a proportional monetary buyout of the remaining term.

### Amah Ivriyah

The *mishnah* notes that the *amah ha'ivriyah* has a special status. She is a minor girl indentured by her father. (An adult woman apparently has no mechanism to indenture herself; similarly, minor boys have no such track. Only adult men and minor girls have defined paths into *eved ivri* status.) The *amah ha'ivriyah* acquires her freedom also upon the appearance of *simanim* — physical signs of puberty. She has an additional path not available to the adult male: the institution of *yi'ud*, whereby the *adon* or his son may marry her, transforming the indentured arrangement into a marital one. *Tosafot* return to this point repeatedly in comparing the acquisition of an *amah ha'ivriyah* to the mechanisms of marriage, and the comparison proves illuminating throughout the earlier part of the *perek*. From the father's perspective, the arrangement provides an opportunity for his daughter to marry into a prosperous family — a context that must be understood against the backdrop of its time, even as it engages obvious tensions with contemporary sensibilities regarding child labor and child marriage.

### Eved Nirtza

The *mishnah* further mentions the *eved nirtza*, the pierced-ear servant. After six years of service, if the servant declares that he loves his master and does not wish to go free, the *adon* brings him to the doorpost and pierces his ear with an awl. The servant then acquires the status of *eved nirtza*, which is distinct from ordinary *eved ivri* in that it does not expire after six years; instead, the *eved nirtza* is released only at the *yovel* year or upon the death of the *adon*. He cannot buy his freedom out early, and this status can only be acquired by a *mecharu beit din*, not a *mocher atzmo* — a distinction that will be explored further. The *midrash* notes that Rabbi Hertz, in his *Chumash* commentary, observes that the final law in Hammurabi's Code addresses what to do when a slave runs away, while the first law in *Parshat Mishpatim* addresses what to do when a slave wishes to remain — a juxtaposition that reflects the Torah's aspiration that the master's household be so humane and generous that the servant might genuinely prefer to stay.

---

## Eved Ivri Kinyan

### Non-Jew Case

The Gemara asks: *eved ivri nikna be'chesef — minalan?* How do we know that an *eved ivri* can be acquired with money? The derivation begins, perhaps surprisingly, with the case of a Jew sold to a non-Jew. The *pasuk* in *Parshat Behar* discusses a situation where a Jew has been purchased by a non-Jewish resident (*ger toshav*) and his relatives wish to redeem him: *mikesef miknato* — from the money of his purchase price, implying he was acquired through money in the first place. For a non-Jew, this is not remarkable, since all acquisitions by non-Jews work through *kesef*; the non-Jewish system of *kinyanim* operates primarily on a financial-monetary basis. But this still leaves the primary case — a Jew indentured to a fellow Jew — underived.

### Amah Extension

The Gemara turns to *amah ha'ivriyah*: *ve'hifdah* — a verse in the *parsha* of *amah ha'ivriyah* speaks of redeeming her freedom proportionally (*migra'at pidyonah*), implying she was originally acquired for money. The connection to *kesef* is thus established for the *amah ha'ivriyah*. This is bolstered by the analogy to marriage: just as she may be acquired (*mekadshah be'chesef*) through money for the purpose of *kiddushin*, so too she is acquired (*maknya be'chesef*) through money for the purpose of indenture. But this still does not directly establish the rule for the adult male *eved ivri*.

### Primary Source

For the primary case of an adult male *eved ivri* sold to a fellow Jew, the Gemara turns to *Devarim*: *ki yimacher lecha achicha ha'Ivri o ha'Ivriyah* — when your Jewish brother or sister is sold to you. The verse then says *ve'avadcha sheish shanim* — he shall serve you six years. *Makish eved Ivri le'Ivriyah* — the adult male is explicitly connected in this verse to the *amah ha'ivriyah*, and the rules derived for her (including acquisition by *kesef*) are extended to him. This establishes the *mecharu beit din* case.

### Mocher Atzmo

The *mocher atzmo* case requires separate derivation. The Gemara invokes a *gezeirah shavah*: *yalif sachir sachir* — the word *sachir* (hired worker) appears in the *eved ivri* context both in *Vayikra* (where *Parshat Behar* describes *mocher atzmo*) and in *Devarim* (where the *mecharu beit din* case is described). This verbal analogy equates the two cases, extending the rules of acquisition by *kesef* to *mocher atzmo* as well.

For the view that does not employ the *gezeirah shavah* of *sachir sachir*, the Gemara offers an alternative: *amar kra ve'chi tassig* — a verse in *Parshat Behar* beginning with "if his hand reaches" adds an additional gloss to the prior discussion. *Mosif al inyan rishon, veyilmad elyon mitachton* — the upper passage (the case of a Jew sold to a non-Jew) and the lower passage (the case of a Jew sold to a fellow Jew) appear in the same broader literary unit of *Parshat Behar*, and through contextual proximity — a principle the Gemara describes as *zeh ke'ein semichut parshiyot* — one learns from the other. This is a literary rather than strictly logical principle: two adjacent paragraphs about the same subject illuminate each other. It is looser than a true *heikesh* but functions similarly, and reflects a recognition that the Torah's arrangement of material is itself an interpretive tool.

---

## Two Types Compared

### Tanna Kamma View

The Gemara presents a *braita* that enumerates the distinctions between *mocher atzmo* and *mecharu beit din* according to the *tanna kamma*. These distinctions are largely rooted in a careful reading of the *pshat* of the relevant *psukim*, and reflect a view that the two categories of *eved ivri* are genuinely different legal institutions, not merely two paths into the same status.

### Six Year Limit

*Hamocher atzmo nimkar le'shesh ve'yater al shesh* — a person who sells himself into indentured servitude may agree to a term longer than six years. Since the arrangement is essentially a voluntary contractual business deal between two parties, the Torah's six-year limit does not apply to him; he may agree to whatever terms he chooses. *Mecharu beit din eino nimkar ela le'shesh* — but a person sold by the *beit din* against his will for theft can only be sold for a maximum of six years. This is a Torah-imposed limit on an involuntary punitive transaction; the Torah specifically circumscribes it with *ve'avadcha sheish shanim*.

### Nirtza Only

*Hamocher atzmo eino nirtza* — a person who voluntarily sold himself cannot have his ear pierced to become an *eved nirtza*. The institution of *eved nirtza* — and the entire emotional and social scenario of the slave who has genuinely found a home in his master's household — applies only to the *mecharu beit din* case, where the servant was thrust into the arrangement against his will and may, over six years, come genuinely to prefer it.

### Severance Gifts

*Mocher atzmo ein ma'anikim lo* — upon release from self-imposed servitude, no severance gifts are provided. *Mecharu beit din ma'anikim lo* — upon the completion of a *beit din*-imposed term, the *adon* is obligated to provide the freed servant with provisions: produce, food, and money (*ha'anek ta'anik lo*). The rationale is clear: the *mecharu beit din* servant was someone who was so poor that he could not even repay stolen goods. At the end of his term, his debt is discharged but he has nothing. Without this endowment, he faces an immediate return to destitution with no resources to restart his life — and perhaps temptation to steal again. The Torah's mandatory severance gift addresses this directly.

### Shfachah Rights

*Mocher atzmo — ein rabo moser lo shifcha kna'anit* — if a man sold himself voluntarily, his *adon* cannot provide him with a *shifcha kna'anit* to marry and produce children who would themselves become *avadim*. *Mecharu beit din — rabo moser lo shifcha kna'anit* — in the *beit din*-imposed case, the *adon* may provide him with a *shifcha kna'anit*, and the children born of that union would be *eved kna'ani*. This is the institution of *yelid bayit* — slaves born in the household — which the Torah explicitly addresses.

The distinction reflects the different legal characters of the two arrangements: *mecharu beit din*, being closer to a form of court-imposed servitude for criminal restitution, carries the fuller range of the Torah's slave laws, including the ability of the *adon* to arrange the servant's domestic life. *Mocher atzmo*, being closer to an employment agreement entered voluntarily, does not carry those features.

### Rabbi Elazar View

*Rabbi Elazar* disagrees with all of these distinctions: *zeh ve'zeh eino nimkar ela le'shesh, zeh ve'zeh nirtza, ve'zeh ve'zeh ma'anikim lo, ve'zeh ve'zeh rabo moser lo shifcha kna'anit* — both categories are subject to a maximum six-year term, both can become *eved nirtza*, both receive severance gifts, and both may be provided with a *shifcha kna'anit*. *Rabbi Elazar* collapses the distinction between *mocher atzmo* and *mecharu beit din*, treating *eved ivri* as a single unified institution.

### Amoraim Resolution

The *Amoraim* initially assumed that the *machloket* between the *tanna kamma* and *Rabbi Elazar* reflects a disagreement about whether to apply the *gezeirah shavah* of *sachir sachir*. On this reading, the *tanna kamma* does not apply the *gezeirah shavah* and therefore sees the two *psukim* — in *Vayikra* and *Devarim* — as addressing genuinely different cases (*mocher atzmo* and *mecharu beit din* respectively), each with its own distinct rules. *Rabbi Elazar*, who does apply the *gezeirah shavah*, equates the two and sees a unified system.

*Amar Rav Tavyumi mishmeih de'Abaye*: the *Amoraim* reject this framework. In fact, both *tannaim* agree that the *gezeirah shavah* of *sachir sachir* is operative. Their dispute lies elsewhere — in the interpretation of specific verses. According to the *tanna kamma*, the verse *ve'avadcha sheish shanim* limits only *mecharu beit din*, not *mocher atzmo* (*zeh ve'lo mocher atzmo*). *Rabbi Elazar* reads *ve'avadcha lecha ve'lo le'yoresh* — the verse teaches that the *eved ivri*'s obligation runs to the specific *adon* and does not transfer to his heirs — rather than imposing the six-year limit exclusively on *mecharu beit din*.

Additional distinctions in the *braita* — such as *eved ivri* service not being inherited by the *adon*'s son — will continue to be worked through in the following session, with the Gemara tracing how each *tanna* derives or does not derive each particular rule.

---

---

# Kiddushin 15

## Three Torah Sources

### Daf Overview

The present daf picks up at the bottom of Kiddushin 14b, at the line *mai lav beha kamipalgi*. We have moved on from the *kinyan* of a woman and a *yevama* — topics bound up with marriage, though addressed in the context of *kinyanim* — and we now turn to the *kinyanim* of other persons. We are not yet dealing with the acquisition of a non-Jewish slave (*eved kna'ani*), where the person is treated more fully as property while retaining human status; that discussion lies ahead. Rather, we are concerned with the *eved ivri* and the *amah ivriyah* — the Hebrew slave — where ownership is not full ownership of the person as such, but ownership *lema'aseh yadav*, of the person's labor.

The *mishna* established that the way an *eved ivri* is acquired is through *kesef*. The *gemara* demonstrated that this applies both to the case of someone sold by the court and to someone who sells himself. Specifically: one can observe the *kesef* mechanism in the case of a daughter sold by her father (itself related to the case of *makhruhu beit din*, sold by the court, because the man stolen and sold to repay his theft), and one can transfer this to the case of *mokhher atzmo*, self-sale, through a *gezeirah shavah*. That background was established on the previous daf.

### Three Contexts

The Torah discusses the sale of Jewish slaves in essentially three locations. The opening of *Mishpatim* addresses the *amah ivriyah* — the minor girl sold by her father — and *hanimkar bignivato* — the man sold because he burgled and cannot repay. *Devarim* continues the discussion of the male slave who goes free after six years, and the various laws attending his release, including the ladening with gifts. Finally, in *Behar* at the end of *Vayikra*, within the broader framework of *shmita* and the jubilee year, the Torah discusses a person who sells himself — either to a fellow Jew or to a non-Jew.

### Categories & Link

These sources give rise to two principal categories: *makhruhu beit din*, the case in *Mishpatim* and *Devarim*, and *mokhher atzmo*, the case in *Behar*. The *gemara* asked: how do we know that the rules derived from *makhruhu beit din* — such as acquisition through *kesef* — carry over to the case of *mokhher atzmo*? The answer introduced was the *gezeirah shavah* of *sakhir sakhir*: both cases describe the slave as being like a hired hand, and this terminological link allows us to equate the two categories and transfer *halachot* between them. However, the *gemara* immediately complicated this by noting that if *sakhir sakhir* is disputed, we might need a different source. The *gemara* explored an alternative derivation based on the case of sale to a non-Jew. This is the background. The daf now focuses on the central question: do we in fact make this *sakhir sakhir* link between *mokhher atzmo* and *makhruhu beit din*?

---

## Tanna Kamma Distinc (III)tions

### Gezeirah Shavah Question

The *gemara* frames the discussion as a potential dispute over the *gezeirah shavah* of *sakhir sakhir*. The *tanna kamma* of a *baraita* cited at the end of the previous daf enumerated numerous differences between *makhruhu beit din* and *mokhher atzmo* as they appear in the *pesukim*. The *gemara* now asks: is this dispute really about whether to make the *gezeirah shavah* at all — that is, does the *tanna kamma* reject the equation of the two categories root and branch, while Rabbi Eliezer accepts it?

### Baraita Overview

The *baraita* sets out the position of the *tanna kamma* alongside that of Rabbi Eliezer. The *tanna kamma* holds that a series of *halachot* mentioned in the Torah in connection with *makhruhu beit din* do not apply to *mokhher atzmo*: the six-year limit on servitude, the rite of ear-piercing when the slave declares *ahavti et adoni*, the obligation to laden the slave with gifts upon his release, and the master's permission to give the slave a non-Jewish maidservant with whom to cohabit and produce children (the case associated with *ahavti et adoni et ishti ve'et banai*). According to the *tanna kamma*, none of these apply to *mokhher atzmo*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that they do apply, and the *gemara* initially reasons that Rabbi Eliezer must be relying on the *sakhir sakhir* equation to transfer these *halachot* from one category to the other, while the *tanna kamma* does not accept that equation.

---

## Sakhir Sakhir Debat (III)

### Tavyumi on Abaye

The *gemara* now resists this framing. Rav Tavyumi cites Abaye: in fact, everyone may fundamentally hold of the *gezeirah shavah* of *sakhir sakhir*. The *sakhir sakhir* link may well be universally accepted — indeed, it was already used to establish that acquisition by *kesef* applies to *mokhher atzmo*, and perhaps other *halachot* are derived from it as well. The dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer need not be about whether to make the equation at all. Rather, it may be about how to read specific limiting words within each of the relevant *pesukim*.

---

## Tanna Kamma Distinc (III)tio…

### Six Year Limit

The *gemara* proceeds to work through each of the four differences in turn. It begins: what is the *tanna kamma*'s reason for holding that *mokhher atzmo* is not sold for six years — that is, that the six-year limit on servitude applies only to *makhruhu beit din*? The answer: the Torah says regarding *makhruhu beit din*, *ve-avadcha sheish shanim* — "and he shall serve *you* six years." The word *avadcha* — "your slave," with the possessive suffix *cha* — functions as a limiting word (*miut*), restricting the law to this case and not extending it to *mokhher atzmo*.

---

## Sakhir Sakhir Debat (III)

### Reframing Debate

This brings the *gemara* to its reframing of the entire dispute. The disagreement between *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer is not about whether the *sakhir sakhir gezeirah shavah* exists. Both may accept the fundamental equation. The question is instead how to interpret the limiting words embedded in the relevant *pesukim*. The *tanna kamma* reads each limiting word as excluding *mokhher atzmo*; Rabbi Eliezer reads each of those same words as conveying a different legal point while leaving *mokhher atzmo* included.

---

## Tanna Kamma Distinc (III)tio…

### Eliezer on Avadcha

What does Rabbi Eliezer do with *avadcha*? He reads it not as excluding *mokhher atzmo* but as addressing the question of inheritance: *avadcha* — he serves *you*, not your heir. The *halacha* is that a slave does serve the master's son, since that is understood as a continuation of the father's ownership; but the slave would not be transferred to a brother, a father, or any other type of heir. This, Rabbi Eliezer argues, is the more natural reading of the word *avadcha* — it is restricting transmission to collateral heirs, not excluding the category of *mokhher atzmo*.

The *gemara* then addresses the fact that the word *avadcha* appears more than once in the relevant passage. The phrase *mishneh sechar sakhir avadcha sheish shanim* — "a double wage of a hired hand, he served you six years" — is invoked. The *tanna kamma* might argue this second *avadcha* is an additional limiting phrase. Rabbi Eliezer responds that this second *avadcha* is not generating a new *halacha* at all; rather, it is the Torah addressing the master, reminding him how much work the slave performed on his behalf so that the master should not begrudge giving the parting gifts. It is a moral exhortation to the master, not a legal restriction.

### Ear-Piercing Limit

The *gemara* turns to the second difference: ear-piercing (*retzi'ah*). Why does the *tanna kamma* hold that *mokhher atzmo* cannot undergo the ear-piercing ceremony? The Torah says, in the context of *makhruhu beit din*: *ve-ratza adonav et ozno ba-martzei'a* — "his master shall pierce his ear with an awl." The word *ozno* — "his ear," with the possessive suffix — is the limiting word: *ozno shelo velo ozno shel mokhher atzmo*. It applies to this case and not to the case of self-sale. Thus the *tanna kamma* holds that *retzi'ah* is restricted to *makhruhu beit din*.

### Ozno Analysis

Rabbi Eliezer, however, reads *ozno* not as a limiting word excluding *mokhher atzmo* but as the source for a *gezeirah shavah* — specifically, the link between the ear mentioned here and the ear mentioned in the context of the *metzora*, where the ritual is performed on the right ear. Rabbi Eliezer taught in a *baraita*: how do we know that the ear-piercing of the slave is performed on the right ear? Because it says here *ozen* and it says there (by the *metzora*) *ozen*, and just as there it is the right ear, so too here it is the right ear. This is why the Torah wrote *ozen* — to generate the *gezeirah shavah*.

This raises an obvious objection: if the *gezeirah shavah* is derived from the word *ozen* (without the suffix), then the limiting function was supposed to be carried by *ozno* (with the suffix *vav*). The *gemara* addresses this: if that were so, the Torah could simply have written *ozen* — why write *ozno*? The additional letter tells us something, and the *tanna kamma* says it excludes *mokhher atzmo*.

Rabbi Eliezer would reply that *ozno* is needed for a different exclusion: *ozno velo oznah* — his ear and not her ear, meaning the rite applies to the male *eved ivri* sold by *beit din* and not to the *amah ivriyah* sold by her father. The *tanna kamma* can extract the exclusion of the *amah* from elsewhere — from *v'im yomar ha'eved*, where the word *eved* (masculine) already excludes the female — and so the *vav* of *ozno* is free to exclude *mokhher atzmo*. Alternatively, the *tanna kamma* derives "while he is still a slave" from *eved*, and derives "not the *amah*" from *ha'eved* (the definite article), leaving *ozno* to exclude *mokhher atzmo*. The back-and-forth turns on precisely how many exclusions each word can carry and which readings of the text are considered operative.

### Gifting Limited

The *gemara* arrives at the third difference: the obligation to laden the slave with gifts (*ha'aneik ta'anik lo*) upon his release. What is the *tanna kamma*'s reason for holding that this does not apply to *mokhher atzmo*? The Torah says by *makhruhu beit din*: *ha'aneik ta'anik lo* — "you shall surely laden him." The word *lo* — "him" — is a limiting word: *lo velo le-mokhher atzmo*. It applies to this one and not to the person who sold himself.

This is a striking observation: the man sold by *beit din* was a *ganav*, a thief; yet he receives the parting gifts, while the person who chose to sell himself does not. The conceptual distinction behind this collection of differences is worth pausing on, though the *gemara* does not spell it out here.

### Wages Debate

The *gemara* then raises a complication with a different reading of *lo*. One might suggest that *lo* comes not to exclude *mokhher atzmo* but to exclude the heirs: *lo velo leyorshav* — "to him and not to his heirs." If the master dies before giving the gifts, his estate has no obligation; the gifts are personal to the slave. But the *gemara* challenges this: the Torah itself describes the slave as a *sakhir*, a hired hand — and wages owed to a hired hand do pass to his heirs. The *gemara* reasons: just as a worker's wages go to his heirs, so too here, *mah sakhir ploni leyorshav af hai ploni leyorshav*. The *gemara* is thus unwilling to read *lo* as excluding the heirs, since the Torah's own framing of the slave's work as hired labor would require the gifts to be treated as wages and to devolve to the heirs.

Interestingly, the Gra excises this entire passage. Rashi has it, Tosafot has it, but the Gra evidently holds that the gifts are not wages the slave has earned and to which he is entitled; they are a special Torah-mandated award. Therefore, they would not pass to the heirs. But our *gemara* insists: the Torah says the slave worked for you like a hired hand, he worked double, and therefore these gifts are treated as wages that would pass to the heirs.

### Lo Creditor Reading

The *gemara* therefore proposes a different understanding of *lo*: *lo velo le-ba'al chovo* — "to him and not to his creditor." Unsurprisingly, a man in this situation likely has other creditors. One might have thought — given that we generally hold like Rabbi Natan — that a creditor of the slave could approach the master directly and demand that the gifts be transferred straight to him, bypassing the slave. As the *braita* of Rabbi Natan teaches: if Reuven owes Shimon a hundred, and Shimon owes Levi a hundred, Levi can go directly to Reuven and demand payment — and the verse *venatan la'asher asham lo* ("and he shall give it to the one to whom he is liable") supports this. Tosafot has an extended discussion about whether we *pasken* that way.

The *gemara* says *lo* comes to tell us: in this case, the creditor cannot make that demand. The gifts must pass through the slave's own hands. There is a significance to the act of giving and receiving these gifts — *lo*, specifically to him — and the creditor cannot short-circuit that by seizing them from the master directly.

Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, uses *lo* to address this creditor problem rather than to exclude *mokhher atzmo*. He thereby applies the parting gift obligation to *mokhher atzmo* as well. The *tanna kamma*, who uses *lo* to exclude *mokhher atzmo*, must explain differently why the creditor cannot intercept: he simply does not hold of Rabbi Natan's principle altogether — *be'alma nami lo sevira lan ke-Rabbi Natan* — and therefore needs no exclusion.

### Maidservant Limit

The fourth and final difference: the master's ability to give the slave a non-Jewish maidservant (*shifcha kena'anit*) with whom to cohabit and produce children. The Torah says by *makhruhu beit din*: *im adonav yiten lo isha* — "if his master gives *him* a wife." Again the word *lo* is the limiting word: *lo velo le-mokhher atzmo*. The master can do this only in the case of *makhruhu beit din*.

### Double Wage & Force

Rabbi Eliezer reads *lo* here differently: *lo be'al korcho* — even against his will. That is, *lo* is not excluding *mokhher atzmo*; it is telling us that the master can compel the slave to cohabit with the maidservant even if he is unwilling. This is obviously morally troubling from any contemporary vantage point, but the *gemara* proceeds with the analysis.

How does Rabbi Eliezer know the master can compel this? From a different *pasuk*, as a *braita* teaches: *ki mishneh sechar sakhir avadcha sheish shanim* — "for a double wage of a hired hand, he served you six years." What does "double wage" mean? A regular hired hand works only during the day; an *eved ivri* works both day and night, thus performing a double wage's worth of labor. Does this literally mean the slave works around the clock? The *gemara* itself rejects this: the Torah says *ki tov lo imach* — that it should be good for him in your household, including equal provisions and housing. Rabbi Yitzchak therefore explains: working "at night" means the slave works for the master's benefit at night through cohabiting with the maidservant to produce slave children for the master's household. That is the "night work" — and it is this *pasuk* that tells Rabbi Eliezer you may compel him (*be'al korcho*).

The *tanna kamma* responds: if that were the only source, I would have read *mishneh sechar sakhir* as establishing only that the cohabitation can occur — but perhaps only if the slave is willing. The word *lo* therefore comes to tell you that it can be done even against his will. And since *lo* carries that legal force, it cannot simultaneously serve to exclude *mokhher atzmo*.

Tosafot raises the question: if *lo* tells us it can be done against his will, what is *mishneh sechar sakhir* teaching? Tosafot answers — in parallel to what was said earlier about *hartza'at adon* — that it is not generating a new *halacha* but rather reminding the master of the slave's substantial work, so that the master does not begrudge giving the parting gifts. According to the *tanna kamma*, by contrast, *mishneh sechar sakhir* does establish the permissibility of compelled cohabitation, and *lo* restricts the entire provision to *makhruhu beit din*.

---

## Sakhir Sakhir Debat (III)e…

### Fundamental Link

Having worked through all four differences, the *gemara* now states its conclusion explicitly: perhaps everyone accepts the *sakhir sakhir gezeirah shavah* as a matter of fundamental principle. The differences between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer are not about whether the two categories are linked, but about how to read the specific limiting words in each relevant *pasuk*. Each difference reflects a disagreement over whether a given word (*avadcha*, *ozno*, *lo*) is excluding *mokhher atzmo* or conveying some other legal or homiletical point.

If that is so, then the earlier framing of the dispute — that the *tanna kamma* does not make *sakhir sakhir* and Rabbi Eliezer does — is not sustained. The *gemara* therefore asks: who, then, is the *tanna* who fundamentally does not hold of the *sakhir sakhir gezeirah shavah*?

---

## Elazar ben Yaakov

### V'shav Argument

The *gemara* answers: it is the *tanna* of the following *braita*. The verse *veshav el mishpachto ve'el achuzat avotav yashuv* — "and he shall return to his family and to his ancestral inheritance he shall return" — appears in *Vayikra* in the section dealing with *mokhher atzmo* and speaks of his going free at the *yovel*. Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov asks: to which case does this verse refer? If it refers to *mokhher atzmo*, that is already the subject of the entire *parsha* — no further verse is needed. If it refers to the *nirtza*, the slave who had his ear pierced and chose permanent servitude, that too is already covered elsewhere (as the *gemara* will explain). The verse must therefore be speaking of *makhruhu beit din* — a person sold by *beit din* who has served two or three years (not exactly two or three, but prior to completing his term) before the *yovel* arrives and frees him.

From this derivation — the fact that a separate verse is needed to include *makhruhu beit din* in the *yovel* freedom — the *gemara* infers that Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov does not hold of the *sakhir sakhir gezeirah shavah*. If he did, the fundamental equation of the two categories would have already implied that *makhruhu beit din* is freed at *yovel*, since *mokhher atzmo* is. The very need for an independent verse to achieve that inclusion shows that for Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, the categories are not fundamentally linked.

### Yovel Exception

The *gemara* once again pushes back. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says: one can accept *sakhir sakhir* and still require an additional verse for the *yovel* case. Even if we equate the categories in principle, one might have thought that *makhruhu beit din* — sold because he committed an *aveira*, because he was a *ganav* — should not benefit from the *yovel* release. The *yovel* provides a kind of extraordinary freedom that breaks the normal schedule of servitude; perhaps a person who landed in servitude through criminal behavior should be penalized and not receive this benefit. *Hu de-avid issura, eima nikansei.* Therefore, even with a *sakhir sakhir* link, an additional verse (*veshavtem ish el achuzato*) is needed to tell us that *makhruhu beit din* does indeed go free at *yovel*.

### Two V'shavtem

The *gemara* then traces the source for the *nirtza*'s inclusion in *yovel* freedom. A *baraita* is cited: *veshavtem ish el achuzato ve-ish el mishpachto tashuvu* — "and you shall return, each man to his inheritance, and each man to his family you shall return." This is a second *veshavtem* verse, distinct from the first. Applying the same logic as before: if it speaks of *mokhher atzmo*, that is already clear from the entire *parsha*. If it speaks of *makhruhu beit din*, that was already covered by the first *veshavtem* verse. Therefore this verse must be addressing the *nirtza* — the slave who chose to remain after his six years were up and had his ear pierced — specifying that even he goes free at the *yovel*, if the *yovel* arrives two or three years (loosely speaking) into his extended servitude.

The word *ish* in this second verse is what signals the *nirtza*: *eizeh davar she-noheg be-ish ve-eino noheg be-isha* — what is a *halacha* that applies to a man and not to a woman in the context of slaves? It is *retzi'ah*, ear-piercing. We already established that *retzi'ah* applies only to the male. The verse therefore is addressing the *nirtza*, including him in *yovel* freedom.

### Necessity Argument

The *gemara* establishes that both verses are necessary. It was necessary to write the inclusion of *makhruhu beit din* because one might have said: a person sold by *beit din* did not choose this situation and is presumably still seeking his freedom; he may not have had the opportunity to go free, and the *yovel* ought to release him. But perhaps the *nirtza* is different — he chose to remain, he declared *ahavti et adoni*, and perhaps he should not be freed at *yovel* as a kind of penalty for forgoing his earlier freedom. Therefore we needed a verse to include the *nirtza*.

Conversely, it was necessary to write the inclusion of the *nirtza* because one might have said: a person sold by *beit din* who has not yet completed even the basic six-year term has not "served out" his time. Perhaps it would be unfair to the master for *yovel* to free him before he has provided the full labor for which the master acquired him. Therefore we needed a verse to include *makhruhu beit din* as well. *Tzricha.*

### Reconciliation

The two *veshavtem* verses thus divide their labor: one includes *makhruhu beit din*, one includes *nirtza*. Each is necessary precisely because there is an independent reason to have excluded the case it covers.

### L'olam Resolution

The *gemara* closes this section by addressing the apparent contradiction between *va-avado le'olam* — "he shall serve him forever" — and the *veshavtem* verse that grants the *nirtza* freedom at *yovel*. If we had only *le'olam*, we would understand it literally: permanent servitude, no *yovel* release. But *veshavtem* overrides this. Conversely, if we had only *veshavtem* telling us the *nirtza* goes free, without *le'olam*, we would not know the duration of his servitude between the piercing and the *yovel*. We might have thought: just as the initial servitude was six years, so too the post-piercing servitude would be six years, and at the end of that additional six years he would go free regardless of *yovel*. *Le'olam* therefore tells us: absent *yovel*, he works indefinitely — *olamo shel yovel*, "forever" in the *yovel* context means until the next *yovel*. Both verses are thus required: *le'olam* to tell us there is no fixed endpoint short of *yovel*, and *veshavtem* to tell us that *yovel* does in fact release him.

---

## Rabbi Non-Jew Case

### Rabbi's Position

At the very end of 15a, the *gemara* finally identifies a *tanna* who clearly does not hold of the *sakhir sakhir* equation: it is Rabbi (Judah the Prince). A *braita* at the top of 15b cites the verse *ve-im lo yiga'el ba-eleh* — "and if he is not redeemed through these" — in the context of someone who has sold himself to a non-Jew. Rabbi states: *ba-eleh hu niga'el ve-eino niga'el be-sheish* — through these means (i.e., redemption by relatives) he may be redeemed, but his servitude to the non-Jew does not terminate automatically at the end of six years. This is surprising: one would think that a non-Jew should have *less* of a claim over a Hebrew slave than a Jewish master, not more. Yet Rabbi reads the verse as teaching that the six-year release that applies to self-sale to a Jew does not apply to self-sale to a non-Jew.

### Kal Vachomer

Rabbi supports this with a *kal va-chomer*. When a Jew sells himself to another Jew, there is no obligation on relatives to redeem him (*ge'ulat kerovim* does not apply), and yet his servitude ends after six years. By a *kal va-chomer*, when a Jew sells himself to a non-Jew — where *ge'ulat kerovim* does apply (the relatives have a *mitzvah* to redeem him and, provided the non-Jew is subject to Jewish authority, can compel the transaction), and where in addition the slave has the right *megara pidyono ve-yotzei*, to reduce his outstanding term and go free — should he not certainly be freed after six years? The argument is compelling: greater protections exist in the case of sale to a non-Jew, so surely the six-year rule should apply there too. Nevertheless, Rabbi says: *talmud lomar ba-eleh, ba-eleh hu niga'el ve-eino niga'el be-sheish* — the verse teaches that his only avenue for release is redemption through relatives, not the passage of six years.

### Rav Nachman Counter

The *gemara* again applies the now-familiar move: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says that even Rabbi could in principle hold of the *sakhir sakhir gezeirah shavah* between *mokhher atzmo* and *makhruhu beit din*. The reason Rabbi does not make the *kal va-chomer* to extend the six-year release to sale-to-a-non-Jew is not that he rejects the fundamental equation of the two main categories — it is that a verse explicitly creates an exception for this specific case.

### Yigalenu Limit

The *gemara* identifies that verse: *yigalenu*, "one shall redeem him." This word restricts the applicability of *ge'ulat kerovim* to the case of sale to a non-Jew and excludes it from the case of self-sale to a Jew. If *sakhir sakhir* fundamentally equates self-sale to a Jew and sale by *beit din*, and if *ge'ulat kerovim* applied to self-sale to a Jew just as it applies to sale to a non-Jew, then why did Rabbi argue in his *kal va-chomer* that there is no *ge'ulat kerovim* by sale to a Jew? Because *yigalenu* restricts the redemption-by-relatives provision specifically to the non-Jew case and excludes self-sale to a Jew. Rabbi thus uses *ba-eleh* to exclude the six-year release in the non-Jew case, and *yigalenu* to exclude *ge'ulat kerovim* from the Jew case — and he can hold *sakhir sakhir* throughout.

---

## Yossi & Akiva

### Braita Intro

Having examined Rabbi's position, the *gemara* asks: who is the *tanna* who disagrees with Rabbi — that is, who holds that a person sold to a non-Jew *does* go free after six years? The answer: Rabbi Yossi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva. A *braita* is cited presenting their dispute.

### Yossi View

Rabbi Yossi HaGlili holds: *ba-eleh l'shichrur* — when it is the relatives who redeem the slave from the non-Jew, the slave goes free. *Beshar kol adam l'shibbud* — but when some other person (not a relative) redeems him, the slave does not go free. The stranger can force the non-Jewish master to sell the slave (compel the transaction, since the non-Jew is under Jewish authority), but the redeemed slave then must work for this stranger-redeemer — he has effectively been sold to a new Jewish master — until the six-year term or *yovel*. The value of this is still real: the slave is out of the hands of a non-Jew. But he does not immediately regain his freedom.

### Akiva View

Rabbi Akiva holds the mirror image: *ba-eleh l'shibbud* — when it is the relatives who redeem him, the slave must work for them. *Beshar kol adam l'shichrur* — but when a stranger redeems him, he goes free immediately. This is counterintuitive: relatives, who have a *mitzvah* to redeem and can compel the non-Jew, nevertheless end up holding the slave in servitude, while a stranger who redeems him out of pure goodwill grants him freedom? The logic will emerge from the *gemara*'s discussion of *svara*.

### Three Geulahs

The *gemara* traces how the dispute arises from the text. The relevant passage contains three distinct categories of redemption: *o dodo o ven dodo yigalenu* — the uncle or cousin redeems him; this is *ge'ulat kerovim*. *O hisiga yado* — or his own hand reaches the means; this is *ge'ulat atzmo*, self-redemption. *Ve-nig'al* — and he shall be redeemed; this functions as a third category, *ge'ulat acherim*, redemption by others. The fact that this third grammatical form appears in the verse establishes that a stranger may compel the redemption and the non-Jew must accept it.

### Yossi Reasoning

With *ge'ulat atzmo* — self-redemption — positioned in the middle between the two, the question becomes: to which of the flanking categories is *ge'ulat atzmo* connected, and which connection determines who goes free? Rabbi Yossi HaGlili holds *mikra nidrash lefanav* — the verse is interpreted by reference to what precedes it. The earlier category, *ge'ulat kerovim*, is linked to *ge'ulat atzmo*. Just as when one redeems oneself one goes free, so too when relatives redeem: *mah ge'ulat atzmo le-shichrur af ge'ulat kerovim le-shichrur*. Others (*ge'ulat acherim*), not linked to *ge'ulat atzmo*, result in servitude.

### Akiva Reasoning

Rabbi Akiva holds *mikra nidrash le-acharav* — the verse is interpreted by reference to what follows it. The later category, *ge'ulat acherim*, is linked to *ge'ulat atzmo*. Just as self-redemption leads to freedom, so too redemption by others: *mah ge'ulat atzmo le-shichrur af ge'ulat acherim le-shichrur*. Relatives (*ge'ulat kerovim*), not linked to *ge'ulat atzmo*, result in servitude.

### Ba'eleh Limiting

The *gemara* asks: if the entire debate is about which flanking category is linked to *ge'ulat atzmo*, why do they invoke the word *ba-eleh* at all? The *gemara* explains: without *ba-eleh*, one might say the verse is read in both directions — both the earlier and later categories are linked to *ge'ulat atzmo*. Then *all* forms of redemption would result in freedom. *Ba-eleh* tells us this is not so — only some of the categories enjoy the same status as *ge'ulat atzmo*. The question then is which ones, and the answer is not derivable from *ba-eleh* itself.

### Svara Debate

This leads to the *gemara*'s conclusion: the debate between Rabbi Yossi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva is ultimately grounded in *svara* — in reasoning and logic — rather than in a purely textual disagreement about the direction of interpretation. *Ba-eleh* establishes that not all categories are equal, and the reading direction (*lefanav* or *le-acharav*) may reflect the underlying *svara* rather than generating it.

### Yossi Svara

Rabbi Yossi HaGlili's *svara*: it makes sense that redemption by others results in servitude. *De-i amrat le-shichrur havay memna ve-lo parki* — if you say that a stranger's redemption leads to freedom, then strangers will simply not bother redeeming the slave. Strangers have no *mitzvah* to redeem and no self-interest in doing so; offering them the "reward" of enslaving the redeemed person to themselves gives them an incentive to act and at least gets the slave out of non-Jewish hands. The relatives, who have an obligation, will redeem — and the slave goes free. Thus the system works: relatives are incentivized by obligation, others by self-interest, and the slave ultimately benefits.

### Akiva Svara

Rabbi Akiva's *svara*: it makes sense that redemption by relatives results in servitude. *De-i amrat le-shichrur kol yoma ve-yoma azil u-mezabin nafsheh* — if relatives' redemption leads to freedom, and relatives are obligated to redeem, then a penniless person with wealthy relatives would repeatedly sell himself to a non-Jew and pocket the sale price, knowing his relatives are obligated to free him at their expense. This is precisely the kind of abuse of system that must be prevented: like the famous example of offering bounties for pests and thereby incentivizing people to breed the very pests one seeks to eliminate. Servitude to relatives therefore deters the abuse. Strangers, by contrast, have no obligation — their redemption is wholly voluntary and unexpected — so if one chooses to act out of pure generosity and the slave goes free, there is no systemic incentive for abuse.

---

## Rabbi & Chachamim

### R. Chiya Quote

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: the dispute described above — between one view that some redeemers free the slave and others subject him to servitude — is the position of Rabbi Yossi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva. But there is a third view.

### Chachamim View

The Chachamim hold *hakol le-shichrur* — in all cases, whether relatives or strangers redeem the slave, the result is freedom. There is no distinction between categories of redeemer; every redemption from the non-Jew results in the slave going free.

### Rabbi Position

The Chachamim in this context is Rabbi himself — not the same position he held in the earlier *braita* regarding the six-year release, but specifically on this question of who is *Chachamim* here. Rabbi does not use *ba-eleh* as a limiting word in the context of *ge'ulat kerovim* versus *ge'ulat acherim*. He uses *ba-eleh* entirely for his earlier teaching — that servitude to a non-Jew does not end at six years. Therefore the verse about all three categories (*ge'ulat kerovim*, *ge'ulat atzmo*, *ge'ulat acherim*) is read in both directions, both forward and backward, meaning *all* forms of redemption are equated with self-redemption — and all result in freedom. *Umikra nidrash bein lefanav bein le-acharav.*

### V'yatza Yovel

What does Rabbi then do with the verse *ve-yatza bi-shnat ha-yovel* — "he shall go free in the year of the jubilee"? This verse, which speaks of *yovel* freedom for the slave sold to a non-Jew, is applied by Rabbi to a specific circumstance: a non-Jew who is under Jewish control (*she-yeshno tachat yadecha*). Because such a non-Jew is subject to our authority, one might think we would exercise that authority to free the slave even before *yovel* — perhaps immediately. The verse therefore tells us: even in that case, we act within the law. We do not abuse our position of power; we wait for *yovel*. Alternatively, one might ask whether the *yovel* release applies even to a non-Jew *not* under our control — but that question answers itself: we cannot impose our laws on someone beyond our reach. The verse therefore addresses only the case where the non-Jew is within our authority, and its teaching is that we nonetheless act with restraint and do not deploy that authority to override the legal framework.

---

---

# Kiddushin 16

## Kinyanim Overview

### Progression Overview

Today's daf is 16 and we have moved on from the discussion of how a woman is acquired or acquires herself, and how a *yevama* represents a similar type of scenario. We now turn to other acquisitions, and this *perek* is really about *kinyanim* broadly. The progression moves in stages: we begin with the *kinyan* of a woman through marriage, which, as we have discussed, may have evolved from something more purely *kinyan*-based to something more centered on personal status. From there we turn to the *kinyan* related to a Jewish slave, the *eved Ivri*, and then we will proceed to the *eved Kena'ani*, and eventually to animals and inanimate objects.

### Eved Ivri Concept

The *kinyan* of a woman through marriage is followed by the *kinyan* of the *eved Ivri*, which is emphatically not an ownership of the person as property, but rather an ownership of the rights to the person's labor — *ma'asei yedeihem*. The *eved Kena'ani*, by contrast, does involve ownership of the person as property, though even there the Torah's innovation is that the slave retains recognition as a human being — a point not to be taken for granted in the ancient world. The *eved Ivri* thus occupies a middle position: the master acquires the right to compel labor, but does not acquire the person as an object of property.

---

## Shtar Kinyan Source

### Mishna Teaching

The *Mishna* already established *kesef* as a mode of acquiring an *eved Ivri*, and the Gemara derived the source for that. We now turn to the second mode: *shtar*. The Gemara on 16a, five lines from the top, asks: *uv'shtar — minalan?* Where do we derive that an *eved Ivri* or *amah Ivriyah* can be acquired through a document?

*Amar Ulla amar kra: im acheres yikach lo* — the verse, speaking of the *amah Ivriyah* whose master takes an additional wife, says that the master may not diminish the first wife's *she'era kesuta ve'onata*, the conjugal and material obligations due to her. The Gemara uses this verse to make a comparison: *hekisha hakatuv le'acheres* — the Torah links the original acquisition of the girl as a slave to the subsequent taking of a wife. Just as a wife can be acquired through a *shtar* — *mah acheres maknya b'shtar* — so too an *amah Ivriyah* is acquired through a *shtar* — *af amah Ivriyah maknya b'shtar*.

### Marriage vs Slave

This analogy immediately raises a question. The comparison is between acquiring an *amah Ivriyah* and acquiring a wife through *kiddushin*. But who writes the *shtar*? This is not a trivial matter. Consider the scenario: I am purchasing a young girl from her father. Do I write a *shtar* saying *bitcha knuyah li* — your daughter is acquired by me — and hand it to the father? Or does the father write *biti mechura lach* — my daughter is sold to you — and give it to me?

By *kinyan karka*, the seller writes the *shtar*. The logic is clear: a *shtar* can serve as proof of a transaction, and the purchaser is the one who needs that proof. So when land is sold, the seller writes *sadi mechura lach*. By contrast, in *kiddushin*, it is the husband who writes the document — *harei at mekudeshet li*, or in the context of the father's daughter, *harei bitcha mekudeshet li*.

### Two Shtar Models

There are thus two distinct models. The first is the *shtar mechira* model, where the seller writes the document, as by the sale of land. The second is the *shtar kiddushin* model, where the acquirer writes it. These are not merely formal differences — they reflect two fundamentally different conceptions of what the transaction is. If the *amah Ivriyah* acquisition is modeled on *kiddushei ishah*, it should be the master writing the *shtar*. If it is modeled on the sale of property, it should be the father writing it.

The relevance of this distinction to the derivation is direct: the verse *im acheres yikach lo* compares the sale of the daughter to the taking of a wife through *kiddushin*. This comparison is compelling only if the same party writes the *shtar* in both cases — namely, the acquirer. If the father writes the *shtar*, the analogy to *kiddushin* collapses, and the basis for deriving *kinyan shtar* from *im acheres yikach lo* disappears entirely.

### Rav Huna vs Chisda

The Gemara records a dispute on precisely this point. *Shtar amah Ivriyah — mi kotvo?* Rav Huna says: *adon kotvo*, the master writes it. Rav Chisda says: *av kotvo*, the father writes it.

According to Rav Huna, who holds that the master writes the *shtar*, the comparison to *kiddushei ishah* is apt and the derivation works cleanly. According to Rav Chisda, who holds that the father writes it — reflecting the property-sale model — the derivation from *im acheres yikach lo* cannot stand. A different source must be found. It is to supply that alternative source that Rav Acha bar Yaakov introduces the verse *lo tetzei k'tzeit ha'avadim*.

---

## Lo Tetzei Derivation

### Lo Tetzei Meaning

*Lo tetzei k'tzeit ha'avadim* — she shall not go free like slaves go free. The plain sense of this verse, as Chazal understand it, is that a Jewish slave — whether male or female — does not go free when the master knocks out an eye or destroys a limb, as an *eved Kena'ani* does. For an *eved Kena'ani*, loss of an eye or a tooth triggers freedom. For an *eved Ivri*, it does not.

This may seem unjust, but there is an important halakhic consideration. If the master knocks out the eye of a Jewish slave, the slave does not go free, but the master does owe substantial monetary compensation for the injury. The slave may then use that compensation to purchase their own freedom.
