If a thief stole something worth a thousand and has sufficient assets to pay back the principal (*keren*) but not the double payment (*kefel*), he is not sold into slavery to cover the outstanding penalty. Further: *begneivato v'lo b'zimamo* — he is sold for his own theft, but not if he is an *ed zomem*, a conspiring witness who testified that someone else owed a penalty and was shown to have lied. Even though the *ed zomem* must pay *ka'asher zamam la'asot l'achiv* — whatever he plotted to do to his fellow — being sold into slavery does not apply to him. And crucially: *keivan shenimkar pa'am achat shuv i ata rashai l'mokhro* — once he has been sold one time for a particular theft, he cannot be sold again. The singular *begneivato* implies a single act of being sold.

So the *eved ivri* is also subject to a form of non-resale restriction, at least in the context of *genevah*. How does this square with the *baraita*'s implication that an *eved ivri* can be resold while an *amah ivriyah* cannot?

Rava resolves this: *lo kashya, kan b'gneivah achat, kan b'shtei gneivot* — there is no contradiction; the two cases are different. The distinction concerns whether we are speaking of one *gneivah* or two. Here Tosafot and Rashi read the resolution in opposite directions, and the difference tracks a textual variant in the Gemara.

According to Tosafot's reading: for a *single* act of theft (*gneivah achat*), if the value of the thief's service does not cover the full amount owed, he can be sold multiple times — sold, completes his term, is sold again — until the debt is paid off. This is consistent with the singular *begneivato*: it is one *gneivah*, and he keeps being sold for that one act. However, for a *second* act of theft — a separate *gneivah* — he cannot be sold. He has already entered the condition of *eved ivri* once, and that experience and its lessons are held to be sufficient; a new theft does not reset his eligibility for a second enslavement.

Rashi reads it in precisely the reverse: for one *gneivah*, even a large one, he can only be sold once — one sale per act of theft. But for each separate *gneivah* from a separate party, he can be sold once per offense.

Abaye responds to Rava's formulation by noting that the word *begneivato* in the verse actually suggests multiple possible readings and that the plain language implies a broad scope. Abaye therefore reformulates the resolution differently: *kan b'adam echad, kan b'shnei bnei adam* — the distinction is not between one *gneivah* and two, but between whether the theft was from one person or from two different people. According to Tosafot's reading of Abaye's position, if someone steals once or multiple times from a single person, it is all treated as a single category of *gneivah* from that person, and the person may be sold — and resold — for that entire category. But if he has stolen from a second, different person, he cannot be sold for that second offense. Rashi reads Abaye's resolution in the opposite direction.

A further *baraita* reinforces the analysis with concrete cases. If one stole something worth a thousand and is himself worth five hundred, he can be sold and sold again (*nimkar vechozer venimkar*) until the debt is covered — since for one *gneivah* multiple sales are permitted. If one stole something worth five hundred and is himself worth a thousand, *eino nimkar klal* — he is not sold at all. It would be unjust to compel someone to serve six years of slavery when the market value of that service exceeds the debt; there is no mechanism for partial terms of servitude. One is either sold for the full six years or not sold at all.

The Gra's variant text (*girsa*) reads *nimkar v'eino chozer venimkar* — sold but not resold — which is the foundation for Rashi's contrary reading. The analysis presented here follows the standard text as Tosafot reads it.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer takes an even more restrictive position, one that Rava acknowledges as logically compelling even if it leads to a near-total elimination of the practice. Rabbi Eliezer says: *im haya gneivo keneged mimkaro nimkar* — the thief is only sold into slavery if the value of his six-year service is *exactly* equal to the value of what he stole. If the *gneivah* is worth more than his service, he is not sold (everyone agrees on this). But if his service is worth more than the *gneivah*, Rabbi Eliezer also says he is not sold.

The logical basis for Rabbi Eliezer's position, as Rava articulates it, is entirely parallel to the reasoning underlying the universally agreed-upon case. Everyone agrees that if the thief is worth a thousand and the theft was worth five hundred, he is not sold — because the verse says *v'nimkar bignevato*, "he is sold *for* his theft," and the Gemara reads this as requiring that the entirety of the sale value goes toward paying off the theft. If only half his sale value goes to the theft, that is not selling him *for* his theft in the required sense. By precisely the same logic, Rabbi Eliezer argues, if the theft is worth a thousand but his service is only worth five hundred, he is not sold — because again, he would be sold for only half his theft. Selling him would not pay off the *gneivah* in full, and the verse requires that being sold suffice to discharge the debt. Rava comments: *beha zachinhu Rabbi Eliezer lerabbanan* — Rabbi Eliezer's logic outshines the rabbis here, in the sense that the textual reasoning is fully consistent and compelling, even though in practice it means that an *eved ivri* sold for *genevah* becomes an almost theoretical category.

### Forced Redemption

Returning to the *baraita*'s final clause — *umifdin otah al karcho*, that the *amah ivriyah* is redeemed against someone's will — Rava initially understands this as meaning against the will of the *master*: one can compel the master to accept the return of the purchase price and release her. But Abaye rejects this reading. Forcing back a redemption against the master's will — returning his money and recovering the slave — is already applicable to an *eved ivri* through the mechanism of *giron kesef*. There is nothing distinctive about the *amah ivriyah* in that respect. Furthermore, Abaye notes, if it means forcing the master to accept an IOU rather than actual payment, that too is untenable: *nakit marganita beyadei, nehavi lei chaspa?* — the master is holding a pearl in his hand; are we going to force him to accept a pottery shard? The father who sold his daughter presumably had no money to begin with; any IOU he could offer would be essentially worthless.

Abaye therefore reinterprets: *be'al korcho de'av* — the forced redemption is against the will of the *father*. If the father has available funds, he can be compelled to use them to redeem his daughter from slavery. The motivation is *mishum pgam mishpacha* — the concern for family honor. Having a daughter in servitude reflects badly on the entire family, and the relatives — or the father himself, per Rashi — can be legally coerced to undo it.

The Gemara then raises an objection: if this is the reasoning, why not similarly coerce the family to redeem a male *eved ivri* who sold himself? The answer: *hadar azil umazvin nafshieh* — he would simply turn around and sell himself again. Forcing a buyback accomplishes nothing if the person can immediately repeat the act.

The same objection seems to apply to the *amah ivriyah*: if the father is forced to redeem her, could he not immediately resell her? This is precisely where the earlier ruling becomes operative. The Gemara answers: *katani einah nimkeres ushenit* — we have already established that an *amah ivriyah* cannot be resold. Therefore, compelling the father to redeem his daughter is a meaningful and lasting act: once he buys her back, he cannot sell her again, and the family honor is permanently restored. By contrast, there is no corresponding restriction preventing an *eved ivri* from reselling himself, so forcing a redemption of a male slave would accomplish nothing permanent.

Tosafot sharpens this by disagreeing with Rashi about *who* is being compelled. Tosafot understands the compulsion as being directed not at the father but at the other family members — along the lines of the biblical provision that a kinsman may redeem a sold relative (*ben dodo o dodo yigalenu*). The family members are compelled to act for the sake of communal honor. The concern about the father simply pocketing the proceeds and reselling his daughter does not arise, because the resale is prohibited.

This position, the Gemara notes, is the view of Rabbi Shimon — which will be elaborated in the discussion of who may be resold and under what conditions.

---

## Selling Daughter Rules

### Father's Resale Rights

A *baraita* now addresses the father's authority to sell his daughter and the limits on that authority. The baseline rule is: *mocher adam et bito le'ishut veshoneh* — a man may betroth his daughter (sell her for purposes of *ishut*, marriage) and repeat the act. How is this possible? As long as the daughter remains a minor (*ketanah*) and has not yet entered *nisuin* (full marriage), she remains under her father's authority. If she was betrothed (*kiddushin* was performed) but the betrothal was dissolved through divorce or death of the betrothed before *nisuin*, she returns entirely to her father's control and he may betroth her again. Thus multiple betrothals are possible while she remains a minor.

The *baraita* further states: *leshifchuto veshoneh* — he may also sell her as a slave and repeat this. If she was sold and then went free — for example, through the completion of six years, by *yovel*, or through *misas ha'adon* — but she is still a minor (*ketanah*), the father may sell her again. Similarly: *le'ishut achar shifchut* — he may also arrange her marriage after she has been a slave. All of these are permitted.

The one explicit prohibition in this *baraita* is: *lo leshifchut achar ishut* — he may not sell her as a slave after she has already been in a state of marriage (*ishut*). Going from the status of a wife to the status of a slave represents a profound diminution of standing, and the Torah prohibits this path.

### First Dispute Source

This is the position of the *tanna kamma*. The Gemara will derive it from the verse *lo yimshol l'mochrah b'vigdo bah* — "he shall not have authority to sell her in her betrayal" (or "in his garment over her") — a phrase whose precise reading lies at the heart of the tannaic dispute.

According to the *tanna kamma* (identified as Rabbi Akiva in the subsequent analysis), the word *bigdo* is read as *beged* — garment — which, in the idiomatic language of marriage (as in the passage in Megillat Rut where spreading one's cloak symbolizes marriage), refers to the act of marriage itself. The verse is thus saying: once he has spread his cloak over her — once she has been in a state of *ishut* — he may no longer sell her. This produces the prohibition of *shifchut achar ishut*.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon extends the prohibition: *keshem she'ein adam mocher et bito l'shifchah achar ishus, kach ein mocher et bito l'shifchah achar shifchah* — just as one may not sell a daughter as a slave after she has been in a state of marriage, so too one may not sell her as a slave after she has already been in a prior state of slavery. For Rabbi Shimon, once the daughter has undergone either *ishut* or *shifchut*, a subsequent sale into slavery is forbidden. The only path that remains available is selling her into *ishut* again, since the prohibition is specifically against entering *shifchut* a second time after any prior "sale" — whether that prior sale was *ishut* or *shifchut*.

This is the position underlying the earlier ruling that the father cannot resell the *amah ivriyah* after she has been redeemed, and it explains why forcing the family to redeem her is an effective and permanent remedy.

### Bigdo Textual Debate

The disagreement among the *tannaim* turns on how to read the word in the verse. The text as written (the *masorah*, or *kesiv*) is *bagdo*, without a *yud*, which in rabbinic reading yields *bagad* — betrayal, treachery. This textual reading (*yesh em l'masores*) produces the prohibition of *shifchut achar shifchut*: once the father has betrayed his daughter by selling her into slavery once, he may not do so again. The verse is warning against a second betrayal following the first.

The word as read aloud (the *mikra*, or *keri*) is *bigdo*, with a *yud*, which, as Rashi explains, corresponds to *beged* — garment — the image of marriage. This oral reading (*yesh em l'mikra*) yields the prohibition of *shifchut achar ishut*: once he has wrapped her in the garment of marriage, she may not be sold into slavery.

### Three Positions

The three positions thus map onto distinct approaches to the verse. Rabbi Akiva rules *yesh em l'mikra* and derives only the prohibition of *shifchut achar ishut*. Rabbi Eliezer rules *yesh em l'masores* and derives only the prohibition of *shifchut achar shifchut*. Rabbi Shimon holds *yesh em l'mikra v'gam l'masores* — both readings are legally operative simultaneously — and therefore derives both prohibitions: neither *shifchut achar ishut* nor *shifchut achar shifchut* is permitted. For Rabbi Shimon, the daughter who has once experienced either marriage or servitude may never again be placed into slavery by her father.

This synthesis accounts for the position attributed to Rabbi Shimon throughout the preceding discussion, including the ruling that an *amah ivriyah* cannot be resold and that it is therefore effective — and appropriate — to compel the family to redeem her.

---

---

# Kiddushin 19

## Yi'ud: Erusin or Nisu'in?

### Rava's Core Question

The daf opens in the middle of 18b, in the context of a broader discussion of the *ama ivriya* — the Hebrew maidservant sold by her father while still a minor. A central feature of that institution is *yi'ud*: the possibility that the master, or his son, may designate her as a wife, effected either by the words *im livno yiyadena* or *asher lo ye'ada*, using the original purchase money as *kesef kiddushin*. The remainder of today's material is devoted entirely to working through the legal ramifications of *yi'ud*.

Rava bar Avuh opens with a pointed question: *yi'ud nisuin osa o erusin osa* — does *yi'ud* create full marriage (*nisuin*) or merely betrothal (*erusin*)? The question is structurally parallel to an earlier discussion about *kiddushei bi'ah*, where the same issue arose: since that form of kiddushin involves immediate physical intimacy, does it bypass the *erusin* stage and go straight to *nisuin*? Here the concern is analogous. The girl is already living in the master's home as a slave. When he performs *yi'ud*, designating her as his wife, does that act produce full *nisuin* — given that she is already present in his household — or is it only *erusin*, leaving *nisuin* as a separate subsequent stage?

The practical difference — the *nafka mina* — is considerable: does he inherit her if she dies? If he is a *kohen*, may he become *tamei* for her? May he annul her vows? All of these are consequences of *nisuin*, not of *erusin* alone. Does the obligation of *she'era kesuta ve'onata* — her sustenance, clothing, and conjugal rights — take effect immediately upon *yi'ud*, or only after a further step? All of these questions hinge on the answer.

### Shifcha Achar Ishut

The *Gemara* offers a first attempt at resolution: *ta shema*, come and hear. The Torah prohibits what we discussed on the previous daf — either *shifcha achar shifcha* or *shifcha achar ishut*, depending on how one reads the verse. One reading of *be'vigdo vah* — interpreting the word as *beged*, garment — is that once the master has "spread his garment over her," he may no longer sell her. This prohibits selling her as a slave after *yi'ud* has already created a marital bond.

Now, if the master performs *yi'ud* and subsequently dies, the *Gemara* notes that he cannot then sell her again — but that he *could* perform *yi'ud* again, meaning he could be *mekadesh* her. This raises the critical difficulty: if *yi'ud* created *nisuin*, then once *nisuin* has occurred, the father has no further authority over her whatsoever — *kivan de'niset shuv ein le'aviha reshut bah*. Why would the Torah need a special verse to prevent the father from reselling her? If she is fully married, she is already entirely out of his domain. The very need for a verse to forbid this act seems to imply that she remains under some residual paternal control — which is only possible if *yi'ud* created only *erusin*, not *nisuin*.

This appears to be a compelling proof. However, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak deflects it. He argues that *be'vigdo vah* in this context is not discussing *yi'ud* at all — it is discussing a completely separate scenario. The *braita* is teaching that if a father first gave his daughter in ordinary *kiddushin* to a man, and that man subsequently died, the father may no longer sell her as a slave. It is *not* addressing the case where she was initially sold as a *shifcha* and then received *yi'ud*. This is admittedly a strained reading of the *braita*, but it neutralizes the proof. The discussion of her being returned to her father's authority is not evidence about the nature of *yi'ud* — it concerns a case of ordinary *kiddushin* where the father loses the right to sell her thereafter.

### Braita Reinterpreted

The *Gemara* now presents a *braita* that initially appears unrelated to the *erusin*-versus-*nisuin* question but is in fact being mined for a proof. The *braita* records a dispute: one opinion holds that the father may not sell his daughter to close relatives (where *yi'ud* would be impossible, since *kiddushin* with a relative does not take effect), while Rabbi Eliezer permits this. All agree, however, that the father *may* sell her to a man who is prohibited from marrying her by a *lav* but for whom *kiddushin* would nonetheless be valid if performed — such as a *kohen gadol* marrying an *almana*, or a *kohen* marrying a *gerushah*. Even though such a marriage is forbidden, *kiddushin* in those cases is *tofes*, legally effective, and therefore *yi'ud* remains a theoretical possibility.

The *Gemara* asks: this is still trying to resolve the original question of whether *yi'ud* creates *erusin* or *nisuin*, yes — and keeps working through the implications.

### Almanah/Gerushah Proof

The *Gemara* now asks about the *almana* case more closely. How does this girl come to be an *almana* in the first place? If she married herself while a minor, the *kiddushin* would not have been valid — a minor cannot contract her own marriage. It must therefore be that her father previously gave her in *kiddushin* to some man, that man died, and now she is an *almana*. But in that case, how can the father now sell her as a *shifcha* at all? That would be *shifcha achar ishut* — selling her into servitude after she has already been in a marital bond — which is prohibited according to the *tanna* we have been following!

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by proposing that the scenario works according to Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *ma'ot harishonot lav le'kiddushin nitnu* — that the original purchase money was not designated as *kesef kiddushin*. Under this view, when the father initially sold his daughter, that act was purely a sale into servitude. The *kiddushin* occurred only later, through the act of *yi'ud* performed by the master — an independent transaction between the master and the girl in which the father played no role. Accordingly, the father never sold her *le'ishut*. The *ishut* happened separately, on its own. When the master dies, the father is therefore not in the position of someone who sold his daughter into marriage. He sold her into servitude, period. The subsequent marital bond was created independently. And that is why it is now permissible to discuss him selling her again — to a *kohen* or *kohen gadol* — because it would be *shifcha achar shifcha*, not *shifcha achar ishut*. The father was never the one who created the *ishut*.

### Ma'os Rishonos Debate

The deeper issue now emerges. Was the original purchase money — the *ma'ot rishonot* — the *kesef kiddushin*, or was it the remainder of the service still owed? The question matters enormously for whether the father was ever a party to the *kiddushin*.

The suggestion had been that the entire discussion of selling an *almana* or *gerushah* to a *kohen* works only according to Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda — who holds that the original money was *not kesef kiddushin*, and therefore the father was not the one who married her off. But the *Gemara* notes that there is a view — that of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — that even Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda may agree that it is the original money that serves as *kesef kiddushin*. If so, the father effectively did marry her off, and the problem of *shifcha achar ishut* returns. How then can the *braita* discuss him selling her as an *almana* or *gerushah* to a *kohen*?

The *Gemara*'s answer is that the scenario follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds the opposite of what we have been assuming: according to Rabbi Eliezer, *shifcha achar ishut* is actually permitted — it is *shifcha achar shifcha* that is prohibited. This resolves the difficulty neatly: if *shifcha achar ishut* poses no barrier, the father can sell her regardless of whether the original money was *kesef kiddushin*.

### Yi'ud = Erusin

Having worked through these preliminary difficulties, the *Gemara* now moves toward a definitive resolution. The *Rambam* rules that *yi'ud* creates only *erusin* — which is indeed where the dominant weight of the *Gemara*'s proofs has pointed throughout this discussion. The critical argument is this: the very fact that we are discussing scenarios where, after *yi'ud*, the father retains sufficient control to sell his daughter again or to contract a new marriage for her — all of this presupposes that after *yi'ud* she remains only an *arusa*, not a full *nisuah*. If *yi'ud* had created *nisuin*, she would have been entirely removed from her father's domain and none of these subsequent discussions would have any traction.

The *Gemara* does attempt one further rejoinder: perhaps one can distinguish between *nisuin* effected by the father and *nisuin* effected by the girl herself — *nisuin didah* versus *nisuin de'aviha*. But the *Gemara* rejects this distinction immediately. The reason a father loses authority over his daughter after *nisuin* is not because he performed a particular act that now prevents a subsequent act. It is the simple reality that she has become part of another man's household. Whether the *nisuin* was arranged by her father or arose independently through *yi'ud*, the result — her integration into another household — would be the same. Therefore the distinction cannot be sustained, and the proof stands: *yi'ud* creates only *erusin*.

---

## Conditions for Yi'ud

### Minor Son Question

Reish Lakish now raises a new question: *mahu she-ye'ayeid adam le'veno katan* — can a father perform *yi'ud* designating the *ama ivriya* for a son who is himself a minor? The Torah says *im livno yiyadena* — he may designate her for his son. Does "his son" mean any son, however young? Or does the son have to be an adult?

This question has a structural uniqueness. In ordinary *kiddushin*, a minor boy can never be the subject of a *kiddushin* arrangement. A girl can be married off while a minor, because her father acts on her behalf. But a minor boy cannot enter *kiddushin*: he cannot perform the act himself (lacking legal capacity), and there is no *shlichut le'katan* — an agent cannot act on behalf of a minor. Therefore, in ordinary law, *kiddushei katan* — a minor boy being betrothed — simply does not exist as a Torah institution. The question here is whether the unique Torah institution of *yi'ud*, which explicitly places the father in the active role, changes this calculus. The father himself is performing the *yi'ud* — perhaps the Torah permits it even for a minor son, since the father is the actor.

Two positions are suggested. One reads *beno* expansively — "his son, any son," even a *katan*. The other argues *beno dumya dideyh*: the son must parallel the father — just as the father is an adult, so too must the son be an adult. The logic is that while the father performs the act, what is fundamentally occurring is the establishment of a marital bond for the son, and a minor cannot be a party to such a bond.

### Minor Marriage Proof

Rabbi Zeira proposes a proof from a verse in the context of adultery: *ish asher yinaf et eshet re'ehu* — a man who commits adultery with his neighbor's wife. The verse specifies *ish* — a man — to exclude a minor: a minor who commits an act of adultery is not subject to the capital penalty. Similarly, the phrase *asher yinaf et eshet re'ehu* — adultery with a man's wife — excludes *eshet katan*, the wife of a minor: one who commits adultery with the wife of a minor is not liable.

But this immediately raises a question: where does one ever encounter the concept of "the wife of a minor"? For the Torah to need to exclude it, the institution must exist in some form. And if *yi'ud* can create a marital bond even for a minor son, that would be precisely such a case. The *Gemara* infers: if the Torah is excluding *eshet katan* from the laws of adultery, it implies that such a status exists — and the source of that status would be *yi'ud* performed by the father for his minor son. This would prove that *yi'ud* can indeed be performed for a *katan*.

### Yibum Alternative

Rav Ashi counters with an alternative source for *eshet katan*: *yibum*. If a man dies and his surviving brother is a boy between nine and thirteen years old, the physical act of *bi'ah* creates *yibum* — levirate marriage — even without intent, since *yibum* does not require conscious decision-making in the way that ordinary *kiddushin* does. If the mere physical act of intercourse, performed even by a minor over the age of nine, creates a valid marital bond through *yibum*, then the Torah's exclusion of *eshet katan* from the laws of adultery addresses precisely this scenario. It need not be addressing *yi'ud* at all. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the verse does not prove anything about *yi'ud* for a minor son — the *yibum* scenario sufficiently explains the Torah's need for that exclusion.

### Rashi/Tosafot Debate

A fundamental dispute between Rashi and Tosafot emerges here, concerning what the verse is actually teaching — the *kamashmalan* — in the *yibum*-of-a-minor case.

Rashi holds that if a boy of nine performs the act of *yibum* with his *yevamah*, the *yibum* is fully valid: she is his wife in every legal sense — he inherits her, he may become *tamei* for her, and so forth. *De'mid'oraita chazei lei* — she is biblically bound to him through the *zika*, and his act of *bi'ah* completes the acquisition. The *kamashmalan* of the verse is therefore not that the marriage is invalid, but rather that despite the validity of the marriage, there is no liability for adultery in such a case. The reasoning appears to be that since the husband is not yet a full adult, the marriage — while legally real — has not yet manifested as a complete marital reality, and therefore the capital punishment for adultery does not apply.

Tosafot disagrees sharply. Tosafot reads the verse as teaching that the marriage itself is not a Torah-level marriage at all. What might have appeared to be a valid *yibum* — because there is a *zika*, there is the physical act, there is the *yevamah* — is in fact only rabbinic in force. *Kamashmalan d'eino koneh ela mi'derabbanan* — the acquisition is only rabbinic. The verse teaches that on the Torah level, such a *yibum* does not create a marriage. Under this view, the practical consequences diverge dramatically from Rashi's: according to Tosafot, if another man subsequently has relations with this woman, she does not need a *get* — since there was no Torah-level marriage — whereas according to Rashi she is fully married and would require a *get* or *chalitzah*.

### Rabbi Aivo's Rule

Returning to the substance of *yi'ud* itself, the *Gemara* cites a statement of Rabbi Aivo in the name of Rabbi Yannai: *ein yi'ud ela be'gadol, ein yi'ud ela mi'da'as* — *yi'ud* can only be performed for an adult son, and it can only be performed *mi'da'as*. The *Gemara* asks: why state both conditions? Is this not redundant?

The *Gemara* answers that Rabbi Aivo is giving a reason rather than two separate rules: the reason *yi'ud* requires a *gadol* is precisely *because* it requires *da'as* — conscious awareness or consent. Since *da'as* is required, and a *katan* cannot supply the requisite *da'as*, it follows that the son must be an adult. The two clauses function together as principle and rationale.

This raises a further question about the nature of *da'as* in this context. Does it mean merely that the son must be informed, or does it mean that the son is the true principal in the *kiddushin* — that the father acts only as his authorized representative? The Rambam rules that the son must grant his father explicit permission to perform the *yi'ud* on his behalf. Under that reading, the father is genuinely acting as the son's agent, and the son's *da'as* is the operative one. This would explain why the son must be an adult: only an adult can authorize an agent, and only an adult can be the party entering into marriage.

### Girl's Da'as Required

Having established the requirement of the son's *da'as*, the *Gemara* now turns to a separate question: does the girl herself need to be part of the process in some meaningful way? Must *yi'ud* be performed with her knowledge?

### Abaye's Source

Abaye son of Rav Avuha derives this from the verse itself: *asher lo ye'adah* — "that he did not designate her" — which he reads as a positive requirement: *melamed shetzarich le'ya'adah*, the verse teaches that he must designate her, meaning he must make the *yi'ud* known to her. Rashi explains the term as *lashon dei'ah* — an expression of knowledge or awareness — indicating that she must be informed.

### When Kiddushin Occurs

The *Gemara* then explains the *yi'ud* requirement by connecting it to Abaye's teaching: *be'kiddushei yi'ud ve'aliba de'Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda de'amar ma'os rishonot lav le'kiddushin nitnu*. Why does this requirement of her *da'as* specifically arise according to Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda? Because if we follow the position that the original purchase money is the *kesef kiddushin* — that the *kiddushin* was effected at the time of the original sale by the father — then the girl need not be involved. The father is the active party, and in ordinary *kiddushin* effected by the father, the daughter need not be informed. But according to Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda, the original money was *not kesef kiddushin*, and the *kiddushin* occurs later through the remaining service owed to the master — a transaction that takes place between him and her directly, without the father. Since the father is out of the picture and the *kiddushin* is happening between the two of them, she must be made part of the process, which requires at minimum that she be informed.

### Rav Nachman's View

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, however, argues that even if one holds that the original money *is* the *kesef kiddushin* — even according to the majority view — there remains a special scriptural requirement that the girl be informed. *Shani hacha de'amar Rachmana ye'adah* — here the Torah itself says "he designated her," imposing a unique condition on *yi'ud* that does not apply in ordinary *kiddushin*. Even though technically the *kiddushin* flows from the money given to the father, the Torah nonetheless demands that when *yi'ud* is actually performed, the girl must be made aware. It is a *gezeirat hakatuv* — a scriptural decree unique to this institution.

The Rambam rules simply that a man cannot perform *yi'ud* on the *ama ivriya* — either for himself or for his son — except *mi'da'atah*: with her awareness. Whether *da'atah* means she must actively acquiesce, or merely that she must be informed, remains somewhat open. The Rambam does not state that she can refuse and invalidate the *yi'ud*, which suggests that *da'atah* means notification rather than consent. The analogy to *mi'un* — a rabbinic mechanism by which a minor girl can reject a marriage — is instructive: since *mi'un* is a rabbinic institution, one cannot import it into this context to argue that she must agree on a Torah level.

---

## Ma'os Rishonos Question

### Rabbi Yosi's Position

Having woven the *ma'ot rishonot* debate through multiple earlier discussions, the *Gemara* now sets out Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda's position explicitly. It is cited from a *braita*: the Torah juxtaposes *ye'adah* (designation) and *hepdah* (redemption) — *asher lo ye'adah*. From this juxtaposition Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda derives that *yi'ud* can only be performed when there is still enough time remaining in the girl's service for her to redeem herself.

### Prutah Requirement

*Tzarich she'yish'heh bayom kedei fidyah* — there must be enough remaining on the day of *yi'ud* to constitute a *prutah*'s worth of service. Just as the girl can redeem herself by buying back her remaining service with a *prutah*, the master can perform *yi'ud* using that same *prutah* of remaining service as the *kesef kiddushin*. But if there is no service left — if the six years are at their final instant and there is not a *prutah*'s worth of labor remaining — *yi'ud* cannot be performed.

*Mikan amar Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda:* if there is enough time left in the day for her to perform a *prutah*'s worth of service, she is *mekudeshet*; if not, she is not. And the *Gemara* draws the explicit conclusion: *alma kasvar ma'ot rishonot lav le'kiddushin nitnu* — this demonstrates that in Rabbi Yosi's view, the original purchase money was not designated as *kesef kiddushin*. The *kiddushin* is being effected only through the remaining service, and that is why a *prutah*'s worth of remaining service is indispensable.

### Rav Nachman Counters

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak again presents the counter-position: one need not conclude that Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda rejects the *ma'ot rishonot* as *kesef kiddushin*. One can maintain that even he holds the original money becomes *kesef kiddushin*, and nonetheless require a *prutah* of remaining service. *Shani hacha de'amar Rachmana ve'hepdah* — it is a *gezeirat hakatuv* arising from the juxtaposition of *ye'adah* and *hepdah*. The Torah is imposing an independent condition: *yi'ud* may only be performed when redemption remains a live option — i.e., when at least a *prutah* of service remains. But the *kesef kiddushin* itself is still the original money; the *prutah* of remaining service is not itself the *kiddushin* but rather a threshold condition mandated by the verse.

---

## Yi'ud Extends Normal Law

### Minor Daughter Kiddushin

The *Gemara* now uses the framework established by *yi'ud* — particularly the mechanism through which *kiddushin* can occur without the father being the active party — to derive a broader ruling about ordinary *kiddushin*. The question under consideration is whether an underage daughter can herself accept *kesef kiddushin*, given that her father has signaled his approval. This touches directly on the *yi'ud* case: according to Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda, the *kiddushin* occurs between the master and the girl directly, without the father. She is a *ketanah*, yet the *kiddushin* is valid. How is that possible?

### Father's Authorization

Rav Amram cites Rav Nachman: *amar adam le'vito ketana, tzei ve'kabeli kiddushayich* — a father can instruct his underage daughter to go and accept *kesef kiddushin* on his behalf. The daughter goes, receives the money from the prospective husband, and the *kiddushin* is valid. This ruling is derived from the logic of *kiddushei yi'ud*: since we must explain how *yi'ud* creates valid *kiddushin* even when the father is not the active party and the girl is a *ketanah*, the answer must be that the father's intent combined with her physical act of receiving is sufficient. And once we establish that principle, we can apply it to ordinary *kiddushin* as well.

### Tosafot Problem

Tosafot raises a significant difficulty: how can a minor girl effect a *kinyan* — an acquisition — of the ring or money? The problem is not merely one of *shlichut* (agency); even setting aside the inability of a minor to be an agent, the fundamental issue is that a *katan* or *ketanah* has no capacity for *kinyan*. Acquisition requires legal capacity, which a minor lacks. How then can the girl's receiving of the *kesef* constitute a valid *kinyan*, even if the father has authorized it?

### Two Da'asos Model

Tosafot resolves this through the concept of *da'as acheres makneh oso* — a transfer effected by the *da'as* of another party. Two distinct mental acts combine through the medium of the girl's hand. The prospective husband provides the *da'as* to transfer the object to her — his intent to convey the ring makes the transfer effective even without her independent capacity. Her hand serves as the physical vehicle through which the ring passes. At the same time, the father provides the *da'as* that she should be married — his intent constitutes the operative will behind the *kiddushin* itself. She does the act of receiving, the husband provides the *da'as* for the transfer of the object, and the father provides the *da'as* for the *kiddushin*. These two *da'asos* work through her hand, and together they constitute a valid *kiddushin*.

This model is precisely what explains *kiddushei yi'ud* according to Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda: when the father sold his daughter into servitude with the implicit expectation of *yi'ud*, he provided — at the time of the original sale — the *da'as* that if the master wished to marry her, he consented to it. When the master later performs *yi'ud*, the girl receives back the service still owed to her (which serves as the *kesef kiddushin*), and the combination of the father's earlier *da'as* and her act of receiving creates the valid *kiddushin*.

### Loan as Kesef

Rava cites Rav Nachman with a further application of this framework: *ha'mekadesh be'milveh ve'yesh lo mashkon mekudeshes* — if a man had lent money to a woman and held a *mashkon* (collateral) from her, and he subsequently was *mochel* (waived) the debt in the context of *kiddushin*, she is *mekudeshes*. The *hana'ah* — the benefit she receives from the waiver of her debt — serves as the *kesef kiddushin*.

### Mashkal Analogy

The *Gemara* explains the application of this case through the *mashkon*. Tosafot reads it as follows: one might have thought that when the creditor still holds the *mashkon*, there is insufficient *gemirut da'as* — finalization of intent — to constitute a proper *kiddushin*. After all, even though he declared the debt waived, he has not yet returned her collateral. Perhaps the *mochel* is not complete, and therefore the *hana'ah* is insufficient to serve as *kesef kiddushin*. The ruling teaches that even in such a case, *mekudeshes* — the *kiddushin* is valid.

The source for this ruling is again the framework of Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda. *Lav amar Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda ma'ot rishonot lav le'kiddushin nitnu* — the original money is not the *kesef kiddushin*; it is the remaining service that serves as *kesef kiddushin*. That remaining service is effectively a debt owed to the master: she owes him labor, and *hi gufa mashkon hi* — she herself is the collateral. Her presence in his household, her ongoing service, constitutes the security for the "debt" of labor. When he performs *yi'ud* and is *mochel* the remaining service, he is using that waiver — with her as the *mashkon* — as the *kesef kiddushin*. *Ve'ki meshayar bah shaveh prutah miyad havei kiddushin* — and from this case we can learn that the parallel scenario of a loan with a *mashkon* also works. The *Gemara* acknowledges that the analogy is not perfectly tight — in the *mashkon* case the creditor holds the woman's object as collateral, while in the *yi'ud* case the woman herself is the collateral — but the principle is being established.

---

## Yi'ud Procedure

### Yi'ud Declaration

The *Gemara* now sets out the mechanics of how *yi'ud* is performed: *omer lah bifnei shnayim harei at mekudeshet li, harei at me'oreset li* — he declares before two witnesses that she is betrothed to him. This is the standard *erusin* declaration, made in the presence of two valid witnesses, as required for any *kiddushin*. The *Gemara* adds that this can be performed even at the very end of the six years — *afillu b'sof shesh*, even *samuch le'shkiat hachama*, within moments of sunset on the last day. From that point on, *noheg bah minhag ishut ve'eino noheg bah minhag shifcha* — he treats her as a wife and no longer as a slave.

### Rabbi Yosi Condition

Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda reiterates his condition: *im yesh she'hut bayom kedei la'asot imo shaveh prutah, mekudeshes; ve'im lav, einah mekudeshes* — she is *mekudeshes* only if, at the time of *yi'ud*, there remains enough time in the day for her to perform a *prutah*'s worth of service; if not, the *yi'ud* does not take effect.

### Mashkal Delayed Effect

The *Gemara* then introduces a *mashal* — an analogy: *le'omer le'ishah hitkadshi li me'achshav ve'le'achar shloshim yom* — "be married to me from now, and it shall take effect in thirty days." If another man attempts to betroth her within those thirty days, she is nonetheless *mekudeshes la'rishon* — betrothed to the first man. Since the *kiddushin* was stated to begin *me'achshav*, from now, it has already commenced, and a subsequent betrothal cannot override it.

Rav Acha b'rei d'Rava explains that this *mashal* is addressed specifically to the Rabbis — the position of *chachamim* who hold that the original money is the *kesef kiddushin*. For the Rabbis, *kiddushei yi'ud* works precisely like *me'achshav ve'le'achar zman*: the money changes hands at the time of the initial sale — *me'achshav* — and the *kiddushin* is fully realized only years later at the time of *yi'ud* — *le'achar zman*. The two events are bound together: the first provides the *kesef*, and the second completes the *kiddushin*.

### Why Mashkal Matters

The *Gemara* asks *peshita* — isn't this obvious? If it began with the original money, of course a subsequent act cannot override it. The *Gemara* answers: *mah d'teima hala lo amar lah me'achshav* — one might have thought that since the master never explicitly said *me'achshav* at the time of the original sale, and since he had not yet even decided at that moment that he wished to perform *yi'ud*, perhaps the whole *kiddushin* takes effect only at the moment of *yi'ud* and is entirely prospective. Under that reading, anything occurring before the *yi'ud* declaration would not be subject to the earlier money at all. The ruling therefore teaches: *kamashmalan* — when he ultimately performs *yi'ud*, the *kiddushin* is treated retroactively as having begun when the money changed hands, analogous to *me'achshav*, and the entire sequence is bound together.

### No Interference Rule

The practical consequence follows directly: if during the period between the initial sale and the *yi'ud* declaration, a third party attempts to betroth this woman, the subsequent *kiddushin* does not take effect. Just as in the *me'achshav ve'le'achar shloshim yom* case the earlier *kiddushin* prevails, so too in *yi'ud* — once the master ultimately declares *yi'ud*, the *kiddushin* is treated as having begun when the money was first paid, and any intervening attempt by another man to create *kiddushin* with her is void.

---

---

# Kiddushin 20

## Original Money vs. Servi…

### Yi'ud Timing

Daf 20 continues the discussion of *eved ivri*, picking up in the middle of 19b. The central question concerns which money constitutes the *kesef kiddushin* for *yi'ud*: is it the original purchase price, or is it whatever value of service remains at the time the master decides to perform *yi'ud*? One practical difference is whether *yi'ud* can be performed even when less than a *perutah*'s worth of service remains. The *gemara* addresses this through a series of *braitot* that examine the related question of when, precisely, the *kiddushin* process begins.

If the original money is the *kesef kiddushin* — even though that characterization is only confirmed retroactively when the master chooses to perform *yi'ud* — the question arises: what happens if another man attempts to betroth the girl during the interval between purchase and *yi'ud*? The *braita* rules that the second man's *kiddushin* would not take effect if the master ultimately proceeds with *yi'ud*. The transaction is treated as though the master had declared at the moment of purchase, *"at mekudeshet li me'achshav"* — you are betrothed to me from now — with completion deferred to the moment of *yi'ud*. Even though no such declaration was made, and even though the master had not yet made up his mind, the structure functions like a *me'achshav u-le'achar zman*, locking out any intervening *kiddushin*. This is a significant *chiddush* in understanding how the *kesef kiddushin* operates when it is identified with the original purchase money.

### Father's Marriage

A second *braita* addresses a related scenario. A man sells his daughter as an *amah ivriyah* and then, before the master has had the opportunity to perform *yi'ud*, the father goes and betroths her to another man — to Shimon. The *braita* states: *sichek ba-adon u-mekudeshet lashani* — he laughs in the face of the master, and she is betrothed to Shimon. This ruling, that Shimon's *kiddushin* does take effect, is attributed to Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda.

### Kesef Kiddushin Dispute

The reasoning follows directly from Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda's position on the nature of the *kesef kiddushin*. In his view, the *kesef kiddushin* for *yi'ud* is not the original purchase money but rather the remainder of the service — the value of the labor still owed. Since no *kiddushin* process has yet commenced under this view, the father retains the ability to betroth his daughter to another man, and that betrothal is fully binding.

The *chachamim*, by contrast, rule that the master may still perform *yi'ud* — *im ratza leyayeid, meyayeid* — because they hold that the original money serves as *kesef kiddushin*, and retroactively, if *yi'ud* is performed, that original money renders the earlier *kiddushin* as though it had been made *me'achshav*. Shimon's *kiddushin* therefore does not take hold. If the master does not perform *yi'ud*, she would be betrothed to Shimon. The entire question is thus *tluim ve-omdim* — suspended and contingent on the master's eventual decision.

### Mashal Comparison

The *gemara* then introduces a *mashal*: the situation is comparable to a man who says to a woman, *harei at mekudeshet li le'achar shloshim yom* — you are betrothed to me after thirty days — without the addition of *me'achshav*. If another man betroths her during those thirty days, she is betrothed to the second man, because the first man's declaration contains no operative *me'achshav* to lock out intervening *kiddushin*.

The *gemara* asks: *mashal le-man* — whose position does this *mashal* illustrate? It cannot be the *rabbanan*, since they allow the master to still perform *yi'ud* and thereby override Shimon's *kiddushin*. Rav Acha the son of Rava therefore concludes that the *mashal* illustrates the position of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda.

The *gemara* then clarifies the added value of this *mashal*. One might have thought: even according to Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, since the master has the power to perform *yi'ud* at any moment he chooses — unlike the thirty-day case where a fixed interval makes it clear that nothing is operative — perhaps the ever-present possibility of *yi'ud* should be sufficient to lock out Shimon even without a *me'achshav*. The *mashal* comes to teach that we do not say this. According to Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, since the *kesef kiddushin* is only the remainder of the service and no *kiddushin* has yet taken effect, the father may betroth her to Shimon and it is binding — notwithstanding the fact that *yi'ud* could have been performed at any moment.

The two positions thus produce symmetric but opposite results: according to the *chachamim*, using the original money as *kesef kiddushin* is sufficient to function as *me'achshav* even without an explicit declaration, blocking Shimon's *kiddushin*. According to Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, even the open-ended and ever-present possibility of *yi'ud* does not block Shimon, because until *yi'ud* is actually performed, nothing has begun.

---

## Stipulation vs. Yi'ud

### No Yi'ud Stipulation

A third *braita* raises yet another configuration. A man sells his daughter as an *amah ivriyah* and stipulates with the master at the time of sale: *al menat shelo leyayeid* — on the condition that there will be no *yi'ud*. She is sold for service only; the master is not to marry her. The question is whether such a stipulation can validly exclude *yi'ud* from the institution of *amah ivriyah*.

### Meir vs. Rabbanan

Rabbi Meir rules that the stipulation is upheld — *niskayem ha-tnai*. The *rabbanan* disagree: if the master subsequently wishes to perform *yi'ud*, he may do so — *im ratza leyayeid, meyayeid* — because the stipulation has no force.

### Void Stipulation

The *rabbanan*'s reasoning is grounded in the principle of *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah*: one who stipulates against the way the Torah has defined an institution — *kol ha-matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah, tna'o batel* — the stipulation is void.

### Marriage Obligations

The *gemara* then raises a challenge to Rabbi Meir's position from a *braita* dealing with marriage. If a man betroths a woman on condition that he has no obligations of *she'er, kesut, ve'onah* — sustenance, clothing, and marital relations — the ruling is that the *kiddushin* takes effect but the stipulation is void: *harei zo mekudeshet ve-tna'o batel*. This too is the position of Rabbi Meir. If a man fundamentally intends to perform *kiddushin*, the *kiddushin* takes effect. But he cannot alter the Torah-defined parameters of the institution. It is a package; if you enter it, you accept the whole of it. How then can Rabbi Meir permit the stipulation against *yi'ud*?

### Yehuda's Position

Before resolving the tension regarding Rabbi Meir, the *gemara* notes the intermediate position of Rabbi Yehuda: *be-davar she-be-mamon, tna'o kayam* — a stipulation against a monetary obligation is valid. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between *onah*, which is a personal obligation and cannot be stipulated away, and the obligations of *she'er* and *kesut*, which are financial in nature. Since financial obligations are the sort of thing a person can waive — they are akin to a debt — the Torah leaves them subject to the parties' agreement.

This is analogous to the law of a *shomer*: the Torah sets default liability rules for a *shomer chinam* and a *shomer sachar*, but a person may stipulate to expand or contract those defaults, precisely because they are monetary. One way to understand this is that the Torah's rules for a *shomer* represent presumed contractual defaults — they reflect what most people intend absent explicit agreement — and explicit contrary terms simply override those defaults. Applied to marriage, Rabbi Yehuda reasons that while the personal obligation of *onah* cannot be contracted away, the financial obligations of maintenance and clothing can be.

Rabbi Meir takes the stricter view: even monetary stipulations against Torah-defined institutional obligations are void. The challenge, then, is how Rabbi Meir can simultaneously hold that a stipulation against *yi'ud* is valid in the *amah ivriyah* case. The answer lies in the position of Chizkiyah, addressed in the following section.

---

## Le'Amah Derasha

### Chizkiyah's Derasha

The *gemara* introduces Chizkiyah's teaching to resolve the apparent inconsistency in Rabbi Meir's position. The Torah uses the phrase *ki yimkor ish et bito le'amah* — when a man sells his daughter as a maidservant. The word *le'amah* is superfluous, and Chizkiyah derives from it: *pe'amim she'eino mochrah ela le'amah bilvad* — there are circumstances under which the sale is purely for service, without any accompanying right of *yi'ud*. The Torah thus itself contemplates a version of the institution in which *yi'ud* is absent. This is not, in Chizkiyah's reading, a stipulation that overrides the Torah; it is a distinct institutional form that the Torah itself authorizes.

This resolves the tension in Rabbi Meir's position. Rabbi Meir does not allow parties to modify an institution by stipulating against the Torah's definition. But Chizkiyah teaches that the Torah itself provides for two forms of the *amah ivriyah* arrangement: one that includes the potential for *yi'ud*, and one — *le'amah bilvad* — that does not. Rabbi Meir therefore holds that the stipulation works not because the parties have overridden the Torah, but because the Torah itself validates this alternative form.

### Pasuk Allocation

The *rabbanan* do not accept Chizkiyah's reading. They understand the institution as a single package — *amah ivriyah* always comes with the right of *yi'ud* — and therefore a stipulation against *yi'ud* is void. What, then, do the *rabbanan* do with the word *le'amah*? The *gemara* explains that they require it for a different teaching: *melamed she-mochrah li-pesulim* — it teaches that a father may sell his daughter to someone who is *pasul* for marriage, meaning someone whom the Torah prohibits her from marrying at the level of a *lav*, such as a *kohen* who would be marrying a *gerushah*, or a *mamzer*.

This is a significant ruling: even though the sale into *amah ivriyah* is predicated on the possibility of *yi'ud*, and *yi'ud* with a *pasul* would be forbidden, the Torah nonetheless permits the sale. The institution is not dissolved by the fact that *yi'ud* is practically barred. The prohibition gets in the way of exercising the right, but it does not change the institutional structure. This is precisely the distinction the *rabbanan* draw: you cannot stipulate to change the institution, but circumstances can prevent the exercise of a right without voiding the institution itself.

The *rabbanan* understand the two cases as follows. When a father sells his daughter to a *pasul* with no stipulation, the institution is intact; *yi'ud* simply cannot be exercised. When a father stipulates against *yi'ud* with someone who is not a *pasul*, he is attempting to alter the institution — and that the *rabbanan* reject. For Rabbi Meir, the calculus runs in the opposite direction, as will become clear.

### Eliezer's Reading

Rabbi Eliezer offers a different allocation of the *pesukim*. He argues that there is no need for the word *le'amah* to teach the permissibility of selling to a *pasul*, because that can already be derived from another verse: *im ra'ah be'einei adoneha asher lo ye'adah* — if it is evil in the eyes of the master such that he does not perform *yi'ud*. Rabbi Eliezer reads *im ra'ah* as referring to a halachically problematic marriage — *she-ra'ah be-nisu'eha*, that there is something wrong with the marriage. The verse is thus already describing the case of a *pasul*, where the master cannot perform *yi'ud* because the marriage would be forbidden, and yet the sale has taken effect. From this verse alone one learns that a sale to a *pasul* is valid. The word *le'amah* is therefore available for a larger *chiddush*: *melamed she-mochrah li-krovim* — even a sale to a relative, where *yi'ud* would not merely be forbidden but would be halachically ineffective (*kiddushin* not being *tofes* at all among *arayot*), the sale is nonetheless valid.

### Kal VaChomer

The *gemara* asks: why is a *pasuk* needed to permit the sale to *pesulim*? A *kal va-chomer* would seem to suffice: if *kiddushin* itself takes effect *be-di'avad* even when it involves an *issur lav* — as in the case of a *kohen* who marries a *gerushah* — then certainly a sale, which does not yet constitute *kiddushin*, should be valid. The *gemara* responds that the *kal va-chomer* fails because it is not symmetric. The father's power in the context of marriage is broader than his power in the context of sale: a father can betroth his daughter even when she is a *na'arah*, whereas he can only sell her when she is a *ketanah*. Since his power in selling is more limited, one might have thought he cannot sell her to a *pasul*. The verse *le'amah* therefore explicitly teaches that he can.

### Institution vs. Fact

The final point in this section concerns the question of *krovim* and the mirror-image positions of Rabbi Meir and the *rabbanan*. The *rabbanan* hold that *krovim* — relatives for whom *kiddushin* would be entirely ineffective — are excluded, and a sale to them is not valid. But a sale to a *pasul* — where *kiddushin* would be *tofes be-di'avad* — is permitted, because the institution remains intact; only the exercise of *yi'ud* is blocked by circumstance. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, permits even a sale to *krovim*, reading *im ra'ah be'einei adoneha* to cover that case as well.

For Rabbi Meir, the picture is striking and, as the *gemara* acknowledges, quite strange. Rabbi Meir uses *le'amah* to teach that a father may stipulate against *yi'ud*, producing an institutional form of *amah ivriyah* that is purely for service. He uses *im ra'ah be'einei adoneha* to teach the permissibility of selling to a *pasul*, mirroring where Rabbi Eliezer learns *krovim*. But Rabbi Meir holds like the *rabbanan* that a sale to *krovim* is invalid.

The asymmetry is genuinely puzzling. Rabbi Meir permits the parties to define the institution without *yi'ud* through stipulation, yet holds that the institution cannot validly exist when *yi'ud* is simply impossible due to the *karov* relationship. The *rabbanan* are internally consistent in the opposite direction: they prohibit the stipulation because the institution is indivisible, yet permit the sale to *krovim* because the institution is intact and only the circumstances prevent *yi'ud*. Rabbi Meir's position — that deliberate exclusion works but factual impossibility does not — is, as the *gemara* itself notes, quite difficult to understand intuitively.

---

## Father vs. Son

### Father/Son Rule

The *gemara* now addresses a specific *braita* that states: one may sell his daughter to her grandfather (the father of the seller) but may not sell her to her brother (the son of the seller). A second *braita* states that one may not sell to either. The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: the second *braita*, which prohibits both, follows the *rabbanan* who hold that *krovim* are excluded categorically. The first *braita* — which permits the sale to the grandfather but not to the brother — requires an explanation of whose view it represents.

### Yi'ud Possibility

The *gemara* concludes: *le'olam ke-Rabbanan* — the first *braita* also follows the *rabbanan*. But the *rabbanan* concede in the case of the grandfather — *modu Rabbanan heicha de-ika tzad yi'ud* — because there, while the master himself (the grandfather) cannot perform *yi'ud* with his own granddaughter, his son can. If the seller has a brother — that is, another son of the grandfather who is not a *karov* to the girl — *yi'ud* remains structurally possible. The institution is therefore intact, and the sale is valid.

This reasoning prompts further questions. What if the grandfather has no other son, or no son old enough to perform *yi'ud* within the six-year term? Does the structural availability of *yi'ud* in the abstract suffice, or must *yi'ud* be practically possible in the specific circumstances? The *gemara* does not resolve this, and it remains an open question.

---

## Yovel Context

### Rambam Yovel

At this point, a fundamental contextual question arises: when did the laws of *eved ivri* actually apply? The Rambam (*Hilchot Shemitah ve-Yovel*, chapter 10, *halacha* 9) rules explicitly: *be-zman she-ha-yovel noheig, noheig din eved ivri* — the institution of *eved ivri* is operative only when the *yovel* is operative. When the *yovel* does not function, none of these laws apply. The *yovel* ceased to be operative already before the end of the First Temple period, from the time of the Assyrian exile under Sancheriv, when the northern tribes were displaced and the requirement of having all the tribes settled in the land — a precondition for *yovel* — was no longer met. Accordingly, by the latter part of the First Temple era, the laws of *eved ivri* were no longer practically applicable. The extended discussion of the *gemara* is thus theoretical in its halachic application, though not diminished in its moral and conceptual weight.

---

## Treatment Rights

### Begapo Yavo

The *gemara* now turns to a new *braita* examining the personal rights of the *eved ivri*. The verse states: *im be-gapo yavo, be-gapo yeitzei* — if he comes in by his body alone, he leaves by his body alone. The *gemara* will explore what this means in practice.

### Eliezer ben Yaakov

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov reformulates the principle as: *yechidi nichnas, yechidi yeitzei* — he enters alone, he exits alone. The *gemara* asks what distinguishes this formulation from the first.

### Rava's Reading

Rava explains *be-gapo yavo, be-gapo yeitzei*: if he enters whole in body, he leaves whole in body. The verse teaches *she-eino yeitzei be-roshei evarim* — that he does not go free on account of loss of limb, as a *eved kena'ani* would. If a master knocks out the eye or tooth of a *eved kena'ani*, the slave goes free. The *eved ivri* does not obtain freedom on this basis. This might appear to disadvantage him, but in fact it works in his favor: the master must pay the full range of injury compensation applicable to a free person — *tza'ar, sheves, ripuy, boshet* — and that payment may well be sufficient for the *eved ivri* to purchase his own freedom outright, leaving him with money to spare. The verse clarifies that bodily injury is compensated but does not of itself terminate the servitude.

### Abaye's Question

Abaye challenges Rava: is this teaching not already derived from the verse *lo yeitzei ke-tzeit avadim* — he shall not go free as slaves go free — which was studied earlier? Why does this verse need to add anything?

### Injury Compensation

The *gemara* answers: if we had only the earlier verse, one might have thought that the rule works differently for the *eved ivri* — that he both goes free and receives compensation for the injury. The verse *be-gapo yavo be-gapo yeitzei* therefore teaches definitively that bodily injury does not serve as a basis for freedom at all. He is compensated, but he does not go free on that account.

---

## Wife & Children

### Shifcha Provision

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — *yechidi nichnas, yechidi yeitzei*, he enters alone and exits alone. If the *eved ivri* enters with a wife and children, the master provides him with a *shifcha kena'anis* to produce slave children from the union. If he enters without a wife and children, the master does not provide a *shifcha kena'anis*. The provision of a *shifcha* is thus conditioned on the *eved* already being a married man when he enters service.

Viewed from the perspective of the wife, this arrangement is deeply uncomfortable: a husband who has sold himself into servitude due to poverty is now, as part of that servitude, given another woman. The *gemara* does not address this perspective directly. There is also the implicit suggestion that this arrangement carries within it a quality of *chotei niskar* — the wrongdoer benefiting from his transgression — in that the very poverty that forced the man into servitude now enables him a form of license he did not previously have. This too the *gemara* leaves unresolved.

---

## Redemption Price

### Value Increased

A new *braita* takes up the question of the redemption price when an *eved ivri* seeks to buy back his freedom before the end of his term. *Nimkar be-maneh ve-hishbi'ach ve-amad ma'asayim* — he sold himself for a hundred and his value rose to two hundred. How do we calculate the price of redemption? *Minayin she-mechashvinan lo ela maneh* — how do we know we use the original purchase price? The verse states *mi-kesef miknato* — from the money of his purchase. The redemption is calculated against the original price, prorated for the remaining years.

### Value Decreased

The converse case: *nimkar be-ma'asayim ve-hichsif ve-amad maneh* — he was sold for two hundred but his value declined to a hundred. *Minayin she-ein mechashvinan lo ela maneh* — how do we know we use the current, lower price? The verse states *ke-fi shanav yashiv et ge'ulato* — according to his years he shall return his redemption. This verse directs us to calculate based on what the remaining years are currently worth.

### Lower Price

The principle that emerges is that we always apply whichever of the two verses yields the lower redemption price — *lekula*. If the original purchase price is lower (because his value rose), we use the original. If the current market value is lower (because his value fell), we use the current. The question of why we consistently apply *lekula* rather than *lechumra* — always taking the higher price — is addressed in the following section.

---

## Lekula Principle

### Abaye's Boast

The question of why we read the *pesukim* toward leniency is prompted by a famous exchange. Abaye, in a moment of scholarly confidence, declared: *hareini ke-ven Azzai be-shukei Tiveria* — I am like Ben Azzai in the marketplaces of Tiberias. Ben Azzai was renowned as a towering figure of learning, and Abaye was effectively issuing an open challenge: ask me anything. One of the *rabbanan* immediately responded with the question: the two *pesukim* can be read either *lekula* — always using the lower price — or *lechumra* — always using the higher. What determines that we read them *lekula*?

### Torah's Concern

The *gemara* answers: *mide de-hava Rachmana legabei* — we know that the Torah expresses concern for the welfare of the *eved ivri*. Given this orientation, we assume the Torah intends the reading that is more favorable to him.

### Ki Tov Lo Imach

The source for the Torah's concern is a *braita* that many will know from earlier learning: *ki tov lo imach* — it should be good for him with you. The verse mandates that the *eved ivri* be treated as an equal. *Imach be-ma'achal* — equal in food; *imach be-mishteh* — equal in drink. The master may not eat fine white bread while the slave eats bran bread; may not drink aged wine while the slave drinks new wine; may not sleep on soft cushions while the slave sleeps on straw. The accommodations must be equivalent. From this the *gemara* derives: *kol ha-koneh eved ivri ke-koneh adon le-atzmo* — whoever purchases a *eved ivri* is as if he has purchased a master for himself.

### Buying Master

This teaching carries within it a subtle note of censure directed at the buyer: be aware of what you are taking on. The person you are purchasing is not someone you may treat with contempt or deprive of dignity. He must have what you have.

### Tosafot Pillow

*Tosafot* raises a challenge: the formulation says *adon* — master, not peer. How can he be merely equivalent? *Tosafot* resolves this with a passage from the Yerushalmi. Suppose the master has only one pillow. If he sleeps on it himself, he is not fulfilling *ki tov lo imach* — he is treating himself better than the *eved*. But if he neither sleeps on it himself nor gives it to the *eved*, that is *midat Sedom* — the attribute of Sodom: causing harm to another without any benefit to oneself. Since he is not using the pillow, there is no justification for depriving the *eved* of it. Therefore, he must give it to the *eved*. The result is that the *eved* ends up with better treatment — and that is why the *gemara* calls it *ke-koneh adon le-atzmo*: in the final reckoning, the *eved* may actually come out ahead.

---

## Treatment vs. Price

### Strict Redemption

The *gemara* entertains a counterargument. Perhaps the Torah's concern for the *eved ivri*'s welfare, expressed through *ki tov lo imach*, applies only to his treatment while in servitude — *ki heichi de-lo litzta'er lei*, so as not to cause him suffering. But when it comes to the redemption price, perhaps we should be strict — *nachmir alav* — and require him to pay the higher amount.

### Sin Leads to Slavery

What would motivate applying stringency at the redemption stage? The *gemara* invokes a teaching of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina: *bo u-re'eh kama kasha avka shel shevi'it* — come and see how grave is even the dust of *shevi'it* transgression. A person who engages in commerce with *shevi'it* produce — not even the primary prohibition, merely a lighter *issur aseh* — sets himself on a path of decline. Because he pursued profit by disregarding *halacha*, the consequence unfolds measure for measure.

### Downward Spiral

The teaching traces the descent through the *parshiyot* of *Behar*: he sells his movable property, as the verse states *bi-shnat ha-yovel tashuvu ish la-achuzato*, juxtaposed to *ve-chi timkeru mimkar la-amitecha*. Then he sells his fields — *ki yamuch achicha u-machar me-achuzato*. Then his home — *ve-chi yimkor beit moshav ir choma*. The *gemara* then introduces, from *Mishpatim*, the sale of his daughter — *ve-chi yimkor ish et bito le-amah* — even though that *parshah* is not found in *Behar*. The *gemara* explains that a person in this position would sooner sell his daughter than borrow with interest, because the two remaining options are selling his daughter or taking an interest-bearing loan. Finally, having sold everything, he sells himself — *ve-chi yamuch achicha ve-nimkar lach* — and if he still has not repented, he may wind up sold to a non-Jew, and ultimately to the service of a pagan temple, *nimkar la-avodat kochavim atzmah*.

### Awareness Stages

The *gemara* notes a shift in language between the stages. After the sale of movable property, it says *lo hirgish* — he was not sensitive, he did not perceive that his poverty resulted from his *aveirah*. After the subsequent stages, the language shifts to *lo ba l'yado* — the awareness did not come to him. Why the difference?

### Repeated Sin

The *gemara* cites Rav Huna: *kivan she-avar adam aveirah ve-shanah bah, hutrah lo* — once a person has committed a transgression and repeated it, it becomes permitted to him. The *gemara* immediately clarifies: not literally permitted, but *na'asit lo ke-heter* — it becomes psychologically as if permitted. The first time, there was a reasonable expectation that the person would have been *murgash* — sensitive, aware — and would have recognized the causal connection between his transgression and his punishment. He was not. By the time he has descended further, the expectation of awareness is far lower; it is no longer surprising that awareness did not come to him. The phrasing of *lo ba l'yado* reflects this diminished expectation — of course it did not come to him; he is already so far gone.

---

## Daughter vs. Interest

### Economic Logic

The *gemara* explains why a man in this spiral would choose to sell his daughter before taking a loan with *ribbit*. When a daughter is sold, the debt she represents decreases over time — *barta migre'ah ve-nafkah* — as she works off her term of service, her redemption price diminishes. The trajectory is toward resolution. A loan with interest, by contrast, only compounds — *ha mosifa ve-azla* — the debt grows continuously. The practical calculation therefore favors selling the daughter over borrowing with interest, even though morally neither reflects well on the person's situation.

This is not a moral endorsement. Rather, it is an economic observation embedded within a trajectory of failure and sin. The inclusion of the daughter's sale in this sequence — drawn from *Mishpatim* into the context of *Behar* — itself conveys the gravity of the situation. That a man should be reduced to selling his daughter is presented not neutrally but as a marker of how far one can fall through the progressive neglect of *mitzvot*.

---

## Redemption Mandate

### Stone After Fall

Returning to the question of whether we should be strict on the redemption price because of the *chet* that brought the *eved* to this position: perhaps, since this person has descended all the way to the service of a pagan temple, we should simply seal his fate — *eima lidchi even achar ha-nofel*, let us throw a stone after the one who has already fallen. This idiom evokes the image of *sekilah* — pushing someone off a cliff and then throwing a stone on top of them — and is the Talmud's way of articulating the impulse to give up on someone who has fallen so far.

### Acharei Nimkar

The *gemara* rejects this: *talmud lomar, acharei nimkar ge'ulah tihyeh lo, echad me-echav yig'alenu* — after he is sold, redemption shall be his; one of his kinsmen shall redeem him. Even at this lowest point, the Torah mandates our responsibility to redeem him. The obligation does not expire with his degradation.

### Mandate Conclusion

Given this strong redemptive mandate, the *gemara* concludes, it follows that the Torah intends to make redemption as accessible as possible — and therefore the lower of the two prices applies. A Torah that commands us to redeem him must intend that the price of redemption not be set at the maximum. The principle of *lekula* is thus not merely a formal reading of competing *pesukim*; it flows from the Torah's fundamental orientation toward enabling the *eved ivri*'s return to freedom.

---

## Two Psukim

### Value Increased

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a direct derivation from the *pesukim* themselves: *im od rabot ba-shanim, le-fihem yashiv ge'ulato mi-kesef miknato* — if there are many years, he shall return his redemption according to them from the money of his purchase. The word *rabot* — many or increased — refers not to the number of years remaining but to the increase in his value *over the years*. If his value has increased during the years of his service — *nitraba kaspo ba-shanim* — we use *mi-kesef miknato*, the original purchase price, which is the lower amount.

### Value Decreased

Conversely, *ve-im me'at nish'ar ba-shanim* — if his value has decreased over the years — *ke-fi shanav yashiv et ge'ulato*, the redemption follows his current value, which is the lower amount. In both cases, the operative *pasuk* directs us to the figure that is more favorable to the *eved*. The two *pesukim* thus work in tandem: one covers the case of rising value, the other covers falling value, and in each case the result is the lower price.

### Pshat Rejected

The *gemara* considers an alternative reading: perhaps the *pesukim* simply refer to how many years remain in the six-year term. If many years remain, use the purchase price; if few years remain, use the current price. The *gemara* rejects this as the correct reading. If the Torah meant only *shanim* — years — it would have written simply *shanim*. The use of the phrase *ba-shanim* — in the years, over the course of the years — indicates a change in value *over time*, not merely the quantity of remaining years. *Nitraba kaspa ba-shanim* — his value increased over the years — or *nitmeit kaspa ba-shanim* — his value decreased over the years — is what is being indicated by the distinctive phrasing.

### K'Sinai Derasha

Rav Yosef closes the discussion with a remarkable accolade: *darshinhu Rav Nachman le-hani kra'ei ke-Sinai* — Rav Nachman interpreted these *pesukim* as if the interpretation came directly from Sinai. It is a fitting conclusion to a discussion that began with Abaye's boast of being like Ben Azzai in the marketplaces of Tiberias. In the event, it is Rav Nachman — not Abaye — who produces the decisive reading of the *pesukim*, and not a word of Abaye's brilliant answer appears in the *gemara*'s resolution.

---

## Moral Synthesis

### Moral Tensions

The *gemara* on this *daf* presents the institution of *eved ivri* within a carefully constructed moral frame that holds two orientations in tension simultaneously. On one hand, there is censure. The teaching of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina traces a downward spiral from the violation of *shemitah* law — not even the primary prohibition, but its secondary dust — through the progressive loss of property, dignity, and autonomy. Each stage is marked by the failure to perceive, or later even to be capable of perceiving, that sin is the cause of the descent. Selling one's daughter appears in this sequence as one of the lowest points before the final degradation of selling oneself, and the moral weight of that inclusion is unmistakable.

On the other hand, the Torah's response to this situation is not abandonment or additional punishment. The mandate *acharei nimkar ge'ulah tihyeh lo* — after he is sold, redemption shall be his — asserts that even at the bottom of the pit, the obligation of kinship and community toward the fallen person does not expire. And the principle of *ki tov lo imach* — that the *eved ivri* must be treated as an equal, fed the same food, given the same drink, afforded the same shelter, and in the edge case described by *Tosafot*, actually given priority — transforms the institution from one of domination into something closer to its opposite. *Kol ha-koneh eved ivri ke-koneh adon le-atzmo*: the buyer takes on a master, not a servant.

These two strands — the moral censure embedded in the path that leads to servitude, and the radical demands of dignity and ease of redemption placed upon the master — do not resolve into a single clean principle. The *gemara* holds them together. The *eved ivri* has, in the fullest sense, brought this upon himself through repeated, unrepentant transgression. And yet the Torah's response is not to make his bondage harsher or his redemption harder, but to surround him with obligations of equal treatment and to mandate his redemption at the lowest possible price. The institution of *eved ivri* thus encodes within its very laws a kind of redemptive compassion — a social and halachic structure that acknowledges moral failure while refusing to use that failure as license for cruelty or indifference.

---

---

# Kiddushin 21

## Partial Redemption

### Rav Huna's Question

The daf opens on 21b, picking up mid-discussion of the *eved Ivri*. The most recent topic had established that when redeeming a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew, the redemption amount is calculated based on years of service remaining, priced at the lesser of the original purchase price or the current market value. The Gemara had also articulated, in terms that are partly *aggadata* and partly *halacha*, that one who purchases an *eved Ivri* must treat him at least as well as himself — a pointed disincentive.
