The *parsha* of Behar makes clear that selling oneself into slavery is a consequence of the most desperate circumstances, and yet even when a person has fallen so low as to sell himself to *ovdei avodah zarah* — to a household of idolatry — the obligation to redeem him remains.

It is worth pausing here to note the precise scope of the Torah's explicit provisions. The Torah specifies that relatives bear an obligation to redeem in only two cases: where a person sells a *sdeh achuza* (an ancestral field), and where a person sells himself into slavery to a non-Jew. The cases of a house sold in a walled city and of a Hebrew slave sold to a fellow Jew are not addressed explicitly. These gaps will drive much of the Gemara's subsequent inquiry.

The daf begins with a question posed by Rav Huna bar Hinena to Rav Sheshet: *eved Ivri hanimkar le-ovdei kochavim* — a Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew — can he be redeemed *lachatza'in*, partially, or not? The question is grounded in a potential *gezerah shavah*: the word *ge'ulato* appears both in the context of the *sdeh achuza* and in the context of the *eved Ivri* sold to a non-Jew. By the *sdeh achuza*, the verse says *u-matza k'dei ge'ulato* — he must find the sufficient funds for full redemption — implying that only the complete amount suffices, and partial redemption is ineffective. Should we apply this rule via *gezerah shavah* to the *eved Ivri* as well, or does the *gezerah shavah* function only to import leniencies and not stringencies?

### Rashi's View

Before the Gemara develops its own scenario, it is worth noting that Rashi understands *nigal lachatza'in* in a rather striking way. Rashi explains that the question is whether, if a slave has managed to accumulate funds sufficient to buy back only half his remaining value, he can pay that amount and thereby reduce his remaining term of service by half. In other words, if four years remain and he can pay the equivalent of two years, can he simply buy back two years and go free after two years rather than four? That is Rashi's reading — and it is quite radical. As we will see, the Gemara's actual scenario operates differently.

### Price Fluctuation Case

The scenario the Gemara itself develops is as follows. Suppose a slave has four years of service remaining, currently valued at 100. He pays 50 — half the current value. Then the market rises and he is now worth 200. How much must he pay to complete his redemption? If the initial payment of 50 constituted a genuine partial buyback — if *nigal lachatza'in* applies — then he has already purchased back half of himself. The remaining half is now worth 100 (half of 200), and that is all he must pay. His total outlay is 150. If, however, partial redemption is invalid and that initial payment of 50 had no legal effect, he must now pay the full 200 to redeem himself — less the 50 already advanced, meaning an additional 150, for a total of 200.

### Abaye's Analysis

Abaye then develops both the lenient and stringent dimensions of *nigal lachatza'in*. Consider the lenient case: the slave was purchased for 100. He pays 50 (half the value), and then the market rises so that he is now worth 200. If the initial payment counted as a partial buyback, he only owes an additional 100 to complete his redemption. If it did not, he must pay an additional 150.

The Gemara, however, immediately raises a difficulty with this scenario: we have already established that one always calculates the redemption price at the *lesser* of the original purchase price and the current market value. So even without the partial buyback concept, if the market has risen to 200 but the purchase price was only 100, you go by the purchase price of 100 — the partial payment question would be irrelevant.

### Abaye's Analysis (continued)

The Gemara therefore refines the scenario to make the question meaningful: the slave was originally purchased at 200 (the market was high), then the market dropped and he paid 50 when his value had fallen to 100, and now the market has recovered to 200 again. In this situation, both the original purchase price and the current market value are 200 — so the lesser-of-two-values rule provides no relief. Now the question of partial redemption becomes decisive. If his earlier payment of 50 constituted a valid partial buyback, he has already paid for a portion of himself at the favorable lower price, and the remaining amount owed is correspondingly reduced. If that payment had no effect, he faces the full 200 (less what he deposited). This is the scenario — analogized to a mortgage — where the partial redemption question carries real halachic weight.

### Lesser Price Rule

This explains the Gemara's point that the lesser-of-two-values rule, while important, does not resolve the *nigal lachatza'in* question in every case. Where the market has fluctuated and returned to the original sale price, both benchmarks converge and the slave must look to whether his installment payment constituted a meaningful partial buyback.

### Complex Scenario

The structure also explains what the Gemara means by the *stringent* side of *nigal lachatza'in*. Suppose the slave was purchased for 200 and pays 100 immediately (half his value at the time). Then the market falls and he is worth only 100. If the initial payment of 100 counted as a partial buyback, he has bought back exactly half of himself — but at the then-current price. The remaining half is now worth only 50, so he pays another 50 and goes free, for a total outlay of 150. If, however, the partial payment had no legal effect, the 100 he gave was simply held in escrow, and since his full value has now dropped to 100, that 100 is sufficient to redeem him entirely. He ends up paying exactly what he gave — 100 total — which is *less* than the 150 he would pay under the partial buyback model. So here, *nigal lachatza'in* would actually work to his detriment.

### Market Timing

The Gemara's point is that if partial redemption is valid, a slave can engage in strategic market timing: accumulate funds, monitor his own market value, and purchase back portions of himself when prices are favorable. The Gemara does not, however, resolve the underlying question — whether *nigal lachatza'in* is valid for an *eved Ivri* sold to a non-Jew. What it establishes is that the question is real and consequential, and that Rashi's understanding (that partial payment reduces one's remaining years of service) differs from the Gemara's own scenario (which frames the question as one of financial accounting for the redemption sum).

---

## Walled Cities Halakha

### Extending Paradigm

The same question — *nigal lachatza'in* or not — is then posed with respect to a house sold in a walled city: *ha-mocher bayit be-vatei arei chomah*, can it be redeemed partially? Again the *gezerah shavah* of *ge'ulato ge'ulato* from the *sdeh achuza* is invoked, arguing that just as the ancestral field cannot be redeemed halfway, so too the walled-city house cannot be. Or perhaps the *gezerah shavah* imports the rule only in one direction?

Rav Sheshet answers that the matter can be resolved from the *drasha* of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one may borrow money to redeem (*loveh ve-goel*) and that one may redeem halfway (*goel lachatza'in*) — two distinct rules — in the case of *makdish sadeh*, a field one has consecrated to the Temple treasury.

The Gemara cites the *baraita*: from the verse *im gaol yigal ish* (Vayikra 27) — the doubled language — we learn *melamed she-loveh ve-goel ve-goel lachatza'in*: one may borrow money and redeem, and one may redeem in installments. This stands in contrast to the rule for *sdeh achuza*, where *u-matza k'dei ge'ulato* teaches that you may not borrow (the money must be one's own, newly acquired) and you may not redeem partially.

### Rabbi Shimon Logic

Rabbi Shimon then provides the underlying rationale. By the *sdeh achuza*, the seller is in a position of strength: *im higia yovel velo nig'ala chozeret le-ba'alah ba-yovel* — if the field is not redeemed by the *Yovel*, it reverts to the owner anyway. Because the seller will recover the property regardless, the Torah does not need to be lenient with him beforehand — it can afford to make redemption harder (only full amount, only own money). By contrast, by *makdish sadeh*, if the field is not redeemed before *Yovel*, it goes to the *Kohanim* permanently. The seller's position is weak. And it is precisely because his position is weak — *hura kocho* — that the Torah compensates by making redemption easier: *she-loveh ve-goel ve-goel lachatza'in*.

### Strength Comparison

The Gemara then applies this logic to *batei arei chomah*: a house in a walled city that is not redeemed within the first year is permanently forfeited — *nechlat* — to the purchaser. The seller's position is extremely weak. Therefore, following Rabbi Shimon's logic of counterbalancing: since his position is so weak, the Torah should grant him the rights of partial redemption and borrowing. This is the power of *darshinan ta'ama de-kra* — reasoning from the underlying principle of a verse to apply it to cases not explicitly mentioned.

The comparison across categories is illuminating. By *sdeh achuza*, the buyback window runs from year 3 until *Yovel* (the first two years being closed to buyback). By *batei arei chomah*, the buyback window is only year 1. By *makdish sadeh*, the buyback window runs from the moment of consecration all the way through *Yovel* — the largest possible window. Rabbi Shimon's logic runs: a larger buyback window means a stronger position, hence more stringent conditions; a smaller window means a weaker position, hence more generous conditions.

### Baraita's Logic

A *baraita*, however, presents the opposite logic. By *sdeh achuza*, the seller has strength — the field returns at *Yovel* — and yet the halacha is stringent (full amount, own money). By *makdish sadeh*, the seller's position is weak — he loses it at *Yovel* — so one might have argued by *kal va-chomer* that the rules should be even stricter. But the doubled language *gaol yigal* teaches that in fact the rules are more lenient. This *baraita*'s logic is the mirror image of Rabbi Shimon's: it reasons that where the category is already strong, the accompanying rules are strict; where it is weak, one might expect still stricter rules — but the verse intervenes to grant leniency.

The *baraita* also invokes *batei arei chomah* as part of its argument structure: even though one can redeem a house in a walled city within the first year (which sounds like strength), nevertheless the halacha is stringent there (no borrowing, no partial redemption). This shows that the ability to buy back does not automatically generate the favorable rules — and therefore even the stronger case of *makdish sadeh* would not logically derive those rules without a verse.

### Rabbanan vs. Rabbi Shimon

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction simply: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. One *baraita* represents the position of the Rabbis, the other reflects Rabbi Shimon. The Rabbis hold that strength goes with strength and weakness goes with weakness — a category that is already weak in one respect will also be weak in terms of redemption rights. Rabbi Shimon holds a counterbalancing logic: a category that is weak in one respect deserves to be given *more* redemption rights, to offset the disadvantage. Accordingly, under Rabbi Shimon, *batei arei chomah* — whose one-year window is a severe limitation — is precisely the category where borrowing and partial redemption are permitted. Under the Rabbis, that same weakness means those rights are withheld. Two *beraitot*, two opinions.

---

## Four Categories Analysis

### Rav Acha Challenge

Rav Acha son of Rava challenges the *baraita*'s argument to Rav Ashi. The *baraita* had used *batei arei chomah* as a proof-case showing that even a category with buyback rights (the one-year window) lacks the special privileges of borrowing and partial redemption. Rav Acha's challenge: *mah le-mocher bayit be-vatei arei chomah she-ken hura kocho le-goel le-olam* — the walled-city house is categorically weak because after year 1, the owner can *never* buy it back. That is a uniquely severe weakness that does not characterize *makdish sadeh* at all. By *makdish sadeh*, the owner can redeem at any point up to *Yovel* — *yafeh kocho le-goel le-olam* — so its redemption window is the strongest of all three categories. One should not need a verse to tell me that the strongest category has the most generous rules; it should follow logically.

The implication: the *baraita*'s use of *batei arei chomah* as a baseline for weakness is flawed, because *batei arei chomah* is uniquely weak in a way that *makdish sadeh* is not. And *sdeh achuza* has its own distinct weakness — it cannot be redeemed in the first two years. Neither weakness of the other two applies to *makdish sadeh*, which is strong across all dimensions.

### Weakness Elimination

Rav Acha the Elder responds to Rav Ashi: *nihadar dina ve-teiti mi-ma'atzad* — cycle through all the cases. *Sdeh achuza* proves that even where the category is strong (returns at *Yovel*), the rules are strict. Ah, but perhaps the *sdeh achuza*'s rule derives from its own weakness — that it cannot be redeemed immediately. And *batei arei chomah* proves that even when there is an immediate buyback right, the strict rule applies. But perhaps that case's strictness derives from the weakness of permanent forfeiture after year 1. Each case has its own distinct weakness, and neither weakness applies to the other case. *Lo re'i zeh ke-re'i zeh* — the unique characteristics of each case differ from the other.

### Generic Halakha

The Gemara therefore proposes a *tzad ha-shaveh*: the common denominator between *sdeh achuza* and *batei arei chomah* is that both appear in the Torah's *parsha* of forced redemptions (*she-nig'alin*), and both require the full amount from one's own funds. Perhaps this is simply a generic rule — whenever something is subject to a forced redemption framework, it cannot be done with borrowed money and cannot be done partially. From this common denominator, one might have derived the same rule for *makdish sadeh* without a verse. The verse *im gaol yigal* is therefore needed to override this inference and teach that *makdish sadeh* is the exception.

### Year Two Factor

Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari presses further against the *tzad ha-shaveh*: *mah le-hatzad ha-shaveh she-bahen she-ken ein kocho le-goel be-shana shniya* — what is common to both of those cases is that neither can be redeemed in the second year. The *sdeh achuza* cannot be redeemed in years 1 and 2; *batei arei chomah* can only be redeemed in year 1, so year 2 is also closed. *Makdish sadeh*, however, can be redeemed in year 2 — in fact, in every year. That is its strength. And it is that strength — the openness of year 2 — that is the common weakness of the other two, and which would logically entitle *makdish sadeh* to the lenient rules. So once again, one should not need a verse.

### Ravina's Argument

Ravina responds: *Eved Ivri yokhiach* — the Hebrew slave sold to a non-Jew is the counterexample that collapses this argument. An *eved Ivri* sold to a non-Jew can be redeemed throughout the full term of his service, including in year 2 — and yet, the halacha (as established earlier in the Gemara via *gezerah shavah* or via the language of *v'nigal kulo*) is that he cannot be redeemed partially and cannot be redeemed with borrowed money. So here is a fourth category — one that *can* be redeemed in year 2, whose window is as broad as *makdish sadeh*'s — and yet it carries the stringent rule. The proposed common denominator (inability to redeem in year 2) therefore cannot be the rationale for the strict rule, because this category lacks that characteristic and yet is equally strict. The strict rule is thus a general feature of all forced redemption frameworks, *makdish sadeh* is the lone exception, and the verse *im gaol yigal* is genuinely necessary to establish that exception.

---

## Relatives' Redemptio (II)

### Relatives Redeem Houses?

Rav Huna bar Hinena poses yet another question to Rav Sheshet: *ha-mocher bayit be-vatei arei chomah* — a house in a walled city — *nigal le-krovim o ein nigal le-krovim*? Can it be redeemed by relatives, or not?

To appreciate the question, one must recall what *ge'ulas krovim* means in practice. The Torah's provision that relatives may redeem is not merely about the family's right to offer money; it is about the legal compulsion placed on the purchaser to accept that money and release the property. A stranger's offer can be declined, but a relative's redemption is binding. The question is: does this power of *ge'ulas krovim* extend beyond the two cases where the Torah mentions it explicitly — *sdeh achuza* and *eved Ivri* sold to a non-Jew — to include *batei arei chomah*?

Again, the *gezerah shavah* of *ge'ulato ge'ulato* from *sdeh achuza* is invoked: just as an ancestral field is not redeemed halfway but *is* redeemed by relatives, so too might we say that the walled-city house is not redeemed halfway and *is* redeemed by relatives. Alternatively, perhaps the *gezerah shavah* was only meant to carry over the *lachatza'in* rule, not the *krovim* rule.

Rav Sheshet answers: the house in a walled city is *not* redeemed by relatives. Without an explicit verse establishing *ge'ulas krovim* for this category, it does not apply.

### Gezerah Shavah

The Gemara immediately challenges this ruling from the verse *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu la-aretz* — "give redemption in everything." What new law does this teach? The proposal: *le-rabot battim ve-eved Ivri* — to include houses and the *eved Ivri* (sold to a Jew) within the framework of *ge'ulas krovim*.

### Inclusive Pasuk

The Gemara entertains this reading: does *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu* extend the scope of *ge'ulas krovim* to *batei arei chomah* and to an *eved Ivri* sold to a Jew? The Gemara initially entertains this and asks *mai lav* — isn't that exactly what the verse is doing?

### Scope vs. Obligation

The Gemara deflects: *lo* — the verse is not extending the scope to new categories. *Batei chatzer* — houses in unwalled cities — are already explicitly comparable to fields by the verse *al sdei ha-aretz yeichashev*, so they do not need a new derivation. And the verse *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu* is not extending *ge'ulas krovim* to *batei arei chomah* at all; rather, it is deepening the *obligation*. It establishes not merely that relatives *may* redeem (a *reshut*), but that they *must* redeem (a *chovah*). The scope remains limited to *sdeh achuza* and *eved Ivri* sold to a non-Jew; the verse adds obligatory force within those categories.

The Gemara then notes the grammatical difficulty with this reading: the word *be-chol* in *u-vekhol ge'ulah* seems naturally to indicate extension of scope (in *all* cases), not deepening of obligation within existing ones. This tension is flagged as a *kashya* — a difficulty that is left standing.

---

## Obligation & Hebrew (II)

### Right vs. Obligation

A *baraita* directly addresses whether relatives' redemption is a *reshut* (a right, discretionary) or a *chovah* (an obligation). The verse *ve-ga'al et mimchar achiv* — "and he shall redeem his brother's sale" — might indicate an obligation. Or perhaps it confers only a right?

### Rabbi Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua derives from the verse *ve-ish ki lo yihiyeh lo go'el* — "a man who has no redeemer" — that relatives may choose not to redeem. This verse contemplates a scenario where a man has relatives but none of them step forward. Since the Torah acknowledges this possibility and addresses what happens in that case (the slave redeems himself when he accumulates sufficient funds), it implicitly confirms that relatives are not obligated — they have a *reshut*, a right to redeem but not an obligation. *She-hareshut be-yado* — the choice is theirs.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer reads *ve-ga'al et mimchar achiv* as establishing a *chovah* — an actual obligation. Then what does *ve-ish ki lo yihiyeh lo go'el* mean? The Gemara resolves: it does not mean he literally has no relatives, since virtually everyone has relatives (*ve-chi yesh adam be-Yisrael she-ein lo go'alim?*). Rather, it describes a situation where no relative is willing to step up — *zeh she-yesh lo ve-eino rotzeh likach* — i.e., one whose relatives are shirking their obligation. And the verse then tells us that even in such a case, the slave himself can eventually redeem himself. Rabbi Eliezer uses *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu* not to extend scope but to establish that the obligation of redemption is universal across the enumerated cases: *ha-katuv kva'o chovah*.

---

## Relatives' Redemptio (II)

### Yigalenu Repetitions

The Gemara turns to another potential source for extending the scope of *ge'ulas krovim*. In the *parsha* dealing with a Jew who sells himself to a non-Jew, the word *yigalenu* appears three times: *o dodo o ven dodo yigalenu*, *o mi-she'ar besaro yigalenu*, *o hisiga yado ve-nigal*. Why three repetitions? The *baraita* proposes: *le-rabot kol ha-ge'ulot she-nig'alu ke-seder ha-zeh* — to include all redemptions that follow this order, i.e., to extend the framework of *ge'ulas krovim* to other categories as well.

The Gemara asks: *mai lav* — doesn't this include *batei arei chomah* and *eved Ivri* sold to a Jew? The Gemara deflects: no, the repetitions are not extending the scope. *Batei chatzerim* and *sdeh achuza* are already explicitly covered. Then why the three repetitions of *yigalenu*? As Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: *karov karov kodem* — to establish the order of priority among relatives. The Torah is teaching that closer relatives take precedence in the obligation to redeem. The verse *ha-karov elav yigalenu* in the *sdeh achuza* section already indicates that a closer relative is preferred, but it does not specify the detailed order. The threefold repetition of *yigalenu* by the case of the *eved Ivri* sold to a non-Jew — *o dodo o ven dodo yigalenu, o mi-she'ar besaro yigalenu* — establishes the specific hierarchical order of which relatives redeem first.

So both potential scope-extensions — *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu* and the triple *yigalenu* — are reinterpreted as doing other work: one establishes the degree of obligation, the other establishes the order of relatives. Neither actually extends *ge'ulas krovim* to the two unaddressed categories.

---

## Obligation & Hebrew (II)

### Rabbi's Teaching

The question of *ge'ulas krovim* for an *eved Ivri* sold to a Jew is taken up next. According to Rabbi (Rebbi), the answer is clear and explicit. Rebbi had taught: *mi she-eino nigal be-eleh nigal be-shesh* — only one who is not redeemed by relatives is released in six years. The converse is equally true: an *eved Ivri* sold to a Jew, who does go out after six years, does *not* go out via *ge'ulas krovim*. Rebbi thus explicitly excludes the Hebrew slave sold to a Jew from the framework of *ge'ulas krovim*. The ruling is: *lo miphrik* — he is not redeemed by relatives.

### Slaves to Jews

The question of *ge'ulas krovim* for an *eved Ivri* sold to a Jew is, however, a live dispute among the Rabbis who have not articulated Rebbi's position. The Gemara asks: do the Rabbis apply a *gezerah shavah* of *sachir sachir* — linking the *eved Ivri* sold to a Jew to the one sold to a non-Jew — and thereby extend *ge'ulas krovim* to the former? Or does *yigalenu* (stated regarding the slave sold to a non-Jew) function exclusively: *le-zeh ve-lo le-acher* — only for this category and not for the other?

The Gemara once again cycles through *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu* and the triple *yigalenu* as potential sources for extending the scope. And once again the Gemara pushes back: *batei chatzerim ve-sdeh achuza be-hedya ksiv* — these are already explicit, and the proposed scope-extensions are doing other work.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi clarifies the final move. The verse *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu* establishes — according to the Gemara's conclusion — that by *eved Ivri* sold to a non-Jew, the relatives' redemption is a *chovah*, not merely a *reshut*, and this ruling holds *even according to Rabbi Yehoshua*. That is a notable shift: Rabbi Yehoshua holds that *ge'ulas krovim* is generally a *reshut* (as in the case of *sdeh achuza*), yet even he agrees that by an *eved Ivri* sold to *ovdei kochavim* it rises to the level of *chovah*. As Rashi explains: *de-lo yitma be-ovdei kochavim* — so that he not become assimilated among the gentiles. The urgency of that concern generates an obligation that the less urgent cases do not.

### Final Conclusion

The Gemara's final resolution: the two potential scope-extending derivations — *u-vekhol ge'ulah titnu* and *yigalenu yigalenu yigalenu* — are both reinterpreted as doing internal work within the two categories that the Torah already mentions. The *bechol* verse deepens the obligation in those categories; the triple *yigalenu* establishes the hierarchical order of *karov karov kodem* — the closer relative redeems first. Neither verse extends *ge'ulas krovim* to *batei arei chomah* or to an *eved Ivri* sold to a Jew. According to the conclusion of the Gemara, those two categories remain outside the scope of *ge'ulas krovim*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 22

## Nirtza Overview

### Nirtza Freedom

The *mishnah* on Kiddushin 22 turns to the *nirtza* — the *eved ivri* whose ear is pierced and who thereby commits to extended service beyond the initial six-year term. The *mishnah* states: *ve'hanirtza nikneh birtziah* — the one who has his ear pierced is acquired through that act of piercing, and he then works until the *yovel*. The *gemara* cites the verse: *veratza adonav et ozno bamarzea* — his master shall pierce his ear with an awl.

The *mishnah* further teaches that the *nirtza* acquires his freedom in two ways: through the *yovel* and through the death of the master. The source for freedom at *yovel* is the explicit verse in *Behar*. The source for freedom upon the master's death is the phrase *va'avado* — serve *him* — followed by *velo es haben velo es habas*, meaning not the son and not the daughter. The Rambam notes that *le'olam* does not independently teach that service continues until the *yovel*; rather, it is forced into that reading by the explicit *pasuk* in *Behar*. The *nirtza* relationship, unlike the six-year term which carries the character of *schirus* (hired work), involves a more total form of ownership — and correspondingly, the death of the master brings it to an end in a way that differs from the ordinary six-year arrangement, where service can in certain circumstances continue for the master's son.

### Piercing Tools

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *ein li ela marzea* — I would only know that an awl is valid. The *tanna* then asks: how do we know to include *hasol* (which Rashi identifies as a piece of wood), *hasira* (a thorn), *hamachat* (a needle), *hamakdeach* (some other type of piercing implement), and *hamichtav* (a stylus)? The answer is *talmud lomar velakachta* — the word "and you shall take" comes to include anything that can be taken by hand. This is the position of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda.

Rabbi, however, takes a different view: *mah marzea meyuchad shel matechet af kol shel matechet* — just as the awl is specifically of metal, so too anything valid for this purpose must be of metal, excluding the wooden implements mentioned above. The *baraita* adds a further point: *davar acher* — *hamartzea lehavi hamarzea hagadol* — the definite article *ha-* in *hamartzea* comes to include even a large awl, though the precise significance of this will emerge below.

### Piercing Location

Rabbi Elazar Yudan Beribbi — Rashi explains that *beribbi* denotes a man of prestige — taught that when the piercing is performed, it is done only in the *milsa*, the soft hanging lobe of the ear, not in the cartilage or main body of the ear itself.

The *chachamim* disagree and adduce a compelling proof: *ein eved ivri kohen nirtza mipnei shena'aseh ba'al mum* — a *kohen* who is an *eved ivri* does not undergo the *retziah* because it would render him a *ba'al mum*. Now, if the piercing were done in the lobe — as one would do for an earring — it would not disqualify a *kohen* from Temple service. The fact that the *halacha* excludes a *kohen* because of *ba'al mum* is therefore proof that the piercing is done in the ear itself, in the place where a permanent hole does indeed constitute a disqualifying blemish. The principle is stated directly: *ein retziah ela begova shel ozen* — the piercing is only in the height, that is, the upper body, of the ear.

The Ramban connects this discussion to the matter of the large *marzea*: once the possibility of using a large awl is introduced, the question of *ba'al mum* for a *kohen* becomes acute. Rabbi Elazar Yudan Beribbi's response was that the *retziah* must therefore be in the lobe. The *chachamim* counter that the *halacha* excluding a *kohen* from *retziah* entirely proves the location is precisely where a *ba'al mum* can result.

### Metal vs. Other

The *gemara* now addresses the underlying hermeneutic dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda. What exactly divides them?

*Rebbi doresh klal uprat* — Rabbi employs the hermeneutic of *klal u'prat u'klal*, general-specific-general. In the verse, *velakachta* is a *klal* (general statement); *marzea* is the *prat* (specific); and *be'ozno uvadelet* — the ear and the door — constitutes a return to the general. The operative rule is: *klal u'prat u'klal iy ata dan ela ke'ein haprat* — one may include only what resembles the specific case. Since the *marzea* is of metal, anything of metal qualifies, and nothing else does.

The mechanics of this principle are worth pausing on. When a *klal* is followed by a *prat* alone — general then specific — the result is that we follow the specific. Similarly, a *prat* followed by a *klal* — specific then general — leaves us with the general. It is only when the pattern is general-specific-general that the principle of *ke'ein haprat* applies: one generalizes, but only to what is similar in kind to the specific item named. By identifying the *marzea* as the controlling *prat*, and metal as its defining characteristic, Rabbi concludes that any metal implement is valid.

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, *doresh ribui u'miut* — employs the hermeneutic of expansion and contraction. He reads the same words but frames them not as *klal* and *prat* but as *ribui* (expansive language) and *miut* (contracting language). *Velakachta* expands; *marzea* contracts; *be'ozno uvadelet* expands again. When the structure is *ribui-miut-ribui*, the result is *riba hakol* — nearly everything is included. What is excluded? *Miet sam* — something that achieves the piercing not through a pointed implement but through an entirely different mechanism, such as burning with acid. The contracting term does not define a category of similar items; it merely excludes what is most dissimilar. Because the middle term functions as a contraction rather than a specification, it does not require that other valid implements resemble the *marzea* in material. Wood is therefore not excluded under this reading.

The conceptual difference is subtle but real. Under *klal u'prat u'klal*, the specific term anchors the interpretation — everything valid must be *like* it. Under *ribui u'miut u'ribui*, the middle term only contracts the outer expansiveness; it does not define the genus. This places the *ribui u'miut* method one step further toward inclusion than *klal u'prat u'klal*.

### Big Martzea

The *gemara* inquires: *mai mashma* — how does one derive from the word *hamartzea* (with the definite article) that it includes a large awl? The answer is by analogy to Rava's principle regarding *gid hanasheh*: just as *asher kaf hayarech* — "the thigh" — singles out the prominent one, the right thigh, so too *hamartzea* singles out the prominent *marzea*, the significant or large one. The *gemara* then returns to the positions of Rabbi Elazar Yudan Beribbi and the *chachamim* as already analyzed above, affirming that the *halacha* excludes a *kohen* from *retziah* because of *ba'al mum*, which in turn proves the piercing is performed in the upper portion of the ear.

---

## Kohen Restrictions

### Kohen Nirtza

Having established that a *kohen eved ivri* cannot become *nirtza* because it would render him a *ba'al mum*, the *gemara* asks where the prohibition against making him a *ba'al mum* comes from in the first place. There is indeed a prohibition against creating a *mum b'kodashim* — a blemish in sacrificial animals — but what is the source for the prohibition against causing a *kohen* to become a *ba'al mum*, even though such a blemish would disqualify him from *ha'avoda*?

Rabba bar Rav Shila answers from the verse: *veshav el mishpachto* — he shall return to his family. This refers to the *eved ivri* going free at *yovel*, and the *gemara* understands it as meaning *lemuchzak sheb'mishpachto* — he must return to the status he held within his family before his servitude. Since a *kohen eved ivri* who becomes *nirtza* would be pierced in the upper ear and rendered a *ba'al mum*, foreclosing his return to priestly service, the verse's requirement that he be restored to his prior status prohibits this outcome.

### Kohen & Shifcha

The *gemara* now poses a fresh question: *eved ivri kohen mahu sheyimsor lo rabo shifcha kna'anit* — may a master assign a non-Jewish female slave to a *kohen* who is an *eved ivri* for the purpose of fathering children? The Torah permits a master to do this for an ordinary *eved ivri* (as stated: *im adonav yiten lo isha*), but the question is whether this permission extends to a *kohen*.

The case is a *chiddush* to begin with: ordinarily there is a prohibition against a man having sexual relations with a non-Jewish slave, rooted in the verse *lo yikadesh velo yikadesha*. The Torah's permit for the *eved ivri* overrides this *issur*. Does this override apply equally to a *kohen*, or do the *kohen*'s additional *mitzvos* — particularly the restrictions on the women he may marry or engage with — place him outside the scope of this permission? The Torah's focus in those laws is on marriage, and while this arrangement is not formal *kiddushin*, it approximates a quasi-marital relationship; *chazal* might well understand this woman to fall within the category of *zona* as they apply it to a *kohen*.

Rav says *mutar* — it is permitted. Shmuel says *assur* — it is forbidden.

### Challenge to Shmuel

Rav Nachman challenged the report of Shmuel's ruling: *ki havisos b'bei Mar Shmuel b'askamderi itatlisos* — when you were in Shmuel's house you must have been distracted (Rashi says *askamderi* refers to cards; the *Aruch* reads it as playing with puppies). You weren't paying attention, because had you been, you would have immediately challenged Shmuel. The challenge is straightforward: *chachamim omrim ein eved ivri kohen nirtza mipnei shena'aseh ba'al mum* — the *chachamim* teach that a *kohen eved ivri* cannot become *nirtza* because it would make him a *ba'al mum*. But why is that the *only* reason he cannot become *nirtza*? If Shmuel were right that a *kohen* cannot be given a *shifcha kna'anit*, then the *kohen eved ivri* could never satisfy the condition of *ahavti et adoni et ishti ve'et banai* — which, as we will see, requires that he actually have been given a slave wife and fathered children — and so the inability to become *nirtza* would have an entirely different and more basic cause. The fact that the *chachamim* locate the sole disqualification in the *ba'al mum* concern proves that the other preconditions *can* be met for a *kohen* — and that means the *shifcha kna'anit* is permitted to him. *Ve'su lo midi* — there is nothing more to say: Shmuel's position is untenable.

### Yefat To'ar

Still in the vein of a *kohen*'s sexual restrictions, the *gemara* asks: *kohen mah b'yefas to'ar* — may a *kohen* take a *yefat to'ar*, a captive woman from the battlefield whom he desires? The Torah describes this as a *chiddush* — a special permission extended to soldiers — and the same structural question applies: does this *chiddush* apply equally to a *kohen* and to a *yisrael*, or do the *kohen*'s additional *mitzvos* (particularly regarding forbidden women) exclude him?

Rav again says *mutar*; Shmuel again says *assur*.

The *gemara* then introduces a crucial distinction. As to *biah rishonah* — the first act of sexual relations — *de'chulei alma lo peligi deshari*: everyone agrees it is permitted. The reason: *lo dibrah Torah ela keneged yetzer hara* — the Torah speaks only in concession to the evil inclination. The lust of the moment, the heat of battle, the desire expressed in the verse *vachashakta bah* — all of this demands some concession, and the Torah provides it equally to *kohen* and *yisrael* alike.

The dispute between Rav and Shmuel concerns *biah shniyah* — the second act of sexual relations. Rav says *mutar*: once the Torah permitted this woman, the permission holds; *ishtarei ishtarei* — what was permitted was permitted. Shmuel says *assur*: by the time of the second act, the woman has gone through the process described in the *pesukim* — she cried for her parents, mourned her prior life, and converted — *de'hava lah giyores*, she has now become a *giyores*. And a *giyores* is precisely one of the women forbidden to a *kohen*, since *chazal* understood *zona* (one of the categories the *kohen* may not marry) to include a *giyores*. Whatever the Torah permitted was the *yefat to'ar* as a non-Jewish captive; it did not and could not permit the *kohen* to marry a *giyores*, which is a distinct and ongoing *issur*.

An alternative formulation of the dispute reverses the terms: according to *ika d'amri*, everyone agrees the *biah shniyah* is forbidden to a *kohen*, since by then she is a *giyores*; the dispute is whether the *biah rishonah* is permitted. Rav holds it is, since the Torah's concession to *yetzer hara* applies to *kohen* no less than to *yisrael*. Shmuel holds it is not: *kol heikha delo karinan beih ve'aveisa el toch beisecha lo karinan beih vera'isa bashivyah* — wherever the complete process (taking her home, completing the marriage) is not available to a man, the initial permission of *vera'ita bashivyah* never applied to him at all. For a *kohen*, since the *biah shniyah* and formal marriage are foreclosed, the Torah never extended the first concession either.

### When Sex Occurs

This discussion raises a deeper question about exactly when in the *pasuk*'s sequence the two acts of *biah* occur. The *pesukim* in *Devarim* read: *vera'ita bashivyah eshet yefat to'ar vachashakta bah velakachta lecha le'ishah veheveisa el toch beisecha* — and then only *ve'achar ken tavo eleha uvealtah* — and afterwards you may come to her and possess her. On a straightforward reading, all sexual relations occur after the entire process: bringing her home, the mourning period, and implicit conversion. The phrase *velakachta lecha le'ishah* means "take her to be your wife," initiating the process, not consummating a sexual act.

Yet *chazal*'s framework of *biah rishonah* before the conversion process requires locating a first act of sex somewhere prior to *veheveisa el toch beisecha*. The *gemara* understands this from *lo dibrah Torah ela keneged yetzer hara* combined with *vachashakta bah* — the lust of the moment demands an outlet that the Torah acknowledges. The exact verse from which *biah rishonah* is derived at the battlefield remains somewhat oblique, but the conceptual structure is that the Torah could not have withheld all concession from the man at the height of his desire.

The *baraita* addresses this through the phrase *besha'at shivyah* — at the moment of captivity — which anchors the first act to the battlefield. The word *melamed shelo yichtzenah bamilchamah* — he should not press/force her *bamilchamah* — is then difficult to interpret if one holds that the first act of sex does occur there. Three explanations emerge from the *rishonim*. The Rambam understands it to mean he should not do it there in the open battlefield but should take her somewhere more removed, though still before the formal process begins. A second approach attributed to the Re'em holds that *lo yichtzenah bamilchamah* means the Torah's permission for the first act of sex is conditional on her consent — she must agree at that moment, making it not an act of violent rape even if the context is inherently coercive. A third opinion understands it as limiting the first act to a single occurrence.

### Yetzer Hara Concession

Rashi's position, however, stands apart from all of these. Rashi reads *melamed shelo yichtzenah bamilchamah* straightforwardly: do not have sexual relations with her in battle at all. Wait until she has been brought home and completed the full process. On this reading there is no *biah rishonah* in the battlefield; all sexual relations occur after the *giyurus* is complete. The Torah's concession to *yetzer hara* lies not in permitting immediate sex on the battlefield but in establishing a formal process that channels the desire toward a legitimate outcome rather than leaving the woman as a sexual slave. The distinction between *biah rishonah* and *biah shniyah* for the *kohen* would then not be a chronological before-and-after conversion, but rather a matter of whether the Torah intended to permit even a single act (given the *kohen*'s prohibitions) or only ongoing marital relations — with the answer perhaps being that once is thinkable but the ongoing marriage is not.

The *Yerushalmi* actually records both of these as distinct opinions among the *tana'im*, which maps onto the debate between Rashi and the other *rishonim* in the *bavli*.

### Lesser of Two Evils

On 22a, the *gemara* articulates the underlying logic of the *yefat to'ar* concession through a vivid analogy: *mutav sheyochlu Yisrael basar temutos shechutos ve'al yochlu basar temutos neveilos* — better that Jews should eat meat from an animal that was going to die and was slaughtered while still alive, than that they should eat the meat of an animal that died without *shechita* and became a *neveilah*. The image is striking: a *treifa* on the verge of death, slaughtered at the last moment — the meat is technically *mutar*, but no one is pleased with the situation. The alternative, allowing it to die and become *neveilah*, is worse. So too here: the Torah fashions a barely-permissible path — forced *giyurus*, a quasi-consensual union — because the alternative, a man simply taking a non-Jewish woman as a permanent sexual slave or intermarrying with her outside of any conversion process, would be worse.

This line has been invoked by *poskim* in later generations when confronted with situations where the only available option is undesirable but the alternative is even more prohibited.

### Conversion Prevention

The Ramban develops a more structured account of what *issur* the Torah is protecting against. The verse says *vachashakta bah velakachta lecha le'ishah* — the man actually wants to *marry* this woman, not merely have a momentary encounter with her. The real danger is that without the Torah's intervention, he would keep her and marry her as a non-Jewish woman, violating *lo titchaten bam* — the prohibition of intermarriage. The Torah therefore channels the desire through a process of *giyurus*, even if effectively compelled, that places the union on a halakhically legitimate footing. The *biah rishonah*, too, is part of this framework: it is not purely an independent concession to *yetzer hara* but the beginning of a process that leads to a permissible marriage rather than an ongoing prohibited one. The Ramban further notes the element of *eishes ish*: the *baraita* states *va'afilu eishes ish* — even a woman married to a non-Jewish man is included in the Torah's permission. While the halakhic status of non-Jewish marriage vis-à-vis Jews is complex — the institution is recognized as part of *sheva mitzvos bnei Noach* but does not create a Jewish-law *issur* of *eishes ish* for a Jewish man — the Ramban explains that this is not a technical halakhic point. Rather, the Torah is emphasizing how far the concession extends: even in a case that is more *mechuar*, more morally degraded — tearing a woman from her husband — the Torah permits the process because the alternative (permanent forbidden cohabitation) is worse.

---

## Declaration & Conditions

### Timing of Declaration

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: the verse says *amar yomar ha'eved* — the slave shall say, shall say — teaching that he must make his declaration twice. Moreover, if he declared at the *beginning* of the six years and not at the end, *eino nirtza* — he does not undergo *retziah*. The source is *lo etzei chofshi* — he must say "I do not wish to go free" at the *moment of going free*, meaning at the conclusion of the six years.

Conversely, if he declared only at the end and not at the beginning, he also cannot become *nirtza*. The reason given is *shene'emar ha'eved* — it must be said *ke'shehu eved*, while he is still a slave. This initially seems strange, since at the end of six years he is still technically a slave. The *gemara* then poses the obvious objection: *atu sof shesh lav eved hu* — at the end of six years is he not a slave?

This leads directly to Rava's explanation.

### Last Penny Standard

Rava resolves the apparent contradiction: *bitchilas pruta achrona bsof pruta achrona* — the terms "beginning" and "end" refer not to the beginning and end of the six-year period, but to the beginning and end of the *last penny's worth* of service. When enough time remains that the master still has a monetary claim worth at least a *pruta* against the slave, the slave is fully an *eved* — but he is not yet at the *sha'at yetziah*, the moment of imminent departure. Once the slave has entered the last unit of time — the final hour or fraction of time worth less than a *pruta* — he is at the cusp of freedom and satisfies *lo etzei chofshi*, but he is no longer fully *ha'eved* in the complete proprietary sense.

To satisfy *both* requirements simultaneously, the declaration must be made at the precise juncture: before the last *pruta*'s worth expires (so that he is still fully an *eved*) and after all prior conditions — wife and children — are already in place. The precision required here is striking, and one senses that the halakha is not designed to make the path to *nirtza* an easy one.

### Wife & Children

A *baraita* sets out additional conditions. If the slave has a wife and children (the *shifcha kna'anit* and the children born from that union) but his master does not, *eino nirtza* — the process cannot proceed. The source is *ki ahevcha ve'et beisecha* — "because he loves you and your household" — implying the master must also have a household that parallels his own.

Conversely, if the master has a wife and children but the slave does not, *eino nirtza* — he cannot say *ahavti et adoni et ishti ve'et banai*. As noted above, this is precisely why the *gemara* proved that even a *kohen eved ivri* must be permitted a *shifcha kna'anit*: the *only* reason the *chachamim* gave for excluding a *kohen* from *nirtza* was *ba'al mum*, proving that the preliminary stage of wife and children is available to him.

### Love & Health

The conditions extend to the relational and physical. If the slave loves his master but his master does not love him, *eino nirtza* — the verse *ki ahevcha* ("because he loves you") requires the master's affection to be genuine. If the master loves the slave but the slave does not love his master, *eino nirtza* — the verse *ki tov lo imach* ("for it is good for him with you") must be true, and it cannot be if the slave is not genuinely content. The slave may have pragmatic reasons for wishing to remain — he loves his wife and children, he has no prospects outside — but if he cannot sincerely say he loves his master, the *retziah* is unavailable.

Similarly, if the slave is ill and his master is not, *eino nirtza* — *ki tov lo imach* cannot be said when he is suffering. If the master is ill and the slave is not, *eino nirtza* — *imach* requires good conditions on the master's side as well. The case of both being ill simultaneously is posed as a *ba'aya* by Rav Bibi bar Abaye: is *imach* a requirement of equality, such that if both are equally ill the condition is met, or does *ki tov lo* mean that the situation must be genuinely good — not merely ill together? The *gemara* leaves this as *teiku*.

### Equal Treatment

A *baraita* then unpacks the phrase *ki tov lo imach* in its material dimensions, and this passage is one of the most celebrated in this entire sugya. *Imach bema'achal* — with you in food; *imach bemishte* — with you in drink; *imach belo'in* — with you in lodging. The slave must receive exactly what the master provides for himself:

*Shelo tehei atah ochel pas nekiyah vehu ochel pas kivar* — you may not eat fine white bread while he eats coarse bran bread. *Atah shoseh yayin yashan vehu shoseh yayin chadash* — you may not drink aged wine while he drinks new wine. *Atah yashen al gabei mochin vehu yashen al gabei teven* — you may not sleep on a featherbed while he sleeps on straw.

From here the *gemara* derives the famous principle: *mikan amru kol hakoneh eved Ivri kekoneh adon le'atzmo* — whoever acquires an *eved Ivri* is as if he has acquired a master for himself. The Ramban sharpens this: if there is only one pillow in the house, giving it to oneself would create an inequality, violating *imach*; throwing it away so neither has it would be *middat Sedom*. The slave therefore takes precedence — he receives the single pillow. In that sense the *eved Ivri* is not merely the master's equal but, where resources are limited, his superior.

### Support Obligations

A further *baraita* addresses the master's obligations toward the slave's family. The verse *veyatza imach hu uvanav imo* — he shall leave you, he and his sons with him — prompts Rabbi Shimon to ask: if he was sold into slavery, who sold his sons? They were not sold. Yet the verse says they leave with him at *yovel*, implying they were present throughout the servitude. *Mikan sherabo chayav bemezonos banav* — from here we learn that the master was obligated to provide for the slave's children throughout the period of service.

An identical structure applies to the wife: *im ba'al ishah hu veyatza ishto imo* — if he was married, his wife leaves with him. Rabbi Shimon again asks: who sold his wife? The answer: *mikan sherabo chayav bemezonos ishto* — the master must support the wife as well.

The *gemara* explains why both rulings are necessary. Had the Torah stated only the obligation regarding children, one might have said the wife can find employment and feed herself. Had it stated only the wife, one might have said that since it is not customary for a woman *lehadori* — to go door to door begging — the master need not provide for children, who can beg. Each case is therefore independently required.

---

## Ear-Piercing Mechanics

### Through Ear & Door

A *baraita* analyzes the precise procedure of the *retziah*. Had the verse said only *be'ozno uvadelet* — in his ear and in the door — one might have thought: place his ear against the door and then pierce into the door only, the ear being merely positioned nearby. The word *be'ozno* forces us to require that the ear itself be pierced. But then, had the verse said only *be'ozno*, I might have thought: pierce the ear first, then separately make a hole in the door and align them. *Talmud lomar be'ozno uvadelet* — both together — teaches: *dokeir veholech ad shemmagi'a etzel dalet* — one pierces through the ear and continues until reaching the door. The ear must be pressed against the door, and a single act of piercing passes through both.

### Standing Door

One might have thought the door need not be standing and attached; perhaps even a detached door panel would suffice. *Talmud lomar mezuza* — the verse's juxtaposition with *mezuza* teaches: *mah mezuza me'umad af dalet nami me'umad* — just as a *mezuza* is only called by that name when the doorframe stands in its permanent upright position, so too the door for the *retziah* must be standing, properly installed.

### Ear at Sinai

Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai offered a famous *mashal* — Rashi understands *kemin chomer* as "like a fragrant mixture," meaning a beautifully composed explanation; Tosafot understand it as "like a story" — to illuminate why the ear specifically is the organ chosen for piercing.

*Mah nishtanna ozen mikkol ha'evarim shebaguf* — why was the ear singled out from all the organs of the body? The Holy One, blessed be He, declared: *ozen sheshame'ah koli al har Sinai besha'ah she'amarti ki li benei yisrael avadim velo avadim la'avadim* — the ear that heard My voice at Sinai when I said "the children of Israel are My servants and not servants to servants" — *vehalach zeh veqana adon le'atzmo* — and yet this person went and acquired a master for himself. That ear must be pierced.

The irony is layered: the very foundation of *mishpatim*, which begins with the laws of slavery, is prefaced by *anochi Hashem Elohecha asher hotzetecha me'eretz mitzrayim mibbeit avadim* — I freed you from a house of slaves. The first substantial legislation after *maamad har Sinai* concerns how one frees one's slave after six years. Yet this slave chooses to perpetuate his bondage — and his ear, which heard the proclamation of freedom, is marked accordingly.

### Door as Witness

Rabbi Shimon b'Rebbi offered a parallel *mashal* focusing on the door and doorpost rather than the ear. *Mah nishtanna dalet umezuza mikkol kelim shebabayit* — why were the door and doorpost chosen from all the vessels of the house? The Holy One, blessed be He, declared: *dalet umezuza shehayu edim bemitzrayim besha'ah shepasachti al hamashkof ve'al shetei hamezuzot* — the door and the doorpost were witnesses in Egypt when I passed over the lintel and the two doorposts. *Ve'amarti ki li benei Yisrael avadim velo avadim la'avadim vehotzetim me'avdut lecherut* — I declared they are My servants and freed them from slavery to freedom. *Vehalach zeh veqana adon le'atzmo* — and this one went and acquired a master for himself. *Yeratza bifneihem* — let him be pierced before them, before these witnesses to his people's redemption, witnesses to the fact that he should not be enslaving himself again.

The *mashal* of Rabbi Shimon prompts reflection on the distinction between the initial six-year period and the *retziah*. For the first six years, the slave was a *gannav* who could not pay his debt — he did not choose slavery freely, or he was driven to *moker atzmo* by economic desperation. One can understand, if not excuse, that first entry into servitude. But to then choose *ve'avado le'olam* — to serve forever — is something else entirely, something that demands a symbolic act before these ancient witnesses to say: this choice runs against everything your history and your God intended for you.

---

---

# Kiddushin 23

## Eved Knaani: Kesef, Shta…

### Eved Knaani Status

The *daf* opens by situating the *eved Knaani* within a broader taxonomy of *kinyanim*. The *mishnah* has just concluded its treatment of *kiddushei isha*, *yibum*, and *eved Ivri* — forms of acquisition or obligation that pertain to persons with varying degrees of legal personhood. The *eved Knaani* represents an altogether different category. On one hand, he is treated as fully fungible property: if an object is placed upon an *eved Knaani*, it is as though it were placed on the master's chattel, and the master acquires it through *kinyan chatzer*. On the other hand, the *Torah* insists on a revolutionary principle — this slave remains a human being. He goes free if the master destroys his eye or tooth; in certain circumstances the master may even be *chayav misa*. This dual status, simultaneously property and person, is the defining tension of the entire *sugya*.

### Three Kinyanim

The *mishnah* states: *eved Knaani nikneh be-kesef u-ve-shtar u-ve-chazakah* — a *Canaanite slave* is acquired through money, a legal document, and *chazakah*, an act of taking possession. The *mishnah* further establishes the mechanisms by which the slave may acquire his own freedom. *Ve-koneh et atzmo be-kesef al yedei acheirim* — he may be redeemed through money provided by others, provided the master agrees to accept it. The dynamic here is analogous to *kesef kiddushin*: the amount is entirely at the master's discretion, but once the agreed-upon sum changes hands, the slave goes free.

Regarding the *shtar*: *u-ve-shtar al yedei atzmo, divrei Rabbi Meir* — a writ of manumission (*shtar shichrur*), in which the master writes *harei ata ben chorin*, is delivered directly to the slave. Whether this precludes delivery to others is a question to be resolved in the *gemara*.

*Ve-chachamim omrim: be-kesef al yedei atzmo* — the Sages hold that the slave may redeem himself even with his own money, *u-ve-shtar al yedei acheirim* — and the writ may be delivered through others. The *mishnah* adds: *u-vilvad she-yihyeh ha-kesef mi-shel acheirim* — even when the slave is himself handing money to the master, that money must have originated with others. This is not self-contradictory: *al yedei atzmo* means he himself is the one delivering the payment, but since any money he earns automatically belongs to his master, the only money he can legitimately call his own is money given to him by outsiders — for example, as a gift explicitly designated for him rather than for his master.

### Comparison to Karka

The *gemara* asks *minalan* — what is the biblical source for acquiring an *eved Knaani* through *kesef*, *shtar*, and *chazakah*? The derivation comes from the verse *ve-hisnachaltem otam li-vneichem achareichem la-reshet achuzah* — you shall bequeath them to your children after you as hereditary property (*Vayikra* 25:46). The *katuv* equates the slave to an *sdeh achuzah*, an ancestral field: just as land is acquired through money, document, and *chazakah*, so too is an *eved Knaani*. The comparison to *karka* is deliberate and carries broad halakhic consequences, as throughout *Shas* there is a recurring discussion of whether an *eved Knaani* shares the legal status of *karka* in various contexts.

One might raise the objection: if the *eved Knaani* is like a field, perhaps he should also return to his original owner in the *Yovel*, just as an *sdeh achuzah* does. The *gemara* responds with the verse *le-olam bahem ta'avodu* — you shall work them forever. Unlike *eved Ivri*, for whom the word *le-olam* implied release at *Yovel* given an additional *pasuk*, here there is no such indication, and so the slave remains a permanent acquisition. Crucially, however, he is acquired in the same manner as land — by *kesef*, *shtar*, and *chazakah*. It is also worth noting that *chazakah* did not appear among the methods of acquiring an *eved Ivri*: that *chazakah* — the most demonstrative act of asserting property-like control — is specific to *eved Knaani* underscores just how fully he is treated as property.

### Chalipin Method

A *baraita* adds: *af be-chalipin* — an *eved Knaani* may also be acquired through *chalipin*, whether through an actual exchange of objects or through the symbolic handkerchief transaction in which the acquiring party takes the handkerchief and thereby effects the transfer of ownership. Why did the *tanna* of the *mishnah* omit this? *Milta de-leita be-metaltelin katani, milta de-ita be-metaltelin lo katani* — the *mishnah* wished to list only those modes of acquisition that are distinctive to *karka* and not to *metaltelin* (movable goods). *Chalipin* works for both *karka* and *metaltelin*, and even works for *karka* — though notably not for *ishah* — so it does not belong to the set of *karka*-specific *kinyanim* that the *mishnah* seeks to highlight. The outer *tanna* of the *baraita*, who does include *chalipin*, was willing to broaden the list to anything that works for *karka*, even if it also works for *metaltelin*.

---

## Meshicha & Chazakah

### Shmuel on Meshicha

*Amar Shmuel: eved Knaani nikneh bi-mshichah* — Shmuel holds that an *eved Knaani* may be acquired by *meshicha*, that is, by physically dragging him toward the buyer. This is unmistakably a *kinyan* of *metaltelin*, not of *karka*. The *gemara* defines how it works: *takfo u-va etzlo kna-o* — if you grabbed hold of him and pulled him, you acquire him; *kara-o u-va atzlo lo kna-o* — if you merely called him and he came on his own, you did not acquire him. This distinction will require explanation shortly.

### Why No Meshicha?

The *gemara* observes that Shmuel's ruling coheres with the *mishnah*'s silence on *meshicha*: since *meshicha* is a *kinyan* of *metaltelin*, the *mishnah* — which limited itself to *kinyanim* distinctive to *karka* — naturally omitted it. By the same logic, the outer *tanna* of the *baraita*, who included *chalipin*, still restricted his list to methods that operate for *karka* as well; *meshicha* does not apply to *karka*, so even that *tanna* would not have included it. The omission is thus explained across all opinions. Everyone concedes, it seems, that *meshicha* works — but the *mishnah* and *baraita* were organized around a different taxonomic concern.

### Dehumanization Debate

This is, however, a striking *chiddush* of Shmuel's, and it is worth pausing over its conceptual significance. The *mishnah* grounds the acquisition of an *eved Knaani* in the *pasuk* comparing him to *karka*. Why is *karka* the operative comparison? One might suggest that *karka* was chosen precisely because of the theological resonance of land-ownership: *la-Hashem ha-aretz*, the earth belongs to God; no one truly owns land absolutely, it reverts in *Yovel*. There remains an irreducible gap between the landowner and his land. Movable property is different — once it is in your pocket, in your house, under your full control, the ownership is total and the gap disappears. To treat an *eved Knaani* as *karka* would thus mean that he is never fully objectified; the master's ownership, like ownership of land, retains an element of incompleteness. By contrast, *kinyanim* of *metaltelin* — *meshicha*, *hagbahah* — assert a kind of absolute, intimate dominion that more completely reduces the slave to an object. Shmuel's move to permit *meshicha* therefore deepens the dehumanizing logic rather than ameliorating it, even if Shmuel's intent was purely technical.

### Animals vs. Slaves

This conceptual tension is sharpened by a *baraita* that the *gemara* cites in the context of *meshicha* by animals. How does *meshicha* work for an animal? Grabbing it by the hoof, the hair, the saddle, the saddlebag, the bit, or the bell around its neck constitutes *mesira*. As for *meshicha* itself: calling the animal and having it come, or striking it with a stick so that it runs — once it lifts a leg and takes a step, the acquisition is complete. According to some *tannaim*, it must travel a distance equal to its full height. The critical point is that for animals, calling and having the animal come *does* work as *meshicha*. Why does the same not apply to a slave?

### Will & Personhood

*Behema da'atah de-marah azlah* — an animal has no independent will; when it comes in response to a call, it is simply responding instinctively to the controller's directive, and so the controller's *da'at* is driving the movement. *Eved da'atah de-nafsheih azlah* — the slave, however, decides to listen. Even in a condition of servitude, even where the choice is severely constrained, the slave exhibits something that looks like will, like personhood. Calling him and having him come does not demonstrate that you have taken him as an object under your control, because he is still the one choosing to move toward you. To objectify him — to make him, for the purposes of *kinyan*, like a piece of movable goods — you must physically seize him and drag him. And yet that very act of seizing and dragging is, as observed above, far more dehumanizing. The rule that *meshicha* requires physical dragging thus rests on an acknowledgment of the slave's subjectivity, even as the *kinyan* itself treats him as an object.

### Minor Slave Exception

*Amar Rav Ashi: eved katan ke-vehema dami* — if the slave is a minor, we do not assume he is exercising genuine will; he is more like an animal in this regard. Accordingly, if you call a minor slave and he comes, that would constitute a valid *meshicha* for purposes of acquisition.

---

## Chazakah Examples

### Service Acts

*Tanu rabbanan: keitzad be-chazakah* — the Rabbis teach how *chazakah* functions for an *eved Knaani*. For *karka*, *chazakah* is performed by improving or working the land, such as plowing or repairing a fence. For a slave, the demonstrative act goes in one direction only: the slave performs an act of personal service for the master. The *baraita* enumerates examples: removing the master's shoe (*hin'ilo*), carrying the master's bathing implements to the bathhouse (*holich keilav acharav le-veit ha-merchatz*), undressing the master (*hifshito*), bathing him (*hirchitzo*), anointing him with oil (*sacho*), scraping him (*gerado*), dressing him again (*hilbisho*), and putting his shoe back on. The preponderance of bathhouse scenarios likely reflects the deeply personal, servile nature of the service required — these are acts that only one who stands in a relationship of submission would perform for another.

Whether this list is exhaustive or merely illustrative — whether, for instance, having the slave mow a lawn would also suffice — is not explicitly resolved, though the pattern suggests that any act of personal service would qualify.

### Higbiho & Gevira

The *baraita* continues: *higbiho* — if he lifted him up — *kna-o*, he acquires him. The *gemara* initially finds this ambiguous. *Rabbi Shimon* objects: *lo tehei chazakah gedolah me-hagbahah* — *chazakah* should not be superior to *hagbahah*, which after all effects acquisition in all contexts (*hagbahah konah be-chol makom*). *Rav Ashi* clarifies: the *higbiho* in the list means *higbiho hu le-rabbo kna-o* — the slave lifted the master, which is consistent with the pattern of the slave performing a service. But if the master lifted the slave, *lo kna-o* — that would not constitute *chazakah*. Rabbi Shimon's objection, then, is precisely that if the master lifts the slave, that should work as *hagbahah* — the same *kinyan* that operates for all movable goods. This is, in miniature, the same debate as Shmuel's broader claim: *Rabbi Shimon* among the *tannaim* was already arguing for the applicability of *kinyanei metaltelin* to an *eved Knaani*.

### Bia & Chazakah

Having established that the slave lifting the master constitutes a valid *chazakah*, the *gemara* raises a provocative *hava amina*: *ela me'atah shifchah Knaanit tikneh be-viah* — might sexual intercourse with a female slave constitute a *chazakah* for her acquisition? The reasoning, formally at least, follows from the prior case: in the act, the slave's body supports and effectively elevates the master's body, which could be characterized as a form of *hagbahah*. Moreover, she is performing a kind of service.

### Rejection of Bia

The *gemara* rejects this on the basis that the standard logic of *chazakah* through lifting requires that the act be one-sided: *zeh neheneh ve-zeh mitzta'er* — one party benefits while the other is burdened. Ordinary *hagbahah* is uncomfortable for the one being made to lift; it demonstrates the master's power by imposing effort on the slave. In the case of *bi'ah*, the *gemara* says *zeh neheneh ve-zeh neheneh* — both parties experience pleasure, which disqualifies it from the structure of *chazakah*. The *gemara* then considers whether *shelo ke-darka* (anal intercourse) might change the analysis, since the *gemara* assumes the woman does not derive pleasure from that act. *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba de-min Archei* challenges even this assumption, asking how we know that both parties do not in fact experience pleasure in that act. The *gemara* responds: since the verse uses the formulation *mishkevei ishah*, which is the source for equating *shelo ke-darka* with *ke-darka* across *kol ha-Torah kulloh*, if *ke-darka* does not work for this purpose, *shelo ke-darka* does not either. The entire *hava amina* is, as one must acknowledge, deeply disturbing — not least because it proceeds without directly confronting the reality of rape — but the *gemara*'s technical rejection is firm.

---

## Hindua Case

### Ger Death Scenario

The *gemara* presents a famous case study. *Rav Yehuda Hindua* — *Rashi* explains that *Hindua* renders *Kush*, translated variously as Ethiopia or India, meaning he was a convert from a distant land — was a *ger* who had no heirs, having converted without subsequently having children. He became gravely ill and was clearly near death. *Mar Zutra* came to pay a *bikkur cholim* visit and observed that the man was *takif leih alma* — the world had seized him, meaning he was at the very threshold of death.

The halakhic significance of the moment is immediately apparent. When a *ger* dies without heirs, his property becomes ownerless — *hefker*. His slaves, who had been owned by him, are at that instant no longer owned by anyone, and can therefore acquire themselves as *benei chorin*. To prevent this, a potential acquirer must already be in the middle of a valid *chazakah* at the precise moment of death, so that there is no intervening moment in which the slave becomes free.

*Mar Zutra* therefore said to the slave of *Rav Yehuda Hindua*: take off my shoe (*shalof li masanai*) and bring it to my house (*ve-amtinhu le-veitei*). The journey to the house would take some twenty minutes. If the *ger* died while the slave was in the middle of this act of service, the slave would have had no moment of freedom — he passes directly from performing *chazakah* for *Mar Zutra* without ever becoming ownerless.

### Adult vs. Minor

*Ika d'amri*: some say the slave was an adult (*gadol*). In that reading, *Rashi* explains, the moment the master dies, the adult slave transitions immediately to the control of the living — he is transferred over. *Ve-ika d'amri*: others say the slave was a minor (*katan*). The *Rashi* text reads *u-de-lo ke-Abba Shaul* — not in accordance with *Abba Shaul* — though most other *rishonim* have the *girsa ke-Abba Shaul*.

The *baraita* is cited: if a *ger* died and Jews subsequently seized his property, and among that property were slaves — whether adult or minor — they acquire themselves as *benei chorin*, because there was a gap in time between the death and the seizure. Even a minor slave can acquire himself in that gap. This is the position of the *tanna kamma*. *Abba Shaul* dissents: only adult (*gedolim*) slaves acquire themselves, because an adult has a *yad* — a capacity for legal acquisition of himself. Minors lack that *yad*, and so if there is a gap, their status remains unresolved and anyone who takes possession of them at that point acquires them.

### Tosafot Logic

*Tosafot* and many other *rishonim* read the *girsa* as *ke-Abba Shaul*, and offer a different explanation for why *Mar Zutra* had to be in mid-*chazakah* at the moment of death. Even according to *Abba Shaul*, where a minor cannot acquire himself in the gap, *Mar Zutra* still needed to be in possession at that precise instant — not to prevent the slave from acquiring himself, but to prevent another person from beating him to the acquisition. The story thus reflects a race against other potential claimants, not only against the slave's own potential freedom.

### Gadol vs. Katan

*Tosafot* goes further, however, and argues that the case *must* have involved a *katan*, not a *gadol* — and that this is precisely the point of the reading *ke-Abba Shaul*. Even if *Mar Zutra* had been performing *chazakah* at the exact moment of death, a *gadol* would nonetheless go free. At a deep halakhic and conceptual level, an adult's ownership of himself takes precedence over any *chazakah* being performed upon him at that very moment. The slave's fundamental self-possession reasserts itself the instant the master dies, overriding even a concurrent act of external acquisition. Only in the case of a *katan*, who according to *Abba Shaul* cannot acquire himself, does the *chazakah* of another party prevail. This reading gives the case sharp halakhic logic: the story works only if the slave is a minor, and only according to *Abba Shaul* who holds that minors cannot acquire themselves.

---

## Rabbi Meir Debate

### Rabbi Meir Rules

The *mishnah* now turns to the mechanisms of self-redemption, and here *Rabbi Meir* and the *Chachamim* fundamentally disagree. According to *Rabbi Meir*: *be-kesef al yedei acheirim* — redemption by money requires that the money come from others, not the slave himself; *u-ve-shtar al yedei atzmo* — and the writ of manumission must be delivered directly to the slave. The *gemara* must establish what case is contemplated here and why these particular rules follow.

### No Slave Money

The *gemara* works through *Rabbi Meir*'s position. Is the case one where the third party pays the money without the slave's knowledge or consent (*shelo mi-da'ato*)? A difficulty arises immediately: *Rabbi Meir* holds *chov hu le-eved she-yetzei mi-yad rabo le-cheirus* — that liberation may actually be a *chov*, a detriment, from the slave's perspective. A freed slave takes on additional obligations, loses certain privileges, and may be worse off in various ways; therefore one cannot say *zachin* (operate on someone's behalf without their consent) when it is not clear that freedom is a benefit. A third party cannot receive a *shtar shichrur* on behalf of the slave unless the slave has agreed. So the redemption through third-party money must in fact be *mi-da'ato* — with the slave's knowledge and consent.

What, then, is the *chiddush* of the *mishnah*? *Al yedei acheirim in, adidech atzmo lo* — the news is that only others' money can redeem him; his own money cannot. *Alma ein kinyan le-eved belo rabbo* — according to *Rabbi Meir*, a slave has no proprietary capacity independent of his master. Any money he earns belongs to the master automatically; he cannot possess money in his own right.

### Gito ve-Yado

This raises a sharp question. If the slave cannot own anything — since his hand is, as it were, like his master's hand — how can the master give him a *shtar shichrur* directly? Anything placed in the slave's hand is as though it were placed in the master's own hand. The answer is *gito ve-yado ba'im ke'echad*: in the very moment that the *shtar shichrur* reaches the slave's hand, he simultaneously acquires it and acquires himself. The manumission and the acquisition happen as a single instantaneous event, so there is no logical problem of the slave's hand being an extension of the master's at the moment of receipt. This is the *chiddush* of the *mishnah*'s ruling that *shtar* is *al yedei atzmo* — even though he cannot normally own anything, he can receive his own *shtar shichrur* by virtue of this principle.

But the *mishnah* then seems to be read as excluding third-party delivery of the *shtar*: *al yedei atzmo* but not *al yedei acheirim*. That is puzzling: since the slave has agreed to be freed (*mi-da'ato*), why can a third party not receive the *shtar* on his behalf? The *gemara* brings a *baraita*: *be-shtar al yedei atzmo ve-lo al yedei acheirim, divrei Rabbi Meir* — only *al yedei atzmo*, explicitly excluding others. The reason emerges from the subsequent analysis.

### Abbaye: Kesef Shelo M'Da…

*Amar Abbaye le-olam shelo mi-da'ato* — Abbaye proposes a fundamental reorientation: in fact, the third-party money works even *without* the slave's consent. *Ho'il ve-kana-o be'al korcho, makni-o be'al korcho* — since the slave was originally sold against his will, he can be freed against his will. The act of purchasing a slave is done without requiring the slave's agreement, and therefore the parallel act of purchasing his freedom is likewise valid without his agreement.

### Sale-Freedom Parallel

The conceptual architecture of Abbaye's argument is that the *kesef* that acquires and the *kesef* that frees are the same kind of instrument doing the same kind of work; the slave's will is simply not a variable in money transactions involving him. It is a striking and somewhat counterintuitive move — freedom is normally something one would want — but Abbaye's point is structural: the *kinyan* logic of *kesef* operates identically in both directions.

The *gemara* challenges: if so, why not free him with a *shtar* delivered by a third party *shelo mi-da'ato* as well, since he was acquired by a *shtar* against his will? *Ha-i shtar la-chud ve-ha-i shtar la-chud* — no, a *shtar* of sale is fundamentally different in character from a *shtar* of manumission. They cannot be equated across the two contexts. By contrast, money is money: *tiv'a mi-chad hu* — it is all the same coin. So the symmetry argument works for *kesef* but not for *shtar*. The conclusion under Abbaye: the *mishnah* is describing a case *shelo mi-da'ato*; third-party *kesef* works even without the slave's consent; third-party *shtar* does not.

### Rava: Master Accepts

*Rava* offers an alternative explanation for why third-party *kesef* works without requiring *zachin*. *Kesef kabbalat rabbo garma lo* — in a *kesef* redemption, what actually effects the liberation is the master's acceptance of the money. The third party who provides the funds is not, in the halakhic sense, *representing the slave* — he is simply providing the instrument. The master's act of taking the money is the operative moment of freedom. Therefore the principle of *zachin* — which governs representation of a person's interests — is never implicated. No one needs to act as the slave's agent, because the slave is not the actor in this transaction.

*Shtar kabbalat acheirim garma lo* — a *shtar*, however, effects liberation through the act of receipt. The natural recipient is the slave himself; if a third party receives it instead, that third party is necessarily acting as the slave's representative, which requires *zachin* and therefore the slave's prior consent. Under Rava's formulation, then, *shtar al yedei acheirim* would work *mi-da'ato* — if the slave agrees, a third party can certainly receive the *shtar* on his behalf. But it will not work *shelo mi-da'ato*, because representation requires consent.

---

## Sages Position

### Slave's Own Money

*Ve-chachamim omrim: be-kesef al yedei atzmo* — the Sages hold that a slave may redeem himself with his own money. This immediately implies a foundational disagreement with *Rabbi Meir*: the *Chachamim* maintain that a slave can indeed own money, at least in certain circumstances, independently of his master.

### Kesef Both Ways

The *gemara* asks whether *al yedei atzmo* is exclusive — only his own money, not others'.
