This seems unlikely: the *Chachamim* hold that freedom is a *zachut* and that *zachin le-adam shelo be-fanav* — one may act on another's behalf when it is clearly to his benefit, even without his knowledge. Surely others could also provide the money. The *gemara* resolves: *mai al yedei atzmo, af al yedei atzmo* — the *mishnah*'s formulation means "even through his own money," not "exclusively through his own money." The *chiddush* of the *Chachamim* is the ruling that *yesh kinyan le-eved be-lo rabbo* — a slave can own property in his own right, making self-redemption through his own funds possible. Third-party money certainly also works under the *Chachamim*'s view.

### Shtar by Others

For *shtar*, the *Chachamim* say *al yedei acheirim* — the writ is delivered to others. The *gemara* interprets this as meaning others can receive it on his behalf — which is straightforwardly explicable by *zachin*: since freedom is a *zachut*, third parties can receive the *shtar* for the slave's benefit without his even being present.

### Gito ve-Yado Q

But this raises a sharp question. The *Chachamim* hold that a slave *can* own money. If so, they presumably also accept *gito ve-yado ba'im ke'echad*, since that principle is needed to explain how the slave can receive his own *shtar*. Why then does the *mishnah* under the *Chachamim*'s position say *al yedei acheirim* rather than allow both? If *al yedei acheirim* means "even *al yedei acheirim*" — i.e., additionally to *al yedei atzmo* — then the *mishnah* should have formulated it to cover both together. But if *al yedei acheirim* means "only *al yidei acheirim*," then why can the slave not receive the *shtar* himself, given that the *Chachamim* recognize both his capacity for ownership and the principle of *gito ve-yado*?

### Rabbi Shimon

The *gemara* answers: *ve-Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar hi* — this reflects the position of *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*, as taught in a *baraita*: *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar omer: af be-shtar al yedei acheirim ve-lo al yedei atzmo* — the *shtar* may only be delivered to others, not directly to the slave. This is a distinct position that requires its own explanation, which *Rava* will provide.

### Three Core Issues

*Ve-shalosh machlokos ba-davar* — there are in fact three independent debates embedded in this *mishnah*, though the *rishonim* differ on how exactly to align them. The first is the question of *zachin* versus *chov*: are the *Chachamim* correct that freedom is a *zachut* (permitting third-party action without consent), or does *Rabbi Meir* have the better of the argument that it is a *chov* (requiring the slave's consent)? The main practical consequence of this debate is whether *shtar al yidei acheirim* can work without the slave's consent. The second debate concerns whether a slave can own money at all: *Rabbi Meir* says *ein kinyan le-eved be-lo rabbo*, the *Chachamim* say *yesh kinyan*. This determines whether *kesef al yidei atzmo* is possible. The third debate is whether *gito ve-yado ba'im ke'echad* applies — whether the slave can receive a *shtar* directly and thereby acquire himself simultaneously. This governs *shtar al yidei atzmo*. *Rashi* reads the *Chachamim* as actually endorsing both *al yidei atzmo* and *al yidei acheirim* for *shtar*, with the *mishnah*'s phrasing *al yidei acheirim* merely alluding to the minority position of *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* rather than endorsing it.

### Get Analogy

*Amar Rava: mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar?* — why does *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* hold that you cannot give the *shtar* directly to the slave? *Gamar lah la-mah me-ishah* — he derives it by analogy to the *get* given to a woman. *Mai ishah — ad she-yotzi get li-reshut she-eino shelo* — when a husband gives a *get*, he gives it to a domain that is not his own. The woman is a separate legal entity, outside the husband's *reshut*. *Af eved nami — ad she-yotzi get li-reshut she-eino shelo* — so too the *shtar shichrur* must be given to a domain outside the master's own. The slave himself, being entirely within the master's legal domain, cannot be that recipient; the *shtar* must be given to a third party who genuinely stands outside the master's ownership. Although there is the principle of *gito ve-yado ba'im ke'echad*, *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — and by extension *Rava*'s explanation — holds that the slave's hand does not attain true independence of domain in the relevant sense: the woman in the *get* is not the property of the husband to the same degree that the slave is the property of the master, and this distinction makes the analogy work in a specific direction. This point is noted as requiring further development.

---

---

# Kiddushin 24

## Gito v'Yado Principle

### Mishna Dispute

The present sugya picks up in the middle of the discussion on 23a concerning *eved kenaani* — how a Canaanite slave is acquired and, more precisely, how a slave acquires his own freedom. The *mishnah* records a *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* on this question. Rabbi Meir holds that a slave may acquire his freedom *bekesef al yedei acherim* — through money paid by others on his behalf — or *uvishtar al yedei atzmo* — by personally receiving a *shtar shichrur*, a document of freedom, from his master. The *chachamim* appear to disagree, holding *bekesef al yedei atzmo* — that the slave himself may hand the money over — but *uvishtar al yedei acherim* — that the *shtar shichrur* must be received through another person.

The *shakla ve-tarya* that preceded this point on 23a suggested that there may in fact be a third opinion embedded in the *mishnah* — that of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. On this reading, the *chachamim* actually permit the slave to acquire his freedom through either money or a *shtar* on his own, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is the one who specifically requires that the *shtar shichrur* be received *al yedei acherim*, through someone other than the slave himself.

### Rava's Question

It is against this backdrop that the *gemara* opens with the last two words of 23a: *bayei Rava le-Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — Rava poses a question directed at the position of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The question is: *eved kenaani ma hu sheyaseh shaliach lekabel gito miyad rabo* — can a Canaanite slave appoint a *shaliach* to receive his *get* of freedom from his master?

The framing of the question turns on a *gezeirah shavah*. The law of slave manumission is derived from the law of divorce through a verbal analogy on the word *la* — appearing in both contexts — linking the freeing of a slave to the *get* given to a woman. Since a woman may appoint a *shaliach* to receive her *get* on her behalf, one might think a slave should likewise be able to do so. But Rava presses further: *o dilma ishah de'ihi matzi mekabel giteh shaliach nami matzi mashvei* — perhaps a woman can appoint a *shaliach* precisely because she herself has the capacity to receive her own *get*. *Eved de'ihu lo mekabel giteh* — but a slave, according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who does not have the capacity to receive his own *get shichrur* directly — *shaliach nami lo matzi mashvei* — would likewise be unable to appoint a *shaliach* to receive it for him.

The underlying assumption seems to be that this conclusion would be absurd, that surely a slave should be able to appoint an agent. After posing the question, however, Rava resolves it himself: *la-la me-ishah* — the *gezeirah shavah* connecting the slave's freedom to a woman's divorce does in fact extend to this, and therefore the slave is compared to a woman in the relevant respects.

It is worth pausing to appreciate how a principle worked out in Masechet Gittin resurfaces here. The rule of *gito v'yado ba'im k'echad* — that the slave's *get* and his acquiring hand come simultaneously — is central to understanding why Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that the slave cannot receive his own *shtar shichrur* directly. This is precisely why Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion is of particular interest, and why tracking opinions across different *masekhtot* is essential to a full understanding of any given *sugya*.

### Shaliach Limitation

This brings into view a more general principle — that a *shaliach* cannot be empowered to perform an act that the person appointing him could not perform himself. This rule is derived from Masechet Nazir (daf 12) and applies broadly to the laws of *shlichut*.

### Kohanim Shlichut

The *gemara* connects this to a famous question raised by Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua, which appears in Masechet Nedarim: *hani kohanei shluchei de-rachmana ninhu* — are the *kohanim* agents of God, or are they agents of *Bnei Yisrael* when they perform the *avodah*? The question is framed precisely in terms of this principle of *shlichut*: *mi ika midi de'anan lo matzinan avdinan ve'ihu matzi avid* — is there any act a *shaliach* can perform that the person appointing him could not perform himself? Since a *Yisrael* cannot perform the *avodah*, and the *kohanim* do perform it, the *kohanim* cannot be agents of *Bnei Yisrael*. They must therefore be *shluchei de-rachmana* — agents of God. The practical *nafka mina* raised in Masechet Nedarim concerns whether a *kohen* may perform the *avodah* for someone who is *mudar hana'ah* from him — that is, if the *kohen* is acting as his agent, the prohibition would apply, whereas if the *kohen* is God's agent, it would not.

### Slave vs. Woman

The *gemara* draws a distinction between the *sugya* here and the *sugya* in Nedarim. A *Yisrael* has no connection to *korbanot* whatsoever — *Yisrael lo shaychei b'torat korbanot klal* — and therefore there is no basis for any principle of *shlichut* that could apply to him with respect to the *avodah*. By contrast, *eved shayach begittin* — a slave is fully connected to the notion of his bill of freedom. The slave is not categorically excluded from the legal framework in the same way a *Yisrael* is excluded from performing the *avodah*.

### Friend's Get Shichrur

A *baraita* is cited to illustrate this distinction: *nirin hadevarim she'ha'eved mekabel gito shel chaveiro miyad rabo shel chaveiro* — it appears from the logic of the matter that a slave may receive his fellow slave's *get shichrur* from that fellow slave's master, acting as an agent for his friend. *Aval lo miyad rabo shelo* — but he cannot receive his own *shtar shichrur* from his own master. The reason is not that a slave is categorically incapable of receiving a *get shichrur*, but rather the specific problem of *kol ma shekana eved kana rabo* — whatever a slave acquires, his master acquires. Therefore, if the slave were to receive his own *get shichrur* into his own hand, it would be as if the master were giving it back to himself, and the slave would never actually receive it. This is the very logic of *gito v'yado ba'in k'echad* — the slave's *get* and his acquiring hand come as one — which Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar does not accept, and which is therefore the crux of his distinctive position.

---

## Conditional Gifts

### Kol Mah Shekana

The *gemara* now shifts from the *sugya* of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and returns to the original *machloket* in the *mishnah* between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim*. The *chachamim* had said that while the slave may pay his own freedom through money, *uvlvad sheyehei hakesef mishel acheirim* — the money must nonetheless belong to others. This requires explanation: if the slave can hand the money over himself, why must the money belong to someone else?

The *gemara* raises the possibility that the *machloket* turns on the underlying question of *kol ma shekana eved kana rabo* — whatever a slave acquires, his master acquires. Does this mean a slave is entirely incapable of acquiring anything for himself, or might there be some qualified form of independent acquisition?

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *gemara* initially proposes that Rabbi Meir holds *ein kinyan l'eved belo rabo* — a slave cannot acquire anything without it immediately transferring to the master. Similarly, *ein kinyan l'isha belo ba'ala* — whatever a woman acquires transfers to her husband. On this reading, Rabbi Meir maintains there is simply no independent avenue of acquisition available to the slave.

### Chachamim Position

The *chachamim*, on this initial reading, would hold *yesh kinyan l'eved belo rabo* — a slave can have independent acquisition, and similarly *yesh kinyan l'isha belo ba'ala* — a woman can acquire independently of her husband. This is why the *mishnah* needed to specify that the money must belong to others: since the slave can in principle have his own property, one might have thought he could use his own funds, so the *mishnah* tells us that even according to the *chachamim* the money cannot be the slave's own.

### Rabbi Elazar

Rabba bar Rav Sheshet in the name of Rav Sheshet, however, rejects this framing entirely. He maintains that in truth everyone — both Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* — agrees that *ein kinyan l'eved belo rabo*, a slave cannot acquire anything without it transferring to the master, and *ein kinyan l'isha belo ba'ala* as well. The *machloket* must therefore concern something else.

The case under discussion, Rav Sheshet argues, must involve a third party who goes to the slave and says: *al menat she'ein lerabcha reshut bo* — here is money on the condition that your master has no rights to it. The donor is attempting to circumvent *kol ma shekana eved kana rabo* by building in a condition that the master should not acquire it.

Rabbi Elazar then refines the case still further. It cannot simply be that someone gives the slave money hoping the slave will use it to buy his freedom through a subsequent transaction, because everyone would agree that the slave's momentary acquisition of the money would immediately vest in the master. Rather, the operative case according to Rabbi Elazar is one where someone hands money to the slave while simultaneously declaring *al menat sheteitzei bo l'cheirut* — on the condition that you go free through this. The third party is not giving the slave money to hold; he is attempting to purchase the slave's freedom by transferring funds directly to the slave, with the freedom as the condition.

### Ownership Dispute

Given this framing, the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* becomes clear — and, striking, almost counterintuitive. Both agree that whatever the slave acquires goes to the master. The question is whether that very mechanism can serve as the vehicle for the slave's freedom.

Rabbi Meir holds: *ki amar lei kani kani eved v'kani rabo* — when the donor says "acquire it," the slave acquires and therefore the master acquires, *v'chi amar lei al menat lo klum ka'amar lei* — and the condition *al menat* is legally void. One cannot impose a condition that subverts the fundamental nature of the slave relationship. The condition therefore has no legal force, and the money simply passes to the master.

The *rabbanan* hold that *keivan d'amar lei al menat ahanei lei t'nai* — once the donor formulates the condition, the condition does have operative legal force, and through this mechanism the slave may go free. The *rabbanan* understand that the slave acquires the money as an extension of the master, and that this is precisely what makes the freedom possible — he acquires it for the master, and simultaneously goes free. As one might observe, it is almost the reverse of what one expects: the slave acquires his freedom *precisely because* he has no independent legal standing. His acquisition being the master's acquisition is what allows the third party's directed gift to function as a purchase of freedom.

It should be noted that the analogy to a married woman, while related, is not identical. A married woman has various layers of ownership — reserved assets, *shibudim*, *peirot* — that distinguish her situation from that of an *eved kenaani* in important respects. An *eved kenaani* has no independent legal standing in any domain analogous to a free person; the principle of *kol ma shekana eved kana rabo* is far more comprehensive than anything that applies to a married woman. Similarly, none of this applies to an *eved Ivri* — a Hebrew slave — who retains full personhood and legal standing. In Masechet Bava Metzia, in the discussion of *eilu metzi'os*, the *eved Ivri* is listed among those who retain ownership over found objects, which illustrates the fundamental halakhic distinction between the two categories of slavery.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni

### Woman & Chomesh

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* that appears to contradict the positions of both Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* as they have been understood: *ein ishah podeh Ma'aser Sheni belo chomesh* — a woman may not redeem *Ma'aser Sheni* without paying the *chomesh*. By way of background: normally, *Ma'aser Sheni* produce is to be brought to Yerushalayim and eaten there. If the distance is too great or the quantity too large, the Torah permits redeeming the produce onto money — but when one redeems one's own *Ma'aser Sheni*, a *chomesh* — a surcharge of one-fifth of the final amount, which works out to 25% of the original value — must be added. The *chomesh* functions as a kind of penalty on using redemption rather than physically transporting the produce. The statement that a woman *must* pay the *chomesh* implies that she is acting as an agent of her husband when redeeming *his* produce, and therefore the exemption that might apply to her does not.

### Rabbi Meir Woman

Against this, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar transmits an opinion in the name of Rabbi Meir: *ishah podeh Ma'aser Sheni belo chomesh* — a woman may redeem *Ma'aser Sheni* without the *chomesh*, treating her as sufficiently independent of her husband in this context that she is not considered his agent.

### Case Analysis

The *gemara* immediately interrogates what the actual case is. If we are dealing with the husband's money and the husband's *Ma'aser Sheni* produce, then she is plainly performing her husband's *shlichut*, and the first position — that she must pay the *chomesh* — clearly applies. If we are dealing with her own money and her own *Ma'aser Sheni*, then there is a *drasha* in the Torah — *ish amar Rachmana velo ishah*, the Torah says "a man" to exclude a woman — which might exempt her from the *chomesh* entirely. Rashi understands this exclusion to mean *ish mi-maasero amar Rachmana velo ishah mi-maaser ba'alah* — a man pays the *chomesh* when redeeming his own *Ma'aser Sheni*, but a woman is considered like an outsider with respect to her husband's *Ma'aser Sheni*, and therefore is not subject to the *chomesh*. Tosafot, by contrast, connects the exemption to the broader question of *talmud Torah* and the verse *ve-lamadeta* that appears in the context of *Ma'aser Sheni*, understanding the obligation of *chomesh* to be bound up with the *mitzvah* dimension of eating *Ma'aser Sheni* — a *mitzvah* from which women may be exempt. The question of how intrinsic the *chomesh* is to the *pidyon* of *Ma'aser Sheni* generally — whether it is simply part of the *mitzvah* or a separable surcharge — underlies this dispute between Rashi and Tosafot.

In any event, neither of those simple cases generates the interesting *machloket*. The *gemara* therefore looks for a case that would produce the apparent contradiction to the positions on *eved kenaani*. It arrives at the following: someone else comes to the woman and gives her money, saying *al menat sheteitzei bo la-cheirut* — that is, on the condition that she use it specifically to redeem the *Ma'aser Sheni*. This is the precise parallel to the case of the slave. And yet here, Rabbi Meir appears to hold that the condition *does* work — that the woman can use this designated money to redeem the *Ma'aser Sheni* without *chomesh* — while the *chachamim* appear to hold that it does not work and she must pay *chomesh*.

This is directly contradicted by what we saw in the context of the slave, where Rabbi Meir said conditions do not work and the *chachamim* said they do. Hence: *rami de-Rabbi Meir a-de-Rabbi Meir, rami de-Rabbanan a-de-Rabbanan* — there is an internal contradiction in Rabbi Meir's position and an internal contradiction in the *Rabbanan*'s position.

One proposed resolution is *ipcha shamina lehu* — we simply heard the two sources with their attributions reversed, and by flipping one of them the contradiction disappears. Abaye endorses this: *ipoch* — reverse them. But Rava objects: *l'olam lo sipoach* — one should not simply reverse *mishnayot* and *baraisos* to make them fit. There must be an organic distinction that resolves the apparent tension.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava proposes that the two cases are not actually parallel. In the *Ma'aser Sheni* case, he specifies: *dhacha b'ma'aser d'asya mibei nasha askinan* — we are dealing with *Ma'aser Sheni* that the woman has inherited from her father's estate, where she has no brothers and is the sole heir. In this case, the *Ma'aser Sheni* produce belongs entirely to her, not to her husband. It is not, therefore, a case of someone giving her designated funds to redeem her husband's *Ma'aser Sheni*; rather, she is redeeming her own *Ma'aser Sheni* with her own inherited property.

### Ma'aser Ownership

But Rava goes further, pointing to what he regards as the more fundamental *machloket*: *Rabbi Meir l'taimei d'amar Ma'aser mamon hekdesh hu* — Rabbi Meir holds that *Ma'aser Sheni* belongs to *hekdesh*, that is, it is property of God. Consequently, *velo kanei lei ba'al* — the husband does not acquire the woman's *Ma'aser Sheni* when she inherits it, because it was never truly hers as ordinary property to begin with. Therefore, when she redeems it, she is acting on her own account, and Rabbi Meir's exemption from *chomesh* makes sense.

The *rabbanan*, by contrast, hold *mamon hedyot hu* — *Ma'aser Sheni* is ordinary personal property, *v'kanei lei ba'al* — and therefore the husband acquires it when she inherits it. When she redeems it, she is acting as her husband's agent — *shlichusa d'ba'al ka'avda* — and the *chomesh* therefore applies to her.

This is a remarkable *machloket* with broad implications. *Ma'aser Sheni* occupies a unique place among the various categories of *hekdesh* and *kodshim*. Unlike *terumah*, where the produce belongs to the owner and must be transferred to the *kohen*, *Ma'aser Sheni* — on Rabbi Meir's view — belongs to God, and the owner must go to Yerushalayim to eat it there, in a sanctified space, because that is where it belongs. Yet *Ma'aser Sheni* is distinct from *korbanos* and other *kodshim* in that it may be eaten by *Yisraelim* and is subject to redemption and transfer in ways that most *hekdesh* is not — it is a more fluid form of *kedushah*, yet retains at its core an obligation that originates from God. It is similar in some ways to *bechor* and *ma'aser behemah*, while remaining distinct.

---

## Injury Mechanisms

### Tooth & Eye

A *baraita* is cited: *yotzei beshein ve'ayin u-roshei evarim she-einan chozrin* — a slave goes free when his master knocks out his tooth or his eye, and also through injury to the tips of limbs that do not grow back. There are twenty-four such tips, which also carry significance in the laws of *nega'im*, where the tips of limbs cannot be examined for *tzara'at* from a single vantage point. The explicit biblical source covers only *shen* and *ayin* — tooth and eye. The question is therefore raised: from where do we derive that injury to the tips of other limbs also triggers the slave's freedom?

The *gemara* answers: *dumya de-shein ve'ayin* — by analogy to tooth and eye. *Ma shein ve'ayin mum she-bagalui ve-einan chozrin* — just as tooth and eye are visible blemishes that do not grow back, *af kol mum she-bagalui ve-einan chozrin* — so too any visible blemish that does not grow back.

### Klal U'Prat

Before accepting this, the *gemara* considers a series of hermeneutical alternatives. One might argue that since both *shen* and *ayin* are explicitly mentioned in the Torah, they function as *shnei ketuvim ha-ba'im ke-echad* — two verses that arrive together with the same teaching — and the rule is *ein melamdin*, one cannot derive a generalization from two explicit cases that cover the same ground. The *gemara* responds that both cases are independently necessary. Had the Torah written only *shein*, one might have thought even a milk tooth — *shein she-yanak bah*, a tooth that grew in while the child was still nursing — would suffice. The inclusion of *ayin* tells us that the paradigm is something that is *nivra imo*, created with the person from birth. Conversely, had the Torah written only *ayin*, one might have read the paradigm as limited to limbs present from birth, excluding teeth that grow in later. *Tzricha* — both are necessary, and therefore the two cases do not function as redundant examples that prevent generalization.

Another hermeneutical path is proposed and rejected: perhaps the verse should be read as *klal u-prat* — general and specific — such that *ki yakkeh* is the general and *shein ve'ayin* is the specific, which would *limit* the application to tooth and eye only. The *gemara* notes, however, that the verse concludes with *le-chofshi yishalchenu* — "he shall send him free" — which adds a second general term. The structure therefore becomes *klal u-prat u-klal*, and by the rules of this hermeneutic, the concluding general term expands the application beyond the specific examples in the middle. The expansion is still constrained, however: *ei ata dan ela ke-ein ha-prat* — the generalization must conform to the nature of the specific examples.

### Specific Examples

What defines the category shaped by the *prat*? *Mum she-bagalui ve-einan chozrin* — a visible blemish that does not grow back — is one dimension. But the *gemara* adds a further qualification: *batel m'melachto* — the injury must also render the affected limb unable to perform its normal function. A tooth that has been knocked out cannot chew; an eye that has been blinded cannot see. Any injury to the body that is visible, permanent, and disabling in this way falls within the category.

Two concrete examples are provided by a *baraita*: if the master pulled the slave's beard and thereby dislocated the slave's jaw — *talash b'zikano v'dildel bo etzem* — the slave goes free, because a dislocated jaw is visible, does not heal on its own, and prevents normal eating. Similarly, if the master struck the slave's arm and it withered — *hikahu al yado v'tzamtah* — but eventually the arm healed, the slave does *not* go free, because the injury was not permanent. The *baraita* makes this explicit: *ein eved yotzei bo l'cheirut*. This concrete ruling serves to limit the scope of *klal u-prat u-klal*, anchoring the requirement of *eino chozer* — that the injury must be one that does not heal — as an essential qualification.

### Tannaim Dispute

With the scope of liberating injuries established, the *gemara* turns to a deeper dispute: does the injury itself effect the slave's freedom automatically, or does it merely create an obligation on the master to issue a *get shichrur*? A *baraita* records the full range of *tanna'itic* opinion. Rabbi Shimon holds that for all such injuries — including tooth and eye — the slave goes free but *requires* a *get shichrur*: the injury creates an obligation, it does not itself accomplish the manumission. Rabbi Meir holds the opposite: *eino tzarich* — no *get shichrur* is required; the injury itself liberates the slave. Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Tarfon agrees with Rabbi Meir.

The *gemara* also records the view of the *machri'im lifnei chachamim* — those who adjudicated before the *chachamim* — who adopt a split ruling.

### Chachamim Compromise

*Nir'in divrei Rabbi Tarfon b'shein ve'ayin* — the reasoning of Rabbi Tarfon appears correct with respect to tooth and eye, *shehatorah zachta lo* — because the Torah itself explicitly granted the slave his freedom through these specific injuries, and therefore the injury itself is the operative mechanism. *Ve-divrei Rabbi Akiva b'sha'ar eivarim* — but with respect to other limbs, whose inclusion is derived only through the *midrash* of the *chachamim* rather than being explicit in the Torah, Rabbi Akiva's position appears correct: a *get shichrur* is still required.

The *gemara* notes that to call the derivation for other limbs *midrash chachamim* — as opposed to explicit Torah — is not to call it merely rabbinic. The *drasha* from *klal u-prat u-klal* does carry *de'oraita* force. Nevertheless, what is learned through *drashot* has a somewhat lesser degree of textual explicitness than what is stated plainly in the *pesukim*, and the *Rambam* is particularly attentive to this distinction — though calling it purely rabbinic would be an overstatement. This reflects a broader *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish about whether the majority of Torah is *Torah she-bichsav* or *Torah she-ba'al peh*, and whether *drashot* are uncovering something latent in the written text or transmitting an oral tradition that was subsequently anchored to verses.

As for the substance of the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon: Rabbi Shimon derives from a *gezeirah shavah* of *shiluach-shiluach* — the freeing of a slave compared to the divorce of a woman — that just as a woman requires a *shtar*, so too a slave requires a *shtar*. Rabbi Meir, by contrast, reads the phrase *le-chofshi yishalchenu* as indicating that at the moment of the injury the slave is *already* free — *hava lei chofshi me'ikara* — and no subsequent document is needed to accomplish what the injury itself has already accomplished. On this view, the injury does not merely obligate the master to free the slave; rather, by injuring the slave in this way, the master has forfeited his position as slave master entirely, and the slave goes free as a direct consequence.

---

## Direct vs. Indirect

### Direct Contact

A new *baraita* is introduced that addresses the question of what type of injury triggers a slave's freedom. *Hikeihu al eino v'sima'ah* — if the master struck the slave's eye and blinded it, *al ozno v'chershah* — or struck his ear and deafened it — *eved yotzei bahen l'cheirus* — the slave goes free. The injury here is a direct physical contact to the affected organ, even though the resulting damage is to the function of the organ rather than to its physical structure. Striking the eye and causing blindness, or striking the ear and causing deafness, constitutes the kind of visible, permanent, functional loss that brings the slave his freedom.

### Non-Contact Injury

By contrast, *keneged eino v'eino ro'eh* — if the master did something in front of the slave's eye such that the slave lost his sight without any physical contact to the eye — *keneged ozno v'eino shomei'a* — or caused the slave to go deaf through some non-contact means — *ein eved yotzei bahen l'cheirus* — the slave does not go free. The *baraita* thus distinguishes between a direct physical blow to the organ and a non-contact mechanism that produces the same functional result.

### Sound Damage

This distinction prompts an immediate challenge from Rav Shemen to Rav Ashi: does this mean that *kol* — sound — has no physical force in halacha? Is non-contact acoustic injury simply a legal nullity? Surely not, since a *baraita* recorded by Rami bar Yechezkel in the context of Bava Kamma addresses precisely this: a chicken that inserts its head into a glass vessel and crows inside it, shattering the glass without any contact — according to Sumchos, the owner pays full *nezek*. And Rav Yosef transmits from *bei Rav* that if a horse whinnies or a donkey brays and the sound breaks vessels inside the house, the owner pays *chatzi nezek*. Whether one follows Sumchos (full payment) or the *rabbanan* (half payment), the point stands that sound-induced property damage does create liability for *nezikin*. Why, then, should non-contact acoustic injury to a slave not suffice to free him?

### Person vs. Object

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty with a crucial distinction: *shani adam dekivan debar daat hu ihu miv'it nafsheih* — a person is different, because being a *bar daat*, a person with awareness, the victim is in some sense involved in the act of being injured. The precise nature of this involvement is elusive. It is not that the slave is actively complicit in his own hearing loss, but somehow the victim's status as a *bar daat* — as a person with legal consciousness and awareness — distinguishes the case from that of a *kli*, a glass vessel, which has no such standing. The *gemara* does not spell out the mechanism in full, but the distinction operates to mean that non-contact injury to a person has a different halakhic character than non-contact damage to an object.

### Blowing Baraita

A final *baraita* is cited to crystallize the distinction: *hamav'it chavero patur midinei adam ve-chayav b'dinei shamayim* — one who startles another person and causes injury is exempt from human courts but liable in the heavenly court. Then the specific case: *taka be'ozno ve'chershah patur* — if one blows into someone's ear and deafens him, without holding the person, he is exempt. *Achazo ve-taka be'ozno ve'chershah chayav* — but if he held the person and then blew into his ear and deafened him, he is liable. The holding of the victim converts what would otherwise be a non-contact acoustic injury into one with a sufficient element of physical contact to create liability. This *baraita* neatly encapsulates the principle that non-contact injury to a *bar daat* occupies a different legal category — and, by extension, that only direct physical injury to the relevant organ suffices to free a slave through the mechanism the Torah established for *shen* and *ayin*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 25

## Eye/Tooth Damage

### Usability Standard

The daf opens on 24b, several lines before the text widens, with a *baraita* addressing the *eved kena'ani* and the question of when damage to an eye or tooth entitles him to freedom. The *tana* teaches: if the master struck the slave's eye and it became dim (*hikah lo eino*), or struck his tooth and it became loose (*shino venadeda*)—without totally knocking it out or gouging it entirely from the body—the measure is functional usability. *Im yachol lehishtamesh bahen achshav*, if it is still usable, he does not go free; *ve-im lav*, if it is no longer usable, he does go free. Precisely what threshold of residual vision or stability constitutes "usability" is left open, but the operative principle is clear: functionality, not structural completeness, governs.

### Pre-existing Conditions

A second *baraita* addresses the mirror image: what if the slave's eye was already dim before the master's act, and the master then brought it from dim to totally blind? Or the tooth was already loose, and the master then knocked it out entirely? Again the measure is usability. *Im yachol lehishtamesh bahen kevar*—if the eye or tooth was still usable beforehand, then by taking it from usable to unusable the master has crossed the threshold and the slave goes free. *Ve-im lav*—if it was already unusable beforehand, he does not.

### Necessity of Both Cases

The *gemara* asks why both directions need to be taught, since both reduce to the same principle. The answer is that each case is genuinely surprising without the other. Had we only heard the first case—going from full sight to functionally blind—one might reason that this applied only because the master caused a radical deterioration: *mishum d'me-ikara nehora bari ve-hashta nehora kakhisha*. But where the eye was already barely usable to begin with, perhaps even bringing it to total blindness would not suffice to free the slave. Conversely, had we only heard the second case—bringing an already-dim eye all the way to total blindness—one might think that applied only because he reduced the slave to absolute zero (*samya l'gamre*). But where the master merely brought a functioning eye down to a non-functional but not totally sightless state, one might think the slave does not go free. *Tzericha*: both cases are necessary.

---

## Intent & Act Nature

### Accidental vs. Intention…

The *gemara* next presents a *baraita*: what if the master himself was a doctor, and the slave asked him to apply an ointment to his eye (*lechkhol lo eino*), or to treat a tooth (*lachator lo shino*), and in the course of this therapeutic intervention the master accidentally blinded the eye or knocked out the tooth? The *baraita* rules: *sicheik b'adon ve-yatzah le-cheirut*—the slave laughs in his master's face and goes free. The unintended result governs; the therapeutic purpose does not shield the master.

### Intent Requirement

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents. He reads the word *ve-shichatah*—"and he destroys it"—in the relevant verse as describing not merely the result but the nature of the act: *ad she-yitkavein le-shachtah*, only when the master intended to destroy. This would exclude a therapeutic act that accidentally causes injury. Critically, an intentional act of violence—say, striking the slave in the face and thereby knocking out a tooth—would still qualify, even if the master was not specifically aiming at the tooth, because the act is fundamentally a destructive one directed at the slave's body. What is excluded is an act that is therapeutic in character and accidentally produces a harmful result.

The *Rabbanan* who do not require destructive intent must account for the word *ve-shichatah*. They respond: *mibaei lei le-khidatanya*—the word is needed to teach the ruling of Rabbi Elazar.

### Fetus Case

Rabbi Elazar teaches: if a man inserted his hand into the womb of his maidservant during childbirth, attempting to assist in delivering the baby, and in doing so accidentally blinded the eye of the fetus, he is *patur*—the child does not go free. The reason: *amar kra ve-shichatah, ad she-yitkaven le-shachtah*. Here the man was not relating to the eye at all—he was trying to extract the fetus and was not even aware of, let alone directing his actions toward, the eye of the unborn child.

This raises a subtle distinction. If a master punches a slave in the face and knocks out a tooth, he did not intend the tooth specifically—he intended the face. Yet this would presumably qualify because hitting the face in that region is, in the words of the *gemara*'s framework, something like a *psik reisha*: the tooth is within the scope of the violent act. By contrast, reaching into the womb to assist in a birth is not in any way directed at the eye of the fetus. One is not even aware of being near that area. That categorical difference is what the *Rabbanan* derive from *ve-shichatah*.

### Veshichatah Debate

The *gemara* clarifies the underlying dispute. The *Rabbanan* read *ve-shichatah* as establishing that even they require some connection between the act and the injured limb—the fetus case is exempt because there is no connection whatsoever. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reads the same word as requiring positive destructive intent. *Ve-idach*: one position derives from the doubled form *shachat ve-shichatah* an additional teaching; the other holds that no such *derasha* from the doubled form is operative (*shachat ve-shichatah lo darish*). Rashi's treatment of the case where someone hit nearby and the slave was startled or frightened (*mav'it*) fills in the bracketing question of what it means to strike "in the vicinity" rather than directly.

---

## Visible Limbs

### Complete Removal

Rav Sheshet introduces a further ruling: *harei she-hayeta eino smuya ve-chitatah*—if the slave's eye was already functionally blind and the master then gouged it out entirely (*chitatah*, removing it from the socket), the slave goes free. This is surprising, since there has been no functional change; the slave could not see before and cannot see now. Nevertheless, *mechusar eivar hu*—he is now missing a limb, and that structural change to the body is itself sufficient. The principle is that the loss of an external limb, even one that was already non-functional, effects the slave's freedom.

### 24 Limb Heads

The *gemara* supports this from a *baraita* that itself draws on the laws of *tzara'at*: *tamim ve-zachrut be-vehemah ve-ein tamim ve-zachrut be-ofot*—the requirements of being unblemished and male apply to large animal sacrifices but not to bird sacrifices. One might therefore think that a bird with a withered wing, a severed leg, or a gouged-out eye would still be valid for a sacrifice. The verse says *min ha-of*—from the birds, implying not all birds—excluding a bird that is *mechusar eivar*, lacking a limb. Rashi emphasizes that this applies *af al gav de-sumya me-ikara*, even if the bird was already blind beforehand, since bird sacrifices may be blemished—yet the final act of removing the eye is still considered a substantive change that renders it *mechusar eivar*.

The *gemara* then introduces the twenty-four *rashei evarim*, the twenty-four limb heads of the human body that do not contract *tum'at michya* (the sign of *tzara'at* at a healed spot) because of their sloped or protruding nature, which prevents the entire spot from being visible to the *kohen* simultaneously. These are: the ten fingertips, the ten toetips (totaling twenty), the tips of the ears (twenty-two), the nose (twenty-three), and the top of the penis (twenty-four). By a woman, the nipples replace or supplement the last entry. Rabbi Yehuda adds the male nipples; the *chachamim* do not consider them sufficiently protruding.

The *baraita* then teaches: *u-vichulam eved yotzei bahen la-cheirut*—by all of these, a slave goes free if the limb is cut off or destroyed. These twenty-four, plus the eye and the tooth already taught in the *mishnah*, constitute the catalog of external limbs. The connection to the *eved* is not the *tzara'at* logic of sloped visibility, but the identification of what counts as an external, visible part of the body.

Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi says in the name of Rav: if the slave had an extra finger and the master cut it off, the slave goes free. Rav Huna qualifies: *ve-hu she-nisperet al gav ha-yad*—only if the extra finger is counted in continuity with the other fingers of the hand, so that one would count "one, two, three, four, five, six" running continuously. If the extra digit protrudes in a way that clearly places it outside the normal row of fingers, it is not considered a finger of the hand, and cutting it off would not free the slave.

### Testicles Query

This leads to the famous exchange. The elders of Nazunya stopped attending Rav Chisda's *shiur*. Rav Chisda sent Rav Hamnuna to inquire why, and rather than simply imposing a sanction, Rav Hamnuna asked what was troubling them. They said: we asked him a question and he did not resolve it—if he cannot answer our questions, why should we attend? Rav Hamnuna invited them to ask him their question.

They asked: *eved she-seiraso rabo be-beitzim*—if the master castrated the slave by crushing the testicles, does this qualify as *ke-mum she-ba-galuye*, a blemish on a visible limb? The question rests on the following tension: on one hand, the principle is that the master must have injured an external, visible limb. On the other hand, while the testicles are located externally in the sense of not being inside the body cavity, they are not fully visible in the way that a finger or an eye is—they are, as Rashi puts it, *tluyim be-kis ve-nikarim mi-bachutz*, suspended within the scrotal sac and discernible from outside, but not exposed in the way that would make the injury itself plainly visible. Rav Hamnuna did not know the answer.

### Hamnuna's Mission

Rav Hamnuna returned to Rav Chisda with the elders' question unanswered. The irony was palpable: Rav Chisda had sent him saying "have you ever asked me something I didn't answer?"—and here was exactly such a question. Rav Chisda told him: *matnisa ba'u minach*—what they asked you is effectively answered by a *mishnah*.

### Castration & Tongue

The *mishnah* cited lists the twenty-four *rashei evarim* and then adds: *Rabbi omer af ha-sirus*—even castration causes the slave to go free. *Ben Azzai omer af ha-lashon*—and cutting off the tongue.

The *gemara* asks: what castration does Rabbi mean? If it refers to the penis (*gid*), that was already included in the twenty-four *rashei evarim* as the *geviyah*. It must therefore be *sirus de-beitzim*—castration by the testicles. This is the answer to the elders' question: the *mishnah* itself treats the testicles as a visible limb, at least according to Rabbi.

The *gemara* then turns to the tongue. Rabbi said *af ha-sirus* and did not mention the tongue; Ben Azzai said *af ha-lashon*. Does this mean Rabbi would not free a slave whose tongue was cut off? The *gemara* answers: *Rabbi omer sirus ve-lo mibaye lashon*—when Rabbi says castration, cutting the tongue goes without saying, since the tongue is at least as visible as the testicles if not more so; you can actually see the tongue, whereas you never fully see the testicles themselves. Ben Azzai, by saying *af ha-lashon*, is disagreeing not with Rabbi but with the *tana kamma*'s list of twenty-four—he is adding the tongue to that list. The testicles, in Ben Azzai's view, do not qualify.

This produces an initially puzzling reading of the text, since Ben Azzai's statement comes after Rabbi's and uses the word *af*, "even." One might expect that Ben Azzai is adding to Rabbi's position, making him more inclusive. But the *gemara* reads it the opposite way: Ben Azzai is more restrictive than Rabbi (excluding the testicles), and *af ha-lashon* adds the tongue not to Rabbi's enumeration but to the *tana kamma*'s original twenty-four. The reason Ben Azzai was appended to the end rather than placed before Rabbi in the sequence is a principle about oral texts: *tana samakh le-de-Rebbe ve-kav'ah, ve-tani mishna lo zaz mi-mkomo*—once the text was learned and memorized in a certain form, it was not rearranged even when a later opinion needed to be integrated. Ben Azzai's view was tagged onto the end even though the resulting *af* is somewhat confusing.

---

## Tongue Status

### Tumah Context

Having established that the tongue is treated as an external limb for purposes of freeing the slave—at least according to Rabbi—the *gemara* now examines whether the tongue is consistently classified as external or whether its classification shifts depending on the legal context. Ulla states: *hakol modim bi-lashon le-inyan tum'ah de-galuye hu etzel sheretz*—everyone agrees that for purposes of contracting *tum'ah* through contact with a *tamei* object, the tongue is considered external. The relevant principle is that *tum'at maga*, becoming *tamei* through contact, requires touching with an external part of the body. If one were to hold a piece of *neveilah* entirely inside one's mouth without any external surface touching it, one would not become *tamei*. But if the tongue touches the *tamei* object, that counts. The reason: *asher yiga bo amra rachmana*—the verse speaks of touching (*nega'*), and the tongue is a natural instrument of touching. From the perspective of *nega'*, the tongue is external—it is how one touches things.

### Tvilah Context

By contrast, Ulla continues, for purposes of *tvilah* in the *mikvah*, everyone agrees that the tongue is considered internal (*ke-tamun dami*) and does not require direct contact with *mikvah* water. The reason: *ve-rachatz besaro ba-mayim amra rachmana*—the verse says one should wash one's *basar*, one's flesh, with water. Just as one's flesh is external (*mibar*), so everything that requires water contact must be external. The tongue, kept inside the mouth and not exposed the way the skin is, does not fall into that category.

The conceptual distinction emerges clearly: when the question is one of *nega'*—an act of touching—the tongue qualifies as external, because touching is something done with a tongue. When the question is one of the body's surface being contacted by water, analogous to skin, the tongue does not qualify. Rashi adds an additional practical dimension: one cannot expose the entire surface of one's tongue to water even if one tried, whereas any act of touching can be performed with any part of the tongue. This further explains why the two contexts yield opposite conclusions.

### Maidservant Story

A challenge arises: does Rabbi truly hold that the tongue is internal for purposes of *tvilah*? After all, the *gemara* recounts: *ma'aseh be-shifchato shel beis Rebbe*—there was an incident with a maidservant in Rabbi's household who immersed in the *mikvah*, and when she emerged there was a bone (*etzem*) between her teeth. Rabbi required her to immerse again. This seems to imply that the interior of the mouth must be free of interposition—that the *mikvah* water must in some sense be capable of reaching inside the mouth.

### Natural Cavities

The *gemara* resolves this: *ne-hi de-vi'at mayim lo be'inan, makom ha-rauy la-vo bo mayim be'inan*—we do not require that *mikvah* water actually enter the oral cavity, but the cavity must be fit for water to enter (*rauy la-vo*), free of any *chatzitzah* that would impede it. This is the principle of *beit ha-starim*: concealed orifices and natural cavities—the inside of the ear, beneath the eyelid, the oral cavity, and similarly *beit ha-kamatin*, the natural folds of the body—do not require the water to actually make contact, but they must not be blocked. The bone between the maidservant's teeth was a *chatzitzah* preventing the cavity from being *rauy* for water contact, which is why Rabbi required a second immersion.

### Potential vs. Actual

This leads to the broader question: when does *halakha* require that an act actually occur, and when is it sufficient that the act could occur? The parallel principle is that of Rabbi Zeira: *kol ha-rauy le-vilah ein vilah me'akevet bo*—anything capable of being mixed with oil (in the context of a *mincha* offering) does not require that the mixing actually occur; but anything incapable of being mixed requires division into separate offerings. The *gemara* applies this logic to *tvilah*: the *beit ha-starim* need not have water contact it, but it must be capable of being contacted.

Tosafot raises the pointed question: how do we know that "fit for" is sufficient rather than requiring the act itself? By analogy, one might argue that a *lulav* only needs to be "fit for" being held, without actually holding it—which is absurd. Tosafot answers that the distinction lies in how the Torah frames the obligation. Where the Torah says *you shall do* an act, the act must occur. Where the Torah describes the *nature* of an object—as when *mincha* is described as *balul ba-shemen*, mixed with oil, rather than saying "you must mix it"—it is sufficient that the object be of that character in potentia. Regarding *beit ha-starim* in *tvilah*, the tension between *kol besaro* (which seems to include even hidden areas) and the comparison to the hand (*ma yadav mi-bora'ei, af kol mi-bora'ei*, requiring external surfaces) is resolved by the intermediate category: the *beit ha-starim* must be *rauy* for water but need not actually be contacted.

Some *rishonim* find Tosafot's explanation insufficient, noting that the obligation of *tvilah* is phrased as an act (*ve-rachatz*), not a description of character. They therefore hold that the requirement of *beit ha-starim* being *rauy* is only *de-rabbanan*. This has significant practical implications: Rav Ovadia Yosef's leniencies in *sheilos* involving blocked orifices often rest on this position, allowing greater latitude when combined with other *shitot*, even though as a general rule a *de-rabbanan* concern is not automatically waived even *be-di'eved*.

---

## Testicles Visibility

### Blemish Verse

The *gemara* now returns to the question of whether crushing the testicles constitutes a visible *mum*, framing it as a dispute among *tanna'im*. The verse in *Vayikra* enumerates blemishes that disqualify an animal: *ma'uach, ve-katus, ve-nasuk, ve-karus*—crushed, bruised, severed, or cut. According to Rabbi Yehuda, all of these refer to injuries of the testicles (*kulam be-veitzim*).

### Testicle Blemish

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagrees: *kulam be-gid*—all of these terms refer to the penis, not the testicles. For Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, an injury to the testicles does not constitute a visible blemish because the testicles themselves are not a visible limb in the relevant sense. While the scrotum is external, the testicles inside it are not exposed in the way that the penis is, and therefore injuries to them—not involving removal of the scrotum itself—do not register as blemishes on a visible limb.

### Yosi's Position

Rabbi Yosi takes a middle position: *ma'uach ve-katus af be-veitzim*—crushing and bruising apply even to the testicles, but *nasuk ve-karus be-gid, be-veitzim lo*—severance and cutting apply only to the penis, not to the testicles. At first glance this seems backward: severance (*nasuk*) and cutting (*karus*) seem more dramatic and visible than mere crushing. The resolution, as Rashi explains (*de-minkar tefei*), is that crushing produces a visible change in the shape and appearance of the scrotal area, while internal severance of the testicles within the scrotum may not produce any external sign at all. Rabbi Yosi is thus distinguishing not by severity of the injury but by whether the injury is externally discernible. The crushing is visible in its effect on the outside; the detachment is internal and therefore not a blemish on a visible limb.

This raises an important conceptual point about the two legal contexts. For the *eved*, the question is whether the *limb* is external and visible—if the testicles qualify as a visible limb, then any significant injury to them frees the slave. For the animal *mum*, the question may instead be whether the *injury* is externally visible. These are not the same question, and one must be careful about directly equating the *tanna'im*'s positions in one context with the other.

---

## Animals Kinyan

### Mishna Modes

Having concluded the *sugyot* relating to human beings as objects of acquisition—whether as wives through *ishut* or as *eved kena'ani* who, though fully property in some respects, retain a human identity—the *gemara* transitions to the acquisition of animals. The *mishnah* teaches: *behema gasa nikneit be-mesira*, a large animal such as a cow or horse is acquired by *mesira*, the handing over of the reins or lead; *ve-ha-daka be-hagbaha*, a small animal such as a sheep or goat is acquired by lifting (*hagbaha*). This is the position of Rabbi Meir.

### Hagbaha Dispute

Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* disagree: *behema daka nikneit be-meshicha*—a small animal is acquired by *meshicha*, pulling or leading, not by *hagbaha*. This sets up a central analytical question about the hierarchy of *kinyanim*. *Hagbaha* is considered the most powerful form of acquisition: lifting an object demonstrates total physical mastery and control. *Meshicha*—causing the animal to move—is a lesser act. If *hagbaha* is possible with a small animal (one can lift a sheep), why does the *mishnah* according to Rabbi Meir specify *hagbaha*, and why do the *chachamim* prefer *meshicha*?

The key principle is one of hierarchy. If *hagbaha* is specified, it means *hagbaha* and not the weaker *meshicha*. If *meshicha* is specified, it means even *meshicha* suffices. The *chachamim*'s position that *meshicha* works for small animals implies that *meshicha* is sufficient even though *hagbaha* would certainly also work. The debate is whether we demand the superior *kinyan* when it is available, or whether a lesser one is adequate.

---

## Rava's Position

### Shmuel Challenge

The *gemara* reports that Rava gave a public *drasha* in the town of Kimchunia stating that a large animal is acquired by *meshicha*. Shmuel encountered Rav's students and challenged this: did Rav really say *meshicha* for a large animal? The *mishnah* says *mesira*, and Rav himself was known to rule *mesira*. What is Rava doing?

### Alignment Question

The *gemara* answers that Rava had retracted his earlier position. He now held *meshicha*, aligning himself with the *chachamim* as quoted in a *baraita*: *ve-chachamim omrim zo va-zo nikneit be-meshicha*—the *chachamim* rule that both large and small animals are acquired by *meshicha*.

### Shimon Opinion

Rabbi Shimon, however, takes the most demanding position: *zo va-zo be-hagbaha*—both large and small animals require *hagbaha*. Since *hagbaha* is at the top of the hierarchy, those who specify it mean *only* hagbaha. The practical difficulty this creates—particularly for animals that cannot be lifted—will be addressed shortly.

---

## Animals Kinyan (II)

### Rashi's Hierarchy

Rashi's analysis of the *mishnah*'s term *mesira* illuminates the broader debate about hierarchy. Rashi explains that *mesira* means specifically the handing over of reins or a saddle, and that *meshicha* would *not* constitute a valid *kinyan* for a large animal in this view: *aval meshicha lo maknya de-ein darkah be-chach lilech lefanav*. The reason Rashi gives is striking: large animals do not walk in front of you—they are led, with the owner handing control forward. *Meshicha*, in Rashi's understanding, means driving the animal from behind, which is not how large animals normally move. Accordingly, *mesira* is not merely a weaker form of *meshicha*; it is the uniquely appropriate act for large animals, while *meshicha*—pushing from behind—is the natural mode for small animals like sheep and goats.

Tosafot disagrees with this hierarchy. For Tosafot, *meshicha* is clearly the stronger act—you do more than merely hand over a lead, you actually cause the animal to move. *Mesira* without movement is a lesser demonstration of control. The debate between Rashi and Tosafot thus goes to the heart of how we define the hierarchy: Rashi holds *mesira* is higher for large animals because it is the appropriate and meaningful act; Tosafot holds *meshicha* is always higher because movement demonstrates greater mastery. On Tosafot's reading, when the *mishnah* says *mesira* for large animals, it means even *mesira* suffices—*meshicha* would certainly also work. On Rashi's reading, *mesira* means *mesira* and not *meshicha*, because the latter is simply not an appropriate act for a large animal.

It is worth noting that these positions need not entail a strict universal hierarchy. It is possible to hold that *mesira* is appropriate exclusively for large animals and *meshicha* exclusively for small ones, with neither strictly including the other—mutual exclusivity based on contextual appropriateness rather than rank. But the *gemara*'s general framework tends toward hierarchy, and the debate among *rishonim* largely proceeds on that assumption.

---

## Elephant Hagbaha

### Rav Yosef Query

The difficulty with Rabbi Shimon's position—requiring *hagbaha* for all animals—becomes acute when Rav Yosef challenges it: *ela me'ata, pil le-Rabbi Shimon be-meh yikneh?*—according to Rabbi Shimon, how would one acquire an elephant? No human being can lift an elephant, so *hagbaha* seems practically impossible.

### Abaye Solutions

Abaye offers two answers. First, *be-chalifin*—one could use *kinyan sudar*, the symbolic exchange of a kerchief, to effect the acquisition. Second, *i nami be-schirut mekomo*—one could rent the space the elephant occupies, a mechanism that somehow effects acquisition of the elephant itself. The second answer envisions something like placing stools or bundles beneath the elephant so that it stands upon objects belonging to the purchaser.

### Vessels & Bundles

The *gemara* explores whether the elephant standing on the buyer's objects constitutes a valid *kinyan*. This would require the buyer's vessels (*kelim*) to effect acquisition even while located in the seller's domain. The *gemara* answers that the case is one where the elephant is standing in a *simta*, a public alleyway, where a buyer's *kelim* are recognized as capable of effecting acquisition. Alternatively, the answer involves *chavilei zemorot*—bundles of vines placed for the elephant to step on.

### Rise vs. Lift

Rashi and Tosafot dispute what the bundle answer accomplishes. For Rashi, placing bundles under the elephant so that it steps on them and rises three *tefachim* off the ground constitutes a form of *hagbaha*: the buyer caused the animal to rise, even without physically lifting it. Rashi apparently holds that *hagbaha* does not require the buyer to personally hoist the animal, only that the animal is elevated by the buyer's act. Tosafot prefers a different reading: the bundles are elephant food placed high up, causing the elephant to rear up on its hind legs to reach the food. This too is a form of induced rising. However, Tosafot's answer raises its own difficulties: whether an elephant can meaningfully "jump," and more fundamentally, whether causing an animal to raise part of its body is equivalent to the *kinyan* of *hagbaha*. The conceptual problem is the same in both accounts—did the buyer perform *hagbaha*, or merely cause the animal to move in a way that resembles it?

---

## Kinyan Hierarchy

### One vs. Multiple

The concluding discussion raises a question that cuts across the entire preceding analysis: when multiple *kinyanim* are valid for a given transaction, does the existence of a superior *kinyan* preclude using an inferior one? Or do multiple valid modes coexist, any one of which may be used at will?

### Kinyan Mitzvot

The *Rashbam* articulates the challenge with characteristic sharpness: *ve-chi kinyanim mitzvot hen she-ein la'asot ela min ha-muvchar?*—are *kinyanim* like *mitzvot*, such that one is obligated to perform only the most distinguished option? The question is deliberately provocative. When we speak of performing a *mitzva* *min ha-muvchar*, from the finest available, we are talking about a religious obligation where the quality of the act reflects on one's service of God. But a *kinyan* is a legal mechanism for transferring ownership—a tool, not a religious duty in that sense. To say one must use the superior *kinyan* when available seems to misunderstand the nature of the institution. This striking formulation of the Rashbam is left for further discussion.

---

---

# Kiddushin 26

## Kinyanim Hierarchy

### Jumping Elephants

Two matters from the previous session warrant brief revisitation before proceeding to the *mishna*. The first concerns *Tosafos*' reading of the *Gemara*'s discussion of bundles of twigs. According to *Rashi*, the case involves walking on top of the twigs, such that one gets the elephant to move off the ground — a form of *hagbaha* that, notably, does not require actually lifting the object clear of the surface. *Tosafos*, by contrast, understands the case differently: one holds a twig with a leaf aloft and the elephant leaps for it. The difficulty, of course, is that elephants do not jump — a point confirmed by those who follow the writings of Natan Slifkin on the natural world. Whether *Tosafos* had ever observed an actual elephant is itself an open question. One proposed defense of *Tosafos* — that the discussion concerns an elephant on a trampoline — may be taken for what it is worth.

### Hierarchy Debate

The second point concerns the hierarchy of *kinyanim*. When the *Gemara* states that a particular *kinyan* works for a given type of object, the implication is that lower-ranked *kinyanim* do not. So when one says *hagbaha* works for *behemah dakah*, the point is that *meshichah* and *mesirah* do not. Understanding which *kinyan* is considered stronger is therefore crucial. When the *Gemara* states that *mesirah* works for *behemah gassah*, is that an exclusive statement — *mesirah* and not *meshichah* — as *Rashi* reads it? Or does it mean that even *mesirah* suffices, and certainly *meshichah*? The direction of the hierarchy matters. Once *halacha* accepts that multiple *kinyanim* work in a given case, one may in principle use whichever is available.

### R. Tam's Objection

A position attributed to the *Rashbam*, however, goes further: in certain cases where both *mesirah* and *meshichah* are available, one is obligated to perform *meshichah* — the stronger *kinyan* — and doing the weaker one would be insufficient. *Tosafos* records *Rabbeinu Tam*'s sharply worded objection to this. The relevant passage in *Tosafos* begins approximately ten lines before the end of that *Tosafos*, at the word *l'miknayei*. The *Tosafos* reads: since *meshichah*, which is the more distinguished *kinyan*, is available in a place such as a *simta*, it would be inappropriate — *lav orach d'ara* — to effect the acquisition through *mesirah*, which is the inferior *kinyan*. Then *Rabbeinu Tam* poses his famous challenge: *v'chi mitzvos hein* — are *meshichah* and *mesirah* commandments, such that performing one is *mevatlo* the other, and one is required to perform the *mitzvah min hamuvchar*, the most distinguished option? The point is incisive: *kinyanim* are not ritual acts whose relative merit carries normative weight. If both are ruled valid in a given case, why should one be compelled to choose the stronger one? The act either transfers ownership or it does not.

### Ownership Demonstration

The conceptual logic underlying the *Rashbam*'s position, however, is not without merit. The underlying purpose of a *kinyan* is to demonstrate *ba'alus* — ownership. If a stronger demonstration of ownership is available, then performing the weaker one in its presence may not constitute a meaningful act of ownership at all. *Mesirah*, according to *Tosafos*, is indeed a relatively weak form of demonstration: merely holding the reins is not the same as drawing an object toward oneself or lifting it. When the stronger forms of demonstrating ownership are available, *mesirah* in that context may be insufficiently meaningful — not because of any ritual hierarchy, but because relative to what could have been done, it does not signify genuine control. In isolation, *mesirah* can work; when better options are present, the act may not rise to the level of a meaningful expression of ownership.

This gives rise to a broader conceptual point. One might think of ownership as binary — either the transfer occurred or it did not — like a switch being flipped. But the *Rashbam*'s view suggests a more graduated picture, where the meaningfulness of the act of acquisition is itself context-dependent. Whether the *halacha* follows this graduated view or the binary one is part of what the debate between *Rabbeinu Tam* and the *Rashbam* is really about.

---

## Land with Money

### Achrayut Defined

The *Gemara* now moves from *metaltelin* — from animals in particular — to land. The *mishna* at the top of 26b reads: *nechasim sheyesh lahem achrayut niknim b'kesef b'shtar uv'chazakah* — property that bears liens is acquired through money, through a document, and through *chazakah*. The phrase *nechasim sheyesh lahem achrayut* is the older, more antiquated formulation for real estate. In later usage this becomes simply *karka*, but this *mishna* employs the earlier idiom, a detail that reflects the age and tightness of this collection of *mishnayot*. As noted when beginning *Masechet Kiddushin*, this series of *mishnayot* — organized around a single theme of degrees of *kinyanim*, moving through women, slaves, Hebrew slaves, *eved kena'ani*, and various categories of property — represents a very early and tightly organized collection.

*Nechasim sheyesh lahem achrayut* means land and real estate because real property serves as collateral: when a loan is made, a lien attaches to the lender's land. The *mishna* states that such property is acquired by *kesef*, *shtar*, and *chazakah*.

### Three Methods

There is, incidentally, a significant debate regarding what *kesef* means in this context. Normally one would assume it refers to payment of the full purchase price. But the parallel to *kiddushei isha* — where *kesef* is fulfilled symbolically by a single *perutah* — raises the question of whether paying the first *perutah* toward the purchase of land itself constitutes *kinyan kesef*. Two conceptual frameworks present themselves. One could say the full payment is technically required, but as soon as a single dollar is paid, we treat it as though the remainder has been paid and the seller has lent the buyer the balance — so the outstanding amount is a loan, not an unpaid purchase price. Alternatively, one could say that any partial payment effects the *kinyan* immediately. The analogous discussion in *Bava Kamma* regarding a merchant who has not yet received full payment — whether such an outstanding debt is a *halva'ah* subject to *shemitah* annulment or an unpaid commercial obligation — is equally relevant. The fundamental question here is whether the model of *kiddushei isha*, where the first *perutah* is sufficient, teaches that the same symbolic sufficiency applies to land, or whether land is fundamentally different and requires the full purchase price.

The *mishna* continues: *u'v'shtar* — with a document, which as the *Gemara* will explain means the seller writes *sadi mechurah lach* and hands over the document. And *uv'chazakah* — through taking possession, which will be discussed in its own right. The reason *karka* requires these distinct forms of *kinyan* rather than the intuitive forms used for *metaltelin* is conceptually clear. *Metaltelin* is movable: one can draw it toward oneself, lift it, carry it into one's home. Ownership of chattels is demonstrated by physical control — the object is on one's person, in one's house, in one's domain. The principle *kol mah shetachat yad adam harei hu shelo* — whatever is under a person's control is presumed to be his — explains why *meshichah*, *hagbaha*, *yad*, and *chatzer* all work for movables: they all express meaningful physical control.

Land, by contrast, cannot be lifted or drawn toward oneself. Simply standing on someone else's land does not demonstrate ownership. The *kinyanim* for land therefore focus on the act of exchange itself — *kesef* is transactional, *shtar* is transactional, and *chazakah*, while touching on something more like control, is still a momentary act rather than an ongoing state of possession. This is why the law of land requires these particular modes.

The *mishna* goes on: *nechasim she'ein lahem achrayut ein niknin ela b'meshichah* — chattel that bears no liens is acquired only through *meshichah*. Though *hagbaha* would obviously also work, and *mesirah* was applicable in certain cases involving animals, the general rule for inanimate movables is *meshichah*. Then: *nechasim she'ein lahem achrayut niknin im nechasim sheyesh lahem achrayut b'kesef b'shtar uv'chazakah* — chattel can be acquired together with land through the same modes that acquire land. The *Gemara* will address whether the chattel must be physically present on the land for this to work.

The *mishna* then adds a further dimension: *v'zokakin et hanechasim sheyesh lahem achrayut l'hishava aleihem* — the chattel can drag the land into the orbit of an oath. Normally, no oath is taken regarding land; oaths are taken only regarding chattel — as in *modeh b'miktzat* or disputes about objects entrusted for safekeeping. But through the mechanism of *gilgul shvuah*, once someone is obligated to take an oath regarding chattel, that oath can roll forward and encompass land as well. So the relationship between land and chattel is bidirectional: land can pull chattel along in the act of acquisition, and chattel can pull land along into the domain of oaths.

### Money Source

The *Gemara* asks: *b'kesef m'nalan* — what is the source that land is acquired with money? *Chizkiyah* answers: *amar kra sadot b'kesef yiknu* — the verse says fields shall be purchased with money, a passage in *Yirmiyah*.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges: perhaps the verse requires both money *and* a document, since the verse continues with instructions to write a document, seal it, and have witnesses sign it. The *Gemara* responds with a grammatical argument: if the verb *yiknu* appeared at the end of the verse, one might read money and document together as a joint condition. But since *yiknu* appears immediately after *b'kesef* — *sadot b'kesef yiknu* — the acquisition is effected by the money alone. The subsequent instructions to write a document are, in the context of that verse, purely evidentiary: *shtar re'ayah b'alma hu* — the document is merely for proof. The document can, of course, also serve as the operative mode of acquisition in other circumstances, but in this verse it is not what effects the transaction.

A natural question arises: why not derive the rule from the *pesukim* regarding *Avraham*'s purchase of the cave of *Machpeilah*, where money is also paid for land? *Tosafos* explains that the *Gemara* prefers not to draw from that episode because it involves a transaction with a non-Jew, and the rules of *kinyan* for non-Jews may differ.

### Rav's Condition

*Rav* now introduces an important qualification: *lo shanu ela b'makom she'ein kotvin shtar* — the rule that money alone suffices applies only where it is not the local practice to write a document. In a place where writing a document invariably accompanies every land transaction — *makom shekotvin shtar* — money alone does not effect the *kinyan*.

*Rashi* explains this as a *gemar da'at* issue. If the universal practice in a given locale is that a document of sale always accompanies the transaction, then even if technically money could suffice, the parties' own expectations define when ownership is finalized. Since the seller does not consider the transaction complete until the document is transferred, there is no *gemar da'at* on the seller's part until that occurs — *lo samcha da'atei d'lokach ad d'nakat shtra*. One interpretation of this principle focuses on cases where the practice recognizes that the transaction is simply not concluded without a document, making it a formal condition. Another reading, suggested here, goes further: even if the document functions technically as *re'ayah*, if registering the transfer is so universally expected that no one considers ownership to have moved until that step is completed, then the *gemar da'at* is correspondingly delayed.

The *Gemara* adds: *v'ei parish parish* — but if the parties explicitly state that the money alone will effect the *kinyan*, it works. Money is fundamentally valid; the default expectation in a document-writing locale merely shifts the assumption, and that assumption can be overridden by explicit agreement.

### R. Idi Bar Avin

This leads to the practice of *Rav Idi bar Avin*: whenever he purchased land, he would declare — *amar ei baina b'chaspa ikni, ei baina b'shtar ikni* — "if I choose, the money shall effect the acquisition; if I choose, the document shall effect the acquisition." His reasoning was straightforwardly strategic. If the money changed hands first (as is typically more convenient than drafting a document), he could retroactively declare that the *kinyan* took effect at the moment of payment — thereby locking in the transaction and preventing the seller from retracting. Alternatively, if he wished to preserve his own right to withdraw after the money had been paid but before the document was drafted, he could declare that the document would be the operative *kinyan*, leaving him free to retract in the interim.

This practice reflects a broader principle about *kinyanim*: they are not rigid ritual acts but instruments of *gemar da'at*, and the parties' articulated intentions can shape which act carries operative weight. This is consistent with the concept of *kinyan situmta* — where the accepted commercial practice of a given community can itself constitute a valid *kinyan*, provided genuine *gemirus da'at* is present. In the diamond trade, for instance, the declaration *mazel u'bracha* is understood as the operative signal that the deal is concluded, enforceable before a *beit din*.

What is perhaps the larger *chidush* of *Rav Idi bar Avin*'s practice is the idea that one party can reserve the right to determine retroactively which act constituted the *maaseh kinyan*. This is a more unusual claim than simply preserving a right of retraction, since it concerns the characterization of which act, among acts that have already occurred, carries the legal weight of the transfer.

---

## Land with Document

### Document Source

The *Gemara* turns to the second mode: *u'v'shtar m'nalan* — what is the source for acquisition of land by document? One might initially suggest deriving it from the instruction in the same verse of *Yirmiyah* to write a document and seal it — but the *Gemara* already established that in that context the document is merely evidentiary. The operative source is instead a different verse in the same passage: *va'ekach et sefer ha'miknah* — "and I took the book of purchase." The document is called the *sefer ha'miknah* — the instrument of acquisition — indicating that the document itself effects the transaction.

### Shmuel's Limit

*Shmuel* now introduces a parallel limitation to *Rav*'s ruling about money: *lo shanu ela b'shtar matanah* — the rule that a document alone suffices applies only to a gift. *Aval b'mecher lo kanah ad sheyiten damim* — but in a sale, one does not acquire until money actually changes hands.

The reasoning again tracks *gemar da'at*. A gift, by definition, involves no expectation of payment; the document alone fully expresses the donor's finalized intention. In a sale, however, the seller expects payment, and without receiving it, has not achieved the settled state of mind — the *gemar da'at* — that the transaction is concluded. The document alone, in the context of a sale, does not suffice.

### Hamnuna Challenge

*Rav Hamnuna* challenges *Shmuel* from a *braita*: *b'shtar keitzad* — how is the acquisition by document accomplished? One writes on paper or even on a shard of pottery — *al haniyar o al hacheres* — the phrase *sadi mechurah lach* or *sadi netunah lach*, "my field is sold to you" or "my field is given to you," and *harei zu mechurah u'netunah* — it is thereby sold or given. Crucially, the *braita* treats *mechira* and *matanah* together, implying that a document alone works even in a sale — directly contradicting *Shmuel*.

### Desperate Seller

*Rav Hamnuna* himself resolves the challenge he raised: *b'mocher sadehu mipnei ra'atah* — the *braita* addresses the special case of someone who is desperate to sell his field because it is worthless or has been on the market for a very long time. In such a case, the seller has *gemar da'at* even without receiving payment — he is sufficiently eager to conclude the transaction that the document alone suffices. In the standard case, where the seller's field is desirable and commands a fair price, the seller is not reconciled to the transaction until he actually receives the money, and so the document alone is insufficient.

### R. Ashi Reinterp.

*Rav Ashi* offers a different reading of the *braita* entirely. He reinterprets the two phrases — *sadi netunah lach* and *sadi mechurah lach* — not as two alternative scenarios but as a single transaction.
