The *gemara* is effectively saying that the scenario where the most tenuous possible "payment" occurs is the one in which *kinyan kessef* is most firmly operative.

Rashi already notes that logically the *shor* and *chamor* of the *mishnah* could just as well be placed in the *kli* category rather than *peirot*, which would dissolve the entire problem for Rav Nachman. But the deeper issue is conceptual: the *gemara* is applying to the plain barter case of the *mishnah* a set of categorical distinctions — *matbei'a*, *peirot*, *kli* — that properly belong to the *sugya* of *kinyan sudar*, where the *kinyan* is not a simple exchange of goods but a formal act of symbolic commitment. The conflation of barter and *kinyan sudar* under a single framework produces the interpretive contortions the *gemara* undertakes here.

The *gemara* concludes the passage regarding Reish Lakish, who holds that *meshicha meforeshet min ha-Torah* — the requirement of *meshicha* for *metaltelin* is explicitly derived from the Torah, and he does not share Rabbi Yochanan's view that *kinyan kesef* retains biblical force. For Reish Lakish, the Rav Nachman reading of the *mishnah* is simply impossible — there is no *kinyan kesef* to invoke. Reish Lakish must therefore read the *mishnah* as a case of *chalifin* with *peirot*, and is therefore compelled to hold like Rav Sheshet that *peirot* do indeed work for *chalifin*.

---

## Reshus Gavoa vs. Hedyot

### Kesef vs. Chazaka

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishnah*, again in archaic language: *reshus ha-gavoah be-kesef u-reshus ha-hedyot be-chazakah*. The *mishnah* uses the older terminology of *reshus gavoah* — the domain of the Most High — for what is elsewhere called *hekdesh*, and *reshus hedyot* — the domain of the ordinary person — for what is called *chulin*, non-consecrated property. *Hekdesh* acquires through money (*kesef*); a layperson acquires through *chazakah* — meaning physical possession, which in practice means *meshicha* for *metaltelin* and *chazakah* for *karka*.

### Amirah Principle

The *mishnah* adds a further statement: *amiraso le-gavoah ki-mesiraso le-hedyot* — one's verbal declaration to the Most High is equivalent to physical delivery to an ordinary person. If I declare an ox to be a *korban olah*, or declare that my house is *hekdesh*, those words immediately transfer the status and ownership of the object to the *Beit HaMikdash*, without any physical act of *kinyan* being required. Contrast this with a transfer to another person, which requires either *meshicha* (for *metaltelin*) or *chazakah* (for *karka*).

### Gizbar Example

The *Tanna'im* expand on the principle of *reshus gavoah be-kesef*. A *braita* teaches: *gizbar she-nasan ma'ot be-behemah* — a Temple treasurer who paid money for an animal acquires that animal for *hekdesh* immediately upon payment, *afilu behemah be-sof ha-olam kanah* — even if the animal is at the other end of the world. By contrast, *u-ve-hedyot lo kanah ad she-yimshoch* — an ordinary person does not acquire until he performs *meshicha*. The application of *kinyan kesef* to *hekdesh* is thus unlimited by the physical proximity of the object.

### Kedusha & Ownership

One might initially ask whether this rule serves *hekdesh*'s interests. After all, we noted earlier that the reason the Sages replaced *kinyan kesef* with *kinyan meshicha* for ordinary transactions was to protect the buyer: if the buyer has already paid but not yet taken possession, and the seller has no incentive to safeguard the goods, the buyer bears the loss when something goes wrong. Does the same concern not apply to *hekdesh*?

This question sets up the discussion that follows. The *mishnah*'s statement that *amiraso le-gavoah ki-mesiraso le-hedyot* reflects a broader point about the nature of *hekdesh* property. When an animal or house is designated as *hekdesh*, two distinct legal dimensions are implicated: the *kedusha* — the sacred status — and the ownership. By a *korban*, such as an animal declared an *olah*, the primary dimension is the sacred status: it is not fundamentally a transaction of ownership that drives the designation, but the imposition of a new intrinsic status on the object. One who misuses *hekdesh* property violates the prohibition of *meilah* — misappropriation of sacred property — which is about the violation of the sacred status, not merely a property offense.

But when someone declares his house *hekdesh*, the primary intent is typically to make a donation to the *Beit HaMikdash*. There the ownership dimension is more central. Yet even there, the Torah derives from the verse *ish ki yakdish et beito kodesh la-Shem* — a man who declares his house holy to God — that the verbal designation alone effects both the sacred status and the transfer of ownership simultaneously. This is the power of *amirah le-gavoah*: words that create *kedusha* are also words that transfer ownership, and no separate physical act is required.

---

## Price Changes

### Mashchu Case

The *gemara* now explores a set of cases involving fluctuating market prices in the context of *hekdesh* transactions, and these cases reveal the precise way in which *hekdesh*'s acquisition rules are structured in its favor.

The first case: *mashchu be-maneh, ve-lo hispik lifdoto ad she-amad be-masayim* — a buyer did *meshicha* on an item priced at a hundred from *hekdesh*, but before he paid the money (*pidyon* — the redemption payment that removes the *kedusha* from the object), the market price rose to two hundred. Who owns the object?

Since *hekdesh* acquires through *kesef*, and no money has yet been paid, *hekdesh* still owns the object despite the buyer having performed *meshicha*. The *meshicha* accomplishes nothing: it does not finalize the transfer from *hekdesh* because *hekdesh* does not go by *meshicha*. Consequently, *hekdesh* is entitled to demand *masayim* — two hundred — before releasing the object. The buyer cannot claim the object at the original agreed price. The source is *ve-nasan ha-kesef ve-kam lo* — the object is acquired when the money is given.

### Padahu Case

The second case is the inverse: *mashchu be-masayim, ve-lo hispik lifdoto ad she-amad be-maneh* — the buyer did *meshicha* when the item was worth two hundred, and before paying, the price dropped to a hundred. Now the buyer might reason: the sale was never final (no *kesef* has been paid), so I will only pay a hundred. The *halacha* is that he must pay two hundred. *Mah ta'ama? Lo yehei koach hedyot chamur me-hekdesh* — a layperson should not have greater legal force than *hekdesh*. If in an ordinary transaction the buyer could insist on a lower price after price fluctuation when the sale was not final, that would give the ordinary counterparty rights that *hekdesh* lacks. The rules are structured so that *hekdesh* is never placed at a disadvantage relative to a layperson.

The principle that emerges from the first two cases is that the *kinyanim* for *hekdesh* are stacked in *hekdesh*'s favor. *Hekdesh* uses whichever mode of acquisition — *kesef* or *meshicha* — works to its benefit in the specific situation.

### Mihu She-Para

The third case reverses the starting point: *padahu be-masayim, ve-lo hispik limshacho ad she-amad be-maneh* — the buyer paid two hundred in cash but had not yet performed *meshicha* when the price dropped to a hundred. The obvious implication of *hekdesh*'s ownership rules: *kinyan kesef* was effected by payment, and so the buyer owns the object and cannot demand a refund. He paid two hundred, the sale is complete, and the lower price is irrelevant.

But the next case is surprising. *Padahu be-maneh, ve-lo hispik limshacho ad she-amad be-masayim* — the buyer paid a hundred in cash, and before performing *meshicha*, the price rose to two hundred. One might expect *hekdesh* to invoke *meshicha*: since *meshicha* was never performed, and *hekdesh* can use whichever *kinyan* is most advantageous, perhaps *hekdesh* can now declare the sale incomplete on the basis that no *meshicha* was performed, and demand two hundred. The *gemara* rejects this.

### Limits on Hekdesh

*Mah she-pada paduy* — what has been redeemed is redeemed. The payment of a hundred was effective, and *hekdesh* cannot retroactively demand more. The *gemara*'s reasoning: *atu hedyot lav be-mi she-para kai?* — even in a transaction between ordinary people, if the buyer has paid money and the seller now wishes to back out before *meshicha* is performed, the seller does not escape consequence-free. The seller who reneges after receiving cash is subject to the *mi she-para* curse: may the One who exacted punishment upon the generation of the Flood and upon all those who violated their commitments exact punishment from one who does not stand by his word.

*Hekdesh*, like an ordinary person, is bound by the moral commitment implicit in having received cash. Even though *hekdesh* retains the technical right to insist on *meshicha* as the completing act, it cannot exercise that right in circumstances where doing so would be seen as reneging on a commitment already evidenced by the exchange of money. As it was put: *yado shel hekdesh al ha-elyona* — the advantage is always with *hekdesh* — but that principle cannot be used to permit the *Beit HaMikdash* to act as a scoundrel. *Hekdesh* must honor its commitments, and once cash has been accepted, backing out on the basis of subsequent price increases falls within the conduct that even ordinary commercial morality forbids.

---

---

# Kiddushin 29

## Mitzvot haben al av

### Overview & context

Daf 29 of Kiddushin marks a significant transition in the sugya. We have been moving through an extended discussion of *kinyanim* — the various modes of acquisition — organized with the systematic, categorical precision that characterizes these early *mishnayot*. Having covered *kol hana'aseh damim be'acher* and *reshut gavoah*, the Mishnah now pivots entirely, bringing the same organizational rigor to bear on a different domain: *mitzvot* and the categories of obligation that define who must perform them.

### Mishnah categories

The Mishnah on 29a opens with a characteristically compressed formulation — the sort of strange, almost elliptical locution one finds in particularly early *mishnayot*. It presents four categories, each defined by the intersection of the type of obligation and the gender of the obligated party.

The first category: *kol mitzvot haben al ha'av, anashim chayavin venashim peturot* — all the *mitzvot* of the child upon the father, men are obligated and women are exempt. The second: *vechol mitzvot ha'av al haben, echad anashim ve'echad nashim chayavin* — all the *mitzvot* of the father upon the child, whether men or women are equally obligated. The third: *vechol mitzvot aseh shehazman grama, anashim chayavin venashim peturot* — all positive *mitzvot* caused by time, men are obligated and women are exempt. The Rambam already notes that this rule has approximately as many exceptions as it has clear instances; whether it is a genuinely descriptive principle derived from the particulars or a prescriptive rule that dictates the particulars is itself a major question. The fourth category: *vechol mitzvot aseh shelo hazman grama, echad anashim ve'echad nashim chayavin* — non-time-bound positive *mitzvot* obligate men and women equally. And finally: *vechol mitzvot lo ta'aseh, bein shehazman grama bein shelo hazman grama, echad anashim ve'echad nashim chayavin* — all negative commandments, whether time-bound like *Shabbat* or not time-bound like the prohibition of *chazir*, obligate men and women equally, with three exceptions: *mibal takif*, *u'val tashchit*, and *u'val titama lametim*, the last of which applies specifically to male *kohanim*.

### Gemara interprets

The Gemara immediately asks: what does *kol mitzvot haben al ha'av* mean? If it means all the *mitzvot* that a child is obligated to perform toward a parent — that is, obligations running from child to parent — then why would women be exempt? That cannot be right, because a *braita* explicitly teaches otherwise. The verse states *ish immo ve'aviv tirau* — each man shall fear his mother and father — and the *Midrash Tannaim* derives: I know only that a man is obligated; how do I know a woman is as well? Because *tirau* is in the plural, implying two — both men and women are equally obligated in fearing and honoring their parents.

Rav Yehuda therefore reframes the Mishnah: *kol mitzvot haben hamutallot alav* — the *mitzvot* of the child that are laid upon the parent, meaning parental obligations directed *toward* children. Those, says the Mishnah, are the obligations of fathers toward sons: *anashim chayavim venashim peturot*, men are obligated and women are exempt.

### Kibbud av va'em

With this clarification in place, the structure becomes clear. *Kibbud av va'em* — the child's obligation toward parents — falls under the second category: *echad anashim ve'echad nashim chayavin*. Both men and women, both boys and girls, adult children of all kinds, are equally obligated to honor both father and mother. The asymmetry in the Mishnah applies solely to the parental side: it is fathers, not mothers, who bear the specific duties toward sons that the Gemara is about to enumerate.

## Braita: paternal duties

### Five obligations

The Gemara now turns to a *braita* that spells out concretely what these paternal obligations consist of. *Ha'av chayav bivno* — the father is obligated with respect to his son — in five specific ways: *lemolo*, to circumcise him; *ulfidoso*, to redeem him (*pidyon haben*); *ulilamedo Torah*, to teach him Torah; *ulehashio ishah*, to arrange his marriage; and *ulilamedo ummanus*, to teach him a trade. Some add a sixth: *af lehashito bamayim*, to teach him how to swim — a basic survival skill, the sort of competency that in earlier eras was genuinely life-saving.

It is worth noting that the *braita* does not mention the general obligation of *chinuch* — training a child to perform *mitzvot*, to recite *brachot*, to shake a *lulav*, to light candles, to observe negative commandments. Yet other sources make clear that *chinuch* is also primarily the father's obligation, though there is some discussion as to whether the mother shares in it as well.

### R. Yehuda on trade

Rabbi Yehuda sharpens the obligation of teaching a trade with a striking formulation: *kol she'eino melamed es beno ummanus melamdo listus* — anyone who does not teach his son a trade is as if he teaches him banditry. The Gemara immediately clarifies: surely no one actually teaches their child banditry. Rather, *ke'ilu melamdo listus* — it is *as if* he did, because by failing to provide his son with a legitimate livelihood, he leaves him with no honest means of sustaining himself. The hyperbole carries a moral charge — apparently the obligation to teach one's son a trade was not being taken seriously enough, and Rabbi Yehuda found it necessary to dramatize the stakes.

## Brit Milah analysis

### Father's obligation

The Gemara now unpacks each obligation in turn. *Lemolo* — where do we know that circumcision is the father's obligation? From the verse *vayamol Avraham es Yitzchak beno* — Abraham circumcised Isaac his son. Abraham's act establishes the paradigm. As for how we know this applies to future generations, the school of Rabbi Ishmael will provide the answer shortly.

### Fallback obligations

The Gemara then establishes a hierarchy of fallback obligations. *Veheicha d'la malye avuha mechayavei bei dina lemimalye* — if the father has not circumcised his son, the *beis din* becomes obligated, because the verse says *himmol lachem kol zachar* — you shall have circumcised for you all males — addressing the community collectively. The community bears responsibility to ensure that all Jewish males are circumcised; if the father fails, that obligation reverts to the public.

If *beis din* likewise fails to act and the child reaches adulthood uncircumcised, *mechayev ihu lemimhal nafshei* — he is now obligated to circumcise himself, derived from *ve'arel zachar asher lo yimmol besar orlaso venichresa* — an uncircumcised male who does not circumcise his foreskin shall be cut off. The very fact that he bears punishment for failure to circumcise demonstrates that he carries a personal obligation to do so.

A notable feature of this hierarchy is that it moves from father to community to self — the mother is not named as an intermediate or backup obligant. This stands in contrast to the story of Tzipporah, who performed the *bris milah* herself. It is important to distinguish between two separate questions: who is capable of executing the act (which the Tzipporah story addresses and which the Gemara in Avodah Zarah discusses), and who bears the halakhic obligation to ensure that the act is performed (which is our question here). On the latter question, the mother appears to be written out of the hierarchy entirely. There is, however, a Rashi elsewhere and a *Mareh Or Zarua* suggesting that the mother does bear an obligation after the father — which raises interesting practical questions, such as whether a single mother performing the *milah* for her son may recite the *bracha* of *lehachniso bivriso shel Avraham Avinu* in her own right as mother, or perhaps only as a representative of the community standing in place of *beis din*.

### Women excluded

How do we know that the mother bears no obligation? *D'ksiv kaasher tziva oso Elohim* — because the verse says as God commanded *him*, Abraham — *oso v'lo osa*: him and not her, not Sarah.

### Tanaic proof

But this is the verse about Abraham and Sarah in their own generation. How do we know it serves as the binding model for future generations? The school of Rabbi Ishmael taught: *kol makom shenemar tzav eino ela zeirus miyad ul'doros* — whenever the Torah uses the root *tzav* (command), it signals both urgency — encouraging alacrity in performance — and applicability to all future generations. This is demonstrated by two verses: *v'tzav es Yehoshua v'chazkeihu v'amtzeihu* (command Joshua, strengthen and encourage him) illustrates the urgency component, and *min hayom asher tziva Hashem v'halah l'doroseichem* (from the day God commanded and onward, for your generations) establishes the multigenerational dimension. Since the verse about Abraham's circumcision of Isaac uses *tziva*, the exclusion of the mother encoded there — *oso v'lo osa* — carries forward to all generations.

## Pidyon HaBen

### Hierarchy of duty

The Gemara turns to *pidyon haben*. The source is *kol bechor banecha tifdeh* — all the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. As with *bris milah*, a hierarchy applies: the father redeems the son, and if the father does not, *michayiv ihu l'mifreikeih l'nafsheih* — the son must redeem himself as an adult, derived from *padoh tifdeh* — you shall surely redeem, implying a personal obligation if the parental one goes unfulfilled.

One significant difference from the *bris milah* hierarchy is worth noting: unlike circumcision, there is no communal obligation that all firstborn sons be redeemed. *Pidyon haben* is an obligation running between father and son; if the father fails, the obligation passes directly to the son himself, without an intermediate stage of communal responsibility.

### Bidirectional logic

How do we know that a woman is not obligated to redeem her son? The Gemara reads *tifdeh tipadeh* — you shall redeem, you shall be redeemed — as establishing a bidirectional principle: *kol shemitzveh lifdos es atzmo mitzveh lifdos es acherim* — whoever is obligated to redeem themselves is obligated to redeem others; *v'chol she'eino mitzveh lifdos es atzmo eino mitzveh lifdos acherim* — whoever is not obligated to redeem themselves is not obligated to redeem others. Since a woman is not subject to redemption herself, she is therefore not obligated to redeem her son.

### Logical deduction

But this raises a prior question: how do we know a woman is not obligated to redeem herself? The Gemara applies the same principle in the other direction: *kol she'acherim mtzuvim lifdoso mitzveh lifdos es atzmo* — if others are obligated to redeem you, you are obligated to redeem yourself. Conversely, *v'chol she'ein acherim mtzuvim lifdoso eino mitzveh lifdos es atzmo* — if no one else is obligated to redeem you, you are not obligated to redeem yourself. The child's obligation to self-redeem exists precisely because the parent's obligation went unfulfilled; where no parental obligation existed in the first place, no self-redemption obligation can arise.

### Daughters excluded

This brings us to the foundation of the entire chain: how do we know that a daughter's parents are not obligated to redeem her? From the verse itself — *kol bechor banecha tifdeh* — *banecha v'lo bnosecha*: your sons and not your daughters. Daughters are not subjects of *pidyon haben*; therefore no one is obligated to redeem them; therefore they are not obligated to redeem themselves; and therefore they are not obligated to redeem others, including their own sons.

The logic works neatly from the end backward. *Banecha v'lo bnosecha* establishes that daughters are not redeemed. *Tifdeh tipadeh* then establishes, in one direction, that those not obligated to be redeemed are not obligated to redeem themselves, and in the other direction, that those not obligated to redeem themselves are not obligated to redeem others. The entire structure of exclusion rests on the initial textual exclusion of daughters from the category of those who must be redeemed.

## Self vs. son debate

### Self first

The Gemara now presents a new *braita*: *hu lifdot u'vno lifdot, hu kodem livno* — if a man must redeem himself (because his father did not do so) and must also redeem his son (as a father), and he lacks the resources to do both, he redeems himself first. This position rests on the principle that one's own personal obligation takes precedence: *mitzva degufei adifa* — an obligation relating to one's own body or status comes first. There is also a chronological logic: presumably the obligation to redeem oneself predates the birth of one's son.

### R. Yehuda: son first

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *beno kodmo* — his son comes first. The conceptual argument is elegant. The father's personal obligation to be redeemed was *originally* on his father; his father failed to fulfill it. The obligation that falls *natively* on this man — the one that is properly his own — is his obligation to his son. Thinking in generational terms: Abraham's obligation was to Isaac; Isaac's obligation was to Jacob. If we are speaking of Isaac, his primary obligation as a father is to Jacob, and his obligation to himself exists only as a derivative of his own father's failure.

### Five sela'im case

Rav Yirmiyahu then reframes the entire dispute, revealing that it is more limited in scope than it initially appears. He says: *hakol modim* — everyone agrees — that if there are only five *sela'im* available (enough for only one *pidyon haben*), *hu kodem livno* — he redeems himself first. *Mitzva degufei adifa* — one's personal obligation takes precedence. This is not what the Gemara seemed to be saying before, but that is the resolution: the dispute between the first opinion and Rabbi Yehuda does not concern the case where there is only enough for one payment.

### Ten sela'im lien

The dispute, Rav Yirmiyahu explains, concerns a case where there are ten *sela'im* — five in cash and five in encumbered property (property upon which creditors hold a lien). The question turns on a fundamental halakhic principle: *milveh haktuva baTorah kaktuva bishtar damya* — does a Torah obligation create a lien on property, just as a written loan document (*shtar*) does?

Rabbi Yehuda holds that it does. On this view, from the moment this man became obligated to redeem himself (say, from Bar Mitzvah), the *kohanim* collectively acquired a lien on his property for five *sela'im*. He subsequently borrowed money from another creditor, Reuven, who also acquired a lien on the same property — but later in time. Rabbi Yehuda therefore says: use the five *sela'im* in cash to redeem your son (fulfilling that obligation first), and the *kohen* will then collect the five *sela'im* from the encumbered property, displacing Reuven's later lien, thus satisfying both obligations. As Rashi explains, the father is entitled to direct his liquid assets to his son's redemption because his son's obligation is primary; it then works out that the *kohanim* can enforce their earlier lien against the encumbered property, leaving Reuven, unfortunately, unable to collect. Rashi's reading, as Tosafot notes, creates some tension — the rationale invoked to justify directing cash to the son (son's obligation is primary) seems to cut against the very premise that self comes first — and Tosafot offers an alternative reading of the Gemara accordingly.

The Rabbis hold that *milveh haktuva baTorah lav kikesuvah bishtar damya* — a Torah obligation does not create a property lien. Therefore the *kohanim* have no prior lien, the five encumbered *sela'im* are of no help to them, and the man must simply choose between redeeming himself and redeeming his son with whatever cash he has. In that situation, *mitzvas degufei adif* — his own obligation takes precedence.

## Pidyon vs. Regel

### Son redeemed first

The Gemara presents another case of competing obligations: *lifdos es beno v'la'alos laregel* — if one must choose between redeeming his son and making the pilgrimage (*aliyah laregel*) to the Temple. The majority view: *podeh es beno v'achar kach oleh laregel* — redeem your son first, then make the pilgrimage.

### R. Yehuda rationale

Rabbi Yehuda, in what at first looks like a reversal of his earlier position (where he prioritized the son), now says the opposite: *oleh laregel v'achar kach podeh es beno* — go on pilgrimage first, then redeem your son. But here there is no contradiction with his earlier ruling, because this is not a question of self versus son but of two distinct obligations. His reasoning: *shezu mitzvah overes v'zu mitzvah einah overes* — *aliyah laregel* is a time-bound obligation that will pass; if you miss the *regel*, you cannot make it up. *Pidyon haben* can be performed later when you acquire the means.

### Verse order logic

The Gemara is satisfied with Rabbi Yehuda's rationale. But what is the Rabbis' rationale for prioritizing *pidyon haben*? *De'amar kra kol bechor banecha tifdeh, v'hadar v'lo yera'u fanai reikam* — the Torah places the verse of redemption before the verse commanding the pilgrimage offering. The sequential order of the *pesukim* itself dictates the priority: first take care of your son's redemption, then address the pilgrimage.

## Multiple firstborns

### Plural sons proof

A new *braita* asks: how do we know that if a man has five firstborn sons from five different wives, he is obligated to redeem all of them? From *kol bechor banecha tifdeh* — the word *kol* (all) indicates that the obligation extends to multiple firstborn sons.

### Peter rechem logic

One might think this is obvious — surely if you have five sons each of whom is a *bechor*, you redeem all five. But there is a genuine question here. *Peter rechem tala Rachmana* — the Torah defines *bechor* status by reference to the opening of the womb, making it a status belonging to the mother's womb, not the father's lineage. So each of these five sons is indeed a *bechor* to his respective mother. The question is whether one also applies the principle of *reishis ono* — the first of his strength — drawn from the laws of inheritance, where *bechor* status is determined by the father. If both conditions were required, a man who already has a son from one wife could never have another *bechor* from a subsequent wife. The Gemara teaches: *ka mashma lan* — no, *bechor* for purposes of *pidyon haben* is determined solely by the mother. Hence a man may have multiple sons who each independently carries *bechor* status, and he is obligated to redeem each of them.

## Talmud Torah obligation

### Father teaches son

The Gemara now turns to the obligation of *Talmud Torah*. The father is obligated to teach his son Torah, derived from *v'limadtem osam es beneichem* — you shall teach your sons. If the father does not teach his son, *mechayav ihu lemigmar nafsheih* — the son, upon becoming an adult, is obligated to learn on his own. This is derived from *ulimadtem* — you shall learn — read not as *v'limadtem* (you shall teach) but as an obligation to learn, implying that if no one taught you, you must teach yourself.

### Sons not daughters

How do we know the obligation is specifically toward sons and not daughters? From *v'limadetem osam es beneichem* — *banecha v'lo bnosecha*: your sons and not your daughters.

### Learn-teach logic

But this only establishes that there is no obligation to teach daughters. How do we derive the mother's exemption from the obligation to teach Torah altogether? The Gemara constructs the same bidirectional logic used for *pidyon haben* and *bris milah*. *Kol shemetzuveh lilmod metzuveh lelamed* — whoever is obligated to learn is obligated to teach. *V'chol she'eino metzuveh lilmod eino metzuveh lelamed* — whoever is not obligated to learn is not obligated to teach.

### Women's exemption

And how do we know a woman is not obligated to learn Torah herself? The same structure applies in the other direction: *kol she'heim metzuvim lelamdo az metzuveh lelamed es atzmo* — if others are obligated to teach you, you are obligated to teach yourself. *Kol she'ein heim metzuvim lelamdo ein metzuveh lelamed es atzmo* — if others are not obligated to teach you, you are not obligated to teach yourself. And since *v'limadetem osam es beneichem* — *banecha v'lo bnosecha* — others are not obligated to teach daughters Torah, daughters are therefore not obligated to teach themselves, and therefore not obligated to teach others.

### Modern discourse

This is, of course, the foundational *Gemara* for one of the most consequential halakhic debates of the modern era. Beginning in the 1950s — with Rav Soloveitchik on one side and the Lubavitcher Rebbe among others on another — and continuing through decades of responsa and scholarly discussion, the question of women's exemption from *Talmud Torah* has generated an enormous body of literature. Many approaches have been proposed: drawing distinctions between *Torah she'bichsav* and *Torah she'be'al peh*; arguing that even if women are exempt from the pure *mitzvah* of *limud Torah* for its own sake (*Torah lishmah*), they are obligated to learn all the Torah necessary for the observance of the many *mitzvot* they do perform — which amounts to a great deal of Torah; and arguing further that learning Torah is an integral part of one's basic relationship with *Hakadosh Baruch Hu* and religious life generally, leaving women's de facto learning obligation not so different in scope from men's. One area where the tension becomes particularly acute is when both spouses wish to devote themselves entirely to full-time Torah study — at which point the technical contours of the exemption become practically significant.

### Sinai context

It is worth noting the broader *midrashic* and *peshat* context that complicates any simple application of this technical exemption. The Torah in *Devarim* repeatedly emphasizes that at *Ma'amad Har Sinai* everyone was present: men, women, and children. *Chazal* themselves underscore this: *koh tomar l'veis Yaakov v'sageid livnei Yisrael* — the *Midrash* reads *l'veis Yaakov* as referring specifically to the women, who were addressed at Sinai first. Similarly, the requirement of *Hakhel* explicitly gathers *anashim nashim v'hataf* — men, women, and children — to hear the Torah read. These sources create a picture of women's deep and primary engagement with Torah that sits in genuine tension with the formal technical exemption, and it is this tension that animates the ongoing debate. The statement in *Sotah* about a father who teaches his daughter Torah — *k'ilu melamdah tiflus* — has also been subject to extensive analysis, with many authorities drawing careful distinctions about what precisely that statement prohibits and what it permits or even encourages.

## Self vs. son Torah

### Self first

The Gemara now applies the same self-versus-son framework to *Talmud Torah*. If a man has not been fully educated in Torah and must choose between studying himself and providing for his son's Torah education, *hu kodem livno* — he comes before his son.

### R. Yehuda condition

Rabbi Yehuda refines this: *im beno zariz ummulach u'tamudo mitkayem beyado, beno kodmo* — if his son is sharp, subtle, and retains what he learns, then his son's learning takes precedence. The underlying principle here is not simply a question of whose obligation is primary but of which investment will yield the greater result. When father and son are equivalently capable, the father's own obligation to himself comes first. But when the son clearly has superior capacity — when his learning will be more productive and enduring — then directing resources toward the son's education takes priority.

### Rav Yaakov story

The Gemara illustrates this with the story of Rav Yaakov, the son of Rav Acha bar Yaakov. Rav Acha sent his son Rav Yaakov to learn from Abaye. When Rav Acha subsequently came to visit, *chazi d'lo havi mechadidun shmatei* — he saw that his son's learning was not sharp; the material was not crisp and precise in his grasp. Rav Acha said to him: *ana adif minach, tuv at d'eizal ana* — I can learn better than you; you stay, I will go learn. The story illustrates that the default assumption had been to send the son — but once the father assessed that his own learning would be more productive, he reasserted his own priority. This is somewhat different from the pure formulation of Rabbi Yehuda's position: rather than saying "I will send my son unless I find I am better," Rav Acha defaulted to sending his son and reversed course only upon discovering his son's deficiency.

### Demon episode

The Gemara then appends a narrative connected to the same setting. *Shama Abaye d'ka havi ati* — Abaye heard that Rav Acha the father was coming. There was a *mazik* — a malevolent spirit — in Abaye's *beit midrash*, *d'chi havi ailei bitrei afilu biyemama havi mitzkei* — such that even when two people entered together, even during the daytime (when such spirits are normally constrained), they were harmed. Abaye instructed that no one should provide Rav Acha with lodging, *efshar d'mitracheish nisa* — perhaps a miracle would occur. Rav Acha was accordingly forced to sleep in the *beit midrash*. The *mazik* appeared to him in the form of a seven-headed serpent. With each prostration that Rav Acha made in prayer, one of the heads fell off — *kol kria d'kara, nassar chad reishei* — until the spirit was vanquished. In the morning he told the students: *ilo lo itrachish nisan sakintan* — had a miracle not occurred, you would have endangered me by forcing me to sleep there.

## Summary

### Duties recap

The sugya of 29a covers, with remarkable density, the core obligations a father bears toward his son: *bris milah*, *pidyon haben*, *Talmud Torah*, arranging marriage, and teaching a trade. In each case, the obligation is directed specifically from father to son — not from mother to son, not from father to daughter, and not from mother to daughter.

### Gender patterns

The textual grounds for excluding women and daughters follow a consistent pattern throughout the *sugya*. For *bris milah*, the exclusion derives from *kaasher tziva oso* — commanding him alone — extended to all generations by the principle that *tzav* implies future applicability. For *pidyon haben*, the chain runs through *banecha v'lo bnosecha* to *tifdeh tipadeh* and back, locking women out on both sides of the redemption relationship. For *Talmud Torah*, *banecha v'lo bnosecha* generates an analogous chain excluding women from the obligation to be taught, to teach themselves, and to teach their sons. There exist minority opinions — a Rashi and the *Mareh Or Zarua* — suggesting that the mother may carry at least a backup or secondary obligation in *bris milah*, which opens interesting questions for edge cases; but the dominant framework throughout this *sugya* is one of consistent textual exclusion.

### Balancing rules

Running through all of these obligations is a second layer of analysis: how to balance competing duties when resources are limited. The tension between one's personal obligation and one's filial obligation is resolved differently in different cases. For *pidyon haben*, the baseline rule is that one's personal obligation (*mitzva degufei adifa*) comes first — though Rabbi Yehuda's position introduces the generational framing that complicates this, and Rav Yirmiyahu's reconciliation confines the dispute to the case of ten *sela'im* with encumbered property. For *Talmud Torah*, personal study generally comes first, but Rabbi Yehuda introduces the aptitude condition — if the son's capacity is superior, the son's learning takes precedence — illustrated concretely by the story of Rav Acha and his son. And when *pidyon haben* competes not with personal obligation but with *aliyah laregel*, the majority prioritizes the non-repeatable obligation of redemption, while Rabbi Yehuda prioritizes the time-sensitive *mitzvah overes* of the *regel*.

# Kiddushin 30

## Torah vs. Marriage

### Tanu Rabbanan

The daf under discussion is daf 30, and we continue in the middle of a rich and multifaceted *mishnah* dealing with a father's obligations to his son. The preceding material covered *bris milah*, *pidyon haben*, and *talmud Torah*, and the shiur now turns to continue exploring *talmud Torah* and related themes.

The *gemara* on 29b opens with a *beraita* introduced by *tanu rabbanan*: between learning *Torah* and getting married — *lilmod Torah v'lisa isha* — which takes priority? This question is no longer about the parental obligation per se, but about competing priorities a young man faces, analogous to earlier questions such as whether one redeems oneself or one's son first, or whether one teaches oneself or one's son first.

### Torah First

The *beraita*'s answer is unambiguous: *yilmod Torah v'achar kach yisa isha* — first learn *Torah*, and only afterward get married. The reasoning is implicit but clear: once married, a man takes on a range of obligations and responsibilities that will inevitably compromise the time and energy available for *Torah* study. Marriage is a weighty undertaking, and one should therefore front-load one's *Torah* learning before assuming those burdens.

It should be noted that implicit in this statement is an assumption of a lifelong, ongoing responsibility to learn. The *gemara* had previously described the father's obligation to educate his son as a kind of foundational primary education — and indeed noted that if the father failed to teach, the son must teach himself. Yet the broader *ethos* of the rabbis is captured in *vehagita bo yomam valailah* — constant, perpetual engagement with *Torah*. The verse *v'shinnantam l'vanecha v'dibarta bam b'shivtecha b'vetecha u'v'lechtecha vaderech* gestures toward this unceasing obligation, even if its precise *halachic* parameters have not yet been fully articulated. The priority given to *Torah* over marriage reflects this assumption: one should be learning as much as possible, growing as much as possible, before taking on responsibilities that will curtail that growth.

### Exception

The *beraita* acknowledges a qualification: *v'im iy efshar lo b'lo isha* — if it is truly impossible for him to manage without a wife, whether for emotional reasons or, as the *gemara* will make explicit shortly, because of the pressure of sexual thoughts (*hirhurei aveira*), then *yisa isha v'achar yilmod Torah* — he may marry first and learn afterward. The hierarchy is not absolute. If a man genuinely needs to marry in order to function, that need takes precedence, but the ideal sequence remains *Torah* first. It is worth noting that the obligation to keep learning is ongoing regardless of when one marries.

---

## Shmuel vs. Yochanan

### Marriage First

The *gemara* then records a striking ruling: *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* — the *halacha* is *nosei isha v'achar yilmod Torah*, marry first, then learn *Torah*. This is the direct opposite of the *beraita* just cited. The question immediately arises: how can Shmuel issue a ruling against an explicit *beraita*?

### Millstone

Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, sides with the *beraita*, and expresses his position with a memorable image: *reichaim b'tzavaro v'ya'asok baTorah?* — you have a millstone around your neck and you think you can learn *Torah*? Once a man shoulders the *ol parnassah*, the yoke of family responsibilities and the need to earn a living, when will he ever find time to learn? Therefore, *Torah* must come first; marriage, with all its weight, must wait.

### V'lo Pligi

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *v'lo pligi* — they do not actually disagree. *Ha lan v'ha lahu* — this ruling applies to us, and that ruling applies to them. Shmuel's ruling is directed at the Jews of Babylonia, while Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is for the inhabitants of *Eretz Yisrael*. This resolution requires explanation, and *Rashi* provides it.

---

## Bavel vs. EY

### Rashi's Explanation

*Rashi*'s explanation is unquestionably the *pshat*. In Babylonia, scholars would leave home and travel to *Eretz Yisrael* to study *Torah*, and in doing so they would effectively abandon their wives and children for extended periods. The *gemara* at the beginning of *Gittin* records this phenomenon vividly: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, writing from *Eretz Yisrael* to those in Babylonia whose husbands had come to learn and left their families behind, invokes the verse *vayitnu et hayeled b'zonah v'et hayaldah machru bayayin* — they have handed their children over to prostitution, as the abandoned families were left without support or supervision. The picture is stark: the pursuit of *Torah* in *Eretz Yisrael* sometimes came at an enormous cost to family life back in Babylonia.

### Babylonian Model

Beyond the geographic dynamic, there is a deeper conceptual difference in how the two communities understood the value of marriage itself. Many Babylonian *gemaras* describe the value of marriage in instrumental terms: marriage protects the husband from sin, provides an outlet for desire, frees him from domestic distraction so he can learn *Torah*, and supplies a kind of domestic infrastructure supporting his learning. In this framework, marriage serves the man's *Torah* study. It is thus consistent that in Babylonia the ruling would be to marry first: get married, satisfy your needs, and then go and learn *Torah* — even if that means eventually leaving your wife and household for extended periods.

### Monogamy/Polygamy

This difference in the conceptualization of marriage is also bound up with a broader sociological distinction. Babylonia, influenced by the surrounding Sassanid culture and still reflecting the biblical model, maintained polygamy, at least among the wealthy. *Eretz Yisrael*, shaped by Roman cultural norms, had moved toward monogamy. This historical difference has long-term consequences: Babylonian Jewish culture eventually flowed into *Sefarad*, where Jews lived among Muslims, and polygamy persisted in those communities. *Eretz Yisrael*'s culture flowed into *Ashkenaz*, embedded in Roman-Christian lands, where monogamy was the norm. This divergence is reflected in the *Yerushalmi*, which essentially assumes monogamy, while the *Bavli* assumes polygamy.

When marriage is understood as exclusively between one man and one woman — a genuine partnership — one thinks of it in terms of mutual obligation and intrinsic value. When the surrounding culture permits multiple wives, the perception of marriage shifts: a wife is more a member of the household than a full partner, and marriage is more easily framed in utilitarian terms.

### EY Model

In *Eretz Yisrael*, by contrast, the *gemara*s describe marriage in far more intrinsic terms. A man who is not married lacks *simcha*, lacks *shalom*, is in some fundamental sense incomplete. Marriage is a primary responsibility in itself, not merely a means to some other end. It follows that once a man in *Eretz Yisrael* marries, those obligations become paramount — *reichaim b'tzavaro*, as Rabbi Yochanan puts it. You cannot then simply leave your wife and go learn *Torah*. Therefore, the prescription for *Eretz Yisrael* is: learn your *Torah* first, because once you are married, that is your primary responsibility and it cannot be subordinated to learning. In Babylonia, by contrast, the attitude was more permissive: marry first, but one may still leave and devote long stretches of time to *Torah* study, since family obligations do not hold the same absolute priority.

*Rashi* reads the *gemara* this way straightforwardly. *Tosafot*, scandalized by what seems to be an endorsement of abandoning one's wife and children, attempts a complicated re-reading of the *gemara* — but *Rashi*'s reading is clearly the *pshat*. The tension this generates — between the all-consuming obligation of *talmud Torah* and a man's obligations to his family — remains unresolved in the *gemara* and is, of course, entirely alive today in communities where husbands learn in *kollel* while wives work and fathers are substantially absent from domestic life. The *Rambam* wrote sharply in his *Peirush HaMishnayot* on *Pirkei Avot* against making *Torah* into a *kardom lachpor bo* — a shovel to dig with — and against communal financial support for scholars. Yet the trade-off between *talmud Torah* and family responsibility is precisely what this *gemara* identifies as the defining difference between Babylonia and *Eretz Yisrael*.

---

## Marriage Age

### Rav Huna Story

The *gemara* continues within this general context of *talmud Torah* and marriage. The following story: *Rav Chisda* was in conversation with *Rav Huna*, singing the praises of *Rav Hamnuna* — *adam gadol hu*, a tremendous *talmid chacham*. *Rav Huna* replied: the next time he is with you, bring him to me. When *Rav Hamnuna* was presented to *Rav Huna*, *Rav Huna* noticed that he was not wearing a *sudra* — the kind of turban or head-covering worn by married men. He asked: *mai ta'ama lo parist sudra?* Why are you not wearing this? *Rav Hamnuna* replied: *de-lo nessivna* — because I am not yet married. At that, *Rav Huna* turned his face away and refused to look at him: *ad nessivta* — I will not look at you until you are married. The gesture was dramatic, even harsh.

### Ben Esrim

The *gemara* explains *Rav Huna*'s severity: *Rav Huna l'ta'ameih* — this was consistent with his known position. He had stated that *ben esrim shana ve-lo nasa isha, kol yamav ba-aveira* — a man who reaches twenty without having married has spent all his days in sin. The *gemara* immediately qualifies this: literally in sin? No — *ella eima kol yamav b'hirhur aveira* — he has spent all his days besieged by sexual thoughts.

### God's Wait

*Rava* adds: *v'chen tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* — and the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught similarly. Until the age of twenty, God sits and waits — *nu*, when will this person get married? Once a person reaches twenty and has still not married, *amar tippach atzmotav* — let his bones be blasted! The parental quality of the image is striking: a kind of divine exasperation at a son who ought to have already acted.

### Rav Chisda

*Rav Chisda* adds his own personal testimony: *hai de'adifna mikhavray, denasivna beshis'ar* — the reason I surpassed my colleagues in religious achievement is that I married at sixteen. Had I married at fourteen, *ha'amina lesatan girei be'einecha* — I could have said to the *satan*, arrows in your eyes! Marrying young eliminated the *yetzer hara* as a factor entirely.

This entire set of statements reflects a very much instrumental, utilitarian view of marriage: its function here is to provide an outlet for sexual desire, freeing the man to focus on *Torah* and *avodat Hashem*. There is no talk here of partnership, companionship, or intrinsic fulfillment — this is fully consistent with the Babylonian framework described earlier.

It is worth noting that the *Rambam* in *Hilchos Kiddushin* picks up on this *gemara* and gives it a striking *halachic* formulation. He states that from the age of seventeen onward, a man becomes obligated in the *mitzvah* of *peru u'revu*, and once he reaches twenty without having married, *harei ze over u'mevattel mitzvas asei* — he has actively negated a positive commandment. This is a remarkable claim. One would expect that as long as the man eventually has children, he has only postponed the *mitzvah* rather than negated it — *bittul* implies a definitive failure, not a delay. Yet the *Rambam* frames it in terms of *bittul*, hinging on the age of twenty established in our *gemara*. He does, however, create an exemption: if one is deeply engaged in *Torah* study and fears that marriage will derail his learning by imposing the necessity of earning a livelihood, then *osek bemitzvah patur min hamitzvah* — being engaged in one *mitzvah* exempts one from another.

The *Rambam*'s use of the language *bittul mitzvas asei* in this context is puzzling in two respects. First, the *gemara* itself frames the concern in terms of *hirhurim*, not *bittul mitzvah*. Second, the standard model of *bittul* applies when one has definitively failed to perform something, not when one is merely pushing it off. That said, the *Rambam*'s position does carry practical implications: any community that does not actively push its young men to marry by age twenty is either not ruling in accordance with the *Rambam* or maintaining that the concept of *bittul mitzvah* is contingent on it being the *right time* — and that the appropriate time is itself part of the framing of when the *mitzvah* applies.

---

## Parental Guidance

### Age Range

The *gemara* then records a teaching of *Rava* addressed to *Rav Natan bar Ami*: *al tzavarei devareich* — literally "on the necks of your sons" — meaning, keep the pressure on, maintain the weight of encouragement on your son, *mi-shitz'ar ve-ad esrim ve-tartin* — from sixteen to twenty-two. The image of the weight on the neck deliberately echoes *reichaim b'tzavaro* from earlier — but here it is a productive pressure, parental effort to guide a son toward marriage.

### Two Views

A second opinion is recorded: *ve-amre lei mi-tamne-isrei ad esrim ve-arba* — from eighteen to twenty-four. The pressure apparently should not start before sixteen or eighteen because the son would be too young, and should not continue beyond twenty-two or twenty-four because past a certain point it becomes counterproductive — the son stops listening and the relationship deteriorates. This is framed as a *machloket* between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemiah, tied to the verse *chanoch la-na'ar al pi darko* — train the child according to his path. *Rashi* notes that while *chanoch* suggests a general sense of *chinuch* and upbringing, the ages given make clear that marriage is the primary subject. And indeed the next topic in the *mishnah* is a father's obligation to marry off his son.

---

## Father's Obligation

### How Far Teach

Returning now to *talmud Torah* proper, the *gemara* asks: *ad hachan chayav adam le-lammed et beno Torah* — until what point is a person obligated to teach his son *Torah*? The question concerns not only the content of the education but also its generational extent.

### Zevulun Example

*Rav Yehuda* says in the name of *Shmuel*: like *Zevulun ben Dan* — a person known at that time — whose grandfather (*avi aviv*) had taught him *mikra u-mishnah* — *Tanakh* and *mishnayot* — *ve-Talmud, halachos ve-aggados*, the entire range of learning. Everything. So on first reading, the obligation would seem to include teaching one's son the full breadth of *Torah*: the text of the written Torah, the received traditions, the analytical *shakla ve-tarya* of the *Talmud*, the *halachic* rulings, and the *aggadic* material.

### Mikra Only

The *gemara* immediately raises an objection from a *beraita*: *limmdo mikra ein melammdo mishnah* — once you have taught him *Tanakh*, you have no obligation to teach him even *Mishnah*. This is a significant *chiddush*. Your entire parental educational obligation is fulfilled with *mikra* alone. You are not even required to provide basic rabbinic literacy. The verse *v'shinnantam l'vanecha v'dibarta bam* refers, after all, to *mikra* — that is what existed when the verse was given.

### Rava's View

*Rava* then sharpens this further: *mikra* here means only the *Torah* — the Five Books — not even *Nevi'im u-Ketuvim*. That is the outer limit of the parental obligation. The *gemara* then reconciles the *Zevulun ben Dan* example: the point of invoking *Zevulun ben Dan* was not to define the *content* of education, but to establish its *generational* scope — specifically, that the obligation extends even to grandchildren, as we will see. The reading is thus *ke-Zevulun ben Dan ve-lo ke-Zevulun ben Dan*: like *Zevulun ben Dan* in the sense that the obligation extends to grandchildren, but not like him in that the content is not everything — only *mikra*.

This limitation to *mikra* is genuinely surprising. The natural response is that what is being defined here is the parental obligation of primary education, which is distinct from and far narrower than a person's independent lifelong obligation of *talmud Torah*. When the *gemara* earlier said that if the father didn't teach, the son must teach himself, it appears to be referring to this foundational primary education. A person's own ongoing obligation to learn is clearly understood as far more expansive — *vehagita bo yomam valailah*, after all — even if the precise contours of that obligation remain to be worked out fully. It is also worth noting, as one participant observed, that *mikra* may have been the only content that was realistically accessible in written form, making it the only component of education every father could provide regardless of his own level of learning.

---

## Grandsons

### Debate

The *gemara* now addresses whether the obligation to teach extends to grandchildren. A *beraita* argues that it does not: *ve-limadetem osam et beneichem* — you shall teach *your sons*, *ve-lo benei beneichem* — not your grandsons. On this reading, the obligation is one generation only.

### Generations

But then the *gemara* asks: how do we account for the verse *ve-hodastem l'vanecha u-le-venei vanecha* — you shall inform your sons and your sons' sons? One answer given is that the second verse is not a separate obligation but an expression of consequence: if you teach your son *Torah*, it is as though you have taught all future generations, because the chain of transmission continues. *Kol ha-melamed et beno Torah, ma'aleh alav ha-kasuv ke-ilu limdo lo u-le-veno u-le-ven beno ad sof kol ha-doros* — teaching your son effectively plants *Torah* in an unbroken chain unto all generations. This is a powerful idea: education has a compounding effect through time.

The *gemara* then resolves the tension by appealing to another *tanna* who reads the two verses differently: the verse *ve-limadetem* — teaching your sons — tells us your sons are obligated; the verse *ve-hodastem* — informing sons and sons' sons — extends the obligation to grandsons as well. The exclusion of daughters is derived separately: *beneichem ve-lo benoteichem*.

### Grandson = Sinai

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* then adds a remarkable statement: *kol ha-melamed et ben beno Torah, ma'aleh alav ha-kasuv ke-ilu kiblah mi-Har Sinai* — whoever teaches his grandson *Torah*, the verse treats him as though he received it directly from *Har Sinai*. The prooftext: *ve-hodastem l'vanecha u-le-venei vanecha* is placed immediately adjacent to *yom asher amadta lifnei Hashem Elokecha be-Chorev* — the day you stood before God at *Sinai*.

The grammatical referent of "he received it from *Har Sinai*" is ambiguous — it could refer to the grandson, who by receiving *Torah* from his grandfather is connected to that unbroken chain stretching back to *Sinai*, or it could refer to the grandfather, who by teaching his grandchildren demonstrates that he understands Torah transmission as a multigenerational obligation rooted in *Sinai* itself. Teaching a grandchild does something that teaching a child does not: it shows that the passing down of *Torah* is not merely an individual parental act but a chain of responsibility that reaches back through history. The grandfather who teaches his grandchild places himself within that chain in a uniquely vivid way.

---

## Chiya Story

### Handkerchief

The *gemara* relates the following story. *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* came upon *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — a sage of *Eretz Yisrael* — who had thrown a simple cloth (*disna*) over his head, not bothering to wear a proper *sudra*, and was hurrying to bring his young child to *beis knesses* — the school-house. People asked him: *mai kulei hai?* What is all this? Why did you rush out without properly dressing?

### Ve-Hodastem

He replied: *mi zutar mai deksiv — ve-hodastem l'vanecha*, immediately followed by *yom asher amadta lifnei Hashem Elokecha be-Chorev?* Is it a small thing what the Torah says — that teaching your children is juxtaposed with the day you stood at *Sinai*? In other words: taking a child to school is not a trivial domestic errand. It is an act that participates in the grand tradition of *Torah* received at *Sinai* and transmitted through the generations. To delay it, or to depute it to someone else, or to pause to dress properly first — none of that is appropriate when the obligation is this weighty.

There is perhaps a subtle irony here as well. Recall that the *sudra* was the garment that identified a man as both a *talmid chacham* and a married man — its absence in the story of *Rav Hamnuna* was the marker of his unmarried state. Here, *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — himself clearly learned and presumably married — prioritizes the physical act of getting his child to school over the formality of proper dress. The contrast may be intentional: the outward markers of status are subordinated to the actual performance of parental educational obligation, which is itself the mark of genuine *talmud Torah* in *Eretz Yisrael*.

---

## Personal Practice

### Before Eating

*Rav Safra* reports in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya*: from that point on, *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* would not taste even a bit of food in the morning until he had reviewed with a child the *pesukim* they had learned the previous day and added a new *pasuk* — *umosefei*. That is, his practice was to first fulfill the obligation of teaching a child *Torah* before attending to his own eating. Whether this refers specifically to his own child or to any child under his care is not entirely precise from the context, but the thrust is clear: the obligation of *talmud Torah* with children takes priority over one's personal needs and forms the first act of the day.

### Beis Midrash

Similarly, *Rabba bar Rav Huna* would not eat anything in the morning until he had brought the child to the *beis medrash*. The personal practice of these sages illustrates how seriously they understood the parental obligation of *talmud Torah* — not as a background duty but as the day's first priority.

---

## Shinnantam

### Three Parts

*Rav Safra* also transmits a teaching in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya* based on the verse *v'shinnantam l'vanecha*: *al tikrei v'shinnantam ela v'shillashtam* — do not read it as *shinnantam* but as *shillashtam* — divide into three. The double *nun* in *shinnantam* signals not merely repetition but a tripling. From this: *le'olam yeshalesh adam shenotav* — a person should divide his years, or as the *gemara* clarifies, his days, into three: *shlish be-mikra, shlish be-mishnah, u-shlish be-Talmud* — one third to *Tanakh*, one third to *Mishnah*, and one third to *gemara*.

### Daily Division

The *gemara* objects: how can one divide one's *years* into thirds when one does not know how long one will live? The answer: *lo tzricha leyomei* — one should divide one's *days*, not one's lifetime. *Rashi* understands this as dividing the days of the week: two days to *mikra*, two days to *Mishnah*, two days to *gemara*, with *Shabbos* perhaps for *chazara* or rest.

*Tosafot* challenges *Rashi*'s reading: if dividing by weeks, you still face the same problem — what if you die in the middle of a week, before having completed all three sections? *Tosafot* therefore concludes that the division must be within each day itself: every single day, one third to each. This is the basis for the practice, codified by Rav Amram Gaon and preserved in some communities today, of reciting a passage of *mikra*, *Mishnah*, and *gemara* each morning before *pesukei dezimra* — a brief but daily *kiyum* of this tripartite obligation.

*Tosafot* then raises a further difficulty in the name of *Rabbeinu Tam*: in practice, the overwhelming focus of Jewish learning at every stage has been *gemara*. How is it possible to justify spending a full third of one's learning time on *mikra* and another third on *Mishnah*? *Rabbeinu Tam* answers by appeal to a principle stated in *Sanhedrin*: the Babylonian *Talmud* is called *belulah* — mixed — because it is interwoven with *Tanakh*, *Mishnah*, and *gemara* together. When you learn *Bavli*, you encounter *mishnayot*, *beraitot*, and occasional citations of *pesukim*. This admixture is what makes the *Bavli* a vehicle for satisfying all three components simultaneously.

### Rambam

The *Rambam* in *Hilchos Talmud Torah*, chapter 1, *halacha* 11, takes the *gemara*'s ruling very literally. He rules that one is obligated to divide one's study time into thirds — *shlish baTorah shebikhtav*, *shlish baTorah shebe'al peh*, and a third for independent analysis: *yavin veyaskil acharit davar mereshito* — understanding the conclusions from their premises, drawing inferences, applying the principles through which *Torah* is expounded. This last third is what is called *gemara*. The *Rambam* illustrates: if a person works at a trade three hours a day, he has nine hours available for learning. Of those nine, three go to *Torah shebikhtav*, three to *Torah sheba'al peh*, and three to analysis.

But the *Rambam* then substantially modifies this ruling: *bameh devarim amurim betechilat talmudo shel adam* — this applies at the beginning of a person's learning, when he is still building his foundational knowledge and skills. Once he has grown in *chochmah* and has mastered the written *Torah* and the received traditions, *yikra be'ittim mezumanim Torah shebikhtav vedivrei hashemuah kedei shelo yishkach* — he should review *Torah shebikhtav* and *Torah sheba'al peh* occasionally so as not to forget them — *v'yifneh kol yamav le-Gemara bilvad* — but all of his real learning should be devoted to *gemara*. This ultimately brings the *Rambam* very close to *Tosafot*'s conclusion: the mature scholar's obligation is primarily the study of *gemara*, with the tripartite division applying to the formative years of education. The irony, noted in the shiur, is that the *Rambam* himself famously described his own exhausting daily schedule as a court physician in the letter he wrote later in life — a schedule that left him almost no time for Torah study beyond an hour on *Shabbos*.

---

## Sofrim

### Why Sofrim

The *gemara* transitions with a seemingly abrupt *lefikach* — therefore — which *Rashi* acknowledges is a new independent topic. The early sages were called *sofrim* — *shehayu sofrim kol otiyot shebaTorah* — because they would count all of the letters in the *Torah*.

### Halfway Points

The *gemara* then lists several calculations attributed to these *sofrim*. The large *vav* in the word *gachon* — in the verse about creatures that go on their belly in *Vayikra* — is said to be the midpoint of the letters of the *sefer Torah*. The phrase *darosh darash* — which we just recently encountered in *Shemini* — is said to be the midpoint of the words of the *Torah*. The word *vehitgalach* is said to mark the midpoint of the *pesukim*. Turning to *Tehillim*: the *ayin* of *ya'ar* in the verse *yecharsmena chazir miyaar* is said to be the midpoint of the letters of *Tehillim*; the verse *vehu rachum yechapeir avon* marks the midpoint of its *pesukim*.

### Precision

*Rav Yosef* raises a question about the *vav* of *gachon*: is it on this side or that side of the midpoint — meaning, with an odd total number of letters, is the *vav* itself the exact middle, or does it fall just before or just after? His interlocutor suggests: let us bring a *sefer Torah* and count. *Rav Yosef* responds by citing another case where this was actually done — a case mentioned by *Rabbah bar bar Chanah* — suggesting it is at least possible to undertake such a count.

### Limited Knowledge

But then the *gemara* deflates both the historical claims and the proposal: *inhu bki'ei b'chaseros v'yesiros, anan lo bki'inan* — the earlier generations had precise knowledge of whether words were written *malei* or *chaser* — fully spelled or defective — and could therefore count letters exactly. We, by the time of the *Amoraim*, no longer possess that precision. Our *sifrei Torah* may not be exactly correct in every *chaser* and *malei*, and therefore we cannot validate or replicate these counts. This admission by the *gemara* is significant: it explicitly concedes that even in the *Amoraic* period, the exact orthography of the *Torah* text was not perfectly known. The *baalei hamesorah*, the Masoretes — most famously the *Ben Asher* family — only completed the systematic cataloging of every letter, vowel, and cantillation mark around the fifth or sixth century, well after this period, in order to fix the text precisely. This uncertainty also dispenses with any naive confidence in Bible codes or letter-count-based exegesis: the *gemara* itself acknowledges that the precise letter count was not reliably known.

---

## Counting Pesukim

### Numbers

The *gemara* similarly questions the count of *pesukim* in the *sefer Torah*. *Rav Yosef* asks about *vehitgalach* — the alleged midpoint of *pesukim* — whether it falls on this or that side of the divide. *Abaye* responds that for *pesukim*, unlike letters, we ought to be able to count: let us just do it. The *gemara*'s response is: *bpsukei nami lo bki'inan* — we are also not expert in counting *pesukim*.

A *beraita* records: the *sefer Torah* contains 5,888 *pesukim* — whereas our current count comes to approximately 5,845, a discrepancy of about forty. *Tehillim* has eight more *pesukim* than the *Torah*, and *Divrei HaYamim* has eight fewer.

### Regional Variations

The reason for uncertainty about *pesukim* is then made clear: *Rav Acha bar Adda* reported that in *Eretz Yisrael*, what we read as a single *pasuk* was divided into three separate *pesukim*. The example given is the verse *vayomer Hashem el Moshe hinei anochi ba eilecha be'av he'anan* — which could be divided at *he'anan*, then at *ba'avur yishma ha'am b'dibri imcha v'gam becha ya'aminu l'olam*, and finally at *vayageid Moshe et divrei ha'am el Hashem*. Different regional traditions of where *pasuk* divisions fall mean that even the count of *pesukim* cannot be determined with certainty. The divergence between Babylonian and *Eretz Yisrael* manuscripts was apparently significant enough to make such counts unreliable.

---

## Warrior Imagery

### Sharp Words

The *gemara* returns to the verse *v'shinnantam l'vanecha* to derive a different teaching. *Tanu rabbanan*: *v'shinnantam l'vanecha* — the word *shinnantam* connotes sharpness, from *shinnun*, sharp. The teaching: *she-yihyu divrei Torah mechuddadim b'ficha* — the words of *Torah* should be sharp in your mouth. If someone asks you something, you should not hesitate or stumble — *al tegagaym ve-tomar lo*, do not mumble — but answer immediately, with fluency and confidence.

### Like Sister

The *gemara* cites the verse *emor la-chochmah achoti at* — say to wisdom: you are my sister. Your knowledge of *Torah* should be as intimate and immediate as your knowledge of your own sister — or, as an alternative *drasha*, as certain as the prohibition of your sister is to you. Either way, the image is of knowledge so internalized that it admits no hesitation.

### Arrows

A series of verses is then brought to expand on the theme of sharpness. *Koshrem al etzbe'otecha katvem al lu'ach libbecha* — bind them to your fingers, inscribe them on the chambers of your heart. *Torah* should be fully internalized, in the blood. Then: *ke-chitzim be-yad gibbor ken bnei ha-ne'urim* — like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are the children of one's youth. *Rashi* interprets this as referring to one's learning — the *Torah* one acquires is one's "children," and what one learns while young is particularly sharp and durable. *Ve-omer chitzei gibbor shenunim* — the arrows of the warrior are sharp. *Ve-omer chitzeycha shenunim ammim tachteycha yippolu* — your arrows are sharp, nations fall beneath you. *Ve-omer ashrei ha-gever asher millei et aspato me-hem* — praised is the man who fills his quiver with these arrows, who fills himself with *Torah* knowledge that is sharp and ready.

### Enemies

*Lo yevoshu ki yedabberu et oyvim ba-sha'ar* — they will not be embarrassed when they speak with enemies in the gate. The *gemara* asks: *mai et oyvim ba-sha'ar?* What does it mean to speak with enemies in the gate? *Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* answers: *afillu ha-av u-vno, ha-rav ve-talmido* — even father and son, even a master and his student, when they are *oskim ba-Torah be-sha'ar echad* — engaged in *Torah* in the same space — *na'asim oyvim zeh la-zeh*. They become enemies to one another: they argue, they contest, they push back. Anyone who has sat in a *beis medrash* during a heated *chavrusa* session recognizes this dynamic. The formality of deference to a father or teacher does not apply within the walls of *Torah* debate; there, one argues for the truth without deference.

### Love

And yet — *v'aynam zazim misham ad shenasim ohavim zeh la-zeh* — they do not leave that encounter until they have become lovers of one another. The argument is entirely *lishma* — for the sake of truth — and so when it is over, there is no residual bitterness, only affection. The prooftext: *et vahev b'sufah* — from the *sefer milchamot Hashem*, the Book of the Wars of God. *Al tikrei b'sufah ela b'sofah* — do not read it as "in a whirlwind" but as "at its end" — *vahev* is related to *ahavah*, love. At the end of the wars of *Torah*, love follows.

Several dimensions of this passage are worth remarking upon. First, there is the martial, warrior imagery attached throughout to *talmud Torah* — arrows, quivers, warriors, enemies. As scholars of rabbinic literature have observed, this seems to be a deliberate refashioning of an activity that might otherwise be coded as passive or non-masculine into something heroic and vigorous. The rabbis mobilize an entire armory of imagery to invest *Torah* study with aggression, strength, and martial valor. Second, notice how far we have traveled from the initial framing: the father's obligation to provide his son a *mikra* education, which was presented as a relatively limited parental duty, gives way, in these *aggadic* passages, to a far more totalizing vision — knowledge that must be perfectly sharp, arguments that are like arrows, devotion so complete that one becomes a warrior for *Torah*. The *gemara* does not fully reconcile these different framings, and how the limited parental obligation relates to the vast personal obligation remains an open question.

---

## Torah Remedy

### Mashal

The *gemara* closes with an *aggadic* passage of striking beauty and psychological acuity. The verse says *v'samtem et divrei eileh asher anochi m'tzavcha hayom* — the word *v'samtem* is read as *sam tam*, a complete remedy, a perfect antidote. *Nimshla Torah k'sam chayim* — the *Torah* is compared to a potion of life. A *mashal*: a man struck his son a great blow and then placed a bandage (*rtiya*) on the wound. He said to him: my son, as long as this bandage is on your wound, you may eat and drink whatever you wish, bathe in hot or cold water, and you need not fear any ill effect — this bandage will protect you against all of it. But if you remove the bandage, *harei hi ma'aleh numi* — the wound will fester and become infected.

### Tavlin

God speaks to Israel in the same terms: *bni, barati yetzer hara* — I created the *yetzer hara*, which is the blow. *U-varati lo Torah tavlin* — but I also created the *Torah* as its *tavlin*, its antidote, its spice and remedy.

### Protection

*Ve-im atem oskim ba-Torah einchem nimsarim beyado* — if you are engaged in *Torah*, you will not be delivered into its power. The verse cited: *halo im teitiv se'eit* — if you do good, meaning if you learn *Torah*, you will carry yourself above it, you will conquer the *yetzer hara*. *Rashi* understands *se'eit* as implying elevation — you will be raised above it.

### Without Torah

But if one does not engage in *Torah*: *atem nimsarim beyado* — you are delivered into the hands of the *yetzer hara*. *Lapetach chatat rovetz* — it crouches at the door, waiting. *V'lo od ela shekol masa u-matano bach* — and furthermore, its entire attention, its whole enterprise, is directed at you: scheming, working, seeking entry. *Ve'eilecha teshukatoi* — its desire is toward you. And yet — *ve-im ata rotze ata moshel bo, shene'emar ve'ata timshol bo* — if you so choose, you can be master over it.

The *gemara* will continue from this point, taking up the challenge of the *yetzer hara* and *Torah* as its antidote.

---

---

# Kiddushin 31

## Yetzer Hara & Torah

### Yetzer Hara Nature

The *daf* opens five lines down from where we left off, with a *tanu rabanan* that addresses the *yetzer hara* with striking directness. *Kashe yetzer hara she'afilu yotzro kara ra* — the *yetzer hara* is so formidable that even its Creator called it evil, as it is written: *ki yetzer lev ha'adam ra mine'urav*. This is worth pausing on. The entire opening of *Bereishit* is structured around *ki tov* — God surveys creation and pronounces it good. The one thing that receives the designation *ra* is what human beings carry within them. That inversion is deliberate and sobering.

Rabbi Yitzchak adds: *yitzro shel adam mitchadesh alav bechol yom* — the *yetzer hara* renews itself against a person every single day, as the verse says *rak ra kol hayom*, it is evil the whole day. And Rabbi Shimon ben Levi goes further still: *yitzro shel adam mitgaber alav bechol yom u'mevakesh hamito* — it grows stronger each day and seeks to destroy you, as it is written, *tzofeh rasha latzadik u'mevakesh lehamito*.

What emerges from these statements is not merely a description of natural sinful impulse but something more vivid and almost personified — a force with creativity, strategy, and malicious intent. This is not simply the *pshat* of a human being's natural lustful drives; the Gemara is drawing on imagery closer to that of a figure who, like a little devil on one's shoulder, is actively scheming to bring a person to ruin. The *yetzer hara*, in this framing, is relentlessly innovating against you, which means the response must be equally dynamic.

### Divine Help & Torah

The Gemara then states: *ilmalai Hakadosh Baruch Hu ozro, ein yachollo* — were God not there to assist, a person could not withstand the *yetzer hara*, as the verse says, *Elokim lo ya'azvenu veyado*, God will not abandon him to its hand. This is a striking and somewhat uncomfortable claim. It implies that on one's own, the deck is already stacked against you. There is no simple resort to free will as a sufficient counterbalance — without divine assistance, one is simply outmatched.

This raises a genuine conceptual tension. The Jewish conception typically holds that we possess both a *yetzer hara* and a *yetzer hatov*, and that the capacity for moral choice is genuinely ours. This is not original sin; one does not start out in a state of depravity requiring external salvation. Yet the Gemara insists that at some fundamental level, unaided human striving is insufficient. One way to read this less troublingly is through the principle the Gemara elsewhere articulates: *haba letaher mesay'in oto* — one who comes to purify himself is aided from Above. God does not do it for you; rather, once you exert your own free will and take the first steps on the right path, divine assistance arrives to *chazek*, to strengthen and sustain that effort. On this reading, the Gemara may be offering *chizuk* to someone who feels they are constantly failing — reminding them that the effort to do right, however imperfect, will be met and supported. The Torah itself, given just before this passage, is presented as the divine instrument: *sam tam*, a perfect elixir, the tool provided by God to combat the *yetzer hara*.

It is also worth noting, as one participant in the discussion observed, that there is a tendency in contemporary Orthodox discourse to focus almost entirely on human choice and responsibility, with relatively little explicit acknowledgment of the idea that God is present to assist and strengthen us. The prayers carry this message, but ordinary religious discourse often does not. The Gemara here offers a corrective, however challenging its metaphysics may be.

### Beit Midrash Solution

*Tana debei Rabbi Yishmael* offers an arrestingly direct prescription. *Beni, im pagah becha menuval zeh* — my son, if this abominable thing takes hold of you — *moshchehu leveit hamidrash*, drag it to the *beit midrash*. Make the *yetzer hara* your *chavruta*, as it were. *Im even hu nimoach* — if it is stone, it will dissolve; *veim barzel hu mitpotzetz* — if it is iron, it will shatter. The verse cited is *halo ko devarai ka'esh neum Hashem* — are not My words like fire — *uchefatish yifotzetz sela*, and like a hammer that shatters rock.

*Tosafot* notes a textual difficulty: the verse speaks of the hammer shattering, but the Gemara applies it to the metal being destroyed. *Tosafot* proposes reading it as *al yedei sela*, by means of the rock — or alternatively, separates the two images: the fire melts the metal, and the hammer shatters the stone. It is admittedly a difficult reading of the *pasuk*, but the homiletical point stands. A complementary verse is then cited — *hoy kol tzame lechu lamayim*, come all who are thirsty to water — and *avanim shachaku mayim*, stones are worn away by water, suggesting that sustained immersion in Torah will erode even the hardest resistance.

The circle thus closes: *talmud Torah* is not merely a religious obligation or a form of intellectual cultivation; it is the essential weapon in a daily existential battle. The *chidush* of the *yetzer hara* — its capacity for constant innovation and renewal — demands a corresponding *chidush* in Torah learning as its antidote.

---

## Father's Obligations

### Marry Off Son
