The Gemara turns from the *aggadeta* of *yetzer hara* and *Torah* to the father's specific obligations toward his son — including, notably, the obligation to marry him off: *le'hashio isha*. The source (*manalan*) is the verse *kechu nashim veholidu banim uvanot, ukechu livneichem nashim, ve'et benoteichem tenu la'anashim* — take wives, have sons and daughters, take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to men.

What is immediately striking is that this *pasuk* appears to obligate the father toward both sons and daughters in the matter of marriage. The Gemara notes *bishlama beno beyado* — I can understand regarding the son, because in theory the father acts as the initiating party on his son's behalf. But then it says *ella bito beyado hi* — and his daughter is in his hand — which must rank as one of the more ironic statements in this entire *sugya*, given that we learned earlier that a father may actually marry off his daughter against her will, while he cannot do the same for his son. The *Gemara* answers: *leiten lah midai velilbasheih nechasaya, ki heichi dekaftzu alei inshi* — give her gifts, clothe her in ornaments, so that men will be attracted to her and wish to marry her. The father's obligation regarding his daughter, then, is to provide a suitable dowry and presentation, making her a desirable match.

The irony here is layered. Throughout this *masechta*, the father's obligations have been defined as applying to sons, not daughters. Yet here, with barely a pause, the Gemara reads the *pasuk* as extending to daughters as well, without flagging the tension. The deeper irony is that while the father legally has the power to contract his daughter's *kiddushin*, he cannot similarly contract his son's marriage — yet the framework of initiative and representation is mapped onto the son's case as if the father were the active party. As the Gemara elsewhere established, *ish mechazir achar aveidato* — it is the male who pursues; so the father, representing his son, can initiate inquiries and pursue a match, whereas representing his daughter, he can only make her attractive enough to receive such pursuit.

### Teaching Trade

The Gemara then addresses the obligation to teach a trade: *lelamdo omanut*. The source is *re'eh chayim im ishah asher ahavta* — see life with the woman that you love. The Gemara reads this on two levels: if *ishah* means a literal wife, then just as one is obligated to marry off one's son, so too must one teach him a livelihood. If *ishah* is a metaphor for Torah — Torah as the *ishah*, the other woman with whom a man lives his life, a motif Boyarin has explored in his analysis of both the militaristic and romantic metaphors for *talmud Torah* — then just as one must teach Torah, one must also teach a trade.

Rabbi Yehuda sharpens this: *kol she'eino melamdo omanut melamdo listut* — whoever does not teach his son a trade teaches him banditry, or as the Gemara immediately clarifies, *ke'ilu melamdo listut* — it is as if he teaches him banditry, because without a livelihood, what will the child do? The *Gemara* asks what Rabbi Yehuda adds beyond the *Tanna Kamma*, and answers: *de'agmarei iska* — the *Tanna Kamma* might have been satisfied with teaching the son commerce, buying and selling. Rabbi Yehuda insists on an actual *omanut*, a manual trade, because commerce depends on market conditions and may not always sustain a person, whereas a skilled trade — plumbing, tailoring, carpentry — will always find need.

That the value of a specific manual trade is not merely theoretical was brought into sharp relief in the discussion that followed. One member of the group noted that her relative survived the Shoah because his work as a tailor gave him skills the Nazi regime could use; another shared that his knowledge of plumbing was what kept him alive in the camps. *Kol she'eino melamdo omanut melamdo listut* takes on a dimension of literal life and death that no abstract analysis can match.

As for the formal status of these obligations — to marry off one's son, to teach a trade — the sources being cited are from *Navi*, not from explicit Torah commands, and one might question whether these even rise to the level of *mitzvah derabbanan* in a strict sense. They feel more like broad parental responsibilities subsumed under the general obligation to raise a child properly, akin in spirit to *chinuch* — training one's children in the *mitzvot* — but oriented toward life in the world rather than life as a Torah Jew.

### Swimming & Safety

Some authorities add a further obligation: *af lehashito banahar* — to teach one's son to swim in the river. *Mai ta'ama? Chayutei hee* — because it is a matter of preserving life. The ability to swim is presented as a basic life-saving skill a parent is obligated to transmit. Indeed, as was noted in passing, some universities to this day will not grant a degree to a student who cannot swim — an echo of this ancient recognition that swimming is not a luxury but a survival competency.

---

## Filial Obligations

### Sons & Daughters Equal

The Gemara now pivots decisively to the second major subject of the *amud*: the filial obligations of children toward parents — *kibbud av va'em*. The *mishnah* states *kol mitzvat ha-av al ha-ben* — all obligations of the father upon the son — and the Gemara initially asks what this means. If it refers to the obligations a father has toward his son, does it follow that women are equally obligated in those parental duties? That cannot be right, since we already established that a mother, unlike a father, is not obligated in *brit milah* or *pidyon haben*.

Rav Yehuda resolves this: the *mishnah* must be read as *kol mitzvat ha-av ha-mutelet al ha-ben la'asot le-aviv* — all obligations that a child owes to a parent — and these fall equally on *echad anashim ve-echad nashim*, both sons and daughters. The *baraita* confirms this: *ish ish imo ve-aviv tira'u* — the plural *tira'u* implies that two people are addressed, both the man and the woman.

### Married Women Exemption

The *baraita* then asks: if the plural *tira'u* includes both men and women, why does the verse emphasize *ish*, man? The answer: *ish she-yesh be-yado la'asot, isha she-ein be-yada la'asot* — a man generally has more capacity to act on behalf of his parents, whereas a married woman's primary obligations run to her husband's household. *Mipnei she-yesh reshut acherim aleha* — because others have authority over her. This does not exempt her from the obligation; it acknowledges that her opportunity to fulfill it is often constrained.

*Tosafot* makes a point worth emphasizing here: legally, a married woman's domestic duties to her husband are only *derabbanan*, not *de-oraita*. The *de-oraita* obligation itself does not subordinate a wife to household service. Yet even *Tosafot* acknowledges that as a practical matter, *einah metzuya etzel avia ela etzel ba'alah* — a married woman's home is her husband's home, not her father's, and her time and energy flow accordingly.

There is an irony here that was pointed out: while the Gemara frames men as having more *opportunity* to honor parents, lived experience frequently reverses this. It is typically the daughter — or the daughter-in-law — who bears the primary burden of caregiving for aging parents, whether her own or her husband's, even in contemporary society with its more egalitarian ideals. The Gemara's theoretical framework and social reality have long been in productive tension on this point.

Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav clarifies that this asymmetry applies only to a married woman. If a woman is divorced — or never married — *shneihem shavin*, her obligation is equal to her brother's. The baseline, then, is genuine equality.

---

## Parents = God

### Honor Parallel

The Gemara now presents a series of scriptural parallels that equate the obligations owed to parents with those owed to God. *Ne'emar kabeid et avicha ve'et imecha* — honor your father and mother — and *ne'emar kabeid et Hashem mehonecha* — honor God from your wealth. *Hishvah hakatuv kevod av va'eim likvod hamakom* — the Torah has equated honoring parents with honoring God.

### Reverence Parallel

Similarly: *ne'emar ish imo ve'aviv tira'u* — revere your mother and father — alongside *ve'et Hashem elokecha tira ve'oto ta'avod* — you shall revere God and serve Him. *Hishvah hakatuv morat av va'eim lemorat hamakom* — the reverence due to parents is equated with the reverence due to God.

### Cursing Parallel

And: *ne'emar mekaleil aviv ve'imo mot yumat* — one who curses his father or mother is put to death — alongside *ish ish ki yekaleil elohav venasa chet'o*, cursing God being treated as a capital offense. *Hishvah hakatuv birchat av va'eim lebirchat hamakom* — the Gemara uses the euphemism *birchat* (blessing) for cursing in both cases, equating them. *Aval behaka'ah* — as for one who strikes a parent being put to death — there is no parallel, since striking God is simply impossible. *Vechein badin* — and it makes sense that parents are thus equated with God.

### Three Partners

Why does this equation hold? *She-shelosha shutafin hein ba'adam* — because three partners participate in the creation of a human being: *Hakadosh Baruch Hu ve'aviv ve'imo*, God, father, and mother. And the Gemara adds: *bizman she'adam mechabeid et aviv ve'et imo, amar Hakadosh Baruch Hu, ma'ala ani aleichem ke'ilu darti beineichem vechibduni* — when a person honors his father and mother, God says: I regard it as if I dwelt among them and they honored Me.

---

## Motivation Debate

### Gratitude Model

The equation of honoring parents with honoring God is weighty, and it invites the question: what is the underlying rationale for this comparison? The intuitive reading is one of gratitude. Parents brought you into the world; they gave you everything. You owe them honor, and recognizing that debt models for you the even greater honor owed to God, who created the entire universe, created your parents, and is the ultimate source of everything you have received. On this reading, the connection moves from the immediate and human — the visceral sense of owing something to those who nurtured you — to the theological: a *kal vachomer* that your gratitude toward parents should extend all the more to God.

### Awe Model

Gerald Blidstein, in his careful study *Honor Thy Father and Mother*, argues for a different reading. He suggests that the comparison is not primarily about the ethics of gratitude — that model being rooted in human experience and then applied upward to the divine. Rather, Blidstein sees the connection as running along a distinctly religious axis: what governs the relationship to parents is *awe*. The same quality of *yirah* — the sense of utter otherness, of one who is at a higher level, of standing before a creator whose act exceeds anything you could fully comprehend — that characterizes a properly religious relationship with God is what should characterize the relationship with parents. It is not about giving back what you owe; it is about the *rimon* of standing before those who brought you into being, which mirrors the awe of standing before the Creator of all being.

On this alternative reading, the motivational structure is reversed. It is not that we learn from the parent-child relationship how to relate to God; rather, the religious sensibility of awe and reverence that we cultivate toward God is the very sensibility that should shape how we stand before our parents. Parents, as creators, partake of something of the divine creative act, and our response to them should draw on the same deep well. As one participant put it: the obligation to parents is not ethically driven out of a sense of debt, but motivated by a deep sense of awe and reverence — the same disposition that enables genuine *davening* and authentic engagement with *Hashem*.

---

## Practical Principles

### Action Over Feeling

Raising the equation of parents with God immediately prompts a question about cases where the equation feels strained — where parents were absent, neglectful, unkind, or worse. The Torah's response, as we will see worked out in the Gemara, is not to address internal states at all. The *Torah* does not command you how to feel about your parents. It commands how to act. Whether you feel respect or not, you behave in ways that demonstrate honor. Whether you regard your parents as deserving of it or not, you perform the actions that constitute *kavod* and *yirah*. This is a fundamental principle, and it stands in interesting contrast to many other relational obligations in Jewish law: here, the action itself is not sufficient either (as we will see at the end of the *amud*), but the baseline is action, not sentiment.

### Self-Care Priority

What about genuinely abusive parents — those who have caused real psychological or emotional harm? Here a critical principle applies, drawn from the broader category of *mitzvot bein adam l'chaveiro*: *chayecha v'chayei chavercha chayecha kodmin* — your life and your friend's life, your life comes first. The first person you are obligated to is yourself. Where maintaining a relationship with one's parents causes genuine harm to one's psychological well-being, the obligation to self-protection is prior. A person in such a situation is not merely *permitted* to maintain distance; they may be *required* to do so, because *kibbud av va'em* cannot override the primary obligation to protect oneself.

This is not a license for avoidance whenever relationships are difficult. *Kibbud av va'em* does demand real personal and financial extension. But where the threshold of genuine harm is crossed, self-care takes precedence — and that is a halachic principle, not merely a pastoral accommodation.

### No Love Command

One further observation deserves notice. The Torah commands honoring parents. It commands fearing and revering them. It prohibits cursing or striking them. What it conspicuously does not command is *love*. There is no *ve'ahavta* directed toward parents. Whether this reflects a recognition that love cannot be commanded, or that the relational framework here is one of awe and duty rather than affection, is itself a rich question — but the absence is notable and worth sitting with.

---

## Natural vs. Commanded

### Natural Tendencies

*Rebbi* teaches: *galui veyadua lifnei mi she'amar vehayah ha'olam she'ben mechabeid et imo yoseir mei'aviv* — it is revealed and known before the One who created the world that a son shows more honor to his mother than his father. Why? *Mipnei she'meshadelto bidvarim* — because she encourages him, nurtures him, draws him close with words. *Rashi* renders this with a sense of gentle persuasion, even seduction.

The underlying dynamic is clear: the mother is classically the nurturer, the father the authority figure. Toward the nurturer, the natural human response is warmth, care, and the desire to do well by her — that is *kavod*. Toward the authority figure, the natural response is the stepping back, the sense of distance, the slight apprehension — that is *yirah*.

### Torah's Reversal

Precisely because these tendencies are natural, the Torah intervenes to counterbalance them. *Ulefikach hikdim Hakadosh Baruch Hu kibbud av le'kibbud em* — therefore God placed *kavod av*, the honor of the father, before *kavod em* in the verse *kabeid et avicha ve'et imecha*. The command is directing you to extend to your father the honor that comes less naturally. Similarly: *galui veyadua lifnei mi she'amar vehayah ha'olam haben mityarei me'aviv yoter me'imo* — a son more naturally has reverence for his father, in part because *biglal shemelamdo Torah*, the father embodies the authority of Torah instruction. Therefore the verse *ish imo ve'aviv tira'u* places the mother first — to direct you to give your mother her due *yirah*, which comes less naturally.

This is a general principle that the *Sifrei* draws out explicitly: sometimes the command of *kibbud av va'em* requires you to do precisely what does not come naturally. That is, in part, why it requires a command at all. And it may also illuminate why the Torah does not command love — not because love is unimportant, but because in some relationships, love comes naturally and does not need legislation, while the more formal postures of honor and reverence may not.

---

## Causing Anguish

### God Withdraws

The Gemara presents an inversion of the earlier promise. If honoring parents leads God to say *ke'ilu darti beineichem vechibduni* — it is as if I dwelt among them and they honored Me — then causing parents anguish produces the opposite. *Bizman she'adam mita'er et aviv ve'et imo, amar Hakadosh Baruch Hu: yafeh asiti shelo darti beineihem* — when a person causes anguish to his father and mother, God says: it is good that I did not dwell among them. *She'ilmalei darti beineihem, tzi'aruni* — for had I dwelt among them, they would have caused Me anguish. The implication cuts two ways: such behavior amounts to a rejection of the divine presence, and also signals that if this is how they treat their parents — those who stand in relation to God — then they would have treated God no differently.

This also raises a question about the precise contours of *kibbud av va'em*. The Gemara earlier cited the case of *Dama ben Netina* who would not disturb his sleeping father — clearly a form of not causing *tza'ar*. But what of adult children who make life choices their parents disapprove of? Is causing parental unhappiness through one's own legitimate choices a violation of *kibbud av va'em*? There is a meaningful distinction between directly doing something offensive or disrespectful to a parent and simply living one's life in ways the parent does not prefer. The former may implicate *tza'ar*; the latter generally does not.

### Secret Sins

The Gemara digresses — though the connection to divine presence makes it feel organic. *Kol ha'over aveirah beseter, ke'ilu dochek raglei Shechinah* — whoever commits a sin in private is as if he pushes God's feet out of the world. The verse: *hashamayim kis'i ve'ha'aretz hadom raglai* — the heavens are My throne and the earth My footstool. God's feet, as it were, rest on this earth; to sin in secret is to implicitly deny that God's presence extends here. One who sins publicly at least demonstrates, however perversely, that he knows he is being observed but does not care. One who sins in secret suggests that he believes God cannot see — that God has no presence in this private space — and thereby pushes *Shechinah* out of the world.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds: *assur le'adam sheyelech arba amot bekoma zekufa* — a person may not walk four *amot* with a fully upright posture, *melo kol ha'aretz kevodo* — for the entire earth is filled with God's glory. To stride with exaggerated erectness is to assert one's own primacy, to crowd out the awareness of divine presence.

### Head Covering

From this emerges the practice of Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: *lo masgei arba amot begillui harosh* — he would not walk four *amot* with an uncovered head. *Amar: Shechinah lemalah meroshi* — he said, the *Shechinah* is above my head. This is the textual basis for the *kippah* — not a formal prohibition, but a *minhag* rooted in the continuous awareness of divine presence overhead.

Returning to the broader context: the Gemara has now constructed a world in which the presence of God is mediated, in part, through parents. The *Shechinah* dwells with those who honor their parents; it withdraws when they cause anguish. And the same sensibility that makes a person aware of *Shechinah* above their head — that constant consciousness of being in the presence of something greater — is precisely what *kibbud av va'em* is meant to cultivate toward one's parents.

---

## Competing Demands

### Father Precedence

The Gemara now enters a halachic case study. A certain son of a widow approached Rabbi Eliezer: *aba amar hashkeini mayim, ve-ima omeret hashkeini mayim* — both my father and my mother are asking me to bring them water. *Eizeh mehem kodem* — which takes priority? Rabbi Eliezer answered: *anach kvod imcha va-asei kvod avicha* — set aside your mother's honor for the moment and attend to your father's honor. *She-atah ve-imcha chayavim bi-chvod avicha* — for both you and your mother are obligated in your father's honor.

This ruling reflects a principle that has been developing throughout the Gemara. While sons and daughters are fundamentally equally obligated in *kibbud av va'em*, and while *kavod* and *yirah* are equally owed to both parents, the case of competing simultaneous demands must be resolved when the parents are in a marital relationship. In a patriarchal household, the father is the head; the mother herself owes *kavod* to the father in certain respects. Just as a married daughter's obligations to her parents may yield to her obligations to her husband, so the mother's claim on the child's immediate service may yield to the father's, not because the mother is less important, but because the household hierarchy places the father's demands first when they directly conflict.

### Divorced Mother

The same questioner then approached Rabbi Yehoshua and posed the same scenario. After receiving the same answer, he pressed: *Rebbi, nitgarsha mahu* — what if my mother is divorced? In that case, she is no longer in a position of owing *kavod* to the father; the marital hierarchy that made the father's claim prior no longer operates. What then takes precedence?

### Harsh Response

Rabbi Yehoshua's response is arresting: *mi-bein risei eynecha nikar she-ben almana atah* — from between your eyelashes it is clear that you are the son of a widow. *Rashi* explains that his eyelashes had fallen out from crying — he was an orphan. Rabbi Yehoshua was rebuking him for asking a question framed in personal terms — *aba amar, ima omeret*, my father says, my mother says — when he had no living father. He was asking as if it were a real dilemma when it was not.

Rabbi Yehoshua then told him: *Hattel lahen mayim besefel vekakei lahen ketarnagolim* — pour water in a bowl and cluck at them like chickens, let them come drink from it. The image is, to say the least, jarring. Treating this as a mocking dismissal seems pastorally inexplicable when addressed to an orphaned child. Whatever Rabbi Yehoshua's precise intent, the halachic upshot is clear: where parents are divorced, there is genuinely no principled resolution to competing demands. There is no hierarchy that straightforwardly applies, and the child must exercise judgment — or, in a sense, the *halacha* simply does not give a clear answer.

This absence of resolution is itself significant. The area of *bein adam l'chaveiro* — and *kibbud av va'em* is paradigmatically such an area — does not lend itself to the kind of precise, context-independent ruling that governs *lulav* or *tefillin*. Human relationships are too complex, too contextual, too varied. The Gemara is, in part, teaching that moral judgment must fill the gaps that halachic specificity cannot reach. And this is one reason the Gemara here moves so readily between *aggadah* and *halacha* — because neither alone is sufficient to capture the full demand being made.

---

## Two Drashot

### Ulla's Drasha

Ulla the Elder delivered a *drasha* at the gates of the house of the *Nasi*. The verse: *yoducha Hashem kol malchei aretz ki sham'u imrei picha* — all the kings of the earth will acknowledge You, God, because they heard the words of Your mouth. The plural *imrei picha*, words of Your mouth, rather than the singular *ma'amar*, is noted. When God declared *anochi* and *lo yihiyeh lecha* — I am the Lord your God and you shall have no other gods — *amru umot ha'olam: lechvod atzmo doresh*, the nations said: He demands this for His own honor; there is no universal moral principle at work, just self-aggrandizement. *Kevan she'amar kabeid et avicha ve'et imecha* — but when God then commanded honoring one's father and mother, *chazru v'hodu lema'amarot harishonot* — they came back and acknowledged the validity of the first commandments. For now they recognized that there is a genuine and universal moral principle underlying the obligation to give honor and recognition to those who bring you into the world and do for you. The divine demand for honor is of a piece with that same principle; it is not self-serving but deeply grounded.

### Rava's Drasha

Rava offers a parallel *drasha* from a different verse: *rosh devarcha emet* — the first of Your words is true. But is only the first true and not the last? Rather, *misof devarcha nikar she'rosh devarcha emet* — from the end of Your words it becomes clear that the first was true. When the *aseret hadibrot* conclude with honoring one's father and mother, it retroactively validates the opening claim *anochi Hashem* — for the same divine voice that demands honor of God also demands honor of parents, confirming that the framework is coherent and principled throughout.

---

## Dama ben Netina

### Lost Fortune

In response to the question of how far *kibbud av va'em* extends, Ulla directs: *tze'u ur'u mah asah oved kochavim echad be-Ashkelon, ve-Dama ben Netina shemo* — go see what a certain non-Jew in Ashkelon did. His name was *Dama ben Netina*, and his story is one of the most famous in this entire *sugya*.

The Sages sought merchandise — precious stones for the *ephod* of the *Kohen Gadol* — for which they were prepared to pay six hundred thousand *dinarin* in profit to *Dama*. (Rav Kahana's version raises the figure to eight hundred thousand.) The key to his storeroom lay under the pillow beneath his sleeping father's head. *Ve-lo tzi'aro* — and he would not disturb him. He forfeited a fortune rather than interrupt his father's sleep.

This story made an impression far beyond its immediate lesson about *kibbud av va'em*. There is embedded within it a profound statement about the sanctity of another person's sleep — *gezelat sheina*, the theft of someone's sleep — as something close to inviolable. The Kabbalistic and *mussar* literature picks up on this dimension, and this story is in many ways its source.

The question of where the prohibition falls halachically is also interesting. Is refusing to disturb a sleeping parent a dimension of *kavod* — providing for his needs, including the need for undisturbed rest? Is it an expression of *mora* — reverence, which involves not treating the parent as an object to be instrumentalized for one's own purposes? Both framings are plausible, and the story does not resolve the question, though it makes the ideal vivid and unforgettable.

One might also wonder: what if the father had woken up and said, "You didn't rouse me for *six hundred thousand dinarin*?" The Gemara does not raise this, presumably because *Dama ben Netina* was not Jewish and his father was not obligated in *kibbud av va'em* toward *Dama*. But it is a reasonable question about the limits of deference.

The non-Jewish exemplar is itself significant. The message is at once universal and *kal vachomer*: if a Gentile without the obligation of *kibbud av va'em* as a commanded *mitzvah* can reach such heights, how much more is demanded of one who is obligated? Beyond the *kal vachomer*, there is a recognition that this value — the reverence and care owed to those who brought you into the world — is part of the moral fabric of humanity, accessible and recognizable across religious boundaries. And the Gemara's use of a non-Jew as the model for this Jewish practice carries its own implicit message about the universality of the underlying moral truth.

It is also worth noting what *Dama ben Netina* is providing: the precious stones for the *ephod*, the garment of the *Kohen Gadol*, central to the religious life of all *Klal Yisrael*. The non-Jew who models *kibbud av* is also the one who enables the religious service of the entire Jewish people. The convergence is striking.

### Divine Reward

The story continues: *le-shanah acheret natan Hakadosh Baruch Hu secharo* — the following year, God provided his reward. *Shenoldah lo parah adumah be-edro* — a *parah adumah* was born in his flock. When the Sages of Israel came to him, *Dama* said: I know you would pay me any price in the world for this animal. *Ela* — but I ask only this: *oto mammon she-hifsadeti bishvil kibbud abba* — the same sum I lost in the honor of my father. Nothing more. His reward matched exactly what he had relinquished.

The *parah adumah* is itself charged with symbolism: it is the paradigmatic *chok*, the statute whose rationale is withheld. That the reward for an act of pure moral devotion — forfeiting enormous profit out of reverence for a sleeping father — comes through the most inscrutable of all *mitzvot* is perhaps not accidental.

### Commanded Principle

The Gemara now cites Rabbi Chanina's principle, which contextualizes the entire story: *gadol metzuvah ve'oseh mishe'eino metzuvah ve'oseh* — one who is commanded and does is greater than one who is not commanded and does. This is the framework within which the exemplary behavior of *Dama ben Netina*, a non-Jew, must be understood. As remarkable as his conduct was, those who are commanded in *kibbud av va'em* and fulfill it are at a higher level — not because they are personally superior, but because the commanded act is more deeply desired and demanded by God.

*Rashi* explains that being commanded actually creates greater resistance — the external obligation generates a kind of counter-pressure that makes compliance harder — and therefore greater reward. A more general formulation: if the act is *commanded*, it reflects that God desires it more intensely, and therefore the person who performs it under obligation achieves something higher.

This principle opens onto a broader question that the story of *Dama ben Netina* uniquely illuminates: what happens to the moral vitality of an obligation once it is formalized as a religious command? The non-Jew, unburdened by the command, could reach those heights perhaps precisely because his motivation remained purely moral. For the Jew, the challenge is to maintain that moral force and inner drive even after the act has been overlaid with the structure of religious obligation. The story of *Dama ben Netina* keeps that moral ideal vivid and present, which may be precisely why it is told in this context.

---

## Rav Yosef Blind

### Initial Hope

The Gemara presents a remarkable personal disclosure from Rav Yosef, who was blind. He said: *meireisha hava amina* — at first I used to think — *man de-hava amar li halacha ke-Rabbi Yehuda, de-amar suma patur min hamitzvot* — if someone were to tell me that we rule like Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a blind person is exempt from *mitzvot*, *avidna yoma tava lerabbanan* — I would make a *Yom Tov* for the Torah scholars. Why? *Dela mipakedna, ve'avidna* — because I am not commanded, and yet I perform the *mitzvot*; I thought that being an unconstrained volunteer would bring me *greater* reward than being an obligated performer.

### Reversal

*Ha de-shames leha de-amar Rabbi Chanina* — but now that I have heard Rabbi Chanina's ruling, that *gadol metzuvah ve'oseh yoter mishe'eino metzuvah ve'oseh*, the one who is commanded is greater — *vehashta adaraba* — it is now the opposite. Now Rav Yosef says: if someone were to tell me that *we do not rule like Rabbi Yehuda* — that I am indeed obligated — that is when I would make the *Yom Tov*, because being obligated means my reward would be greater. Rav Yosef's reversal captures with great poignancy how deeply the principle of *metzuvah ve'oseh* reorders one's understanding of religious merit.

---

## Mother's Assault

### Public Assault

*Ki asa Rav Dimi amar* — when Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael* he reported: once *Dama ben Netina* was wearing a golden embroidered *sirkon* — some kind of fine toga or garment — and was seated among the great men of Rome. *U-va'at immo* — his mother came. *Vekara'aso mimenu* — she tore it off him. *Vetapcha lo al rosho* — she struck him on the head. *Veyarka lo befanav* — and she spat in his face. *Velo hichlima* — and he did not embarrass her.

The contrast with the earlier story is instructive. In the case of the sleeping father, *Dama* demonstrated *kavod* — honor — by not disturbing him, by treating his father's repose as paramount even at enormous personal cost. Here, with his mother, he demonstrates *mora* — reverence and self-restraint — by absorbing a public humiliation without retaliation or shaming her. The Gemara noted earlier that a son more naturally shows *kavod* to his nurturing mother and *mora* to his authoritative father. In both these stories, *Dama ben Netina* performs the *less* natural act: honor toward the father, restraint and reverence toward the mother.

---

## Attitude Principle

### Feeding Example

The *amud* concludes with a teaching that synthesizes everything the Gemara has been building toward. *Tani Avi berei de-Rav Avo: yesh ma'achil le'aviv pasyoni vetordo min ha'olam* — there is one who feeds his father fattened pigeons — a genuine delicacy — and through doing so drives him from the world, from any share in the *olam ha-ba*. *Veyesh mat'chino bereichayim umevi'o lechayei ha'olam haba* — and there is one who causes his father to grind at a millstone and through this brings him to the life of the *olam haba*.

The *Yerushalmi* supplies the context. In the first case: a son feeds his father beautiful dishes day after day, and one day the father asks where such fine food comes from. The son replies: "What do you care, old man? Just chew and eat." In the second: the father is called to perform some compulsory service for the king — dangerous, degrading — and the son says: "You stay here and work the millstone; I'll go do the service for the king," thereby protecting his father at personal risk and cost.

### Respect Demonstration

The principle is clear and far-reaching. We have discussed, and will discuss further, the specific actions that constitute *kavod* and *yirah* — providing food and drink, not occupying a parent's seat, not contradicting them publicly, accompanying and serving them. But the Gemara here insists that performing those very actions is not sufficient to fulfill *kibbud av va'em*. It depends entirely on how they are done — what they communicate, what attitude they express.

You can provide the finest meals with complete contempt and disdain. That is not *kibbud av va'em*; it may in fact be a desecration of it. You can perform none of the prescribed acts and yet do the single greatest *kiyum* of *kibbud av va'em* through an act of self-sacrifice that places your parent's welfare above your own.

This is where *kibbud av va'em* diverges fundamentally from most areas of *halacha*. When we put on *tefillin*, the attitude with which we do so does not affect whether we have fulfilled the obligation. The precise physical act, performed correctly, is *yotzei*. Here, the same physical act can be fulfilled or violated depending entirely on what it expresses. *Kavod* is not a checklist; it is a posture, a communication, a demonstration. And that is why the constant movement in this *sugya* between *halacha* and *aggadah*, between the specific rulings and the moral stories, is not incidental. The aggadic dimension — the stories of *Dama ben Netina*, the Gemara's images of God withdrawing when parents are caused anguish, the equation of parents with God — is not ornamental. It is the very substance of what *kibbud av va'em* requires.

---

---

# Kiddushin 32

## Kibbud Stories

### Avimi's Deference

The daf opens at the last line of 31a with a *tanna* attributed to Avimi the son of Rabbi Abbahu: *yesh ma'achil le'aviv pisyoni v'tardo min ha'olam, v'yesh mat'chino b'reichayim u'mevi'o l'chayei ha'olam ha'ba* — there are those who feed their parents pheasants and thereby drive them from the world, and there are those who make their parents grind behind a millstone and thereby bring them to *olam ha-ba*. As Rabbi Linzer discussed the previous day, this opening statement captures the deep subjectivity — or rather, the essential need for context — in understanding the obligations of *kibbud av va'em* and *mora em va'av* in a way that other *mitzvot* perhaps do not require. The same act can honor or humiliate depending on the relationship and the circumstances.

Immediately following, Rabbi Abbahu himself offers a living example: *ke-gon Avimi brei* — my son Avimi exemplifies the fulfillment of the *mitzvah* of *kibbud*. The *gemara* then details precisely how. Avimi had five *benei samchei* — the term is somewhat ambiguous; it may mean sons who had received *semicha*, or more plausibly sons who were already grown and dependent on his table — in his father's lifetime. Yet whenever Rabbi Abbahu would come to visit, Avimi himself would run to the door and open it, calling out "Yes, yes, I'm coming" until he reached the threshold. He did not delegate this act of *kibbud* to his own grown children but insisted on performing it himself.

This narrative touches on something worth noting: the overwhelming majority of *gemara* stories about *kibbud av va'em* concern adult children navigating the care of aging, and in some cases declining, parents — not teenagers relating to middle-aged parents. Avimi had a household of his own to manage. And according to *Tosafot*, Rabbi Abbahu lived in *Eretz Yisrael* while Avimi lived in *Bavel*, meaning these visits were infrequent, which makes Avimi's scrupulous deference all the more striking.

### Vigil & Merit

The *gemara* continues with a second episode. One day, Rabbi Abbahu asked Avimi for a glass of water. By the time Avimi returned, his father had already dozed off. Rather than waking him or setting the water down and leaving, Avimi stood vigil beside him until he woke on his own. The *gemara* records that as a result of this act, *ista'yei miltei* — he merited to expound the *mizmor* of *Mizmor l'Asaph, Elohim nitzav b'adat el* — which is, as it happens, the *shir shel yom* of that very day. The connection drawn between *kibbud av va'em* and the relationship between human beings and God runs as a quiet current beneath this entire sugya.

*Tosafot* raises a separate question about which *Mizmor l'Asaph* is intended here — *Mizmor l'Asaph, Elohim bau goyim b'nachalatecha* presents an alternative — and the *rishonim* engage with the textual question at length, though that discussion is set aside here.

### Mother vs Father

The next narrative introduces Rabbi Yaakov bar Abuha — a name which itself prompts a brief observation, since *bar Abuha* means "son of his father," and one always wonders in the *gemara* whether *Abba* was a proper name or a term of address substituted for a parent whose name one could not directly invoke. Rabbi Yaakov bar Abuha posed his question to Abaye: *ke-gon ana* — let me offer my own example. When he would return from the *beis midrash*, his father would pour him a glass of wine, and his mother would mix it with water. What should he do? His parents were being deferential to him, and both had prepared something for him.

Abaye's answer is instructive: accept the drink from your mother, but do not accept it from your father, *de-keivan de-bar Torah hu chalsha datei* — because your father is himself a Torah scholar, and he will be more pained if his son accepts the drink from him. The role reversal here is striking on multiple levels. These are parents serving their son the way the son is supposed to be serving them. And the complicating factor is precisely his status as a *talmid chacham* — his father's honor for Torah learning is entangled with the familial dynamic in a way that cannot be easily separated. Each of these episodes could sustain extended psychological and *halachic* analysis; the *gemara* presses forward.

### Tarfon's Footstool

The *gemara* then turns to the well-known story of Rabbi Tarfon, who would lie down on the floor each time his mother needed to get into or out of bed, serving as a living footstool. *De-chol eimat de-hava baei lemisik le-purya gachin ve-salik lei* — whenever she needed to ascend to her bed, he would crouch down and she would step up on him; and whenever she needed to descend, she would step down upon him. Whether his mother was infirm or simply unable to manage the height of the bed on her own, the image is vivid and deliberate.

When Rabbi Tarfon came to the *beis midrash* and spoke proudly of this practice, the response was immediate and sobering: *adayin lo higata le-chatzi kibbud* — you have not yet reached half of what *kibbud* requires. The standard set by the *gemara* is this: *klum zarka arneki be-fanecha le-yam ve-lo hichlamta* — have you reached the point where if she threw your wallet into the ocean in front of you, you would not be shamed or angered?

### Wallet Test

This wallet question becomes a *sugya* in its own right for the *poskim*: how much financial loss and how much personal humiliation is a child obligated to absorb without reacting? These are actually two separate questions. *Rashi* reads the test primarily as a question of public embarrassment — the shame of allowing a parent to treat one this way before others. But the financial dimension is also real: a parent destroying your property, in public or in private, tests the inner composure that *kibbud* demands. Both threads will return later in the *daf*.

### Rav Yosef Rising

A brief but vivid vignette follows. Rav Yosef, upon hearing the sound of his mother's footsteps approaching, would say: *ekum mikamei Shechina de-asya* — I am rising before the *Shechina* that is coming. The analogy between honoring one's mother and receiving the divine presence appears here not as a homily but as the stated reason for Rav Yosef's own practice.

### Orphanhood Blessing

This leads into one of the more striking statements in the *gemara*. Rabbi Yochanan said: *ashrei mi she-lo chamman* — fortunate is one who never saw them. *Rashi* explains the difficult word but the meaning is arresting: better perhaps never to have had parents than to have had them and failed so consistently at the *mitzvah* of *kibbud*. The *gemara* then explains this in terms of Rabbi Yochanan's own biography: *ki ivarta imeh meis aviv, ki yeladtih misa imeih* — when his mother was pregnant with him, his father died; when she gave birth, his mother died. He was orphaned from the outset. In a deeply ironic sense, he never had the opportunity to fail at *kibbud av va'em* — and this is offered, somewhat ruefully, as a kind of grace. One can read this either as a psychological justification that Rabbi Yochanan constructed for himself, or as a genuine *gemara* observation about the extraordinary difficulty of the *mitzvah* and the near-impossibility of fulfilling it perfectly.

The same was true of Abaye, the *gemara* continues — *ve-khen Abaye*. A trope emerges: the orphaning of great *amora'im* is not merely biographical detail but seems to suggest that greatness and deprivation were intertwined, and that these sages were spared the burden of potential failure at *kibbud av va'em* precisely through their loss. But then the *gemara* immediately challenges this: *eyni ve-ha-amar Abaye amra li em* — doesn't Abaye constantly quote his *em*? The resolution: *hahi amar bnitei havei* — that was his nurse, his adoptive mother who raised him. The question of how *halacha* regards adoptive parents is genuinely significant, and the *poskim* take it seriously. The principle of *melamdo Torah k'megadlo* — that one who teaches another Torah is considered as though he raised them — points in the same direction: those who form us and nurture us carry a kind of *kibbud* weight that approximates, and in some cases equals, that owed to biological parents.

### Rav Asi's Flight

The concluding narrative in this section is among the most humanly complex in the *daf*. Rav Asi had an elderly mother. She asked him for jewelry; he provided it. She asked for a husband; he said he would look. She asked for a husband as handsome as him — and at that point he fled to *Eretz Yisrael*. He subsequently heard that she had followed him. He came before Rabbi Yochanan and asked: *mahu l'tzeit me-Eretz la-chutz la-Aretz* — may I leave *Eretz Yisrael* and go back to *chutz la-Aretz*? Rabbi Yochanan answered: *asur* — forbidden. He then asked: what if I am going to greet my mother? Rabbi Yochanan said: *eyni yodeia* — I do not know. The *gemara*'s implication is that Rabbi Yochanan sensed something complicated in the story; the question about going to visit his mother was not quite candid.

Somewhat later, Rav Asi returned and reported that Rabbi Yochanan had blessed him: *Ha-Makom yachzirekha l'shalom* — God should return you safely. He then went to Rabbi Elazar and related what had happened. Rabbi Elazar responded: *chas v'shalom mirtach rattach* — *Rashi* explains this as Rabbi Elazar's worry that Rabbi Yochanan would be angry at him for effectively ruling against him. But the ambiguity is genuine: who exactly would be angry at whom? Rabbi Elazar nonetheless concluded that if Rabbi Yochanan had offered a *berakha*, he clearly was not planning to get angry: *v'im ita de-rattach lo hamvarkh lakh* — if he were truly angry, he would not have blessed you.

Then, in mid-deliberation, Rav Asi heard that his mother's coffin was being brought. *Amar: i yadai lo nafki* — if I had known, I would not have left. She had died in *Bavel* and was being transported for burial, and someone else — presumably other family members — had already attended to everything. The weight of what he had failed to do, failed to witness, failed to participate in, settles over the story without commentary. She died alone, in some sense, while he was negotiating the *halacha* of whether to go back to her.

---

## Halakhic Framework

### Kibbud & Mora

The *gemara* now transitions from narrative to systematic *halachic* formulation. A *beraita* is cited: *tanu rabbanan mechabdo be-chayav u-mechabdo be-moto* — there is an obligation of *kavod* toward one's parents both during their lifetime and after their death. The *gemara* asks: how does one fulfill *kavod* during the parent's lifetime? The answer: if you are about to go do something in your parent's service, you may not say "send me along for my own sake" or "speed me up for myself" — *ela kulhu bi-shvil abba* — everything is framed as being done for the parent.

After death, *kavod* takes the form of how you transmit teachings received from them. You may not say simply "this is what my father said" — you must say *kach amar abba mori ha-reini kaparat mishkavo* — "thus said my father, my teacher, for whose resting place I am an atonement." The *gemara* qualifies: *ve-hanei milei toch shneim asar chodesh* — this formulation applies only within the first twelve months. After that, one says *zichrono l'vracha l'chayei ha'olam ha'ba*.

The phrase *ha-reini kaparat mishkavo* carries genuine ambiguity. It has become associated with the practice of saying *kaddish* and attending *minyan* regularly after a parent's passing — a way of acting on their behalf in the post-mortem realm, whether understood as easing their passage through *Gehinnom* or as adding merit toward *olam ha-ba*. *Rashi* reads the phrase in its more severe sense — may all evil due to them befall me instead — while a more positive reading frames it as *le-ilui nishmat*, that the child's good deeds are beneficial to the deceased parent's soul. Many of the mourning practices that are normative in *Ashkenazi halacha* flow from *Chasidei Ashkenaz*, and both readings are consistent with that tradition.

### Name Change

The next *beraita* addresses the *chacham* teaching publicly: *chacham meshaneh shem aviv ve-shem rabo* — when quoting one's parent or teacher, a scholar must alter how he refers to them. He cannot simply say "Rabbi so-and-so said this" but must say "my *rebbe* said such and such." The *turgaman* — the one who sits beside the lecturer and repeats the teaching aloud, more slowly and with elaboration — is exempt from this requirement.

But whose father and whose teacher are meant? If it is the *turgaman*'s own father, the *gemara* objects: *atu turgaman lav bar chiyuva hu* — is a *turgaman* somehow exempt from showing *kavod* to his parents? Rather, Rava clarifies: it is the *chacham*'s father and the *chacham*'s teacher whose names must be modified — not the *turgaman*'s. The *chacham* has that specific relationship of honor to express; for the *turgaman*, whose function is clarity of transmission, the obligation to modify names does not apply in the same way. The practical illustration involves Mar bar Rav Ashi: when he taught, he would refer to his father simply as *Abba Mari*, while the *turgaman* would repeat the teaching by name — *kach amar Rav Ashi*.

### Mora vs Kibbud

The *gemara* now formally distinguishes between the two separate *mitzvot*: *mora* and *kibbud*. What constitutes *mora*? *Lo omed bimkomo, velo yoshev bimkomo, velo soter devarav, velo machrio* — do not stand in the parent's place, do not sit in the parent's place, do not contradict or overturn their words. The formulation *soter devarav* — literally "demolish his words" — is noteworthy. What constitutes *kibbud*? *Ma'achil u-mashkeh malbish u-mechaseh machnis u-motzi* — providing food, providing drink, clothing (*malbish* referring to daytime clothing, *mechaseh* to nighttime coverings), and transportation, bringing the parent to where they need to go and returning them.

This formal framework raises a broader *halachic* question: how literally must these categories be applied? If a parent is not particular about which chair he sits in, but is deeply sensitive about something else entirely, does *mora* require technical adherence to these specific categories, or does it mean cultivating the actual relational state of reverence — adapting its expression to what truly affects this particular parent in this particular context? Major *halachic* works on *kibbud av va'em* have been written taking both more formalist and more contextual approaches, and this tension is genuine.

### Money Source

The *gemara* then raises the question of *mishel mi* — whose money must pay for all of the obligations of *kibbud*? The children bear the responsibility to ensure their parents have food, clothing, shelter, and transportation; but must the children pay for this from their own resources?

Rav Yehuda says: *mishel ben* — from the child's own property. Rav Natan bar Oshaya says: *mishel av* — from the parent's property. On the latter view, parents are expected to have prepared financially for old age; once they are no longer able to manage their own affairs, the children administer the parental resources appropriately. The *rabanan* told Rabbi Yirmiyah — or some say, his son — that the *halacha* follows *mishel av*: it is the parent's money that funds the obligations of *kibbud*.

### Lost Money

But a *meitivei* is raised: the *pasuk* says *kabbed et avicha ve'et imecha*, and in *Mishlei* it says *kabbed et Adonai mehoncha* — honor God from your wealth. Just as honoring God requires *chisron kis*, actual financial expenditure and loss, so too *kibbud* of parents must involve *chisron kis*. If the obligation is *mishel av*, what does the child actually lose? The *gemara* answers: *le-bittul melacha* — the financial loss is in lost wages, the time taken away from work in order to care for the parent. This is a genuinely different conception of *chisron kis*: not the direct expenditure of funds, but the opportunity cost of time. One might compare it to other contexts in *halacha* where refraining from productive work — *bittul melacha* — is treated as a form of financial sacrifice.

### Ma'aser Ani

A *beraita* is then brought: two brothers, two business partners, a father and son, a teacher and student — *podin ze la'ze ma'aser sheni u-machilin ze la'ze ma'aser ani* — they may redeem each other's *ma'aser sheni* (avoiding the additional *chomesh* that applies when one redeems one's own) and they may feed each other *ma'aser ani*. The case of *ma'aser ani* is where the *gemara*'s argument turns sharp.

If we were to say the obligation of *kibbud* is *mishel ben* — from the child's own resources — then feeding one's parents with *ma'aser ani* would constitute *poreia chovo mishel aniyim*: paying off your own financial obligation to your parents using money that belongs to the poor. *Kibbud av va'em* is not merely a pious aspiration; it is a *chov*, a genuine legal obligation, and satisfying that obligation with charity funds designated for others is improper. The *gemara* responds: perhaps the *beraita* addresses surplus beyond the actual *ma'aser* — extra produce that was set aside but not technically *ma'aser ani*. And even so, Rabbi Yehuda in the *beraita* is pointed: *tavo me'eira l'mi she-ma'achil et aviv ma'aser ani* — a curse on one who feeds his father *ma'aser ani*. The final note: even if technically permitted, *zeila bei milta* — it is simply not appropriate. The spirit of *kibbud* is not satisfied by finding technical workarounds.

---

## Extremes & Tests

### Eliezer's Standard

The *gemara* returns directly to the wallet question introduced in the Tarfon narrative. A *beraita* asks: how far must *kibbud av va'em* extend? Rabbi Eliezer answers: *k'dei she-yitol arnaki v'yizrakenu l'yam b'fanav v'eino machlimo* — to the extent that if your parent took your wallet and threw it into the sea in front of you, you would not become upset. This is the measure of *kibbud*.

One might ask: does this preclude later legal recourse? Can the child not sue for damages? The *gemara* does not address that directly here, but the emotional and behavioral standard is clear: in the moment, there can be no anger and no shaming of the parent. If the obligation is *mishel ben*, the money belongs to the child, and the parent is simply destroying the child's property. The test is whether the child's composure holds even then.

This connects back to the *gemara* from twenty *dafim* earlier, in the *sugya* of *harei at mekudeshet li* — where a woman takes the *kiddushin* money and throws it into the sea. Does that act represent acceptance and exercise of ownership, or rejection? Who would be entitled to hire divers to retrieve it? The emotional and legal parsing of who owns a thrown object, and what that act means, surfaces across multiple *sugyot* in this tractate.

The *gemara* then raises: *ve-eima be-mishel av* — perhaps we can explain the wallet test from the perspective of *mishel av*. If the money is the parent's money to begin with, why would the child get angry? The *nafka mina* would be in the case of *ra'uy le-yorsho* — property that the child stands to inherit. Even if the parent is spending their own money, a child who knows they will one day inherit that estate might resent seeing it wasted. The wallet test thus applies even in the *mishel av* framework: the child must not become angry even when witnessing the squandering of what they might eventually inherit.

### Huna's Test

This leads to one of the most unsettling stories on the *daf*: *ve-chi ha de-Rabbah bar Rav Huna de-Rav Huna kara shirai de-anpai Rabbah berei* — Rav Huna tore an expensive silk garment in front of his son Rabbah. *Ve-amar eizil achezi i ratach i lo ratach* — and Rav Huna said: I am going to go and see whether he gets angry or not. He was testing his son's *kibbud av va'em*.

This is a striking story, and the *gemara* immediately recognizes its *halachic* problems. First: perhaps Rabbah will get angry — and then *ka avar al lifnei iver* — Rav Huna has set up a situation in which his own son is caused to sin. You do not set traps designed to make people transgress. Second: even if we say Rav Huna was confident Rabbah would not get angry and had pre-emptively been *mochel* on being bothered, there remains *bal tashchit* — the prohibition against wantonly destroying objects of value. Third: if Rabbah knew his father was deliberately testing him, perhaps he would not get angry precisely because he understood it was a test — in which case the test proves nothing.

The *gemara* resolves each objection in turn, though the resolutions have a somewhat forced quality. On the *lifnei iver* problem: *de-machil lei* — Rav Huna must have already signaled some kind of forgiveness, perhaps indicating to Rabbah in advance that this was a test and that anger would not constitute a genuine transgression in context. On *bal tashchit*: *de-avad lei be-pumbeioni* — he tore it in the hem, in a place where a tailor could repair it and the value would not be diminished. It looked dramatic but caused no actual material loss. On the problem of Rabbah knowing it was a test: *de-avad lei be-sha'at retichei* — Rav Huna did it at a moment when Rabbah was already emotionally agitated, already primed to react, making the self-restraint genuinely tested.

One reasonable reading of the story is that Rav Huna was simply not thinking clearly — an elderly man behaving erratically — and the *gemara* is working to retroactively justify actions that were in the moment instinctive rather than calculated. This would itself be a kind of commentary on the earlier observation about elderly parents whose behavior may reflect cognitive or emotional decline.

There is an extended *sugya* within this section about a case from *Sanhedrin*: Rabbi Yechezkel asked his son Rami about what happens when those condemned to *sreifah* become mixed among those condemned to *sekilah*. Rabbi Shimon holds they should all receive *sekilah*, on the grounds that *sreifah* is more severe — the lesser punishment is applied. Rav Yehudah, the son, responded: *Abba, lo titnaya hachi* — Father, don't teach it this way. He proposed an alternative rationale: since the majority of those present are *niskalin*, the rule of *rov* governs, and there is no need to appeal to relative severity of punishment at all. His father pushed back from the *seifa* of the *mishna*, where the *chachamim* seem to require the severity-based rationale. Rav Yehudah held that the *seifa* represents the *chachamim* responding to Rabbi Shimon, pressing him on his own terms — and so *rov* remains the primary principle while the severity-comparison belongs to the internal *machloket* between Rabbi Shimon and the *chachamim*.

The entire discussion is brought here specifically because of the mode of speech: Rav Yehudah said to his father, *lo titnaya hachi* — don't teach it like this. That directness is what occasions Shmuel's rebuke in the following subsection.

### Shmuel Rebuke

Shmuel addressed Rav Yehudah — calling him by the nickname *Shinena*, which may refer to his sharpness in learning or to his broad smile — and said: *lo teima lei le-avuch hachi* — do not speak to your father this way. A *beraita* is cited: if you see your father violating a matter of Torah, do not say *Abba avarta al divrei Torah* — Father, you have transgressed the Torah. Rather say: *Abba, kach katuv ba-Torah* — Father, it is written thus in the Torah. The deferential formulation presents the teaching without accusation.

But even that formulation, the *gemara* pushes further, might cause the parent *tza'ar* — distress — to be told that the Torah says something that contradicts what they just did. Therefore the most refined approach: *ela omer lo Abba mikra katuv ba-Torah kach* — say, Father, there is a *pasuk* that reads such-and-such. Do not even frame it as "this is written in the Torah" with its implicit weight of accusation; simply cite the verse. Whether a given practice is *d'oraita* in the explicit sense or derived through *drashot* is itself a layered question — the *Rambam* in *Sefer Ha-Mitzvot* and *Peirush Ha-Mishna* is careful to distinguish between what is literally written in the Torah and what is derived through rabbinic interpretation, even when the latter carries *de'oraita* weight. But the *halachic* principle here is clear: deferential speech toward a parent who is erring requires the softest possible framing.

---

## Prioritization

### Father vs Mitzvah

Elazar ben Masya raises a case: his father asks him for a glass of water, and at that same moment he has a *mitzvah* to perform. Should he set aside *kibbud av* and go do the *mitzvah*? His reasoning: *she-ani ve-abba chayavim be-mitzvah* — both my father and I are equally obligated in this *mitzvah*. Since the father is no less obligated than the son, the son need not subordinate himself to serve his father when an equal obligation beckons. The force of the question depends on the nature of the *mitzvah* as well — a *mitzvah overes*, one that will expire if not done immediately, poses the case more acutely than one that can wait.

### Delegation Rule

Issi ben Yehuda offers a more nuanced principle: *im efshar le-mitzvah le-asos al yedei acherim, te'aseh al yedei acherim, vayeilechu be-kibbud av* — if the *mitzvah* can be performed by others, let others do it, and you go fulfill *kibbud av*. The category of *mitzvah efshar la'asot al yedei acherim* — a *mitzvah* that others can discharge — versus a *mitzvah* that only you personally can fulfill appears across many *halachic* contexts. A *mitzvah shebegufo* or a *mitzvah* for which you bear a specific personal obligation cannot be handed off; nobody else can hear the *megillah* on your behalf. But communal obligations, or tasks that any qualified person can do, can in principle be delegated — and in such cases, *kibbud av va'em* takes precedence.

This principle has been applied in serious contemporary *halachic* discussions, including in *chardal* communities regarding whether a *yeshiva* student may serve as an EMT or volunteer medic during his *yeshiva* years. If there are other qualified individuals who can serve, it may be argued that ambulance work is a *mitzvah efshar la'asot al yedei acherim*, and the student's primary obligation is to remain in learning. Other communities reason differently, and the *gemara* explicitly records *beraitot* about *yeshiva* students joining military campaigns when necessary. The tension between different categories of obligation, and the finite hours in a day, is precisely what the *gemara* is navigating throughout this material.

### Matna's Ruling

Rav Matna provides the *pesak*: *halacha k'Isi ben Yehuda* — the *halacha* follows Issi ben Yehuda. When a *mitzvah* can be performed by others, *kibbud av va'em* takes precedence and the child must attend to the parent's needs. When the *mitzvah* is one that only the child can perform — *kibbud av va'em* yields.

---

## Teacher's Honor

### Forgiveness Limits

Rav Chisda (as reported through a chain of transmission: Rav Yitzchak bar Shila citing Rav Matna citing Rav Chisda) establishes a fundamental asymmetry: *ha-av she-machal al kevodo, kevodo machul* — if a parent forgives their own honor, waives the *kibbud* owed to them, that honor is indeed forgiven. The *mitzvah* is the parent's to waive. But *ha-rav she-machal al kevodo, ein kevodo machul* — if a teacher forgives their honor, that forgiveness is not effective. The honor owed to a teacher cannot be extinguished simply because the teacher consents.

The reason is embedded in the nature of the obligation. The *beraita* already established that *ein kavod ela Torah* — there is no honor except for Torah. The honor you show your teacher is not ultimately about the person; it is about the Torah they represent and transmit. And because it is *kavod ha-Torah*, not merely *kavod ha-rav*, the teacher cannot personally waive something that is not wholly theirs to waive.

Rav Yosef dissents: *afilu ha-rav she-machal al kevodo, kevodo machul* — even a teacher who forgives their honor has forgiven it. His proof: *va-Adonai holech lifneihem yomam* — God led the entire camp of Israel through the desert, and by doing so, God was in a sense *mochel* on God's own *kavod*, descending to lead and to serve. If God could be *mochel* on divine honor, a teacher can certainly waive their own.

### Torah Ownership

Rava responds sharply: *heichi hashta? Hatam Hakadosh Baruch Hu alma dilei, ve-Torah dilei, machil likra. Hacha Torah dilei hi?* — How can you compare? There, God's world and God's Torah — so God can waive the honor. But here, is the Torah really the teacher's Torah?

This challenge is then answered by Rava himself, who resolves it with a counterintuitive move. He cites the verse *u've-Torato yehgeh yomam va-lailah* — and in *his* Torah he meditates day and night. The possessive *Torato* is interpreted as meaning that a person who truly engages with Torah acquires it as their own — it becomes *his* Torah. And therefore the honor a student shows a teacher *is* directed at the teacher's own Torah, not merely at something borrowed from God. On this reading, Rava affirms — rather than overturns — the position that the teacher's honor is genuine and personal, and therefore the teacher *does* have the right to waive it. The *sugya* thereby comes to rest on a view close to Rav Yosef's, though the reasoning is refined: the teacher's Torah is genuinely theirs because they have acquired it through total immersion, and they may therefore be *mochel* on the *kavod* that flows from it.

---

## Standing & Status

### Wine & Standing

The *gemara* closes with a pair of narratives about standing as a form of honor. Rava was serving wine at his son's wedding. Rav Papa and Rav Huna the son of Rabbi Yehoshua were present, and they stood up before Rav Mari and Rav Pinchas the son of Rav Chisda — but they did not stand before Rava. Those present said: *hani rabbanan rabbanan, ve-hani rabbanan lav rabbanan* — those are real rabbis, and those are not real rabbis. Rava was offended. The story illustrates both the social stakes of the standing-up obligation and the judgment being made in real time about who merits such recognition.

### Hidur Rising

Similarly, Rav Papa was serving wine at the wedding of his son Abba Mar — whose name was likely Papa bar Papa, giving rise to the title *Abba Mar brei* — and he poured wine for Yitzchak his son and for Rav Yehudah, but did not stand up for them. Those present were offended. Yet the *gemara* notes: *afilu hachi hidar mavdei* — even so, they performed a *hidur*. A *hidur* is a partial rising, a gesture of deference that falls short of full standing — one begins to rise without fully completing the motion. This qualified rising is recognized as a meaningful intermediate form of honor, distinct from both full standing and complete indifference.

Here the *daf* concludes.

---

---

# Kiddushin 33

## Rav Mochel on Kevodo

### Rav Mochel - Intro

The *daf* opens on 33b, picking up where the previous session left off — namely, the question of whether a *rav* can be *mochel* on his *kavod*. The Gemara had already established that a father can waive honor owed to him, but the case of a *rav* is more complex. A *rebbe* does not merely represent himself; he embodies *kevod hatorah*. One might therefore argue that even if he personally does not object to being treated without ceremony, the *Torah* he represents demands that others show him respect regardless. Nevertheless, the Gemara concludes with a powerful statement about the nature of *Torah sheba'al peh* and the personal investment it entails. Because *Torah* becomes genuinely one's own through the process of learning and transmission — one has, in a real sense, an ownership stake in it — a *rav* can indeed be *mochel* on his *kavod*. The very intimacy of that ownership is what grants him the standing to waive the honor.

### Even After Mechila

Yet the Gemara's conclusion is not that the obligation disappears entirely. The line that opens this session reads: *afilu hachi hiddur me'avad leh ba'ei* — even so, some form of *hadarta* must still be shown. The *Rambam* leaves this deliberately open-ended: even if the *rav* has been *mochel*, his students remain in a curious state of being simultaneously exempt and obligated. They are exempt from the full requirement, yet still bound to demonstrate some gesture of respect. *Rashi* is characteristically precise: *linua me'at ke'ilu rotze la'amod mipanav* — one should shift slightly, as if intending to rise. Anyone familiar with *yeshiva* culture will recognize what is being described — the partial rising from one's seat, the so-called tush-move, which is not mere social awkwardness but an expression of this very *halakhic* balance. The *rebbe* has waived the full honor; his standing as a representative of *Torah* cannot, however, be entirely ignored. The partial gesture embodies that equilibrium precisely.

### Nasi Cannot Mechel

With that established, Rav Ashi introduces a further distinction. Even according to the opinion that a *rav* may be *mochel* on his *kavod*, a *nasi* cannot do so: *nasi shemachal al kevodo ein kevodo machul*. The *nasi* in this context refers to the role of the exilarch in *Eretz Yisrael* — a uniquely combined office of political and religious leadership, embodied most famously by *Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi* and his descendants. This convergence of authority is distinctive to *Eretz Yisrael*; in *Bavel* the political and rabbinic leaderships were separate institutions.

The Gemara's reasoning seems to be that certain institutions of authority are so fundamental to the structure of society that no individual can simply choose to dissolve them. The framework of social order — the subjection of persons to governance and law — is not a personal privilege that the leader may surrender at will. Just as the Gemara in *Pirkei Avot* teaches that one should pray for the welfare of the government because without it people would consume one another, the authority of the *nasi* represents something too structurally necessary to be quietly waived.

### Rabban Gamliel Story

The Gemara raises an objection from a *baraita*: *Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua*, and *Rabbi Tzadok* were reclining at a *beis hamishteh* celebrating the wedding of *Rabban Gamliel's* son. *Rabban Gamliel* — who was himself the *nasi* — was moving among the guests and pouring their drinks. The host serving drinks was a known practice, but the *nasi* doing so represents at minimum a degree of *mechila* on his *kavod*; one who insists on the dignity of his position does not take on a serving role toward others.

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

*Rabban Gamliel* offered the cup to *Rabbi Eliezer*, who refused to accept it. He would not allow the *nasi* to occupy a role of service toward him, even at the *nasi's* own initiative. *Rabban Gamliel* then offered it to *Rabbi Yehoshua*, who accepted. *Rabbi Eliezer* challenged him: *mah zeh Yehoshua? Anu yoshvim v'Rabban Gamliel omeid umashkeh aleinu?* — How can we remain seated while the *nasi* stands and serves us?

*Rabbi Yehoshua* responded by invoking a greater precedent: *matzinu gadol mimenu sheshimash* — we have found someone even greater than *Rabban Gamliel* who served others. *Avraham* was the *gadol hador*, the greatest of his generation, and yet *v'hu omeid aleihem* — he stood over his guests and served them. Nor can one deflect this by saying that *Avraham* knew they were angels and therefore this was somehow exceptional — *k'arviyim nidmu lo*, they appeared to him as ordinary Arabs. Yet he served them. All the more so, *Rabbi Yehoshua* argued, we should be willing to allow *Rabban Gamliel* to attend to us.

One might note that a distinction exists: *Avraham* was a *gadol hador* but not technically a *nasi* in the institutional sense, and the question of whether *mechilas kavod* applies specifically to political authority is somewhat separate from the question of how great a person is. Moreover, while the guests *Avraham* served were not members of his own clan, the analogy is not exact. Still, it is the argument *Rabbi Yehoshua* deploys.

### Tzadok's Critique

*Rabbi Tzadok* then offered a striking counter-critique that reframes the entire conversation. *Ad masai atem manichim kevodo shel Makom v'atem oskim bichvod habriyos?* — For how long will you set aside the honor of God and occupy yourselves with the honor of human beings? If one wants to invoke a precedent for serving those beneath oneself, the proper model is not *Avraham* but *Hakadosh Baruch Hu* Himself. God causes the winds to blow, the clouds to rise, the rain to descend, the earth to bring forth produce — He effectively sets the table for every creature. If God, who is the ultimate authority, provides for every human being in this direct and personal fashion, then surely *Rabban Gamliel's* attending to his guests involves no compromise of his position.

This argument carries interesting implications. On one reading, *Rabbi Tzadok* is saying that *Rabban Gamliel* is not actually being *mochel al kevodo* at all — acting in a manner that provides for and serves others is not a diminishment of one's authority; it is a *Godly* act, an expression of *vehalchata bidrachav*. On another reading, even if such service could in theory be considered *mechila*, it is entirely legitimate because God Himself models it. Either way, the Gemara concludes from this episode that a *nasi* apparently can be *mochel* — and Rav Ashi's statement is therefore reformulated: even according to the opinion that a *nasi* who waives his honor has indeed waived it, a *melech* cannot do so.

### King Cannot Mechel

The verse invoked for the *melech* is *som tasim alecha melech* — you shall place upon yourself a king, with the word *alecha* ("upon you") signifying that the king's authority must always remain elevated over the people. His *aima*, his commanding presence, must be constant and may not be dissolved. The Gemara draws an analogy to practical governance: just as certain roles in civil society carry enhanced legal protections precisely because the stability they represent cannot be treated lightly, so too the authority of the *melech* cannot be compromised through personal *mechila*. This is ultimately about what is necessary for society to function — *u-mitpallel lishloma shel malkhut* — and no individual, not even the king himself, may unilaterally dissolve that.

---

## Scriptural Basis

### The Pasuk

Having concluded the discussion of *mechilas kavod*, the Gemara now turns to the biblical foundation of the entire subject. *Tanu rabbanan* — the Sages taught in a *baraita*: *mipnei seiva takum ve-hadarta pnei zaken ve-yareta me-elokecha ani Hashem* — before the hoary head you shall rise, and you shall honor the elderly, and you shall fear your God, I am the Lord. At first glance, the verse sounds like a command to respect the elderly broadly. The *baraita* will now analyze precisely what it requires and from whom.

### Tanna Kamma View

The *tanna kamma* begins with a potential misreading: *yakhol afilu mipnei zaken ashmai* — perhaps the verse obligates one to rise even before an elder who is wicked, or more neutrally in the view of *Tosafot*, one who is simply unlearned. The *talmud lomar* is the word *zaken* itself. *Seiva* emphasizes white hair and age, but *zaken* carries a different meaning: *ve-ein zaken ela chakham* — *zaken* denotes a sage. The prooftext is *asfa li shivim ish miziknei Yisrael* — gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel — with the phrase *asher yadata ki hem ziknei ha'am* suggesting that what God *knows* about them, the quality that identifies them as *ziknei ha'am*, is not merely their age but their recognized wisdom and authority. Age alone is therefore insufficient; *zaken* in the *pasuk* means a Torah sage, and *seiva* is understood in light of that.

### R. Yosei HaGlili

*Rabbi Yosei HaGlili* agrees that *zaken* means a sage, but arrives there differently: *ein zaken ela mi shekanah chochmah* — *zaken* refers to one who has *acquired* wisdom. *Rashi* notes the play on words: *ze kanah* — this one acquired. The prooftext is *Hashem kanani reishit darko*, the emphasis falling on the root *kinyan*, acquisition.

The *baraita* then asks: *yakhol ya'amod mi-panav mi-makom rachok* — perhaps one must rise even from a great distance? The *talmud lomar* is *takum ve-hadarta* read together — the rising and the honoring are linked. Several inferences flow from this pairing. First, *takum* is qualified by *ve-hadarta*: a rising that constitutes genuine honor (*hiddur*) is one performed in proximity, not from across the room. Second, the question arises whether *ve-hadarta* refers to something entirely independent of *takum* — perhaps lavishing the sage with gifts. The *talmud lomar* answers: *ma kima she-ein ba chisron kis af hiddur she-ein bo chisron kis* — just as rising costs nothing, so too the *hiddur* required involves no monetary expenditure. Honor is expressed through gesture and manner, not through financial outlay.

Third, might one be obligated to rise inside a bathhouse or while using a toilet? Again *takum ve-hadarta* — *lo amarti kima ela be-makom she-yesh hiddur*, rising is only required in a context where *hiddur* is socially operative. In a bathhouse, particularly the inner section where all are unclothed, the social distinctions that give *kavod* its meaning are suspended. Everyone is reduced to the same fundamental human condition; the context does not support the kind of status-based respect the verse demands. Indeed, the *halakha* holds that one does not even yield one's place in a bathhouse entrance to show deference — in that setting, social standing simply does not assert itself the same way.

Finally, *yakhol yaatzim einav mi-panav she-lo yirehu* — perhaps one may close one's eyes so as not to see the sage and thereby avoid the obligation. The *talmud lomar* invokes the conclusion of the *pasuk*: *ve-yareta me-elokecha* — you shall fear your God. This phrase always signals a *davar ha-masur la-lev*, something known only to the heart and hidden from others. Closing one's eyes to avoid seeing the sage is precisely such an act — it is visible to God alone, and therefore the obligation to fear God applies directly to it.

### Issi ben Yehuda

*Issi ben Yehuda* reads the verse differently: *mipnei seiva takum*, and *afilu kol seiva be-mashma* — the word *seiva* includes any person of white hair, any elder. The obligation to rise is not limited to Torah sages; it extends to any elderly person on the basis of age alone.

### One or Two Categories

With three positions before it — the *tanna kamma*, *Rabbi Yosei HaGlili*, and *Issi ben Yehuda* — the Gemara asks whether the first two are in fact distinct. *Rabbi Yosei HaGlili hainu Tanna Kamma* — aren't they saying the same thing? Both hold that *zaken* means a sage. The Gemara answers: *ika beinaihu yanik ve-chakkim* — the difference is a young Torah sage. For the *tanna kamma*, both dimensions are necessary: *seiva* and *zaken* combine, meaning an older person who is also a sage. A young prodigy, however brilliant, does not qualify. For *Rabbi Yosei HaGlili*, wisdom acquired (*zeh kanah chochmah*) is sufficient on its own, independent of age.

### Tanna Kamma vs. R. Yosei

The Gemara probes further: what is *Rabbi Yosei HaGlili's* reason for separating *seiva* and *zaken* into distinct terms if in the end only *zaken* — the sage — matters? *Ei salka da'atakh k'de-amar tanna kamma* — if you thought like the *tanna kamma*, the Torah could have simply written *mipnei seiva zaken takum ve-hadarta*, combining them cleanly. *Mai shna d'palginhu rachmana* — why did the Torah separate them? *Le-meimra d'hai lav hai v'hai lav hai* — to indicate they are distinct categories.
