The *Gemara* establishes the rule: *kol she-yeshno be-hashchatah yeshno be-hakafah* — whoever is subject to the prohibition of destroying the beard is also subject to the prohibition of cutting the sidelocks. Since women are not subject to *hashchatah* (the beard prohibition), they are not subject to *hakafah* (the sidelocks prohibition) either.

But this raises the immediate question: how do we know women are not subject to *hashchatah* in the first place? Two answers are offered. The first is *sevara* — simple logic. The *Torah* is evidently addressing men, since the beard is a characteristic of men. Even if there are rare exceptions, the *Torah*'s presumed audience is those who naturally have beards. The second is textual: the verse says *pe'at zekanecha* — in the singular — rather than *pe'at zekhanchem* in the plural. The shift from the plural *roshchem* to the singular *zekanecha* is deliberate. *Zekanecha* — your beard, singular — means your beard and not your wife's beard (*ve-lo zikan ishtecha*). Since the verse itself limits the beard prohibition to a single male addressee, the entire prohibition is addressed to men alone.

### Sevel Logic

The principle linking *hashchatah* and *hakafah* is derived from the juxtaposition within the verse itself: both the sidelocks and the beard appear together, and the *Gemara* reads this as establishing that the scope of one prohibition tracks the scope of the other. Whoever is subject to destroying the beard is subject to cutting the sidelocks; whoever is not subject to the former is not subject to the latter. Since women are excluded from *hashchatah*, they are likewise excluded from *hakafah*.

### Braita Challenge

The *Gemara* then introduces a challenge from a *braita*: *zikan ha-ishah ve-ha-saris she-he'elu sei'ar harei hen ke-zakan le-chol divreihem* — a beard grown by a woman or a eunuch (who would not normally grow facial hair) is treated as a beard for all their purposes. If so, this seems to contradict our *mishnah*, since the *braita* implies that the woman's beard carries full halachic status — presumably including the prohibition against shaving it.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye resolves this firmly: the *braita* cannot be referring to the prohibition of *hashchatah*. That women are exempt from *hashchatah* — from the beard-shaving prohibition — is beyond question. Abaye invokes an additional basis beyond the *sevara* and *zekanecha* analysis: a *gezeirah shavah* linking *pe'at* in the *Yisrael* verse to *pe'at* in the *kohanim* verse. By the *kohanim*, the *Torah* says *bnei Aharon* — only the sons, not the daughters — and the verse concerning the beard of the *kohanim* uses the same word *pe'at* as the verse concerning *Yisrael*. By the *gezeirah shavah*, what applies to *kohanim* — i.e., that the prohibition is limited to men — applies equally to *Yisrael*. Since the *kohanim* are unambiguously only men, and the beard prohibition for *Yisrael* is linked to it by *gezeirah shavah*, the *Yisrael* prohibition is likewise limited to men.

### Kal Vachomer Question

The *Gemara* interrupts Abaye's reasoning with a sharp question: if we accept that *bnei Aharon* applies throughout the entire section addressing *kohanim* — covering *tumah*, *korcha*, and *pe'at zekanam lo yigaleichu* — then why do we need the *gezeirah shavah* at all? We could simply derive by *kal va-chomer*: if *kohanim*, who are subject to greater *mitzvah* obligations and more stringent demands than an ordinary *Yisrael*, are limited to men (*bnei Aharon ve-lo bnot Aharon*) for the beard prohibition — then for *Yisrael*, who are subject to fewer obligations, certainly it should be limited to men as well.

### Gezerah Shavah Scope

Abaye's response is that without the *gezeirah shavah*, he would have said *hifsik ha-inyan* — the context was interrupted. That is, *bnei Aharon* at the beginning of the section applies only to the *tumah* prohibition immediately following; by the time the *Torah* reaches the beard prohibition later in the section, the limiting phrase no longer applies, and the beard prohibition would apply equally to men and women. If so, the *kal va-chomer* would also fail, since there would be nothing on the *kohanim* side limiting it to men with respect to *pe'at ha-zakan*.

This is where the *gezeirah shavah* becomes essential. The very existence of the *gezeirah shavah* — the shared word *pe'at* linking the *Yisrael* and *kohanim* verses — signals that there is something to learn from one to the other. If the *kohanim* verse were also men and women (because *bnei Aharon* didn't extend that far), there would be nothing to learn. The fact that the *Torah* invites a *gezeirah shavah* forces us to conclude that there is a meaningful difference between the two cases, and the only meaningful difference is the restriction to men. Therefore, the *gezeirah shavah* itself tells us that *bnei Aharon* does extend through the entire section, including the beard prohibition.

The *Gemara* then asks: even granting that *hifsik ha-inyan* is a real concern, could the *gezeirah shavah* not be teaching something else entirely — not the restriction to men — while the beard prohibition by *kohanim* would still apply to women? And it answers: yes, because the *gezeirah shavah* is indeed needed for something else as well.

### Tashchit Definition

The *gezeirah shavah* between *pe'at zekanam lo yigaleichu* (by *kohanim*) and *lo tashchit et pe'at zekanecha* (by *Yisrael*) is also needed to clarify the definition of what type of shaving is prohibited. *Tashchit* — destruction — implies getting to the root, cutting destructively at the surface; but it does not specify the instrument. *Yigaleichu* — shaving, cutting with a blade — implies a blade instrument but does not specify that it must destroy at the root. Each verse alone is incomplete: *tashchit* alone might include plucking with tweezers (*malket u-rahitani*), since that destroys the hair at the root. *Yigaleichu* alone might include scissors (*misparayim*), since scissors cut with a blade-like action.

The *Gemara* resolves this through the combination: *ha-keitzad, giluach she-yesh bo hashchatah* — what is the prohibited form? A shaving that both involves a blade and destroys at the root. *Havei omer zeh ta'ar* — that is a razor blade (*ta'ar*). Scissors do not destroy at the root; tweezers do not involve a blade-style shaving. Only a razor blade satisfies both conditions simultaneously. This is the halachic basis for the opinion that an electric shaver, which operates by a scissors-type action rather than a blade-against-skin action, might not violate *bal tashchit*.

So the *gezeirah shavah* serves a double purpose: it limits the prohibition to men (via the *bnei Aharon* extension), and it defines the nature of the prohibited act as razor-blade shaving only.

### Braita Purpose

Returning now to the *braita* that stated a woman's beard is treated as a beard for all purposes: if it does not refer to *hashchatah*, what *halacha* does it convey? Mar Zutra initially suggests it refers to *tumat nega'im* — the impurity of *tzara'at* on the beard. The *Gemara* responds that *tumat nega'im* is explicit in a *pasuk*: *ve-ish o ishah ki yihyeh vo nega be-rosh o ve-zakan* — a man or a woman who has a spot on the head or beard. No *braita* is needed to teach something already in the verse.

Mar Zutra then suggests the *braita* addresses *taharat nega'im* — the purification process. The *Gemara* dismisses this as well: once she is subject to *tumah* just like a man, she is obviously subject to the corresponding *taharah* process.

The *Gemara* then settles on the correct reading: the *braita* is needed to clarify how to read the verse *ish o ishah ki yihyeh vo nega be-rosh o ve-zakan*. One might naturally read it as follows: *ish o ishah* — a man or a woman — *ki yihyeh vo nega be-rosh*, if there is a spot on the head; *o ve-zakan*, or — in the case of a man — on the beard. Under this reading, the reference to *zakan* reverts to *ish* only, and *isha* is mentioned only in connection with the head, not the beard. The *braita* comes to teach that this reading is incorrect: a woman's beard, if she has one, has the full status of a beard for purposes of *tzara'at* impurity — *harei hen ke-zakan le-chol divreihem* means for this purpose. The *braita* thus does not conflict with the *mishnah*'s ruling that women are exempt from *bal tashchit*; it addresses an entirely separate question regarding *nega'im*.

---

## Bal Yikrechu

### Isi's Teaching

The *Gemara* now presents a teaching of Isi: *af bal yikrechu nashim pturot* — women are also exempt from the prohibition of *bal yikrechu korcha* — making a bald spot on the head as a sign of mourning (*lo tasimu korcha bein eineichem la-met*). This is a separate prohibition from the beard shaving, derived from a separate verse, and Isi teaches that it too does not apply to women.

### Banim Atem

The exegetical basis is the verse in Devarim: *banim atem la-Hashem Elokeichem, lo titgodedu ve-lo tasimu korcha bein eineichem la-met* — "you are children of the Lord your God; do not cut yourselves and do not make a bald spot between your eyes for the dead." Isi reads *banim* — sons — as limiting: *banim ve-lo banot le-korcha*. Sons, not daughters, are the subject of the *korcha* prohibition. This is a deliberate narrowing of the prohibition to men, derived from the masculine noun *banim*.

### Korcha vs Gedida

However, the *Gemara* immediately asks whether this limitation also applies to *gedida* — lacerations in the flesh, which is also mentioned in the same verse (*lo titgodedu*). Perhaps *banim ve-lo banot* limits women's exemption to that prohibition as well?

The *Gemara* answers no, because of the continuation of the verse: *ki am kadosh atah la-Hashem Elokecha* — "for you are a holy people to the Lord your God." This phrase, *am kadosh*, encompasses everyone — *am* is the entire people, men and women alike — and it provides the basis for the prohibition of *gedida*. Therefore, the prohibition of lacerations in the flesh applies to women equally.

The question then becomes: why do we include women in *gedida* from *am kadosh* but exclude them from *korcha* based on *banim*? The answer is the scope of each prohibition. *Gedida* — lacerations in the flesh — applies to any part of the body, whether in an area of hair or not (*she-yeshnah be-makom se'ar u-velo be-makom se'ar*). It is a broader prohibition. *Korcha* — a bald spot — applies only in an area of hair (*she-einah ela be-makom se'ar*). It is a more limited prohibition. Therefore, from *banim ve-lo banot* we exclude women from the narrower prohibition, and from *ki am kadosh* we include women in the broader one.

We will continue on *Shabbat* with the full analysis of Isi's position.

---

---

# Kiddushin 36

## Korcha & Women

### Issi's View

The *gemara* picks up at the very bottom of 35b, continuing the discussion of the scope of *mitzvot* as they apply to women and men. The established principle is that all negative prohibitions apply equally to both, with the exception of the shaving and cutting of the forelocks, the shaving of the beard, and the *mitzvah* of *tuma* for *Kohanim*. We are now also dealing with the position of *Issi*, who holds that the prohibition of making a bald spot on one's head — *korcha* — likewise does not apply to women.

### Banim v'lo Banot

The *gemara* raises an initial challenge to *Issi*'s position. The verse introducing the prohibition of *korcha* opens with the phrase *banim atem la-Shem Elokeichem* — "you are children of the Lord your God" — immediately before prohibiting the making of a bald spot or a laceration. *Issi* reads *banim* and not *banot* as excluding women from *korcha*. But the *gemara* asks: *ve'eima banim ve-lo banot bein le'korcha bein le'gedida* — why not say that the exclusion of women applies equally to both the bald spot and the laceration? After all, both appear in close proximity to the same phrase.

The *gemara* answers: *ve'hachi ksiv Am Kadosh atah la-Shem Elokecha bis'rita hu d'chsiv* — the end of the verse, from which *Issi* derives the inclusion of women in the prohibition of laceration, speaks specifically of *s'rita*. *Rashi* explains that *s'rita* refers to a laceration made with the hand rather than with an implement such as a knife, as distinct from *gedida*. One might then ask: since *s'rita* and *gedida* appear in different verses, perhaps women should be excluded from both based on *banim* and not *banot*? The *gemara* replies: *ksavar Issi s'rita u-gedida achas hi* — *Issi* holds that *s'rita* and *gedida* are in substance the same prohibition. Therefore the verse employing the phrase *Am Kadosh* comes to include women in that single prohibition of laceration, and women are correspondingly excluded only from *korcha*.

### Abaye's Gezeira

At the top of 36a, the *gemara* presents *Abaye*'s derivation of *Issi*'s position: *Abaye amar hainu ta'ama d'Issi, de-gamar korcha korcha mi-Bnei Aharon* — he learns it through a *gezeira shava* of *korcha-korcha* from the passage dealing with *Bnei Aharon*. The Torah states separately, regarding the *Kohanim*: *lo yikrechu korcha be-rosham u-fe'at zekanam lo yegalechu* — they shall not make a bald spot on their head nor shall they shave the corners of their beards. This parallel prohibition is linked by the shared term *korcha* to the prohibition incumbent upon all of Israel.

Because the verse concerning *Bnei Aharon* says *banim* — sons — this naturally implies the exclusion of daughters. *Abaye* argues: *mi-Bnei Aharon mah le-halan nashim peturot af kan nashim peturot* — just as the prohibition for *Kohanim* is limited to the males and not the females, so too the parallel prohibition for all Israel is limited to men and not women.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: if *Issi* is already relying on the formulation *Bnei Aharon ve-lo bnot Aharon*, he has no need for a *gezeira shava* at all. Once we know that female *Kohanim* are exempt from *korcha*, we could simply apply a *kal va-chomer*: if women are excluded even among *Kohanim* — who bear additional *mitzvot* — then certainly women among ordinary Israelites should be excluded. *Mah Kohanim she-ribba bahem ha-katuv mitzvot yetirot Bnei Aharon ve-lo bnot Aharon, Yisrael lo kol she-ken* — all the more so for non-*Kohanim*.

The *gemara* responds: *ilmalei gezeira shava hava amina hifsik ha-inyan* — had there been no *gezeira shava*, one might have thought that the language *Bnei Aharon* does not apply to *korcha* in that passage because there is a textual interruption between the introduction of *Bnei Aharon* and the eventual verse prohibiting the bald spot. The *gezeira shava*, by linking the two passages, tells us there is something to be learned from the connection, and what is learned is the limitation: *banim* and not *banot*. Without the *gezeira shava*, the interruption in the text would have prevented that inference.

The *gemara* then pushes further: but now that there is a *gezeira shava*, let us say the interruption nonetheless applies, and do not derive the exclusion of women from it. The *gezeira shava* must simply be telling us something else — namely, what we learn in the *baraita*. The question is therefore: what is the *gezeira shava* of *korcha-korcha* actually accomplishing?

### Gezeira Details

The *gemara* explains the full content of the *gezeira shava* as presented in the *baraita*. The verse by *Kohanim* reads *lo yikrechu korcha be-rosham* — they shall not make a bald spot on their head. One might have thought that making multiple bald spots constitutes only a single prohibition. *Talmud lomar korcha* — the singular form *korcha* teaches that one is liable for each individual bald spot, *le-chayev al kol achat ve-achat*.

Why then does the verse add the word *be-rosham*, "on their head"? Because the verse for Israel reads *lo titgodedu ve-lo tasimu korcha bein eineichem la-met* — do not make a laceration and do not place a bald spot between your eyes for the dead. One might have thought that the prohibition of *korcha* is limited specifically to the area between the eyes. *Talmud lomar be-rosham* — "on their head" teaches that the prohibition extends across the entire head, *le-chayev al kol ha-rosh ke-vein einav*.

These two details — liability for each separate bald spot, and application to the whole head — might have been thought to apply only to *Kohanim*, who bear additional *mitzvot*. So how do we know they apply to Israel as well? *Ne'emar kan korcha ve-ne'emar le-halan korcha* — the same term appears in both contexts, and through the *gezeira shava* we derive that just as by *Kohanim* one is liable for each bald spot and across the entire head, so too by Israel. And in the reverse direction, just as by Israel the prohibition is specifically in the context of mourning a dead person, *al ha-met*, so too by *Kohanim* the prohibition is limited to the context of mourning a dead person.

This *gezeira shava* of *korcha-korcha* is thus carrying a great deal of substantive content. The *gemara* therefore argues that it is already fully occupied with these teachings, and one cannot assume it is additionally teaching the exclusion of women. The question becomes: how does *Abaye* then derive the exclusion of women from the *gezeira shava*?

### Double Karcha

The *gemara* resolves this in favor of *Abaye*: *im ken nichtov kra kerach* — if the Torah merely wanted to convey those teachings, it could have written *kerach* rather than *korcha*. The fact that both the verse for *Kohanim* and the verse for Israel use the form *korcha* — with the additional *heh* — signals that there is yet another *gezeira shava* embedded in the text, a secondary derivation. And that secondary *gezeira shava* is what teaches us the limitation of *banim* and not *banot*: the exclusion of women from the prohibition of *korcha* as derived from *Bnei Aharon ve-lo bnot Aharon*. This is *Issi*'s reason, as reconstructed by *Abaye*.

### Rava's Tefillin

*Rava* offers an entirely different derivation of *Issi*'s position: *de-yalif bein eineichem mi-tefillin* — he derives the exemption of women from *korcha* through an analogy to *tefillin*. The verse for Israel says *lo tasimu korcha bein eineichem la-met* — do not place a bald spot between your eyes. The same phrase *bein eineichem* also appears in the context of *tefillin*. Since women are exempt from *tefillin*, we derive by analogy — *mah le-halan nashim peturot af kan nashim peturot* — that women are also exempt from the prohibition of *korcha*.

### Abaye v. Rava

The *gemara* then inquires into each *amora*'s reasons for rejecting the other's approach. *Rava mai ta'ama lo amar ke-Abaye* — why did *Rava* not accept *Abaye*'s derivation? *Kerach karcha lo mashma lei* — he does not accept that the difference in spelling between *kerach* and *korcha* generates a second *gezeira shava*. He remains troubled by the distance in the text between the introduction of *Bnei Aharon* and the eventual discussion of *korcha*, and therefore finds *Abaye*'s approach unconvincing.

Conversely, *v'Abaye mai ta'ama lo amar ke-Rava* — why did *Abaye* not accept *Rava*'s derivation from *tefillin*? *Tefillin gufayhu mei-hacha gamir lah* — because the very rule that *tefillin* are placed on the upper part of the head, corresponding to where hair grows above the forehead and opposite the space between the eyes, is itself learned from the passage about *korcha*. The *gezeira shava* of *bein eineichem* was originally employed to teach something about *tefillin*: *mah le-halan makom she-osim korcha be-govah shel rosh, af kan makom hanacha be-govah ha-rosh* — just as the bald spot between the eyes is understood to refer to the top of the head where hair grows, so too the placement of *tefillin* is on the top of the head. The *rishonim* raise the question of whether one *gezeira shava* can simultaneously teach two separate laws, and the conclusion is that once a *gezeira shava* is focused on clarifying the meaning of a word — in this case, what *bein einav* means — it cannot simultaneously pivot to teach an entirely separate *halacha* such as the exemption of women.

The *gemara* then asks: since both *Abaye* and *Rava* derive the exclusion of women from *korcha* through means other than the opening phrase *banim atem la-Shem Elokeichem*, what do they do with that phrase? The answer is that *Abaye* and *Rava* both require that phrase for an altogether different teaching, as presented in the *baraita* that follows.

## Banim Atem

### Children Status

The *gemara* transitions to a broader discussion of the phrase *banim atem la-Shem Elokeichem*. According to *Abaye* and *Rava*, this phrase cannot be used to derive the exclusion of women from *korcha* since they each have alternative derivations for that. The phrase is instead required for the teaching of the *baraita*: *banim atem la-Shem Elokeichem, bi-zman she-atem nohagim minhag banim atem keruim banim* — when you conduct yourselves as children, you are called children of God.

### R. Yehuda

This is the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*: *ein atem nohagim minhag banim ein atem keruim banim, divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — when you do not conduct yourselves as children, you are not called children. The implication is that the title is conditional on appropriate behavior, and that engaging in idolatrous practices such as the very rituals of laceration and bald spots — which the *Torah* is here prohibiting — would forfeit the relationship.

### R. Meir

*Rabbi Meir* takes a strikingly more compassionate view: *bein kach u-vein kach atem keruim banim* — either way, you are called children of God. This reading seems especially fitting for a period of reflection and repentance, as *Rabbi Meir* insists that the parent-child relationship between God and Israel is never truly severed.

### Scriptural Proofs

The *gemara* presents multiple scriptural proofs in support of *Rabbi Meir*'s position. The verse *banim sechalim hem* — "they are foolish children" — demonstrates that even foolish children retain the designation of children. The verse *banim lo emun bam* — "children without trustworthiness" — shows that even when Israel acts without faithfulness they are still called children. The verse *zera me-re'im banim mash'chitim* — "an evil seed, children who deal corruptly" — shows that even when Israel engages in corruption, which the *gemara* reads as *avoda zara* in line with the usage of *shichet amcha*, they are still called children. And finally, *v'haya bi-mkom asher ye'amer lahem lo ami atem ye'amer lahem bnei Kel chai* — "in the place where it is said to them 'you are not my nation,' it will be said to them 'you are the children of the living God'" — showing that ultimately, even when the most severe divine rejection seems to apply, Israel will still be recognized as God's children, and indeed as children without any negative qualifier, fully restored to their ideal relationship.

## Korban Service

### Mishna Overview

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishnah* dealing with acts associated with *korbanot* from which women are excluded. The *mishnah* enumerates: *ha-smichot ve-ha-tnufot ve-ha-hagashot* — placing the hand on the offering, waving it, and bringing it to the altar — along with *kmitzot*, *haktarot*, *melikot*, *kabalot*, and *hazayot* — taking the handful, burning it, slaughtering the bird with the fingernail, receiving the blood, and sprinkling the blood. All of these, the *mishnah* states, *nohagim ba-anashim ve-lo ba-nashim* — apply to men and not to women. The first two items — *smicha* and *tnufa* — pertain to the owner of the *korban*, while the remaining acts are those performed by the *Kohanim*, from whom female descendants of *Kohanim* are similarly excluded.

### Smicha

The *gemara* derives the exclusion of women from *smicha* from the verse *Daber el Bnei Yisrael ve-samach* — speak to the children of Israel, and he shall place his hand. *Bnei Yisrael somchim ve-ein bnot Yisrael somchot* — only the sons of Israel, not the daughters. The *gemara* notes that *Tosafot* raises the broader question of whether women may nonetheless perform *smicha* on a voluntary basis — a significant debate with implications extending beyond this particular act to the general question of women's participation in *mitzvot* from which they are technically exempt. *Ramban* similarly raises the question of whether every instance of the phrase *Bnei Yisrael* in the Torah is meant to exclude women, noting that the phrase appears in many contexts — but for its purposes, *Chazal* understand it as limiting this act to men.

### Tnufa

For *tnufa*, the waving of the *korban*, the verse reads *Daber el Bnei Yisrael ve-henif* — and they shall wave. The derivation is parallel: *Bnei Yisrael menifim ve-ein bnot Yisrael menifot* — only the sons of Israel wave, not the daughters.

### Hagasha & Kmitza

For *hagasha* — the bringing of the *mincha* to the corner of the altar — the verse reads *Ve-zot torat ha-mincha, hakrev otah bnei Aharon* — this is the law of the *mincha*, the sons of Aaron shall bring it. *Bnei Aharon ve-lo bnot Aharon* — the sons and not the daughters. For *kmitza* — the taking of the handful — the verse reads *ve-heviah el bnei Aharon ve-kamatz* — and he shall bring it to the sons of Aaron and they shall take the *kmitza*. Again, *bnei Aharon ve-lo bnot Aharon*.

### Haktara & Melika

For *haktara* — burning the offering on the altar — the verse reads *ve-hiktiru oto bnei Aharon* — the sons of Aaron shall burn it. For *melika* — the slaughtering of the bird with the fingernail — the verse reads *u-malak ve-hiktir* — he shall cut it and burn it on the altar. The *gemara* notes that *melika* is juxtaposed to *haktara* — *ve-hukash melika le-haktara* — and since *haktara* requires *bnei Aharon* and not *bnot Aharon*, so too *melika* is limited to male *Kohanim*.

### Hazayot

For *hazayot* — sprinkling — the *gemara* is careful to identify which act of sprinkling is meant. If it refers to the sprinkling of the ashes of the *Para Aduma*, the verse explicitly specifies *Elazar*, a named individual, and even though we rule that a *Kohen Gadol* is not strictly required for this act, the explicit naming of a *Kohen Gadol* makes the exclusion of women obvious. Similarly, if it refers to the inner sprinklings on the *Mizbe'ach ha-zahav* — the golden altar — the verse speaks of *ha-Kohen ha-Mashiach*, the anointed *Kohen*, i.e., the *Kohen Gadol*, which again makes the exclusion self-evident. The *mishnah* must therefore be referring to something less obvious: the sprinkling of the blood of a bird offering, where the *Torah* uses the language of *hazayah* rather than *zerikah* because the quantity of blood is too small for the standard act of throwing.

This case is derived through a *kal va-chomer* from an ordinary animal offering. *U-mah ben tzon she-lo kava lo Kohen li-shechitato* — for a sheep or cattle, the slaughter itself does not require a *Kohen* and can be performed even by a woman, yet *kava lo Kohen le-hazayato* — the throwing of the blood still requires a *Kohen*, explicitly derived from *bnei Aharon ve-lo bnot Aharon*. *Ben of she-kava lo Kohen le-melichato* — a bird offering, where even the slaughter requires a *Kohen* to perform it personally, *eino din she-kava lo Kohen le-hazzatah* — it is certainly a logical inference that the sprinkling of its blood likewise requires a *Kohen*, and therefore also excludes women.

## Sota & Nezirah

### Rav Elazar Question

The *mishnah* concludes with the exceptions: *chutz mi-minchat Sotah ve-nezirah she-hen menifot* — excluding the *mincha* of the *Sotah* and the *nezirah*, which they wave themselves. *Rav Elazar* said to *Rabbi Yoshiya* of his generation: do not sit down until you explain to me this *shemata*. *Minayin li-minchat Sotah she-te'unah tenufah* — from where do we derive that the *mincha* of the *Sotah* requires waving, and moreover that the *Sotah* herself waves it?

### Sota Yad-Yad

*Rabbi Yoshiya* responds: *be-gufeih ketiv ve-henif et ha-mincha* — it is written explicitly in the passage of the *Sotah* that the *mincha* is waved. But *Rav Elazar* clarifies his question: he already knows the *Kohen* waves it. What he wants to know is *tenufah bi-ve'alim me-nayin* — from where do we know that the owner herself, the woman, waves it? The answer: *atya yad yad mi-shelamim* — this is derived through a *gezeira shava* of *yad-yad* from *shelamim*. In the passage of the *Sotah*, the verse reads *ve-lakach ha-Kohen mi-yad ha-ishah* — the *Kohen* shall take from the hand of the woman, and then he waves it. By *shelamim*, the verse reads *yadav tevinah* — his hands shall bring it, which means the owner waves it.

### Sota Shelamim

From this *gezeira shava*, both passages illuminate each other in a mutual derivation. By the *Sotah*, it is explicit that the *Kohen* waves it — he takes it from her hand and waves it. This teaches us that by *shelamim* as well, not only does the owner wave it, but the *Kohen* also waves it alongside the owner. In the reverse direction, by *shelamim* it is explicit that the owner waves it — *yadav tevinah*. This teaches us that by the *Sotah* as well, the owner, that is, the woman herself, waves it — *mah le-halan be'alim af kan be'alim*.

### Holding Together

The *gemara* then asks *ha keitzad* — how exactly is this accomplished in practice, given that there is one physical item being waved? *Kohen meniach yado tachat yad be'alim u-menif* — the *Kohen* places his hand beneath the hands of the owner and they wave together. *Tosafot* raises the question of how precisely this is understood: does "beneath" mean the hands are in direct contact with one another, in which case there is no concern about *negiah* but there might be a concern about whether the *Kohen*'s hand constitutes a *hefsek* — an interposition — between the owner's hand and the vessel? Or does "beneath" mean that the owner holds the vessel near its rim while the *Kohen* holds it near its base? *Tosafot* presents both possibilities.

### Nezirah Kaf-Kaf

Having established the *Sotah*'s obligation and the manner in which it is fulfilled, the *gemara* notes: *ash'kechan Sotah — nezirah me-nayin* — we have found a source for the *Sotah*, but from where do we derive the same for a *nezirah*? The answer: *atya kaf kaf mi-Sotah* — through a *gezeira shava* of *kaf-kaf*, the hand, linking the passage of the *nezirah* to that of the *Sotah*. Just as by the *Sotah* both the *Kohen* and the owner wave it together, so too by the *nezirah* both the *Kohen* and the owner wave it together, and the *nezirah* herself participates in the waving of her own offering.

---

---

# Kiddushin 37

## Intro & Mitzvot Categori…

### Perek Theme

The *daf* before us is 37, and we pick up with a *mishna* appearing at the bottom of 36b. The broader theme of this *perek* is the construction of categories: first, the categorization of the various modes of acquisition (*kinyanim*), and now a categorization of *mitzvot* according to who and where they obligate. The *perek* calls to mind the *ain bein* passages in *Megilla*, which sweep across a wide scope of material. There may also be a linguistic thread — the *kol* construction, as in *kol mitzvas haben al ha'av* — but the dominant organizing principle seems to be simply the *perek*'s ambition to sort broad classes of things into coherent categories. It is, notably, the longest *perek* in *Shas*.

### Gender to Geography

Having covered the division of *mitzvot* between men and women, the *mishna* now transitions to a second axis of categorization: which *mitzvot* are geographically restricted to *Eretz Yisrael*, and which apply wherever one happens to be.

---

## Mitzvot Teluyot Ba'aretz

### Mishna Text

The *mishna* states: *kol mitzva she'hi teluya ba'aretz eina noheget ela ba'aretz* — any *mitzva* that is dependent on the land applies only in the land of Israel. *Ve'she'eina teluya ba'aretz noheget bein ba'aretz uvein bechutz la'aretz* — and what is not dependent on the land applies whether inside or outside of the land of Israel.

### Orlah & Kilayim

The *mishna* immediately carves out two exceptions: *chutz min ha'orlah vehakilayim* — *orlah* and *kilayim* apply even outside the land, despite being land-based *mitzvot*. *Orlah* refers to the prohibition on fruit during the first three years of a tree's planting; *kilayim* refers to the prohibition on crossbreeding seeds.

What is striking here is the relative legal weight of these two exceptions. *Orlah* outside *Eretz Yisrael* is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, while *kilayim* outside *Eretz Yisrael* is only *derabbanan*. Intuitively, one might have expected *kilayim* to carry the heavier extra-territorial force, since the prohibition on mixing species is not obviously tethered to the sanctity of the land — it parallels other forms of *kilayim* such as crossbreeding animals or mixing wool and linen. *Orlah*, by contrast, is closely linked in the *Torah* to *neta reva'i*, the fourth-year fruits brought to the *Beit Hamikdash*, and would seem on its face to belong to the category of *kedushat ha'aretz*. Yet the *halacha* inverts one's expectations: *orlah* outside the land carries the weight of *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, while *kilayim* is merely *derabbanan*.

The further implication of the *mishna's* phrasing is important. By explicitly listing *orlah* and *kilayim* — one of which is only *derabbanan* — as the exceptions that apply in *chutz la'aretz*, the *mishna* implies that everything else does not apply outside the land even at the *derabbanan* level. This is a significant point that will bear on later discussion.

### R. Eliezer on Chadash

*Rabbi Eliezer* adds: *af chadash* — even *chadash*, the prohibition on new grain before the *omer* is brought on the sixteenth of *Nissan*, applies outside the land of Israel. This position sets up the central dispute of the *sugya*.

---

## Teluyah Definition

### Peshat Proposal

The *gemara* opens by asking: *mai teluya u'mai she'eina teluya* — what does it mean for a *mitzva* to be "dependent" on the land, and what does it mean to be "not dependent"? The initial proposal is that *teluya* means that the relevant verse explicitly conditions the *mitzva* on entering the land — *kol mitzva sheketiv bah bi'ah* — while a *mitzva* that does not say "when you come into the land" is not so restricted.

### Tefillin Objection

The *gemara* immediately challenges this reading: *va'harei tefillin u'peter chamor dekesiv bahen bi'ah* — both *tefillin* and *peter chamor* (the redemption of the firstborn donkey) are explicitly conditioned in the verse on entering the land, yet both apply equally inside and outside of *Eretz Yisrael*. The verse in *Shemos* 13 — *vehayah ki yeviacha Hashem el eretz hakenani* — introduces both the *mitzva* of the firstborn and, ultimately, *tefillin*, within the frame of the entry into the land. If the proposed criterion were correct, these *mitzvot* should not apply in *chutz la'aretz* — or at the very least, one might argue they apply only *derabbanan* outside the land. But the *mishna* forecloses even that escape: since *kilayim* is only *derabbanan* outside the land and yet is listed explicitly as an exception, the implication is that everything not listed does not apply even *derabbanan*. We know from the *gemara* itself that the Sages of *Bavel* wore *tefillin*, so *tefillin* plainly applies in *chutz la'aretz* at the full *d'oraita* level.

### Rashi's Answer

There is a famous *Rashi* on the *Torah* — picked up by the *Ramban* — which is relevant here. On the *pasuk* in the second *parasha* of *Shema* — *vesamtem es devarai eileh al levavchem ve'al nafshechem* — *Rashi* explains: *af acharei shetiglu heyu metzuyanim bemitzvot* — even after you go into exile, distinguish yourselves with *mitzvot*: put on *tefillin*, affix *mezuzot* — *kedei shelo yihyu lachem chadashim keshetachzoru* — so that these practices will not seem foreign to you when you return. *Rashi* then cites the verse *hatzivi lach tziyunim*.

The *Ramban* is struck by this: can one really say that *tefillin* and *mezuzot* are merely "practice" for the real performance back in the land? For the *Ramban*, this *Rashi* opens onto his broader theological position that even *mitzvot* that are *chovat haguf* — personal obligations — find their true and ideal fulfillment in *Eretz Yisrael*. The *Torah* does not envision Judaism as an abstract religion that happens to include, as an adjunct, a homeland; the *Torah* of *Devarim* imagines a nation living as a people in their land. *Galus* is called exile for a reason — it is not the natural condition. So even though it is true that *mitzvot ha-teluyot ba-guf* apply in *chutz la'aretz*, that is not the ideal mode of their performance.

Some have been so unsettled by *Rashi's* formulation — that *tefillin* and *mezuzot* are essentially preparatory exercises for return — that they have proposed emending the text of *Rashi* to read *terumos u'maasros* instead of *tefillin u'mezuzot*. But that emendation is not authentic; *Rashi* is drawing on the plain sense of the *pesukim*, which speak about going into exile and then say *vesamtem es devarai eileh...uktavtem al mezuzos beiseicha* — with *tefillin* and *mezuzah* explicitly in view, followed by *lema'an yirbu yemeichem al ha'adamah*.

What makes this *gemara* striking is that it presents as a mere *havah amina* what *Rashi* treats as the *peshat* of the *pesukim* — that *tefillin* might be restricted to *Eretz Yisrael*. The *gemara* ultimately rejects that reading, but the underlying intuition that all *mitzvot* find their home in *Eretz Yisrael* is very much present.

---

## Chovat Haguf & Karka

### Rav Yehuda's Principle

*Rav Yehuda* resolves the question by reframing it entirely. The distinction, he says, is not about how the verse is phrased, but about the nature of the *mitzva* itself. *Kol mitzvah she'hi chovat haguf noheget bein ba'aretz bein bechutz la'aretz* — any *mitzva* that is a personal obligation applies everywhere. *Chovat karka* — a land-related obligation — applies only in *Eretz Yisrael*, with the exceptions of *orlah* and *kilayim*. One need not search the *pesukim* for contextual cues; one simply looks at the reality of what the *mitzva* demands. Does it engage you as a person? Then it applies everywhere. Does it engage the earth and its produce? Then it is restricted to the land of Israel.

### Midrash Source

The *gemara* asks *minah hani milei* — what is the source? The *tanna'im* teach: *eileh hachukim vehamishpatim asher tishmerun la'asot ba'aretz* — these are the laws you shall observe to perform in the land. The *midrash* unpacks this: *eileh hamidrashot* — these are the *midrash*-derived teachings; *vehamishpatim eileh hadinim* — these are the civil laws; *asher tishmerun* — that you shall guard — *zo mishnah*, that refers to the learning and transmission of the laws; *va'asot* — to perform — *zu ma'aseh*, that is the actual practice. Then *ba'aretz* — in the land.

One might think from this that all *mitzvot* apply only in the land — *yakhol kol hamitzvot kulan lo yehu nohagot ela ba'aretz*. The *gemara* therefore brings the continuation of the verse: *kol hayamim asher atem chayim al ha'adamah* — all the days that you live on the land. There is a certain irony in the interpretive move here: the phrase *al ha'adamah* ties the text to the land, yet *Chazal* read *kol hayamim* — all times — to indicate that the obligation is universal. After the text has spoken broadly and narrowly, one must determine what falls into each category.

### Avodah Zarah Paradigm

The operative teaching that follows is: *tzei u'lemad* — go and look at the opening subject of that passage, which is *abed tave'dun et kol hamekomot asher avdu sham hagoyim et eloheihem* — you shall destroy all the places where the nations worshipped their idols. *Mah avodat kokhavim meyuchedet she'hi chovat haguf* — just as destroying *avodah zarah* is a personal obligation that *noheget bein ba'aretz bein bechutz la'aretz* — applies in all places — so too everything that is a *chovat haguf* applies everywhere.

The choice of *avodah zarah* as the paradigm is itself ironic on multiple levels. First, the very phrase *kol hayamim asher atem chayim al ha'adamah* that anchors the teaching in the land is immediately followed by a *mitzva* that is at once personal and, in its fullest expression, fundamentally territorial. The obligation to destroy *avodah zarah* in *Eretz Yisrael* is heightened — *chayav attah lishrosh achareiha*, one must uproot it completely, pursuing it even beneath the surface. The *pesukim* speak clearly about clearing the land so that it becomes one's own national home. The intuition that if one is in India and encounters an idol one is obligated to smash it does not emerge naturally from reading those *pesukim* in context.

Second, read *Masechet Avodah Zarah* in its entirety, and one would never arrive at the conclusion that there is a positive *mitzva* to destroy *avodah zarah* — because the historical realities of Jewish life under Roman rule required the wholesale practical suspension of that obligation. Scholars and academics have commented extensively on this. And yet the *gemara* here uses *avodah zarah* destruction as the quintessential model of a *chovat haguf* that applies everywhere. The double irony — of a text anchored in *al ha'adamah* teaching universal personal obligation, instantiated through a *mitzva* whose real scope is territorial and whose practical observance was historically bracketed — is difficult to miss.

---

## Chadash Dispute

### Tanna Kamma Position

The *tanna kamma* holds that *chadash* applies only in *Eretz Yisrael*. To understand this position, one must look at the relevant *pasuk*: *lechem vekali vekarmel lo tochlu ad etzem hayom hazeh...chukat olam ledoroteichem bechol moshvoteichem* — you shall not eat bread or parched grain or fresh grain until that very day...it is an eternal statute for your generations in all your dwellings. The phrase *bechol moshvoteichem* — in all your dwellings — might seem to extend the prohibition everywhere. The *tanna kamma* reads it otherwise: *moshav le'achar yerusha veyeshiva mashma* — *moshav* means after you have already inherited and settled the land. Thus *bechol moshvoteichem* means once you are settled in the land, not wherever you happen to dwell. On this reading, the prohibition was not even operative during the first fourteen years after entry — the years of conquest and division — because the land was not yet *moshav*, not yet truly settled.

What makes this practically significant is the agricultural reality of *chutz la'aretz*. In *Eretz Yisrael* there is essentially one wheat season, and the harvest comes naturally around the time the *omer* is brought; one would have to make a special effort to create a problem of *chadash*. But in the diaspora — in France, Germany, and elsewhere — grain was planted in spring, took root after the *omer*, and came to market around *Rosh Hashana*. For those who hold that *chadash* applies in *chutz la'aretz*, that grain would be forbidden for the following six months, until the next *omer*. This creates an acute practical challenge that the *rishonim* had to confront head-on.

### R. Eliezer Position

*Rabbi Eliezer* reads *bechol moshvoteichem* in its plain sense: *bechol makom she'atem yoshvim* — wherever you dwell. On this reading, *chadash* applies outside *Eretz Yisrael* just as it does within it. The *gemara* establishes that *Rabbi Eliezer* is being *machmir* — his position is the stricter one — and that the *tanna kamma* is the more lenient position, restricting *chadash* to the land.

---

## Chadash Dispute (II)

### Nesachim & Central Altar

*Abaye* identifies the *tanna kamma* as *Rabbi Yishmael*, and frames the entire dispute around a broader hermeneutical principle. *Rabbi Yishmael* holds that whenever a verse combines both the language of *bi'ah* — entering the land — and *moshav* — dwelling — the combination restricts the obligation to *le'achar yerusha veyeshiva*, after the land has been inherited and settled. He derives this principle from the laws of *nesachim* — the wine, flour, and oil libations that accompany sacrifices. The relevant *pasuk* in *Shelach Lecha* reads *ki tavo'u el eretz moshvoteichem va'asitem isha l'Hashem* — when you come to the land of your dwellings and bring a fire-offering to God. *Rabbi Yishmael* holds that individuals did not bring *nesachim* on a *bamat yachid* in the *midbar*; only the communal *bamah gedolah* had *nesachim*. Since the verse says *lachem* — in the plural, indicating communal offering at the *bamah gedolah* — and that was already operative in the *midbar*, the *chiddush* of the *pasuk* must be that individual *nesachim* will now be brought — but only once the land is settled. Given this, *moshvoteichem* cannot mean "wherever you dwell" in the sense of individual locations throughout the land; it must mean "after your settlement is complete." And this principle, says *Rabbi Yishmael*, generalizes: wherever the *Torah* combines *bi'ah* and *moshav*, it means only after the first fourteen years of conquest and settlement.

---

## R. Yishmael vs. Akiva

### R. Yishmael's Rule

*Rabbi Yishmael's* general hermeneutical principle is thus: *kol makom shene'emar bo moshav eino ela le'achar yerusha veyeshiva* — wherever the *Torah* uses the language of dwelling in combination with entering the land, it means only after the land has been inherited and settled. When the *pasuk* on *chadash* says both *ki tavo'u* — when you come — and *bechol moshvoteichem*, the combination limits the prohibition to *Eretz Yisrael* after settlement, not to wherever Jews may dwell.

### Shabbat Objection

*Rabbi Akiva* objects: *harei Shabbat shene'emar bah moshvot* — but *Shabbat* also uses the language of *moshvot*, and *Shabbat* applies everywhere, both inside and outside *Eretz Yisrael*. The *pasuk* reads *Shabbat hi l'Hashem bechol moshvoteichem* — it is a *Shabbat* to God in all your dwellings. Clearly, *moshvoteichem* there means wherever you dwell, not only in the land after settlement.

### Response on Shabbat

*Rabbi Yishmael* responds on two levels. First: *ana bi'ah u'moshav ka'amina* — my principle applies only when the verse contains both the language of entering and the language of dwelling. *Shabbat* mentions only *moshvot*, without *bi'ah*, and therefore does not fall under my rule. Second — and in any case — *Shabbat kal vachomer hi*: even if one were to argue from the word *moshvot* alone, we know *Shabbat* applies in *chutz la'aretz* from a *kal vachomer*: if *mitzvot* that are lighter apply outside the land, how much more so the weightier *mitzva* of *Shabbat*.

The *gemara* notes that *Rabbi Yishmael's* response is actually a compound reply — *chada ve'od ka'amar lei* — he is saying one thing and additionally another: first, that *Shabbat* is categorically irrelevant to his rule because it lacks the *bi'ah* language; second, that even if it were relevant, the *kal vachomer* would resolve it independently.

---

## Chadash Halakha Today

### Mishna Conflict

The question of how to rule practically on *chadash* outside *Eretz Yisrael* is complicated by a conflict between the *mishna* in our *masechta* and a *mishna* elsewhere. The *mishna* in *Kiddushin* presents the restriction of *chadash* to the land as a dispute between *Rabbi Eliezer* and the *tanna kamma*, suggesting we might simply rule like the *tanna kamma* — and therefore like *Rabbi Yishmael* — that *chadash* does not apply in *chutz la'aretz* even *derabbanan*. That would be the most straightforward and lenient resolution.

The problem is the last *mishna* in *Orlah*, which states unambiguously: *ha-chadash asur min ha-Torah bechol makom* — new grain is forbidden by *Torah* law everywhere. No dispute, no qualification. A number of *rishonim* attempt to rule like the *tanna kamma* in *Kiddushin* on the grounds that the position of *Rabbi Eliezer* there is a *da'as yachid*. Others argue that the *stam mishna* in *Orlah* — situated in the primary discussion of these issues — must be dispositive and cannot be overridden by a *da'as yachid* in *Kiddushin*, especially given the principle of *stam ve'achar kach machlokes*.

### Tosafot on Chadash

*Tosafot*, at the bottom of 36b, does not resolve the dispute between the two *mishnayot* but states plainly: *venira de-chadash noheig bizman hazeh* — it appears that the prohibition of *chadash* applies in our times, meaning in the diaspora. He does not elaborate on whether this follows *Rabbi Eliezer* or is derived from the *mishna* in *Orlah*. Instead, he proceeds directly to practical guidance.

### Rov & Safek Sefeika

*Tosafot* writes: *ul'kach yesh lehizaher she'im adam yode'a bevadai she-se'orim nizre'u achar zman hakravas ha-omer* — one should be careful that if one knows with certainty that grain was planted after the *omer* was brought, i.e., after the sixteenth of *Nissan*, one should not eat from it. However, *u'missafek ein le'asur kol ha-se'orim* — in cases of doubt, one should not prohibit all grain, *keivan d'rov se'orim nizre'u kodem tet-zayin b'Nisan* — since the majority of grain was planted before the sixteenth of *Nissan*, and one may therefore follow the *rov*.

*Tosafot* mentions *se'orim* — barley — specifically, likely because the most pressing practical challenge involved beer, which was pervasive in the diaspora communities and from which people could not easily abstain. The *issur* of *chadash* does not apply to benefit (*hana'ah*), but one may not eat it.

There is a certain irony in the structure of this *hetter*. *Chadash* is an *issur d'oraita*, and normally a *safek* in a *d'oraita* prohibition would not suffice to permit; here it is an assertion of *rov* that carries the weight. One must ask whether that assertion is truly accurate and whether the *rov* is *mevurrar* — established — or relies on an approximation. In practice, it seems that many *rishonim* began with the reality that communities could not avoid eating the grain, and worked backward to find justification.

Beyond *rov*, some *rishonim* developed a *safek sefeika*: perhaps the grain came from last year's supply, and even if from this year, perhaps it took root before the *omer*. Though one might argue that these two doubts collapse into a single question — was it *yashan* or *chadash* — the *rishonim* maintained this framework as a further basis for leniency in combination with other factors.

Additional arguments proposed by various *rishonim* include: ruling entirely like the *tanna kamma* that *chadash* does not apply in *chutz la'aretz*; arguing that *chadash* grown by non-Jews is exempt; and the position of the *Aruch Hashulchan* that grain of a second wheat season — which could never be fit for the *omer* — should never have been subject to the *chadash* prohibition in the first place, limiting the concern to the primary wheat season only. Against the exemption for non-Jewish-owned grain, the *Yerushalmi* itself closes the door: it explains why *challah* is not listed alongside *chadash* in the *mishna* — because *challah* does not apply to grain owned by non-Jews — implying that *chadash* as listed does apply to grain owned by non-Jews.

### Modern Context

The practical landscape has changed significantly in the modern era. For centuries, communities maintained the permissive practice because there was simply no way to know with certainty the origin of grain — whether it had taken root before or after the *omer*. The arguments from *rov* and *safek sefeika* were, at least in part, post-hoc rationalizations of a practice driven by practical necessity.

Today, however, detailed information is available about grain lots and their planting schedules. It is possible to determine, based on barcodes or lot information, precisely when a given batch of grain took root and whether it qualifies as *yashan* or *chadash*. The availability of this information raises serious *halachic* questions about whether one may continue to rely on *rov* or *safek sefeika* when the facts are in principle ascertainable. The most straightforward *halachic* resolution — and the one that avoids all of these complexities — would be to rule definitively like the *tanna kamma* against *Rabbi Eliezer*, holding that *chadash* does not apply in *chutz la'aretz* even *derabbanan*. Whether the *stam mishna* in *Orlah* forecloses that option remains the underlying difficulty.

---

## Orlah & Wine

### Orlah Problem

*Tosafot* raises an equally pressing question about *orlah* in the diaspora. Since *orlah* applies in *chutz la'aretz* as a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, and since virtually all vineyards propagate new vines by attaching shoots to existing root systems — a process that, if it constitutes a new planting, would make the new growth subject to the three-year *orlah* prohibition — how has it been historically permissible to drink wine from diaspora vineyards? *Tosafot* notes that one cannot rely on *rov* here as one might in other cases, because the majority of vines are indeed propagated this way.

### Mavrich Solution

*Tosafot* cites *Rabbeinu Shimshon* — the *Rash mi-Shantz* — who investigated the matter by actually speaking with farmers and viticulturists. What he found was that the process being used was not *markiv* — true grafting, where a shoot is severed and joined to a different root — but rather *mavrich* — layering, where a shoot is bent underground and trained to emerge elsewhere, while still remaining physically attached and connected to the original vine. Crucially, *she'einam chotchim ha-zmorah min ha-sadan* — they never actually sever the shoot from the trunk. It remains drawing nourishment from the old vine throughout.

The legal implication is decisive: *im kein hu yonek od min ha-zkeinah* — since it is still drawing from the old vine, it retains the legal status of the old plant. A shoot that is not severed is not a new planting; *orlah* does not commence.

### Yerushalmi Source

The *Yerushalmi* provides the source for this distinction: *ha-mavrich bizman she-yonek min ha-zkeinah patur min ha-orlah* — when the layered shoot still draws from the old vine, it is exempt from *orlah*. Once it is severed and no longer drawing, it becomes subject to the full *orlah* counting.

### Signs of Attachment

The *Yerushalmi* also provides a physical sign by which one may determine whether the layered vine remains attached. *Keshe-ha-zmorah yoneket min ha-zkeinah harei hem notim letzad acher* — when the shoot is still drawing from the old vine, the leaves turn away from it; *u-cheshe-posek harei hem notim letzad ha-zkeinah* — once it is severed and stops drawing, the leaves turn back toward the old vine. The mnemonic offered is charming: *de-hai man de-achil me-chavrei ba'ei le-istakulei bei* — one who eats from another person's table is a little embarrassed to look directly at them. So too, the shoot that is still feeding off the old vine averts its leaves. Whether this botanical observation fully maps onto modern viticulture is another question, but that is the tradition as *Tosafot* records it.

---

## Nesachim Debate

### R. Yishmael View

The *gemara* now clarifies the foundational disagreement between *Rabbi Yishmael* and *Rabbi Akiva* that drives the *chadash* dispute. *Rabbi Yishmael savar lo keruvu nesachim ba-midbar* — *Rabbi Yishmael* holds that individuals did not bring *nesachim* on a *bamat yachid* in the *midbar*. Only the communal *bamah gedolah* received *nesachim* during the wilderness period.

### Yishmael's Consequence

Given this starting point, the *chiddush* of the *pasuk* in *Shelach Lecha* — *ki tavo'u el eretz moshvoteichem* — is that upon entering the land, individuals will for the first time bring *nesachim* on their individual *bamot*. Since the *pasuk* is introducing this novel permission or obligation, *moshvoteichem* cannot mean "wherever you are currently located," because individuals were not bringing *nesachim* anywhere; the *pasuk* must mean after you have settled and conquered the land — *le'achar yerusha veyishiva*. The verse does not broaden the geographic scope of *nesachim*; it defers their onset until after settlement is complete.

### R. Akiva View

*Rabbi Akiva savar keruvu nesachim ba-midbar* — *Rabbi Akiva* holds the opposite: individuals already brought *nesachim* on a *bamat yachid* in the *midbar*. The communal obligation was already operative in the wilderness.

### Akiva's Consequence

If *nesachim* were already being brought individually in the *midbar*, the verse *ki tavo'u el eretz moshvoteichem* cannot be introducing something new — individuals were already bringing *nesachim*. The *chiddush* must therefore be something else: you will continue to bring *nesachim* even on an individual *bamat yachid* after you enter the land. And since it is telling you that individual *bamot* remain valid in the land, *moshvoteichem* must mean *bechol makom she'atem yoshvim* — wherever you dwell. For *Rabbi Akiva*, the word *moshvoteichem* naturally carries the broader geographic meaning, and it is from this foundation that he argues against *Rabbi Yishmael's* restrictive reading — including, by extension, on the question of *chadash*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 38

## Chadash Overview

### Winter vs. Spring Wheat

Today's *daf* is 38, continuing the discussion of *mitzvot hatluyot ba'aretz* and picking up where we left off on the topic of *chadash*. By way of introduction, it is worth clarifying the practical application of *chadash* to the wheat situation in the United States. Winter wheat is planted in the fall, grows through the winter, and begins to be harvested around spring. Because it takes root over the winter — before the *omer* is brought — it never presents a *chadash* problem: by the time it is ready to come to market, the *omer* has already been brought, and the *omer* is effective from the moment the grain has taken root. The problem arises specifically with spring wheat, which is planted in the spring after the *omer* is brought, takes root after the *omer* is brought, and comes to market around *Rosh Hashanah*. That spring wheat remains *asur* until the following *pesach*, until the next *omer* is brought.

As for the practical proportion: approximately 70 to 80 percent of wheat grown in the United States is winter wheat, so the argument that the *rov* is *yashan* is correct. However, different wheat varieties have different qualities — gluten content and rising characteristics differ — and so it is not always possible to assume that a given flour is entirely from one type. Some all-purpose flours may be a blend. Pizza dough, by contrast, is almost invariably winter wheat, chosen specifically for its rising qualities, which is why pizza establishments can readily rely on *yashan*. The winter wheat is what gets one out of the *chadash* problem.

### Contradiction Issue

One might ask why no one seems to address the apparent contradiction between all these *sugyot* and the verse in *Kohelet*, which states *ein chadash* — there is nothing new. The response offered is simply: *ain chadash* — there you go.

### Mixing Chadash/Yashan

A practical question arises about mixing: if flour that is *chadash* is blended with *yashan* flour by a producer, can one rely on *bitul*? The answer is that one cannot simply rely on *bitul* here, because *chadash* is a *davar sheyesh lo matirin* — something that will eventually become permitted on its own, namely after the next *omer* is brought. A *ta'arovet* of *chadash* with *yashan* therefore does not permit the mixture. One might try to argue along the lines of *kol deparish meruba parish* — treating whatever comes to hand as presumptively from the majority — but the matter is complicated.

---

## Rabbi Yishmael & Binyan…

### Tanna Contradiction

The *Gemara* picks up on 37b. By *chadash* the *pasuk* states: *lechem vekali vekarmel lo tochlu ad etzem hayom hazeh ad havi'achem es korban elokeichem, chukas olam ledoroseichem bechol moshavoseichem* — bread, parched grain, and fresh ears you shall not eat until this very day, until you bring the offering of your God, an eternal statute throughout your generations in all your dwelling places. The question is what *bechol moshavoseichem* means. Does it mean wherever you dwell — even in *chutz la'aretz* — as Rabbi Eliezer holds? Or does it mean after you have settled the land, as Rabbi Yishmael holds regarding *nesachim*, linking *moshavoseichem* to the concept of having taken possession and settled?

*Abaye* notes that a *tanna* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael contradicts another *tanna* from that same school. The teaching he introduces runs as follows: *ho'il vene'emru biyot batorah stam* — since the *Torah* frequently speaks of *ki savo el ha'aretz* without further specification — *ufaret lecha hakatuv be'achat mehen le'achar yerusha veyeshiva* — and in one place it specifies that the obligation applies only after taking possession and settling — *af kol le'achar yerusha veyeshiva* — we derive that all instances of *ki savo*, even without the added phrase *veyarashta veyashavta*, mean after you have settled the land. In other words, in one place the *Torah* explicitly links entry to settlement, and that serves as a paradigm for every other usage of *ki savo* throughout the *Torah*.

### Binyan Av Hermeneutic

The hermeneutical mechanism here is *binyan av*: one clear case in the *Torah* — where entry is explicitly conditioned on *yerusha veyeshiva*, possession and settlement — serves as a model for all other cases, establishing that *ki savo* never means the mere act of crossing the border but always implies the completed process of conquest and settlement after the fourteen-year period. The specific examples are the *pasuk* by the king — *ki savo el ha'aretz veyarashta veyashavta bah* — and the *pasuk* by *bikkurim* — similarly, *ki savo el ha'aretz veyarashta veyashavta*, followed by *velakachta mereishit kol pri ha'adamah*. Both specify that the relevant obligation applies only after taking possession and settling.

### Two Verses Together

The opposing *tanna* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael disagrees. His argument is that you cannot use this as a *binyan av* because the condition *yerusha veyeshiva* is spelled out explicitly in two separate *pesukim* — by the king and by *bikkurim* — and the rule is that *shnei ketuvim haba'im ke'echad ein melamdin*: when the *Torah* makes two cases explicit, those two cases are to be understood as exceptions, not as paradigms from which to generalize. According to this view, the default meaning of *ki savo* is immediate entry, and both the king and *bikkurim* are spelled out precisely because they would otherwise have been understood as applying immediately.

The first *tanna* responds with *tzrichi* — both *pesukim* are necessary and neither is superfluous. He argues that had the *Torah* written only the case of the king without *bikkurim*, one might have concluded that while the general rule requires settlement, *bikkurim* is an exception — since the fruits of the land are immediately available upon entry, one might have thought *bikkurim* should apply at once. Therefore the *Torah* had to clarify that *bikkurim* too follows the general rule and applies only after settlement. And had the *Torah* written only *bikkurim* without the king, one might have assumed that a king is needed from the outset — since waging the wars of conquest requires a king — and therefore the obligation to appoint a king applies immediately. Therefore the *Torah* had to clarify that even appointing a king is only after settlement. Each case is necessary, but they are not exceptions; they are confirmations that the rule of settlement applies even in contexts where one might have thought otherwise.

### Challah Comparison

The *tanna* who holds that the two explicit *pesukim* create exceptions then pushes back further. He says: the *Torah* could have written only the case of the king, and I could have inferred *bikkurim* on my own — *umah Melech d'lichbosh acharei yerusha veyeshiva, Bikkurim lo kol shekein* — if even appointing a king, who is normally needed to wage war, is only after settlement, how much more so *bikkurim*, which is simply bringing the first fruits. The fact that *bikkurim* was spelled out again signals that it is an exception, confirming that the general rule of *ki savo* means immediately upon entry.

The first *tanna* replies that this inference fails because of *challah*. By *challah*, the *Torah* uses the word *bevo'achem* — when you come — and the *Gemara* elsewhere derives that *challah* applies immediately upon entry into the land, without waiting for settlement. Since *bikkurim* and *challah* are closely analogous — both are considered a form of *terumah*, both are *matanot* given to the *kohen*, and both are called *reishit* — I would have naturally equated them and concluded that *bikkurim*, like *challah*, applies immediately. Therefore the *Torah* had to specify separately that *bikkurim* too requires prior settlement, and this specification is not to mark *bikkurim* as an exception but to prevent me from placing it in the category of *challah*. The general rule remains that *ki savo* means settlement, and *bikkurim* is clarified as part of that rule, not as a departure from it.

What remains relevant to us regarding *chadash* is that in both approaches, *moshavoseichem* means after you have settled — as opposed to the entirely different reading that *moshavoseichem* means wherever you dwell, which would entail that *chadash* applies immediately in *chutz la'aretz*. Regardless of which hermeneutical approach one takes within the debate above, the question of whether *chadash* applies outside the land depends on which meaning of *moshavoseichem* one adopts.

---

## Moshvoteichem Meaning

### Shabbat Application

The *Gemara* now transitions: *hashta de'amarta chovat haguf noheget bein ba'aretz bein bechutz la'aretz* — now that we have established that personal obligations apply in *chutz la'aretz* — *moshvoteichem dichtav rachmana gabei Shabbat lama li?* Why does the *Torah* say *bechol moshvoteichem* by *Shabbat*? The *pasuk* reads *Shabbat hi l'Hashem bechol moshvoseichem*. If *moshvoseichem* normally signifies after you've settled the land, then writing it by *Shabbat* is completely inappropriate — *Shabbat* obviously cannot be a condition on settlement. And if it means wherever you dwell, that too is obvious regarding *Shabbat*, since everyone knows it applies everywhere.

The *Gemara* answers: *itzterich* — it is necessary. *Salka da'atach amina* — one might have thought, since *Shabbat* is written in *Parshat Emor* in the same passage as the other *mo'adim*, that perhaps it would require a process of sanctification parallel to the other festivals, which depend on *kiddush hachodesh* — the declaration of the new month — to determine when they occur. Perhaps *Shabbat* would similarly require some form of declaration to make it holy. *Ka mashma lan* — the *Torah* therefore teaches, through the phrase *bechol moshvoseichem*, that *Shabbat* has no dependence on what takes place in the land of Israel. It applies automatically, without any aspect of sanctification — emphasizing that it is entirely independent of any centralized process. This is why even though it is obvious that *Shabbat* applies everywhere, the *Torah* still had to write *bechol moshvoseichem*.

### Chelev Vedam

The *Gemara* continues to other *mitzvot* where the *Torah* uses the phrase *bechol moshvoseichem*, examining in each case why that phrase is necessary. By *chelev vedam* — fat and blood — the *Torah* says *bechol moshvoseichem*. Why is this necessary? The prohibition on *chelev vedam* is clearly not land-based; of course it applies everywhere. The *Gemara* answers: *salka da'atach amina* — since the prohibition of *chelev vedam* appears in the context of *korbanot*, one might have thought that *chelev* and *dam* are only forbidden because they belong on the *mizbe'ach*, and that therefore the prohibition would apply only when there are *korbanot*. And as for the *chelev* of a *chaya* — a non-domesticated animal — which cannot be sacrificed on the *mizbe'ach*, one might have thought it is entirely permitted. *Ka mashma lan* — the *Torah* therefore teaches through *bechol moshvoseichem* that the prohibition applies in all places and at all times, entirely independent of the context of the *Mikdash*.

### Matzah Umaror

Similarly, by *matzah umaror* the *Torah* states *bechol moshvoseichem tochelu matzot*. Why is this necessary? *Salka da'atach amina* — the *pasuk* itself establishes *matzah* and *maror* in the context of the *korban pesach* — *al matzot umerorim yochelohu* — and one might have concluded that *matzah* and *maror* are obligatory only when the *Pesach* offering is brought, and not otherwise. *Ka mashma lan* — the phrase *bechol moshvoseichem* teaches that *matzah* applies even in exile, even after the *churban Beis HaMikdash*, even when one is not in the land of Israel and even when there is no *korban pesach*. This is of course directly relevant to our own practice. The irony is not lost that *maror* in fact does not apply today independently of the *korban pesach*, and the *Gemara* elsewhere derives the continuing obligation of *matzah* from a separate *pasuk*. But the principle established by *bechol moshvoseichem* is that *matzah* is not contingent on the context of the *Mikdash*.

### Tefillin & Peter Chamor

By *tefillin* and *peter chamor*, the *Torah* uses the phrase *ki savo el ha'aretz* — when you come to the land — followed by the instruction regarding the firstborn donkey and the commandment of *tefillin*. These *mitzvot* are plainly not limited to coming into the land. So why does the *Torah* phrase them in terms of entry? The *Gemara* answers that we need the phrase for what the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches: *asei mitzvah zo she'bishvilah tikanes la'aretz* — perform this *mitzvah*, for in its merit you will enter the land. The reference to entry is not to say that *tefillin* and *peter chamor* apply only after entry; rather, it is a reversal of the usual dependency. These *mitzvot* are the merit by virtue of which one merits entry into the land.

---

## Chadash in Israel

### Omer Necessity

The *Gemara* now returns to *chadash* directly. *Bishlama lema'an de'amar moshav kol makom she'atem yoshvim mashma* — according to the view that *moshav* means wherever you dwell, and *chadash* therefore applies in *chutz la'aretz* like Rabbi Eliezer holds, one can understand the *pasuk* in *Yehoshua*: *vayochlu me'avur ha'aretz mimocharat haPesach* — they ate from the produce of the land from the day following *Pesach*. On the reading that *chadash* applies everywhere, they could not eat the new grain of the land until the *omer* was brought — *mei'ikara lo achol* — and only after that could they eat. *Alma akrivu omer ve'hadar achol* — this implies the *omer* was in fact brought and the eating followed. According to *Chazal*, something happened on the sixteenth of *Nissan* — evidently the *omer* was brought in the traveling *Mishkan* — and that permitted eating from the new grain. This reading coheres with the position that *chadash* applies in *chutz la'aretz* and applies in Israel immediately upon entry, requiring the *omer* before any new grain may be consumed.

### Settlement Timing

But consider the alternative: *ela lema'an de'amar le'achar yerusha veyeshiva* — according to the view that *bechol moshvoseichem* by *chadash* means after you've settled the land. In that case, when *Yehoshua* and the Jewish people had just entered the land, the *issur chadash* had not yet taken effect. So *neichlu le'altar* — why did they not simply eat the new grain immediately upon crossing the Jordan? The *Gemara* answers: *lav mitzterichi* — they simply did not need it. It was coincidence that they waited until the sixteenth of *Nissan*, and this had nothing to do with the *omer*.

Why did they not need the grain? Because *dichtiv uvnei Yisrael achlu es haman arbaim shana ad bo'am el eretz noshevet* — they ate the *man* for forty years until they came to the settled land. But a problem arises: one *pasuk* says they ate the *man* until they came *el eretz noshevet* — implying they ate it until after they entered — while another says they ate it *ad bo'am el ketzei eretz Canaan* — until they reached the edge of the land of *Canaan*, suggesting they stopped before entering. *Ha keitzad* — how do we reconcile these?

The *Gemara* resolves: *beshiva be'Adar meis Moshe* — Moshe died on the seventh of *Adar*. The *man* stopped falling when Moshe died, when the people were at the cusp of entering. But they continued eating from that last supply of *man* — one day's portion, which sustained them — for the following thirty-seven days until they actually entered the land. Both *pesukim* are thus true: the *man* stopped falling at the edge of *Canaan*, and yet they were still eating it when they came *el eretz noshevet*. This is the resolution to the apparent contradiction.

The relevance for our question is as follows: if *chadash* applies *bechol moshvoseichem* everywhere and immediately — including in the land of Israel from the moment of entry — then one must explain why they did not eat the new grain immediately upon crossing. The answer is that they still had *man* and did not need it. The *omer* was then brought on the sixteenth, and only after that did they eat from the new grain. But if *moshavoseichem* means only after settlement, they were already permitted to eat the new grain upon entry, and they simply happened not to need it until the sixteenth because they were still sustained by the *man*.

### Mahn Narrative

A separate *braisa* addresses the chronology of the *man* itself. *Uvnei Yisrael achlu es haman arbaim shana* — they ate the *man* for forty years. Did they really eat it for a full forty years? In fact it was forty years minus thirty days, since the *man* did not begin to fall on the day they left Egypt but only a month later. How then can the *Torah* say forty years? *Ela lomar lach* — the *Torah* is telling us that the cakes they had taken out of Egypt — *ugah shehotziu miMitzrayim ta'amu bahem ta'am man* — tasted like the *man*. So it was as if they had been eating the *man* for forty years, because even in the first month, before the *man* fell, the cakes they were eating had the taste of *man*.

### Chronology Timeline

Another *braisa* establishes the precise chronology. *Beshiva be'Adar meis Moshe, beshiva be'Adar nolad* — Moshe was born and died on the seventh of *Adar*. How do we know he died on the seventh of *Adar*? From the *pasuk* stating that Moshe died in the plains of *Moav*, combined with the *pasuk* that the people mourned him for thirty days in the plains of *Moav*. Then the book of *Yehoshua* opens with God commanding Yehoshua following Moshe's death: *moshe avdi meis ve'atah kum avor* — Moshe my servant has died, now arise and cross. And soon after: *ivru bekerev hamachane vetzivu es ha'am — hachinu lachem tzeidah ki be'od shlosha yamim ta'avru es hayardein* — prepare yourselves provisions, for in three days you will cross the Jordan. And then: *veha'am alu min hayardein be'asor lachodesh harishon* — the people came up from the Jordan on the tenth of the first month. Working backwards from the tenth of *Nissan*: subtract thirty days of mourning and three days of preparation, and one arrives at the seventh of *Adar*. That is how we know Moshe died on the seventh of *Adar*. And how do we know he was born on that date? Because Moshe said *ben me'ah ve'esrim shana anochi hayom* — I am one hundred and twenty years old today — and the principle is that the righteous live out the full measure of their years, filling out the year entirely, as the *pasuk* states *et mispar yamecha amaleh* — the number of your days I will fill. Therefore Moshe died on the same day he was born.

---

## Three Mitzvot Debate

### Rabbi Shimon View

*Tanya Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai omer* — Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches: *shalosh mitzvot nitztavu Yisrael bichnisatan la'aretz venoheget bein ba'aretz bein b'chutz la'aretz* — three *mitzvot* were commanded to Israel upon their entry into the land, and yet they apply both in the land and outside the land. Those three are *chadash*, *orlah*, and *kilayim*. They began with entry into the land, but once they began to apply, they apply everywhere — including *chutz la'aretz*. He thus agrees with Rabbi Eliezer that *chadash* applies in *chutz la'aretz*.

He then reasons as follows: *umah chadash she'ein issuro issur olam ve'ein issuro issur hana'ah veyesh heter l'issuro noheg bein ba'aretz bein b'chutz la'aretz* — *chadash* is the weakest of these three prohibitions. Why? Three reasons. First, *ein issuro issur olam* — the prohibition is not permanent; the grain that begins as *chadash* becomes *mutar* once the *omer* is brought. Second, *ein issuro issur hana'ah* — *chadash* is not forbidden in *hana'ah*; you may not eat it but you may derive benefit from it. Third, *veyesh heter l'issuro* — it has a mechanism of permission: not only does the *issur* end with time, but if the *omer* is brought on the sixteenth it becomes *mutar* even on the sixteenth itself — in effect, half a day early. Rashi understands *yesh heter l'issuro* as essentially a stronger formulation of the first point — that the *omer* creates a *heter* even within the *issur* period. *Tosafot* offers several alternative explanations. In any case, even with all these leniencies, *chadash* applies in *chutz la'aretz*. 

*Kilayim she'issuran issur olam* — *kilayim*, by contrast, is always forbidden; it does not become permitted with time. *Ve'issuran issur hana'ah* — it is forbidden even in *hana'ah*. *Ve'ein heter l'issuran* — there is no mechanism of permission. *Eino din she'yanogu bein ba'aretz bein b'chutz la'aretz* — how much more so should *kilayim* apply in *chutz la'aretz*. And *orlah* has two of these three stringencies — it is not *issur olam* in the same sense, since while the fruit of those first three years remains permanently forbidden, the tree itself eventually yields permitted fruit — and it too therefore applies in *chutz la'aretz*.

Importantly, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai appears to be saying not merely that *chadash*, *orlah*, and *kilayim* apply rabbinically in *chutz la'aretz*, but that they apply *de'oraita*. This is a significant point and stands in contrast to the positions that will emerge from the *Mishnah* later.

*Tosafot* raises a pointed objection from this line of reasoning. If *chadash* applies *de'oraita* in *chutz la'aretz* and is demonstrably the weakest of these three prohibitions, then by a straightforward *kal vachomer* all the other *mitzvot hatluyot ba'aretz* — *tevel*, *terumah*, *ma'aser*, and so on — should also apply *de'oraita* outside the land. *Tosafot* answers that the *kal vachomer* can be challenged: *chadash* is unique in that it cannot be annulled through a *she'eilah* — a *halakhic* inquiry dissolving the status — whereas *terumah* and *ma'aser* can in principle be reversed through such inquiry, since they acquire their status through a human act of designation.
