But the question is in some ways more striking than any particular answer: if one takes Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position fully seriously, it opens the door to an expansive view of which agricultural *mitzvot* apply everywhere.

### Rabbi Elazar View

Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon takes the opposing position: *kol mitzvah shenitztavu Yisrael kodem knisatam la'aretz noheget bein ba'aretz bein b'chutz la'aretz* — any *mitzvah* that applied before they entered the land is not land-dependent and therefore applies outside the land as well. But *le'achar knisatam la'aretz* — anything that applied only upon entering the land, such as *chadash*, *orlah*, and *kilayim* — *einah noheget ela ba'aretz* — applies only in the land of Israel. He thus disagrees with his father and takes the position that these three are categorically limited to the land of Israel, since they are precisely the type of obligations that came into effect only with entry and are fundamentally land-dependent.

### Exceptions: Loans & Slav…

Rabbi Elazar does, however, identify two exceptions: *chutz min hashmattat kesafim veshiluach avadim* — the annulment of loans in the *shemittah* year and the freeing of slaves in the *yovel* — *she'af al pi shenitztavu le'achar knisatam la'aretz, noheget bein ba'aretz bein b'chutz la'aretz* — even though these were commanded with reference to entry into the land, they apply both inside and outside. The question, which the *Gemara* will now address, is: why are these two specifically carved out as exceptions? If they are personal obligations with no inherent connection to the soil, why would it even occur to anyone to limit them to the land?

---

## Shemittah & Release

### Loans Dependency

The *Gemara* asks: *hashmattat kesafim chovat haguf hi* — annulling loans is a personal obligation, so of course it applies outside the land. Why does Rabbi Elazar need to spell this out as an exception? The *Gemara* answers: *lo nitzrecha ela l'chidetanya* — the ruling is necessary because of what we learn in a *braisa*. *Rabbi omer*: *v'zeh devar hashemittah shamot* — this is the matter of *shemittah*, release — *bishtei shemittot hakatuv medaber* — the *Torah* here is speaking of two types of *shemittah*. *Achat shemitat karka ve'achat shemitat kesafim* — one is the release of the land from agricultural labor, and the other is the cancellation of loans. The principle established is: *bizman she'atah meshamet karka, atah meshamet kesafim* — when *shemitat karka* applies, *shemitat kesafim* also applies. *Bizman she'ei atah meshamet karka, ein atah meshamet kesafim* — when *shemitat karka* does not apply, neither does *shemitat kesafim*.

From this dependency, one might have reasoned: *bemakom she'atah meshamet karka atah meshamet kesafim uvemakom she'ein atah meshamet karka ein atah meshamet kesafim* — perhaps the annulment of loans applies only where *shemitat karka* is geographically practiced, namely in the land of Israel. Therefore it would be *mutar* to maintain loans in *chutz la'aretz* even during a *shemittah* year, since *shemitat karka* does not operate there. This is not an unreasonable reading; indeed, a number of *Rishonim* held that *shemitat kesafim* outside the land is not even *de'rabbanan* in a full sense but merely a *minhag chasidut*, and historically people in the Rishonic period sometimes barely bothered with writing a *pruzbul*.

Against this, the *Gemara* answers: *talmud lomar ki kara shemittah l'Hashem mikol makom* — the *Torah* teaches that *shemittah* is declared for God from every place. The word *mikol makom* signifies that the cancellation of loans operates regardless of geographic location — even in *chutz la'aretz* where *shemitat karka* does not apply. What *shemitat kesafim* does require is that *shemitat karka* is being practiced in Israel; the dependency is temporal, not geographic. When *shemittah* is operative in Israel, the annulment of loans applies everywhere. When *shemittah* is not operative in Israel — for instance, because *yovel* is not practiced, which in turn requires that *kol yoshveiha aleha* — all inhabitants dwell upon it — the annulment of loans does not apply even in Israel, let alone outside it. This condition has not been met since *Sancheriv* exiled the ten tribes, toward the end of the era of the first *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Slaves Release

Similarly, *shiluach avadim chovat haguf hi* — freeing slaves is a personal obligation, so of course it applies in *chutz la'aretz*. But the *Gemara* notes the *salka da'atach amina*: the *Torah* states *ukratem dror ba'aretz lechol yoshveiha* — you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants thereof. *Ba'aretz in, bechutz la'aretz lo* — one might have read this as limiting the freeing of slaves to the land of Israel. *Talmud lomar yovel hi mikol makom* — the *Torah* teaches that it is the *yovel*, regardless of location. *Im ken mah talmud lomar ba'aretz?* What then is the function of the word *ba'aretz*? *Bizman shehadrur noheg ba'aretz, noheg bechutz la'aretz* — when freedom is proclaimed in Israel, it applies outside Israel as well. *Bizman she'ein dror noheg ba'aretz, eino noheg bechutz la'aretz* — if *yovel* is not operative in Israel for whatever reason, it does not apply outside of Israel either. The structure is identical to *shemitat kesafim*: the obligation is not geographically confined to Israel, but it is triggered by and dependent on the practice in Israel.

### Theological Framework

This pattern invites a broader theological reflection. The *Gemara* is operating throughout with a lens that divides *mitzvot* into soil-based obligations, on one hand, and personal obligations, on the other — assuming that the former are naturally limited to Israel while the latter apply everywhere. But this framing is itself worth questioning. As Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's formulation makes clear — and as the cases of *shemitat kesafim* and *shiluach avadim* illustrate — there is a category of *mitzvot* that are not literally soil-based but are deeply national in character, tied to an experience of Israel that generates obligations even in *chutz la'aretz*, yet only when that experience is actively taking place in Israel.

This points toward what the *Ramban* articulates: the *Torah* does not fundamentally conceive of Judaism as a universal religion whose *mitzvot* are practiced wherever one happens to live. Rather, the *Torah* and its *mitzvot* are the laws of the Israelite people living in the land of Israel. Any other state of being — exile — is not a natural or normative condition but an aberration. The *chiddush* in this framework is not that some *mitzvot* are limited to the land; it is that any *mitzvot* apply in *chutz la'aretz* at all. The question of which *mitzvot* are soil-based and therefore limited to Israel is, in a sense, the wrong starting point. The prior question is why anything should apply outside Israel.

---

## Status Categories

### Mishna Statuses

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishnah* in *Orlah*. *Hachadash assur min hatorah bechol makom* — *chadash* is forbidden by Torah law everywhere. This *stam Mishnah* reflects the position of Rabbi Eliezer, and it is the operative *halakhic* question whether we rule in accordance with this *stam Mishnah* and apply *chadash de'oraita* in *chutz la'aretz*. *Orlah halakhah* — *orlah* is a *halakhah*, the precise meaning of which the *Gemara* will now debate. *Vekilayim midivrei soferim* — *kilayim* is rabbinic.

### Halachot Medinah

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* — Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says that the word *halakhah* by *orlah* means *hilchot medinah* — a very interesting formulation that Rashi interprets as meaning something like an accepted practice, something the people took upon themselves in *chutz la'aretz* rather than a legislated rabbinic enactment from above. The word *noheg* captures this — it is the practice, the custom, rather than a formal decree. This would make *orlah* in *chutz la'aretz* weaker even than a standard *de'rabbanan*.

### Halacha L'Moshe

*Ulla amar Rabbi Yochanan* — Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *halakhah* here means *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — a tradition handed down orally from Sinai. This is weightier than a rabbinic enactment; it carries the authority of an ancient tradition even though it is not written explicitly in the *Torah*.

### Safek Distinctions

The practical difference between these two positions is illustrated by comparing the laws of *safek orlah* and *safek kilayim* in *chutz la'aretz*. *Safek orlah* in the land of Israel is forbidden — *safek de'oraita lechumra*. In *Surya*, which has a certain intermediate status due to the conquests of *David HaMelech*, *safek orlah* is *mutar*. And in *chutz la'aretz*, not only is *safek* permitted but one may even go down and purchase from the orchard owner even knowing that some of the trees are *orlah* and some are not — *yored velokeach* — as long as one does not directly witness the seller picking specifically from the *orlah* tree. This represents a significant leniency, almost resembling a form of willful ignorance.

Regarding *kilayim* in *chutz la'aretz*, the *Mishnah* in *Kilayim* describes a case of a vineyard planted with vegetables, and a vegetable stand selling from what appears to come from inside the vineyard, right at the edge of the public road. In the land of Israel this is forbidden. In *Surya* it is *mutar*. In *chutz la'aretz*, one may even observe the seller picking from the mixed planting directly, as long as one does not pick it oneself — *yored veloket ubilvad shelo yilkot beyad*. This is a striking leniency: even witnessing the act of picking directly from what is almost certainly *kilayim* does not prevent purchase, as long as there remains some degree of personal remove.

Ulla's argument is: *bishlama l'didi de'amina halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — if *orlah* is *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* and *kilayim* is *de'rabbanan*, it makes sense that there would be different thresholds for leniency in cases of *safek*. A *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* is weightier than a *de'rabbanan*, and the levels of stringency in the *safek* cases reflect this difference. *Ela l'didach* — but according to Rav Yehuda, who says *orlah* is *hilchot medinah* — a practice even weaker than a *de'rabbanan* — why would there be any different standards at all? Both should be at the same level of leniency. The fact that there is a discernible difference in *halachic* stringency between *safek orlah* and *safek kilayim* in *chutz la'aretz* thus supports Ulla's position that *orlah* is *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* and not merely an accepted regional practice. This point will be developed further in the next *daf*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 39

## Orlah vs. Kilayim

### Intro: Orlah/Kilayim

We begin at the bottom of 38b, picking up the thread of which prohibitions apply in *eretz yisrael* and which apply in *chutz la'aretz*. The *mishna* in *Orlah* teaches that *chadash* is *assur min hatorah* everywhere — that is the position of Rabbi Eliezer, and we have already discussed how we *pasken* that question for *chadash* in *chutz la'aretz*. The *mishna* then states that *orlah* is *halacha* and *kilayim* is *divrei soferim* — that is, *d'rabbanan*.

The question is: what does *halacha* mean in this context? One opinion, that of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, understands it as *hilchos hamedina* — adopted local practice, or at most *d'rabbanan*. The competing position understands *halacha* to mean *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, which would give *orlah* considerably more weight than a mere *d'rabbanan*. The *sugya* now proceeds to demonstrate that *orlah* is indeed weightier than *kilayim*, by examining how each handles the question of *safek* — doubtful cases — in *chutz la'aretz*.

### Ulla's Challenge

Ulla raises the question directly to Rav Yehuda: *bishlama ledidi* — according to my position, that *orlah* is *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, I can explain why the *mishna* distinguishes between a doubtful case of *orlah* and a doubtful case of *kilayim*, treating the latter more leniently than the former. *Orlah* is *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* while *kilayim* is *d'rabbanan*, and thus their respective treatments of *safek* differ accordingly.

But according to your view, Rav Yehuda, that both are *d'rabbanan*, why should there be any difference between them in cases of *safek*? The *mishna* should either make them equally strict or equally lenient — but not treat them differently.

### Leniencies Compared

To appreciate the force of Ulla's challenge, we must look carefully at what the *mishna* actually teaches. In a case of *safek orlah* in *eretz yisrael*, it is *assur* — the land itself is *d'oraita*. In *Surya* — the lands adjacent to Israel conquered by David — it is *mutar*, because the prohibition there is only *d'rabbanan*. In *chutz la'aretz* proper, it is even more lenient: *yored velokei'ach* — one may go down into the orchard and purchase from the seller there, provided only that one does not actually witness the seller picking directly from the *orlah* tree itself. One does not even need to ask. The level of *safek* required is remarkably minimal — as long as it is not blatantly apparent that the fruit came from that tree.

When we turn to *kilayim*, the *mishna* presents a parallel structure but with a notably greater leniency in *chutz la'aretz*. The case discussed is a vineyard in which vegetables have been planted — rendering those vegetables *kilayim* — with a small produce stand right outside selling the very same vegetables. In *eretz yisrael* this is *assur*; in *Surya* it is *mutar*. But in *chutz la'aretz*, the leniency goes even further: *yored veloket* — one may actually observe the seller picking the vegetables directly from the vineyard and still purchase and eat them. As Rashi explains at the top of 39a: *delo assru be-chutz la'aretz ela es hazoreya o es haloket beyadayim* — the only prohibition in *chutz la'aretz* falls on the one who planted the *kilayim* or the one who personally picks it. One who merely purchases — even having watched the picking occur — is permitted.

So we have two extreme *kulos*, but *kilayim* is more lenient still: by *orlah* one cannot witness the picking; by *kilayim* one can. Ulla's argument is that if both are *d'rabbanan*, they should be treated identically. Why is one permitted to witness the picking for *kilayim* but not for *orlah*?

### Shmuel Amends Mishna

Shmuel, who is precisely the one who taught that *orlah* in *chutz la'aretz* is *hilchos hamedina* — effectively *d'rabbanan* — concedes Ulla's point entirely. He instructed the *rabanana* to amend the *girsa* of the *mishna* so that both *orlah* and *kilayim* carry the same ruling. Either both prohibit witnessing the picking — i.e., the stricter version — or both permit witnessing the picking as long as one does not personally do the picking. Since Shmuel holds them to be at the same level, the *mishna* must reflect uniform treatment, and he accordingly emends the text to achieve that consistency.

### Mar Brei D'Ravina

Mar brei d'Ravina takes the more lenient of the two positions. He teaches: *zeh vezeh yored velokei'ach* — in both cases one may even watch the picking occur directly, *ubilvad shelo yilkat beyado*, as long as one does not pick it oneself. This presumably reflects his agreement with Shmuel's view that both *orlah* and *kilayim* stand at the same level, and if they are both *d'rabbanan*, one might as well adopt the more lenient ruling for both.

### Shivi's Proposal

Shivi said to Shmuel — calling him *aryoch*, apparently a term meaning something like "the great one" or "the lion," which may derive from the same root as *aryoch melech Elasar* — *sfeik li v'ana eichol*: make it a *safek* for me and I will eat it. Rashi explains: *sfeik li likot shelo bifnai sheyisafek etzli v'ana eichol uv'Orlah ka'i* — go ahead and pick when I am not present, so that there will be a genuine *safek* as far as I am concerned, and I will eat it. This is actually the stricter of the two positions: it does not permit witnessing the picking for *orlah*, but it does show a practical workaround for a Jew who has, say, an apple orchard in its third year. The seller picks when the buyer is not present, thereby maintaining the technical requirement that one not witness the picking directly.

### Exchange of Picking

Rav Avya and Rabba bar Bar Chana went one step further and would exchange the picking of doubtful produce between one another — each one picking for the other, so that neither was in the presence of his own orchard's picking. This is a practical mutual arrangement that achieves the same result as Shivi's proposal but between two parties acting in concert.

### Pumbedita's Leniency

The *charifei d'Pumbedita* — the sharp ones of Pumbedita, whom Rashi identifies as Ha'eifa u'Ramibi, the sons of Rechava — took a far more sweeping position: *ein orlah b'chutz la'aretz*, there is simply no *orlah* in *chutz la'aretz* whatsoever. This was the predictable endpoint of the slippery slope: once the leniencies are extended far enough, someone will ultimately make the blanket declaration that the prohibition does not apply at all.

---

## Yochanan's Response

### RavYehuda Reports

Rav Yehuda sent word to Rabbi Yochanan, who was in *eretz yisrael*, reporting that the scholars of Pumbedita were declaring *ein orlah b'chutz la'aretz* — that *orlah* does not apply at all outside the Land. Rabbi Yochanan's response was forceful and multidimensional. First, *setom sefeika*: silence the *safek*. Now that people are sliding into the position that *orlah* does not apply at all, one must stop publicizing the various leniencies in cases of *safek*, lest the teaching of those leniencies serve as the gateway to the blanket denial of the prohibition. Second, *v'abeid vadah*: actively destroy any produce that is a *vaday* case of *orlah*. Third, *v'hachreiz al peiroteihen she-te'unin genizah*: announce publicly that the fruit of those who engaged in these arrangements — the exchange of picking and similar tactics — requires *genizah*. And finally, regarding anyone who says *ein orlah b'chutz la'aretz* outright: *lo yiheyeh lo nin v'neched* — he should have no descendant. This is strikingly severe rhetoric, and reflects Rabbi Yochanan's alarm at how far the leniency had traveled.

The *gemara* then asks: upon which authority were the scholars of Pumbedita relying? If they were making the blanket statement that *orlah* does not apply at all in *chutz la'aretz*, they presumably had a tannaitic source for that position.

### Rabbi Eliezer Tradition

Indeed, there is such a tradition: *Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yossi omer mishum Rabbi Yossi ben Durmaska she-amar mishum Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili she-amar mishum Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri she-amar mishum Rabbi Eliezer ha-Gadol* — an unbroken chain of authorities going back to Rabbi Eliezer the Great: *ein orlah b'chutz la'aretz*. It is worth pausing to note that this itself is a remarkable feature of the *sugya*: if one holds that anything which is a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* is never subject to debate — as the Rambam maintains — then the very fact that Rabbi Eliezer is denying that *orlah b'chutz la'aretz* exists at all presents a difficulty, whether one frames it as a debate about whether it is a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* or as a flat rejection of that category's application here.

### Contradiction Resolved

The *gemara* immediately notes an apparent contradiction: we have a *mishna* in which Rabbi Eliezer says *af he-chadash* — even *chadash* applies outside the Land, in the context of a list that includes *orlah* and *kilayim*. If Rabbi Eliezer holds *ein orlah b'chutz la'aretz*, why does he seem to be adding *chadash* to a list that includes *orlah*? The resolution offered is to emend the *mishna*: remove the word *af* and read it as saying that Rabbi Eliezer holds that only *chadash* applies in *chutz la'aretz* — *orlah* and *kilayim* do not apply — whereas the *stam* view of the *mishna* holds that all three apply. This way, the two attributed statements of Rabbi Eliezer are brought into alignment.

### Halacha L'Moshe Claim

Rav Assi teaches in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *orlah b'chutz la'aretz halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*. This is a reiteration of Rabbi Yochanan's position — a strong stance that treats the application of *orlah* outside the Land as a law transmitted directly from Sinai, not merely a rabbinic practice or local custom.

### Zeira's Objection

Rav Zeira raises an objection to Rav Assi: how can you claim this is *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*? But we have the *mishna* that teaches *safek orlah ba'aretz assur, be-Surya mutar, u-vechutz la'aretz yored velokei'ach* — all these extensive leniencies in cases of *safek*! If *orlah b'chutz la'aretz* is a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, how can there be such extraordinary leniency even in what amounts to a near-*vaday* case? Rav Assi was momentarily speechless — *ishtomem kesha'a chada* — he was dumbfounded.

### Safek Mutar Solution

Then Rav Assi recovered: *eima kach ne'emar* — perhaps this is precisely how the *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* was formulated: *sveika mutar, vadai assur* — in a case of *safek* it is permitted, in a case of *vaday* it is forbidden. The *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* itself incorporated this leniency for *safek* as an intrinsic part of its content.

There are two significant observations to make here. First, note that Rav Assi does not say he has a clear transmitted tradition that the *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* included this *safek* provision; rather, he says *eima kach ne'emar* — "let us say it was stated this way." He is reconstructing the content of the *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* from what the *mishna* teaches, rather than recalling an unbroken explicit tradition about it. This itself raises questions about what it means to invoke *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — whether it always reflects a clearly remembered transmission or whether it can be a category that is inferred and in some measure reconstructed.

Second, Rav Zeira's question implicitly assumes that *safek d'oraisa l'chumra* should apply to a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — that if this has Sinaitic authority, one should be strict in cases of doubt. And indeed, the Rambam holds that the principle of *safek d'oraisa l'chumra* is itself only *d'rabbanan* — that as far as the *torah* is concerned, *safek d'oraisa l'kula*. Yet this *gemara* seems to proceed on the assumption that Sinaitic authority calls for stringency in *safek*, requiring a special built-in provision to permit leniency. One possible way of resolving this tension is to note that what may have been troubling the *gemara* is not the abstract principle of *safek l'kula* but rather the extraordinary practical extremity of the leniency — a situation so attenuated that it barely qualifies as a *safek* in any meaningful sense, such as buying from a seller when one knows the orchard contains *orlah* trees but simply did not witness the picking. That kind of manipulated or fictional *safek* may be what prompted the objection, quite apart from any general principle about *safek d'oraisa*.

This question — whether *safek* in a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* is *l'chumra* or *l'kula* — is discussed among the *rishonim*; if memory serves, the Ran or Rabbeinu Yona addresses it somewhere. It connects to the broader question of the weight of *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* relative to *d'oraisa* prohibitions in general.

A further note is worth adding about the category of *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* itself. The Rambam held that whatever is truly *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* was never debated — and he enumerated approximately thirty such items in the *gemara*. He used this framework in part as a response to the Karaite challenge: how can you claim an unbroken oral tradition when everything is debated? The Rambam's answer was that virtually all of *torah she-ba'al peh* was never directly transmitted as bottom-line *halachos* but rather as hermeneutic principles and an empowerment to interpret; that interpretation, applied by different minds in different circumstances, naturally generates debate. The one domain in which actual content was transmitted intact is *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, where there should be no *machlokes*. The problem, as this *sugya* illustrates, is that there plainly *is* debate even over some of those traditions. In addition, there are places in the *gemara* where the phrase *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* appears to be used rhetorically — the *Mishnah Yadayim* is one example — for matters that cannot literally be Sinaitic laws. The Rosh makes this observation explicitly. The Netziv, in his introduction to the *She'iltos*, discusses how certain *rishonim* understand the term *hilchasa* when it appears after a *gemara* dispute: Rashi reads it as *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, while others understand it as an ancient *d'rabbanan* whose reason was forgotten, without any claim that it goes back to Moshe. These questions of when the phrase is literal and when it is rhetorical are treated in modern scholarship as well.

---

## Kilayim Distinctions

### Lashes for Kilayim

We now turn to *kilayim* specifically. Abba teaches in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lokin al kilayim de-var Torah* — one receives lashes for *kilayim* as a biblical prohibition. The immediate response from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yossi is a challenge: but we have an explicit *mishna* — *ha-kilayim mi-divrei sofrim*! *Kilayim* is rabbinic! The entire thrust of our *sugya* up to now has been that *kilayim* is *d'rabbanan*. How can Rabbi Yochanan say one gets lashes, which is a punishment reserved for biblical violations?

### Harkavah vs. Seeds

The resolution: *lo kashya, kan b'kilai kerem kan b'harkava* — there is no contradiction because we are dealing with two entirely different categories. The *mishna*'s statement that *kilayim* is *d'rabbanan* refers to *kilayim* of seeds — mixing different seeds in a field. But there is another form of *kilayim*: *harkavat ilan* — grafting one tree onto another. This form is more analogous to the crossbreeding of animals (*harva'at behema*), since it involves direct physical manipulation of living organisms rather than simply planting seeds in proximity. It is this category — *harkavat ilan* — for which one receives lashes even in *chutz la'aretz*, based on a teaching of Shmuel.

Shmuel derives this from the verse *et chukotai tishmoru* — you shall observe My statutes. The unusual word order (*et chukotai*, placing the object first) implies that these *chukim* are ancient, pre-existing the moment of their formal biblical statement. The next verse reads: *behemtecha lo tarbia kilayim, sadecha lo tizra kilayim* — you shall not crossbreed your animals with *kilayim*, and you shall not sow your field with *kilayim*. The derivation proceeds as follows: just as *behemtecha* refers to crossbreeding animals, so too *sadecha* here is read not at the level of *peshat* (planting seeds) but through *derash*, as referring to something analogous — grafting trees. And just as crossbreeding animals applies equally in *eretz yisrael* and in *chutz la'aretz*, so too grafting trees (*harkavat ilan*) applies *bein ba'aretz bein be-chutz la'aretz* — wherever one is.

There is a further dimension to this derivation: the antiquity implied by *et chukotai* suggests that these prohibitions predate the giving of the *Torah* at Sinai — they go back to the *benei Noach*. According to this position, even non-Jews are prohibited in crossbreeding animals and grafting trees, as these are counted among the *sheva mitzvos benei Noach*. The Rambam rules accordingly: *hamarkiv ilan be'ilan... harei zeh lokeh min haTorah bechol makom bein ba'aretz bein bechutz la'aretz* — one who grafts tree onto tree receives lashes from the *Torah* in every location, whether in *eretz yisrael* or in *chutz la'aretz*.

As for the word *sadecha* — "your field," which sounds possessive and might suggest the prohibition is limited to one's own land in *eretz yisrael* — the *gemara* resolves this by saying *hahu le-ma'uti zera'im she-ba-chutz*: *sadecha* is used specifically to exclude *kilayim* of seeds in *chutz la'aretz*, which is indeed not prohibited there at the biblical level. So the verse operates on two levels simultaneously: the *peshat* level (*lo tizra*, seeds, *sadecha*, limited to *eretz yisrael*) and the *derash* level (grafting, analogous to crossbreeding, which applies universally). Rashi's comment here is striking: *chutza la'aretz lo chasmu lachem min hashomayim* — outside the Land, heaven has not sealed off for you [the fruit of grafted trees]. The fruit itself remains permitted even where the act is forbidden.

### Biblical Sources

The two verses that govern these prohibitions are *behemtecha lo tarbia kilayim* — your animals you shall not crossbreed — and *sadecha lo tizra kilayim* — your field you shall not sow with mixed species. The hermeneutic reading of *sadecha* as parallel to *behemtecha* allows the prohibition to travel from the planting of seeds (its *peshat* meaning) to the grafting of trees (its *derash* meaning), and simultaneously the comparison to animal crossbreeding establishes that the prohibition is geographically unlimited. The *peshat* reading of seeds, by contrast, is confined by *sadecha* — "your field," meaning *eretz yisrael* — to the Land.

### Rav Chanan/Anan

Rav Chanan and Rav Anan were walking along a road when they observed a man planting seeds together. Rav Anan suggested: *neisei mar nishmasei* — let us go and put him in *cherem*, for he is transgressing the prohibition of *kilayim* in *chutz la'aretz*. His companion replied: *lo chavir su* — it is not clear to you what the *halacha* is. The exchange was not finished, however. They then saw another man planting wheat and barley inside a vineyard. Again Rav Anan suggested putting him in *cherem*. Again: *lo tzahiri tu* — it is not clear to you. The *gemara* explains that we do not rule like Rabbi Yoshiya, whose stringent definition of the act of *kilayim* would apply here.

### Rabbi Yoshiya's Rule

Rabbi Yoshiya holds: *ad she'yizra chittah u'se'orah ve'chartzan be'mapoles yad* — a person does not transgress the prohibition of planting *kilayim* unless he plants wheat, barley, and a grape seed all simultaneously, in a single action. Planting wheat and barley alone does not constitute the prohibition of *kilayim* of the vineyard according to his view, because a vineyard requires the grape to be present as part of the act. Given this ruling — especially in the lenient context of *chutz la'aretz* — there is no basis for putting the man in *cherem*.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot works through the relationship between the two types of *kilayim* with precision. First: Rabbi Yoshiya's requirement of all three seeds simultaneously — wheat, barley, and a grape seed — applies specifically to *kilayim hakerem*, *kilayim* of the vineyard. By contrast, *kilayim zeraim* — the prohibition of mixed seeds in a field, without a grapevine — requires only two different species and is violated by planting any two species together.

This raises an obvious question: even if the man planting wheat and barley in the vineyard has not violated *kilayim hakerem* (since he did not include a grape seed simultaneously), why is he not liable for *kilayim zeraim*? After all, he has planted two different seeds together. Tosafot addresses this with a clever reading of the verse. *Karmecha lo tizra kilayim* — your vineyard you shall not sow with *kilayim* — implies that in order to constitute *kilayim hakerem*, the *kilayim* must already exist before it comes into the vineyard; that is, one must bring the two grains together with the grapevine simultaneously, as a combined act. By contrast, *sadecha lo tizra kilayim* — your field you shall not sow with *kilayim* — does not carry the same implication, because a *sadeh* is simply a field, requiring no additional element to define it. Planting two seeds in a field is sufficient to create *kilayim zeraim*. But something that is already a vineyard is only a *kerem* by virtue of the grapes, not a plain *sadeh*. Therefore, when wheat and barley are planted inside an existing vineyard, it may not qualify as *kilayim zeraim* since the location is a *kerem*, not a plain *sadeh*.

The *halacha* follows Rabbi Oshaya, as Tosafot concludes: one may plant under a vine as long as all three seeds were not planted simultaneously, and *kilayim zeraim* does not apply in *chutz la'aretz* at all.

### Rav Yosef Practice

Rav Yosef would mix seeds together and plant them. Rashi adds: *v'lo b'kerem* — not in a vineyard. This reflects his position that *kilayim zeraim* does not apply in *chutz la'aretz* and therefore planting two different seeds together in a field outside *eretz yisrael* is not prohibited.

### Abye Distinguishes

Abaye challenges: but the *mishna* says *ha-kilayim mi-divrei sofrim* — *kilayim* is rabbinic! Even if we allow *kilayim zeraim* in *chutz la'aretz*, should it not at least be prohibited rabbinically? The response: *lo kashya, kan b'kilai kerem, kan b'kilai zrayim* — there is no difficulty, because we must distinguish sharply between the two. *Kilayim hakerem* — the vineyard mixture — is of such severity that even in *eretz yisrael* the produce is *assur behana'ah*, and therefore the rabbis extended its prohibition to *chutz la'aretz* as well. *Kilayim zeraim* — the mixing of seeds — is never *assur behana'ah* even in *eretz yisrael*; accordingly, the rabbis made no such extension, and it is not prohibited in *chutz la'aretz* at all.

### Summary of Rules

Let us now draw together the full picture that emerges from this *sugya*. In *eretz yisrael*: *kilayim hakerem* is biblically prohibited, both the act and the produce, which is *assur behana'ah*. *Kilayim zeraim* is prohibited as an act but the produce is not *assur behana'ah* — one may eat the fruit or vegetables that grew from mixed seeds. Outside *eretz yisrael*: crossbreeding animals is biblically prohibited — a *d'oraita* prohibition with no consequence for the produce (one may use a mule). Grafting trees (*harkavat ilan*) is similarly a *d'oraita* prohibition — but again, with no consequence for the produce: the fruit of a grafted tree is entirely permitted. *Kilayim hakerem* in *chutz la'aretz* is rabbinically prohibited, but only in the narrow definition of Rabbi Yoshiya — planting all three seeds (wheat, barley, and grape) simultaneously. *Kilayim zeraim* in *chutz la'aretz* is not prohibited at all, neither biblically nor rabbinically.

The only prohibition that renders produce *assur behana'ah*, whether in *eretz yisrael* or *chutz la'aretz*, is *kilayim hakerem* — and this is why the *mishna* discussing doubtful *kilayim* specifically chose the case of vegetables growing near a vineyard. The Rambam in *Ma'achalos Assuros*, chapter 13, reflects this: among the prohibitions that are of the *Torah* with respect to the produce of the earth, he lists *chadash*, *kilayim hakerem*, *tevel*, and *orlah* — not *kilayim zeraim*.

### Hybrid Fruits OK

This last point has important practical implications. Hybrid fruits — nectarines, tangelos, and similar products of botanical grafting or selective cultivation — are not *assur behana'ah* and are entirely permitted to eat. The reason is that *kilayim zeraim* never renders produce forbidden even where the act is prohibited, and *harkavat ilan*, while prohibited as an act even in *chutz la'aretz*, similarly carries no consequence for the fruit. One may make a *bracha* and eat the fruit of a grafted tree without any *halachic* concern. The only category of hybrid that would raise a concern regarding the produce is *kilayim hakerem*, which requires the specific combination of grain and grapevine — a scenario that does not describe the commercially available hybrid fruits of our time.

One detail does remain somewhat puzzling: that one should have a *d'oraita issur* such as *harkavat ilan* with no *gezeirah* extending the prohibition to the produce. Compare, for example, *basar b'chalav*, where some *rishonim* explain that the *Torah* prohibited eating the mixture precisely because there had to be some tangible consequence to the act of cooking them together. Here, by contrast, the act is gravely prohibited and yet the fruit emerges entirely permitted. Perhaps the explanation is that the concern of *kilayim* is the act of disrupting the divine order of creation through unnatural combination, rather than the product of that combination — and therefore the prohibition attaches to the act, not to its fruit.

---

## Reward/Punishment

### Mishna: One Mitzvah

We now turn to what is a welcome *aggadic* interlude — though it opens into some of the deepest theology in the tractate. The *mishna* states: *kol ha'oseh mitzvah achas metivin lo u'ma'arichin lo yamav v'nochel et ha'aretz* — whoever performs even one *mitzvah*, good is extended to him, his days are lengthened, and he inherits the land. *Nochel et ha'aretz* is linguistically picking up the theme of *eretz yisrael* that has dominated the preceding discussion, whether it is meant literally, metaphorically, or simply as a literary echo. And the passage concludes with the negative: whoever does not perform even one *mitzvah* receives none of these benefits. The literary structure also continues the *kol* formulation we have seen throughout — *kol mitzvos ha'av al ha'ben*, *kol mitzvos aseh she'hazman gerama*, and now *kol ha'oseh mitzvah* — now turning from the categorization of *mitzvos* to the power of performing a single one.

### Mishna Peah

This *mishna* appears to be in tension with the first *mishna* of *Peah*, which specifies a particular list of *mitzvos* for which one eats the fruit of the reward in this world: *kibbud av v'em, gemilus chasadim, hachnasat orchim, havaa't shalom bein adam l'chavero*, and *talmud Torah keneged kulam*. (The inclusion of *hachnasat orchim* in some versions is itself subject to textual question.) If any single *mitzvah* yields reward in this world, as our *mishna* in Kiddushin implies, what is distinctive about the list in *Peah*? Conversely, if the *Peah* list is exhaustive, then our *mishna* seems to overclaim.

It is worth pausing to note that the *mishna* in *Peah* may not be making a purely theological claim about divine reward. It is entirely possible to read *ochel peiroteihem ba'olam hazeh* as describing the natural and pragmatic fruits of those specific *mitzvos* — the person who honors parents, does acts of kindness, brings peace between people, and engages in *Torah* study will experience the concrete benefits of those behaviors in this world, quite apart from any supernatural reward. Research on human happiness consistently finds that acts of generosity toward others yield greater personal satisfaction than self-directed spending. The intrinsic payoff of these particular *mitzvos* may be precisely what the *mishna* is pointing to. The *gemara*, however, reads the conflict textually — the language of reward and its this-worldly versus other-worldly character — and proceeds to resolve it on those terms.

### Rav Yehuda Balance

Rav Yehuda resolves the tension by reframing the *mishna* entirely: *kol oseh mitzvah achas yeseira al zechuyosav meitivin lo* — the *mishna* is not saying that the reward for performing a *mitzvah* is delivered in this world. Rather, it is describing what happens when a person is at exact equilibrium — fifty percent merits, fifty percent demerits — and this one additional *mitzvah* tips the scale in his favor. In that case, *meitivin lo*, and it is as though he fulfilled the entire *Torah*. And correspondingly, the person who fails to perform one *mitzvah* when he is at fifty-fifty tips his scale in the negative direction. This reading confines the *mishna*'s applicability to the specific and relatively rare scenario of a precisely balanced accounting — which is a much narrower and less dramatically satisfying claim than a straightforward reading would suggest.

The question then becomes: what distinguishes the *mitzvos* listed in *Peah*, where this-worldly reward is promised even without the fifty-fifty precondition? The *gemara* answers in the name of Rav Shmaya: if one of those *mitzvos* from *Peah* is already among your fifty percent of merits, then it functions as a slight additional weight — you do not need a separate extra *mitzvah* to tip the scale, because that particular *mitzvah* itself carries additional weight. Our *mishna* then describes the case where none of the *Peah* mitzvos are part of your fifty percent, and you need an additional act to tip the balance.

### Baraita Opposites

The *gemara* then raises a further challenge from a *baraita* that teaches the precise opposite of what our *mishna* predicts. The *baraita* states: *kol she-zechuyosav merubin me-avonosav me-arin lo* — whoever has more merits than sins, it is done badly for him, *ve-domeh ke-mi she-saraf kol ha-Torah kullah* — and he will appear as though he burned the entire *Torah*; his suffering will be so severe that it will look as though he committed the greatest sins imaginable. Conversely, *kol she-avonosav merubin mi-zechuyosav meitivin lo* — one whose sins outweigh his merits will have it well in this world — *ve-domeh ke-mi she-kiyyem kol ha-Torah kullah* — and it will look as though he fulfilled the entire *Torah*.

This, of course, is the classic theodicy invoked to explain *tzaddik ve-ra lo*: God cleans the slate of the righteous through suffering in this world, and rewards the wicked in this world so as to deny them any credit in the world to come. But it directly contradicts our *mishna*, which promises that doing a *mitzvah* leads to good outcomes.

### Abye Days Theory

Abaye's resolution — and Tosafot's reading of Abaye is cleaner than Rashi's here — is that these opposing outcomes operate on the level of individual days rather than one's entire life. The *mishna* in Kiddushin describes the overall trajectory of one's life: a *tzaddik* will ultimately have it good and a *rasha* will ultimately have it bad. But the *baraita* describes what happens on any given day: there will be specific days on which the *tzaddik* suffers greatly — as though he had done the worst things imaginable — and specific days on which the *rasha* prospers remarkably. The two sources are thus not in conflict; they describe different timeframes.

### Rabbi Yaakov

Rava offers a different resolution entirely: the *baraita* that teaches these counterintuitive outcomes reflects the view of Rabbi Yaakov, because *de-ammar sechar mitzvah be-hai alma lekka* — Rabbi Yaakov maintains that there is no reward for *mitzvos* in this world whatsoever. All reward is reserved exclusively for the world to come. According to Rabbi Yaakov, the *tzaddik* suffering in this world is not a theodicy requiring explanation — it is simply the expected state of affairs. This world is not where the divine accounting is settled. Our *mishna* in Kiddushin, which speaks of this-worldly reward, reflects the majority view; the *baraita* reflects the position of Rabbi Yaakov.

### Problem: Tzaddik Vra Lo

Rabbi Yaakov's position is articulated in a *baraita* that explores it through concrete cases. Rabbi Yaakov says: there is not a single *mitzvah* written in the *Torah* alongside its stated reward where the real fulfillment of that reward does not depend on *techiyas hamessim* — the resurrection of the dead — rather than this-worldly realization. Consider *kibbud av v'em*, which promises *lema'an ya'arichun yamecha u-le'ma'an yitav lach*. Consider *shilluach haken*, which likewise promises *lema'an yitav lach ve-ha'arachta yamim*. Now consider the following case: a father tells his son to go up to a tower and bring down some chicks. The son goes up, performs *shilluach haken* by sending away the mother bird, takes the chicks, and on the way down falls and dies. *Heichen tovas yamav shel zeh? Ve-heichen arichas yamav shel zeh?* Where is the good that was promised? Where is the length of days? This is the problem of *tzaddik ve-ra lo* in its starkest and most personal form.

### Solution: Olam Haba

Rabbi Yaakov's answer is sweeping and unambiguous: *lema'an yitav lach* — to the world that is entirely good; *lema'an ya'arichun yamecha* — to the world that is entirely long. Every promise of reward in the *Torah* refers to *olam haba*, a world that is *kullo tov* and *kullo aroch*. There is no commitment in the *Torah* to reward in this world. This resolution eliminates the problem entirely by relocating its terms: the promises are real, but they belong to a different register of existence altogether.

### Hypothetical Challenge

The *gemara* immediately probes this answer. Perhaps, it suggests, the case Rabbi Yaakov describes — where someone performs two *mitzvos* and immediately suffers a fatal accident — is purely hypothetical, and in reality it never happens that way. Perhaps everyone who has ever honored their parents and performed *shilluach haken* has in fact lived long. If so, Rabbi Yaakov has built his theology on an imagined scenario that has no real-world instantiation.

The response is that *Rabbi Yaakov maiseh chaza* — Rabbi Yaakov actually witnessed such an event, and therefore he knows it is not hypothetical. The *gemara* continues probing: perhaps the young man died because he was harboring sinful thoughts at the time, and it was those thoughts, not the failure of the promise, that caused his death. To this the *gemara* responds: *machashavah ra'ah ein ha-kadosh baruch hu metzarfah le-ma'aseh* — God does not combine a sinful thought with an act and punish a person for it. Mere thought does not constitute transgression.

Perhaps, then, he was harboring thoughts of *avodah zarah* — for which there is a biblical source (*lema'an tpos es beis yisrael be-libbam*) suggesting that even the contemplation of idolatry can be held against a person? To this the *gemara* effectively says: if anything, that actually reinforces Rabbi Yaakov's point. *I-sal-ka da'atach sechar mitzvah be-hai alma* — if you truly believed that *mitzvos* are rewarded in this world — *ammai lo aggen mitzvah aleh ke-heichi de-lo leyessi lidei hirhur* — then the *mitzvah* he was in the midst of performing should have protected him from having that idolatrous thought in the first place. The very fact that the *mitzvah* failed to protect him is itself evidence that *mitzvos* carry no this-worldly protective guarantee. The real world does not work the way a naive reading of the *Torah*'s promises would suggest, and therefore those promises must be referring to something beyond this world entirely. We will pick up from here in our next *shiur*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 40

## Reward Theology

### Mishna Rewards

The daf opens at the bottom of 39b, following a sequence of *mishnayot* categorizing *mitzvot*. The *mishna* there promises that whoever performs a *mitzvah* is *nochal et ha'aretz* — he inherits a portion of the World to Come — and, further, that he reaps the rewards of his deeds in this world as well. This claim stands in some tension with the *mishna* in *Pe'ah*, which identifies only a specific set of *mitzvot* for which one enjoys the fruits of his labor in this world. The *Gemara* had attempted various harmonizations, including the suggestion that God evens out the accounts over the course of a lifetime — some days of blessing, some of tragedy — so that, broadly speaking, one's life reflects one's deeds. That is how *Tosafot* reads the passage. But the *Gemara* then raises the deeper question: is there not a fundamental theological debate lurking here?

### R. Yaakov Position

The *Gemara* introduces the famous position of Rabbi Yaakov, encapsulated in the phrase *schar mitzvah be-hai alma leka* — reward for a *mitzvah* in this world simply does not exist. All the Torah's promises of reward are promises for the *olam ha-ba*. This principle represents a fundamental resolution of the challenge of *tzaddik ve'ra lo* — the suffering of the righteous — by relocating all recompense to the next world. The paradigmatic case that compelled Rabbi Yaakov to articulate this position is the child who obeys his father, performs *shiluach ha-ken*, and then falls from the ladder and dies. He fulfilled two *mitzvot* for which the Torah explicitly promises long life, and yet he perished. Even if one insists this particular case never occurred, the scenario is realistically conceivable — and our honest reckoning with the world demands that we acknowledge it. The Torah's promises, then, must be understood as directed toward *olam ha-ba*.

### Maharsha Solution

The *Maharsha* raises a pointed difficulty against Rabbi Yaakov's position. One can plausibly reinterpret broad promises like *ve-ha'arachta yamim le-ma'an yitav lach* as referring to *olam ha-ba*, but what does one do with the very concrete and specific *blessings* and *curses* enumerated in the Torah — things like *yakecha Hashem bashechin uvakadachas*? These cannot be casually redirected to the next world. The *Maharsha* therefore proposes a crucial distinction: these detailed promises operate at the level of the *tzibur* — the community as a whole. When an entire people is meritorious or sinful, those national promises are fulfilled in this world. But the challenge of *schar ve-onesh* — particularly *tzaddik ve'ra lo* — is acutely felt at the individual level, not the communal one. The *Maharsha* is careful to situate the terms of the *Gemara*'s discussion without resolving the broader and more searing questions that communal tragedies — including those most recent to us — thrust upon this framework.

---

## Shlichei Mitzvah

### Not Injured

The *Gemara* now introduces a new apparent difficulty. Rabbi Elazar teaches: *shluchei mitzvah einam nizokin* — those who go out to perform a *mitzvah* are not injured along the way. This statement seems to operate in a very practical, this-worldly register: those engaged in *mitzvot* enjoy divine protection from harm. But this immediately creates a tension: if we have just concluded, following Rabbi Yaakov, that all the Torah's promises of benefit are for *olam ha-ba*, how do we account for Rabbi Elazar's teaching, which plainly implies protection in this world? And more concretely — what happened to the child who fell from the ladder? He was engaged in a *mitzvah*, and yet he was harmed.

### Fixed Danger

The *Gemara* offers an initial resolution: *hatam be'halichatan shani* — the case of the child was different, because he was on his way *back* from the *mitzvah*, not in the midst of performing it. But the *Gemara* immediately rejects this, since Rabbi Elazar explicitly extends the protection to both going and returning — *lo be'halichatan velo be'chazirasom*. The *Gemara* therefore offers a different answer: *sula ra'ua hava* — the ladder was rickety. The principle is *dekevia hezeika* — where there is a fixed and established danger, one cannot rely on a miracle for protection. *Vechol heicha dekevia hezeika lo samchinan anisa* — wherever there is a fixed and predictable risk, we do not depend on a *nes* to save us. Rabbi Elazar's guarantee of protection applies to unexpected, unforeseeable harm — not to situations where the person has voluntarily entered into objectively dangerous circumstances. This principle also carries a significant implication for the original puzzle: the Torah's promise of long life cannot be invoked by someone who acts negligently and exposes himself to unwarranted risk. One cannot cite divine protection as a license for recklessness.

### Samuel Example

The *Gemara* offers a scriptural illustration of this principle from the story of Samuel. When God commanded Samuel to anoint David as king, Samuel cried out: *eich elech ve-shama Shaul ve-harogani* — how can I go, when Saul will hear and kill me? Samuel was engaged in a *mitzvah* of the highest order — anointing a king at God's direct command. Why did he not simply rely on the principle that *shluchei mitzvah einam nizokin*? The answer is *kevia hezeika shani* — the danger was real and fixed. Saul's murderous jealousy was not an unlikely or unforeseeable hazard; it was a concrete and predictable threat. Rabbi Elazar's protection is from the unexpected; it does not generate miracles in the face of genuine, established danger. One might ask whether Samuel's very fear represents a failing, given the principle in another context that *mora lo ya'aleh al rosho*. A distinction can be drawn: being afraid and taking necessary precautions is not the same as being paralyzed by fear. But the question is not easily dismissed.

---

## Acher Apostasy

### Rav Yosef

The *Gemara* now introduces a dramatic statement from Rav Yosef: *ilmalei darsha Acher lehai kra ke-Rabbi Yaakov bar barteh lo chata* — had Acher, Elisha ben Abuya, known how to interpret the relevant verse the way Rabbi Yaakov, the son of his daughter, interpreted it, he would not have sinned. Several things are striking here. First, this passage attributes Acher's apostasy to a theological failure — his inability to reconcile what he witnessed in the real world with the Torah's apparent promises of reward. This sits alongside the famous account in *Chagigah* that attributes his heresy to his experiences in *pardes*, to what he beheld in the supernal realm. One may suggest that both are true — that his mystical experience planted seeds of doubt, which were then watered by his encounter with manifest injustice in the world; or conversely, that his shattering experience of injustice made him vulnerable to a misreading of what he had seen on high. But on the reading presented here, what ultimately drove Acher to apostasy was his inability to interpret the Torah's promises in the way Rabbi Yaakov had — as directed toward *olam ha-ba* rather than this world. Second, a student noted — and this is confirmed by *Tosafot* — that Rabbi Yaakov was in fact Acher's grandson, the son of his daughter. The poignancy of this is unmistakable: the very theological resolution that might have saved the grandfather was articulated by the grandson, who wrestled with the same agonizing question and remained within the fold.

### Acher Stories

The *Gemara* then asks: *ve-Acher mai hu* — what precisely did Acher witness that broke him? Two accounts are offered. Some say he witnessed the very case we discussed — a child being sent by his father to perform *shiluach ha-ken*, who then died. Others say it was something altogether different and more visceral.

### Chutzpit

The second account describes what Acher saw regarding the tongue of Chutzpit the Meturgeman, one of the martyrs of the Hadrianic persecution. *De-hava garer lei davar acher* — a pig was dragging it through the refuse heaps. Acher exclaimed: *amar peh she-hefik margaliot* — the mouth from which pearls once emerged, the mouth of the greatest teacher, *yelachech afar* — shall now be licking the dust? For Acher, this was the final rupture. Where were God's promises? Where was justice? His faith shattered, *nafak chata* — he went out and sinned. The *Gemara* presents this as the alternative to the first account, though, as noted, both experiences may have contributed cumulatively to his collapse. What is clear is that his crisis was genuinely theological — the apparent refutation of divine justice in the most brutal possible terms — and that his tragedy lies in not having possessed the interpretive key that his own grandson would later articulate.

---

## Active vs. Passive

### Rami Contradiction

Rami bar Tuvia bar Rav Kisna posed a contradiction to Rava. The *mishna* states that the four categories of people who possess all the relevant merits — one who does a single *mitzvah* — are benefited thereby. The formulation *assah in, lo assah lo* implies that only active performance generates merit; passive non-performance does not. Yet a *baraita* states: *yashav ve-lo avar aveirah* — if a person simply sits and passively refrains from transgression, *notnin lo sechar ke-oseh mitzvah* — he is rewarded as though he performed an active *mitzvah*. This seems to imply that one can accumulate *mitzvot* simply by staying home and doing nothing objectionable — a conclusion that is both intuitively strange and in direct contradiction with the *mishna*.

### Temptation Resistance

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction with a crucial distinction. *Hatam kegon she-ba'at davar aveirah leyado ve-nitzal himena* — the *baraita* does not describe a person who merely happened not to sin because the opportunity never arose. It describes a person to whom the temptation came, who encountered the pull of transgression directly, and who found the strength to resist. This is not simply the absence of a bad act — it is an act of moral fortitude, and it therefore earns a reward equivalent to performing a positive *mitzvah*. The analogy is instructive: a *mitzvat lo ta'aseh* normally means one simply refrained from doing something wrong, which is quite different from actively doing something good, much like a *mitzvat aseh*. But when genuine temptation presents itself and one overcomes it, that resistance itself constitutes an act — an act of the will and character that carries the weight of positive performance.

To illustrate this, the *Gemara* cites the case of Rav Chanina bar Pappa. A certain *matronita* — a Roman woman of rank and power — propositioned him. The power differential made direct refusal dangerous. He uttered a certain mystical word, causing his body to be covered with boils and sores, rendering himself repugnant so that she would leave him alone. She, however, also possessed knowledge of mystical arts, and she reversed his condition, healing him. Now without recourse, Rav Chanina fled and hid in a certain *bei banei* — a bathhouse that was known to be so haunted by *mazikin* that even two people entering it in daytime would be harmed. He preferred the company of demons to the risk of succumbing to her. The next morning, the rabbis asked him who had protected him through the night. He replied that two of Caesar's soldiers had guarded him. The rabbis immediately drew the inference: *shema davar ervah ba le-yadcha ve-nitzalta himeno* — perhaps you were confronted with sexual temptation and were delivered from it? For the tradition teaches: *kol ha-ba davar ervah le-yado ve-nitzal himeno, osin lo nes* — anyone to whom sexual temptation comes and who is saved from it, a miracle is performed on his behalf. And of course, that is precisely what had occurred.

---

## Temptation Stories

### R. Tzadok

The *Gemara* introduces a verse: *gibbore koach osei devaro lishmoa be-kol devaro* — mighty ones who do God's word, who hearken to the voice of His word. This is read as a reference to those who display heroic valor in resisting temptation — *kegon Rabbi Tzadok ve-chaverav*, like Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues.

Rabbi Tzadok was similarly propositioned by a *matronita*. Recognizing that direct refusal was dangerous — she was a powerful woman, and the word *matronita* alone signals her social power — he played for time. He said: *chalash li libbai*, my heart is weak, *lo matzinna*, I do not have the strength for such relations; *ika midi le-meichal*, do you have something to eat? She replied that there was forbidden food in the house — pork. His response was striking: *mai nafka mina de'avid ha achul ha* — what difference does it make? One who does this will eat this. If I am to be brought so low as to violate one prohibition, I might as well be brought low enough to violate another as well. This can be read on multiple levels: as a lament about the gravity of what she was asking, or as an attempt to communicate to her the weight of what she was demanding — that for him, both acts are equivalent sins against God. She apparently misread him, taking him at face value and going to heat up the pork. *Salik ve-yativ be-gavah* — he rose and sat inside the oven itself. He was prepared to die rather than transgress. She asked him, *mai hai* — what is this? He replied: *de'avid ha nafil be-ha* — one who commits such a sin falls into such a fire. He would face *gehinnom*. Her response was remarkable: *ei yadei kulei hai lo tza'artich* — had I known it was so weighty to you, I would not have put you through this.

### Rav Kahana

Rav Kahana was a wicker-basket seller. A *matronita* propositioned him while he was in a compromised position — unable to simply refuse. He told her: *izil ikashit nafshai* — let me go make myself presentable. He went up to the roof, and from the roof he fell — or more precisely, he jumped — to the ground below. The *Gemara* records that he fell, but given the context and the parallel with Rabbi Tzadok's act, it appears that these rabbis were prepared to take their own lives rather than transgress. This raises significant *halachic* and theological questions: the principle of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* — be killed rather than transgress — applies when an external agent threatens death unless you violate a prohibition, but taking one's own life proactively is a different matter. The *Ashkenazi* *rishonim* grappled with precisely this question in the context of the Crusades. Whether the prohibited act here constitutes *giluy arayot* — which would create a *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* obligation — is itself debated among the *rishonim*. But in any case, the *Gemara*'s framing presents this as a heroic act beyond what might normally be expected.

Elijah appeared and caught Rav Kahana in mid-air. Elijah remarked with a kind of celestial complaint: *atrachtan arba mea parsa* — you made me travel four hundred *parsa* to catch you. Rav Kahana replied: *mi garim li? lav aniyuta?* — what caused this to me? Was it not my poverty? I have to sell wicker baskets for a living, and that exposes me to this kind of encounter. The response came: Elijah gave him a basket full of gold coins. The rescue and reward are connected — his heroic resistance was not only acknowledged but compensated.

### Heroic Resistance

One might ask what connects these narratives to the *pasuk* cited: *gibbore koach osei devaro lishmoa be-kol devaro*. The word order is curious — it says they *do* God's word and then *hearken* to it. Doing before listening? The *Maharsha* reads this as a precise *diyuk*: *lishmoa be-kol devaro* refers not to the person doing but to God — if you are *gibbore koach* who do God's work, then God *listens* to your voice, God hearkens to your cry. That is why these rabbis who displayed such fortitude were answered with miraculous intervention. There is also a reading in which *lishmoa be-kol devaro* describes a depth of internalization — not merely performing the deed but hearing and feeling the moral and religious imperative so profoundly that it provides the inner strength for these extraordinary acts of resistance when demanded.

It is worth noting that these stories invert a familiar cultural script: it is the women who are the aggressors and the men who resist, an echo of the Yosef narrative. Whether this represents a conscious literary parallel or a subversion of assumed gender roles in the world of temptation, the *Gemara* makes clear that the capacity for moral heroism in the face of powerful temptation is what it means to be among the *gibbore koach* of whom the *pasuk* speaks.

---

## Specific Rewards

### Bird Sending

The *Gemara* returns to the theme of reaping rewards in this world. Rava posed a contradiction to Rav Nachman from the *mishna* in *Pe'ah*: *eilu devarim she-adam oseh otam ve-okhel peiroteihem ba-olam ha-zeh ve-ha-keren kayemet lo la-olam ha-ba* — these are the things a person does and eats their fruits in this world while the principal remains for the world to come. The list comprises honoring one's father and mother, acts of lovingkindness, bringing peace between people, and Torah study — *keneged kulam*, which outweighs them all. For each, a *pasuk* is cited demonstrating this-worldly reward: *kibbud av va-em* carries *lema'an ya'arichun yamecha u-lema'an yitav lach*; *gemilut chasadim* carries *rodef tzedakah va-chesed yimtza chayyim tzedakah ve-khavod*; making peace is connected through a *gezeirah shavah* of *redifah* linking *bakesh shalom ve-rodfehu* with *rodef tzedakah va-chesed*; and *talmud Torah* carries *ki hi chayyecha ve-orech yamecha*. But then — why is *shiluach ha-ken* not included? The Torah explicitly promises *lema'an yitav lach ve-ha'arachta yamim* for sending away the mother bird! The *Gemara*'s answer that *tana ve-shayer* — the list is simply incomplete — is immediately challenged: the *mishna* opens with *eilu devarim*, "these are the things," implying an exhaustive enumeration.

### Five Mitzvot

Rava then cites Rav Idi's explanation, which provides the underlying principle governing the list's selection. The *pasuk* in question is *imru tzaddik ki tov ki peri ma'alaleihem yokhelu* — say to the righteous who is good, that they will eat the fruit of their deeds. The operative phrase is *tzaddik ki tov*, and the *Gemara* now unpacks its significance: *vechi yesh tzaddik tov ve-yesh tzaddik she-eino tov* — is there indeed a righteous person who is good and one who is not? Yes: *tov la-shamayim ve-labriyot zehu tzaddik tov* — one who is good to God and to other human beings is a *tzaddik* who is good; *tov la-shamayim ve-ra la-briyot* — one who is scrupulous in his religious obligations but who treats his fellow human beings poorly — *zehu tzaddik she-eino tov*, that is a *tzaddik* who is not good.

This is a striking *Gemara* with profound religious implications. It gives a name to a phenomenon many observe: the person who is *frum* in the ritual domain but morally deficient in the interpersonal one. The *Gemara* does not deny his status as *tzaddik* — it acknowledges the religious dimension — but it identifies the absence of the *tov*. And the theological point follows directly: the *mitzvot* that yield fruit in this world are precisely those that make one a *tzaddik ki tov* — acts that are not merely between the person and God, but that generate genuine goodness in the world. *Kibbud av va-em*, *gemilut chasadim*, *havaat shalom* — these are acts that concretely improve the lives of real people. *Shiluach ha-ken* is a legitimate *mitzvah* for which one is indeed rewarded, but it is a *mitzvah* between person and God; it does not generate goodness in the human world in the same way, and therefore it was not included in this particular list. The list is not exhaustive of all *mitzvot* rewarded in this world — it is a curated list of *mitzvot* whose reward flows naturally from the goodness they create.

---

## Tzaddik Ki Tov

### Good vs. Righteous

The distinction between *tzaddik tov* and *tzaddik she-eino tov* merits further reflection. The categories represent, in one framing, the distinction between vertical piety — the relationship between person and God — and horizontal piety — the relationship between person and fellow. A person may be exemplary in the former and deficient in the latter. The *Gemara* does not collapse the categories, but it insists that truly reaping the fruits of one's deeds in this world is connected specifically to the *tzaddik ki tov* — the person whose righteous acts are also good, that is, acts that create genuine benefit in the world.

There is another way to read the *tov* here: not merely morally good, but *creating goodness in the world*. If one's *tzidkut* is a *tzidkut* of goodness in this world — acts that concretely help people, that improve reality, that ripple outward — then the reward in this world is not simply God's direct recompense but the natural consequence of having created a better world. The people one helped are real; the kindness one showed has effects; the peace one fostered endures. The reward is, in a sense, built into the very nature of the deed.

### Rasha Ra

The parallel formulation concludes the *derashah*: *oi la-rasha ra* — woe to the wicked evil one, *ki gemul yadav ye'aseh lo* — for the deeds of his hands shall be done to him. The *Gemara* asks: *vechi yesh rasha ra ve-yesh she-eino ra* — is there a wicked person who is evil and one who is not evil? Yes: *ra la-shamayim ve-labriyot hu rasha ra* — one who sins against God and against other human beings is a *rasha ra*; *ra la-shamayim ve-eino ra la-briyot* — one who transgresses against God but is good to people — *zeh rasha she-eino ra*, that is a transgressor who is not evil. The *Gemara* notes that the Hebrew word *rasha* already carries a moral connotation — it implies wickedness beyond mere transgression — so one might speak of a good transgressor, a person who violates religious norms but who is genuinely kind and beneficent toward others.

---

## Merit Dividends

### Merit Structure

A *Tosefta* in *Pe'ah* now elaborates the underlying structure of reward and punishment, developing a contrast between the handling of good deeds and bad deeds. *Ha-zechut yesh la keren ve-yesh la peirot* — merit, the reward for a good deed, has both principal and dividends. The principal is deposited, as it were, for *olam ha-ba*, while the dividends — the fruits — are enjoyed in this world. The *pasuk* is again *imru tzaddik ki tov ki peri ma'alaleihem yokhelu* — they will eat the fruit of their deeds, implying reward beyond the mere act itself, the dividends of the principal investment.

### Sin Structure

Sin, by contrast, is treated differently. *Aveirah yesh la keren ve-ein la peirot* — a sin has only principal, not dividends. You are paid back for the sin itself, but punishment does not ramify and extend indefinitely beyond it. The *pasuk* is *oi la-rasha ra ki gemul yadav ye'aseh lo* — *lo*, to him specifically, the pay-back of his own hands. The word *lo* signals a payment calibrated to the act, not extended beyond it.

### Bearing Fruit

However, the *Tosefta* confronts a contradicting verse: *ve-yokhelu mi-peri darkam u-mi-mo'atzoteihem yisbe'u* — they will eat from the fruits of their paths and be sated from their scheming. This speaks of *fruit* in the context of the wicked — implying that the wicked too can suffer the extended consequences of their sins. The resolution is the same principle encountered earlier in the discussion of *tzaddik ki tov*: *aveirah she-osah peirot yesh la peirot* — a sin that bears fruit, that has a real-world impact beyond the individual act, *yesh la peirot* — there the punishment extends accordingly. *Ve-she-einah osah peirot ein la peirot* — if the sin is contained and does not ramify into harm for others, punishment is limited to the sin itself. This is a precise parallel to the structure of reward: just as good deeds that generate goodness in the world earn dividends, bad deeds that generate harm in the world incur extended punishment. *Rashi* explains this to include cases where one's sin leads others to sin as well — the public transgressor who gives others license to follow his example. The underlying principle is consistent: real-world impact, in either direction, changes the magnitude of one's account.

---

## Thought Ethics

### Good Thoughts

The *Gemara* now turns to a related distinction — between good thoughts and bad thoughts. *Machshava tova mitzarfah l'ma'aseh* — God joins a good thought to a deed, crediting it as if one had acted. The source is *az nidbru yirei Hashem ish el re'ehu vayakshev Hashem vayishma vayikasev sefer zikaron lifanav liyirei Hashem ulchoshvei shmo* — those who feared God spoke one to another, and God listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear God and *choshvei shemo* — those who think about His name. Rav Assi derives: *afilu chashav adam la'asot mitzvah ve-ne'enas ve-lo asah* — even one who intended to perform a *mitzvah* but was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, *ma'aleh alav ha-katuv ke-ilu asah* — Scripture accounts it to him as though he had done it. The critical qualifier is *ne'enas* — he was compelled by circumstance, not by a change of heart. A person who genuinely intended to perform a *mitzvah* and truly tried, but was thwarted by external forces, receives full credit. The formulation does not apply to one who thought about performing a *mitzvah* and then thought better of it.

### Bad Thoughts

The treatment of bad thoughts is markedly asymmetrical. *Machshava ra'ah ein Hakadosh Baruch Hu mitzarfah l'ma'aseh* — God does not join a bad thought to a deed. One is not punished merely for having entertained sinful thoughts. The *pasuk* is *avon im ra'iti be-libi lo yishma Hashem* — if I see iniquity in my heart, God does not listen — meaning God does not punish for mere thought. However, another verse says: *hineni mevi el ha'am hazeh ra'ah peri machshavotam* — I will bring evil to this people, the fruit of their thoughts. This appears to contradict the first: here people *are* punished for their thoughts. The resolution follows the same logical structure used earlier: *machshava she-osah pri* — a thought that bears fruit, that becomes an action, *Hakadosh Baruch Hu mitzarfah l'ma'aseh* — then God does join it to the deed and punishment is extended to include the thought. *Machshava she-ein bah pri* — a thought that does not produce action — *ein Hakadosh Baruch Hu mitzarfah l'ma'aseh* — is not joined to the deed and incurs no punishment.

### Idolatry

A further verse complicates this picture: *le-ma'an tfos et beit Yisrael be-libam* — in order to seize the house of Israel by their hearts. This appears to describe punishment for thought itself, independent of action. Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains: *hu be-avoda zara hu de-chtiv* — this verse refers specifically to *avoda zara*, idolatry, which is an exceptional case. *Chamura avoda zara ke-neged kol ha-mitzvot* — idolatry is as weighty as all the *mitzvot* combined; *kol ha-kofer bah ke-modeh be-chol ha-Torah kulah* — whoever repudiates idolatry is as though he has affirmed the entire Torah; and correspondingly, whoever embraces it, even in thought, has in some fundamental sense rejected everything. One may ask whether the exceptional treatment of *avoda zara* reflects the sheer gravity of the act, making even the thought a form of the transgression, or whether it reflects the *Rambam*'s view that *avoda zara* is fundamentally about belief rather than act — so that the thought itself, the very considering of other deities, already constitutes a departure from God. On that reading, there is no clean separation between the thought of *avoda zara* and *avoda zara* itself.

### Habitual Sin

The *Gemara* now introduces a related principle from Rav Huna. *Keivan she-adam avar aveirah ve-shanah bah, hutrah lo* — once a person has committed a sin and repeated it, it becomes permitted to him. The *Gemara* immediately asks: does it literally become permitted? *Ela na'aseit lo ke-heter* — no, it becomes in his own mind and experience as though it were permitted. Once a person has transgressed repeatedly, the sense of prohibition has eroded; the act no longer feels off-limits or taboo. The consequence for the laws of thought is direct: for a habitual sinner, the plan to sin is itself punishable, because at this stage the gap between planning and doing has effectively closed. If a person who has violated a prohibition twice is now planning to do so again, his restraint at any given moment is most likely circumstantial — not a genuine act of resistance, but merely a missed opportunity. *Rashi* states this explicitly: at this stage, if someone did not commit the sin, it was probably only because the opportunity was not available. Therefore God counts the plan as the act. This contrasts with the general rule — for the ordinary person, who has not habituated himself to a given sin, planning to transgress does not incur punishment if the action is not carried out.

---

## Sin Privacy

### Private Sin

Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Chanina: *noach lo le-adam she-ya'avor aveirah be-seter ve-al yechallel shem Shamayim be-farhesya* — it is better for a person to commit a transgression in private than to desecrate God's name in public. The principle is rooted in the danger of *chillul Hashem* — of the public disgrace and its consequences. When a visibly observant person sins openly, the transgression is not merely a violation between himself and God; it becomes a *davar she-osah peirot*, a sin that bears fruit, that impacts how others see God and Torah, and potentially licenses others to transgress as well. Better to commit one *aveirah* than two. The *pasuk* offered is from *Yechezkel*: *ish gilulav lechu avdu ve-achar im einchem shome'im elai ve-et shem kodshi lo techallalu* — go worship your idols if you will not listen to Me, but do not desecrate My holy Name.

### Anonymity

Rav Ilai HaZaken elaborates with practical instruction: *im ro'eh adam she-yitzro mitgaber alav*, if a person sees that his *yetzer hara* is overpowering him, *yeilech le-makom she-ein makirim oto* — let him go to a place where he is not recognized, *ve-yilbash shechorim ve-yitkaseh shechorim* — dress in dark clothes and cover himself in dark clothing, *ve-ya'aseh mah she-libbo chafetz* — and do as his heart desires, *ve-al yechallel shem Shamayim be-farhesya* — but he shall not desecrate God's name publicly. *Rashi* notes that dressing in black and covering oneself signals mourning or social marginality, prompting others to keep their distance and thus affording anonymity. Some *rishonim*, citing *Rabbeinu Chananel*, suggest that the process itself — donning dark clothing, going to an unfamiliar place — will diminish the desire; but the plain meaning of *ya'aseh mah she-libbo chafetz* does not support reading this as mere misdirection toward the intended act. No license is being granted; the person is still sinning. What is being addressed is the *manner* of sinning, given that the sin will occur in any case.

This teaching raises practical questions that echo through later *halachic* discussion. If the availability of a private sinning option removes the only social barrier that might have prevented the sin entirely, then the advice is counterproductive. The case of the *yarmulke* in the movie theater — a question put to Rav Moshe Feinstein — captures exactly this tension: should one remove the *kippah* to avoid *chillul Hashem*, or keep it on in the hope that it will deter further transgression? Both considerations are real, and the resolution is not obvious.

### Theological Problem

The *Gemara* now raises the deeper objection. *Ein makifin be-chillul Hashem*, we are told elsewhere. But more fundamentally: is sinning in private really a solution? *Ve-hatanya: kol shelo chas al kavod kono ra'uy lo shelo ba la-olam* — anyone who does not show concern for God's honor is unworthy of having come into the world. Rav Yosef identifies the person described here as *zeh ha-over aveirah be-seter* — one who sins in private. The theological problem is acute: sinning in private, under the assumption that only other people can observe you, demonstrates either a belief that God cannot see you in private or a greater concern for human perception than for divine perception. It is a form of *chillul Hashem* in itself — a practical denial of God's omniscience or a statement about one's hierarchy of concerns.

### Ability Distinction

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — ha de-matsi kayif lei le-yitzrei, ve-ha de-la matsi kayif lei le-yitzrei* — it is not difficult: the two teachings refer to two different situations.
