If a person *has the ability to overcome his *yetzer hara** and restrain himself, then choosing to sin in private is itself a theological transgression. The privacy is what gives him license; without it, he would not sin. In that case, sin in private is *chillul Hashem*, because it demonstrates that one's real deterrent is social rather than divine. If, however, a person genuinely *cannot* overcome his *yetzer hara* and will commit the sin in any case, then at least doing it privately limits the damage — the sin does not become a *davar she-osah peirot*, does not spread, does not license others. In that case, the private sin, while still a transgression, spares the public the *chillul Hashem*. The difficulty, practically speaking, is that we rarely know which category we are in — and the very act of choosing the private option often shapes which category we occupy.

---

## Chillul Hashem

### Unbalanceable

The *Gemara* turns to a teaching from a *mishna* cited from elsewhere: *ein makifin be-chillul Hashem, echad shogeg ve-echad mezid* — we are not *makif* regarding *chillul Hashem*, whether the transgressor acted unintentionally or intentionally. Two interpretations of *makifin* are offered. Mar Zutra says: *she-ein osin ke-chanvani* — God does not extend credit; *hakafah* means putting on account, as a storekeeper might do for a trusted customer. *Chillul Hashem* is not deferred — it is collected immediately. Mar berei de-Ravina interprets *makifin* differently: *she-im hayta shekula machra'at* — even if a person's merits and demerits are perfectly balanced, *chillul Hashem* tips the scales. It is not balanced out by other merits. A person who is otherwise fifty-fifty but has a *chillul Hashem* on his account does not remain fifty-fifty — the scale tilts toward liability. *Chillul Hashem* is, in this sense, unbalanceable: it cannot be offset by accumulated merit on the other side.

---

## Half-Balance

### Fifty-Fifty

The *Gemara* now presents a teaching from the Rabbis that has direct thematic connection to the preceding discussion: *le-olam yir'eh adam atzmo ke-ilu chetzyo chayav ve-chetzyo zakai* — a person should always see himself as though he is half liable and half meritorious. This is a remarkable psychological and theological prescription. The stakes of every single act are thereby made vivid: no one may coast on accumulated credit, and no one may despair at accumulated debt.

### One Act

The teaching continues: *asa mitzvah achat*, if he performs one *mitzvah*, *ashrav* — praised is he, *she-hichria atzmo le-chaf zechut* — for he has tipped the scales in the direction of merit. *Avar aveirah achat oy lo*, if he commits one sin, *she-hichria atzmo le-chaf chova* — he has tipped the scales toward liability. The verse offered is *ve-chotei echad ye'aved tova harbe* — one sinner, or one sin, destroys great good. *Bishvil cheit yechidi she-chata, oved mimenu tovot harbe* — through a single sin, one loses great good. The weight of a single act — in either direction — is not diminished by the lifetime of acts that precede it.

### Majority Rule

Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon adds the communal dimension: *lefi she-ha-olam nidon achar rubo, ve-ha-yachid nidon achar rubo* — the world is judged according to its majority, and the individual is judged according to his majority. The question is always: overall, is this person — is this world — a good one? And because both the individual and the world should be seen as standing precisely at fifty-fifty, a single act by a single person carries maximal weight. *Asa mitzvah achat, she-hichria et atzmo ve-et kol ha-olam le-chaf zechut* — one *mitzvah* tips both the individual and the entire world toward merit. *Bishvil cheit yechidi she-asah zeh, ibeid mimenu u-mi-kol ha-olam tovah harbe* — through a single sin, a person can bring himself and the entire world into deficit. The analogy to electoral politics is apt: a single vote in a single precinct that shifts a state and determines an election is only decisive because the underlying distribution was already so close. The teaching assumes that closeness as the baseline.

---

## Final Day

### Righteous Rebellion

The *mishna* — or rather Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's teaching in this context — introduces a startling claim: *afilu tzaddik gamur kol yamav u-marad b'acharonah, ibeid et ha-rishonot* — even a person who was entirely righteous all his days, if he rebels at the end, he loses all the earlier good. The verse is *tzidkat ha-tzaddik lo tatzilenu be-yom pish'o* — the righteousness of the righteous person will not save him on the day of his transgression.

### Wicked Repentance

The symmetrical case: *afilu rasha gamur kol yamav ve-asah teshuvah be-acharonah, ein mazkirin lo shuv rish'o* — even a person who was entirely wicked all his days, if he repents at the end, his wickedness is no longer recalled. The verse is *ve-rish'at ha-rasha lo yikashel bah be-yom shuvo me-rish'o* — the wickedness of the wicked person will not cause him to stumble on the day he returns from his wickedness.

### Gemara Challenge

The case of *teshuvah* at the end of life is, in one sense, consonant with the tradition's understanding of *teshuvah*'s power. One may still ask how it accounts for real harm caused to others over a lifetime — but at least between the individual and God, the tradition insists that *teshuvah* is always efficacious. The case of last-day rebellion is far more troubling. The *Gemara* presses the obvious difficulty: *ve-nehevei ke-mechtza avonot u-mechtza zachuyot* — let the person at least be considered fifty-fifty! He has ninety years of righteous deeds and one day of rebellion. Why should that single day of rebellion render him entirely wicked and destroy all prior merit?

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish answers: *b'toheh al ha-rishonot* — we are speaking of a case where, on that final day, the person *regrets* his earlier righteous life. He does not merely rebel; he retroactively repudiates the good he had done. This is the inverse of *teshuvah*. *Teshuvah* is effective because genuine regret retroactively undoes the past — the sinner says, had I known better, I would not have done those things, and this sincere retroactive rejection changes the status of the earlier acts. In the same structural logic, a righteous person who ends his life saying, what was the point of all my years of righteousness? I should have lived for pleasure — has retroactively rejected his earlier deeds. By his own declaration, those deeds no longer represent who he truly was. The deeds are, in a sense, disowned.

The question remains, however, and it presses equally on the *teshuvah* side of the ledger: what of the real-world effects of those years? The Torah one taught, the kindnesses one performed, the peace one brought — those affected real people and had real consequences. Can a change of heart at the end retroactively undo what was concretely accomplished? This is one of the deep unresolved tensions in the theology of *teshuvah* and its inverse, and the *Gemara* does not offer a clean resolution.

---

## Three-Fold Cord

### Non-Sinners

The final *mishna* of the first *perek* opens with the phrase *kol* — anyone — and describes those who are engaged in *mikra*, *mishna*, and *derech eretz*: *lo bimehera hu chote* — such a person does not sin quickly. The three elements are worth distinguishing. *Mishna* represents *halacha* — the practical, apodictic teaching of how to live; it is the normative structure of Jewish life. *Mikra* represents the religious connection — engagement with *Tanach* as a mode of connecting to God, to the narrative of the covenant, to the prophetic voice. And *derech eretz* — productive engagement with the world, a profession, real involvement in the workings of human life — keeps one connected to reality and, in its way, also keeps one from sin. The verse cited is *ve-ha-chut ha-meshulash lo bimehera yinatek* — the three-fold cord is not quickly broken.

### Outsiders

The inverse: *ve-khol she-eino lo be-mikra ve-lo be-mishna ve-lo be-derech eretz, eino min ha-yishuv* — whoever lacks all three is not part of settled society. Without a connection to God through *mikra*, without the normative structure of *halacha* through *mishna*, and without genuine engagement in the productive world, a person is on the margins — not really integrated into the fabric of the community.

---

## Tree Parable

### Tzaddik Tree

Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok concludes the *perek* with a parable. *Lamma tzaddikim nimshalim ba-olam ha-zeh le-ilan* — why are righteous people in this world compared to a tree? The tree is rooted in a place of *tahara* — purity — but one branch extends into a place of *tuma*. *Niktzatz nofo* — cut that branch back, *ve-kulo omed be-makom tahara* — and the whole tree stands in purity.

### Suffering Purpose

*Kacha Hakadosh Baruch Hu mevi yissurin al tzaddikim ba-olam ha-zeh kede sheyirshu ha-olam ha-ba* — so too, God brings suffering upon righteous people in this world so that they may inherit the World to Come. The *tzaddik* is essentially rooted in *olam ha-ba* — that is where he truly belongs, that is his real soil. The suffering he experiences in this world trims away whatever has extended into the wrong place. It is not injustice but restoration — returning the *tzaddik* to the fullness of what he truly is, so that when he arrives at *olam ha-ba* he is fully himself. The verse: *reshitcha mitzar va-achritcha yisgeh me'od* — your beginning will be constrained, but your end will flourish greatly.

### Rasha Tree

The inverse parable: *ve-lamma resha'im domim ba-olam ha-zeh le-ilan* — why are the wicked in this world compared to a tree? Their tree is rooted in a place of *tuma*, but a single branch extends into a place of *tahara*. *Niktzatz nofo* — cut that branch back, *ve-kulo omed be-makom tuma* — and the entire tree stands in impurity. *Kacha Hakadosh Baruch Hu mashpia lahem tova la-resha'im ba-olam ha-zeh kede le-hordam le-darga tachtona* — God showers the wicked with goodness in this world in order to bring them to the lowest levels of *gehinnom*. The small branch of goodness — whatever genuine good they had — is trimmed away, and what remains is the root: the core of what they truly were. The verse: *yesh derech yashar lifnei ish ve-achritah darkhei mavet* — there is a path that seems straight before a man, but its end is the ways of death.

With this *Gemara*, the first *perek* of *Kiddushin* comes to a close — a chapter dense with theology: the nature of reward and punishment, the challenge of righteous suffering, the weight of individual acts on the cosmic scale, and the relationship between who we are and what we do, in this world and in the next.

---

---

# Kiddushin 41

## Merit & Mitzvot

### Intro & Prior Mishnah

Daf 41 opens at the very bottom of 40b, in the last of the narrow lines, continuing a discussion about the weight of *mitzvot* and their consequences for the individual. The previous *mishnah* had addressed anyone who performs a single *mitzvah*, enumerating the great good that follows, and conversely, the grave consequences of failing to perform one. The *Gemara* there interpreted this somewhat narrowly — the case of someone exactly balanced at fifty-fifty, for whom a single *mitzvah* tips the scales. That may seem like a narrow reading, since the *mishnah* appears to assign enormous weight to any single *mitzvah* regardless of context. But the *Gemara*'s framing is itself profound: if one is trained to regard oneself as always standing at perfect equilibrium — exactly half merit, half demerit — then every *mitzvah* one is about to perform carries enormous consequence, as does every *mitzvah* one neglects.

### Learning & Character

The *mishnah* that follows shifts from *mitzvot* in the narrow sense to a broader triad: *mikra*, *mishnah*, and *derech eretz*. One who is engaged with all three, the *mishnah* teaches, will not quickly sin — *lo bimhera hu chotei*. The three components map onto distinct dimensions of religious life. *Mikra* — Tanakh — orients a person toward God; it is a framework of religious consciousness. *Mishnah* corresponds to *halakhah*, the legal-observational dimension. *Derech eretz* admits of two interpretations. One reading, associated with the *Rambam* and developed extensively in his writings, is that *derech eretz* means having a livelihood, being embedded in the real world of labor and production — a corrective to the insularity that purely theoretical study can produce. The *Rambam* speaks at length about the dangers of being supported by the community without engaging in productive work. A second reading, which the *Rambam* himself gives in his *Perush HaMishnayot*, understands *derech eretz* as proper conduct between people — good character traits and refined interpersonal behavior. On this reading, the triad encompasses intellectual-religious formation (*mikra*), legal observance (*mishnah*), and character (*derech eretz*).

The *mishnah* is not primarily about reward in this world or the next; it is about what protects a person and keeps him on the right path. Without these three elements, the *mishnah* concludes, one is *eino min hayishuv* — not part of civilized society. With that framing in place, the *Gemara*'s next movement is natural: having discussed *mitzvot*, *mikra*, *mishnah*, and *derech eretz*, it turns to the question of which among them is most fundamental.

---

## Talmud vs. Maaseh

### Question in Lud

The *Gemara* at the close of 40b records the following: Rabbi Tarfon and the elders were reclining in the upper chamber of the house of Nitzah in Lud — an almost Haggadah-like setting, evoking the famous scene in Bnei Brak. The question posed before them was: *talmud gadol o ma'aseh gadol* — which is greater, learning or doing?

### Tarfon vs. Akiva

Rabbi Tarfon answered that *ma'aseh* — action, performance of *mitzvot* — is greater. Rabbi Akiva answered that *talmud* — learning — is greater.

### Consensus Reached

The assembly then reached a consensus: *talmud gadol sheh-hatalmud meivi lidei ma'aseh* — learning is greater, because learning brings one to action. The formulation is striking. The reasoning offered in support of *talmud*'s greatness is itself an argument that *ma'aseh* is the ultimate goal. Learning is declared superior not because it has independent, intrinsic primacy, but because it is the instrument that generates action. At the axiomatic level, then, it almost sounds as though *ma'aseh* is what matters most — *talmud* is a supremely important *hechsher mitzvah*, a preparatory act that makes the real thing possible.

### Tosafot's Question

This tension is precisely what *Tosafot* identifies. The *Tosafot* opens with *teimah* — a difficulty — drawn from a *Gemara* at the end of the first chapter of Bava Kamma. There, Rabbi Yochanan washed his hands after using the bathroom, put on *tefillin*, and taught the following: at a *hesped*, a eulogy, we say *kiyyem* — this person fulfilled a life of *mitzvos* — but we do not say *limeid*, that he taught Torah. The *Gemara* there asks: but since we say *talmud gadol she-hatalmud meivi lidei ma'aseh*, shouldn't it be an even greater compliment to say that someone taught? Why would *limeid* not be said?

Rashi explains the *Gemara*'s question there as follows: *mi nitlah b'mi? kattan nitlah b'gadol* — the lesser depends on the greater. Since the *Gemara* says *talmud meivi lidei ma'aseh*, that actually betrays the fact that *ma'aseh* is the fundamentally superior category. If so, and we are willing to praise someone as a *ba'al ma'asim*, a person of *mitzvos*, should we not be all the more willing to praise him as someone who learned Torah — since *kiyyem* is already the greater compliment? The implication, then, is that *ma'aseh* is genuinely *gadol*, and the *Gemara* in Bava Kamma takes our *Gemara* as evidence of exactly that. *Tosafot* presses this: from that *Gemara*, it appears that declaring *talmud meivi lidei ma'aseh* actually concedes the supremacy of *ma'aseh* — so which is it?

---

## Hierarchy Analysis

### Personal vs. Teaching

*Tosafot* resolves the tension by distinguishing between different contexts. The key line is: *ha l'migmar ha l'agmurei* — this applies to one's own learning, that applies to teaching others. *Klomar*: if the comparison is between your own private learning and your own performance of *mitzvot*, then *ma'aseh* is indeed preferable. *L'migmar l'didei vadai ma'aseh* — when it comes to your own learning for yourself, doing is certainly more important. But when the comparison is between *ma'aseh* and teaching others — *l'agmurei achrinei vadai adif tfei mi-ma'aseh* — teaching others is at a higher level still, and that is why we do not routinely say *limeid* at a *hesped*, since not everyone reaches that level. The result is a hierarchy: one's own private learning is the lowest tier; performing *mitzvot* is the next; and teaching others is the highest religious achievement of all. If you must choose between going to perform a *mitzvah* and going to open a *Gemara* for your own study, you perform the *mitzvah*. But if you must choose between a *mitzvah* and delivering a *shiur*, you deliver the *shiur*.

### Pedagogy Approach

A second interpretive approach within *Tosafot* reframes the *Gemara*'s question entirely. Perhaps the debate was not about axiomatic religious priority at all, but about pedagogy — what is the right course of religious education for someone just beginning? Should one first focus on learning, or on doing more *mitzvos*? The answer, under this reading, is that one should learn first — *ein am ha-aretz chasid*, an unlearned person cannot be truly pious — spend time learning the *Mishnah Berurah*, understand what is required, and then translate that into action. But for someone who has already learned, *ha-ma'aseh tov yoter mi-limmud* — doing is better than further private study. This approach maintains the hierarchy: ultimately it is about doing; learning is the vehicle that brings it about.

### Talmud Gadol

On this reading, to say *talmud gadol* means only that learning is the practically superior starting point, not that it is axiomatically supreme. *Ma'aseh* remains the end; *talmud* is the preferred means, because *talmud* brings to *ma'aseh* while *ma'aseh* does not reciprocally bring to *talmud*. This is a practical preference, not a statement of fundamental ontological superiority.

---

## Talmud Torah Theology

### Talmud Torah Keneged

This question does not rest here. For those who invest their entire lives in *yeshiva* and *kollel*, in uninterrupted learning and teaching, the formulation *talmud meivi lidei ma'aseh* raises a serious challenge. It is worth noting that *talmud Torah keneged kulam* — as it appeared in yesterday's *Gemara* — did not mean that the most important *mitzvah* to perform is *talmud Torah*. The context of that list was *ochel peiroteihen ba-olam hazeh* — things whose benefits one enjoys in this world. *Talmud Torah keneged kulam* in that context may simply mean that among all the things whose reward one reaps in this world, learning Torah produces the most such reward — precisely *because talmud meivi lidei ma'aseh*, because that learning translates into doing, shapes character, and transforms one's relationship to other people. It is not necessarily a declaration that learning is intrinsically the most important *mitzvah*; it may mean that learning is the most generative.

### Kodashim Question

Rabbeinu Yonah raises a pointed challenge: if it is all about *ma'aseh*, if the whole purpose of learning is to translate into action, then why do we learn *Masechet Kodashim* — the entire *Seder Kodashim*? Why do we learn all these *masechtos* dealing with laws that are simply not actionable today? One answer offered is that even abstract *halacha* translates into *yirat shamayim* and shapes character traits. But Rabbeinu Yonah's answer is notably not that *talmud Torah* is valuable even without *ma'aseh* — his answer remains firmly within the framework that learning's purpose is ultimately to shape a religious life.

This position finds expression in the *mishnah* in *Pirkei Avot*: *lo ha-midrash hu ha-ikar ela ha-ma'aseh*. Interestingly, Rabbeinu Yonah himself — who elsewhere argues that learning must translate into doing — interprets that line from *Pirkei Avot* quite differently. He reads it as: you do not primarily influence and teach people through what you say. You influence them through what you do. The injunction is not about the hierarchy of learning versus action in the abstract, but about the mechanism of religious influence: modeling through behavior is more powerful than instruction through speech.

### Two Readings

There is a second, fundamentally different way of reading our *Gemara* — one that does not subordinate learning to action. On this reading, both *talmud* and *ma'aseh* are *mitzvos*, each intrinsically important. The debate is simply: which *mitzvah* is greater — shaking a *lulav* or learning *Gemara*? And the answer is that learning *Gemara* is greater because it is, as it were, a *twofer*: you fulfill the *mitzvah* of *talmud Torah* and you also generate other *mitzvos*. Shaking a *lulav* does not typically lead to additional *mitzvos*; learning does. On this reading, *talmud* does not begin at a lower level than *ma'aseh* and earn superiority only through its instrumental power. Rather, it starts at an equal level and then surpasses *ma'aseh* because it also carries the capacity to bring about additional doing. These are two genuinely distinct theological positions regarding the relationship between *talmud Torah* and *mitzvos* — and this *Gemara* sits at the heart of that debate.

---

## Yosi's Chronology

### Timeline of Mitzvot

The *Gemara* continues with a *baraita*: Rabbi Yosi says *gadol talmud she-kodam la-challah arbaim shanah* — learning is great in that it preceded the *mitzvah* of *challah* by forty years. The Torah commanded *challah*, but the actual performance of that *mitzvah* did not begin until the Jewish people entered the land. Between the giving of the Torah and the first *challah* taken was forty years. For *terumot u-ma'asrot*, 54 years, since those *mitzvos* began only after fourteen years of conquest and settlement following entry into the land. For *shemitah*, 61 years — fourteen years of entering and settling the land, then beginning to count the seven-year *shemitah* cycle. For *yovel*, 103 years — since *yovel* takes effect at the beginning of its fiftieth year, *kasavar yovel mi-techilaso hu mashmit*, meaning the effect of *yovel* kicks in at the start of year fifty, which falls at the end of 49 years of counting after the 54-year baseline, yielding 103.

### Learning Precedence

The point is that just as learning preceded the doing — the Torah was taught and studied long before these *mitzvos* could be performed — so too, judgment and reward for learning come first. This connects to a principle of Rav Hamnuna: *ein techilat dino shel adam ela al divrei Torah* — the first thing a person is judged for is his learning of Torah, as derived from the verse *peter mayim reshit madon*. And correspondingly, just as one is judged first for learning, one is rewarded first for learning: *va-yiten lahem artzos goyim va-amal le'umim yirashu* — God gave them the lands of the nations and the labor of the peoples — *ba-avur yishmeru chukav ve-torasav yintzoru* — because they observed His commandments and guarded His Torah.

The verse links guarding Torah with observing the commandments, and the order matters. The predominant sense throughout this section is not that learning and doing are two entirely unrelated categories ranked independently, with learning simply declared more important. The sense, rather, is that they are tightly related — one leads to the other — and the one that serves as the gateway and generative force is the one for which judgment and reward come first. As noted, that does not preclude the alternative reading, in which learning has equal intrinsic value *plus* additional instrumental value, making it overall superior. But the texture of this *Gemara* leans toward the view that the connection between learning and doing is constitutive, not incidental.

---

## Social Exclusion

### Unfit Witness

The *Gemara* now turns to the social and legal consequences of failing to engage with *mikra*, *mishnah*, and *derech eretz*. Rabbi Yochanan rules: *kol she-eino lo be-mikra ve-lo be-mishnah ve-lo be-derech eretz — pasul le-eidus* — one who is not engaged in learning in any form, not connected to *halakhah*, and lacking decent character traits or a productive livelihood, is disqualified from testimony. The disqualification is *mi-d'rabanan*, but it reflects the view that such a person stands so far outside the structures of normative society that his reliability cannot be assumed.

### Marketplace Eater

A *baraita* adds: one who eats in the marketplace is like a dog — *ha-ochel ba-shuk harey ze domeh le-kelev* — since dogs eat publicly without social inhibition. Some say this disqualifies one from testimony. Rabbi Idi bar Avin rules that the *halacha* follows that view. The *Maharsha* is skeptical that this literally means eating in public, and suggests it refers to grabbing food from a stall — though as the *Maharsha* himself notes, that would simply make the person a *gazlan*, which raises its own questions.

### Character & Fruit

Bar Kappara taught: *ragzan* — an angry person — *lo alta b'yado ela ragzanuto* — gains nothing from his anger but the anger itself. It produces no positive fruit. This connects back to the earlier discussion about *oseh pri* — what does a *mitzvah* or *aveirah* produce in the world? The *ragzan*'s anger produces nothing of value; whatever *pri* it yields is, so to speak, an ulcer. By contrast, a good person — *adam tov* — *mati'imin oto mi-pri ma'asav*, is rewarded with the fruit of his actions. The discussion here is no longer primarily about *mitzvos* and their formal reward but about character itself — what a person's way of being generates in the world.

### Complete Avoidance

Finally, *v'chol she-eino lo be-mikra ve-lo be-mishnah ve-lo be-derech eretz* — one who has no learning, no observance, and neither good character nor a productive livelihood — *dur hana'ah mimenu*: one should make oneself *mudar hana'ah* from such a person, as if by *neder*, keeping maximum distance. The prooftext is *u-v'moshav leitzim lo yashev* — wherever such a person will be found, it will be a gathering of mockers, a place of wasted time and trivial pursuit. This brings the first section of the daf to a close with a rich portrait: beginning from the enormous weight of any single *mitzvah*, moving through the relationship between learning and doing, and arriving at what these values produce — or fail to produce — in a person's character and in their place within society.

---

## Kiddushin Intro

### Mishnah Recitation

With *Hadran alach ha-ishah nikneis*, the massive first chapter — the longest in all of *Shas* — concludes, and the new *perek* begins. The opening *mishnah* announces: *ha-ish mekadesh bo u-v'shlucho* — a man betroths a woman directly or through his agent. *Ha-ishah mitkadeshet bah u-v'shluchah* — a woman may be betrothed directly, by receiving the money herself, or through her agent. The language shifts notably from the previous chapter's *kinyan* terminology: the *Gemara* later observes that *kinyan* was *lishnah d'kra* — the biblical vocabulary — whereas *kiddushin* is the rabbinic conceptualization of the institution.

### Father's Right

The *mishnah* adds: *ha-ish mekadesh et bito k'she-hi na'arah bo u-v'shlucho* — a father has the right to marry off his daughter when she is a *na'arah*, whether he does so directly or through an agent. This is a significant *chiddush*, since one might have thought that a father who is acting not as principal but as representative of his daughter's interest could not further delegate that authority to an agent. The *mishnah* teaches that he can.

The *na'arah* stage — a legally defined period of roughly six months following the onset of physical maturity at age twelve — might seem like an oddly narrow category to specify. But it is extensively developed in *halacha* because the Torah repeatedly invokes the status of *b'neureha beis aviha*, treating this transitional period as legally significant across many contexts. The *pshat* of the *pesukim* may not have conceived of it as a six-month window; *Chazal* derived that formal limitation. But regardless of the precise derivation, it is the critical period of marriageability and transition, dense with legal consequence.

---

## Personal Action

### Why Mention Both

The *Gemara* asks the obvious question: *hashta bi-shlucho mekadesh, bo miba'ya* — if a man can betroth through an agent, does it even need to be stated that he can do it himself? Of course he can do it personally. So why does the *mishnah* mention both? Rav Yosef answers: *mitzvah bo yoter mibishlucho* — to teach that it is preferable to perform the act personally. The mention of both modes is not redundant; it is instructive. The *mishnah* includes the *bo* — the personal performance — precisely to convey that while the *shlucho* is entirely valid, the *bo* is the preferred mode.

### Body Engagement

This principle extends well beyond *kiddushin*. Rav Safra would char the head of the fish or animal himself in preparation for *Shabbos*; Rava would salt the fish himself — despite these being great *Amoraim* whose time was extraordinarily valuable. They engaged their bodies personally in *kvod Shabbos* because *mitzvah bo yoter mi-bishlucho* is a general principle. Rashi explains: *dechi asi gufa be-mitzvot, mekabel schar tvei* — when one engages one's own body in a *mitzvah*, one receives greater reward. But this is not simply an accounting of additional brownie points for greater effort. The deeper point, connected to the earlier discussion of *ochel peiroteihem*, is that personal engagement produces a different kind of connection. When you personally do something, it impacts you differently — it enters your *kishkes*, as it were. The *mitzvah* becomes more real, more embodied, more yours. That is what it means to engage one's very person in the act.

### Man's Prohibition

Some say — *ika de-amri* — that for the man, failing to perform personally is not merely suboptimal but rises to the level of an actual *issur*. The source for this is a ruling of Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav, which the *Gemara* will now introduce: *assur le-adam she-yekadesh isha ad she-yirena* — a man is forbidden to betroth a woman until he has seen her first. This generates an *issur* dimension to the use of an agent when it would result in betrothing a woman one has never seen.

---

## Seeing the Woman

### Rav's Statement

Rav Yehudah says in the name of Rav: it is forbidden for a man to betroth a woman until he has seen her. This was entirely realistic as a concern in a society where betrothal was often arranged through intermediaries, sometimes without any prior meeting between the parties. Sending an agent to perform the act of *kiddushin* could easily mean that the man has never set eyes on his future wife.

### Lest Repulsion

The reason given is: *shema yireh bah davar maguneh ve-titganeh alav* — lest after the marriage he find something repulsive about her and she become repulsive to him. This would violate the obligation of *ve-ahavta le-re'acha kamocha* — love your neighbor as yourself — which extends to one's wife as a fellow human being.

### Marriage Context

One might initially find this rationale somewhat flat — is the whole basis for spousal affection merely the generic commandment to love one's neighbor? But the *Gemara* must be read against its social context. This is not a society in which marriage is primarily an emotional or romantic institution. The scenario being addressed is one where the first time a man might see his wife is at the moment of betrothal, when he hands her the ring. In such a world, where romantic love plays little role in the formation of marriages and people often remain married under deeply imperfect conditions — because divorce, while technically available, involves a *ketubah* payment and carries social weight — it remains genuinely important to ensure that the couple can at minimum regard each other without visceral repulsion. The *ahavah* invoked here is not the *ahavah* of romance; it is the baseline of human decency one owes to any fellow person. And yet there is something profound in insisting on even that baseline. Even in a society where marriage is fundamentally a practical institution, where couples may live together for decades without deep emotional connection, the rabbis are concerned that something as elemental as mutual contempt should not be the starting point.

---

## Men vs. Women

### Women Allowed

The *Gemara* clarifies a textual point about the *mishnah*: when it states *mitzvah bo yoter mi-bishlucho*, this was said specifically about the *seifa* — the latter clause — regarding the woman. *Ha-ishah mitkadeshet bah u-v'shluchah* — for her, it is a *mitzvah* to participate personally, but if she chooses to use an agent, *issur leit bah* — there is no prohibition. For the man, *ika de-amri* that there is an *issur* dimension; for the woman, there is no such *issur*.

### Reish Lakish

Why is there no concern on the woman's side about *ve-ahavta le-re'acha kamocha* — that she might find her husband repulsive? Because of the principle of Reish Lakish: *tav lemeitav tan du mi-lemeitav armelu* — better to sit in tandem than to live as a widow, better to be married, even imperfectly, than to live alone. The presumption is that women are willing to settle to a greater degree than men. Even if a woman does not find her husband particularly appealing, she will not experience the same degree of visceral antagonism that would result on the man's side. Therefore the concern that generates the *issur* for the man — that he will find her repulsive and this will corrode the marriage — does not apply with equal force to the woman.

The *Gemara* acknowledges that this principle carries implications beyond the sociological. The presumption that women are more tolerant of imperfect situations has, in other contexts, fed into a certain passivity around issues of *agunah* — a motivation to not be proactive about resolving situations where a woman is unable to receive a *get*, on the assumption that she can tolerate the circumstance. That is a significant and troubling extrapolation, and the *Gemara*'s observation here about differential marital dynamics should not be read as an endorsement of those downstream applications.

---

## Marriage as Mitzvah

### Language Question

The use of the term *mitzvah* — *mitzvah bo yoter mi-bishlucho* — raises a fundamental question that the *Gemara* has now prompted. The previous chapter analyzed *kiddushin* through the lens of *kinyanim*, commercial-legal transactions. But now the text speaks of *mitzvah*. Why should getting married be a *mitzvah*? If the earlier analysis framed it as an economic institution — the acquisition of a wife — then the language of *mitzvah* seems incongruous, just as one would not invoke *mitzvah bo yoter mi-bishlucho* when purchasing a boat.

### Rishonim Dispute

This prompts a genuine debate among the *Rishonim*. Many *Rishonim* hold that marriage is not a *mitzvah* per se. The majority of those who do consider it a *mitzvah* classify it as a *hechsher mitzvah* — a preparatory act that enables the fulfillment of *pru urvu*, the *mitzvah* to be fruitful and multiply. This is a natural fit: just as *kvod Shabbos* is not itself a Torah-level *mitzvah* but is a *hechsher* for *Shabbos*, so too *kiddushin* may be a *hechsher* for *pru urvu*. The counterargument, raised by the *Rosh*, is that one fulfills *pru urvu* even through children born outside of marriage — even through a *mamzer* — so that *kiddushin* cannot technically be a *hechsher* for the *mitzvah* if the *mitzvah* can be fulfilled without it.

### Rambam's View

The *Rambam*'s position is notably complex. When the *Rambam* discusses the *mitzvah* of *pru urvu*, he frames it as a two-part *mitzvah*: first, to marry a woman, and second, to have children with one's wife. He thus embeds marriage within the *mitzvah* of *pru urvu* itself — at least as the primary mode of fulfillment. Whether the *Rambam* would say one fails to fulfill *pru urvu* entirely through children born out of wedlock is not fully resolved in his writings. The *Rambam* also emphasizes an *issur* dimension: relations outside of marriage are forbidden, and thus one must marry before having children. On that reading, the *mitzvah* to marry is really a necessary condition for avoiding an *issur*, which makes the language of *mitzvah bo yoter mi-bishlucho* somewhat difficult to apply.

### Two Stages

A third dimension of the *Rambam*'s position draws attention to a structural *chiddush* of the Torah: marriage is a two-stage process. Before the Torah, one would proceed directly to living together. The Torah introduces the requirement that *kiddushin* precede *nisuin* — commitment must precede cohabitation. The *Rambam* makes a great deal of this distinction. One way to understand its significance is as follows: if marriage were defined entirely by the lived reality of the relationship — by the daily experience of life together — then any period of difficulty, conflict, or estrangement would undermine the marriage at its foundations. But if there is a prior commitment, a formal contractual bond that precedes and is independent of the lived reality, then the marriage has an anchor that can survive difficult periods. The couple committed before they began living together, and that commitment remains even when the current experience of the marriage is challenging. The *mitzvah* on the *Rambam*'s third reading would then be: when you wish to marry, do so in the manner that the Torah established — go through *kiddushin* first, then *nisuin*, honoring the structure the Torah created.

Practically speaking, it is the first reading — *kiddushin* as *hechsher* for *pru urvu* — that best supports the language of *mitzvah bo yoter mi-bishlucho*, with its parallel to *kvod Shabbos*. The other readings are harder to fit into that mold. It is also worth noting that the formulation *mitzvah bah yoter mi-bishlucha* is applied to the woman as well, even though *pru urvu* is formally the *mitzvah* of the man and not the woman according to standard *halachic* ruling — suggesting the term *mitzvah* may be used here in a looser, less technically precise sense.

The *Gemara* in *Yevamos* discusses whether a man who has already fulfilled *pru urvu* should nonetheless remain married after his wife's death. One answer given there is *lo tov heiyot ha-adam levado* — it is not good for a person to be alone, a value rooted in *Bereishit*. That fundamental human dimension of marriage — the value of shared life — is not captured by the formal *halachic* language of *mitzvah* and *hechsher mitzvah*, but it is real and acknowledged, even if it does not generate formal *halachic* terminology in the present context.

---

## Minor Daughter

### Minor Prohibition

The *mishnah* states that a father betroths his daughter when she is a *na'arah*. The *Gemara* reads this as implying: when she is a *na'arah*, yes — but when she is a *ketanah*, a minor, he should not do so. This supports the ruling of Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav (with some attributing it to Rabbi Elazar): *assur le-adam she-yekadesh et bito ke-she-hi ketanah* — it is forbidden for a father to betroth his minor daughter.

### Consent Required

The reason is: *ad she-tigdal ve-tomar bi-ploni ani rotzah* — she must grow up and say, "I want to marry this specific person." Marriage requires her mature, personal assent to this particular man, and that is simply impossible when she is a minor.

### Adult vs. Minor

*Tosafot* anticipates an obvious question: if we earlier said that a woman can betroth through an agent without having seen the man, relying on the principle that women are willing to settle — *tav lemeitav tan du mi-lemeitav armelu* — why is it *assur* for a father to betroth his minor daughter? *Tosafot* draws a critical distinction. When an adult woman says, "Go find me a husband," she is making a conscious, autonomous decision to accept whoever her agent selects. She has effectively consented in advance to the arrangement and to whatever outcome it produces, and we trust that she will make her peace with it. But a minor never made any such declaration. She never agreed to be betrothed to an unknown party through her father's choice. In the adult woman's case, her willingness to settle was expressed through her own decision to delegate; in the minor's case, no such expression of consent ever occurred. Therefore the concern — that she will find her husband repulsive and the marriage will be deeply troubled — applies on her end as well, and it is *assur*.

### Tosafot Modern

*Tosafot* then adds a poignant comment: *ve-achshav she-anu nogahin le-kadesh benoteinu afilu ketanot* — in our time, we do betroth our daughters even when they are minors. *Haynu mishum she-be-chol yom ve-yom ha-galut mitgaber aleinu* — because each day the exile presses harder upon us. With the Crusades and the mounting persecutions, if a father has the means *now* to provide his daughter with a dowry — *nadan* — and secure her future, *shema le-achar zeman lo yiheyeh sipek be-yado ve-teshev bito agunah le-olam* — lest a time come when he lacks the means and his daughter remains an *agunah* forever, without a husband to protect and provide for her. *Tosafot* thus acknowledges the practice as a deviation from the ideal, justified only by the desperate circumstances of exile.

This passage also raises a broader point. The Torah is replete with cases of fathers marrying off daughters — *natati et biti la-ish hazeh* and similar formulations appear throughout. Yet *Chazal* look at all of this and say it is *assur le-chatchila*. This reflects an important methodological principle: not everything that appears in the Torah, even repeatedly and without any critical framing, should be read as a *mitzvah* or a *le-chatchila* ideal. *Chazal* were capable of recognizing that the Torah sometimes accommodates social realities without endorsing them as the preferred norm.

---

## Agency Sources

### Divorce Source

Having discussed *shlichut* in the context of the *mishnah*, the *Gemara* now asks: *shlichut minalan* — what is the source that one can appoint an agent at all? The *baraita* derives it from the verse about divorce: *ve-shilcha mi-beito* — he shall send her from his house. From the word *ve-shalach* — the active sending — we learn *melamed she-oseh shaliach*, that a man can appoint an agent to give the *get*. This establishes *shlichut* in the context of *girushin*.

### Grammar Rules

From the same verse, the *Gemara* reads *ve-shalcha* — taking the final *heh* without its *mappik*, converting the verb to feminine — to teach *melamed she-ossa shaliach*, that the woman can appoint an agent to receive the *get* on her behalf. And from yet another reading of *ve-shalach ve-shalcha*, the *Gemara* derives *melamed she-shaliach oseh shaliach* — that an agent can in turn appoint a sub-agent. (The full complexity of whether *milei mimsran le-shaliach* limits this in the context of *gittin* is not the *Gemara*'s focus here.)

That establishes *shlichut* from *girushin*. But how do we know *shlichut* works for *kiddushin*?

### Terumah Source

One might suggest simply learning *kiddushin* from *girushin*, but the *Gemara* rejects this: *mah girushin she-ken yeshnan be-al korchah* — *girushin* can be effectuated against the woman's will. A one-sided transaction in which one party holds all authority is structurally simpler: when you are fully in control, it is more obvious that you can delegate. *Kiddushin*, by contrast, requires a meeting of minds between two parties; neither side holds unilateral power. The capacity to delegate in such a context is less obvious and cannot simply be inferred from *girushin*. The *Gemara* therefore derives *shlichut* for *kiddushin* from a different verse: *ve-yatz'ah ve-hayta* — she shall go out and become [the wife of another man]. The *Gemara* reads *havaya* (becoming a wife) as parallel to *yetziah* (leaving through divorce): *mah yetziah mashvei shaliach, af havaya nami mashvei shaliach* — just as you can appoint an agent for divorce, so too for betrothal.

For *terumah*, the *Gemara* derives *shlichut* from the verse *gam atem* — "also you" — in the context of separating *trumat ma'aser*. The word *gam* — "also" — is read to include one's representative: *le-rabot et ha-shaliach*, even your agent counts as "you" in this context.

### Why Different

Why not simply learn *shlichut* for *kiddushin* from *girushin*, and for *terumah* from *girushin* as well? Because each of these domains has distinctive characteristics that make a simple derivation impossible. *Girushin* involves a fundamentally one-sided, passive transaction; *kiddushin* is bilateral and active. *Terumah* involves *kedushah* — a sanctity — that *girushin*, a secular matter, lacks. These differences mean that each domain requires its own source for *shlichut*, which the *Gemara* will now elaborate systematically.

---

## Korban Pesach

### Pesach Scenario

The *Gemara* introduces a third domain of *shlichut* through a *mishnah*: a group — *chabura* — that has pooled to bring a *korban Pesach* together finds that their lamb has run away. They send one member: *tze u-vakesh u-shchot aleinu* — go find it and slaughter it for us. He goes, finds the lamb, and *shechts* it at the *Beit Hamikdash*. Meanwhile, unsure whether he will succeed, they go and purchase another lamb and *shecht* it as well. The *mishnah* works out the rules for which *korban* is valid depending on the order of events — but for the *Gemara*'s purposes, the *case* establishes that the members of the *chabura* can appoint one of their number as *shaliach* to *shecht* the *korban Pesach* on behalf of all.

But why is this even notable? In practice, only one person *shechts* for each group — no one imagines ten people holding the knife together. The distinction lies in the proof: the verse says *ve-shachatu oso kol kehal adat Yisrael bein ha-arbayim* — all the congregation of Israel shall *shecht* it. The *Gemara* asks: does the entire congregation literally *shecht*? Of course not — *eino shocheit ela echad* — only one person *shechts*. *Ela mikan she-shlucho shel adam ke-moto* — this teaches that an agent is like the person himself.

### Kodashim Logic

The *chiddush* of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's derivation is this: if the *pasuk* had simply said one person *shechts* for the household, one might read that as the basic *structure* of the *mitzvah* — the *korban Pesach* just works that way, one person *shechts* on behalf of the group, not as agency but as the fundamental mode. But the *pasuk* says *kol ha-kehal* — the entire congregation — each individual — must *shecht*. That is an individual obligation. And yet individual *shechita* is clearly not what happens; one person *shechts*. The only explanation is that this one person is discharging each individual's personal obligation through *shlichut*. That is the proof.

---

## Set Theory Logic

### Kodashim Traits

Having established *shlichut* in three domains — *girushin*, *terumah*, and *korban Pesach* (*kodashim*) — the *Gemara* asks why each cannot simply be derived from the others, making the separate sources unnecessary. The answer lies in the distinctive characteristics of each domain, and the *Gemara* works through the logic systematically.

*Kodashim* (as represented by the *korban Pesach*) has three notable features: it involves *kedushah* (holiness), it is governed by *machshava* (thought — one can sanctify a *korban* and affect its legal status through intention alone), and *ma'aseihem al yedei shaliach* — actions in the *Beit Hamikdash* are routinely performed through representatives, the *kohanim* acting on behalf of the owners. This third feature means *kodashim* is an environment where the use of agents is the norm, not the exception, which makes it less surprising that *shlichut* would apply there.

### Terumah Traits

*Terumah* shares two of these features: *kedushah* (it is a sanctified portion given to the *kohanim*) and *machshava* (one can designate a portion as *terumah* through thought or speech alone, without a formal physical act). However, *terumah* does not have the feature of *ma'aseihem al yedei shaliach* — the routine delegation of all actions to representatives — in the same way *kodashim* does. The owner's own act of separation is the primary mode.

### Girushin Traits

*Girushin*, by contrast, is essentially *chol* — secular. It involves no *kedushah* whatsoever. The *get* is not a sanctified object; the divorce is not a religious sanctification in the sense of *terumah* or *kodashim*. *Girushin* also has no element of *machshava* affecting the legal status of the transaction — it is a formal legal act, not one governed by intention in the way that sanctification is.

### Universal Application

The *Gemara* thus applies set theory. One cannot learn *shlichut* universally from any two domains that share a distinctive characteristic, because one might argue the shared characteristic is what enables *shlichut* in those domains. *Kodashim* and *terumah* both share *kedushah* and *machshava* — so learning from them together does not prove *shlichut* applies where neither is present. *Terumah* and *girushin* together share a characteristic on the other end: they are both at a level of holiness *less than* that of *kodashim* — and one might argue that *shlichut* requires a lower threshold of holiness than full *kodashim*. That shared feature prevents learning the rule universally from this pair.

But *girushin* and *kodashim* share *no* common characteristic. *Girushin* is *chol*; *kodashim* is the highest level of *kedushah*. *Girushin* has no *machshava*; *kodashim* does. *Girushin* has no routine delegation through agents; *kodashim* does routinely involve agents. Since these two domains share absolutely nothing, and yet *shlichut* applies to both, the principle must be universal — it applies regardless of the presence or absence of any of these features. The *Gemara* concludes accordingly: *shlichut* is established universally from the combination of *girushin* and *kodashim*. The *Gemara* then notes that tomorrow's discussion will address why, given this, the independent verse for *terumah* was nonetheless necessary.

---

---

# Kiddushin 42

## Sources of Shlichut

### Three Sources

The present daf deals with the institution of *shlichut* — agency — and three distinct biblical sources from which it is derived. The first is the law of *terumah*, where the verse reads *gam atem*, "even you," which is understood to include a *shaliach*. The second is *gerushin* (divorce), where the verse *veshilach veshilchah mibeito* — literally, "he shall send her out of his house" — is read as authorizing the appointment of an agent. The third is *korban Pesach*, where the verse states *veshachatu oto kol kehal adat Yisrael bein ha'arbayim*, "and the entire congregation of Israel shall slaughter it at dusk." Since every individual is obligated and yet every individual plainly did not perform the *shechita*, the obvious inference is that one person slaughtered on behalf of each household — a paradigmatic act of agency.

The *gemara* had already observed, on the previous daf, that two of these three sources — *korban Pesach* and *gerushin*/*kiddushin* — together suffice to establish *shlichut* across the full range of *halacha*. From *kodshim* alone one could not learn *gerushin*, since *gerushin* operates through thought (intention), whereas *kodshim* requires a physical act. And from *gerushin* alone one could not learn *kodshim*, for the reverse reason. By anchoring the principle in both extremes, everything between them is included. The question that follows, then, is why the Torah also needs the verse in *terumah*.

### Why Terumah Needed

The *gemara* picks up on 41b with the question: *ve'ella atem gam atem lama li* — why is the phrase *atem gam atem* in the *terumah* context needed at all, if *shlichut* can already be derived from *korban Pesach* and *gerushin*?

### Gam Atem - Like You

The *gemara* answers by invoking the teaching of Rabbi Yannai: *gam atem* does not come merely to affirm that a *shaliach* can separate *terumah*. That much might be derived elsewhere. Rather, it comes to define the parameters of a valid *shaliach* — specifically, to require that a *shaliach* be *like you*. As the *gemara* formulates it: *mah atem bnei berit af shluchaichon bnei berit* — just as you are members of the covenant, so too must your agent be a member of the covenant. A non-Jew cannot serve as one's *shaliach*. The verse teaches not the existence of *shlichut* but its qualifications.

### Learning From Logic

The *gemara* then pushes further: why is a verse even necessary to exclude a non-Jew? Cannot this be derived through logic, from the principle stated by Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan? Rabbi Yochanan taught that a slave cannot serve as a *shaliach* to receive a *get* on behalf of a woman from her husband, *lefi she'eino betorat gittin vekiddushin* — because the laws of marriage and divorce simply do not apply to him. The principle is that one cannot serve as an agent in a legal domain that is categorically inapplicable to oneself.

This principle readily explains the exclusion of a slave from *gittin* and *kiddushin*, since those laws do not govern a slave at all. And yet a slave is nonetheless *bnei berit* — he is within the covenant, partially obligated in *mitzvot*, and could in principle serve as an agent in other contexts. He can, for instance, separate *terumot u'maasrot* on behalf of someone or conduct a commercial transaction as a *shaliach*. The category-exclusion rule of Rabbi Yochanan thus accounts for why a slave cannot represent a woman in the receipt of a *get*, without requiring a special verse.

### Non-Jew Terumah

Given this logical principle, why would a verse be required to exclude a non-Jew from serving as a *shaliach* for *terumah*? A non-Jew is not subject to the laws of *terumah*, so surely the same logic applies: since *terumah* does not apply to him, he cannot be an agent for it. The *gemara* responds that the situation is actually more nuanced. Unlike the slave by *gittin*, a non-Jew is not categorically outside the orbit of *terumah*. The *mishnah* teaches: *ha'oved kochavim veha'kuti she'tarmu terumatan terumah* — if a non-Jew or a Samaritan separated *terumah*, that separation is halachically valid. Rashi notes that this assumes the non-Jew's ownership and processing of the grain do not exempt it from the obligation; but granted those assumptions, a non-Jew can in fact validly separate *terumah*. Since a non-Jew is thus "in the category" of *terumah* in some sense, one might conclude that he can also serve as a *shaliach* for *terumah* — *eima shaliach nami avid*. The verse therefore comes to exclude him.

### Resolution

The *gemara*'s resolution points toward a dual requirement. There are in fact two distinct conditions for valid *shlichut*: first, the *shaliach* must be Jewish — he must be *bnei berit* — even if the relevant domain of law applies to him in some form (as with the non-Jew and *terumah*, or with commercial transactions generally). Second, even if the *shaliach* is *bnei berit* and fully within the covenant, he cannot serve as agent in a legal domain categorically inapplicable to him — as with the slave and *gittin*. The verse *gam atem* establishes the first condition; the logical principle of Rabbi Yochanan establishes the second.

### Rabbi Shimon

The *gemara* notes that according to Rabbi Shimon, this entire construction collapses. Rabbi Shimon holds that when a non-Jew separates *terumah*, the separation has no legal status — it is not *terumah*. The *mishnah* records the dispute: the *tanna kamma* holds that the *terumah* of a non-Jew causes *dima'a* (if mixed into other produce, it confers upon it the restricted status of *terumah*) and one who eats it inadvertently must pay *chomesh*; Rabbi Shimon exempts. According to Rabbi Shimon, a non-Jew is simply outside the category of *terumah*, and there would be no basis for thinking he could serve as a *shaliach* for it. So why is *gam atem* needed?

The *gemara* explains that even according to Rabbi Shimon, the verse serves a necessary function — albeit a different one — which leads into the next discussion.

---

## Word 'Atem' Exclusions

### Atem Excludes

Before the word *gam* appears in the verse — which the *gemara* uses to include a *shaliach* — there is the word *atem*, "you," which functions as a limiting term. The *gemara* records: *atem ve'lo arisim, atem ve'lo shutafin, atem ve'lo apitropus* — "you" and not sharecroppers, "you" and not partners, "you" and not an overseer. None of these individuals can separate *terumah* on behalf of the owner. A sharecropper can separate on his own portion, not on the owner's. A partner can separate on his own share, not his partner's. An *apitropus* — a guardian or overseer, including one appointed over orphans — lacks the authority to separate *terumah* on behalf of the principal. The word *atem* similarly excludes *hatoreim terumah chaveiro* — someone who simply separates another person's *terumah* without authorization.

All of these are individuals who have some relationship or connection to the owner or the property, yet are not the owner himself and not his appointed agent.

### Question on Shaliach

This raises a natural difficulty. If the word *atem* is so restrictive — excluding sharecroppers, partners, overseers, and others who have genuine connections to the property — one might conclude that a *shaliach* too is excluded. After all, a *shaliach* is not the owner himself; *atem* would seem to indicate that only the owner may act.

### Gam Includes Shaliach

The word *gam* — "even" — resolves this. *Gam atem*, "even you," extends the category to include a *shaliach*. The verse does two things simultaneously: through *atem* it restricts to the principal and excludes various connected but unauthorized parties; through *gam* it expands to include the one person who is authorized — the *shaliach*. This is the second explanation of why *gam atem* is needed even given the other biblical sources for *shlichut*: without it, one might have excluded the *shaliach* from *terumah* precisely because the word *atem* emphasizes the personal nature of the act.

---

## Korban Pesach Shlich (II)

### Rabbi Yonatan's Use

The *gemara* now takes up a difficulty that arises from a different direction. It was assumed above that the *korban Pesach* verse — *veshachatu oto kol kehal adat Yisrael* — teaches the principle of *shlichut* in the domain of *kodshim* (sacred things). But this works only according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who reads that verse as establishing agency for the *shechita*. According to Rabbi Yonatan, that same verse is expended on an entirely different law, and cannot simultaneously teach *shlichut*.

The *baraisa* records: Rabbi Yonatan asks, how do we know that in principle all of Israel can fulfill their obligation through a single *korban Pesach*? He answers from the same verse — *veshachatu oto kol kehal adat Yisrael* — noting that the verse speaks of all of Israel slaughtering "it" (singular), implying that one sacrifice could serve the entire nation. The implication is that not every individual needs to eat a *kezayis* in order to be *yotzei*, since if all of Israel shared one small lamb, most would receive far less than a *kezayis*.

This is not the standard view, which holds that the entire purpose of *korban Pesach* — unlike other sacrifices, whose primary end is the *mizbeach* — is the eating. Accordingly, not eating a *kezayis* would normally render one not *yotzei*. (Indeed, the unique status of *korban Pesach* as an eating-focused sacrifice is evident in the law that if it is offered in a state of *tumah*, it is also eaten in *tumah*, an exception made precisely because eating is its essential purpose.) Rabbi Yonatan nonetheless derives from the verse that even a *kezayis* is not strictly required. The *gemara* opens 42a with his formulation: *minalan shekol Yisrael kulan yotzin b'Pesach echad*, "how do we know that all of Israel can fulfill their obligation through one *Pesach*?" — and answers from this verse.

### No Shlichut From Pesach

If that is what the verse teaches — that all of Israel can share one *korban Pesach* and one need not eat a *kezayis* — then the verse has been "used" by Rabbi Yonatan for that *derashah*, and cannot simultaneously serve as the basis for *shlichut* by *kodshim*. The *gemara* therefore asks: *shaliach dikdash minalei* — from where, according to Rabbi Yonatan, do we derive that *shlichut* applies to sacred matters? We know it from *gerushin*, we know it from *terumah*, but those do not establish the principle for *kodshim*. *Kodshim* is the most stringent domain; if we lack a source there, the principle of agency may not apply to it at all.

### Scene Shows Shlichut

The *gemara* answers: *minei* — you learn it from the case itself. Even if the stated *point* of the verse is to teach that one need not eat a *kezayis*, the verse nonetheless *describes* a scenario in which all of Israel own a single lamb and one person performs the *shechita* on behalf of everyone. That is a real instance of *shlichut* depicted in the text, even if it is not the *derasha*'s primary teaching. The *scenario* itself demonstrates the concept of agency in *kodshim*.

---

## Korban Pesach Shlich (II)

### Co-Ownership Problem

The *gemara* rejects this solution: *vidilma shani hatam de'isai shutfus begavaihu* — perhaps there it is different because everyone has a partnership, a shared ownership, in the *korban Pesach*. When all members of a household jointly own the same lamb, the fact that one person performs the *shechita* on behalf of all the others does not prove anything about general *shlichut*. The co-owners are already united in a single enterprise; one of them representing the group follows naturally from that shared ownership. This is fundamentally different from a situation in which a wholly unrelated individual is appointed as one's agent — where there is no pre-existing connection or joint stake — and then acts on the principal's behalf.

*Tosafot* raises an obvious question: why did the *gemara* not ask this objection earlier, on the previous daf, when it used the *korban Pesach* as a source for *shlichut* without qualification? *Tosafot* answers that the discussion on the previous daf was not positing that all of Israel owned one *korban*. Rather, it was describing the standard practice: each family or group brings their own *korban*, and a single designated *shochet* performs the *shechita* for every group — you bring me your *korban* and I will slaughter it, and you bring me yours and I will slaughter it. In that scenario, the *shochet* does not share ownership with any of the groups for whom he slaughters. That is genuine *shlichut* even without a co-ownership connection. It is only here, where the *gemara* is speaking about all of Israel sharing one lamb, that the objection of *shutfus* — joint ownership as a potentially sufficient explanation — becomes relevant.

This discussion touches on a deeper conceptual distinction about the nature of agency. The kind of representation that flows from co-ownership or joint enterprise creates what might be called a corporate identity: the group is a single unit, and one member acts as the mouthpiece or representative of that unit. This is categorically different from the classical model of *shlichut*, in which an individual appoints an unrelated third party as his personal agent and the agent's act is legally attributed to the principal.

### Two Psukim

The *gemara* then considers whether a different verse from the *korban Pesach* narrative can provide the required source. The purchase of the *korban Pesach* is described as well: *veyikchu lahem ish seh l'veit avot* — one person takes a lamb on behalf of the household. Here, before the purchase is made, no one yet has joint ownership; the joint ownership only comes into being *through* the act of acquisition. So this person is acquiring on behalf of everyone before anyone has become a co-owner, which looks more like genuine *shlichut*.

But the *gemara* presses the same objection: *vedilma hatam nami de'islei shutfei begavaihu* — perhaps even there, since these are all members of the same household and are all ultimately going to become co-owners together in this enterprise, their shared connection is sufficient to explain the representation without requiring a general principle of *shlichut*.

The *gemara* responds with a different argument: *im ken trei kraei lama li* — if both verses (the one about *shechita* and the one about purchase) describe only cases of pre-existing connection and shared enterprise, why are two verses needed? If neither teaches anything beyond what the other already teaches by virtue of the *shutfus* rationale, one would be superfluous. The extra verse must therefore be doing additional work — teaching that *shlichut* applies even in the absence of any special connection or co-ownership. However, the *gemara* immediately deflects this argument as well: *ki dehachi*, the purchase verse is not superfluous, because it is needed for the teaching of Rabbi Yitzchak.

---

## Shlichut Models

### Co-Owner Model

The co-ownership problem discussed above reflects a broader conceptual distinction between two models of representation. When a group of people share ownership of an object and one member of the group acts on behalf of all — performing the *shechita*, conducting the negotiation, making the decision — that individual is not necessarily functioning as a personal agent of each member individually. Rather, the group constitutes a single unit, and the person is the operative arm of that unit. The force of the act derives from the group's collective ownership and shared stake. This explains why one cannot derive general *shlichut* from the *korban Pesach* scenario: the case may merely illustrate how a joint enterprise operates, not how an individual appoints a stranger to act on his behalf.

### Shliach Tzibbur Model

This same conceptual distinction arises in a striking context discussed here. The only place in all of the *mishnah* where the principle *shlucho shel adam k'moso* — a person's agent is like himself — is stated explicitly is the *mishnah* in *Brachot* concerning the *shliach tzibbur*. And yet the *shliach tzibbur* presents an apparent paradox: the *gemara* elsewhere holds that one must pray for oneself and cannot discharge one's obligation through another's prayer. If a person simply stands and listens while the *shliach tzibbur* recites *Shemoneh Esrei*, intending to be *yotzei* through him as one would be *yotzei* through a personal agent, many authorities hold that this does not work. How, then, did the institution of *shliach tzibbur* function historically — particularly for those who were illiterate and could not pray independently?

The resolution is that the *shliach tzibbur* does not function as a personal agent of each individual congregant. He is not discharging each person's individual obligation as though he were that person's *shaliach*. Rather, the congregation as a whole constitutes a single corporate entity, and the *shliach tzibbur* is the voice of that entity — the mouthpiece through which the community as a single unit addresses God. He represents not each individual but the *tzibbur* itself.

### Silent vs. Repeated

This distinction corresponds to the difference between the silent *Shemoneh Esrei* and its repetition. The silent *Shemoneh Esrei* is *tefilla b'tzibbur* — an individual praying in the presence of a congregation. Each person is fulfilling a personal obligation as an individual, albeit within a communal setting. The repetition of *Shemoneh Esrei*, by contrast, is *tefilat ha'tzibbur* — the prayer *of* the congregation. The individual is no longer acting as an individual at that point; the community as a collective unit is praying through its representative. This is precisely the model that illuminates why the *korban Pesach* scenario may not prove general *shlichut*: *isley shutfei begavaihu*, they all share ownership of the sheep, and the one who performs the *shechita* represents the entire household as a single unit. *Sha l'veit avot* — a lamb for a household — means everyone has joint ownership, and one person is the operative arm of that household as a unit. This says nothing about how one individual unconnected to another may appoint that other as his personal agent.

---

## Iyakchu Lahem Ish

### Purchase on Behalf

Having exhausted the *shechita* verse, the *gemara* turns to the purchase verse: *veyikchu lahem ish seh l'veit avot* — one person takes a lamb on behalf of the household. The argument is that before the purchase, there is no joint ownership; the person is acquiring on behalf of others, which looks like genuine *shlichut*.

### Connection Objection

The *gemara* counters, as noted above, that even this case may be explainable through the lens of shared enterprise and pre-existing connection: perhaps they all gave him the money, perhaps they are already bound together as a household unit, and the representation flows from that shared context rather than from a general principle of *shlichut*.

### Why Two Psukim

If both verses — the *shechita* verse and the purchase verse — are limited to cases with pre-existing connection, neither would prove general *shlichut*. And yet two verses have been written. One of them, on this reading, would be entirely superfluous. That superfluity should be redirected to teach the general principle of *shlichut* even without connection. But the *gemara* closes off this move.

### Superfluous Pasuk

The *gemara* explains: *hahu me'ish lefi ochlo nafka* — the exclusion of minors from representing others in the acquisition of the *korban Pesach* is derived from the phrase *ish lefi ochlo* ("each man according to his eating"), where *ish* — man — already implies that a *katan* cannot take possession for others. If the exclusion of minors is derived from that *ish*, then the *ish* in *veyikchu lahem ish seh l'veit avot* is not needed for that purpose and is superfluous — and that superfluity is redirected to teach general *shlichut*. Without a second source for the *katan* exclusion, however, there would be no superfluity in the purchase verse, and no basis for deriving *shlichut* from it.

### Rabbi Yitzchak

Rabbi Yitzchak had stated the principle: *ish zocheh ve'lo katan zocheh* — a man can acquire possession, but a minor cannot. The *gemara* invokes the teaching of Rabbi Yitzchak in connection with the purchase verse. *Tosafot* raises the question: why does one need a verse specifically here, by *korban Pesach*, to teach that a minor cannot acquire? This is a general principle — *ein yad le'katan*, a minor has no legal capacity for *kinyan*. *Tosafot* answers: by *korban Pesach* one might have thought it was different. A minor can eat from the *korban Pesach* — *salka da'atach ho'il de'shayach ba'achilat pesachim* — and can register as part of a group (*leihimanot alav*), participating in the offering even without owning it himself. One might therefore have thought that since a minor has a genuine connection to the *korban Pesach* through eating, perhaps he can also acquire it for others. The verse therefore specifies *ish* to teach that only an adult can effect an acquisition on behalf of others; a minor, though he can be part of the group through enrollment, cannot serve as the acquiring agent for others.

This interplay is of particular interest on the eve of Pesach. Minors — *ketanim* — stand at the center of the *Seder* experience, and indeed they can genuinely participate in the *korban Pesach* by joining a group. Yet the legal capacity to acquire the sacrifice on behalf of others belongs only to an adult.

Given that *ish lefi ochlo* already teaches that a minor cannot acquire for others, the word *ish* in *veyikchu lahem ish seh l'veit avot* is superfluous for that purpose. That superfluous *ish* is then the source for general *shlichut* in *kodshim* — teaching that even where there is no pre-existing co-ownership or connection, one person may act as the agent of another.

---

## Other Shlichut Contexts

### Nasi Land Division

The *gemara* now introduces a teaching of Rav Gidel in the name of Rav: *minayin she'shlucho shel adam k'moso* — from where do we derive that a person's agent is like himself? The verse cited is *v'nasi echad nasi echad*, from the account of the division of the Land of Israel, where one prince from each tribe participated in the allocation on behalf of his entire tribe. To the degree that any representation of individual tribal members was required, it was performed by the *nasi*.

The *gemara* then asks why this verse should be considered the source for *shlichut* at all, given the other sources already discussed. But more fundamentally, it questions the premise.

### Minors Represented

*Ve'tisabra* — does this actually make sense? Is the division of the land through tribal princes really a case of *shlichut*? *V'ha ketanim lav bnei shlichus ninhu* — minors cannot appoint a *shaliach*. Yet minors were certainly included in the tribal allocation, receiving their portions through the *nasi*. If this were *shlichut*, it could not have applied to them — a minor lacks the legal capacity to appoint an agent.

### Zchiyah Not Shlichut

The *gemara* therefore reframes the teaching. What the verse by the division of the land teaches is not *shlichut* but rather *zechiyah* — the principle that one may take possession of something on behalf of another, even not in the other's presence, and even when the other is a minor. The teaching is reformulated: *minayin she'zachin le'adam she'lo bifanav* — from where do we know that one may acquire on behalf of another not in his presence?

The distinction between *zechiyah* and *shlichut* is conceptually significant. *Shlichut* requires appointment by the principal and depends upon the principal's legal capacity to appoint. *Zechiyah* operates differently: when an act is unambiguously to someone's benefit, a third party may act on that person's behalf without formal appointment, and without the other's capacity to appoint being a prerequisite. In this sense *zechiyah* is simultaneously more limited — it applies only when the benefit is clear and unambiguous — and more expansive — it does not require the formalities of *shlichut* and can operate even for a minor.

The *gemara* then presses this framing as well. *Zechus hu lo* — is it really an unambiguous benefit? *Hachova nami ika* — there is also a potential detriment. The *nasi* did not merely hand each person a gift; he determined which portion of the land each person received. *De'ika de'nicha lei behar ve'lo nicha lei bevika* — one person might have preferred the mountain, another might have preferred the valley. Determining which specific portion someone receives is not a pure benefit; it involves judgment calls and tradeoffs. This therefore cannot be the paradigmatic case of *zechiyah* either.

---

## Orphans & Trustees

### Apotropus Appointed

The *gemara* finally settles on a more precise characterization of what the verse teaches. It is not general *shlichut* and not general *zechiyah*; rather it establishes a specific principle: *minayin le'yisomim she'bau lachlok b'nichsei avihen she'bezdin mamidin lahem apitropus l'chov u'lizkos* — from where do we know that when orphans (minors) come to divide their father's estate, the *beit din* can appoint a guardian (*apitropus*) to act on their behalf, with the authority to make tradeoffs that may involve both benefit and detriment? This authority is derived from the *nasi*'s role in dividing the land of Israel.

The parallel is instructive. The division of *Eretz Yisrael* was not purely beneficial for every individual in every respect; it involved allocations that some would have preferred differently. Yet it was conducted by the *nasi* on behalf of the entire tribe, including those who could not represent themselves. The authority to make such consequential, judgment-laden decisions on behalf of others — including those who lack legal capacity — derives from the fact that the representative was appointed by a higher authority. In the case of *Eretz Yisrael*, that authority was divine. In the case of orphans dividing an estate, the parallel authority is *beit din*.

Rav Nachman bar Shmuel states the practical rule: when minors come to divide their father's estate, *beit din* appoints an *apitropus* and chooses a good portion for them — meaning the trustee attempts to achieve a fair and beneficial distribution for everyone under his charge.

### No Protest After

Once the orphans reach majority, Rav Nachman rules in his own name: *im higdilu einam yecholim limchos* — they cannot protest the division that was made on their behalf. The principle invoked is *mah koach beit din yafeh*: if the court-appointed division could be undone the moment the orphans grew up and decided they were unhappy, the authority of the court would be rendered meaningless. A division backed by *beit din* is binding even against the future objection of those who were represented.

### Beis Din Authority

This contrasts with the ordinary principle applicable to *zechiyah she'lo bifanav*: when someone takes possession of an object for an absent party and that party is subsequently informed, the party can refuse the acquisition — *macha'ah* — if they did not want it. The presumption that the acquisition was beneficial can be overridden once the party expresses otherwise. But a court-appointed trustee's decision operates differently; it carries the authority of *beit din*, and the orphans' later preference cannot undo what was done under that authority.

### Error Exception

A difficulty arises from a *mishnah* elsewhere. The *mishnah* teaches that when judges assess property values in order to authorize a creditor's seizure, and their assessment was off by a sixth or more — *shepichasu shtus o hosiru shtus* — the resulting transaction is void. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: the transaction stands, because voiding a court's assessment would undermine the authority of *beit din* — *mah koach beit din yafeh*. Rav Huna bar Chinena reported that Rav Nachman himself ruled in accordance with the *chachamim* (i.e., that the transaction is void). But Rav Nachman also said, in the context of the orphans, that one cannot protest a court-appointed division — on the same grounds of *mah koach beit din yafeh*. The *gemara* asks: does Rav Nachman really hold consistently by the principle of *mah koach beit din yafeh*, or does he apply it selectively?

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — ha detau, ha delo tau* — it is not difficult.
