Rav Huna in the name of Rav rules: *mema'enes l'ma'amaro v'einah mema'enes l'zikatoh* — she performs *mi'un* in response to Shimon's *ma'amar*, but not merely in response to the *zika* bond alone. *Ma'amar* is the act by which a *yavam* — the surviving brother — performs a form of *kiddushin* with the *yevamah* while she awaits *yibum* or *chalitza*. If Shimon does *ma'amar*, that introduces an additional dimension; if he does not, the situation is different.

### Triple Remedy

If Shimon performed *ma'amar*, the *Gemara* specifies: *tzricha get v'tzricha chalitza v'tzricha mi'un* — she requires all three from Shimon. Each is explained separately.

She needs a *get* — *shema nitratza ha'av bekiddushei sheini* — because perhaps the father did not accept the first marriage to Reuven, but he did accept the *ma'amar* of Shimon. If the father accepted Shimon's *ma'amar* as valid *kiddushin d'oraita*, then Shimon has truly married her and must give her a *get* to release her.

She needs *chalitza* — *shema nitratza bekiddushei rishon* — because perhaps the father accepted the original marriage to Reuven. In that case, there is a genuine *zika* between her and Shimon as the surviving brother, and Shimon must perform *chalitza* to release her from that bond.

She needs *mi'un* — *shema lo nitratza lo bekiddushei rishon velo bekiddushei sheini* — because perhaps the father accepted neither marriage, in which case she was never truly married to anyone. The *get* and the *chalitza* would then both be legally meaningless — performed only as *chumrot*. The *mi'un* signals this uncertainty and prevents people from drawing the erroneous inference that the *chalitza* confirms a real *d'oraita* marriage and that if Shimon were to betroth her sister, the *kiddushin* would not take effect — *ein kiddushin tofsin b'achota*.

### Chalitza Alone

If Shimon did *not* perform *ma'amar*, the ruling is simpler: *einah tzricha ela chalitza bilvad* — she needs only *chalitza*. The logic is that there are only two relevant scenarios: either the father accepted the marriage to Reuven, in which case there is a real *zika* and Shimon needs *chalitza*; or the father did not accept it, in which case Shimon has no connection to her at all. Since Shimon did no *ma'amar*, there is no third scenario involving Shimon's own *kiddushin* — and therefore no need for a *get*.

One might ask: should she not also need a *mi'un* even in this case, to signal that the *chalitza* was of uncertain necessity and prevent people from concluding that Shimon marrying her sister would not be *chal*? The *Gemara* answers: *hakol yodim achot chaluza d'rabbanan* — everyone knows that the sister of a *chalutzah* is forbidden only *d'rabbanan*, not *d'oraita*. Reish Lakish establishes this in Yevamot: the sister of a *grusha* (divorced woman) is forbidden *d'oraita*, but the sister of a *chalutzah* is forbidden only *midivrei sofrim*. Accordingly, even if observers see a *chalitza* here and conclude that there was a genuine *zika*, they will also know that any subsequent *kiddushin* to her sister would take effect *d'oraita* — there is no risk of a false inference that would permit a prohibited union or negate a valid one. The *mi'un* is therefore unnecessary when there was no *ma'amar*.

## Ravina Dispute

### Father & Son

The *Gemara* now introduces a case that frames Ravina's broader rejection of the *nitratza ha'av* concern. Two men were drinking wine together under an awning in Bavel. One took a cup of wine, gave it to the other, and said: *mekadsha li bartech livri* — let your daughter be betrothed to my son. Here the man who accepted the wine had the authority to marry off his daughter; there is no question about that side of the transaction. The issue is that the man giving the wine was acting on behalf of his son without having been appointed as the son's *shaliach*. Could we say — by parallel to the *nitratza ha'av* reasoning — that perhaps when the son finds out he will be pleased with the marriage, and that retroactive acceptance will make the father's action valid?

Ravina says no: *shema nitratzei haben lo amrinan* — we do not invoke the concern that the son may come to accept it. The *Gemara* presents the reason on behalf of the rabbis who explained Ravina's position: *de'av bekiddushei bito bechol dehu nicha lei* — a father has a low threshold for accepting whatever arrangement his daughter has entered into, because, as the *Gemara* characterizes it, *detav lemeitav tan du* — it is preferable for a woman to be partnered than to be alone, and fathers tend to embrace opportunities to see their daughters settled. But *aval gavra dayek venasiv* — a man is exacting and discerning about who he marries.

### Gender Presumption

There is therefore an asymmetry between the two cases. For a daughter: the father's presumed willingness to accept after the fact provides at least some basis — however thin — for the *nitratza ha'av* concern. For a son: no comparable presumption exists. The son is expected to care deeply about his choice of spouse and cannot be presumed to accept whatever was arranged without his input.

Furthermore — and this is a second, independent reason — even if the son were inclined to accept what the father did, that acceptance alone would be insufficient. To marry on someone's behalf, one must be a *shaliach*; retroactive willingness does not substitute for the proper appointment of agency. This applies regardless of one's views on the *nitratza ha'av* concern: *ubein eino birshut aviv lekadesh lo isha shelo bishlucho* — the father does not have the standing to marry for his son without having been formally designated as a *shaliach*.

### Ravina Rejects

The *Gemara* makes explicit what this case implies: *befirush amar mar d'lo savar lah l'ha d'Rav u'Shmuel* — Ravina explicitly stated that he does not accept the ruling of Rav and Shmuel. And since the discussion in the *Gemara* has been framing the son's case as parallel — in some ways — to a *shidduchin* scenario (the son had been expressing interest in the girl, which created a context of presumed desirability, analogous to prior *shidduchin* with the daughter), Ravina's rejection extends even to cases where *shidduchin* preceded the event. We do not invoke *nitratza ha'av* even then.

## Bizayon Exception

### Vegetables Case

Even from the perspective of Rav and Shmuel — who do invoke the *nitratza ha'av* concern — not every case of self-*kiddushin* by a *ketanah* triggers it. Ravina articulates an important limitation. A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace. Ravina rules: *afilu man d'amar chaishinan shema nitratzei ha'av, hani mili derech kavod* — even according to those who hold that we are concerned the father may have been *meratze* after the fact, that concern applies only when the original *kiddushin* was performed in a respectful manner. *Aval hacha derech bizayon* — when the betrothal was done in a degrading manner, we have no concern at all that the father would ever come to accept it.

### Bizayon Definition

Rav Acha of Difti asks Ravina: *bizayon d'mai* — what constituted the degradation here? Was it the object — a mere bundle of vegetables — or was it the setting — the public marketplace? The distinction matters practically: *nafka mina d'kadesh b'chaspa beshuka* — if he betrothed her with money but in the marketplace, or with a bundle of vegetables but in a private home, which of these constitutes *derech bizayon*? Ravina answers: *idei v'idei derech bizayon hu* — both constitute degradation. Either the object or the setting, taken alone, is sufficient to render the betrothal a *derech bizayon*, removing it from the scope of the *nitratza ha'av* concern.

## Public Commitment

### Wife Persuasion

The *Gemara* presents a case reminiscent of one discussed in tractate Nedarim. A father wanted to marry his daughter to his own relative. His wife disagreed and insisted that the daughter be married to her brother — the father's brother-in-law. The wife prevailed: *kafstei* — she pressed him until he conceded and agreed. They then celebrated with a party, announcing the engagement to the wife's brother. And then, while everyone was eating and drinking, the husband's own relative came up to the second floor and gave the daughter *kesef kiddushin* — betrothing her himself, exactly as the father had originally wanted. The question is whether we invoke *nitratza ha'av*: the father clearly had preferred this match all along and only reluctantly agreed to the other arrangement.

### Abaye Finality

Abaye rules that we do not invoke *nitratza ha'av* here. He invokes the verse *she'erit Yisrael lo ya'asu avlah velo yedabru kazav* — the remnant of Israel will not act perversely or speak falsehood. Once the father gave his word and committed to the other match — and especially once he made that commitment at a public gathering, announcing the engagement — we do not fear that he will reverse himself. The public commitment constitutes a moral and social bond that forecloses the *nitratza* concern.

### Rava Expense

Rava adds a further condition: *chazakah ein adam torach beseuda umafsidah* — there is a presumption that once a man has gone to the trouble and expense of making a party, he will not allow that effort to be wasted. It is not merely the announcement that removes the concern; it is the concrete investment in a celebration. The practical difference between Abaye and Rava is a case where the announcement was made publicly but no party with actual expense took place — *delo tarach*. Abaye would say that even the announcement alone suffices to preclude the reversal; Rava requires that actual expense have been incurred.

## Final Pesak

### Tosafot Rules

The *sugya* concludes with the question of how to rule. Do we follow Rav and Shmuel — who require both *get* and *mi'un*, limited perhaps by Rav Nachman to cases of *shidduchin* and further qualified by the exceptions for *bizayon* and public commitment — or do we follow the line of Ulla and Ravina, who reject the *nitratza ha'av* concern entirely? Tosafot rules explicitly — *befirush amar mar lo sevira lei deShmuel* — and cites Rav Alfas as ruling in the *She'iltot* of Rav Achai that the *halachah* follows Ravina. The rationale is that Ravina was a later authority — *batra* — representing the *sof hora'ah* at the close of the Talmudic period. Rav Ashi, too, concurred. Accordingly: *ein tzarich lo get velo mi'un* — she requires neither a *get* nor a *mi'un* — *va'afilu shidduchu* — even if *shidduchin* had preceded the event. The *nitratza ha'av* concern is entirely set aside.

### Father Absent

A separate question remains: what if the father is not present at all — not because he is dead, but because he has traveled abroad for an extended period? In that case, the *She'iltot* holds that the *ketanah* can enter into a *kiddushin d'rabbanan* — not *d'oraita*, which is never available without the father, but a rabbinic marriage with the status of *mi'un* as the mode of exit. The reasoning parallels the case of a true orphan: *kedin yetomah de'ein lah av detaknu rabbanan kiddushin mishum hefker* — the rabbis instituted *kiddushin* in such cases to prevent the girl from being treated without dignity or taken advantage of. When the father is overseas and effectively unavailable, she is in a comparable position: *v'zu she-halchah l'medinat hayam, harei hu k'yetomah mishum hefker* — this girl, with her father overseas, is like an orphan in terms of the concern that she will be treated as *hefker*. A *kiddushin d'rabbanan* is therefore permitted under such circumstances.

### Remote Marriage

Rav Menachem Me'yuni dissents. He does not accept that a *kiddushin d'rabbanan* can be effected in the father's absence when the father is alive. He cites a specific case: a man traveled to a distant land and left behind a young daughter; she was married off; and Rav Menachem ruled that the marriage could not be maintained. His reason goes beyond a mere disagreement about whether *kiddushin d'rabbanan* applies — he raises a new concern: *chaishinan shema y'kadshana aviha l'ish acher bimkom shehu* — we must fear that the father, wherever he is, has in the meantime married her off to some other man. How then can we permit this marriage to stand?

Rabbeinu Tam responds sharply: if one takes that concern seriously, then even after the father dies the girl could never marry, because perhaps the father had betrothed her to someone while abroad, unknown to anyone here. The *Gemara* does not treat such unknowable possibilities as legally operative concerns. We are not afraid of what an absent father may have done without our knowledge.

The upshot is a layered picture: when the father is present and the *ketanah* marries herself off, the final ruling — following Ravina, Rav Ashi, Rav Alfas, and Tosafot — is that nothing is required, not a *get* and not a *mi'un*, even with prior *shidduchin*. When the father is absent and alive, there is a serious dispute about whether a *kiddushin d'rabbanan* can exist at all, with an additional concern, raised by Rav Menachem, about what the father may have arranged independently. The *sugya* thus ties together the speculative legal question with which it began and a practical reality that the *Rishonim* clearly recognized as pressing in their own communities.

---

---

# Kiddushin 45b

## Ketana, Father Away

### Setup

The *gemara* picks up in the middle of 45b with a case involving a *ketana* — a minor girl — whose *kiddushin* was performed with her father's knowledge and approval. Whether the father himself arranged the match or she acted on her own initiative in a way that made his assent clear, the binding character of the *kiddushin* is not in question; the father was demonstrably on board. Subsequently, however, *ve-halach aviha le-medinat ha-yam* — the father traveled to a distant land — and while he was away, *ve-amda ve-niset*, she proceeded to *nisuin*.

### Nisuin & Da'at

The resulting question is whether *nisuin* performed *she-lo le-da'at aviha* — without the father's knowledge or consent — is legally effective. This raises two analytically distinct considerations. First, one might argue that *nisuin* is categorically different from *kiddushin* as a form of *kinyan*: *kiddushin* creates the marriage as a matter of law, whereas *nisuin* translates it into lived reality, and might therefore require less of the formal *da'at* ordinarily demanded of a *kinyan*. On the other hand, *nisuin* is precisely the moment when the minor daughter passes out of her father's legal control and into her husband's domain. Even if an adult woman's *nisuin* requires less formal *da'at* than an initial *kinyan*, one would expect that a *ketana* cannot make that transition — from the father's authority to the husband's — without the father's explicit consent. The *nafka mina* is multiple and concrete: whether she may eat *terumah* if her husband is a *kohen*, and whether if she dies her husband inherits her estate, along with the full range of reciprocal financial obligations that attach to full *nisuin*.

### Rav's Position

*Amar Rav: ochelet be-terumah ad she-yavo aviha ve-yimcheh.* Rav holds that she is presumed to be a *nesuah* and may eat *terumah* until her father returns and objects. The presumption runs in favor of the *nisuin* being valid; the father, knowing that *kiddushin* had taken place and having approved it, can be assumed to acquiesce in the natural continuation to *nisuin*. Should he return and protest — presumably while she is still a *ketana* or *na'arah* and within the window of paternal authority — he can retroactively undo the status of *nesuah*.

### Rav Asi's Position

*Rav Asi amar: eino ochelet.* Rav Asi disagrees. His concern is *shema yavo aviv ve-yimcheh* — the father might protest upon returning — and therefore one cannot presume the *nisuin* valid. The consequence is stark: *ve-nimtza zara ochelet be-terumah le-mafreia* — were she eating *terumah* and the father then protested, she would retroactively have been a non-*kohen*'s wife consuming *terumah* improperly.

### Rav's Stringency

Although Rav's theoretical ruling permits her to eat *terumah*, the *gemara* records that *havei uvda ve-chash leh Rav le-hadei Rav Asi* — in a practical case that arose, Rav was stringent in accordance with Rav Asi's position and did not permit her to eat. Some *rishonim* understand this to mean that Rav did not abandon his ruling but simply exercised *chumra* in practice. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak clarifies that Rav himself is the one who held, as a matter of law, that she could eat *terumah*; it is merely that when an actual case presented itself, he deferred to the stricter view of Rav Asi.

### Inheritance & Safek

*Amar Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak u-modeh Rav: she-im metah einah yorshah.* Even Rav concedes that if she were to die, her husband would not inherit her estate. Despite holding that she has sufficient status as a *nesuah* to eat *terumah*, Rav acknowledges that the *nisuin* is not certain enough to transfer property: *uki mamona be-chezkas mara* — the money remains in the presumptive possession of its original owner, and one does not transfer an estate on the basis of a doubtful *nisuin*.

This creates an apparent tension: if Rav is prepared to concede a *safek* as to whether there is *nisuin* — sufficient doubt that he will not allow property to transfer — how can he simultaneously permit her to eat *terumah*? Here Rashi and Tosafot both point to an important underlying principle. According to the *Bavli*, the right of a *kohen*'s wife to eat *terumah* derives *mid'oraisa* already from *kiddushin* alone, without waiting for *nisuin*; the requirement that she first undergo *nisuin* before eating *terumah* is only *mid'rabanan*. Therefore, Rav and Rav Asi may agree that her status as a *nesuah* is a *safek* — and indeed both accept that framework — but when it comes to the *d'rabanan* restriction, Rav is willing to be lenient. Tosafot further clarifies that even according to Rav Asi, the practical reasons for the *gezera* do not apply in the same way here, since she is already living with the man; Rav Asi's position is therefore a form of *lo plug* rather than a strict application of the underlying rationale.

---

## Elopement Cases

### Kidushin Good, Nisuin Not

The *gemara* now turns to a different configuration: *niskadsha le-da'at ve-niset she-lo le-da'at*, with *avia kan* — the father present. The *kiddushin* was performed with the father's knowledge, but the *nisuin* was not. The distinction from the prior case is that there the father was simply absent and could not be consulted; here the father is available and his response — or rather his lack of explicit response — is the crux of the matter. She has, it seems, acted behind his back, and when he found out, said nothing. The question is how to interpret that silence.

### Huna: Silence = No

*Rav Huna amar: eino ochelet.* She may not eat *terumah*. Even though Rav permitted eating when the father was away in a distant land, *hasam hu de-leika le-av* — there the father was simply unreachable, and we could presume he would be accepting when he eventually learned of it. But *aval hacha de-ika le-av* — here the father is present and presumably has now learned what occurred. His silence cannot be read as acquiescence. *Hai de-ishtik mirtach ratach* — one who falls silent in this situation may well be simply too angry to speak.

### Yirmiah: Silence = Yes

*Rav Yirmiah bar Abba amar: ochelet.* She may eat. Even Rav Asi, who would not permit eating when the father was far away on grounds that *shema yavo aviv ve-yimcheh*, said so only because *hatam hu de-shema yavo aviv ve-yimcheh* — when the father is absent, the concern is that upon returning he will raise an objection. But *aval hacha mi-de-shatik, isnochi asnach lei* — here, where the father is present and has heard what happened and said nothing, that silence is itself an indication of acceptance. The general principle of *shtika ke-hoda'ah* — silence functions as acknowledgment — supports the inference that a person who genuinely objects would say so; one who remains silent has made his peace, however reluctantly.

### Ulla's Analysis

As the *gemara* itself notes, there is a structural asymmetry in these two positions. The stance of Rav Yirmiah bar Abba is coherent: ordinarily we fear the father will protest when he hears the news, but actual silence in the face of known facts changes that presumption. By contrast, Rav Huna's position seems to move in the opposite direction — starting from a presumption that the father would approve when absent, yet interpreting his silence once present as anger and opposition. Ulla observes that the position of Rav Yirmiah, who was Rav Huna's student, appears considerably more consistent.

---

## Total Elopement (III)

### Ulla Rejects

Moving to the most extreme scenario — *niskadsha she-lo le-da'at avia ve-niset she-lo le-da'at avia ve-avia kan* — both the *kiddushin* and the *nisuin* were performed entirely without the father's knowledge, and he is present. Rav Huna holds *ochelet*, she may eat; Rav Yirmiah bar Abba holds *eina ochelet*, she may not. Ulla characterizes Rav Huna's position here as *ke-chometz la-shinayim u-ke-ashan la-einayim* — intolerable, like vinegar on the teeth or smoke in the eyes.

### Logical Inference

The *gemara* articulates why. In the immediately preceding case — where *kiddushin* was done with the father's knowledge and only the *nisuin* was without — Rav Huna himself said she could not eat, reading the father's silence as opposition. How then, in the more extreme case where even the *kiddushin* was done without his knowledge, can one say she may eat? *Hashta u-mah hatam... amrat lo ochlah, hacha lo kol she-ken* — if even when the *kiddushin* was clearly valid and the father was silent about the *nisuin* alone, Rav Huna said no, surely when neither act was done with his knowledge, the answer must be no all the more. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *nirin divrei talmid* — the position of the student (Rav Yirmiah bar Abba) appears more logically compelling.

---

## Total Elopement (III)

### Rava Reinterprets

Rava, however, defends Rav Huna's position by offering a more nuanced reading of the underlying logic. *Mai ta'ama de-Rav Huna: ho'il ve-na'asah be-ma'aseh yatom be-chayei av* — the reason is that this girl has conducted herself as though she were an orphan in her father's lifetime. Two major life events — *kiddushin* and *nisuin* — have occurred without any paternal involvement or reaction. The absence of any assertion of authority across both events is itself a form of relinquishment. The father, by allowing the pattern to continue unchallenged, has in effect yielded his position and left her to make her own decisions. His silence is not opposition in this case; it is acquiescence born of having ceded control entirely.

### Setup

The contrast with the prior case now becomes clear: when the *kiddushin* was performed under his auspices and with his approval, there was never a moment when he had stepped back from his role. His silence about the *nisuin* alone would then read against a backdrop of active, continuing paternal authority — and that silence is harder to interpret as acceptance of something done behind his back. But when both acts proceed without him and he says nothing, the cumulative picture is that he has let her be.

---

## Elopement Cases (II)

### Rava Defends Huna

This is the key to Rava's defense of Rav Huna. When the *kiddushin* was done *le-da'at av* and only the *nisuin* was not, the father has never forfeited his standing. His silence regarding *nisuin* is therefore ambiguous — and Rav Huna reads it as tacit objection, in keeping with the view that *mirtach ratach*. But when neither act was within his purview, the father has effectively allowed his daughter to function as though she had no father, and the consistent pattern of non-response amounts to a relinquishment of control. Rava thus reconciles Rav Huna's two rulings by identifying the relevant variable not as whether there was one unapproved act or two, but rather whether there was any prior basis of paternal authority that was then bypassed.

---

## Conclusion on Ketana

### Both Can Object

*Amar Rav: bein hi u-vein aviha yecholim limchot.* Rav states that in the case of a *ketana* who was betrothed without her father's knowledge, both the father and the daughter herself are capable of objecting and thereby invalidating the *kiddushin*. This statement should be read in context: Rav had previously held that such *kiddushin* creates a concern (*chashash*) of valid betrothal — *shema yitratze ha-av* — meaning that if the father acquiesces, the *kiddushin* might take effect. What Rav now clarifies is the other side of that picture: if the father explicitly objects, that *chashash* evaporates entirely. And not only the father — the daughter, too, can object.

---

## Total Elopement (III)

### Huna: Yes

In the case of full elopement — *kiddushin* and *nisuin* both *she-lo le-da'at ha-av*, with the father present — Rav Huna holds that she may eat *terumah*.

### Yirmiah: No

Rav Yirmiah bar Abba holds that she may not eat *terumah* in this case.

---

## Conclusion on Ketana (II)

### Rashi's Limitation

Rashi understands the daughter's right to object as temporally limited: she can only object prior to the father finding out about the *kiddushin*. Once the *kiddushin* is known to the father, the question of its validity passes into his domain, and her prior acceptance of the *kiddusin* money can no longer be undone by her protest. The reasoning is that before the father learns of it and before his reaction can ratify the *kiddushin*, her ongoing willingness remains a live factor; once she retracts before that window closes, the acceptance is undermined and the *kiddushin* cannot take effect.

### Tosafot Clarification

Tosafot clarifies the scope of the entire preceding discussion. When Rav said earlier that we are *choshesh shema yitratze ha-av*, that concern applies specifically *be-stama she-shama ve-shatak* — when the father heard and was initially silent. The *sugyot* about interpreting the father's silence are thus unified: the entire discussion addresses the ambiguous case of an unexplained non-reaction. *Aval heicha de-michah gila be-da'ato* — if the father explicitly objected, his intent is manifest and there is no *kiddushin*; if he explicitly accepted, the *kiddushin* is valid. The interpretive work only begins when the father's response is silence.

### Explicit Intent

When the father makes his position clear — whether by explicit approval or explicit objection — his stated intent governs the validity of the *kiddushin*. The debates among Rav, Rav Asi, Rav Huna, and Rav Yirmiah bar Abba all operate within the space of ambiguity created by silence alone.

---

## Torah Case Analysis

### Torah Source

Chiya bar Rav challenges Rav Asi by grounding the case in a *pasuk* from the Torah. The verse in question — *im ma'en yema'en aviha* — concerns the case of the seducer, where the father refuses to give his daughter in marriage to the man who seduced her, and the man must therefore pay fifty *kesef*. Chiya bar Rav reads this case as the precise scenario the *gemara* has been discussing: a *ketana* or *na'arah* who underwent what amounted to *kiddushin* without her father's prior knowledge, with the father now reacting.

### Deriving Daughter's Right

From the *pasuk* alone, only the father's right to refuse is explicit — *ein li ela aviha, hi atzma minayin?* How do we know the daughter herself may refuse? The *midrash* derives this from the doubled language of *im ma'en yema'en*, reading the repetition as an inclusion — *mi-kol makom*, from whatever source, a refusal is valid. This would suggest that her objection also carries legal force in the case of *kiddushin she-lo le-da'at aviha*, and would support Rav's position that *bein hi u-vein aviha yecholim limchot*.

### Rav's Interpretation

Rav, however, deflects this argument: *lo tizul batar ipcha — yacholni le-shannoye lach k'gon she-pita le-shem ishus*. The *pasuk*, Rav insists, need not be understood as a case of *kiddushin* at all. The more straightforward reading is that the seduction occurred *she-lo le-shem ishus* — not in the context of marriage — and the sexual act was simply that, with no accompanying *kinyan kiddushin*.

### No Kiddushin Here

If that is the case, why does the Torah need to tell us that the father can refuse? Of course the father can refuse to allow his daughter to marry this man — the father's authority over whom his daughter may marry is a fundamental premise that requires no *pasuk*. The *gemara* therefore explains that the *pasuk*'s point is not to establish the father's authority to veto the marriage but rather to specify the financial consequence: even when the father refuses and the marriage does not take place, the seducer must still pay the fifty *kesef — amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: lomar she-meshalem knas ke-meputah*. The *pasuk* teaches the law of the *knas*, not a ruling about *kiddushin*.

### Seduction L'Shem Ishus

Rav Asi then responds: *ee hachi* — if that is indeed the reading — *hainu de-tanina etzlo: mahor yimharena lo le-ishah she-tzricha himenu kiddushin*. The language *mahor yimharena lo le-ishah* implies that a formal act of *kiddushin* now needs to take place, which confirms that no *kiddushin* had yet occurred — consistent with Rav's reading that the seduction was not *le-shem ishus*. Abaye, however, addresses the reading in which the seduction *was* for the sake of marriage — and on that reading, *mahor yimharena lo le-ishah* would mean that a new *kiddushin* must now be performed with the father's explicit approval: *tzricha kiddushin le-da'at aviha*.

### Tosafot's Question

This resolution raises a question that Tosafot presses. If the daughter can refuse, what does her refusal accomplish in practical terms? Consider the scenario as Rav reads it: the seduction was not *le-shem ishus*, the father has the right to refuse the marriage, and if the father refuses, the seducer pays fifty *kesef*. Now suppose the daughter objects. Does her objection prevent the marriage from going forward? Normally a *ketana* or *na'arah* has no independent right to veto a match her father has sanctioned. Is it really possible that simply because she was seduced she now acquires that right?

### Tosafot's Solutions

Tosafot offers two answers. The first, which Tosafot itself finds problematic, is that her refusal does not actually prevent the marriage but does obligate the payment of the *knas* — the fifty *kesef* — as though the father had refused, even if the wedding ultimately proceeds. Tosafot acknowledges the strangeness of this: presumably the father and husband could simply coordinate so that the daughter refuses, the *knas* is paid to the father, and the marriage goes forward regardless. The second and preferable answer is more straightforward: *nafka mina heicha de-ba aleha ve-achar kach nityatmah* — the daughter's refusal is operative in a case where the father has since died. Once there is no father to exercise paternal authority, *mahani miun didah le-akeiv she-lo tehei ishto* — her own objection can now function to block the marriage entirely. The broader point, which the *gemara* never fully resolves, is that once *chazal* recognized the daughter's right of refusal, the precise circumstances in which it is operative — when the father is present, when he has approved, and what weight her voice carries — remain somewhat underdeveloped.

---

## Multiple Dates Case

### Separate Statements

The *gemara* now turns from the dynamics of *kiddushin* of a *ketana* to a *mishna* dealing with the mechanics of *kesef kiddushin* in the case of an adult woman. The *mishna* records: *ha-omer le-ishah hiskadshi li be-tamarah zo hiskadshi li be-zo* — a man who says "marry me with this date, marry me with this date," separately, offering each date with its own declaration. *Im yesh be-achas mehen shaveh perutah mekudeshet* — if any single one of them is worth a *perutah*, she is betrothed; *ve-im lav einah mekudeshet* — and if not, she is not, even if their combined value reaches a *perutah*. Since each statement of *hiskadshi* constitutes a separate act, the dates do not combine.

### Combined Statement

If instead he said *b'zo u-v'zo u-v'zo* — "with this and this and this" — combining everything into one declaration, then *im yesh shaveh perutah be-chulan mekudeshet*, if together they are worth a *perutah*, she is betrothed; *ve-im lav einah mekudeshet*, and if not, she is not. Here the single composite statement ties all the dates into one act of *kiddushin*, and their values aggregate accordingly.

### Eating While Given

The *mishna* then adds: *haysah ochelet rishonah rishonah* — if she was eating each date as he placed it before her — *ve-einah mekudeshet ela im ken yesh be-achas mehen shaveh perutah* — the combined-statement rule does not apply, and one of the dates by itself must be worth a *perutah*. Even in the composite-statement case, the fact that she is consuming each date as it is offered changes the legal analysis.

### Why Eating Matters

The *gemara* asks: on which clause of the *mishna* does this final condition apply? And why does the act of eating matter at all?

### Textual Ambiguity

*Ilei'ma areisha* — if the clause about eating applies to the first case, where he says *hiskadshi* separately before each date, then the condition seems redundant: even without the eating, each date must individually be worth a *perutah*, since the statements were never combined. Why would eating change or add anything? The *gemara* therefore proposes *ela aseifa* — the clause applies to the final case of the combined statement. But even then, the question presses: if she was eating the dates as he gave them, why can she not be betrothed on the basis of their combined value?

---

## Milveh Concept

### Rabba & Shmuel

Rabba and Shmuel both hold *le'olam areisha* — the clause about eating applies to the first case, where each date carries a separate *hiskadshi* declaration. The apparent redundancy is resolved as a *lo miba'ya* construction.

### Objective Value

The *gemara* explains: it goes without saying that when she leaves the dates in front of her — *manacha* — and one of them is worth a *perutah*, she is betrothed, and if not, she is not. But one might have thought that when she is eating each date eagerly as it is placed before her — *ho'il u-mekarva hana'asa*, since she derives immediate pleasure from it — perhaps even a date worth less than a *perutah* suffices, on the theory that she has demonstrated by her conduct that she values it at *perutah* or more. *Ka mashma lan* — the *mishna* teaches that this is not so; the requirement remains an objective valuation of *shaveh perutah*. Tosafot notes that this is a rather weak *chidush*, since an earlier passage in the *gemara* had already established clearly that subjective satisfaction cannot substitute for the minimum objective value, but the answer stands.

### Rabbi Ami

Rabbi Ami offers a different reading: *le'olam seifa* — the eating clause does apply to the last case, the combined statement. And his explanation resolves the structural difficulty by reinterpreting the phrase *im yesh be-achas mehen shaveh perutah*: it does not mean that any one of the dates needs to be worth a *perutah*, as the plain reading would suggest. Rather, it means *ad she-yavo be-achrona shaveh perutah* — the last date given must itself be worth a *perutah*.

### Act Completion

The logic is as follows. When he says "this and this and this," the act of *kiddushin* is not complete until the final word of the declaration. At the moment the declaration is complete, all the dates he gave beforehand have already been consumed. Those earlier dates no longer exist in any concrete form; they are, at best, outstanding obligations — money she would owe him if the *kiddushin* were to fail. Something given as *kesef kiddushin* that would have to be returned if the *kiddushin* does not take effect functions as a loan, a *milveh*, not as a present object. And one cannot effect *kiddushin* with a *milveh*. The only item that is concretely present and not yet consumed at the moment the declaration is finished is the last date. Therefore, only if that final date is worth a *perutah* can the *kiddushin* take effect.

### Milveh Invalid

*Amar Rava: shema mina mi-de-Rabbi Ami tlat.* From Rabbi Ami's reading of the *mishna*, Rava draws three inferences. The first: *shema mina ha-mekadesh be-milveh eina mekudeshet* — since the *mishna*'s analysis treats the eaten dates as *milveh* and therefore ineffective for *kiddushin*, we learn that marrying with a *milveh* does not work. This will be the subject of extended subsequent *gemara*.

### Milveh + Perutah

The second inference: *shema mina ha-mekadesh be-milveh u-perutah da'ata a-perutah*. Suppose a man says to a woman: "I marry you with the hundred dollars you owe me — keep that debt — and with this penny." The *milveh* component cannot serve as *kesef kiddushin*; the question is whether the penny alone can carry the act. One might argue that since he invoked the *milveh* as part of the package and that part is invalid, the entire declaration is compromised. Alternatively, the *milveh* drops out as irrelevant, and the concrete *perutah* before her does the work — provided that both parties are focused on it. The *gemara* phrases this as *da'ata a-perutah* (and in parallel passages *da'ateih*), indicating that the mental focus of both parties on the concrete *perutah* is what allows the *kiddushin* to function despite the invalid *milveh* component.

### Milveh vs Matana

The third inference concerns the status of the money in the first place. *Maot be-alma chozrin* — when *kesef kiddushin* is given and the *kiddushin* fails to take effect, the money must ordinarily be returned. This is the premise of calling the early consumed dates a *milveh*: they would need to be returned if the *kiddushin* did not go through. Tosafot raises the question of whether this premise is itself self-evident. What if we were to say instead that *kesef kiddushin* is a *matana* — a gift — regardless of whether the *kiddushin* takes effect? If the eaten dates were hers to keep in any event, we would not frame them as a debt; we might rather say she owns them outright and the subsequent dates are simply part of one ongoing *kinyan*. Tosafot argues that if the money were indeed a *matana*, the *mishna* itself would be inexplicable: there would then be no reason why the last date specifically must be worth a *perutah*, since the aggregate of everything she received — all hers in any event — could simply combine to meet the threshold. The fact that the *mishna* requires the last date to carry a *perutah* only makes sense if the earlier dates are a *milveh* and thus disqualified from serving as *kesef kiddushin*. Rava's third inference is therefore that the premise of *maot chozrin* — money given for *kiddushin* must be returned if the *kiddushin* fails — is the correct one.

---

## Sister Marriage Case

### Setup

The *gemara* now presents a vivid illustration of these principles. *Ha-mekadesh achoto* — a man who attempts to betroth his own sister, saying *harei at mekudeshet li be-taba'at zo*. The *kiddushin* is of course void. The question is what happens to the ring.

### Rava: Return It

*Rava amar: maot chozrin* — she must return the ring; it is a *milveh*, and he retains legal title. *Ve-gamar ve-nasan le-shum pikadon* — and the legal framing of what occurred is that he gave it to her as a deposit, a *pikadon*, held on his behalf.

### Why Pikadon

But if that is what he intended, why not simply say outright: "hold this for me"? *Savar lo mekablah* — she would refuse. By framing it as *kiddushin*, even a transparently void *kiddushin*, the ring passes into her hand. The practical purpose is to get the object into her possession while preserving his legal ownership, rather than seeking her cooperation in an ordinary bailment.

### Shmuel: Gift

*U-Shmuel savar: maot matana.* Shmuel holds the ring is a gift. *Adam yodeya she-ein kiddushin tofsin be-achoto* — he obviously knew that *kiddushin* cannot take effect with one's own sister, *ve-gamar ve-nasan le-shum matana* — and so his giving of the ring, whatever form it took, was in substance a gift. Again the *gemara* asks: why not simply say "this is a gift"? *Savar kesifa lei milsa* — it would be embarrassing for her to receive it framed as a gift, so the form of *kiddushin* provides a face-saving vehicle for the transfer.

### Ravina's Question

Ravina challenges the underlying logic of this entire dispute. If all parties understand that the *kiddushin* is void — and indeed everyone knows that *kiddushin* with one's sister is invalid — then the debate between *milveh* and *matana* might seem academic. Both Rava and Shmuel agree that no valid *kiddushin* has occurred; the only question is the legal characterization of the transfer itself.

---

## Hallah Case

### Flour Not Hallah

The *gemara* introduces a parallel case. *Ha-mafrish chalato kemach* — one who separates *challah* while the grain product is still flour, before it has become dough. *Challah* can only be designated from dough, not from flour; the separation is therefore legally ineffective, *eino challah*.

### Kohen Keeping

*Ve-gezel be-yad kohen* — if the flour was nonetheless given to a *kohen*, and the *kohen* retained it, that would constitute theft. This is the position of the *gemara*. The challenge to Shmuel is immediate: *naima adam yodeya she-ein mafrishin challah kemach* — according to Shmuel's principle, since everyone knows that *challah* cannot be taken from flour, the transaction should be read as a *matana* and the *kohen* should be entitled to keep the flour.

### Confusion Risk

The *gemara* responds: *shani hasam de-nafik churba mineih* — that case is different because permitting the *kohen* to keep the flour would cause serious harm. If the *kohen* retains it, he will conclude that the separation was in fact valid *challah*.

### Partial Knowledge

But this concern seems to contradict itself: if everyone knows you cannot take *challah* from flour, why would the *kohen* draw a false conclusion? The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between knowing a rule and understanding its reason. *Yada de-ein mafrishin challah kemach ve-eino yodea tama mai* — people know that one is not supposed to separate *challah* from flour, but they do not necessarily know *why*. They may think the reason is only *tircha de-kohen* — an inconvenience to the *kohen*, who would have to convert the flour to dough — and that perhaps the separation is valid *be-di'eved*. If the *kohen* is then permitted to keep the flour, they will infer that the separation did take effect retroactively.

### Force Return

To prevent this confusion, the flour must be returned. Allowing the *kohen* to retain it would implicitly signal that the *challah* designation was valid, leading people to draw incorrect halachic conclusions.

### Hydroponics Parallel

The *gemara* then asks why the same concern does not prevent a comparable ruling in the case of *terumah min ha-nakuv al she-eino nakuv* — terumah taken from produce grown in a perforated pot on behalf of produce grown in an unperforated pot. Produce grown without a perforation in the pot is not biblically obligated in *terumah*, so the designation is technically invalid. Nevertheless, the *halacha* there is that the *kohen* may keep the produce, though he may not eat it until *terumah* has been properly separated from another source: *de-tehavei terumah ve-lo tochal ad she-yotzi aleha terumah u-ma'aser mi-makom acher*. Why does this not create the same confusion?

### One vs Two Vessels

*Bitrei mane tsaytei, be-chad mana lo tsaytei* — with two vessels, people will listen and understand; with one vessel, they will not. In the hydroponics case, there are two distinct containers involved — the perforated and unperforated pots — and the distinction between them is tangible enough that people can comprehend why the *terumah* taken from one does not cover the other. Knowing that two vessels were involved, they will accept the teaching that the *kohen* must separate again and will understand that the original designation was somehow incomplete. By contrast, in the flour case there is only one vessel and one substance throughout; telling the *kohen* that he may keep the flour while insisting that it is not really *challah* will not register. People will simply take the *kohen*'s possession as confirmation that the separation was valid. Therefore, in the flour case, the only way to prevent the false inference is to demand return of the flour entirely.

---

---

# Kiddushin 46

## Ketana Shelo L'Da'as Avi…

### Father Travels Abroad

The *gemara* on 45b deals with the case of a *ketana* whose *kiddushin* was performed with her father's knowledge — whether the father himself arranged the marriage or whether she entered into it herself with his clear approval. The central question concerns what happens next: *vehalach aviha limedinas hayam* — the father subsequently travels to a distant country — and then *ve'amda venises* — she proceeds directly to *chuppah* without the father's knowledge or consent. Do we presume that since the *kiddushin* was *leda'as aviha*, he would naturally be pleased that the *nisuin* took place whenever it did? Or do we say that the *chuppah* without his explicit approval is problematic?

This raises a deeper conceptual question about the nature of *nisuin* as a *kinyan*. On one hand, one might argue that *chuppah* is less a new act of *kinyan* and more the translation of an already-established legal status into a factual living arrangement, and therefore requires less *da'as* than an entirely new *kinyan*. On the other hand, *nisuin* is precisely the moment when a *ketana* or *na'arah* leaves her father's *reshus* and enters her husband's *reshus*. Even if in the case of an adult woman *nisuin* requires somewhat less formal *da'as*, here one cannot imagine that she can transition out of the father's control without his approval. Several *nafka minas* attend this question: can she eat *terumah* if her husband is a *kohen* — since a wife of a *kohen* may eat *terumah* only once she is a *nesu'ah* — and does her husband inherit her estate if she dies?

### Rav vs. Rav Assi

The *gemara* records the following dispute. *Amar Rav ocheles biterumah* — Rav holds that she is presumed to be a *nesu'ah* and may eat *terumah* if her husband is a *kohen*, and this presumption holds *ad sheyavo aviha veyimcheh* — unless and until the father returns and objects. If the father protests, retroactively she will not have been a *nesu'ah*, at least for so long as she remains a *ketana* or *na'arah* under his authority.

Rav Assi disagrees: *eina ocheles*, she may not eat *terumah*, *shema yavo aviha veyimcheh* — because we are concerned the father may object when he returns, and if he does, it will turn out retroactively that she was a non-*kohen*'s wife eating *terumah*, a *zar* eating *terumah l'mafre'a*. The question is whether we begin from a presumption that the father will likely approve, or whether we begin from a posture of concern.

The *gemara* records that there was an actual incident — *hava uvda v'chash lah Rav l'ha d'Rav Assi* — and Rav was *machmir* in practice like the position of Rav Assi. Some *Rishonim* understand that Rav did not actually rule like Rav Assi; he simply adopted the stringent position as a practical matter, while maintaining that *min hadin* — strictly speaking — she is permitted.

### Okki Mamona B'Chezkas

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak reports a concession that qualifies Rav's position significantly: *u'modeh Rav she'im mesa eina yorshah* — Rav concedes that if she were to die, her husband does not inherit her. Even though Rav considers her *nesu'ah* enough to permit the eating of *terumah*, the *nisuin* is not sufficiently established to transfer her estate to the husband upon her death. The reason is *oki mamona b'chezkas mareih* — money, or property, remains in the possession of its original owner under conditions of doubt. Since it is uncertain whether there is *nisuin*, we do not remove property from her estate and transfer it to him.

This creates an apparent tension: if Rav concedes enough doubt about the *nisuin* that he will not allow the property to transfer, how does he permit her to eat *terumah* on the basis that she is a *nesu'ah*?

### Terumah vs. Yerusha

The resolution offered by Rashi and Tosafot is grounded in the distinction between *mide'oraisa* and *miderabbanan*. According to the Bavli, from the moment of *kiddushin* the wife of a *kohen* may eat *terumah* by Torah law — she does not need to be a *nesu'ah* for this. The requirement that specifically a *nesu'ah* may eat *terumah* — to the exclusion of an *arusin* — is a *miderabbanan* enactment. Accordingly, both Rav and Rav Assi agree that her status as a *nesu'ah* is a *safek*. When it comes to the Rabbinic question of *terumah*, Rav is willing to be lenient. When it comes to the Biblical matter of *yerusha*, where property can only be transferred with certainty, he is not.

Tosafot adds a further point: one might ask why Rav Assi is concerned about this *miderabbanan* restriction at all, given that the practical rationale behind the Rabbinic enactment — namely that an *arusin* who lives separately might bring *terumah* back to her father's non-*kohen* household — does not apply here, since she is living with her husband. Tosafot answers that the Rabbis made the enactment without drawing internal distinctions — *lo plug* — and therefore even in this case the formal rule applies.

---

## Father Present, Silent

### Kiddushin Yes, Nisuin No

The *gemara* now turns to a variation: the *kiddushin* was *leda'as aviha* — her father knew of and approved the *kiddushin* — but the *nisuin* took place *shelo leda'as aviha*, and the father is present, *v'aviha kan*. Presumably the father found out after the fact and said nothing. What is the legal status of his silence?

### Silence: Approval or Obj…

Rav Huna says: *eina ocheles* — she may not eat *terumah*. Even accepting Rav's position that when the father is in a distant country we presume he would approve, *hasam hu d'lo isei l'av* — that is only because the father is not present, and in his absence we may assume he will be satisfied when he learns of it. But here, *d'isei l'av* — the father is present. He heard about the *nisuin* and said nothing. *Hai de'ishtik mirtzach ratach* — his silence reflects smoldering anger; a man too upset to speak should not be understood as having acquiesced.

Rav Yirmeya bar Abba disagrees: *ocheles*. Even granting Rav Assi's position that when the father is far away we are concerned he will object — *hasam hu d'shema yavo aviha veyimcheh* — that is because there is an open question whether he will protest. But here, *de'ishtik, isnuche ishnach leh* — he heard and said nothing, which we interpret as acceptance. The principle of *shtika k'hoda'ah* — that silence in the face of a known fact constitutes a form of assent — supports this reading. Normally, we would expect an opposed party to say something.

This leads to a striking analytical observation. The position that makes intuitive sense is Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's: if one begins from a presumption of concern (Rav Assi's approach), silence that follows upon hearing changes the calculus, since a person who genuinely objects would speak up. What is harder to understand is the reverse switch in Rav Huna's reasoning: if one begins from a presumption that the father will be fine with it (Rav's approach), how does the fact that he heard and said nothing make things *worse* than when he was simply absent? The idea that silence signals rage rather than approval seems strained when the baseline presumption is benign.

### Both Acts Unknown

The *gemara* now advances to a more extreme scenario: *niskadsha shelo leda'as aviha venisas shelo leda'as aviha v'aviha kan* — both the *kiddushin* and the *nisuin* were performed without the father's knowledge, and the father is present. Again, the assumption is that once he found out, he was silent. Here Rav Huna says *ocheles* — she may eat — while Rav Yirmeya bar Abba says *eina ocheles*. The positions are now reversed from the previous case.

Ulla is sharply critical of Rav Huna's ruling here. He invokes the verse: *k'chometz l'shinayim u'k'ashan l'einayim* — like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes — to convey how intolerable this position is. The argument is stark: in the *immediately preceding case*, where the *kiddushin* was definitely valid and performed with his knowledge, and only the *nisuin* was done without him — yet Rav Huna there said the father's silence signals objection and she *cannot* eat — how can it be that here, where the father was not even present for the *kiddushin*, his silence now somehow signals approval?

### Nachas B'Ma'aseh

Rava defends Rav Huna with a different rationale. *Mai ta'ama d'Rav Huna? Ho'v'na'aseh b'ma'aseh yatom b'chayei av* — this girl has been conducting herself as though she has no father. Two major events in her life — *kiddushin* and *nisuin* — have occurred without his knowledge or involvement, and he has reacted to neither. In such a pattern of behavior, where the daughter consistently acts autonomously and the father consistently fails to assert his authority, we interpret the cumulative passivity as an implicit relinquishment of control. He has essentially made his peace and decided to let her make her own decisions.

The contrast with the previous case is now coherent: when the *kiddushin* was firmly established under his auspices and authority, and only the *nisuin* was done without him, he has never done anything to signal that he was stepping back from his paternal role. His silence regarding the *nisuin* alone is therefore reasonably read as resistance. But when he allowed *both* acts to occur without reaction, the pattern itself speaks — and we conclude he has, in effect, yielded.

---

## Father's Direct Response

### Bein Hi U'Vein Aviha

The *gemara* now returns to the original case: *ketana sheniskadsha shelo leda'as aviha* — a *ketana* who entered into *kiddushin* without her father's knowledge. This was the primary focus of the previous *sugya*, and the conclusion of Rav and Shmuel was that there is a *chashash kiddushin* — one is concerned that *kiddushin* may have taken effect — on the possibility that the father will retroactively approve, *shema yisratzeh ha'av*. What was never clarified there, however, is: what happens when the father actually responds?

Rav now addresses this directly: *bein hi uvein aviha yecholim limchos* — both the daughter and the father can prevent the *kiddushin* from taking effect, or conversely can ratify it. This is, on the surface, somewhat surprising. We already know that if the father objects, there is no concern — that is obvious. The new information is that *she* can also object. But how? She was the one who accepted the *kiddushin*. She is a minor, so what does her objection mean?

Rashi explains that her objection is only effective if it occurs *before* the father finds out. She accepted the money; the father will hear of it tomorrow; but if before he does she retracts, she has cut off the possibility of ratification before it could crystallize. The act of acceptance is undermined by her subsequent retraction before the father's knowledge can validate it.

Tosafot offers a broader reading: she may be able to object even *after* the father approves, on the theory that the father's approval is premised on her also being agreeable. However, Tosafot is vague on the outer limits of this — does she have an indefinite window to object? — and this reading is admittedly difficult, since she was the one who originally accepted the *kiddushin*.

### Shtika vs. Micha

Tosafot clarifies the relationship between this ruling and everything that came before. When Rav earlier said there is a *chashash* that the father will approve — *chaishinan shema yisratzeh ha'av* — that ruling was specifically in a case of *stam*, where the father heard and was silent, *sheshama v'shatak*. The entire preceding *sugya* was about how to interpret paternal silence. But where the father explicitly objects — *micha, gila b'da'ato* — he has disclosed his position and the *kiddushin* is certainly void. Similarly, if he explicitly approves, it is certainly valid. The debate about silence is thus the operative center of the preceding discussion, which now becomes clear in retrospect.

### Daughter's Miun

The right of the daughter to object constitutes a form of *miun* — refusal — in the context of a *ketana*. It is a different mechanism than ordinary *miun*, since according to Rav there is at least a *chashash kiddushin d'oraisa*. According to Rav Assi, however, only the father can object — *aviha v'lo hi* — which is the more standard position. The father's authority over his minor daughter's marriage is the default; the daughter's power of objection is the exceptional ruling that requires derivation.

---

## Seduction & Torah

### Midrash on Seduction

Rav Huna (or, in another version, Chiyya bar Rav) presents a challenge to Rav Assi from the Biblical passage dealing with *mefuta* — the case of a man who seduces a *na'arah*. The verse states *im ma'ein yema'ein aviha lesitta lo* — if the father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the seducer must pay fifty *kesef*. The *gemara* asks: from where do we know that *she* can also refuse? The answer derived by *midrash* is from the doubled language of *ma'ein yema'ein* — a doubling that implies both the father's refusal and hers. The underlying assumption of the question is that the Torah case involves a *kiddushin* of sorts — the seduction was *leshum ishus*, for the purpose of marriage, and the act of intimacy constituted *kiddushei bi'ah*, with the father's knowledge now a condition of validity. This is precisely analogous to the cases we have been discussing.

### Pita Shelo L'Shum

Rav deflects the challenge: *lo teizil basar ipcha* — do not seek complications. *Yacholni lshinuyei lach lchula* — I can answer you in a way that resolves everything. Specifically: *kegon shepita shelo lshum ishus* — the seduction in the Biblical case was not for the purpose of marriage. The man simply seduced her for the sake of intimacy, not as an act of *kiddushin*. Accordingly, what the Torah is addressing when it says the father can refuse is not refusal of *kiddushin*, but refusal of the proposed marriage after the fact — since of course the father controls whom his daughter may marry, the case tells us the legal consequence of that refusal, namely that the seducer pays fifty *kesef*.

### Maher Yimarena

Rav Ashi then interjects: *ei hachi hainu dtanyana, maher yimarena lo l'isha shetricha heimenu kiddushin* — this reading actually makes good sense of the verse that follows, which says *maher yimarena lo l'isha*, meaning he must now marry her. The implication is that he still needs to perform *kiddushin*, which confirms that no *kiddushin* had yet taken place — the seduction was indeed *shelo lshum ishus*. Some *Rishonim* read *ei hachi hainu dtanyana* not as a sharp question but as an expression of approval — "ah, now it fits perfectly" — though others understand it as a genuine challenge.

### Tzricha Kiddushin L'Da'as

The *gemara* then raises the alternative reading: *ve'ei pita lshum ishus kiddushin lama li* — what if the seduction *was* for the purpose of marriage? In that case, the act of intimacy constituted *kiddushei bi'ah*. What then does *maher yimarena lo l'isha* mean? Abaye answers: *tzricha kiddushin leda'as aviha* — the verse teaches that even if the father chooses not to object and allows the marriage to proceed, a new act of *kiddushin* must be performed, this time with the father's knowledge and proper approval from the outset. This is admittedly strange — if the act of seduction already constituted *kiddushin* and the father ratifies it, why is another *kiddushin* required? The answer seems to be that the Torah is insisting on a fully proper, formal process even where the prior act has a degree of legal standing.

### Miun & Knas

The case of the daughter's refusal now requires closer attention. On the reading that the seduction was *shelo lshum ishus*, if the father objects and she does not marry the seducer, he pays fifty *kesef*. But the verse also implies she can refuse. What does her refusal accomplish, given that she is a *ketana* or *na'arah* still under her father's authority?

Tosafot addresses this in two ways. The first answer is that her *miun* — her refusal — does not prevent the marriage from taking place if the father wants it to proceed. *D'keivan d'avia rotzeh she'tehei ishto, eino yachola l'akeiv* — if the father wishes to marry her off, she cannot block it. Rather, what her refusal accomplishes is to trigger the payment of *knas*: just as the father's refusal causes the seducer to pay, so too her refusal, even if the marriage ultimately proceeds, causes the payment. This leads to what seems like an odd outcome: could the father and daughter coordinate — the father consents to the marriage, the daughter refuses, they collect the *knas* and she marries the man anyway?

Tosafot's second and better answer is that her refusal is operative specifically in the case where the father has died before the matter is resolved. *D'hashta mehani miun didah l'akeiv she'lo tehei ishto* — in the absence of a father, her refusal is what prevents the marriage from taking effect. This is more coherent: once there is no father, she is the one in whose hands the decision rests, and her *miun* then has full legal force. The general question that is never fully resolved, however, is what it means to speak of the daughter's right of refusal when a father is present and she is still a *ketana* or *na'arah* — under normal circumstances, she simply has no such right.

---

## Multiple Objects

### Separate Statements

The *gemara* turns to a *Mishnah* dealing with the case of a normal adult woman entering into *kiddushin*. If a man says to a woman *hiskadshi li b'tmara zo, hiskadshi li b'zo* — "be betrothed to me with this date, be betrothed to me with this date" — giving her separate objects with a separate declaration for each, the rule is: *im yesh b'achas meihen shaveh prutah mekudeshes* — if any one of them was individually worth a *perutah*, she is *mekudeshes*; if not, she is not, even if all of them combined would equal a *perutah*. Since each declaration constitutes a separate act of *kiddushin*, the objects cannot be combined.

### Combined Statements

If, however, he said *b'zo u'v'zo u'v'zo* — "with this and this and this" — without repeating the declaration between each object, then *im yesh shaveh prutah b'kulam mekudeshes* — as long as they collectively amount to a *perutah*, she is *mekudeshes*. Since the single declaration covers all the objects together, they combine into one act.

### Eating While Giving

A third case: *haysa ocheles rishona rishona* — if she was eating each date as he placed it in front of her, *einah mekudeshes ad she'tehei b'achas meihen shaveh prutah* — she is not *mekudeshes* unless one of the objects is individually worth a *perutah*. The reason for this rule is the focus of the subsequent *gemara*.

The *gemara* first asks who the *tana* is who holds that saying *hiskadshi, hiskadshi* between each object is what breaks the statements into discrete acts. Rabbah answers that it is Rabbi Shimon, who holds the same principle in the context of *shvuos*: if one says "a *shvuah* I do not owe you, and a *shvuah* I do not owe you," those are separate oaths with separate *korbanos* for false swearing. But if one says "a *shvuah* I do not owe you or you or you," that is one oath. The same logic applies here.

### Areisha L'Olam

The *gemara* then asks on which clause of the *Mishnah* the eating case applies. If we say it is the first clause — the case of separate *hiskadshi* declarations — the point of mentioning eating is unclear. In that case even without eating, if one of the dates was worth a *perutah*, she would be *mekudeshes*, and if not, not. Why add the detail of eating? Rav and Shmuel both say *le'olam areisha* — it goes on the first clause — and the *Mishnah* employs the rhetorical device of *lo mibaya*: it goes without saying that if the dates are simply lying before her, the rule is that each needs to be worth a *perutah*; the *chidush* is that even when she is eating them eagerly, demonstrating immediate enjoyment — *ho'il u'mekarva hana'atah* — one might have thought that her enthusiasm itself signals acceptance even for less than a *perutah*. The *Mishnah* teaches that this is not so: a *perutah* of objective value is still required. Tosafot notes that this is a relatively weak *chidush*, since the earlier *gemara* made clear that *kiddushin* requires an objectively recognized *perutah*, not a subjective sense of value.

### Aseifa L'Olam

Rabbi Ami offers the more natural reading: *le'olam aseifa* — it goes on the last clause, the combined-statement case. The *Mishnah*'s rule that "one of them must be worth a *perutah*" means specifically the *last* one. Here is the logic: when a man says "with this and this and this," the act of *kiddushin* is not complete until the final object is given. By that time, she has already eaten the preceding dates. Those earlier dates no longer exist as concrete objects; they have been consumed. Consequently, the man cannot "marry her" with those dates in their current non-existent form — to do so would be *mekadesh b'milveh*, marrying with a debt, which is invalid. However, the last date, which has not yet been eaten at the moment the statement concludes and the act is completed, is present before her. If that last date is worth a *perutah*, the *kiddushin* takes effect on the basis of that concrete object.

### Shma Mina Tlat

Rava then draws three inferences from Rabbi Ami's explanation. *Shma mina hamekadesh b'milveh einah mekudeshes* — first, it is confirmed that one who performs *kiddushin* using a debt (a *milveh*) accomplishes nothing, since Rabbi Ami does not challenge the premise of the question but rather redirects which date is operative.

*U'shma mina hamekadesh b'milveh u'prutah da'atah a'prutah* — second, if a man says "marry me with the hundred dollars you owe me and with this additional penny," does it work? One might argue that since he framed it as both the debt and the coin, and the debt portion is invalid for *kiddushin*, perhaps the coin does not stand alone either. Rava infers from Rabbi Ami's ruling that in such a case, both he and she are understood to be focusing on the concrete *perutah* before them — *da'atah a'prutah* — and the *milveh* component drops away as legally inoperative, leaving the *perutah* as the effective *kesef kiddushin*.

*Shma mina ma'os be'alma chozrin* — third, the very fact that we describe the earlier consumed dates as a *milveh* implies that money given as *kesef kiddushin* that does not result in valid *kiddushin* must be returned. If the money were simply a *matanah* — a gift — there would be no reason to call it a *milveh* at all.

### Mkvadesh B'Milveh

Tosafot raises a question on this third inference: is Rava not simply reading his assumption back out of his conclusion? The question *u'milveh hi* was posed as a challenge, and now we are deriving from Rabbi Ami's non-response that yes, it is a *milveh*. But what if the money was treated as a *matanah*? Tosafot argues that the distinction is legally significant: if the money given during the sequential date-giving is understood as a *matanah* regardless of whether *kiddushin* ultimately takes effect, then she owns each date the moment she receives it. In that case, there is no conceptual gap between the early dates and the later ones — she already owns them, and there is no "debt" relationship to speak of. Accordingly, the entire combined statement could be viewed as one integrated act, and the collective value might suffice for *kiddushin*. The only way to explain why the *Mishnah* requires one specific date to be worth a *perutah* by itself is through the *milveh* framework: since those earlier dates might need to be returned if *kiddushin* fails, they are conceptually debt rather than concrete present property, and *kiddushin* cannot rest upon them.

---

## Invalid Kiddushin Cases

### Sister Marriage

The *gemara* now presents a clearer case: *hamekadesh achoto* — a man who "betroths" his sister, declaring *harei at mekudeshes li b'tabaat zu*. This obviously cannot take effect. The question is: does she return the ring?

### Money Returns

Rav says *ma'os chozrin* — the money must be returned. The reasoning is *adam yodea she'ein kiddushin topsin b'achoso, v'gamar v'nasan lshum pikadon* — he knows perfectly well that *kiddushin* cannot take effect with his sister, so his act of giving the ring is to be understood as a deposit, as placing the object in her hands for safekeeping. The *gemara* asks: if that is what he intended, why not simply say so explicitly? The answer is *savar lo mikabla* — he was concerned she would refuse to accept it if framed that way, so the *kiddushin* language was a pretext to get the ring into her hands. Since the underlying intention was a deposit, it must be returned.

### Money as Gift

Shmuel disagrees: *ma'os matanah* — the money is a gift. *Adam yodea she'ein kiddushin topsin b'achoso, v'gamar v'nasan lshum matanah* — knowing that no *kiddushin* can take effect, his act of giving must be interpreted as an outright gift. The *gemara* similarly asks: if so, why not say explicitly it is a gift? *Savar ksifa lei milsa* — it would be embarrassing. Framing it as a gift is socially awkward, whereas the *kiddushin* framing allows the ring to pass into her possession without the discomfort of one party explicitly giving the other a gift in this context. The practical effect is that she keeps it.

---

## Challah & Terumah Cases

### Challah Flour Case

Ravina challenges Shmuel's position with a parallel case: *hamfrish chalato kemach* — one who separates *challah* while the grain is still flour rather than dough. This is invalid; *challah* cannot be separated until the dough stage. *Eino challah* — it does not take effect as *challah*. And yet, if the flour was given to a *kohen*, we say *v'gezel b'yad kohen* — it is theft in the *kohen*'s possession; the *kohen* must return it. But why, according to Shmuel?

### Confusion Risk

The *gemara* applies Shmuel's logic: everyone knows that *challah* cannot be separated from flour, so why not say the person gave it as a *matanah*, and let the *kohen* keep it? The *gemara* answers: *shani hasam d'nafi churbah minei* — this case is different, because allowing the *kohen* to keep the flour would lead to a serious problem. *Zimnin d'is lei l'kohen pachos m'chamesh rivayim kemach* — there may come a time when the *kohen* has slightly less than the minimum quantity of flour obligated in *challah*. He then takes the flour you gave him — which he believes is already *challah* — and mixes it with his own supply. Now the combined quantity exceeds the threshold and is genuinely obligated in *challah*, but he thinks no *challah* need be separated because he believes a portion of the mixture already is *challah*. *V'asi l'meichal b'tevel* — he will eat the bread when it is still *tevel*, since true *challah* was never separated.

The *gemara* then challenges this reasoning: you just said that everyone knows you do not separate *challah* from flour — so why would the *kohen* be confused? The answer distinguishes between knowing the rule and understanding its legal consequence. People know that one is *not supposed to* separate *challah* from flour, and they assume the rationale is *mishum tircha dekohen* — so as not to burden the *kohen* with having to convert flour to dough himself. But they do not know with certainty what happens *bedi'avad* if it was done anyway. They may think it worked after the fact, especially since the *kohen* is *mochel* on his own *tircha*. Therefore, if we allow him to keep the flour without requiring return, people will conclude it really did work, leading to the error described.

### Hydroponic Terumah

The *gemara* proposes an alternative solution: rather than requiring the *kohen* to return the flour, perhaps declare it simultaneously *challah* and not-*challah* — allow him to keep it but require him to separate *challah* again from another source before eating. A precedent exists for this kind of dual status. The *gemara* cites a case: *min hanakuv al she'eino nakuv* — one takes *terumah* from produce grown in a pot with a hole (which is biblically obligated) on behalf of produce grown in a pot without a hole (hydroponic produce, which is not fully biblically obligated). The *terumah* separated in this way has an ambiguous status. The ruling is: *terumah* — it is treated with the stringency of *terumah* — *velo tochal ad sheyotzi alei terumah uma'aser mimmakom acher* — but it cannot be eaten until additional *terumah* and *ma'aser* are separated from another source. The *kohen* keeps the produce but must separate again. Why not do the same with the flour?

### Bitrei Mani vs. Echad

The *gemara* answers with a distinction of considerable practical subtlety. *Bitrei mani tzyat, b'chad mana lo tzyat* — with two vessels they will understand; with one vessel they will not. The hydroponics case involves produce from two conceptually distinct categories — pots with holes and pots without holes are recognizably different situations. When told that the *kohen* can keep the produce but must separate again, the recipient intuitively grasps that there is something unusual about the provenance of this particular produce, and the dual treatment makes sense to him.

### Return vs. Re-Separate

But in the flour case, everything is *chad mana* — one vessel, one undifferentiated mass. If we tell the *kohen* he can keep the flour but must separate *challah* again, he will not understand why. As far as he can see, the flour he holds is *challah*, full stop — and the instruction to separate again will strike him as incomprehensible. He will not internalize the message that the original separation was invalid; he will simply think the requirement to re-separate is an inexplicable imposition. Under these conditions, the confusion is not adequately addressed by requiring re-separation. The only solution that genuinely communicates the invalidity of the original act is insisting on return. Therefore, in the flour case, the *kohen* must return the flour; in the hydroponic case, he may keep the produce but must separate again.

---

---

# Kiddushin 47

## Multiple Dates

### Intro: Dates & Shaveh

The discussion opens in the context of the *mishnah* dealing with a man who counts off individual dates — or similar objects — one by one, saying "marry me with this, and with this, and with this," and the question whether each date constitutes a separate act of *kiddushin* or whether they are combined into one act, such that collectively they might satisfy the requirement of *shaveh perutah*. We pick up on the bottom of 46b, approximately twenty lines from the bottom, at the line beginning with the word *bechamna*.

### Money: Gift or Loan?

At this point the *gemara* temporarily moves away from the question about counting off the dates and raises a different question: if a man performs *kiddushin* and for some reason the *kiddushin* does not take effect, must the woman return the money? Is the money to be treated as a gift — a *matanah* — or as a *pikadon*, an entrusted object held in trust? Obviously, if he stated his intention explicitly, there is no question. The issue is how to interpret the transaction legally when nothing further was said.

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The *gemara* frames the question as a debate between Rav and Shmuel, using the case of a man who betroths his sister — a *kiddushin* that everyone understands is entirely invalid. Does she return the money or may she keep it? Rav holds she must return it, which seems to be the straightforward position: why should we read into the transaction a new gift? Shmuel, however, holds that she may keep it.

### Challah Analogy

The *gemara* challenges Shmuel's position from a case involving one who separates *challah* from flour — that is, before it has become dough — and gives it to a *kohen*. This is similarly a transaction that everyone should understand is ineffective. The *halakhah* is that the *kohen* must return the flour; he does not get to keep it. This appears to support Rav's position.

### Shmuel's Reasoning

The *gemara* explains that according to Shmuel, the reason the *kohen* must return the flour is not because of any general principle about invalid transactions, but rather to prevent confusion about the law. If the *kohen* keeps the flour, the *ba'al habayit* or the *kohen* himself might come to think the *challah* separation was valid, leading to further violations. The flour is therefore returned as a way of reinforcing that it was not effective *challah*. Shmuel's broader position — that recipients may generally keep what was given in such contexts — remains intact; it is only the specific concern about legal confusion that mandates return here.

### Alternative: 2nd Separat…

The *gemara* then asks: within the logic of Shmuel's reasoning, why not find an intermediate solution? Let the *kohen* keep the flour, but instruct him to separate *challah* again from it — or, equivalently, once it becomes dough. That would signal to everyone that the original separation was invalid, and the *kohen* would still benefit from keeping the flour. The *gemara* supports this suggestion by noting that the *kohen* would be willing to listen (*metzayet*) to such an instruction.

### Why Alt. Fails

The problem, says the *gemara*, is the *ba'al habayit*. Even if the *kohen* would listen to us and separate *challah* a second time, the *ba'al habayit* will not see that second separation. From his perspective, he gave flour, the *kohen* kept it, and the transaction is done. He will now believe his own obligation has been discharged and will proceed to eat his remaining dough while it is still *tevel* — untithed produce. This creates a serious violation. Therefore, returning the flour to the *ba'al habayit* is the only way to prevent the confusion.

### Owner's Knowledge

The *gemara* then raises what seems like an obvious objection: surely everyone knows that one does not separate *challah* from flour before it becomes dough — the *ba'al habayit* knows this! The *gemara* responds with a subtle but important distinction: *yodeia v'eino yodeia* — he sort of knows, but not fully. He knows the norm is not to do it. However, he does not know the underlying reason. He assumes the prohibition is merely a matter of not burdening the *kohen* with the extra work of turning flour into dough, and since the *kohen* here was willing to accept the flour (*tircha d'kohen kablah*), he may conclude that *bedi'avad* — after the fact — the separation might have been valid.
