Because his understanding is incomplete and his error is therefore plausible, we must return the flour to correct any possible misconception.

### Hydroponic Plants

The *gemara* continues exploring alternative solutions. It asks: why not tell the *ba'al habayit* that the *kohen* may keep the flour, but that the *ba'al habayit* must separate *challah* a second time? This is modeled on a known case: one who takes *terumah* from hydroponic plants intending it to apply to produce grown in the soil. In that case, the *kohen* keeps the hydroponic produce, and the owner is instructed to separate a second time. So too here, perhaps the *ba'al habayit* can be instructed to separate again. The *gemara* rejects this parallel: in the hydroponic case, the two items are *trei minei* — fundamentally different categories — and for that reason the owner accepts that the first separation did not cover the second type and willingly separates again. But in the case of flour and dough, it is essentially the same substance. There is no reason apparent to the owner why he should have to separate a second time if the *kohen* is keeping the flour. He will not listen, and the desired effect will not be achieved.

### Challenge: Same Object

The *gemara* presses further: is it really true that a person will not listen to a second separation when the same type of object is involved? Is there no precedent for that?

### Watermelon Precedent

The *gemara* answers its own challenge from a *mishnah*: one who separated a gourd (*kishut*) as *terumah* and it turned out to be bitter, or a watermelon and it turned out to be sour (*avatiach ve-nimtzet saruach*) — the *kohen* keeps what was given, and the owner must separate again. Here it is all the same category — all watermelons — yet we say the separation was effective and the owner must repeat it. This would seem to show that even from a single type, people do listen to a second separation.

### Distinction: Biblical Va…

The *gemara* distinguishes this case. Even in the watermelon situation, it is not clear that people will actually comply with the instruction to separate again. But it does not matter, because even if they do not listen, the first *terumah* is *min ha-Torah* valid — it is biblically effective *terumah de-Oraita*. Since the sour watermelon is still, at least nominally, somewhat edible, the separation takes effect *bedi'avad*. If they fail to separate again, we are not left with a complete violation, because the first separation was already biblically sound. The flour case is entirely different — there the first separation was not valid at all, and if the owner does not separate again, the dough will be eaten as *tevel*. Therefore, the watermelon precedent does not apply.

### Leviticus Source

How do we know that separating from the inferior on the superior — *min ha-ra al ha-yafeh* — takes effect *bedi'avad*? Rabbi Ila derives this from the verse: "You shall not bear sin when you take the *chelbo* — the best of it — as *terumah*" (Leviticus). The implication is that if you do not take from the best — that is, if you take from the inferior on the superior — you will have sinned. As the *gemara* reasons, the concept of bearing sin (*nesi'at cheit*) only makes sense if the act was legally effective. If the bad-on-good separation had no legal force whatsoever, there would be nothing to bear sin over: one tried to do something wrong but achieved nothing. The fact that the *pasuk* speaks of *cheit* demonstrates that the act did take hold — it was a valid but sinful *terumah*.

It is worth noting that *Tosafot* raises a significant question here, since there is an entire discussion in *Temurah* about the general principle of *kol milta de-amar Rachmana la ta'avid i avid mahani o lo mahani* — whether an act performed in violation of a Torah prohibition takes legal effect. The cases vary: some prohibited acts do achieve their intended legal effect (*arayot*, for instance, are *chal*), while others do not (*issurei lav* generally are not *chal*). *Tosafot* asks how the *gemara* here can draw the inference it does without accounting for that general debate. He explains that even according to those who hold that a prohibited act may be punishable without taking effect, in this specific case the *gemara* understands from the structure of the *pasuk* itself that the only way the actor incurred a *cheit* is if the *terumah* was in fact *chal*. The generalization is fair, but the broader question is independently debated.

In summary: according to Shmuel, if someone betroths his sister, she gets to keep the money, because in principle parties may retain what was given in an invalid transaction. The *kohen* must return the flour only because specific concerns about legal confusion — on the part of either the *kohen* or the *ba'al habayit* — require it, and none of the proposed intermediate solutions adequately addresses those concerns.

---

## Back to Mishnah

### Bezo Vezo Vezo Case

Rava now returns to the *mishnah* at the top of 47a. The question is: when does the rule apply that if she eats individual dates as they are handed to her, those eaten dates cannot be counted toward the *shaveh perutah*? Rava specifies: this is only where the man said *bezu uvezu uvezu* — "with this, and with this, and with this" — designating each date separately as he gives it.

### Eating: Last Date Only

In the *bezu uvezu uvezu* case, if she eats each date as he hands it to her, the problem is that the act of *kiddushin* is not complete until the man finishes his statement. Each date eaten before that final moment has already been consumed — it is no longer present when the act of *kiddushin* is definitively concluded. Those dates are therefore analogous to a *milveh*: they were given, but they are no longer around at the legally significant moment. The only date that counts is the last one — the one still in existence when his statement concludes — and that final date must itself be worth a *perutah*.

### Collective: All Combined

The case is different, says Rava, when the man says *ba'elu* — "marry me with these" — using a collective formulation while indicating the entire group of dates in his hand. He then hands them to her one by one and she eats each as it is given. Even so, she is *mekudeshes*. Why? Because the moment he completed the statement *ba'elu*, the entire group was already designated as *kesef kiddushin*. The act of *kiddushin* was definitionally complete at that moment. Everything she subsequently receives, she receives as her own property — *ki ka'achla midida ka'achla*, when she eats it, she eats what is already hers. There is no *milveh* problem, because there is no longer any ambiguity about whether these dates are *kesef kiddushin*. They were so designated before she received the first one.

This is the precise significance of the *chiddush*: in the *bezu uvezu uvezu* scenario, where each date is described individually and the act of *kiddushin* is not complete until the end, the earlier dates are consumed before the transaction is finalized and cannot be counted collectively. In the *ba'elu* scenario, all dates are declared as a unit at the outset, and even if each one is worth only a fifth of a *perutah*, they combine to satisfy the requirement — because they were all labeled as *kesef kiddushin* before any was given.

### Baraita: Ba'elu

The *gemara* notes that a *baraita* supports Rava's position. The *baraita* reads: if a man says to a woman, "marry me with an acorn, a pomegranate, and a nut" (*hitkadshi li be'alon be'rimon u've'egoz*) — or if he says *ba'elu*, "with all of these" — and collectively they are worth a *perutah*, she is *mekudeshes*; if not, she is not. Then the *baraita* continues to the case of *bezo uvezu uvezu* with eating: if she took each and ate it as it was given, she is *mekudeshes* only if one of them is worth a *perutah*.

### Question: Ba'elu?

The *gemara* asks: in the first case of the *baraita* — the acorn, pomegranate, and nut — what exactly is the case? If the man said "either with the acorn, or with the pomegranate, or with the nut" (*o be'alon o be'rimon o be'egoz*), how could it suffice for them to be collectively worth a *perutah*? He spoke in the disjunctive — he named one at a time. But if we read it as simply listing them together (*be'alon be'rimon u've'egoz*), then that is identical to *bezu bezu bezu* — individual labeling — not a *ba'elu* formulation. So in what sense is the opening case of the *baraita* a *ba'elu* case?

### First Case: No Distincti…

The *gemara* resolves this: the first clause of the *baraita* (*be'alon be'rimon u've'egoz*) is simply an example of how *ba'elu* works — it is explaining the *ba'elu* case by specifying what kind of items might be included. The formulation is *perusha kampfaresh* — an explanatory gloss, not a distinct case. Understood this way, the *baraita*'s structure becomes clear: first it presents the *ba'elu* scenario and rules that collective worth suffices; then it presents the *bezu* scenario with eating and rules that one individual date must be worth a *perutah*. The eating clause appears only in connection with the *bezu bezu bezu* case — not the *ba'elu* case — which is precisely what Rava argued.

### Rav Ami vs. Rav

One might ask: why was it necessary to attribute this *baraita* to Rava's position at all, given that the same point was made yesterday by Rav Ami? To understand this, one must recall the prior discussion. The *mishnah* presented two main structures: first, where each *kiddushin* was a separate statement — *hitkadshi li bezo, hitkadshi li bezo, hitkadshi li bezo* — and second, where the man said *bezu uvezu uvezu*, treating them as a group. The *mishnah* then added the case of *ochelet* — eating — and the question was: to which of the two structures does the eating clause belong?

Rav Ami said that *ochelet* modifies the *bezu uvezu uvezu* case. When she eats each date as it is named individually in one continuing statement, those eaten dates become *milveh*-like, and only the last one counts. This is what the *baraita* makes explicit: *bezo natla ve'achaltu, bezo natla ve'achaltu* — she took and ate, she took and ate — and the conclusion is that one of them must be a *shaveh perutah*.

Rav and Shmuel, by contrast, held that *ochelet* modifies the first structure — the case of separate *hitkadshi li* statements. On their reading, each *hitkadshi li bezo* is already a complete and independent act of *kiddushin*, and the eating clause teaches only the *chiddush* that even if she derives immediate benefit by eating the date, the *kiddushin* still requires a *shaveh perutah*. But this is no real *chiddush*: of course if any one of the separate acts is worth a *perutah* it works. And indeed the *baraita*'s language — explicitly describing eating date by date within a single continuing sequence — clearly tracks Rav Ami's reading, not Rav and Shmuel's.

### Baraita: Rabbi View

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty by attributing the *baraita* to the position of Rebbi. Rebbi holds — in a parallel *sugya* concerning *pigul* intentions (*kol ke-zayit ke-zayit u-ke-zayit u-k-zayit trata ha-vei*) — that even when the conjunctive *vav* is used to link items, each is still treated as a separate act. It does not matter whether one says *ke-zayit ke-zayit* or *ke-zayit u-ke-zayit*; each remains independent. Analogously, according to Rebbi, even *bezu uvezu uvezu*, despite the connecting *vav*, is treated not as a collective but as a series of separate acts of *kiddushin*.

This means that the eating clause in the *baraita*, though textually attached to the *bezu uvezu uvezu* sequence, is functioning according to Rebbi's framework where each *bezo* is a separate act — like the *hitkadshi li bezo, hitkadshi li bezo* case of Rav and Shmuel. The *chiddush* is then: not that one must wait for the last date, but that as long as any one of them was worth a *perutah* when accepted, that act of *kiddushin* is valid. The *baraita* accordingly does not require specifically the *last* date to be a *perutah*, but *one of them* — because each acceptance was its own independent transaction. In this way, the *baraita* can be reconciled with Rav and Shmuel's reading after all, provided we understand it as authored according to Rebbi's view.

---

## Mekadesh B'Milveh

### Basic Question

The *gemara* now turns to a sustained discussion of a fundamental question: *ha-mekadesh be-milveh* — can a man betroth a woman using a debt she owes him? She owes him a hundred dollars; he says, keep the money, you are *mekudeshes* to me. He has not given her anything new — he has merely remitted an existing obligation. One might argue that the benefit she receives from the forgiveness of the debt (*mechilat ha-chov*) has a real monetary value, and that value could function as *kesef kiddushin*. But that would be a different act entirely — he would need to say explicitly, "marry me with the value of my waiving this debt" (*be-hana'at mechilat milveh*). What he has actually said is, "keep the money you owe me, and with that money you are *mekudeshes* to me." The question is whether that formulation is effective.

It is worth noting a contrast that clarifies the issue: if instead of lending money, he had lent her an object — say, a phone — and then said "keep the phone and be *mekudeshes* to me with it," that would work, because the object remains legally his throughout the loan. Money is entirely different, and that difference is the crux of the upcoming analysis.

### Rav's Position

Rav rules: *ha-mekadesh be-milveh einah mekudeshes* — one who betroths a woman with a loan does not effect valid *kiddushin*. The reason is the principle *milveh le-hotza'ah nitnah* — a loan is given to be spent. As soon as the money leaves the lender's hand, it is no longer his. The borrower owns that specific currency outright; all that remains in the lender's domain is an abstract right to repayment.

### Money vs. Object

The *chiddush* here is the sharp distinction between money and other objects. When a person lends money — even if the borrower has not yet spent it, even if the bills are still sitting in the borrower's hand — those bills are no longer the lender's property. He cannot demand them back. He cannot give them to someone else. He has nothing concrete left: only an abstract debt owed to him. This is *milveh le-hotza'ah nitnah*: the money is given with the understanding that it will be spent, and legally it transitions to the borrower's ownership immediately upon receipt. By contrast, a borrowed object (*shoel*) remains the lender's property throughout the period of the loan — the lender can demand its return, and the object itself is still his to dispose of. If he says to the woman, "keep the object I lent you and be *mekudeshes* to me," he is genuinely giving her something that was his. With money, he is not.

### Mechirah Contradiction

The *gemara* introduces an apparent contradiction. A *mishnah* dealing with land purchase (*mechirah*) seems to indicate that *kiddushin be-milveh* can work. If Rav's principle is absolute — the loan money is never the lender's to give — then it should fail equally in any transactional context, whether *kiddushin* or sale of land. Why, then, does the *mishnah* in *mechirah* suggest otherwise?

### Special Case: Short Paym…

Rav Nachman resolves this by introducing a completely different scenario. The *mishnah* in question is not addressing the classic *mekadesh be-milveh* case that Rav ruled on. Rather, says Rav Nachman citing Rav Huna, it deals with a case of *maneh chaser* — a short payment. A man said to a woman, "marry me with a hundred dollars (*maneh*)," she took the money and counted it, and it came up five short — only ninety-five. The missing five is in the nature of a *milveh*: he owes her the remainder. Does the *kiddushin* work?

### Debate: Embarrassment

This is the subject of the *tanna'im*'s debate. One opinion holds that the *kiddushin* is invalid because the woman is *kesifa lah milta le-mitba'ei* — she is embarrassed to demand the remaining five dollars from her betrothed. Because of this social pressure, even if she said yes, she did not fully and genuinely accept the arrangement. Her consent was tainted by the fact that she felt unable to press her legitimate claim.

### Gmar Da'at Principle

The other opinion holds that she is not embarrassed to ask, and therefore her acceptance reflects genuine *gmar da'at* — a complete and decisive resolve. The underlying principle is that *kiddushin* requires that the woman truly and fully accept what is being offered. If she is being placed in a position where she cannot freely assert her rights, her apparent consent lacks the necessary decisiveness. If, on the other hand, she genuinely trusts she will receive what is owed and freely agrees, the *kiddushin* is valid despite the shortfall.

This also explains why the case of land purchase (*karka*) works according to both opinions. In a commercial transaction between two parties who are not entering a marriage, neither would hesitate to sue for the outstanding amount. There is no *kesifa* in a business deal; the buyer will unambiguously demand what is owed. Therefore, in that context, *gmar da'at* is unquestionable and the transaction succeeds.

### Threshold Cases

The *gemara* then explores the thresholds of this principle. If the shortfall is enormous — say, ninety-nine dollars short out of a hundred — she will obviously demand the rest, since the discrepancy is so glaring that embarrassment is out of the question. In that case, *gmar da'at* is present and the *kiddushin* may work. If the shortfall is only five dollars out of a hundred, the embarrassment argument applies. These threshold cases help define when *kesifa* operates and when it does not.

### Rav Elazar Case

The *gemara* now raises the case stated by Rav Elazar: a man says "marry me with a hundred dollars" (*hitkadshi li be-maneh*) and gives her only one dinar — a small down payment — saying he will complete the payment later. Does this work?

Rav Elazar rules: *harei zu mekudeshes ve-yashlim* — she is *mekudeshes*, and he should complete the payment. The *gemara* asks: does this accord with only one side of the *tanna'im* debate? If giving ninety-five and owing five might not work because of *kesifa*, does giving only one dinar and owing the rest pose the same problem?

The *gemara* answers no: the two situations are inverse in the relevant dimension. When he gave ninety-five and owed five, the shortfall is small and the woman is embarrassed to ask for it — *kesifa* is operative. When he gave only one dinar and owes ninety-nine, the gap is so enormous that there is absolutely no expectation that she would absorb the loss. She will obviously press for the remainder — *lo kesifa lah milta* — and therefore her *gmar da'at* in accepting the *kiddushin* is unimpaired. Rav Elazar's case thus sidesteps the *tanna'im* debate entirely and is acceptable to both opinions.

### Pikadon Baraita

The *gemara* now cites a *baraita* about *pikadon*: if a man says to a woman, "marry me with the entrusted object (*pikadon*) that I have in your possession" — say, a bag of grain she is watching for him — and she agrees, and then goes to retrieve it and discovers it was stolen or lost. If something worth a *perutah* remains, she is *mekudeshes*; if nothing remains, she is not. By contrast, continues the *baraita*, in the case of a *milveh* — a loan — even if nothing of the original money remains, she is *mekudeshes*.

This *baraita* is striking, because it directly contradicts Rav's position. According to Rav, even with the full amount of the loan still in her possession, *kiddushin be-milveh* does not work — *milveh le-hotza'ah nitnah*. The *baraita*, however, seems to say the *milveh* case works even better than the *pikadon* case.

### Baraita Positions

The *baraita* thus presents two views. The first (the *tanna kamma*) says: *pikadon* requires a *perutah* to remain, but *milveh* works even with nothing left. This is the opposite of Rav's position. The second view, that of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir, is that *milveh* is like *pikadon*: something of the original money must remain for the *kiddushin* to work.

Both views are, to varying degrees, in tension with Rav. One says *milveh* works completely (even better than *pikadon*); the other says it works if some money remains — still more permissive than Rav, who says it fails even when the entire amount is still in her possession.

### Text Corruption

Rava intervenes with a striking move: *hamishabeshta hi* — the text of this *baraita* is corrupt. He argues that the *baraita* as received cannot be internally coherent. His argument proceeds as follows: what is the *pikadon* case? If she accepted liability for the object (*kibla aleha achrayus*), then if it is lost or stolen she owes the man the money — making her, in effect, a *milveh* debtor. In that case, the *pikadon* scenario where nothing is left should work just as well as the *milveh* case, and the *baraita*'s distinction collapses. If she did not accept liability (*lo kibla aleha achrayus*), then she owes him nothing when the object is lost, and indeed the *kiddushin* can only work if something physical remains. But in that case, why does the *baraita* draw the contrast to *milveh* at all? It should simply distinguish within the *pikadon* case itself: if she accepted liability, it works even without a remainder; if not, it requires a remainder. The fact that the *baraita* instead contrasts *pikadon* with *milveh* in the *sefa* reveals an internal incoherence, demonstrating that the text has been corrupted.

### Corrected Baraita

Rava therefore proposes a corrected reading of the *baraita*: *ela tani hachi* — read it this way instead. In the case of *milveh*, even if something of the original amount remains (*af al pi she-nishtayer heimena shaveh perutah*), she is *einah mekudeshes*. This is the exact reversal of the *baraita*'s original formulation, and it aligns precisely with Rav's ruling: *milveh le-hotza'ah nitnah* — the loan money is entirely the borrower's from the moment it is given, and even if the bills have not yet been spent and are still physically present, the lender has no ownership claim over them and cannot use them to effect *kiddushin*.

### Shimon b. Elazar

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing Rabbi Meir, maintains his counter-position: *milveh harei hu ke-pikadon* — a loan is like an entrusted object. If some of the original money remains, it can function as *kesef kiddushin*. This is a principled disagreement with the *tanna kamma*'s position as corrected by Rava, and by extension with Rav. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that the loan money does not instantly and completely transfer to the borrower; while some of it persists in its original physical form, it retains some connection to the lender's ownership and can therefore serve as a vehicle for *kiddushin*.

---

## Loan Ownership Debate

### Two Views

The *gemara* now examines the underlying conceptual dispute that drives the *mekadesh be-milveh* debate. There are two views on when exactly a loan transitions out of the lender's ownership. According to the first view — which is Rav's — the transfer is immediate: the moment the money enters the borrower's hand, it belongs to the borrower fully. *Milveh le-hotza'ah nitnah* means not merely that the money is destined to be spent, but that it is already no longer the lender's at the instant of transfer. According to the second view — associated with Shmuel's formulation — the money only becomes the borrower's when he actually begins to spend it (*hotza'ah*). Until that moment, the bills remain, in some meaningful sense, the lender's property.

### Application

If Shmuel's view is correct — that the lender retains ownership until spending begins — then *mekadesh be-milveh* could potentially work as long as none of the money has yet been spent. The lender would be giving the woman something that is genuinely still his: those specific bills, which have not yet crossed into the borrower's ownership by virtue of being spent. This is what Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's position (*milveh ke-pikadon*) is premised on: since the money may still be the lender's property, it can serve as *kesef kiddushin* just as an object in a *pikadon* relationship can.

### Retraction Rights

Rava reports that he found the Rabbis of Rav's academy (*rabbanan de-vei Rav*) sitting and discussing this very point. They offered a different way to frame the debate: *milveh bi-reshut be'alim le-chazarah* — the question is whether the loan, while still in the borrower's possession unspent, remains within the lender's domain for purposes of *retraction* (*chazarah*). Can the lender say, "I changed my mind, give me back my twenty dollars"? One opinion holds that he can — the loan is still *bi-reshut be'alim* before being spent, and just as a lender can recall an unspent loan, he can also use those funds as *kesef kiddushin*. The other opinion holds that the transfer is immediate and irrevocable: from the moment of lending, the money is out of the lender's domain entirely, and he has no right of retraction.

### Sheol Analogy

Rava challenges this framing by raising the case of *shoel* — one who borrows an object (not money). A *shoel* is fully liable (*chayav be-onassin*) from the moment he takes possession of the object, even though the object itself remains the lender's property throughout the loan. The *gemara* notes: *lo gara mi-shoel* — the money-borrower should certainly not be less liable than the object-borrower. Just as the *shoel* accepts full liability for loss and *oness* (force majeure) at the moment of taking possession — even though the lender could in principle demand the item's return — so too the money-borrower should be fully liable from the moment he receives the funds, regardless of whether ownership has technically transferred.

### Refined Position

Rava therefore corrects the Rabbis' framing. The debate cannot be about liability for *onessin* — everyone agrees the borrower is liable for any loss from the moment he receives the money. A *shoel* accepts liability as soon as he takes possession, even before he begins using the item, and the money-borrower is certainly no less liable. The debate, Rava clarifies, must therefore be exclusively about *chazarah* — retraction rights — and its implication for *kiddushin*: can the lender reclaim the specific bills before they are spent, thereby still owning them in a sense that allows him to give them as *kesef kiddushin*?

### Abstract vs. Physical

This brings the discussion to its sharpest formulation. At what moment does the concrete, physical ownership of the specific currency dissolve into an abstract debt obligation? Everyone agrees that this transition occurs — certainly before the last coin is spent, and certainly before the obligation is discharged. The question is whether it occurs immediately upon transfer of the bills (*milveh le-hotza'ah nitnah*, Rav's view), or only when the borrower actually begins spending the money (Shmuel's view, and the basis for Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's leniency). Once the money is fully abstracted into a debt — regardless of how much currency remains physically in the borrower's possession — the lender can no longer marry the woman with it, because he has nothing concrete left to give. The entire *sugya* of *mekadesh be-milveh* thus turns on this precise question of when abstract debt replaces physical ownership.

---

---

# Kiddushin 48

## Milveh Le'hotza'ah Nitnah

### Marrying with Milveh

The daf opens in the middle of an extended discussion that began on 47b: can a man betroth a woman using a *milveh* — not by waiving a loan she owes him, but by in some sense "returning" the money she borrowed? The complication is that the money may no longer be considered his at all. This is the principle of *milveh le'hotza'ah nitnah*: once a lender hands over cash, that cash belongs to the borrower, who merely owes an abstract debt in return. If so, when the man says "be betrothed to me with this money," he is attempting to betroth her with something that is already hers — and that cannot constitute *kesef kiddushin*.

This is Rav's position: *mekadesh bimilveh* does not work. The Gemara has been defending Rav by arguing that the principle of *milveh le'hotza'ah nitnah* is actually undisputed, and that the only open question is precisely *when* the money ceases to be the lender's — whether immediately upon transfer or only once the borrower begins to spend it.

### Money Becomes Hers

The Gemara's resolution is that everyone agrees the money becomes the borrower's property once it is handed over. What the *tannaim* may disagree about is a narrower question: at what point is the transaction irreversible from the lender's perspective, and at what point can the money be said to have fully passed out of his domain? The practical consequence of *milveh le'hotza'ah nitnah* is that by the time the man attempts to use the loan as *kesef kiddushin*, the money is already hers. He cannot marry her with what is already in her possession.

### Nafka Minas

Beyond the question of *kiddushin* itself, the Gemara identifies two *nafka minas* — practical differences — between the position that the money passes immediately upon transfer and the position that it passes only when she begins to spend it. The first *nafka mina* is liability for losses: if a wind blows the money out of her hand before she has spent any of it, whose loss is it? The second *nafka mina* is *chazarah* — whether the lender can retract and demand his money back before she begins spending it.

### Liability vs. Ownership

The Gemara argues that on the question of liability for losses, both positions would actually agree that she becomes liable immediately upon receiving the money. The reasoning is drawn from the laws of *she'elah*: when one borrows an object, one does not become its owner — the object remains the lender's — yet the moment it passes into the borrower's physical control, the borrower becomes a *sho'el* and is fully liable for any damage or loss. The same logic applies here: even if the money does not yet fully belong to her, once she has taken physical possession she bears the status of a *sho'el* and absorbs any losses. The genuine point of disagreement, then, is only the second *nafka mina*: whether the lender retains the right to retract before she begins spending the money.

---

## She'elah - Borrowed Hatc…

### Rav Huna's View

This analysis leads directly to a statement of Rav Huna: *hasho'el kardom me'chavero — bika bo kena'o; lo bika bo — lo kena'o*. If one borrows an axe from a friend, once one begins chopping with it, one "takes possession"; if one has not yet begun chopping, one has not taken possession. The Gemara here uses the word *kana* — acquisition — but it is worth clarifying what this means, since the axe obviously remains the lender's property throughout. What Rav Huna means by "taking possession" is, at minimum, the point from which the owner can no longer retract — and possibly also the point of full liability, though as we will see, liability begins earlier.

The question the Gemara raises is whether Rav Huna's position represents only one side of a tannaitic debate. After all, we just established that in the context of loans, there are two views on when the lender loses the right to retract — either immediately upon handing over the money, or only once the borrower begins spending. Is Rav Huna, who says the borrower of the axe does not "take possession" until he begins using it, simply adopting one side of that debate?

### Loans vs. Objects

The Gemara rejects this framing: *ad kan lo peligi ela bemilveh* — the tannaitic debate applies only to a monetary loan, not to a borrowed object. The reason is rooted in the fundamental nature of each transaction. A monetary loan is structured precisely so that the borrower will spend the specific coins and return different ones; from the moment the lender hands over the cash, he has in some sense relinquished his hold on those particular coins. One could therefore argue that his proprietary claim dissolves immediately. A borrowed object, by contrast, must be returned in its original form — *dehadra be'eina*, it comes back as itself. The lender's sense of ownership over that specific object remains intact throughout the loan period. Consequently, *divrei hakol* — by universal agreement — the borrower of a physical object does not extinguish the lender's right to retract until the borrower actually begins using it.

This also helps explain why the Gemara ruled the way it did on the monetary loan: the position that the lender loses his claim *immediately* upon handing over cash is grounded in the uniqueness of money, not in a general principle applicable to all forms of lending.

### Immediate Liability

Tosafot raises a complementary point. The Gemara earlier justified immediate liability for losses in the context of a monetary loan by analogy to borrowed objects — as soon as the object passes into the borrower's control, the *sho'el* is liable. Tosafot notes that the same logic must apply in the case of the borrowed axe: the moment it passes into the borrower's physical control, he is liable for any damages, even before he begins using it. This is in fact the source of the principle in the loan case. So in both the monetary loan and the borrowed object, liability for *onsin* — accidents and losses — attaches immediately upon transfer, even though the question of *chazarah* and full proprietary transfer may differ. The Gemara does not spell this out explicitly in this context, but Tosafot makes clear that the cases are parallel in this respect.

---

## Tannaitic Debate?

### Shtar Chov Cases

Having settled the internal logic of *milveh le'hotza'ah nitnah* and its comparison to *she'elah*, the Gemara pivots to the central project of this sugya: can the ruling that *mekadesh bimilveh* is ineffective be shown to reflect a tannaitic debate, or is it universally agreed upon? The Gemara now attempts — in several stages — to locate a *machloket tannaim* that maps onto this question.

The first attempt introduces a *baraita* with two cases. In the first, a man betroths a woman by handing her a *shtar chov* — a document of debt. In the second, others owe him money and he authorizes her to collect on his behalf, thereby transferring the debt to her. Rabbi Meir holds she is betrothed (*mekudeshet*); the Sages hold she is not (*einah mekudeshet*). At first glance, particularly in the second case — where a concrete right of collection is being conferred — this looks like a genuine debate about whether a debt can function as *kesef kiddushin*, and thus a debate about *mekadesh bimilveh*.

### Whose Debt?

The Gemara zeroes in on the first case: what exactly is the *shtar chov* being handed over? If it is a document recording a debt that others owe the man — *shtar chov de'acheirim* — then that is simply a restatement of the second case, and the two cases collapse into one. The Gemara therefore entertains the possibility that the first case involves a *shtar chov deidah* — a document recording a debt that *she* owes *him*. In that case, by handing her the IOU, the man is effectively telling her to keep the money she owes him. That *would* be *mekadesh bimilveh*, and the tannaitic debate would map directly onto the question of whether such betrothal works.

The Gemara ultimately rejects this reading — it is unlikely that the *baraita* would use a single list to debate two logically distinct categories (her debt to him versus third parties' debt to him) without distinguishing between them. Instead, the Gemara concludes that both cases involve debts owed to the man by *others*, and the debate concerns entirely different sub-questions about how such a debt is transferred. The debate, in other words, is not really about *kiddushin* at all.

### Document Transfer

With the *baraita* now read as involving only third-party debts, the Gemara asks: what exactly do Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagree about? When there is a written *shtar chov*, the mechanism of transfer is *otiyyot niknot bimesirah* — the rights embedded in a debt document are acquired by physically handing over the document. Rabbi says this is sufficient; the Sages (*Rabbanan*) say that mere transfer of the document is not enough — one must *both* write a supporting document (formally recording the new creditor) *and* hand over the *shtar*: *ad she'yichtov ve'yimsor*.

On this reading, the case involves a man who handed her the *shtar* but did not write supporting documentation. Rabbi Meir, following the opinion of *Rabbi* (Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi) that handing over the document suffices, holds she is *mekudeshet*. The Sages, who require both acts, hold she is not. This is a debate about the mechanics of *kinyan* in document transfers — not about *kiddushin*.

### Rav Pappa's Line

A second resolution is offered: perhaps everyone rejects Rabbi's position and agrees that both handing over and writing are required. On this reading, the man performed *both* acts — he handed her the document *and* wrote supporting documentation — but the question is whether the supporting documentation contained the precise formula required by Rav Pappa. For Rav Pappa rules: *hai man de'zavin shtar le'chavrei tzarich le'michtav lei — knei lach ihu ve'chol shibudei* — when transferring a debt document, the supporting text must explicitly state "take possession of it and all its liens." One side of the debate holds that this precise formulation is indispensable; the other holds it is not. Once again, the dispute has nothing to do with the law of *kiddushin*.

### Shmuel's Mechilah

A third resolution involves an entirely different dimension of the problem. Assume everyone agrees with Rav Pappa that the required formula was written, and that the transfer was fully executed. The Gemara now invokes Shmuel: *ha'mocher shtar chov le'chaveiro ve'chazar u'machalo — machul*. If one sells a debt document to another person, and the original creditor subsequently forgives the debt — *mochel* it — the forgiveness is legally effective, and the purchaser can no longer collect. The reasoning, at its core, is that a debt is fundamentally a personal obligation between debtor and original creditor. What passes to the buyer is not the debt itself in some fully abstracted sense, but rather the right to step into the creditor's position — perhaps as a kind of agent or substitute. Since the original creditor's claim never fully dissolves, he retains the power to be *mochel*.

Tosafot offers a related but differently framed explanation: *kinyan shtarot lav mi'de'orayta* — the transfer of debt documents has no biblical basis, only rabbinic. Therefore the rabbinic mechanism of transfer is not strong enough to fully uproot the original creditor's power (*lo alim le'afkuei koach harishon*). The conceptual formulation offered in the shiur — that the debtor fundamentally still owes the original creditor, and the buyer merely acquires some right to collect through or in place of that creditor — captures the same insight.

How is Shmuel's rule relevant to *kiddushin*? Even if the woman receives a fully transferred *shtar chov* of real market value, the original creditor retains the power to forgive the debt and leave her with nothing. This affects the *quality* of what she receives as *kesef kiddushin*.

### Samchat Da'ata

This leads to the concept of *samchat da'ata* — settled confidence in the object of betrothal. The Gemara raises the possibility that even though the transferred debt has genuine market value (discounted, of course, for the risk of *mechilah*), the woman's lack of confidence in her ability to collect may itself be a disqualifying factor for *kesef kiddushin*. This is a striking argument: that something with real monetary worth, which could be sold on the open market for a price reflecting its discounted value, might nevertheless fail to operate as *kesef kiddushin* because of an anxiety about its ultimate collectibility.

The Gemara presents two levels of debate. The first is simply whether one holds like Shmuel at all — whether the original creditor genuinely retains the power to forgive. If not, the transferred debt is fully hers and *samchat da'ata* is unproblematic. The second level, introduced as an alternative framing, accepts that everyone holds like Shmuel, and asks instead whether the specific context of betrothal is different. Here the Gemara distinguishes between selling a field with a transferred debt — where no one, presumably, would feel confident, since the seller might turn around and forgive the debt to benefit the debtor at her expense — and the case of betrothal. The argument for *samchat da'ata* in betrothal is romantic but legally grounded: *meimar amra — lo shavik leididi u'machil le'achrinei* — she reasons that he would not deprive her, his new wife, by doing a favor for a third party. One opinion holds that this confidence is real and legally operative; the other holds that even in betrothal, the woman cannot be assumed to feel truly secure, and therefore the anxiety remains. Either way, the underlying debate is not about *kiddushin* per se but about the transferability of debt instruments and the reliability of *mechilah* — and the tannaitic *machloket* has not yet been established as a debate about *mekadesh bimilveh*.

---

## Oral Loans Transfer

### Ma'amad Shloshtan

The Gemara turns to the second case in the *baraita*: the oral loan (*milveh al peh*) — a debt owed by a third party that is not recorded in any document. Here even the mechanism of *otiyyot bimesirah* is unavailable. The Gemara invokes Rav Huna in the name of Rav: *maneh li be'yadcha — tenahu li'ploni bema'amad shloshtan* — if all three parties are present — the original creditor, the debtor, and the intended recipient — and the creditor says "that hundred you owe me, give it to so-and-so," the recipient (*koneh*) acquires the debt. This is a special form of *kinyan* — *ma'amad shloshtan* — enacted by the Sages for precisely this situation. The Gemara further notes, drawing on Tosafot's analysis, that this mechanism has an important advantage over the written transfer: Shmuel's rule of *mechilah* may not apply. When all three stand together and the creditor explicitly steps out of the picture, the new recipient is not merely a collector on behalf of the original creditor — the original creditor has, in some conceptual sense, fully substituted the recipient into his own position. He is out; the new party is in. Accordingly, the original creditor may no longer be *mochel* the debt.

### Oral vs. Physical

If *ma'amad shloshtan* is a fully effective transfer, why would it not work as *kesef kiddushin*? The debate, the Gemara says, is whether one accepts Rav Huna's ruling at all — and, if one does, whether it applies to oral debts as well as to objects in safekeeping (*pikadon*). One view holds that *ma'amad shloshtan* works only for a *pikadon* — a physical object being held — because it is easier to conceptualize the transfer of a physical thing when all parties are present and in agreement. A monetary debt, being an abstract obligation, cannot be transferred by this mechanism. The other view holds that there is no distinction: *lo shna milveh velo shna pikadon* — whether it is a debt or a physical deposit, *ma'amad shloshtan* works, and therefore she can be betrothed with it.

Once again, what appears to be a debate about betrothal is in reality a debate about the laws of transfer. The Gemara has now exhausted the *baraita*'s two cases — the *shtar chov* and the *milveh al peh* — without finding a genuine tannaitic *machloket* about *mekadesh bimilveh* itself.

---

## Shtar Kiddushin

### Document Witnesses

The Gemara regroups and tries a different *baraita*. The case now involves *shtar kiddushin* — betrothal by document — specifically the scenario of *hiskadshi li beshtar*: a man says to a woman, "be betrothed to me with this document." The document is not a *shtar chov* at all; rather, it is the classic *shtar kiddushin*, the written declaration *harei at mekudeshet li*. The *baraita* records a three-way dispute. Rabbi Meir says she is not betrothed; Rabbi Eliezer says she is betrothed; the Sages evaluate the monetary worth of the paper itself — if the paper is worth a *perutah*, she is *mekudeshet*; if not, she is not.

The Gemara asks: what exactly is the *shtar* in this case? If it is a *shtar chov* of money others owe him, there is an immediate contradiction: in the earlier *baraita*, Rabbi Meir said she *is* betrothed; here Rabbi Meir says she is *not*. The positions would be reversed. Therefore, the Gemara concludes, the case here cannot be a third-party debt document. It must be something else — and that opens the door to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reading.

### Witness Requirements

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes: *keivan shekidsha beshtar she'ein lo eidim* — the case is where the man betrothed her with a *shtar kiddushin* that has no signed witnesses. This is a classic debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer — not about loans, but about the law of *shtarot*. Rabbi Meir holds *edei chasimah karsi* — the signed witnesses on a document are what give it legal force; without their signatures, it is not a valid *shtar*. Rabbi Eliezer holds *edei mesirah karsi* — it is sufficient that witnesses observed the handing over of the document; signatures are not required.

On this reading, Rabbi Meir says she is not betrothed because the unsigned *shtar* has no legal standing. Rabbi Eliezer says she is betrothed because the witnesses were present at the moment of delivery. The debate is the identical *machloket* these two *tannaim* conduct throughout the laws of *gittin* and *shtarot* — it has been transplanted here into *kiddushin*, but it is not a debate unique to betrothal.

### Paper's Value

The Sages' position — evaluate the paper — requires explanation. Rashi notes a difficulty: if the Sages are uncertain whether to follow Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Eliezer, then without a *perutah*'s worth of paper, she should be *safek mekudeshet* (doubtfully betrothed), not definitively *einah mekudeshet*. Rashi therefore emends the conclusion: with a *perutah*-worthy paper she is *vadai mekudeshet*; without it, the matter is unresolved.

A further question arises: why would the Sages evaluate the paper at all, given that the man was not attempting to betroth her with the value of the paper — he was attempting *kiddushei shtar*? The answer appears to be that because there is a real possibility that the *shtar* worked as a genuine *shtar kiddushin* (following Rabbi Eliezer), and because the paper itself has monetary value, the Sages treat it as potentially doubling as *kiddushei kesef*. If the *shtar kiddushin* route was possibly effective, then the paper's monetary value provides an additional basis for betrothal. But if the *shtar* was definitively invalid and the paper was worth less than a *perutah*, there would be no betrothal on either ground.

### Shelo Lishmah

The Gemara offers an alternative framework for the same dispute. Setting aside the witness question, the debate may instead concern *lishmah* — whether a *shtar kiddushin* must be written specifically with *this* woman in mind. The scenario: a man writes out a *harei at mekudeshet li* document in advance, before identifying his intended bride, and later produces it on a date. Is such a document valid?

This question was raised by Reish Lakish.

### Lishmah Required

Reish Lakish formulated the question as a *beia*: does the principle of *havayah liyetzi'ah makishna* — comparing betrothal to divorce — require that a *shtar kiddushin* be written *lishmah*, just as a *get* must be written *lishmah* (derived from *ve'chasav lah*, "and he shall write for her")? Or does one instead compare one form of *kiddushin* to another — *havayah le'hadadi makishna* — in which case, since *kiddushei kesef* (monetary betrothal) requires no *lishmah* (money is not minted with a specific woman in mind), *kiddushei shtar* similarly requires none?

The Gemara reports that after posing the question, Reish Lakish himself resolved it: *veyatze'ah ve'hayetah — makish havayah liyetzi'ah* — the comparison to divorce is the operative one, and *lishmah* is required for a *shtar kiddushin*. The tannaitic debate in the *baraita* would then be between one who accepts Reish Lakish's conclusion and one who does not. Rabbi Meir, requiring *lishmah*, rules she is not betrothed when the document was written *shelo lishmah*. The other opinion, presumably Rabbi Eliezer, does not require *lishmah* and holds she is betrothed. This reading has an additional advantage: it preserves the exact same Rabbi Meir / Rabbi Eliezer pairing as the previous explanation, lending it structural coherence.

### Lishmah Lo Mida'atah

The Gemara pushes further. What if everyone agrees with Reish Lakish that *lishmah* is required, and the document *was* written with this specific woman in mind — but without her knowledge or awareness? This is the case of *lishmah ve'shelo mida'atah*: he writes *harei at mekudeshet li* while thinking of her specifically, perhaps months before proposing, without her having any idea.

Would this satisfy the *lishmah* requirement? The question has conceptual depth. A *get* need not be written with the wife's knowledge — divorce is a unilateral act and she is entirely passive. But *kiddushin* is different: she must consent, and she is, in some sense, a party to the transaction. Moreover, there is a subtle structural point: in a standard sale, the *shtar* is written by the *seller*. In betrothal, the man writes *harei at mekudeshet li* — yet it is the woman who is in the position of the seller (she is "selling" herself into the marital bond). Since she is the functional *ba'al hashtar*, one could argue that the document must emerge with her awareness, if not by her hand.

### Amoraim Dispute

This question is the subject of a dispute among *Amoraim*: Rabbah and Ravina hold she is *mekudeshet* — the document is valid even without her awareness. Rav Papa and Rav Sharvya hold she is *einah mekudeshet* — the lack of her awareness is disqualifying. The tannaitic *baraita* may reflect this very debate, with Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim divided on whether the woman's awareness at the time of writing is a precondition for a valid *shtar kiddushin*.

In any case, the Gemara has now demonstrated that the tannaitic debate in the *baraita* is about the internal requirements of *kiddushei shtar* — witness signatures, *lishmah*, or the woman's awareness — and not about *mekadesh bimilveh*. The attempt to locate *mekadesh bimilveh* in a tannaitic dispute has again come up empty.

---

## Labor as Kiddushin

### Jewelry Service

The Gemara makes one final attempt to root *mekadesh bimilveh* in a tannaitic debate, this time using a case involving labor. A woman approaches a man who is a jeweler and says: fashion for me earrings, rings, and bracelets from my gold and silver — *ve'ekadesh ani lach* — and in exchange for your service, I will be betrothed to you. He performs the work and hands the finished jewelry back to her. Has he given her anything? The answer requires careful analysis. Her gold is still her gold — it was never his. The increase in value that his workmanship produced belongs, in the ordinary case, to the owner of the raw material. All that he has rendered is his labor. The question is how to characterize the legal relationship between that labor and the proposed betrothal.

### When Debt Incurs

A three-way structure emerges in the *baraita*. Rabbi Meir says: *keivan she'asah — mekudeshet* — once he completes the work and presumably hands over the jewelry, she is betrothed. The Sages say she is not betrothed *until money reaches her hands* (*ad sheyagia mamon leyadah*). The Gemara immediately interrogates what "money" refers to. If it means the jewelry itself — the physical objects now completed and returned — then does Rabbi Meir's position imply she is betrothed even *before* the jewelry is handed back? That would be startling: what exactly has she received at that earlier moment that could serve as *kesef kiddushin*?

### Schirus Timing

The Gemara's resolution introduces a crucial conceptual distinction: *yeshnah li'skhirus mitechilah ve'ad sof* versus *einah li'skhirus ella besof*. Does the wage debt accrue continuously from the very beginning of the work — so that by the time the job is done, what exists is a loan (the accumulated debt for services already rendered)? Or does no debt come into being at all until the work is completed and handed over — in which case, at the moment of completion, the craftsman is giving her the *service itself* rather than forgiving a debt?

This is the pivot on which the entire case turns. If the debt was accruing all along (*yeshnah mitechilah ve'ad sof*), then at the moment of completion, the only thing the man can do is forgive the debt she owes him — which is *mekadesh bimilveh*, and which everyone agrees does not work. If the debt arises only at the end (*einah ella besof*), then at the moment of completion the man is giving her his service as a gift — not forgiving a pre-existing debt but providing something new and concrete — and *that* could work as *kesef kiddushin*.

On this reading, Rabbi Meir holds *einah li'skhirus ella besof*: the service is given at the end and is a genuine gift of value. The Sages hold *yeshnah mitechilah ve'ad sof*: by the time he is done, it has always been a debt, and *mekadesh bimilveh einah mekudeshet*. The tannaitic debate, then, is not about *mekadesh bimilveh* per se — everyone may agree that does not work — but about when the wage obligation crystallizes.

### Artisan's Share

The Gemara offers yet another reading. Assume everyone holds *yeshnah li'skhirus mitechilah ve'ad sof* — the debt accrues from the beginning — and assume everyone agrees that *mekadesh bimilveh* is invalid. The remaining debate concerns *uman koneh be'shvach keli*: does the craftsman acquire a proprietary share in the enhanced object by virtue of his labor?

This principle holds that when an artisan improves an object and is being paid for the job rather than by the hour, he does not merely become a creditor of the owner. Instead, he acquires a partial ownership stake in the improved object proportional to the enhancement his work produced. He must then, as it were, "sell" that stake back to the owner upon completion. If *uman koneh be'shvach keli* applies, then what the jeweler transfers to the woman at the end of the job is not simply a forgiven debt but a tangible proprietary interest — his partial ownership in the finished ring — and *that* is a real and concrete object of value that can serve as *kesef kiddushin*.

Rabbi Meir holds *uman koneh be'shvach keli*: the artisan owns a share in the ring, and what he gives her is that ownership stake — genuine *kesef kiddushin*. The Sages hold *eino uman koneh be'shvach keli*: he owns nothing in the ring, all he has is money owed to him, and giving it up is *mekadesh bimilveh*.

### Milveh U'Perutah

The Gemara adds one further layer. Assume everyone agrees *uman koneh be'shvach keli* does not apply, and *yeshnah li'skhirus mitechilah ve'ad sof* does apply, so the artisan has only a monetary debt and cannot betroth her with it. Nevertheless: what if, out of affection, he added a small precious stone of his own — something not contracted for, not part of the original agreement? Can he betroth her with that addition?

This is the case of *milveh u'perutah*: a large loan being forgiven (which cannot work) combined with a small concrete addition of actual value (which potentially could). The debate is whether *da'atei aperutah* — his intention, and halachic characterization, is focused on the concrete *perutah*-sized addition — or whether *da'atei amilveh* — the dominant element is the loan he is forgiving, and the small addition is legally trivial, swept up in and overshadowed by the invalid larger transaction. This parallels, though does not perfectly replicate, the earlier question of whether the paper in a *shtar kiddushin* can function as *kesef kiddushin* when the man's primary intent was betrothal by document.

### Past/Future Labor

The tannaitic parallel is now made explicit. A *baraita* records: *bischar she'asisi imach — einah mekudeshet*: "with the wages you owe me for labor I have already performed" — she is not betrothed. This is straightforwardly *mekadesh bimilveh*. *Bischar she'e'eseh imach — mekudeshet*: "with the wages you will owe me for labor I will perform" — she is betrothed, according to the *Tanna Kamma*. This corresponds to the view that *einah li'skhirus ella besof* — no debt exists yet, and the service to be rendered is a genuine future gift.

Rabbi Natan disagrees: even *bischar she'e'eseh imach* does not work — once performed, it will always have been a debt. Rabbi Yehuda Nasi goes further and rules that *both* formulations fail, whether past or future labor. However, Rabbi Yehuda Nasi adds: *ve'im hosif lah nofach mishelo — mekudeshet* — if he added something of his own, she is betrothed.

The Gemara maps out the internal structure. Between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Natan, the debate is *yeshnah li'skhirus mitechilah ve'ad sof* versus *einah ella besof*. Between Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yehuda Nasi, the debate is *milveh u'perutah*: Rabbi Natan holds *da'atei amilveh* even when a *perutah* is added; Rabbi Yehuda Nasi holds *da'atei aperutah* and the small addition rescues the transaction.

### Final Ruling

In each stage of the *baraita*, the Gemara works to show that *nobody* is actually debating *mekadesh bimilveh* on its own terms. The *Tanna Kamma* who permits future-labor betrothal is not saying *mekadesh bimilveh* works — he is saying no debt existed yet, so this is not *milveh* at all. Rabbi Yehuda Nasi who permits when a *nofach* is added is not saying *mekadesh bimilveh* works — he is saying the small concrete addition is what effects the *kiddushin*. The Gemara thus arrives at its conclusion: *mekadesh bimilveh einah mekudeshet* — a man cannot betroth a woman with an existing monetary debt she owes him. This ruling is undisputed. All of the tannaitic debates that appeared to bear on the question turn out, upon careful analysis, to concern something else entirely — and Rav's position stands as universally accepted *halacha*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 49

## Object Misrepresentation

### Mishnah Overview

The daf begins in the middle of 48b, continuing the discussion of topics relating to the act of *kiddushin*. The *Mishnah* presents a series of cases in which the object or condition of *kiddushin* turns out to be different from what was specified. The *Mishnah* says: *hiskadshi li be-cos ze shel yayin ve-nimtza shel devash* — if a man says to a woman, "Marry me with this goblet of wine," and it turns out to be filled with honey; or conversely, he said honey and it turned out to be wine. Similarly, *bedinar ze shel kesef ve-nimtza shel zahav* — with this silver *dinar* and it is found to be gold; or he said gold and it was found to be silver. And finally, *al menat she-ani ashir ve-nimtza ani* — on the condition that I am wealthy and he turns out to be poor; or he said poor and turns out to be wealthy. In all of these cases, the *Mishnah* rules *eina mekudeshet* — the *kiddushin* is not valid.

This applies even in the cases where, by any objective measure, the woman received something better than what was promised — gold instead of silver, a wealthy husband instead of a poor one. The reasoning is that the condition was not met, regardless of whether the deviation was for the better or for the worse.

### Conditions vs. Objects

The *Mishnah* presents two analytically distinct categories of misrepresentation. The first involves the object given to effect the *kiddushin* — the goblet or the *dinar* — where the specific item turned out to be different from what was named. The second involves the *al menat* formulation, an explicit conditional stipulation about the man's personal status or circumstances. When a man says *al menat she-ani ashir*, "on the condition that I am wealthy," and it emerges that he is not, that is more obviously problematic: he stated a condition, and the condition was not satisfied. Yet the *Mishnah* treats the object cases similarly. Even when the woman received something of greater value than what was specified, the *kiddushin* is invalid because it was different from what was stated.

### R. Shimon: Leshevach

Rabbi Shimon disputes this ruling in cases where the deviation is *leshevach* — an improvement. *Rabbi Shimon omer: im hita'a leshevach, mekudeshet* — if she was misled and it turned out to be better, the *kiddushin* is valid. This applies both to the object of *kiddushin* (the coin or goblet) and to the personal condition (*al menat*). The *Gemara* will now examine each category in turn.

---

## Goblet Definition

### Three Baraitot

Before addressing the substantive debate, the *Gemara* first establishes what is included when one says "with this goblet." Three *baraitot* are cited, and they appear to contradict one another. The first holds *bo u-ma she-besocho* — the goblet and what is inside it. The second holds *bo ve-lo ma she-besocho* — the goblet alone, not its contents. The third holds *be-ma she-besocho ve-lo bo* — the contents alone, not the goblet itself. The *Gemara* resolves this by saying the three *baraitot* are not in dispute; they address three different circumstances: *ha be-maya, ha be-chamra, ha be-tziara* — one refers to water, one to wine, and one to fish brine or a similar preserved substance.

### Rashi's Cases

Rashi explains the three cases as follows. If someone says "this goblet of water," the water is entirely inconsequential — no one gives a gift of water. The focus must therefore be on the goblet itself. If someone says "this goblet of wine," the wine is meaningful, but Rashi notes that in common usage people say "here is a glass of wine," and the recipient drinks the wine and returns the glass. Just as one who offers a guest a glass of wine does not intend to give away the vessel, so too here — the gift is the wine, not the goblet. If, however, someone says "this jar of fish brine" (*tziara*), the analogy shifts: one who gives a jar of preserves does not expect the recipient to empty it and return the container. The item comes together with what it is stored in, and therefore in that case the reference is to both.

---

## Wine/Vinegar Debate

### Gemara's Question

The *Gemara* now focuses on Rabbi Shimon's position regarding the object of *kiddushin* and raises a pointed question. *Ve-lait lei le-Rabbi Shimon yayin ve-nimtza chametz, chametz ve-nimtza yayin, shneihem yecholim lachzor bahem?* — Does Rabbi Shimon not hold that if someone goes to a storekeeper and asks to purchase wine and receives vinegar, or asks for vinegar and receives wine, either party may retract? This is a standard principle: even if one receives something of greater value than what was requested — wine instead of vinegar, which is cheaper — either party can undo the transaction, because the buyer's desire was for a specific item, not simply for maximum value. Someone might need vinegar for a recipe and have no use for wine. The item's identity matters independently of its monetary worth.

If that is true, asks the *Gemara*, then even according to Rabbi Shimon, if a man says "marry me with this silver *dinar*" and it turns out to be gold, she should not be *mekudeshet* — because perhaps she wanted silver specifically. The *Gemara* thus presses: *ika de-nicha lei be-chaspa ve-lo nicha lei be-dahava* — there are those who prefer silver and not gold, just as some prefer vinegar and not wine. How then can Rabbi Shimon validate the *kiddushin* when the object is different from what was stated, even if the substitute is of greater worth?

### Tosafot Distinction

*Tosafot* offers a distinction. When it comes to objects, there is a genuine basis for preferring one type over another regardless of value — a craftsman making jewelry might specifically want silver, not gold. The case of money as a pure monetary instrument — where the only consideration is value — is different. If, for instance, a man said "marry me with a check for one hundred *dinars*" and gave a check for two hundred, that would obviously be valid even according to the *Rabbanan*, since there is no reason to prefer less money over more. The debate in the *Mishnah* arises precisely because the specific material of the coin — silver versus gold — may carry independent significance beyond mere monetary value, just as wine and vinegar do.

The *Gemara* nevertheless presses this question conceptually, observing that even Rabbi Shimon should be troubled by the parallel to the storekeeper case. There is something slightly counterintuitive in the *Gemara's* assumption that a woman accepting *kiddushin* is analogous to a buyer at a shop — she is not acquiring the object for its own sake in the way a customer purchases vinegar for a recipe. Yet the *Gemara* frames the two cases as structurally parallel, and that framing drives the subsequent analysis.

---

## Abaye's Shaliach

### Woman's Shaliach

The *Gemara* cites Rav Shimi bar Ashi, who reports that he found Abaye explaining this *Mishnah* and Rabbi Shimon's position to his son. Abaye's resolution is as follows. The case in the *Mishnah* is not one in which the man handed an object directly to the woman and it turned out to be different from what he stated. In that straightforward scenario, all would agree that the *kiddushin* is invalid — even Rabbi Shimon — because there is no basis to assume she would accept something other than what was specified. Rather, the *Mishnah* is dealing with a case in which the man appointed a *shaliach*: *amar lei le-shlucho, haveini dinar shel kesef, ve-lech ve-kadesh li et isha plonit* — "bring me a silver *dinar* and go betroth this woman on my behalf." The *shaliach* then went and used a gold *dinar* instead. In that scenario, the woman received exactly what she received — she had full *da'at*. The question is whether the man's original instruction to the *shaliach* is understood as a precise specification (*kefida*) or merely as a general direction (*mareh makom*).

### Makpid vs. Mareh Makom

The debate between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon is framed as follows: *mar savar kefida, u-mar savar mareh makom hu lo* — one holds that when the man specified silver, he was *makpid*, exacting, and therefore the *shaliach* exceeded his authority by substituting gold; the other holds that specifying silver was merely *mareh makom* — showing the *shaliach* the direction, indicating that silver is sufficient, while not excluding the possibility of giving something more. According to the view of *mareh makom*, since the *shaliach* gave more than the minimum required, the *kiddushin* stands.

### Language Objection

The *Gemara* objects that this reading cannot be correct. If the scenario involves the man's *shaliach*, the *Mishnah* should have used the language *hiskadshi lo* — "be married to him" — referring to the man who sent the *shaliach*. The *Mishnah* instead uses *hiskadshi li* — "marry me" — which is the language of the man speaking directly. Moreover, if it says "it turned out to be gold" (*nimtza shel zahav*), this implies it was always gold and never misrepresented — the *shaliach* simply chose to use gold. These linguistic difficulties show that Abaye's reading cannot be the correct interpretation of the *Mishnah's* language.

---

## Rava's Reading

### Woman Appoints

Rava, together with Rabbi Hiyya bar Abbin — whom the *Gemara* identifies as the *arya she-bachevraya*, the lion of the group — offers an alternative reading. *Hacha be-mai askinan:* the scenario involves a *shaliach* appointed not by the man but by the woman. The man had previously approached the woman and said, "Marry me with a silver *dinar*." She told him she needed to think about it. She then appointed a *shaliach* and said to him: *tzei ve-kabel li kiddushin mi-ploni she-amar li hiskadshi li be-dinar shel kesef* — "Go and accept *kiddushin* on my behalf from that man who told me to be betrothed to him with a silver *dinar*." The *shaliach* went, and the man gave him a gold *dinar* instead. The *nimtza* — "it turned out to be" — refers to the wrapping (*d'katzir be-vavlisa*): the coin was wrapped up, and when it was unwrapped it was discovered to be gold.

### Identification Question

This reading preserves the *Mishnah's* language — the woman appointed the *shaliach*, and the language *hiskadshi li* reflects the man's original words that she is quoting to the *shaliach*. The debate between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon now concerns the woman's intent when she gave instructions to her *shaliach*. Did she mean that the *shaliach* must accept specifically a silver *dinar* (*kefida*)? Or was she simply identifying which man she was referring to — "the man who offered me a silver *dinar*" being her way of pointing out the specific individual (*mareh makom*)? If the latter, then the silver was merely her way of directing the *shaliach* to the right man, and if that man chose to give gold, there is no reason to think she would object. Just as one might say "the man in the purple suit said he would betroth me" — and if the *shaliach* finds him in a different suit, that is obviously immaterial — perhaps mentioning silver was similarly just a way of identifying who was being discussed. Rabbi Shimon holds this reading; the *Rabbanan* hold that she was *makpid* on the silver itself.

One might ask why her *da'at* should be more flexible simply because a *shaliach* was involved. The *Gemara* does not fully resolve this, but the implication seems to be that when a person empowers a *shaliach* to act in a matter, there is a degree of latitude granted that would not exist in a direct transaction. The specific designation given to the *shaliach* may function more as identification than as a binding specification.

---

## Three Tannaim

### Abaye Reports

Abaye reports that three *Tanna'im* share the principle of *mareh makom* — that when one gives instructions to a *shaliach*, the specification may be understood as pointing a general direction rather than imposing a strict requirement. These three are Rabban Shimon, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rabbi Elazar. The concept of *mareh makom* is not invented for our *Mishnah*; rather, the *Gemara* borrows it from a recognized dispute about the latitude of a *shaliach*. The introduction of this language into the analysis of our *Mishnah* signals that the *Gemara* understands it to be an application of this broader principle.

### Get Analogy

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position emerges from a *Mishnah* dealing with *gittin*. There are two types of *get*: a *get pashut*, which is a flat document with the witnesses signing at the bottom, and a *get mukushar*, which is a folded and sewn document, traditionally associated with the special concern for a *kohen* who cannot remarry a divorcée and therefore should not divorce hastily. To slow down the process, the *get mukushar* required writing on every other line, folding the blank line over the written line and sewing it shut, repeating this for each line — a laborious process — with the witnesses signing on the back of those folds. The *Mishnah* in *Gittin* establishes that a *pashut get* has witnesses signing inside (at the bottom) and a *mukushar get* has witnesses signing outside (on the back). If these are switched — a *pashut* with witnesses on the back, or a *mukushar* with witnesses inside — both are invalid according to Rabbi Hanina. Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel says a *mukushar* with witnesses inside is valid because it can simply not be sewn, and then it would function as a *pashut*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says *hakol ke-minhag ha-medina* — everything follows the practice of the region.

### Get Decision

The *Gemara* asks: does this principle not say anything new? We know the proper form for each type. Rav Ashi clarifies: the statement *hakol ke-minhag ha-medina* applies in a specific case — where a man instructed a *shaliach* to write one type of *get*, and the *shaliach* wrote the other. The debate between *kefida* and *mareh makom* applies only when both types of *get* are in common use in that locale. If the region uses only one type and the *shaliach* wrote the other, all agree this is *kefida* and the *shaliach* exceeded his authority. *Ki pligi* — the dispute arises when both *pashut* and *mukushar* are accepted in that place — *be-atra d'nahigi bein be-pashut bein be-mukushar* — and the man said to write a *pashut*, and the *shaliach* wrote a *mukushar*. One opinion (*kefida*) holds the *shaliach* deviated from the instruction; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view (*mareh makom*) holds that since both are locally acceptable, the man was merely pointing to the simpler option, and if the *shaliach* chose the more involved form, he acted within the scope of the mandate.

---

## Shaliach Conclusion

### Limits of Doctrine

The *Gemara* establishes that the principle of *mareh makom* applies specifically when the *shaliach* does *more* than what was asked — he chose the more elaborate form, the more valuable coin, the more difficult option. If the *shaliach* does *less* than was asked, or switches laterally to something of equal or different character, all agree the principal is *makpid*. The only space for the debate between *kefida* and *mareh makom* is when the *shaliach* exceeds the instruction in a way that could plausibly be understood as fulfilling the original intent more amply. This sets the parameters within which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling and Rabbi Shimon's ruling in our *Mishnah* operate.

---

## Three Tannaim (II)

### R. Elazar Case

The third of the three *Tanna'im* cited by Abaye is Rabbi Elazar, whose position derives from a *Mishnah* dealing with *gittin* as well. The *Mishnah* states: *ha-ishah she-amrah, hitkabel li giti mi-makom ploni* — a woman said to a *shaliach*, "Go and accept my *get* on my behalf from such-and-such a location" — that is, from a specific place where her husband agreed to meet. *Ve-kiblah et gitah mi-makom acher* — and the *shaliach* went and accepted the *get* at a different location. The *tanna kamma* holds this is *pasul* — invalid — because her instruction specified a particular place, and accepting it elsewhere is a deviation. *Ve-Rabbi Elazar machshir* — Rabbi Elazar validates it. *Alma kasavar mareh makom hu lo* — Rabbi Elazar holds that by naming the location, the woman was merely pointing the *shaliach* toward where her husband would be, not requiring that the exchange happen at precisely that street corner. It is worth noting that this is likely the case where the phrase *mareh makom* originated in its literal sense — showing the place — before being applied metaphorically to other cases of general direction-giving. Unlike the *get* and *kiddushin* cases above, where one option was more valuable than the other, here the question is simply a different location — neither easier nor harder, just different. Yet Rabbi Elazar's principle of *mareh makom* encompasses even this: the instruction was directional, not constitutive. By analogy, when the woman in our *Mishnah* says "the man who offered me a silver *dinar*," Rabbi Shimon applies the same logic — she was identifying the man, not mandating the metal.

---

## Conditions Analysis

### Ulla's Position

The *Gemara* now turns to the second part of the *Mishnah* — the *al menat* cases of rich and poor — without formal announcement. Ulla states: *machloket be-shvach mamon* — the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Rabbanan* is limited to the case where the man's financial situation turns out to be better than stated, i.e., he is rich rather than poor. Here the *Gemara* does not invoke the wine-and-vinegar argument against Rabbi Shimon. The logic is more intuitive: on the assumption that a woman would generally prefer a wealthy husband, Rabbi Shimon holds that if the *al menat* condition fails because the man is *more* than he represented, the *kiddushin* is valid. The *tanna kamma's* objection in this case may simply be formalistic — the condition was stated and not met — rather than based on any genuine concern that she preferred poverty.

### Yichus Objection

However, Ulla continues: *aval be-shvach yichusin, divrei hakol eina mekudeshet* — but if it turns out that the man has higher *yichus* — better lineage or personal status — than he represented, all agree she is not *mekudeshet*. Why? *Masana de-rav mi-kara'i lo ba'ina* — "a shoe bigger than my foot, I do not want." The woman could say: I am not capable of filling that role. A man of higher status — a *kohen* when she expected a *Yisrael*, or a *Yisrael* when she expected a *mamzer* — imposes expectations and social obligations she never agreed to. She may genuinely not want to be the wife of someone whose status she cannot match or whose position creates discomfort or tension within the marriage. Better *yichus* is not straightforwardly *leshevach* from the woman's perspective, and therefore even Rabbi Shimon agrees the *kiddushin* does not stand.

### Baraita Agreement

A *baraita* confirms this: *modeh Rabbi Shimon she-im hita'ah le-shvach yichusin she-eina mekudeshet* — Rabbi Shimon himself concedes that if the misrepresentation was an improvement in personal status, she is not *mekudeshet*. This is not a case of Rabbi Shimon being overruled; it is his own stated position. The distinction he draws is between objective material improvement — greater wealth — and the more complex category of status, where individual preference and social dynamics render the calculus uncertain.

---

## Rav Ashi Inference

### Silence Proof

Rav Ashi argues that this conclusion — that Rabbi Shimon's disagreement is limited to the case of wealth and does not extend to *yichus* — can be inferred from the language of the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* that immediately follows our *Mishnah* deals with cases such as *al menat she-ani kohen ve-nimtza levi, levi ve-nimtza kohen, natin ve-nimtza mamzer, mamzer ve-nimtza natin* — conditions about tribal and legal status — and rules *eina mekudeshet*. Notably, Rabbi Shimon does not voice any disagreement in that *Mishnah*. Rav Ashi argues: *ve-lo paligi Rabbi Shimon* — Rabbi Shimon's silence indicates that he agrees with the ruling in those cases. Since he expressly disagreed in the case of wealth earlier, his failure to speak up when the *Mishnah* discusses *kohen*, *levi*, and *mamzer* demonstrates that he concedes those cases entirely.

### Objection

Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges this inference. He notes that the later *Mishnah* also includes a case of *al menat she-yesh li bat o shifcha megudelet* — on the condition that I have an older daughter or maidservant capable of helping in the household — and again Rabbi Shimon does not disagree. But this is surely a case of financial benefit, not *yichus*. If Rabbi Shimon only fails to disagree regarding *yichus*, we would have expected him to reassert his position regarding the daughter or maidservant. His silence there undermines the inference from his silence in the *kohen*/*levi* cases.
