One could argue, says Mar bar Rav Ashi, that Rabbi Shimon simply didn't repeat his position because *he already stated it* regarding wealth, and *hu ha-din le-seifa* — the same ruling applies to all the cases of wealth, including the daughter and maidservant. If so, his silence in the *kohen*/*levi* cases is equally uninformative.

### Gemara Response

The *Gemara* responds: *hatam idi ve-idi shvach mamon* — both the case of wealth and the case of having a daughter or maidservant belong to the same category of material benefit. It is entirely natural for Rabbi Shimon to remain silent in the later *Mishnah* regarding those cases, since he already stated his position — having a helpful household member falls under the same principle as financial wealth, and the ruling is identical. But the case of *kohen* and *levi* is *shvach yichusin* — a fundamentally different category. Were Rabbi Shimon to disagree there as well, he would have needed to say so explicitly. *Ei ita de-palig litni* — if he disagreed, he should have said it. His silence in that qualitatively distinct context is therefore meaningful, and Rav Ashi's inference stands.

### Megudelet Definition

The *Gemara* then offers an alternative answer (*iba'it eima*) that approaches the matter differently. One might reconsider what *megudelet* means. The simple reading takes it to mean a grown (*gedolah*) daughter or maidservant — an adult who can be useful around the house, which is indeed a material benefit analogous to wealth. But the *Gemara* asks: *mai megudelet?* What if *megudelet* does not mean simply an adult? *Tosafot* explains — and this reading is the more compelling one — that *megudelet* means a hairdresser. And why would having a hairdresser in the house be a problem rather than a benefit? Because *lo nicha li de-shakeila mili minai ve-azla ve-ganya kammai shivvutei* — the wife can say: I do not want her to take my personal matters and go spread them among the neighbors. A hairdresser, by the nature of her work, talks while she works and shares what she hears. Rashi's version of this concern is that an important woman (*gedolah* in the sense of prominent) would feel comfortable circulating socially and carrying information. Either way, having such a person in the household is not straightforwardly a benefit for the wife — it introduces the risk of her private affairs becoming public. In this reading, the *megudelet* case is analogous to *yichus*, not to wealth: it is something that may appear to be an improvement but which the woman may legitimately not want. This explains why Rabbi Shimon does not disagree there either.

---

## Personal Traits

### Reader Condition

Having addressed the *al menat* cases involving social status and wealth, the *Gemara* now turns to conditions involving personal traits and scholarly achievement. A *baraita* discusses each in turn. *Al menat she-ani kraina* — on the condition that I am a reader. The minimum that satisfies this condition is *keivan she-kara shelosha pesukim be-veit ha-knesset* — if he has received an *aliyah* and read three *pesukim* in the synagogue, the condition is met and she is *mekudeshet*. Reading three verses publicly demonstrates basic literacy; a high level of scholarship is not implied by the word *kraina* used without further qualification.

Rabbi Yehudah, however, says *ad she-yikra ve-yitargem* — he must be able to read and also do *Targum*, the Aramaic translation. The *Gemara* asks: does this mean he can translate freely in his own words? Surely not — the *Gemara* recalls that Rabbi Yehudah himself ruled that one who translates a verse *ke-tsurato*, in an overly literal fashion, is a liar (*badai*), and one who adds his own embellishments to the accepted translation is a blasphemer. The authorized *Targum* is the traditional *Masorah*-based translation; to deviate from it in either direction is a distortion of the Torah's meaning. The *Gemara* resolves this: *ela mai targum — targum didan*, the *Targum* referred to is the accepted traditional one, understood to be *Targum Onkelos*.

The *baraita* further distinguishes: *va-hanei milei de-amar lei kraina* — these standards apply when a man says *kraina*, "I read" — an unqualified claim to basic reading ability. But if he says *kara ana* — I am a reader in the full sense, a *ba'al korei* — then the condition is only satisfied *ad de-kari Oraita, Nevi'ei u-Chtuvei be-didkuka* — if he can read the entire *Tanakh* with precision and grammatical accuracy.

### Learner Condition

*Al menat she-ani shoneh* — on the condition that I am a learner. Here, *shoneh* has the connotation of *Mishnah*, the core oral tradition. Hezekiah says the condition is met if one knows *halachot* — basic legal rulings. Rabbi Yochanan says *Torah*, meaning *Midrash Torah*, i.e., the *midreshei halacha* — the halachic midrashim (*Sifra*, *Sifrei*, *Mechilta*) that derive law exegetically from Scripture. A *baraita* confirms this, with Rabbi Meir specifying *halachot* and Rabbi Yehudah specifying *Midrash*. The *Gemara* reconciles Rabbi Yochanan's position with Rabbi Yehudah's — *mai Torah, Midrash Torah* — what he meant by "Torah" is the *midrashic* exposition of the Torah's laws.

Here again the *baraita* distinguishes based on how the man phrases his claim. *Va-ani midi de-amar lah tanina* — this applies when he says *tanina*, "I learn," in a general sense. But if he says *tana ana*, "I am a *tana*" — implying the role of those whose entire function was systematic memorization and transmission of the oral law — then *ad de-tani hilchata, Sifra, Sifrei, ve-Tosefta*: he must have mastered all the *halachot*, all the *midrashei halacha*, and all the *Tosefta*.

### Student Condition

*Al menat she-ani talmid* — on the condition that I am a *talmid*. Here *talmid* refers not to memorization but to *Talmud* — analytical engagement with the material. The minimum for this condition is not the standard of a Shimon ben Azzai or Shimon ben Zoma, who bore the title of *talmidim* despite being the greatest scholars of their generation (having never received *semikhah*). Rather, the standard is: *kol she-sho'alin oto be-chol makom davar echad be-limudo ve-omer* — one whom you can ask about anything from a field he has studied, and he is able to answer and explain it. Rashi reads this generously: if in even one area of learning he can answer questions competently, the condition is satisfied. *Va-afilu be-Masechet Kallah* — even in the relatively accessible tractate of *Kallah*.

### Sage Condition

*Al menat she-ani chacham* — on the condition that I am a *chacham*. Again, the standard is not the level of the sages of Yavneh — Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues. Rather, the condition is met by *kol she-sho'alin oto davar chochmah be-chol makom ve-omer* — anyone who can be asked a matter of analytical wisdom in any field and is able to respond. Rashi notes, significantly, that this need not even be a matter of Torah learning specifically: if a man claims to be a *chacham* in physics, or mathematics, or any field of knowledge, and he can demonstrate analytical competence in that field when asked, the condition is satisfied. *Chochmah* is not restricted to Torah scholarship.

---

## Moral Traits

### Valiant

*Al menat she-ani gibbor* — on the condition that I am valorous. The standard is not the level of Avner ben Ner or Yoav ben Tzeruyah, the great military commanders. Rather, *kol she-chaverav mis-yar'im heimenu mipnei gevurato* — anyone whose friends are afraid of him because of his physical strength and formidability. Even if it later turns out that in absolute terms he is not a strong man, if his social circle regards him as someone not to be crossed, the condition is considered met.

### Rich

*Al menat she-ani ashir* — on the condition that I am wealthy. Again, not the standard of Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom or Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, men of legendary wealth. Rather, *kol she-bnei iro mechabdim oto mipnei oshro* — anyone whom the people of his town honor and respect on account of his wealth. Relative standing in one's social context defines *ashir* for purposes of this condition.

### Righteous

*Al menat she-ani tzaddik* — on the condition that I am righteous. Here the ruling is striking: *afilu rasha gamur, mekudeshet* — even if the man was known to be a complete *rasha*, she is *mekudeshet*. Why? *Shema hirhir teshuvah be-da'ato* — perhaps at that very moment, he had a thought of repentance. This is the first case in this series that introduces the word *shema* — "perhaps." The implication of the *poskim* is therefore that she is *safek mekudeshet* — doubtfully betrothed — not definitively *mekudeshet* as in the other cases, where a minimum threshold was simply defined. Here the status rests on a possibility.

This passage is the basis for Rav Soloveitchik's discussion in *Al Ha-Teshuvah*. He notes that full *teshuvah* — which absolves the sin — requires *viduy peh*, verbal confession; *charatah*, genuine remorse; *kabbalah le-atid*, commitment to the future; and *meratze chaveiro*, reconciliation with the wronged party. But the *Gemara* here is addressing something different: not the mechanics of atonement but the transformation of personal identity. A person can undergo a sudden, profound inner transformation — going from *rasha* to *tzaddik* in an instant — even without any external process. The man did not say "on the condition that I have done *teshuvah*"; he said "on the condition that I am a *tzaddik*." Perhaps, at the moment of his betrothal — finding the right woman, sensing a turning point in his life — he has become, at that moment, who he claimed to be.

### Wicked

*Al menat she-ani rasha* — on the condition that I am wicked. *Afilu tzaddik gamur, mekudeshet* — even if the man was known to be a complete *tzaddik* his entire life, she is *mekudeshet*. *Shema hirhir devar avodah zarah be-da'ato* — perhaps at that moment, he had a thought of idol worship. A person who has been wholly righteous throughout his life is not immune to a sudden internal turn. As the principle goes, *al ta'amin be-atzmecha ad yom mosecha* — do not trust yourself until the day of your death. The soul's moral condition at any given instant cannot be assumed from its history. This case, like the previous one, yields only *safek mekudeshet*.

---

## Agadic Homily

### Distribution

Having traversed the territory of rich and poor, wise and foolish, righteous and wicked, the *Gemara* closes this sugya with an *aggadic* passage distributing the qualities discussed throughout the world. Ten measures of *chochmah* — wisdom — came down to the world: nine were taken by *Eretz Yisrael* and one by the entire rest of the world. Ten measures of *yofi* — beauty — came down: nine were taken by *Yerushalayim* and one by the rest of the world. Ten measures of *ashirut* — wealth — came down: nine were taken by the early Romans (*Roma'im kadmonim*) and one by the rest of the world. Ten measures of *aniyut* — poverty — came down: nine were taken by *Bavel*, where the *talmidei chachamim* lived in great poverty, and one by the rest of the world. Ten measures of *gasut* — haughtiness — came down: nine were taken by *Elam* and one by the rest of the world.

### Elam's Haughtiness

The *Gemara* objects: was haughtiness not a trait of *Bavel*? The verse in Zechariah describes two winged women carrying an *eifah* — a large measure — between heaven and earth, and the angel explains they are bringing it to build a house in the land of *Shinar*. Rabbi Yochanan explains: *zu chanufah ve-gasut ha-ruach she-yardu le-Bavel* — this represents flattery and haughtiness, which descended to *Bavel*. The *Gemara* reconciles: yes, it came down to *Bavel*, but then *ishtarvovei hu de-ishtarvov le-hasam* — it rolled and made its way to *Elam*. The house was never built in *Bavel*; it was carried onward. The language *livnot lah bayit* — "to build her a house" — without the house ever having been completed confirms the inference.

But this raises a further question: does haughtiness not belong to *Bavel* after all? The principle *siman le-gasut aniyut* — poverty is a sign of haughtiness — would locate haughtiness in *Bavel*, which we just said took nine measures of poverty. The *Gemara* resolves: the poverty meant here is *aniyut de-Torah* — poverty in Torah. When a person is haughty, he is self-satisfied with his learning and never genuinely applies himself; he does not give himself over to teaching others or to the self-sacrifice that real *Torah* mastery demands. This is the *aniyut* associated with *gasut*. The proof is the verse applied by Rabbi Yochanan to *Elam*: *achot lanu ketanah ve-shadayim ein lah* — "we have a young sister and she has no breasts." This refers to Elam: *she-zacheta lilmod ve-lo zacheta lelamed* — those who merited to study but never merited to teach, because their haughtiness precluded them from attaining the depth and humility that genuine transmission of Torah requires.

### Other Traits

The *Gemara* continues the catalogue. Ten measures of strength (*gevurah*) came down: nine were taken by the Persians. Ten measures of lice (*kinim*) came down: nine were taken by the Medes. Ten measures of *nega'im* — leprous afflictions — came down: nine were taken by pigs. Ten measures of licentiousness (*znut*) came down: nine were taken by Arabia. Ten measures of brazenness (*azut*) came down: nine were taken by Meshan. Ten measures of idle chatter (*sicha*) came down: nine were taken by women. Ten measures of drunkenness (*shikhrut*) came down: nine were taken by the Ethiopians. Ten measures of sleep (*shena*) came down: nine were taken by slaves, and one by the rest of the world — and here the *Gemara* concludes the discussion.

---

---

# Kiddushin 50

## Status Conditions

### Kohen/Levi Cases

Daf 50 opens at the very bottom of 49b with a new *mishnah*. The *mishnah* presents a series of cases in which a man betroths a woman by stating a condition regarding his personal status — *al menat she'ani Kohen venimtsa Levi*, on the condition that I am a *kohen* and he is discovered to be a *levi* — or the reverse, on the condition that I am a *levi* and he turns out to be a *kohen*.

### Natin/Mamzer Status

The *mishnah* continues: *natin venimtsa mamzer*, on the condition that I am a *natin* — a Gibeonite, a lower rank of personal status — and it turns out he is a *mamzer*; or *mamzer venimtsa natin*, he declared himself a *mamzer* and turned out to be a *natin*. In each pair, the first-mentioned status is the more preferred or higher-ranking one. The pattern holds throughout: whether the condition stated was better than the reality, or worse, the *kiddushin* does not take effect.

### Town vs. City

The *mishnah* goes on: *ben ir venimtsa ben krach*, he said he lived in a town and it turned out he lived in a city, or *ben krach venimtsa ben ir*, a city-dweller who turns out to live in a town. Since the town is listed first — as the preferable condition — the *mishnah* is implicitly expressing that it is better to live in a town than in a city. Rashi explains: *yeshivat krachim kasha* — city living is difficult. The city is a place of markets, noise, high rents, and crowds. Of course, precisely those features lead many people to prefer city life, which makes this an interesting reflection of the *mishnah*'s social assumptions.

### Bathhouse Proximity

The *mishnah* continues with conditions relating to amenities: *al menat sheyesh li bayit karov lemerchats venimtsa rachok*, on the condition that my house is close to the bathhouse, and it turns out to be distant — or the reverse, distant and it turns out to be close. Either way, the condition was not fulfilled as stated.

### Household Help

Similarly: *al menat sheyesh li bat o shifcha megudelet*, on the condition that I have a daughter or a maidservant who is an adult — reading the straightforward *pshat*, someone who can assist with the household (though the *gemara* earlier had offered a different reading of this phrase) — and he does not, or he says he does not have such help and it turns out he does.

### Sons Condition

The *mishnah* further addresses: *she'ein li banim*, on the condition that I have no sons. This is a preferred status from the wife's perspective, since it means there will be no other heirs — specifically sons — competing with her future children for the inheritance. Again, whether he stated he has sons and does not, or stated he has none and does, the condition is unfulfilled and the *kiddushin* does not take effect.

Strikingly, the *mishnah* does not explicitly conclude with *eina mekudeshet* — she is not betrothed. That ruling is apparently presumed from the previous *mishnah*. It is also worth noting that Rabbi Shimon, who argued in the previous *mishnah* that fulfillment of a condition in the better-than-promised direction should be valid, does not dispute this *mishnah* — because as the *gemara* explained, in matters of personal status, "better" is not necessarily better. Perhaps one does not want a spouse of a higher status than anticipated. That is how the *gemara* resolved the matter there.

### Internal Intent Invalid

The *mishnah* then adds a critical new principle: *af al pi she'amra belibi haya lehitkadesh lo af al pi chen eina mekudeshet* — even if the woman says, "In my heart I had already decided to marry him regardless; I didn't care whether he was a *kohen* or a *levi*, I love him and the condition was irrelevant to me" — she is still not married. Once a condition is articulated, it becomes the legally binding framework of the *kiddushin*. The *mishnah* adds that *vechen hi shehit'athu* — the same applies in reverse, if she is the one who misrepresented a stated condition.

It is worth noting that the *mishnah* frames the issue in terms of deception — *leta'u* — but the *gemara* consistently does not focus on the wrongfulness of deception as such. The operative point is not the moral dimension of misleading the other party; it is that something was stated as a condition, and that condition was not met. The primary innovation here is that even an explicit disclaimer of internal indifference — "I didn't care about that condition" — has no legal effect. What is legally binding is what was said. This leads directly into one of the most consequential principles in the entire *Shas*.

---

## Devarim Shebalev

### Aliyah Sale Case

The *gemara* introduces the foundational discussion of the principle of *devarim shebelev einam devarim* — that unarticulated intentions have no halakhic weight. The case that opens the discussion: *hahu gavra dezavin lenichsei ada'ata lemisak le'Ara deYisrael* — a man sold his property with the intent of making *aliyah*. Rashi emphasizes that the property in question was his home. The man had a plan — to sell everything and move to Eretz Yisrael — but critically, *u-ve-idna de-zavin lo amar velo midi*, when he actually sold the property he said nothing to anyone about this plan. It did not work out and he did not make *aliyah*, and he is now effectively homeless. Can he reverse the sale?

### Rava's Principle

*Amar Rava: havei devarim she-ba-lev*. Rava rules that the unarticulated intent — the assumption that the sale was contingent on his *aliyah* plans — constitutes *devarim she-ba-lev*, and *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*: things in the heart, things that are never articulated, carry no halakhic weight. The sale stands.

The *gemara* then asks: *minalei le-Rava ha?* — where does Rava derive this principle? The natural candidate is our own *mishnah*, which prompted the discussion, but the *gemara* works through several possible sources to determine which most cleanly establishes the principle.

### Sacrifice Forced

The *gemara* proposes a source from the top of 50a. In the beginning of *Vayikra*, the *pasuk* states *yakriv oto* — he shall bring it — which is read as a superfluous phrase alongside *zachar tamim yakrivenu*. The *mishnah* derives from this: *melamed she-kofin oto* — you may compel a person to bring a *korban* if he made a *neder*. But the *pasuk* also states *lirtzono* — it must be of his own will. How can one be both compelled and willing? *Kofin oto ad she-yomar rotzeh ani* — you compel him until he says, "I consent." He says the words verbally, even as it is evident he did not wish to do this. The *gemara* notes the apparent difficulty: *libeih lo nicha lei* — in his heart he clearly does not want to. Yet we accept his verbal declaration. Does this not prove *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*?

### Challenge to Principle

The *gemara* pushes back: *ve-dilma shani hatam de-anan sahadei de-nicha lei be-khaparah* — perhaps there it is different, because we can say that in truth he wants the atonement. Even if it took some arm-twisting, deep down he actually desires what he is ultimately being led to do. He wants to be reconciled with his obligations, and in that sense his verbal statement does align with his real desires, once we factor in what a person truly wants.

This points to a deeper issue. The principle of *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* is not merely an evidentiary claim — that we cannot verify what someone was thinking. It is a substantive legal principle: even if we somehow know with certainty what the person was thinking, it has no halakhic effect. But the *gemara* here is suggesting that in the sacrifice case, perhaps what the person says actually does reflect what he really wants — so it is not a pure case of discounting the inner state.

### Get & Slave Freedom

The *gemara* then turns to the continuation of that *mishnah*: *ve-khen ata motzei be-gitei nashim u-ve-shichrurei avadim — kofin oto ad she-yomar rotzeh ani*. The same principle applies to a *get* and to the freeing of a slave: when *beis din* determines that a *get* must be given or a slave freed, the man is compelled until he says *rotzeh ani*. This is directly relevant to the *agunah* problem — if *beis din* were to apply compulsion and obtain a verbal declaration of consent, it would be valid, something that cannot practically occur in certain jurisdictions but is theoretically operative in Israel. The principle is that once he says *rotzeh ani*, his internal reluctance is legally irrelevant.

### Yetzer Hatov Defense

Yet the *gemara* deflects this proof as well: *ve-dilma shani hasam mishum de-mitzvah lishmo'a divrei chachamim* — perhaps there, too, it is different. Since *beis din* is compelling him, we can say that deep down he wants to do the right thing; his *yetzer hatov* wants to comply with the ruling of *chachamim*, and it is only his *yetzer hara* that resists. The Rambam develops this idea at length — that every person fundamentally desires to fulfill his religious obligations, and *beis din*'s compulsion is simply helping the *yetzer hatov* overcome the *yetzer hara*. Under this reading, what the person ultimately says truly reflects his genuine inner will, and the case thus does not cleanly prove *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*.

### Woman Assumed Kohen

Rav Yosef then proposes a different source: *ha-mekadesh es ha-isha ve-amar kasavur hayisi she-hi kohenes ve-harei hi levaya* — a man betroths a woman and says after the fact, "I thought she was the daughter of a *kohen*" — the *mishnah* calls her a *kohenes* rather than *bat kohen* — "and it turns out she is the daughter of a *levi*." Or the reverse: he thought she was a *levaya* and she was a *kohenes*, or poor and she is wealthy, or wealthy and she is poor. In all these cases, *mekudeshes mipnei she-lo hit'ahu* — the *kiddushin* is valid because she did not deceive him. Again, the *mishnah* emphasizes deception, but the *gemara*'s consistent focus is on the distinction between what was articulated and what was merely assumed. He thought she was a *kohenes* — but he said nothing. His assumption is entirely internal and legally irrelevant. *Kasavur hayisi* — "I thought" — does not constitute a condition. This seems to be a strong proof for *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*.

### Stringency Objection

Abaye, however, objects: *dilma shani hasam de-lechumra* — perhaps there it is different, because there we are discounting the inner intent in the direction of *chumra*, of stringency. We refuse to treat her as unmarried based on his claim of what he was thinking — because we want to play it safe, not because inner intentions are always irrelevant. To truly prove *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*, one would need a case where inner intent is discounted even *le-kula* — even in the direction of leniency. Discounting intent in the stringent direction could simply be a matter of caution, not a statement about the irrelevance of inner states.

### Woman's Indifference

Abaye therefore offers his own proof — from the *mishnah* itself. *Bakulam af al pi she'amra belibi hayah le-hiskadesh lo af al pi chen einah mekudeshes* — in all these cases, even if the woman says she didn't care about the condition, she is not married. Here, she is saying "I would have married him regardless" — and we discount that to rule *lekula*, that she is not married. We are ignoring her stated inner indifference and declaring the *kiddushin* void. This is discounting *devarim she-ba-lev* in the lenient direction. Surely this proves the principle?

### Stated Negates Internal

The *gemara* responds: *ve-dilma shani hasam de-kivan de-asni lav kol kaminei de-akei lei letna'ei* — perhaps there it is different, because since a condition was explicitly stated, she cannot use her inner thoughts to negate it. *Kivan de-asni* — since he articulated a condition, she cannot come and say "in my heart I didn't care about that." Inner intent cannot override an explicit verbal stipulation. This is a narrower principle than what Rava wants to establish: not that *devarim she-ba-lev* are never legally relevant, but that *devarim she-ba-lev* cannot negate something that was explicitly stated.

The question, then, is how to prove the broader principle — that even in cases where nothing was said at all (as in the man who sold his property planning *aliyah* without articulating that intent), the unarticulated intent is legally void.

### Shaliach & Windowsill

The *gemara* reports that Rav Chiya bar Avin brought this question before Rav Chisda, who brought it before Rav Huna, and they found support from the following *me'ilah* case. If a person says to his *shaliach*, "Bring me the money from the windowsill" — *havi li min hachalon* — and from a certain box — *umin hadeluskema* — and the *shaliach* does so and spends the money, and it turns out the money was *hekdesh*, the *ba'al habayis* has committed *me'ilah*. The principle of *shlichus* applies in *me'ilah* — the *shaliach* acted on his behalf, so the *ba'al habayis* bears the liability. Now, the *ba'al habayis* claims: *lo haya li belibi ella al ze* — "I only meant the money on this side of the windowsill, not the other side." The *shaliach* took from the other side. Does this matter?

### Shaliach Proof

*Keivan shehevi lo mize ba'al habayis ma'al* — it does not matter. Even though the *ba'al habayis* is articulating what he says he was thinking, the *shlichus* was fulfilled and he has committed *me'ilah*. This is an ideal proof for *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* for several reasons. First, there is nothing here that contradicts what was said — there was no explicit statement about which side of the windowsill; the inner thought is not being deployed to negate anything articulated. Second, the question of *kula* versus *chumra* is not straightforwardly applicable here — either the *ba'al habayis* brings the *korban* or the *shaliach* does. Third, we are completely discounting what the *ba'al habayis* says he was thinking, even if we believe him entirely. *Ella lav mishum de-amrinan devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim.*

### Korban Escape Doubt

The *gemara* raises one more challenge: *ve-dilma shani hatam delimeiftar nafshia mikorban ka'ati* — perhaps we discount his claim not because *devarim she-ba-lev* are legally irrelevant, but because we suspect he is lying. He wants to escape liability for the *korban* and is fabricating a story about which side of the windowsill he meant. If so, we are discounting him because we do not believe him — not because his inner state would be irrelevant even if sincere.

### Easier Escape Routes

The *gemara* answers: *hava lei lemeimar mezid hava* — if he only wanted to escape the *korban*, he had easier things to say. He could have claimed to have acted intentionally — *mezid* — since a deliberate act of *me'ilah* does not carry the *korban* obligation. But *la avid inish demashvi nafshia rashi'a* — a person will not declare himself a *rasha*, will not portray himself as someone who deliberately misappropriated *hekdesh* funds, just to avoid a *korban*. Alternatively, *hava lei lemeimar nizkarti* — he could have said, "I remembered it was *hekdesh* while the *shaliach* was on the way, but by then I had no way to recall him." The *braita* establishes: *nizkar ba'al habayis velo nizkar shaliach — shaliach ma'al* — if the *ba'al habayis* remembered and the *shaliach* did not, the *shaliach* bears the liability. So the *ba'al habayis* had a clean, costless way to escape — and he did not use it. His claim about the windowsill therefore cannot be dismissed as motivated by self-interest. We believe him — and we still discount it. *Devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*, even when sincere.

### Exceptions Overview

Having established the principle, it is important to note that there are significant exceptions — cases where *devarim she-ba-lev* do carry halakhic weight.

### Self-Evident Exception

One major exception is called *devarim she-ba-lev kol adam* — intent that is self-evident from the circumstances to any reasonable person. Even if something is not explicitly articulated, if the context makes it entirely clear what a person must have intended, that intent may be given legal weight. This opens a broad area of discussion, but the basic idea is that when there is no need to access someone's private thoughts — when the circumstances themselves make the intent obvious — we are not truly in the domain of unarticulated inner states. Related to this are cases where a person makes an elliptical statement — as at the beginning of *Nedarim*, where someone says "I will be" as a *nazir* walks by, and we understand from context what was meant. There the full sentence is being completed from external evidence, not from speculation about private thought. Situations involving clear external compulsion also raise questions about how much weight to give the verbal statement versus the evident reluctance, though as we saw, the *gemara* earlier seemed to indicate that compulsion does not restore legal weight to inner states.

### One vs. Two-Sided

A further and very important distinction emerges from the Rambam, and the *Tosafot Rid* as well: the principle of *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* applies with particular force in two-sided transactions — a sale, a betrothal, an appointment of a *shaliach* — where there is another party whose interests and reasonable expectations must be protected. It would be deeply unfair to that other party if halakhic outcomes could be affected by the unarticulated private thoughts of one side. However, in more one-directional acts — giving a gift, delivering a *get*, where the act is essentially emanating from one side — there may be greater readiness to consider *devarim she-ba-lev*. Others among the *rishonim* frame the distinction not in terms of one-sided versus two-sided transactions, but in terms of how self-evident the intent is from the circumstances. In any case, the core principle — that purely private, unarticulated intentions that no one had access to cannot be given halakhic meaning — is firmly established by this *gemara*.

---

## Aliyah Condition Met?

### Went, Didn't Settle

The *gemara* now turns to a related case, this time assuming that the man did articulate his intent when selling his property. *Hahu gavra dezavin le-nikhsei ada'ata le-misak le-ara de-Yisrael* — he sold his property because he was planning to go up to Eretz Yisrael and said so. Unlike the previous case, the assumption here is that something was stated. He went — *salik* — attempted to make *aliyah*, but *ve-lo istadar lei* — he could not find a place to live, could not get settled, and returned. The condition was stated; was it met?

### Rava: Settling Intent

*Amar Rava kol de-salik ada'ata le-meidar hu* — Rava rules that when a person says he is selling in order to go up to Eretz Yisrael, he means to go up and settle there. *Ve-ha lo istadar* — and since he did not manage to settle, the intent was not fulfilled and the sale is reversed.

### Alternative: Going Only

*Ika de-amri* — some say the opposite ruling in Rava's name: *ada'ata le-misak ve-ha salik* — he said he was going to go, and he went. The condition of going was satisfied; the fact that he did not ultimately settle is beside the point. These are two competing interpretations of what his stated intent meant.

### Never Went Case

A further case: *hahu gavra d'zavin l'nichsei ada'ata l'misak l'Eretz Yisrael* — another man sold his property planning to go up to Eretz Yisrael. *Lesof lo salik* — in the end he changed his mind and never went. Does he have the right to reverse the sale?

### Option to Go

*Amar Rav Ashi: ibai salik* — Rav Ashi responds: who is stopping him? He can still go. The sale cannot be reversed simply because he has decided not to exercise the option. He retains the ability to fulfill the intent; he is simply choosing not to. *Ika de-amri: ibai lo salik* — some formulate it as: well, if he wants to, nothing prevents him from going. Both formulations say essentially the same thing: the option remains available.

### Impossible Travel

The *gemara* asks: *mai beinaihu* — what is the practical difference between the two formulations? *Ika beinaihu d'ishlei unsa be'orcha* — the difference emerges when travel is genuinely impossible, such as when road conditions make the journey truly impracticable. According to the formulation "who is stopping him," there is now an answer — something genuinely is stopping him — and the sale may be nullified. But according to the formulation "if he wants to, he can go," the implication is that so long as it is at all possible, the option exists and the sale stands. A legitimate external impediment, however, might nullify it.

### External vs. Central

This case raises a striking question that is addressed by the *rishonim*. Since when is a person compelled to fulfill such a condition? Normally, if I sell you a plot of land on the condition that I walk around the block, I may freely choose whether to walk or not — and my choice determines whether the sale stands. Why then does the *gemara* respond "who is stopping you? Go!" — implying he must go? The answer, developed by *Tosafot*, Ramban, and others, turns on a fundamental distinction between two types of conditions.

### Formal vs. Fundamental

When a condition is *external* to the basic intent of the transaction — such as "this sale will take effect if I walk around the block" — it is a technical device layered on top of the transaction. The person may fulfill it or not at will, but if he wants to use the condition to undo the transaction, he must have satisfied all the formal requirements of *mishpetei tna'im* — the formal rules of conditions modeled after the stipulation of *Bnei Gad u-Vnei Reuven*: the condition must be doubled, the positive stated before the negative, and so forth.

When, however, the reason for the transaction is itself central to the person's fundamental *da'at* — as when someone sells his home *because* he intends to make *aliyah*, and that intent is what motivates the entire transaction — we are not dealing with an external conditional device. We are speaking about the core of what the person wanted to do. In that case, there is no need to satisfy the formal *mishpetei tna'im*, because this is not a formal condition at all — it is an expression of what the transaction fundamentally was about. But by the same token, as long as the underlying intent remains achievable — as long as he could still make *aliyah* — the transaction reflects a genuine, intact *da'at*, and simply choosing not to act on it does not unwind what was done. The formal question of whether to fulfill the condition is replaced by the substantive question of whether the fundamental premise of the transaction has genuinely failed.

These discussions yield two major and interconnected principles. First, *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*: purely unarticulated intentions — even if sincerely held and even if we somehow know them — have no halakhic significance in transactions, particularly two-sided ones. Second, even when things are articulated, the legal analysis of what was said depends on whether it constitutes a formal external condition subject to technical *tna'im* requirements, or whether it expresses the fundamental *da'at* of the transaction. These are among the most consequential principles in the entire *Shas*.

---

## Shaliach Location

### Different Location

The *gemara* turns to a new *mishnah*: *ha'omer lishluchо tze vekadesh li isha plonis bemakom ploni vehalach vekideshah bemakom acher* — a man says to his *shaliach*, "Go betroth this woman for me in such-and-such place," and the *shaliach* goes and finds her in a different place and betroths her there. The *mishnah* rules: *eina mekudeshet* — she is not betrothed. The *shlichus* was limited to that particular place.

### Mareh Makom

This ruling reflects the principle of *makpid* — that when a person specifies a location as part of a *shlichus*, we treat him as genuinely insisting on that location, not merely as indicating where the woman can be found. This is in contrast to the principle of *mareh makom* — merely indicating the woman's whereabouts as a point of reference, which would not be a binding limitation on the *shlichus*. The *mishnah* establishes: if the location was articulated as part of the act of *shlichus*, it is a substantive requirement, not a mere *mareh makom*. A dissenting *tanna* does appear in the parallel discussion regarding *get*, though not explicitly here in the *kiddushin* context.

### Get Location

The *mishnah* also teaches the parallel rule regarding *get*: *ha'omer tnu get l'ishti bemakom ploni unesanu lah bemakom acher — pasul* — if a man says to give his wife a *get* in a specific place and it is given in a different place, it is invalid. But if he says "she is in such-and-such place" and the *get* is given elsewhere, *kasher* — it is valid. There the reference to a location was purely *mareh makom*, indicating where the woman could be found, not a substantive condition of the *shlichus*.

### Marriage Reputation

Why does specifying the location matter in the context of *kiddushin*? The *gemara* explains: *dekureva ka'asi* — the man is trying to bring her close, to marry her. When he specifies a place, it is because *behai asra rachmu li velo mamlu mili aluy* — in that neighborhood or community, people know him favorably and will speak well of him. He does not want the *shaliach* to approach her in a place where people might speak poorly of him and cause her to refuse. He is genuinely insisting on the location, not merely indicating where she might be found.

### Divorce Embarrassment

Why must the parallel rule also be taught by *get*? The *gemara* explains that one might have thought that when it comes to *get*, where *delerichuka ka'asi* — the man is trying to push her away — perhaps *lo ikphas leh* — he does not particularly care where it happens, since she has no say in accepting a *get* and no one can obstruct it. So perhaps even an explicit mention of location is only *mareh makom* in the context of *get*.

Conversely, one might have thought that a man is more *makpid* about the location of a *get* than of *kiddushin*. Rashi explains: *delivzi shemegareshes ishto g'nai hu lo* — the act of divorcing one's wife carries a certain disgrace for the man, an embarrassing reflection on the failure of the marriage. He may have strong feelings about where this humiliating event occurs — *behai asra nicha leh denivzi* — this is a place where he can tolerate the embarrassment, whereas elsewhere he would be much more sensitive. So one might have thought he cares more acutely about the location of the *get* than of the *kiddushin*. Since the reasoning cuts in different directions, the *mishnah* must teach the rule in both contexts. The underlying principle remains: when the location is articulated as part of the *shlichus*, it is binding; when it is merely a *mareh makom*, it is not.

---

## Vows Condition

### Pre-Marriage Vows

The *mishnah* presents another category of conditions: *hamekadesh es ha'isha al menas she'ein aleha nedarim venimtzu aleha nedarim* — if a man betroths a woman on the condition that she has no outstanding *nedarim*, and *nedarim* are found, *eina mekudeshet* — the *kiddushin* is void.

### Void Pre-Nisuin

If the *nedarim* are discovered before *nisuin* — before the full marriage is consummated — then the condition was explicitly unfulfilled and the *kiddushin* simply does not take effect, consistent with everything we have learned.

### No Ketubah Post-Nisuin

If, however, the man made this condition, they proceeded to *nisuin*, began living together, and only then discovered the *nedarim*, the situation is different. *Kensah stam venimtzu aleha nedarim — teitzei belo kesuvah* — if he married her without having explicitly made the condition and *nedarim* are found, or if the condition was made but discovered only post-*nisuin*, she must leave — but without a *kesuvah*. She receives no *kesuvah* because the marriage violated what was stipulated; however, she still requires a *get*.

### Nisuin Nullifies

Why does she need a *get* even though the condition was not met? This is based on the principle of *ein adam oseh beilaso beilas zenus* — we assume that a man does not wish for his act of marital intimacy to be treated as promiscuous. Once they proceeded to *nisuin* and consummated the marriage, there is a reasonable assumption — or at least a real possibility — that by proceeding he effectively waived the condition. Given that possibility, we treat her as genuinely married and requiring a *get*, though she loses her *kesuvah* since the condition was violated.

### Agunah Solution

This *mishnah* raises the broader question of *tna'i bekiddushin* as a proposed solution to the *agunah* problem. One suggested approach is to build a condition into the *kiddushin* itself — stipulating that if the couple separates and no *get* is given under certain circumstances, the *kiddushin* will be retroactively void. The question that this *mishnah* directly implicates is: once the couple begins living together, does the *nisuin* and subsequent cohabitation automatically constitute a *bittul* of the *tna'i*? Or can the condition be explicitly formulated in a way that survives the *nisuin*? This is one of the central practical complications in evaluating that proposed solution.

### Blemishes Condition

The *mishnah* then states a parallel case: *al menas she'ein lah mumim venimtzu bah mumim* — on the condition that she has no physical blemishes, and blemishes are found. If discovered before *nisuin*, *eina mekudeshet* — the *kiddushin* is void. *Kinasa stam venimtzu bah mumim — teitzei belo kesuvah* — if discovered after *nisuin*, she leaves without a *kesuvah* but still requires a *get*, for the same reasons discussed above. The *mishnah* adds: *shekol hamumim haposlim bakohanim poslim banashim* — all the blemishes that disqualify *kohanim* from service similarly disqualify women under this type of condition — a striking and far-reaching statement that the *gemara* does not elaborate upon here.

---

## Savlonos Gifts

### Insufficient Money

The final *mishnah* of the daf addresses: *hamekadesh shtei nashim beshaveh perutah* — a man who betroths two women with a single *perutah* between them, each receiving only half a *perutah*, which is insufficient for valid *kiddushin* — or *isha achas bepachas mishaveh prutah*, one woman with less than a *perutah*. In these cases the *kiddushin* obviously does not take effect.

### Savlonos as Kiddushin

The *mishnah* then introduces the central question: *af al pi sheshalach savlonos achar kach einam mekudashos* — even if he subsequently sent *savlonos*, the traditional gifts sent by the groom to the bride's family after *kiddushin*, she is still not betrothed. Two possible concerns motivate the question. One — emphasized by Rashi — is whether the *savlonos* themselves might constitute new *kesef kiddushin*, functioning as a fresh act of betrothal. The other, which fits other parts of the *gemara* more naturally, is whether the sending of *savlonos* should lead us to assume that some valid act of *kiddushin* occurred that we do not know about, since *savlonos* typically follow *kiddushin*.

### Based on Initial

The *mishnah* resolves both concerns: *she'machmat kiddushin harishonim shelach* — the *savlonos* were sent on account of the initial *kiddushin*, invalid as it was. The man thought his *kiddushin* had taken effect, and that is why he sent the *savlonos*. They are therefore not a new act of *kiddushin*, and they do not indicate that some other valid *kiddushin* occurred — they are simply the natural continuation of what he (mistakenly) believed had already happened.

The same principle applies to *vechen katan shekiddesh* — a minor who performed *kiddushin* and then, after reaching majority, sent *savlonos*. She remains unbetrothed for the same reason: the *savlonos* are explained by the prior invalid act.

### Why All Cases

The *gemara* asks: *u'tzricha* — why must the *mishnah* teach all three cases — two women with one *perutah*, one woman with less than a *perutah*, and the case of the *katan*?

If only the case of two women with one *perutah* were taught, one might think: since a full *perutah* was paid, the man assumed it was valid, so obviously the *savlonos* are not a new *kiddushin*. But in the case of less than a *perutah* — *aval pachas mishaveh prutah* — perhaps he knew very well that an amount below a *perutah* is invalid, and when he sent *savlonos* he intended them as a new act of *kiddushin*. The *mishnah* teaches us that even there, we do not assume this.

Conversely, if only those two cases were taught, one might think that in cases involving money, men generally do not know or pay attention to the precise threshold — but when it comes to a *katan*, *hakol yodim she'ein kiddushei katan klum* — everyone knows that the *kiddushin* of a minor is entirely invalid. So when, after reaching adulthood, he sends *savlonos*, perhaps we should assume he knew his earlier act was void and now intends the *savlonos* as a new *kiddushin*. The *mishnah* teaches that even in that case we do not assume this. Without evidence of a new act of *kiddushin*, we attribute the *savlonos* to the earlier invalid act, and no new betrothal is established.

### Concerned About Savlonos

The *gemara* now presents an *amoraic* debate that stands in some tension with the *mishnah*. *Rav Huna amar chosheshin lesavlanos* — Rav Huna rules that when *savlonos* are sent, we are concerned about the possibility of a prior *kiddushin*. *Vechen amar Rabbah chosheshin lesavlanos* — Rabbah agrees. There is a major debate among the *rishonim* about what exactly this means. Rashi understands it to mean that we are concerned the *savlonos* themselves were intended as *kesef kiddushin*. Many *rishonim* resist this reading, pointing out that valid *kiddushin* requires explicit articulation of *harei at mekudeshet li* and the presence of witnesses. They prefer to read the concern as follows: the sending of *savlonos* — which are traditionally sent after *kiddushin* — raises the possibility that some valid *kiddushin* occurred beforehand that we simply do not know about.

### Resolves Contradiction

Rabbah then anticipates the apparent contradiction with our *mishnah*: if we are concerned about *savlonos*, how does the *mishnah* say *einam mekudashos*? Abaye answers: *hatam kideiktani ta'ama* — there, the *mishnah* itself explains why there is no concern: *she'machmat kiddushin rishonim shelach* — the *savlonos* are accounted for by the prior invalid *kiddushin*. The man sent them because he thought the first *kiddushin* had worked. That eliminates the evidentiary weight of the *savlonos*. But Rav Huna and Rabbah are addressing a different scenario: where *savlonos* are sent with no prior known *kiddushin* at all. In that case, we are concerned that a valid *kiddushin* took place beforehand.

### Savlonos Indicate Kiddus…

*Ika de'amrei* — there is an alternative version of the exchange, in which Rabbah does not present the *mishnah* as a problem at all. Rather, he reads the *mishnah* itself as the source of his ruling. The *mishnah* says the *savlonos* are not a concern *because* the prior *kiddushin* explains them — *hacha hu detai*, in the *mishnah*'s case he is mistaken in thinking the prior act was valid. *Ha be-alma havei kiddushin* — but normally, when *savlonos* are sent without any preceding invalid act to account for them, we would assume that they reflect a prior valid *kiddushin*. Abaye, in this version, pushes back and says the *mishnah*'s point was that we need no concern whatsoever — not even where *savlonos* appear without any context — since the idea that *savlonos* indicate prior *kiddushin* is not self-evidently true, given that in some communities *savlonos* are sent before *kiddushin*.

### Practice Dependent

*Amar Rav Pappa* — the conclusion depends on local practice. *Be-asra demikadshi vehadar mesavli* — in a place where *kiddushin* comes first and *savlonos* follow, if we see *savlonos* being sent, *chassinan* — we are concerned that a *kiddushin* has taken place. *Mesavli vehadar mikadshi* — if the local practice is to send *savlonos* before *kiddushin*, *lo chassinan* — there is nothing to be concerned about.

### Kiddushin First Usually

The *gemara* notes that the ruling for the case where *kiddushin* typically precedes *savlonos* might seem self-evident — of course we are concerned. The ruling is therefore necessary for a more nuanced situation.

### Savlonos First Usually

If the practice is to send *savlonos* first, there is obviously no concern, since seeing *savlonos* tells us nothing about whether *kiddushin* has occurred.

### Majority Practice

The novelty of the ruling applies where the *majority* practice in a community is for *kiddushin* to precede *savlonos*, but a minority practice the reverse. One might have thought: this person sent *savlonos* and we know no *kiddushin* occurred — perhaps he is from the minority who do things in reverse order. The *gemara* rules that because of the weight of *eshes ish* — the gravity of a woman being considered a married woman — we do not attribute the *savlonos* to the minority practice. We follow the majority and are concerned that *kiddushin* already took place.

### Ketubah Writing

A parallel question is then asked: *hukhzak shtar kesuvah bashuk mahu* — if it becomes known that a *kesuvah* was written for a woman, does that indicate that *kiddushin* has already taken place? Rav Acha bar Rav Huna poses this question to Rava. The questioner wonders whether the writing of a *kesuvah* should be treated like the sending of *savlonos* — as evidence of a prior *kiddushin*. Rava responds with some skepticism: why should we simply assume, because a *kesuvah* was written, that *kiddushin* has occurred? Perhaps the *kesuvah* was written in preparation, and perhaps other explanations exist.

### Ketubah Practice

*Amar Rav Ashi* — again the answer depends on local practice. *Be-asra demikadshi vehadar kisvi kesuvah* — in a place where the standard practice is for *kiddushin* to occur before the *kesuvah* is written, and we hear that a *kesuvah* was written, *chassinan* — we are concerned that *kiddushin* has taken place. *Kasvi vehadar mikadshi* — in a place where the *kesuvah* is typically written before *kiddushin*, *lo chassinan*.

### Sofer Availability

The *gemara* notes that the ruling for the case where *kiddushin* typically precedes the writing of the *kesuvah* might again seem obvious. The ruling is necessary for a case where *delo shakhiakh safra* — a *sofer* is not readily available. One can imagine a perfectly reasonable scenario: a man intends to marry, has not yet performed *kiddushin*, but a *sofer* happens to be available now and may not be available for months. So he has the *kesuvah* written in advance. Surely, one might think, we should assume this is what happened rather than concluding that *kiddushin* has already occurred.

### Ashes Ish Concern

The *gemara* rules that this reasoning does not override the standard practice. Since the norm in that community is to write the *kesuvah* only after *kiddushin*, even the plausible scenario of an early *kesuvah* written for the sake of *sofer* availability does not remove the concern. Just as with *savlonos* — where we follow the majority practice and do not assume this person belongs to the minority that sends *savlonos* first — here too we follow the standard practice, and the concern that *kiddushin* has already taken place, with all the gravity of *eshes ish*, leads us to treat the situation accordingly until we can investigate further.

---

---

# Kiddushin 51

## Savlanot & Kiddushin

### Rav Huna Intro

The sugya opens on 51b, approximately fifteen lines from the top, with a teaching introduced by the formula *itmar*: Rav Huna said, *choshishin lesavlanot* — we are concerned that gifts sent after an engagement (*savlanot*) may constitute or indicate an act of *kiddushin*. This teaching must be understood against the backdrop of the preceding *mishnayot*, which dealt extensively with conditional *kiddushin* and the principle of *devarim shebalev einam devarim* — that unexpressed mental reservations do not legally alter what has transpired. The immediately preceding *mishnah* had established that when an original act of *kiddushin* was defective — worth less than a *perutah*, for instance — we do not reinterpret subsequent gifts as a new and valid *kiddushin*. Now, Rav Huna addresses a different scenario.

Rashi's formulation is precise: the case requires that there first be some engagement context — *mi sheshidach be'isha venitratzes*, a man courted a woman and she agreed — and then, *vekadam veshilach savlanot beyadayim*, he went ahead and sent these gifts. In this situation, where no prior defective *kiddushin* preceded the gifts, Rav Huna says we are concerned — *choshishin* — that the *savlanot* themselves may constitute or indicate *kiddushin*.

### Rashi v. Tosafot

There is a fundamental interpretive dispute between Rashi and Tosafot regarding the nature of this concern. According to Rashi, the question is whether the *savlanot* themselves function as an act of *kiddushin* — that is, the man may have intended them to serve as the formal act. According to Tosafot, that is not the question at all; rather, the concern is evidentiary: since it was customary to send such gifts only after *kiddushin* had taken place, the presence of *savlanot* may serve as evidence that a prior, valid *kiddushin* occurred, even if no one witnessed it. These two readings produce meaningfully different legal frameworks, and various passages in the *gemara* appear to support one or the other position.

### Rava & Abaye

Rava concurs with Rav Huna: *vechen amar Rava, choshishin lesavlanot*. But Rava immediately anticipates the obvious challenge from the *mishnah*, which states, *af al pi sheshilach savlanot acher mikan eina mekudeshet* — even if he sent *savlanot* after the fact, she is not married. Rava himself raises this and says we must ask about it: *amar Rava umosivinan ashmatin*.

Abaye resolves the tension: *hatam kedetani ta'ama, shemachmat kiddushin rishonim shilach* — in the *mishnah*'s case, the reason the *savlanot* are not *kiddushin* is that they came in the wake of a prior defective *kiddushin* which framed their meaning. The sender was relying on the original (flawed) act; the *savlanot* are understood as consequent to that first attempt. In our case, by contrast, no defective *kiddushin* preceded the gifts, and so either the gifts may signal a valid *kiddushin* took place or may themselves constitute one.

There is a second formulation in the *gemara* — *ika de'amri*, some say — in which Rava himself argues from the *mishnah*'s reasoning to support his own position. The *mishnah* specifies the rationale: *shemachmat kiddushin rishonim shilach*, the gifts were sent on account of the prior *kiddushin*. This implies that the only reason the *savlanot* are harmless in the *mishnah*'s case is because of that framing. But *ha b'almam hava kiddushin* — in a normal case without that framing, they would indeed constitute *kiddushin*. This version reads more congenially with Rashi's position, since it suggests the *savlanot* themselves become an act of *kiddushin* rather than merely serving as evidence of one.

In any event, the operative word throughout is *choshishin* — we are *concerned*, not *certain*. This is a *chashash*, not a definitive ruling. The practical implication is that such a woman would require a *get* as a precaution, but one would not, for example, treat intimacy with another man as definite adultery subject to the severest penalties.

### Cultural Context

The *gemara* then records: *mai havah alah* — what was the conclusion? Rav Pappa answers that the concern depends on local custom. *B'atra demikadshi vehadar mesabli* — in a place where the practice is to perform *kiddushin* first and only then to send gifts, *chashinan*, we are concerned. If the *savlanot* were sent and there was no known *kiddushin*, the cultural context tells us that such gifts are sent only after *kiddushin*, so their presence creates concern that a *kiddushin* occurred. By contrast, *misavli vehadar mikadshi* — in a place where gifts are sent before the *kiddushin* as the local custom — obviously the gifts create no concern; they are simply the customary pre-betrothal gifts.

The *gemara* adds a nuanced case: *lo tzericha deruba mikadshi vehadar misavli u'miuta misavli vehadar mikadshi* — what if most people in the community first perform *kiddushin* and then send gifts, but a minority does it in reverse? One might think to be lenient by ascribing this particular case to the minority practice. The *gemara* rejects this: since ninety percent of the community first does *kiddushin* and then sends gifts, when these gifts appear without a documented *kiddushin*, we follow the majority and are concerned.

This principle is worth pausing over. The *chashash* applies specifically because the *savlanot* belong to a category of gift that is culturally understood as given after *kiddushin*. This is what Rav Pappa is contributing. The point is not merely that he sent a gift in a general engagement context; it is that he sent a particular kind of gift that in this community is exclusively or predominantly associated with the post-*kiddushin* stage. Only in that specific cultural configuration does the concern arise.

One might wonder whether this applies to the modern engagement ring. As it happens, the engagement ring is paradigmatically *misavli vehadar mikadshi* — it is given before the *kiddushin*, not after it — so it would not raise this concern. The relevant scenario would have to involve a gift that in a given community is the customary token sent after an act of *kiddushin* has already occurred.

---

## Ketubah Evidence

### Ketubah Question

The *gemara* now records a query from Rav Acha bar Rav Huna to Rava: *huchzak shtar ketubah bashuk* — it became known in the marketplace that a *ketubah* had been written for a certain woman. *Mahu* — does this constitute evidence that *kiddushin* must have occurred?

Rashi explains the case as one where people saw the woman's *ketubah* document. The question is whether the existence of a known *ketubah* is sufficient grounds to treat the woman as *eshet ish*. Tosafot views this as the strongest proof for their reading of the entire *savlanot* discussion — this case is clearly about evidentiary inference rather than about the *ketubah* itself functioning as an act of *kiddushin*.

Rava responds sharply: *vechi mipnei shemachzik shtar ketubah bashuk nachzik ba k'eshet ish* — just because a *ketubah* is circulating in the marketplace, we are going to treat her as a married woman? The implication is that without further context, this alone would be insufficient. But the *gemara* then proceeds to explore what the actual conclusion was.

### Rav Ashi Answer

Rav Ashi provides the resolution, and the parallel to the *savlanot* discussion is unmistakable: *b'atar d'mikadshi vehadar katvi* — in a place where the custom is to perform *kiddushin* and only then to write the *ketubah*, *chashinan*. The presence of a written *ketubah* creates a concern that she is *mekudeshet*. *Katvi vehadar mikadshi* — where writing the *ketubah* precedes *kiddushin*, as is our practice today, *lo chashinan*. There is no concern.

The *gemara* presses: if it is obvious that in a place where *kiddushin* precedes *ketubah* writing we would be concerned, what is the *chiddush*? The answer: *lo tzericha d'lo shchiach safra* — the case concerns a place where scribes are not readily available. One might say: perhaps this man intended to marry in three months but happened to get the *ketubah* written now while the scribe was in town. *Mah d'teima safra hu d'isrami* — perhaps the scribe just happened to be available and so the *ketubah* was written early. The *gemara* rejects this reasoning: since the norm is that writing follows *kiddushin*, the presence of a written *ketubah* creates sufficient concern to treat the woman as a *safek mekudeshet*, even if there is a possible innocent explanation.

---

## Two Sisters Issue

### Mishna Rule

The *gemara* transitions to a new *mishnah*. *Ha-mekadesh isha u-vitah* — if a man attempts to betroth a woman and her daughter, *o isha ve-achotah* — or two sisters, *ke-achas* — simultaneously, *einan mekudashot* — neither is married. The scenario is that he gave the money to effect *kiddushin* on behalf of two women at once — perhaps through an agent who accepted on behalf of both — without having identified one as primary.

The *mishnah* then records: *ma'aseh be-chamesh nashim, u-va-hen shtei achayot* — there was a case involving five women, among them two sisters. A man picked a basket of figs, *ve-she-la-hen haytah* — which belonged to them, *ve-shel shevi'it haytah* — and it was *shemitah* produce (a detail we will revisit), *ve-amar harei kulchen mekudashot li be-kalkalah zo* — and he declared, "Behold, all of you are betrothed to me with this basket." One woman accepted the basket on behalf of all of them. *Ve-amru chachamim ein ha-achayot mekudashot* — the Sages ruled that the sisters are not married.

### Torah Source

*Menani mili* — from where is this rule derived? Rami bar Chama cites the verse: *isha el achotah lo tikach litzror legalot ervatah aleha be-chayeha* — "A woman to her sister you shall not take, to be a rival, to uncover her nakedness in her lifetime." Rami bar Chama reads this as establishing that at the very moment when they would become *tzarot* — rivals — the *kiddushin* cannot take effect even for one of them: *be-sha'at she-na'asu tzarot zo le-zo lo yiheye lecha likuchin afilu be-achas mehen*.

### Karet Problem

Rava challenges this derivation. The verse continues: *ve-nichretu ha-nefashot ha-osot mi-kerev amam* — those who do this are subject to *karet*. But *karet* for violating the prohibition of a sister's wife applies only if one is actually married to her sister first. If the *kiddushin* never takes effect for either sister, then there is no violation carrying *karet* — you have not married anyone. *Ei kiddushin lo tafsi bah, karet mi mechayav?* The verse must therefore be speaking of the sequential case: you married one sister, do not have relations with the other — and that would incur *karet*. The verse is not addressing simultaneous *kiddushin* at all.

### Rabba's Principle

Rava therefore concludes: *kra bezu achar zo* — the verse addresses the sequential case. So what is the source for the *mishnah*'s rule that simultaneous *kiddushin* of two sisters fails? *Umatnisin keRabbah* — the *mishnah* follows Rabbah's famous principle: *kol she'eino bezu achar zo, afilu bevat achas eino* — anything that cannot work sequentially cannot work simultaneously either.

The logic is elegant. If Reuven is married to Rachel and then attempts to betroth Leah (her sister), it would not take effect — the second *kiddushin* is prohibited because he is already married to the first sister. Therefore, when he attempts to do both at once, since there is no sequential ordering — no way to determine which is "first" and which is "second" — and since for whichever one is treated as "second" the *kiddushin* categorically cannot take effect, the result is that it takes effect for neither.

---

## Ma'aser Parallels

### Ma'aser Grain

Abaye challenges Rabbah's principle with a case from the laws of *ma'aser*. The *mishnah* teaches: *hamarbeh bema'aser, peirotsav metukkanim uma'asrotav mekulkalim* — if one separates more than the required tenth as *ma'aser*, his produce is rectified (*metukkan*) but his *ma'aser* is disqualified (*mekulkal*). The case: you have ten units of grain and you separate two units as *ma'aser*, when only one unit was required. One of those two units properly functions as *ma'aser* and fixes the nine remaining units; the other is merely grain from the *tevel* pile, and now the two units of designated *ma'aser* are a mixture of true *ma'aser* and *tevel*.

Abaye's challenge: just as with two sisters, you cannot take *ma'aser* sequentially from the same pile after you have already taken it — the second designation would not work. So when you take both units simultaneously, since one of them cannot function as *ma'aser*, why does the *mishnah* not say that neither does? Why not apply Rabbah's principle and say both units remain *tevel*?

### Ma'aser Solution

The *gemara* answers: *shani ma'aser d'ita l'chatzayim* — *ma'aser* is different because it can take effect on half of each grain. *D'ei amar tikadesh palga d'chitata, kadsha* — if one were to say that half of each grain kernel should be sanctified, that would work. Therefore, in the case of excess *ma'aser*, there is no need to conceptualize the two units as competing: one can instead understand all two hundred kernels (across both units) as having their *ma'aser* sanctity distributed across the whole — half of every single kernel, across the entire combined pile, is *ma'aser*. Since the sanctity can apply fractionally and uniformly to the whole, there is no question of "which unit is first and which is second." The entire pile is addressed simultaneously as a unified whole.

This is precisely what distinguishes it from the two sisters: you cannot say half of each sister is married to you. The *kiddushin* must attach to one specific person, and since you have not identified which one, and the sanctity cannot distribute fractionally, the paralysis of undetermined ordering means it takes effect for neither.

### Behema & Toda

The *gemara* then presses with *ma'aser behema* — the animal tithe. Unlike grain *ma'aser*, *ma'aser behema* cannot take effect on half an animal, *d'leita l'chatzayim*. And it also cannot work sequentially: once the tenth animal has been designated *ma'aser*, if an eleventh walks out, it is not *ma'aser*. So if two animals walk out of the gate simultaneously when the tenth was expected, and you call both of them "ten," why does the *gemara* say *asiri ve-achad asar me'uravin zeh be-zeh* — ten and eleven are mixed, meaning one is *ma'aser* and one is not, and we simply do not know which — rather than saying, by Rabbah's principle, neither is *ma'aser*?

The *gemara* answers: *shani ma'aser behema d'ita b'ta'ut* — *ma'aser behema* is different because it can take effect even through error. If you miscounted — calling the ninth animal "ten," or the tenth "nine," the eleventh "ten" — the *mishnah* teaches that all three nonetheless acquire *kedushah*. This is because to some degree *ma'aser behema* is defined by the objective fact of being the tenth animal, not entirely by the owner's conscious designation. Since the sanctity arises somewhat automatically, the fact that you erroneously called two animals "ten" does not eliminate it from both; one of them objectively is the tenth, and therefore *ma'aser behema* attaches to one of them — we simply cannot determine which.

This, too, distinguishes it from the two sisters. There, the *kiddushin* depends entirely on the person's intentional act and his identification of a specific woman; there is no objective fact of "being the tenth" that would cause *kiddushin* to take effect automatically on one of them despite the ambiguity.

### Toda Dispute

The *gemara* next considers the *korban toda* — the thanksgiving offering — accompanied by forty loaves. *D'leita b'ta'ut* — the *kedushah* of the loaves does not take effect through error; and *v'leisa b'zeh v'zeh* — once you have slaughtered the *toda* and sanctified forty loaves, additional loaves cannot become *kadosh*. So if someone slaughtered a *toda* with eighty loaves rather than forty, this should present the exact same challenge to Rabbah's principle: since the second forty cannot be sanctified once the first forty are done, and since both sets are presented simultaneously with no specified ordering, why should any forty be sanctified?

On this very question, *Chizkiyah* and Rabbi Yochanan dispute. Chizkiyah says: *kadshei lei arbaim mitoch shmonim* — forty of the eighty are sanctified; we simply do not know which forty. Rabbi Yochanan says: *lo kadshei lei arbaim mitoch shmonim* — none of them are sanctified. Rabbi Yochanan is consistent with Rabbah's principle; but Chizkiyah appears to contradict it. How do we explain Chizkiyah?

### Intent Resolution

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing cases based on the person's stated or implied intent. *Hakol modim* — everyone agrees that if the person explicitly said "forty of the eighty should be sanctified," *kadshi* — it works. He is not trying to sanctify all eighty; he specified forty, and forty are sanctified — we simply do not know which ones. Similarly, *lo yikdeshu arbaim ela im ken kadshi shmonim* — if he said "I will not sanctify forty unless it works for all eighty," everyone agrees it does not work, since it categorically cannot work for all eighty, and he conditioned the partial sanctification on the whole.

*Lo nechelku ela bistam* — the dispute between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan concerns only the ambiguous case, where the person said nothing explicit. *Mar savar l'achrayus ka mechaven* — Chizkiyah holds that we assume the person's underlying intent was to sanctify forty and have the other forty as backup, so forty are sanctified. *U'mar savar l'korban gadol ka mechaven* — Rabbi Yochanan holds we assume the person wanted to make an unusually large offering of all eighty, and since that cannot work, none are sanctified.

The upshot for our discussion is clear: the *toda* case does not refute Rabbah's principle in any straightforward way. Where intent is explicit and directed only at forty, everyone agrees forty are sanctified; where intent is directed at all eighty, everyone agrees none are. Only in the ambiguous case — *bistam* — do Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan part ways, and that debate concerns what presumption to apply when the person's mind is simply unknown. And crucially, the assumption of the two-sisters *mishnah* is that he intended both — so the case maps cleanly onto the position that neither is sanctified.

---

## Ayin Mesurin L'Biah

### Rava's Rationale

Having established Rabbah's principle as the basis for the *mishnah*'s ruling that simultaneous *kiddushin* of two sisters is invalid, the *gemara* now asks: *veRava lama lei leshnuyei keRabbah* — why did Rava need to explain the *mishnah* on the basis of Rabbah's principle at all? Rava himself holds a broader and more fundamental position — *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah* — that a *kiddushin* which cannot ultimately be consummated does not take effect at all. If that is Rava's general principle, then the *mishnah*'s case — where a man does not know which sister he has married and therefore can never permissibly have relations with either — should be invalid not because of the simultaneous nature of the attempt, but simply because any *kiddushin* that can never lead to *bi'ah* is not *kiddushin*.

*Lidvarav deRami bar Chama ka'amar* — the *gemara* answers that Rava was responding within the framework of Rami bar Chama's derivation. Rami bar Chama had attempted to derive the *mishnah*'s rule from a verse, and Rava showed that Rami's verse doesn't support the simultaneous case. Rava then supplied Rabbah's principle as the textual basis for the *mishnah* even according to those who might not accept his own principle of *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah*. In other words, Rava was arguing conditionally: even if you reject my general principle, you can still derive the *mishnah*'s ruling from Rabbah's principle. My own principle provides an additional and independent basis.

### Abaye v. Rava

The *gemara* now states the dispute directly. *Itmar: kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah* — a *kiddushin* that cannot be consummated. *Abaye amar: havi kiddushin* — Abaye holds it still takes legal effect. *Rava amar: lo havi kiddushin* — Rava holds it does not.

The paradigm case is the man who attempted *kiddushin* with one of two sisters without specifying which. Since he can never determine which one he married, and since having relations with either one risks violating the prohibition of *issurei arayot* — she might be his wife's sister, or he might be violating the prohibition by having relations with the non-married sister — his *kiddushin* can never permissibly translate into *bi'ah*. Rava says: this means no *kiddushin* took effect at all. Abaye disagrees: the *kiddushin* is in some sense real; we simply do not know to whom it applies, and both women require a *get*.

### Scriptural Basis

Rava grounds his position in a verse. *Rava bar Hina asbra li* — Bar Hina explained the derivation to me: *ki yikach ish isha u'be'alah* — "When a man takes a woman and has relations with her." The verse juxtaposes *yikach* (taking/betrothal) with *u'be'alah* (consummation), implying that a valid *kiddushin* must be one capable of leading to *bi'ah*: *kiddushin hamesurin l'biah havu kiddushin* — only a *kiddushin* that is "given over" to *bi'ah* constitutes *kiddushin*. *Kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah, lo havu kiddushin*.

### Tosafot Nuance

Tosafot raises an obvious difficulty with Rava's principle: according to Rava, should *kiddushin* in cases of *issurei lavin* — prohibitions carrying lashes rather than *karet*, such as a *kohen* marrying a *grushah* or a *kohen gadol* marrying a *widow* — not also fail, since these unions cannot be permissibly consummated? Yet the *gemara* elsewhere is clear that such *kiddushin* takes effect.

To resolve this, Tosafot refines the principle. The operative category of *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah* is not simply any *kiddushin* where *bi'ah* happens to be prohibited. Rather, it is specifically a case where it is the act of *kiddushin itself* that creates the *issur bi'ah*. In the case of two sisters: before any *kiddushin* occurs, there is no prohibition on having relations with either woman. It is only because he performed (or attempted) *kiddushin* with one of them that the other becomes prohibited as his wife's sister. The *kiddushin* generates the very *issur* that makes consummation impossible.

By contrast, in the case of a *kohen* and a *grushah*, the *issur* preexists and is independent of the *kiddushin*. The woman's status as a *grushah* was established before he ever betrothed her; his act of *kiddushin* did not create the prohibition. In such cases, the *kiddushin* takes effect despite the prohibition.

This also clarifies a distinct scenario: suppose a woman might be a man's sister but it cannot be determined — perhaps because her mother's relationship history is unknown. If he were to perform *kiddushin* with her, would that be a *safek kiddushin* or null *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah*? According to Rashi's broader reading, it might be categorized as *einam mesurin l'biah* since he can never permissibly have relations with her. According to Tosafot's refinement, it would be a *safek kiddushin* — because the prohibition on his potential sister preexists and is wholly independent of his act of *kiddushin*. His betrothal did not create the *issur*; it was always there. Therefore Tosafot's principle does not apply, and she would be *safek mekudeshet*.

---

## Five Women Story

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now tests Rava's principle against the *mishnah* itself. *Tnan: hamkadesh isha u'vitah o isha v'achotah k'achat, einan mekudashot* — both are not married. The *mishnah* implies: *ha achat* — if he married only one, without specifying which, she would be *mekudeshet*. But this seems to contradict Rava directly: such a *kiddushin* cannot lead to *bi'ah* and should therefore be null. *Tiufta d'Rava* — this is a decisive refutation of Rava's position.

The *mishnah*'s concluding case involves five women including two sisters, a basket of figs, *shemitah* produce, and the declaration *harei kulchen mekudashot li be-kalkalah zo* — "All of you are betrothed to me with this basket," accepted by one woman on behalf of all. The Sages ruled that the sisters are not married — implying the other three are.

### Rava's Reading

Rava responds: *v'letameich eima seifa* — let us examine the end of the *mishnah* carefully. The case in which the three non-sisters are *safek mekudashot* is the *mishnah*'s conclusion. But if we take the declaration at face value — *harei kulchen*, all five of you — then this is the case of *at v'chamor lo kana*: if one attempts to transfer ownership jointly to a valid recipient and an invalid one (classically, a person and a fetus not yet born), the entire transaction fails for the valid recipient as well, since the package cannot be divided. Similarly here, if he tried to marry all five and it failed for two of them, why would it work for the other three?

Therefore, Rava argues, the *mishnah*'s end-case must be read as *d'amar lehu achat mikem* — he said "one of you," not "all five of you." He was attempting to betroth one unspecified woman from the group of five. In that case, three of the five could be *safek mekudashot* — any one of the three non-sisters might be the intended bride — while neither sister qualifies.

### Position Logic

This reading creates an asymmetry between the beginning and end of the *mishnah*. *L'Rava kashya reisha* — for Rava, the beginning of the *mishnah* is difficult: it says *ke-achas*, at the same time, implying the problem is the simultaneity.
