But according to Rava, even attempting *kiddushin* with one unspecified sister — without simultaneity — should also fail, since it would be *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah*. The beginning of the *mishnah* seems to identify the *ke-achas* as the operative defect.

*V'l'Abaye kashya seifa* — for Abaye, the end of the *mishnah* is difficult. Reading the end as "one of you," Abaye must explain why neither sister would be married even in that case, since according to Abaye, *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah* does take effect — the sisters should at least be *safek mekudashot*.

### Abaye's Reading

*Abaye metaretz l'taameih, Rava metaretz l'taameih* — each resolves the other's difficulty according to his own position. Abaye explains the *mishnah* as follows: *hamkadesh isha u'vitah o isha v'achotah k'achat, einan mekudashot* — only if he attempted to marry both at once do neither become married. *Achat me'isha u'vitah o me'isha v'achotah, mekudeshet* — if he attempted to marry only one, without specifying which, she is in principle *mekudeshet* (as a *safek*). However, *ve'im amar hara'uya l'vi'ah titkadesh li* — if he explicitly stipulated that the one who is permissible to him should be betrothed, then *eina mekudeshet*, since there is no way to know who qualifies, and this *kiddushin she'eino masur l'vi'ah, d'hava lei kiddushin she'eino masur l'vi'ah*.

For the five women case, Abaye reads the man's statement as implicitly including *hara'uya li mikem titkadesh li* — one of you who is fit for me should be betrothed to me. Since the sisters are not "fit" for him in the sense that there is no *bi'ah* possible, they are excluded, and the ruling that they are not married is explained. This reading is something Abaye inserts into the text because Rava's reading of the *mishnah* forced the case into the "one of you" framework — Abaye simply adds the further specification.

Rava, in turn, explains the beginning of the *mishnah*: *hamkadesh achat me'isha u'vitah o achat me'isha v'achotah, na'aseh k'mi shekidesh isha u'vitah v'isha v'achotah k'achat* — attempting to betroth one unspecified member of a forbidden pair is legally equivalent to attempting to betroth both simultaneously. Even though in reality he only tried to betroth one, the indeterminacy makes it as if he tried to betroth both at once, and therefore neither is married.

---

## Unspecified Daughter

### Baraita Rule

The *gemara* brings a further challenge to Rava from a *baraita*: *hamkadesh et bito stam* — if a man betroths off "my daughter" without specifying which daughter. *Eina bogeres bichlal* — his adult daughters are obviously not included, since a father has no legal authority to betroth an adult daughter on her behalf. *Haketanot bichlal* — the minor daughters, however, are included; the *baraita* implies that one of the minor daughters is *safek mekudeshet*.

This is a direct challenge to Rava. If there are multiple minor daughters and the father did not specify which one he was marrying off, this is structurally identical to the two-sisters case: *kiddushin she'ein mesurin l'vi'ah ninhu* — the groom can never know which daughter he married, and therefore can never permissibly have relations with any of them. *U'visyufta deRava* — this appears to be a decisive refutation of Rava.

### Rava's Limit

Rava responds: *hacha bemai askinan keshein sham ela gedola u'ktana* — the *baraita* addresses a case where there is only one adult daughter and one minor daughter. In that scenario, it is obvious that the *kiddushin* was accepted for the minor daughter, since the father has no authority over the adult. There is no ambiguity whatsoever; the groom knows exactly whom he married. This is entirely unlike the two-sisters case.

The *gemara* challenges: the *baraita* uses the plural *bogeros* and *ketanot*, implying multiple daughters of each type. Rava deflects: *mai bogeros bogeros de'alma* — the plural "adult daughters" is a general formulation referring to the category of adult daughters that any person might have, not to this particular father having many adult daughters. In this case, we read it as: his one adult daughter is excluded, and his one minor daughter is the one who is *safek mekudeshet*. The *gemara* then asks, *ei hachi mai lemimra* — if there is only one minor daughter, what is the *chiddush*? It is entirely obvious.

### Shaliach Scenario

The *gemara* suggests a more nuanced reading: *hacha bemai askinan deshavisa shaliach* — the *baraita* addresses a case where the adult daughter had appointed her father as her *shaliach*, her agent, to arrange her *kiddushin*. In that case, one might think the father would betroth off the adult daughter first: after all, he is acting as her *shaliach*, and perhaps his acceptance of the *kiddushin* was on her behalf. The ambiguity is real — was this the minor daughter (his primary charge) or the adult daughter (whose *shaliach* he is)? *Mahu d'teima ki mekabel kiddushin adaita dideihu ka mekabel* — one might think he accepted the *kiddushin* with the adult daughter in mind, since she is older and the pressure to see her settled is perhaps greater.

### Priority Rule

*Ka mashma lan dela shavik inish midi de'is lei hana'ah minei* — the *baraita* teaches us that a man does not set aside something from which he derives benefit in order to do something else first. The father benefits financially from the *kiddushin* of the minor daughter — the *kesef kiddushin* goes to him in that case. He would therefore not prioritize the adult daughter's *kiddushin*, from which he receives no such benefit, over the minor daughter's.

The *gemara* then considers: what if the adult daughter said, "Father, you may keep the *kiddushin* money for yourself"? *Mahu d'teima ki mekabel kiddushin adaita dideihu ka mekabel* — perhaps even then he might betroth the adult daughter first. The *gemara* rejects this: *afilu hachi lo shavik inish mitzvah deramya alei ve'avid mitzvah dela ramya alei* — even so, a person does not set aside a *mitzvah* that is incumbent upon him and perform instead one that is not. The father bears a primary obligatory *mitzvah* to marry off his minor daughters; for his adult daughter, any help he provides is supererogatory. He would therefore always marry off the minor daughter first. The result is that the *baraita* does not challenge Rava — and the debate between Abaye and Rava over *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'biah* will continue into the next session.

---

---

# Kiddushin 52

## Rava's Position

### Rava's Principle

The sugya continues from where we left off on 51b, in the middle of Rava's position regarding *kiddushin she'eina mesura l'via* — a betrothal that cannot ultimately lead to consummation. Although *kiddushin* ordinarily precedes *nisuin* by a considerable period, Rava holds that if the *kiddushin* can never translate into a permissible marital relationship, it is not a valid *kiddushin* to begin with.

A clarification is necessary at the outset. As Tosafos already notes, there are prohibited relationships — *isurei lavin*, such as a *kohen* marrying a *gerusha* — where the couple is forbidden from having relations, yet the *kiddushin* takes effect regardless. Rava's principle is confined to *isurei kareis*: if the relationship would carry the penalty of *kareis*, everyone agrees the *kiddushin* does not take effect at all. The contested terrain is the case where the *kiddushin* itself would be valid but uncertainty about the identity of the woman makes consummation perpetually impossible.

### Two Sisters Case

The paradigmatic example is a man who betroths one of two sisters without knowing which one he has married. Rava's contention is that in such a case, neither woman requires a *get mi'safek*. Since he can never have relations with either — doing so might mean sleeping with his wife's sister — the *kiddushin* is fundamentally defective. The doubt itself prevents the *kiddushin she'eina mesura l'via* from ever taking effect.

### Abaye's View

Abaye disagrees with Rava's position. Thus far, the evidence presented in the sugya has consistently cut against Rava, though Rava has managed to respond to each textual challenge. The Gemara now continues pressing the point.

---

## Mi Sheyeish Lo

### Scenario Setup

The Gemara introduces a *braisa*: *mi sheyeish lo shtei kitei banot mi'shtei nashim* — a man who has two sets of daughters from two wives, each wife having borne him multiple daughters. The man declares that he married his older daughter — *kidashti et biti hagdola* — to a particular man, but he cannot remember which daughter he meant. Several possibilities present themselves: he may have meant the oldest among the children from his first wife, or the older one from his second wife's children, or even a younger daughter from the first wife who is nonetheless older than the oldest daughter of the second wife.

### Get Requirements

The ruling — this is the position of Rabbi Meir — is that *kulan asurot*: all of these daughters are potentially married to this man and require a *get*, with the single exception of the youngest daughter of the second wife, *katanat sheba-ktanot*, whom the father could not possibly have meant when he said "my older daughter."

This case seems to pose a strong challenge to Rava. Here is a situation precisely analogous to marrying one of two sisters — the *choson* cannot have relations with any of the daughters because whichever one is truly his wife, the others are potentially her sisters. Yet the *kiddushin* is treated as taking effect *mi'safek*. If Rava were correct, none of them should require a *get* at all.

### Initial Knowledge

The Gemara deflects the proof: *hacha b'mai askinan — keshehukru u'levasof nisarvu*. The case is not one where the father never knew which daughter he intended. Rather, at the moment of *kiddushin* he knew precisely which daughter he had in mind, and only afterward did he forget. The *kiddushin* therefore took effect validly at the moment it was performed — when it was *mesura l'via* — and the subsequent confusion does not retroactively undo it.

### Linguistic Proof

The Gemara adds a textual confirmation: *deika nami d'katani eini yodea* — the *braisa* uses the first-person "I do not know," meaning the father currently does not know, rather than the impersonal *eino yaduia*, "it is not known" — which would indicate it was never known. This linguistic precision supports the interpretation that knowledge existed initially and was subsequently lost.

### Rabbi Yose Contrast

But if so, the Gemara asks, what is the *chiddush* of the *braisa*? If the father once knew and merely forgot, it seems obvious that all the daughters would require a *get*. The Gemara answers: *le'apokei mid'bei Rabbi Yose*. The *chiddush* is that Rabbi Meir disagrees with Rabbi Yose's position.

### Allowing Doubt

Rabbi Yose would reason that if a person says "my older daughter" and that is the only detail he can recall, we assume he meant it in the most unambiguous sense — the oldest of all his daughters. The reasoning is *lo machis inish nafshei li'sefeika*: a person does not allow himself to enter into such a state of doubt. If "older daughter" were ambiguous in your own mind, you would have been more precise in your formulation so you could remember. The very fact that you remember only "older daughter" implies you meant it to refer to one clearly identifiable person.

Rabbi Meir rejects this assumption. *Ka mashma lan demachis inish nafshei li'sefeika* — people do in fact allow themselves to use loose formulations and wind up in precisely this kind of doubt. Therefore, all the daughters remain candidates, and all require a *get* save the youngest of the youngest. That is the *chiddush*.

---

## One of Two Sisters

### Marriage Scenario

The Gemara presents another challenge: *mi shekidesh achas mi'shtei achayot v'eino yodeia eizeh kidesh* — a man married one of two sisters but does not know which one he married. Again, we are invited to read this as a case where he never knew, which would make it a direct refutation of Rava.

### Get Solution

The ruling is *nosein get lazo v'get lazo* — he must give a *get* to each sister, since each one is in a state of *safek* betrothal to him. This appears once more to demonstrate that *kiddushin she'eina mesura l'via* takes effect.

### Knew Then Forgot

The Gemara again deflects: *hacha b'mai askinan — keshehukru levasof v'nisrefu*. Once more, the case involves a situation where the identity was known at the outset and subsequently forgotten. The linguistic indicator is the same: *eini yodea* rather than *eino yaduia*.

The Gemara then asks again: if that is so, what is the *chiddush*? The answer is: *seifa itzterichah lei* — the *braisa* is needed for what follows, namely the complex laws of *chalitza* and *yibum* that arise if the husband dies without the confusion having been resolved.

---

## Yibum/Chalitza

### Death Case

The *braisa* continues: if this man — who was married *mi'safek* to one of two sisters — dies, and he has one surviving brother, that brother must perform *chalitza* with both women, since one of them is his brother's widow and requires either *yibum* or *chalitza*.

### Multiple Brothers

If there were two brothers, the ruling is *echad choleitz v'echad miyabeim* — one brother performs *chalitza* and the other may perform *yibum*. Furthermore, if they both already went ahead and married both sisters — *im kadmu v'kanesu* — we do not remove them from the marriage.

### Achot Zekukato

Why can a single brother not simply perform *yibum* with one of the sisters directly, without first performing *chalitza* for the other? Because before *chalitza* is performed, both brothers maintain a *zikah* — a levirate bond — to both women. If a brother were to perform *yibum* with one sister while that *zikah* remains intact, he might be marrying *achot zekukato* — the sister of a woman to whom he is already quasi-bonded. That is prohibited.

The mechanics of two brothers work as follows. Suppose brother A performs *chalitza* for sister 1. This removes the *zikah* that both brothers held toward her. Brother B, who did not himself perform the *chalitza*, has no *achot chalutzato* issue. He is therefore free to perform *yibum* with sister 2. Since it was brother A who did the *chalitza*, sister 1 is *achot chalutzato* only with respect to brother A — not to brother B. Brother B's *yibum* with sister 2 is therefore unproblematic.

If, however, the brothers had not first done *chalitza* and both simply proceeded to marry the two sisters — *kinsu* — the fact that *achot zekukato* is only a *d'rabbanan* prohibition, combined with the fact that the *zikah* dissipates once the marriages are performed, means we allow the marriages to stand after the fact.

### Already Married

The principle established is: once they are already married, *ein motzi'in osam mi'yadam* — we do not remove them from their marriages.

### Proper Sequence

The proper sequence is therefore explicit: *davka michlatz v'hadar yabumi* — specifically, *chalitza* must precede *yibum*. If one brother does *yibum* first and only then the other does *chalitza*, it does not work, *d'ka paga b'achot zekukato* — because the brother doing *yibum* before the *chalitza* was performed would be engaging with the sister of a woman to whom he still has a *zikah*. This is the genuine *chiddush* of the passage — a *halacha* in the laws of *yibum*, not a ruling about *kiddushin she'eina mesura l'via*.

---

## Two Men Two Sisters

### Mixed Marriage

The Gemara moves to yet another challenge: *shnayim shekidshu shtei achayot v'zeh eino yodeia eizo kiddesh v'zeh eino yodeia eizo kiddesh* — two men, who are not brothers, each married one of two sisters. Each man married one sister and each does not know which sister he married. Once again, the assumption is that this means the men never knew.

### Get Distribution

The ruling is that each man must give a *get* to both women. Man A might be married to Rachel or to Leah, so he must give a *get* to each. Similarly for Man B. Rachel and Leah cannot remarry until they have received a *get* from each man, since either one might be married to either man. Each man thus gives two *gittin*, one to each of the two women.

Once more the Gemara answers that this too is a case of *keshehukru levasof v'nisarvu* — initially known, subsequently forgotten. The *seifa itzterichah lei* — and the real novelty of the ruling emerges in the more complex scenarios that follow.

### Unequal Brothers

If both men die, and each leaves a surviving brother, each brother must perform *chalitza* for both women. But the *braisa* then introduces an asymmetric case: one man left one brother, and the other left two brothers. The single brother — let us call him B' — performs *chalitza* for both women and thereby removes himself entirely from the scene. Only once B' has stepped off entirely are the two brothers of the other man — A' and A'' — in a position analogous to the earlier case of two brothers with two sisters: one performs *chalitza* and one performs *yibum*.

### Sequence Req.

The sequence is critical. B' must first perform *chalitza* for both women before A' and A'' can proceed with their *chalitza* and *yibum*. If A' and A'' were to act before B' performed his *chalitza*, one of the two women would be a *yevamah* — a levirate widow obligated to either B' — who has not yet released her. Marrying her before that *chalitza* is performed constitutes the prohibition of *yevamah la'shuk* — a levirate widow going out into the marketplace. Only after B' has performed *chalitza* for both women can the remaining two brothers proceed.

Once again, the Gemara notes: *aval yabumei v'hadar michlatz lo* — if the two brothers of the first man were to perform *yibum* and *chalitza* before B' removes himself, it would not work, *d'ka paga b'yevamah la'shuk* — because one of these women is still awaiting her *chalitza* from B'. The *halacha* being taught here is the required sequence in a complex *yibum* case — not a ruling about *kiddushin she'eina mesura l'via*.

---

## Five/Five Case

### Non-Specific Marriage

The Gemara now arrives at what it treats as decisive. It cites a teaching of *Tiviumi*: one man has five sons, another has five daughters. The father of the sons declares: *achas mi'bnotecha mekudeshet l'echad mi'banai* — one of your daughters is married to one of my sons.

### Get Requirements

The ruling: *kol achas v'achas tzrichah chamishah gittin* — each of the five daughters requires five *gittin*, one from each of the five sons. Since no one knows which daughter was married to which son, every daughter is in a state of *safek* betrothal to every son.

### Death Adjustment

If one of the sons dies, each daughter now requires four *gittin* from the surviving sons and *chalitza* from one of them — since she might have been betrothed to the deceased son, triggering levirate obligation. Crucially, she does not need *chalitza* from all four surviving brothers — any one brother performing *chalitza* suffices. One brother thus both gives a *get* (as he might be her husband) and performs *chalitza* (as he might be her deceased brother-in-law's *yavam*).

### Non-Specific Language

What makes this case decisive is the precise language of the declaration: *achas mi'bnotecha l'echad mi'banai* — one of your daughters to one of my sons. The statement is non-specific from the outset. There is no question of "initially knew and then forgot." The marriage was constituted in entirely unspecified terms — and it takes effect. This directly refutes Rava: even *kiddushin she'eina mesura l'via*, formed when the identity of the parties was never specified and consummation could never take place with any particular woman, is nonetheless valid.

### Rava Refuted

The Gemara declares: *tiyuvta d'Rava tiyuvta* — Rava is definitively refuted. As a general rule in *Shas*, the formulation *tiyuvta d'peloni tiyuvta* signals a complete rejection of that position and a ruling against it. Only on rare occasions does the Gemara say *tiyuvta v'hilchasa* — a refutation followed nonetheless by a ruling in keeping with the refuted position — and that itself prompts the Gemara to ask how such a thing can be. Here, the rejection is unambiguous.

### YAL KGAM Acronym

The Gemara then states: *v'hilchata k'vosei d'Abaye b'Ya'al Kegam* — although we generally rule like Rava in disputes with Abaye, there are six cases where we rule like Abaye, and they are encoded in the acronym *Ya'al Kegam*.

The *yud* stands for *yeiush shelo mi'da'as* — the question treated in the second chapter of Bava Metzia of whether giving up hope of recovering a lost object, had the owner known it was lost, constitutes valid *yeiush* even if he did not consciously despair. The *ayin* stands for *eid zomem* — whether a witness who is rendered a *zomem* is disqualified retroactively from the time he gave his testimony, not merely from the time the counter-witnesses testified against him. The *lamed*, though there is some debate about this position, stands for *lechi ha'omed mei'eilav*. The *kuf* — the case before us — stands for *kiddushin she'eina mesura l'via*: we follow Abaye that such a *kiddushin* takes effect. The *gimmel* stands for *gilluy da'as b'get*, the question of whether implicit indications of intent are operative even without explicit statement — a matter discussed in the context of *gittin* and the principle of *devarim she'belev*. The *mem* stands for *mumar ochel neveilot l'tei'avon* — whether someone who transgresses a particular prohibition due to *yetzer hara* rather than as an ideological rejection of *halacha* is disqualified as a witness. That is Rashi's account of the six; Tosafos offers a slightly different list.

It is worth noting, as Tosafos observes at the conclusion of his discussion of *Ya'al Kegam*, that there are other cases where the ruling follows Abaye against Rava — such as *techilaso bi'fshia v'sofo b'ones* — that are not included in the acronym. Tosafos resolves this by citing the *Halachos Gedolos*, who suggests that the *hilchata* ruling in that case was not part of the original text of the Gemara but was appended by the *Rabbanan Savorai* or the *Geonim* after the *chatimas ha'Shas*. This is a broader phenomenon: certain *hilchata* rulings that appear embedded in the Aramaic of the Gemara were actually added by post-*siyum* editors whose glosses were subsequently absorbed into the received text. The fact that some rulings following Abaye are not in *Ya'al Kegam* is thus explained as those rulings having been formulated after the original editing of the Talmud.

One final structural observation: the father of the five daughters could marry off his daughters to one of the five sons because he has the legal right to betroth his daughters. But the father of the five sons — what authorizes him to participate? One must say that each son appointed his father as his *shliach*: whichever woman you choose for me, I accept.

---

## Five Women/Figs

### Marriage Scenario

The Gemara now returns to the *ma'aseh* — the incident involving five women and the basket of figs that opens the mishnah. A man took figs and used them to attempt to betroth all five women simultaneously, with two sisters among the group. Rav declares: *shema mina mimatnisin arba* — our mishnah teaches four *halachos*. However, he adds: *v'nakad Rav b'yadei tlas* — he only has clear rulings for three of them, because the mishnah's teaching regarding the fourth remains ambiguous to him.

### Shemita Works

The first *halacha*: *hamekadesh b'peiros shevi'is mekudeshes* — betrothal effected with the fruit of *shemita* is valid. The *chiddush*, as Rashi explains, lies in the prohibition against conducting business with *shemita* produce — *v'hayesa shabbat ha'aretz lachem le'ochla*, the Torah specifies the fruit is for eating. One might have thought that using *shemita* fruit as the medium of a transaction renders the *kiddushin* invalid, or that it constitutes prohibited commerce. The mishnah teaches that even so, the transaction is effective, and this use does not carry the characteristics of prohibited *s'chorah* with *shemita* fruit.

### No Stolen Goods

The second *halacha*: *kidsha b'gezel eina mekudeshes* — betrothal with stolen property does not take effect. Since the man picked the women's figs and returned them as the medium of *kiddushin*, the only reason it worked was that it was *shemita* — when the fruit was *hefker* and he was legally entitled to take it. Had it not been *shemita*, returning their own figs to them would not have constituted valid *kesef kiddushin*, even though he stole the goods from the very women he wished to marry.

### Woman as Agent

The third *halacha*: *ishah na'asis shliach la'chaverta* — a woman can serve as an agent for another woman to receive *kesef kiddushin* on her behalf, *afilu b'makom shena'asis lah tzara* — even in a case where the agency results in the woman becoming her co-wife. One might have thought that implicit consent to serve as *shliach* could not be assumed in such a circumstance, particularly since the woman accepted the *kiddushin* for herself at the same time without explicitly declaring herself an agent for the others. The mishnah teaches that she does serve as their agent nonetheless.

### Ambiguous Position

The fourth matter: the mishnah presumably has something to say about *kiddushin she'eino masur l'via*, since two of the women were sisters. However, Rav cannot determine what the mishnah is teaching on this point because the case admits two readings. If the man was attempting to marry both sisters simultaneously, then the mishnah's ruling that they are not married reflects the straightforward prohibition against marrying two sisters — not any principle about *kiddushin she'eino masur l'via*. In that reading, the mishnah would imply that ordinary *kiddushin she'eino masur l'via* — where only one sister was intended — would in fact work, consistent with Abaye. Alternatively, if the man was attempting to marry each sister separately without knowing which was which, then the sisters being unmarried would support Rava's position. Because the mishnah is susceptible to both readings, Rav cannot extract a clear ruling from it about *kiddushin she'eino masur l'via*.

### Rav's Inference

What Rav does extract — and what he presents as the mishnah's clear teaching — are the three *halachos* above. The fourth point remains, as far as Rav is concerned, unresolved.

---

## Gezel in Kiddushin

### R. Yochanan

When Rabbi Zeira ascended to *Eretz Yisrael* and related this discussion to Rabbi Yochanan — the inference that Rav drew from the mishnah about *gezel* — Rabbi Yochanan responded with evident interest: *mi amar Rav haki*? Did Rav really say this? The Gemara initially reads this as an expression of surprise that Rabbi Yochanan seemingly agrees. Rabbi Yochanan's own position is: *gazel v'lo ni'yashu ha'be'alim — shneihem einam yecholim l'hakdish* — if an object was stolen and the owners have not yet despaired of its recovery, neither the thief nor the owner can sanctify it.

The thief cannot sanctify it because it is not his. The owner cannot sanctify it — and here is the genuine *chiddush* of Rabbi Yochanan — because even though the owner retains legal title, the object is no longer under his control, and one cannot perform acts of sanctification over an object that is not in one's domain. By analogy, one cannot use an object to betroth a woman if one does not own it.

### Braita Proof

But the Gemara raises a challenge from a *braisa*: *kidsha b'gazel, b'chamas u'vigniva, o shechataph sela mi'yadah v'kidshah — mekudeshes* — if one betrothed a woman with stolen goods, with extorted money, or seized a coin from her hand and used it to betroth her, the betrothal is valid. This seems to directly contradict the principle that *kiddushin* with stolen property does not work.

### Stolen from Her

The Gemara resolves: *hasam b'gezel deidah* — that case involves property stolen from the woman herself. The reasoning is that when she accepts the object back from the thief in the context of a declaration of *kiddushin*, we interpret her acceptance as a waiver — she is *mochelet* the object to him, allowing him to use it as *kesef kiddushin*.

### Implicit Willingness

The Gemara then examines this resolution more carefully. From the *braisa* itself, it appears that the opening clause — *kidsha b'gazel, b'chamas u'vigniva* — is stated in general terms, without specifying that the stolen goods belonged to the woman. Does this not indicate that even generically stolen goods can effect *kiddushin*? The Gemara answers: *perushei ka mefareish* — the end of the *braisa* is not adding a new case; it is explaining the opening clause. The meaning is: what kind of stolen goods are we speaking of? The case where he seized a coin from her own hand. Generic stolen goods from a third party do not work.

### Intent Distinction

The Gemara now notes a remaining difficulty: our mishnah with the figs, as Rav interpreted it, establishes that even returning stolen goods from the woman herself does not effect *kiddushin* — the figs worked only because it was *shemita* and they were *hefker*. How then can the *braisa* say that seizing her coin and using it for *kiddushin* works? The answer: *ha d'shaddikh v'ha d'la shaddikh* — the distinction depends on whether *shidduchim*, a prior engagement process, had taken place. If the *kiddushin* is being performed in the context of an established betrothal arrangement, the woman's acceptance of her own goods back can be construed as an implicit waiver — she intends to let him have them so he can use them for the *kiddushin*. Without that prior context, the most natural reading of her taking back the coin is that she merely wants her property returned; there is no basis for inferring that she is extending a waiver. The mishnah's case of the figs took place without any such prior arrangement, which is why it would not have worked absent *shemita*.

---

## Ownership Disputes

### Woman Bathing

The Gemara now presents a series of practical cases testing the boundaries of *kiddushin* effected with another's property. In the first: a woman was washing her feet in a basin of water. A man came, seized a coin from someone else's hand, and threw it to her, declaring *mekudeshes li* — be married to me. The case came before Rava.

Rava ruled: *leis d'chash lah l'ha d'Rabbi Shimon* — we do not rule in accordance with Rabbi Shimon's position that ordinary *gezeila* — brazen robbery committed openly — creates a presumption of *yeiush ba'alim*, that the owners have despaired of recovering the stolen property. Rabbi Shimon's reasoning would be that the bold, public nature of the theft signals to the victim that recovery is hopeless, and thus *yeiush* is presumed. If *yeiush* had occurred, and the coin then passed to the woman — constituting *shinui reshuyot*, a change of domain — the combination of *yeiush* and *shinui reshuyot* might in principle allow the transaction to take effect, since the woman would acquire the coin cleanly and could not be required to return it.

The logic deserves elaboration: if there is *yeiush* followed by *shinui reshuyot*, the original owner's claim against the woman lapses, even though the thief still owes him compensation. In that case, the woman would be holding a coin she lawfully possesses, and the *kiddushin* might be valid. But since we do not follow Rabbi Shimon's presumption of *yeiush* in cases of *gezeila*, we cannot assume *yeiush* occurred, the coin remains fully stolen property, and the *kiddushin* does not take effect.

### Sharecropper

In the second case: a sharecropper betrothed a woman with a bundle of onions taken from the owner's field before the crop had been formally divided. He came before Rava. Rava said to him: *man achlah lach* — who was *mochel* to you, who permitted you to do this? The onions were not yet the sharecropper's to give. Although he would eventually be entitled to a percentage of the crop, that entitlement only crystallizes at the time of division.

### Bundled Crops

However, the Gemara qualifies this ruling: *v'hanei milei b'muza* — this applies only when the sharecropper took a random handful. If the produce had already been made into bundles — *kisha* — then one can say: *ana shakilna kisha, shakul at kisha* — I'll take one bundle, you take one bundle. Where produce has been gathered into units that lend themselves naturally to division, the sharecropper may perform an impromptu mini-division on the spot, taking one bundle as his share. That is regarded as a legally operative preliminary division rather than unauthorized taking. But to grab a handful before any such bundling has occurred is simply stealing from the owner's undivided crop.

### Beer Vessel

The third case: a beer-maker — someone who received dates from an owner, fermented them into beer, and was entitled to a portion of the proceeds — betrothed a woman with a vessel belonging to the owner, which had been used for storing the beer and had absorbed its flavoring. The owner of the beer came, found him, and said: why did you give from that vessel? You should have given from a better one — apparently the more saturated vessels were more prized. The question was whether the owner's comment could be construed as retroactive consent to the act.

Rava ruled: *lo amru k'lach etzel yafot ela bi'truma bilvad* — the principle that saying "you should have taken the better ones" signals consent applies only in the context of *truma*, not here.

### Terumah Parallel

The operative *braisa*: if someone entered another person's field without permission and separated *truma* from the produce — *taram shelo bi'reshut* — when does the *truma* take effect? If the owner is distressed by it, treating it as theft, the *truma* is invalid. If not, it is valid. How do we determine his attitude? If the owner arrives, finds the situation, and says *k'lach etzel yafot* — you should have taken from the better produce — and there genuinely is better produce available, we take the statement at face value: he is indicating that he would have wanted better *truma* taken on his behalf, and this signals acceptance. If there is no better produce, the comment is read as biting sarcasm — his way of expressing displeasure at having his best grain consecrated without his consent — and the *truma* is invalid. And if the owner himself joins in the harvesting alongside the agent, the *truma* is valid regardless.

### Terumah vs. Kiddushin

Why does the "you should have taken the better ones" principle apply to *truma* but not to *kiddushin* with the owner's vessel? Because in the case of *truma*, the owner has an independent obligation to separate *truma* from his grain. When he speaks approvingly of what was done — provided the words can be read as genuine — we interpret them as indicating he ratifies the act, since it discharges an obligation he was in any event required to fulfill. By contrast, in the *kiddushin* case, no one obligated the beer-maker to use the owner's vessel to betroth a woman. Whatever the owner says in response to finding what happened, we cannot read it as endorsement. *Mishum kisufa de'avad* — the owner says what he says out of embarrassment for the beer-maker, not wishing to shame him publicly. It would be unreasonable to interpret social courtesy as legal consent.

### No Permission

The ruling: *v'eina mekudeshes* — the betrothal is invalid. The beer-maker used property that was not his and for which he had no authorization. Whatever the owner subsequently said cannot transform unauthorized use into permitted use, and therefore the *kiddushin* does not take effect.

---

---

# Kiddushin 53

## Kodshei Kodashim

### Opening

We pick up today with the *Mishnah* on 52b, a remarkably rich one that touches on several distinct categories of sanctified property and the question of whether any of them can serve as the object of *kiddushin*.

### Hamikadesh Bechelko

The *Mishnah* opens: *hamikadesh bechelko bein kodshei kodashim bein kodashim kalim* — if someone betroths a woman using his portion in either *Kodshei Kodashim* or *Kodashim Kalim*, she is not betrothed. The broader context of this *Mishnah* concerns not merely whether the object used for *kiddushin* has a *shaveh perutah* in the simple market-value sense, but deeper questions about the nature of ownership and the halachic status of the object being transferred.

To situate the discussion: a *kohen* who performs a *kiddushin* using his portion in a *Kodshei Kodashim* offering — for instance, his share of the meat of a *chatat*, which may only be eaten by male *kohanim* and only within the *Azarah* — is attempting to use that meat as a transactional object. Similarly, *Kodashim Kalim*, such as the meat of a *shlamim*, which may be eaten throughout Jerusalem by both *kohanim* and *Yisraelim* of either gender, is likewise the subject of the *Mishnah*'s ruling. In both cases: *lo kadesh*, the *kiddushin* does not take effect.

### Temple Layout

To appreciate why, it is worth mapping the relevant areas of the *Beit HaMikdash*. At the innermost sanctum stood the *Kodesh Kodashim* and the *Heichal*, fronted by the *Ulam*. Proceeding outward, one entered the *Azarah*, which comprised the *Ezras Kohanim* and the *Ezras Yisrael*. Beyond that lay the *Ezras Nashim*. The *Kodshei Kodashim* may never leave the *Azarah* for any purpose; the *Kodashim Kalim* may be eaten throughout Jerusalem. These distinctions will bear heavily on later discussions about the practicability of the *Mishnah*'s case.

### Mishulchan Gavoa

The *Gemara*'s short formulation for why neither category of *korban* portions can effect *kiddushin* is: *mishulchan gavoa ka zachu* — he is eating off of God's table. Even though the *kohen* has every right to eat that meat, it is not his meat. He has a right to eat *from* the meat that came, figuratively, from the *Mizbe-ach*; it is not his in any proprietary sense. Accordingly, he cannot use it to betroth a woman.

### Maaser Sheni/Hekdesh

The *Mishnah* then turns to two additional cases. First, *Maaser Sheni*: whether he betrothed the woman with *Maaser Sheni* fruit or money knowingly or unknowingly — *bein beshogeg bein bemezid* — the *kiddushin* does not take effect, according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: if it was unintentional (*shogeg*), it does not work; if it was intentional (*mezid*), it does. Second, *hekdesh*: if the object used for *kiddushin* was sanctified property — say, an object he had consecrated to the *Beit HaMikdash* and subsequently forgotten about — Rabbi Meir rules that if it was done intentionally (*mezid*), the *kiddushin* works; if unintentionally (*shogeg*), it does not. Rabbi Yehuda rules precisely the reverse: *shogeg* works, *mezid* does not.

This is a striking arrangement. By *Maaser Sheni*, Rabbi Yehuda says *mezid* is the operative case for valid *kiddushin*. By *hekdesh*, Rabbi Meir says *mezid* is operative. The two are exact mirror images of each other, and a great deal will need to be unpacked about the role of *shogeg* and *mezid* in each context. But the *Gemara* begins with *Kodshei Kodashim* and *Kodashim Kalim*.

One student raises a question about whether the *Mishnah* might be discussing *Maaser Sheni* money (*maaser kesef*) rather than produce — an interesting point, but not the subject of the current discussion. Another notices a shift in language: the *reisha* of the *Mishnah* uses *lo kadesh* rather than *eina mekudeshet*. This linguistic asymmetry is worth noting and will recur.

The *Gemara* raises an initial challenge: perhaps the *Mishnah* does not accord with the position of Rabbi Yosi HaGalili. A *Baraita* teaches that the verse *u-ma'ala ma'al b'Hashem* — which concerns one who swears falsely to deny possession of his neighbor's property, thereby using God's name to perpetrate a theft — is extended by Rabbi Yosi HaGalili to include *Kodashim Kalim*, because *Kodashim Kalim* is still considered the property of its owner (*mamono*). The argument: if Michael consecrates his sheep as a *shlamim*, entrusts it to someone for safekeeping, and that person falsely swears he never received it, is that person liable under this *parasha* of false oaths? Rabbi Yosi HaGalili says yes — because the verse's inclusion of *b'Hashem* extends the prohibition even to sanctified property, and *Kodashim Kalim* of all sanctified categories is the one most retaining its character as the owner's property (*Kodashim Kalim mamon ba-alim hem*).

According to Rabbi Yosi HaGalili, then, if someone consecrated a sheep as a *shlamim* and damages it, he would be liable to pay. If it is still his property, why should the *Mishnah*'s ruling that one cannot use it for *kiddushin* be in tension with Rabbi Yosi HaGalili's view?

The *Gemara* answers: *ki ka-amar Rabbi Yosi HaGalili mechayev* — Rabbi Yosi HaGalili only holds the animal belongs to you while it is still alive, prior to being offered. *Aval le-achar shechita lo* — once it has been slaughtered and offered, even according to Rabbi Yosi HaGalili, the principle of *mishulchan gavoa ka zachu* applies. One might think that after the slaughter, when one is actually eating and benefiting from the meat, one's proprietary connection would be stronger rather than weaker. But the *Gemara* is saying the opposite: at the moment the animal is offered on the *Mizbe-ach*, the owner has given it to God. Whatever portion returns to him in the form of meat is now received from God's table — it is God's bounty extended to the *kohen* or the owner, not the owner's own property reverting to him.

This does leave a conceptual puzzle — *v'tzarich iyun* — since intuitively, one's rights and practical control over the animal seem *less* clear before the offering than after, when one is actively eating it. Yet the principle stands: the living animal is still yours, the offered meat is not.

The *Mishnah* itself supports this reading: *deika nami diktani hamekadesh bechelko* — the *Mishnah* says "his *portion*," implying a share in the already-divided meat, which presupposes that the offering has already taken place. Thus *shma mina*, we can confirm the *Mishnah* is speaking post-offering.

One further linguistic puzzle: why does the *Mishnah* here say *lo kidesh* rather than *eina mekudeshet*? This question is noted and left for further examination of the different textual readings (*girsaot*).

---

## Rabbi Meir vs Yehuda

### Sumchos Story

The *Gemara* now presents a striking narrative. The *Mishnah* as we have it is anonymous (*stam*), and *stam Mishnah* is Rabbi Meir. But behind the surface of the *Mishnah* lies a live dispute. *Tanu rabanan*: after Rabbi Meir's death, Rabbi Yehuda said to his students, "Do not allow Rabbi Meir's students to enter here." His reasoning: *mipnei shekantarnin hen* — they are troublemakers. *V'lo lilmod Torah hen ba-im* — they are not coming sincerely to learn. *Ela lekofachni behalachot hen ba-im* — they come to challenge me, to show off their dialectical virtuosity, not out of genuine pursuit of *halacha*.

Despite this prohibition, *Sumchos* — one of Rabbi Meir's most distinguished students — forced his way in and declared: "Here is what Rabbi Meir taught me: *hamekadesh bechelko bein kodshei kodashim bein kodashim kalim lo kadesh*." Once again, notably, *lo kadesh* rather than *eina mekudeshet*.

### Yehuda's Response

Rabbi Yehuda became angry at his own students for having allowed Sumchos in, and he questioned why this case was worth discussing at all. His challenge: *Kodshei Kodashim* cannot leave the *Azarah*. Women, Rabbi Yehuda presumes, have no business being in the *Azarah*. Therefore this entire case — a woman receiving *kiddushin* with *Kodshei Kodashim* — is a pure impossibility, a theoretical construct with no *halacha le-ma'aseh* application whatsoever. Far from reflecting genuine Torah inquiry, raising such a case proves, in Rabbi Yehuda's view, that Rabbi Meir's students are simply engaging in intellectual gamesmanship.

### Yosi Defends Case

Rabbi Yosi would not let this stand. He reasoned that if he stayed silent, it would effectively dishonor Rabbi Meir's entire approach to learning. *Tifei Torah mah tehei aleiha* — what will become of the honor of Torah? He therefore rose to defend the case on three grounds. First: *v'chi ein adam masur lekabel kiddushin l'vito b'Azarah?* — perhaps a man is betrothing off his minor daughter, and *he* is the one in the *Azarah*, receiving the *kiddushin* on her behalf — no woman need be present at all. Second: *v'ein isha asuya la-asos lah shaliach lekabel kiddusheha b'Azarah?* — can a woman not appoint a male agent (*shaliach*) to receive her *kiddushin* within the *Azarah* on her behalf? Third: *v'od dachaka v'nichnesa mah hi?* — and if she forced her way in, what would the *halacha* be? — a pointed echo of Sumchos himself having forced his way into the *beit midrash*.

### Women in Azara

This brief exchange opens a window onto a broader and theologically weighty question: what was the status of women in the *Azarah*? The *Gemara* seemingly assumes women were not normally present in the *Azarah* proper — that it was essentially male space. *Rashi* states explicitly, citing the first chapter of *Keilim*, that women cannot enter the *Azarah*. *Tosafos*, however, sharply disagrees and says *Rashi* was not careful here (*v'lo dak*): nowhere is it stated that women are forbidden from entering the *Azarah*. *Tosafos* marshals several proofs: the *Mishnah* in *perek Kol HaPesulim* states that a woman may perform *shechita* of *kodashim* — which requires being in the *Azarah*; and both the *Sotah* and the *Nezirah* must enter the *Azarah* to perform *tenufah* with their *korbanot*, as they cannot send a representative for that rite.

*Tosafos* therefore reformulates the question: the issue is not that a woman cannot enter the *Azarah*, but rather that a woman entering the *Azarah* for the purpose of getting married there would be unusual and inappropriate — *milsa d'lo sh'chicha*, an uncommon and undignified circumstance — and it is the combination of a woman's presence and that particular purpose that strikes Rabbi Yehuda as absurd. All the *rishonim* and *poskim* accept *Tosafos*' position that women do enter the *Azarah* when bringing *korbanot* and similar occasions; the *Ezras Nashim* exists not as an exclusionary barrier but as a designated area. What remains is a question of degree: does a woman require a specific reason — like bringing a *korban* — to enter the *Azarah*, or is only a completely trivial or inappropriate purpose insufficient justification?

This discussion carries real relevance for the question of *mechitzah* in synagogues. Some authorities ground the requirement for a *mechitzah* in the model of the *Beit HaMikdash*, where the *Ezras Nashim* was separate from the *Ezras Yisrael*. The *Gemara* here has been read as suggesting the *Azarah* proper was exclusively male space. But even according to *Tosafos*' reading — which is the accepted view — there remains a presumption that the *Azarah* was predominantly male space during worship, with women entering only for specific ritual needs. Even Rav Moshe Feinstein, in addressing the question of whether a woman may enter an all-male *shul* without a *mechitzah* to say *Kaddish*, permitted it in principle while noting that in *Lita* women would do precisely that, standing in the back without incident.

The resolution of the case is in any event clear: Rabbi Yosi's three answers demonstrate that a woman receiving *kiddushin* in the *Azarah* is neither impossible nor purely theoretical. A father, an agent, or even an intrepid woman herself could place the scenario squarely within the realm of *halacha le-ma'aseh*, and the discussion is eminently worthwhile.

---

## Biblical Sources

### Baraita Dispute

A *Baraita* at the bottom of 52b records the dispute directly: Rabbi Yehuda says *mekudeshet* — the *kiddushin* takes effect; Rabbi Yosi says *eina mekudeshet* — it does not. Rabbi Yehuda thus consistently fights against Rabbi Meir's position: not only should we be discussing the case, but Rabbi Meir is wrong — she *is* betrothed. Rabbi Yosi sides with Rabbi Meir: *eina mekudeshet*.

### Two Interpretations

Rabbi Yochanan observes: *shneihem mikra echad darshu* — both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi derive their positions from the very same verse: *vezeh yiheyeh lecha mikodesh hakodashim min ha-esh* — "and this shall be yours from the holy of holies, from the fire" — referring to the *kohen*'s portion in the *chatat* meat. Rabbi Yehuda reads the word *lecha* — "to you" — as granting broad proprietary rights: this is yours, to use as you will, within whatever constraints govern its consumption. If you can find a legitimate use for it beyond eating it yourself, you may do so. Rabbi Yosi, by contrast, reads *ke-esh* — "like the fire." Just as fire is there to consume, this portion too is solely for consumption. You have no ownership over it in any sense beyond eating it; it is *mishulchan gavoa*, God's table.

### Nimmnu v'Gamru

Rabbi Yochanan then reports, at the top of 53a: *nimnu ve-gamru* — they took a vote and reached a binding conclusion. *Hamekadesh bechelko bein kodshei kodashim bein kodashim kalim lo kadesh* — whether the betrothal was made with a portion in *Kodshei Kodashim* or even *Kodashim Kalim*, it does not take effect. The principle of *mishulchan gavoa* applies across the board: none of it is yours.

### Rav's Position

Rav disagrees: *adayin hi machlokes* — no vote was taken and no conclusion was reached; Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda remain in dispute, and there persists a position that one may indeed have a valid proprietary interest in the *korban* portions sufficient to effect *kiddushin*.

Abaye, however, aligns himself with Rabbi Yochanan: *ke-vasei de-Rabbi Yochanan mistabra* — it is more reasonable that Rabbi Yehuda ultimately reversed his position. The evidence for this comes from a *Baraita* drawn from the *Sifra* — *Toras Kohanim*, the *Tannaitic* commentary on *Vayikra* — whose anonymous author (*stam Sifra*) is assumed to be Rabbi Yehuda himself.

---

## Sifra Evidence

### Menachot Division

The *Baraita* asks: *minayin she-ein cholkin mincha kineged zvachim* — how do we know that when dividing *korbanos* among the *kohanim* at the end of the day, one may not swap a *mincha* offering against animal sacrifices? One might imagine that a *kohen* who prefers vegetarian food could say to his colleague: give me your share of the *mincha* and take my share of the meat in exchange. The answer derives from the verse: *v'chol mincha asher te'afeh ba-tanur l'chol bnei Aharon tihyeh ish ke-achiv* — every *mincha* shall belong to all the sons of Aaron, each equal to his brother. This teaches that each *korban* must be divided equally among the *kohanim*, and no one may substitute his portion in one type of offering for another's portion in a different type.

### No Swapping Rule

One might argue that the prohibition on swapping a *mincha* for animal sacrifices is specifically because a *mincha* can never fully substitute for an animal sacrifice in most contexts (*shelo bau tachteihem be-dalus*). But perhaps one could swap a *mincha* for bird sacrifices, since a *mincha* does substitute for a bird on the sliding-scale *korban* for the destitute. The *Sifra* counters this with a separate verse: *v'chol na-aseh ba-markheshet ul'chol benei Aharon tihyeh* — another instance of the same formulaic phrase applied to a different type of *mincha*, teaching that this type of swapping is also forbidden. The repetition is instructive: each additional invocation of "to all the sons of Aaron" comes to exclude a different proposed form of exchange.

### No Cross-Type Division

The *Sifra* continues to elaborate. Perhaps one cannot swap a *mincha* for animal sacrifices because one involves flour and the other blood (*hallu minei damim ve-hallu minei kemachim*), but perhaps bird sacrifices and animal sacrifices could be swapped since both involve blood. Another verse forecloses this. Perhaps *menachos* of different types could be swapped among themselves — surely one baked *mincha* could be exchanged for another baked *mincha*, since they are in the same category. Yet another verse prohibits this. Perhaps a *machavat mincha* — a hard, fried wafer — could be exchanged for another *machavat mincha*, since they are identical in type. The *Sifra* rules even this out, deriving from yet another verse that even within the same sub-genre, you cannot combine all offerings of that type and distribute them globally. Each individual *korban* must be divided among the *kohanim* equally — every offering brought that day must be apportioned separately.

### No Ownership Proof

The logical consequence of this *Sifra* passage is decisive. If a *kohen* cannot even swap his portion in one *mincha* for his colleague's portion in a different *mincha* of exactly the same type, he plainly has no real proprietary rights over his portion. If it were truly *his* property, he could do with it as he wishes — trade it, sell it, use it. The fact that no such latitude exists demonstrates that the *korban* portions do not belong to the *kohanim* in any meaningful sense of ownership. And if they have no ownership, they cannot use those portions to effect *kiddushin*.

Since the *stam Sifra* is Rabbi Yehuda, this passage demonstrates that Rabbi Yehuda ultimately conceded the point and agreed with Rabbi Meir: *chazar bo*. This is what the *Gemara* earlier meant by *nimnu ve-gamru*.

### Lechem Hapanim Story

Rava challenges this conclusion. He cites a *Baraita* that describes the period following the death of Shimon HaTzaddik, when the divine blessing that had rested upon the *Lechem HaPanim* — which had sufficed to satisfy all the *kohanim* — departed. The showbread now produced no miraculous satiety, and each *kohen* received only a tiny portion. The *Baraita* says the *tzenu-im* — the modest, self-effacing *kohanim* — would withdraw their hands rather than scramble for a slightly larger crumb. *Ve-hagargarnim* — the ravenous ones — *cholkin*, would divide it. Rava initially reads *cholkin* as meaning they would subdivide and trade among themselves, implying that the *kohanim* did exercise proprietary rights over the *Lechem HaPanim* and could arrange exchanges — which would seem to support Rav's position that there remains a valid sense of ownership.

### Chotfim Clarified

The *Gemara* resolves this by reinterpreting the word *cholkin*. *Mai cholkin? Chotfin* — "dividing" here does not mean trading or swapping portions across different *korbanos*. It means grabbing. The *Baraita*'s continuation confirms this: *ma'aseh be-echad she-chataf chelko ve-chelek chaveiro* — there was an incident where someone grabbed not only his own portion but his colleague's as well, and he was called *ben hamtzan* — "the grabber" — for the rest of his life. That is what *cholkin* describes: jostling for a larger share within the same *korban*, not exchanging portions across different offerings.

*Tosafos* adds a further nuance: even according to the view that you may not swap portions across different *korbanos*, it remains permissible to reassign your portion *within* a single *korban* — if you received your share of one *mincha* and you choose to give it to a colleague, that is a permissible act of generosity, not a prohibited trade. What is forbidden is substituting your portion in one *korban* for your colleague's portion in a different one. The *Lechem HaPanim* story describes no such cross-*korban* exchange; it describes pure grabbing within the same offering. Accordingly, it provides no support for the notion that *kohanim* have proprietary ownership over *korban* portions sufficient to use them for *kiddushin*.

The conclusion stands: *stam Sifra* Rabbi Yehuda, and he says in the clearest possible terms that there is no right of division or exchange with regard to *korban* portions — proving that even Rabbi Yehuda in the end agrees one cannot betroth a woman with them, whether the offering is *Kodshei Kodashim* or *Kodashim Kalim*.

---

## Maaser Sheni Status

### Rabbi Meir on Maaser

The *Mishnah* states: *Maaser Sheni bein beshogeg bein bemezid lo kadesh divrei Rabbi Meir* — whether knowingly or unknowingly, *Maaser Sheni* does not effect *kiddushin*, according to Rabbi Meir.

### Yehuda Disagrees

Rabbi Yehuda says: if it was done unknowingly (*shogeg*), it does not work; if it was done knowingly (*mezid*), it does.

### Kodesh La-Hashem

Where does Rabbi Meir derive his position? The *Gemara* cites Rav Acha son of Rava, speaking in the name of the *Gemara* — meaning in the name of accepted tradition in the *beit midrash*: the verse *v'chol maaser ha-aretz mi-zera ha-aretz mi-pri ha-etz la-Hashem hu* — "and all the *maaser* of the land, from the seed of the land and from the fruit of the tree, belongs to God" — together with the characterization *kodesh la-Hashem*, "holy to God." The combination means *Maaser Sheni* is not yours; you are eating God's produce. Just as with *korban* portions the operative concept was *mishulchan gavoa ka zachu*, here the parallel formulation is *mamon gavoa hu* — it is entirely God's property — and you cannot use it to betroth a woman.

### Kodesh Distinctions

The *Gemara* tests this logic by considering several other items that carry similar designations. *Trumat ma'aser* is called *trumas Hashem* — yet the *Mishnah* implies that one can use *terumah* to effect *kiddushin*. The *Gemara* distinguishes: *trumas Hashem* means it is God's *terumah* in the sense that God commanded it be given, not that it belongs to God. It is given to the *kohen* and remains his property. *Challah* carries the language *titnu la-Hashem* — "give it to God" — but it lacks the word *kodesh*, which would indicate that it is fully God's. *Shevi-it* produce carries the phrase *kodesh tihyeh lachem* — "it shall be holy to you" — but lacks the phrase *la-Hashem*. And while one *pasuk* equates the Jewish people to *terumah* and calls Israel *kodesh la-Hashem*, that is metaphorical; the *Gemara* notes this usage pertains to the Jewish people, not to actual *terumah*.

One might object that the metaphor implicitly confirms that *terumah* itself is *kodesh la-Hashem*. The *Gemara* accepts this logical inference but adds: even granting that *terumah* carries the designation *kodesh la-Hashem*, the verse by *Maaser Sheni* adds the crucial word *hu* — "it is" — specifically: *la-Hashem hu*. *Ravin Sava* explains in front of Rav that *hu* signifies permanence of status — it remains God's, with no movement away from that state. The combination of *kodesh*, *la-Hashem*, and *hu* in the *Maaser Sheni* verse places it in a uniquely inviolable category of divine ownership. That is Rabbi Meir's source.

### Mamon Gavoa

Thus, according to Rabbi Meir, *Maaser Sheni* is *mamon gavoa hu* — completely God's property, not yours. You may eat it, but eating it does not make it yours in a proprietary sense; you are partaking of God's *maaser*, and you have no right to transfer it to another.

---

## Intent Analysis

### Woman's Consent

Having established why Rabbi Meir holds *Maaser Sheni* never effects *kiddushin*, the *Gemara* turns to why Rabbi Yehuda draws a distinction between *shogeg* and *mezid*. Rabbi Yehuda fundamentally disagrees with Rabbi Meir's characterization of *Maaser Sheni* as *mamon gavoa*; in Rabbi Yehuda's view, *Maaser Sheni* belongs to the owner. If so, why should the distinction between knowing and unknowing matter at all?

The key insight is that the *shogeg/mezid* distinction here is not about the man's state of knowledge but about the woman's. If a man betroths a woman with what appears to be an ordinary apple and it turns out to be *Maaser Sheni* fruit, she faces a significant burden she never accepted: that apple cannot be eaten at home; it must be brought to Jerusalem. Had she known this, she would not have agreed to receive it as her *kiddushin*. We therefore presume — as a matter of *umdena*, an assessment of intent — that she would never have consented had she understood what she was receiving. Accordingly, when she is in a state of *shogeg*, the *kiddushin* fails. But if she knows it is *Maaser Sheni* and agrees nonetheless, then she has knowingly accepted the conditions — she is willing to take the apple to Jerusalem — and the *kiddushin* takes effect.

One might ask, as a *nafka mina* from knowing whose consent is the operative factor: if in practice the woman later says she would not have minded, does that change the outcome? *Rashi* notes that this is indeed the practical implication.

### Rav Yeimar

Rav Yeimar offers a clean resolution to the puzzle Rabbi Yochanan raised — which case involves only one unwilling party, and which involves both? By *Maaser Sheni*, according to Rabbi Yehuda, *the man has no problem* using his *Maaser Sheni* fruit for *kiddushin*. On the contrary, he benefits from it: *de-mitparka minei* — he is thereby relieved of the obligation to schlep the fruit to Jerusalem himself. The woman, however, would not have wanted it had she known. Thus *shogeg* does not work because of the woman's presumed non-consent, while *mezid* works because she knew and agreed.

### Me'ilah Concern

By *hekdesh*, the analysis is different. Here, *traveihu lo nicha lehu* — neither party would have consented had they known. Why not? *Lo nicha lehu de-nafik hekdesh le-chulin al yadeihu* — neither would have wanted to be the instrument by which consecrated property was transferred to non-sacred use, thereby transgressing the *issur me'ilah*. When the transaction is done unknowingly (*shogeg*), we presume retroactively that neither party would have wanted to participate in an act of *me'ilah* — and so the *kiddushin* is void. It is only when done intentionally (*mezid*) — when both parties knew it was *hekdesh* and proceeded anyway — that Rabbi Meir considers the *kiddushin* valid, since at that point both parties accepted the transaction with full knowledge of its nature. We will continue tomorrow with further analysis of why *shogeg* fails in these two cases and other approaches to understanding the interplay between intent and the underlying halachic status of *Maaser Sheni* and *hekdesh*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 54

## Meir vs. Yehuda

### Intro: Two positions

The discussion in our *daf* actually begins toward the end of 53b, where the *Gemara* is working through a *Mishnah* that records two distinct disputes — one concerning *ma'aser sheni* and one concerning *hekdesh* — and the divergent positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda. By *ma'aser sheni*, Rabbi Meir holds that one can never use it to betroth a woman, because it is *mammon gavoh* — it belongs to God, not to the individual owner. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees in principle and allows it, but rules that the betrothal is invalid in a case of *shogeg*, when the parties acted unwittingly. Thus, according to Rabbi Yehuda, the unwitting case is worse. By *hekdesh*, the positions are reversed: Rabbi Meir holds that if one betroths a woman with *hekdesh* funds knowingly (*mezid*), it is effective, but unwittingly (*shogeg*) it is not. Rabbi Yehuda again takes the opposite view.

The challenge, then, is to explain what principle underlies each position. The *Gemara* frames the question in terms of who would not have wanted the transaction had they known the true nature of the funds. The key distinction is whether it was the woman alone who would have objected, or whether both parties would have objected — since the presence of a *ta'us*, an error that undermines the consent of both parties, voids the transaction entirely.

### Yirmiyah's answer

Rabbi Yirmiyah's initial resolution is that for *ma'aser sheni*, only the woman would have objected had she known, because accepting *ma'aser sheni* as her *kiddushin* money would obligate her to schlep the funds to Jerusalem before she could benefit from them. The man, however, would not have minded — if she was willing to accept *ma'aser sheni* and make the journey to Jerusalem, he would be perfectly content to have married her on those terms. Accordingly, the transaction is voided by *shogeg* because her consent was compromised.

By *hekdesh*, Rabbi Yirmiyah explains, neither party would have wanted the transaction had they known the funds were *hekdesh*. Both parties would have realized they were committing *me'ilah* — misappropriating consecrated property — and neither would have wished to be party to that transgression. The woman would not want to be implicated in the violation of *hekdesh*, and the man would not want to spend *hekdesh* funds in order to contract a betrothal. Since both parties are in *ta'us*, neither one's consent was genuine, and the transaction is entirely void.

Rashi notes a further implication: the relevant question of whose *ta'us* undermines the transaction depends on whom you would ask — meaning, in principle, one might think these presumptions about unwillingness are case-sensitive and could be rebutted by the actual parties. Nevertheless, the basic framework stands.

### Yaakov reverses

The *Gemara* now picks up approximately twelve to fifteen lines into 53b, with the position of Rabbi Yaakov, who says *ipcha mistabra* — the opposite makes more sense. Rabbi Yaakov argues that by *ma'aser sheni* as well, both parties would have objected had they known. The woman, as before, would not have wanted the schlep to Jerusalem. But Rabbi Yaakov adds: the man also would not have wanted to give her *ma'aser sheni* had he known, *mishum onsa de'orcha* — on account of the burden of the journey. Rashi's initial reading is that perhaps the woman would not be fully betrothed until the *ma'aser sheni* actually arrived in Jerusalem intact and could be consumed, leaving open the possibility that if the funds were lost along the way she would not be *mekudeshet*. Tosafot rejects this reading entirely and insists that the betrothal takes effect immediately regardless of what happens subsequently. Rashi himself offers the more persuasive explanation: even if the man bears no formal legal liability if something goes wrong along the way, he would not have wanted to give her something that she could only benefit from after a difficult journey to Jerusalem — because she would come back to him with legitimate grievances if anything went wrong. She had a *schlep*, the funds rotted or were lost, and now she is unhappy with him. The man, therefore, would also have preferred not to initiate such an arrangement.

So Rabbi Yaakov concludes that by *ma'aser sheni* both parties would have objected, and thus the *ta'us* is bilateral. This leaves him with a more difficult question about *hekdesh*: we understand why the woman would not have wanted to be party to a violation of *hekdesh* — she would not want the consecrated property to be profaned *al yadah*, through her. But why would the man have objected? Rabbi Yaakov raises the rather striking point that, from the man's perspective, if it turned out he accidentally used *hekdesh* funds and in the process managed to betroth a woman without spending his own money — well, perhaps he would not have minded all that much. He committed *me'ilah b'shogeg*, which is unfortunate, but he got a betrothal at no personal cost. The *Gemara* notes this candidly: *d'nafka itatta mimeila* — the woman came out of the *me'ilah*, as it were, at no expense to him.

The *Gemara* itself acknowledges that Rabbi Yirmiyah's original answer seems the more compelling one — that by *ma'aser sheni* the problem is fundamentally hers, and by *hekdesh* it is a problem for both — but Rabbi Yaakov's position is recorded as the reverse. In any case, the underlying logic of both answers is that the transaction fails in *shogeg* when we can say that the relevant parties, had they known, would not have wanted to go forward — because without that genuine *da'as*, no transaction takes effect.

---

## Ta'us & Kiddushin

### Rava's question

At this point the *Gemara* records a question posed by Rava to Rav Chisda. We have established, operating within Rabbi Yirmiyah's explanation, that the woman is not *mekudeshet* when *hekdesh* is used *b'shogeg* — because had the man known, he would not have wanted to spend *hekdesh* money, and thus the transaction was a *ta'us* from the start. Since the act was done in error, and had either of them known they would not have proceeded, the entire transaction is treated as if it never took place.

Rava's question is: if the woman is not betrothed because the transaction was void on account of *ta'us* — if no legal act of acquisition occurred — then how could the money possibly have become *chullin*? The man physically handed the woman some funds, but if we say the transaction never legally took effect, then there was no genuine transfer of possession. If there was no legal transfer, then there was no act of *me'ilah*. And if there was no *me'ilah*, the money did not exit the domain of *hekdesh* into *chullin*. This is Rava's sharply posed question: *ma'os heichi yeitz'u l'chullin* — how did the money ever become *chullin*?

### Void transaction

The answer given is direct: if the woman is not betrothed, then the transaction never took place. The money changed hands physically, but it was never legally taken into the woman's possession. Since no valid act of acquisition occurred, no act of *me'ilah* occurred either, and the money does not become *chullin*.

This response, however, immediately generates a further problem. If one never commits *me'ilah* when spending *hekdesh* funds *b'shogeg* — because in every such case we can say the person would not have wanted to spend the funds had they known, and therefore the transaction is always void — then it seems to follow that there can *never* be *me'ilah* involving the misuse of *hekdesh* funds through a spending transaction when the act was unintentional. That is precisely the opposite of the standard presumption about *me'ilah*, which assumes that the classic case of *me'ilah* is *b'shogeg*, the unwitting misuse of consecrated property. How can Rav Chisda's answer be correct?

Rav Chisda replies: indeed, the same logic applies to a sale. Rav Chiya bar Avin posed this directly: *b'mecher mai* — what if one used *hekdesh* funds to make a purchase without knowing they were *hekdesh*? Rav Chisda responds: *af b'mecher lo kanah* — even in a case of purchase, nothing is acquired. Because the buyer, had he known, would not have wanted to make the transaction, it is treated as void, there was no genuine acquisition, and therefore no *me'ilah* occurs.

This is a remarkable position. It implies that *me'ilah* through the spending or transferring of funds can never occur *b'shogeg*, since any such transaction will be retroactively void on the grounds that the party would not have agreed had they known the truth. One might then ask: is there ever *me'ilah b'shogeg* at all? The answer is yes — but only in cases where *me'ilah* does not depend on a transaction. If someone ate *hekdesh* food without knowing, or anointed themselves with *hekdesh* oil, or used *hekdesh* oil to light their lamp — these are cases of directly benefiting from *hekdesh* without any transactional element. There, *me'ilah* occurs *b'shogeg*, and the object may exit *hekdesh* into *chullin* to whatever extent it can. But where the *me'ilah* would consist of transferring ownership of funds through a transaction, *shogeg* renders it void and no *me'ilah* takes place.

### Storekeeper case

The *Gemara* now raises a challenge from a *braita* that distinguishes between a *chanvani* (storekeeper) and a *shulchani* (money changer) — a *braita* presented explicitly as the position of Rabbi Meir. The case runs as follows: I hold *hekdesh* funds, having forgotten they are *hekdesh*, and I give them to someone to watch for safekeeping. If the recipient is an ordinary *baal habayit*, a homeowner, he has no implicit authorization to use the funds regardless of whether I hand them to him loosely or in a sealed bundle. If he uses them on his own initiative, the *me'ilah* is his. However, if I give the funds to a money changer, and I hand them to him loosely — loose coins given to a money changer signal, by common practice, that he may use them in his business and simply repay me equivalent funds — then I am considered to have implicitly authorized his use of those funds, and I am the *mo'el*.

The debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda in this *braita* concerns the intermediate case: a storekeeper. Storekeepers also typically have loose change available for making change with customers. If I give a storekeeper loose funds and he uses them, is he acting with my implicit authorization — making me the *mo'el* — or is he acting on his own, making himself the *mo'el*? Rabbi Meir holds the storekeeper is like the ordinary homeowner (*chanvani k'baal habayit*) and the storekeeper is liable. Rabbi Yehuda holds the storekeeper is like the money changer (*chanvani k'shulchani*) and I am liable.

This *braita* poses a direct challenge. The *braita* is framed entirely within a scenario of *shogeg* — neither the depositor nor the recipient knows the funds are *hekdesh* — and yet *me'ilah* is treated as occurring. Both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree that *me'ilah* takes place; they only debate *who* committed it. This seems to flatly contradict the position we have been developing in the name of Rabbi Meir, that there can be no *me'ilah b'shogeg* through a transaction.

The *Gemara* offers a resolution: Rabbi Meir is not speaking in his own voice in this portion of the *braita*. He is responding *l'divrav d'Rabbi Yehuda* — within the framework of Rabbi Yehuda's position. As if to say: I, Rabbi Meir, fundamentally hold that no *me'ilah* occurs through a *shogeg* transaction because any such transaction is void. But *you*, Rabbi Yehuda, who believe that *me'ilah* does occur through spending *b'shogeg* — at least concede to me that in this case the storekeeper acted on his own authority, like a homeowner. To which Rabbi Yehuda replies: no, even on my view, the storekeeper is like the money changer, and the depositor is responsible. The entire debate about the storekeeper is therefore internal to Rabbi Yehuda's framework, with Rabbi Meir only arguing within that framework while maintaining his own fundamental position.

The *Gemara* acknowledges this is a strained reading, since the plain meaning of the *braita* strongly suggests both opinions accept that *me'ilah* occurs in such a case. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* will continue developing this position of Rabbi Meir.

### Rav rejects position

Rav himself pulls back from this framework. *Chazinu al kol tzedadim shel Rabbi Meir* — we have examined every position of Rabbi Meir from every angle. And we have never found Rabbi Meir articulating the extreme position that *hekdesh b'shogeg ein mitchalel, b'meizid mitchalel* — that *hekdesh* is only desanctified when the misuse is intentional and never when it is unintentional. This would be the exact inverse of what we understand about *me'ilah*. The classic, fundamental case of *me'ilah* is *b'shogeg*; when you bring the *korban me'ilah*, the entire institution is predicated on unwitting misuse. To say that unintentional misuse of *hekdesh* funds through a transaction never constitutes *me'ilah* is, to Rav, an astonishing and unattested position.

It is worth noting that Rabbi Meir does have a *chiddush* regarding *me'ilah b'meizid*. As Tosafot observes, Rabbi Meir derives from the *parasha* of *Sotah* — *ish ki tisteh ishto u-ma'alah vo ma'al* — that *me'ilah* can apply even to intentional violations. The standard ruling is that *b'meizid* the funds do not exit *hekdesh* into *chullin*; Rabbi Meir says they do. So Rabbi Meir's position, properly understood, is an expansion of *me'ilah* to include the *mezid* case — not an elimination of *me'ilah* in the *shogeg* case. The claim that Rabbi Meir abolishes *me'ilah b'shogeg* for transactional misuse is, according to Rav, nowhere to be found and would be an incoherent reading.

How, then, does Rav explain our *Mishnah*, in which Rabbi Meir rules that a woman is not betrothed when *hekdesh* is used *b'shogeg*? The *Gemara* proposes that the *Mishnah* is discussing a very specific case: *bigdei kehunah she-lo balu* — the garments of the priesthood that have not yet worn out. If someone attempted to betroth a woman with a priestly garment — perhaps he was a *kohen* who possessed such a cloak — and did so unwittingly, then Rabbi Meir rules there is no *me'ilah* and consequently no *kiddushin*. But this is due to a special exemption specific to *bigdei kehunah*, not a general principle about transactional *me'ilah b'shogeg*.

---

## Priestly garments

### Unworn garments

Why is there a special exemption for *bigdei kehunah* from *me'ilah b'shogeg*? The *Gemara* explains: *ho'il v'nitnu lihanis bahem* — since *kohanim* are given permission to derive benefit from these garments. The garments of the *kehunah* are *hekdesh*, but *kohanim* are authorized to wear them and benefit from them in the course of the *avodah*. Because there is a standing allowance for benefit, there is a corresponding latitude that extends to their incidental use.

### Heavenly angels

The *Gemara* then invokes one of the most celebrated principles in all of *halacha*: *she-lo nitna Torah l'malachei ha-shareit* — the Torah was not given to the ministering angels. A *kohen* cannot be held to the standard that the instant the *avodah* concludes, he must strip off his priestly garments immediately. If he lingered two minutes after the close of the day, still wearing his *bigdei kehunah* while chatting with a colleague, it would be absurd to say he committed *me'ilah* for those two minutes of inadvertent benefit. The Torah is given to human beings operating within human norms. Therefore, a general exemption from *me'ilah* applies to *bigdei kehunah* when the use is unintentional — the latitude given for their ordinary and necessary use extends to cover incidental overlap.

This principle — *she-lo nitna Torah l'malachei ha-shareit* — appears in a number of halachic contexts, including discussions of microscopic organisms that are halachically invisible. It is always an expression of the same idea: the Torah calibrates its demands to the realities of human life and human perception.

### Worn-out distinction

The *Gemara* then investigates this principle by looking at a *braita* concerning worn-out priestly garments: *kotonos kehunah shebalu, mo'alin bahem, divrei Rabbi Meir* — if the priestly cloaks have worn out and are no longer in use, Rabbi Meir says *me'ilah* applies to them. The *Gemara* initially wonders whether to read this broadly — as if there would be *me'ilah* regardless of whether they were worn out or not. The answer is *lo, balu davka* — no, the ruling is specifically about worn-out garments.

The distinction is essential: the entire basis for the exemption from *me'ilah* was that these garments are objects in active use by *kohanim*, and the Torah grants a certain latitude in the context of that active use. Once the garments have worn out and are no longer being worn, they are simply property of *hekdesh*, removed from active priestly service. Perhaps the *Mikdash* will repurpose the fabric, sell the raw material, or use it for wicks.
