Whatever the case, the kohen's personal authorization to wear them has lapsed, and the special exemption no longer applies. They revert to the status of standard *hekdesh* property, and ordinary rules of *me'ilah* apply.

What, then, does Rabbi Yehuda say about *bigdei kehunah* that are still in use? Rashi explains that Rabbi Yehuda would hold that even though there is a standing allowance for *kohanim* to benefit from these garments, that allowance was specifically circumscribed: it covers the *kohen* wearing his garments too long after the *avodah*, but it does not extend to misusing the garment in some entirely different way — such as using it to betroth a woman. For Rabbi Yehuda, the limited allowance does not create a blanket immunity from *me'ilah* in every other conceivable context of misuse. This, then, is how Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir diverge on the specific case of *bigdei kehunah* within our *Mishnah*.

### New vs. old coins

The *Gemara* now examines an analogous case involving Temple funds: *mo'alin b'chadatin v'ein mo'alin b'atikin* — one is liable for *me'ilah* with new *shekalim* but not with old *shekalim*. The background is as follows. Beginning in *Adar*, people would donate their annual half-*shekel* to the *Beit HaMikdash* for the purchase of communal sacrifices in the coming year. These new funds — the *chadatin* — would be drawn upon in three collections throughout the year to buy *korbanos*. If someone failed to donate in time and contributed a *shekel* from a prior year, those older funds — the *atikin* — were designated for a different purpose: municipal and Temple infrastructure needs, such as building and repairing the walls of Jerusalem and its towers, and other city needs. Rashi describes this as *kol tzorchei tikkun ha'ir* — all manner of maintenance of the city.

Now, funds used to build the walls of Jerusalem are something from which ordinary people will naturally benefit — shade, shelter, protection. This is analogous in some respect to *bigdei kehunah*, in that there is an allowance for benefit built into the purpose of these funds. The question the *Gemara* poses is: does that allowance create a blanket exemption from *me'ilah* in the same way we are arguing it does for *bigdei kehunah*? If I accidentally took those old *shekalim* and spent them on something entirely unrelated to the walls of Jerusalem, would there be *me'ilah*?

*Ta shema* — the *braita* states: *mo'alin b'chadatin* — the new *shekalim* are subject to *me'ilah*, *v'ein mo'alin b'atikin* — but not the old *shekalim*. Then Rabbi Meir says: *mo'alin af b'atikin* — even the old *shekalim* are subject to *me'ilah*. Rabbi Meir further invokes the rule of *shiyarei halishka*: leftover funds from the collection designated for purchasing *korbanos*, which were not drawn upon in that year, were allocated to these same communal infrastructure needs. Rabbi Meir holds that even those *shiyarei halishka* funds remain subject to *me'ilah*.

This poses a significant difficulty. If Rabbi Meir is the one insisting on *me'ilah* even when funds are earmarked for communal use from which the general public will benefit — which is an even more permissive context than *bigdei kehunah* — how can we maintain the reading that it is specifically Rabbi Meir in our *Mishnah* who exempts from *me'ilah* due to the allowance given to *bigdei kehunah*? The logic should run the other way: if even the old *shekalim* and *shiyarei halishka* are subject to *me'ilah* despite their broad allowances for public benefit, then certainly there should be *me'ilah b'shogeg* with *bigdei kehunah*.

### Fallen wall stones

The *Gemara* then brings a further *braita*: *avnei Yerushalayim shenashru, mo'alin bahen, divrei Rabbi Meir* — if stones fall from the wall of Jerusalem, Rabbi Meir says there is still *me'ilah*. This is precisely the question that arose regarding the old *shekalim*: once there is a broad allowance for people to benefit from the walls, can we say that when stones tumble off and someone uses them to build their own house — not realizing the stones belong to the *Beit HaMikdash* — there is *me'ilah*? Rabbi Meir says yes, there still is.

This again contradicts the attempt to explain our *Mishnah* as a case where Rabbi Meir grants blanket exemption from *me'ilah* because a limited allowance was given. The *Gemara's* response in both cases is the same: *lo teima Rabbi Meir, ella eima Rabbi Yehuda* — remove Rabbi Meir's name wherever it appears in these *braitot* and replace it with Rabbi Yehuda. It is Rabbi Yehuda who maintains *me'ilah* in these cases, and Rabbi Yehuda who takes the stricter position that a limited, purpose-specific allowance does not create broad immunity.

This answer is, as the *Gemara* itself implicitly acknowledges, a significant stretch. The approach of reading *bigdei kehunah* as a hyper-specific exception and then reversing all the attributed names to maintain internal consistency becomes increasingly strained — particularly because the general thrust of the other sources suggests that the more lenient position on the walls of Jerusalem and *shiyarei halishka* is precisely the one we should be attributing to Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Meir.

Further complicating matters: the *Gemara* observes that Rabbi Yehuda's approach would require saying that the walls of Jerusalem retain *kedushah*, and that stones fallen from those walls remain *hekdesh* subject to *me'ilah*. But we know from a *Mishnah* in Nedarim that Rabbi Yehuda holds the opposite. If one says a loaf of bread shall be like a lamb, or like the wood of the altar, or *k'Yerushalayim* — like Jerusalem — Rabbi Yehuda rules it is not a valid *neder*, because Jerusalem does not have the type of personal-property *kedushah* that can be invoked in a *neder*. Even if one says the correct formula — *k'Yerushalayim*, with the comparative *kaf* — Rabbi Yehuda rules it is ineffective, because Jerusalem's *kedushah* is not of the operative kind. This strongly implies that Rabbi Yehuda does not treat the walls of Jerusalem as possessing the same *hekdesh kedushah* as Temple property, which would mean that assigning him the position that fallen wall-stones are subject to *me'ilah* is inconsistent.

The *Gemara* resolves this final tension with *trei tanna'im aliba d'Rabbi Yehuda* — there is a dispute among *tanna'im* about what Rabbi Yehuda's position actually entails. Some hold Rabbi Yehuda denies *kedushah* to the walls of Jerusalem entirely; others attribute to him a view that the walls do retain *kedushah* and *me'ilah* applies when their use is taken outside the permitted parameters. The *Gemara* is ultimately threading a very fine needle to maintain the interpretation that our *Mishnah* addresses only the narrow case of *bigdei kehunah*, rather than accepting the broader reading that Rabbi Meir fundamentally rejects transactional *me'ilah b'shogeg* altogether. And yet, as the *Gemara* will make clear in the next section, it is precisely that broader reading — however extreme — that is in fact Rabbi Meir's genuine position.

---

## Halachic ruling

### Follow Meir: Me'aser

With the analysis of the competing frameworks now complete, the *Gemara* turns to how we rule in practice. Rav Adda bar Ahava states: *halacha k'Rabbi Meir b'ma'aser* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Meir regarding *ma'aser sheni*. This means that *ma'aser sheni* is *mammon gavoh* — it belongs entirely to God — and one can never use it to betroth a woman, under any circumstances.

### Kerem revai proof

The basis for ruling like Rabbi Meir on *ma'aser sheni* is that a *stam Mishnah* aligns with his position. The *Gemara* identifies this *stam* in the laws of *kerem revai* — the fruit of a vineyard in its fourth year.

### Shammai vs. Hillel

The *Mishnah* records a debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the status of *kerem revai*. Beit Shammai holds that *kerem revai* does not require the addition of a *chomesh* — the twenty percent surcharge added when one redeems *ma'aser sheni* — and does not require *bi'ur*, the removal of the produce from one's home in the third and sixth years of the *shemita* cycle. Beit Hillel holds that it does require both *chomesh* and *bi'ur*, treating it consistently like *ma'aser sheni*. In a further point of dispute regarding the gifts to the poor: Beit Shammai holds that the normal gifts to the poor apply to *kerem revai* — specifically *peret* (individual grapes dropped during harvest) and *olelot* (unripe or inferior clusters) — while Beit Hillel says *kulo l'gat*, it goes entirely to the winepress, with no portion left for the poor.

The *Gemara* explains the reasoning. Beit Hillel derives the similarity to *ma'aser sheni* from a *gezeirah shavah*: *kodesh-kodesh*. The verse by *kerem revai* says *kodesh hilulim l'Hashem*, and by *ma'aser sheni* the word *kodesh l'Hashem* also appears. Beit Shammai does not accept this *gezeirah shavah*. Beit Hillel's ruling that all the fruit goes to the winepress, leaving nothing for the poor, follows directly from their view that *kerem revai* is like *ma'aser sheni* — and since *ma'aser sheni* is *mammon gavoh*, it is not the owner's money in a meaningful sense, which means the owner does not bear the personal obligation to leave gifts to the poor from it. If it were his money — as Rabbi Yehuda maintains — then it would remain his property subject to those obligations, and he would need to leave the gifts to the poor. Beit Hillel's ruling that no gifts to the poor apply thus presupposes that *ma'aser sheni* is *mammon gavoh* — exactly the position of Rabbi Meir. Since Beit Hillel constitutes the *stam* ruling and the *halacha* follows them, this establishes that we rule like Rabbi Meir on *ma'aser sheni*.

### Follow Yehuda: Hekdesh

Conversely, Rav Adda bar Ahava states: *v'halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda b'hekdesh* — we follow Rabbi Yehuda regarding *hekdesh*. This is the classic, standard position on *me'ilah*: *b'shogeg* the money exits *hekdesh* and becomes *chullin*, and the woman is *mekudeshet*; *b'meizid* the money does not exit *hekdesh* and she is not *mekudeshet*. Here too the ruling is supported by a *stam Mishnah*.

The *Mishnah* in question: one had *hekdesh* funds and, without realizing it, sent a competent adult — not a minor, not someone of diminished capacity — as a *shaliach* to spend those funds. The *shaliach* was sent to a storekeeper to make a purchase. Before the *shaliach* reached the storekeeper, he remembered that the funds were *hekdesh* — meaning both the sender and the *shaliach* were now *b'meizid*. In that case, *chanvani mo'el l'ch'sheyotzi* — the storekeeper commits the *me'ilah* when he receives and uses the money, because the storekeeper is *b'shogeg*. The *Gemara* clarifies that the case is one in which both the sender and the *shaliach* recalled, so both are *b'meizid*, the money did not exit *hekdesh* through either of them, and when the unsuspecting storekeeper uses the funds, his *shogeg* act is what causes the money to become *chullin* and constitutes the *me'ilah*. This perfectly illustrates the principle of Rabbi Yehuda: *shogeg* causes the money to exit *hekdesh*, *meizid* does not. And since this *Mishnah* operates on that assumption without attribution, it functions as the *stam* that establishes the *halacha* like Rabbi Yehuda for *hekdesh*.

---

## Contradiction: chullin s…

### Rav Pappa's question

With the ruling now established — we follow Rabbi Meir that *ma'aser sheni* is *mammon gavoh*, and we follow Rabbi Yehuda that *me'ilah* with *hekdesh* funds operates in the standard manner, *b'shogeg* desanctifying the money and *b'meizid* not — Rav Pappa addresses a difficulty to Abaye. We have ruled according to Rabbi Yehuda's framework on *hekdesh*: if one uses *hekdesh* money to betroth a woman *b'shogeg*, the *me'ilah* is effective, the money becomes *chullin*, and the *kiddushin* works. If done *b'meizid*, the money does not become *chullin* and the *kiddushin* fails.

But compare this to a *Mishnah* in Tractate *Me'ilah* involving a *balan*, a bathhouse keeper. If someone pays a bathhouse keeper for entry using *hekdesh* funds without realizing it (*b'shogeg*), the *me'ilah* takes effect, the donor is liable, and the money becomes *chullin*. If he did it *b'meizid* — knowingly — the money does not become *chullin*.

So far this is consistent with Rabbi Yehuda and our ruling. But Rav Pappa identifies a genuine tension: by *kiddushin*, we say that if the man intentionally (*b'meizid*) gives *hekdesh* money to betroth a woman, the money becomes *chullin* and the betrothal is effective — that is Rabbi Meir's position which governs the *kiddushin* case in the *Mishnah*. Yet by the bathhouse keeper, *b'meizid* it does not become *chullin*. Why should the intentional use of *hekdesh* funds produce different outcomes in these two cases — effective desanctification leading to valid *kiddushin* in one instance, and failure to desanctify in the other?

This is the question with which the *daf* concludes, and which will be taken up in the subsequent session.

---

---

# Kiddushin 55

## Maaser Sheni & Hekdesh

### Maaser Sheni Status

We resume in the middle of 54b, having just established the ruling that we follow *Rabbi Meir* on the question of *maaser sheni*. The position is that *maaser sheni* is *mamon gavoah* — God's money — and not the private property of the individual. The basis for this ruling is a *stam mishna* reflecting the position of *Beit Hillel*, which holds that one does not distribute the gifts of the poor — *peret u'olelot* — from *neta reva'i*, since *neta reva'i* shares the laws of *maaser sheni*. The logic is that if it is truly God's money, one cannot use it to betroth a woman, because one cannot effect *kiddushin* with property that does not genuinely belong to oneself.

### Me'ilah Distinctions

When it comes to *hekdesh* and *me'ilah*, however, the ruling follows *Rabbi Yehuda*. The many *mishnayot* in Masechet Me'ilah demonstrate that when one uses *hekdesh* funds, one transgresses *me'ilah b'shogeg* — unwittingly — and does not transgress *me'ilah b'mezid* — intentionally. *Rabbi Meir* takes precisely the reverse position: *me'ilah* can occur *b'mezid*, and moreover, when it comes to monetary transactions involving *hekdesh* funds, *me'ilah* does not occur *b'shogeg*, because had one known one was transacting with sacred funds, one would not have wanted the transaction at all, and the transaction is therefore void. The *stam mishna* in Me'ilah goes against *Rabbi Meir* and follows *Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Stam Mishna Logic

Thus the general picture is: by *maaser sheni*, the *stam mishna* reflects *Rabbi Meir*; by *me'ilah*, the *stam mishna* reflects *Rabbi Yehuda*.

---

## Three Mishnayot Challenge

### Redeeming Maaser Sheni

The *gemara* now raises a series of challenges. Having said we rule like *Rabbi Meir* that *maaser sheni* is *mamon gavoah*, the *gemara* cites the following *mishna* with the words *v'ha tnan* — but do we not teach? The *mishna* states: *HaPodeh Maaser Sheni shelo* — one who redeems his own *maaser sheni* — adds a fifth to its value. This applies *bein mishelo bein shenitan lo b'matanah* — whether the produce is his own or whether it was given to him as a gift, and he now wishes to redeem it rather than carry the fruit to Jerusalem.

### Gift-Giving Problem

The difficulty is immediately apparent: if someone can give their *maaser sheni* to another person, and that other person genuinely owns it to the point of being required to add a fifth upon redemption, it sounds very much as though *maaser sheni* belongs to its owner as private property, transferable at will. The *gemara* asks: *mani* — who is the author of this *mishna*? If it is *Rabbi Meir*, how can one give it as a gift? *V'amar maaser mamon gavoah hu* — he holds it is God's money. One may have the right to bring it to Jerusalem and eat it there, but it is not one's property to transfer to someone else.

### Tevel Resolution

The *gemara* answers: *la, l'olam Rabbi Meir* — no, the *mishna* can still reflect *Rabbi Meir*'s view. *V'hacha b'mai askinan k'de'yahiv lei b'tevel* — what are we dealing with? A case in which the original owner gave the produce to the recipient while it was still *tevel* — before *trumot u'maasrot* had been separated. The giver said, in effect, here is some of my crop; take it, and you handle the separation of tithes. The *maaser sheni* thus never belonged to the first person in its final sanctified form; it was given as *tevel*, and it was the recipient who rendered it *maaser sheni* through his own act of separation.

One might press the point: even at the stage of *tevel*, the future *maaser sheni* already exists within the produce in potential — why does that not prevent transfer? The *gemara* responds that this *tanna* holds the position of *matnas shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu d'mi'an* — that gifts not yet separated are treated as though they already have been. On this view, before separation, the grain is simply *tevel*, an undifferentiated whole; the future *maaser sheni* does not have independent status yet, and therefore the entire *tevel* belongs to the owner to transfer. Once transferred, the recipient separates the tithe, and it is his own *maaser sheni* that emerges from his own produce. The *mishna* is therefore entirely consistent with *Rabbi Meir*.

On the related question of why *me'ilah* does not apply to *maaser sheni*: *me'ilah* applies only to things sanctified to the *beit hamikdash* — a *korban*, or something dedicated to *bedek habayis*. *Maaser sheni* has *kedushah*, but it is *kedushah* of a different type — the obligation to eat the produce in Jerusalem. It is a categorically distinct form of sanctity.

### Neta Reva'i Case

The *gemara* then attempts again: *ta shma* — come hear. Another *mishna* teaches: *hapodeh neta reva'i shelo* — one who redeems his own *neta reva'i*, his fourth-year fruit — adds a fifth. This applies *bein mishelo bein shenitan lo b'matanah*, whether the fruit is his own or was given to him as a gift. The implication is that ownership of *neta reva'i* can genuinely be transferred between individuals.

Critically, the *tevel* answer does not apply here. Fourth-year fruit does not exist as *tevel* and then become *neta reva'i* through an act of separation. Everything that grows in the fourth year of the vine or tree immediately has the status of *neta reva'i* — or *kerem reva'i* — which *Beit Hillel* treats as equivalent to *maaser sheni*. There is no prior stage at which the fruit is merely *tevel* that can be transferred before acquiring its sacred status. Yet the *mishna* states that it can be given as a gift and genuinely acquired by the recipient. This appears to be an unambiguous *stam mishna* like *Rabbi Yehuda*, who holds *maaser sheni* is *mamon hedyot*.

### Smadar Answer

The *gemara* again insists: *la, l'olam Rabbi Meir* — the *mishna* can be explained as reflecting *Rabbi Meir*'s position. *V'hacha b'mai askinan kegon d'yahiv lei k'shehu smadar* — we are dealing with a case in which the owner transferred the vines to the recipient while the grapes were still in the unripe *smadar* stage, before they had developed into actual fruit. Since they had not yet become a *pri*, they had not yet acquired the status of *neta reva'i*. While they remained *smadar*, they were still ordinary property, and the owner could transfer them freely. The recipient then came to own the vines at the point the grapes ripened into *neta reva'i*, and so it is his own *neta reva'i* that he redeems. This reading diverges from the position of *Rabbi Yosi*, who holds that even at the *smadar* stage the fruit is already considered a *pri* and therefore already *orlah*-relevant — the present explanation cannot proceed according to *Rabbi Yosi*.

The irony is not lost: the natural reading of both *mishnayot* supports *Rabbi Yehuda*. These explanations are genuine *kvetches*. Nevertheless, because a *stam mishna* like *Rabbi Meir* exists, the *gemara* prefers to reinterpret those *mishnayot* as compatible with *Rabbi Meir* rather than acknowledge two *stamim* in favor of *Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Meshichah Sale

The *gemara* tries a third time. Another *mishna* in *maaser sheni* states: *mashach heimenu maaser b'selah* — someone pulled *maaser sheni* into his possession at the agreed price of one *selah*, performing *meshichah*, the formal act of acquisition. But *velo hispik lifstoso ad she-amad bish'tayim* — before he got around to completing the redemption by handing over the money, the market value of the produce doubled. The *mishna* rules *noten selah umistaker besela* — he pays the original agreed price and profits the difference. *U'maaser sheni shelo* — and the *maaser sheni* is his.

The underlying mechanics require some analysis. The act that determines the purchase price is the *meshichah*: once he performed *meshichah*, the transaction was legally finalized at the price agreed upon at that moment. Even though the money has not yet changed hands — and handing over the money would constitute the act of *pidyon*, redemption — the sale price was set at *meshichah*, and any subsequent change in market value does not alter his obligation. He pays the original *selah*, and the *kedushah* of the *maaser sheni* transfers onto that money.

### Meshichah Logic

Now the *gemara* identifies the problem. *Mani* — who is this *mishna* going like? If it is *Rabbi Meir*, there is a fundamental difficulty. *Rabbi Meir* holds *maaser sheni* is *mamon gavoah*. If so, there can be no *mechira*, no sale. The transaction cannot be treated as a commercial exchange finalized by *meshichah*, because *meshichah* effects acquisition only when ownership can genuinely be transferred. If it is God's money and not the seller's private property, *meshichah* is meaningless. What can happen is only *pidyon* — redemption — and *pidyon* takes effect at the moment the money is handed over, by the verse *v'nasan es hakesef vekam lo*, one gives the money and it is established. If that is the operative moment, then when the money is handed over and the value has risen to twenty, the redemption must be calculated at the current value of twenty. The fact that *meshichah* finalizes the transaction and locks in the lower price demonstrates that this is a genuine sale, treating *maaser sheni* as *mamon hedyot*. This is, apparently, an unambiguous *stam mishna* like *Rabbi Yehuda*.

The *gemara* concedes: *ella l'olam Rabbi Yehuda* — fine, this *mishna* is *Rabbi Yehuda*. 

---

## Eduyos Authority

### Two vs One

At this point the *gemara* recalibrates. *Ve'hacha chad stama ve'hacha trei stami* — here we have one anonymous *mishna* like *Rabbi Yehuda*, and elsewhere we have two *stam mishnayot* like *Rabbi Meir*. The first two *mishnayot* — the *tevel* case and the *smadar* case — were reinterpreted through strained but technically possible readings; the *meshichah* case is conceded to *Rabbi Yehuda*. But the *mishna* about *Beit Hillel* and *peret u'olelot* from *neta reva'i* appears both in Masechet Ma'aser Sheni and again in Masechet Eduyot, giving us two *stamim* aligned with *Rabbi Meir* against one with *Rabbi Yehuda*. We rule by the majority.

### Eduyos Weight

The *gemara* then raises a sharper objection: *mai li chad stama mai li trei stamei* — what difference does it make whether a *stam* appears once or twice? If a *stam mishna* carries authority because it represents *Rebbe*'s final ruling, why should mere repetition amplify that authority? The same *mishna* appearing in two places should not count as two separate votes.

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* therefore offers the true basis for the ruling: *ho'il ve'isnan bi'vchirasa kevasei* — since we have a *stam mishna* like *Rabbi Meir* in the chosen *masechet*, in the *masechet* of choice. That *masechet* is Eduyot. The *mishnayot* of Masechet Eduyot carry greater weight than *mishnayot* elsewhere, because Eduyot is a tractate of authentic, carefully preserved testimonies and traditions. A *stam mishna* in Eduyot therefore carries special authority that tips the balance in favor of *Rabbi Meir*.

### Authority Tension

There is a striking irony embedded in this ruling. Masechet Eduyot was taught, according to the *gemara*, precisely when the doors of the *beit midrash* were opened to all — when *Rabban Gamliel* was replaced as head and a more inclusive policy was adopted. The *mishna* records that on that day the benches had to be multiplied to accommodate the flood of new students. Even ordinary craftsmen — weavers, for instance — came forward and transmitted authentic traditions they had preserved. The very tractate whose *stamim* carry the highest halachic weight was compiled under maximally populist circumstances, admitting testimony from people who would not normally have been considered *talmidei chachamim*. Yet what they transmitted carries more authority, not less. This tension — between elitist and populist sources of authority — runs deep through the structure of *halacha*, and echoes in the ongoing question of how much weight to give communal practice against canonical sources, or canonical sources against communal practice.

This is why we rule that *maaser sheni* is *mamon gavoah*, following *Rabbi Meir*, even though the natural reading of several *stam mishnayot* supports *Rabbi Yehuda*.

---

## Wandering Animal

### Animal Types

We now turn to a new topic introduced at the opening of 55a, drawn from a *mishna* in Shekalim. The *mishna* teaches: *behemah shenimtzes miYerushalayim leMigdal Eder* — an animal found wandering in the area between Jerusalem and Migdal Eder, approximately fifteen kilometers south of the city, and within a comparable radius in every direction. *Zcharim olos* — if it is a male, we presume it is an *olah*. *Nekeivos zivchei shelamim* — if it is a female, we presume it is a *shelamim*. The reasoning behind these presumptions is that in the vicinity of Jerusalem, where animals were brought constantly for *korbanot*, and where private individuals generally did not raise livestock within the city itself, a wandering animal is most likely a sacrificial animal.

### Male Ambiguity

The *gemara* immediately interrupts with a question: it is true that all *olos* are male, but it does not follow that all males are *olos*. A *shelamim* can also be male. Why, then, when we find a male animal, do we not also consider the possibility that it might be a *shelamim*?

### Monetary Obligation

*Rabbi Oshaya* explains: *hacha bavo lachov bidmeihem askinan* — what the *mishna* is dealing with is not simple identification of the animal's status, but a situation in which a *tzaddik*, a conscientious person who found this animal, wishes to ensure that the *kedushah* is properly handled and is willing to incur personal monetary obligation to do so. The male has the possibility of being an *olah*, and the female can only be a *shelamim*. The question is what practically to do with such an animal — and that is what the *mishna* and the subsequent *gemara* discussion are working out.

---

## Me'ilah B'Mezid

### Rashi Dual Dedication

*Rabbi Oshaya*'s resolution of the *mishna* invokes the position of *Rabbi Meir*: *Rabbi Meir hi de'amar hekdesh b'mezid mitchalel* — it is *Rabbi Meir* who holds that *hekdesh* can be desacralized and transferred to *chullin* even through an intentional act. On *Rashi*'s reading, the procedure works as follows. Since the male animal might be either an *olah* or a *shelamim*, the *tzaddik* takes two separate piles of money, each equal to the animal's value. He declares: if this animal is an *olah*, I am transferring its *kedushah* to pile A, and I am simultaneously dedicating pile B as a *shelamim* as a voluntary gift; if this animal is a *shelamim*, I am transferring its *kedushah* to pile B, and I am simultaneously dedicating pile A as an *olah* as a voluntary gift. The result is that one pile carries the transferred *kedushah* and the other carries his own voluntary dedication — one is an *olah* and one is a *shelamim* — and the animal itself is redeemed. Both the *olah* and *shelamim* obligations are thus fulfilled, covering whichever the animal actually was.

### Tosafot Theft

*Tosafot* reads the mechanism differently, and while this reading is probably closer to the *pshat* of the *gemara*, it is striking enough that one can understand why *Rashi* sought an alternative. According to *Tosafot*, the *tzaddik* — precisely because he wishes to properly resolve the animal's status — takes the animal for himself. This is an act of *me'ilah*. He is fully aware of what he is doing; it is *b'mezid*. According to *Rabbi Meir*, *hekdesh b'mezid mitchalel* — this intentional act of *me'ilah* removes the *kedushah* from the animal and renders it *chullin*. The *tzaddik* then contributes both an *olah* and a *shelamim* to the *beit hamikdash* from his own funds, thus ensuring that the *beit hamikdash* receives its due regardless. He has, in effect, exposed himself to the transgression of *me'ilah* in order to resolve the animal's problematic status — hence the phrase *bavo lachov bidmeihem*, coming to incur an obligation commensurate with their value.

### Kedusha Removal

The *gemara* raises the obvious difficulty: even granting *Rabbi Meir*'s position that *me'ilah b'mezid* can remove *kedushah*, that principle was articulated with respect to *hekdesh* funds — money or property owned by the *beit hamikdash*, which is *bedek habayis*. *Bedek habayis* is essentially the *beit hamikdash*'s bank account: the institution owns the asset and can dispose of it as it sees fit. It is understandable that an act of misappropriation could sever that ownership relationship and render the object *chullin*.

But an animal dedicated as a *korban* has *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic sanctity. Its *kedushah* does not consist merely in being owned by the *beit hamikdash*; rather, the *korban* itself, in its very identity, is sacred. Why would an act of *me'ilah*, even *b'mezid*, have the power to remove a *kedushah* that defines the object's essential nature? The question becomes: does *me'ilah b'mezid* extend to *kedushat haguf*?

---

## Kedushat HaGuf

### Multiple Me'ilot

The *gemara* brings a *mishna* that bears directly on this question. The *mishna* states: *ein moel achar moel b'mukkdashim ella b'vehema u've'klei shares bilvad* — one cannot do multiple acts of *me'ilah* on the same sanctified object, except in the case of an animal (*korban*) or the sacred vessels (*klei shares*). The reason one generally cannot transgress *me'ilah* twice on the same object is that once *me'ilah* has been committed, the object exits *kedushah* and becomes *chullin* — there is nothing sacred left to misuse a second time. The exception for animals and *klei shares* demonstrates that these objects, possessing *kedushat haguf*, retain their *kedushah* even after an act of *me'ilah*. Multiple individuals can ride upon a *korban* animal or drink from a sacred golden goblet, and each one commits *me'ilah*, because the *kedushah* of these objects is not extinguished by being misused.

### Survival Question

This *mishna* poses a sharp problem. If *kedushat haguf* survives even *me'ilah*, how can *me'ilah b'mezid* be said to remove the *kedushah* from this wandering animal? The very *mishna* just cited teaches that *kedushat haguf* persists through *me'ilah*.

### Strength of Act

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between the positions of *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir*. *Rav amar Rabbi Yehuda hekdesh b'shogeg mitchalel kedushat haguf lo mitchalel* — *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that *hekdesh* goes out to *chullin* only *b'shogeg*, not *b'mezid*, and moreover, *kedushat haguf* never goes out to *chullin* through *me'ilah* at all. One then asks: why should *Rabbi Meir* disagree on this latter point? Even if *Rabbi Meir* extends the effect of *me'ilah* to *b'mezid*, why should that change the rule regarding *kedushat haguf*?

The *gemara* answers with a crucial conceptual distinction. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, *me'ilah* operates only *b'shogeg*. An inadvertent misuse is, inherently, a weak act — one did not intend it, did not consciously strive to appropriate or to desacralize. Because the act is weak, it can sever a relationship of ownership (*kedushat damim*, the *beit hamikdash*'s proprietary claim), but it cannot penetrate and negate a *kedushah* that defines the object's very identity. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, the *mishna*'s rule that *kedushat haguf* survives *me'ilah* is entirely coherent: *me'ilah b'shogeg* is simply not a strong enough act to dislodge something so fundamental.

But according to *Rabbi Meir*, *me'ilah* can occur *b'mezid* — and *me'ilah b'mezid* is qualitatively different. When a person consciously, deliberately intends to remove an object from the domain of the *beit hamikdash* and take it into his own possession — *hacha ka michaven la'apukeia lechullin*, here he is intending to bring it out to *chullin* — that is an act of a fundamentally stronger character. It is, in a sense, the most aggressive possible form of appropriation. And according to *Rabbi Meir*, an act of that strength is sufficient to negate even *kedushat haguf*. The intuition is compelling: if any act is going to change the status of something intrinsically holy, it would be a maximally intentional, deliberate effort to desacralize it, not an accidental stumble.

The *gemara* further develops this: *amar lei hahu me'rabbanan, Rabbi Yaakov shemei, kal vachomer* — one of the rabbis, a figure named *Rabbi Yaakov*, argued from a *kal vachomer*: if *kodshei kodashim*, the most holy things, can be brought out to *chullin* through *me'ilah b'mezid* according to *Rabbi Meir*, then *kodashim kalim* — things of lesser sanctity, like a *shelamim*, which the owner himself will eat — should certainly be susceptible to losing their *kedushah*, since their sanctity is of a lower order and therefore more easily displaced. One might have thought the reverse: that a lower level of *kedushah* is more resistant to removal because it is less fragile. But the *kal vachomer* presses the other direction — lesser *kedushah* yields more readily, not less.

This is confirmed in a *baraita*: *amar Rabbi Chama b'Rabbi Yaakov amar Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina, haya Rabbi Meir omer* — *Rabbi Meir* used to say: *hekdesh b'mezid mitchalel, b'shogeg ein mitchalel, echad kodshei kodashim v'echad kodashim kalim* — *hekdesh* goes out to *chullin* through intentional *me'ilah*, not through inadvertent *me'ilah*, and this applies equally to *kodshei kodashim* and to *kodashim kalim*. The *kal vachomer* is then stated explicitly.

### Sin Objection

*Rabbi Yochanan* was astounded by the reading of *Rabbi Oshaya*: *V'chi omrim lo l'adam amod v'chata bishvil shetizkeh* — does one tell a person, "Go and sin so that things will work out properly with this animal"? Could the *mishna* actually be instructing someone to commit *me'ilah* deliberately as a matter of course?

---

## Blemish Solution

### Male Procedure

*Rabbi Yochanan* therefore offers an entirely different reading of the *mishna*, free of any intentional transgression. *Mamtin lo ad sheyista'eiv* — one simply waits until the animal develops a *mum*, a blemish. Once it has a *mum*, it can be redeemed without restriction. Having redeemed the blemished animal, one then brings two substitute animals and makes a conditional declaration: if this wandering animal is an *olah*, I am transferring its *kedushah* to animal A, and I am voluntarily dedicating animal B as a *shelamim*; if it is a *shelamim*, I am transferring its *kedushah* to animal B, and I am voluntarily dedicating animal A as an *olah*. One then brings both animals. The *tzaddik* is out the cost of two animals, but no transgression has occurred.

### Three Animals

The *gemara* immediately challenges: why only two animals? *Dilma todah hi* — perhaps the animal is a *todah*, a thanksgiving offering, which is a subspecies of *shelamim* that can be brought by a male or female animal. One would then need a third animal to cover this possibility. *D'meisei nami todah* — fine, bring three animals. But *v'ha ba'ya lechem* — a *todah* requires bread loaves to accompany it. *D'meisei nami lechem* — bring the bread as well. If the animal turns out to be a *todah*, the *kedushah* transferred to the corresponding animal plus its bread; if not, the extra animal and bread were a voluntary *todah* dedication.

### Age Requirement

The *gemara* then asks: *v'dilma asham hu* — perhaps it is an *asham*, a guilt offering, which is male, presents a more serious problem because an *asham* cannot be brought as a voluntary *nedavah*. The *gemara* answers: *asham ben shtei shanim* — an *asham* must be two years old. Since the case in the *mishna* involves a one-year-old animal, the possibility of *asham* is excluded by age. The *gemara* further raises the possibility of *asham metzora* or *asham nazir*, both of which require one-year animals, but these are dismissed as uncommon enough to set aside — *lo shchiach*.

### Pesach and Bechor

*V'dilma pesach hu* — perhaps it is a *pesach* offering, which is also one year and male. The *gemara* answers that *pesach bizmano*, in its proper season, *miz'harei zehirei bei* — people are careful with their *pesach* animals, and one need not be concerned about a stray *pesach* wandering unattended. *V'shelo bizmano* — and if we are past the time of *pesach*, a *pesach* that was not offered in its time reverts to the status of a *shelamim*, and *shelamim* is already covered.

*V'dilma bechor u'maaser ninhu* — perhaps it is a *bechor* or *maaser beheimah*, both of which are male and one year old. The *gemara* answers: *g'mai hilchasa l'michli'inhu b'muman* — the established *halacha* for both *bechor* and *maaser* is that once they develop a *mum*, the owners may eat them outside the *beit hamikdash* without further ceremony. Since one is already waiting for a *mum*, this scenario is automatically handled: if the animal turns out to be a *bechor* or *maaser*, the owner simply eats it once the *mum* appears. *Hacha nami b'muman mi'achli* — here too, one eats it upon the *mum*.

### Female Status

The *gemara* turns to the second part of the *mishna*: *nekeiva zivchei shelamim* — if it is a female, it is treated as a *shelamim*. The *gemara* initially questions why one cannot simply bring it directly — but the problem is *dilma todah hi*, it might be a *todah*, which is also female. Fine, one brings a *todah* as well and covers the bread requirement. But then: *v'dilma chatas hi* — perhaps it is a *chatat*, which is also female and which cannot be brought as a voluntary *nedavah*. If this animal might be a *chatat*, one cannot simply bring it as a *shelamim*.

The *gemara* notes that a *chatat* must be in its first year of life — *chatas bas shnata* — and accordingly, if the found female animal is two years old, the *chatat* possibility is eliminated. But if it is one year old, *ishtakach bas shnata mai* — what then?

### Cell Confinement

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* in which *Chananya ben Chachinai* teaches that a one-year-old female goat — *ez bas shnata l'chatas* — evokes the verse's language for a *chatat*. The *gemara* immediately asks: but perhaps it is not a *chatat* at all — perhaps it is a *shelamim*? *Ella amar Abaye: k'chatas* — *Abaye* answers that it must be treated as a *chatat*. What does that mean in practice? *Konas'la l'chippa v'hi mesa mei'aleha* — one confines it in a cell and allows it to die on its own. There is no offering one can bring for it, since one cannot voluntarily bring a *chatat* that does not correspond to a specific obligation. Any other *kedushah* the animal might have — if it were a *shelamim* — can be transferred conditionally to substitute animals and dealt with through *olah* and *todah* dedications, allowing those to proceed, while the animal itself is left in confinement until it dies.

---

---

# Kiddushin 56

## Me'ilah & Ma'aser Sheni

### Recap Me'ilah

We pick up at the very bottom of 55b, where a *tanu rabbanan* opens a new section of the *gemara*. The preceding discussion had centered on a case of an animal found outside of Jerusalem whose identity as a particular type of *korban* was uncertain. That uncertainty served as an occasion to explore the position of Rabbi Meir, who holds that *me'ilah be'mezid* — intentional misappropriation of consecrated property — is halachically effective. The *gemara* had raised the possibility that according to Rabbi Meir, *me'ilah be'mezid* could operate even against something possessing *kedushat haguf*, intrinsic sanctity, since the power of a willful act might be sufficient to divest even a *korban* of its consecrated status. Under the ordinary rule, *me'ilah* does not remove *kedusha* from an object with intrinsic sanctity. The *gemara* further noted that this question would apply regardless of whether the animal in question was *kodshei kodashim* or *kodshei kallim*, with arguments running in both directions.

### Ma'aser Sheni Status

To step back and provide the broader framing: several days earlier, the *gemara* had addressed the foundational dispute over the status of *ma'aser sheni* — whether it is *mammon gavoah*, God's property, or *mammon hedyot*, the individual's own property encumbered with *kedusha*. The *gemara* concluded that by *ma'aser sheni* we rule like Rabbi Meir, who holds it is *mammon gavoah*, and that by *me'ilah* we rule against Rabbi Meir, rejecting the view that *me'ilah be'mezid* is halachically operative. Both issues, however, were explored in their own right regardless of the practical ruling. Now the *gemara* returns to the *ma'aser sheni* question and proceeds to examine several consequential and intricate *halachot* that arise from it.

---

## Animal Purchase Ban

### Rule: No Animal Purchase

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *ain lokchin behema b'dmei ma'aser sheni* — one may not purchase an animal with *ma'aser sheni* money. This prohibition applies outside of Jerusalem. Within Jerusalem, one may certainly purchase an animal and either slaughter it for its meat or bring it as a *korban*, since *ma'aser sheni* money is designated for food. The question is why one cannot purchase an animal outside of Jerusalem with that money.

### Rashi Explanation 1

Rashi offers two explanations. His first is that the only things one may bring to Jerusalem are the original fruit itself or the money to which it was transferred; one may not purchase other items outside and transport them in. According to this view, the animal purchase is invalid because the mechanism of *ma'aser sheni* transfer requires either the original produce or its monetary equivalent, not a further exchange.

### Tosafot Challenge

Tosafot challenges Rashi's first explanation by pointing out that it is in fact permissible to transfer *ma'aser sheni* to money and then use that money to purchase food, which one then brings to Jerusalem in place of the original fruit. It is not the case that only the original fruit or the original money may be brought — other food purchased with that money is equally valid. If so, Tosafot cannot understand why purchasing an animal outside of Jerusalem should be inherently problematic, given that one could simply slaughter it or bring it as a *korban* upon arrival. Rashi's first rationale, Tosafot argues, is thus without basis.

### Rashi Explanation 2

Rashi therefore offers a second explanation: the problem is that an animal driven on foot to Jerusalem will lose value in transit. Unlike other goods that can be transported without deterioration, a sheep or cow walked along the road will become less healthy, less fat, and therefore worth less upon arrival. The *ma'aser sheni* money thus suffers a loss. This is a rabbinic concern — the practical devaluation of the sacred funds.

### Tosafot Explanation

Tosafot adds a third explanation, also a secondary rabbinic concern. If one purchases an animal with *ma'aser sheni* money and then delays bringing it to Jerusalem, the animal may give birth, and its offspring would also carry the status of *ma'aser sheni*. One could quickly find oneself responsible for entire flocks encumbered with *kedushat ma'aser sheni*, which creates obvious practical difficulties and potential for abuse. For one reason or another, then — whether the animal's devaluation during transport or the proliferation of *ma'aser sheni* offspring — the Sages prohibited purchasing animals outside Jerusalem with *ma'aser sheni* funds.

---

## Unwitting Purchase

### Shogeg: Sale Reversed

The *gemara* moves to the top of 56a: *ve'im lakach bishogeg* — if one purchased an animal unwittingly, not realizing he was using *ma'aser sheni* money, then *yachzeru damim limkomam*, the sale is reversed. The money is returned to the seller, the animal is returned to the buyer, and the transaction is undone.

### Mekach Taos Principle

Rashi explains that this reversal is grounded in the principle associated with Rabbi Yehuda: had the buyer known he was using *ma'aser sheni* money, he certainly would not have wanted to violate this rabbinic restriction. Since, had he known, he would not have agreed to the transaction, the sale is treated as a *mekach ta'os* — an erroneous transaction — and is therefore void. This principle was already encountered earlier in the *sugya*, and here it applies straightforwardly.

---

## Mezid: Intent & Transfer

### Mezid Rule

The *gemara* now addresses the case of intentional purchase: *bemezid ta'aleh vetachel bamakom* — if he knew what he was doing and violated the prohibition anyway, the animal acquires *kedushat ma'aser sheni*, and he should bring it to Jerusalem and consume it there with that *kedusha*. What is done is done; the appropriate response is to move forward and treat the animal as having assumed the sanctity of the money used to purchase it.

### Rabbi Yehuda Limit

Rabbi Yehuda, however, qualifies this rule. He asks: *bameh devarim amurim* — when does this ruling apply? Only when the buyer was *bimitkaven velakach techila leshem shelamim* — when he intentionally purchased the animal with the conscious purpose of having its *kedusha* transfer, and with the plan to bring it to Jerusalem and eat it there with *kedushat ma'aser sheni*.

### Shelamim Use Case

The natural and obvious case Rabbi Yehuda envisions is the following. A person buys a sheep with *ma'aser sheni* money; the sheep takes on *kedushat ma'aser sheni*. He could simply slaughter it and eat the meat as *ma'aser sheni* food in Jerusalem. But since he is going to Jerusalem anyway, he takes the opportunity to bring it as a *shelamim*, thereby fulfilling his obligation to bring a *korban* while still retaining the ability to eat the meat — since a *shelamim* cannot be an *olah*, which would require burning the entire animal and preclude eating it. This double purpose is entirely appropriate, and in such a case Rabbi Yehuda's rule applies: proceed, bring the animal up, eat it in Jerusalem.

---

## Profane Transfer Concern

### Problem Scenario

Rabbi Yehuda continues: *aval bimitkavein lehotzi ma'os ma'aser sheni lechulin* — but what if the buyer's intention was not to transfer the *kedusha* to the animal but rather to spend the *ma'aser sheni* money and obtain a *chulin* animal in exchange? In this scenario, the buyer wishes to have steaks in his backyard rather than travel to Jerusalem, and he "sticks" the seller with the *ma'aser sheni* money. The seller, for his part, has agreed to this arrangement — perhaps because he is being offered more than he would ordinarily receive for the animal.

### Tosafot Reading

Tosafot's reading of this passage — which is clearer than Rashi's — presents a contrast between two intentional scenarios. In the first, the buyer knowingly transfers the *kedusha* of the money to the animal; he intends to bring a *shelamim* or eat the animal in Jerusalem with *kedushat ma'aser sheni*, and the transaction functions as an intentional and legitimate transfer of *kedusha*. In the second, the buyer knowingly spends the *ma'aser sheni* money — *lehotzi*, to spend it — in exchange for a *chulin* animal, deliberately avoiding the *kedusha* obligation and leaving the seller holding the *ma'aser sheni* money without a corresponding transfer of *kedusha* to the purchased object.

The phrase *lehotzi ma'os ma'aser sheni lechulin* thus means: to spend the *ma'aser sheni* funds in a transaction designed to yield *chulin* goods, while the money retains its *kedusha* in the seller's possession. The buyer intends to avoid the *kedusha* obligations entirely, and the seller may be complicit or simply uninformed.

### Misuse Risk

This scenario is deeply problematic. The *ma'aser sheni* money belongs in Jerusalem — it must be spent on food there, or its *kedusha* must transfer to something that will serve that purpose. By structuring the transaction as the buyer did, the money is diverted from its intended purpose. There is a real concern of *zilzul ma'aser sheni* — a degradation or misuse of the sacred funds. The seller may take the money and, thinking or hoping that the *kedusha* has been lifted, use it for ordinary purposes. The buyer has no intention of bringing anything to Jerusalem.

### Reversal Solution

Accordingly, in this scenario — *bein shogeg bein mezid*, whether the buyer was *shogeg* or *mezid* in a relevant sense — the sale must be reversed. The *gemara* notes that *shogeg* here refers to a buyer who did not even realize he was using *ma'aser sheni* money at all, in which case *mekach ta'os* applies directly. The *mezid* case refers to a buyer who knew it was *ma'aser sheni* money and intentionally structured the deal to keep the animal as *chulin* while leaving the seller with the encumbered funds. In both cases, *yachazir damim limkomam* — the sale is reversed. The Rabbis do not approve of this arrangement, and the reversal of the sale is the remedy. The concern is clear: the money is being diverted from its sacred purpose, and the seller may well misuse it.

This resolution is halachically sufficient, and the practical enforceability is a separate matter. The general principle is that by firmly establishing the halachic ruling, communal pressure and individual conscience play their role. Moreover, it is rarely a case of pure, calculating wickedness — most situations are more ambiguous, and the ruling creates the framework within which people are expected to act.

---

## Kiddushin Exception

### Kiddushin Valid

The *gemara* now raises a comparison to the *mishnah* before us: *Rabbi Yehuda omer bemezid kideish* — if one intentionally used *ma'aser sheni* money to betroth a woman, the *kiddushin* is valid. Here, too, the *ma'aser sheni* money retains its *kedusha* in the woman's hands — there is nothing for the *kedusha* to transfer to, since a woman is not a food item that can be eaten in Jerusalem.

### Why No Reversal?

This raises a pointed question. The woman is in an analogous position to the seller of the animal: she has received *ma'aser sheni* money, and in the back of her mind she might rationalize — as the animal seller might — that the *kedusha* has left the money and she can use it freely. The same concern of *zilzul ma'aser sheni* should apply. So why does the *gemara* not demand that the *kiddushin* be reversed, just as the animal sale is reversed? It is clearly a less drastic remedy to reverse a sale than to void a *kiddushin* — the latter would leave a woman thinking she is unmarried when she may not be, with all the attendant consequences for *ishut*. And yet, there is still a conceptual question: if the same misuse concern exists, why does it not generate at least a demand for reversal?

### Woman Knows Status

Rabbi Elazar answers: *isha yoda'at she'ein me'os ma'aser sheni mischallin al yadah, v'ola v'ochla b'Yerushalayim* — the woman knows that *ma'aser sheni* money does not lose its *kedusha* through her receipt of it, and she therefore intends to go up to Jerusalem and spend it properly there. But this is not simply because she is a woman receiving *kiddushin* money — the key factor is that she is a *chavera*, a member of that scrupulous, learned subgroup that is expert in precisely these laws. The term *chaver* or *chavera* does not denote scholarly achievement per se but rather membership in a community distinguished by its careful practice of these *halachot*. Because she is a *chavera* and is *yoda'at* — she knows — we trust that the money will be used properly and do not demand reversal.

This answer is, in a sense, a limiting principle: the case of *kiddushin* in the *mishnah* is not a general rule but a specific case premised on the woman's knowledge. The real rule, applicable across all scenarios, is that wherever we fear the money will be misused, we demand reversal. The *kiddushin* case is bracketed off as exceptional not primarily because of the severity of undoing a marriage — though that is surely also a factor — but because of the presumption that a *chavera* will handle the funds properly.

---

## Non-Food Purchases

### Challenge Posed

Rav Yirmiyah now challenges this framework. He raises the case of purchasing non-food items with *ma'aser sheni* money: *beheima tmei'a, avadim, v'karka'os* — a non-kosher animal, slaves, or land. In all of these cases, the *kedusha* of the *ma'aser sheni* money obviously cannot transfer, since *kedusha* can only transfer to food items. The money therefore retains its *kedushat ma'aser sheni* in the seller's hands.

### Presumption of Knowledge

Rav Yirmiyah's point is this: if the buyer knows that *kedusha* cannot transfer to non-food items — and this should be common knowledge, since the *halacha* that *kedusha* transfers only to food is well established — then by the same logic we applied to the *chavera* who received *kiddushin* money, the seller should be presumed to know that the money retains its *kedusha* and should handle it accordingly. If that presumption of knowledge justified not reversing the *kiddushin*, it should equally justify not reversing the sale of a non-food item.

### Gemara Response

The *gemara* responds that in fact one may not purchase these non-food items with *ma'aser sheni* money — *ein lokchim beheima tmei'a avadim v'karka'os b'me'os ma'aser sheni afilu b'Yerushalayim*, not even in Jerusalem. However, if one did purchase such items, there is an alternative remedy rather than reversal: *v'im lakach yochal k'negdan*.

---

## Yochel K'Negdan

### Non-Food Remedy

*Yochal k'negdan* — the buyer must spend an equivalent sum on food and eat it in Jerusalem. He is not required to reverse the sale; instead, he personally undertakes the obligation that the *ma'aser sheni* money was supposed to fulfill. This alternative remedy applies when the sale of a non-food item cannot be reversed.

### Interpretation Debate

There is a *machlokes* among the *ba'alei haTosafos* regarding the precise mechanics of *yochal k'negdan*. One view holds that when the buyer spends his own money in Jerusalem on food, the *kedusha* of the original *ma'aser sheni* money — still sitting with the seller — transfers onto the buyer's new expenditure, and the seller's money thereby becomes *chulin*. The other view holds that the seller's money remains *kodesh* and must still find its way to proper use; the buyer's *yochal k'negdan* expenditure is a *knas* visited upon him but does not automatically discharge the seller's *ma'aser sheni* obligation. Either way, the buyer must spend equivalent money and eat it in Jerusalem; the question of whether this action discharges the *kedusha* on the seller's funds remains the subject of dispute.

---

## Decision Framework

### Solutions Differ?

At this point, the *gemara* confronts an apparent inconsistency. We seem to have different legal solutions for different types of objects: reversal for a kosher animal, *yochal k'negdan* for non-food items, and nothing at all for *kiddushin*. The *gemara* asks why these distinct solutions apply to these distinct object types.

### Seller Presence Key

Shmuel answers: *keshebarach* — the distinguishing factor is not the type of object at all, but whether the seller is present. If the seller has fled or is otherwise unavailable, it is impossible to reverse the sale. In that case, *yochal k'negdan* is the only available remedy. If the seller is present, reversal is possible and is the preferred remedy.

### Decision Chart

The *gemara*'s framework thus yields the following decision structure. The first question is: does the recipient know that the *ma'aser sheni* money retains its *kedusha* and will use it properly? If yes — as in the case of the *chavera* who receives *kiddushin* money — no remedy is necessary and the transaction stands. If no — the normal case, in which we fear the money will be misused — then we proceed to the second question: is the seller present? If present, we reverse the sale. If not present, we apply *yochal k'negdan*. The differences between the *mishnah*'s cases involving a kosher animal, a non-kosher animal, and *kiddushin* are not intrinsic to those categories but reflect these underlying circumstantial differences that happen to characterize each typical scenario.

---

## Why Reverse?

### Default Question

The *gemara* presses further. Given that both reversal and *yochal k'negdan* are available remedies when the seller is present, why is reversal treated as the default? Why not simply apply *yochal k'negdan* in all cases?

### Fine the Seller

The *gemara* answers: *kansinan lemocher* — we impose a penalty on the seller. Reversal is the means by which this penalty is administered. When the seller is present, he is held accountable, and reversal — forcing him to undo a transaction he sought to complete — is the appropriate sanction.

### Seller More Eager

Tosafot explains why the seller is the one penalized rather than the buyer. If the remedy were *yochal k'negdan* rather than reversal, the seller would clearly prefer that outcome: he has already sold his animal or property, and the buyer is the one burdened with the obligation to spend equivalent money in Jerusalem. *Yochal k'negdan* is a *knas* on the buyer. Reversal, by contrast, is a *knas* on the seller, who is forced to undo the very transaction he was eager to complete. Moreover, there is a general presumption that the seller is always more eager to sell than the buyer is to buy — the seller wanted to be rid of his goods, and reversing the sale frustrates that interest. Thus, when the seller is present, reversal is the appropriate mechanism.

---

## Rectify Location

### Seller as Enabler

At this point the *gemara* introduces the famous principle: *lav achbara ganav ela chura ganav* — it is not the rat that steals, it is the hole it escapes through. The seller, by being available and willing to transact with *ma'aser sheni* money, provided the very opportunity that enabled the misuse. Without the seller's participation, the buyer could not have diverted the sacred funds. In this sense, the seller is the enabling condition, the "hole," and bears responsibility accordingly.

### Buyer More Culpable

The *gemara* itself, however, pushes back against this reasoning. After all, *ve'ee lav achbara chura mai ka'avad* — what good would the hole have done without the rat? The buyer is the one who actually possessed the *ma'aser sheni* money, who chose to spend it in this improper manner, who sought to obtain *chulin* goods while leaving the seller with encumbered funds. He is, if anything, the more culpable party — the one whose act we would most naturally identify as the *aveira*. Why then do we penalize the seller rather than the buyer?

### Rectify Not Punish

The *gemara* resolves this with the word *mistavra* — it stands to reason. Both the buyer and the seller are complicit; both parties participated in the problematic transaction, and arguments can be made for penalizing either. But the *gemara* shifts the frame: *kol heicha de'ika issura hatam kansinan* — wherever the problem currently resides, that is where we focus our intervention. And where is the problem? The *ma'aser sheni* money is now with the seller. That money has *kedusha*; it does not belong where it is. The goal is not to punish individuals but to rectify the situation — to return the money to a position where it can fulfill its sacred purpose. Since the money is in the seller's hands, we address that situation directly by reversing the sale and returning the money to the buyer, from whom it must then properly make its way to Jerusalem. The asymmetry of penalty is thus not really about culpability at all; it is about where the money is and what needs to be done about it.

---

## Issurei Hana'ah

### Six Categories

With the *ma'aser sheni* and *me'ilah* discussion concluded, the *gemara* now transitions to a new *mishnah*. We move from objects that are *kodesh* — sanctified — to a different category: *issurei hana'ah*, objects from which one is forbidden to derive any benefit. These are not objects possessing *kedusha* in the manner of *ma'aser sheni* or *hekdesh*, but objects that the Torah has placed entirely beyond the realm of permissible use.

### Object Examples

The *mishnah* enumerates several categories. *Orla* is fruit from the first three years of a tree's growth. *Kilai hakerem* refers specifically to the mixture of grape vine with other grain crops; a *kilayim* of two grain species without the vine would not render the produce forbidden, but the combination of vine with grain does. The *shor haniskal* is an ox sentenced to stoning because it gored a human being. The *eglah arufah* is the heifer whose neck is broken in the ritual performed when a murder victim is found outside a city. *Tziporei metzora* are the birds used in the purification process of the *metzora*. *Se'ar nazir* is the hair of the *nazir* that is shaved upon the completion of the *nezirut* period. *Peter chamor* is the firstborn of a donkey. *Basar bechalav* is meat and milk cooked together. And *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* are non-sanctified animals slaughtered in the *Beit HaMikdash*. All of these are *assurim behana'ah*.

### Kiddushin Invalid

If one attempts to betroth a woman using any of these objects — *hamikadesh be'orla eino mekudeshet* — the *kiddushin* is invalid. The reason is that these objects are legally valueless: since one may not derive benefit from them in any recognized way, they carry no legal market value, and *kiddushin* requires transfer of an object worth at least a *perutah*.

### No Status Transfer

A crucial distinction marks off *issurei hana'ah* from *kedushat ma'aser sheni*: *kedusha* can transfer. If I sell a *ma'aser sheni* item, the money I receive takes on the *kedusha*. With *issurei hana'ah*, no such transfer occurs. If one transgresses and sells a cheeseburger to another person for ten dollars, having violated the prohibition against deriving benefit from *basar bechalav*, the ten dollars received is entirely *mutar* — plain, ordinary money, free of any forbidden status. The *issur hana'ah* does not follow the proceeds. Therefore, if one uses that ten dollars to betroth a woman, the *kiddushin* is valid: the money is perfectly ordinary, and the *isur* on the original item does not encumber the sale proceeds.

---

## Tosafot Discussion

### Market Value Q

Tosafot raises a significant question on the *mishnah*'s rule that *kiddushin* with *issurei hana'ah* is invalid. The assumption is that such objects are valueless. But Tosafot points out that *chazal* permit deriving benefit from *issurei hana'ah* in a non-standard manner — *shelo k'derech hana'aso*. For instance, olives that have not yet ripened can be used for medicinal purposes in a non-food application. Since there is some category of permissible use, however narrow, someone might be willing to pay something for the item. If so, the object does carry some market value, and *kiddushin* with it should in principle be valid.

### Value Answer

Tosafot's first answer is that the quantity in question simply does not reach *shaveh perutah*. Even if theoretically someone would pay something for the object because of its limited non-standard use, the amount of the object being used in the *kiddushin* is insufficient to constitute a *perutah*'s worth of value via that restricted use. Only if one had enough of the substance to generate a full *perutah* of value through that unusual channel would *kiddushin* be potentially valid.

### Awareness Answer

Tosafot's second answer introduces a different principle. Even granting that enough of the substance is present to be worth a *perutah* through non-standard use, if the woman is unaware that her use of the object is restricted to this unusual mode — if she assumed she was receiving something she could use normally — then the *kiddushin* is void as a *mekach ta'os*. She never would have agreed to the *kiddushin* had she known she was receiving something with such a limited and atypical form of permissible use. This answer effectively transforms the *mishnah*'s ruling from a categorical legal statement about the valuelessness of *issurei hana'ah* into a circumstantial rule dependent on the woman's awareness.

### Rashba: Lawful Valuation

The Rashba offers what is likely the most straightforward *pshat* in the *mishnah*, and it cuts through both of Tosafot's answers. Tosafot's two answers effectively concede that if there is enough of the substance and if the woman is aware of the restricted use, one could marry a woman with *issurei hana'ah* — which is plainly not what the *mishnah* is saying. The Rashba therefore takes a more fundamental position: it is irrelevant what someone might actually pay for an *issur hana'ah* object. The law defines these objects as valueless. Since the Torah forbids any benefit that we would legally recognize as *hana'ah*, there is no legally cognizable value. Whatever a buyer might actually pay for such an object reflects a transaction between private parties that we do not prohibit — but it does not alter the legal classification of the object's value. As a matter of *halacha*, the object's value is zero. *Kiddushin* performed with a legally valueless object is invalid, regardless of what private market conditions might dictate.

---

## Sources & Proofs

### Orlah Source

The *gemara* now undertakes to trace the biblical sources for each of the *issurei hana'ah* listed in the *mishnah*. Beginning with *orla*: *ba'orlah minalan* — from where do we derive that *orla* is forbidden in benefit? A *beraita* is cited: the *pasuk* says *orlah lo ye'achel* — the uncircumcised fruit shall not be eaten. From this verse alone, I would know only that eating it is forbidden. How do I know that benefit is also prohibited — that one cannot use it for dyeing, or for fuel for a candle? The answer comes from the continuation of the verse: *va'araltem arlato* — make it entirely off-limits, as though it were uncircumcised. This language of total exclusion — *lirabot et kulam* — extends the prohibition to all forms of benefit.

### Kilai Source

For *kilai hakerem*: *bekilai hakerem minalan* — from where do we know this is forbidden in benefit? Chizkiyah cites the verse *pen tikdash* — lest it become sanctified. Chizkiyah reads this not as *tikdash* (become holy) but as *pen tukad esh* — lest it be deserving of burning by fire. This reading implies total prohibition: an object deserving to be burned is one from which no benefit may be derived.

### Rav Ashi Read

Rav Ashi proposes an alternative reading of *pen tikdash*: take it literally as *pen yihyeh kodesh* — lest it become like something holy. And since holy things — *hekdesh* — are forbidden in benefit, the same should apply to *kilai hakerem*.

### Objection

The *gemara* objects to Rav Ashi's reading. *Kedusha* is not a perfect analogy, because an object possessing *kedusha* can have that *kedusha* transferred to money, whereupon the original object becomes *chulin*. If *kilai hakerem* were truly analogous to *kodesh*, one might think that transferring its "status" to money would render the original produce permissible — which is clearly not the case.

### Resolution

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ela k'deChizkiyah* — better to adopt Chizkiyah's *drasha* of *pen tukad esh* rather than the *kedusha* analogy. An object deserving to be burned is absolutely off-limits, and this resolves the difficulty raised against Rav Ashi's reading.

---

## Shor Haniskal

### Neveilah Status

For the *shor haniskal*: *shor haniskal minalan* — from where do we know the stoned ox is forbidden in benefit? A *beraita* begins by noting that the verse commands *sakol yisakel hashor* — the ox shall certainly be stoned. Once stoned, the ox is a *neveilah*, an animal that did not undergo proper *shechita*. And a *neveilah* is already forbidden in eating.

### Redundancy Q

If so, why does the Torah add *velo ye'achel et besaro* — and its flesh shall not be eaten? We already know from the *neveilah* status that eating is forbidden. What does this additional prohibition accomplish?

### Slaughter Teaching

The *beraita* explains: *she'im shechato le'achar shenigmar dino assur ba'achilah* — to teach that even if one slaughtered the ox properly after the death sentence was pronounced — thereby circumventing the *neveilah* status and producing what would otherwise be ordinary slaughtered meat — it is nevertheless forbidden to eat. The ruling of *shor haniskal* takes effect at the moment the *gmar din* is rendered; from that point forward, all the *halachot* of *shor haniskal* apply, including the eating prohibition, regardless of how the animal subsequently dies.

### Benefit Source

But that addresses the eating prohibition. For the forbidden benefit aspect: *talmud lomar u'va'al hashor naki* — the verse adds that the owner of the ox is *naki*, clean. The *gemara* cites Shimon ben Zoma's *drasha*: this is like the expression *yatza ploni naki minichasav* — that person was cleaned out of his possessions, he had no benefit from them at all. The phrase *ba'al hashor naki* thus teaches that the owner is "cleaned out" — he retains no benefit whatsoever from the ox, meaning all *hana'ah* from it is forbidden.

---

## Lo Ye'achel Rule

### Standard Rule

Rabbi Eliezer articulates a general principle: *kol makom shene'emar lo ye'achel, lo tochal, lo tochlu* — whenever the Torah uses the formulation "shall not eat" in any of its conjugations, the verse includes *both* the prohibition on eating and the prohibition on deriving benefit: *echad issur achilah ve'echad issur hana'ah bemashma*. The standard biblical prohibition to not eat encompasses the full prohibition on benefit.

### Exception Case

The only exception is where the *pasuk* itself explicitly permits benefit. The example is *neveilah*: the Torah says one may not eat a *neveilah*, but then adds *lager asher bish'arecha t'tnena va'achalhah o machor l'nochri* — you may give it to the resident alien or sell it to a foreigner. This explicit permission to sell demonstrates that benefit is permitted. Absent such explicit permission, *lo ye'achel* includes the prohibition on *hana'ah*.

### Shor Application

The *gemara* now applies this principle back to the *shor haniskal* and raises a difficulty. Given Rabbi Eliezer's rule that *lo ye'achel* always implies *issur hana'ah*, why did the *gemara* need the *drasha* of *ba'al hashor naki* to derive that *hana'ah* is forbidden? Let the extra *lo ye'achel et besaro* itself teach us the prohibition on *hana'ah*!

The resolution: Rabbi Eliezer's principle applies when the eating prohibition itself was derived from the *lo ye'achel* of that very verse. But for the *shor haniskal*, the eating prohibition did not derive from *lo ye'achel et besaro* — it was already established from the *neveilah* status, which flows from *sakol yisakel*. Since the eating prohibition was independently derived from a different source, the *lo ye'achel* cannot serve double duty by additionally teaching *issur hana'ah*; the extra *lo ye'achel et besaro* must therefore be doing something else entirely. And what does it teach? *Af al gav deshachatei ke'ein basar assar* — even if the ox was slaughtered and has the character of ordinary meat, it remains forbidden. That is the *chiddush* of the phrase *et besaro*. The source for *issur hana'ah* must therefore come from elsewhere — and that source is *ba'al hashor naki*, which teaches that the owner is entirely cleaned out and retains no benefit whatsoever.

---

---

# Kiddushin 57

## Shor Haniskal

### Mishna Overview

The *daf* before us — Kiddushin 57 — opens at the bottom of 56b, dealing with the *mishna* that lists items forbidden in benefit (*issur hana'ah*), and therefore if a man attempted to betroth a woman using any of them, she is not *mekudeshet*, since such items carry no legally transferable value. Among the cases discussed is the *shor haniskal* — the ox condemned to stoning because it killed a person — which remains forbidden in benefit even if it was subsequently *shechted*, rather than actually stoned.

### Mar Zutra Challenge

The *gemara* raises a challenge — *matkif lah* Mar Zutra: when the *Torah* says that even its flesh (*besoro*) is forbidden, perhaps that applies only where one performed something akin to stoning itself — for instance, where one sharpened a stone into a blade and used it to slaughter the animal, *damechzei kisekila*, it resembles stoning. But if one simply used an ordinary knife, perhaps that would render the animal permitted.

### Slaughter Methods

The *gemara* responds on two grounds. First, *mi saki b'oraisa kesiv* — the *Torah* nowhere specifies a knife, and therefore there is no halakhic basis for distinguishing between one method of *shechita* and another; if one type renders the animal permitted, so should any other. Second, there is an explicit *braisa*: one may *shecht* with any implement — *bein betzur bein bezechuchis bein bekurmis shel kano* — whether with a rock, a piece of glass, or a reed splinter. The methods are legally equivalent, and the challenge collapses.

## Et Particle Debate

### Dual Prohibitions

The *gemara* now observes that both the prohibition of eating (*issur achila*) and the prohibition of benefit (*issur hana'ah*) are derived from the same phrase — *lo ye'achel es besoro*, its flesh shall not be eaten. Given that, what further need is there for the phrase *u'va'al hashor naki*, "and the owner of the ox shall be clean" — which has also been used to teach that the owner derives no benefit?

### Skin Benefit

The answer is that *u'va'al hashor naki* is needed to establish that one may not derive benefit even from the hide. Without it, one might have reasoned from *lo ye'achel besoro* — the word *besaro*, its flesh, is what is written — that the flesh is forbidden but the skin is permitted, and one could therefore produce leather from it. The phrase *u'va'al hashor naki* closes that possibility.

But what of those *tannaim* who deduce something else from *u'va'al hashor naki* — for instance, that one does not pay half-damages (*chatzi kofer*) or compensate for miscarried fetuses (*demei vlados*) in the case of a goring ox — and thus do not use that phrase to teach the prohibition on the skin? From where do they derive that the skin too is forbidden in benefit?

The answer is: from the word *es* — *es besoro* — the particle *es* coming to include *hamatfel lebesoro*, something that is secondary or attached to the flesh, namely the skin. And the opposing position — the one that does derive the skin prohibition from *u'va'al hashor naki* — does not employ the *et* particle hermeneutically at all.

### Shimon Ha'amsuni

This introduces one of the most striking passages in the *gemara*. At the top of 57a, a famous *braisa* is cited: Shimon Ha'amsuni — and some say Nechemia Ha'amsuni — would systematically interpret every instance of the particle *es* in the *Torah* to indicate an inclusion, something additional being taught. This was his organizing principle across the entire *Torah*.

*Keivan shehigia le'es Hashem Elokecha tira* — until he reached the verse commanding fear of God — *perash*, he withdrew. He could not bring himself to say that anything could be compared to or included alongside fear of God. His students immediately raised the obvious problem: *kol esin shedarashta mah tehei aleihem* — if this particular *es* teaches nothing, does that not undermine every other instance you have interpreted? Is the hermeneutical principle now invalidated retroactively?

His response was remarkable: *keshem shekibalti sachar al hadrisha kach kibalti sachar al haprisha* — just as I received reward for the interpretations, so too I will receive reward for the retraction. There is a question of how far this concession actually goes. One reading is that he means: I still believe all those other interpretations are true; I simply cannot in good conscience force this one, and if my inability to answer here casts doubt in people's minds about my other teachings, so be it — my intellectual honesty demands no less. The other, more radical reading is that *sachar al haprisha* means he was willing to surrender all those teachings entirely, rather than compromise on a *drasha* he did not believe. That would make the gesture even more extraordinary — the full sacrifice of a lifetime's learning in service of *emes*.

### Rabbi Akiva Resolution

*Ad sheba Rabbi Akiva v'limed* — until Rabbi Akiva came and taught that *es Hashem Elokecha tira l'rabos talmidei chachamim*: the *es* particle in that verse comes to include *talmidei chachamim*, whose fear and awe bears at least an analogical relationship — obviously not equivalence — to the awe of God, inasmuch as they represent and transmit His *Torah*. One elegant reading of this episode is that it was precisely Shimon Ha'amsuni's act of *perisha*, his public withdrawal rather than offering a forced answer, that made possible Rabbi Akiva's insight: only a tradition that demonstrates such radical commitment to *emes* could produce *talmidei chachamim* genuinely worthy of being mentioned alongside the awe of God.

## Egla/Metzora Analogy

### Egla Arufah

The *gemara* proceeds to ask: from where do we know that the *egla arufa* — the heifer whose neck is broken as part of the unsolved murder ritual — is forbidden in benefit? The answer given in the name of the school of Rabbi Yannai is: *kapar kesiv bah k'kodshim* — the *Torah* uses the language of atonement (*kapar*) in connection with the *egla arufa*, and therefore it operates on the same principle as sacrifices, which are forbidden in benefit.

### Tzippurei Metzora

Regarding the *tzippurei metzora* — the birds brought as part of the purification process for a *metzora* — the source is derived from a *braisa* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael. The *braisa* formulates a parallel structure: inside the *Beis Hamikdash*, the *Torah* mentions something that is *machshir* (changes the status of the *metzora*, namely the *asham* brought by the *metzora*) alongside something that is *mechaper* (provides atonement, meaning all other *korbanos*). The same pairing appears outside the *Beis Hamikdash*: something *machshir* (the birds of the *metzora*) alongside something *mechaper* (the *egla arufa*).

### Parallel Structure
