The logical structure is a *gezeira shava* of principle: just as inside the *Beis Hamikdash* the *machshir* — the *metzora's asham* — is treated like the *mechaper* and is forbidden in benefit, so too outside the *Beis Hamikdash* the *machshir* — the *metzora's* birds — is treated like the *mechaper*, and since the *egla arufa* is forbidden in benefit, so too the birds are forbidden in benefit.

## Metzora Birds Timeli (II)

### Yochanan/Lakish

An *amoraic* dispute now turns on the question of precisely *when* the *tzippurei metzora* become forbidden in benefit. Rabbi Yochanan holds: *mishe'as shechita* — from the moment of *shechita*. One bird is slaughtered and the other is dipped in its blood and water and released; the act of *shechita* is what triggers the prohibition. Reish Lakish holds: *mishe'as lekicha* — from the moment of purchase.

It is worth noting — as *Rashi* and most *Rishonim* understand — that the sent bird also acquires forbidden status at some point, but ultimately becomes permitted once sent free. According to Reish Lakish, both birds become forbidden from the moment of purchase; the released bird subsequently regains its permitted status upon release. According to Rabbi Yochanan, both become forbidden from the moment of *shechita*, and the released bird then regains permitted status. *Rashi*'s alternative reading — that according to Rabbi Yochanan only the slaughtered bird ever becomes forbidden while the sent bird was never forbidden — does not accord easily with the plain language of the *mishna*, which lists "the birds of the *metzora*" without distinction.

Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning is simply that *shechita hi d'asra lah* — it is the act of *shechita* that creates the forbidden status. Reish Lakish's reasoning is that we derive the prohibition of the *metzora* birds from *egla arufa*. The *egla arufa* is forbidden *michayim* — while still alive — just as sacrifices become forbidden while still alive. Therefore, the *metzora* birds are likewise forbidden while still alive, and since they are alive at the time of purchase, from that point the prohibition takes effect.

## Egla Timeline

### Yannai Memory

The *gemara* now turns to the *egla arufa* itself: when precisely does it become forbidden? Rabbi Yannai says: *gvul shamati bah v'shachachti* — I recall that there is a significant point in the process that triggers the prohibition, but I no longer remember which point.

### Wadi Descent

The colleagues — *chavraya* — propose: *yeridasah lenachal eisan hi osartah* — it is the descent into the *nachal eitan*, the wadi, that renders it forbidden. This is a concrete, explicit moment described in the *Torah*, making it the natural candidate for the triggering event.

### Consistency Test

The *gemara* then asks: if the *egla arufa* is not forbidden from the moment of purchase, should we apply that reasoning consistently to the *metzora* birds — and say that they too are not forbidden from the time of purchase?

### Two Moments

The *gemara* rejects this: *hachi hashta? hasam is lei gvul achrina hacha leis lei gvul achrina* — the situations are not parallel. The *egla arufa* has its own distinct moment — the descent to the wadi — which is explicitly referenced in the *Torah*. The *metzora* birds have no such equivalent moment. And as *Rashi* points out, while the *Torah* says nothing analogous to the descent of the wadi by the birds, it does say explicitly that the birds must be purchased (*tikach*), thereby establishing the moment of acquisition as the operative trigger. Each has its own moment, but both become forbidden while still alive.

## Metzora Birds Timeli (II)

### Braisa Proof

Rabbi Yochanan now challenges Reish Lakish from a *braisa*. The *braisa* expounds: *kol tzippor tehorah tocheilu lerabos es hameshulachas* — "every pure bird you may eat" includes the sent-out bird, teaching that it is permitted in benefit. And *vezeh asher lo socheilu meihem lerabos es hashechutah* — the extra formulation teaches that the slaughtered bird is forbidden in eating — and by extension, given the *mishna*, in benefit.

Now, Rabbi Yochanan presses: if according to Reish Lakish the bird was already forbidden from the time of purchase — *michayim asura* — why does the *braisa* derive the prohibition specifically from the moment of *shechita*? If it was already forbidden before *shechita*, why would the text focus on that moment?

Reish Lakish's response is that this teaching is necessary nonetheless: one might otherwise have thought that the *metzora* birds are like *kodashim*, where the animal begins forbidden while alive but then *shechita* comes and renders it permitted (*mashchita umachshira*). The *braisa* therefore teaches that no — the *shechita* does not change its status to permitted; the bird remains forbidden even after the ritual has been performed on it.

### Status Resolution

The *gemara* then brings another challenge to Reish Lakish, this time from a *mishna*: *shachat venimtzah tereifah* — if one of the *metzora* birds was slaughtered and found to be a *tereifah*, one takes a replacement pair for the second bird, *veharishonah muteres bahana'ah* — and the first bird (the one found to be *tereifah*) is permitted in benefit. Like any *tereifah*, it does not carry the forbidden status of the *metzora* birds, because ultimately it was not used.

The challenge to Reish Lakish is sharp: if the bird was forbidden from the time of purchase, it was already forbidden before being slaughtered. Why, then, when its *shechita* fails because it is a *tereifah*, would it revert to being permitted? It was already forbidden!

The *gemara* resolves this: the case here is where the *tereifah* defect was found *bevnei me'eha* — in its internal organs — meaning a congenital defect, an organ that was missing from birth. Such an animal was never fit to serve as one of the *metzora* birds at all, and therefore *kedushah* never took effect upon it — *delo chalah kedushah klal*. Even according to Reish Lakish, who holds that the prohibition takes effect at purchase, if at the very moment of purchase the bird was already a *tereifah* by virtue of a congenital defect, the *kedushah* never attached. This is different from a case where the animal became *tereifah* only later — whether at the moment of *shechita* or subsequently — in which case, since it was whole at the time of purchase, the prohibition would have taken effect then and would remain in force even if the *shechita* ultimately failed.

### Improper Shechita

A further *tosefta* challenges Reish Lakish: if one performed the *shechita* without having the cedar wood, the hyssop, and the red string present — *shelo be'ezov ushelo be'erez ushelo bishni tola'as* — Rabbi Shimon rules that since it was slaughtered without fulfilling its commandment properly (*shelo kemitzvato*), the bird is permitted in benefit.

The *gemara* explains the dispute: *ad kan lo pligi ela* — the entire disagreement turns on whether *shechita she'eina re'uya* — a *shechita* that is not properly constituted — counts as a *shechita* for purposes of conferring the forbidden status, or not. Crucially, both disputants agree that it is *shechita* that gives the bird its status; they disagree only about whether this particular defective *shechita* accomplishes that. One holds that *shechita she'eina re'uya shema shechita* — even an improper *shechita* is still called *shechita* and triggers the prohibition, since the animal was set aside (*huktza*) for the *mitzvah*. The other holds that *shechita she'eina re'uya lo shema shechita* — such a *shechita* does not count and therefore does not confer the status.

The *gemara* concludes that this is a *tannaitic* dispute (*tannai hi*), and Reish Lakish aligns himself with the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which — as cited earlier — derives the birds' prohibition from *egla arufa* and therefore holds that they are forbidden *michayim*, from the time they are alive. That position belongs to Rabbi Yishmael's school, while those *tannaim* who ground the prohibition in *shechita* form the opposing view. The existence of that *tannaitic* disagreement means the challenge to Reish Lakish from the *tosefta* does not compel him.

## Sent-Out Bird Status

### Living Animals

The *gemara* now turns to a different question: is the sent-out bird permitted in benefit? The starting premise, offered in the name of Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, is that *lo matzinu ba'alei chayim she'asurin* — we do not find that living animals acquire a status of *issur hana'ah*. The ordinary rule is that forbidden statuses attach when an animal dies or is slaughtered, not while it is still alive. On that basis, since the sent-out bird remains alive, it should be permitted.

### Exceptions

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak immediately challenges this: what about an animal that was *muktza* or *ne'evad* — set aside for or actually worshiped as *avodah zarah*? These are living animals and they are forbidden. Rabbi Yirmiyah adds: what about an animal that performed *biah* in the presence of witnesses (*rovei'a venirba be'eidim*)? That too is a living animal which the *Torah* requires be put to death — and presumably it is forbidden in benefit even while alive. One could equally have cited the *shor haniskal* from our own *mishna*, which is forbidden from the time of *g'mar din*.

### Most vs. All

The *gemara* therefore qualifies the principle. The formulation is adjusted: *lo matzinu rov ba'alei chayim she'asurin* — it is not that no living animal ever acquires forbidden status, but that *most* living animals do not. These exceptional cases exist, but they are exceptions. The operative assumption, where we have a choice between deeming the living bird permitted and deeming it forbidden, is that living animals ordinarily do not carry *issur hana'ah*, and that is why we default to permitting the sent-out bird.

### Field Analogy

Rabbi Yishmael's school provides a textual basis: the *Torah* says *v'shilach al pnei hasadeh* — and he shall send it out over the face of the field. *Mah sadeh mutar, af hai nami mutar* — just as a field is free for use, so too this bird is permitted.

### Geographic Requirement

The *gemara*, however, questions whether the word *sadeh* really comes to teach that the bird is permitted. Perhaps the term is needed for a different *braisa*: *sadeh* means you cannot stand in Yafo and throw it into the Mediterranean, nor stand at the edge of the wilderness and fling it into the desert, nor stand outside a city and send it back into the city. Rather, you must stand within a city and send it out beyond the city wall, with an open field beyond. The word *sadeh* teaches a geographic requirement for how and where the bird must be sent, not that it is permitted in benefit. The *gemara* replies: if that were all, the text would not need the definite article — *hasadeh*. The extra *hei* teaches two things: *shema mina tarti*, both the geographic requirement and the permissibility of the bird.

### Rava Answer

Rava offers a simpler and more elegant answer: *lo amra Torah shlach l'takalah* — the *Torah* does not issue a command that would create a stumbling block. If the sent-out bird were forbidden in benefit, then after the ceremony no one would know which specific bird it was, and someone might find it and eat it, unknowingly transgressing. The *Torah* would not design a commandment that predictably leads people into transgression.

## Examples Series

### Nezir Hair

The *gemara* continues its survey of cases of *issur hana'ah*. Regarding the hair of a *nazir* — *bsar nazir* — the source is the verse *kadosh yihiyeh gadel pera sear rosho*, "holy shall be the growth of his hair." From the word *kadosh*, one derives that the hair is forbidden in benefit.

One might ask: perhaps *kodesh tofes es damav v'yotze l'chulin* — perhaps holiness works here the way it does with sanctified objects, where one can redeem them so that the money becomes holy and the object returns to ordinary status? The *gemara* answers: *mich'dinan kodesh kadosh k'rinan*. Though we read the word as *kodesh* for purposes of the *drasha*, the actual word written is *kadosh* — and here *Rashi* identifies a crucial distinction between a noun and an adjective. *Kodesh* is a noun, a status of sanctification that can in principle be transferred to money through redemption. *Kadosh* is an adjective, a descriptive quality inherent to the thing itself. An adjective cannot be redeemed away from the object it describes; it adheres to the thing and cannot be detached by transferring it to money. The hair of the *nazir* is intrinsically described as holy — it is not that holiness was assigned to it as a transferable status.

### Peter Chamor

Regarding the *peter chamor* — the firstborn donkey that was not redeemed — our *mishna* appears not to accord with the view of Rabbi Shimon. A *braisa* records a *tannaitic* dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the *peter chamor* is forbidden in benefit; Rabbi Shimon permits it. The *mishna* reflects Rabbi Yehuda's position.

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha clarifies: this dispute — and the *mishna*'s ruling of forbidden benefit — applies specifically *l'achar arifa*, after the donkey's neck has been broken because the owner did not redeem it with a lamb. On that everyone agrees it is forbidden. The dispute apparently concerns its status prior to that point.

### Basar B'Chalav

For *basar b'chalav*, the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives the *issur hana'ah* from the fact that the verse *lo tivashel gdi b'chalev imo* — do not cook a kid in its mother's milk — appears three times in the *Torah*. One occurrence teaches the prohibition of eating, one teaches the prohibition of cooking, and one teaches the prohibition of deriving benefit.

### Shimon Yehuda

The *mishna*'s ruling does not accord with the view of Rabbi Shimon Yehuda, who holds that *basar b'chalav* is forbidden in eating but permitted in benefit. His proof is from a juxtaposition: the *Torah* places *lo tivashel gdi b'chalev imo* adjacent to the verse *v'anshei kodesh tihiyun li*, "you shall be holy people to me," followed immediately by *u'vasar basadeh tereifah lo tocheilu lakelev tashlichun oto* — do not eat meat of a *tereifah* in the field; throw it to the dog. The *tereifah* is forbidden in eating but permitted in benefit — you may throw it to a dog, meaning you may derive benefit from it. Since the passage about *basar b'chalav* is juxtaposed to the *tereifah*, we learn: *ma lehalan assur b'achila u'mutar b'hana'ah, af kan assur b'achila u'mutar b'hana'ah* — just as *tereifah* is forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit, so too *basar b'chalav*. The *halacha* does not follow this view; we rule *basar b'chalav* is forbidden even in benefit.

## Chulin B'Azara

### Parallel Argument

The *gemara* now arrives at what is arguably the most complex case in the *mishna*: *chulin shenishchatu b'azara*, ordinary (*chulin*) animals slaughtered in the *Beis Hamikdash*. The source for this prohibition is not immediately obvious, since no verse explicitly addresses it.

Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Meir offers a structural parallel: the *Torah* implies *shchot li besheli v'shelcha beshelcha* — slaughter My things in My place, and your things in your place. We know from the prohibition of *shchutei chutz* that *kodshim* must be slaughtered inside the *Beis Hamikdash*; slaughtering them outside renders them forbidden in benefit. By parallel, *chulin* must be slaughtered outside the *Beis Hamikdash*: *ma sheli beshelcha assur, af shelcha besheli assur* — just as My things [slaughtered] in your place are forbidden, so too your things [slaughtered] in My place are forbidden.

### Karet Distinction

The *gemara* immediately probes whether *karet* applies to *chulin b'azara* by the same analogy: *ma sheli beshelcha anush kares, af shelcha besheli anush kares?* The *gemara* rejects this by citing the verse *v'el petach ohel moed lo hevio l'hakriv korban l'Hashem v'nichrat* — one who fails to bring a *korban* to the *Beis Hamikdash* and instead slaughters it outside incurs *karet*. The verse specifies *korban* — a sacrifice. *Al korban anush kares v'ein al chulin shenishchatu b'azara anush kares*: *karet* applies only to a *korban* slaughtered outside, not to *chulin* slaughtered inside.

But this creates a difficulty for the original analogy: since *chulin b'azara* does not carry *karet* while *shchutei chutz* does, the parallel is imperfect — *ika l'mifrach* — the analogy can be challenged. One can argue that the severity of the *kodshim* case (which includes *karet*) warrants the *issur hana'ah* there, but the absence of *karet* for *chulin b'azara* means the parallel does not compel us to apply *issur hana'ah*.

### Abaye Derivation

Abaye therefore offers an independent derivation. The *Torah* uses the formulation *v'shachat... v'shachato... v'shachat oso* — three separate mentions of *shechita* in connection with *shelamim* (peace offerings). Given that a single mention suffices to teach the law, why the repetition?

### Five-Step Logic

Because the *Torah* also states *ki yirchak mimcha hamakom v'zavachta* — when the *Beis Hamikdash* is distant from you, you may slaughter and eat. The implication: *berichuk makom ata zove'ach v'ee ata zove'ach bemakom karov* — it is when you are far from the *Beis Hamikdash* that you slaughter *chulin*; you do not slaughter *chulin* when you are close to the *Beis Hamikdash*, meaning inside it. *Prats le-chulin shelo yishchatu ba-azarah* — this excludes *chulin* from being slaughtered in the *azarah*. But from this verse alone, one might have thought the prohibition applies only to *tmimim* — unblemished animals that are fit to be brought as *korbanos*. And even if one would extend it to animals with blemishes (*ba'alei mumim*), on the grounds that they belong to the same general category (*min hamachshir*), one might not extend it to wild animals (*chaya*), and certainly not to birds, since birds are not brought as *shelamim* and are slaughtered differently.

### Shechut Repetitions

The three-fold repetition of *shechita* by *shelamim* — *v'shachat, v'shachato, v'shachat oso* — comes to close each of these gaps progressively: only *shelamim* are slaughtered in the *azarah*, not *chulin*, not blemished animals, not *chaya*, and not birds. And the phrase *ki yirchak... v'zavachta v'achalta* — when far away, you shall slaughter and eat — implies further: *mah she'ata zove'ach berichuk makom ata ochel, v'ee ata ochel mah she'ata zove'ach bemakom karov* — what you slaughter far from the *Beis Hamikdash* you may eat; what you slaughter inside the *Beis Hamikdash* you may not eat. This establishes the prohibition on eating *chulin b'azara*. The same three-fold repetition applies again to extend this eating prohibition to all the same categories — blemished animals, wild animals, and birds.

### Tereifa Parallel

Finally, the question remains: perhaps *chulin b'azara* is merely forbidden in eating, but one may derive benefit — for example by throwing it to dogs? Here the *gemara* derives from the verse *lakelev tashlichun oso*, referring to *tereifah*: *oso ata mashlich lakelev v'ee ata mashlich lakelev chulin shenishchatu ba-azarah* — it is the *tereifah* that you throw to dogs; you do not throw *chulin b'azara* to dogs. The juxtaposition with *tereifah* — which may be fed to dogs and thus is permitted in benefit — teaches by exclusion that *chulin b'azara* may not. That is how we derive that *chulin b'azara* is forbidden not only in eating but in benefit entirely.

---

---

# Kiddushin 58

## Intro: Assur B'Hana'ah

### Opening Context

The daf opens in the midst of a discussion about objects that are *assur b'hana'ah* — forbidden to derive benefit from — and whether a man who attempts to betroth a woman using such an object achieves a valid *kiddushin*. The Gemara has been working through the relevant cases systematically, and the primary focus at this point is *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah*.

### Chullin Ba'azarah

*Chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* refers to non-sanctified animals — ordinary *chullin* — that were slaughtered within the *Beis HaMikdash* courtyard. This act is prohibited, and the resulting meat is forbidden in benefit. The question is both how we know the act is prohibited and how we know the prohibition extends to *hana'ah*.

### Pasuk Source

The Gemara derives both dimensions from the *pasuk* that speaks of slaughtering and eating meat outside the *Beis HaMikdash*: *ki yirchak mimcha hamakom — vezavachta ve'achalta* — "when the place is distant from you, you shall slaughter and eat." The implication is that if one is *within* the *Beis HaMikdash*, one may not slaughter and one may not eat. Additional *psukim* extend the prohibition to all types of animals slaughtered there — even blemished ones, even species that could never be brought as a *korban*. From this web of verses the Gemara establishes both the prohibition of the act and the forbidden status of the meat that results.

---

## R. Shimon vs. Chachamim

### Braita: R. Shimon

The Gemara cites a *braisa* that introduces a dissenting voice. *Hamkadesh b'peter chamor, b'basar bechalav, uvchullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* — one who betroths a woman using a firstborn donkey that has not yet had its neck broken, or with meat and milk cooked together, or with *chullin* slaughtered in the *azarah* — *Rabbi Shimon omer mekudeshet*: Rabbi Shimon holds that the betrothal is valid in all three cases. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, say she is not betrothed.

### Logic of Positions

Rabbi Shimon's position in each case has a traceable basis. With respect to *peter chamor*, an earlier *braisa* already established that according to Rabbi Shimon, a firstborn donkey is not forbidden in benefit while still alive — only after its neck is broken does it take on a more restricted status, analogous to *eglah arufah*. The case here would concern the living donkey, where Rabbi Shimon is consistent with his own position. As for *basar bechalav*, a position attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda — that meat and milk are permitted in benefit — was cited the previous day. Rashi notes that *Rabbi Shimon le'shitaso* implies this is the standard Rabbi Shimon, namely Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, though some read his *girsa* as referring specifically to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda. Either way, there is a *tanna* who holds that *basar bechalav* is permitted in benefit.

### Not Biblical

The most striking element of the *braisa* is what it implies about *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah*: if Rabbi Shimon rules that a woman is betrothed through such meat, the Gemara draws the conclusion that *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah leRabbi Shimon lav de'oraisa* — for Rabbi Shimon, the prohibition is not biblical. As Rashi explains: *kasavar issuro lav de'oraisa, lo issur shechitah velo issur hana'ah* — Rabbi Shimon holds that neither the prohibition of the slaughter itself nor the prohibition of deriving benefit is of biblical force. Importantly, Tosafot notes in several places that saying the prohibition is not *de'oraisa* need not mean the act itself carries no biblical violation. It may mean specifically that the *status* of the meat produced — the consequence — is not biblically prohibited, even if the act of slaughtering it in the *azarah* might itself still be problematic on some level.

---

## Lav De-Oraisa Issue

### Rashi Explains

Rashi's comment establishes that when the Gemara says *lav de'oraisa*, it is making a claim about the resulting status of the meat: neither the prohibition against performing the slaughter nor the prohibition against deriving benefit from the outcome rises to a biblical level for Rabbi Shimon. The implication — that the prohibition is rabbinic — is what the Gemara acknowledges and what generates the next problem.

### Rabbinic Prohibition

This raises a pointed question: if the meat of *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* is only rabbinically forbidden in benefit according to Rabbi Shimon, can it nevertheless be used for *kiddushin*? The question has two competing frameworks. On one view, from the Torah's perspective the meat retains real value — it is edible flesh from which benefit can in principle be derived — and a woman who receives it has received something of value, so the marriage should take effect. The Rabbis' prohibition is a superimposed restriction, but it does not alter the Torah-level reality of the object. On the other hand, one might argue that the Rabbis have the power to affect ownership and can declare an object effectively worthless in order to enforce their enactment, or alternatively that within an observant community, an object that no one is permitted to purchase or use has no practical monetary value — *de facto* rather than *de jure*. The prohibition's practical effect collapses the object's market value to zero, regardless of its theoretical worth.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot addresses this directly. The Gemara in the chapter *Kol Sha'ah* quotes a teaching of Rav: one who betroths a woman from the sixth hour onward on *erev Pesach* — when *chametz* becomes forbidden in benefit — *ein chosheshin le'kiddushin*, the *kiddushin* does not take effect. This applies even with the type of hard wheat (*chitei de'kurdenayta*) whose *chametz* status is only rabbinic — *de'einam assurim ela mi'de'rabanan*. This appears to be a clear ruling that a rabbinically forbidden object cannot effect *kiddushin*, even when the prohibition is only rabbinic. The question then is how to reconcile this with Rabbi Shimon's ruling that *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* — which is only rabbinically prohibited according to him — can nevertheless be used for *kiddushin*.

---

## Tam vs. Rashi

### Tam Position

Tosafot resolves the tension by distinguishing between two types of rabbinic prohibition, following the view of Rabbeinu Tam. The case of the hard wheat on *erev Pesach* — in the sixth hour — is technically rabbinic, but Rabbeinu Tam explains that it sits within the immediate ambit of a biblical prohibition. The wheat itself may be genuine *chametz*; the only reason the prohibition at that specific moment is rabbinic is that the sixth hour has not yet fully elapsed. In a matter of minutes, the very same wheat will be forbidden *de'oraisa*. That proximity to, and structural position within, a biblical category gives the rabbinic prohibition a weight it would not otherwise carry. The Rabbis, in extending the prohibition to the sixth hour, are extending a biblically established category — and that extension participates in the stringencies of the biblical category, including the effect of rendering the object valueless for *kiddushin*.

### Rashi Position

Rashi, by contrast, reads the Gemara in *Pesachim* differently. On his reading, the wheat in question is not genuine *chametz de'oraisa* at all; the rabbinic prohibition there does not operate as an extension of the biblical category. Instead, the object itself is simply rabbinically prohibited — which might appear to make Rashi's position more permissive. Yet Tosafot acknowledges Rashi's reading and still must grapple with the question of how *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* differs.

### Extension Doctrine

Tosafot's resolution draws a structural distinction. When the Rabbis create a prohibition that is an *extension* of a biblical category — even if the particular case being prohibited is not itself biblical — the object is treated as carrying the full weight of the biblical prohibition, including being considered devoid of monetary value for *kiddushin*. By contrast, when the Rabbis create a prohibition that is entirely new, *whole cloth* — something that has no analogue or root in any biblical prohibition — the object is not stripped of its value, and a *kiddushin* effected with it would be binding. *Chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah*, on this analysis, is a standalone rabbinic category with no biblical counterpart, and therefore even if forbidden, it does not render the object worthless. The *chametz* of the sixth hour, however, is structurally part of the biblical *chametz* framework, and therefore carries biblical weight into the *kiddushin* analysis — even where the specific prohibition at that hour is only rabbinic.

---

## Burning Challenge

### Mar Yehuda Challenge

Mar Yehuda encountered Rav Yosef and Shmuel bar Rabba — the son of Rabba bar bar Chana — standing at the entrance of Rabba's academy and posed a sharp challenge. The *braisa* just discussed attributes to Rabbi Shimon the position that *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* allows *kiddushin* — implying that the prohibition is not biblical. Yet another source also attributed to Rabbi Shimon states: *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah yisarefu* — such meat must be burned. And not only that, but even a *chayah* — a deer or similar animal that could never be brought as a *korban* — must be burned if slaughtered in the *azarah*. Rashi explains the significance of the burning: ordinarily, things forbidden in benefit are buried, not burned. Burning is a special stringency reserved for disqualified *kodashim*. The reasoning is that when a *chullin* animal is slaughtered in the courtyard and cannot be eaten, observers will assume it is a disqualified sacrifice — and disqualified sacrifices are burned. The extension to a *chayah*, a species with no conceivable connection to any sacrifice, pushes this further: even there, the meat must be burned. This level of stringency suggests the prohibition is treated as fully biblical. How, then, can Rabbi Shimon simultaneously say the woman is betrothed when *kiddushin* is performed with such meat? Rav Yosef and Shmuel bar Rabba had no answer and were silenced.

### Rava Responds

They went before Rava, who was dismissive — calling them troublemakers — suggesting he had already explained this. His resolution: *hacha b'mai askinan? kegon shenishchata venimtza trefa* — the case in which Rabbi Shimon permits *kiddushin* is where the animal was slaughtered and then discovered to be a *treifah*, or was known to be a *treifah* when slaughtered. This is not a standard case. In a standard case of *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah*, Rabbi Shimon would agree that the meat is *assur b'hana'ah*.

### Shechita She'eina

The key principle underlying Rava's resolution is *shechita she'eina re'uya* — a slaughter that does not render the meat permissible. This principle was introduced the previous day: if the slaughter does not achieve its purpose of permitting the meat for consumption — because the animal was a *treifah* — then halachically the act is not categorized as a valid *shechita*. It therefore does not trigger the prohibition of *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah*, because that prohibition is predicated on an act of *shechita* having occurred, and a *shechita she'eina re'uya* is not such an act. The resolution is not an artificial narrowing of the case but is directly grounded in an explicit *braisa*.

---

## Treifah Status

### Known/Discovered Treifah

A *braisa* addresses the case explicitly: *hashochet et hatrefa* — one who slaughters an animal known to be a *treifah* — and *vehen hashochet venimtza trefa* — one who slaughters and then finds the animal to be a *treifah* upon examining the organs — *vezeh vezeh chullin ba'azarah* — and both cases involve *chullin* slaughtered in the *azarah*.

### R. Shimon vs. Chachamim

*Rabbi Shimon matir b'hana'ah* — Rabbi Shimon permits benefit — because the act constitutes *shechita she'eina re'uya*: since the animal was a *treifah*, the *shechita* did not accomplish its purpose of rendering the meat permissible, and therefore halachically no act of *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah* occurred. The *Chachamim*, however, forbid benefit: *osrim* — they hold that physically the act of slaughter was performed, the animal was indeed killed through *shechita* in the *azarah*, and it does not matter that the animal was a *treifah*. The physical act triggers the prohibition regardless. This *braisa* confirms that Rava's *oikimta* is not an ad hoc narrowing but rather reflects an explicit controversy that maps precisely onto the case — and this is why Rava referred to it as something he had already established.

---

## Money Transfer

### Status Transfer

The Gemara now pivots away from the entire list of *issurei hana'ah* to address a new question. What happens when one takes a forbidden object and sells it, thereby obtaining money? The act of sale was itself a transgression — but what is the status of the proceeds? The answer the Gemara establishes is that the status does *not* transfer. The meat and milk was *assur b'hana'ah*; one transgressed by converting it to money; but the money itself is fully one's own, unrestricted by any prohibition. One may use these proceeds to betroth a woman, and the *kiddushin* takes effect.

### Avodah Zarah

The Gemara asks: how do we know the status does not transfer? The answer: *midigallei rachmana b'avodat kochavim* — because the Torah explicitly states by the case of an idol: *vehayita cherem kamohu* — "you shall be under the ban like it." The phrase *kol she'ata mehaya mimenu* — anything that arises through it — acquires the status of the idol. So if one sells an idol, the money received carries the idol's forbidden status. This could suggest a general principle that selling any forbidden object transfers its *issur* to the proceeds. The Gemara rejects this: far from a general rule, the idol case is the exception.

### Two Verses Rule

The exception is proven by the principle of *shnei ketuvim haba'im ke'echad*: when the Torah teaches the same rule in two separate cases, it is signaling that these cases are the *exceptions*, not examples of a general rule. The two cases are *avodah zarah* and *shevi'is* — Sabbatical year produce — where the Torah separately establishes that the forbidden status transfers to whatever is exchanged for it. Because both cases are stated explicitly, we conclude that the *rule* is the opposite: for all other *issurei hana'ah*, the status does *not* transfer to the proceeds of a sale.

---

## Shemitah Transfers

### Redemption Model

The basis for including *shevi'is* among the exceptions is a verse: *yovel hi, kodesh tihye lakhem* — "it is the Jubilee year, it shall be holy to you." Just as something that is sanctified (*kodesh*) transfers its status to whatever it is redeemed into — and the original object is thereby desanctified — so too *shemitah* produce transfers its *kedushah* to whatever one obtains in exchange for it. One might then think that, as with *pidyon*, once the status transfers to the money, the original produce loses its *kedushah*. Against this the Torah says *tihye* — "it shall be" — *b'havayatah tehei*: it retains its sanctity. The original *shemitah* produce never exits its status.

### Last Object Rule

The Gemara illustrates through a chain of exchanges: if one takes *shemitah* fruit and exchanges it for meat, both the original fruit and the meat now carry *kedushat shevi'is* — meaning they must be consumed before the time of *biur* and cannot be used for other purposes. If one then exchanges the meat for fish, the meat exits the status and the fish take it on. Fish exchanged for wine: the fish exit, the wine enters. Wine exchanged for oil: the wine exits, the oil enters. The rule is *acharon acharon nitpas beshevi'is*: each successive exchange — the *last* object in the swap — carries the *shemitah* status. And *peri atzmo assur*: the original fruit itself always retains its status regardless.

### Exception Parallels

The Gemara's position that *shemitah* and *avodah zarah* are the two exceptions raises a certain conceptual question. *Shemitah* is not, at least at its core, an *issur hana'ah* in the standard sense — it is a *kedushah* status that governs how produce must be treated and consumed. It might seem more natural to include only *avodah zarah* as the single exception to the rule that status does not transfer, since *avodah zarah* is the paradigmatic case of an object forbidden in benefit. One could reasonably suggest that the analogy between *shemitah* and *avodah zarah* works because of the *biur* stage — after the time of *biur*, *shemitah* produce that has not been destroyed does become *assur b'hana'ah*, and perhaps it is from that angle that the Gemara makes the comparison. Regardless, the operative conclusion is clear: only by these two does the status transfer; for everything else, the proceeds of a sale are permitted.

---

## Mishnah: Terumot

### Objects Listed

The final *mishnah* of the chapter takes up a new category of objects that can be used for *kiddushin*: *hamekadesh b'terumos u'b'maasros u'b'matnos b'mei chatas u'b'eifer parah harei zo mekudeshes v'afilu Yisrael* — one who betroths with *terumah*, with *ma'aser*, with priestly gifts, with water used in the *parah adumah* purification process, or with the ashes of the *parah adumah* — the woman is betrothed, and this applies even if the man is a non-kohen.

### Priest Gifts

The *matanot* referred to are the portions of a slaughtered animal that must be given to a *kohen* — the *zero'a*, the cheeks, and the maw — as obligated by the Torah. *Terumah* and *ma'aser* are the portions of one's grain that must be given to a *kohen* and *levi* respectively. The initial analysis suggests these cases are relatively straightforward: *ma'aser* and priestly gifts carry no inherent sanctity that would restrict their use, and *terumah*, even if the woman cannot eat it herself, could be resold to a *kohen*. On this surface reading, the *mishnah* seems obvious — if one possesses *terumah*, it has market value and can be given in *kiddushin*. The Gemara, however, will complicate this picture.

### Chatas/Parah

The more intriguing cases are the *mei chatas* — water that has been or is to be mixed with the ashes of the *parah adumah* — and the *eifer parah adumah* itself — the ashes of the red heifer used in the purification ritual. These raise genuine questions: are these objects *assur b'hana'ah*? Do the ashes of an animal used for an elaborate purification ritual carry any forbidden status if applied to a non-purification purpose? If one possesses this water or these ashes, can they be sold? And in what scenario does one use them to betroth a woman? The Gemara will address these questions directly.

---

## Tovas Hana'ah

### Ulla's Position

Ulla offers a teaching that reframes how the entire *mishnah* is to be understood: *tovas hana'ah einah mamon* — the benefit one receives from the ability to choose which *kohen* or *levi* to give an obligatory gift to is not considered monetary value. This statement implies that Ulla understands the *mishnah* to be teaching precisely the case where the man does not own the *terumah* outright but has merely separated it and must give it away — the interest Ulla is addressing is not ownership of the object but the privilege of deciding its recipient.

### Separation Context

The scenario Ulla envisions is *hamafrish terumah mitvalo* — a man who has separated *terumah* from his grain, which he is now obligated to give to a *kohen*. He cannot keep it himself. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah*, on Ulla's reading, is about what exactly this man gives the woman when he betroths her with this *terumah*.

### Choice Benefit

What the woman receives, on this reading, is not the *terumah* in a full proprietary sense — she too must ultimately give it to a *kohen* — but rather the right to choose *which* kohen receives it. That privilege of selection — *tovas hana'ah* — is what Ulla characterizes as *einah mamon*, not genuine monetary ownership. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah* would then be that despite the man's lack of full ownership in the object, the *kiddushin* takes effect. This makes the *mishnah* a genuinely novel ruling rather than an obvious case.

---

## Rav Abba Challenge

### Contradiction

Rav Abba challenges Ulla. If *tovas hana'ah einah mamon* — if the right to choose the recipient is not monetary — then how can the *mishnah* rule that the woman is betrothed? *Kiddushin* requires the man to give the woman something of genuine monetary value, at minimum a *perutah*'s worth. If the man has no real ownership stake in the *terumah*, what has he given her?

### Easy Answer

Ulla's response is that the *mishnah* need not be read in the case Rav Abba assumes. The easy reading — which Ulla rejects as too trivial — is that the man actually *owns* the *terumah*. A non-*kohen* can come to own *terumah* in several ways: he might have purchased it from *kohanim* as a commercial venture, he might have inherited it from a relative who was a *kohen*, or similar scenarios. If the man owns the *terumah* outright, the case is obvious — *terumah* has market value, it can be sold to *kohanim*, and using it for *kiddushin* is a straightforward application of giving the woman an object of value. This reading, Ulla argues, trivializes the *mishnah*.

### Rashi Critique

Rashi makes the point explicit: the reason we cannot be satisfied with the easy case is that it renders the *mishnah* unremarkable. Of course one can betroth with an object one owns, even if it is *terumah*. The *mishnah*'s ruling demands a harder case to be interesting and to constitute a genuine *chiddush*. Therefore the *mishnah* must be speaking of a more complex scenario — which is what the Gemara proceeds to establish.

---

## Inherited Tevel

### Tevel Inheritance

The harder case the Gemara identifies: a *Yisrael* who inherited *tevel* — grain from which *terumos u'maasros* have not yet been separated — from his maternal grandfather, who was a *kohen*. He himself is not a *kohen*, since *kehunah* follows the father's lineage. Nevertheless, because of his grandfather's status, there is a potential claim to the *terumah* embedded in the *tevel*.

### Gifts Present

The operative principle: *matanot shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damyan* — gifts that have not yet been separated are considered as though they have been separated. The terumah exists in potential within the *tevel*, and a *kohen* who owns *tevel* is considered, on this view, to have already staked his claim to the *terumah* portion even before the physical act of separation.

### Grandfather's Claim

Because the grandfather was a *kohen*, his claim to the *terumah* portion of his *tevel* was already established during his lifetime, on the principle that *matanot shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damyan*. When the grandson inherits this *tevel* and separates the *terumah*, he is not separating *terumah* that is owed to any other *kohen* — he is separating *terumah* that was already owned by his grandfather, which he has now inherited. He may keep it himself. This is the genuinely novel case of the *mishnah*: the grandson is considered an actual owner of the *terumah* — not through *tovas hana'ah*, but through the inherited status — and betrothing with it is therefore effective. Ulla's point, then, is preserved: *tovas hana'ah einah mamon*, and the *mishnah* is not speaking of a case of mere *tovas hana'ah* but of real ownership transmitted through the grandfather.

---

## Chiyya to Huna

### Direct Question

Rav Chiyya bar Avin posed a direct question to Rav Huna: *tovas hana'ah mamon o eino mamon?* — is the benefit of choosing which recipient to give an obligatory gift to considered monetary value or not?

### Huna Answers

Rav Huna pointed to the *mishnah*: *tanitua* — you have learned it. *Hamekadesh b'terumah u'v'ma'aser u'v'matnot b'mei chatas u'v'eifer parah harei zo mekudeshes v'afilu b'Yisrael* — he understood the *mishnah* as Ulla had understood it, that the case involves a man who has separated *terumah* and must give it to a *kohen*, and whose right to choose the recipient constitutes the value given to the woman. From the fact that she is betrothed, Rav Huna concluded that *tovas hana'ah mammona*.

### Clarification Issue

Rav Chiyya pressed back: but haven't you already explained the *mishnah* as the case of a *Yisrael* who inherited *tevalim* from his maternal grandfather the *kohen* — a case of genuine ownership, not mere *tovas hana'ah*? If the *mishnah* was explained away as a case of real ownership, it cannot serve as a proof that *tovas hana'ah* is *mamon*.

### Rav's Deflection

The response: *hutzat* — that explanation, the maternal grandfather case, is excluded from serious consideration, or alternatively, it designates the speaker as following the approach of a scholar from *Hutzal*. The exchange becomes uncomfortable: Rav Chiyya took *hutzat* as an insult, implying he was not fit to be in the *beis midrash*. The speaker clarified that he meant *hutzat* in reference to the approach of Rav Assi of *Hutzal* — a buffering of the offense. But the underlying point stands: Rav Huna's answer is that the *mishnah* should be read in its primary sense as a case of *tovas hana'ah*, and that reading demonstrates *tovas hana'ah mammona*.

---

## Theft Debate

### Theft Case

The Gemara introduces a related dispute to probe the question of *tovas hana'ah* and monetary ownership further. If one steals *tevel* — grain from which *terumos u'maasros* have not been separated — from a non-*kohen*, how much must the thief repay? The owner would eventually be obligated to give away a portion: at minimum approximately 2% as *terumah* and 10% as *ma'aser*. Does the thief owe the full face value, or only the value of the portion the owner could actually retain?

### Positions

Rabbi holds: *meshalem lo d'mei tevelo* — the thief pays the full value of the *tevel*. Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda holds: *ein meshalem lo ella d'mei chullin shebo* — the thief pays only the value of the *chulin* portion — approximately 88% of the total.

### Benefit = Ownership?

The Gemara initially suggests this may reflect the debate about *tovas hana'ah*: Rabbi, who requires full payment, may hold that *tovas hana'ah mammona* — the owner's right to choose which *kohen* and *levi* receives the gifts constitutes genuine monetary ownership, and therefore the full value of the *tevel* belongs to him. Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda, who requires payment only for the *chullin* portion, may hold that *tovas hana'ah eino mamon* — the owner has no monetary stake in the portions destined for *kohen* and *levi*, and the thief owes nothing for them. Rashi's reading of this position is striking: it would mean that *tovas hana'ah mammona* implies full ownership of the face value of the object — not merely that the owner has *some* stake, but that he is considered the complete owner of those portions, able to demand their full market value.

---

## Matanot Status

### Reframing

The Gemara then offers an alternative framework in which the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda does not actually turn on the question of *tovas hana'ah* at all. Rather, all parties could agree that *tovas hana'ah eino mamon*. The dispute instead concerns the application of the principle *matanot shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damyan* — whether gifts that have not yet been separated are considered as though they already have been — to a specific factual scenario.

### Rabbi: Pre-owned

On this reading, Rabbi holds that *matanot shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damyan* — the obligatory portions are considered already separated and already owned by the eventual recipient. The owner of the *tevel*, on this view, already fully owns the entire hundred bushels because the *terumah* and *ma'aser* portions within it are treated as though they had already been separated and allocated to him — that is, if his ancestor was a *kohen* who owned the grain, the *terumah* was already his. Hence the thief must pay the full value.

### R.Y.B.Y: Not Pre-owned

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda disagrees: *matanot shelo hurmu* are *not* like *shehurmu* — the obligatory gifts have no legal existence until physically separated, and until that moment the owner has no claim to those portions. Therefore the thief owes only for the portions the owner actually owns — the *chullin* part.

---

## Thief Penalty

### Penalty Rationale

The Gemara ultimately rejects the interpretation that the dispute is about ownership — whether *tovas hana'ah* or *matanot* — and instead explains Rabbi's ruling as a rabbinic penalty. Even if technically the owner of the *tevel* has no monetary claim to the portions destined for *kohen* and *levi*, the Rabbis imposed a penalty on the thief: *kansuha rabbanan le'ganav* — they fined the thief — requiring payment of the full value.

### Escape Logic

The reasoning: if the thief only had to pay 88 dollars on 100 dollars' worth of stolen grain, he would escape any obligation to the *kohen* and *levi* whose portions he effectively consumed. Any *kohen* or *levi* who came to claim his share would be told: prove that you are the specific *kohen* or *levi* to whom this grain was going to be given. They cannot prove it, and the thief walks away without paying the full social debt his theft incurred. The Rabbis found it intolerable that a thief could steal a hundred dollars' worth of grain and walk away having paid only 88. Therefore, despite the owner's limited technical ownership of the obligatory portions, the thief is penalized and must pay the full value to the owner.

### Shmuel Alternative

An additional resolution: one might say that everyone agrees with Shmuel's principle — *chitah achas poteres es hakari* — even a single grain of *terumah* exempts the entire pile, meaning the owner theoretically could separate only the smallest possible amount of *terumah* and retain nearly the full 90% *chullin* portion. Under this view, the dispute is not about ownership at all, but about the proper calculation of repayment given different assumptions about how much the owner would actually give away in practice versus what he was technically obligated to give.

---

## Chatas Service

### Payment Void

The Gemara now turns to the final cases in the *mishnah*: *mei chatas* and *eifer parah adumah* — the water and ashes used in the purification ritual of the *parah adumah*. The Gemara challenges from a *braisa*: *ha'notel sachar ladun — dinav bateilin* — one who accepts payment for rendering judgment voids his rulings. Similarly, *l'ha'id — eidaso beteilah* — a witness who accepts payment voids his testimony. And then the relevant case: *l'hazos u'l'kadesh — memav mei mearah v'eifro eifer mikleh* — one who accepts payment for performing the *hazayah* (sprinkling of the purification water) or for the *kiddush* (mixing the ashes into the water) — his water is considered like water drawn from a swamp (not *mayim chayim* as required) and his ashes are like ordinary cooking ashes. The ritual is entirely voided. The reason, as Tosafot explains, is that one may not accept payment for performing a *mitzvah*; doing so invalidates the act, at least rabbinically. This creates an obvious problem: how can the *mishnah* say one may betroth a woman with *mei chatas* or *eifer parah*, if accepting benefit from performing these acts voids the ritual and is itself prohibited?

### Forbidden Acts

Abaye resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — kan b'sachar hava'ah u'milui v'kan b'sachar haza'ah v'kiddush* — there is no difficulty. The *braisa* that voids the ritual refers to payment for the *mitzvah* acts themselves — *hazayah* (sprinkling) and *kiddush* (mixing the ashes with the water). These are the ritual acts that constitute the *mitzvah*, and one may not be compensated for performing them. Our *mishnah*, however, refers to something entirely different.

### Permitted Service

The permitted acts for which payment may be accepted — and with which *kiddushin* may be effected — are *hava'ah u'milui*: transporting the ashes and drawing the water. These are logistical services, not *mitzvah* acts. The *Beis HaMikdash* required people to carry ashes from one location to another and to draw water for use in the *parah adumah* process. These tasks are physical labor, not ritual acts, and one may legitimately charge for them. In whatever scenario the man provides this service to the woman rather than to the *Beis HaMikdash* directly — and she compensates him through *kiddushin* — the betrothal takes effect, because he has given her something of genuine value: his service.

### Language Check

Abaye adds that this resolution is also *dika* from the language of the *mishnah* itself: *hacha b'mei chatas u'b'eifer parah* — the *mishnah* says "water" and "ashes" — referring to the objects transported and drawn, not to the acts of sprinkling or mixing. The contrasting *braisa* explicitly states *l'hazos u'l'kadesh* — "for sprinkling and for mixing" — highlighting that the prohibition targets the ritual acts themselves, while the *mishnah*'s permissive ruling concerns the preparatory physical services. *Shema minah* — this distinction is confirmed by the precise language each source chooses to employ.

*Hadran alach ha'ish mekadesh.*

---

---

# Kiddushin 59

## Agent Acts for Himse (II)

### Mishnah Case

The third *perek* opens with the following case: a man says to his friend, "Go and betroth a woman for me," and the friend goes and betroths her for himself. The *mishnah* rules that she is married — *mekudeshet* — to the second man, the one who acted as the emissary. The act works, whatever its ethical dimensions.

### Tosafot Chiddush

Tosafot immediately raises the obvious question: what is the *chiddush* here? Surely it is self-evident that if a man performs an act of *kiddushin* with his own money and in his own name, the marriage is valid. Tosafot answers by specifying the precise scenario the *mishnah* is addressing. At the moment of betrothal, the agent declared to the woman that so-and-so had sent him to betroth her to him — *Ploni shlachani l'kadeshach lo* — and then, in the very same breath, turned and said to her, *harei at mekudeshet li*, "You are betrothed to me." In such a case, one might have thought that when he said *li* — "to me" — she could not tell whether he meant himself or whether he was speaking in the voice of the *meshaleach*, representing the one who sent him. If she were genuinely confused and believed she was being betrothed to the one who sent him, the marriage would be a *kiddushei ta'ut*. Tosafot therefore adds that the *mishnah* is teaching a case where *hi yada'at* — she knew — that he meant himself. But the deeper *chiddush* is the rejection of a *hava amina* that we might read *li* as spoken in the principal's voice: we do not say that. When the agent says *li*, he speaks in his own voice, not that of the one who appointed him.

A natural question arises: why does the *mishnah* require that she subjectively understood him? Generally in *halacha* we assess matters objectively — *dvarim shebalev einam dvarim* — we do not ask what she thought he meant, but what the words or circumstances objectively signify. The answer seems to be that the language here is genuinely ambiguous in context, given that the agent had just been speaking as a representative of the *meshaleach*. That objective ambiguity is precisely why the *mishnah* must specify the scenario in which the meaning was clear.

---

## Rama'ut Discussion

### Braita Rama'ut

The *mishnah*'s ruling — that the marriage is valid — says nothing explicit about the moral dimension. A *braita* fills the gap: *mah she-asah asui*, what he did is done and stands, *ela she-nahag bah minhag rama'ut* — but he conducted himself with deceptive and faithless behavior toward the one who sent him.

This is worth pausing over, because the ethical weight of the critique depends heavily on the specific circumstances. The *mishnah* uses the phrase *isha plonit* — a specific, named woman — which means the principal had a particular woman in mind, not merely a general mandate to find someone suitable. That makes the betrayal considerably more concrete. The agent was not simply stumbling upon a woman while on an errand; he was dispatched with a particular mission regarding a particular woman and then diverted that mission to his own benefit.

Even so, the situation is not entirely simple. If the first man and this specific woman had no existing relationship beyond the principal's expressed interest, one might wonder how severe the *rama'ut* truly is. The *gemara* will also raise the principle of *shema yikdemenu acher* — the fear that someone else will seize the opportunity — which suggests that urgency can sometimes change the calculus. And the woman's own preference, while not foregrounded in the *gemara*, is not entirely absent from the moral picture.

As for the *mishnah* itself, the *gemara* notes that although it does not explicitly invoke the language of *rama'ut*, the word *halach* — "and he went" — carries a connotation of going off and doing something underhanded. The *tanna* of the *mishnah* encodes the moral critique in the choice of word, while the *braita* makes it explicit.

---

## Agent Acts for Himse (II)

### Friend vs. Agent

The *gemara* then asks: why does the *mishnah* describe the one sent as *chavero* — his friend — while an earlier *mishnah* in the previous *perek* described a similar figure as *shlucho*, his agent? The *gemara* answers that each formulation carries its own *chiddush*, and both were necessary.

In the present *mishnah*, which uses the language of *chavero*, the *chiddush* is this: one might have thought that only when you formally appoint an *agent* — someone you have explicitly commissioned, on whom you rely, from whom you expect full performance of the task — does his acting for himself constitute *rama'ut*. That is because *samcha da'atei*, you have placed full confidence in him; you feel you have discharged your responsibility. But if you merely ask a favor of a friend — if you said casually, "If you happen to be passing by and you get the chance, see if you can arrange this for me" — then perhaps there is less of a sense of binding obligation, and the friend who acts for himself would not be a *ramai*. The *mishnah* teaches that even in that case it is the wrong thing to do.

Rashi clarifies the distinction between *chavero* and *shaliach*: the friend was asked in an incidental way — if you happen to find yourself near her, perhaps you could arrange this on my behalf — not sent on a formal mission. Nevertheless, the *mishnah* tells us, even that informal request creates enough of a moral obligation that diverting it to one's own benefit is considered *rama'ut*.

The earlier *mishnah*, which uses *shlucho*, teaches a different *chiddush*: that if you send a formal agent to betroth a woman in a specific location, and he betroths her elsewhere, the *kiddushin* does not take effect. One might have thought that if you are sent on a mission, the specification of a location is merely *mareh makom* — a helpful pointer about where to find the woman — and that you retain latitude to act wherever you encounter her. The *mishnah* teaches otherwise: if a location was stipulated, only that location falls within the *shelichut*, and an act performed elsewhere is outside its scope entirely.

The broader point is that the nature of the relationship — whether the person is a paid agent on a formal commission or a friend asked a casual favor — can shape the moral weight of the betrayal and the scope of the *shelichut*, even if in all cases the person technically holds the legal power to perform the act.

---

## Rama'ut Discussion (II)

### Rabin Chasida Story

The *gemara* now records the story of Rabin Chasida — the righteous one, and presumably *chasida* here is not merely a family name — who went to betroth a woman on behalf of his son. His son had presumably made his father a *shaliach* for this purpose; Tosafot addresses the awkwardness that a son would be so bold as to ask his father to serve as his agent in this matter, and suggests the father may have volunteered. In any case, when Rabin Chasida began speaking with the woman, he decided to betroth her for himself.

The *gemara* asks: does this not violate the *braita*'s ruling that acting for oneself in such circumstances is *rama'ut*? The *gemara* answers: the situation was that the woman's family would not give her to the son — he was not *chashuv* enough for her — but they were pleased to give her to the father, who was a far more distinguished person. So the agent's taking her for himself was not, in that context, taking something away from his principal, because his principal could not have obtained it regardless.

### Duty to Inform

Even granting that the switch was substantively acceptable — because the family would not have agreed to the original match in any event — the *gemara* insists: *ibaya lei la-aduyei*, he should have informed his son before proceeding. The obligation to inform is more than a courtesy. It prevents the experience of betrayal that arises when someone discovers, without warning, that the person they trusted to act on their behalf has instead acted for himself. Even if the explanation that follows is entirely legitimate, the shock of the discovery is itself a form of harm. Moreover, informing the principal formally terminates the *shelichut*; the agent announces that the original mission cannot be fulfilled, and only then proceeds on his own behalf. Without that communication, the transition from acting as representative to acting for oneself happens invisibly, and that invisibility is its own form of *rama'ut*.

### Shma Yikdemenu Acher

The *gemara* explains why Rabin Chasida did not stop to inform his son: *savar ad hacha ve-hacha ati inish achrini mekadesh lah* — he calculated that by the time he could send word to his son and wait, another suitor would come and betroth her first. The principle of *shema yikdemenu acher* — the concern that delay will cost the opportunity entirely — justified acting without prior notification. This woman was evidently sought after, and the window was narrow. Under those circumstances, the *gemara* accepts the failure to inform as excusable.

---

## Land & Competition

### Rav & Land Deal

The discussion of *rama'ut* extends naturally from marriage to commerce. Rabbah bar bar Chana gave money to Rav and said: go buy me this plot of land. Rav went and bought it for himself. The *gemara* again invokes the *braita*: is this not *minhag rama'ut*? And again the *gemara* answers that the land was owned by powerful men — *alimei* — who showed honor and deference to Rav, and who would sell the land to Rav but would not have sold it to Rabbah bar bar Chana, even at Rav's request. Only Rav himself could acquire it; the principal could not have obtained it through any means.

And again: *ibaya lei la-aduyei* — Rav should nevertheless have informed Rabbah bar bar Chana of the situation before proceeding. The *gemara* answers in the same terms: *savar ad hacha ve-hacha ati inish achrini zavnin lah* — Rav calculated that by the time he sent word, someone else would purchase the land. This was hot property, the opportunity was fleeting, and the delay required to inform his principal would have cost him the acquisition entirely.

### Rabbi Abba Case

A related but distinct case follows. Rav Giddel had been *mehapeich* — actively engaged in negotiating the purchase of — a certain plot of land. Rabbi Abba came along and purchased it. This is importantly different from the previous cases: Rabbi Abba was not a *shaliach* for Rav Giddel. He was simply another person, acting entirely for himself, with no prior relationship of agency or mission. Each man was, as it were, acting on his own behalf.

The *gemara* does not apply the *braita*'s critique of *rama'ut* to Rabbi Abba directly. The *gemara* reserves that critique specifically for situations where one was charged with acting on another's behalf. Here it is a case of open competition.

Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who brought the matter to Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha. Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha waited until Rabbi Abba came to the pre-*Yom Tov* lectures — the *pirka d'yarcha kalla* — and confronted him indirectly. He posed the case: what do we say about a poor person who is in the process of trying to seize a piece of cake — *ani mehapech becharara* — and someone comes and snatches it from under his nose? Rabbi Abba answered immediately: *nikra rasha*, the one who takes it is called a *rasha*. Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha then said: so why did you do exactly that?

Rabbi Abba replied that he had not known Rav Giddel was in negotiations; the seller had not informed him. Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha then said: in that case, now that you know, give the land to Rav Giddel. Rabbi Abba said he would not sell it — it was the first plot of land he had ever purchased, and divesting oneself of one's first property is a bad *siman*. But he offered to give it to Rav Giddel as a gift.

Rav Giddel would not take the gift, for it is written *ve-sonei matanot yichyeh* — one who hates gifts will live; he would not accept what he could not earn himself. Rabbi Abba would not use the land, because Rav Giddel had been engaged in trying to purchase it and he had unwittingly cut him out. The result: *lo mar nachis lah velo mar nachis lah* — neither this one nor that one would enter the land, and it came to be called *ar'a de-rabbanan*, the land of the rabbis, as it was given over to the use of the *benei yeshiva*. A story of everyone trying to do the right thing, at the conclusion of a discussion about people doing the wrong thing.

### Tosafot: Metziah

The case of *ani mehapech becharara* raises a deeper question about when it is and is not appropriate to seize an opportunity that someone else had their eye on — in a context where no *shelichut* exists at all. Tosafot notes the tension with the *halacha* of *metzia*: the law of found objects seems to be that even if you spotted a lost object first, if I physically seize it before you do, it belongs to me. Why would seizing a cake or a plot of land be any different?

Tosafot, citing Rabbeinu Tam, offers an important distinction. The prohibition on *mehapech becharara* applies specifically in two types of cases: where a person is trying to profit from an ownerless or available thing and you compete with them for the same opportunity, as in the case of Rav Giddel and the land; or where a person is trying to purchase a particular item and you swoop in and buy it first. These are analogous to the case of Rav Giddel — *dumya de-Rav Giddel* — and are called *rasha* for the same reason: go and find another opportunity for yourself, rather than interfering with your fellow's engagement.

But if the object is a true *metziah* — a lost object on the street — then there is no equivalent alternative. There is only one such object, only one such opportunity. If you do not grab it, you will not find another. In that case, it is genuinely every man for himself, and there is no prohibition.

This maps onto an interesting parallel in the context of marriage. The very first *daf* of *Kiddushin* compared the act of finding a wife to finding a *metziah*. If a particular woman is unique — if there truly is no equivalent — then the zero-sum nature of the situation may change the moral analysis. By contrast, where the matter is purely commercial and similar opportunities exist, interfering with another person's active engagement is considered a form of *resha'a*.

Tosafot extends this reasoning to a further case: the prohibition of *yored le-umanuto shel chaveiro* — entering into another person's trade or livelihood. If a person has cast nets for fish, one may not begin casting nets in the same area, even though the fish are ownerless *hefker*. The reason is that this is not a case of grabbing an isolated windfall opportunity; the other person has established a business, and you are interfering with that business. The relevant category is not *metziah* but *umanuto* — the ongoing livelihood of the other.

### Employment Ethics

Tosafot draws an explicit practical application from this analysis, citing a ruling of Rabbeinu Yitzchak: it is forbidden for a tutor to approach a homeowner who already employs a different tutor and offer to take the position. The existing tutor is already engaged, and the one seeking to displace him should go find his own employment elsewhere rather than interfering with that *parnassah* arrangement.

However, if the homeowner himself indicates dissatisfaction and signals that he is looking for a replacement, then of course one may compete for the position. And, Tosafot adds, another homeowner may approach the already-employed tutor and try to hire him away — because the second homeowner can say: *eino ritzoni ela lazeh*, I want specifically this person, not just any tutor, since this one seems to me most likely to benefit my son. That rationale — I cannot simply find a functionally equivalent alternative — is precisely what removes the prohibition.

This parallels the logic applied to marriage: one cannot simply say to the person who wants a particular woman, "go find someone else," because in the world of persons, each individual is unique. The zero-sum nature of the situation justifies acting in one's own interest even at another's loss — provided one is not acting in violation of a prior commitment or an existing agency relationship.

---

## After 30 Days

### Thirty-Day Condition

The *mishnah* moves to a second case, which is joined by the word *ve-chen* — "and similarly." A man says to a woman: *harei at mekudeshet li le-achar shloshim yom* — you are betrothed to me as of thirty days from now. If another man came and betrothed her within that thirty-day window, she is betrothed to the second man. The *mishnah* further distinguishes the case where the first man said *me-achshav u-le-achar shloshim yom* — from now and taking effect in thirty days — in which case if another man betroths her within that period, her status is *mekudeshet ve-eina mekudeshet*, doubtfully betrothed, because it is unclear how much the formula "from now" advances the effect of the *kiddushin*. In that state of uncertainty, a *bat Yisrael* betrothed to a *kohen* or a *bat kohen* betrothed to an *Yisrael* may not eat *terumah*, as the respective marital status is unresolved.

### Money Consumed

The *gemara* asks: what is the law if no second man came and betrothed her within the thirty days, but the money — or ring — given at the time of the original *kiddushin* was consumed or spent before the thirty days elapsed? Does the *kiddushin* take effect at the end of the thirty-day period?

### Rav & Shmuel

Rav and Shmuel both rule: she is betrothed — *mekudeshet* — even though the money has been consumed. The *chiddush* of this ruling is striking, because ordinarily when a legal *kinyan* is structured to take effect after a period of time, some remnant of the original act of acquisition must still be present when that time arrives. If a person says "I will own your cow in thirty days" and draws the cow into his property, but on day thirty the cow is wandering in *reshut ha-rabbim*, the *kinyan* does not take effect. The original act must still have a surviving presence when the transaction is supposed to finalize.

### Original Kesef

The *gemara* explains why the thirty-day *kiddushin* is different. *Hanei zuzei lav l'milveh damu ve-lav l'pikadon damu* — this money is neither a loan nor a deposit.

It is not a *pikadon*, because if it were, the money would remain in the man's ownership, held in trust by the woman; loss of the money would be the man's loss, and no money remaining would mean nothing left with which to effect the *kiddushin*. But here the money was given into the woman's possession outright — if it is lost, it is her loss. That is not a *pikadon*.

Nor is it a *milveh*, a loan. A loan is money transferred for the borrower to spend, with an obligation to repay an equivalent sum. One cannot effect *kiddushin* with a loan — *ein mekadesh be-milveh* — because there is nothing concrete with which to betroth; you are merely forgiving a debt. That too does not apply here.

What was given was *kesef kiddushin* from the very first moment — money delivered to the woman specifically in the capacity of *kiddushin*, with the understanding that it would take effect later. Because it was originally given with the full force of *kesef kiddushin*, the memory of that act is not erased even if the physical money no longer exists. The woman received it as *kiddushin*, and if the *kiddushin* does not go through, she would be obligated to return it; that lingering reality of the transaction is sufficient to keep the original act "present" in the relevant sense. One is not marrying her with money that no longer exists at the moment the thirty days arrive; one is marrying her with the money that was originally given to her as *kesef kiddushin*, and the fact that it no longer physically exists does not erase the significance of that original act.

---

## Woman Retracts

### R. Yochanan

The *gemara* now asks: what is the law if no second man came, and the woman herself retracted — *chazrah bah* — before the thirty days were up? Since the *kiddushin* has not yet taken effect, can she withdraw from it?

Rabbi Yochanan rules that she can retract — *chozeret*. The reasoning is *ati dibbur u-mevatel dibbur*: her words negate his words. Until the *kiddushin* takes effect, the entire transaction is still in the realm of speech and declaration; it has not been actualized. Words can therefore undo words.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish disagrees: she cannot retract. *Lo ati dibbur u-mevatel ma'aseh* — words cannot negate an act. Although the *kiddushin* has not yet taken effect, the *ma'aseh kiddushin* — the physical act of handing the ring or money to the woman — has already been performed. That act cannot be undone by mere words.

### Get Comparison

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the law of *terumah*: if a householder appoints an agent to separate *terumah* on his behalf and then verbally revokes the appointment before the agent has acted, the *terumah* is invalid — *ein trumato trumah*. Here, both the appointment and the revocation were purely verbal — *dibbur u-mevatel dibbur* — and the revocation is effective. The same should apply in the case of *kiddushin*.

Reish Lakish counters: the case of *kiddushin* is different, because *nesinas ma'ot le-yad ishah ke-ma'aseh dami* — the transfer of money into the woman's hands is equivalent to an act. There was a concrete physical transaction, not merely an exchange of words. Words can void words, but words cannot void an act.

### Get Analysis

Rabbi Yochanan presses further with the case of *get*: if a man sends a messenger to deliver a *get* to his wife, and then sends a second messenger after the first saying "the *get* I gave you is void," it is indeed void — *harei ze batel*. Here, a physical *get* was placed in the agent's hand — an act was performed — yet a verbal declaration is sufficient to void the agency. This parallels the case of *kiddushin*, where money was placed in the woman's hand and she now verbally retracts.

Reish Lakish responds: there is a crucial distinction. *Kol kamma de-lo mata gitta le-yadah, dibbur hu* — as long as the *get* has not reached the wife's hand, the entire arrangement is still only words in the relevant sense. The act that transforms legal status — *gerushin* — has not yet taken place. Placing the *get* in the agent's hand is a preparatory step, not the actualization of the divorce. Since the status-changing act has not occurred, the transaction remains in an abstract state and words can still void it. But in the case of *kiddushin*, placing the ring in the woman's hand *is* the act of *kiddushin* — the *ma'aseh* was complete, even though the *kiddushin* has not yet taken effect. That completed act cannot be reversed by words alone.

---

## Thought vs. Action

### Vessel Completion

Reish Lakish himself now raises a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from the laws of *tumah* and vessels. The *mishnah* teaches: *kol ha-kelim yordim lidei tumatan be-machshava* — all vessels acquire susceptibility to *tumah* through thought. When a craftsman is fashioning a vessel, the question of when the vessel is "complete" — and therefore susceptible to *tumah* — is determined by the craftsman's intention. If he decides in his mind that the vessel is finished, it is finished and can become *tamei* from that moment, even without any further physical action.

However, *ve-ein olim mi-tumatan ela be-shinuy ma'aseh* — vessels do not lose their susceptibility to *tumah* except through a change in action — actually reworking the vessel. If a craftsman has already decided in his mind that the vessel is complete, he cannot simply think "I want to continue working on it" and thereby un-make the vessel's status as a complete vessel. He must actually go back and physically resume work on it.

The principle derived from this: *ma'aseh motzi miyad ma'aseh u-miyad machshava* — an act can reverse either a prior act or a prior thought. *Machshava eina motzi'ah lo miyad ma'aseh ve-lo miyad machshava* — thought reverses neither a prior act nor even a prior thought. This seems to directly contradict Rabbi Yochanan's position: even thought cannot reverse thought, so certainly words should not be able to reverse *kiddushin*.

### Maaseh Motzi

Rabbi Yochanan responds: the domain of *tumah* is sui generis. *Shani machshava de-tuma de-chi ma'aseh damya* — thought regarding *tumah* is treated as equivalent to an act. This is derived from the *drasha* of Rav Pappa, who noted the tension between the written and read forms of the verse *ki yutan*: water placed passively on seeds renders them susceptible to *tumah* provided the owner was *nicha lei* — pleased about it. The owner's positive disposition toward the water having touched the seeds is treated as though he himself had placed the water on them. Thought and will, in the domain of *tumah*, have the legal force of action.

Because thought in the *tumah* context functions as an act, when the craftsman decides in his mind that the vessel is finished, that is legally equivalent to performing an act of completion. And since thought-as-act cannot be reversed by mere thought, it takes a physical act of resuming work on the vessel to undo that status. This is entirely specific to *tumah*; it does not establish a general principle that thought cannot reverse thought, and therefore has no bearing on the *kiddushin* question, where Rabbi Yochanan holds that words — in a domain where there is no such equivalence to acts — can indeed reverse prior words.

### Rav Zavid Case

The *gemara* notes that Rav Zavid taught this entire dispute in the context of a different case. Rather than the case of conditional *kiddushin* taking effect after thirty days, he applied the debate to the following scenario: a woman appointed an agent to accept *kiddushin* on her behalf — *natna reshut li-shlucha le-kadsha* — and then went and betrothed herself before the agent acted. If she acted first, her own *kiddushin* is binding; if the agent acted first, his *kiddushin* on her behalf is binding.

### Void Agent

The *gemara* then asks: what if she did not betroth herself, but simply verbally retracted her appointment of the agent — *chazrah bah* — without performing any act? Can she void her agent with words?

Rabbi Yochanan says she can retract: *ati dibbur u-mevatel dibbur*. Reish Lakish says she cannot: *lo ati dibbur u-mevatel dibbur*.
