Reish Lakish's position here is, as noted, quite extreme: a woman could announce before witnesses that she is revoking her agent's authority, and yet the agent could theoretically proceed to marry her off. Tosafot grapples with this and attempts to limit the scope of Reish Lakish's ruling.

---

## Terumah & Get

### Terumah Negation

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the *terumah* case: if one appointed an agent to separate *terumah* and verbally revoked the appointment before the agent acted, *ein trumato trumah* — the agent's *terumah* is invalid. This is a case where appointment was verbal and revocation was verbal, and the revocation was effective — *ati dibbur u-mevatel dibbur*.

### Rav Response

Rav responds on behalf of Reish Lakish: no — *hacha be-mai askinan ke-gon she-kadam ba'al ha-bayit ve-taram mi-kalav*, the case is where the householder himself went ahead and performed the act of taking *terumah* from his own vessels first. The revocation was not purely verbal; it was effected by an action — the householder taking *terumah* himself before the agent could act. This is a case of *ma'aseh mevatel shelichut*, an act terminating the agency, not words terminating the agency. Reish Lakish's principle — that words cannot void a prior arrangement — remains intact, because the effective revocation here was through action, not speech.

By extension, a woman wishing to void her agent for *kiddushin* would have to perform an act — such as betrothing herself to someone else — not merely declare verbally that she revokes the agency.

### Get Negation

Rabbi Yochanan then raises the *get* case again: a man sends a *shaliach* with a *get* for his wife and subsequently sends a second messenger to tell the first that the *get* is void — *batel hu*. This is purely verbal revocation of an agency that involved a physical act of handing over the *get*. Yet it is effective.

### Get Contingent

Reish Lakish's earlier answer applies here too: *kol kamma de-lo mata gitta le-yadah, dibbur hu* — as long as the *get* has not reached the wife's hand, the entire arrangement is still in the realm of the abstract and contingent. The act of *gerushin* has not been performed. The delivery of the *get* to the agent was preparatory, not the completion of any legal change in status. Before any status has changed, words can still void words.

### Hilcheta Ruling

Despite this defense, the *gemara* concludes: *tiyuvta de-Reish Lakish tiyuvta* — Reish Lakish is refuted by the *get* case. And the *gemara* rules: *ve-hilcheta ke-vateih de-Rabbi Yochanan va-afilu be-kamaita* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yochanan, and not only in the case of voiding an agent with words, but even in the original case of thirty-day conditional *kiddushin*. Even there, where a physical act — the giving of the ring or money — has already been performed, since the *kiddushin* has not yet taken effect, the woman can retract with words before the thirty days elapse.

---

---

# Kiddushin 60

## Voiding Pending Kiddushin

### Dibbur Mevattel Dibbur

The daf opens by returning to the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerning a case where a man designates that the effect of *kiddushin* will take place later — he gives the money now, but the *kiddushin* is not to take effect immediately. The question is whether such an arrangement can be voided through words alone, or whether some *ma'aseh* is required. The principle at stake is *ati dibbur u-mevattel dibbur* — can speech negate speech?

The underlying tension is that while Reish Lakish concedes that purely verbal acts can be negated verbally — appointing a *shaliach*, for instance, is a verbal act and can therefore be verbally revoked — the present case involves an actual *ma'aseh*: money was physically handed over as *kiddushin*. The question is to what degree that act is considered legally operative when its effect has been postponed, and whether it therefore falls into the category of *ma'aseh* or remains merely in the domain of *dibbur*.

### Reish Lakish's Versions

The *Gemara* presents two versions of Reish Lakish's position. In the first, he disputes only the case of the postponed monetary act. In the second, far more striking version, he disputes even the case of a woman who designated a *shaliach* to receive *kiddushin* on her behalf — arguing that she cannot verbally revoke the appointment. This position is difficult to the point of being untenable: it would mean a woman could be married against her will. Tosafot grapples with this reading, but the *Gemara* clearly concludes that it cannot be correct. If a woman designates a *shaliach*, she may verbally void the *shlichus*.

### Hilchesa Ke-Rabbi Yochan…

The *Gemara* records a definitive contradiction to Reish Lakish — *tiuvta de-Reish Lakish tiuvta* — demonstrating that a *shaliach* appointment can indeed be verbally revoked. And then the *Gemara* goes further: *ve-hilchesa ke-Rabbi Yochanan ve-afilu be-kameita* — we rule like Rabbi Yochanan even in the first version of the dispute, even where money was physically given with the effect designated to take place thirty days later. Even that can be verbally voided before it takes effect.

The *Gemara* anticipates the objection: *shani nesinas mammon le-yad ha-ishah de-kama'aseh dami* — the actual giving of money into a woman's hands is like a real act. Nevertheless, the ruling stands: *afilu hachi ati dibbur u-mevattel dibbur*. As long as the *kiddushin* has not yet taken effect, words can void it.

### Status Change Analysis

The *Gemara* explains why. The classic case in which *dibbur* cannot negate a *ma'aseh* involves a situation where a status change has already occurred — for instance, once an object has been rendered a finished vessel, it becomes susceptible to *tum'ah*, and a subsequent mental intention to resume work on it is irrelevant, because the status has already changed. Here, by contrast, although money was given, no halachic status has yet changed. The woman's status has not shifted; the man's status has not shifted; everything has been projected into the future. Since nothing has yet been concretized halachically, the entire arrangement remains in the domain of *dibbur*, and words suffice to void it.

---

## Get vs. Shaliach Voiding

### Conflicting Piskei Din

The *Gemara* immediately raises a contradiction: *kashya hilchesa a-hilchesa*. On one hand, we have just established that we rule like Rabbi Yochanan — an arrangement to take effect later can be verbally voided. On the other hand, we also hold *hilchesa ke-Rav Nachman*, that in the case of voiding a *shaliach ha-get*, we rule like Rav Nachman. What was that ruling?

The case, discussed in Gittin, is as follows: a man sent a *shaliach* to deliver a *get* to his wife, then chased down the *shaliach* and verbally revoked the *shlichus*. The question is whether, having voided the *shaliach*, he may reuse the *get* document itself. Rav Nachman says yes; Rav Sheshet says no. We rule like Rav Nachman. But how is this consistent with our ruling that a verbal voiding dissolves everything? If the writing of the *get* is analogous to giving money to the woman's hands — both are acts done now with effect designated for later — then just as the *kiddushin* is voided, the *get* should be voided as well, and could not be reused.

### Get Remains Valid

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction directly: *nehi d'batlei mishum shlichus mishum get lo batlei* — yes, you voided the *shlichus*, but you did not void the *get* itself. The two are entirely separate. One might ask why: in both cases, has not the decisive act been done now, with effect pending?

The answer lies in a crucial distinction. When money is given for *kiddushin* with a postponed effect, nothing new has been created. The money remains money; the woman's status is unchanged; the man's status is unchanged. The act has been suspended in abstraction. But when a *get* is written, the act of writing creates something concrete here and now — this piece of paper acquires the halachic status of a *get*. That is a genuine *ma'aseh*, analogous to designating an object as *terumah* or rendering an item a completed vessel. The writing transforms the document's status in the present moment.

### Maasah Analysis

This distinction clarifies the ruling. Because the *get* document itself has undergone a status change — it has become a *get* — that status cannot be dissolved through words alone. The voiding of the *shaliach* affects only the agency, not the instrument. The *get* document remains fully valid, and may be reused. By contrast, the giving of *kiddushin* money with a postponed effect created no present status change whatsoever, and therefore *ati dibbur u-mevattel dibbur* applies in full. The two rulings are thus entirely consistent.

---

## Me'achshav U'Le'achar Zm…

### Rav: Safek Le'olam

The *Gemara* now turns to the precise case under discussion in the *Mishnah*: a man says *me-achshav u-le'achar sheloshim yom* — "as of now and after thirty days." A second man then comes and betroths this woman before the thirty days have elapsed. What is the legal status of both *kiddushin*?

Rav rules: *mekudeshet ve-einah mekudeshet le'olam* — she is betrothed and not betrothed, and this status of uncertainty is permanent. The *safek* — does she belong to man number one or man number two — never resolves. Even after day thirty arrives, the uncertainty endures.

### Shmuel: Tenai Logic

Shmuel disagrees: *mekudeshet ve-einah mekudeshet ella ad sheloshim yom* — the uncertainty lasts only until day thirty. After that, *paka kiddushei sheni ve-gamri kiddushei rishon* — man number two's *kiddushin* lapses, and man number one's *kiddushin* takes full effect.

Shmuel's reasoning is that the phrase *me-achshav u-le'achar sheloshim yom* functions as a *tenai* — a condition. The meaning is: "You are betrothed to me as of now, provided that day thirty arrives" — or more precisely, provided that nothing intervenes to prevent it (neither party dies, neither reverses). When day thirty does arrive and the *tenai* is satisfied, the *kiddushin* takes effect retroactively from the moment it was given. During the intervening period, therefore, the *safek* is genuine — perhaps the *tenai* will not be satisfied, perhaps man number one will withdraw or die — so man number two's *kiddushin* is uncertain. But once day thirty arrives and the *tenai* is fulfilled, all uncertainty dissolves in favor of man number one.

### Language Interpretation

Rav's position, by contrast, is that the phrase is genuinely ambiguous — not about subjective intent, but as a legal matter. The language could mean either: "as of now, with day thirty as a *tenai*" (Shmuel's reading), or: "not really as of now — when he added *u-le'achar sheloshim yom*, he effectively retracted the *me-achshav* and meant *le-achar sheloshim yom* alone." On this reading, the two readings are mutually exclusive extremes — either entirely now (retroactively upon fulfillment of the *tenai*) or entirely later — and we cannot determine which was meant. Therefore the *safek* is permanent: *mekudeshet ve-einah mekudeshet le'olam*.

The *Gemara* notes that this debate maps directly onto a *tannaitic* dispute. The *braita* records: *me-hayom u-le'achar mita get ve-eino get* — "from today and after I die, this is a *get* and is not a *get*" — *divrei Chachamim*. A man on his deathbed attempting to spare his wife from *yibum* says the *get* should take effect now, assuming he dies. The *Chachamim* hold it is uncertain — perhaps he meant *me-achshav* as a *tenai*, perhaps he retracted and meant *le-achar mita* only, in which case there is no valid *get*. *Rabbi* says: *kazeh get* — it is certainly a *get*, meaning Rabbi reads it definitively as *me-achshav*.

Rav thus parallels the *Chachamim*; Shmuel parallels Rabbi. The *Gemara* explains why it is insufficient to simply state their positions as *psak* in one of the two cases: the contexts differ in a legally significant way. In *kiddushin*, the man is eager to create the relationship and might be presumed to prefer an earlier effective date; in *gittin*, the man is distancing himself and might be less eager, making the "later" reading more plausible. And in the *get* case, there is an additional pressure toward the immediate reading — because a *get le-achar mita* is legally impossible — that does not exist in *kiddushin*, where *kiddushin* taking effect after thirty days is perfectly valid. Hence both cases are independently necessary.

Abaye then raises a further case under Rav's framework: *ba echad ve-amar lah harei at mekudeshes li me-hayom u-le'achar lamed yom, u-va acher ve-amar lah harei at mekudeshes li me-hayom u-le'achar esrim yom*, and a third man who says *me-hayom u-le'achar asara yamim*. The ruling: *mi-rishon u-mi-acharon tzricha get, mi-emtzai eina tzricha get*. She requires a *get* from man number one and from man number three, but not from man number two.

The logic is straightforward: *mima nafshach* — whatever you say. If all three statements constitute a *tenai*, then all three take effect retroactively as of the moment of *kiddushin*, and man number one, having acted first, wins. Man number two and man number three are both excluded; she needs only a *get* from man number one. If, conversely, all three statements mean the effect is genuinely delayed, then whoever's designated date arrives first prevails — that is man number three, whose ten-day period expires first. Man number one and man number two are excluded; she needs only a *get* from man number three. Either way, man number two — the *meatzai*, the middle one — is never the winner.

The *Gemara* asks: isn't this obvious? Why state it? The answer is this: one might have thought that the phrase *me-achshav u-le'achar zman* has no single fixed legal meaning, but rather that each individual speaker might have meant it differently — man number one meaning *me-achshav*, man number two meaning *le-achar zman*, and so forth. If that were so, any one of them could have been the operative *kiddushin*, and all three would require a *get*. The *Gemara* therefore teaches that this is not the case. A legal phrase has one fixed meaning, not a range of personal interpretations. We may not know yet which of two possible fixed meanings it carries, but it carries only one. Whatever the phrase means, it means the same thing for every person who uses it. This is a foundational principle: *devarim she-belev einam devarim* — subjective intent that departs from the objective legal meaning of a term is legally inert. The legal system demands fixed meanings for its operative language.

---

## Three Kiddushin Case

### Case Setup

Having established that the phrase *me-achshav u-le'achar zman* carries a single fixed legal meaning — even if we remain uncertain what that meaning is — the *Gemara* also finds that the uncertainty itself has been resolved by Abaye's analysis. Rav's position is that the phrase is permanently ambiguous as between two binary alternatives: either entirely now or entirely later. Shmuel's position is that it unambiguously means *me-achshav* with a *tenai*, so that all uncertainty dissipates once day thirty arrives.

### Get Requirement Logic

The case of three sequential *kiddushin* — man number one designating effect after thirty days, man number two after twenty days, man number three after ten days — illustrates the consequences of Rav's view. Since the phrase is either-or, the same either-or applies identically to all three. If it means now for one, it means now for all; if it means later for one, it means later for all. This produces the clean *mima nafshach* analysis: the middle man is excluded under both possibilities.

### Fixed Legal Meaning

The deeper lesson is about the nature of legal language. One might have thought, as the *Gemara* entertains, that since we are ultimately trying to understand what the speaker intended, it is possible for different speakers to have meant different things by the same phrase. But a legal system cannot function on that basis. The same term must carry the same legal meaning regardless of the speaker's internal state. This principle aligns with *devarim she-belev einam devarim* — unspoken thoughts cannot alter the legal effect of spoken words. The contrast with *nedarim* and *nezirut* is instructive: those are one-sided obligations where the subjective intent of the obligating party carries greater weight, operating under the inverse principle of *ad she-piv ve-libo shavin*. But in bilateral transactions like *kiddushin*, legal objectivity is paramount: what the term means halachically is what governs, regardless of what any individual speaker may have privately intended.

---

## Ongoing Process View

### Shivura Metaphor

The *Gemara* now introduces a third interpretive framework, presented by Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *afilu me'ah tofsim bah* — even a hundred men could be betrothed to this woman under *me-achshav u-le'achar sheloshim yom*. Rav Assi transmits the same ruling in Rabbi Yochanan's name.

This is a striking statement. It does not mean — Rashi is explicit on this — that there is a *safek* as to which one of a hundred men married her, such that any one of them might have been the operative betrothal. Rather, it means literally that all hundred could be simultaneously betrothed to her. The mechanism is explained by Rav Mesharshiya son of Rav Ami: *shavtah nafshah ki-sharga d'livni* — she made herself like a row of bricks, *de-chol chad ve-chad ravcha le-chavreih shavik* — each brick leaving space for the next one alongside it.

The brick-row metaphor captures a third reading of *me-achshav u-le'achar sheloshim yom* that is distinct from both Rav's and Shmuel's. This phrase does not mean either "now" (with a *tenai*) or "later" (with a retraction of *me-achshav*). It means that the *kiddushin* is a continuous process: it begins now and concludes after thirty days. It is not a binary event — a switch that is either on or off — but an ongoing, partially-actualized state. During the thirty-day period, the woman is not fully betrothed to man number one, but she is not unbetrothed either. The process is underway. When man number two arrives and says *me-achshav u-le'achar esrim yom*, she is not yet fully married, and so his *kiddushin* too can take hold. Just as bricks are laid in overlapping rows, each man's *kiddushin* begins before the previous one has fully concluded, and the partial availability of the woman at each moment allows the next *kiddushin* to attach.

### Partial Marriage Status

Tosafot raises what seems a natural objection: elsewhere we have established that if a man says "half of you is betrothed to me," the *kiddushin* does not take effect, because a woman cannot be half-married. How, then, can Rabbi Yochanan say that all hundred men are betrothed to her — is she not fractionally married to each?

Tosafot's answer distinguishes the two cases precisely. In the "half of you" case, the man leaves over a portion of the woman herself — he does not marry the full person. That is the defect: *kiddushin* requires taking the whole person, and if you attempt to marry only half of her, nothing takes effect. Here, by contrast, each man marries her completely — *lo sheyar be-gufa ha-ishah kelum ela gemurin kulam* — he did not leave over any part of her person; he married her in full. It is only that the marriage has not yet fully actualized, that the process is still ongoing. He left over time, not personhood. Since the remainder is temporal rather than personal, his *kiddushin* is not defective — it simply has not yet completed. And because it has not yet completed, the next man finds enough unresolved space to enter.

---

## Get L'achar Mita Debate

### Get After Death

The *Gemara* applies Rabbi Yochanan's framework — *kiddushin* as ongoing process — to the *get* case. The case of *me-hayom u-le'achar mita get ve-eino get*, a man on his deathbed who says "from today and after I die," produces a different result under Rabbi Yochanan's model than under Rav's or Shmuel's.

If the *get* is an ongoing process that begins now and concludes after the man dies, then by the time the process concludes — at the man's death — it arrives at a moment when the *get* cannot take effect, because a *get* must take effect while the husband is alive. The process started, but did not complete. Therefore, according to Rabbi Yochanan, there is no *safek* here at all: this is simply not a valid *get*. The woman is a widow, not a divorcée.

The halachic consequence is significant. If she is a widow, *yibum* should apply. The *Mishnah* records: *choletzes ve-lo mityabemes* — she performs *chalitza* but does not undergo *yibum*. This is fine according to Rav, whose position generates genuine *safek* — perhaps the *get* was valid, perhaps not. It is also fine according to Shmuel, who aligns with the *Rabbanan* of the *braita*. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, there is no *safek* — she is definitively not divorced. Why, then, does she not simply undergo *yibum*?

Rava proposes: *get lehotzi'a u-mita lehotzi'a* — the *get* removes her from the husband's domain, and death likewise removes her from that domain. Perhaps the *get* initiated ninety-eight percent of the severance, and the death completed the remaining two percent — *ma she-shiyyer get gamar mita*. Abaye rejects this reasoning: *get motzi'a me-reshut yavam, mita machneset le-reshut yavam* — a *get* removes her from the domain of a potential *yavam*; death brings her into that domain. The two operate in opposite directions. Death cannot complete the process of a *get*.

### Get Models Applied

Abaye therefore says: yes, according to Rabbi Yochanan, she is definitively not divorced. The ongoing process did not complete before the husband died, and therefore there is no *get* at all. She is a widow and should by rights undergo *yibum* — or *chalitza*. The reason we do not permit *yibum*, and instead require *chalitza*, is not intrinsic to this case.

### Gezeira M'shum Leshon

The reason is a *gezeira*: *gezeira mishum me-hayom im mati harei zeh get* — a protective ordinance against confusing this case with a different one. If a man says "from today *if* I die" — *im mati* — the *get* is unambiguously valid. This is a clear *tenai*: the *get* takes effect now on the condition that he dies from this illness. According to Rabbi Yochanan, this would be a complete, valid *get*, and there would be no *yibum* at all. Were we to permit *yibum* in the case of *me-hayom u-le'achar mita* — where the *get* failed because the process did not complete — people might confuse the two cases and permit *yibum* even in the *im mati* case, where she is definitively divorced and *yibum* would be *arayot*.

The *Gemara* then asks the reverse: since we require *chalitza* in the *me-hayom u-le'achar mita* case, should we not also require *chalitza* in the *me-hayom im mati* case — as a *gezeira* lest the cases be confused in the other direction? The answer: if we require *chalitza* in the *im mati* case, people will conclude that the *get* was doubtful, leading them to permit *yibum* there. And *yibum* in the *im mati* case, where the *get* is valid, would be catastrophic. The *Gemara* responds: so too with our *gezeira* — requiring *chalitza* in the *me-hayom u-le'achar mita* case might lead to *yibum*. But the *Gemara* dismisses this: *tityabbem ve-ein bekach kelum* — in the *me-hayom u-le'achar mita* case, *yibum* is in principle permitted; we merely said not to do it for reasons of confusion. If requiring *chalitza* there leads someone to do *yibum*, that is not a disaster, because *yibum* is fundamentally valid in that case. By contrast, permitting *yibum* in the *im mati* case — where she is divorced — would be genuinely catastrophic.

The upshot is a three-way framework for *me-achshav u-le'achar sheloshim yom*: Shmuel holds it is unambiguously a *tenai*, uncertainty resolving at day thirty; Rav holds it is permanently ambiguous between "entirely now" and "entirely later"; and Rabbi Yochanan, via Ulla, holds it is an ongoing process — beginning now and concluding later — with all the attendant consequences for *kiddushin* and *get*.

---

## Al Menas Conditionality

### Mishnah Cases

The *Gemara* moves to the next *Mishnah*, which deals with *al menas* — conditional *kiddushin*. *Ha-omer le-ishah harei at mekudeshes li al menas she-etten lach masayim zuz* — "you are betrothed to me on the condition that I give you two hundred *zuz*." The *Mishnah* rules: *harei zo mekudeshes ve-hu yitten* — she is betrothed, and he must give. If he stipulated *al menas she-etten lach mikan ve-ad sheloshim yom* — within thirty days — then *nasan lah be-soch sheloshim yom mekudeshes, ve-im lav einah mekudeshes*. Further cases: *al menas she-yesh li masayim zuz* — on the condition I have two hundred *zuz* — she is betrothed if he does indeed have them. *Al menas she-arech masayim zuz* — on the condition I show you two hundred *zuz* — she is betrothed if he shows her, provided *ve-im her'ah lah al ha-shulchan einah mekudeshes* — if he showed her money on the table (Rashi: belonging to a money-changer, not his own), she is not betrothed, because it is evident he did not mean to show her someone else's money.

### Tenai Timing Debate

The operative question the *Mishnah* leaves unresolved — and which is now the subject of an *amoraic* dispute — is the precise meaning of *ve-hu yitten*. Does it mean "as of now, provided that he eventually gives" (a *tenai*, taking effect retroactively from the moment of *kiddushin*), or "when he gives" (taking effect only at the moment the money is transferred)?

Rav Huna rules: *ve-hu yitten — tenai havei, mekayem tna'eih ve-azil* — it is a *tenai*; he fulfills his condition whenever he fulfills it, but the *kiddushin* dates from now. Rav Yehuda rules: *lich'she-yitten — lich'yaiv havei kiddushin, hashta miha lo havei kiddushin* — only when he gives the money does the *kiddushin* take effect; as of now, it does not.

The *nafka mina* is immediate: if she accepted *kiddushin* from a second man before the first gave the money. According to Rav Huna, she was already betrothed to man number one from the outset, so the second *kiddushin* is ineffective. According to Rav Yehuda, since no *kiddushin* yet exists, the second *kiddushin* is valid.

### Kiddushin vs. Geirushin

The parallel *Mishnah* in *Gittin* presents the same question in the context of divorce. A man says: *harei zeh gittech al menas she-titni li masayim zuz* — "here is your *get*, on the condition you give me two hundred *zuz*." The *Mishnah* rules: *harei zo megureshes ve-hi titten* — she is divorced as long as she gives the money. Rav Huna applies the same reasoning: *ve-hi titten — tenai havei*, it is a *tenai*, and upon fulfilling the *tenai* she is retroactively divorced from when the *get* was given. Rav Yehuda says: *lich'she-titten* — only when she gives.

The *nafka mina* in the *get* case is the *Gemara*'s focus: the *get* is torn or lost before she gives the money. According to Rav Huna, this is no problem — the *tenai* can be fulfilled later, and the effect retroacts; the *get* need not be physically present at the moment of fulfillment. According to Rav Yehuda, since the *kiddushin* or *get* only takes effect at the moment of the condition's fulfillment, the operative instrument — money or document — must still exist at that moment. A *get* that has been destroyed cannot take effect even if the condition is later satisfied.

The *Gemara* notes that both cases must be stated independently, because there are contextual reasons to presume different intentions in each. In *kiddushin*, the man is seeking to bring the woman closer, which suggests eagerness to have the *kiddushin* take effect immediately — favoring Rav Huna's reading. But one might argue that the woman's reluctance to ask for money she was promised (*de-ichasfa lah le-mitbahyei*) means she would insist the *kiddushin* not take effect until payment is received — perhaps favoring Rav Yehuda. In *gittin*, the man is distancing himself and might prefer a delayed effect; but one might argue that he is not embarrassed to demand payment (*de-ihu lo kasif lei le-mitbah*) and therefore does not need to hold the *get*'s effect hostage to receipt of funds, again favoring Rav Huna's reading. Each case presents independent considerations, and therefore each must be stated.

---

## Al Menas Proof Texts

### Get Validity Proof

The *Gemara* now marshals decisive evidence in favor of Rav Huna. The first *braita*: a man says *harei zeh gittech al menas she-titni li masayim zuz* — even if the *get* is torn or lost, *harei zo megureshes* — she is divorced, as long as she gives the money. She should not, however, remarry until she has done so — not because she is not yet divorced, but because she must ensure she can satisfy the *tenai*. This *braita* clearly treats the *get* as taking effect from the moment of giving, with the condition functioning retroactively — precisely Rav Huna's position.

A second *braita* reinforces this: a man gives his wife a *get al menas she-titni li masayim zuz* and then dies. *Natna ein zekuka le-yavam* — if she gave the money and fulfilled the *tenai*, she is divorced and not subject to *yibum*. *Lo natna zekuka le-yavam* — if she did not give it, the *tenai* was not fulfilled and she is a widow subject to *yibum*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds: she may give the money to his brother, his father, or another relative — the *tenai* can be satisfied even post-mortem, by giving to heirs. The debate between *tanna kamma* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is only whether *li* — "to me" — includes heirs. But both agree that the *tenai* can be satisfied after the man's death, and the *get* then takes effect retroactively to when it was given. This is a clear proof that *al menas* functions as a *tenai* that retroacts — *dkulei alma miha tnai havei*.

These two *braitas* constitute a *tiuvta* — a decisive contradiction — to Rav Yehuda.

### Consensus on Al Menas

Rav Yehuda deflects by arguing that both *braitas* may reflect only the position of Rabbi, who holds *kol ha-omer al menas ke-omer me-achshav dami* — whoever says "on the condition" is as if he said "as of now." This is Rav Huna's position, attributed here to Rabbi. Perhaps, Rav Yehuda claims, the *Rabbanan* dispute Rabbi and hold that *al menas* means *le-achar zman*, and he rules like the *Rabbanan*.

Rav Zeira then reports a tradition that resolves the matter entirely. When he was in Bavel, he had understood this to be a dispute between Rabbi and the *Rabbanan* — Rabbi holding *me-achshav*, the *Rabbanan* disputing. But when he made *aliyah* to Eretz Yisrael, he found Rabbi Assi sitting and teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ha-kol modim be-omer al menas ke-omer me-achshav dami* — everyone agrees that *al menas* means *me-achshav*. It is not Rabbi's lone opinion. There are no *Rabbanan* who dispute it. The claim that there exists a dissenting view regarding *al menas* has no basis.

### Dispute Scope Limited

The only genuine dispute, Rabbi Yochanan reports, is the case of *me-hayom u-le'achar mita* — and there, the debate is recorded in the *braita*: *get ve-eino get divrei Chachamim; Rabbi omer kazeh get*. That ambiguous construction — "from today and after my death" — is genuinely disputed. *Al menas* is not.

The *Gemara* then addresses Rav Yehuda's position directly: if the *Rabbanan* dispute Rabbi even regarding *al menas*, why does the *braita* record their debate specifically around *me-hayom u-le'achar mita*? Why not state the dispute regarding *al menas* and let us infer from there? The answer is *koach d-hetera adif* — it is preferable to demonstrate the force of the permissive ruling. Rabbi's position is strongest precisely in the hard case — *me-hayom u-le'achar mita*, where the language seems to push toward a later effect — and it is *koach d-hetera* to show that even there, Rabbi considers it a valid *get*. Conversely, demonstrating the force of the *Rabbanan*'s restrictive view in the easy case of *al menas* would serve no such purpose.

The upshot is clear: *al menas* universally means *me-achshav*. Nobody disputes this. The only case in which there is a genuine *tannaitic* dispute about whether a designation means now or later is *me-hayom u-le'achar mita* — the ambiguous formulation that stands at the center of all the debates traversed in this *daf*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 61

## Al Menat Conditions

### From Now Until 30 Days

The *daf* opens toward the bottom of 61b, a little before the *mishnah*, picking up a theme established in the preceding discussion. There we had been dealing with a man who says "this is your *get* from now and after thirty days," where a range of possibilities arose concerning whether the formula meant the *get* took effect immediately, whether there was ambiguity about the intended moment, or whether it described some ongoing mode of effectuation. The comparison was to *kiddushin*, not *get*, and the preceding *mishnah* had established the principle *kol ha'omer al menat ke'omer me'achshav damei*: whoever uses the *al menat* formulation is treated as though he said "from now." That position is clearly associated with Rebbe, and while there is a minority voice suggesting the matter is subject to debate, the overwhelming weight of evidence treats it as a consensus ruling.

We now turn to the next case: *al menat she'etayn lecha mi'kan v'ad shloshim yom* — "I am betrothing you on the condition that I give you two hundred *zuz* from now until thirty days." He must give the money within thirty days, or the *kiddushin* does not take effect. The *Gemara* raises the possibility that this is so obvious it need not be stated — *peshita*. The response: one might have thought that the phrase "within thirty days" is not strictly part of the condition itself but is rather an expression of self-encouragement, a kind of personal pledge to act promptly, while the operative *tnai* remains only the giving of two hundred *zuz*. The *Gemara* therefore clarifies that the time limit is indeed part of the condition itself, and failure to perform within thirty days leaves her not *mekudeshet*.

### Ownership of Zuz

The *mishnah* then takes up: *al menat she'yesh li matayim zuz* — "on the condition that I have two hundred *zuz*." If he does indeed have two hundred *zuz*, she is married. The plain reading of the *mishnah* implies that if he does not have it, she is definitely not *mekudeshet*. But this raises an immediate difficulty: how does one prove a negative? If you look in his wallet and find nothing, how can you be certain there is no money hidden elsewhere? A *braita* makes this explicit — *chashinan shema yesh lo*: we are concerned that perhaps he does have two hundred *zuz* tucked away somewhere.

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha b'kiddushei vadai, ha b'kiddushei safek* — the *mishnah* means she is not *definitely* married, while the *braita* clarifies she is not definitely *unmarried* either. When one cannot establish whether a *tnai* has been satisfied, the result is *safek mekudeshet* — a state of doubtful betrothal, which is of course the worst of both worlds. She cannot freely remarry without a *get*, yet she is not definitively bound to this man.

### Showing Money

The *mishnah* next addresses *al menat she'arech matayim zuz* — "on the condition that I show you two hundred *zuz*." If he shows her the money, she is married. But the *Gemara* immediately adds: *tana lo niskaven ela l'harot mishelo* — the implicit meaning of "show you" is "show you that I have it," specifically from his own funds. He cannot show her money belonging to others and count that as fulfillment of the condition.

This is a significant interpretive point. Technically the words "show you" were satisfied — he showed her money. Yet the *Gemara* reads in an implicit qualification that he never explicitly stated: the money must be his own. This is not *devarim shebalev* — a subjective, unexpressed intention that the law generally disregards — because there is an objectively understood context that any normal person would appreciate. When someone says "I will show you two hundred *zuz*" in the context of betrothal, the universal understanding is that he is demonstrating his capacity to provide, not merely producing coins that happen to be nearby.

The *Gemara* then rules: *v'im her'ah al hashulchan einah mekudeshet* — if he showed her money on the table of a money-changer, she is not *mekudeshet*. *Peshita* — obviously. The case that actually requires the ruling is the following: *d'af al gav d'nakat damei b'iska* — he is holding money given to him to invest. Here there is a genuine *hava amina*: the money is not wholly unrelated to him; he has investment rights, will earn a share of the profits, and in a sense manages the funds. Nevertheless, since it was never his money to begin with — it was entrusted to him by others for investment purposes — showing it does not satisfy the condition. His demonstrating that he oversees a large investment portfolio does not constitute showing that he has two hundred *zuz* of his own.

### Land as Condition

The parallel case for land follows: *al menat she'yesh li beit kor afar* — on the condition that he has a plot of land measuring a *beit kor*, which *Rashi* defines as seventy-five thousand square *amot*. If he has it, she is *mekudeshet*; if he does not, she is not. When he specifies a location — *al menat she'yesh li b'makom ploni* — she is only married if the land is in that precise location. Land elsewhere does not satisfy the condition. The *Gemara* addresses the possibility that he might argue: the land is functionally equivalent, the only difference is distance, and he pledges to exert the extra effort in traveling to it — *ana tarchana u'maitina*. The *Gemara* rejects this: the location was part of the explicit condition, and he cannot discount what he stated clearly.

This raises a broader question that runs throughout this section: when does context allow us to *add* something unstated, and when does it allow us to *discount* something that was stated? When he says "show you" and we read in "mine," we are supplementing an implicit understanding that nobody would contest. But when something was stated explicitly — a specific location, a specific time frame — context alone does not suffice to say he did not really mean it or that no one should care. There is a meaningful distinction between using context to fill a gap and using it to override an express term. The latter requires a far higher threshold, and even if the deviation seems trivial in practice, the condition as stated remains binding.

### Showing Land

The *mishnah* also takes up *al menat she'arecha beit kor afar* — on the condition that he shows her a *beit kor* of land — with exactly the parallel structure to the money case. *Tana: lo niskaven ela leharot mishelo* — when he says "show you," he means show you mine. If he shows her land in a valley that he does not own, she is not *mekudeshet*. The operative *hava amina* here involves the case of a *distura* — a sharecropper. This is a stronger case than the money analogy, because the man never said "I'll show you my land" — he said "I'll show you a *beit kor* of land." One might argue that a sharecropper demonstrating that he has means of agricultural support for the family has in substance fulfilled the promise. Yet the *Gemara* rules that even here, the implicit meaning of "show you" is that it must be land he fully owns.

What is striking is the degree to which we read the word "mine" into a statement that never used it. He said he would show her; we infer he meant to demonstrate that he possesses. And the inference is so powerful that even partial ownership — sharecropping rights, investment stakes — does not suffice. The *tnai* was for full ownership, even though those exact words were never spoken.

---

## Beit Kor Definition

### Hekdesh & Crevices

Having established that a *beit kor* is the relevant land measurement in the *kiddushin* case, the *Gemara* takes up a more fundamental question: what exactly constitutes a *beit kor*? The answer is less obvious than it first appears, because land is rarely perfectly flat, and the treatment of irregular topographical features — crevices and rocks — differs depending on the legal context in which the measurement arises.

The *Gemara* opens with the *hekdesh* case. When one sanctifies a field during the *yovel* period, the *Torah* establishes a fixed redemption rate: fifty *shekel kesef* for every plot of land on which one plants a *chomer* of barley seed — that is, for every *beit kor*. The relevant rule from the *mishnah* is: if the field contains crevices ten *tefachim* deep or rocks ten *tefachim* tall, they are not measured together with the field — *ein nimdadim imah*. If they are less than that, they are measured with it.

*Rashi* understands *nimdadim imah* to mean that the measurement literally follows the contour of the terrain — up and over the rock, down into the crevice — so that the total measured area includes those features. Others understand it more simply: features below the threshold are treated as if they are flat and included in the overall area, while those above the threshold are subtracted from the total.

The *Gemara* asks: why does it matter whether the crevices and rocks are included in the measurement or not? Even if they are excluded from the main field and treated as separate sanctified spaces, the owner said "I am sanctifying this land," and everything within the field's borders is in principle sanctified — either as part of the field or as its own unit. What is the *nafka mina*?

The answer lies in the redemption structure. The fixed fifty *shekel* rate applies per *beit kor*. If the field was exactly a *beit kor* and you subtract the crevice, you no longer have a *beit kor* subject to the fixed rate — you have a slightly-less-than-*beit kor* field and a separate crevice that is not a field at all. The slightly-smaller field gets redeemed at the proportional rate (which follows from the *Torah*'s use of the word *sadeh*, teaching that even partial plots are assessed proportionally). But the rock or water-filled crevice, as a non-plantable space, is not a *sadeh* and gets redeemed not at the standard rate but at market value.

*Mar Ukva bar Chama* then specifies: the entire discussion of *hekdesh* concerns crevices filled with water — *nikaymei d'maya* — which are not plantable. The comparison with rocks supports this: just as rocks cannot be planted, we are dealing with features that are inherently non-agricultural.

### Plantability Standard

This introduces the governing principle for the *hekdesh* case: **plantability**. Whether a topographical feature is included in the *beit kor* or treated as a separate unit depends on whether it can be farmed. A crevice filled with water cannot be planted; if it is deep enough to constitute its own space (ten *tefachim*), it is not a *sadeh* and is excluded. If it is shallower, the *Gemara* explains: *hani nagnei d'ara mikru* — it is treated as a basin of the land, an integral topographical feature of an otherwise cultivable field. Similarly, a shorter rock is called *shidra d'ara* — the spine of the land — a natural feature within a plantable field, not a separate space.

The logic is coherent: a field need not be perfectly uniform in every square *amah* to be called a *sadeh*. Minor topographical variation is part of what a field is. But once a feature becomes deep or tall enough to constitute its own independent space — its own *reshut* — it is evaluated on its own terms. If those terms yield a non-plantable space, it falls outside the category of *sadeh* and is redeemed differently.

### Mechira Standard

The *Gemara* then turns to the corresponding rule in *Bava Batra* for a sale — *mechira* — which, as anticipated, follows a meaningfully different standard. The *mishnah* there addresses the case where one says *beit kor afar ani mocher lach* — "I am selling you a *beit kor* of land" — and the field contains crevices ten *tefachim* deep or rocks ten *tefachim* tall. There too, they are *ein nimdadim imah* — not measured with the land, and the seller must make up the shortfall with additional flat land.

But *Ukva bar Chama* rules: *af al pi she'ein mele'im mayim* — even if the crevices are not filled with water. Unlike the *hekdesh* case, where plantability is the criterion, here the exclusion applies even to a dry, theoretically plantable crevice.

*Pappa* explains the rationale: *lafi she'ein adam rotzeh sheyiten et ma'otav b'sadeh achat v'teira'eh lo kishnayim ushlosha mekomot* — a person does not want to spend money on what he understands to be one field and then find himself working two or three separate spaces. Even if the deep crevice is technically cultivable, it requires separate attention, separate plowing, separate harvesting — a distinct agricultural operation. The buyer was expecting to purchase a coherent, unified working unit, and a field fragmented by deep crevices does not deliver that. The standard here is not formal plantability but the **reasonable expectation of the buyer** — what a person of ordinary sense would have meant and understood when agreeing to purchase a *beit kor*.

The underlying distinction between *hekdesh* and *mechira* is therefore conceptual. Redemption from *hekdesh* is governed by the *Torah*'s formal definition of a *sadeh*: so long as the land as a whole qualifies as a field — meaning it is predominantly plantable — the technical definition controls. There is no "meeting of minds," no subjective expectation to assess; the question is whether the land fits the Torah's category. A *mechira*, by contrast, is an agreement between two parties, and it is therefore governed by what each party reasonably understood the transaction to include. Economy of use, ease of harvest, and the coherence of the agricultural unit are all part of what the buyer was expecting to receive.

### Kiddushin Standard

This sets up the *Gemara*'s question regarding our case: *hacha mai* — which standard applies when a man says "I will show you a *beit kor*" as a condition of *kiddushin*? Do we compare it to *hekdesh* or to *mechira*?

One might argue that *kiddushin* resembles *mechira*, since it too involves a meeting of minds between two parties, and the woman might reasonably have expected a field that she could work as a coherent unit rather than one fractured by deep crevices. This argument mirrors the one the *Gemara* just made on behalf of the buyer: she could say she did not anticipate the extra difficulty. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* rules that as long as the crevice is not filled with water and is therefore plantable, the condition is satisfied. The man can say: *ana tarchana u'zarna u'maitina* — I will invest the extra effort, I will plant the crevice, I will bring in the yield. If the land is plantable — even if demanding — he has demonstrated that he has a *beit kor* of agricultural land to his name, and the *tnai* is met.

This result is instructive alongside what was said earlier about location. When the condition was not satisfied — when he claimed land in location A and the land was actually in location B — he could not say "don't worry, I'll do the extra traveling." That is a case where the condition was genuinely unmet and he was proposing to compensate for its non-fulfillment. Here, by contrast, the question is definitional: *is* this a *beit kor* or not? Under the applicable standard — plantability — it is. He is not waiving or compensating for a failed condition; he is asserting that the condition has in fact been met under the correct measure, and that he will personally absorb whatever extra labor that entails.

---

## Double Condition

### Rabbi Meir Principle

The *Gemara* now moves to one of the most consequential debates in the laws of *tnai*: the doctrine of *Rabbi Meir* concerning the proper formulation of a conditional. *Rabbi Meir omer: kol tnai she'eino k'tnai bnei Gad u'vnei Reuven, eino tnai* — any condition that is not formulated like the condition that *Moshe* made with the tribes of Gad and Reuven is not a valid condition. If the condition is defective, it is simply ignored and the underlying act — the *kiddushin*, the sale, the *get* — takes effect unconditionally.

The biblical source is the negotiation in *Bemidbar* where *Moshe* tells the tribes of Gad and Reuven: if you go armed before your brothers, you will receive the land of *Gil'ad*. And it is written: *v'im lo ya'avru chalutzim* — and if the armed men do not cross over, then they will receive with you in the land of *Kena'an*. The positive side of the condition was stated, and then the negative side was explicitly stated as well. *Rabbi Meir* derives from this that a valid *tnai* requires the formulation of **both** consequences — the positive outcome if the condition is met and the negative outcome if it is not. This is the *tnai kaful*, the doubled condition.

### Logic Explanation

The logical basis for this requirement is genuine and worth noting. In propositional logic, "if P then Q" does not entail "if not P then not Q." What it entails is the contrapositive: "if not Q then not P." The two are not equivalent. If one says "you are betrothed to me if I give you two hundred *zuz*," that statement alone does not logically imply that if he fails to give the money she is not betrothed. Strictly speaking, the non-fulfillment of the antecedent leaves the consequent indeterminate. Only by stating the negative explicitly — "and if I do not give you two hundred *zuz*, you are not betrothed" — does the condition operate symmetrically and unambiguously govern both outcomes.

This is not how most people speak in ordinary conversation, but *Rabbi Meir* holds that when it comes to legal acts as powerful as *kiddushin* — where the *ma'aseh* carries enormous weight and its undoing requires extensive formulation — only a rigorously complete statement of the condition suffices to make the *ma'aseh* contingent.

### Three Requirements

*Rashi* identifies three requirements derived from the *tnai b'nei Gad u'vnei Reuven*, of which the *mishnah* places primary emphasis on the *tnai kaful*:

The first is *tnai kaful* — the double condition, as described. Both the positive and negative outcomes must be articulated.

The second is *tnai kodem l'ma'aseh* — the condition must be stated before the act. If he says "you are betrothed to me — if I give you two hundred *zuz*," the act (*kiddushin*) is stated first and the condition appended afterward. Since primacy has been given to the act, the condition is not strong enough to prevent it from taking effect. The underlying principle is that the *ma'aseh* is so powerful a legal event that in order for a condition to subordinate it completely, the conditionality must be established from the very outset. Stating the act first gives it an unqualified primacy that a subsequent condition cannot overcome.

The third requirement is *hein kodem l'lav* — the affirmative outcome must be stated before the negative. One must say "if I give you, you are betrothed; if I do not give you, you are not betrothed" — not the reverse. If one ends by stating the positive outcome, the act is again given the last word, imparting to it a kind of finality that undermines the conditionality. *Rabbi Meir* requires that the condition be framed so that the act's contingency is expressed in every way possible: it comes second, its positive outcome is stated first, and the negative consequence is made explicit.

The formula that satisfies all three: *im etayn lach matayim zuz, harei at mekudeshet li; v'im lo etayn lach, einech mekudeshet li* — "if I give you two hundred *zuz*, you are betrothed to me; and if I do not give you, you are not betrothed to me." The *tnai* precedes the *ma'aseh*, the *hein* precedes the *lav*, and both sides are stated.

It is notable that every case in the preceding *mishnayot* — formulated as *al menat she'etayn lach matayim zuz*, *titkadshi li* — places the act before the condition, violating *Rabbi Meir*'s rule of *tnai kodem l'ma'aseh*, and none of them include a *tnai kaful*. Those *mishnayot* are not according to *Rabbi Meir*, and it is a legitimate question whether we *pasken* like him across all three requirements or only in some of them — particularly *tnai kaful*, which has stronger reason to be followed.

### Rabbi Hanina Position

*Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel* disagrees with the premise that the doubled formulation in *Bemidbar* was necessary to teach the doctrine of *tnai kaful*. He holds: *tzarich hadavar l'omro* — there was a specific reason *Moshe* had to state the negative side, but it was not to establish a general principle requiring repetition. Had *Moshe* not stated "and if they do not cross over," one might have inferred that the tribes would receive nothing at all — *afilu b'eretz Kena'an lo yinchalu*. The explicit statement was necessary not to articulate the consequence of non-fulfillment of the positive *tnai* (that was already implicit), but to inform them that they would nonetheless retain a portion in *Eretz Kena'an*. The repetition was doing positive work — granting a consolation benefit — not negative work establishing a rule of formulation.

On *Rabbi Hanina*'s view, therefore, a single-sided *tnai* is perfectly valid. The non-fulfillment of a stated condition implicitly negates the act; explicit repetition is not required.

### Pessukim Analysis

The *Gemara* examines this dispute through a careful reading of the relevant *pesukim*. *Rabbi Meir* challenges *Rabbi Hanina*: if the purpose of the negative formulation was merely to grant them a portion in *Eretz Kena'an*, it would have sufficed to say *im lo ya'avru v'ne'echzu b'tochachem* — if they do not cross over, they will be settled among you. That alone would establish their entitlement to a share among the rest of *Bnei Yisrael*. Why does the verse need to add *b'eretz Kena'an*? The extra words, says *Rabbi Meir*, are limiting: they specify *only* the land of *Kena'an*, thereby explicitly negating the earlier promise of *Gil'ad*. This demonstrates that without such explicit negation, the original promise would have remained in effect — proving that a *tnai kaful* is necessary.

*Rabbi Hanina* responds: had the *Torah* not said *b'eretz Kena'an*, the word *b'tochachem* would have been understood to mean among you in *Gil'ad* — a shared portion in the Transjordanian territory — and would not have conveyed any entitlement to *Kena'an* at all. The phrase *b'eretz Kena'an* was therefore necessary to specify that they receive a portion in *Kena'an* proper, not merely a share in *Gil'ad*. The non-receipt of all of *Gil'ad* in the case of non-fulfillment was already obvious from the simple logic of the condition and required no statement.

*Rabbi Meir* counters: *b'tochachem kol heicha d'ato lachu mashma* — "among you" means wherever you have, encompassing both *Gil'ad* and *Kena'an*. Had it said only *im lo ya'avru v'ne'echzu b'tochachem*, one would have understood that they receive equal shares everywhere — in *Gil'ad* and *Kena'an* alike. *B'eretz Kena'an* is therefore restricting: they get *Kena'an* and not *Gil'ad*. That restriction constitutes an explicit rejection of the original promise of *Gil'ad*, and without it, the original *tnai* would not have been negated.

### Meir vs Hanina

The fundamental disagreement can now be sharpened. *Rabbi Meir* holds that without the explicit negation embedded in *b'eretz Kena'an*, the original promise of *Gil'ad* would have remained in force even if the condition went unfulfilled. The entire doubled formulation was therefore necessary to negate the original *tnai* — establishing the general rule of *tnai kaful*. *Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel* holds that the negation of the original *tnai* was already implicit; the affirmative statement of the *tnai* is sufficient to generate, by implication, its negative consequence. The doubled language served the entirely different purpose of conferring a positive benefit — a portion in *Kena'an* — that would not otherwise have been granted.

### Inheritance Parable

To illustrate his position, *Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel* offers a *mashal*. A man on his deathbed distributes his estate among his sons. He says: Reuven shall inherit such-and-such a field; Shimon shall inherit such-and-such a field; and Levi, if he gives two hundred *zuz* to the estate, shall inherit field number three. If he had stopped there, one might have worried that Levi is disinherited entirely if he fails to give the money. The father therefore adds: if he does not give, he shall inherit together with his brothers among the remaining assets. *Mi garam lo l'yerash im echav b'shar nechasim? Kefelo garam lo* — what enabled him to share with his brothers in the remainder? The repetition — the doubled statement — did that. The parable's point: the doubled language was needed not to prevent the original promise from standing in the absence of fulfillment, but affirmatively to confer a benefit that would not otherwise have existed.

### Final Resolution

The *Gemara* notes a tension between the parable and the earlier language of the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* had stated that without the repetition, one might have inferred *she'afilu b'eretz Kena'an lo yinchalu* — that they would not have received *any* share in *Eretz Kena'an*. This suggests that *venachazu b'tochachem* alone would have given them a share in *Gil'ad* (not *Kena'an*), and only *b'eretz Kena'an* extended that to *Kena'an* as well. But the parable implies the repetition only helped with *shar nechasim* — the remainder — not with the primary promised asset.

The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *lo kashya — ha mikamei denamlei Rabbi Meir venachazu, ha levatar denamlei Rabbi Meir venachazu*. The answer turns on the phrase *venachazu* itself. Before the specification *b'eretz Kena'an*, the phrase *venachazu b'tochachem* already established, on its own, that they would receive a share in *Gil'ad*. Then *b'eretz Kena'an* added that they would also receive a share in *Kena'an*. For *Rabbi Hanina*, the logic of a single *tnai* already negated their exclusive claim to all of *Gil'ad* without any need for the doubled language; both subsequent phrases served only to specify and expand the positive benefits they would retain. For *Rabbi Meir*, this entire scaffolding was necessary precisely to overcome the force of the original unrepeated promise — which, without explicit negation, would have continued to entitle them to all of *Gil'ad*. The *sugyah* on the parsing of the *pesukim* is thus complete, and the *shiur* will continue tomorrow with the working out of *Rabbi Meir*'s doctrine of *tnai kaful* in its practical applications.

---

# Kiddushin 62

## Tnai Kaful Debate

### Opening & Context

The daf begins in the middle of 61b, picking up the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel concerning whether the requirement of a *tnai kaful* — a double condition — can be derived from the condition set by Bnei Gad and Bnei Reuven, and whether, absent an explicit statement of the negative clause, one should assume the act is binding even if the condition is not met.

Before entering the *sugyah* proper, it is worth noting the broader framing of the debate. Rabbi Meir's position is articulated in two distinct ways in the rabbinic literature. One formulation is the technical halachic principle: *kol tnai she-eino ke-tnai Bnei Gad u-Bnei Reuven eino tnai* — any condition that is not structured like the condition of Bnei Gad and Bnei Reuven is not a valid condition. That is a claim about *hilchos tna'im*, about what makes a stipulation legally operative in the context of a halakhic act. The second formulation, however, is purely linguistic: *miklal lav ee ata shomea hen u-miklal hen ee ata shomea lav* — from the positive you cannot infer the negative, and from the negative you cannot infer the positive. That principle has nothing to do with formal legal conditionality. It is a claim about how language works and how rigorously we should apply formal logic to ordinary speech. The *gemara's* strategy in the passages that follow — moving through a series of *psukim* from across the Torah — strongly suggests it is this second, linguistic dimension that is primarily at issue, even as Tosafot throughout the *sugyah* attempts to read everything through the narrower lens of *tnai kaful* in the technical halachic sense.

### Bereishit Example

The *gemara* opens with a *bishlama* formulation: it makes sense according to Rabbi Meir that the verse in Bereishit 4 states, *im tetiv se'et v'im lo tetiv la-petach chatat rovetz* — if you do good you will be uplifted, and if you do not do good, sin crouches at the door. According to Rabbi Meir, who holds that you cannot infer the negative from the positive, it was necessary to state both sides explicitly.

The *gemara* then asks: and according to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, who maintains that the negative is indeed implied by the positive, why did the verse need to state the negative side at all? The answer is: *itzterich* — it was necessary. Without the explicit negative clause, one might have thought that *im tetiv agra* — if you do good you are rewarded — and *im lo tetiv*, if you do not do good, *lo agra ve-lo dina* — you simply receive no reward, but no punishment either. In other words, Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's point is not that the negative clause is superfluous, but that it carries additional information beyond the mere negation of the positive. Without it, we would know only that one does not receive what was promised in the first clause; we would not know that the opposite consequence actively applies. This distinction — between the absence of reward and the imposition of punishment — is precisely what necessitates stating the reverse.

### Sotah Case

The *gemara* turns to a verse from the *sotah* passage: *im lo shachav ish otach v'im lo satit tuma tachat ishech hinaki* — if no man has lain with you and if you have not strayed from your husband, you will be cleansed. The verse does not state the converse — that if you did stray you will be punished. According to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, this is the expected pattern: you need not state the flip side. The negative of the first clause implies only that you will not receive what the first clause promised, but does not by itself indicate a positive punishment.

But according to Rabbi Meir, who requires the double condition, why does the verse omit the explicit reverse? The *gemara* answers: *hinaki ketiv* — the word *hinaki* is written *chaser*, defectively, without the expected *yud*. Rabbi Tanchum teaches that this orthographic anomaly is intentional, allowing the verse to be read as a *drasha* of *chinaki* — you will be strangled. The flip side is thus hidden within the *pasuk* itself. The word that says "you will be cleansed" simultaneously implies "you will be strangled," and Rabbi Meir can maintain that without such a device, the verse would have been deficient.

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, for his part, also explains why the verse required even the implicit suggestion of *chinaki*: without it, one might have thought that *im lo shachav* — if she is innocent, she is cleansed — but *im shachav*, if she committed adultery, *lo hinaki ve-lo chinaki* — she neither gets cleansed nor strangled, merely violating a prohibition without incurring the *sotah* punishment. The verse therefore encodes the punishment even within its conditional structure.

It is worth pausing here. The *gemara*'s movement through these verses — Bereishit, Vayikra, the *sotah* passage — makes clear that what is being examined is not only a formal rule of *tnai kaful* in the domain of *kiddushin* or *gittin*, but a broader question of how conditional language functions. When a verse says "if X then Y," does the reader know what happens in the case of not-X? From a strict logical standpoint, the implication does not follow. From the standpoint of ordinary language, it often does. Rabbi Meir holds the stricter logical position; Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel holds that ordinary language entitles one to infer the reverse, but only in the limited sense that the positive result of the first clause will not obtain — nothing more.

### Abraham's Oath

The *gemara* next cites the episode of Avraham's oath to his servant in Bereishit 24. Avraham adjures his servant not to take a wife for his son Yitzchak from the daughters of Canaan, and instructs him to go to Avraham's homeland. He then says: *v'im lo taveh ha'isha lalechet acharecha v'nikita mishvuati* — and if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you will be cleansed of my oath. And similarly, *v'im lo yitnu lach* — if they do not give her to you. According to Rabbi Meir, it makes sense that the verse spells out the condition under which the servant would be released from the oath, because without stating it explicitly one could not have inferred it.

The *gemara* notes that the passages being cited include both Avraham's original formulation and the servant's later repetition of it to Lavan, treating them as part of the same narrative unit.

Tosafot raises a pointed question: this is not really a *tnai* in the formal halachic sense at all. Avraham did not say "you are bound by the oath if X and released if not-X." He issued a direct oath — you shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. The case of *v'nikita mishvuati* — being released from the oath — is a separate matter, not a classically structured condition. Tosafot asks: *ma inyan zeh etzel machlokes* — what does this have to do with the dispute? If Avraham had not spelled out the conditions of release, the servant might simply have assumed he was bound by the oath unconditionally, whether he succeeded or not. The fact that the release had to be stated explicitly tells us something, but Tosafot is uncertain whether it tells us the same thing as the dispute about *tnai kaful*.

The *gemara*'s answer is that according to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, even he concedes that the release conditions needed to be stated, because otherwise one might have assumed: if the parents are willing but the girl herself is not, bring her against her will. The verse therefore had to say *v'im lo taveh ha'isha* — if the woman herself is unwilling — to make clear that her refusal alone, independently of her parents' objection, is sufficient grounds for the servant's release. Similarly, *v'im lo yitnu lach* — even if she is willing but her family objects — that too suffices. Neither side's objection alone, without the other's, would have been assumed to constitute a legitimate out without explicit statement.

The *gemara*'s handling of this passage makes it clear, again, that what is at stake is not primarily a technical rule about the structure of a halakhic *tnai*, but rather a question about what we can and cannot infer from the language of conditionality in its broadest sense.

---

## Verse Support

### Blessings/Curses

The *gemara* continues to marshal biblical support for Rabbi Meir's position, turning to the *tochachah* passages in Vayikra. The verse states: *im bechukotai telechu* — if you follow my statutes, then all the blessings enumerated will come upon you. The Torah then separately states: *v'im bechukotai timasu* — but if you despise my statutes, then the curses will follow. According to Rabbi Meir, one cannot infer the curses from the mere absence of the blessings; the negative clause must be stated explicitly.

According to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel: why state both? The *gemara* answers that without the explicit negative clause, one would have known only that failing to follow the *mitzvos* means you do not receive the promised *bracha* — but one would not know that something actively bad happens. The punishment is not implied by the mere absence of the reward. That is precisely why the verse must say it: *lo bracha v'lo klalah* — no blessing and no curse — is what one would have assumed; the explicit statement is necessary to convey that the curse actively follows.

The same analysis applies to the verses in Yeshayahu: *im tovu ushmartem tuv ha'aretz tocheilu* — if you desire and obey, you will eat of the good of the land; *v'im temanu u-meritem cherev tukhallu* — but if you rebel, you will be consumed by the sword. Again, without the second clause, one would have known only that the reward is withheld, not that a punishment is incurred.

At this point the *gemara* briefly digresses to explain the phrase *cherev tukhallu* — "the sword will consume you" — which presents an unusual grammatical structure. Rava explains that this refers to *milcha galulanita nahama d'se'arei akusha u-vatzli* — coarse salt, hard barley bread, and onions. The teaching is that plain hard bread with salt and onions is as harmful to the body as swallowing swords, so that *cherev tukhallu* denotes eating food that tears up the body from within.

### Sotah Drasha

The *gemara* returns to the *sotah* passage in greater depth. The verse reads: *im lo shachav ish otach v'im lo satit tuma tachat ishech hinaki* — and you will be cleansed. The verse presents only the positive outcome of innocence; it does not explicitly state what happens if she did sin. This supports Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel: you do not need to state the negative clause; you only need to specify the positive, and the implication is that failure to meet the condition means failure to receive what the positive clause promised — in this case, cleansing.

But according to Rabbi Meir, the verse should have spelled out *chinaki* — strangling — as the reverse. The *gemara* answers, as noted above, that *hinaki ketiv* — the word is written *chaser* — allowing for the *drasha* of *chinaki* to be embedded within the text. Rabbi Meir can thus maintain his position: the reverse is stated, just in an encoded form.

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel then explains why even according to his view the hint was necessary: without it, one might have assumed that *im shachav* — if she did commit adultery — *lo hinaki v'lo chinaki* — neither cleansed nor punished in the specific way the *sotah* ceremony implies, but merely in violation of a general prohibition. The encoded word *chinaki* therefore adds: no, the specific *sotah* punishment does apply.

### Parah Adumah

The *gemara* then cites the laws of *parah adumah* purification. The verse states: *hu yitchata bo bayom hashlishi u-vayom hashvi'i yithar* — he shall purify himself on the third day and on the seventh day, and he will be cleansed. The verse then adds: *v'im lo yitchata bayom hashlishi u-vayom hashvi'i lo yithar* — and if he does not do so on both the third and seventh days, he will not become pure. According to Rabbi Meir, it makes sense that the verse states both sides: without the negative clause, one could not infer that failure to do both invalidates the purification.

According to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel: why must both sides be stated? The *gemara* answers that without the negative clause, one might have thought the requirement of day three and day seven is a *lechatchila* but not strictly necessary *bedi'eved*. Perhaps if one performed the purification only on day three or only on day seven, it would still be effective after the fact. The negative clause teaches that both days are indispensable: absence of either renders the purification invalid.

### Heifer Details

Having cited the *parah adumah* verse in the context of the *tnai kaful* debate, the *gemara* pauses to expound on two additional phrases in those laws that might appear redundant. The verse *viyazeh ha-tahor al ha-tamei bayom hashlishi u-vayom hashvi'i* — the pure one shall sprinkle on the impure person on day three and on day seven — why does the Torah repeat this specification after already having stated it?

The *gemara* explains: without this repetition, one might have thought that "day three" and "day seven" function merely to exclude day two and day six — that is, one cannot shorten the purification period below three and seven. But one might then have assumed that extending the period would be acceptable: doing the sprinkling on day three and day eight, for instance, would be fine since one is adding days of purification rather than subtracting them. The repetition teaches that there can be no variation — neither shorter nor longer — only precisely day three and day seven.

Similarly, another verse — *v'chiteo bayom hashvi'i* — why does it need to specify cleansing on the seventh day after already establishing the requirement? The *gemara* explains that without this verse one might have thought the full regimen of day three and day seven is necessary only for *kodashim* — sacred foods — but that for *terumah*, perhaps one day alone would suffice. The additional verse teaches that the full requirement applies uniformly.

This extended explication of the *parah adumah* passage is the *gemara*'s own, not directly tied to the Rabbi Meir–Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel dispute, but it follows naturally from the verse cited in that context. Its presence here reinforces the observation that the *gemara* is treating the *tnai kaful* debate not merely as a technical legal question but as an entry point into broader questions of how language and conditional structures operate across the full breadth of Torah.

---

## Tnai Kaful Debate (II)

### Tosafot Analysis

Having worked through the *sugyah*, the *gemara* notes — and Tosafot presses — that it is not entirely obvious how these biblical examples relate to the formal dispute about *tnai kaful* in halakhic contexts. The *gemara* concludes its treatment of the *parah adumah* verse and the *tnai kaful* debate by returning to Tosafot's broader concern.

Tosafot asks a pointed question (*teima*): the verse *hu yitchata* — what does this have to do with the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel? After all, in many places in the Torah it says *rachatz bamayim v'taher* — he shall wash in water and be purified — and there is no felt need to add "and if he does not wash, he will not be purified." The act is described as achieving a result; its negative is obviously implied. So how does the *parah adumah* verse, which seems similarly descriptive, become relevant to the debate?

Tosafot answers: *d'lo dami* — these are not comparable. When the Torah says *rachatz bamayim v'taher*, it is phrased as a *mitzvah*, a command. Since God commanded this act, it is self-evident that failure to perform it means failure to achieve the result. There is no conditional reading possible; this is simply the mechanism by which the thing works. But the verse *hu yitchata bayom hashlishi* — "he shall purify himself on day three and on day seven, and he will be purified" — reads slightly differently. The phrasing, Tosafot observes, is more suggestive of a condition: *michdi ketiv hu yitchata — d'havei k'ilu ketiv im yitchata bo yithar* — it is as though the text said "if he purifies himself, he will be purified." Had it said *yitchata v'yithar* in direct sequence, it would read as a command with a consequence; instead the formulation carries a conditional flavor. And it is precisely this conditional flavor that brings it within the orbit of the Rabbi Meir–Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel dispute.

What Tosafot is doing here is distinguishing three categories. The first is the classic *tnai* structure: "if X then Y" — an explicit condition where one might ask whether Y obtains even in the absence of X. The second is the descriptive: "doing this act achieves this result." There, obviously, the absence of the act means the result is not achieved; no inferential problem arises. The third is the command: "you must do X and Y will follow." There too, as Tosafot notes, the logic is clear — it is a *mitzvah*, and not performing it obviously forfeits the result.

The middle, descriptive category is where the dispute becomes interesting. When a verse describes what an act accomplishes rather than commanding it or conditioning it, and when its phrasing tilts slightly toward the conditional, that is where Rabbi Meir insists the negative clause must be stated, and Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel insists it is sufficiently implied. The *parah adumah* verse sits in this middle zone, which is why the *gemara* brings it.

The larger picture that emerges from the full *sugyah* is this: Rabbi Meir's position is not merely a technical rule about the formal structure of *tna'im* in *kiddushin* and *gittin*. It reflects a sustained commitment to strict inferential discipline — a refusal to assume that the converse of a statement is implied by the statement itself. That principle has implications across legal acts, biblical narrative, divine promise, and ritual law. And that is precisely why the *gemara* ranges so far afield in illustrating it.

At the same time, it is worth noting that there remain substantial unresolved questions about Rabbi Meir's position: whether it applies as a general linguistic rule or only to formal halakhic *tna'im*; whether other requirements of *tna'im* — such as *tnai kodem l'ma'aseh* (the condition preceding the act) or *hen kodem la-lav* (the positive clause preceding the negative) — are accepted by Rabbi Meir, disputed, or simply not addressed in this *sugyah*. The *gemara* here focuses exclusively on *tnai kaful*; the full picture of *hilchos tna'im* remains to be assembled from elsewhere.

---

## Error & Deception

### Unspoken Conditions

The *mishnah* presents a series of cases in which a man betroths a woman under a certain assumption that turns out to be mistaken. He thought she was a *kohenet*, she turns out to be a *leviya*. He thought she was a *leviya*, she is a *kohenet*. He thought she was poor and she is wealthy. He thought she was wealthy and she is poor. In all these cases, the ruling is *harei zu mekudeshet* — she is nonetheless betrothed, fully and validly. The reason given is *mipnei shelo hit'atu* — because she did not deceive him. He deceived himself. The assumption was in his mind, unspoken, and no explicit condition was attached to the *kiddushin*.

It is worth noting a small but telling point in the *mishnah*'s language. The categories — *kohenet*, *leviya*, wealthy, poor — are presented symmetrically. One might assume a *kohenet* or a *leviya* is always preferred, but the *mishnah*'s symmetry suggests otherwise: different men have different preferences and different concerns, and neither status is presumed superior to the other.

### Devarim Shebaleiv

The operative principle is *devarim she-b'lev einam devarim* — matters that remain in the heart, unexpressed, are not halakhically operative. A condition or assumption that is never articulated cannot render the act conditional. Since the man's belief about her status was never stated as part of the *kiddushin* transaction, it has no legal force, and the *kiddushin* stands.

### Complexities

The *mishnah*'s ruling, however, leaves significant questions unaddressed. The *mishnah* identifies two distinct elements: the absence of deception, and the absence of articulated conditions. But these can come apart in important ways, and the *gemara* does not fully explore the resulting complexity.
