The Gemara rejects this: *lo shavik inish midi d'is lei hana'ei minei v'avid midi d'leis lei hana'ei minei* — a person does not abandon something that benefits him in favor of something that does not. When a father marries off his *ketanah*, he retains the *kesef kiddushin* — the ring or money given by the *mekadesh* — for himself. When he acts as *shaliach* for his adult daughter, the *kesef kiddushin* goes to her. He therefore has a financial incentive to be marrying off the *ketanah* rather than the *bogeret*.

### Father's Obligation

The Gemara presses further: what if even the adult daughter told the father that he may keep the *kesef kiddushin* for his efforts? Would we not then presume, absent any financial differential, that the *bogeret* is the intended bride? The Gemara answers that even so, the father's presumed intention remains the *ketanah*. The reason is not financial but moral and legal: *lo shavik inish mitzvah d'ramya alei v'avid mitzvah d'lo ramya alei* — a person does not set aside an obligation that rests upon him in order to fulfill one that does not.

The Torah places the responsibility for an underage daughter squarely on her father. In the world the Talmud presumes, a daughter moves directly from *beit aviha* — her father's home — to *beit ba'alah* — her husband's home. There is no normative period of independent adult life without either a father's or a husband's protection. Once a girl reaches *bogeret* status, she acquires her own legal standing and can manage her own affairs; she is, in a sense, no longer fully under her father's jurisdiction. The *ketanah*, however, is entirely his responsibility. He is obligated to ensure that she transitions properly from his household into a marriage. That obligation weighs on him and constitutes the priority: he will, as it were, take care of his own obligations first.

### Two Daughter Groups

The Mishnah then addresses a more complex case. A man has two groups of daughters — one group from an earlier wife and a second group from a later wife. He says, "I betrothed my *gedolah* — my oldest," but then cannot remember precisely whom he meant. The ambiguity the Mishnah describes is striking: did he mean the oldest of the older group? The oldest of the younger group — who is the oldest within that set? Or the youngest of the older group — who is nonetheless older than the oldest of the younger group?

The Mishnah walks through the parallel case using the word *ketanah* — youngest — with the same structure.

### Rabbi Meir's Approach

Rabbi Meir holds that all daughters who could in any sense be called *gedolah* are potentially betrothed and therefore *asur* — all, that is, except for the very youngest of the younger group. Rabbi Meir's reasoning is that a person is willing to use a term loosely and allow themselves to enter into a state of ambiguity. If he remembers saying "*gedolah*," he may well have been using that label in a relative sense — anyone who is older than someone else might be called *gedolah*. As long as a daughter has someone younger than her, she can bear that label. Rabbi Meir does not expect precision in such a memory, and the result is that the uncertainty sweeps broadly.

### Rabbi Yosi's View

Rabbi Yosi takes the opposite position: *kulan mutarot chutz min hagedolah shebagedolot* — they are all permitted except for the oldest of the oldest group. Rabbi Yosi reasons that a person does not get themselves into ambiguity (*lo machzik inish nafshei besafeka*). If what he remembers is the word *gedolah*, he must mean the most specific and unambiguous referent of that word — the daughter who is oldest in the clearest sense, the oldest of the oldest group. Anything less definite would not have registered in his memory under that label.

### Pesach Comparison

The Gemara notes that there is an apparently parallel debate elsewhere. If someone takes a *neder* forbidding himself from something *ad pnei HaPesach* — until the "face" of *Pesach* — what does that mean? The Mishnah cited there states: Rabbi Meir says *asur ad sheyagia* — forbidden until *Pesach* arrives; Rabbi Yosi says *asur ad sheyeitzei* — forbidden until *Pesach* departs. But this seems to be the reverse of their positions in our Mishnah. Here, Rabbi Meir holds that the term can refer to many things and thus extends the prohibition broadly; there, Rabbi Meir seems to take the narrower reading, and Rabbi Yosi the broader one.

The Gemara initially suggests that the names may have been accidentally reversed in transmission — *muchlefet hashita* — and that a *baraita* records the positions in the correct order consistent with our Mishnah.

### Abaye's Precision

Abaye offers a fundamental clarification of the debate in our Mishnah. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi, he says, applies specifically to the case of *shtei kitei banot* — two distinct groups of daughters. The crucial feature of two groups is that membership in the older group itself confers the label *gedolah* on every daughter within it. A daughter in the older group can be called *gedolah* not because she is the oldest individual, but because she belongs to the *kat hagedolah* — the older cohort. This is what allows the ambiguity to extend beyond a single individual.

By contrast, if there is only one group of daughters — say, four daughters in a single family unit — then *gedolah* means the oldest and *ketanah* means the youngest, full stop. A middle daughter would be called by her name. The label *gedolah* or *ketanah* attaches unambiguously only to the extremes. In that case, there is no dispute: everyone agrees that *gedolah* means precisely the oldest, and *ketanah* precisely the youngest.

### Three Daughters Test

Rav Adda bar Masna challenges Abaye: if the debate applies only when there are two groups, and within those groups the label *gedolah* attaches to everyone in the older cohort, then what if there are three daughters in the younger group rather than two? The middle one of the younger group would seem ambiguous — she could arguably be called *gedolah* relative to the youngest, but she cannot be the *gedolah* of the younger group in any straightforward sense. Should she then be *mutar*?

Abaye responds that the Mishnah is best read as presupposing exactly two daughters in the younger group. This is evident from the Mishnah's own language: it says that the father does not know whether he meant *gedolah shebakedolot*, *gedolah shebaketanot*, or *ketanah shebagedolot* — but says nothing about a middle daughter in either group. If there were three in the younger group, the Mishnah would have needed to mention the middle one as a case of ambiguity. Since it does not, the case must be that there are only two in each group.

### Pesach Resolution

Returning to the *Pesach* case, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua asks Rava: if the entire debate in the Mishnah rests on the two-group structure — which allows the label *gedolah* to attach to an entire cohort rather than a single individual — why does the *Pesach* case generate a parallel dispute? The days of *Pesach* are all in one group; there are not two cohorts of days. According to Abaye, only one day should clearly be called the *pnei haPesach*, just as only one daughter in a single group can unambiguously be called *gedolah*.

The Gemara resolves this by clarifying that the *Pesach* case involves an entirely different type of dispute. The debate there is not about whether a person enters into ambiguity or remembers things loosely — it is a purely linguistic question about the meaning of the word *pnei*. One view (*mar savar*) holds that *pnei* means "before" — *ad kamei Pischa* — and so the prohibition lasts until *Pesach* begins. The other view holds that *pnei* derives from *mifnei* — to turn away or pass — and so the prohibition lasts until *Pesach* has passed. The two Amoraim are therefore debating the semantic content of a single word, not the psychological question of how loosely people use descriptive labels or whether they tolerate ambiguity. Once this distinction is clear, the apparent parallel with the daughters case dissolves entirely, and the positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi in our Mishnah stand on their own terms without needing to be reversed.

---

## He Said / She Said

### His Claim Alone

The Mishnah presents a series of cases in which the two parties to an alleged *kiddushin* give contradictory accounts. The first: a man says to a woman, *kidashtich* — "I betrothed you" — and she says, *lo kidashtani* — "you did not betroth me." The result is asymmetric. He is *asur* to her relatives — he cannot marry her mother, her daughter, her sister — because he is bound by his own statement. She, however, is entirely *muteret*: she is not bound by his statement and may marry whomever she wishes, including his own relatives. One person's claim cannot impose a status upon another person.

### Her Claim Alone

The reverse: she says he married her, and he says he did not. Now she is *asurah* to his relatives — and, more immediately, she cannot marry any other man, since she is claiming she is already married. He, however, is *mutar* to her relatives, since he denies the marriage. She has bound herself by her own words; she has not bound him.

### Different Targets

The Mishnah then introduces cases in which the two parties do not even agree on who was betrothed. He says, "I betrothed you," and she says, "No — you betrothed my daughter." Each party is bound only by their own statement. He is *asur* to the mother's relatives (since he claims he married her), but *mutar* to the daughter's relatives (since he makes no such claim about her). The mother is *muteret* to his relatives (since she does not claim to be married to him), and the daughter is also *muteret* to his relatives, because a mother's claim about her daughter's betrothal does not bind the daughter.

### Mother vs. Daughter

The final case reverses the parties: he says, "I betrothed your daughter," and she says, "No — you betrothed me." Again, each is bound only by their own claim. He is *asur* to the daughter's relatives, *mutar* to the mother's relatives. She is *asurah* to his relatives because she claims the marriage, and the daughter remains *muteret* to his relatives since she said nothing.

The underlying principle throughout is simple: *you are bound by your own statement, and your statement cannot bind another person*.

### Why Believe Whom

The Gemara asks why these cases need to be stated explicitly rather than derived from each other. The answer illuminates the asymmetry between male and female claims. When a man says he married a woman, it costs him relatively little: his only immediate *issur* is with respect to her close relatives. He remains free to marry other women; no sweeping prohibition falls upon him. Since his statement is so inexpensive, *gavra lo ikhpat lei u'mikrei amar* — men will make such statements casually — and we have no strong reason to extend its legal effect to bind anyone else.

By contrast, when a woman says she is married to a man, she is making an extraordinarily consequential claim. She is effectively declaring herself *asurah* to every other man in the world. No one would make such a statement carelessly or frivolously. The inherent weight of her claim gives it credibility: *lo havi amra l'meisar nafsha b'krovateih* — she would not make that statement, imposing such a severe restriction upon herself, unless it were true. One might therefore argue that even the man should be bound — that at minimum he should not be permitted to marry her relatives, since she has given such a compelling self-incriminating statement. The Gemara concludes, however, that even this reasoning does not suffice to make something *asur* upon another person on the basis of one party's unilateral claim.

### Mother's No Power

The case of the mother who claims that her daughter was betrothed raises a natural question: the Torah empowers a father to betroth off his underage daughter, but grants no such authority to the mother. Might we nonetheless say that rabbinically, the mother should be believed enough to impose some restriction upon her daughter? The Gemara states that no such rabbinic authority exists — the mother's claim does not bind the daughter even rabbinically. The *chiddush* of the Mishnah in including this case is precisely to tell us that we do not extend the father's Torah-level power to the mother on a rabbinic basis.

### Pesach & Get

The Gemara then addresses the practical consequence in the case where she claims to be married and he denies it. Shmuel holds: *mevakshin mimenu litten get* — we ask him, as a matter of propriety and compassion, to give her a *get*. She has put herself in a bind by her own statement; she can now not marry anyone else. Even though he is not halakhically compelled to do anything, it is proper to request that he give her a *get* and thereby free her from her self-imposed status.

### Request vs. Coercion

Rav's position initially appears to be that we *force* him to give a *get* — *kofin*. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between Rav and Shmuel by showing that they are not disputing but complementing one another. Shmuel's statement establishes that we request a *get* from him. Rav adds: *v'im natan get mei-atzmo* — if he gives the *get* on his own initiative, without being asked or pressured by the *beit din*, that act constitutes an implicit admission that he was in fact married to her. Having admitted the marriage through the voluntary *get*, we then *force* him to pay her *ketubah*.

The practical implication is notable: a man in this situation would be well advised to give the *get* only in response to the *beit din's* request, and not spontaneously. A voluntary *get*, given before any such request, reads as an admission of the marriage and opens him to a compelled *ketubah* payment. The Gemara presents this without editorializing, though the underlying logic is clear.

---

## Witnesses Requirement

### Rav Yehuda's Rule

The Gemara now turns to what is, in many respects, one of the most consequential *sugyot* in the entire tractate for contemporary *hilchos kiddushin*. Rav Yehuda states: *hamekadesh be'ed echad ein chosheshin lekiddushav* — if a man performs *kiddushin* with only one witness present, we have no concern that the *kiddushin* is binding. The marriage is without legal effect.

### Constitutive vs. Evident…

This rule is clear in its practical import, but its conceptual basis is ambiguous. Does the requirement for two witnesses mean that their presence is necessary to *prove* the *kiddushin* occurred — so that if everyone already agrees it happened, one witness might suffice? Or does it mean that the presence of two kosher witnesses is *constitutive* of the *kiddushin* itself — without them, the act simply does not take effect as a *kiddushin*, regardless of how confident everyone is that it occurred? The test case is clear: both parties fully admit that *kiddushin* took place, and one witness corroborates them. We have no factual doubt whatsoever. Is this *kiddushin* binding?

### Rav Yehuda Uncertain

Rav Yehuda himself, when asked this precise question, could not resolve it. He vacillated — *lo pashat b'yadei* — and left the question open. Whether two witnesses are required as a constitutive element of *kiddushin* or merely as an evidentiary mechanism for proving it remained, for him, genuinely uncertain.

### Shmuel's Clear Position

Rav Nachman, citing Shmuel, provides an unambiguous answer: *hamekadesh be'ed echad ein chosheshin lekiddushav, va'afilu shneihem modim* — even if both parties fully admit to the *kiddushin*, without two witnesses present the *kiddushin* is not legally binding. Shmuel's position is that witnesses are not merely evidentiary — they are constitutive. Without them, the act of *kiddushin* does not take legal effect.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges this from the very Mishnah we have been studying. The *he said / she said* cases in the Mishnah — which occupy a significant portion of the tractate — appear to operate without any mention of witnesses. A man says he betrothed a woman; she denies it; the Mishnah determines who is bound by what. If *kiddushin* requires two witnesses to be legally binding, the Mishnah's entire framework of claims and counter-claims should be irrelevant: without witnesses, no *kiddushin* occurred, end of discussion. The fact that the Mishnah engages extensively with whose statement binds whom seems to presuppose that *kiddushin* can be legally effective without two witnesses present and actively testifying.

### One Witness Present

The Gemara resolves Rava's challenge by reinterpreting the Mishnah's scenario. The cases in the Mishnah do not presume an absence of witnesses. Rather, the Gemara reads the Mishnah as operating in a case where the claimant asserts that witnesses were present at the time — *kidashtich bifnei ploni u'ploni* — but those witnesses are not currently available to testify. They have, as the Gemara puts it, gone overseas (*halchu lahem limdinat hayam*). The legal question is then not whether *kiddushin* requires witnesses, but rather: given that someone claims witnesses were present, how much do we credit that claim? Each party is bound by their own statement regarding an alleged act they themselves assert was properly witnessed, even though those witnesses cannot currently be produced.

### All Cases Presume Witness

This resolution has far-reaching implications. Every one of the Mishnah's cases — not just the current ones but all the earlier discussions about who is believed regarding marriage — must be understood as involving a claim that witnesses were present, even though those witnesses are not currently being called to testify. The Mishnah is not operating in a world without witnesses; it is operating in a world where witnesses existed at the time but are unavailable now. This is, the Gemara notes, a significant reinterpretation of the entire series of *mishnayos*, and it is precisely what Shmuel's position requires.

### Seclusion as Witnesses

The Gemara then raises a further challenge from the debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* regarding a man who divorced his wife and later spent the night with her at an inn. *Beit Hillel* holds that a second *get* is required — suggesting that the encounter may have constituted new *kiddushin*; *Beit Shammai* holds it does not. The Gemara initially considers whether this debate might hinge on the question of one witness versus two, with the positions of *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* mapping onto different views of evidentiary sufficiency.

### What Witnesses See

The Gemara immediately recognizes that this reading does not hold up under scrutiny. If witnesses directly observed them having intercourse, *Beit Shammai* would have no grounds to say no second *get* is needed. And if there were no witnesses at all, *Beit Hillel* would have no basis to require one. The debate cannot be about the number of witnesses. It must concern something else.

The Gemara resolves this: the case involves witnesses who observed the couple entering into *yichud* — seclusion together — but who did not directly witness any sexual act. The legal and factual question is whether *eidei yichud* — witnesses to seclusion — are treated as *eidei biah* — witnesses to intercourse — and thereby constitute evidence of a new act of *kiddushin*.

### Beis Shammai

*Beit Shammai* holds: *lo amrinan hein hein eidei yichud hein hein eidei biah* — we do not treat witnesses to seclusion as equivalent to witnesses to intercourse. Seclusion alone, without prior sexual history between the parties, does not allow us to presume that intercourse occurred, and therefore no new *kiddushin* is created.

### Beis Hillel

*Beit Hillel* holds the opposite: *amrinan hein hein eidei yichud hein hein eidei biah* — where the couple had previously been married and had engaged in intercourse, witnesses seeing them enter seclusion together are treated as if they had witnessed the sexual act itself, and this constitutes evidence of a new *kiddushin* requiring a new *get*.

### Consensus on Virgins

Both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* agree, however, that if the couple had been divorced after *eirusin* — betrothal without consummation — and had therefore never had sexual relations, then witnesses to seclusion are not treated as witnesses to intercourse, and no second *get* is required. The reasoning: *she'ein libo gas bah* — without the prior intimacy of a consummated marriage, we cannot presume that an incidental overnight encounter would naturally lead to intercourse. The debate between the two schools thus concerns not the requirement for witnesses, but the evidentiary and presumptive weight to be assigned to what those witnesses actually saw.

---

---

# Kiddushin 65

## Chazakah & Yibum Belief

### Abaye's Clarification

The daf opens mid-*sugya*, carrying over from the previous discussion on 64b. The *mishna* had established that a husband is believed when he says on his deathbed that he has sons or no brothers — statements that would free his wife from *yibum* — but is not believed when he says the opposite, claiming he has brothers or no sons, which would obligate her in *yibum*. The rule appeared to be that he is believed to free her but not to bind her, without an explicit rationale. The *gemara* then cited a *braita* quoting Rebbe to that effect — *ne'eman lehatir ve'eino ne'eman le'asor* — and contrasted it with the position of Rebbe Natan, who held that the husband is believed both ways, at least in the scenario where he had said the freeing statement at the time of *kiddushin* and retracted it on his deathbed.

Abaye now clarifies the underlying logic. Our *mishna*, he says, is dealing with a case where *de'lo muchzak lan b'achi v'lo muchzak lan bivani* — we have no established presumption that he has brothers or sons. Given this starting point, if he says he has children, he is believed, because his statement reinforces the *chazakah* — our baseline presumption that she is *mutar*, not obligated in *yibum*. If he says he has brothers, he is not believed — *lav kol kimeinei de'asar lah akoli alma* — it is not within his power to make her forbidden to the world on his say-so alone.

### Status Quo Principle

The essential principle that emerges is not that the husband is believed to produce a *heter* and disbelieved to produce an *issur* in the abstract. Rather, the *gemara* frames it in terms of the *chazakah*: a person is believed when his statement is consistent with the prevailing presumption, and is not believed when his statement contradicts it. If what he says reinforces her status of being *mutar*, of course we believe him. If she already has a *chazakah* of being *mutar* and he now claims she is *assur*, he is not believed — he does not have the power, through his bare assertion, to override an established presumption and render his wife obligated in *yibum*.

The *braita* involving Rebbe Natan addresses a different factual configuration: *de'muchzak lan b'achi v'lo muchzak lan bivani* — we had reason to presume he had brothers, though no sons were known. In this setting, the woman was presumed obligated in *yibum* before the marriage. He then said at the time of *kiddushin* that he had no brothers, and the *gemara* considers why we believed him then, even against the prevailing presumption.

### Rebbe Natan Reconciliation

The answer is *mah lo leshaker*: why would he lie? One might think he was lying simply to induce her to marry him, promising she would not be bound by *yibum*. But that reasoning fails, because *matsi patarna lach b'gita* — he could simply have promised to give her a *get* that would take effect before his death, rendering the *yibum* question moot regardless. Since he had an alternative means of achieving the same practical result, there is no compelling motive for the lie, and therefore we believe him at the time of *kiddushin*, even to the point of shifting the *chazakah* in her favor.

### Mah Lo Leshaker Logic

This is the critical juncture. The first *mah lo leshaker* — his statement at the time of *kiddushin* — was powerful enough that Rebbe holds it was *k'eidim dami*, like the testimony of witnesses, and *asu eidim akrei chazakah* — it completely uprooted the prior *chazakah*. She is now fully presumed to be free of any *yibum* obligation. Then, on his deathbed, he says the opposite: he has brothers after all. Now Rebbe and Rebbe Natan divide.

Rebbe holds that the first *mah lo leshaker* was so powerful that it totally shifted the presumption. She is now presumed *mutar*, and he cannot overturn that new *chazakah* on his deathbed with a bare claim — especially since the *mah lo leshaker* logic does not apply in reverse. At the deathbed, why would he lie? One cannot say he had no alternative means to bind her; perhaps he is simply trying, in his final hours, to make her life difficult. There is no analogous argument eliminating his motive to lie, and therefore his retraction carries no weight against the established presumption.

Rebbe Natan disagrees. He holds the first *mah lo leshaker* was *k'chazakah dami* — it was like a *chazakah*, sufficient to neutralize the prior presumption, but not sufficient to establish a new one in the opposite direction — *v'lo atei chazakah v'akrei chazakah l'gamrei*. The original presumption was not completely erased, only suspended. When, on his deathbed, he reverts to the original presumption, he is in effect reinforcing what was there to begin with, and Rebbe Natan believes him.

### Mah Lo Leshaker Context

The *gemara*'s larger move, as one steps back, is to neutralize what appeared to be an absolute position of Rebbe Natan — that the husband is simply believed to make his wife obligated in *yibum*. That is not what Rebbe Natan says at all. Even according to Rebbe Natan, if the woman has a full *chazakah* of being *mutar*, the husband is not believed on his bare word to make her *assur*. The only case where Rebbe Natan believes him is precisely because his deathbed statement is reinforcing — even if only partially — a pre-existing *chazakah* that was never fully extinguished. The *mishna* and Rebbe Natan are thus not fundamentally at odds.

The broader application of *mah lo leshaker* — which functions here similarly to *migo*, though the *rishonim* debate the precise relationship between the two concepts — is that it can shift a *chazakah* but only within limits defined by whether it truly eliminates a plausible motive to deceive. At the time of *kiddushin*, the logic is compelling. On the deathbed, it is not — and without it, the man's statement cannot prevail against whatever *chazakah* is in place.

---

## Unspecified Daughters

### Adult vs. Underage

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishna* concerning cases where a father marries off his daughter without specifying which daughter he means. The *mishna* states that *hamakadesh et bito stam* — one who betroths his daughter in general, without designation — *ein babogres bechlal*: the statement does not encompass daughters who have already reached the age of *bogeres*, i.e., who are more than twelve and a half years old and fully mature, because the father no longer has the halachic authority to betroth an adult daughter. The *gemara* will probe what this is teaching us and then turn to the more complex cases.

The *gemara* asks: if there are multiple underage daughters, are they all potentially betrothed by his unspecified statement? This raises the issue of *kiddushin she'einam mesurin l'viah* — a *kiddushin* that can never culminate in consummation, because the husband would never know which daughter he actually married, and any act with one might be a violation with the sister of his actual wife. The *gemara* resolves this by saying the *mishna* is discussing a case where the father has only one underage daughter and one adult daughter — *ein sham ela gedola u'ketana*. The use of the plural form referring to adult daughters is not an indication that this specific father has multiple adult daughters; it simply describes the general class of daughters in such matters.

### Father's Priority

But if there is only one underage daughter and one adult daughter, and the father is empowered to betroth both — since, as the *gemara* considers, the adult daughter may have appointed him as her *shaliach* — why assume the unspecified betrothal refers to the younger one rather than the older?

The *gemara* offers two reasons. First, *lo shavik inish midi d'isleih hana'ah minei v'avid midi d'lo isleih hana'ah minei* — a person does not abandon what yields him benefit and act instead on what yields him none. When a father betroths his underage daughter, he retains the *kesef kiddushin*; when he betroths his adult daughter, the money belongs to her. Even if the adult daughter waived her share as compensation for his efforts as *shaliach*, a second consideration applies: *lo shavik inish mitzvah d'ramya alei v'avid mitzvah d'lo ramya alei* — he would not set aside an obligation incumbent upon him in favor of one that is not. While his daughter is a minor, she is under his guardianship and it is his responsibility — indeed his *mitzvah* — to ensure she is married and protected. The Torah envisions a girl passing directly from *beis aviha* to *beis ba'alah*; the rabbis carve out a space for the adult woman who has not yet married, but that scenario does not exist in the Torah's own framing. The father's presumptive priority is therefore to marry off his younger daughter, and the unspecified statement is read accordingly.

### Two Groups Ambiguity

The *mishna* then introduces the more elaborate case: a man had daughters from two wives — sequentially, not simultaneously — and thus has two groups of daughters, an older cohort and a younger cohort. He says he betrothed *biti hagedola* — his older or oldest daughter — and then cannot remember which daughter he meant. The *mishna* enumerates the possibilities: did he mean the oldest of the older group? The older of the younger group? Or the youngest of the older group, who is nonetheless older than the oldest of the younger group?

According to Rabbi Meir, all of the daughters are *asuros* — forbidden to all other men until the matter is clarified — except for the youngest of the younger group, *chutz min haketana shebaketanos*, because no interpretation of the word *gedola* could possibly apply to her. According to Rabbi Yosi, all are *mutaros* except for the oldest of the oldest group, *chutz min hagedola shebagedolos*, because when a person uses the word *oldest* they mean it in its most precise and unambiguous sense.

The case is then presented in reverse: he said *biti haketana*, my younger or youngest daughter, and cannot remember which he meant. Rabbi Meir says all are forbidden except the oldest of the oldest group; Rabbi Yosi says all are permitted except the youngest of the youngest group.

### Meir vs. Yosi

The *gemara* asks whether it is necessary to state both cases — the *gedola* case and the *ketana* case. It concludes that both are necessary. If we only knew the *gedola* case, one might think Rabbi Meir holds his position only there — because any daughter who is older than someone else can be called *gedola* — but that when the father says *ketana*, surely he means the unambiguous youngest, and even Rabbi Meir would agree with Rabbi Yosi. Conversely, if we only knew the *ketana* case, one might think Rabbi Yosi holds his position only there, but that for *gedola* — a more positive and freely used descriptor — even Rabbi Yosi might agree that it could refer to a wider range, aligning with Rabbi Meir. Therefore both cases must be stated, showing that they debate both.

The underlying question is whether people speak or remember in ways that create ambiguity. Rabbi Meir holds that they do — *machnis inish nafshei l'safeka* — a person will record a memory as "oldest" even if that word does not uniquely identify the intended person. Rabbi Yosi holds the opposite — *lo machnis inish nafshei l'safeka* — a person would not characterize their memory with a term that leaves them in a state of genuine doubt; if he remembers *oldest*, he means it in its most determinate sense.

### Abaye's Two-Group Theory

A *braita* then presents an apparently reversed debate concerning *nedarim*: regarding the *neder* formulation *ad p'nei hapesach* — until the face of *Pesach* — Rabbi Meir says it means until *Pesach* arrives and Rabbi Yosi says it means until *Pesach* departs, which appears to be the exact inverse of their positions in the *mishna*. Rabbi Chanina bar Avdimi cites Rav: *muchlefet hashita* — the names are inverted in one source, and a *braita* indeed presents the *Pesach* positions consistently with the *mishna*, so that the same underlying logic governs in both cases.

Abaye then provides an important clarification of the *mishna* itself: *machlokes bishtei kitei banot* — the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi applies specifically to the case where there are two distinct groups of daughters. In that situation, any daughter from the older group can be described as *gedola* because she belongs to *hakat ha-gedola*, the older set, and thus the label is not anchored solely to the single oldest individual. This is what opens the possibility, under Rabbi Meir's reading, that multiple daughters could fall under the description.

By contrast, says Abaye, if there were only one group — say, four daughters from a single wife — *amtza'is bishmah kari lah*: the middle daughters would simply be called middle daughters. *Gedola* would refer unambiguously to the oldest, and *ketana* unambiguously to the youngest. The ambiguity Rabbi Meir identifies arises only because the two-group structure licenses a broader use of the term: she is *gedola* meaning she is from the older group, not that she is the single oldest individual.

### Rav Adda Challenge

Rav Adda bar Matna challenges Abaye: if his theory depends on the two-group structure, what happens if there are three daughters in the younger group rather than two? According to Abaye, the word *gedola* in the context of the younger group should attach only to the oldest daughter within that younger group, since she is the one who can be labeled *gedola* as its leading member. But then the *mishna* should permit the middle daughter of the younger group — why does it list her among the forbidden ones?

Abaye's response is that the *mishna* is indeed speaking of a case where there are only two daughters per group — *ein sham ela gedola u-ketana* — and this is further confirmed by the internal logic of the *mishna* itself: if there were three daughters in the younger group, the *mishna* would have needed to mention ambiguity about the middle daughter of that group, yet it does not. The *mishna*'s silence on that possibility is itself evidence that no such middle daughter exists in the case under discussion.

The *gemara* then presses: if that argument from silence works for the younger group, it should equally prove the absence of a middle daughter in the older group. The response is that the two situations are not parallel. In the older group, the *mishna* explicitly states that both the oldest and the youngest of that group are *assur* — so of course any middle daughter there is also *assur* and need not be separately listed. In the younger group, by contrast, the *mishna* says only the oldest daughter of that group is *assur*, implying that anyone younger within that group is *mutar* — so if a middle daughter existed, she would need to be mentioned as *assur*, and her absence from the list demonstrates she does not exist.

### Pesach Neder Parallel

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua raises a challenge to Abaye from the *Pesach* *neder* parallel: the case of *ad p'nei hapesach* was presented as analogous to the daughters debate, but if Abaye is correct that the daughters debate turns on the two-group structure, the *Pesach* case does not fit that framework. The days of *Pesach* are one continuous sequence — one group — not two distinct groups. So why should any intermediate day be understood as a potential *face* of *Pesach* that creates ambiguity?

The *gemara* responds that the *Pesach* debate is not actually about the same question at all. It is not a question of whether language creates ambiguity by being applicable to multiple members of a group; it is a linguistic dispute about the word *pnei* itself. One opinion holds *ad p'nei hapesach* means *ad kamei Pesach* — until before *Pesach*, i.e., until it arrives. The other holds it derives from *lipanot*, to turn away or depart — the Aramaic *mipanei*, to pass — meaning until *Pesach* has concluded. The debate is purely about the semantic range of the word *pnei*, not about the structure of groups or the breadth of ambiguous descriptors. The *Pesach* case and the daughters case thus involve distinct conceptual issues, and the apparent parallel between the two debates should not be overstated.

---

## He Said/She Said

### He Says/She Denies

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishna* presenting a series of conflicting claims about whether a betrothal occurred. The core principle governing all the cases is that a person's statement binds himself but cannot, through his words alone, obligate another person.

In the first case: a man says to a woman *kidashtich* — I betrothed you — and she says *lo kidashtani* — you did not betroth me. The rule is *hu assur bikrovoteha v'hi muteres bikrovav*: he is forbidden to marry her close female relatives — her mother, sister, daughter — since his own statement binds him, while she is free to marry his relatives, because his unilateral assertion cannot impose a prohibited status upon her.

### She Says/He Denies

In the reverse case: she says *kidashtani* — you betrothed me — and he says *lo kidashtich* — I did not. He is free to marry her relatives, since he made no claim. She, however, is forbidden to his relatives — and indeed, more basically, she is forbidden to any other man entirely, since she herself is asserting that she is married. Her own statement binds her, but it cannot impose any restriction upon him.

### Daughter vs. Mother

The third case: he says *kidashtich* to the mother, and she says *lo kidashta ela et biti* — you did not marry me, you married my daughter. He is forbidden to the mother's relatives — since he claimed the mother — but the mother is free to marry his relatives, since she does not claim to be married to him. He is permitted to marry the daughter's relatives, since he never claimed to have married her. And the daughter — *haktana muteres bikrovav* — the daughter is free to marry his relatives, because the mother's claim that the daughter is married to him does not bind the daughter.

### Mother vs. Daughter

The fourth case is the mirror image: he says *kidashti et bitchich* — I married your daughter — and the mother says *lo kidashta ela oti* — no, you married me. He is forbidden to the daughter's relatives, since he claimed her. The daughter is free to marry his relatives, since no claim was made about her and she made none about herself. He is free to marry the mother's relatives, since he never claimed her. The mother is forbidden to his relatives, since she claims to be married to him.

### Low Cost Principle

The *gemara* asks why it is necessary to state both the case where he makes a claim and the case where she makes a claim — are they not obvious? The response is that one might have thought differently in each direction. When the man says he married a woman, one could argue: *gavra lo ichpat lei u'mikrey amar* — for him, the cost of such a claim is so low that he might simply say it casually, without it being a sincere or reliable statement. After all, during *kiddushin* — as opposed to *nisu'in* — the betrothal does not immediately impose an obligation of *ketubah*, and the man's restriction is primarily limited to her close relatives. The *gemara* teaches us that even so, his statement is taken seriously and does bind him.

### Mother's Claim Invalid

Regarding the case where the mother claims the daughter is married: one might have thought that just as the Torah grants the father authority to effect and attest to the *kiddushin* of his minor daughter — *heimnu rachmana l'av* — the rabbis might extend analogous, if lesser, authority to the mother rabbinically, so that her claim would bind the daughter at least on a rabbinic level. The *mishna* teaches that this is not so. The mother is simply not believed with respect to the marriage status of her daughter — not biblically and not rabbinically — and her statement creates no prohibition upon the daughter at all.

### Get Debate

The *gemara* then records a dispute between Rav and Shmuel concerning the second case — where she claims he married her and he denies it. Shmuel says *m'vakshin mimenu litein get* — we ask him to give a *get* as a matter of good will, since her own statement has rendered her unable to marry any other man, and a *get* would release her. Rav adds: *im natan get mei'atzmo* — if he gives a *get* on his own initiative, unprompted by the court's request, *kofin oto litein ketubah* — we treat that act as an admission that they were married and compel him to pay her *ketubah*.

The *gemara* initially reads these as conflicting opinions and asks how one can *force* him to give a *get*, since writing a *get* would make her his divorcee and prevent him from marrying her relatives — a concrete cost to him that he might legitimately resist. The resolution is that Rav and Shmuel are not contradicting each other but building upon one another — *sh'maita d'adu adadei* — Shmuel establishes that we ask, and Rav adds that if he gives spontaneously, that is taken as an admission, with the consequence that the *ketubah* becomes enforceable. The practical lesson that emerges is that a man in this situation would be well advised to wait for the court's formal request before giving the *get*, rather than acting voluntarily, so that his act of generosity is not construed as a legal admission.

---

## Witnesses Requirement

### One vs. Two Witnesses

The *gemara* now arrives at what may be the most consequential legal question in the entire tractate, one that has taken sixty-four *dappim* to reach: whether the presence of kosher witnesses is constitutive of *kiddushin* — whether without such witnesses the act of *kiddushin* simply does not take effect as a matter of *halacha*, even if everyone present acknowledges that the betrothal occurred.

Rav Yehuda states: *hamikadesh b'ed echad ein chosheshin lekiddushav* — if a man betroths a woman before only one witness, the *kiddushin* is not binding and we have no concern that it took effect.

### Constitutive Question

This formulation immediately prompts a question that was posed to Rav Yehuda himself: *shnayim hamodim mai* — what is the rule when both parties agree? The question is probing the theoretical foundation of the witness requirement. Is the requirement evidentiary — do we need witnesses to prove that the betrothal occurred? Or is it constitutive — do we need witnesses in order for the act of *kiddushin* to achieve legal standing at all, irrespective of whether anyone doubts what happened? If both parties agree, and a single witness corroborates them, there is no evidentiary question — the act is not in doubt. If the *kiddushin* is still invalid in that case, it must be because witnesses are constitutive. Rav Yehuda's answer on this point was *rafya bidei* — it was unresolved in his hand, and he could not give a decisive ruling.

The question is then resolved by Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: *hamikadesh b'ed echad ein chosheshin lekiddushav v'afilu shneihem modim* — even if both parties fully agree that the betrothal occurred, without two witnesses it is not binding. The requirement for witnesses is constitutive, not merely evidentiary.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges this ruling from the *mishna* we have just studied — the *he said/she said* cases. That *mishna* discusses scenarios where one party claims a betrothal occurred and the other denies it, with no mention of witnesses at all. If witnesses are constitutive — if without two witnesses there is simply no *kiddushin* — then the *mishna* makes no sense. If witnesses were present, how is anyone *mutar*? The witnesses themselves establish the marriage. If witnesses were not present, how is anyone *assur*? There is no binding *kiddushin* without them.

It must therefore be the case, argues Rava, that the *mishna* is operating in a scenario with one witness — and with one witness combined with one party's admission, that combination is sufficient to generate at least a partial status. So it appears that one witness plus an admission does constitute *kiddushin*, which would contradict Rav Nachman's ruling in the name of Shmuel.

### Witnesses Presumed

The *gemara* resolves this by re-reading the *mishna*: *kegon de'amar lah kidashtich bifnei ploni u'ploni vehalchu lahem lemedinas hayam* — the *mishna* is discussing a case where the man says "I betrothed you in the presence of so-and-so and so-and-so," explicitly claiming that two witnesses were present, even though those witnesses are not here to testify now. The *mishna* does not depict a situation where there were objectively no witnesses; rather, it depicts a situation of contested claims where witnesses are alleged but inaccessible.

This reading has sweeping implications for everything that came before. All the *mishnayos* throughout the tractate that discuss who is believed about a betrothal — the father's claim about his daughter, the man's claim at the time of *kiddushin*, all the *he said/she said* cases — must be understood as cases where witnesses are claimed to have been present, even though they are not being produced at the moment. Without that background assumption, none of those cases are legally coherent. The *gemara* has therefore quietly transformed the interpretive framework for the entire preceding discussion.

### Beis Shammai/Hillel

The *gemara* then tests Rav Nachman's ruling against a *braita* about a man who divorced his wife and later shared lodgings with her at an inn. The question is whether we are concerned that they renewed their *kiddushin* through intercourse — *kiddushei biah*. Beis Shammai say no second *get* is required; Beis Hillel say one is.

The *gemara* initially suggests that this debate might hinge on the testimony of a single witness, but quickly recognizes a much simpler explanation: *hacha b'mai askinan k'gon d'ika eidei yichud v'leika eidei biah* — the case involves witnesses to *yichud*, to the fact that the two entered seclusion together, but no witnesses to intercourse itself. The debate between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel is not about the numerical sufficiency of witnesses but about the legal weight of *eidei yichud*: do witnesses to seclusion function as witnesses to intercourse — *hen hen eidei yichud hen hen eidei biah* — or not?

Beis Shammai hold that *eidei yichud* do not constitute *eidei biah*, and therefore no new *kiddushin* has been established. Beis Hillel hold that when the couple has a prior history of marital intercourse, witnesses to their entering seclusion are treated as equivalent to witnesses to intercourse, and a new *kiddushin* through *biah* has thereby taken effect, requiring a second *get*. Both schools agree, however, that if the couple had never consummated their original marriage — *niseis min ha'erusin* — *eidei yichud* would not be treated as *eidei biah*, because *ein libo gassah bah*: without the prior intimacy, we cannot presume they acted upon the seclusion.

The *gemara* concludes that this entire *braita* has nothing to do with the question of one versus two witnesses, and therefore poses no challenge to Rav Nachman's ruling. The question of how many witnesses are required for *kiddushin* to be constitutive remains firmly established as requiring two — and the question of what those witnesses must have observed is a separate matter, one that the debate between Beis Hillel and Beis Shammai illuminates. That discussion will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 65b

## Witnesses & Kiddushin

### One Witness & Agreement

The central question animating this sugya is whether witnesses play a merely evidentiary role in *kiddushin* — that is, whether they are needed only to prove that the betrothal occurred — or whether they are constitutive of the act itself, such that without witnesses, the *kiddushin* simply did not take place. A further dimension of this question concerns whether one witness might suffice when both parties acknowledge that the *kiddushin* occurred. If the couple themselves agree, one might reason that the evidentiary function is already satisfied by their mutual admission, rendering a second witness superfluous.

### Rav & Rabbah Rulings

The *gemara* opens with a clear and emphatic ruling. In the name of Rav, Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta states: if a man performs *kiddushin* with only one witness, *ein chosheshin lekidushav* — there is no concern whatsoever that any *kiddushin* has taken place. Crucially, this applies *va'afilu shenehem modim* — even if both parties agree that the betrothal occurred. The mutual admission of husband and wife cannot substitute for the requirement of two witnesses.

Rabbah bar Rav Huna then repeats this ruling, attributing it to *Bei Dina Rabba* — "the great court." The *gemara* asks: who is this great court? The answer is Rav himself. An alternative version of the tradition has Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav directly, in which case *Bei Dina Rabba* refers to Rebbi. In either formulation, an authority of the highest stature stands behind this position, and its force extends even to the rabbinic level — that is, it is not merely a *de'oraita* invalidation. This matters enormously in practice, because any requirement of a *get* carries grave consequences for the woman, and the rabbis were deeply reluctant to impose one without firm grounding.

### Two Men, Woman Bundle

A challenge is raised from the following scenario: two men arrive from overseas together with a woman and a bundle of belongings. Each man claims the woman as his wife, the other man as his slave, and the bundle as his property. The woman, for her part, claims both men as her slaves and the bundle as hers. The ruling is that she requires two *gittin* and may collect her *ketubah* from the bundle.

The immediate question is why she should need a *get* from either man, given that he is merely making a claim without witnessed proof. The *gemara* investigates: if each man had witnesses to his marriage, her counterclaim would carry no weight against their testimony. It therefore concludes that the case must involve one witness per claimant — and since one witness for one man is effectively cancelled by one witness for the other, we are back to the position of mutual, unwitnessed claims. *Ela le-mishrei le-alma de-kulei alma lo peligi de-sharya* — to permit her to the general public, everyone agrees she is free. The requirement of two *gittin*, then, is not a genuine *halachic* demand but a practical mechanism: only if one of the men voluntarily gives a *get* would she be entitled to collect her *ketubah* from the contested bundle. The *chiddush* is that of Rabbi Meir, who holds that movable property (*metaltelin*) is subject to the *ketubah* lien. The case thus does not prove that one witness effects *kiddushin*; rather, the absence of any objective proof means that no *get* is truly required, and the question reduces entirely to the disposition of the assets.

A final practical note: the *gemara* is very reluctant, absent clear necessity, to declare that a woman requires a *get*, given the devastating consequences in practice — the contemporary reality of *agunah* being the most acute expression of that concern.

## Proof vs. Constitutive

### Kahana vs. Pappa

The *gemara* now asks *mai havya alah* — what is the bottom line of all this analysis? Two positions emerge. Rav Kahana rules *ein chosheshin lekiddushin* — there is no concern at all; *kiddushin* performed with a single witness is entirely without effect. Rav Pappa rules *chosheshin lekiddushin* — he is still somewhat concerned, perhaps at the level of rabbinic stringency.

### Rav Ashi's Challenge

Rav Ashi presses Rav Kahana: what is the source for his confident ruling that a single witness effects no *kiddushin* whatsoever? The most natural source would be a *gezeirah shava*: the Torah uses the word *davar* in the phrase *al pi shenei edim yakum davar* — testimony is established by two witnesses — and the same word *davar* appears in the phrase *ki matza bah ervat davar*, which concerns marital and personal status matters. From this verbal analogy, one might derive that the two-witness requirement applies to *davar she-be-erva* — matters of personal status — just as it applies to monetary matters.

But here the challenge bites: by monetary matters, the rule is *hoda'at ba'al din keme'ah edim dami* — a litigant's own admission is equivalent to a hundred witnesses. The debt exists whether or not there were witnesses present; the witnesses serve only to prove it in court. If the need for two witnesses in *kiddushin* is derived from the monetary domain, why not draw the same inference — that if both parties admit the *kiddushin* occurred, their admission should function like witnesses, and the *kiddushin* should be valid?

### Money vs. Status

The answer given is fundamental: *hatam lo kachaiv l'achrinei hacha kachaiv l'achrinei* — there is a crucial difference. When a borrower admits a debt, he harms only himself. His admission is therefore fully effective. But when a husband and wife admit to a *kiddushin*, they are harming others. The husband's admission restricts the wife vis-à-vis all other men; the wife's admission restricts the husband from her relatives; and other men in the world are now prohibited from marrying her under pain of adultery. Matters of personal status have societal ramifications that reach far beyond the admitting parties, and therefore personal admission — *hoda'at ba'al din* — cannot substitute for objective, external testimony.

Yet one might observe that this argument proves only that admission is insufficient as proof; it does not yet prove that witnesses are constitutive — that without them, the act did not occur at all. The gap between "we require a higher standard of proof" and "without witnesses, nothing happened" is a substantial one, and it is a point that troubles the *acharonim*. The *gemara* itself, they note, never fully bridges that gap.

### Edei Beirur Kiyum

This brings us to the conceptual heart of the discussion: the distinction between *edei beirur* and *edei kiyum*. *Edei beirur* — proof witnesses — serve only to establish in the eyes of the court that something happened. If everyone is honest and the fact is admitted, witnesses of this type are redundant. *Edei kiyum* — constitutive witnesses — do something altogether different: they make the act happen. Without their presence, the act is a legal nullity, regardless of what the parties intended or admit.

By monetary matters, witnesses are *edei beirur*. The obligation exists independently of whether anyone witnessed it; the witnesses merely allow us to enforce it. By *kiddushin* and *gittin*, witnesses are *edei kiyum* — without them, the marriage or divorce did not occur.

There is, however, a further debate among the *acharonim* about precisely how to conceptualize the *edei kiyum* function. One view holds that witnesses are still fundamentally evidentiary, but because *kiddushin* is *chav l'achrinei* — it impacts broader society — a society that cannot verify its occurrence cannot recognize it. In the absence of proof, the act did not, as a social-legal matter, happen. A second view holds that the witnesses do something categorically different: they formalize and give gravity to the act. Just as one cannot be executed without witnesses and *hatra'ah*, the weight and solemnity of *kiddushin* demands the formal presence of witnesses as a constitutive element of the act.

The *nafka mina* between these two views is whether witnesses hidden behind a bush — unknown to the bride and groom — would suffice. If witnesses are fundamentally there to prove that the act occurred, then hidden witnesses accomplish exactly that. If, however, witnesses must be part of formalizing the act and impressing its gravity upon the parties, their concealment might be fatal. The *Ktzot* in *Choshen Mishpat* engages this question extensively, drawing on a *machloket Rishonim* about precisely this scenario.

### Property Division

Mar Zutra and Rav Adda Sava, the sons of Rav Mari bar Issur, divided their inherited property between themselves without witnesses. They came before Rav Ashi with a question: does *al pi shnei edim yakum davar* — the Torah's requirement of two witnesses — mean that the division is simply invalid without witnesses? Or is the entire function of witnesses in monetary matters only to prevent subsequent denial, and since neither party intends to back out, the division stands?

### Abaye Liars Principle

Abaye answered them with the formulation that became the classic expression of the *edei beirur* principle: *lo ivru sahadei ella leshakrei* — witnesses were created (*nivre'u*) only for liars. The entire purpose of witnesses in monetary matters is to prevent dishonest parties from denying what occurred. In a world of honest parties who both affirm what happened, witnesses add nothing and are not required to validate the act. This is *edei beirur* in its purest form. And the implicit contrast with *kiddushin* and *gittin* could not be sharper: there, the witnesses are *edei kiyum*, and their absence means the act never happened, honest parties notwithstanding.

One might draw an interesting parallel to *malkut* and capital punishment, which similarly require both witnesses and *hatra'ah*. There, too, *hoda'at ba'al din* does not work. Whether the witnesses and *hatra'ah* in those cases are there to establish guilt evidentiary or to constitute the particular character of a defiant, warned transgression is a parallel conceptual question — one that mirrors the *edei beirur/edei kiyum* debate and is left here as a worthy avenue for further study.

## One Witness & Silence

### Forbidden Fat Case

Abaye now introduces a series of cases in which a single witness is believed when the person he testifies against remains silent. The first: one witness says to a person, *achalta cheilev* — you ate forbidden fat (*chelev*) inadvertently. The person says nothing. The *gemara* rules: *ne'eman* — the witness is believed, and the person would be obligated to bring a *korban*. A supporting *baraita* confirms this: if the accused says *lo achalti* — I did not eat it — he is exempt. The *ta'ama de'amar lo* — the reason is because he denied it. But *ha ishtik meheiman* — if he was silent, the witness is believed and the *korban* is required.

### Grain Purity Case

Abaye continues: one witness says to a person, *nitme'u taharotecha* — your grain has become *tamei*. The person is silent. The witness is believed, and the grain may not be eaten in a state of *tahara*. Again, a parallel *baraita* is cited: if one witness says the grain became *tamei* and the owner contradicts him, the grain is *tahor*. The reason is because he said otherwise; had he been silent, the single witness would have been believed.

### Ox Bestiality Case

A third case: one witness says *shorcha nirva* — your ox was used in an act of bestiality. The owner is silent. The witness is believed, and the ox is disqualified from being brought as a *korban*. Note that without two witnesses, the ox would not be stoned — the capital penalty for the animal requires two witnesses — but the prohibition on bringing it as a *korban* is triggered even by a single witness coupled with the owner's silence. A *baraita* confirms: animals used in sin or that killed a person *al pi ed echad* — based on one witness — or *al pi ba'alim* — based on the owner's admission — are disqualified from the altar. The *gemara* asks: what does *al pi ed echad* mean if the owner already admitted? It must mean the owner was silent, and silence functions as admission.

### Three Cases Analysis

The *gemara* then performs a *tzrichuta* — explaining why all three cases needed to be stated. In the *chelev* case, silence is clearly an admission: *dei lav dekimlei benafshei de-avad* — if he truly did not know he had eaten the forbidden fat, he would not remain silent, because the consequence of his silence is that he must bring a *korban*. And no one would bring a *korban* they were not certain they were obligated to bring, since that would constitute *chullin ba-azarah* — bringing non-sacred animals into the Temple precincts in a sacred context. His silence thus unmistakably signals acknowledgment.

In the grain case, one might think the silence is not admission — perhaps he reasons he will simply eat the grain on a day when he is *tamei* and suffer no loss, making his silence meaningless. The case therefore needed to be stated to show that since he does lose access to the grain on days when he is *tahor*, his silence is indeed an admission.

In the ox case, one might think silence means nothing — perhaps he never intended to bring the ox as a *korban* anyway, so he sustains no real loss by remaining silent. That case also needed to be stated.

### Tosafot Silence Distinct…

This *tzrichuta* leads Tosafot to a crucial interpretive conclusion: the operative legal mechanism in all three cases is not that the single witness is believed in his own right, but that the owner's silence is read as an admission. The witness functions as the prompt for an admission; it is the admission itself that carries legal weight. A critical *nafka mina* follows: if the owner says *eini yode'a* — I don't know — this is not silence, and therefore not admission, and the witness would not be believed. Similarly, if the witness testifies about something that occurred in the owner's absence — where silence cannot possibly constitute acknowledgment — the witness would likewise not be believed.

Tosafot also raises a broader question: given the principle of *ed echad ne'eman be-issurin* — a single witness is ordinarily believed regarding matters of prohibited status — why do these cases require the owner's silence at all? The answer seems to lie in the fact that all three cases involve a direct economic consequence to the owner of the property in question. This is qualitatively different from the general rule about *issurin*, where the witness is speaking about the status of an item without directly threatening the owner's assets. When a witness's testimony would force the owner to incur a loss — sacrificing an animal, discarding grain, losing the use of an ox — additional indicia of reliability are required, and the owner's own silence provides that assurance.

## Personal Status & Witnes…

### Wife Adultery Case

The *gemara* now poses the question that the preceding analysis has been building toward: *ishto zinta be-ed echad veshotek* — a single witness tells a man that his wife committed adultery, and the husband remains silent. What is the law?

To understand the stakes, a preliminary distinction must be drawn. If the husband himself declares that his wife committed adultery, the consequence is that he is bound by his own statement and must divorce her — but since he is exercising what is always his unilateral right to divorce, this is not considered *chav l'achrinei* in the relevant sense. He must, however, pay the *ketubah*, since there is no objective proof of the transgression. Now: what if a single witness makes this claim and the husband says nothing?

The single witness cannot be believed in the ordinary sense for matters of personal status. The principle of *ed echad ne'eman be-issurin* does not apply to *davar she-be-erva* — matters concerning marital and sexual status — which require two witnesses even for purposes of proof, not merely for the constitutive function discussed above.

### Abaye Rava Debate

Abaye rules *ne'eman* — the witness is believed, and the husband would be required to divorce his wife. Rava rules *eino ne'eman* — *havay davar shebe'ervah ve'ein davar shebe'ervah pachos mishnayim*: this is a matter of *ervah*, and matters of *ervah* require a minimum of two witnesses.

Tosafot explains the debate in terms of the distinction developed in the preceding section. Abaye reads the husband's silence as an admission. Since the husband is always personally bound by his own admission regarding his wife's fidelity, and since his silence functions as admission, the result is that he must divorce her — not because the external witness is believed as a formal matter of *davar she-be-erva*, but because the husband himself has constructively admitted the fact. Rava, by contrast, holds that the legal mechanism here is not silence-as-admission but the credibility of the external witness, and that credibility is simply insufficient for *davar she-be-erva*. Without two witnesses, the testimony cannot establish the wife's transgression, and the husband has no obligation to act.

### Blind Tanna Story

Abaye adduces a compelling source for his position. He notes: *dehava samya dehava mesader masneisa kamei deMar Shmuel* — there was a blind man who served as Shmuel's *tanna*, memorizing and reciting the Tannaitic traditions in the *yeshiva*. One day this man was running late. Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch him. The messenger took one route to his house while the *tanna* arrived by another, so they did not meet. In the meantime, the messenger — having arrived at the *tanna*'s house in his absence — witnessed the man's wife engaged in an act of infidelity. When the messenger returned to Shmuel and reported what he had seen, the *tanna* came before Shmuel and asked: must I divorce my wife?

This case is structurally revealing. The husband was not present and therefore could not have been silent in any meaningful sense. There is no question of *shtikat ke-hoda'ah* here. The entire question is about the weight of a single, unopposed witness in a matter of personal status, absent any admission. Shmuel ruled: *im meheman lach* — if you trust him, *zil apkah* — go divorce her; *va'i lo lo tipik* — if not, do not divorce her.

Abaye reads *im meheman lach* as meaning: if you know him to be reliable in the sense of not being a *gazlan* — that is, if there is no specific reason to doubt him — then you treat an unopposed single witness as sufficient to compel divorce. This would be a striking ruling: even absent any admission, an unopposed *ed echad* can operate in a matter of *davar she-be-erva*.

### Rava Rebuttal

Rava reads Shmuel's ruling entirely differently. *Im meheman lach ke-bei trei zil apkah* — if you trust him *as much as* two witnesses, then you must divorce her. This is not about the ordinary credibility of a single witness in the absence of contradiction. It is about a special and exceptional personal trust, equivalent to ironclad certainty, that this specific person would never lie. In the absence of that extraordinary trust, the testimony of a single witness in a matter of *davar she-be-erva* carries no legal weight whatsoever. The woman's marital status remains unchanged, and no divorce is required.

## King Yannai Narrative

### Yannai Feast Scheme

Abaye now seeks a further proof-text, this time from a striking historical *baraita* — a passage that has a parallel in Josephus and has attracted the attention of historians. The *baraita* recounts: King Yannai went to the region of Kochlit in the wilderness and conquered sixty cities. Upon his triumphant return, he was filled with great joy and summoned all the sages of Israel. He said to them: our ancestors, when they were engaged in building the *Beit HaMikdash*, ate salted foods (*meluchim*) in their poverty — let us likewise eat salted foods in memory of them. In a striking contrast, these humble foods were served upon golden tables. There is a *mishibud lige'ulah* quality to the moment — a deliberate juxtaposition of former deprivation and present glory.

At the feast, one man was present who is described in almost biblical literary language as a *latz*, a mocker — evil and scheming. His name was Elazar ben Po'ira. He approached King Yannai and said: *libam shel Perushim alecha* — the hearts of the Pharisees, meaning the sages, are against you. They do not support you.

### Yehuda Challenge

Yannai asked what he should do to test this claim. Elazar advised him: wear the *tzitz* — the golden headplate of the *Kohen Gadol* — and observe the reaction of the sages. (The *gemara* notes in passing the debate between Rashi and Tosafot about whether a *Kohen Gadol* is permitted to wear *bigdei kehunah* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, and whether the *tzitz* — which the Torah describes as to be worn *tamid*, always — carries a special dispensation to be worn continuously. Neither question is the *halachic* focus here.)

One elder at the feast, named Yehuda ben Gedidya, spoke up — not very astutely, as it turned out: *rav lecha keter malchut* — the crown of kingship is sufficient for you, Yannai. *Hanach keter kehunah lezar'o shel Aharon* — leave the crown of *kehunah* for the descendants of Aaron. The reason he offered was that there had been a rumor that Yannai's mother had been taken captive at Modi'im. If true, this would have disqualified her from her *kohen* husband, rendering Yannai a *chalal* — someone of compromised priestly lineage — and unfit to serve as *Kohen Gadol*.

### Mother Captivity Rumor

The *baraita* states: *vayivukash hadavar velo nimtza* — the matter was investigated and nothing was found to substantiate it. The rumor had not been established. Nevertheless, Yehuda ben Gedidya's remark caused enormous offense, and *vayibadlu chachmei Yisrael beza'am* — the sages of Israel were separated, driven out in the king's fury. Perhaps their silence at Yehuda's outburst was read as complicity.

### Sages Destruction

Elazar ben Po'ira then pressed his advantage, saying to Yannai: if this were merely an ordinary person (*hedyot she-be-Yisrael*), what was done to Yehuda ben Gedidya would be appropriate. But you are a king and *Kohen Gadol* — is this the treatment you deserve? (The parallel in Josephus fills in the gap: the sages had imposed lashes on Yehuda ben Gedidya for *motzi shem ra*, and Elazar was arguing that this trivial penalty demonstrated the sages' fundamental disrespect for the king's dignity.)

When Yannai asked what he should do, Elazar replied: *romsem* — destroy them. Yannai asked: but what will become of the Torah? Elazar answered: *harei keruchah umunachat bekeren zavit* — it is rolled up and sitting in the corner. Any person who wishes to study may come and study. The Torah scroll is still there; kill the sages and the Torah survives.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak observes: *miyad nizreka bo apikorsus* — immediately a spirit of *apikorsus* took hold of Yannai. What was his *apikorsus*? That he should have responded: *tinach Torah shebikhtav, Torah she-be-al peh mai* — granted, we still have the Written Torah; but what of the Oral Torah? Who will transmit it? By remaining silent at Elazar's answer, Yannai implicitly accepted the premise that the Written Torah alone suffices — a denial, in effect, of the entire tradition of *Torah she-be-al peh*. It is worth noting that *apikorsus* in the *gemara* in Sanhedrin is specifically defined as *mevazeh talmidei chachamim* — contempt for the sages and their authority — which makes its deployment here particularly pointed.

### Shimon Restoration

*Miyad* — immediately — *vayahargu kol chachmei Yisrael* — all the sages of Israel were killed. *Vehaya ha-olam mishtomem* — the world was desolate and bereft. This continued until Shimon ben Shatach — who had been hidden away, reportedly because he was the brother of Yannai's wife — emerged and *hechzir et ha-Torah le-yoshnah*, restored the Torah to its former state. Some connect this restoration to the tradition that Shimon ben Shatach was instrumental in establishing primary Jewish education, ensuring that all children would be educated from a young age — a fitting counterpoint to the catastrophic loss described here.

### Evidence Analysis

The *gemara* now asks: what exactly was the evidentiary situation regarding the rumor about Yannai's mother? The *baraita* says it was investigated and dismissed. But what kind of investigation was this?

If two witnesses had originally testified that she was taken captive, and then two witnesses contradicted them, the result should be a standoff — *mai chazit disomkhat ahanei somkhat ahanei* — why do we credit one pair over the other? Rashi suggests that even in a two-against-two standoff, Yannai's status might remain in doubt, because while the mother had a *chezkat kashrut* going in her favor, Yannai himself — as the child whose status is the operative question — may never have had an established presumption of priestly fitness to fall back on. But this is itself a difficult position, since our intuition is that two witnesses against two witnesses should simply neutralize one another.

Abaye's reading of the story is that the evidence was one witness against one witness or one witness unopposed — and since an unopposed single witness is believed even in matters of *davar she-be-erva*, the rumor initially gained traction until it was directly contradicted.

## Unopposed Witness Conclu…

### Rava Position

Rava rejects Abaye's reading of the story entirely. He maintains *le'olam trei vetrei* — it was in fact two against two. The reason the claim was dismissed rather than left in doubt is explained by reference to the principle of *edei hazamah*: the second pair of witnesses did not simply testify to a different version of events, but rather told the first pair *atem einkem yecholim* — you could not have been there to see what you claim, because you were elsewhere with us. When witnesses are subjected to *hazamah* — a direct challenge to their physical presence at the scene of the alleged event — their testimony is not merely contradicted but completely annulled. Therefore the original two witnesses were entirely discredited, and nothing remained of the accusation.

Alternatively, Rava offers the explanation of Rabbi Yitzchak: *shifcha hachnisu tachteha* — a maidservant was substituted for Yannai's mother in captivity. The second pair of witnesses did not contradict the first pair but completed the account: yes, she was taken, but she was subsequently rescued and a maidservant was swapped in her place. In this reading, the testimony of the second pair does not cancel the first but resolves the situation into a positive outcome.

### Abaye Position

The debate concludes in a state of tension. Abaye holds the bold position that an unopposed single witness is believed even in personal status matters — *davar she-be-erva* — such that a husband confronted with such testimony and remaining silent would be compelled to divorce his wife. Rava holds that for *davar she-be-erva*, two witnesses are always required, whether for the constitutive function that creates the act of *kiddushin* or *gittin*, or for the evidentiary function of proving that a personal-status fact occurred. A single witness, even one who goes wholly unopposed, cannot satisfy that threshold. The *halacha* will follow Rava — as it nearly always does against Abaye — and the requirement of two witnesses for *davar she-be-erva* stands in full force. The discussion continues on the following *amud*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 66

## Witnesses in Kiddushin

### Central Question

The daf opens in the middle of a sustained inquiry into one of the most fundamental questions in the laws of *kiddushin*: are witnesses merely required to *prove* that a marriage took place, or are they constitutive of the act itself — such that without witnesses, no *kiddushin* occurs at all? This distinction carries enormous practical weight. If witnesses serve only a probative function, then one might argue that where both parties openly acknowledge the marriage, their mutual admission substitutes for testimony. But if witnesses are constitutive — if their presence is what makes the act of *kiddushin* happen — then no degree of mutual consent can compensate for their absence.

The Gemara had been testing this question by examining various cases: a husband claiming marriage while his wife denies it (where are the witnesses?), and the dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel regarding a divorced couple discovered together in an inn (where witnesses to the seclusion raise the question of whether they stand in for witnesses to the act itself). Throughout, the thrust of the discussion has been that witnesses are not optional — without them, the *kiddushin* did not take place.

### Rav's Position

The Gemara now presents a direct ruling, transmitted by Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav: *ha-mekadesh be-ed echad ein chosheshin le-kiddushav* — one who performs *kiddushin* with only a single witness present need not be concerned; no *kiddushin* has occurred. Critically, the ruling adds *ve-afilu shneihem modim* — even if both parties, the man and the woman, mutually agree and acknowledge that the marriage took place, it makes no difference. Without two witnesses, nothing happened.

### Rabbah bar Rav Huna

Rabbah bar Rav Huna then offers a parallel formulation: one who performs *kiddushin* with only one witness — *Beidina Rabba amrei ein chosheshin le-kiddushav* — the great *beis din* rules there is no concern. The Gemara asks: who is this *Beidina Rabba*, this great *beis din*? The answer: Rav. That is, the earlier authority, Rav himself, is being identified as the source of this ruling, lending it still greater weight.

### Textual Variants

The Gemara then records an alternative version of the transmission: *ve-ika de-amrei*, some say the chain runs differently — Rabbah bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rav that the great *beis din* rules there is no concern. In this reading, Rav is explicitly named, and the *Beidina Rabba* he references is identified not as Rav but as Rebbi — the Nasi, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi. Either way, the ruling emerges with formidable authority: whether it is Rav himself or Rebbi standing behind it, the dominant voice in the Gemara is unambiguous that *kiddushin* performed with only one witness is of no legal effect whatsoever.

---

## Two Men, One Woman

### The Scenario

The Gemara now introduces a counter-challenge from Rav Achdevai bar Ami. Two men arrive from *medinas ha-yam* — from overseas — accompanied by a woman and a bundle of property. The first man claims: "This is my wife, this is my slave, and this is my luggage." The second man claims: "This is my wife, that is my slave, and that is my bundle." And the woman herself declares: "Both of you are my slaves, and the bundle is mine." It is a remarkable scenario, made all the more pointed by the fact that no one simply says "three people arrived" — two people come *with* a woman, and she is listed alongside the luggage.

### The Ruling
