The *halacha* in this case is: *tzerichah shnei gittin* — she requires a *get* from each of them — *ve-gomer kesuvahsah min ha-chavilah* — and she may collect the value of her *kesuvah* from the bundle. Each man's claim that she is his wife creates at least a conditional obligation: if he is to give her a *get*, he must pay her *kesuvah*, and *mima nafshach* she is entitled to collect that amount from the disputed bundle, since each man acknowledges the luggage came with the woman he claims to have married.

### Case Clarification

The Gemara immediately asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If each man has witnesses establishing that the woman is his wife, how can her claim that both are merely her slaves have any standing at all? The presence of witnesses to *kiddushin* should overwhelm her counterclaim. The Gemara considers the possibility that each man has one witness — but then the witnesses neutralize one another, and we are back to square one. There is no objective basis for requiring her to obtain a *get* at all, since a man's bare claim that a woman is his wife does not, by itself, impose upon her the need for a *get*. Indeed, the Gemara confirms: *ela lemishrei le'alma dechulei alma lo peligi desharya* — she requires no *get* to remarry, as there is no objective halachic basis for such a requirement.

What then is the case actually saying? The scenario is best understood as one in which the claims are all a matter of he-said-she-said, with no standing witnesses available at the time of judgment. In such a case, no one can compel anyone to do anything. The only practical resolution is: if one of the men voluntarily gives her a *get* — why he would, given that he is not halachically required to, remains unclear, but if he does — only then would she be entitled to collect her *kesuvah* from the bundle.

It is worth noting the contemporary weight of this discussion. The Gemara is extremely reluctant to say a woman requires a *get* without clear halachic basis, precisely because of the consequences for the woman: she would be *asurah le-kohen*, he would be *asur bi-krovah*, and the specter of *agunah* looms over any unnecessary imposition of *get* requirements.

### Rabbi Meir's Chiddush

If no *get* is actually required and the entire scenario is contingent on voluntary action, what is the *chiddush*? The Gemara explains: the novel ruling here follows Rabbi Meir, *de-amar metalteli mishta'abdi le-kesuvah* — Rabbi Meir holds that movable property is subject to the lien of a *kesuvah*. The innovation is not about the *get* requirement or the witness question per se, but about the eligibility of the bundle — *metaltelin*, chattel — to serve as collateral for collecting a *kesuvah*. According to Rabbi Meir, one need not hold real estate to pay a *kesuvah*; movable goods suffice.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Kahana & Papa

The Gemara now asks: *mai hava alah* — what is the practical upshot of all this discussion? Despite the weight of amora'ic opinion that two witnesses are required, it has proven difficult to adduce clear Tannaitic support for the rule. Rav Kahana therefore rules: *ein chosheshin le-kiddushin* — no concern whatsoever; *kiddushin* with one witness simply did not occur. Rav Papa, however, says: *chosheshin le-kiddushin* — he remains somewhat concerned. Even if the *kiddushin* may not be fully valid, Rav Papa is unwilling to declare it entirely without effect.

### Gezeirah Shavah

Rav Ashi then challenges Rav Kahana directly: what is the source for your position? You must have derived it through a *gezeirah shavah* — a verbal analogy — between the word *davar* appearing in *al pi shnayim edim yakum davar* (the requirement for two witnesses in monetary cases) and the word *davar* in *ki matza bah ervat davar* (pertaining to personal status and *davar she'be'ervah*). The analogy imports the two-witness requirement from monetary law into the domain of personal status.

But this raises a powerful objection: in monetary matters, *hoda'as ba'al din ke-me'ah edim dami* — a litigant's own admission is equivalent to the testimony of a hundred witnesses. If I acknowledge that I owe someone money, the debt stands even without any witnesses to the original transaction. Witnesses in monetary law are *edei beirur* — their function is purely probative, to prevent lying and establish facts in court. If the parties are honest and admit the reality, no witnesses are needed. If this is the model from which the *kiddushin* requirement is derived, why should not the same logic apply there? If husband and wife both acknowledge the marriage, why should that admission not suffice?

### Beirur vs. Kiyum

The Gemara's response is sharp: *lo k'chayev l'achrinei hacha k'chayev l'achrinei* — there, in monetary law, when I admit a debt I am only harming myself. Here, when a man and woman admit to a marriage, they are imposing consequences on others. The woman's admission restricts her to this man; other men are now forbidden to her, and relations with them would constitute adultery. His admission restricts him from her relatives. The marriage, unlike a private debt, is not a transaction between two parties only — it ramifies throughout society.

This reasoning, however, only explains why personal admission is insufficient as a *standard of proof*. It does not yet prove that witnesses are *constitutive* — that without them the *kiddushin* literally did not occur. This gap is noted by the *acharonim* as something the Gemara never fully closes: we begin from monetary law where witnesses serve only to prove that something happened, and we arrive at the conclusion that in *kiddushin* and *gittin* the act does not even occur without witnesses — which is a far more radical claim.

There is indeed a significant debate among *acharonim* about how to conceptualize this. One approach holds that even in *kiddushin* the witnesses are fundamentally *edei beirur* — their role is probative — but because the act *chav le-achrinei*, because it impacts all of society, an act that cannot be proven in the requisite manner is treated as if it did not happen. Another approach holds that witnesses are genuinely constitutive of the act: *kiddushin* is so weighty a transaction that it requires the formal presence of witnesses to give it legal reality, in the same way that some acts require a justice of the peace.

A practical *nafka mina* between these two approaches concerns the case of witnesses who were hidden — watching from concealment — without the bride and groom's knowledge. If witnesses are merely probative, it should not matter whether the parties knew they were present; the fact can be proven. But if witnesses are constitutive — if they formalize and give weight to the act — perhaps the parties must be aware of their presence. This question is in fact debated among the *rishonim*, and the *Ketzos ha-Choshen* in *Choshen Mishpat* is among the primary places where the competing views are laid out, alongside a *teshuvah* of the Rashba.

A practical corollary: the Rema in *Even HaEzer* notes that since the Gemara did not entirely reject the possibility that *kiddushin* with one witness and mutual admission might carry some weight, one should *lechatchila* take it seriously if the situation arises — particularly in cases involving potential *agunah* concerns. Rav Moshe's responsa address precisely this scenario (a case of a teenager who said *harei at mekudeshet li* before only one witness), and the answer is nuanced: we are somewhat concerned *lechatchila*, but not to the point of treating the woman as requiring a *get* in the face of serious hardship.

---

## Witnesses & Monetary Law

### Asset Division

The Gemara now addresses a parallel case that further develops the conceptual framework. Mar Zutra and Rav Ada Saba, sons of Rav Mari bar Issur, had divided their assets — presumably a partnership or an inheritance — without any witnesses present. They came before Rav Ashi with a fundamental question: when the Torah says *al pi shnayim edim*, does that mean witnesses are necessary even to effectuate a valid division of assets? That is, if nobody wishes to back out and both parties acknowledge what was done, must the division be repeated with witnesses? Or were witnesses created only to prevent subsequent denial?

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye answers with one of the most important and oft-cited principles in halachic literature: *lo ivru sahadei ela le-shakrei* — witnesses were created only for liars. The sole purpose of witnesses in monetary matters is to protect against dishonest denial. In a world of universal honesty, witnesses would be unnecessary. Since neither party here is interested in reneging, the division stands entirely without witnesses.

### Framework

This ruling crystallizes the distinction that underlies the entire sugya. In monetary law, witnesses are *edei beirur* — probative instruments designed to establish facts against potential denial. The act itself — the loan, the division, the sale — exists independently of whether witnesses were present. Hoda'as ba'al din works precisely because the underlying obligation is real regardless; witnesses merely allow us to prove it in court. *Edei kiyum*, by contrast, are constitutive: without them, the act itself has no legal existence.

This framework also raises fascinating parallels with capital law, where formal witnesses and *hatra'ah* — forewarning — are equally required. Are those requirements merely evidentiary — to establish that the act was truly willful — or are they part of what defines the gravity of the act itself? The question of whether witnesses and *hatra'ah* make an act *deserving* of punishment by constituting its character, or merely allow us to *prove* it, maps precisely onto the debate about *edei beirur* versus *edei kiyum* in the domain of *kiddushin*.

---

## Single Witness Cases

### Contaminated Terumah

The Gemara now presents a series of cases in which Abaye rules that a single unopposed witness is believed. A single witness tells someone *nitme'u taharosecha* — your pure items, your *terumah* grain, have become *tamei* — and the owner is silent. Abaye rules: *ne'eman* — the witness is believed, and the grain may not be eaten. A supporting *baraisa* confirms: if the owner actively contradicts the witness — saying *lo nitme'u* — the grain is *tahor*. The reason the grain is *tahor* in the contradicted case is that he said no; the implication is that had he been silent, the witness would have been believed.

### Korban Obligation

Abaye offers a second case: a single witness tells someone *achalta chelev* — you ate forbidden fat — *be-shogeg*, unintentionally, and the owner is silent. The witness is believed and the person must bring a *korban*. Here too the *baraisa* confirms: if the person says *lo achalti* — I did not eat — he is exempt. The implication is that silence would have obligated him.

### Animal Status

A third case: a single witness tells someone *shorcha nirva* — your ox was used in an act of bestiality — and the owner is silent. The witness is believed, and the ox is disqualified from use as a *korban*. A *baraisa* teaches that animals disqualified through sin — whether through bestiality (*nirva*) or through having killed a person (*shehemit*) — are disqualified *al pi ed echad* or *al pi baalim*, on the basis of a single witness or the owner's own admission. The Gemara notes: if the owner is admitting, that is the second category (*al pi baalim*). The case of a single witness must therefore be the case where the owner is simply silent — and silence suffices.

### Why Three Cases

The Gemara explains why all three cases are necessary: *tzricha*. Each case presents a scenario where one might have thought the silence is not a meaningful admission. In the *korban* case, silence seems clearly an admission — the owner would never remain silent if he did not know he had eaten *chelev*, because bringing an unnecessary *korban* would constitute *chullin ba-azarah*, which no one would risk. Hence his silence is unmistakably an acknowledgment. But one might have thought that in the *terumah* case, silence is not meaningful, since the owner might reason: even if the grain is *tamei*, I can eat it during my own days of *tum'ah* — no real loss. The Gemara counters: he does lose the ability to eat it while *tahor*. And one might think the ox case requires no admission at all, since the owner may not have been planning to bring this particular animal as a *korban* anyway — why would he care if it is disqualified? All three cases are needed to establish that in each context, the silence does constitute a meaningful admission.

### Tosafos Analysis

Tosafos draws from this *tzrichusa* a significant principle: what the Gemara is really crediting in these cases is not the weight of the single witness per se, but rather the owner's silence read as an admission. If the Gemara were simply recognizing the witness's credibility as a matter of *ed echad ne'eman be-issurin*, no *tzrichusa* would have been necessary. The reason we need all three cases is that each requires us to carefully establish that silence in that specific context is indeed an admission.

This yields an important *nafka mina*: if the owner says *I don't know* rather than remaining silent, the witness is not believed — because the admission that underlies the ruling is absent. Similarly, if the witness testifies about something that occurred while the owner was elsewhere and had no way of knowing about it, silence cannot be read as admission, and the witness's testimony alone does not suffice.

This analysis also intersects with the question of why *ed echad ne'eman be-issurin* does not simply operate here on its own. In these cases, the witness is telling someone something about their own property, effectively imposing a financial consequence — the grain must be discarded, the animal cannot be sold as a *korban*. That is more akin to a monetary imposition than to a simple status ruling, and it is not obvious that the ordinary rule of *ed echad ne'eman be-issurin* applies where the consequence is a direct loss to the owner. Tosafos introduces additional factors here as well, such as whether the person was in a position to have done something about the outcome — as in the case of an animal given to be slaughtered, where the *shochet* who declares it *treif* is more readily believed because he could have handled the *shechita* differently.

---

## Wife & Adultery

### The Case

The Gemara now introduces the central case of the broader discussion: *ishto zinsa be-ed echad ve-shotek* — a single witness testifies to a man that his wife committed adultery, and the man is silent. What is the law?

Before addressing the ruling, it is worth situating this within the broader framework. If a man himself declares that his wife committed adultery, the halachic consequence is not that the court objectively establishes adultery — his unilateral declaration cannot do that, as it is *chav le-achrinei*. Rather, he is bound by his own words and must divorce his wife, though he remains obligated to pay her *kesuvah* since there is no objective proof. By contrast, a single witness to adultery would not ordinarily be credited in matters of personal status — *davar she'be'ervah* requires two witnesses even to prove it. The question here combines these issues: a single witness speaks, the husband says nothing. What now?

### Abaye vs. Rava

Abaye says: *ne'eman* — the witness is believed, and the husband must divorce his wife. Rava says: *eino ne'eman* — he is not believed. *Havei davar she'be'ervah ve-ein davar she'be'ervah pachos mi-shnayim* — this is a matter of *ervah*, and no matter of *ervah* can be established with fewer than two witnesses.

Tosafos offers an elegant framework for understanding what is actually being disputed. Abaye and Rava agree that personal status matters require two witnesses for objective halachic effect. They disagree about what this case actually is. Abaye reads the husband's silence as an admission: he is not contesting the witness, which is tantamount to saying he himself acknowledges his wife committed adultery — and just as a man's own statement about his wife's adultery binds him to divorce her, so too here. Rava, by contrast, does not read silence as admission in this context. This case is about the credibility of an unopposed single witness in a matter of *davar she'be'ervah* — and such a witness simply cannot carry the requisite halachic weight, regardless of whether anyone contradicts him.

### Reframing

The distinction is sharp and consequential. For Abaye, the operative mechanism is *shtika ke-hoda'ah* — silence as admission — and the admission of a party binds him to consequences he would bear from his own declaration. For Rava, the operative question is the inherent credibility of the witness's testimony in a *davar she'be'ervah* matter, and a single witness — even unchallenged — cannot establish *davar she'be'ervah*.

---

## Blind Man Story

### The Setup

Abaye now attempts to adduce a source for his position. He introduces a story: there was a blind scholar — a *tanna*, one who had memorized Tannaitic material and served as a teaching assistant in the *yeshiva* — who would regularly arrange *mishnayos* before Mar Shmuel. One day he was running late. Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch him. The messenger and the scholar took different paths and missed each other; the scholar arrived at the *yeshiva* and the *shiur* proceeded. When the messenger returned, he reported what he had seen: *ishta zanya* — the scholar's wife had been with another man.

### Shmuel's Ruling

The scholar came before Shmuel and reported what the messenger had said. Shmuel told him: *im meiman lach, zil afkeih* — if you trust this person, go and divorce her. *Ve-i lo, lo tappeik* — and if not, do not divorce her.

### Abaye's Proof

Abaye uses this story to prove his position. Note that this case cannot be explained by silence as admission: the husband was away, the witness reports what he saw, and the husband's lack of response is obviously not an admission — he had no way of knowing what happened. Yet Shmuel appears to rule that an unopposed single witness can obligate the husband to divorce his wife. This is precisely what Abaye holds: an unopposed *ed echad* carries sufficient weight in *davar she'be'ervah* to require divorce, even without any admission from the husband.

### Rava's Reading

Rava reads the story differently. When Shmuel said *im meiman lach* — if you trust him — he did not mean simply "if you know him to be an honest person and not a *gazlan*." He meant: *im meiman lach ke-vei trei* — if you trust him to the degree that you would trust two witnesses — if you have such absolute, ironclad personal confidence in this individual that his word is equivalent to formal testimony. Only in that extraordinary case should you act on his report. This is not a general ruling about unopposed single witnesses; it is a ruling about a case of such unusual personal certainty that it approaches the weight of two witnesses. And even then, Rava would likely maintain, the husband would still need to pay the *kesuvah*, since there remains no objective testimony sufficient to establish adultery in court.

---

## Yannai Story

### The Feast

Abaye's broader proof is derived from a remarkable historical *baraisa* — one with a clear literary quality unusual in Tannaitic texts, and with a known parallel in Josephus. The story concerns King Yannai, one of the Hasmonean monarchs. He sent forces to *Kochalit* in the wilderness and conquered sixty cities there — an achievement he celebrated with great joy upon returning. He summoned all the sages of Israel and told them: our ancestors, in the days when they were preoccupied with building the *Beis HaMikdash*, ate salted fish — the food of poverty. Let us eat salted fish in their memory. Rashi understands this as a gesture of *me-shibbud li-ge'ulah*: a recognition of how far they had come, from grinding poverty to this moment of military triumph, with the food of the past served on tables of gold — *meluchim al shulchanot shel zahav* — a striking and deliberate contrast.

### The Insult

At this feast there was, as the *baraisa* describes in almost scriptural language, *ish echad latz lev ra u-vliya'al* — one person, a mocker, evil-hearted and worthless — *ve-Elazar ben Po'irah sh'mo* — and his name was Elazar ben Poira. He said to King Yannai: the hearts of the Pharisees — the *chachamim* — are against you; they do not support you. Yannai asked: what can I do to test this? Elazar told him: wear the *tzitz* — the golden headplate of the *Kohen Gadol* — and make them stand before you. (There is a dispute among *rishonim* here: Rashi permits wearing *bigdei kehuna* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* based on the principle that the Torah was not given to ministering angels — one cannot demand instant removal of sacred garments after completing the *avodah*. Tosafos restricts this leniency and suggests the *tzitz* may be an exception, as the verse states *ve-hayah al mitzcho tamid* — it shall be upon his forehead always.)

One elder at the feast, Yehudah ben Gedidya, then spoke — unwisely. He said to King Yannai: *rav lecha keter malchut* — the crown of kingship is enough for you; leave the crown of *kehuna* to the descendants of Aharon. His basis was a rumor: *imo nishbis be-Modi'in* — that Yannai's mother had been taken captive in Modi'in, which, if true, would have rendered her unfit as the wife of a *kohen* and Yannai himself a *chalal*, disqualified from priestly service and from the *kehuna gedolah*. The problem was that *vi-yuvakash ha-davar ve-lo nimtza* — the matter had been investigated and nothing had been found to substantiate the claim. Yehudah ben Gedidya's remark was thus not only politically reckless but factually without support.

### The Rumor

The sages at the feast — *vayivadlu chachmei Yisrael be-za'am* — were driven out under the king's displeasure. Rashi explains this as their being expelled from the feast under Yannai's anger; the suggestion is also that their collective silence, their failure to defend Yannai or rebuke the offending speaker more forcefully, made them appear complicit in the insult. From Josephus's parallel account, we know that the sages in fact imposed lashes on the offender for *motzi shem ra* — defamation — but Elazar then argued to Yannai that the punishment was inadequate given the magnitude of the insult to a king and high priest.

### The Conspiracy

Elazar ben Poira then said to Yannai: *im atah shome'a le-atzati* — if you follow my counsel — destroy the sages, wipe them out. Yannai asked: *ha-Torah mah te'ei aleiha* — but what will become of the Torah? Elazar replied: *harei krucha u-munachat be-keren zavis* — it is rolled up and sitting in the corner; *kol ha-rotzeh yilmod yavo ve-yilmod* — whoever wants to learn may come and learn. The written Torah remains; why do you need the sages?

### Heresy & Restoration

The Gemara records: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said that immediately an *apikorsus* — a heresy — entered into Yannai. What was his sin? *De-hava leih le-meimar* — he should have responded: *tenach Torah she-bichtav* — granted, the written Torah remains, *Torah she-be-al peh mah* — but what of the Oral Torah? Who will transmit it? By remaining silent in the face of Elazar's dismissal of the sages, Yannai tacitly accepted the premise that the written Torah alone suffices. Note that *apikorsus* in the Gemara — especially as it appears in Sanhedrin — specifically denotes *mevazeh talmidei chachamim*, contempt for Torah scholars. The term here is thus precise: Yannai's silence was a form of dismissing the indispensable role of the *chachamim*.

The *baraisa* continues: *u-tutzatz ha-ra'ah al yedei Elazar ben Po'irah* — the evil blossomed forth through Elazar ben Poira — *ve-yarequ kol chachmei Yisrael* — and all the sages of Israel were killed. *Ve-hayah ha-olam mishtomem* — the world was desolate. This continued *ad she-ba Shimon ben Shetach* — until Shimon ben Shetach came — who had been hidden away, reportedly under the protection of Yannai's own wife, who was his sister. *Ve-hechzir es ha-Torah le-yoshnah* — and he returned the Torah to its former glory. Some connect Shimon ben Shetach to the establishment of primary education for children throughout the land — an interesting counterpoint to this very story, in that the response to the near-annihilation of Torah scholarship was to ensure that Torah would never again be concentrated only in the hands of a small group of sages who could be wiped out in a single night.

---

## Analysis of Story

### The Question

The Gemara now turns to ask what this story proves. Abaye had invoked it as a source for his position that an unopposed single witness can be credited in matters of personal status. The question is: what was the nature of the evidence about Yannai's mother's captivity, and how exactly was it refuted?

### Evidence Structure

The Gemara considers the possibilities. If two witnesses had testified that she was taken captive, and two others testified she was not, then we have *bei trei u-bei trei* — two against two. What would that produce? In monetary matters, we say they neutralize one another and return to the status quo. But in personal status matters, the analysis is more complex.

### Rashi's View

Rashi's reading is that even if the two sets of witnesses neutralize each other in some sense, the child — Yannai — would remain in *safek*. The mother herself has a *chazkas kashrus* — a presumption of fitness — and so the conflicting testimony leaves her status intact. But Yannai as a child never had an established *chazakah* of priestly fitness in this particular context. Since the case before the court is about the *child's* status, and the child lacks an independent *chazakah* that could resolve the doubt, the result is that Yannai's status as a *kohen* would remain *be-safek*. The *baraisa* says the matter was investigated and nothing was found — Rashi takes this to mean that even in the two-against-two scenario there would have remained a real question, which is why the story is halachically meaningful.

### Gemara's Inference

From here the Gemara draws its inference for Abaye's position: *ela be-echad* — the initial testimony must have been by a single witness. And if the sole reason the case was dismissed is that one or two witnesses contradicted that single witness — *te'ima de-kamachshei lei bei trei* — then in the absence of that contradiction, *meheiman*, the single witness would have been believed. This is Abaye's proof: even in a *davar she'be'ervah* matter — the personal status of the king's mother, which carries enormous ramifications — an unopposed single witness would have been sufficient.

### Rava's Counter

Rava responds: *le-olam trei ve-trei* — in fact, it was two against two from the start. And the reason the case was completely dismissed — rather than leaving Yannai in *safek* — is because the second pair of witnesses employed *edei hazamah*, the mechanism of impeachment. Rather than contradicting the content of the first testimony, they said to the first witnesses: you could not have seen what you claim to have seen — you were elsewhere at that time. *Hazamah* does not merely neutralize; it entirely discredits and removes the first testimony from consideration. Rav Acha bar Minyumi is cited in a parallel context for precisely this principle. Thus the first testimony was not neutralized by equal counter-testimony; it was thrown out entirely, leaving nothing. This is why the *baraisa* says the matter was found to be without basis.

### Alternative Explanation

The Gemara then offers a further alternative: *ve-i ba'it eima, ki de-Rabbi Yitzchak* — if you prefer, explain it like Rabbi Yitzchak, who says *shifcha hichnisu tachteha* — a maidservant was substituted in her place. On this reading, the two sets of witnesses do not contradict each other at all. The first pair testified that Yannai's mother was taken captive — and they were correct. The second pair testified to the rest of the story: yes, she was initially taken, but she was then rescued, and a maidservant was substituted so that the captors would not notice. The second witnesses thus complete and supplement the first testimony rather than contradict it, and the combined account establishes that Yannai's mother had ultimately not been harmed in her personal status.

The daf concludes with the debate between Abaye and Rava unresolved in the text at this point — though of course, as the Gemara will make clear, the *halacha* follows Rava: in all matters of *davar she'be'ervah*, whether to constitute the act or to prove it, two witnesses are required, and even an unopposed single witness does not suffice. For Abaye to maintain that an unopposed *ed echad* is believed in such cases — with consequences as severe as compelling a man to divorce his wife — is, as the Gemara acknowledges, a striking and counterintuitive position, and its implications underscore just how much rides on the foundational distinction between *edei beirur* and *edei kiyum*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 66b

## Abaye-Rava Debate

### One vs. Two Witnesses

The daf opens with a debate between Abaye and Rava concerning the evidentiary standards required in matters of personal status — specifically, whether one witness suffices or whether two are required. The question is not merely about the formal act of *kiddushin* or *gittin*, where it is already established that two witnesses are needed for the act to take effect, but about proof after the fact: can one witness, even an uncontested one, establish a fact bearing on personal status? Abaye holds that one witness would be enough in such circumstances. Rava disagrees, invoking the principle of *ein davar shebiervah pachot mishnayim* — no matter touching on *erva*, personal status, or sexual propriety can be established by fewer than two witnesses. According to Rava, this principle operates in both directions: two witnesses are required both to effectuate such an act and to prove that it occurred.

The scope of the discussion extends well beyond *gittin* and *kiddushin* proper. Among the examples discussed: whether a woman was taken captive, which would render her forbidden to a *kohen*, or whether a woman committed adultery, which would render her forbidden to her husband. In all such cases, Rava insists, the standard of proof remains two witnesses.

### Rava's Principle

The Gemara opens with *mina meimra* — where do we derive this? — and points to a *mishnah* (also found in the *Tosefta*). The citation is introduced with *tennan*, indicating a *mishnah*-level source.

### Mikvah Story

The *mishnah* presents the following case: there was a *mikvah* in a place called Diskim — Rashi understands this as either a personal or a place name — located in Yavneh. The *mikvah* had stood under the presumption (*chazakah*) of being *shalem*, complete, containing the required forty *se'ah* of valid water. At some point, a *chacham* measured it and found it deficient. The question becomes: what is the status of everything done using this *mikvah* since the last time it was verified as complete?

Rabbi Tarfon rules *metaher* — he considers everything done with the *mikvah* to have been valid. His reasoning rests on the principle of *chazakah*: the *mikvah* had an established status of completeness. A doubt about when exactly it became deficient does not override that status; we assume the *mikvah* remained *shalem* until the last possible moment, i.e., until the moment it was found to be lacking. As he articulates it: *mikvah zeh bechezkat shalem hu omed* — this *mikvah* stands in its presumption of completeness. One cannot retroactively undermine it on the basis of uncertainty.

Rabbi Akiva rules *metamei* — he considers everything done since the last verification to be suspect. His reasoning is that there is a competing *chazakah* to consider: *adam zeh bechezkat tamei hu omed* — the person who immersed had a pre-immersion status of *tumah*. That status too is established. The question of whether the person became *tahor* depends entirely on whether the *mikvah* was *kasher* at the time of immersion. Since that is now uncertain, one cannot presume the person's status changed. The doubt cuts both ways, and the question becomes which *chazakah* prevails.

### Kohen Analogy

Unable to resolve the competing *chazakot* directly, Rabbi Tarfon proposes an analogy: *mashal le'omed umakriv al gabbe hamizbeach* — imagine a *kohen* who has been standing and offering *korbanot*, and it then becomes known that he is a *ben gerushah* or *ben chalutzah*, i.e., a *chalal*. In that case, his *avodah* until that point is *kesheirah*. This is not merely a matter of presumption but a special *gezeirat hakatuv*, derived from a *pasuk*, that retroactive invalidation does not apply once the *avodah* was performed in ignorance. Rabbi Tarfon invokes this case to suggest a general policy consideration: just as one cannot issue recall notices invalidating years of priestly service, so too one cannot retroactively invalidate months of *taharot* performed using the *mikvah*.

There is, as the lecturer acknowledges, a notable imprecision in the analogy. The *mikvah* case involves a *safek* — genuine uncertainty about when the deficiency arose — whereas the *kohen* case involves a situation where the *pesul* was present throughout, and we are simply applying a special legal rule that suspends retroactive invalidation. Nonetheless, Rabbi Tarfon's point has a certain policy logic: the societal consequences of wholesale retroactive invalidation support leaning toward the *chazakah* that the *mikvah* remained *kasher*.

### Baal Mum Analogy

Rabbi Akiva responds with a counter-analogy: *mashal l'ma hadavar domeh* — imagine instead a *kohen* offering *korbanot* who is discovered to have a *mum*, a bodily blemish. In that case, his *avodah* is retroactively *pesulah*. This is a striking contrast: one might have supposed that being a *chalal* — lacking the fundamental *kedushat kehunah* — is a more severe disqualification than having a *baal mum*, who in many respects retains *kedushat kehunah* (he shares in the *korbanot*, he is subject to the restrictions of *kohanim*). And yet the *halacha* is precisely the reverse: for the *chalal*, past *avodah* is valid; for the *baal mum*, it is not.

Rabbi Akiva presses the point further. He offers a second distinction: *mikvah pesulah begufa, baal mum pasul begufo* — the *mikvah*'s deficiency is intrinsic to itself, and the *baal mum*'s deficiency is intrinsic to his own body. By contrast, the *ben gerushah* or *ben chalutzah* is *pesul me'acherim* — the disqualification comes from outside, from what his parents did. This structural parallel between the *mikvah* case and the *baal mum* case suggests that the *mikvah* should follow the rule of the *baal mum*, under which retroactive invalidation applies.

Rabbi Tarfon then states the question openly: *nireh l'mi domeh* — let us determine which analogy is more apt. If the *mikvah* case more closely resembles *ben gerushah*, we apply that rule; if it more closely resembles *baal mum*, we apply that rule. Rabbi Akiva then proceeds to argue the comparison systematically: *mikvah pesulah beyachid, baal mum pasul beyachid* — the *mikvah*'s deficiency can be established by a single person's testimony, and the *baal mum*'s deficiency likewise. Whereas *ben gerushah* and *ben chalutzah* — matters of personal status touching on *erva* — require two witnesses. The *mikvah* thus structurally resembles the *baal mum*, not the *ben gerushah*. One therefore applies the *baal mum* rule, and retroactive invalidation follows.

Rabbi Tarfon famously capitulates: *kol haparesh mimcha k'poresh min hachayim* — anyone who separates from you is as one who separates from life itself. The argument was conceded.

### Contested Testimony

The Gemara now takes stock of the actual probative value of this exchange for Rava's principle. The question is: in what circumstance does the *baal mum* case require only one witness? The Gemara asks: *hai baal mum d'pesulah beyachid heichi dami?* — in what scenario does a single person's testimony suffice for a *baal mum*? If the accused is contesting the testimony, we would not ordinarily credit a single witness against a denial. It must therefore be the case — says Rava — that the scenario is one of uncontested testimony: *ela d'shatik*, the *kohen* is not disputing it. And yet even such an uncontested single witness does not suffice for *ben gerushah* or *ben chalutzah*. This demonstrates that in matters of personal status, even uncontested testimony from a single witness is insufficient. Two witnesses are required, and that is Rava's proof.

### Uncontested Testimony

Abaye responds: *l'olam d'ka machish lei* — in fact, the *kohen* is contesting the testimony. So how does the single witness prevail? *D'amar lei shlach achvei* — because the witness can say: if you are telling the truth that you have no *mum*, strip and demonstrate it. The single witness is believed not because the testimony is uncontested in the ordinary sense, but because there is a mechanism for verification: the subject's refusal to demonstrate constitutes corroboration of the witness's claim.

This explains the second distinction Rabbi Akiva drew: *baal mum pesulah begufo* — the *mum* is on the person's body, and is therefore in principle demonstrable. The *mikvah*'s deficiency is similarly intrinsic and demonstrable. Whereas *ben gerushah* and *ben chalutzah* — *pesulah me'acherim* — involve a fact about parentage that cannot be demonstrated physically. If a witness says this man is a *ben gerushah* and the *kohen* denies it, there is nothing to show. Therefore a single witness, even a contested one, does not suffice; two are required.

Abaye's position thus becomes: the distinction is between contested and uncontested testimony, not between one witness and two in the context of personal status per se. When testimony is contested and cannot be demonstrated or refuted, two are needed — as by *ben gerushah*. When testimony can be verified by physical demonstration, one witness may suffice even in a contested setting — as by *baal mum*. But for personal status where no physical verification is possible, one witness — contested or not — is insufficient.

The Gemara concludes that the debate between Abaye and Rava on this point remains unresolved by this source alone. We do *posken* like Rava — *ein davar shebiervah pachot mishnayim* applies both to effectuating and to proving matters of personal status — but the logical proof from this passage is not airtight.

One practical extension of this debate is worth noting: the principle applies not only to cases of invalidation but also in situations where a person must prove something favorable — a woman proving she is divorced, a convert proving the fact of conversion. The standard of proof is accordingly robust.

### Kohen Ben Gerusha

The Gemara closes out this section by establishing the underlying source for the rule that a *kohen* discovered to be a *ben gerushah* or *ben chalutzah* does not have his prior *avodah* retroactively invalidated.

Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel derives it from the verse regarding Pinchas: *v'haytah lo u'l'zaro acharav berit kehunat olam* — it shall be for him and for his descendants after him a covenant of eternal priesthood — which is interpreted to apply *bein zera kasher bein zera pasul*, to both valid and disqualified offspring. Even a *chalal* retains enough of the *kehunat olam* to validate past *avodah* performed in ignorance.

The father of Shmuel derives it from *barech Hashem cheilo u'fo'al yadav tirtzeh* — bless his service-strength and may the work of his hands find favor — understanding *cheilo* as a wordplay on *chulin*, and reading the verse as: even if it turns out there is *chulin* in him — i.e., he is a *chalal* — his *avodah* was *tirtzeh*, found acceptable, until the point of discovery.

Rabbi Yannai derives it from *u'vata el hakohen asher yihyeh bayamim hahem* — you shall go to the *kohen* who is in your days. Obviously one can only go to the *kohen* available at the time; the verse thus validates the *avodah* of whichever *kohen* served during a given period, even if he was later discovered to be disqualified.

For the *baal mum*, the Gemara inverts the derivation. Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel reads *lachen emor hineni noten lo et briti shalom* — the covenant of peace — as applying *kshehu shalem*, only when he is physically complete, unblemished. The word *shalom* in this verse is written with a *vav ketia*, a broken or truncated *vav*, as a scribal tradition indicating that the wholeness the verse describes is conditional on physical integrity. Once there is a *mum*, the condition fails, and past *avodah* is retroactively *pesulah*.

The lecturer acknowledges difficulty with the internal logic of this distinction: intuitively, a *chalal* — who lacks *kedushat kehunah* entirely — seems more fundamentally disqualified than a *baal mum*, who retains *kedushat kehunah* and participates in *korbanot*. And yet the *halacha* holds the *baal mum*'s past *avodah* invalid while validating the *chalal*'s. The best available explanation tracks the distinction between something demonstrable and present — the *mum* was on the body, in principle perceptible — versus something more abstract and genealogical, which could not have been known without information from others. But the lecturer notes that this explanation remains imperfect.

---

## Yichus Rules

### No Aveirah Rule

The next *mishnah* opens the broader inquiry into *yichus* — genealogical status — which encompasses the questions of *kohen*, *levi*, *Yisrael*, *mamzer*, *chalal*, and related categories. The *mishnah* articulates a general principle: *kol makom sheyesh kiddushin v'ein aveirah, havalad holech achar hazachar* — wherever *kiddushin* is binding and no transgression occurred, the child's status follows the father.

### Paternal Descent

The illustrative case: a woman who is a *kohenet*, *leviyah*, or *Yisraelit* marries a man who is a *kohen*, *levi*, or *Yisrael*. The child follows the father's status in all cases, regardless of the mother's status. This is the straightforward application of paternal descent in a permitted marriage.

### Aveirah Rule

The *mishnah* continues: *v'kol makom sheyesh kiddushin v'yesh aveirah, havalad holech achar hapagum* — wherever *kiddushin* is binding but a transgression occurred, the child follows the disqualification. It does not matter whether the *pesul* comes from the father's side or the mother's side; the stigma passes to the child.

### Forbidden Marriages

The illustrative cases of forbidden *kohen* marriages: an *almanah* with a *kohen gadol*, or a *gerushah* or *chalutzah* with a *kohen hedyot*. In these unions *kiddushin* is technically binding (as these are *issurei lavin*, not *issurei karet*), but transgression has occurred. The child does not inherit the precise status of *gerushah* per se, but becomes a *chalal* — disqualified from priestly service and the associated privileges and restrictions. The concept is that the disqualifying status passes on in some form regardless.

### Mamzer Status

Similarly, if a woman who is a *mamzeret* or *netinah* marries a *Yisrael* (or vice versa — a *mamzer* marrying a *bat Yisrael*), *kiddushin* is binding, but the child is a *mamzer*. The principle of *holech achar hapagum* applies directly: the child carries the disqualified status.

### No Kiddushin/Others Poss…

The *mishnah* then addresses a woman with whom *kiddushin* is not binding at all regarding this particular man, but who could be validly married to others: *havalad mamzer*. The child is a *mamzer*. The paradigm case here is a married woman — her husband could marry her, but she cannot create *kiddushin* with this other man. Any issue of such a union, being from *arayot*, is a *mamzer*.

### Matrilineal Descent

The final category: *kol mi she'ein lah lo alav v'lo al acherim kiddushin, havalad kamosah* — any woman with whom no *kiddushin* is possible at all, with anyone, and the child follows the mother's status. The cases: a non-Jewish woman, or a slave. No Jew can contract valid *kiddushin* with either. The child accordingly is not a *mamzer* — that category presupposes a prohibited but potentially valid Jewish marital nexus — but is rather a non-Jew or a slave, following the mother.

This is, as the Gemara will shortly elaborate upon, the foundational principle of matrilineal descent. Where no *kiddushin* can exist, the child's status is determined entirely by the mother.

---

## Rule Exceptions

### Shimon's Challenge

The Gemara immediately challenges the *mishnah*'s framing as a universal principle. Rabbi Shimon asks Rabbi Yochanan: *klala hu?* — is this really a complete and reliable rule?

### Ger-Mamzeret

The challenge: consider a *ger* who married a *mamzeret*. According to some opinions, such a marriage is permitted — a *ger* is allowed to marry a *mamzeret*. If so, there is *kiddushin* and there is no *aveirah*, yet the child is still a *mamzer*. The child follows the *pagum* despite the absence of transgression — which contradicts the first clause of the *mishnah*.

A *baraita* is cited: *ger shenasa mamzeret, havalad mamzer* — if a *ger* marries a *mamzeret*, the child is a *mamzer*. This is the position of Rabbi Yose.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *mi savart masnitin Rabbi Yose hi?* — who says our *mishnah* follows Rabbi Yose? The *mishnah* may reflect the view of Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that a *ger* is not permitted to marry a *mamzeret* in the first place. According to Rabbi Yehudah, such a union involves *kiddushin* with *aveirah*, and therefore the child following the *pagum* is entirely consistent with the *mishnah*'s second clause. The apparent exception dissolves once we assign the *mishnah* to Rabbi Yehudah rather than Rabbi Yose.

### Kol Makom Inclusion

The Gemara then takes up the question of completeness. Even if the *mishnah*'s rule is internally consistent, there are cases that fit the rule but are not listed as examples, and cases that are exceptions to the rule that are also unlisted. How do we account for both?

The Gemara answers with a dual hermeneutical move. The phrase *kol makom* — wherever — at the opening of each clause signals a general principle intended to include additional cases beyond those explicitly listed. The phrase *v'eizu zu* — and which is this? — following each list signals that the list is exhaustive for its particular formulation, thereby implicitly acknowledging that other cases may deviate from the rule.

The Gemara proceeds through candidate cases. A *chalal* who marries a *bat Yisrael*: *kiddushin* is binding, no *aveirah*, and the child follows the father — he is a *chalal*. This is an application of the rule not listed in the *mishnah*. A *Yisrael* who marries a *chalala*: *kiddushin* is binding, no *aveirah*, and the child follows the father — the child is *kasher*, not a *chalala*. This too is an application of the rule not listed.

### Chalal Case

The Gemara asks: if these are applications of the rule, why were they not listed explicitly? The answer is that they cannot be framed neatly within the *mishnah*'s formulation. The *mishnah* lists cases of *kohenet*, *leviyah*, and *Yisraelit* marrying a *kohen*, *levi*, or *Yisrael* — implying that any of these women could marry any of these men. But a *chalala* cannot marry a *kohen*. Were the *mishnah* to include *v'chalala* in the list of women who married a *kohen*, *levi*, or *Yisrael*, it would imply that a *chalala* marrying a *kohen* is among the scenarios — which is forbidden. The *mishnah* cannot include the case without distorting its own framing. This is, as the Gemara acknowledges, a satisfying answer: literary considerations of economy and consistency preclude the explicit listing.

### Framing Problem

This observation generalizes. The *mishnah* is constructed as a tight, elegant set of rules. Cases that fit the rule but require syntactic contortions to include are simply absorbed into the scope of *kol makom* without being named. Cases that are exceptions are similarly handled by *eizu zu*, which marks the list as the intended application rather than an exhaustive catalogue of all possible cases. The strategy is: *tana kol makom l'atuyei* — the *tanna* uses *kol makom* to include unlisted applications; *tana eizu zu l'motei* — and uses *eizu zu* to exclude, or rather to acknowledge, unlisted exceptions.

### Mitzri Generations

Another application of the rule is now introduced from a tradition of Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan: *Mitzri sheini shenasa Mitzrit rishona, benah shelishi havei* — a second-generation *Mitzri* who marries a first-generation *Mitzrit* produces a third-generation child. The background rule is that a *Mitzri* convert may not marry into the Jewish community until the third generation: *dor shelishi yavo lahem bikhal Hashem*. The question is how to count generations when two converts of different generational remove marry each other. The answer: the child's generation is counted by the father's status. A second-generation *Mitzri* father and a first-generation *Mitzrit* mother produces a third-generation child — following the father. This is another application of the rule of paternal descent in a permitted marriage with no *aveirah*. Why was it not listed? The *kol makom* of the *reisha* includes it.

### Converting Nations

A tradition brought in the name of Ravin citing Rabbi Yochanan introduces a case that functions as an exception rather than an application: when members of non-Jewish nations convert, and two converts of different national backgrounds marry — for example, an *Edomi* convert and a *Mitzri* convert — one asks what status their child bears, given that different nations have different generational thresholds for full integration. The rule here, says Ravin, is *halach achar hapagam shebishneihem* — we follow whichever of the two parents carries the greater disqualification, the greater *pagum*. Even if no *aveirah* was committed in the marriage, the child follows the more disqualified parent. This is an exception to the rule that in a permitted marriage one follows the father. It is accounted for by *eizu zu l'motei* — the *eizu zu* formulation acknowledges the existence of such exceptions without enumerating them.

### Category Resolution

The Gemara now resolves how the various cases map onto the categories under Rabbi Yehudah versus Rabbi Yose. According to Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that a *ger* may not marry a *mamzeret*, the union of *ger* and *mamzeret* is one of *kiddushin v'yesh aveirah*, and the child following the *pagum* fits the second clause of the *mishnah*. The *kol makom* of the *reisha* includes the *chalala* and *Mitzri* cases as unlisted applications of paternal descent. The *eizu zu* of both clauses covers the exceptions — most notably the *umot shenitgayru* case of nations that converted.

According to Rabbi Yose, who holds the *ger-mamzeret* union is permitted, that case is an exception: no *aveirah*, yet the child follows the *pagum*. It is covered by *eizu zu* as an unlisted exception. But the Gemara notes that under Rabbi Yose's reading, the *kol makom* of the *seifa* — the clause about *kiddushin v'yesh aveirah* and *holech achar hapagum* — has nothing additional to include. The Gemara deflects: *aidi d'tana reisha eizu zu, tana seifa eizu zu; aidi d'tana reisha kol makom, tana seifa kol makom* — the parallel structure of the *mishnah* requires that each clause employ both formulations, even if in a given clause one of them does no independent work. The literary symmetry of *kol makom* and *eizu zu* appearing in each half of the *mishnah* is itself sufficient justification for their inclusion, regardless of whether both are needed for substantive legal purposes in every case.

---

## Non-Jewish Nations

### Tribal Paternity

The Gemara turns to the governing principle for non-Jews: *b'umos halach achar hazachar* — among the nations, one follows the father in determining tribal identity. The question of national or tribal membership for non-Jews is determined patrilineally.

### Cana'anite Status

The Gemara distinguishes between native *Kena'anim* — members of the seven nations — and non-native *Kena'anim*, those who happen to dwell in the land but whose fathers are not from the seven nations. The legal significance pertains to the laws of slavery: the Torah permits purchasing *Kena'ani* slaves from among the peoples dwelling in the land, but the application of this permission turns on the national identity of the person in question. The Gemara asks: from where do we know that a child born to a *Kena'ani* woman by a foreign father is not considered a *Kena'ani* for these purposes?

### Slavery Proofs

The *talmud lomar*: *vegam mibnei hatoshavim hagarim imachem* — from among the children of the residents who dwell among you — you may acquire them as slaves. The verse distinguishes those who are resident sojourners in the land from native inhabitants. The Gemara understands this distinction as tracking the father's origin: if the father is foreign, the child, though born in the land, is not a native *Kena'ani*. The verse *mehem tiknu* — from them you may acquire — applies to such a child, and the implication is that the child's status is determined by the father's national identity.

### Reverse Case

The reverse case: a *Kena'ani* man who fathers a child with a non-*Kena'ani* woman. The verse *asher holidu b'artzechem* — who were born in your land — is read to indicate that being physically born in the land is not determinative; what matters is whether the father is from *Kena'an*. If the father is a *Kena'ani*, the child is considered to be living in *Kena'an* in the relevant sense, because the child's national identity follows the father. *Aval lo min hagarim b'artzechem* — but not from those who are merely dwelling in the land — distinguishes the case where the father is foreign: that child, though resident in the land, does not carry *Kena'ani* identity.

The Gemara acknowledges the circularity here: the *pesuk* does not explicitly mention the father as the determining factor; rather, the presumption that status follows the father is read into the verse, and then read back out of it as proof. Nevertheless, the result is consistent: for non-Jewish nations, tribal or national identity is determined patrilineally. The discussion of what occurs when such individuals convert — how to reckon the status of a child born to, for example, an *Edomi* convert and a *Moavi* convert — is deferred to the following session.

---

---

# Kiddushin 67

## Two Witnesses Debate

### One vs. Two Witnesses

The sugya opens with the dispute between Abaye and Rava concerning the principle of *ein davar she-be'erva pahot mi-shenayim* — that matters of personal status require no fewer than two witnesses. The question is not merely about the formal act of *kiddushin* or *get*, where two witnesses are needed to constitute the act itself, but about the evidentiary standard required to establish that such an act occurred, or to determine personal status more broadly. Rava holds that two witnesses are required both to effectuate and to prove matters of personal status. Abaye disagrees, maintaining that one uncontested witness suffices for proof even in such matters.

The stakes of this dispute extend well beyond the narrow domain of marriage and divorce. The same standard of proof applies, for instance, to questions of whether a woman was taken captive — which would render her forbidden to her *kohen* husband — or whether a woman committed adultery, which would render her forbidden to her husband entirely.

### Mikvah Case Source

Rava introduces his proof from a *mishnah* (cited also in the *Tosefta*): *Amar Rabbi Shimon* — there was an incident involving a *megurah*, a cistern or body of water, in a place called Diskim (or, as Rashi notes, this may be a personal name rather than a place), situated in Yavneh. This *mikvah* had long stood with a *chezkat shelemah* — a presumption of having sufficient water. When it was eventually measured, it was found to be lacking the requisite forty *se'ah*.

The question that arises is: what is the status of all the purifications performed using this *mikvah* since the last time it was confirmed to be complete? The *mikvah* did not become deficient the very day after the prior measurement. So when did it lose its valid status, and what are the consequences for everything done in the interim?

### Mikvah Dispute

Two *tanna'im* debate the question. Rabbi Tarfon rules leniently: *mikvah zeh be-hezkat shalem hu omed* — the *mikvah* stands with a presumption of being complete. He invokes the principle of *chazakah*: since the *mikvah* had a recognized valid status, one cannot retroactively undermine that status based on mere doubt about when it became deficient. The doubt does not override the *status quo* of the *mikvah* being *shalem*. This is the foundational logic of *chazakah*: we assume the prior status persists until we have definitive evidence that it changed, which means we push the change to the last possible moment — when the measurement was actually taken.

Rabbi Akiva, however, rules stringently. He too invokes *chazakah*, but from the opposite direction: *adam zeh be-hezkat tame hu omed* — the person who immersed had a *status quo* of being *tameh* before entering the *mikvah*. Just as one cannot arbitrarily strip away the *mikvah's* status based on doubt, one equally cannot strip away the person's prior *tumah* status based on doubt. The fundamental question thus becomes a collision of two competing *chazakot*: the *chazakah* of the *mikvah* as valid versus the *chazakah* of the person as *tameh*.

Rabbi Tarfon then introduces a *mashal*: consider a *kohen* who was standing and offering *korbanot*, and it subsequently came to light that his mother had been divorced before marrying his father, making him a *ben grushah* and hence a *challal*. In that case, his *avodah* performed prior to the discovery is declared *ksherah* — valid. Now, admittedly, once we have this information, we know retroactively that he was a *challal* all along. Logically, one might expect his past *avodah* to be invalidated. Yet the *halacha* is that it is not, and the *gemara* will derive this from a *pasuk*. Rabbi Tarfon is invoking this case analogically, perhaps also gesturing toward the practical and societal consequences of the alternative — if a *kohen* at age seventy discovered he was a *ben grushah*, are we to retroactively recall and invalidate everything he performed over the preceding decades? There is reason, policy and otherwise, to affirm the prior status.

### Comparative Arguments

Rabbi Akiva responds with a counter-analogy: consider a *kohen* who was offering *korbanot* and was subsequently discovered to have a *mum* — a bodily blemish. In that case, his *avodah* is *pesulah* — retroactively invalid. This is striking, because intuitively one might have thought the opposite: being a *ben grushah* or *ben chalutzah* is a more fundamental deficiency of status — it goes to the heart of one's *kehuna* — whereas a *ba'al mum* retains his *kedushat kehuna* in every other respect. Yet the *halacha* distinguishes sharply: the *ba'al mum* whose *avodah* is retroactively disqualified, and the *ben grushah* whose *avodah* is retroactively valid.

Rabbi Akiva's point is structural: these two cases generate different legal consequences, so one must ask which case the *mikvah* scenario more closely resembles. And he argues that the *mikvah* case resembles the *ba'al mum* case: just as by a *ba'al mum* a single witness suffices to establish the disqualification, similarly, the deficiency of the *mikvah* can be established by one person — the deficiency is, so to speak, *pesulah bi-gufo*, present in the body of the thing itself. By contrast, the disqualification of a *ben grushah* or *ben chalutzah* — *psulo me-acherim* — derives from others, namely the conduct of the parents, and requires two witnesses.

Rabbi Akiva then formalizes the comparison: *mikvah pasul bi-yachid u-va'al mum pasul bi-yachid* — the deficiency of the *mikvah* is established by one person and the *ba'al mum* is established by one person. But the *ben grushah* and *ben chalutzah* — *psulo bi-shnayim* — their disqualification requires two witnesses. This is precisely the reason the *gemara* introduced this entire passage: to prove that matters of *erva*, of personal status, require two witnesses. He additionally offers a second line of comparison: *mikvah pesulah be-gufah, ba'al mum pasul be-gufo* — the problem is inherent in the body of the *mikvah* or the person, whereas *ben grushah u-ven chalutzah* — *psulo me-acherim* — the problem originates externally, from what others did.

Rabbi Tarfon, unable to counter this reasoning, concedes with characteristic rhetorical flourish: *kol ha-poreish mimcha ke-poreish min ha-chayim* — anyone who separates from you separates from life itself.

### Contested Testimony

The *gemara* then turns to interrogate the precise meaning of the *ba'al mum* case. It asks: *hai ba'al mum she-pesulah bi-yachid heichi dami?* — What exactly is the case where one witness suffices for a *ba'al mum*? If the *kohen* himself is contesting the claim — denying he has a blemish — would we really believe a single witness against him? Surely not. So presumably, says Rava, the case is where the *kohen* is not contesting the testimony — *de-shatik* — and one uncontested witness is believed. And yet, even in that scenario, by a *ben grushah* and *ben chalutzah* two witnesses are still required. This is Rava's proof: even uncontested testimony of a single witness is insufficient for personal status matters; two are always required.

Abaye responds directly — and this is precisely the counterargument that presents itself naturally. Abaye says: *le'olam de-ka machish lei* — actually, we are dealing with a contested case. The *kohen* is denying it. But why, then, do we believe the single witness? Because the witness can say to the *kohen*: *shlach achvei* — strip and show us. If you deny having a blemish, demonstrate it. The single witness is believed even over the *kohen's* objection because the claim is objectively verifiable — the *ba'al mum* is *pesulah be-gufo*, the deficiency is on the body itself, and the *kohen's* refusal to demonstrate substantiates the witness's account.

This is precisely why the comparison to *ben grushah* and *ben chalutzah* breaks down for Abaye. In that case, if the *kohen* contests a single witness's claim that he is a *ben grushah*, there is nothing to show, no demonstration possible. The status derives entirely from a historical fact about the parents — *psulo me-acherim* — and so a contested single witness cannot be believed, because there is no objective verification to demand. Hence, for contested testimony about personal status where there is nothing to demonstrate, two witnesses are required. But for Abaye, this is the reason for the two-witness requirement in the *ben grushah* case, not a general rule that personal status always requires two witnesses.

### Personal Status Rule

The *gemara* does not definitively resolve the dispute at this juncture. Whether the *ba'al mum* case was contested or uncontested remains open — for if the *mum* is internal, there is nothing to demonstrate in any event, making it structurally more similar to an uncontested case, which would restore Rava's proof. The *gemara* then briefly addresses the underlying *halachic* sources for the distinction between *ben grushah* and *ba'al mum*. How do we know a *kohen* discovered to be a *ben grushah* does not have his past *avodah* invalidated? Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel derives it from the *pasuk* concerning Pinchas: *ve-haytah lo u-le-zaro acharav* — the covenant of *kehuna* extends to his descendants, *bein zera kasher bein zera pasul*, whether the offspring is fit or disqualified. The father of Shmuel derives it from the verse *bareich Hashem cheilo* — bless his strength — reading *cheilo* as referring even to *chullin she-bo*, those whose sanctity may be impaired, and *u-po'al yadav tirtzeh* as indicating acceptance of his service through the moment of discovery.

Rabbi Yochanan offers yet another source: *u-vata el ha-kohen asher yihyeh ba-yamim ha-hem* — you shall come to the *kohen* who will be in those days. This teaches that even if it turns out the *kohen* before whom you stood was later discovered to be unfit, the interaction was valid — *zeh kasher ve-nit-chalal*, he was fit and became disqualified thereafter.

Regarding the *ba'al mum*, Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel derives from the continuation of the Pinchas passage: *lachen emor hinni noten lo et briti shalom* — the covenant of *shalom* applies only *ke-shehu shalem*, when he is whole and unblemished, *ve-lo ke-shehu chaser*, not when he is lacking. The word *shalom* in the *pasuk* is written with a broken *vav* — a *vav keti'a* — as Rav Nachman notes, a scribal tradition attested in *Sifrei Torah*, with various traditions as to the precise form. This textual irregularity is the basis for reading *shalom* as *shalem*, and thereby limiting the grant of validity to an unblemished *kohen*.

On the conceptual level, this distinction remains genuinely puzzling. A *challal* has no *kedushat kehuna* at all — he is exempt from all its prohibitions and obligations — while a *ba'al mum* retains his sanctity fully, merely being unable to perform the *avodah*. Yet it is the *challal* whose prior *avodah* is retroactively valid and the *ba'al mum* whose prior *avodah* is retroactively disqualified. One possible line of reasoning, parallel to a point the *gemara* makes in another context, is that the *ba'al mum's* disqualification was present and objectively discoverable — it was there to be seen — whereas the *challal's* disqualification was a matter of hidden historical fact. That which was discoverable and observable carries a greater legal charge. But this remains difficult.

The practical ruling follows Rava — we generally rule *ein davar she-be'erva pahot mi-shenayim* even as a standard of proof. This has significant implications beyond invalidating personal status: a woman seeking to prove she is divorced, or a convert seeking to prove the validity of his conversion, faces the same evidentiary threshold. These remain live questions wherever status must be affirmatively established.

---

## Genealogical Status

### Child Follows Father

The *mishnah* opens with a tripartite framework governing *yichus* — genealogical status — based on the nature of the union between the parents.

The first principle: *kol makom she-yesh kiddushin ve-ein aveira, ha-velad holech achar ha-zachar* — wherever *kiddushin* is binding and there is no transgression, the child's status follows the father. The *mishnah* illustrates this with the most basic case: whether the mother is a *kohenet*, a *leviyah*, or a *yisraelit*, and the father is a *kohen*, *levi*, or *yisrael*, the child inherits the father's tribal and priestly status. A *kohen* father produces a *kohen* child regardless of the mother's background. This is the standard, unexceptional case of a valid and permitted marriage.

### Child Follows Disqualifi…

The second principle: *kol makom she-yesh kiddushin ve-yesh aveira, ha-velad holech achar ha-pagum* — wherever *kiddushin* is binding but the union involves transgression, the child follows the disqualified party. The examples given are the forbidden unions of *kohanim*: an *almanah* with a *kohen gadol*, or a *grushah* or *chalutzah* with a *kohen hedyot*. The child born of such a union does not himself become a *kohen gadol* or a divorcée — rather, the child becomes a *challal*, stripped of the full sanctity of *kehuna*, which is the operative consequence of a forbidden *kohen* union. The conceptual principle is that the stigma of the forbidden relationship attaches to the offspring, regardless of whether the disqualified party is the father or the mother.

### Mamzer Status

The third principle extends this logic to *mamzer* status: if a woman who is a *mamzeret* marries a *yisrael*, or a *yisrael* woman marries a *mamzer*, the child is a *mamzer*. The *kiddushin* in such unions is binding — since the prohibition is an *isur lav* and not an *isur karet* or punishable by death — but the child inherits the disqualified status of whichever parent bears it. This applies symmetrically regardless of whether the *mamzer* is the father or the mother.

### Matrilineal Descent

The *mishnah* then turns to two remaining categories defined by the woman's status. First: *kol mi she-ein lah alav kiddushin aval yesh lah al acherim kiddushin* — a woman with whom *kiddushin* is not binding for this particular man, but who can nonetheless contract valid marriage with others — *ha-velad mamzer*. This is the category of *arayot*, the forbidden incestuous and adulterous relations enumerated in the Torah. For instance, a married woman's union with someone other than her husband produces a *mamzer*, because *kiddushin* cannot take effect with the adulterer, but she remains capable of valid marriage with her husband.

Finally: *kol mi she-ein lah lo alav ve-lo al acherim kiddushin* — a woman who cannot contract valid marriage with anyone — *ha-velad kemotah*, the child follows the mother's status and is not a *mamzer*. The *mishnah* identifies this category as the *vlad shifcha ve-nochrit*, the child of a non-Jewish woman or a slave woman. Since no Jew can contract *kiddushin* with a non-Jewish woman or a slave, and since these women cannot marry any Jew, the child follows the mother entirely — and is either a non-Jew or a slave, not a *mamzer*. This is the *mishnah's* expression of matrilineal descent: where no Jewish *kiddushin* can attach to the mother in any circumstances, the child's status is defined entirely by her.

---

## Rule vs. Exception

### Challenge to Completeness

The *gemara* opens with Rabbi Shimon challenging Rabbi Yochanan: *klala hu?* — Is this general principle truly comprehensive? Does the rule *kol makom she-yesh kiddushin ve-ein aveira ha-velad holech achar ha-zachar* genuinely account for all cases?

### Convert & Mamzeret

Rabbi Shimon immediately identifies a problem. *Harei ger she-nasa mamzeret* — consider a convert who married a *mamzeret*. According to one opinion, a *mamzeret* is permitted to marry a *ger*, making the *kiddushin* binding with no transgression. Yet even in that case, the child is a *mamzer* — *ha-velad holech achar ha-pagum*. Here we have a case of valid *kiddushin* with no *aveira*, yet the child does not follow the father; the child follows the stigmatized party. The *mishnah's* general rule is therefore violated.

A *baraita* confirms: *ger she-nasa mamzeret — ha-velad mamzer*. This is the position of Rabbi Yosi. Rabbi Yochanan's response is that our *mishnah* need not be Rabbi Yosi's view. *Matnitin Rabbi Yehuda hi* — perhaps the *mishnah* reflects Rabbi Yehuda's position. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a *ger* is in fact *forbidden* to marry a *mamzeret* — *ger lo yisa mamzeret*. Under Rabbi Yehuda's view, the union involves transgression — *yesh kiddushin ve-yesh aveira* — and so the child following the *pagum* fits squarely within the *mishnah's* second rule. The apparent exception dissolves once we attribute the *mishnah* to Rabbi Yehuda.

### Klal Inclusion

But the *mishnah* does not list the *ger* and *mamzeret* case explicitly under the second rule, even according to Rabbi Yehuda. Why not? The *gemara* answers: *tanna kol makom le-atuyei* — the phrase *kol makom* functions as a *klal*, a general statement broad enough to include unlisted cases within the scope of the rule. The *mishnah* says *kol makom she-yesh kiddushin ve-yesh aveira* — wherever there is *kiddushin* and transgression — and that formulation is deliberately expansive, encompassing the *ger u-mamzeret* case without explicit mention.

Alternatively, even if the *mishnah* reflects Rabbi Yosi's view, the case of *ger u-mamzeret* would be an exception to the first rule, handled by the word *ve-eizo zu* in the *mishnah's* phrasing, as we shall see.

The *gemara* then raises a further unlisted case: *vaharei challal she-nasa bat Yisrael* — a *challal* who married a *bat Yisrael*. This union involves no transgression — a *challal* is not forbidden to a non-*kohen* woman — and *kiddushin* is fully binding. The child follows the father and is a *challal*. This is a straightforward application of the first rule, yet it is absent from the *mishnah's* list. Similarly, a *Yisrael* who married a *challala* — again, no transgression, binding *kiddushin*, and the child follows the father and is *kasher*. Why were these not listed?

The *gemara* answers: *de-lo pasika lei* — the case cannot be stated cleanly given the *mishnah's* framing. If one tried to extend the list to include *challala*, one would write something like: *kohenet, leviyah, Yisraelit, ve-challala she-niset le-kohen, levi, ve-Yisrael* — but then one is implicitly including the possibility of a *challala* marrying a *kohen*, which is in fact *assur*. The case does not lend itself to the tidy phrasing the *mishnah* prefers, and so it was left out despite being a genuine application of the rule. The *klal* of *kol makom* is understood to encompass it nonetheless.

### Eizehu Exceptions

Now the *gemara* examines the function of *eizehu* — the word *ve-eizo zu* that introduces the specific lists in the *mishnah*. Initially, there is an assumption that *ve-eizo zu* is exhaustive — that it confines the application of the rule to precisely those cases enumerated. If so, any unlisted application would be a problem for the *mishnah's* completeness. Jenna's observation here is apt: at this stage, the *gemara* is working with the premise that *ve-eizo zu* is limiting, before ultimately arriving at the resolution that *ve-eizo zu* serves a different function.

The *gemara* develops the position that *ve-eizo zu* functions not only to define the scope of the rule but to flag exceptions — cases that fall outside the expected application of the rule. By saying "and which cases are these?" and then providing a list, the *mishnah* implicitly acknowledges that the list does not exhaust all possible applications; there are others not mentioned that nonetheless fall under the *klal*. At the same time, the specificity of the list implies that there are scenarios where one might have expected the rule to apply but where it does not. The word *eizehu* thus does double duty: it confirms that the rule applies to the listed cases, and it signals that certain unlisted cases are exceptions.

The overall framework that emerges is this: anything that is an application of the rule not explicitly listed is included under *kol makom*; anything that is an exception to the rule is signaled by *ve-eizo zu*. The two phrases together provide the *mishnah* with the flexibility to be both a general rule and a practically accurate guide.

### Israelite & Challala

Returning to the unlisted cases of *challal* and *Yisrael* — the *gemara* confirms that *tanna kol makom de-reisha le-atuyei*, the *kol makom* of the opening clause serves to include *Yisrael she-nasa challala* and *challal she-nasa bat Yisrael* as applications of the first rule, even though they were not explicitly enumerated. This is the *gemara's* formal resolution for those cases.

### Framing Difficulty

The *gemara* returns to the question of why the *challal* case was not listed explicitly, even though it is a genuine application of the rule. The answer, as established, is that including *challala* in the list of women would require writing a formulation that also implies a *challala* could marry a *kohen* — *ve-challala le-kohen lo chazya* — which she cannot. The *mishnah* cannot phrase it in a single clean sentence without creating a false implication, and so it leaves the *challal* case to be derived from *kol makom*.

### Egyptian Generations

The *gemara* identifies another unlisted case: *Mitzri she-nasa Mitzrit* — an Egyptian convert who married a female Egyptian convert. The *halacha* is that an Egyptian convert may enter the community of Israel (*kahal Hashem*) only from the third generation: *dor shelishi yavo lahem bi-kehal Hashem*. The question is how generations are counted when the parents are of different generational standing within the Egyptian convert lineage.

Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan states: *Mitzri sheni she-nasa Mitzrit rishona — bena shelishi havei* — if a second-generation Egyptian convert married a first-generation Egyptian female convert, the child is a third-generation, and consequently permitted. Generations are counted by the father. This is another application of the rule that the child follows the father — *yesh kiddushin, ein aveira, ha-velad holech achar ha-zachar* — and it is included in the *klal* of *kol makom*.

### Non-Jewish Nations

Ravin, citing Rabbi Yochanan, introduces a principle regarding non-Jews: *be-umot halech achar ha-zachar* — among the nations, the tribal identity of a child follows the father. If a man from one non-Jewish nation has a child with a woman from another nation, the child's nationality is determined by the father. This too is an unlisted application of the rule that status follows the male, and the *gemara* includes it under *kol makom de-reisha le-atuyei*.

### Converted Nations

The same teaching of Ravin continues: *nitgayeru — halech achar ha-pagum she-be-shneihem* — if they converted, the child follows whichever parent bears the more disqualifying status. For instance, if an *Edomi* convert married a *Mitzri* convert — where the *Edomi* is restricted for two generations and the *Mitzri* for three — the child follows the more stringent status. This is a case of *yesh kiddushin, ein aveira* — two converts, permitted to marry one another — yet the child does not follow the father; it follows the *pagum*. This is an exception to the first rule, and the *gemara* includes it under the category of *eizehu* as an unlisted exception.

### Klal & Eizehu Purpose

The *gemara* now consolidates its analysis. According to Rabbi Yehuda — the likely author of the *mishnah* — the *ger u-mamzeret* case is an *aveira*, so it fits the second rule via the *kol makom* of the *seifa*. The *challal* and *Yisrael* cases are applications of the first rule also included in *kol makom*. The exceptions — the converted nations following the *pagum* despite no *aveira*, and possibly the *Mitzri* generation count depending on the ruling — are flagged by *eizehu*.

According to Rabbi Yosi, the *ger u-mamzeret* case is *muttar* and thus an exception to the first rule, included in *eizehu*. The converted nations' cases are likewise exceptions included there. But then the *kol makom* of the *seifa* — the general rule for when there is *kiddushin* and *aveira* — seems to have nothing left to include that is not already listed.
