The *gemara* resolves this by noting: *ayidi de-tana reisha eizo zu, tani seifa eizo zu* — since the *mishnah* uses *eizehu* in the first clause, it maintains the same structural parallel in the second clause, even if the second *eizehu* has no independent work to do in limiting or flagging exceptions there. Similarly, the *kol makom* of the *seifa* mirrors the *kol makom* of the *reisha* for structural reasons, even if — according to Rabbi Yosi — no additional cases need to be drawn in by the *seifa's kol makom*. The *mishnah's* symmetrical structure accounts for the repeated usage of both phrases.

### Non-Jewish Tribal Status

The *gemara* now examines the case of non-Jewish tribal identity in detail, returning to the teaching of Ravin. *Mai be-umot halech achar ha-zachar?* — What is the precise case where among non-Jews the child's tribal identity follows the father?

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *minayin le-echad min ha-umot she-ba al Kena'anit ve-holid ben she-ata rashai liknoto be-eved?* — From where do we know that if a man from the nations (not one of the seven Canaanite nations) fathered a child with a *Kena'anit* woman, that child may be purchased as a slave and is not subject to the prohibition of destruction that applies to the seven nations? The *talmud lomar*: *ve-gam mi-benei ha-toshavim ha-garim imachem, me-hem tiknu* — from those who dwell as sojourners in your land, you may purchase. The *baraita* understands the distinction between "sojourners" and "native" to be defined by the father. If the father is from outside *Kena'an*, the child is not a *Kena'ani*, even if the mother is.

Conversely: if a *Kena'ani* man fathered a child with a non-*Kena'anit* woman — *yachol af eved she-ba al shifcha min ha-umot ve-holid ben she-ata rashai liknoto be-eved?* — perhaps that child is also purchasable as a non-*Kena'ani*? The *talmud lomar*: *asher holidu be-artzechem* — those born in your land, meaning those born into a foreign land whose father identifies them as belonging elsewhere. *Min ha-noladim be-artzechem — aval lo min ha-garim be-artzechem* — you may purchase those born here among sojourners, but not those who genuinely dwell in the land as part of the *Kena'ani* nations. And who belongs to the *Kena'ani* nations? Those whose father is *Kena'ani* — the child follows the father.

The *gemara* acknowledges that what we have done here is read the assumption of paternal identity into the *pesukim* and then read it back out again as a proof — the *pesukim* speak of "born in your land" versus "sojourning in your land" without explicitly mentioning the father, and the determination of which category a child belongs to is being derived from the principle that follows the father. Nonetheless, this is the *tanna'im's* reading, and it establishes that for non-Jewish national identity, status is defined by the father.

The discussion of what happens when such individuals convert — for instance, an *Edomi* convert and a *Moavi* convert, or an *Ammoni* convert, each of whom carries different *halachic* consequences regarding entry into the Jewish community — will continue in the next *shiur*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 67b

## Converts & Lineage

### Restricted Nations

The daf begins towards the end of 67b, with the final lines of the *mishnah* addressing the transmission of *yichus* — lineage status — in cases of marriage between individuals whose marital prospects are in some way restricted. The *mishnah* groups these cases by the nature of the relational status involved and how that status passes to children. Of particular concern here are converts from nations that carry restrictions on who they may marry into the broader Jewish community: the *mitzri* (Egyptian), the *amoni* (Ammonite), and the *moavi* (Moabite). These nations' converts, while permitted to marry *mamzerim* and other converts, face a higher bar before marrying into a community of fully accepted *yichus*.

### 3-Gen Barrier

The *mishnah* states: *nitgaiyru halach achar hapgum shebishneihem* — if both converts, one must follow whichever of the two parties is the more *pagum*, the more restricted. The *gemara* immediately asks: *bemai* — what precise case is the *mishnah* describing? If we suggest it refers to an Egyptian man who married an Ammonite woman, there is no real competing problem: *amoni velo amonit* — the prohibition affecting Ammonites applies only to males. A female Ammonite convert faces no restriction whatsoever in marrying into the Jewish community. This is the same principle underlying the narrative of the Book of Ruth, where Ruth's Moabite origin posed no halachic obstacle to her marriage with Boaz, in keeping with the oral tradition that the exclusions of Ammon and Moab apply only to males.

The *gemara* therefore concludes the *mishnah* must be discussing the reverse: a male Ammonite convert who married a female Egyptian convert. Here both parties carry restrictions, but they operate differently. The male Ammonite's restriction is permanent — his male descendants are perpetually barred from full integration. The female Egyptian convert, by contrast, transmits the *mitzri* status in a non-gendered fashion, such that her descendants face a three-generation barrier. So: *veim zachar havei, hai shadia batrei dideih* — if the couple has a male child, the child follows the father's status and is treated as an Ammonite, with the lifelong restriction; *veim nekeiva havei, shadia batrah didah* — if they have a daughter, she is treated as a second-generation Egyptian. This, then, is the meaning of *halach achar hapgum shebishneihem*: one does not simply take the worst of the two and apply it uniformly. Rather, the *yichus* transmitted depends on the child's gender, each child tracking the more restrictive parent according to their own status.

### Gender-Based Status

This ruling raises a practical question about its modern application: does the three-generation barrier still apply to Egyptian converts today, long after *yetziat Mitzrayim*? The traditional understanding, at least in terms of *halacha*, is that the prohibition is not limited to the generations immediately following the Exodus. Whenever a *mitzri* converts, the three-generation restriction applies afresh. The arithmetic is significant: a convert's children are born Jewish but are second-generation *mitzri*; their children are third-generation *mitzri*; and only the grandchildren of the original convert are fully free of the restriction. Seventy-five years is a long time to carry that particular layer of *yichus* complexity.

## Mamzerut Defined

### Modern Tech

At this point the *gemara* transitions to one of the central discussions in all of *shas* on the question of *mamzerus*: what is the precise link between a prohibited relationship and the status of *mamzer*? It is important to clarify at the outset that a child born out of wedlock between two people who are halachically permitted to marry each other is emphatically *not* a *mamzer*. *Mamzerut* is fundamentally tied — at least according to most *tanna'im* — to the prohibition on the relationship itself. The debate is over which level of prohibition suffices.

The question of advanced reproductive technologies is directly relevant here, since the status of *mamzer* requires an actual sexual relationship. A child conceived through in-vitro fertilization or artificial insemination, according to the majority view among *poskim*, would not be a *mamzer* even if the genetic parents could not halachically have relations. Rav Moshe Feinstein famously took the permissive position on such technologies, marshaling extensive *mekorot* to argue that the administering physician could not be considered the active male party in the halachic sense. The Satmar Rav held the opposite view, maintaining that artificial insemination constitutes a form of adulterous act. Most authorities today follow Rav Moshe's reasoning.

### Tannaim Dispute

Among the *tanna'im*, the question of which prohibited relationships produce *mamzerut* is the subject of a three-way (or four-way) *machloket*. Rabbi Shimon HaTimni holds that *mamzerut* is produced only by *chayvei kraitot* — those forbidden unions punishable by *karet* or by *mitat beit din* (capital punishment). For these relationships, *kiddushin* does not take effect and the child is a *mamzer*. Rabbi Yehoshua takes an even narrower position: only those *arayot* that carry *mitat beit din* — actual capital punishment — create *mamzerut*; those punishable merely by *karet* do not.

### R. Akiva View

Rabbi Akiva holds the most expansive view. His position, encountered already in *Yevamot* and elsewhere, is that *chayvei lavin* — any prohibited relationship carrying a negative commandment — also produces *mamzerut*, because *kiddushin* does not take effect in such cases. There are a small number of prohibited marriages that are *chayvei asei* or *issur asei* rather than *lavin*, but the vast majority involve some form of prohibition. Rabbi Akiva extends the principle of *lo tafsei bah kiddushin* accordingly.

## Kiddushin Failure

### Divorce Passage

The *gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the scriptural source for the rule that a certain category of prohibited union prevents *kiddushin* from taking effect, and that a child born from such a union is a *mamzer*? The *mishnah* had stated: *mi she-ein la alav kiddushin aval yesh la al acherim kiddushin — havlad mamzer* — a *mamzer* is the product of a union in which *this* man and *this* woman cannot be married, but the woman could in principle marry someone else.

The *gemara* cites a teaching transmitted through a chain: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, tracing back through Rabbi Yannai, and also through Rabbi Acha the son of Rava, tracing back to Rabbi Yossi Ha-Gelili. The proof text is the verse in the divorce passage: *ve-yatz'ah mi-beitah ve-halchah ve-haytah le-ish acher* — she may go and become the wife of another man. The *drasha*: *l'acherim v'lo likrovim* — she may marry "others," but not the relatives of her ex-husband. This is not merely a statement that such a marriage would be prohibited; it implies that *kiddushin* would not take effect at all with those *krovim*.

### R. Abba Query

Rabbi Abba challenges this reading: *v'eima l'acher v'lo l'ven* — why not read the exclusion as applying only to the ex-husband's son, rather than to all relatives? The *gemara* responds: *ben b'hedya ketiv beih* — the son is already mentioned explicitly elsewhere, in the verse *lo yikach ish et eshet aviv* — a man may not marry his father's wife. And importantly, the term *lo yikach* — he shall not take — implies not only a prohibition but also an absence of valid *kiddushin*. So the verse using the word *acher* serves a distinct purpose: *shma mina l'acherim v'lo likrovim* — it broadens the exclusion to all relatives.

A further challenge is raised: perhaps both verses refer to the son, one teaching the prohibition *lechatchila* and the other teaching that even *bediavad* the *kiddushin* does not work. The *gemara* responds: *lechatchila m'achot isha nafka* — the prohibition itself is already derived from the case of *achot isha*, the wife's sister. That case becomes the paradigm for the entire category of *arayot* and for the principle that *kiddushin* does not take effect.

### Sister-in-Law

The verse *acher* is therefore understood as teaching that a woman's *kiddushin* does not work with her ex-husband's relatives. The case of *achot isha* — a man's wife's sister — then becomes the *binyan av* (paradigmatic source) from which we extend to all *arayot*: just as *kiddushin* is impossible with one's wife's sister, so too with all forbidden relationships of equivalent or greater severity. This is also the classical source, from the opening of *Yevamot*, for the principle of *tzarat ervah* and the exemption from *yibum*. It is worth noting the tension at the heart of *Yevamot*: the wife's sister (*achot isha*) generates the paradigmatic prohibition on *yibum*, while the brother's wife (*eshet ach*) is precisely where the *mitzvah* of *yibum* is located — a tension that tells us much about how the Torah conceptualizes family structure and inter-clan relations.

## Binyan Av Logic

### Kal Vachomer

From the paradigm of *achot isha*, the *gemara* attempts a *kal vachomer*: *u-mah achot isha b'karet lo tikadesh, chayavei mitot beit din lo kol sheken* — if marriage to one's wife's sister, which carries the punishment of *karet*, renders *kiddushin* inoperative, then certainly relationships punishable by *mitat beit din* — the most severe category — should also preclude valid *kiddushin*. The *kal vachomer* appears straightforward at first glance.

### Weaknesses

However, this *kal vachomer* is not airtight. One might posit that the severity of the death penalty actually reflects the fact that *kiddushin does* take effect — that is, the very reason the Torah requires capital punishment is because the *kiddushin* creates a real bond requiring more drastic severing. If so, the argument that a more severe prohibition must also preclude *kiddushin* is undermined: one could argue the opposite, that greater severity correlates with *kiddushin* being *tofes*. Without an independent intuition about which direction the *kal vachomer* should run, the argument is weakened.

A further challenge: perhaps both the *kal vachomer* source and its target refer only to *achot isha*, with one verse teaching the *lechatchila* prohibition and the other teaching the *bediavad* ineffectiveness of *kiddushin*. If so, the *kal vachomer* cannot be extended at all to other *arayot*. The *gemara* responds: *i hachi nami ashkhachan achot isha, she'ar arayot minalan* — we would then have established the rule only for *achot isha* itself, leaving all other *arayot* without a source.

Additionally, even granting the *binyan av* from *achot isha*, two cases pose a challenge: *eshet ish* and *eshet ach*. For *eshet ach* — the brother's wife — there is a *heter b'makom mitzvah*: the *mitzvah* of *yibum* creates an exception that applies to no other *ervah*. And *eshet ish* — the married woman — has a *heter b'chayei osran*: the prohibition can be removed during the lifetime of the one who created it, through divorce. That reduces the categorical severity of *eshet ish* as an *ervah*, making it a weaker paradigm and undermining the *binyan av*.

### Verbal Analogy

Rabbi Yona — and the tradition also attributes this to Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua — offers a different approach. The summary verse at the end of the *parasha* of *arayot* states: *kol asher ya'aseh mikol hato'evot ha'eleh venichretu* — whoever commits any of these *to'evot* shall be subject to *karet*. This groups all *arayot* together in a single category linked to *achot isha*: *hukshu kol ha'arayot kulehan l'achot isha*. Just as *kiddushin* does not take effect with *achot isha*, so too with all other *arayot* — *af kol ha'arayot kulam lo tafsi bah kiddushin*.

It is worth noting that *Tosafot* in their discussion of *mena hanei milei* addresses at length the relationship between the absence of *kiddushin* and the status of *mamzerut*, asking whether one necessarily causes the other, and concluding that they are tightly bound together — though the precise direction of causation is discussed extensively in *Yevamot* and elsewhere.

## Exceptions

### Niddah Problem

The verbal analogy linking all *arayot* to *achot isha* immediately raises a major difficulty: *i hachi afilu niddah nami* — if we group all *arayot* together, then *niddah* should also be included, since the *Torah* lists the menstruant woman among the *arayot*. Yet everyone knows that a child born to a woman who was *niddah* at the time of conception is not a *mamzer*, and furthermore that *kiddushin* with an unmarried woman who happens to be *niddah* is fully valid. So *niddah* appears on the list of *arayot* but is categorically different.

This distinction is treated at length in related contexts. *Tosafot HaRosh* on *Yevamot* daf 2 confronts the question of whether a wife who was *niddah* at the time of her husband's death would create a *tzarat ervah* situation that exempts co-wives from *yibum*. *Tosafot HaRosh* concludes that *niddah* is not really called an *ervah* in the full halachic sense — even though she appears on the list. This parallels a *Tosafot* in *Sanhedrin* discussing why the laws of *yichud* do not apply with equal stringency between a husband and wife during *niddah* as they do with other *arayot*. Many *achronim*, particularly in the Brisker tradition — the Brisker Rav in his commentary on the *Rambam* — devote attention to the fundamental distinction between *niddah* and the other *arayot*.

*Rashi* here clarifies the case: *im kidesh pnuyah b'imei niddutah* — what if a man betrothed an unmarried woman during her period of *niddah*? The *hava amina* would be that this *kiddushin* fails and any child would be a *mamzer*. As a side note, the separate question of *chupat niddah* — whether *nisuin* can take effect when the bride is *niddah* — is handled differently. Most *rishonim* do not view this as a major halachic obstacle, though the *Rambam* does quote an opinion that *nisuin* does not take hold during *niddah*. In practice, various arrangements are made to avoid having the couple in *yichud* before *niddah* concludes, though the practical logistics can become complex.

The resolution comes from *Abaye*, who states: *hakol modin b'va al haniddah v'al hasotah she'ein havlad mamzer* — everyone agrees that a child born following relations with a *niddah* or with a *sotah* is not a *mamzer*. This applies even to Rabbi Shimon HaTimni, who holds that any *chayav karet* prevents *kiddushin* — he nonetheless concedes that *niddah* is an exception. And it applies even to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *chayvei lavin* produce *mamzerut* — he nonetheless concedes that *sotah* is an exception. A *sotah* — a woman who committed adultery — creates a prohibition (*issur lav*) on her husband resuming relations with her, but a child born from those subsequent relations is not a *mamzer*. (If the child were born from the adulterous relationship itself, that would raise separate questions about paternity, resolved in most cases through the *chazakah* of *rov beilos achar habaal* — the presumption that most of a married woman's intimacy is with her husband.)

Chizkiyah provides the scriptural basis for excluding *niddah*: *utehi niddatah alav* — the verse that describes how a man who has relations with a *niddah* acquires her *tumah* for seven days. The word *tehi* is read as a form of *havayah* (being/marriage), implying: *afilu bish'at niddutah tehei bah havayah* — even during her *niddah* state, the act of *havayah* (i.e., valid *kiddushin*) can apply to her. Hence *niddah* is carved out by explicit scriptural derivation from the general rule that *arayot* preclude *kiddushin*.

### Hekkesh Rule

This raises a methodological question: given that all *arayot* are grouped together by the summary verse, one could equally make the *hekkesh* to connect them all to *niddah* (permissive outcome) or to connect them all to *achot isha* (restrictive outcome). Why choose *achot isha* as the paradigm? The *gemara* answers with a principle: *kula bechumra lechumra makshinan* — when constructing a *hekkesh*, we always link to the more stringent outcome. This is worth noting as a methodological *klal* about how *drashot* operate, even though it has a somewhat arbitrary quality — it is presented as a rule of *drasha* rather than as an application of *safek deoraitah lechumra*, which belongs to a different domain entirely.

### Yevama Proof

Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative derivation via *kal vachomer*: *ma yevama shehi belav lo tafsi bah kiddushin, chayavei mita v'chayavei kraitot kol she-ken* — if a *yevama* (a deceased brother's childless widow), who is only an *issur lav*, cannot contract valid *kiddushin* with anyone other than the *yavam*, then certainly relationships punishable by death or *karet* should preclude *kiddushin* as well. The force of this argument relies on the principle of *yesh zika* — that the bond between the *yavam* and *yevama* begins automatically at the moment of the brother's death, creating something almost like a proto-*kiddushin* that prevents her from being acquired by anyone else. The *kal vachomer* thus runs from the least severe prohibition (*lav*) to the most severe.

### Two-Wives

The *gemara* challenges Rav Acha bar Yaakov's *kal vachomer*: if it holds, it would extend to *all* other *chayvei lavin* as well — a result that contradicts the accepted view that *chayvei lavin* do allow *kiddushin* to take effect. Rav Pappa resolves the issue with a direct proof: *chayevei lavin be-hedaya ktiv behu* — the *Torah* makes explicit that *chayvei lavin* do produce valid *kiddushin*. The source is the passage in *Parshat Ki Teitzei*: *ki tehiyena le-ish shtei nashim ha'achat ahuvah veha'achat snuah* — when a man has two wives, one beloved and one hated. The *gemara* asks: does God play favorites? Rather, *ahuvah ahuvah benisu'eha, snuah snuah benisu'eha* — one wife's marriage is "beloved," meaning halachically favorable, while the other's is "hated," meaning she is someone he is prohibited from marrying — yet the *kiddushin* works. This is direct scriptural proof that *chayvei lavin* are *tofsei bakiddushin*.

## R. Akiva Position

### Issur Aseh

Given that the two-wives passage proves *chayvei lavin* allow *kiddushin*, how does Rabbi Akiva — who holds that *chayvei lavin* do not allow *kiddushin* — interpret that verse? He must hold that it refers to *almana l'kohen gadol*: the case of a High Priest marrying a widow, which is not a *lav* in the ordinary sense. Here it is important to correct a possible misreading of the relevant categories. The prohibition on a *kohen gadol* marrying an *almana* is indeed a *lav* — it is listed explicitly in the verse *almana ugirusha vachalala zonah et eileh lo yikach*. What is an *issur asei*, rather than a *lav*, is the prohibition on a *kohen gadol* marrying a woman who has been sexually active but was not previously married (*beulah* who is not *almana* or *grushah*) — since the positive commandment *ki im betulah m'amav yikach isha* requires him to marry a *betulah*, and the prohibition on *beulah* is a *lav haba m'klal asei*, a prohibition derived from a positive commandment.

For Rabbi Akiva, who maintains that *chayvei lavin* preclude *kiddushin*, the verse *ki tehiyena le-ish shtei nashim* must describe a case where one wife is halachically acceptable and the other is not — but the "not" must fall outside the category of ordinary *lavin* (since Rabbi Akiva holds those don't produce *kiddushin* at all). The only case that fits is *beulah l'kohen gadol*, an *issur asei*, because *issur asei* does allow *kiddushin* even according to Rabbi Akiva. The inheritance law in that passage — that the father cannot favor the son of the beloved wife over the firstborn son of the disfavored wife — would then apply to a *kohen gadol* who married one *betulah* and one *beulah*, producing children from both.

### R. Simai

This reading of Rabbi Akiva's position is associated with Rabbi Simai, whose opinion is cited in a *baraita*: *min hakol haya Rabbi Akiva oseh mamzer chutz m'almana l'kohen gadol* — from all prohibited unions, Rabbi Akiva holds the child is a *mamzer*, except for *almana l'kohen gadol*. In that exceptional case, the Torah says *lo yichalel* — he shall not desecrate — implying that the child of such a union becomes a *chalal*, not a *mamzer*.

The *rishonim* note that this reasoning should extend beyond the *kohen gadol* to a regular *kohen* who marries a *grushah*, since the underlying principle — that the Torah provides a distinct category for priestly offspring of prohibited unions — applies there as well. The child of a *kohen* who marries someone he is forbidden to marry does not become a *mamzer* but a *chalal*.

### Chalal Status

The distinction between *chalal* and *mamzer* is significant. A *mamzer* represents a drastic reduction in *yichus* — from whatever level the parents occupied, the child falls to the most restricted category. A *chalal*, by contrast, represents only one step down from *kohen* status; in practical terms, a *chalal* is comparable in many respects to a regular *Yisrael*. He cannot serve as a *kohen*, cannot eat *trumah*, and is cut off from the priestly lineage — but unlike a *mamzer*, a *chalal* is not restricted in whom he may marry. Interestingly, there is a path back: a *chalal*'s daughter, if she marries a *kohen*, may produce sons who are fully qualified *kohanim* again. The priestly status can be recovered within one generation through the maternal line, which has no parallel for *mamzerim*. The only classical route out of *mamzerus* involved slavery — a mechanism no longer operative.

### R. Shaveiv

Rabbi Shaveiv disagrees sharply with Rabbi Simai's limiting principle. He declares: *bo u'nitzvach al Akiva ben Yosef* — let us take Rabbi Akiva to task. In Rabbi Shaveiv's reading, Rabbi Akiva's position — that *kol she-ein lo biah b'Yisrael havlad mamzer*, every prohibited union produces a *mamzer* — is an almost absurdly sweeping rule that would create *mamzerim* in great numbers, since not everyone observes *halacha*. Rabbi Shaveiv's objection has the character of a *sevara* argument: the sheer breadth of the position makes it untenable. It is also notable that Rabbi Shaveiv does not grant Rabbi Simai's exception for *almana l'kohen gadol* — he holds that even that union produces a *mamzer*. The *gemara* notes the somewhat animated quality of this exchange; similar rhetorical intensity appears elsewhere, such as Reish Lakish's famous protest against Rabbi Yochanan regarding the *hekkesh havayah l'yetziah*.

## Reconciling

### Passage Scope

The *gemara* now reconciles the competing *drashot*. Those who accept Rabbi Akiva's position in the reading of Rabbi Simai — that only *chayvei lavin* (and above) preclude *kiddushin* according to Rabbi Akiva, with the single exception of *almana l'kohen gadol* — must account for the two-wives passage, which Rav Pappa argued demonstrates that *chayvei lavin* do allow *kiddushin*. For Rabbi Akiva, that passage must instead refer to *beulah l'kohen gadol*, which is an *issur asei*. For the *rabbanan* who disagree with Rabbi Akiva, the passage applies more broadly to *chayvei lavin* in general.

The *gemara* works through the four operative categories: *mitat beit din*, *karet*, *lavin*, and *asei*. The alignment is as follows: Rabbi Akiva holds that for *mitat beit din*, *karet*, and *lavin*, there is no *kiddushin*; only *issur asei* allows *kiddushin*. Rabbi Shimon HaTimni holds that *mitat beit din* and *karet* preclude *kiddushin*, while *lavin* and *asei* allow it. Rabbi Yehoshua holds that only *mitat beit din* precludes *kiddushin*. Within these broad categories, various specific exceptions apply: *yevama* falls within *lavin* but is universally agreed to preclude *kiddushin* (based on *yesh zika*); *eshet ach* has a *heter* in the context of the *mitzvah* of *yibum*; *eshet ish* has a *heter* through divorce; and *niddah* and *sotah* are conceded exceptions even by the more stringent *tanna'im*.

### Gender Issue

A further challenge to reading the two-wives passage as referring to *arayot* arises from gender specificity. The passage describes *shtei nashim* — two wives — implying the scenario is one man with two women. But the case of *achot isha*, the paradigmatic *ervah*, would involve a man married to two sisters simultaneously — both women are equally prohibited to him (once he has married one of them). There is no way to configure *achot isha* as "one acceptable and one unacceptable" within the framework the two-wives passage describes. The passage therefore cannot be speaking about *arayot* at all; it must be speaking about a different category of prohibited marriage that still allows *kiddushin*.

### Beulah Case

This leaves *beulah l'kohen gadol* as the only case compatible with Rabbi Akiva's reading of the passage. The verse *ki tehiyena le-ish shtei nashim* is set in a context that says *le-ish* — to a man — rather than *le-kohen*, which is the objection raised against Rabbi Akiva's reading. The *gemara* concludes that Rabbi Akiva's *drasha* is admittedly strained (*baal karkhakh shavkah likra dehavi dakhik umuki anafshei*) — his reading is difficult to fit naturally into the verse, and in this sense the *rabbanan*'s position, which applies the verse more naturally to a broader range of cases, is to be preferred. The *rabbanan* apply the two-wives passage to *chayvei lavin* in general, establishing that those unions do produce valid *kiddushin*, while Rabbi Akiva is forced to restrict the verse to a single, highly specific case in order to maintain his position.

## Slave & Goy

### Shifcha Kiddushin

The *mishnah* addressed a third category: cases where a woman cannot marry *this* man and also cannot marry any Jewish man — the *shifchah* (slave) and the *nochrit* (non-Jewish woman). The *gemara* now asks for the scriptural basis for the rule that the child's status follows the mother in these cases.

Regarding the *shifchah kenaanit*: Rav Huna derives from the verse *shevu lachem poh im hachamor* — Abraham's instruction to Eliezer his servant to stay behind with the donkey at the time of the *akeidah* — the principle that slaves are comparable in some respects to animals: *am hadomeh lachamor*. The *drasha* is that just as animals have no *kiddushin*, slaves — *shifchah kenaanit* specifically — have no *kiddushin* either: *v'shifchah lo tafsei bah kiddushin*. It is a striking and harsh *drasha* to deploy for so fundamental a *halacha*. The broader tendency to assimilate the legal status of non-Jews or slaves to that of animals in certain specific halachic contexts appears in other *sugyot* as well, such as the discussion in *Avodah Zarah* about whether a non-Jewish corpse transmits *tumah be'ohel*, where the verse *atem keruyim adam v'ein ovdei avodah zarah keruyim adam* is invoked in a *machloket tanna'im*. In each such case, the implication is precisely calibrated to the halachic question at hand rather than serving as a global statement.

### Shifcha Children

Having established that *kiddushin* does not take effect with a *shifchah kenaanit*, the *gemara* asks separately: *v'valdah kemotah minalan* — how do we know that the child of a *shifchah* follows the mother's status and remains a slave? The source is: *ha'ishah v'yeladeha tiyeh l'adoneha* — the woman and her children shall belong to her master. This verse addresses the scenario in *parshat mishpatim* where a master gives his *eved ivri* (Hebrew slave) a *shifchah kenaanit* as a wife. Any children born from that union remain with the master as slaves, even when the *eved ivri* goes free. The children follow the mother — the *shifchah* — and stay with her master.

### Non-Jew Kiddushin

The case of the *nochrit* — a non-Jewish woman — is handled next. The *gemara* cites: *lo titchaten bam* — you shall not intermarry with them. This establishes that *kiddushin* does not take effect between a Jewish man and a non-Jewish woman. One might ask whether this verse teaches the impossibility of *kiddushin* or merely a prohibition on an otherwise-valid act. The *gemara* here reads it as *lo tafsei bah kiddushin* — the *kiddushin* simply does not work. *Tosafot* raise the obvious difficulty: *lo titchaten bam* is explicitly addressed to the seven Canaanite nations (*zayin amamim*), not to all non-Jews. *Rashi* responds at length, distinguishing between the seven nations — who are described as deeply entrenched in their *avodah zarah* in a way categorically different from other peoples — and non-Jews outside the Land of Israel, about whom the *gemara* in *Chullin* says: *lav ovdei avodah kochavim hen, ela minhag avoteihem beyadeihem* — they are not true idolaters but merely following ancestral practice. *Rashi* uses this distinction to explain why the prohibition extends to all non-Jews despite the verse's specific context, and *Tosafot* deploy the same reasoning in a number of *sugyot* to argue for more lenient approaches to relations with Christians in medieval Europe.

### Descent Rules

Having established that *kiddushin* is impossible with a non-Jewish woman, the *gemara* asks how we know the child follows the mother: *v'valdah kemotah minalan*? Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai derives this from the verse: *ki yasir et bincha me'acharei* — for he will turn your son away from following Me. The *drasha* is: *bincha habah mi-Yisre'elit karui bincha* — your son born from a Jewish woman is called "your son," *v'ein bincha habah min ha-ovedet kochavim karui bincha* — but your son born from a non-Jewish woman is not called "your son." The non-Jewish mother's child, even though his father is Jewish, is not halachically Jewish. *Ravina* adds: *shma mina ben bitcha habah min ha-oved kochavim karui bincha* — but the son of your daughter born to a non-Jewish man is called your son. That is, your grandchild from a Jewish daughter and a non-Jewish father is Jewish.

*Ravina*'s ruling prompts a question: does this not imply that *Ravina* holds the child of a non-Jewish man or a slave who has relations with a Jewish woman is a *mamzer*? The *gemara* responds: *nehi de-kasher, mamzer lo havi* — granted the child is not fully *kasher*, but he is certainly not a *mamzer*. Rather, he is called *pasul* — specifically *pasul l'kehunah*, disqualified from the priesthood. A Jewish woman who has a child with either a non-Jew or a slave produces a child who is Jewish but who carries this disqualification one generation forward.

### Yifat Toar

The *gemara* extends this discussion to provide the source for those *rabbanan* who do not interpret *lo titchaten bam* as applying to all non-Jewish nations (following Rabbi Shimon's principle of *darish ta'ama dikra*). For them, the proof that *kiddushin* does not take effect with a non-Jewish woman comes from the passage of *yifat to'ar* — the non-Jewish captive woman taken in war. The verse states: *v'achar ken tavo eleiha u-ve'altah* — afterward you may come to her and have marital relations. The word *achar* — afterward, following a waiting period of transformation — implies: *michlal d'meikara lo tafsi bah kiddushin* — that initially, before this process was completed, *kiddushin* with her was impossible. This establishes that in the original state of a non-Jewish woman, *kiddushin* is inoperative.

From this, the *gemara* then derives the principle that the child follows the mother in all such cases. The verse *tihyenah le-ish v'yaldu lo* — when women are married to a man and bear him children — is read as establishing a link: *ke-heicha d'karinan beih 'ki tihyenah' karinan beih 'v'yaldu lo'* — only where valid marriage (*tihyenah*) applies does the attribution of children to the father (*yaldu lo*) follow. Where *kiddushin* cannot take effect — as with the *shifchah kenaanit* and the *nochrit* in her initial state — the children are attributed to and follow the mother, not the father. This is the final and comprehensive statement of the *mishnah*'s rule: the child follows the legally recognized parent, and where only the mother can contract a Jewish legal status, the child's status is determined by hers.

---

---

# Kiddushin 68

## Converts & Yichus

### Opening & Daf

Today's daf is 68, though we begin at the very end of 67b, in the last three narrow lines of that amud.

### Mishnah: Yichus Cases

The *mishnah* under discussion addresses four distinct categories regarding *yichus* — lineage and personal status — examining how the status of children is transmitted when parties of differing legal standing attempt to marry one another. The *mishnah* uses rather striking descriptive language to organize these cases, grouping them by the nature of the union and the resulting *yichus* of the offspring.

### Restricted Nations

One of the cases treated by the *mishnah* concerns individuals who have converted from nations subject to special restrictions on their marital prospects. The nations in question are *Mitzri* (Egyptian), *Ammoni* (Ammonite), and *Moavi* (Moabite). These groups are permitted to marry converts and *mamzerim*, but face a higher standard before they may enter into the fully accepted Jewish community by marriage. The principle stated is *nitgayru, halach achar hapagum shebishneihem* — when both parties convert, one follows the most *pagum* (flawed or restricted) status between the two of them.

The *gemara* immediately asks: *bimai* — what case exactly are we discussing? If we say it is a *Mitzri* man who married an *Amonit* woman, there is a problem: the restriction for Ammonites, as established by *Torah she-be'al peh* and as the background for the entire discussion in *Masechet Yadayim* and for much of *Sefer Rut*, applies only to males (*Amoni velo Amonit*). The female Ammonite is not restricted from marrying into the Jewish people at all — which is precisely why *Rut* was able to marry *Boaz* without any halachic difficulty. Therefore, if an Egyptian man married an Ammonite woman, there is no competing *pagum* on her side, and the formulation *hapagum shebishneihem* — the more restricted of the two — cannot apply.

Rather, the *gemara* redirects: *ela be'Ammoni shenasa Mitzrit* — we are discussing a male Ammonite convert who married a female Egyptian convert. Here, the husband's restriction as an *Ammoni* is perpetual for male descendants, while the wife's restriction as a *Mitzrit* is not gender-specific and applies for three generations. The *gemara* then clarifies how the *mishnah*'s rule operates: *ve'im zachar havei, hai shadia batrei didei* — if they have a male child, that child follows the father's status, meaning the child is treated as a male Ammonite convert, whose restriction is perpetual. *Ve'im nekeivah hava, shadia batar didah* — if they have a female child, that daughter follows the mother's status, treated as a second-generation *Mitzrit*. The children are thus allocated by gender to the respective parental status — not a simple "take the worst of both" rule, but a gender-based bifurcation of *yichus*.

### Three Generations

One might ask: does the three-generation restriction for an Egyptian convert date from *Matan Torah*, applying only to those three generations after the Exodus? The traditional understanding, however, as reflected in *halacha*, is that *mitzvot* are binding for all generations. Any *Mitzri* who converts at any time in history still faces a three-generation barrier before full integration into the mainstream Jewish community. The convert's children are born Jewish, but are second-generation *Mitzri*; their children are third-generation *Mitzri*; and only thereafter are the descendants fully unrestricted. That represents a span of perhaps seventy-five years — a significant ongoing tracking of *yichus*.

---

## Mamzerut & Kiddushin

### Mamzer Definition

The *mishnah* now introduces the third category: *kol she-ein lah alav kiddushin* — any woman for whom there is no *kiddushin* possible with this particular man, but who could in principle marry someone else — *ha-valad mamzer*. The child of such a union is a *mamzer*.

It is important to emphasize at the outset what *mamzerut* is and is not. A child born out of wedlock to two people who are halachically permitted to marry one another is not a *mamzer*. *Mamzerut* is fundamentally linked — at least according to most *tanna'im* — to the prohibition itself upon the marriage. The connection between the prohibited nature of the union and the *mamzer* status of the offspring is what the *gemara* now seeks to establish.

### Four Schools

There is a four-way *machloket* among *tanna'im* on this question. *Rabbi Shimon HaTimni* holds that *mamzerut* arises specifically from *chayavei krisos* — those forbidden relationships (*arayot*) for which the Torah prescribes *karet* or *mitat beit din* (capital punishment). In those cases, the *kiddushin* does not take effect and the children are *mamzerim*. *Rabbi Akiva* takes a far more expansive position: *chayavei lavin* — any prohibited relationship backed by a negative commandment — likewise produces *mamzerut*, because *kiddushin* cannot take hold. *Rabbi Yehoshua* is actually narrower than *Rabbi Shimon HaTimni*, holding that only those *arayot* punishable with *mitat beit din* — actual capital crimes — generate *mamzerut*; *karet* alone is insufficient.

### Sexual Relation

An important clarification: in order for a child to be a *mamzer*, there must be an actual sexual relationship. A child conceived through *in vitro* fertilization or artificial insemination, even from a prohibited union, would not be a *mamzer* in the same sense. This is precisely the axis of a famous dispute among *poskim* regarding advanced reproductive technologies. *Rav Moshe Feinstein* was the permissive opinion on artificial insemination and *in vitro* fertilization, marshaling many *mekorot* in his argument. The *Satmar Rav* was strongly opposed, maintaining that a doctor administering such procedures might be regarded as the active male party in the fertilization and thus the act could be considered adulterous. The consensus among contemporary authorities has generally followed *Rav Moshe*'s reasoning.

### Divorce Pasuk

The *gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for the rule that prohibited unions produce *mamzerut*? *Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*, transmitted through *Rabbi Yannai* and *Rabbi Acha bereih de-Rabba* in the name of *Rabbi Yossi HaGlili*, that the source is the *pasuk* concerning divorce: *ve-yatzah mi-beisah ve-halchah ve-haysah le-ish acher* — the divorced woman leaves and may go become the wife of another man. The *drasha* derives: *le'acherim velo likrovim* — she may marry others, but not close relatives of her ex-husband. This teaches not merely a prohibition but a substantive legal consequence: the *kiddushin* would not take effect at all between a divorced woman and her ex-husband's relatives.

### Rabbi Abba Query

*Matkif lah Rabbi Abba* — Rabbi Abba challenges this derivation. Why not read the *pasuk* more narrowly: she may marry someone else, but specifically not this man's *son* — not *krovim* in general? The *gemara* answers: the prohibition against a son marrying his father's ex-wife is stated explicitly elsewhere — *lo yikach ish et eshet aviv* — and that *pasuk* already teaches that the *kiddushin* would not work in that case. Therefore the phrase *le-ish acher* must be serving an additional purpose, and from it we derive *le'acherim velo likrovim* — she may marry other people generally, but not his relatives.

The *gemara* then considers: perhaps both *pesukim* refer to the son, one teaching the *lechatchila* prohibition and the other the *bedi'eved* invalidity of any attempted *kiddushin*? The response is that we already know from *achot isha* — a wife's sister — that the prohibition itself is established. Therefore the second *pasuk* must be extending the rule of invalid *kiddushin* to *krovim* more broadly.

### Achot Isha Paradigm

*Achot isha* — the wife's sister — becomes the paradigmatic case for the inability of *kiddushin* to take effect among *arayot*. This is the same *achot isha* that appears at the very opening of *Yevamot* and forms the basis for the exemption from *yibum* in the case of *tzarat ervah*. Here it serves as the foundation for the broader rule: just as one cannot legally marry his wife's sister — not merely that it is prohibited but that any attempted *kiddushin* is legally null — so too should the same apply across the spectrum of *arayot*.

### Kal Vachomer

From *achot isha*, the *gemara* attempts a *kal vachomer*: if *achot isha*, which carries the punishment of *karet*, disables *kiddushin*, then *chayavei mitat beit din* — those *arayot* punishable with capital punishment, which are in some ways more severe — should certainly (*lo kol shekein*) also disable *kiddushin*. One questioner raises the point that *achot isha* becomes permitted after the death of the wife, which might seem to reduce the severity of that prohibition. Yet this observation applies specifically to the *yesh la heter b'makom mitzvah* discussion that follows and does not fully undermine the *kal vachomer* as presented here.

### Kal Vachomer Weak

The *kal vachomer* is not without its difficulties. One might argue that the reason the Torah prescribes a harsher punishment for certain *arayot* is precisely because *kiddushin does* take effect there — the severity of the violation is greater because a genuine legal bond was formed. That is, there is no clear intuition about whether it is more *chamur* that *kiddushin* should work or that it should not work. The relationship between severity of punishment and validity of *kiddushin* is not self-evident, and this undercuts the *kal vachomer*.

### Binyan Av

The *gemara* therefore pivots to a *binyan av* from *achot isha*: just as *achot isha* is distinguished by the fact that she is an *ervah*, the violation carries *karet*, and a *korban chatat* if done *be-shogeg* — and *kiddushin* does not take effect — so too any *ervah* sharing those same features (punishment of *karet*, *chatat* for inadvertent violation) should likewise disable *kiddushin*. The formulation is: *mah achot isha miyuchedet she-hi ervah ve-chayavin al zdonah karet ve-shigegata chatat lo tafsei bah kiddushin, af kol she-hi ervah ve-chayavin al zdonah karet ve-shigegata chatat lo tafsei bah kiddushin*.

### Exceptions

Two cases threaten to break this *binyan av*: *eshet ish* (a married woman) and *eshet ach* (a brother's wife). The *gemara* articulates why each is different.

Regarding *eshet ach*: the prohibition against a brother's wife is in a different category because there exists a situation in which marrying her is not merely permitted but obligatory — namely *yibum*, the levirate marriage commanded when a brother dies childless. This *heter b'makom mitzvah* marks *eshet ach* as qualitatively distinct from other *arayot* and prevents us from using the *binyan av* to conclude that *kiddushin* with her never takes effect.

Regarding *eshet ish*: this prohibition can be lifted during the lifetime of the one who created the *issur* — the husband — through divorce. This *yesh lah heter b'chayei osra* makes *eshet ish* a lesser level of *ervah* in one respect, since there is a mechanism for removal. Therefore the *binyan av* from *achot isha* — which has no such escape mechanism in the normal case — cannot straightforwardly extend to *eshet ish*. Notably, the *acharonim* observe that this entire analysis frames the problem of marrying a married woman in terms of *ervah* — the relational prohibition — rather than from the *kinyan* perspective of whether a woman can be legally acquired by two men simultaneously. This appears to stand in some tension with material treated elsewhere in the tractate and generates significant discussion among the *acharonim*.

### Rabbi Yona Drasha

*Rabbi Yona* — or as the *gemara* alternatively identifies him, *Rav Huna bereih de-Rav Yehoshua* — proposes an entirely different approach. Rather than a *binyan av*, he derives the rule from the concluding *pasuk* of the *parasha* of *arayot*: *kol asher ya'aseh mikol ha-to'evot ha-eleh ve-nichreitu* — whoever does any of these abominations shall receive *karet*. This *pasuk* creates a *hekesh* — a textual equation — linking all of the *arayot* together with *achot isha*: *hukshu kol ha-arayot kulan le-achot isha*. Just as *achot isha* disables *kiddushin*, so too, by virtue of this encompassing equation, all *arayot* similarly disable *kiddushin*.

---

## Niddah & Sotah

### Niddah Question

The *binyan av* and the *hekesh* of *Rabbi Yona* both confront a striking difficulty: *i hachi afilu niddah nami* — if this logic holds, then it should also apply to *niddah*. A *niddah* — a menstruant woman — appears in the list of *arayot* and her violation carries *karet*. The *hava amina* would therefore be that if one performed *kiddushin* with an unmarried woman while she is a *niddah*, the *kiddushin* would not take effect and any child born of that relationship would be a *mamzer*.

This is a significant challenge. *Tosafot*, already in the context of the first *daf* of *Yevamot*, grapples with the same issue in a parallel form: if *niddah* is among the *arayot*, then if one of the *tzarot* of the deceased brother was in a state of *niddah* at the time of his death, she might count as a *tzarat ervah*, thereby exempting all the *co-wives* from *yibum*. *Tosafot* resolves this, and *Tosafot HaRosh* on *Yevamot daf 2* goes further, arguing that *niddah* is not fundamentally called an *ervah* in the same sense as the other *arayot*. A similar point is raised by the *Tosafot* in *Sanhedrin* regarding why the laws of *yichud* do not apply with equal stringency between married partners during *niddah* as they do in other *arayot* contexts. The *Brisker Rav*, in his commentary on the *Rambam*, and several other *acharonim* develop the distinction between *niddah* and other *arayot* into a fundamental categorical difference.

One might also note that using *achot isha* as the paradigmatic *ervah* for this entire *drasha* invites a similar objection: *achot isha* becomes permitted upon the death of the wife, which arguably makes it less severe than other *arayot*. The *gemara* does address the analogous concern somewhat earlier, in the framework of *ein lah heter b'chayei osra* vs. *yesh lah heter b'chayei osra*, but *Rabbi Yona*'s formulation reopens the same question and the *gemara* does not fully resolve it.

The case of *kiddushin* with a *niddah* that *Rashi* addresses is *im kidesh pnuya bimei nidutah* — what if a man performed *kiddushin* with an unmarried woman during her period of *niddah*? The *hava amina* is that *kiddushin* would not take effect and the child would be a *mamzer*. Separately, there is also the question of *chuppat niddah* — what happens if the *nisuin* ceremony takes place while the woman is in *niddah*? Most *rishonim* do not view this as a fundamental problem for the *nisuin* itself. The *Rambam* cites an opinion that the *nisuin* does not take full effect and must be redone, though in practice this is addressed through various means — principally by ensuring that the couple avoid *yichud* until after *niddah* concludes.

### Agreement Niddah

*Amar Abaye*: *hakol modim beva'al ha-niddah ve-al ha-sotah she-ein ha-valad mamzer* — everyone agrees that in the case of *niddah* and *sotah*, the child is not a *mamzer*. This means that *Rabbi Shimon HaTimni*, despite holding that all *chayavei krisos* produce *mamzerut*, agrees that *niddah* is an exception. And *Rabbi Akiva*, despite his sweeping position regarding *chayavei lavin*, agrees that *sotah* is an exception. *Sotah* here refers to the situation where a woman has had an adulterous relationship and her husband subsequently has relations with her — that relationship is an *issur lav* for the husband, yet the child of that relationship is not a *mamzer*.

In cases where adultery has occurred and a child is born shortly thereafter, the *chazakah* of *rov beilos achar ha-ba'al* — that most marital relations are with the husband — generally serves to prevent the child from being declared a *mamzer*.

### Chizkiyah Drasha

*Amar Chizkiyah*: the exemption of *niddah* is derived from a specific *pasuk*. The verse *u-tehi nidatah alav* describes the consequence for one who has relations with a *niddah* — he acquires the same seven-day impurity she carries. *Chizkiyah* derives from the word *u-tehi* — the root *lihyot*, which the Torah elsewhere uses to denote the establishment of marriage — that even during her period of *niddah*, *havayah* (a marriage bond) can be established. The *pasuk* thus explicitly permits *kiddushin* to take hold despite the prohibition of *niddah*, notwithstanding the *karet* penalty.

### Chumra Chumra Rule

The *gemara* asks: given that we have a *hekesh* connecting all *arayot* to one paradigm, why did we choose to connect them all to *achot isha* rather than to *niddah*? If we connected them to *niddah*, the result would be permissive — *kiddushin* could take effect even with *arayot*. We could construct an argument in either direction, so why favor the stricter outcome?

The *gemara* answers: *kula b'chumra l'chumra makshinan* — when a *hekesh* can be drawn in either direction, we always draw it toward the stricter (*machmir*) option. This is presented as a methodological rule of *drashot*. The *gemara* does not appear to ground this in the general principle of *safek de'oraita l'chumra*; rather, it seems to be an independent rule governing how textual equations are resolved when there is a choice. The *gemara* suggests it as a rule worth flagging, though its consistent application across *Shas* is a question worth investigating further.

### Rav Acha Kal V.

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* offers a different approach altogether: the exclusion of *niddah* can be derived through *kal vachomer* from *yevamah*. A *yevamah* — a widow required to undergo *yibum* — who goes and attempts to marry a stranger faces only an *issur lav*, the least severe category of prohibition, yet her *kiddushin* with that stranger does not take effect. This is because of the principle of *yesh zikah* — the bond between the *yavam* and *yevamah* begins automatically at the moment of the brother's death, creating something almost akin to a proto-*eshet ish*. If even an *issur lav* can disable *kiddushin*, then *chayavei mitat beit din* and *chayavei krisos* certainly should as well — *lo kol shekein*. 

The *gemara* then challenges: *i hachi she'ar chayavei lavin nami* — if this *kal vachomer* holds, then all other *chayavei lavin* should equally disable *kiddushin*, which would force us to rule like *Rabbi Akiva* that *kiddushin* never takes effect by *chayavei lavin* — a conclusion rejected by the *rabbanan*.

### Two Wives Pasuk

*Amar Rav Papa*: *chayavei lavin* are explicitly proven to allow *kiddushin* to take hold from a *pasuk* in *Parshat Ki Teitzei* — *ki tihyena le-ish shtei nashim ha-achat ahuvah ve-ha-achat senuah* — when a man has two wives, one beloved and one hated. Since God is described as designating one wife as *ahuvah* and one as *senuah*, and we do not say that God plays favorites among permissible relationships, this must mean that the *senuah* wife represents a marriage that was halachically disfavored — i.e., a prohibited relationship — yet the *kiddushin* nonetheless took effect. The *pasuk* thus explicitly contemplates a case where *kiddushin* is valid despite a prohibition: *ahuvah b'nisueha* and *senuah b'nisueha* — one whose marriage is favored in the eyes of heaven and one whose marriage is not, yet both are married.

### Akiva vs Rabbanan

The *rabbanan* — those who disagree with *Rabbi Akiva* — understand this *pasuk* as providing explicit proof that *kiddushin* is effective with *chayavei lavin*. *Rabbi Akiva*, however, holds that *kiddushin* never takes hold by *chayavei lavin*. To what situation, then, does he apply this *pasuk*? *Rabbi Akiva* must restrict it to the case of *almanah le-Kohen Gadol* — a widow marrying the High Priest — which involves not a *lav* but an *issur asei*. The High Priest is commanded *ki im betulah me-amav yikach ishah* — he must marry a virgin from his people. Marrying a widow therefore constitutes a *lav ha-ba mi-chlal asei*, a prohibition derived from a positive commandment, which is regarded as a lower-level prohibition. According to *Rabbi Akiva*, this is the only case in which *kiddushin* takes effect despite a prohibition — because it is merely an *issur asei*.

### Four Categories

At this point the full analytic structure comes into view. There are four categories of prohibited relationships: *issur asei* (positive commandment violation), *chayavei lavin* (negative commandment violations), *chayavei karet*, and *chayavei mitat beit din*. The positions of the *tanna'im* can be charted accordingly. *Rabbi Akiva* holds there is no valid *kiddushin* for *chayavei lavin*, *chayavei karet*, and *chayavei mitat beit din*, but *kiddushin* is effective for *issur asei*. *Rabbi Shimon HaTimni* holds that *kiddushin* is disabled for *chayavei karet* and *chayavei mitat beit din* only. *Rabbi Yehoshua* restricts this further to *chayavei mitat beit din* alone.

In addition, various exceptions apply within these categories. *Yevamah*, despite being merely an *issur lav*, disables *kiddushin* — universally agreed upon. *Eshet ach* has a special *heter* in the context of the *mitzvah* of *yibum*. *Eshet ish* can be released from her status through divorce during the husband's lifetime. *Niddah*, despite carrying *karet*, is universally agreed to allow *kiddushin* to take effect. And *sotah* is universally agreed not to produce *mamzerut* even under *Rabbi Akiva*'s expansive framework.

### Rabbi Simai

*De-tani Rabbi Simai*: Rabbi Simai articulates what he understands *Rabbi Akiva*'s full position to be. *Min hakol hayah Rabbi Akiva oseh mamzer chutz me-almanah le-Kohen Gadol* — *Rabbi Akiva* creates *mamzerut* from all prohibited relationships, with one exception: *almanah le-Kohen Gadol*. The reason is that the Torah explicitly uses the word *lo yechalel* — "he shall not profane" — indicating that in this case the result is *chillul*, a disqualification to *kehunah* status, producing a *chalal* rather than a *mamzer*.

The category of *chalal* is significant. The child of a *kohen* who marries a woman he is forbidden to marry becomes a *chalal* — not a full *kohen*, but not a *mamzer* either. A *chalal* cannot serve in the Temple and cannot eat *terumah*, but may otherwise marry any Jewish woman he wishes. Furthermore, there is a path back: a *chalal*'s daughter who marries a legitimate *kohen* can have sons who are *kohanim* once again. This contrasts sharply with *mamzerut*, from which there is essentially no exit — at least not in a world without slavery, where the one technical mechanism of exit no longer functions.

The *gemara* also notes that this discussion extends naturally to a regular *kohen* who marries a *gerushah* (divorced woman). The child of such a union, on the same logic, would be a *chalal* — a step down from *kohen*, but not as catastrophic as *mamzer*. This distinction — that violations within the priestly framework produce *chalal* status rather than *mamzer* status — is important both practically and conceptually.

### Rabbi Shaveiv

*Rabbi Shaveiv* disagrees sharply with *Rabbi Simai*'s account of *Rabbi Akiva*'s position. *De-amar bo unitzvach al Rabbi Akiva* — let us go and protest loudly at *Rabbi Akiva*, who said *kol she-ein lo biah be-Yisrael ha-valad mamzer* — anyone whom you are forbidden to have relations with, the child is a *mamzer*. *Rabbi Shaveiv* contends that *Rabbi Akiva*'s position creates *mamzerut* even in the case of *almanah le-Kohen Gadol*, without the exception that *Rabbi Simai* introduced. The implication is that *Rabbi Akiva*'s rule, as *Rabbi Shaveiv* understands it, is sweeping and unqualified — and *Rabbi Shaveiv* finds this alarming, as it dramatically expands the population of *mamzerim*. The *gemara* notes this objection carries an almost rhetorical, polemical character — this is a *beit midrash* in which strong disagreement is sometimes expressed with open exasperation, as we have seen elsewhere, such as *Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish*'s famous outburst about the *hekesh* of *havayah le-yitziah*.

The question of how many *Kohanim Gedolim* exist at any given time is relevant here: the *Kohen Gadol* is a singular figure, and the case of *almanah le-Kohen Gadol* affects a vanishingly small number of people. It is therefore striking that this particular case becomes the crux of the dispute between *Rabbi Simai* and *Rabbi Shaveiv*.

### Reconciliation

The *gemara* then works through the reconciliation. If *Rabbi Shaveiv* intends to refute *Rabbi Simai*, his approach is coherent — he is arguing that even *almanah le-Kohen Gadol* produces *mamzerut* and that *Rabbi Simai*'s exception is wrong. But if *Rabbi Shaveiv* is stating his own independent position, what is the *issur asei* case he would apply the *pasuk* of *ki tihyena* to?

The resolution involves a careful re-examination of which category the prohibition of *almanah le-Kohen Gadol* properly belongs to. According to *Rabbi Simai*, *Rabbi Akiva*'s one exception applies to *almanah le-Kohen Gadol* — which involves a *chayavei lav*-level prohibition — and therefore the exception operates within *chayavei lavin*. But the *gemara* ultimately concludes that *Rabbi Simai*'s exception is better understood as applying only to *issur asei*, not to *chayavei lavin* proper.

The deeper point about *issur asei* is that it is an extremely weak level of prohibition — *bitul asei* is the least severe form of violation in the rabbinic hierarchy — and accordingly the case of a *beulah le-Kohen Gadol*, a non-virgin who marries the High Priest, is the paradigm of *issur asei* here. Even *Rabbi Akiva* agrees that *kiddushin* takes effect in such a case and no *mamzerut* results. The *rabbanan*, for their part, apply *ki tihyena* broadly to *chayavei lavin*, establishing that *kiddushin* is effective across that entire category. The contrast between *Rabbi Akiva* and the *rabbanan* thus turns on whether *chayavei lavin* falls on the side of valid or invalid *kiddushin*, with *Rabbi Akiva* placing it in the invalid column and the *rabbanan* placing it in the valid column — and the *pasuk* of *ki tihyena* being interpreted accordingly.

The *sotah* exception under *Rabbi Akiva* similarly remains in place: even according to *Rabbi Akiva*, *sotah* — the adulterous woman whose husband subsequently has relations with her — does not produce *mamzerut*, because the *issur* in her case is specifically constructed around the marital relationship itself and carries its own textual basis for exemption.

---

## Shifcha & Nochrit

### No Kiddushin Ever

The *mishnah* delineates a third major category: *kol mi she-ein lah alav lo kiddushin ve-lo al acherim kiddushin ha-valad k'motah* — any woman for whom there is no possibility of *kiddushin* with this man and no possibility of *kiddushin* with any Jewish man. The two paradigmatic examples are *shifcha Kenaanit* (a Canaanite slave woman) and *nochrit* (a non-Jewish woman). In both cases the child follows the mother's status.

### Shifcha Donkey

*Amar Rav Huna*: the derivation that a *shifcha Kenaanit* cannot contract *kiddushin* is learned from the *pasuk* in *Bereishit* in which *Avraham*, on his way to the *Akeidah*, instructs *Eliezer* and his companion: *shevu lachem po im ha-chamor* — stay here with the donkey. The *midrash* reads *im ha-chamor* as *am ha-domeh la-chamor* — a people similar to a donkey. Since slaves do not have *kiddushin*, they are compared, in this *drasha*, to animals. This is a strikingly harsh comparison, and the *gemara* is clearly aware of the gravity of this formulation. It must be situated within a broader legal framework in which the status of an *eved Kenaani* (Canaanite slave) is treated in certain respects as analogous to property rather than as a fully autonomous legal person with respect to personal-status law. Similar *drashot* appear elsewhere — for example, the discussion in *Avodah Zarah* about whether a non-Jewish corpse conveys *tumah be-ohel*, derived from *adam ki yamut be-ohel* with the *drasha atem k'ruyim adam ve-ein ovdei avodah zarah k'ruyim adam* — and in each case the *gemara* uses a sharp formulation to establish a specific legal category.

### Mother's Status

The *gemara* establishes that *kiddushin* does not apply to a slave. But from where do we know that the child of a *shifcha Kenaanit* follows the mother's status? From the *pasuk*: *ha-ishah vi-yladeha tihyeh le-adoneha* — the woman and her children shall belong to her master. This verse appears in the context of an *eved Ivri* (Hebrew slave) who marries a *shifcha Kenaanit* that his master provided for him; when the *eved Ivri* goes free, his children from the *shifcha Kenaanit* remain with the master as slaves. The explicit language of the *pasuk* establishes that the children follow the mother's status — they remain enslaved because she is a slave. The economic logic here is plain: the capacity to have one's slaves procreate was, within the institution of slavery, a means of generating additional slaves without capture or purchase.

### Non-Jew Marriage

*Nochrit minalan* — how do we know that a non-Jewish woman cannot contract *kiddushin* with a Jewish man and that her children follow her status? *Amar kra lo titchaten bam* — you shall not intermarry with them. The *gemara* derives from *lo titchaten bam* that *kiddushin* cannot take effect with non-Jews.

However, *Tosafot* raises an objection: the *pasuk* of *lo titchaten bam* is specifically addressed to the seven Canaanite nations — the *Zayin Amamim* — for whom there is a distinct and heightened prohibition rooted in their extreme devotion to idolatry. *Rashi* in a long comment further down in the *sugya* — when he discusses *Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai*'s approach of *darish ta'ama de-kra* — distinguishes between these seven nations and other non-Jews precisely on this basis, citing the *gemara* in *Chullin*: *umot she-b'chutz la-aretz lav ovdei avodat kochavim heim, ela minhag avoteihem b'yadeihem* — non-Jews outside of *Eretz Yisrael* are not considered genuine idol worshippers; they simply follow inherited custom. The seven Canaanite nations, by contrast, were deeply and genuinely committed to *avodah zarah*, which is the underlying reason for the heightened prohibition against marrying them. *Tosafot* leverages this distinction in several places to permit closer commercial and social relations with medieval European Christians.

### Severs Jewishness

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai*: the derivation for the children's status follows the mother is taken from *ki yasir et bincha me-acharei* — for he will turn your son away from Me. The *pasuk* addresses the case of a Jewish man who marries a non-Jewish woman: the non-Jewish father-in-law will lead the Jewish son astray into idolatry. From this the *gemara* derives: *bincha ha-ba mi-Yisraelit karuy bincha* — your son born from a Jewish woman is called your son, *ve-ein bincha ha-ba min ha-ovedet kochavim karuy bincha* — but your son born from a non-Jewish woman is not called your son. One generation down, the grandchildren of a Jewish man through a non-Jewish woman are no longer recognized as his children within the Jewish people.

*Rabbi Yishmael* draws a further inference: *ben bitcha ha-ba min ha-oved kochavim karuy bincha* — the son of your daughter born from a non-Jewish man is called your son. That is, the grandchildren of a Jewish woman, even through a non-Jewish father, are still Jewish. The *gemara* then notes that *Ravina* holds that a child born from a non-Jewish man or a slave who had relations with a Jewish woman is not fully *kasher* — *nehi de-kasher lo havi, mamzer lo havi* — meaning the child is Jewish but carries a disqualification (*pasul*), specifically being *pasul le-kehunah*, ineligible for the priesthood. The child is neither fully unrestricted nor a *mamzer*.

### All Nations

The *gemara* presses the point that *lo titchaten bam* applies specifically to the seven Canaanite nations. *She'ar umot minalan* — what is the source for extending the rule to all other nations? *Amar kra ki yasir et bincha lerabot kol ha-mesirim* — the phrase *ki yasir*, "for he will lead astray," is understood to encompass anyone who would draw a Jewish child away from the Jewish people. Any non-Jewish woman who marries a Jewish man creates the same risk, and therefore the same legal consequence — invalid *kiddushin* and children following the mother — extends to all nations.

### Drasha vs Pshat

*Hanicha le-Rabbi Shimon de-darish ta'ama de-kra* — this extension works according to *Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai* because he applies *darish ta'ama de-kra*, interpreting the contextual purpose and meaning of the verse and applying it broadly to all cases that share the same underlying rationale. *Ela le-Rabbanan* — the *rabbanan*, however, do not employ *darish ta'ama de-kra*; they do not generalize from the contextual reason of a verse to expand its legal application. They therefore require a separate source.

### Yefat Toar

For the *rabbanan*, the source is the *pasuk* describing *yefat to'ar* — the captive woman taken in war — which states *ve-achar ken tavo eleha u-ve'altah*, "and only afterward may you come to her and marry her." The phrase *ve-achar ken* — only after a certain process — implies that initially, before this process is completed, *kiddushin* cannot take effect with her. *Michlal de-mei-ikara lo tafsei bah kiddushin* — it is implicit that at the outset she was not subject to *kiddushin*. This establishes, for the *rabbanan*, that *kiddushin* does not apply to a non-Jewish woman.

### Concluding Rule

How do we then know that the child follows the mother? From the *pasuk*: *ki tihyena le-ish ve-yaldu lo* — when a man's wives give birth to him children. *Ke-heicha de-karinan bei ki tihyena karinan bei ve-yaldu lo* — wherever we apply the rule of *ki tihyena* (i.e., wherever a valid marriage bond exists), we also apply *ve-yaldu lo* (the children are attributed to the father). And wherever we cannot apply *ki tihyena* — wherever *kiddushin* does not take effect — the children follow the mother instead.

This concluding principle unifies the entire discussion: *kiddushin* validity and paternal attribution of children are two sides of the same coin. Wherever *kiddushin* works, children follow the father. Wherever it does not, children follow the mother. This is the foundational rule underlying the *mishnah*'s entire framework of *yichus* in these cases.

---

---

# Kiddushin 69

## Matrilineal Descent

### Non-Jewish Mother

The daf opens in the middle of an extremely important discussion rooted in the final point of the preceding *mishnah*: that the child of a *shifcha* — a slave woman — is also a slave, derived from the *pasuk* *ha'isha veyeladeha tihyeh le'adoneha* ("the woman and her children shall belong to her master"). From there, the *Gemara* moves to the *halacha* that the child of a non-Jewish woman and a Jewish man is not Jewish. The *mishnah* does not explicitly address the reverse — a Jewish mother and a non-Jewish father — but the *Gemara* here is the locus classicus for the entire principle of matrilineal descent.

The *Gemara* begins with the question: *nochrit minalan* — how do we know, in the case of a non-Jewish woman, that the child is not Jewish? The answer is *amar kra: lo titchaten bam* — the Torah commands not to intermarry with them, the context being the seven Canaanite nations. From this prohibition we derive that *kiddushin* does not take effect. But *vevalda kamota minalan* — how do we know that the child's status follows the mother?

### Rashi's Interpretation

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*: the verse states *ki yasir et bincha me'acharai* — "for he will cause your son to stray from Me." From this we derive: *bincha haba miyisraelit karui bincha* — your child born from a Jewish woman is called your son, *ve'ein bincha haba min ha'avodat kochavim karui bincha ela binah* — but your child born from a non-Jewish woman is not called your son; rather, he is called her son.

The difficulty is obvious: how does one derive all this from that *pasuk*? The surrounding verses state *bitcha lo titein livno uvito lo tikach livnecha* — do not give your daughter to their son and do not take their daughter for your son — and the reason given is "for he will cause your son to stray from Me." But this is grammatically awkward. If we are talking about giving your daughter to their son, the verse should have said that he — the non-Jewish son-in-law — will cause *your daughter* to stray. And if we are talking about taking their daughter for your son, it should have warned that *she* will cause your son to stray. The verse, as written, says "he will cause your son to stray" — which fits neither case straightforwardly.

Rashi resolves this by reading the verse as follows: the prohibition against giving your daughter to their son is because *he* — the non-Jewish son-in-law — will cause *your grandson* to stray. In other words, the "son" referred to is not your own son but your daughter's son, your grandson. This is significant: it implies that the child of your Jewish daughter and her non-Jewish husband is still *your* grandson, still Jewish — and therefore the concern is that this non-Jewish husband will lead that Jewish grandchild away from God. The reverse inference is then drawn: if a Jewish man fathers a child with a non-Jewish woman, that child is called *her* child, not his, and is therefore not Jewish.

### Rabbeinu Tam's View

Rabbeinu Tam is troubled by the interpretive leap of reading "your son" as "your grandson," since the grandson has not been mentioned in the text. He therefore reads the verse differently. According to Rabbeinu Tam, "he" who will cause "your son" to stray refers not to any future child of the union but to the non-Jewish father-in-law himself. The case in view is your son marrying their daughter, and the warning is that *he* — the father-in-law — will pull your son away from Jewish practice. What the verse thereby teaches about the status of the offspring is that, under this reading, "turning your son away" implies that the children of that union will be non-Jewish — the entire family line is being drawn away. Rashi's reading remains somewhat simpler: the word *bincha* — your son — means your grandson through your daughter, which establishes that the child of a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father is still Jewish.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Returning to the *Gemara*'s derivation: the principle stated by Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is that *bincha haba miyisrael karui bincha* — a child born of a Jewish woman is called your child — *ve'ein bincha haba min ha'ovedet kochavim karui bincha ella benah* — but the child of a non-Jewish woman is not your son but hers. However one parses the grammatical problem in *ki yasir et bincha*, it is from this difficulty that the *Gemara* derives the principle of matrilineal descent. It is worth noting that this is not the most airtight proof; the entire edifice rests on a subtle grammatical anomaly.

### Ravina's Proof

*Amar Ravina shema mina*: Ravina draws an explicit conclusion from this teaching — *ben bitcha haba mi'oved kochavim karui bincha* — the son of your daughter, even if born from a non-Jewish man, is still called your son, and thus is Jewish. This appears to be a complete restatement of what Rabbi Yochanan already said, and *Tosafos* attempts to distinguish them, but functionally both are making the same point: a child of a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father is Jewish. This principle, it bears repeating, was not stated in the *mishnah* itself, which addressed only the case of a non-Jewish mother.

### Mamzer Question

The *Gemara* immediately raises a concern: *neima kasavar Ravina oved kochavim ve'eved haba al bat Yisrael havlad mamzer* — perhaps Ravina holds that the child of a non-Jewish man or slave who fathers a child with a Jewish woman is a *mamzer*? The reasoning is familiar: we know that when *kiddushin* cannot take effect between two parties, the child of their union is a *mamzer*. Since *kiddushin* is clearly not binding between a Jewish woman and a non-Jewish man, why isn't the child a *mamzer*?

This would actually create a strange dynamic: saying the child is non-Jewish is in one sense the more lenient outcome, because the child could simply convert and carry no stigma. Saying the child is Jewish immediately raises the specter of *mamzer* status.

### Psul Status

The *Gemara* resolves this: *nehi de'kasher lo havei mamzer lo havei* — Ravina said neither that the child is fully *kasher* nor that the child is a *mamzer*. As Rashi explains, *mamzer* status arises from a union where both parties could, in principle, marry someone else within *halakha* but are forbidden to each other — as in adultery or incest. In the case of a Jewish woman and a non-Jewish man, the non-Jewish man has no valid *halachic* marriage at all within our framework. This is a categorically different type of forbidden relationship. Therefore: the child is Jewish, but carries a *psul* — a defective status that falls short of full *kashrut* without rising to the severity of *mamzerut*.

What does this *psul* mean practically? Two areas are worth noting. First, there are contexts in the *Gemara* where the status of a person with a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father is considered alongside the status of a *geir*, not because such a person needs conversion — they do not — but because there is a partial analogy in that their Jewish identity has, as it were, a non-Jewish biographical component. Second, and perhaps more immediately practical, there is a significant debate among the *poskim* — addressed in another *Gemara* and not fully spelled out here — about whether a *kohen* may marry a woman born of a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father. This *psul* may give rise to at least a *de'rabbanan* concern in that context. The *Gemara* here does not spell out all the ramifications, but these are the two areas where this intermediate status carries genuine *halachic* weight.

---

## Seven Nations

### All Non-Jews Question

Having established the principle, the *Gemara* now asks: *hahu beshivah goyim ketiv, she'ar umos minalan* — that *pasuk* of *lo titchaten bam*, with its attendant consequences for the status of the child, is written in the context of the seven Canaanite nations. How do we know to apply the same rules to all non-Jews?

The *Gemara* answers: *amar kra ki yasir et bincha* — the verse explains the reason for the prohibition as "he will cause your son to stray," *l'rabos kol hamisirim* — which comes to include all those who would cause such straying. Since the rationale — that the non-Jewish spouse will lead the child away from Jewish identity — applies equally to any non-Jew, the verse's scope is not limited to the seven nations.

### Rabbi Shimon Method

But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *hani l'Rabbi Shimon d'daresh ta'ama dikra* — this works well for Rabbi Shimon, who is willing to use the reason of a verse to redefine its parameters. Rabbi Shimon's method, *darshan ta'ama dikra*, allows the inferred rationale to expand or contract the application of a law. A classic illustration of this principle is the prohibition of *lo tachvol beged almanah* — one may not take a widow's garment as collateral. Rabbi Shimon reads this as applying only to cases where taking the garment would create a problematic situation — such as repeatedly entering a widow's home alone to return the garment each day, raising suspicion — but not to a rich widow, because the rationale does not apply there. Crucially, the rationale itself may vary: even when two authorities agree that *darshan ta'ama dikra* is legitimate, they may disagree entirely about what the *ta'ama dikra* is.
