### Rabbanan Objection

The *Rabbanan*, however, do not use the reason of a verse to redefine its parameters. This does not mean they deny that *mitzvot* have reasons; it means they refuse to allow their own assumption of a reason to override or extend the plain scope of the verse. So *ella l'Rabbanan mai ta'ama* — how do the *Rabbanan* extend the law beyond the seven Canaanite nations?

### Rashi's Resolution

Rashi's approach is that the very inclusion of the phrase *ki yasir et bincha* in the verse is what provides the extension — for *everyone*, including the *Rabbanan*. Had the verse not stated this reason, one might indeed have confined the prohibition and its consequences to the seven nations. But because the Torah itself explicitly provided the rationale, that explicit statement is itself teaching that wherever the rationale applies — any non-Jew who might lead the child astray — the law applies as well. This is not a case of the *Rabbanan* inferring an unstated reason and then using it to redefine the *mitzvah*; rather, the Torah stated the reason explicitly, and that explicit statement carries its own exegetical force as a *ribui* — an expansion. *Tosafos* takes a somewhat different approach, but the upshot is the same.

---

## Yefat Toar Source

### Yefat Toar Intro

The *Gemara* now introduces a second textual basis for the law of matrilineal descent, drawn from a completely different part of the Torah — the *yefat to'ar*, the captive woman taken in war. This case, by definition, involves non-Canaanite nations, since the laws of *yefat to'ar* apply specifically to wars waged against nations *outside* the land. The verse there states *v'acharei ken tavo eleha u'va'alta* — only after the prescribed mourning process does the marriage become valid.

### Kiddushin Bindable

From here the *Gemara* derives a general principle: *kiddushin* must be capable of taking binding effect for the child's status to follow the father. The mechanism is as follows: where *kiddushin* can bind, the children are "his"; where it cannot, they are not.

### Ki Tiheyena L'Ish

The textual peg for this is the verse *ki tiheyena l'ish shtei nashim v'yaldu lo* — if a man has two wives and they bear him children. The *Gemara* reads this as: *kol heicha d'karinan ki tiheyena* — anywhere that the woman can truly be said to "belong to a man" in the full legal sense of *kiddushin* — *karinan beih v'yaldu lo* — the children are considered born to him and follow his status.

### Non-Jewish Mother

Conversely, *v'kol heicha d'lo karinan beih ki tiheyena* — in any case where there is no Jewish man for whom this woman's *kiddushin* would be binding, *lo karinan beih v'yaldu lo* — the children are not attributed to the father. This is not merely a case where *kiddushin* is forbidden but where it is categorically incapable of taking effect with *any* Jewish man. In such a case, the children are not his and are not Jewish.

### Jewish Mother Inference

Notably, this derivation, like the one from *ki yasir et bincha*, establishes only the case of the non-Jewish mother: where *kiddushin* cannot bind, the child is not Jewish. The converse — that the child of a Jewish mother and non-Jewish father *is* Jewish — is not explicitly derived from this verse; that principle rests on the earlier *drasha* of Rabbi Yochanan.

---

## Servant Woman

### Redundancy Challenge

One might ask: if we have already derived from *ki tiheyena l'ish* that where *kiddushin* cannot bind, the child follows the mother — this should cover the case of a *shifcha* as well, since no Jewish man can contract a valid *kiddushin* with a *shifcha*. If so, why do we need the separate verse *ha'isha veyeladeha tihyeh le'adoneha* — "the woman and her children shall belong to her master"? We have already established the principle from elsewhere.

### Braita Case

The *Gemara* answers: *lichdetanya* — as was taught in a *braita* (on 67a). The verse is needed for a specific case: what if a master says to his female slave, *harei at bat chorin* — you are hereby a free woman — *u'vladech eved* — but your unborn child, still in the womb, will remain a slave? Can a master split the freedom of the mother from the slave-status of the fetus?

### Split Debate

*Havlad kamota, divrei Rabbi Yossi HaGlili* — Rabbi Yossi HaGlili rules that you cannot split them: if the mother is freed, the child is automatically freed as well. *Va'chachamim omrim d'varav kayamin* — the *chachamim* say his words stand and the split is valid.

### Verse Unity

*Amar Rava aliba d'Rabbi Yossi HaGlili*: what is the textual basis for Rabbi Yossi HaGlili's position? The verse *ha'isha veyeladeha tihyeh le'adoneha* — the woman *and her children* shall belong to her master — teaches that mother and child are bound together: when the mother is the master's slave, the children are the master's slaves; but you cannot create a situation where the mother is no longer your slave while the unborn child is. The mother and child are a unified legal unit. This is what required the verse: the general principle of matrilineal descent was already derivable from *ki tiheyena l'ish*, but the specific rule that you cannot sever the legal bond between mother and fetus in this way required the verse *ha'isha veyeladeha* explicitly.

---

## Rabbi Tarfon

### Proposal Structure

The *mishnah* concludes the *perek* with a striking proposal: *Rabbi Tarfon omer yakhol ani letaher et hamamzerim* — Rabbi Tarfon says he can "purify" *mamzerim* — not retroactively remove the status, but arrange that their children will not be *mamzerim*. The mechanism is rooted in what was just established. Since the child of a *shifcha* is an *eved* and follows the mother, Rabbi Tarfon proposes: let the *mamzer* marry a *shifcha kena'anit*. Their children will be slaves — *vlad eved* — following the mother. As slaves, they are outside the category of *mamzerut*, which applies only within Jewish status. Then free the children. The freed children are Jewish and not *mamzerim*. Problem solved.

### Rabbi Eliezer

*Rabbi Eliezer omer harei zeh eved mamzer* — Rabbi Eliezer disagrees sharply. The *mamzer* status passes through regardless; the child is worse off than before, now an *eved mamzer*. The reasoning of Rabbi Eliezer, as Rabbi Elazar explains, is derived from the verse *lo yavo lo bikhal Hashem* — the word *lo* (meaning "to him," the *mamzer*) teaches that the stigma always follows: *halach achar psulo*, any future generation traces back to the original *mamzer* regardless of the mother's status. The word *lo* is read as overriding the ordinary rules of lineage — just as normally we follow the father (*l'mishpechotam l'veit avotam*), yet the verse by *mamzer* says even where you would normally not transmit the *psul*, *lo* tells you the *psul* persists.

---

## Rabbi Tarfon (II)

### L'Chatchila Question

A question is raised: when Rabbi Tarfon proposes this solution, is he saying it is permitted *l'chatchila* — that a *mamzer* may proactively seek out a *shifcha* to marry — or only *b'di'eved*, meaning that if it happened, the children would not be *mamzerim*, but one may not initiate the arrangement? There is an underlying *issur* for a *Yisrael* to marry a *shifcha*. A *mamzer* may marry a *giyoret*, since there is no prohibition for a *Yisrael* to marry a *giyoret*, but marrying a *shifcha* is a different matter.

### Gender Difference

The *Gemara* notes an asymmetry between the male and female *mamzer*. The *mishnah* notes that Rabbi Tarfon's interlocutors observed: *tiharta es hazacharim v'lo tiharta es hanekevos* — this solution works for males but not for females. A *mamzeret* who is a female cannot marry a male *eved* and achieve the same result, because the child of a *mamzeret* and a male *eved* would follow the mother — but the mother is Jewish and a *mamzeret*, so the child would be Jewish and a *mamzer*. The solution only works when the *mamzer* is male and the *shifcha* is female, because then the child follows the mother — the *shifcha* — and is an *eved*, breaking the Jewish status entirely, after which the children can be freed.

Rashi explains the practical reason why the solution was unavailable to a female *mamzeret*: she could not go off anonymously and enter into such an arrangement without her family — fathers, brothers — knowing and intervening. A male could, in principle, travel elsewhere and arrange a union with a *shifcha* without attracting attention. But this logic presupposes the arrangement is not entirely above-board, suggesting it might only work *b'di'eved* — after the fact.

### Rabbi Simlai Proof

The *Gemara* brings a proof from a story: the host of Rabbi Simlai — *ushpizchanei de-Rabbi Simlai* — was a *mamzer*. Rabbi Simlai said to him, *ei akdamtach tihartinhu l'vanecha* — had I known you earlier, I could have advised you how to arrange that your children would not be *mamzerim*. The *Gemara* reasons: *ei amart bishlama l'chatchila shapir* — if it is permitted *l'chatchila*, Rabbi Simlai's statement is perfectly coherent; he would have given proactive advice. *Ela ei amart di'eved* — but if marrying a *shifcha* is forbidden and only works *b'di'eved*, how could Rabbi Simlai say he would have *advised* someone to do something prohibited?

The *Gemara* considers a workaround: Rabbi Simlai would have advised the man to go steal something, be sold as an *eved Ivri*, and since an *eved Ivri* is permitted to marry a *shifcha kena'anit*, the *issur* would be circumvented. Rashi notes the obvious problem — stealing is forbidden — but the *Gemara* rejects this solution on independent grounds: *uv'shnei de-Rabbi Simlai eved Ivri mi havai?* The laws of *eved Ivri* only apply when *yovel* is in force, which was not the case in Rabbi Simlai's time.

### Perpetuation Debate

The disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Rabbanan* thus comes into full relief. Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *mamzer* status perpetuates through any union, even with a *shifcha*, based on *lo yavo lo bikhal Hashem* — *halach achar psulo*, the stigma always follows. The *Rabbanan* counter that *kol vlad shebimei shifcha kena'anit kevlad bimei behema dami* — the child of a non-Jewish slave woman is like the offspring of an animal, in the sense that it completely severs any prior lineage-based identity. Just as an animal's offspring has no tribal or family affiliation, the child of a *shifcha* exits the entire framework of Jewish lineage, including *mamzerut*. Once that break is complete, there is nothing for the *mamzer* stigma to attach to.

The distinction is important: we are not merely saying that the child follows the mother's status rather than the father's — which would be the normal matrilineal principle operating within a Jewish framework. Here, because the mother is entirely outside the Jewish legal order, the child's very connection to the father's status is severed at a more fundamental level. This is why the *Rabbanan*'s position is not simply "the child follows the mother's slave status" but the stronger claim that the bond to the father's Jewish identity — including its *psul* — is broken entirely.

### Halacha Conclusion

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel halacha k'Rabbi Tarfon* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Tarfon, and as established, it is *muttar l'chatchila*. A male *mamzer* is permitted, not merely *b'di'eved*, to marry a *shifcha* with the intention of freeing the children and resolving the *mamzerut*. Indeed, Rav Moshe Feinstein has a *teshuvah* in which he considers implementing this in practice as a solution for a *mamzer*, with all the *halachos* attending such an arrangement — the *kiddushin* would not be effected with the *shifcha*, she is *koneh* as a *shifcha*, the same *halachos* of *hilchos niddah* apply since a *shifcha kena'anit*'s obligations in *mitzvos* are equivalent to a woman's, and the children may be freed immediately upon birth without waiting for the mother to be freed.

---

## Ten Yuchasin

### Categories List

The next *mishnah* opens a new *perek* continuing the discussion of *yuchasin* — lineage categories — and their consequences for marriage eligibility. *Asara yuchasin alu miBavel* — ten categories of lineage came up from Babylon with Ezra. The ten are: *kohanei, leviyei, yisraeli* — Kohanim, Levi'im, Yisraelim — *challalim* (children of a Kohen from a forbidden union for *kehuna*, who lack *kedushat kehuna*), *geirim* (converts), *charurei* (freed slaves), *mamzeirim*, *nesinim* (Gibeonites, subject to David HaMelech's *gezera* prohibiting intermarriage within the Jewish nation), *shtuki*, and *asufi*. All of these categories were known and identified among those who made *aliyah* with Ezra.

### First Tier

*Kohanei, leviyei, va'yisraeli mutarin lavo ze baze* — Kohanim, Levi'im, and Yisraelim may all intermarry freely with one another. This group constitutes the first tier.

### Second Tier

*Levi, yisraeli, challali, geirei, ve'charurei mutarin lavo ze baze* — Levi'im, Yisraelim, *challalim*, *geirim*, and freed slaves may all intermarry with one another. The reason Kohanim are excluded: a Kohen may not marry a *chalalah*, and by extension is prohibited from marrying a *gerusha*, a *zonah*, and categories assimilated thereto. A *geir* and an *eved meshuchrar*, having presumably had a sexual life outside of marriage before their entry into full Jewish status, are placed by *halakha* into the category analogous to *zonah* for purposes of *kehuna* marriage prohibitions. Hence this second tier excludes Kohanim, but all others in it may intermarry freely.

### Third Tier

*Geyri ve-charurei im mamzer ve-netini, shtuki va-asufi, kulam mutarin lavo ze baze* — converts and freed slaves may marry *mamzerim*, *nesinim*, *shtuki*, and *asufi*, and all of these may intermarry with one another. The rationale is rooted in the verse *lo yavo mamzer bikhal Hashem* (and similarly *lo yavo lo bikhal Hashem* by the descendants of *mamzerim*): the inner circle of *kehal Hashem* — as understood to exclude those who are not Jewish by birth — means that *geirim* and *meshuchrarim*, despite being fully Jewish, are considered outside the innermost *kehal Hashem* in this restricted sense, and therefore may marry *mamzerim*. This is a striking *halacha* and not without theological complexity, given the competing *pasuk* of *mishpat echad yihyeh lachem kager kaezrach ha'aretz*. But it is the operative *halakha*, and it actually functions as a *kula* in practice for these categories.

### Shtuki Definition

*Ve-eilu hem shtuki* — who is a *shtuki*? It is one who knows who his mother is but does not know his father. The etymology is from *shtak* — silence or "be quiet" — because when the child asks about his father, the mother says nothing, or perhaps tells the child not to ask, or redirects him from the man he might have identified as his father. Rashi notes an alternative reading: the mother may have said *shh* to the child when he pointed at the man currently married to her, indicating that person is not his father.

### Asufi Definition

*Asufi* is *kol sheneesaf min hashuk* — whoever was gathered in from the marketplace. This is the foundling, the child left in a basket and collected, who does not know either parent.

### Safek Mamzer

Both the *shtuki* and *asufi* are treated as *safek mamzerim*. One might wonder: in the case of a *shtuki*, the mother is not a married woman — there is no accusation of adultery. How could the child be a *mamzer* at all, since *mamzerut* requires a union forbidden under penalty of *karet* or death? The answer is that the father could have been a *mamzer* himself — and this is indeed the primary *choshesh*, not incest, which would be a far rarer concern.

The general principle of *yuchasin* operates differently from other areas of *halakha*. In other domains, we often rely on *rov* — the statistical majority — to resolve doubts. Here, we are far more demanding about certainty of lineage. Once a *safek mamzer* status is assigned, the individual is considered a *safek mamzer* and may not marry a *Yisrael* — but may marry a *vadai mamzer* or a *geir*. Interestingly, what appears to be a stringency — calling someone a *safek mamzer* — operates simultaneously as a *kula*: it opens the door to marriages with *mamzerim* and *geirim* that would otherwise be unavailable if the person were simply considered a full *Yisrael*.

The further asymmetry is worth noting: a *safek mamzer* cannot marry a full *Yisrael*, but nor can two *safek mamzerim* marry each other without difficulty, since one might be a *mamzer* and the other not. In practice, they may marry *geirim* and *mamzerim* of either sex.

### Abba Shaul

*Abba Shaul haya korei l'shtuki beduki* — Abba Shaul would call the *shtuki* not *shtuki* but *beduki* — from *bedika*, investigation. Rather than accepting the silence as definitive, Abba Shaul's name for this person suggests that the proper response to uncertainty is inquiry and investigation. The *Gemara* will elaborate on what that means in practice.

---

## Babylonian Ascent

### Aliyah Meaning

The *mishnah* states *asara yuchasin alu miBavel* — ten categories of lineage *came up* from Babylon. The *Gemara* asks: *mai irya d'tani alu miBavel* — why does the *tanna* use the language of "came up"? Why is traveling from Babylon to Eretz Yisrael described as going *up*?

### Eretz Yisrael Higher

The answer: *milta gavita kamashma lan* — it is telling us something about the relative sanctity and elevation of Eretz Yisrael. As the *braita* derives from the verse *v'kamta v'alita el hamakom asher yivchar Hashem Elokecha* — "you shall rise and go up to the place that God has chosen" — we learn that the *Beit HaMikdash* is higher than all of Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands. The verse from *Yirmiyahu* further confirms this: God says that people will no longer praise Him solely as the One who brought Israel up from Egypt, but as the One who brought them up from all the northern lands and all the places to which they had been scattered — *asher he'ela*, "who brought them up" — meaning all those other lands require going *up* to reach Eretz Yisrael.

### Rabbi Elazar

But why specifically mention that they came from *Bavel*? *Mesayei lei l'Rebbi Elazar* — the *mishnah*'s phrasing supports the view of Rabbi Elazar: *lo ala Ezra miBavel ad she'asah k'solet nekiyah v'ala* — Ezra did not make *aliyah* from Babylon until he had made it like sifted flour — *solet nekiyah* — and then went up. That is, Ezra cleaned out Babylon of all those of questionable lineage before departing, so that what remained in Babylon was the refined, identified population, and what he brought to Eretz Yisrael was equally identifiable and categorized.

### Abbayyei Position

*Abaye amar alu me-aleihem* — Abaye holds that they went up on their own initiative. According to Abaye, Ezra identified the lineage categories of the various families in Babylon; once identified as *challal*, *mamzer*, *nasin*, and so on, those individuals found their social position in Babylon untenable and chose on their own to join Ezra on his *aliyah*. Ezra did not force them out; he simply made their status known, and self-interest did the rest.

### Rava Position

*Rava amar he-alum tnan* — Rava holds that the *mishnah*'s language, *alu* (they went up), implies they were *brought up* — that Ezra actively compelled them to leave, against their will if necessary. Ezra controlled the entire process of identification and removal.

### Removal Mechanism

A further layer of disagreement: *iy ba'is eima d'kulei alma is lehu d'Rabbi Elazar* — one can argue that everyone agrees with Rabbi Elazar's essential point, that Ezra's agenda was to clean out Babylon. The dispute is only about the *mechanism*: *mar savar afrushei afrashunihu, m'nafsheihu siliku* — one view is that Ezra merely separated and identified them, and they departed of their own accord; *u-mar savar b'al korcha asikinuhu* — the other view is that he physically compelled their departure.

### Sifted Flour

*Kol ha'aratzot issah l'Eretz Yisrael, v'Eretz Yisrael issah l'Bavel* — Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel articulates the hierarchy: all lands are like *issah* (unkneaded dough — mixed, undifferentiated) relative to Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael itself is like *issah* relative to Babylon. Babylon, having been purged of those of questionable lineage by Ezra, is the most refined — *solet nekiyah*, sifted flour. Eretz Yisrael, while more refined than other lands, still has admixture. All other lands are the most mixed.

This makes intuitive sense according to Abaye's view: since those who went up did so voluntarily after being identified, the process in Eretz Yisrael was less controlled. Ezra could not maintain the same oversight once they had gone up, and over time the clarity of lineage in Eretz Yisrael became diluted again. Babylon, from which they had been removed, remained clean.

### Later Generations

The *Gemara* addresses the tension in Rava's view: if Ezra forcibly controlled the entire process, why isn't Eretz Yisrael also *solet nekiyah*? *Midei yad'inhu l'hahu dara* — in *that* generation, everyone knew everyone's identity. But *l'dara achrina lo yadi* — in subsequent generations, the clarity was lost. Over time, the categories blurred in Eretz Yisrael even though they had been crisply identified when those people arrived with Ezra. Babylon, having been emptied entirely of those categories, remained permanently clean — there was no one left there of questionable status to create confusion. Eretz Yisrael absorbed these people, and once the generation that knew them personally had passed, confusion set in again.

The *Gemara* also addresses a difficulty with Rava's view from the book of Ezra itself: when Ezra encamped at the river Ahava and investigated the people with him, he found that among the *kohanim* and *levi'im*, there were those who could not serve in the *Beit HaMikdash*. If Ezra had been in full control of identifying everyone from the outset, how did this come as a surprise? The answer: *nehi de-izhar bi-psulim* — Ezra had indeed identified who among the people bore stigmatized *yuchasin* statuses (*mamzer*, *nasin*, etc.), but what he discovered at the river was a different matter entirely — Kohanim and Levi'im who, while not bearing those general *psul* categories, were disqualified specifically from Temple service. That was a separate inquiry he had not yet completed. The two categories of disqualification are distinct, and discovering one does not mean the other had been addressed.

---

---

# Kiddushin 70

## Return from Exile

### Opening & Location

Today's daf is daf 70. We pick up in the middle of 69b, approximately fifteen lines down in the wide lines, at the word *minalan* — "from where do we know?" — where the text begins its discussion of *Kohani Leviei VeYisraeli*, the various groups that came up with Ezra from the Babylonian exile.

### Three Groups

The *mishnah* enumerates the different groups that returned with Ezra, and the *gemara* now proceeds to demonstrate that most of what the *mishnah* records is grounded in scriptural testimony. In this sense, the *mishnah* reflects a fairly accurate historical record, even if not every detail is made explicit in the verses. The *gemara* asks: *minalan disliku* — how do we know that members of the *kohanim*, *levi'im*, and *Yisrael* all came up with Ezra?

### Scriptural Proof

The answer comes from the verse: *Vayeshvu hakohanim vehaleviim umin ha'am vehameshorerim vehasho'arim vehanetinim be'areihem vechol Yisrael be'areihem* — "And the *kohanim* and the *levi'im* and from the people and the *meshorerim* and the *sho'arim*" — understood to refer to the *levi'im* who perform the singing or instrumental music and those who guard the gates — "and the *netinim* in their cities, and all of Israel in their cities." The verse thus attests to *kohen*, *levi*, and *Yisrael*. The *netinim* — the Gibeonites — appear here as well, though their discussion comes later in the *mishnah*. Moving forward.

---

## Chalalim

### Gedola Chazaka

The *gemara* turns to *chalalim*, *geirim*, and *charurim* — disqualified *kohanim*, converts, and freed slaves. How do we know *chalalim* — *kohanim* born from forbidden unions who therefore lack *kedushat kehuna* — came up with Ezra? A *braita* is cited: Rabbi Yosi says, *gedola chazaka* — the principle of presumed status is great — as we learn from the following passage in Ezra.

### No Genealogy

The verse reads: *Umibnei hakohanim bnei Chavayah bnei haKotz bnei Barzillai asher lakach mibnot Barzillai haGil'adi ishah vayikarei al shemam* — these are the priestly families that went up from the exile, the sons of Chavayah, Kotz, and Barzillai, named after Barzillai the Gileadite because they had married his daughters and were identified by that name even though they were really his daughters' children. The verse continues: *Eleh bikshu ksavam hamityachasim velo nimtze'u* — these sought their records of lineage and could not find them. The word *yichus* appears here directly: they could not produce documentation to establish themselves as legitimate *kohanim*. As a result, *vayig'alu min hakehuna* — they were pushed out from the *kehuna*, though the word *vayig'alu* is read with the sense of being removed or rejected rather than redeemed.

### Kodshei Kodashim

*Vayomer HaTirshatha lahem asher lo yochlu mikodesh hakodashim ad amod kohen le'urim vetumim* — Nehemiah, who is called by the title *HaTirshatha*, said to them: since you cannot document your *kehuna*, you may no longer eat from the *kodshei hakodashim* — from the sacrificial offerings — until a *kohen gadol* arises with an *urim vetumim*. Since there was no *urim vetumim* in the Second *Beit Hamikdash*, Rashi understands this to mean, in effect, until the coming of Mashiach. They cannot prove their *yichus*, and so they cannot eat from the *korbanot*.

### Terumah Exemption

But the *gemara* then introduces the principle of *gedola chazaka*. He said to them: *harei atem bechezkatchem* — you retain your presumed status. The question is: what were you eating in exile? *Bekodshei hagvul* — you were eating things sanctified outside the *Mikdash*, meaning *terumah*, which is what you had been eating until now. And so, *af kan nami bekodshei hagvul* — here too you may continue eating *terumah*; your *chazaka* is retained.

This is the *chiddush* of Rabbi Yosi: although these *kohanim* could not document their *kehuna* and could not eat from the *korbanot*, they could continue eating *terumah* on the basis of their established presumptive status. There had been no contrary evidence disproving their *kehuna* — only an absence of supporting documentation. All *kohanim* today lack documentation of their lineage, yet we extend them the same *chazaka*. The distinction between *korbanot* and *terumah* here is notable and will be developed further.

### Terumah Jurisdiction

A complication arises, however. There is an opinion — *ma'alin mitrumah le'yichus* — that one who is seen eating *terumah* is thereby presumed to hold full *yichus*, including fitness to bring *korbanot* in the *Beit Hamikdash*. If we allow these *kohanim* to eat *terumah* now that they are in Eretz Yisrael, observers may presume that they are fully qualified *kohanim* and draw incorrect inferences about their status vis-à-vis the *Beit Hamikdash*.

The *gemara* answers: *shani hasam de-rei'a chezkateihu* — their case is different, because their *chazaka* has been weakened. Rashi explains that since a public declaration was made distinguishing those permitted to bring *korbanot* from those who are not, the distinction is already known. People understand that these particular *kohanim* are eating *terumah* on a different basis and will not draw the wrong conclusion. Tosafot adds that since it was publicly known that they had sought their genealogical records and failed to find them, no one would be confused into thinking they held full *yichus*. Either way, the historical event attached a clear and known label: they eat *terumah* but may not be *makriv korbanot*.

This still raises the question: what exactly is *gedola chazaka*? A *chazaka* simply means that the status quo continues in the absence of contrary evidence — so what is so great about this one? The *gemara* answers: *demeikara achal biterumah derabbanan ulevesof achal biterumah de'oraita* — initially, in exile, *terumah* was only rabbinic in force, since *terumah* outside Eretz Yisrael has no biblical standing. But now that they are coming into Eretz Yisrael, their *chazaka* as *kohanim* in the domain of *terumah* carries over into *terumah de'oraita* as well. That is genuinely remarkable: within the world of *terumah*, once a *chazaka* of *kehuna* is established, it applies across all levels of *terumah* obligation.

An alternative answer is then offered: *ve'ibba'it eima le'olam hasam nami bederabbanan achal uved'oraita lo achal* — perhaps they may only eat *terumah derabbanan* even in Eretz Yisrael, meaning produce for which the biblical obligation of *terumah* does not apply. According to Rashi, *terumah de'oraita* applies only to grain, oil, and wine, so any other produce would remain *terumah derabbanan*. Under this reading, they are limited to *terumah derabbanan* in Eretz Yisrael as well, and there is no concern about the *ma'alin mitrumah le'yichus* problem, since that inference applies only when one is observed eating *terumah de'oraita*.

But then what is *gedola chazaka*? The *gemara* replies: when they were in exile, there was no risk that eating *terumah derabbanan* there would ever lead to someone eating *terumah de'oraita*, because there was simply no *terumah de'oraita* outside Eretz Yisrael. But now, *af al gav de'ika lemigzar mishum terumah de'oraita* — even though one might say rabbinically we ought to prevent them from eating even the *terumah derabbanan* of fruits in Eretz Yisrael, lest observers see them eating it and assume they may also eat *terumah de'oraita* of grain — the *chazaka* overrides that rabbinic concern. We do not allow a speculative rabbinic hedge to erode an established *chazaka*.

The *gemara* also addresses a textual difficulty. The verse says *lo yochlu mikodshei hakodashim* — they shall not eat from *kodshei hakodashim*. Does this not imply that they *may* eat everything else, including *terumah de'oraita*? The *gemara* resolves this: the prohibition is against anything called *kodesh* or *kodashim* — which encompasses *terumah* as well — and even the lesser category of *korbanot* such as the *chazeh veshok*, the priest's portion of the *shelamim*, called *trumat hakodashim* in the verse that states a *bat kohen* who marries a non-*kohen* may not eat it. So according to the restrictive reading, they are barred from *terumah de'oraita* and from *korbanot* of all levels, but may continue eating *terumah derabbanan*.

### Chazaka Strength

One might ask: is this not anomalous? The same person is simultaneously a *kohen* for the purposes of *terumah* and not a *kohen* for the purposes of *korbanot*. The entire point of Rabbi Yosi's teaching is precisely that — *gedola chazaka*: a *chazaka* established within a defined domain is operative within that domain even when it cannot be extended to an adjacent one. The *chazaka* was established through the practice of eating *terumah*; there is no parallel practice in the realm of *korbanot* that would generate a corresponding *chazaka* there.

This principle has important practical analogues. A *kohen* today has established a *chazaka* of *kehuna* through his ongoing observance of the laws of *tumah* — avoiding cemeteries, hospitals, and the like — in a way that he has not necessarily established through his marriage conduct. Accordingly, when a leniency is sought in a *tumah* case on the grounds that "perhaps he is not really a *kohen*," such an argument carries much less weight, because his actions have established him as a *kohen* in that domain. In the world of marriage, by contrast, no comparable practice has built up the same *chazaka*, so there may be somewhat more room to introduce doubt. The point, as the *gemara* illustrates here, is that *chazaka* operates through the lens of a particular legal domain, and one cannot automatically transfer it from one domain to another.

It also bears noting what kind of *chalalim* the *gemara* has actually established here. These are not definitively identified *chalalim* — they are *safek chalalim*, *kohanim* who could not prove they had a clean priestly lineage and may therefore have been *chalalim*. They were restricted from the *korbanot*, permitted to continue with *terumah*, and it is this group — those unable to establish their genealogical fitness — that represents the *chalalim* who came up with Ezra.

---

## Gerim & Slaves

### Gerim & Freedmen

The *gemara* turns to *geirim* and *charurim* — converts and freed slaves. How do we know they came up with Ezra? Rav Chisda says, from the verse at the top of 70a: *vechol hanivdal mitum'at goyei ha'aretz aleihem* — all those who separated themselves from the impurity of the nations of the land joined them. These were people who had previously been non-Jews, and their joining the community could only come about through conversion or manumission.

The question of *mamzeirim* follows. The *gemara* cites the verse: *vayishma Sanbalat haChoroni veTuviyah ha'eved ha'Ammoni* — Sanbalat and Tuviyah the Ammonite slave heard. The verse then states: *ki rabbim biYehudah ba'alei shevuah lo* — many in Judah had taken an oath to this Tuviyah. *Ki chatan hu liShechaniah ben Arach* — because he was a son-in-law to Shechaniah ben Arach, a Jew. So this slave had married a Jewish woman. And further: *viYehochanan beno lakach et bat Meshullam ben Berechiah* — and Tuviyah's son Yehochanan had also married the daughter of another Jewish man. These slaves, then, had married Jewish women and presumably had children from those unions — children who would have been *mamzeirim*.

### Intermarriage Issue

But the *gemara* challenges this on several grounds. First, is a child born of a slave and a *bat Yisrael* really a *mamzer*? The *gemara* acknowledges that this holds only according to the opinion that such a child is a *mamzer* — on the grounds that *kiddushin* cannot take effect between them, and a child of a union where *kiddushin* is invalid is a *mamzer*. We do not rule that way; the accepted *halacha* is that such a child is *kasher*, not a *mamzer*.

### Mamzeirim

Even setting that aside, the *gemara* raises further objections. How do we know they actually had children from these marriages? And even if they did, how do we know those children were born in Babylon and then came up to Eretz Yisrael? The verses being cited describe the situation *in Judah* — *biYehudah* — meaning those marriages may have taken place in the land itself. You cannot use those verses to prove that *mamzeirim* from Babylon made the journey with Ezra's group.

The *gemara* therefore derives the point from a different source entirely.

---

## Tel Melach Groups

### Genealogy Proof

The *gemara* turns to the verse: *ve'eleh ha'olim miTel Melach, Tel Charsha, Keruv, Addon ve'Immer* — these are those who came up from Tel Melach, Tel Charsha, and other locations. *Velo yachlu lehagid beit avotam vezar'am im Yisrael hem* — they could not say who their paternal household was, or, as Rashi explains, even from whom they were descended on their mother's side. They could not prove they were Jews at all. So already from the plain meaning of the verse, an entire contingent of the returning exiles could not establish their Israelite identity. They did not claim to be non-Jews; they simply had no way to prove they were Jewish.

### Tel Melach Derasha

Now the *gemara* offers its *derasha*. *Tel Melach* — the name means "mound of salt." These are people whose deeds resembled those of Sodom, which was overturned into a region of salt. According to certain *midrashim*, Sodom was associated with adultery; and so those compared to Sodom had committed adultery, which means their children were *mamzeirim*. So on the level of *derasha*, the first group — those from Tel Melach — represents *mamzeirim*, children of adulterous unions who cannot demonstrate legitimate Jewish descent.

### Shtukim

*Tel Charsha* — *charsha* evokes *cheresh*, silence. This refers to someone who calls out "Abba, Abba!" — who calls for his father — and his mother silences him. She cannot or will not reveal who the father is. That is a *shtuki* — someone whose paternity cannot be established, though his mother is known to be Jewish.

### Asufim

The verse continues: *velo yachlu lehagid beit avotam vezar'am im Yisrael hem* — they could not even establish whether they were from Israel. *Zehu ha'asufi* — this is the foundling, *shene'esaf min hashuk*, one gathered from the marketplace. A *shtuki* does not know his father but knows he is Jewish through his mother. The *asufi* does not even know who his mother was, and so cannot establish Jewish identity at all.

The *netinim*, it should be noted, appeared explicitly in an earlier verse in the passage, so their presence in the returning group is already accounted for. With these derivations, the *gemara* has now covered the complete list from the *mishnah*: *kohanim*, *levi'im*, *Yisrael*, *chalalim*, *geirim*, *charurim*, *mamzeirim*, *shtukim*, *asufim*, and *netinim*.

---

## Intermarriage Ethics

### Leopard Metaphor

The *gemara* now transitions into a more *aggadic* register, directly confronting the social reality described by the *mishnah*. Rabbi Abbahu expounds the phrase *Keruv Addon ve'Immer* from the same verse. *Amar Adon* — the Master, God, said: *yehu Yisrael lefanai chashuvim ke-Keruv* — Israel should be as precious to Me as the cherubim, as the angels. *Vehem samu atzmam ke-namer* — but they made themselves like the leopard, like an untrustworthy, spotted animal. They committed adultery and intermarried inappropriately.

An alternative version of the same *derasha* is also recorded: even though they made themselves like the leopard and acted in this disloyal way, *hen chashuvim lefanai ke-Keruv* — they are still precious before Me as the cherubim. God's love for Israel is not extinguished by their failures. Two readings of the same words, two very different theological endpoints.

### Unequal Marriage

Rabba bar bar Chana then cites a teaching with sharp moral force: *kol hanosei ishah she'einah hogenet lo* — anyone who marries a woman who is not fitting for him — here the context makes clear that "fitting" refers to social and genealogical standing, *yichus* — it is as though he plowed the entire world and sowed it with salt. The imagery is of destruction: you plow the earth to prepare it for seeds, then pour in salt to render it permanently barren. The marriage produces not growth but ruin. The *gemara* finds this reading in the same verse: *ve'eleh ha'olim miTel Melach* — *charsha*, the plowing; *melach*, the salt.

### Marrying for Money

Rabba bar Rav Adda citing Rav then extends this: *kol hanosei ishah leshum mamon* — anyone who marries a woman for money, that is, who accepts a lower *yichus* in exchange for wealth, *havyu lo banim she'einam hogenin* — will have children who are unworthy. The verse cited: *baHashem bagadu ki banim zarim yaladu* — they betrayed God because they bore foreign children. The word *zarim* points to the estrangement from proper lineage and character that results.

One might think the wealth at least is preserved even if the children turn out poorly. Not so. *Atah yochlem chodesh et chelkeihem* — in a month their portion will be consumed. And lest one imagine only the man's portion is lost: *chelkeihem* — both their portions, his and hers. And lest one think the destruction takes a long time: *chodesh* — a month. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: one month comes in and another goes out — in a single month cycle, everything is gone.

### Divine Judgment

The teaching escalates further. Rabba bar Rav Adda citing Rav Sala citing Rav Hamnuna: *kol hanosei ishah she'einah hogenet lo, Eliyahu kofato veHakadosh Baruch Hu rotze'ahu* — whoever marries a woman who is not fitting for him, Eliyahu binds him to the post and God Himself administers the lashes. A *braita* adds: on all such people, Eliyahu writes and God seals — *oi lo leposel et zar'o uvehapogem et mishpachto ulehanosei ishah she'einah hogenet lo* — woe to him who stigmatizes his offspring and degrades his family and marries a woman not fitting for him.

The choice of Eliyahu as the one who writes this writ is significant. Eliyahu is alive in heaven; he is the one who tells God, when asked what he is doing there, that he alone has remained faithful. He is the guardian of fidelity to the covenant. That it is Eliyahu who writes and God who signs reflects a cosmic seriousness attached to this offense.

### Kol Haposel

The *gemara* continues: *vechol haposel pasul ve'eino medaber bishvacho le'olam* — and anyone who stigmatizes others is himself invalid, and never speaks in praise of others. This appears to be part of the writ Eliyahu writes, or perhaps it is the *gemara*'s own observation — in either case, the one who goes around declaring others *pasul* is himself *pasul*, and is the sort of person who only ever criticizes, never praises. And Shmuel sharpens this into the maxim: *bemumo posel* — when someone invalidates another, it is because that very flaw is his own. The classic formulation that emerges is *kol haposel bemumo posel*: whoever disqualifies others shares their disqualification.

A reasonable question arises: does this mean that rabbis who investigate *yichus* and declare certain families *pesulim* are thereby themselves suspect? The answer is clearly not. The teaching addresses the layperson who spreads unfounded slurs, not the rabbinic authority who investigates and adjudicates. Ezra himself identified and categorized all these groups — such inquiry is legitimate and necessary. The *gemara* is concerned with the world in which status-anxiety is high and defamation is easy: someone who casually calls others *pasul* without evidence is revealing something about himself. But that is altogether different from the structured process of communal genealogical investigation.

---

## Nehardea Visitor

### Butcher Incident

The *gemara* now tells a vivid story that will wind its way back to *kol haposel bemumo posel*. A certain man from Nehardea came to Pumbedisa and went to the butcher to purchase meat. He was told to wait — they needed first to serve the attendant of Rav Yehuda bar Yechezkel. The visitor was outraged. He demanded to know who this "Yehuda bar Sheviskel" was to take precedence over him — mocking the name *Yechezkel* by substituting a derogatory term, which Rashi suggests may also carry the meaning of a glutton. When the people reported this to Rav Yehuda, Rav Yehuda placed the man in *nidui* — excommunication — for showing disrespect toward a *talmid chacham*.

They then told Rav Yehuda something further: this man is in the habit of calling people *avdi* — slaves — whenever he is offended. On the basis of this, Rav Yehuda proclaimed: this man is a slave. This declaration rests directly on the principle of *kol haposel bemumo posel*: if he constantly calls others slaves, it is because that stigma is his own.

### Court Summons

The visitor, now placed in *nidui* and declared a slave, was not prepared to let the matter rest. He summoned Rav Yehuda to stand before Rav Nachman's court in Nehardea. A writ of subpoena — a *pitka de'azmana* — was delivered to Rav Yehuda.

### Huna's Advice

Rav Yehuda brought this subpoena to Rav Huna and asked: *eizal o lo eizal* — should I go or not? Rav Huna replied that as a matter of principle, Rav Yehuda had no need to go — *mishum degavra raba at* — because Rav Yehuda was a greater authority than Rav Nachman, and arguably Rav Nachman was outside his proper jurisdiction. However, Rav Nachman was a son-in-law of the house of the *nasi*, and given the honor owed to that family, Rav Huna advised: go. The whole episode had begun as a dispute about respect for authority and precedence, and now that tension was being played out on a larger stage.

### Yehuda Arrives

Rav Yehuda arrived and found Rav Nachman building a *ma'aka* — a fence. Immediately, Rav Yehuda challenged him: does the Master not know the teaching of Rav Huna bar Idi citing Shmuel, that once a person is appointed *parnas al hatzibur* — a communal leader — it is forbidden for him to perform labor in the presence of three people? Rav Yehuda, famously a devoted transmitter of Shmuel's teachings, was wasting no time in demonstrating that Rav Nachman was not only of lower stature but was actively violating a ruling Rav Yehuda knew firsthand. Rav Nachman replied that he was only repairing a small break, minimizing what he was doing.

### Terminology Dispute

But Rav Yehuda immediately pivoted to something else. The word Rav Nachman had used for "fence" was *gundirisa* — an unusual, elevated-sounding term. Rav Yehuda asked: what is wrong with the Torah's word *ma'aka*, or the rabbinic term *mechitza*? Why use this strange word?

Rav Nachman then invited Rav Yehuda to sit, using the word *karpisa* for stool. Rav Yehuda responded: why not use *safsal*, which is the rabbinic term, or *itztaba*, which is what people commonly say? Rav Nachman offered fruit, calling it *estrunga*. Rav Yehuda shot back: Shmuel himself taught that anyone who says *estrunga* has a third of haughtiness in him — use either *esrog*, as the rabbis say, or *esroga*, as people say. Rav Nachman then offered a drink using the word *anvaga*. Rav Yehuda asked: why not *ispargos*, the rabbinic term, or *anfak*, the common word?

The pattern is consistent: Rav Yehuda is showing that at every turn, Rav Nachman is using inflated, affected language — putting on airs — while simultaneously conducting himself in ways unbecoming of his claimed authority. One listener suggested the opposite reading, that Rav Nachman was using common vernacular. But the *gemara*'s logic moves clearly in the other direction: Shmuel's statement that *estrunga* reflects haughtiness confirms that the vocabulary was the problem, not the simplicity.

### Women's Service

Rav Nachman then called for his daughter *Dunag* to pour wine for them. Rav Yehuda stopped him: Shmuel explicitly taught that one may not make use of a woman's services. Rav Nachman protested — she is a minor! Rav Yehuda replied: Shmuel said explicitly, *bein gedolah bein ketannah* — whether a grown woman or a minor.

Rav Nachman then tried a different tack. Perhaps Rav Yehuda would like to send his respects to Rav Nachman's wife, Yalta? Rav Yehuda replied: Shmuel taught *kol be'ishah ervah* — the voice of a woman is *ervah*. If she responds to my greeting I will hear her voice. Rav Nachman then suggested it could be done through an intermediary. Rav Yehuda: Shmuel taught one does not ask after the welfare of a woman even through an intermediary. Through her husband then? Rav Yehuda: Shmuel taught one does not ask after a woman's welfare at all, *klal* — categorically.

This last ruling prompted a challenge from Tosafot: the *malachim* asked *Ayeh Sarah ishtecha* — where is Sarah your wife? Tosafot's distinction, which the lecturer acknowledges is not entirely clear, appears to be between asking how a woman is doing (*she'ilat shalom*) and actively dispatching a message of good wishes — the former being permitted, the latter being what Shmuel prohibits. However this distinction is parsed, the *gemara* treats *kol be'ishah ervah* here as referring to the speaking voice. The *rishonim* note that this is not absolute: in a context where men and women are accustomed to speaking with one another, the speaking voice is not categorically *ervah* — which underscores the broader principle that these categories are contextually sensitive.

### Yalta's Intervention

At this point Yalta, Rav Nachman's wife, sent a message to her husband: dismiss the case and let this man go — *delo nishvach kishar amei ha'aretz* — otherwise Rav Yehuda would reduce Rav Nachman to the level of an ordinary *am ha'aretz*. Rav Yehuda was making Rav Nachman look incompetent at every exchange, and Yalta was sharp enough to see that this needed to end.

### Nachman's Capitulation

Rav Nachman now attempted to recover. He asked Rav Yehuda, *mai shayata demar hacha* — what brings you here? Rav Yehuda was taken aback: you sent me a subpoena! He produced the writ from his jacket and showed it. Rav Nachman responded: *hashta deshuta demar lo gamirna* — I cannot even follow your ordinary conversation, you are so far above me; do you think I would ever send you a subpoena to a *beis din*? *Chas veshalom*, I would never presume to do such a thing!

Nonetheless, since Rav Yehuda had already made the journey, Rav Nachman said they should hear the case — *ki heichi delo lemru machanfe rabbanan ahadadi* — so people should not say that rabbis merely flatter and show favoritism to one another. Rav Nachman asked: why did you put this man in *nidui*? Because he caused pain to a messenger of the rabbis. Why not lashes? Rav responded to similar offenses with lashes; Rav Yehuda explained that *nidui* is actually a more significant and lasting censure. Why did you declare him a slave? *Deragil dekari inshi avdei* — because he habitually calls others slaves. *Vetani kol haposel pasul ve'eino medaber bishvacha le'olam, ve'amar Shmuel bemumo posel* — and the teaching of Shmuel is: when someone disqualifies others, it is because that flaw is his own.

Rav Nachman pressed back: Shmuel's teaching, one might say, means only to be *suspect* of such a person — not to *proclaim* him a slave outright. Is actually declaring someone a slave not taking things too far?

### Hasmonean Claim

While they were still debating this very point, the litigant himself stepped forward and said to Rav Yehuda: you had the audacity to call me a slave? *De'atina mibeit Chashmonai malka* — I descend from the royal Hasmonean house!

### Slave Verdict

Rav Yehuda replied without hesitation: Shmuel taught — *kol de'amar mibeit Chashmonai ka'atina avda hu* — anyone who claims descent from the Hasmonean house is a slave. The entire Hasmonean line was wiped out; the one who assumed their name and perpetuated it was Herod — *Hordos* — who was a slave. So by claiming Hasmonean descent, the man has only confirmed the verdict. The story will continue tomorrow, but Rav Yehuda has, in every exchange, thoroughly demonstrated his authority over Rav Nachman.

---

---

# Kiddushin 71

## Chashmonai Testimony

### Slave Declaration

The daf begins in the middle of 71b, six lines down from the top of the wide text, at the word *Chashmonai*. We are in the midst of a narrative involving Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna, centered on a case of *din Torah* that arose when a certain man came to Pumbedita, insulted Rav Yehuda's attendant, and was himself known to speak disparagingly of others — calling people slaves. In response, Rav Yehuda declared this man to be a slave. The broader backdrop of this story is the principle of *kol haposel bemumo posel* — one who invalidates others does so because of his own defect.

As established in the previous daf, Rav Huna challenged Rav Yehuda's declaration, arguing that even if Shmuel taught *kol haposel bemumo posel*, this teaching should at most make one *choshesh* — cautiously alert — but not empower a formal declaration of slavery. At that very moment, the man in question entered the room and declared indignantly that he was a descendant of *Beit Chashmonai*. Rav Yehuda seized on this: precisely as I said! Because Shmuel himself taught that anyone who claims descent from *Beit Chashmonai* is a slave, since the original Hasmonean dynasty was entirely killed off, and it was only Herod — an Edomite slave — who remained and identified with that lineage. Therefore, any contemporary claim to Hasmonean descent is itself evidence of slave ancestry.

### Kol Haposel Teaching

The Gemara now raises a pointed challenge to Rav Yehuda's reliance on this teaching. Rav Huna said to him: do you not hold by the principle that Rav Abba cited in the name of Rav, who cited it in the name of Rav Huna — who cited it in the name of Rav? This is already somewhat striking: Rav Huna is quoting a teaching transmitted in his own name, from Rav, the classic *bar plugta* of Shmuel. The teaching states: *kol talmid chacham shemoreh halacha uva* — any *talmid chacham* who advances a new legal ruling, *im kodem maaseh amra shomin lo* — if he taught it before the relevant case arose, he is believed. But *im lav ein shomin lo* — if he produces the ruling only at the moment when the case conveniently arises before him, we are somewhat suspicious of it.

This is a remarkable piece of Talmudic skepticism. The Gemara acknowledges that a scholar might fabricate a tradition in the name of his teacher precisely to respond to a case at hand. In our story, the suspicion is compounded: Rav Yehuda was not merely citing a teaching that happened to be relevant — he was invoking it specifically to vindicate his own prior ruling. He declared the man a slave, and now he produces a teaching of Shmuel that justifies that declaration. One might fairly ask: why have we never heard this teaching before?

### Rav Matna Confirms

To this challenge, Rav Yehuda responded: *ha'ika Rav Masna dekay kivasay* — Rav Matna holds like me. Rav Matna can corroborate that this is indeed a teaching of Shmuel. It then happened that Rav Matna, who had not been in Nehardea — the location of these proceedings — for the past thirteen years, arrived that very day. *Hahu yoma* — by pure coincidence, on that exact day, he came to Nehardea.

Rav Yehuda then had to prompt Rav Matna without leading him, and he did so elegantly: do you remember what Shmuel taught *ki kachada* — on that occasion when he was stepping onto the ferry, one foot still on the bank and one foot already on the vessel? The memorable physical circumstance made the teaching verifiable and distinctive. Rav Matna confirmed: *hachi amar Shmuel* — Shmuel said: *kol d'omar midebeis Chashmonai moga chasina avda hu* — anyone who says he descends from the royal house of the Hasmoneans is a slave.

### Woman on Roof

Rav Matna then provided the reason for Shmuel's ruling. He recalled that after Herod's violent overthrow of the Hasmonean house, only one young woman remained from the original dynasty. When she saw what Herod had done — that the entire family had been slaughtered — she went up to the roof, *v'ramya kala*, and called out: let it be known that anyone who claims descent from the house of *Chashmonai* is a slave, for there is no one left. And then, *nafla m'igra umesa* — she fell from the roof and died. With this, the entire Hasmonean lineage was extinguished, and Herod — the Edomite slave — was the only one who identified himself with that heritage.

Rav Yehuda had now been vindicated on all fronts.

### Ketuvot Torn Up

*Achrizu alei d'avda hu* — they announced about this man that he was indeed a slave, exactly as Rav Yehuda had originally declared. The consequences were severe: *hahu yoma akran kama ksuva beNardaa* — on that day, many *ketubot* were torn up in Nehardea.

Rashi explains that the members of this man's family, having now been identified as slaves, could not have contracted valid *kiddushin*, and so those marriages required invalidation. There is an obvious problem, however: the man's testimony applies only to himself — there is no independent, objective evidence that implicates his family members. How could their marriages be invalidated on the basis of his own admission? One commentator resolves this by suggesting that the *ketubot* were torn up for a different reason: he had served as a signatory on those documents, and now that he had been declared *pasul*, his testimony was rendered invalid, requiring the documents to be redrawn. Yet the narrative suggests something more sweeping.

As Rav Yehuda departed Nehardea to return to Pumbedita, the families whose marriages had been disrupted ran after him intending to stone him — literally, stones were in their hands. He turned to them and said: *ei shtiku shtiku* — if you stay silent, stay silent. But if you continue making a fuss, *maglina alaichu* — I will reveal something about you that is even worse. What could be worse than being declared slaves? Shmuel, he said, also taught: *tarti zarayasa ika beNardaa* — there are two families in Nehardea, one called the house of the dove and one called the house of the raven — *v'simanach tamei tamei tahor tahor* — the impure family bears the name of the impure bird, and the pure family bears the name of the pure bird. Those descended from the raven are of invalid lineage — *mamzerim*, slaves, or the like.

How exactly this threat made things worse if they were already declared slaves is somewhat unclear from the text; perhaps the formal *halachic* ruling against the wider family had not yet been made and remained merely a suspicion. Regardless, the message landed. *Shadu alahu rigma* — they threw down the stones they had intended to hurl at him, and so many stones fell into the *Nehar Malka* that they formed a dam in the river.

---

## Invalid Families

### Announced Invalidities

The foregoing story raises an important question: if Rav Yehuda knew about the invalidity of these Nehardean families, why had he been withholding the information? We will return shortly to the principle of *mishpacha keivan shenitm'ah nitm'ah* — once a family's lineage has been submerged, one leaves it submerged. That principle stands in tension with what we have just witnessed. In the present story, the declaration of slavery came only as a response to the man's own behavior — *kol haposel bemumo posel* — and it happened to be borne out. Nevertheless, the Gemara now pivots in the opposite direction, moving into a series of proactive public announcements about people and places of problematic lineage.

*Machriz Rav Yehuda* — Rav Yehuda publicly announced, according to one textual tradition in Pumbedita and according to another in Nehardea: *Ada veYonatan avdi* — these two individuals are slaves; *Yehuda bar Pappa mamzer* — this person is a *mamzer*; *Bati bar Tuvia berama srucha deshakil gitei* — this wealthy man, universally assumed to be of excellent *yichus*, was actually offered a *shtar shichrur*, a deed of manumission, but refused to accept it because of his pride in his high social standing. Nonetheless, he is halachically a slave. Here Rav Yehuda is not merely responding to a case — he is proactively labeling individuals as *pasul*.

### Rava's Declarations

*Machriz Rava beMechuza* — Rava similarly made public announcements in Mechuza, his own city: *Belai Danai Talai Malai Zagai kulam lepsul* — these families are all of invalid status, whether *mamzer*, *avdus*, or some other form of disqualification. Rav Yehuda further identified whole towns: *Gvai* is a corruption of *Givonai* — the inhabitants are really *Givonim*, of problematic lineage. *Durnunisa* is *Darei Netinai* — the village of *Netinim*. The *Netinim* and the *Givonim* are the same. And Rav Yosef added that a suburb of Pumbedita, *Beikvei*, was entirely composed of slaves.

These broad geographic labelings are deeply troubling, moving beyond the identification of individuals to the invalidation of entire communities. The Gemara draws a parallel to the actions of Ezra, who similarly identified and sorted the *psulim* when he returned from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael.

### Slave Intermarriage

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *arba meos avadim, ve'amrei lei arba alafim avadim hayu lo lePishchar ben Imar* — four hundred slaves, and some say four thousand slaves, belonged to a man named Pishchar ben Imar. *Vekulam nitmu bikehuna* — all of them intermarried among *kohanim*. Rashi explains that as slaves of a *kohen*, they were permitted to eat *terumah* and were thus able to pass themselves off as *kohanim*, eventually intermarrying into priestly families. The practical consequence is alarming: a *kohen* we encounter today might actually descend from one of these slaves. But how far does that suspicion extend — should we be suspicious of every *kohen*?

The Gemara offers a suggested marker: *vekol kohen sheyesh bo azus panim eino ela mehem* — any *kohen* who displays brazenness is probably from among these slaves and is not a legitimate *kohen*.

### Abaye's Pushback

Abaye pushes back on this, first noting practically that all of these slave-descended pseudo-*kohanim* can be found in a particular position of authority in a specific locale — they are identifiable. But he then challenges the underlying principle directly. This view, that brazenness is a marker of illegitimate priestly descent, *pliga d'Rabbi Elazar* — contradicts the position of Rabbi Elazar. Rabbi Elazar taught: *im ra'isa kohen b'azus metzach al taharher acharav* — if you see a *kohen* who acts with brazenness, do not suspect thereby that he is an illegitimate *kohen*. The proof is from the verse *v'amcha k'mrivai kohen* — your people are like those who contend with a *kohen*, which indicates that a *kohen* can be contentious; it takes two parties to have a quarrel. So brazenness alone cannot be taken as evidence of disqualified lineage.

We find ourselves, then, in a state of tension: a great deal of labeling and suspecting, with only a small degree of pushback thus far — though the pushback will grow considerably.

---

## Aggada on Lineage

### Divine Presence & Yichus

The Gemara now turns to *aggadic* material bearing on the themes of genealogy and the Divine Presence. Rav Avin bar Rav Adda said in the name of Rav: *kol hanosei ishah she'eino hogenes lo* — anyone who marries a woman of lesser lineage than himself, *kshe'hakadosh baruch hu mashreh shechinaso maid al kol hashvatim v'ein maid alav* — when God causes His *Shechina* to dwell among the people, He testifies on behalf of all the *shevatim* but will not testify about or identify with that family. The verse cited is *shivtei Yah edus l'Yisrael* — the tribes of God, testimony to Israel. The *Shechina* gives testimony about Israel only when they are truly *shivtei Yah*, when the tribal and family structures are properly maintained and not adulterated.

A subtle question arises: does "adulterated" here refer to marrying someone of inferior but still halachically valid status — in which case this *aggadah* is making a sweeping statement about social hierarchy — or does it refer to marrying someone of formally invalid status, a *mamzer* or slave, who would genuinely disqualify the family line? Given the immediate context of the discussion about *mamzeirim* and *avdus*, the latter reading seems more likely, but the text does not foreclose the former.

### Shechina Dwelling

Rabbi Chama in the name of Rabbi Chanina sharpens this further: *kshe'hakadosh baruch hu mashreh shechinaso, ein mashreh ela al mishpachos meyuchasos shebeYisrael* — when God causes His *Shechina* to rest, it rests only upon families of distinguished lineage within Israel. The verse is from Jeremiah: *ba'eis hahi neum Hashem eheyeh l'Elokim l'chol mishpachos Yisrael* — at that time, says God, I will be a God to all the *mishpachos* of Israel. Notably, the verse does not say *l'chol Yisrael* but *l'chol mishpachos* — to all the families, meaning those who have preserved their family distinctions and *yichus*. This is a stronger statement than the previous one; here the *Shechina* does not merely withhold its testimony, but actively does not dwell except upon families of recognized lineage.

### Native vs Convert

Rabbah bar Rav Huna draws a distinction between a native-born Israelite and a *ger*: *zo ma'alah yesh bein Yisrael l'geirim* — there is a level of superiority that the native-born Jew holds over the convert. When Scripture speaks about Israel, it says *v'hayisi lahem l'Elokim v'heimah yihyu li l'am* — I will be for them a God, and they will be for Me a nation. The relationship with God is stated first; it preexists and draws Israel near. When Scripture addresses converts, it says: *mi hu zeh arav es libo l'higeshal elai v'hayisem li l'am v'anochi eheyeh lachem l'Elokim* — whoever stirs his heart to come close to Me, you will be for Me a nation and I will be for you a God. Here the initiative must come from the convert; the divine relationship follows rather than precedes their approach.

Rashi reads this as descriptive: the native-born Jew is born into an existing covenantal relationship that draws him naturally toward God, while the *ger* must first generate the motivation from within himself. One might fairly read this as an extraordinary tribute to the spiritual achievement of the convert — the initiative required is immense. However, the Gemara's framing is plainly hierarchical, and it cannot easily be read otherwise.

### Converts as Scabs

Rabbi Chelbo makes a striking and harsh statement: *kashim gerim le'Yisrael kesappachat* — converts are as difficult for Israel as a scab. The verse is *venilva hager aleihem venispachu al beit Yaakov* — the stranger will cleave to them and be added onto the house of Jacob. The word *venispachu* is connected exegetically to *sappachat*, the skin affliction mentioned among the forms of *tzara'at*.

What does this mean? Rashi, working within the context of tractate Yevamot, explains that converts are sometimes insufficiently conversant with the tradition and may lead others astray. Tosafot, however, connects the statement to the immediately preceding discussion: if the *Shechina* dwells only upon *mishpachos meyuchasos*, then the presence of *geirim* among Israel — who do not have the same chain of *yichus* — diminishes that quality. This is an extremely harsh reading of the concept of *yichus*, one that operates not merely as a halachic category but as a marker of social and spiritual hierarchy.

Tosafot then cites, though without attribution, an interpretation by one Rav Avraham Hager — a man who was himself a convert yet whose interpretation made its way into Tosafot — who read the statement in precisely the opposite spirit: because converts are new to the tradition and approach it with passion rather than complacency, they put to shame the native-born Jews who are not so *medakdek bemitzvot*. This is a beautiful inversion, and Tosafot records it seriously.

There is no question that this entire sugyah on *yichus* sits in considerable tension with a more egalitarian ethos, and equally with other Talmudic passages that speak in glowing terms about *geirim* and invoke the commandments of *ve'ahavtem et hager* and *kager ka'ezrach*. Both currents are present in the Talmud, and the tension between them is real.

---

## Keep It Hidden

### Money Purifies

Continuing at the bottom of amud bet, Rabbi Chama bar Chanina teaches: *kshe'hakadosh baruch hu metaher shvatim* — when God comes to purify the tribes, *shivto shel Levi metaher techila* — He begins with the tribe of Levi. The prooftext is from Malachi: *veyashev metzaref umetaher kesef vetiher es bnei Levi v'zikak osam k'zahav v'chakesef* — He will sit as one who smelts and purifies silver, and He will purify the sons of Levi, refining them like gold and silver, and they will then be able to bring offerings to God in righteousness.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, however, turns this passage on its head: *kesef metaher mamzeirim* — it is money that purifies *mamzeirim*. This is a striking inversion of the imagery. The verse's metaphor of silver purification is reread not as an analogy for genealogical purification but as a literal reference to wealth. Rashi explains the reference: wealthy individuals — for the sake of money — married into the tribe of Levi despite having invalid status, and the point Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is making is not that money literally confers kashrut, but rather that once people have intermarried, the genealogical record is absorbed and everything becomes *kasher* by virtue of being submerged. That is the operative mechanism of purification — not the money itself, but the intermingling that money enabled.

The Ri"f, however, reads *kesef metaher mamzeirim* more literally and more cleverly: the halachic mechanism by which a *mamzer* can produce non-*mamzer* offspring is through marriage to a *shifcha* — a female slave — whose child, being a slave, can then be freed and thereby exits the status of *mamzer* entirely. The money involved is the purchase price of the slave. This is an elegant halachic reading.

### Mixed Family Rule

Rabbi Yitzchak draws out the implication of the verse's closing phrase — *v'hayu l'Hashem magishei mincha bitzdaka*, they will bring offerings to God in righteousness: *tzadaka asa hakadosh baruch hu im Yisrael* — God performed an act of charity for Israel — *shemishpacha shenitme'ah nitme'ah* — that once a family has been submerged into the general population, it remains submerged. This is the principle of *mishpacha shenitme'ah nitme'ah*, written with an *ayin*, meaning merged rather than defiled. God's act of righteousness consists precisely in not requiring Israel to investigate and uproot every genealogical impurity that has been absorbed into the community. If people present themselves as *Levi'im* or *Yisraelim*, and their intermarriage has made it impossible to know otherwise, they are accepted as such.

With this, the Gemara begins to shift explicitly against the mode of proactive identification that characterized the earlier part of the *sugya*. The two tendencies — publicly labeling *psulim* on the one hand, and accepting the status quo on the other — have now both been articulated, and the latter is gaining ground.

---

## Boundaries & Assumpt (II)

### Shmuel's Teaching

The Gemara introduces a teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel that returns to the geographic framework established earlier in the *perek*: *kol ha'aratzos issa l'Eretz Yisrael* — all other lands are like *issa*, dough, compared to Eretz Yisrael. The contrast drawn earlier was that when Ezra departed from Bavel, he left it like *solet nekiyah* — refined, sifted flour, with the bran entirely removed — meaning that all those of problematic lineage had departed with him, and what remained in Bavel was pure. All other lands lack this quality; they are like dough, mixed and unpurified. But *v'Eretz Yisrael issa l'Bavel* — Eretz Yisrael is itself like dough compared to Bavel. Even Eretz Yisrael, which contains *psulim* in known and recorded form, has a less certain pedigree than Bavel overall.

In the time of Rabbi, the question arose whether to reverse this ranking — to say that Bavel had perhaps deteriorated over time and should be considered *issa* relative to Eretz Yisrael. Rabbi responded sharply: *kotzim atem matilim li bein einai* — you are placing thorns in my eyes. Since Rabbi was descended from Hillel, and Hillel came from Bavel, any downgrading of Babylonian *yichus* would undermine Rabbi's own genealogical standing and his claim of descent from the house of David. Accordingly, he deferred the matter to Rabbi Chanina bar Chama, who engaged those raising the challenge and reported: *kach mikubalni mi'Rabbi Yishmael be'Rabbi Yossi she'amar mishum aviv* — this is the tradition I received from Rabbi Yishmael in the name of his father: all lands are dough compared to Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael is dough compared to Bavel. The tradition was thus confirmed independently, which was important precisely because Rabbi himself could not have reported it without appearing self-interested.

### Diversion Strategy

A parallel episode occurred in the time of Rabbi Pinchas. When the same attempt arose — to reclassify Bavel as inferior to Eretz Yisrael — Rabbi Pinchas devised a remarkable stratagem. He told his servants: when I say two things in the *beit hamidrash*, rush me out immediately, carry me out on my stretcher and run. He went in and announced: *ein shechita l'of min haTorah* — the requirement of ritual slaughter for birds is not Biblically mandated; it is only rabbinic. This is a provocative ruling that does not represent the final *halacha*, but it was sufficiently surprising to throw the assembled scholars into a state of confusion and discussion. While they were processing this startling claim, he quickly added: *kol ha'aratzot issa l'Eretz Yisrael v'Eretz Yisrael issa l'Bavel* — and then his servants ran him out on the stretcher before anyone could ask follow-up questions.

The scholars pursued him but could not catch up. When they sat back down and began investigating which families in Eretz Yisrael might be problematic — since Rabbi Pinchas had implied that there were some *psulim* there — they found themselves approaching dangerous territory. *Ad she'higiu l'sakana* — until they reached a point of danger: Rashi explains that they began discovering that some very prominent families might have questionable *yichus*, at which point they realized it was better to stop looking. *U'pirshu* — and they ceased.

---

## Keep It Hidden (II)

### Rabbi Yochanan Stays Sil…

Rabbi Yochanan stated, taking an oath by the *Beit HaMikdash*: *b'yadeinu hu* — it is within our capacity to identify certain families of invalid lineage — *aval mah e'eseh she'gdolei hador nitme'u bo* — but what can I do, since great figures of this generation have already been intermingled with those families? To reveal the invalidity would call into question the *yichus* of major communal figures. And so Rabbi Yochanan kept silent. This is the clearest expression yet of the principle of *mishpacha shenitme'ah nitme'ah*: even when knowledge exists, the decision is made not to deploy it. Rabbi Yochanan *savar lah k'Rabbi Yitzchak* — held in accordance with Rabbi Yitzchak, who taught explicitly: *mishpacha shenitmeah nitmeah* — once a family has been merged in, it stays merged in.

### Forced Status

Abaye notes a corroborating *baraita* from tractate Eduyot: there was a family called *Beit Hatzerifah* on the far side of the Jordan which was actually of valid lineage, but a powerful man named Ben Tziyon used his authority — *b'zroa*, with force — to get everyone to treat them as *pasul*. Conversely, there was another family that was genuinely *pasul*, and Ben Tziyon again used his power to force people to treat them as *kasher*. The *Mishnah* then states: cases like these, *Eliyahu ba l'tamei u'l'taher l'rachek u'l'karev* — Eliyahu will come to set right, declaring the unjustly invalidated to be valid and the unjustly validated to be *pasul*.

The Gemara comments: this *mishnah* about Eliyahu refers specifically to *d'yedian* — situations that are known to be problematic and have been handled improperly. But *aval mishpacha shenitmeah* — when a family's invalid lineage has genuinely been absorbed and lost to public knowledge — *nitmeah*, it stays that way, and no rectification is expected.

### Secret Traditions

A *baraita* then teaches: *oda cheres haysa v'lo ratzu chachamim l'galosa* — there was another invalid family that the Sages did not wish to publicize. Nevertheless, the Sages transmitted this information to their children and students *pa'am achas b'shavua* — once every seven years; some say twice every seven years, so that some record would survive until the time of Eliyahu HaNavi.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rules that the preferable position is once every seven years — the less spoken about such matters, the better. The preference for restraint is reinforced by a *baraita*: if a person says, "I hereby take upon myself *nezirut* on the condition that I will not reveal genealogical problems," we say *yehei nazir v'lo yigaleh mishpachos* — let him be a *nazir* and not reveal the family information. Rather than allowing him to choose between the *nezirut* and disclosure, we direct him to accept the *nezirut* and remain silent.

At this juncture, the Gemara draws an illuminating parallel. Rabbah bar Bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the four-letter Divine name — *shem ben arba otiyos* — the Sages transmitted to their students *pa'am achas b'shavua*, once every seven years; some say twice every seven years. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak again prefers the position of once every seven years, deriving support from the verse *zeh shemi le'olam* — this is My name forever — which is written *le'aleim*, suggesting it should remain hidden. The parallel is pointed: just as the transmission of God's secret name is hedged with restraint and solemnity, so too the transmission of genealogical secrets about invalid families.

Rava once sought to teach the four-letter name publicly to his students. A certain elder stopped him by quoting *le'aleim ksiv* — it is written to be concealed.

Rav Avina raises an apparent contradiction: one verse says *zeh shemi le'olam* — this is My name forever (which we read *le'illum*, hidden), while another says *zeh zikhri* — this is how I am to be remembered. God's response, as it were, is: *lo kshe'ani nikhtav ani nikra* — I am not read the way I am written. I am written with the *yud-keh-vav-keh* but read as *Adon*. The written name is for concealment; the spoken name is for public invocation. The name itself — *shemi* — is *le'aleim*, hidden. The name by which I am addressed — *zikhri* — is known.

The Gemara then describes a progression. Originally, the twelve-letter name of God was transmitted to everyone. Once those who were insufficiently guarded became more numerous and the name began to be misused, it was transmitted only to the *tzenu'in shebekehuna* — the particularly modest among the *kohanim*. These would weave the name into their melodic recitation during *Birkat Kohanim*, blending it into the singing so that the other *kohanim* — who were simultaneously stretching out the four-letter name — could not discern it.

Rabbi Tarfon testified personally: once, when he accompanied his maternal uncle to the *duchan* for *Birkat Kohanim*, he tilted his ear toward the *kohen gadol* — or perhaps, given the chronological difficulties with this testimony, toward a senior *kohen* — and overheard him weaving in the twelve-letter name during the melody.

The forty-two letter name — still more sublime and potent — was transmitted only under stringent conditions: the recipient must be *tzanua* — modest and trustworthy with secrets — *v'anav* — humble — *v'omed bechatzi yamav* — having reached at least the midpoint of life (approximately 35, assuming a lifespan of 70) — *v'eino ko'es* — not given to anger — *v'eino mishtaker* — not prone to intoxication — and *v'eino ma'amid al midotav* — one who does not press his claims insistently when wronged. The reason for these requirements, as Rashi explains, is that such a name carries enormous power to do damage, and a person who cannot control his temper or his drinking might use it to curse another. The reward for those who know the name and guard it with purity is that they become *ahuv lemala* — beloved above — *venichmad lemata* — cherished below — and *nochal shenei olamim*, inheriting both this world and the world to come.

---

## Boundaries & Assumpt (II)

### Ze'iri's Avoidance

Shmuel said in the name of an elder: *Bavel bechezkat ksheira omedet ad sheyivada lecha bameh nifsala* — Bavel stands in the presumption of being kasher unless you know specifically on what basis a given person became *pasul*.
