By contrast, other lands — *bechezkat pasul hein omdot ad sheyivada lecha bamah nichsharah* — stand in the presumption of invalidity unless you know how the person became *kasher*. Eretz Yisrael occupies a middle position: *muchzak lepasul pasul, muchzak lekasher kasher* — if known to be *pasul*, they are *pasul*; if known to be *kasher*, they are *kasher*.

This last formulation seems internally contradictory — it establishes no default. The Gemara asks: *hagufei kashya* — is this not self-contradictory? The statement *muchzak lepasul pasul* implies that absent that knowledge the person is *kasher*, making *kasher* the default; yet *muchzak lekasher kasher* implies the opposite. Rav Huna bar Tachalifa resolves this in the name of Rav: *kan lehasi'o isha kan lehotzi isha miyado* — one clause speaks to permitting him to marry, and the other speaks to compelling a divorce after the fact. Before marriage to someone of distinguished lineage, a man from Eretz Yisrael must establish his *yichus*; but once married, only demonstrated *psul* can undo it. Rashi and Tosafot both connect this to the specific case of marrying into a family of elevated status, not to ordinary marriages — a normal person is not required to prove his lineage before marrying.

Rav Yosef adds: *kol sheyichaso beVavel masi'in lo isha* — anyone whose lineage identifies him as Babylonian, one may marry him off to a woman of good *yichus*. However, *ve'idna de'ika rama'ei chaishinan* — now that there are deceivers who can learn to speak Babylonian even without having Babylonian origins, we are suspicious and this linguistic marker can no longer be relied upon.

The Gemara now relates the story of Ze'iri, who persistently avoided Rabbi Yochanan — because Rabbi Yochanan wished to give him his daughter in marriage. Rabbi Yochanan was from Eretz Yisrael; Ze'iri was from Bavel. One day, they were traveling together and came to a stream. Ze'iri, as the devoted student, carried Rabbi Yochanan on his shoulders through the water. Rabbi Yochanan, frustrated by the persistent evasion, said to him: our Torah of Eretz Yisrael is good enough for you — *oraitin kesheira* — but our daughters are not? What is your reasoning? Are you relying on the *Mishnah* that teaches that ten categories of lineage made the ascent from Bavel with Ezra — *kohanim*, *Levi'im*, *Yisraelim*, and so forth — and inferring therefrom that Bavel is genealogically purer than Eretz Yisrael?

But one cannot infer this from the *Mishnah*, Rabbi Yochanan argues. *Atu Kahanei Levi'ei ve-Yisra'ei kulu siliku?* Just because *psulim* came with Ezra, the *Mishnah* also states that *kohanim*, *levi'im*, and *yisraelim* came with him — but that does not mean they all left Bavel. There are still *kohanim*, *levi'im*, and *yisraelim* in Bavel. And correspondingly, *psulim* also remain in Bavel. You are no better than we are.

The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan had in that moment forgotten the teaching of Rabbi Elazar: *lo ala Ezra miBavel ad she'asah k'soles nekiyah v'alah* — Ezra did not ascend from Bavel until he had made it like refined flour, meaning he specifically removed all the *psulim*, even if he did not remove all the legitimate Israelites.

Ulla came to Pumbedita and visited Rav Yehuda. He observed that Rav Yehuda's son Rabbi Yitzchak was already grown but had not yet married. Rav Yehuda explained: *mi yadana me'heicha yinasiv* — I do not know where to marry him off, because the question of *yichus* is so fraught. Ulla pushed back vigorously: *atu anan mi yad'inan me'heicha kasina?* — Do we even know where we ourselves come from? Perhaps we descend from women who were violated during the *Churban HaBayis*, as the verse in Lamentations attests: *nashim b'Tzion inu b'sulos b'arei Yehuda*. Rav Yehuda responded: but such a union would still produce a *kasher* child halachically. Ulla countered: what about other disqualifying unions that occurred among the first Temple generation — the Gemara cites the verse *ha'shochvim al mitos shen u'sruchim al arsosam*, which Rabbi Abbahu interprets not as a reference to mere indecency but as describing widespread wife-swapping — eating and drinking together, pushing beds together, exchanging wives — *u'masrichim arsoseihem b'shichvas zera she'eina shelahem*, and thereby filling their beds with semen that was not theirs. Given such pervasive adultery in the generation of the first Temple, there are certainly *mamzeirim* embedded in many Jewish family trees. So how does Rav Yehuda know that anyone is pure enough for his son?

### Silence as Yichus

Rav Yehuda acknowledged the point and asked: so what should I do if I still want to find a suitable match? The answer given is: *zil basar shtikusa* — follow the families that are quiet, that do not argue and pick fights. Rashi explains this as based on the premise — whether understood genetically or sociologically — that families of compromised lineage tend toward contentiousness, either as a character trait passed down through their ancestry or as a result of having historically been marginalized by society, cultivating a defensive and argumentative culture.

The people of Eretz Yisrael used a similar method of investigation: *ki matzu bei srei bahadi hadadei* — when two families were in dispute, they would watch to see which one was first willing to be silent, to step back and not press the fight. *Hai meyuchas tefei* — the one more willing to stop fighting has the better *yichus*. What begins as an index of *yichus* becomes, practically speaking, a direct focus on *middos*. The inquiry about lineage has been quietly displaced by an inquiry about character.

Rav states: *shetikutei deBavel hainu yichusa* — the silence of Bavel is itself its *yichus*. The willingness to not fight is not merely a sign of good lineage; it is what the lineage actually means in practice. When challenged that Rav himself went to investigate a certain family, the Gemara clarifies: he did not investigate their genealogical records; he investigated whether they were *shtiki* — non-argumentative. That was his method of verification.

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *im ra'ita shenei bnei adam shemitgarim zeh ba'zeh, shemetz pasul yesh be'echad mehen* — if you see two people perpetually feuding, there is a scintilla of invalidity in one of them, *v'ein manichin oto lidabek bechavertah* — and from Heaven, they are made to quarrel so that the families should not intermarry. It is worth noting that this logic works better if the concern is something like a hereditary disease — both families are carriers and should not intermingle — than if the concern is purely about lineage status, where the problem would apply equally to any marriage partner. Nevertheless, the principle stands: contentiousness is treated as a sign, if not a symptom, of underlying genealogical trouble.

### Bavel Bri'ah

Rav Pappa savya said in the name of Rav: *Bavel bri'ah* — Bavel is healthy, meaning its *yichus* is sound. *Meshan mitah* — this neighboring region is dead, meaning virtually all its inhabitants are of suspect lineage — *mamzeirim* and the like. *Madai mi'idi cholah* — Media is sick, meaning mostly *kasher* but with some *psulim* present. *Ve'Eilam hi goseset* — Elam is like one in the final stages of dying, meaning mostly *pasul* with some *kasher* present. The difference between *cholah* and *goseset* is simply probabilistic: most sick people live, while most of those on their deathbed die.

---

## Geographic Limits

### East/West Limits

The Gemara now turns to the question of the precise geographic boundaries of Bavel — a necessary question given that Bavel has been established as the gold standard of *yichus*. *Ad heichan hi Bavel?* Rav says: until the *Nahar Azak* on the east. Shmuel says: until the *Nahar Yoni*. Rashi identifies this as the discussion of the eastern boundary. The primary territory of Bavel is understood to be bounded by the Tigris and the Euphrates — *bein shenei neharot*, between the two rivers — but the question here is how far the recognized region extends beyond those two rivers in each cardinal direction.

### Northern Limits

Going north along the Tigris: Rav says until *Bagda* and *Avna*. Shmuel says until *Mushchani* — but not including *Mushchani* itself. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba then says in the name of Shmuel: *Mushchani harei hi keGolah* — Mushchani is like *Golah*. In this context, *Golah* is not exile in the pejorative sense but rather a name for Pumbedita, the city most closely associated with purity of *yichus*. So Mushchani is treated as having the status of Pumbedita — genuine Babylonian *yichus*.

### Euphrates Limits

Going north along the Euphrates: Rav says until *Akra deTulbanki*. Shmuel says until the bridge of *Perat*. Rabbi Yochanan says until the crossing of *Gizma*.

Abaye, and some say Rav Yosef, cursed Rav's position for extending the boundary too far north. One might ask: why curse Rav and not Shmuel, whose position went even farther north? The answer given is that the curse applied to Rav *and certainly* to Shmuel — the curser was criticizing those who extended the valid boundary too far, and Shmuel's more expansive position was included by implication.

Alternatively, there is no contradiction at all: when Shmuel made his ruling, the bridge of *Perat* was actually located further south than its current position. The Persians subsequently moved it northward. *Ha'idna hu de'illyuyei Parsa'ei* — it is only now that the Persians have situated it further north, but Shmuel's original designation referred to the lower location, which was actually less expansive than Rav's.

Abaye asked Rav Yosef: what about the western side of the Euphrates — how far east into that territory does the Bavel zone extend? Rav Yosef understood the question to be about the town of *Biram*, located to the east of the *Perat*. He answered: *meyuchasei dePumbedita miBiram nasvei* — people of distinguished *yichus* from Pumbedita used to marry women from *Biram*. So *Biram* is fully within the acceptable zone.

Rav Papa states: *kemachloket leyuchasin kach machloket legittin* — the same disagreement that governs the parameters of Bavel for purposes of *yuchasin* also governs the parameters of Bavel for *gittin*, specifically regarding whether a messenger delivering a *get* from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael must declare *bifanai nechtam* — it was signed in my presence. Since Bavel was as conversant in *halacha* as Eretz Yisrael, this declaration was unnecessary within those borders.

Rav Yosef disagrees: the debate applies only to *yuchasin*. For *gittin*, everyone agrees the boundary is the second lake of the bridge — *Arva Tinyana deGishra* — a known, specific location.

### Chavil Yama

Rami bar Abba teaches: *Chavil Yama techla deBavel* — *Chavil Yama* is the *techeiles*, the finest quality, of Bavel. And within *Chavil Yama*, the cities of *Shunya* and *Guvya* are the crème de la crème. Ravina adds: even *Tzitzura* is included. A *baraita* corroborates: Chanan ben Pinchas said the same — *Chavil Yama techla deBavel*, and *Shunya, Guvya, and Tzitzura* are the finest within it.

Rav Papa then introduces a contemporary qualification: *ve'ha'idna arevu behu Kutai* — in his time, *Kutim* — Samaritans — had intermingled there, diminishing its *yichus*. The Gemara immediately challenges this: *velo hi* — it is not so. The Gemara explains that a certain individual wanted to marry a woman from that region and they refused him, and he then began raising the claim of Samaritan infiltration. Rashi notes that it is very difficult to attribute to Rav Papa the *motzi la'az* of slandering an entire community out of pique at a personal rejection. Rashi therefore prefers the reading that it was a *Kuti* who sought to marry there and was refused, and the episode led to some concern about Samaritan presence — but not substantiated enough to genuinely compromise the *yichus* of *Chavil Yama*.

### Shot Mishat

The Gemara concludes with the location of *Chavil Yama* itself: *Zu Prat DeBorsi* — it is the region of *Prat DeBorsi*. A man who declared himself to be from *Shot Mishat* prompted Rav Yitzchak Nafcha to clarify: *agra d'amshat Shot Mishat bein hanaharot omedet* — the advantage of *Shot Mishat* is that it stands between the rivers, between the Tigris and the Euphrates, and is therefore classic Bavel with good *yichus*.

The Gemara then asks: what exactly constitutes *bein hanaharot* — between the rivers? Abaye said in the name of Rav Chama bar Ukva, who said in the name of Rabbi Yose in the name of Rabbi Chanina: *bein hanaharot kegolah leyuchsin* — being between the rivers is like *Golah*, like Pumbedita, for purposes of *yuchasin*. Any place between the Tigris and the Euphrates has this elevated status.

Rabbi Yochanan specifies: the region of *bein hanaharot* begins from *Dikra* going northward, and extends until the crossing of *Gizma*. But Abaye adds: *retzu'ah nafka* — there is a strip that extends beyond, reaching further north and including *Shot Mishat* within the zone of *bein hanaharot*. Even though *Shot Mishat* lies north of *Dikra*, the strip extension brings it within the territory of Bavel and grants it the status of *bein hanaharot* for purposes of *yuchasin*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 72

## Chalazone Nihavnad

### Rav Ika's Claim

The sugya opens with a statement transmitted through a chain of authorities: *amar Rav Ika bar Avin amar Rav Chananel amar Rav* — Chalazone Nihavnad, a city located in Iran that exists to this day, has the status of *gola* with respect to *yuchsin*. That is, it enjoys the same presumption of genealogical purity as Pumbedita, the paradigmatic *meyuchas* community of Babylonian Jewry.

Before proceeding, it is worth recalling the broader context in which this statement appears. The preceding dappim engaged at length with the question of *yuchsin* — genealogical fitness for marriage — examining which lands could be relied upon, which families could not, and how far the concern for *yichus* could be pressed in practice. Bavel was identified as superior to *chutz la'aretz*, while Eretz Yisrael occupied an intermediate position. Yet the *Gemara* simultaneously pushed back against the entire enterprise, arguing that once a family has become intermingled with *psulim*, there is no way to identify it, and one should neither ask nor tell. Even the role of Eliyahu HaNavi at the end of days was reinterpreted: rather than exposing families of problematic lineage that have already been absorbed into the community, he will address only those cases that remain conspicuously and publicly unresolved. In other words, the *Gemara* has repeatedly and powerfully challenged the practical relevance of *yichus* as a halakhic category — even while nominally maintaining the structure of the *Mishnah's* concern. Against that backdrop, the claim that a specific Iranian city qualifies as *meyuchas* like *gola* is itself notable, and the *Gemara* immediately scrutinizes it.

### Abaye's Challenge

*Amar lei Abaye: lo tetzitzu lei* — do not rely on what Rav Ika bar Avin said. The reason: *yevama hi d'nafla lei hatam* — he had a *yevama*, a sister-in-law whom he was obligated to marry, living in that very city. His claim that Chalazone Nihavnad is *meyuchas* is therefore self-interested and cannot be trusted.

This picks up a theme the *Gemara* developed previously, in which Rav Pappa made a negative claim about a certain place — asserting it had Samaritans intermingled within it — and the *Gemara* suggested this was motivated by the fact that he had been refused permission to marry a woman from there, making it look more like slander born of resentment than an objective report. *Tosafot* notes that it was not actually Rav Pappa himself but someone else, yet the pattern is clear. In that earlier case, one could not trust a negative claim about a place's *yichus* because the claimant had a personal grievance. Here, conversely, one cannot trust a positive claim because the claimant stands to benefit from it. Taken together, these cases leave the reliability of any testimony about a community's *yichus* deeply in question — whether the claim is favorable or unfavorable, some personal motive may be driving it.

One might ask: even if Rav Ika had a personal interest, he was transmitting in the name of Rav Chananel, who transmitted in the name of Rav — surely those earlier authorities had no such interest? The *Gemara* addresses this directly. Rav Ika responded: *atu didi?* — are you accusing me of fabricating this? I said it in the name of Rav Chananel, and Rav Chananel has no *yevama* there; he was not *nogeia ba-davar*. So they went and asked Rav Chananel directly. Rav Chananel replied: *hachi amar Rav* — this is indeed what Rav said, that Chalazone Nihavnad is like *gola* for *yuchsin*. The chain thus traces back to Rav himself — but it now emerges that Rav was the one who had the *yevama* there. The very source of the tradition is compromised by a personal interest.

The episode is a striking illustration of how the *Gemara* refuses to allow *yichus* claims to pass unchallenged. Every positive or negative assessment of a community's genealogical standing is potentially tainted by the claimant's circumstances.

### Ten Tribes Connection

*U-pligi d'Rav Abba bar Kahana* — this disputes the position of Rav Abba bar Kahana, who independently addressed the question of Chalazone Nihavnad by grounding it in a biblical text. Rav Abba bar Kahana cited the verse describing where the Ten Tribes were settled after the Assyrian exile under Sancherev: *va-yanchim ba-Chalach u-va-Chavor nehar Gozan ve-arei Madai* — and he settled them in Chalach, Chavor, the river of Gozan, and the cities of Madai. He then identified each toponym: *Chalach zo Chalazone* — Chalach is Chalazone; *Chavor zo Hadyav* — Chavor is Hadyav; *nehar Gozan ze Ginzak* — the river Gozan is Ginzak; and *arei Madai ze Chemdan ve-chaveroteha* — the cities of Madai are Chemdan and its neighboring cities. An alternative tradition identifies the last location not as Chemdan but as *Nahavnad ve-chaveroteha* — Nihavnad and its neighbors.

The implication is significant. Chalazone and Nihavnad — the very city whose *meyuchas* status was being claimed — are identified as places where the Ten Tribes were exiled and settled. Since the Ten Tribes are understood to have intermingled with the surrounding populations and lost their distinct Jewish identity, these locations cannot be presumed genealogically pure. On the contrary, according to Rav Abba bar Kahana, they are precisely the kind of places one should view with suspicion regarding *yuchsin*.

The *Gemara* then asks about the neighboring cities of Nihavnad mentioned by Shmuel: *krach Moshchi, Chutzki, ve-Rumki*. Rabbi Yochanan adds: *ve-kulam lipsol* — all of these are cities problematic for *yuchsin*.

### Border Cities

The *Gemara* now introduces a further complication from the book of Daniel. The verse *ve-tlat alin be-pumeih bein shinaiha* — three leaves were in its mouth, between its teeth — is expounded by Rabbi Yochanan: *zu Chalazone, Hadyav, ve-Natzivin* — these are the three cities, Chalazone, Hadyav, and Natzivin. *She-pe'amim bole'an u-fe'amim poltetan* — sometimes they are swallowed up by the Persian Empire and sometimes they are expelled from it.

The image is vivid: these cities sit on the border, sometimes absorbed within the empire's control and sometimes outside it, perpetually shifting between jurisdictions, like territory that alternates between two powers. The analogy to border regions that have historically moved between empires — absorbed one year, expelled the next — makes the point concrete. Their unstable political status is directly connected to their uncertain *yuchsin* status: when a community's identity and boundaries are permanently in flux, its genealogical records cannot be relied upon.

The *Gemara* then proceeds with the vision of the bear-like beast, identified by a *baraita* as referring to the Persians — *she-ochlim ve-shotim ke-dov, u-muse'arim ke-dov, ve-ein lahem menuchah ke-dov* — who eat and drink like a bear, are as hairy as a bear, and have no rest like a bear. Rabbi Ami, when he would see a Persian riding, would say: there goes a traveling bear. It is worth noting — as the scholar Yaakov Elman has observed — that this particular set of pejoratives (hairy, fat, bear-like) was itself a Persian slur directed against others; the *Gemara* here applies it back against the Persians themselves, an ironic inversion captured by the principle *kol ha-posel b'mumo posel*.

Rav asked Levi to describe the Persians through a *mashal*. Levi said they resemble the troops of the house of David — meaning they are valorous and powerful. The Chaverin, a nation that came to dominate parts of the region after the Persians and proved far more oppressive toward Jews, are like *malachei chabalah* — angels of destruction. The Ishmaelites are compared to *se'irim shel beit ha-kisei* — the demons of the outhouse. And the Torah scholars of Bavel? They are like the ministering angels — *malachei ha-shareit* — dressed in white, wrapped in their garments, their appearance distinguished and luminous. Rashi elaborates, citing other *Gemarot* that compare the *talmidei chachamim* of Bavel to the vision in Yechezkel of the angel *ish lavush badim*, clothed in linen — because they too would sit wrapped in *sedinim ha-metzuyatzin*, fringed linen garments, like heavenly figures.

---

## Rebbi's Prophecy

### Humanya

*Ki hava nicha nafshia d'Rabbi amar* — as Rebbi lay dying, he was moved to prophetic utterance, and this is what he declared. The first statement: *Humanya ika b'Bavel kulah Amonai* — there is a place in Bavel called Humanya, and it is entirely populated by Ammonites. The halakhic relevance is implicit: the prohibition of *lo yavo Amoni* applies to the male — *Ammoni v'lo Ammonit* — so the concern, while not all-encompassing, is nonetheless a real *yuchsin* issue.

That Rebbi chose to devote his final moments to enumerating these genealogical problems is itself striking. Rebbi was the great champion of Babylonian Jewry's honor — it was he who resisted the claim that Bavel was inferior to Eretz Yisrael in terms of *yichus*. And yet here, on his deathbed, he is cataloguing problems specifically in Bavel. The answer may be that precisely because he otherwise defended Bavel's honor, this transmission had special weight — he was not slandering a community out of bias, but passing down information he felt obligated to disclose at the end of his life, information that might otherwise be lost.

### Misgarya

*Misgarya ika b'Bavel kulah d'mamzeira hi* — there is a place in Bavel called Misgarya that is entirely populated by *mamzerim*. Again, the focus is on Bavel specifically — the very land whose genealogical standing Rebbi had defended throughout his life.

### Birka

*Birka ika b'Bavel, shenei achim yesh sham ha-machlifim neshotehem zeh la-zeh* — there is a place called Birka in Bavel, where two brothers live who swap their wives with one another. The consequence is that all children born of these unions are *mamzerim*, since a married woman who cohabits with another man produces illegitimate offspring. Rebbi identifies Birka as a community bearing this taint.

### Birta deSatya

*Birta deSatya ika b'Bavel, hayom saru me-acharei ha-Makom* — there is a place in Bavel called Birta deSatya, meaning something like the city that strays, and Rebbi declares: today they strayed from God. What occurred? *De-akfei peira be-khifrei be-Shabta* — fish rose to the surface of the pond on *Shabbat*, and the townspeople could not resist the opportunity: *va-azlu ve-tzadu lehu be-Shabta* — they went and caught the fish on *Shabbat*.

The obvious question arises: why does Rebbi include this? The other items in his deathbed disclosure concern permanent *yuchsin* problems — communities with *mamzerim* or *Ammonites* intermingled. A single *Shabbat* violation, whatever its gravity, would not seem to leave a lasting genealogical stain. What is the relevance?

The *Gemara* continues: *ve-shamteinun Rav Akhi berei de-Rabbi Yoshiya* — Rav Akhi the son of Rabbi Yoshiya put them in *cherem* on account of what they had done. But the consequence of this severe communal excommunication was *ve-ishtamad* — they all abandoned the faith. The lesson embedded here is itself a warning: a *cherem* applied to an entire city, based on what may have been prophetic knowledge rather than direct halakhic adjudication, can be counterproductive to the point of catastrophe. The *Gemara* records the outcome in a single phrase, without further editorial comment, leaving the weight of the result to speak for itself.

### Akra de-Agma

*Akra de-Agma ika b'Bavel, Adda bar Ahava yesh bah* — there is a place in Bavel called Akra de-Agma, and in it lives Adda bar Ahava. *Hayom yoshev be-cheiko shel Avraham* — today he sits in the lap of Avraham. Rashi suggests this might mean he has died and ascended to the world of the righteous, but notes the difficulty that Rav Adda bar Ahava was a much later figure than Rebbi. An alternative reading offered by Rashi is that today was his *bris milah* — he was just born, and is thus literally in the embrace of Avraham, as the sandek holds the infant. *Tosafot* proposes that there may have been two figures with the same name. The precise resolution remains uncertain, but the significance of the mention is clear: Rebbi wanted to note that in this place, a figure of great spiritual stature was present.

### Succession of Tzadikim

*Hayom nolad Rav Yehuda b'Bavel* — today, Rav Yehuda was born in Bavel. This statement becomes the pivot for a teaching about the continuity of *tzadikim*: *keshe-mes Rabbi Akiva nolad Rebbe* — when Rabbi Akiva died, Rebbi was born; *keshe-mes Rebbe nolad Rav Yehuda* — when Rebbi died, Rav Yehuda was born; *keshe-mes Rav Yehuda nolad Rava* — when Rav Yehuda died, Rava was born; *keshe-mes Rava nolad Rav Ashi* — when Rava died, Rav Ashi was born. The *Rambam's* text had the formulation *ad she-lo mes Rava nolad Rav Ashi* — before Rava died, Rav Ashi was already born — suggesting the succession is not merely sequential but overlapping.

*Le-lamedakh she-ein tzadik niftar min ha-olam ad she-nivra tzadik kamosohu* — to teach you that a righteous person does not depart from this world until another like him has already been created to take his place. The prooftext is *ve-zarach ha-shemesh u-va ha-shemesh* — the sun rises and the sun sets — read as a statement that before one sun sets, the next has already risen. This is supported by the story of Eli and Shmuel: *ad she-lo kavsah shimsho shel Eli zarchah shimsho shel Shmuel ha-Ramati* — before Eli's light was extinguished, Shmuel's had already begun to shine, as indicated by the verse *ve-ner Elokim terem yichbeh u-Shmuel shochev* — the lamp of God had not yet gone out when Shmuel was lying in the sanctuary, already receiving his prophetic calling.

One might pause over the choice of the word *tzadik*. The chain being traced is not merely a chain of righteous individuals in a general sense, but of generational halakhic leadership — great *rabbinic* figures whose absence would leave a community without guidance. The proof from Eli and Shmuel is instructive in this regard, as Shmuel was Eli's own student. The verse speaks to an overlap, not merely a succession, and the concern is that no generation be left without its guiding light.

The *Gemara* then cites: *tziva Hashem l'Yaakov sevivo tzarav* — God has commanded that Yaakov's oppressors always surround him. Rabbi Yehuda explains: *kegon Humanya l'pum Nahara* — just as Humanya surrounds Pum Nahara, a place inhabited by Jews, closing the circle back to Rebbi's opening statement about Humanya and its Ammonite population.

---

## Pelatya ben Benaya

### Good Version

The *Gemara* cites a verse from Yechezkel: *va-yehi k'hinavi u-Pelatya ben Benaya met* — and it was as I prophesied that Pelatya ben Benaya died, and I fell upon my face and cried out with a great voice, saying, "Ah, Lord God!" This is interpreted as a dispute between Rav and Shmuel. One says the prophet's outcry was *l'tova* — mourning the death of a righteous man. The other says it was *l'ra'ah* — distress that an evil man died too peacefully.

The positive interpretation unfolds as follows. The governor of Mishan — and it is worth noting that Mishan is one of the places previously identified as having problematic *yuchsin* — was the son-in-law of Nevuchadnetzar. After Nevuchadnetzar destroyed the *Beis HaMikdash* and took the Jews captive, the governor sent a message demanding his share of the captives: *mikulei hai shivya d'ayeisis lach reisha d'varta lan* — from all those captives you brought, give us the leadership of the settlement, our portion. Nevuchadnetzar wanted to comply and send Jewish captives to Mishan. Pelatya ben Benaya intervened and said to Nevuchadnetzar: *anan d'chashvinan neiku mikameich hacha* — we Israelites, who are important, should remain here with you, the great king; *v'avdin neizlu l'hasam* — let our slaves go there. By this maneuver, he ensured that the Jewish captives stayed in Bavel rather than being sent to Mishan.

Why was this a kindness? Rashi explains it on two grounds. First, Bavel afforded the Jews far better conditions than Mishan would have. Second, it is generally worse to be a servant of a servant — *avadim l'avadim* — subject to someone who is himself subordinate to a greater power, than to be in the service of the ultimate sovereign. The prophet's anguished cry was therefore a lament: *mi she-asa tova b'Yisrael yamut b'chatzi yamav?* — someone who did such good for Israel should die in the prime of his life?

### Bad Version

The negative interpretation draws on a different passage in Yechezkel. The prophet is brought to the eastern gate of the *Beis HaMikdash*, where he sees twenty-five men, and among them he identifies *Yaazanya ben Azur ve-Pelatya ben Benaya, sarei ha-am* — officers of the nation. He is then brought to the inner courtyard, where again there are approximately twenty-five men — *achoreihem el heichal Hashem u-fneihem kedma* — their backs were toward the sanctuary and their faces toward the east.

The *Gemara* asks: when the verse says their faces were toward the east, is it not obvious that their backs were toward the west? What is the need to specify *achoreihem el heichal Hashem*? *Melamed she-hayu mafri'in atzman u-mitrizin atzman klapei ma'alah* — this teaches that they would expose and relieve themselves in a manner directed toward God, as an act of deliberate desecration and contempt toward the *Heichal*. The prophet's outcry of anguish was therefore not a lament but rather an expression of outrage: *mi she-asa ra'ah zot b'Yisrael yamut al mitato?* — someone who committed such desecration against Israel should die peacefully in his bed?

### Shmuel's Position

*Tistayem b'Shmuel d'amar l'ra'ah* — the *Gemara* proposes to identify Shmuel as the one who holds the negative version. The reasoning: *d'amar Rabbi Chiya bar Avin amar Shmuel, Moshchani harei hi k'gola l'yuchsin* — Shmuel says Moshchani is like *gola* for *yuchsin*. And separately: *Mishan lo chashu lah, lo mishum avdut v'lo mishum mamzerut, ela kohanim she-hayu bah lo hikpidu al gerushot* — regarding Mishan, there is no concern for slave status or *mamzerut*; the only issue is that the *kohanim* there did not guard themselves from marrying divorced women, creating *chalalim*. This is exclusively a *kehuna* concern, not a general *yuchsin* problem.

Now, if according to the positive version, what was sent to Mishan were slaves — not Jews — and Shmuel holds that there are no slave-status concerns in Mishan, this would seem to be no problem at all. But the *Gemara* notes that Shmuel has a principle: *ha-mafkir avdo yatza l'cheirut v'eino tzarich get shichrur* — one who renounces ownership of his slave, the slave goes free without requiring a formal writ of manumission. If the Jewish masters were taken captive and their slaves along with them, the masters' despair of ever regaining their slaves constitutes an implicit renunciation of ownership. *She-ne'emar kol eved ish miknat kasef* — the verse says "slave of a man," meaning only when the *ish* maintains his ownership is the person considered a slave; once effective ownership lapses, the slave is freed.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *l'olam eima lach Shmuel amar l'tova* — you can maintain that Shmuel holds the positive version after all. Even according to Shmuel, slaves were sent to Mishan; and even according to Shmuel, those individuals ceased to be slaves once ownership was effectively abandoned. Therefore Shmuel's statement that Mishan has no slave-status concern is entirely consistent with the positive reading of Pelatya's intervention.

This resolution carries an implicit but striking observation about the scope of the *yuchsin* concern. The *Gemara* is essentially saying that even freed slaves — individuals who, in the previous chapter of the *Mishnah*, are ranked lower than *yisrael* in the hierarchy of marriageability — are treated as having no meaningful *yuchsin* issue once they are technically free. The concern for *yichus* is thus narrowly halakhic, not a broader social or cultural judgment about genealogical quality.

---

## Rabbi Meir vs. Chachamim

### Rabbi Meir's Position

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: zu divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: the entire framework we have been working with — the graduated hierarchy of Bavel as superior to *chutz la'aretz* for *yuchsin*, with all its distinctions and concerns — represents only the position of Rabbi Meir. It is not the consensus view.

This is a remarkable statement. Everything the *Gemara* has developed across the preceding dappim about the superiority of Bavel, the problems of other lands, and the careful distinctions between communities — all of it, according to this formulation, reflects the singular opinion of one Tanna. And this statement comes, pointedly, from Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — the very authority who elsewhere was responsible for many of the most pointed warnings about *yuchsin* problems in specific places.

### Chachamim's View

*Ve-chachamim omrim kol ha'aratzot b'chezkas kashrus hein omdot* — the Chachamim say: all lands stand under a presumption of genealogical fitness. This is a sweeping counter-position. Rather than elaborate hierarchies of *yuchsin* quality between different lands, the Chachamim apply the standard principle of *chazakah* — the ordinary legal presumption that things are as they appear and as they have been — to the question of lineage. Why should a person's fitness for marriage be treated differently from any other matter of personal status, where we simply follow the *chazakah*?

### Amemar vs. Rav Ashi

*Amemar sharei lei l'Rav Huna bar Nasan l'minsav itesa mechoza'ah* — Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Nasan to marry a woman from Chozaya, a place outside of Bavel and therefore in *chutz la'aretz*. Rav Ashi challenged him: *mah da'atach?* — on what basis? You are relying on the statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel that this whole framework is only Rabbi Meir's view. But the houses of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Zevid did not transmit the tradition in these terms — they did not frame it as a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim, but as a settled and unanimous concern.

### Version Disputes

Despite Rav Ashi's objection, Ameimar did not accept it. The *Gemara* records: *afilu hachi lo kibel minei* — even so, he did not accept from him, *mishum d'shmi'a lei me-Rav Zevid d'Naharda'ah* — because he had heard it from Rav Zevid of Nehardea, a different Rav Zevid from the one cited earlier, that this framework of *yuchsin* concerns was indeed only Rabbi Meir's position.

The competing attributions here are themselves revealing. The same essential dispute — whether concern for *yuchsin* across lands is a universal position or merely Rabbi Meir's minority view — is being transmitted differently by different *batei midrash*. The houses of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Zevid (one version) did not transmit the framing as a *machloket*; Rav Zevid of Nehardea (another version) did. This mirrors a broader pattern in the *Gemara's* treatment of *yuchsin* throughout these pages: even on the question of how much to worry about *yuchsin*, there is irresolvable uncertainty about what anyone actually held.

It is also worth noting the internal tension in attributing the limiting formulation — "this is only Rabbi Meir" — to Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel. Throughout the preceding discussion, it has consistently been Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel who transmitted the most pointed statements about *yuchsin* problems: this place is filled with *mamzerim*, that place is problematic, and so on. Yet here it is the same authority who provides the most powerful tool for dismissing the entire apparatus — it is only Rabbi Meir. One possible resolution is that *la matni hachi* — the tradition that this is a dispute of Rabbi Meir versus Chachamim — was itself contested, and different *amoraim* disputed whether Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel actually said it.

One further observation the *Gemara* invites: is Rabbi Meir's concern for *yuchsin* consistent with his general halakhic disposition of *chaish l'miyuta* — being attentive to small minorities and minority possibilities? If so, the Chachamim's counter-position — that everyone has a *chezkas kashrus* — represents simply the standard application of *chazakah*, without any heightened vigilance toward the remote possibility of genealogical disqualification.

---

## Future Purification

### Rabbi Yosi's View

*Tanu Rabbanan: mamzerei ve-netinei tehorim le'atid lavo, divrei Rabbi Yosi* — our Rabbis taught: *mamzerim* and *netinim* will become pure in the future, in the words of Rabbi Yosi. This is a significant claim about the eschatological resolution of personal status issues. *Netinim* — descendants of the Gibeonites who were made Temple servants by David — are disqualified from full membership in the Jewish community, their status a product of circumstances rather than of any sin. And *mamzerim*, however they came to be, bear their status indefinitely. Rabbi Yosi maintains that in the future, both will be purified.

The prooftext is Yechezkel's vision of the messianic era: *ve-zarakti aleichem mayim tehorim u-tehartem* — I will sprinkle pure water upon you and you shall become pure. If God is going to purify Israel from all impurity in the future, that purification must include the removal of these personal status stigmas as well.

### Rabbi Meir's Response

Rabbi Meir disagrees. *Keshe-hu omer mi-kol tumoteichem u-mi-kol gilluleichem* — when the verse says "from all your impurities and from all your idolatries," that specifies the source of the purification: sin and ritual defilement. *Ve-lo min ha-mamzerut* — but not from personal status issues. The word *tumah* refers to moral and ritual contamination; the status of *mamzer* is a halakhic category of personal identity, not a species of ritual impurity, and the verse does not promise its erasure.

Rabbi Yosi responds: *keshe-hu omer ateher etchem* — but then the verse continues with the separate phrase "I will purify you," which is a second, broader statement of purification. *Hevei omer af min ha-mamzerut* — this additional formulation includes even the removal of *mamzerut*.

*Bishlama le-Rabbi Meir*, the verse *ve-yashav mamzer be-Ashdod* is well-understood — in the future, *mamzerim* will be settled in Ashdod, meaning they will be identified and separated, retaining their distinct status even in messianic times. But according to Rabbi Yosi, *mai ve-yashav mamzer be-Ashdod?* Rav Yosef offers a *targum*: *ve-yateivun beit Yisrael le-ruchatzan be-arahon, de-havu damu beh le-nuchrain* — the house of Israel will dwell in security in their own land, they who had been like strangers. The *mamzer* here is a metaphor for Israel's own experience of exile and marginalization — the nation that was itself like a rejected outsider, dwelling in a land not its own, will now return and settle securely. The implication is that just as Israel's status as a stranger is reversed in the messianic era, so too is the *mamzer's* status of exclusion reversed.

There is something poignant in this reading. The *Gemara* is drawing on the profound parallel between the *mamzer's* condition — excluded, marginalized, unable to marry fully into the community — and the Jewish people's condition in exile. Both are described by the same word, and both find their resolution in the same future moment.

---

## Future Purification (II)

### Yechezkel's Vision

The previous discussion of Yechezkel's prophecy continues. Rabbi Yosi's reading of *ve-yashav mamzer be-Ashdod*, rendered by Rav Yosef's *targum* as speaking of Israel's homecoming and security after generations of displacement, frames the entire messianic purification as encompassing the reversal of every form of exclusion — including the status of *mamzer*.

### Halacha K'Rabbi Yosi

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: halacha k'Rabbi Yosi* — Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi. Again this is Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel — the same voice that previously said the entire *yuchsin* framework is only Rabbi Meir's view, and the same voice behind so much of the *yuchsin* discussion across these pages. The package is consistent: we are not particularly concerned about *yuchsin* in the present, and in the future it will all be set right.

The ruling is *halacha k'Rabbi Yosi* even though the subject matter is eschatological — a statement about what will be true *le'atid lavo*. The use of the term *halacha* in this context is itself striking.

### Rav Yosef's Statement

*Amar Rav Yosef: ilmale d'amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel halacha k'Rabbi Yosi, hava ati Eliyahu u-mafik minnan tzvarne tzvarne kolarin* — Rav Yosef said: were it not for the fact that Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel ruled that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi, Eliyahu would have come and extracted from us, group by group, great numbers of people — identifying the *psulim* among us and expelling them from the community.

This is a breathtaking statement. The ruling *halacha k'Rabbi Yosi* is understood not merely as a practical legal decision about the present, but as a decision that effectively reshapes what Eliyahu will do when he comes. Before this ruling, the plan — as one reading of the verses suggested — was that Eliyahu would come and expose all the hidden *psulim*, performing a massive rectification through exclusion. By ruling *halacha k'Rabbi Yosi*, the tradition has changed the trajectory: the future rectification will be one of inclusion and purification, not identification and expulsion.

This is reminiscent of the principle *lo bashamayim hi* — the Torah is not in heaven — but even more radical, because here the *halacha* is not merely overriding a heavenly voice in a present dispute, but actively determining what the heavenly plan will look like in the future. As one participant noted, this is an extraordinary use of the word *halacha* in the context of a question about messianic times — and the audacity of it is clearly the point.

---

## Marriage Status Rules

### Ger and Mamzeret

Having engaged in an extended multi-layered dismantling of the practical concern for *yuchsin* — through arguments about unknowability, through limiting it to Rabbi Meir's minority position, through appeal to future purification — the *Gemara* now pivots decisively to concrete, specific *halachot* about marriage between identified individuals of known status. The previous discussion has effectively cleared the ground; now we address what the rules actually are when the relevant facts are known.

*Tanu Rabbanan: ger nosei mamzeret, divrei Rabbi Yosi* — a *ger* may marry a *mamzeret*, in the words of Rabbi Yosi. *Rabbi Yehuda omer: ger lo yisa mamzeret* — Rabbi Yehuda says a *ger* may not marry a *mamzeret*. The pivot of the dispute is the verse *lo yavo mamzer bi-khal Hashem* — a *mamzer* may not enter the assembly of God. Does that prohibition encompass *gerim* as well? Is a *ger* included in the *kahal* that a *mamzer* cannot enter?

### Chamisha Kahale

The *Gemara* grounds the dispute in a *derashah* on the word *kahal* and its multiple occurrences in the Torah. *Chamisha kahale ketivi* — the word *kahal* appears five times in relevant contexts. Rashi enumerates: *lo yavo mamzer bi-khal Hashem* (once); *lo yavo lo bi-khal Hashem* (again, emphasizing the double exclusion); *lo yavo Amoni u-Moavi bi-khal Hashem* (concerning Ammonites and Moabites); and further instances. Each use of *kahal* is taken to include an additional category of Jews within the prohibited assembly: one *kahal* for *kohanim*, one for *leviyim*, and one for *yisraelim* — establishing that the prohibition on a *mamzer* marrying into the *kahal* applies not only to the inner priestly circles but to the full range of Jewish lineage.

### Vadai vs. Safek

The remaining two uses of the word *kahal* teach that: *v'chad l'mishri mamzer b'shtuki* — one use permits a *mamzer* to marry a *shtuki* (a person of unknown paternity, a doubtful *mamzer*); *v'chad l'mishri shtuki b'yisrael* — and one use permits a *shtuki* to marry into the full Jewish community. The reasoning is that *bi-khal Hashem* means *kahal vadai* — a *definite* assembly, a person of *definite* Jewish fitness. *Kahal safek* — a person whose status is uncertain — is not encompassed by the prohibition. Therefore *lo yavo mamzer bi-khal Hashem* means only a *definite mamzer* may not enter; a person of *doubtful mamzer* status (*shtuki*) may marry a *yisrael*. Correspondingly, the prohibition bars a *mamzer* only from a *definite kahal*; he may marry a *shtuki*, who is only a *safek kahal*.

The practical significance is substantial: *mid'oraita*, a *shtuki* may marry into a *kohen*, *levi*, or *yisrael* family. The *mishnah's* stricter treatment of *shtuki* is *mid'rabbanan*.

### Gerim Outside Kahal

*Kahal gerim lo ikra kahal* — converts were never referred to as *kahal* in the Torah. Therefore, the prohibition of *lo yavo mamzer bi-khal Hashem* does not apply to them as the protected community. A *mamzer* may marry a *giyoret*, and a *ger* may marry a *mamzeret*, because *gerim* were not included in the Torah's designation of *kahal Hashem*. This is Rabbi Yosi's position.

### One Law Argument

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and sources his position in a different verse: *ha-kahal, chuka achat lachem v'la-ger ha-gar* — the assembly: one law for you and for the *ger* who dwells among you. This verse explicitly places the *ger* within the *kahal*, meaning that when the Torah says a *mamzer* cannot enter *kahal Hashem*, the *ger* is included in that *kahal*. Accordingly, a *mamzer* cannot marry a *giyoret*, and a *ger* cannot marry a *mamzeret*.

Rabbi Yosi responds: *chuka achat hefsik ha-inyan* — the phrase *chuka achat* ("one law") interrupts the passage and is a separate statement. The verse says "one law for you and for the *ger*" — meaning certain laws apply equally to both — but it does not mean the *ger* is identified as part of the *kahal* in the genealogical sense.

### Marriage to Kohenet

*Echad ger v'echad eved meshuchrar v'chalal mutarin b'kohenet* — a *ger*, a freed slave, and a *chalal* are all permitted to marry a *kohenet* (the daughter of a *kohen*). This is uncontested. The Torah's marriage restrictions on *kehuna* apply to *kohanim* as men — they may not marry a *giyoret*, a *chalalah*, a divorced woman, or a *zonah*. There is no corresponding restriction on which men a *kohenet* may marry. Since a *ger*, freed slave, and *chalal* each have the same *yisrael* status for purposes of marriage eligibility, they may marry any woman a *yisrael* may marry, including a *bat kohen*.

### Women's Status

*Mesayei lei l'Rav, d'amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: hitir kesherot l'hinasei l'psulim* — this supports Rav's position that *kesherot* — women of fit status — are not restricted from marrying men of *pasul* categories. The entire structure of marriage prohibitions in *kehuna* is directed at the *kohanic* male. A woman, regardless of her father's lineage, bears no independent restriction based on whom she marries, as long as the marriage itself is permitted from his side.

### Zeira Stoned

*Darash Zeira b'Mechuza: ger mutar b'mamzeret* — Rabbi Zeira stood up and publicly taught in Mechuza that a *ger* is permitted to marry a *mamzeret*, in accordance with Rabbi Yosi. *Ragmuhu kulei alma b'etrogaihu* — everyone pelted him with their *etrogim*. The incident apparently occurred during *Sukkot*. Rashi explains that the audience was not actually offended by the permissive ruling itself — being told that something is *mutar* is hardly an insult. What offended them was the underlying *derashah*: Rabbi Zeira's teaching implied that *gerim* were never called *kahal*, that they stand outside the primary designation of the Jewish assembly. For a community with a large *ger* population, this was experienced as a statement of exclusion and diminishment of identity, not as halakhic permission.

### Rava's Strategy

*Amar Rava: mi ika d'darash milta ki hai b'duchta d'shchichei giyorei?* — who would be so careless as to teach this in a place full of converts? Rava himself then taught in Mechuza. He began with: *ger mutar b'kohenet* — a *ger* may marry a *kohenet*. The community was delighted — *tnu b'shirai*, they clothed him in silk garments — for this ruling affirmed the *ger's* full status and his access to the most distinguished women of the Jewish community. Then Rava added: *ger mutar b'mamzeret* — a *ger* may also marry a *mamzeret*. The community objected that he had undermined his first teaching.

Rava replied: *lo d'tava l'chu avdi l'chu* — no, I am doing you good. *Ei bei meihacha nasiv v'ei bei meihacha nasiv* — if he wishes, he may marry from here (a *kohenet*), and if he wishes, from there (a *mamzeret*). The point Rava was making was not that the second ruling is offensive, but that it should be understood as an expansion of opportunity, not as a statement of diminishment. The pedagogical lesson is clear: the same halakhic content, presented in a different sequence and framing, can be received as affirming rather than insulting. One begins by establishing the *ger's* full dignity and standing, and then presents the broader range of his legal options.

### Final Halacha

*Hilkhata: ger mutar b'kohenet u-mutar b'mamzeret* — the practical ruling is that a *ger* is permitted with a *kohenet* and permitted with a *mamzeret*. *Mutar b'kohenet d'huzharu kesherot l'hinasei l'psulim* — the permission with a *kohenet* reflects the rule that women of fit status are not restricted from marrying men of *pasul* category; the restriction of *kehuna* runs only to the *kohanic* male. *U-mutar b'mamzeret k'Rabbi Yosi* — the permission with a *mamzeret* follows Rabbi Yosi's ruling, which is the *halacha l'maaseh*.

---

---

# Kiddushin 73

## Safek D'Oraita Framework

### Safek in Psak

Before entering the *gemara* itself, it is worth pausing on one of the most far-reaching and central *sugyos* in all of practical *psak*: the question of *safek* — doubt — and how halachic authorities navigate it. This question bears on *machlokes*, on cases of genuine uncertainty, and on a vast range of applied *halacha*. The most important foundational source is the Rambam, and understanding his position is indispensable for what the *gemara* on this *daf* is doing.

### Rambam on Safek

The Rambam, at the end of the ninth *perek* of *Hilchos Tumas Meis*, states what he calls a *davar yadua* — a known fact: *she-kol elu ha-tumaos v'kayotzei bahen she-hein mishum safek hare hein shel divreihem* — any *tumah* concern that arises from a case of doubt is itself only rabbinic in origin. And he continues: *v'ein t'me'in min ha-Torah ela mi she-nitma b'tumah vada'is* — the only biblical-level *tumah* is one that is certain. He extends this principle across every domain of *halacha*: *b'tumaos bein b'machalos asuros bein b'arayos v'shabbasos* — *tumah v'taharah*, forbidden foods, *arayos*, and *Shabbos* alike — *ein chosheshin lahem ela mi-divrei sofrim*. According to the Rambam, any case of doubt immediately reduces the prohibition to a rabbinic level.

It is worth noting where these general rules about *safek* find their primary halachic articulation: in the laws of *tumah v'taharah*. This is because a principle derived from *Sotah* — *safek tumah b'reshus harabbim tahor*, that a doubtful impurity in a public space is treated as pure — is applied throughout. The Rambam defines *reshus harabbim* for *tumah* purposes differently than for *hilchos Shabbos*; here, even three people constitute a *reshus harabbim*. In *reshus hayachid*, by contrast, *safek tumah* is *tamei*. Both of these rulings operate at the biblical level. The Rambam's broader point, however, is that beyond these specific *tumah* rules, in all other areas of *halacha* — including the gravest categories of *issur* — doubt itself carries only rabbinic force. The implication that immediately follows is that one would never bring a *korban* for any such doubtful case, since the doubt does not constitute a biblical violation.

### Rashba vs Rambam

That observation precisely is the ground of the *Rashba*'s challenge. In his *Toras HaBayis* — the fourth *bayis*, first *shaar* — the *Rashba* argues at length against what he takes to be the Rambam's position. His objection: we know that when someone has a *safek* about whether he violated a prohibition that would normally require a *korban chatas*, he must bring an *asham talui*. The very institution of *asham talui* demonstrates that the Torah itself is concerned with cases of doubt. The Torah, in the *Rashba*'s view, does not treat *safek* as automatically rabbinic.

The *Rashba* further believes that the Rambam's source for his broad principle is precisely the *gemara* before us — and we will see shortly why. The debate reduces to whether the *gemara*'s treatment of *safek mamzer* is a model for all other cases of doubt in the Torah, or whether it is a unique exception. The *Rashba* takes the latter position, maintaining that *safek mamzer* is a special case and that the Torah's general rule remains that *safek d'Oraita l'chumra* — biblical-level doubts must be treated stringently — and this principle is itself biblical, not merely rabbinic.

### Machlokes & Authority

The Rambam presents a second, distinct *halacha* about how to rule when there is a *machlokes*. In *Hilchos Mamrim*, at the end of the first *perek*, the Rambam rules: *shnei chachamim o shnei batei dinin she-necheleku* — if two sages or two courts disagree — *bizman shelo bizman haSanhedrin*, in a time when there is no centralized authority (as has been the case for some seventeen hundred years), or even in a time when there is a *Sanhedrin* but the matter has not yet been adjudicated before it, then whether the dispute spans one generation or many generations successively, if *im ein lekha yodea lehikan hadin noteh* — if the decisor cannot determine which position the law favors — *beshel Torah halakh ahar hamahmir*, in matters of biblical law one must be stringent, and *beshel soferim halakh ahar hamekel*, in matters of rabbinic law one must be lenient. 

The Rambam's point is that post-*Sanhedrin*, there is no longer any structural rule for resolving *machlokes*. The only operative principle is: leniency for rabbinic matters, stringency for biblical matters. This *Rambam* is much debated, but it is essential to distinguish it clearly from the question of *safek*. The question of what to do when a case itself is in doubt is separate from the question of how to rule when authorities disagree. The two are often conflated, but they are distinct *halachos*.

### Chumra vs Kula

A further complexity arises when applying the rule of *beshel Torah halakh ahar hamahmir*. There are cases — *shiurim* being a prime example — where the very same ruling that is stringent in one application produces leniency in another. Almost any *halachic she'eilah* can be analyzed where the *machmir* position and the *meikil* position each simultaneously generate *kulot* and *chumros* depending on the specific case. This is a critical part of the *halachic* calculus: whether a given ruling is genuinely stringent or genuinely lenient must be evaluated across its full range of applications, not only in isolation.

The famous formulation of Rav Chaim Brisker captures this well. When asked why he was so lenient in *hilchos Shabbos*, he replied: I am not lenient in *hilchos Shabbos* — I am stringent in *pikuach nefesh*. His tendency to permit even arguably Rabbinic violations when there was any medical concern was, in his framing, a *chumra* in the domain of preserving life — which is itself a biblical obligation — not a *kula* in *Shabbos*.

---

## Shtuki Kosher D'Oraita

### Shtuki Kasher

We are now at the second wide line on 73a. *Amar Rava: devar Torah shtuki kasher.* Rava rules that at the biblical level, a *shtuki* — a child whose mother is known but whose father is unidentified — is *kasher* for marriage into the Jewish people. The *mishna* had already discussed the category of *shtuki*, who may be a *mamzer* or a *chalal* without our knowing. Yet Rava's opening claim is that this concern is not biblical in origin. We now need to understand why.

### Rov & Extraction

*Mai ta'ama?* — what is the reason? *Rov kesherim etzlah* — the majority of men who had any relationship with this woman are *kesherim lah*: they are not her relatives, not *mamzerim*, not *netinim*. They are, in other words, men whose children would be fully *kasher*. And *umi'ut pesulim etzlah* — only a minority are *pesulim* to her. 

Now, even if the man who fathered the child came from among those *pesulim*, we can apply the principle of *kol d'parish m'ruba parish*: whenever a person or thing is extracted from its original locale, we follow the *rov*. That is, if the man left his community and came to be with this woman, he separated himself from the majority — and since the majority of men are *kesherim*, we follow that majority and presume the child is *kasher*.

One might ask: why invoke *kol d'parish m'ruba parish* at all? Is this not simply the standard application of *rov*? The *gemara* here addresses one of the central distinctions in the entire topic: the difference between going after the majority of a fixed group versus going after a majority when the individual has left his setting.

### Kavuah Distinction

*Mah amart dilma azlah ihi legabeihu? Havah lei kavuah.* If she left her location and went to him, then the man is stationary — *kavuah* — and a different principle applies: *kol kavuah k'mechetza al mechetza dami*. When the relevant party is fixed in place, we treat the doubt as fifty-fifty rather than as a case governed by the majority. 

The *gemara* thus distinguishes two scenarios. If the man came to her — or if both of them went to a third location — then *kol d'parish m'ruba parish* applies and we follow the *rov*. But if she went to him, his being stationary invokes *kavuah* and the doubt becomes an even split. This contrast between *kol d'parish m'ruba parish* and *kavuah* — between a mobile extraction and a fixed party — is one of the core distinctions in the *sugya* of *rov*, debated extensively by the *Rishonim* and *Acharonim*.

### Mamzer Safek Allowed

Even granting that the case of *kavuah* would leave us with a fifty-fifty doubt, there is a further biblical principle that resolves the matter in favor of *kashrut*. *HaTorah amra lo yavo mamzer* — the Torah says a *mamzer* may not enter the assembly of Israel. But *mamzer vadai hu d'lo yavo* — only a *certain* mamzer is excluded. *Ha mamzer safek yavo b'kahal* — a *safek mamzer* may enter and marry into the Jewish people. 

From this the *gemara* draws a further inference: *b'kahal vadai hu d'lo yavo, ha b'kahal safek yavo* — a *vadai mamzer* is excluded only from a *vadai* Jewish community, but he may marry someone whose *kashrut* is itself *b'safek*. Both conclusions follow from the *drasha* on the verse: a *safek mamzer* may marry a perfectly *kasher* Jew, and a *vadai mamzer* may marry a person whose *kashrut* is uncertain.

It is precisely here that the *Rashba* locates the Rambam's proof. According to the *Rashba*'s reading of the Rambam, the Torah's permission for a *safek mamzer* to marry is the model for the Rambam's general rule that *safek* reduces all prohibitions to the rabbinic level. The *Rashba* himself reads this as a *chiddush* unique to the law of *mamzer* — a special biblical exception — while maintaining that *safek d'Oraita l'chumra* remains a biblical rule everywhere else.

### Rabbis' Yuchsin Upgrade

If *shtuki* is *kasher* at the biblical level, why did the Rabbis restrict him? *Gezeira shema yisa achoto me'aviv* — a *shtuki* does not know who his father is, and so he might unknowingly marry his paternal sister. This is the first proposed reason for the rabbinic prohibition.

### Gezeira Rejection

The *gemara* immediately challenges this reasoning. *Ela me'ata shtuki shtukit lo yisa shema yisa achoto me'aviv* — if we are worried that a *shtuki* might marry his paternal sister, then he should be forbidden to marry even another *shtukis*, a female *shtuki*, since they might share the same father even with different mothers. And one could extend this further: *bat shtukit lo yisa shema yisa achoto me'aviv* — he should not be permitted to marry even the daughter of a *shtukit*, since conceivably her father might also be his father.

The *gemara* rejects each extension: *kol ki hani mezaneu v'azlei?* — are we really to suppose that the same man fathered every *shtuki* in town? And *lo shechiach* — such a scenario is so rare and implausible that we do not build legislation around it. *Hacha nami lo shechiach* — the case of *bat shtukit* is equally implausible. The *gezeira* argument for each of these extensions fails for the same reason.

With all these proposed *gezeiros* rejected, the *gemara* concludes: *ela ma'ala asu b'yuchsin* — the prohibition on *shtuki* is not grounded in any single compelling logical necessity but reflects a rabbinic decision to establish heightened standards in matters of *yuchsin*, lineage. The *Maharsha* at the beginning of this *perek* compares the ten levels of lineage that the Rabbis instituted to the ten levels of *kedusha* in *Eretz Yisrael* enumerated in the first *perek* of *Keilim* — from the land itself inward to the *Beis HaMikdash*. Just as those gradations of sanctity are maintained and protected, so too the Rabbis established tiers of *yuchsin* as a way of heightening the community's awareness and protection of familial status. The Rambam himself, in his *Perush HaMishnah*, traces his own ancestry back many generations, listing rabbis and *dayanim* who preceded him in Spain — a testament to the care families ought to take in preserving knowledge of their lineage.

---

## Asufi Kosher D'Oraita

### Asufi Kasher

Having completed the *sugya* of *shtuki*, Rava turns to the parallel case: *devar Torah asufi kasher* — at the biblical level, an *asufi* is likewise *kasher*. An *asufi* — literally one who has been gathered up — is a foundling of entirely unknown parentage, discovered abandoned in a public place. Unlike the *shtuki*, whose mother is known, the *asufi*'s lineage is completely unidentified. Rava maintains that even this more severe case of unknown parentage does not render the child *pasul* at the Torah level.

### Three-Fold Doubt

*Mai ta'ama? Eshet ish bi'ba'ala talya.* The reasoning begins with the observation that if the mother was a married woman, it is overwhelmingly likely that her husband is the child's father. A married woman's child would therefore be fully *kasher*. The vast majority of women who might abandon a child are married women whose children are presumptively legitimate.

What, then, of the remaining cases? *Mi'ut arusot umi'ut shehalach ba'aleihen limdinat hayam* — the *gemara* identifies two smaller categories: *arusot*, women who are *mekudeshet* but whose marriages have not been consummated, whose child would be a *mamzer* if fathered by another man; and *nesuot* whose husbands had gone abroad for an extended period, such that any child they bore would also be a *mamzer*. To these two categories we add *pnuyah* — an unmarried woman, whose child would be entirely *kasher* regardless of the father — and the case of *demachmat ra'avon*, a woman compelled by famine to abandon a child she could not support.

*Keivan de'ika pnuyah ve'ika nami demachmat ra'avon, hava palga u'palga.* Because there are two plausible scenarios that would produce a *kasher* child and two that would produce a *mamzer*, the *gemara* treats this as a fifty-fifty doubt. One might object that the incidence rates of each scenario are not necessarily equal, but the *gemara*'s point is that there is genuine doubt on both sides — enough to constitute a *safek*.

It is worth appreciating what the practice of abandoning a child in the street meant in the ancient world. It was not equivalent to modern adoption; an infant placed in a public thoroughfare faced severe risk of death unless discovered quickly. Yet in years of famine, parents who felt unable to provide for a newborn and wished to preserve resources for surviving children made this choice — not an excusable one, but an understandable one given the desperation of circumstances. Notably, Rav Chaim Brisker was known as a kind of address for such cases in his own community: parents who could not care for a child knew that the rabbi's doorstep was where to turn, and Rav Chaim reputedly checked his front step throughout the night to ensure no abandoned child was left unattended.

### Asufi as Safek

The same biblical argument that resolved *shtuki* resolves *asufi* as well. *HaTorah amra lo yavo mamzer b'kahal Hashem* — and *mamzer vadai hu d'lo yavo, ha mamzer safek yavo*. Since the worst-case scenario for an *asufi* is that he is a *safek mamzer*, and the Torah explicitly permits a *safek mamzer* to marry into the Jewish people, the *asufi* is *kasher* at the biblical level. Even the *kavuah* concern does not generate anything worse than a fifty-fifty doubt — and a fifty-fifty doubt, as the *gemara* has shown, still falls within the category of *safek mamzer* who may marry a *kasher* Jew.

### Asufi Prohibition

Why then did the Rabbis prohibit the *asufi* from marrying into an established Jewish family? *Shema yisa achoto me'aviv bein me'imo* — perhaps he will unknowingly marry his paternal or maternal sister, since both parents are unknown. *V'chi hanei shadei v'azlei?* — and are we to suppose that all the abandoned children in a city come from the same man and woman? Once again, the *gezeira* is extended to its logical extremes and each extension is rejected as implausible: *lo shechiach, hacha nami lo shechiach*. And once again, the *gemara* concludes: *ela ma'ala asu b'yuchsin* — the Rabbis elevated the standards of lineage beyond what the Torah strictly demands. The *asufi*, like the *shtuki*, is *kasher* d'Oraita, but the Rabbis, as a matter of *yuchsin* policy, restricted his marriage options.

This is a notable moment in the *sugya*. The acknowledgment that these restrictions are rabbinic — not biblical — creates real *halachic* flexibility. Once a prohibition is classified as rabbinic, a further *safek* about whether the category applies at all is sufficient, under *safek d'rabbanan l'kula*, to resolve matters leniently. The *amoraim* in the *sugya* that follows will work hard to narrow the *asufi* category precisely in this spirit.

Regarding contemporary analogues: the question of sperm donation has generated significant *halachic* discussion. Rav Moshe Feinstein, in the first volume of *Igros Moshe*, rules leniently, arguing that *mamzerus* cannot be created through a medical procedure that does not constitute an act of sexual intercourse. The Torah's prohibition and the *halachic* category of *mamzer* are predicated on a prohibited sexual act, and a clinical procedure does not meet that threshold. The Satmar Rav reportedly took the opposing position, and the dispute was fierce. Today, however, the mainstream *poskim* — including in the *Chareidi* world — generally follow Rav Moshe's position, since the alternative is logically untenable: if the parents committed no prohibited *act*, the mechanism for creating *mamzerus* is absent. Rav Moshe supports his ruling with *gemaros* that discuss conception occurring without intercourse — cases the *gemara* itself apparently contemplated. Related but distinct questions arise around egg donation, where the *halachic* identity of the mother becomes a separate dispute, and where the concern shifts from *mamzerus* to *arayos* for the resulting child.

---

## Signs Negating Asufi

### Circumcision Evidence

The *gemara* now turns to a critical practical narrowing of the *asufi* category. *Amar Rav Abba bar Huna: matzu mahul, ein bo mishum asufi* — if the foundling was found to have been circumcised, he does not carry the *halachic* status of *asufi*. The reasoning is that parents who kept the child for eight days, arranged for a *mohel*, and performed the *mila* cannot be said to have abandoned the child in a spirit of utter neglect. The very act of *mila* demonstrates parental care, and a child whose parents exercised such care is presumed to come from a *kasher* family. It is worth noting that this ruling does not depend on the assumption that only Jews performed *mila* in that environment — the point is that the parents' ongoing involvement, evidenced by the *mila*, removes the presumption of abandonment that defines *asufi* status. The *rishonim* already raised the question of whether parents of a *mamzer* would be willing to provide such care, and the answer embedded in this *halacha* is that the stigma and shame attending a *mamzer* are precisely what would lead such parents to avoid investing in the child — making the presence of *mila* an indicator of *kasher* parentage.

### Limb Care Signs

Similarly, *meshofeyhu* — if the child's limbs had been straightened. Newborns in antiquity were sometimes bound to frames to correct bow-leggedness or otherwise align their limbs, a practice Rashi notes continued as recently as the early twentieth century. *Rashi* explains *eivarav mesukanim umeyusharim* — his limbs are adjusted and straightened. If the child shows evidence of this kind of physical care, *ein bo mishum asufi*, he is not classified as an *asufi*, because once again the parents are demonstrably not people who simply cast the child away.

### Anointing & Amulets

Further signs of parental care: *mashuach u'mahul v'kachul* — if the child has been anointed with oil or had eye shadow applied, practices done for infants in that period. *Rami chamra tali pitka* — if the child was bound with medicinal preparations or had an amulet hung about him — *tali kemeia* — or carried some other protective charm, *ein bo mishum asufi*. The logic is consistent: the parents provided for the child's health and protection, which is incompatible with the profile of total abandonment that defines *asufi*. A child found with a vaccination record in a modern setting might be understood analogously — the parents were clearly engaged in the child's care.

### Tree Placement

*Tali b'diklei* — if the child was found hanging in a palm tree, suspended in a basket or swaddled, the *gemara* rules as follows: *ei matya leh chaya, yesh bo mishum asufi* — if it is a location where an animal could reach him, he is an *asufi*, because the parents placed him there for him to be consumed. *V'im lav, ein bo mishum asufi* — if the location was one where no animal could reach him, the parents placed him there to protect him, not to abandon him to death, and he is not an *asufi*.

A variant case involves a *sardita* — a sorb tree, which Rashi identifies using a term meaning a tree known to attract demonic forces when close to a settled area. *Sardita semicha l'mata, yesh bo mishum asufi* — if the sorb tree was close to town, the child is an *asufi* because the proximity of such a tree to populated areas renders it dangerous on account of the demonic presences said to frequent inhabited spaces. *V'im lav, ein bo mishum asufi* — if the tree was far from town, the child is not an *asufi*. Rava offers an alternative explanation: the criterion is simply whether there are many people about — *mishum de'nefishi* — which is in effect the same standard as the synagogue case that follows.

### Synagogue & Public

*Bei knishta smicha lemata, ve'shichichi bei rabim, ein bo mishum asufi* — a child found in a *shul* that is close to the town and regularly frequented by many people is not an *asufi*, because placing a child there is a way of ensuring he will be found and cared for. It is worth noting that in Babylonia, the *shul* was typically located outside the city — a feature of Persian rule or of the practical convenience for people traveling to work — and indeed some of the conventions of Babylonian *davening* reflect this extra-urban placement. *V'i lo, yesh bo mishum asufi* — if the *shul* was not close to town and few people passed through, then leaving the child there is tantamount to abandonment and the child is an *asufi*.

### Non-Asufi Assumption

The thrust of this entire *sugya* is a consistent movement away from classifying children as *asufi*. The *mishna*'s category of *asufi* is narrowed by the *amora'im* at every turn. Whatever grounds can be found to say the child is *not* an *asufi* are embraced. The principle is that *asufi* means truly abandoned — not merely found in the street, but found in circumstances indicating total neglect, with no signs of parental investment whatsoever. Any evidence of care — physical, medical, ritual, or positional — removes the classification. The *gezeira* that motivated the rabbinic prohibition in the first place (*ma'ala asu b'yuchsin*) was itself acknowledged to be not strictly logical; and so the *amora'im* are appropriately reluctant to extend it into cases where any reasonable argument for non-*asufi* status exists. A *safek* about whether the child is an *asufi* at all, once the prohibition is rabbinic, resolves leniently.

### Pit & River Tests

*Hai pira de'sufla, yesh bo mishum asufi* — a ditch used for storing harvested dates, or for storing date pits for animals to lick (since the residual sugar attracts goats and cattle), is a location where a child left there would be an *asufi*. *Chitzra de'nahara, ein bo mishum asufi* — the bank of a river, by the docks where people pass, does not confer *asufi* status, because the parents placed the child there to be found. *Pashrei* — but in another section of the riverbank, further from populated areas and traffic — *yesh bo mishum asufi*, the child is an *asufi* because discovery there is unlikely.

The case of Moshe Rabbeinu naturally comes to mind: found on the bank of the Nile in the middle of Mitzrayim. Of course, Moshe had a *mashgiach* — his sister Miriam stood watch. The *midrashim* in the beginning of *Sotah* elaborate on Miriam's role: she had prophesied Moshe's birth, she confronted her father about his decision, and she watched over the infant with dedication. The *mefarshim* debate what exactly it was she later took issue with — whether it concerned whom Moshe married or whether it involved his separation from his wife — but throughout the narrative Miriam's protective watchfulness over her younger brother is evident.

### Street Edges

*Ve'tzidei reshus harabim, ein bo mishum asufi* — the edges of the public thoroughfare do not constitute *reshus harabim* in the full sense for purposes of *asufi*. As we know from the first *perek* of *Masechet Shabbat*, the sidewalk-like edges alongside storefronts do not share the full status of the *reshus harabim* that occupies the middle of a sixteen-*amah*-wide street; they carry at most the status of *karmelis*. Here too, a child placed at the edge of a public street — against a wall, near a storefront — was placed in a protected and visible location. The parents were trying to ensure he would be found, not leaving him to be trampled. *Yesh bo mishum asufi* only if the child was found in the actual middle of the street, where leaving him constitutes abandonment to death.

---

## Famine & Reclamation

### Famine Leniency

*Amar Rava: uvshanei raavon, ein bo mishum asufi* — Rava rules that during years of famine, a child found in the marketplace does not carry *asufi* status at all. The reasoning is that a family driven by famine to give up a child is not a family that has abandoned the child in the morally and *halachically* relevant sense. However desperate and inexcusable the act, there is a comprehensible motivation — preserving resources for surviving children — that distinguishes this from straightforward abandonment. The presumption, even for a child found in the street during a famine, is that his parents are a *kasher* family acting under impossible circumstances.

### Le'Altar Principle

This raises the question of how Rava's ruling on famine years relates to an earlier opinion. *Ella ki itmar d'Rava aha d'amar Rav Yehuda bar Zavda amar Rav: kol zman shebashuk aviv ve'imo ne'emanim alav* — as long as the child is still in the marketplace, his parents are believed if they appear and claim him. *Ne'esaf min hashuk ein ne'emanim alav* — once the child has been taken in from the marketplace, the parents are no longer believed. The principle underlying this ruling is *le'altar*: the parents are believed only immediately, while the situation is still unfolding and no *shem* has attached to the child.

### Shem Asufi Timing

*Mai ta'ama? Amar Rava: ho'il veyatza alav shem asufi* — once the child has been publicly identified as an *asufi*, that name and status attach irreversibly. It is analogous to *yatza kol* — once the name has gone out, it cannot be undone. The parents who arrive after the fact and wish to reclaim the child cannot undo the *shem asufi* that has already spread.

### Famine Exception

*Ve'amar Rava: uvshanei raavon af al pi shene'esaf min hashuk aviv ve'imo ne'emanim alav* — but in a year of famine, Rava rules that even after the child has been taken in from the marketplace, the parents may appear and reclaim him, and they will be believed. The *shem asufi* that would normally be irreversible does not permanently attach during famine years. The *gemara* clarifies that Rava's ruling addresses precisely the case where *ne'esaf min hashuk* has already occurred — in the normal case that is the point of irreversibility, but in a famine year the parents retain the ability to reclaim the child even afterward. How long afterward this extends — whether days, weeks, or longer — is left open, but the short-term claim is clearly valid.

This has poignant resonance with the realities of post-Holocaust life, where parents and children separated by catastrophe sought to reunite years later, generating real *she'eilos* in *arayos* when people who had grown close discovered they were related. One thinks also of the story of Trotsky's grandson, himself *halachically* Jewish, who discovered that his sister had survived Stalin's purges and flew to Moscow to be reunited with her as she was dying of cancer — a lifetime after their separation.

---
